text: AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents. Large language models (LLMs) possess broad factual knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, but solving complex tasks also requires procedural knowledge about how to act. Existing approaches often represent procedural knowledge through trajectories or bundled skills, limiting flexible reuse across interaction histories. This paper introduces Procedural Atoms, fine-grained and independently applicable units that represent Intent, When, Do, and Avoid guidance. Building on this representation, we propose AtomSD, an Atom-guided Self-Distillation framework in which the learner continually extracts Procedural Atoms from its own successful trajectories and distills them into the evolving policy through Atom-conditioned supervision and task-reward optimization. Comprehensive experiments show that AtomSD consistently outperforms strong reward-based and distillation methods, exceeding the state-of-the-art baseline by up to 9.31 points in average performance. Further analyses demonstrate that the proposed Procedural Atoms provide effective guidance, highlighting the value of atom-level procedural knowledge for policy learning.

Large language models (LLMs) have acquired extensive factual knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, enabling them to tackle increasingly complex tasks across diverse domains (OpenAI et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2026b). However, knowing the relevant facts does not necessarily imply knowing how to act. For example, a model may understand the properties of every reagent in a scientific experiment, yet still fail to execute the experimental procedure correctly. Such failures reflect the difference between declarative knowledge about a domain and procedural knowledge or planning knowledge about how tasks within that domain should be carried out. It becomes particularly consequential when successful behavior depends on sequences of interdependent decisions rather than isolated answers. In such contexts, an agent must determine which operations advance a goal, when their prerequisites hold, how intermediate results constrain later actions, and how its procedure should adapt as conditions change (Shridhar et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023a; Yu et al., 2026b). Therefore, learning reusable procedural knowledge is an important step toward translating the broad capabilities of LLMs into reliable performance in complex tasks.

Toward this goal, existing approaches leverage interaction trajectories to construct and transfer reusable procedural knowledge, broadly following two directions. (1) Organizing trajectories into reusable guidance. Prior work transforms previous interactions into reflections, workflows, skills, or conditional rules that can guide subsequent behavior through prompting (Wang et al., 2025; Mi et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). Such representations abstract beyond individual actions and make past experience accessible across future interactions. (2) Distilling experience into the policy. A second line of work transfers knowledge from demonstrations, feedback, or skill-augmented teacher context into the learner itself, allowing the resulting policy to benefit from this supervision without requiring the same external guidance at inference time (Zhao et al., 2026a; Hübotter et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a; Lu et al., 2026).

Despite their effectiveness, these approaches leave two important questions unresolved. (1) What should be the reusable unit of procedural knowledge? As shown in Figure 1, complete trajectories retain instance-specific objects, observations, and action sequences, while workflows and skills often bundle multiple operations into a single unit of guidance. Both can limit transfer across interaction histories: a new execution may require only a subset of the operations in a previous procedure, or may need to compose operations learned from different experiences. This calls for finer-grained procedural units that can be independently reused and flexibly composed across interaction histories. (2) How should procedural knowledge evolve with the learner? Existing approaches often rely on separately maintained skill libraries or external models to derive and update guidance from interaction trajectories (Mi et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026). However, reusable procedural knowledge should ideally co-evolve with the policy itself: as the learner acquires new capabilities and succeeds on new interaction histories, the knowledge available for subsequent learning should be updated accordingly.
In a word, the aforementioned limitations motivate us to ask: what form of procedural knowledge can be extracted from previous interactions, and continuously distilled as the learner evolves?

To this end, this paper proposes AtomSD, a procedural Atom -guided S elf- D istillation framework that couples continual procedural abstraction with online policy learning. To provide a reusable unit of procedural knowledge, we define a Procedural Atom as a fine-grained and independently applicable unit of procedural knowledge. As illustrated in Figure 1, a Procedural Atom consists of (i) Intent, specifying what the procedure is intended to accomplish; (ii) When, defining its applicability conditions; (iii) Do, specifying an ordered procedure; and (iv) Avoid, identifying operations or failure modes to avoid. With this goal-directed and condition-aware representation, individual Atoms can be selectively applied and flexibly composed across different interaction histories, rather than reused only in complete and inseparable trajectories or bundled workflows. In this way, procedural knowledge can better adapt to new interactions.

To enable procedural knowledge to co-evolve with the learner, AtomSD establishes a self-improving loop through two complementary processes. (1) Online procedural abstraction. At each training iteration, the student acts as its own knowledge extractor, abstracting successful on-policy trajectories into independently applicable Procedural Atoms. By sharing the resulting Atom set within the same task, knowledge extracted from one trajectory can guide other interaction histories, including both successful and failed ones. As the policy evolves, subsequent extraction continually refreshes the procedural guidance to reflect the learner’s growing capabilities. (2) Atom-guided self-distillation. An Atom-conditioned teacher, derived from the student, evaluates the original on-policy trajectories, transforming self-extracted procedural knowledge into token-level supervision across different interaction histories. Through joint reward optimization and self-distillation, this guidance is progressively internalized into the policy, whose continued improvement in turn supports further procedural knowledge discovery.

Comprehensive experiments on widely used benchmarks (Shridhar et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023a; Guo et al., 2025b) demonstrate that AtomSD consistently outperforms six strong reward-based and distillation baselines, while also showing competitive performance against advanced API-based models such as DeepSeek-V4-Pro (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026) and GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026). AtomSD exceeds the state-of-the-art baseline in average performance by up to 9.31 points, with improvements extending to unseen tasks. Further analyses show that fine-grained Procedural Atoms provide compact and effective guidance, validating the design of Atom-guided self-distillation.

Our key contributions are as follows: This paper introduces Procedural Atoms, fine-grained and independently applicable units that support selective reuse and flexible composition of procedural knowledge across interaction histories. AtomSD combines online procedural abstraction with Atom-guided self-distillation, allowing procedural knowledge to be progressively internalized into the policy while co-evolving with the learner.

As shown in Figure 2, this paper proposes Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation as a self-improving loop in which procedural knowledge is continually extracted from on-policy interactions and internalized into the evolving student policy. We define Procedural Atoms as fine-grained functional units of procedural knowledge that capture guidance across four aspects: Intent, When, Do, and Avoid. As training proceeds iteratively, the student policy is updated at each training iteration based on its newly generated on-policy interactions. We formulate each training iteration as one complete self-improving loop consisting of two coupled processes: (1) Online Procedural Abstraction and (2) Atom-Guided Self-Distillation.

We represent an interaction trajectory \tau as a task together with the sequence of observations and actions encountered during execution. From its own successful trajectories, the evolving student serves as the procedural knowledge extractor, abstracting reusable procedures into independently applicable Procedural Atoms.

Formally, an Atom \omega is represented as \omega=\left\langle\iota_{\omega},\mathcal{C}_{\omega},\mathcal{P}_{\omega},\mathcal{B}_{\omega}\right\rangle, where \iota_{\omega} denotes the procedural intent; \mathcal{C}_{\omega}=\{c_{\omega,1},\ldots,c_{\omega,n_{C}}\} specifies the conditions under which the Atom applies; \mathcal{P}_{\omega}=(p_{\omega,1},\ldots,p_{\omega,n_{P}}) defines the ordered procedure to execute; and \mathcal{B}_{\omega}=\{b_{\omega,1},\ldots,b_{\omega,n_{B}}\} captures optional failure modes or inappropriate operations to avoid. Here, the elements of \mathcal{C}_{\omega}, \mathcal{P}_{\omega}, and \mathcal{B}_{\omega} denote the conditions, operations, and avoidance items, respectively, while n_{C}, n_{P}, and n_{B} denote their respective counts. Together, these components characterize what to achieve, when to apply the Atom, how to act, and what boundaries to respect.

To provide fine-grained procedural knowledge for reuse across interaction histories, we atomize successful trajectories and aggregate their Atoms at the task level. Consider the k -th self-improving iteration and a sampled task x in its training batch. Let \theta_{k} denote the student parameters at the beginning of iteration k. For task x, the current student \pi_{\theta_{k}} generates G on-policy trajectories \mathcal{T}_{x}^{(k)}=\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} without access to Procedural Atoms. Within \mathcal{T}_{x}^{(k)}, we identify the successful trajectories as \mathcal{S}_{x}^{(k)}=\{\tau_{i}\in\mathcal{T}_{x}^{(k)}\mid s(\tau_{i})=1\}, where s(\tau_{i})\in\{0,1\} indicates whether \tau_{i} successfully completes task x. The current student then serves as its own procedural knowledge extractor, atomizing each successful trajectory \tau_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{x}^{(k)} using the extraction prompt shown in Figure 8: \displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{i}^{(k)} \displaystyle=\textsc{Extract}\bigl(\pi_{\theta_{k}};\tau_{i}\bigr)=\left\{\omega_{i,r}=\left\langle\iota_{\omega_{i,r}},\mathcal{C}_{\omega_{i,r}},\mathcal{P}_{\omega_{i,r}},\mathcal{B}_{\omega_{i,r}}\right\rangle\right\}_{r=1}^{M_{i}}, where M_{i} denotes the number of Procedural Atoms extracted from \tau_{i}. The trajectory-level Atom sets are then aggregated into the task-level procedural knowledge of the current self-improving loop: \Omega_{x}^{(k)}=\bigcup_{\tau_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{x}^{(k)}}\mathcal{A}_{i}^{(k)}.

The resulting \Omega_{x}^{(k)} aggregates procedural knowledge discovered across successful trajectories while retaining the constituent Atoms as distinct units. It is then shared across all trajectories of task x to provide reusable guidance over different interaction histories, including both successful and unsuccessful ones.

The second process completes each self-improving loop by distilling the procedural knowledge \Omega_{x}^{(k)} extracted from the current student back into its policy. Conditioned on this shared Atom set, the teacher provides token-level procedural supervision over the student’s on-policy interaction histories. Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete self-improving loop executed at each training iteration.

Let \phi_{k} denote the teacher parameters at iteration k. For each trajectory \tau_{i}\in\mathcal{T}_{x}^{(k)} and the j -th student-generated token y_{ij} in \tau_{i}, let h_{ij} denote its preceding token-level interaction history. Given the shared task-level Atom set \Omega_{x}^{(k)} and the teacher prompting template shown in Figure 9, the teacher’s Atom-conditioned token-level support for y_{ij} is defined as q_{ij}^{\mathrm{Atom},(k)}=\pi_{\phi_{k}}\left(y_{ij}\mid h_{ij},\Omega_{x}^{(k)}\right). For each Atom \omega\in\Omega_{x}^{(k)}, the intent \iota_{\omega} and applicability conditions \mathcal{C}_{\omega} provide the basis for identifying relevant Atoms from the current history h_{ij}, while \mathcal{P}_{\omega} and \mathcal{B}_{\omega} provide the corresponding procedural guidance and boundaries. Conditioning jointly on h_{ij} and \Omega_{x}^{(k)} allows the teacher to draw on relevant Atom guidance while providing history-specific token-level supervision, enabling compositional procedural guidance across multiple Atoms.

We convert the Atom-conditioned support from a teacher derived from the student into a token-level internalization signal: \displaystyle A_{ij}^{\mathrm{Atom},(k)} \displaystyle=\operatorname{sg}\!\left[\log q_{ij}^{\mathrm{Atom},(k)}-\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{ij}\mid h_{ij})\right], where \operatorname{sg}(\cdot) denotes stop-gradient. This signal captures the difference between the teacher’s support under the extracted procedural knowledge and the student’s corresponding unguided probability.

In parallel, environment feedback provides a trajectory-level learning signal. For the G trajectories in \mathcal{T}_{x}^{(k)}, we compute the GRPO advantage (Shao et al., 2024) as A_{i}^{\mathrm{RL},(k)}=(R(\tau_{i})-\overline{R}_{x}^{(k)})/\sigma_{x}^{(k)}, where \overline{R}_{x}^{(k)} and \sigma_{x}^{(k)} denote the within-task reward mean and standard deviation. The policy ratio is r_{ij}^{(k)}(\theta)=\pi_{\theta}(y_{ij}\mid h_{ij})/\pi_{\theta_{k}}(y_{ij}\mid h_{ij}). Both learning signals use the same PPO-style clipped surrogate loss (Schulman et al., 2017): \displaystyle\ell_{\mathrm{clip}}\!\left(r_{ij}^{(k)}(\theta),A\right) \displaystyle=-\min\Bigl\{r_{ij}^{(k)}(\theta)A,\operatorname{clip}\!\left(r_{ij}^{(k)}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\right)A\Bigr\}, where \operatorname{clip}(\cdot) constrains the policy ratio to [1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon], and A denotes the corresponding reward or Atom-guided distillation signal. Combining the two signals, the task-level objective is \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{x}^{(k)}(\theta) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{G}L_{i}}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{i}}\Big[\ell_{\mathrm{clip}}\!\left(r_{ij}^{(k)}(\theta),A_{i}^{\mathrm{RL},(k)}\right)+\lambda\,\ell_{\mathrm{clip}}\!\left(r_{ij}^{(k)}(\theta),A_{ij}^{\mathrm{Atom},(k)}\right)\Big], where L_{i} counts valid student-generated tokens in \tau_{i}, and \lambda controls the strength of distillation. The batch objective aggregates these task-level losses according to their valid token counts. Optimizing this objective updates the student from \pi_{\theta_{k}} to \pi_{\theta_{k+1}}, progressively internalizing the procedural knowledge represented by \Omega_{x}^{(k)} into the policy.

The teacher and student are initialized identically, \phi_{0}=\theta_{0}. After optimizing each training iteration, the teacher is updated by exponential moving average (EMA): \phi_{k+1}=\alpha\phi_{k}+(1-\alpha)\theta_{k+1}, where \alpha denotes the EMA decay. The updated student \pi_{\theta_{k+1}} then serves as the basis for procedural abstraction in the next iteration. Repeating this loop continually externalizes procedural knowledge from the evolving learner and distills it back into the policy, allowing procedural knowledge and the policy to co-evolve throughout training.

We evaluate agents’ ability to follow and execute multi-step procedures across four benchmarks. ALFWorld (ALF) (Shridhar et al., 2021) assesses household planning and execution in text-based environments. ScienceWorld (SW) (Wang et al., 2022) requires scientific reasoning through multi-step experimentation. WebShop (WS) (Yao et al., 2023a) evaluates product search and purchasing under user constraints. StableToolBench (STB) (Guo et al., 2025b) assesses tool use through a virtual API environment. We report seen and unseen results separately for ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, denoted by the suffixes -S and -U, alongside test results for WebShop and StableToolBench. Detailed descriptions of the datasets and evaluation subsets are provided in Appendix A.

We use Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026) as backbone models. We additionally evaluate four strong API-based models: DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026), GLM-5.3 (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026), and GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026).

All models interact with the environments using ReAct (Yao et al., 2023b). API-based models are evaluated with ReAct alone. We compare AtomSD with the following categories of methods: (1) Prompting: the initial model with ReAct alone and Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), which additionally incorporates textual reflections from previous attempts without parameter updates; (2) Reward-based RL: GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), which learns from task rewards; (3) Trajectory-guided self-distillation: OPSD (Zhao et al., 2026a), SDPO (Hübotter et al., 2026), and GRPO+OPSD, which use successful demonstrations as privileged teacher context in our setting, with GRPO+OPSD additionally incorporating task rewards; and (4) Skill-guided distillation: Skill-SD (Wang et al., 2026a) and SDAR (Lu et al., 2026), which combine reward optimization with teacher guidance from skills constructed by strong external LLMs. Together, these baselines provide a comprehensive comparison across inference-time reflection, reward-based learning, and trajectory- or skill-guided distillation. We set \lambda=0.001, \alpha=0.95, and \epsilon=0.2 for AtomSD. Detailed training and implementation settings are provided in Appendix B.

For training-based methods, we evaluate checkpoints at the same training step. We report success rate on ALFWorld, average task score on ScienceWorld and WebShop, and solved rate on StableToolBench using the official Final Answer Completeness (FAC) (Guo et al., 2025a). All scores use a 0–100 scale.

Table 1 summarizes the main results, with four key findings. (1) AtomSD improves beyond reward- and demonstration-guided training. AtomSD consistently outperforms GRPO, OPSD, and GRPO+OPSD in average performance at both model scales, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.31 and 5.42 points at 4B and 9B, respectively. This highlights the value of Procedural Atoms beyond reward-only learning, demonstration-guided distillation, and their combination. (2) AtomSD provides broader gains than skill-level distillation. AtomSD outperforms Skill-SD and SDAR on most tasks at both scales, with particularly pronounced gains on ScienceWorld. These results suggest that even skill libraries constructed by stronger external models do not necessarily provide more effective guidance, highlighting the value of fine-grained Procedural Atoms. (3) Improvements generalize to unseen tasks. AtomSD leads on ScienceWorld unseen at both model scales, with improvements also extending to ALFWorld unseen. These results suggest that procedural knowledge learned through AtomSD can generalize beyond seen tasks. (4) AtomSD is competitive with strong LLMs without inference-time reflection. AtomSD surpasses Reflexion by 22.91 and 20.85 points at 4B and 9B, respectively.

AtomSD-9B further exceeds DeepSeek-V4-Pro and trails GPT-5.5 by only 5.39 points in average score, suggesting that internalizing Procedural Atom guidance can reduce reliance on inference-time reflection while narrowing the gap to substantially stronger LLMs. We further provide qualitative case studies in Appendix D.1.

section: Effects of Atom Components and Joint Optimization
text: Figure 3 examines the contributions of Atom components and joint reward optimization. (1) The complete Atom representation provides more effective guidance. Including Intent improves the average score by 15.0 points at 4B and 1.4 points at 9B, while the complete representation outperforms removing both Intent and Avoid by 8.9 and 13.4 points, respectively, with similar trends observed in the training rewards. These results highlight the value of organizing procedural guidance within the complete Atom representation. (2) Explicit avoidance boundaries improve performance at both scales. Removing Avoid reduces the average score by 13.1 points at 4B and 14.0 points at 9B. This further highlights the importance of explicitly representing what to avoid, rather than distilling successful operations alone. (3) Joint optimization strengthens Atom-guided learning. Combining Atom-guided distillation with task rewards improves average performance by 25.3 and 25.1 points over Atom-only training at 4B and 9B, respectively. This supports the design choice of jointly internalizing procedural guidance while optimizing for task completion. Overall, these results show that effective Atom-guided learning depends on both a complete procedural representation and joint optimization with task rewards.

To examine whether the student internalizes Atom guidance, we consider two relevant Procedural Atoms, \omega_{\alpha} and \omega_{\beta}, and evaluate guidance from each individually and in combination. We use GPT-5.5 to identify supported actions and their preceding interaction histories. This analysis covers both same-task and cross-task histories at two training stages, Early and Late. Within each stage, we use a fixed training interval and compare the student checkpoints at its beginning and end using two metrics: (1) maximum-token support change, measuring the relative probability increase of the most-improved action token without Atoms, and (2) guidance-direction agreement, measuring whether Atom-favored tokens change in the same direction after training without Atoms. Detailed definitions and results are provided in Appendix C. As shown in Figure 5, during Early training, maximum-token support (\Delta p/p) increases by 36.9% for 4B and 45.2% for 9B on same-task histories. Agreement with composed guidance from \omega_{\alpha} and \omega_{\beta} reaches 75.0% on cross-task histories for Early 4B and 70.5% for Late 9B. These results support effective internalization of both individual and composed Atom guidance, including across tasks; see Appendix D.2 for a concrete composition case.

To assess whether procedural knowledge benefits from co-evolving with the learner, we replace the evolving student extractor with either DeepSeek-V4-Pro or the frozen initial Qwen backbone. Figure 5 (top) shows that a stronger extractor alone does not yield better performance: DeepSeek-V4-Pro trails AtomSD at 4B and is comparable at 9B. Meanwhile, the evolving student consistently outperforms the frozen extractor in evaluation performance and late-stage rewards at both scales. These results support AtomSD’s co-evolving design: learner improvement refreshes procedural knowledge for distillation, which in turn supports further policy improvement.

To characterize the granularity and compactness of Procedural Atoms, Figure 5 (bottom left) compares lengths using trajectories matched by task and training step across methods. Overall, Atom guidance requires 1.53k prefix tokens, compared with 2.20k for skills and 3.93k for trajectories. At the unit level, individual Atoms average only 0.15k tokens, substantially smaller than skills (0.64k) and trajectories (4.97k). Figure 5 (bottom right) further shows a relatively balanced distribution of the four Atom components across datasets throughout training. These results show that Procedural Atoms provide compact, fine-grained guidance across multiple procedural aspects, supporting selective reuse and composition.

Figure 7 (top) shows that AtomSD’s advantage emerges as training progresses. OPSD improves rapidly early on at both model scales, but its gains subsequently plateau, whereas AtomSD continues to improve and reaches the highest reward toward the end. Figure 7 (bottom) further shows that these gains accompany relatively low token usage and fewer interaction steps during later training at both scales. These results show that Procedural Atoms improve performance with more compact trajectories.

Figure 7 shows that increasing \lambda from 0.001 to 0.01 or 0.1 consistently reduces late-stage training rewards and average evaluation performance at both model scales. This suggests that Atom-guided distillation is more effective when properly balanced with reward optimization rather than simply strengthened, consistent with recent findings on self-distillation in agentic RL (Lu et al., 2026; Kaur et al., 2026).

Figure 5 (middle) compares EMA with fixed and fully synchronized teachers. EMA achieves the highest average evaluation performance at both model scales; the fixed teacher remains competitive, while full synchronization yields lower late-stage training rewards at both scales. These results suggest that EMA balances preserving prior teacher knowledge with incorporating student progress.

Experience-based agents transform interaction histories into reflections, insights, and reasoning memories for reuse in subsequent decisions (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Ouyang et al., 2026), while others leverage embeddings, KV cache, or special tokens to represent memories (Yu et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026c; Wu et al., 2026b). Furthermore, prior work organizes histories into reusable workflows, conditional procedures, and explicit rules, enabling more selective reuse across interactions (Wang et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026a; Mi et al., 2026). A complementary line of work models environment dynamics and action consequences to support planning (Qiao et al., 2024; Kim and Hwang, 2025; Liu et al., 2026b). AtomSD instead uses procedural abstractions as privileged context. Condition-aware Atoms guide policy learning and are progressively internalized into model parameters, without requiring external guidance at inference.

On-policy distillation applies teacher supervision to student-generated trajectories, internalizing privileged knowledge into model parameters (Agarwal et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2026a; Hübotter et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026a). Privileged knowledge can be supplied as explicit textual context or encoded into learned latent representations (Liu et al., 2026a; Ye et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). AtomSD uses independently applicable Procedural Atoms as the unit of privileged supervision, enabling guidance to be composed according to the student’s current interaction history rather than being tied to a specific demonstration trajectory or workflow.

Skill-augmented reinforcement learning optimizes agents’ ability to exploit and improve external skill libraries (Wang et al., 2026b; Xia et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). Skill-conditioned distillation instead uses skill guidance as teacher-side context to train policies that operate without external skill inputs at inference (Lu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026; Lv et al., 2026). AtomSD constructs procedural guidance online from the evolving student’s successful trajectories, without relying on a preconstructed skill library or a separate external model for knowledge extraction. By continually decomposing trajectories into independently applicable Atoms rather than bundled skills, it supports selective reuse and flexible composition while allowing procedural knowledge to co-evolve with the learner.

This paper presents AtomSD, a self-improving framework that transforms successful on-policy trajectories into Procedural Atoms and distills their guidance back into the policy, allowing procedural knowledge to co-evolve with the learner. Comprehensive experiments and analyses show that AtomSD consistently improves agent performance, while fine-grained Procedural Atoms support selective reuse and flexible composition across interaction histories. Our results highlight atomized procedural knowledge as an effective bridge between raw interaction histories and parametric policy learning.

A Jury, Not an Electorate: Label-Free Reliability Estimation for Ensembles of Language Models. An ensemble of language models is a jury, not an electorate. The answers are testimony from witnesses of unknown reliability, and the question is not what the majority said but who is credible. Most ensemble methods assign each expert a fixed reputation, often learned from labels. We ask whether it can instead be inferred from the pattern of agreement and disagreement among the experts. We model the experts as a jury: each question has a latent true answer, each expert reports it with unknown reliability, and those reliabilities are estimated by Expectation Maximisation (EM) from unlabelled answer configurations alone. We show that its decision rule reduces to a log-odds weighted linear score over the experts' answer distributions. What changes is not how the jury votes, but how it learns whom to trust. On a 1560-question benchmark, the jury, with nine experts of up to 3B parameters, performs comparably to the same fusion rule with label-fitted weights, showing no statistically significant advantage from supervision. Instead, it outperforms the best single model with matched self-consistency and the strongest label-free alternative on the full benchmark.

A collection of language models can know more than any one of its members. Models trained at different scales, on different corpora, or for different domains fail in different places, so the answer that one model misses may already be present elsewhere in the pool. The difficulty is not creating diversity, but deciding how to use it when models disagree.

Most existing approaches treat model aggregation like an electorate with known candidates. Each model arrives with a reputation, learned from labelled data or inferred from the query, and the final answer is chosen by applying those reputations to the models’ votes. In that view, credibility is decided before the answers are heard.

We take a different perspective: once all experts have answered, the question is no longer how much we already trust each model, but what their testimony tells us about them. The evidence is the configuration of answers: which answers appear, how strongly they are supported, and which experts agree. A jury can judge who to trust from the testimony itself.

A pool can improve on a plain vote in two separate ways. The first comes from keeping the answer distributions: reducing each expert to its argmax discards the rest of its distribution. The second comes from weighting the experts: even when the distributions are kept, the experts still need to be weighted appropriately. The two are often mixed together, but they are conceptually different. On our benchmark, keeping the answer distributions improves majority voting by 8.4 points, and weighting the experts adds a further 5.5 points. A sample-matched control shows that the first gain comes from the distribution itself rather than from additional test-time sampling.

Our contribution concerns the second gain: learning whom to trust without labels. We separate the effect of retaining the answer distributions from the effects of expert weighting and additional sampling. We use a simple generative model, inspired by Dawid and Skene [8], where each question has a latent true answer and each expert has an unknown reliability. Those reliabilities are estimated by EM from unlabelled answer configurations alone. The model never sees a gold answer. It sees the same training questions as the supervised baselines, but only the experts’ testimony.

Mathematically, the resulting decision rule is not a new family of ensemble methods. With one answer per expert, it reduces exactly to the classical log-odds weighted vote. With answer distributions, it becomes a weighted linear score over those distributions, equivalent to a linear opinion pool when the weights are non-negative and a signed linear fusion otherwise. Neither the vote nor the estimator is new in form: the first is a standard opinion pool, the second is an EM for a classical crowdsourcing model. What this work adds is the adaptation of that model to language-model outputs, and a direct test of whether reliabilities inferred from agreement can replace reliabilities measured on labels.

This allows a direct comparison with the same fusion rule whose weights are fitted from labelled questions, which we call the supervised linear fusion. On a 1560-question benchmark spanning six MMLU subjects, GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, and HellaSwag, nine experts of up to 3B parameters combined by the jury reach 76.9\pm 1.3\%. This is 2.0 points above the pool’s best single expert, with a 95% confidence interval of [+0.5,+3.6], 1.6 points above that expert when it is given the same eight-sample self-consistency on GSM8K ([+0.0,+3.1]), and substantially above the best label-free alternative on the full benchmark. The jury also performs comparably to the supervised linear fusion.

Our contributions are fourfold. We separate two gains that are often mixed together. The first is the use of answer distributions instead of argmax answers, which applies to any method. The second is how the experts are weighted. We adapt the one-coin Dawid–Skene model to ensembles of language models with observed candidate sets and sampled answer distributions, and use it to obtain expert weights for linear fusion without labels. We characterise the resulting rule exactly: on single answers it is the log-odds weighted vote, and on answer distributions a signed linear fusion. This makes the same rule with label-derived reliabilities the natural supervised reference. We also give a closed-form, moment-based identifiability result for the one-coin model with K\geq 3 that does not require any expert to be better than chance. We extensively evaluate the method by ablating its assumptions and comparing it against ten post-hoc combiners under a common full-benchmark protocol, spanning both supervised and label-free methods, including SkillAggregation, with a +2.7 pp margin over its strongest tested variant.
We follow the taxonomy of Chen et al. [4], which divides LLM ensembling into what happens before, during and after inference.

A router maps the query to one model, trained on correctness labels, on reward-model scores, or on human preferences; others cast the choice as a bandit or select a subset by mutual information under a budget. Simple embedding-based routers can also be competitive. This family is complementary to ours: it decides whom to ask, while we decide whom to believe once everyone has answered.

section: During inference: token, span and process fusion.
text: These methods combine models during generation through vocabulary alignment, perplexity-based weighting, span-level cross-scoring, speculative decoding, or process-reward search over partial reasoning chains. They rely on logits or partial generations, while our method only uses final answers.

section: After inference: the family this paper belongs to.
text: Aggregating completed answers splits into two groups. Weighting the experts covers plain majority voting over sampled outputs, unsupervised per-sample quality estimation, diversity-driven subset selection with a learned combiner, and the correlation-aware Optimal Weight and Inverse Surprising Popularity (ISP) rules of Ai et al. [1]. Answer-scoring methods form the smaller group: Jiang et al. [26] rank candidates with a pairwise cross-encoder over their text and then generate a fused answer, Si et al. [43] select among candidates with a supervised model over inter-expert agreement and confidence, and LENS learns per-model confidence from hidden states.

section: After inference: the family this paper belongs to.
text: Our method is a weighted linear fusion of the experts’ answer distributions, with the reliability vector as its only learned content (Section 3). We estimate those reliabilities directly from the experts’ unlabelled answer configurations. Other label-free methods that weight the experts estimate a model’s quality: Smoothie from pairwise distances between outputs, and ISP from second-order agreement statistics that detect answers more popular than predicted. Ai et al. [1] also propose OW-L and OW-I, which estimate each model’s accuracy without labels, from the pairwise agreement table or from ISP’s verdicts used as pseudo-labels, and then apply Optimal Weight; these are the closest published counterparts of our estimator.

section: After inference: the family this paper belongs to.
text: A close reference-free setting is SkillAggregation, which learns to combine multiple LLM judgments without ground-truth labels and accepts both binary and probabilistic estimates. It extends Crowdlayer with a learned context encoder and per-judge skill estimates, including context-dependent skills. Our method fits a restricted generative model to unlabelled answer configurations, yielding log-odds weights for a fixed linear fusion rule.

Combining probability distributions is a classical problem in statistics. With non-negative weights, our rule is Stone’s linear pool; negative log-odds weights instead yield a signed linear fusion. The main alternative is the logarithmic pool, a weighted geometric mean related to the product of experts; the principles distinguishing the two are reviewed by Genest and Zidek [15]. DeGroot’s consensus model instead iteratively averages expert opinions.

In this literature, weights are obtained from experts or fitted on questions with known answers, and equal weighting is often competitive. In our work, the generative model of Section 3 determines the linear-fusion weights, and EM estimates them from agreement alone.
Cascades escalate through models until an answer is accepted, using stopping rules, learned policies, or self-consistency. They address the accuracy-cost trade-off rather than post-hoc aggregation.

Recovering a latent truth and the annotators’ reliabilities jointly, from agreement and without labels, is Dawid and Skene [8]; weighting voters by the log-odds of their accuracy is optimal for conditionally independent voters, with the K -ary form we use given in Ai et al. [1]; conditioning a combination on the input is the mixture-of-experts gate; and Prelec et al. [38] propose the approach for detecting answers that are more popular than predicted.

Section 3.1 shows which answers a weighted vote over the experts’ argmax answers can reach, and identifies two separable sources of improvement. Section 3.2 introduces the generative model and derives the EM updates that estimate each expert’s reliability without labels. Section 3.3 characterises the resulting decision rule, and Section 3.4 outlines the modelling choices.

section: What a weighted vote over argmax answers can and cannot do
text: Fix a question q and let \mathcal{E} be the finite set of experts in the pool. Each expert e\in\mathcal{E} returns an answer a_{e} from a task-dependent answer space \mathcal{A}; only the finite set of distinct answers actually produced, the candidate set \mathcal{V}(q)=\{a_{e}:e\in\mathcal{E}\}\subseteq\mathcal{A}, enters the model. A weighted vote with weights w\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{E}|} returns \hat{y}(w)\;=\;\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{v\in\mathcal{V}(q)}\;\sum_{e\,:\,a_{e}=v}w_{e}. We let w range over \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{E}|} rather than over the simplex because the model-derived weights can be negative for sufficiently weak experts, and the vote and the model should speak about the same object.

section: What a weighted vote over argmax answers can and cannot do
text: A weighted vote over argmax answers can only return an answer in \mathcal{V}(q). Conversely, any v\in\mathcal{V}(q) can be made the winner by assigning all weight to an expert that proposed it. Changing the weights can therefore change which observed answer wins, but cannot enlarge the set of possible winners. Two separable gains lead beyond such a rule: keeping the answer distributions, which can enlarge the reachable set, and weighting the experts better.

section: A working generative model of the answer configuration
text: Rather than score a candidate from features of its supporters, we model how the answers arose. For a question with candidate set \mathcal{V}, let z\in\mathcal{V} be the latent true answer. Each expert e reports it with reliability \pi_{e}, and otherwise reports one of the remaining candidates uniformly: P(a_{e}=v\mid z)\;=\;\begin{cases}\pi_{e},&v=z,\\[2.0pt] \dfrac{1-\pi_{e}}{m},&v\neq z,\end{cases} with m=|\mathcal{V}|-1. When m=0 the pool is unanimous, \mathcal{V} is a singleton, (2) is vacuous and the verdict is that answer; such questions are also excluded from the estimation below, since they constrain no parameter.

section: What \mathcal{V} is, and what the model is defined on.
text: \mathcal{V}(q) is not a fixed label space. It is the set of distinct answers produced by the pool on q: in the greedy regime the distinct argmax answers, and with repeated samples the union of all answers produced by the experts, over which p_{e} is the expert’s empirical frequency. If repeated samples are unavailable, p_{e} reduces to a point mass at the greedy answer; a non-answer is omitted from the likelihood. During fitting and prediction the set is treated as a fixed support, and (2) is a simplified emission model defined on that support: it does not model how the support itself was generated. This matters for what the model can claim. Conditioning on the observed support would itself induce dependence between the experts (if two experts can say A or B and the observed set is \{A,B\}, they are known to disagree), so the conditional independence used below is an assumption of the simplified model, not a consequence of the construction. The error channel is uniform over the alternatives in the support rather than over the task’s full answer space, and a candidate outside \mathcal{V}(q) has probability zero.

section: What \mathcal{V} is, and what the model is defined on.
text: The reliabilities \pi_{e} are therefore reliabilities according to this model, and need not equal the experts’ true probabilities of being correct. Appendix D reports a control in which the support of every multiple-choice question is fixed to its four options instead of being read off the answers.

section: What \mathcal{V} is, and what the model is defined on.
text: The model assumes that, given z, the experts are conditionally independent, so with a uniform prior over \mathcal{V} the verdict is \hat{y}\;=\;\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\;\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\log P(a_{e}\mid z=v).

section: What \mathcal{V} is, and what the model is defined on.
text: This is a restricted form of Dawid and Skene [8]: one reliability per expert rather than a full confusion matrix, and a uniform error distribution over the remaining candidates. We use one reliability per expert, avoiding the O(|\mathcal{E}|\,|\mathcal{V}|^{2}) parameters of a full confusion-matrix model.

The reliabilities are estimated by EM. For a distribution p_{e,q} over \mathcal{V}(q) under the likelihood of Proposition 3, the M-step is \pi_{e}\;=\;\frac{1}{|Q_{e}|}\sum_{q\in Q_{e}}\;\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}(q)}\gamma_{q}(v)\,p_{e,q}(v), where \gamma_{q}(v) is the posterior of the E-step and Q_{e} are the questions e answered. An expert’s reliability is the posterior-weighted mass it placed on each candidate, averaged over questions. For point-mass evidence p_{e,q}=\delta_{a_{e}}, this reduces to \pi_{e}=|Q_{e}|^{-1}\sum_{q\in Q_{e}}\gamma_{q}(a_{e}).
Writing A_{e} for the double sum in (4), the expected complete-data log-likelihood of expert e is A_{e}\log\pi_{e}+(|Q_{e}|-A_{e})\log(1-\pi_{e}); maximising gives \pi_{e}=A_{e}/|Q_{e}|.

The EM updates explain how to estimate the reliabilities without labels. A separate question is whether the distribution of unlabelled responses determines them uniquely. Under task-specified support, as in Appendix D, the model yields the following label-free identifiability guarantee.

Fix a support size K\geq 3 that occurs with positive probability, and condition on questions with |V(q)|=K. Let p_{e} be the empirical distribution of expert e ’s answers sampled according to (2) on that support. Assume (p_{e})_{e\in\mathcal{E}} are jointly observed and conditionally independent given (z,q), with question-independent reliabilities. If at least three experts satisfy \pi_{e}\neq 1/K, then the reliability vector \pi is identifiable from the joint distribution of the (p_{e})_{e\in\mathcal{E}} alone.

The proof in Appendix E reconstructs each reliability from second and third order agreement moments. This guarantee holds even when every expert’s probability of answering correctly is below 1/K, the probability of uniform random guessing. Even when the reliabilities are identifiable, EM may converge to a local rather than a global maximum of the non-concave likelihood.

We initialise \pi_{e}=0.6 for every expert, giving all experts the same positive initial weight. We run a single EM fit with no restarts, stop when no parameter moves by more than 10^{-7} or after 200 iterations, and clip \pi_{e} to [0.02,0.98] to keep the log-odds finite. A 25 -start sensitivity analysis confirms that the reported distributional fit is insensitive to this choice, as the highest-likelihood distributional solution found on every split is the one reached by the default start. The single-answer regime has an additional higher-likelihood degenerate mode (Section B.6). We fit \pi on unlabelled training configurations and freeze it before evaluation; no gold label is used during fitting.
Propositions 2 and 3 characterise how (3) reduces in the two evidence regimes.

With one answer per expert and m\geq 1, \displaystyle\sum_{e}\log P(a_{e}\mid z=v) \displaystyle\;=\;C\;+\!\!\sum_{e\,:\,a_{e}=v}\!\!w_{e}, \displaystyle w_{e} \displaystyle\;=\;\log\frac{\pi_{e}\,m}{1-\pi_{e}}, with C=\sum_{e}\log\frac{1-\pi_{e}}{m} independent of v. Hence (3) coincides with the weighted vote (1).
Substitute (2) and add and subtract \sum_{e}\log\frac{1-\pi_{e}}{m}. ∎
Proposition 2 says that, with single answers, the jury is the Nitzan-Paroush log-odds rule in the K -ary form of Ai et al. [1], with \pi estimated unsupervised instead of read off labels.

Let each expert supply a distribution p_{e} over \mathcal{V} and let its contribution to the log-likelihood be \alpha\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}}p_{e}(u)\log P(a_{e}=u\mid z=v), with \alpha>0 the evidence weight of Section 3.4. Then \displaystyle\hat{y} \displaystyle\;=\;\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\;\sum_{e}w_{e}\,p_{e}(v), \displaystyle w_{e} \displaystyle\;=\;\log\frac{\pi_{e}\,m}{1-\pi_{e}}.

\sum_{u}p_{e}(u)\log P(a_{e}=u\mid z=v)=p_{e}(v)\log\pi_{e}+(1-p_{e}(v))\log\frac{1-\pi_{e}}{m}=C_{e}+p_{e}(v)\,w_{e} with C_{e} independent of v; sum over e, drop the constant, and drop the common factor \alpha, which leaves the argmax unchanged. ∎

Proposition 3 keeps the rule within weighted linear fusion. It remains an inner product between a weight vector and per-candidate evidence. Unlike voting over argmax answers, however, a candidate can win without being any expert’s top choice, so the reachable set can be strictly larger. Together the two propositions show that the method’s learned content is the reliability vector \pi, which determines the expert-specific component of w, making the same fusion rule with label-fitted weights the natural supervised baseline.

The weights are not entirely fixed in advance. Since m=|\mathcal{V}|-1 depends on the answers observed, w_{e}=\log\frac{\pi_{e}}{1-\pi_{e}}+\log m carries a question-level offset shared by every expert, contributing \log m\sum_{e}p_{e}(v) to the score — a multiple of the equal-weight pool. Only the per-expert part is fixed before the answers are seen. Note also that w_{e}<0 whenever \pi_{e}<1/|\mathcal{V}|, in which case the expert is voted against rather than merely ignored. The fusion score ranks candidates but need not be a probability, the posterior \gamma_{q} of (3) remains a probability distribution either way.
Figure 1 puts these pieces together on a toy example: the emission model, the label-free fit of \pi, the log-odds weights and the signed linear fusion.

Let p_{e,q} be the empirical distribution obtained from n samples of expert e. We weight its log-likelihood contribution by \alpha. Setting \alpha=n recovers the multinomial log-likelihood, up to a term independent of the latent answer and the reliabilities. We therefore use \alpha=n as the default: \alpha=8 for the sampled distributions, since the cache holds eight samples per expert and question (Section 4.1), and \alpha=1 for a single greedy answer. As an ablation, we also consider \alpha=1 for a sampled distribution, which treats the whole distribution as one unit of evidence (see Appendix C). At fixed \pi, \alpha does not change the argmax in Proposition 3, because it multiplies every candidate score by the same positive constant. It does, however, change the E-step distribution \gamma, and therefore the fitted reliabilities.

Equation 2 assumes that experts are conditionally independent given the latent answer. To test sensitivity to shared failure modes, we also consider an extension with a second latent variable per question, a lure: a wrong answer toward which a specified group of experts may be jointly drawn. Each expert has a susceptibility parameter controlling its response to the lure. We consider groups defined by pre-training lineage and a pool-wide group (see Appendix C); the independent model remains the default.

This section tests the jury empirically. Section 4.1 describes the benchmark and the evaluation setup. Section 4.2 compares the jury with label-free and supervised baselines and the best single expert, separates the gains from answer distributions and expert weighting, and reports robustness and compute. Section 4.3 examines the modelling choices of Section 3.4 and calibration. Further experimental details and analyses are in Appendices A, B and C.

Our pool contains nine instruction-tuned experts of up to 3B parameters, selected to vary in size, domain, and model family. The goal is to include models that fail in different ways, giving the combiner useful disagreement to exploit. qwen3b is the strongest expert overall (75.0\%) and on multiple choice, while olmo2-1b leads on GSM8K despite being one of the weakest experts overall. The full model list and individual accuracies are given in Appendix A, Table 3.

The benchmark has 1560 questions from four sources: 240 from MMLU (40 from each of six subjects spanning humanities, law and science), 120 GSM8K problems, the only generative slice, 600 ARC-Challenge and 600 HellaSwag questions. Every source is scored 0/1 against a single gold answer (for more details see Appendix A).

Multiple choice is scored in one forward pass from the log-probabilities of the four option letters; GSM8K is answered by chain-of-thought generation, from which the final number is extracted (Appendix A). Besides one greedy answer per expert, the cache holds eight samples per expert per question (T=0.7, p=0.95), i.e. self-consistency sampling applied per expert. These samples give the distribution p_{e} that Proposition 3 consumes. On multiple choice they are draws from a distribution that the single forward pass has already computed, so they cost nothing extra.

Every method is evaluated over ten stratified 50/50 train/test splits of the same cached answers; methods that need labels see only the training half. The jury is fitted on the unlabelled answer configurations of the same training half; fitting it on all configurations would leak no label, but would not be a matched comparison. We report the mean and standard deviation over splits. The ten test sets overlap heavily, so a paired t -test over splits would overstate the evidence. All comparisons therefore use a paired bootstrap over questions with 20{,}000 resamples, where a question’s score for a method is its mean correctness over the splits in which it was held out. Compute is the average number of parameters activated per question, which charges a router for the one expert it calls and a fusion rule for all nine.

The supervised linear fusion uses the fusion rule of Proposition 3 with its reliabilities read off labels. Its reliability for expert e is the accuracy of e ’s greedy answer on the training half. The comparison with the jury is between two ways of estimating the reliabilities of one rule, not against every way of fitting weights from labels. The two estimators also differ in three implementation conventions (see Section A.1).
Table 1 is the main comparison: ten post-hoc combiners re-implemented on this cache and run on the same ten splits with the same experts.

Majority voting is the simplest form of model aggregation: every expert casts one equally weighted vote. Over all nine experts it scores 63.0\pm 1.6\%, twelve points below the best single expert. Replacing the argmax answers with the answer distributions, at equal weights, gives 71.4\pm 1.8\%: a +8.4 -point gain from keeping the distributions, with no weights and no labels. Weighting the experts by log-odds adds a further +5.5 points, reaching 76.9\pm 1.3\%. The first gain is available to any method; the second is where the jury operates, since it must learn from the testimony alone which witnesses to trust.

Table 2 shows that the first gain comes from the distribution not the extra samples. Its middle row is a sample-matched control that uses the same eight samples per expert, at the same cost, but reduces them to their mode before the rule sees them.

The two effects are separable but interact: weighting improves every evidence regime, and retaining the full distribution rather than its sample-matched mode improves every weighting scheme, by 2.2 to 8.3 points.

The supervised linear fusion has the same functional form as the jury, with weights fitted on the labels of the training half. It reaches 76.2\pm 1.4\%, and the jury is +0.6 points above it ([+0.1,+1.2], p=0.02). Conditional on the ten fitted models the difference is small but significant in the jury’s favour. Once the variability of refitting is included as well, the nested bootstrap of Section B.2 gives a difference of +0.6 points with a 95\% interval of [-0.6,+2.0]: no statistically significant difference, and an interval that admits differences of either sign, so not a demonstration of equivalence. On this benchmark, against this baseline, we find no evidence that supervised weight estimation outperforms label-free estimation.
Further supervised comparisons and per-task results are reported in Sections A.1, B.2 and B.3.

On the full benchmark, the greedy jury scores 72.3\%, versus 69.1\% for ISP, and with distributions it reaches 76.9\%, +5.5 over the equal-weight pool ([+4.1,+7.0]) and +7.9 over ISP ([+6.2,+9.6]). On the 1440 fixed-label questions, SkillAggregation reaches 73.2\% with distributions without a labelled development set; even its test-selected upper reference, SkillAggregation-X, reaches 74.0\%, 2.7 points below the jury at 76.6\%. OW-L and OW-I reach 71.3\% and 71.6\% on greedy answers, versus 72.4\% for the greedy jury, with intervals including zero (Section B.4). Most of the gain comes from the minority stratum, where the gold answer is not the unique plurality winner: accuracy rises from 6.2\% for majority voting to 55.5\% for the jury, while the jury also reaches 95.7\% on plurality questions.

qwen3b is the strongest expert overall (75.0\%), and the jury reaches 76.9\%, +2.0 ([+0.5,+3.6], p=0.012). Giving every expert the same eight-sample self-consistency on GSM8K and selecting on the training half again chooses qwen3b on every split, at 75.3\%; the jury remains +1.6 ahead ([+0.0,+3.1], p=0.048). The gain is concentrated on GSM8K, where qwen3b is weakest and olmo2-1b is the strongest expert; there the jury gains 20 points, while on the sources qwen3b already dominates it essentially matches that expert (Section B.1).

Nested resampling leaves the main conclusions unchanged: the jury remains above the equal-weight pool (+5.5, [+2.9,+8.3]) and majority vote (+14.1, [+10.5,+17.8]), while its +0.6 margin over the supervised linear fusion is not significant once refitting is resampled as well ([-0.6,+2.0]; Section B.2).

Across 246 sub-pools, the jury beats the equal-weight pool on 79\%, 98\% and 100\% of the three, five and seven expert pools, and the best expert on 82\%, 96\% and 100\%, respectively; the advantage is therefore not specific to the full nine-expert pool. Section B.5 gives the full breakdown and the \alpha=1 degeneracies.
Sampled variants activate 22.2 B parameters per question versus 14.4 B for greedy variants, because only GSM8K re-runs the models; Figure 2 in the appendix plots accuracy against cost.

Appendix C reports the full checks. Experts agree on wrong answers more often than independence predicts, but the correlated-error extension slightly lowers accuracy, and selective override does not help. The posterior is strongly overconfident (mean top-1 confidence 0.991 versus 76.9\% accuracy; expected calibration error, computed over ten equal-width confidence bins, is 0.223) and requires recalibration before use as a confidence score.

We asked whether an ensemble of language models can work like a jury: infer credibility from testimony rather than be told it in advance. Keeping experts’ answer distributions instead of only their argmax improves majority voting by 8.4 points, and weighting experts adds a further 5.5 points. Our contribution is to the second: showing that a simple generative model, fitted by EM on unlabelled answers, learns expert weights without reading a gold answer.

The resulting jury reaches 76.9\pm 1.3\%, beating the pool’s best greedy expert by 2.0 points, the same expert with eight-sample self-consistency on GSM8K by 1.6 points, and the strongest label-free alternative on the full benchmark by 5.5 points, while performing comparably to the supervised linear fusion, the same rule with weights fitted from labels, with a small edge that is significant conditional on the fitted models but not once the variability of refitting is included. The method therefore provides a label-free estimator of expert weights for linear fusion.

In this work, we used generative AI tools (Codex, Claude) to assist with: (i) checking algebraic steps in the proofs, after the propositions and proof strategies had been developed by the authors; (ii) supporting the implementation of the evaluation code; (iii) editing the manuscript to improve readability; and (iv) identifying relevant literature.

Our evaluation uses a fixed pool of nine models and 1,560 questions, mostly multiple-choice. We test every subset of three, five, and seven experts, providing extensive coverage of combinations within this pool, but not of different underlying models. Most of the gain over the best single expert comes from GSM8K. The absence of a significant supervised advantage under the nested bootstrap does not establish equivalence or generalisation beyond the evaluated setting.

The jury requires outputs from every expert and repeated sampling for generative tasks, increasing inference cost. The comparison with the best greedy expert therefore measures the benefit of the complete system, including additional sampling, rather than aggregation alone.

How to get the best and fairest performance out of your ASR system using activation steering. Activation steering for ASR systems is an underexplored technique in improving both ASR performance and demographic fairness. We investigate two forms of activation steering: paired activation subtraction, and supervised optimization. We find the former to be ineffective at ameliorating ASR performance whatsoever, while the latter is quite effective at deriving steering vectors (SVs) that improve at once overall ASR performance and demographic fairness along such diverse axes as gender, age, and dialect. We also explore what types of data---from the most to the least personal---are necessary for calculating or training SVs. First, we show significant performance in performance from training SVs using an eclectic group of speakers from the same dataset. Furthermore, we find that vectors trained using acoustically similar speakers leads to ASR performances that are competitive or superior to vectors trained on the same speaker, or speakers from the same labeled demographic group. This finding shows that we can harness activation steering for few-shot adaptation given access to a speaker's demography, or zero-shot adaptation to unseen speakers without the need for any labels at all.

Activation steering has recently shown promise in various NLP decoding tasks by provoking models such as LLMs or text-to-speech systems into generating outputs with a particular style. Steering works by adding static vectors that represent any given concept at intermediate model layers, thus influencing the flow of information through the model in broad strokes. Steering is useful for three main reasons: 1) its extremely lightweight architecture—steering vector sets for a model M are at most L\times D parameters, where L and D are the width and hidden size of M respectively. 2) its noninvasive setup—no parameters of M are finetuned. 3) the exceptionally small amount of data required to define or train steering vectors (SVs), in an zero-shot optimization-free or supervised optimization setting.

Recent work has shown the viability of encoder steering for ASR systems. However, little is known about how to steer most effectively for maximal performance and demographic fairness. The main contributions of this work are thus twofold. First, we compare SVs trained using two standard steering techniques: optimization-free subtraction of contrasting activations pairs; and supervised SV optimization. We find the former method is not very effective in ameliorating ASR performance for any speakers. On the other hand, we find supervised optimization to be quite effective at improving both overall performance and demographic fairness. This is a rare and noteworthy combination, as many fairness enhancing approaches compromise overall performance for the sake of greater parity.

Second, we investigate the impact of personalization of SV training data, and in particular the viability of training SVs from similar speakers without demographic labels. We train SGs from several data sources representing decreasing levels of data personalization, from same-speaker data (most personal) up to same-dataset data (least personal). We find nearly every level of training data improves both overall performance as well as demographic fairness. Furthermore, we find unsupervised data selection is competitive or superior to data grouping using demographic or speaker labels, thus demonstrating the ASR systems’ potential for zero-shot adaptation to unseen speakers.

Recent work has introduced activation steering for Whisper-style encoder-decoder ASR systems, showing it to improve performance on under-performing speaker groups (SGs). In essence, they show that steering can work as a domain adaptation or personalization tool—SVs representing particular accents can push the latent space of the model back towards familiar territory without having to train it on this unseen domain. This is a slightly different vantage point from “classical” LLM steering: we are not trying to elicit a semantically definable behavior, rather to reduce transcription error.

Activation steering differs from other parameter-efficient ASR personalization methods such as LoRA on two counts: first, it works only on the inter-layer activation space, and second requires far fewer parameters to train. shows steering to outperform LoRA in the low-resource setting of speech accent adaptation in ASR.

Of the three main techniques for learning steering vectors—pairwise activation subtraction, direct optimization, and sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features—the first two have been shown to reduce transcription error rate for marginalized SGs in ASR systems. SAE feature steering tends to underperform other steering methods, though it has been shown to reduce hallucination in Whisper, That said, utterance-level concept vectors from SAE are unlikely to contribute substantially towards domain adaptation as we can easily calculate multi-dimensionally informative utterance-level vectors by averaging over all latent frames of an utterance, without the the information loss that tends to accompany SAE.

(Some SV settings will probably be most effectively steered at different layers, depending on which layers store more information about the constitution of Oth. is located—for example, gender and dialect information are maximized at different layers).
