Validating the Comparison, Not Just the Scorer: Why Overall Accuracy Can Mislead in Interactive LLM Evaluation. Many LLM studies compare how models respond to different follow-up prompts. For example, one prompt may neutrally ask a model to reconsider, while another insists that an invented film really exists. The difference is used to measure the effect of conversational pressure. An automatic scorer then labels whether each response makes an unsupported factual claim. Researchers commonly validate the scorer with one overall accuracy or $F_1$ score. However, high overall performance can hide prompt-specific mistakes: if the scorer makes more errors after one prompt, the measured difference can be too large, too small, or point in the wrong direction. An audit containing mostly difficult responses can also misrepresent performance in the full study. We derive how such errors alter a prompt comparison and examine the problem using six models, 180 invented-entity questions, and six prompt conditions. In a balanced audit of 288 responses, overall $F_1$ was $.916$. Yet, depending on the prompt, the scorer flagged 2.6%-33.3% of responses that the primary LLM rater judged not to contain an unsupported claim; these prompt-specific estimates were uncertain.

In a second audit, the scorer and two separate LLM raters evaluated the same 300 model-question cases under each prompt. An apparent 9.3-point increase from asserting certainty rather than neutrally asking the model to reconsider fell to 2.3 points under both raters. The primary-rater interval included zero, so it did not establish an increase. Two other prompt comparisons kept their direction under both raters, while an attempted prompt-specific correction remained too uncertain for a firm conclusion. Researchers should therefore validate the exact difference they plan to report, not just the scorer as a whole: audit both prompts on matching cases and include scorer and rater uncertainty in the final result.

Consider an evaluation that asks a model about a film that does not exist. After the model expresses uncertainty, one prompt asks it to reconsider; another insists that the film exists and requests a direct answer. The study compares how often the model makes an unsupported claim after each prompt. If the automatic scorer treats hypothetical answers differently in the two conditions, the measured difference combines model behavior with scoring error. Pooling the conditions can still produce a strong F_{1} because errors in one are hidden by correct labels in the other.

We call each prompt condition an arm and the difference between two arms a contrast. Interactive evaluations use contrasts to support claims about pressure, persuasion, or robustness. The claim concerns the difference, not the scorer’s average accuracy. A scorer can therefore look reliable overall while overstating, understating, or changing the direction of the result (Figure 1).

Sampling and routing add further risks. A hard-case audit can reveal failures without estimating accuracy in the study population. In a hybrid pipeline, rules score some responses while ambiguous ones go to a fallback LLM, or routed LLM judge; prompt wording can change both its errors and how often it is used. We examine these problems in UUP-Bench using six models, 180 questions about constructed nonexistent entities, and six prompt conditions. A 550-response stress audit finds failures, a balanced 288-response audit targets an equal-model population, and a 300-key paired audit compares automatic labels with two independent LLM raters on identical model–item pairs.

We derive how each arm’s false positives and false negatives enter the reported contrast, test same-key comparisons, and show why sparse calibration can leave a correction too uncertain to use. The resulting protocol retains, qualifies, rejects, or quarantines a comparison based on its construct, target population, audit sample, paired evidence, and uncertainty. These analyses are exploratory diagnostics, not a scorer leaderboard.

The concrete problem comes before the notation. The automatic pipeline can add more false positives, or miss more positives, in one arm than in the other. The reported arm difference then combines the outcome contrast with a difference in scoring error.

Let A\in\{a,c\} identify the treatment and comparator. Let Y\in\{0,1\} be the primary-rater label and \widetilde{Y} the automatic-pipeline label. All probabilities refer to a declared target population \mathcal{P} over models, items, prompts, and turns. Define \displaystyle p_{j} \displaystyle=P_{\mathcal{P}}(Y=1\mid A=j), \displaystyle\widetilde{p}_{j} \displaystyle=P_{\mathcal{P}}(\widetilde{Y}=1\mid A=j), \displaystyle\alpha_{j} \displaystyle=P(\widetilde{Y}=1\mid Y=0,A=j), \displaystyle\beta_{j} \displaystyle=P(\widetilde{Y}=0\mid Y=1,A=j). Conditioning on Y gives \widetilde{p}_{j}=(1-\beta_{j})p_{j}+\alpha_{j}(1-p_{j}). Therefore, for \Delta_{a,c}=p_{a}-p_{c} and \widetilde{\Delta}_{a,c}=\widetilde{p}_{a}-\widetilde{p}_{c}, \boxed{\widetilde{\Delta}_{a,c}-\Delta_{a,c}=b_{a}-b_{c}},\qquad b_{j}=\alpha_{j}(1-p_{j})-\beta_{j}p_{j}. Here b_{j} is signed arm bias: false positives raise it, while false negatives lower it. Pooled error constrains a contrast only when it also implies b_{a}\approx b_{c} for the target arms. Even equal sensitivity and specificity can produce unequal bias when prevalence differs. Conversely, an automatic scorer can err often in both arms while preserving their difference. Neither pooled F_{1} nor two per-arm F_{1} values therefore validate a contrast by themselves.

section: Why the audit sample and fallback judge matter
text: Evaluation metrics inherit the way the audit was sampled. Let S=1 mean that a row is included. For sensitivity \mathrm{Se}_{a,S}, specificity \mathrm{Sp}_{a,S}, and audit prevalence \pi_{a,S}, \mathrm{PPV}_{a,S}=\frac{\mathrm{Se}_{a,S}\pi_{a,S}}{\mathrm{Se}_{a,S}\pi_{a,S}+(1-\mathrm{Sp}_{a,S})(1-\pi_{a,S})}. Oversampling predicted positives, difficult responses, selected arms, or routed cases changes \pi_{a,S}. It may also change errors within label groups. A hard-case audit can reveal failures, but it cannot estimate target precision without a justified sampling model and weights. Keeping the scorer version fixed does not make its measured performance transportable, meaning applicable to a different target population.

section: Why the audit sample and fallback judge matter
text: Hybrid evaluation adds another mixture. Rules score some rows, while ambiguous rows go to the routed LLM judge. Let R=1 denote that route, q_{a}=P(R=1\mid A=a), and e_{ar}=E[\widetilde{Y}-Y\mid A=a,R=r]. The second index records the route: e_{a1} is error among routed-judge cases and e_{a0} is error among heuristic-only cases. Averaging over the two routes gives b_{a}=q_{a}e_{a1}+(1-q_{a})e_{a0}. Either route-specific error or the routing share can change arm bias. A pooled hybrid score hides both. This breakdown is descriptive. Harder cases enter the routed LLM judge, so route-specific behavior does not show the causal effect of using that judge.

section: Why the audit sample and fallback judge matter
text: We therefore attach validity to \mathcal{V}=(Y,\ a\!:\!c,\ \mathcal{P},\ \mathcal{S}), where \mathcal{S} is the sampling and weighting plan. A complete record also fixes the automatic pipeline and LLM-rater process. Four separate gates ask whether the arms measure the same construct, whether errors were observed by arm, whether the audit transports to \mathcal{P}, and whether same-key ratings preserve the contrast. Changing arm wording, the label schema, the routed LLM judge, the router, the model mixture, sampling, or the rater process can create a new validation problem.

LLM judges can agree with independent ratings and still have task- and model-dependent bias (Liu et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023). Meta-evaluation usually pools a benchmark and summarizes that agreement. We ask whether signed error preserves one declared prompt comparison. The outcome must also be explicit: factual support, abstention, and uncertainty are different labels (Min et al., 2023; Madhusudhan et al., 2025; Yona et al., 2024). Sensitivity/specificity correction and prediction-powered inference can use LLM-rater labels (Rogan and Gladen, 1978; Angelopoulos et al., 2023). Neither repairs a changed construct or an audit that does not apply to the target cases.

An anonymized companion studies which model–item pairs continue after a Soft cue (Anonymous, 2026). It shares the panel but asks a different question and uses a different empirical analysis. Here we declare the target population first, then ask whether the automatic pipeline preserves the difference between two prompt conditions.

UUP-Bench evaluates Claude Sonnet 5, Gemma 3 4B, Llama 4 Maverick, GPT-5.6 Luna, Qwen3-32B, and Qwen3-8B on 180 constructed nonexistent-entity items (nonreferents) drawn from cities, films, and scientists. We screened names with lexical checks, knowledge bases, and manual review. “Clean” means the retained screened layer; it does not mean perfect undetectability. The six audited arms are Spontaneous, Soft cue, reconsider Neutral, instructional-license Existence, Confidence, and Authority. The positive outcome is an entity-specific unsupported assertion.

Our design assigns four distinct roles. The automatic pipeline applies deterministic and heuristic rules. It sends ambiguous responses to the routed LLM judge, DeepSeek V4 Pro. A separate audit process uses the primary LLM rater (Mistral Large 3 2512) and the secondary LLM rater (MiniMax M3) at T{=}0 with the written unsupported-assertion rubric. The raters see response text and item metadata, but not hypothesis names or automatic labels. The primary LLM rater supplies the comparison labels throughout. Independently collected secondary-rater labels measure disagreement, and we do not adjudicate them into consensus. Neither rater family is otherwise used as an evaluated endpoint or automatic judge, so the audits provide unused-family cross-model evidence. Neither rater is human, and neither supplies ground truth.

The first audit has 550 rated responses and deliberately includes extra pressure-arm and routed-LLM-judge cases. Across it, TP/FP/FN/TN are 111/52/58/329 (P=.681, R=.657, F_{1}=.669). The routed LLM judge handles 264/550=48.0\%. The heuristic-only slice has F_{1}=.762 (n=286), versus.545 for the routed slice (n=264). These values describe a stress sample. Harder cases enter the routed LLM judge, so the difference does not show that routing causes errors.

The representative audit samples 48 clean responses per arm and eight per model, for n=288. It estimates behavior for an equal-model target, not provider traffic, future endpoints, or every prompt mixture. Both LLM raters label a 96-row subset from Neutral, Existence, Confidence, and Authority. They agree on 94/96=.979, with Cohen’s \kappa=.958. Spontaneous and Soft cue have no secondary-rater labels in this representative audit. The 288-row audit and all analyses based on it are exploratory.

section: Audit sampling changes the reported accuracy
text: Precision changes by different amounts when the audit sample changes (Figure 2). Neutral rises from.667 (n=81 hard rows) to 23/24=.958 on 48 representative rows. Authority rises from.633 (n=111) to 28/29=.966, while Spontaneous rises from.684 on 24 hard rows to 27/34=.794. Wilson intervals are wide and often overlap. These summaries describe different sampling plans. They neither test temporal drift nor establish a plan-by-arm interaction.

section: Why errors must be measured by prompt condition
text: The balanced audit makes the pooled-versus-arm problem concrete. TP/FP/FN/TN are 120/18/4/146, agreement is 266/288=.924, and pooled F_{1}=.916. Yet observed arm false-positive rates range from.026 to.333 (Table 1). Existence precision is 15/18=.833 ([.608,.942]), while Authority precision is 28/29=.966 ([.828,.994]). Their FPRs are 3/32=.094 and 1/20=.050. A Fisher test does not find this particular difference significant (p=1.000).

section: Why errors must be measured by prompt condition
text: The FPR analysis uses the 164 rows that the primary LLM rater labels negative. An exploratory linear-probability model includes fixed effects for arm and model and clusters its CR1 covariance by item. It does not reject equal arm FPRs (\chi^{2}_{5}=9.10, p=.1052; 102 item clusters). Of 15 pairwise comparisons, Soft cue minus Spontaneous has the largest model-adjusted difference, -.325 (Holm p=.1572). This imprecise estimate is relative to the primary LLM rater in the audited six-model panel; it neither identifies a cause nor establishes pairwise heterogeneity. Under an independent-proportion approximation, the observed raw extreme needs 20 primary-rater-negative rows per arm. A 10-point difference around.20 –.30 needs 292, before extra costs from model clustering.

section: Why errors must be measured by prompt condition
text: The corresponding unpaired bias diagnostics, (\mathrm{FP}-\mathrm{FN})/48, range from -.042 to +.146. The difference in bias is +.083 for Confidence - Neutral and -.021 for Authority - Existence. Soft cue has three false negatives among ten primary-rater positives, and Existence has one among sixteen, so sensitivity is imprecise. These values diagnose the audit slice; they are not corrected panel effects.

section: Why errors must be measured by prompt condition
text: Existence also fails the construct gate. Its instruction permits hypothetical completion. That changes which answers comply with the prompt instead of merely adding scoring noise to Neutral. In a clean unpaired slice, Authority - Existence is +22.9 points under the automatic pipeline and +25.0 points under primary-rater labels. The hard slice gives -19.0 and -5.0 points. These diagnostics have no contrast interval and are not effect estimates. A separate paired audit of Authority - Existence (registered H3) using primary-rater labels is positive (+.150, item-clustered 95% CI [+.061,+.279], n=100 pairs). H3 remains quarantined because primary-rater labels cannot turn an instructional-license comparator into a neutral pressure contrast.

section: Why errors must be measured by prompt condition
text: Claude Sonnet 5 acts as an alternative automatic judge, not as the secondary LLM rater (Table 6). It rescores the same 288 rows. It agrees with the automatic pipeline on 259/288=.899 and with the primary LLM rater on 273/288=.948; TP/FP/FN/TN are 119/10/5/154 (F_{1}=.941). It repeats the relevant ordering: Neutral precision is 23/23=1.000, and Existence precision is 16/19=.842. This evidence is correlated, not independent. Claude shares the rows, primary-rater labels, and framing, and Claude Sonnet 5 is also an evaluated panel model. The result only shows that the ordering is not unique to one automatic implementation. It adds no independent LLM-rater process or cross-family transport guarantee.

section: Does error change the comparison on the same cases?
text: Per-arm metrics explain error. The same-key contrast check asks the more direct question: does that error change the contrast on identical keys? A seeded, model-balanced audit contains 300 complete clean item–model keys, with 50 per model. The same keys appear in four continuation arms after the same Soft-cue response. Neutral asks for reconsideration. Certainty-only states confidence in the model’s knowledge. Confidence also states that the entity exists and requests an unhedged answer. Existence \times Directness tells the model to assume existence and answer directly. Both LLM raters independently label all 1,200 responses. Item-clustered bootstrap intervals preserve pairing, and the second rater directly tests cross-family sensitivity on the target rows.

section: Does error change the comparison on the same cases?
text: The gate withholds the raw Certainty-only - Neutral headline: automatic +.093 attenuates to primary-rater +.023 ([-.059,+.053]), and the secondary-rater estimate is also +.023. Confidence - Neutral keeps its positive sign but shrinks to +.070 ([+.001,+.112]); the secondary estimate is +.107. Confidence - Existence \times Directness keeps a negative sign, from -.163 automatic to -.167 under primary-rater labels ([-.207,-.081]) and -.190 under secondary-rater labels. No contrast reverses sign. These decisions apply only to the labeled factorial contrasts. They do not repair H3’s changed comparator.

section: Correction does not remove calibration uncertainty
text: After the construct and transport checks, Confidence–Neutral permits a separate-arm diagnostic. We apply a sensitivity-and-specificity prevalence correction (Rogan–Gladen) separately to each arm: \widehat{p}_{j}^{\,RG}=\frac{\widetilde{p}_{j}+\widehat{\mathrm{Sp}}_{j}-1}{\widehat{\mathrm{Se}}_{j}+\widehat{\mathrm{Sp}}_{j}-1}. It changes automatic RD from +.113 to +.032, near the primary-rater value of +.070 (Table 3). A 200,000-draw Beta posterior calculation with a Jeffreys prior carries uncertainty from the target rate, sensitivity, and specificity into the result. It includes zero-FN cells instead of treating an estimated sensitivity of one as known. The interval is [-.146,+.197], with P(\Delta>0)=.685. Forty-eight calibration rows per arm cannot support a precise corrected headline. Prediction-powered inference adds no information because the primary LLM rater labels all 300 target keys. Using the separate 288-row audit as its correction term would require an unsupported transport assumption.

section: Correction does not remove calibration uncertainty
text: LLM-rater uncertainty remains separate from automatic-scorer uncertainty. Across all 1,200 factorial labels, the primary and secondary LLM raters disagree on 57/1200=4.75\%; arm-specific disagreement ranges from 1.7\% to 6.7\%. Their contrast estimates are close: primary/secondary RDs are +.023/+.023, +.070/+.107, and -.167/-.190 (Table 8). This does not identify label error or make either rater preferable. Seven single-label changes among 600 arm labels can move Certainty-only - Neutral to zero. Confidence - Neutral requires 21, and Confidence - Existence \times Directness requires 50 (Table 7). Under illustrative five-point per-arm prevalence-error budgets, the RD bounds are [-.077,+.123], [-.030,+.170], and [-.267,-.067], respectively. The budget marks breakpoints rather than turning disagreement into a ground-truth error rate. Only the third sign survives.

section: How to decide whether a comparison is supported
text: Apply the protocol separately to every intended headline.

Before seeing effects, define the positive label and unit. Reproduce the treatment and comparator prompts. State the pairing key, target models, items, domains, turns, weights, automatic-pipeline and router versions, audit design, and LLM-rater process. Prespecify a meaningful tolerance \epsilon for automatic–primary-rater contrast bias. State whether success means preserving the sign or showing equivalence.

section: 2. Separate target sampling from failure discovery.
text: Draw a probability sample, or an explicitly balanced sample, from both arms. Record inclusion probabilities or target weights. Preserve identical treatment–control keys. A separate hard sample can find failures, but applying its metrics to the target requires a justified model.

Blind LLM raters to hypotheses, expected directions, and automatic labels. Have both raters independently label a declared subset. Report counts, agreement, \kappa, and the adjudication policy. Rater disagreement is outcome uncertainty, not a nuisance to omit.

section: 4. Report errors by arm and route.
text: Publish TP/FP/FN/TN, intervals, prevalence, missingness, and routing shares for each arm. For a hybrid scorer, also report behavior within the rule and routed-LLM-judge routes and the quantities in Equation 5. Pooled F_{1} cannot replace this disclosure.

section: 5. Test the comparison on identical cases.
text: On the target keys and weights, estimate \widehat{\Delta}^{\rm auto}, \widehat{\Delta}^{\rm ref}, and \widehat{d}=\widehat{\Delta}^{\rm auto}-\widehat{\Delta}^{\rm ref} with clustering that matches the design. An unpaired slice is only diagnostic. Here “ref” denotes the primary-rater contrast.

section: 6. Apply four gates and a disposition.
text: Construct asks whether both prompts implement one intended comparison. Observation asks whether the audit measured errors by arm. Applicability (transport) asks whether the audit applies to \mathcal{P}. Same-key asks whether the prespecified contrast rule passes on identical keys. Retain when all gates pass. Qualify when the stronger rule fails but a prespecified weaker sign rule passes. Reject when a sufficiently reliable same-key audit contradicts the raw headline. Quarantine when the construct, LLM-rater process, or audit cannot answer the claim. Correction is eligible only after the first three gates and must carry calibration uncertainty forward. It cannot repair a changed comparator.

Changes to the prompt, label, routed LLM judge, router, model panel, target weights, sampling, or LLM-rater process create a new record. Preserve exploratory status and earlier versions. Do not relabel diagnostics as prospective confirmation.

The case study shows why trust cannot be assigned to an evaluator in the abstract. Pooled F_{1}=.916 coexists with prompt-specific false-positive rates whose differences remain too imprecise to dismiss. The stress and balanced audits describe different groups of cases, and the alternative automatic judge repeats one ordering without providing an independent check. On identical cases, one automatic comparison shrinks to an interval that includes zero, while two keep their direction under both independent LLM raters. The prompt-specific correction moves toward the primary-rater estimate but remains too uncertain to replace it.

Validation should therefore attach to a defined outcome, two prompts, a target set of cases, and an audit sample, together with versioned automatic and LLM-rater processes. Error counts by prompt help explain a problem; same-case ratings test whether the reported difference survives. Neither can rescue prompts that measure different constructs or an audit that does not apply to the target population. The protocol uses explicit decisions instead of a universal F_{1} threshold.

The representative audit supports a local statement: in an equal-model mixture of these six arms, observed FPRs span.026 –.333, but the omnibus does not reject equal arm FPRs and modest variation remains unresolved. The hard audit finds failures under its documented enrichment and routing; it does not estimate a population error rate. The alternative automatic judge shows that the Neutral–Existence ordering is not unique to the automatic pipeline on the same rows. Shared data, framing, and primary-rater labels make this corroboration rather than independent validation.

The factorial audit addresses the reported contrasts more directly. On the same 300 keys, Certainty-only - Neutral attenuates to an interval spanning zero, Confidence - Neutral weakens but stays positive under both raters, and Confidence - Existence \times Directness stays negative under the illustrative rater-error budget. These outcomes justify contrast-specific retain, qualify, or quarantine decisions. They do not identify a globally trustworthy scorer or an error budget for future prompts. Arm correction cannot replace the fully rated estimate because calibration uncertainty is wide and sample dependence is only approximated.

The practical lesson is to match evidence to the decision. For a benchmark prevalence claim, estimate error in the benchmark population. For a difference between prompts, rate matched cases and test whether scoring error changes that difference. If the prompts do not measure the same construct, the LLM ratings are unstable, or the audit does not apply to the target cases, quarantine the result instead of turning pooled agreement into confidence. This discipline keeps automatic evaluation useful while making each score’s limits explicit.

The representative audit has 48 responses per arm and eight per model. Precision, FPR, and especially sensitivity intervals are wide. Its Wilson intervals are row-level descriptive summaries. The exploratory omnibus has 102 primary-rater-negative item clusters, treats six models as fixed, and lacks precision for modest arm differences. Factorial intervals are also exploratory.

The audit labels are uncertain LLM ratings, not human judgments or ground truth. Both rater families are unused among the evaluated endpoints and automatic judges, but cross-family agreement cannot establish correctness. The representative dual subset excludes Spontaneous and Soft cue, disagreements are not adjudicated, and both raters label all 1,200 factorial responses. Sensitivity bounds expose but do not resolve this uncertainty. The “representative” target is only an equal-model mixture of clean nonreferents in six arms. It is not provider traffic, future models, or arbitrary prompts. Hard-sample and route summaries support neither causal nor population claims.

The alternative automatic judge is one correlated frontier model on the same rows. Rogan–Gladen assumes that arm calibration transports to the target and handles overlap only approximately. Its interval rules it out as a replacement headline. The protocol supplies no universal \epsilon, and this retrospective study cannot demonstrate prospective preregistration.
Reproduction materials are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/scorer-validity-53E8/. They include data, code, prompts, metadata, and seeds; no proprietary scorer is claimed.

Overstated automatic evaluation can mislead benchmarks and model comparisons. Arm counts and uncertainty reduce that risk. UUP-Bench uses generated nonreferents, no private conversations, and collision-screened names. Hosted LLM ratings are neither human labels nor ground truth; no human subjects took part. Hosted-call costs were not logged exhaustively, and endpoints are not redistributed.

What Is a Clarification? Estimating Model-Dependent Input Ambiguity. Ambiguous inputs can admit multiple interpretations, each potentially yielding a different answer. Existing work largely treats this ambiguity as a property of the input, yet for a particular language model, only some alternatives may be known and answerable. We therefore distinguish world ambiguity, capturing all alternatives admitted by an input, from model ambiguity, capturing those accessible to the responding model. To characterize these alternatives, we formalize natural-language clarifications through three desiderata: \emph{uniqueness}, \emph{faithfulness}, and \emph{answer equivalence}. We show that these desiderata induce a one-to-one correspondence between valid answers and equivalence classes of clarifications, implying that any interpretation can be represented either by its answer or by the clarifications that uniquely express it. We leverage this correspondence to introduce \circleclar{}, a black-box method that estimates the set of answers available to a model by checking consistency along an answer--clarification--answer cycle. Across open-domain QA and executable Text-to-SQL, \circleclar{} achieves strong recovery of these answer sets. In QA, the recovered support yields the strongest overall performance in model-dependent ambiguity detection and enables effective selection among answering, clarifying, and abstaining.
Together, these results demonstrate the practical value of a model-dependent view of ambiguity and its characterization through an answer-clarification correspondence.

Ambiguous inputs can admit multiple reasonable interpretations, each potentially leading to a different answer. Existing work has largely treated this ambiguity as a property of the input itself. However, when an ambiguous input is presented to a Large Language Model, not every valid interpretation is necessarily accessible and answerable by that model. Consider, for example, the question “Who voiced the snake in the Jungle Book?”. The intended adaptation is unspecified: for the 1967 film, the answer is Sterling Holloway, whereas for the 2016 film, it is Scarlett Johansson. While both interpretations are valid, one model may know both films and their answers, whereas another may know only one. The ambiguity inherent in the question remains unchanged; what changes is how much of that ambiguity is accessible to the responding model.

We therefore propose to distinguish between world ambiguity and model ambiguity (Figure 1). World ambiguity captures the alternatives admitted by the input, independent of any particular model. Model ambiguity instead captures those alternatives that are known and answerable to the responding model. The distinction is consequential: two models can face the same world ambiguity but, because they know different parts of its ambiguity, effectively face different problems. A model that knows several valid alternatives should recognize that committing to one leaves the user’s intent unresolved; a model that knows only one alternative, or none, is in a fundamentally different situation. We therefore ask how to estimate the interpretations and corresponding answers a particular model knows.

To do so, we use natural-language clarifications, which are explicit representations of distinct interpretations of the original input. While such clarifications are widely used in prior work, their precise definition is often omitted. Hence, we propose to characterize valid clarifications through three desiderata: uniqueness: a clarification should admit only a single answer; faithfulness: that answer must also be a valid answer for the original question; and answer equivalence: clarifications that induce the same answer should be treated as equivalent. Our key observation is that, under these desiderata, each valid answer corresponds to exactly one clarification class, thereby providing two complementary representations of the same interpretation (Figure 1 b).

This correspondence suggests a simple way to estimate what ambiguity a model can realize. If a model proposes an answer, expresses the corresponding interpretation through a clarification, and then reliably returns to the same answer under that clarification, the resulting cycle provides additional evidence that this alternative is accessible to the model. We turn this idea into CircleClar, a black-box method for estimating the model-specific set of realizable answers (Figure 1 c). We evaluate CircleClar on open-domain QA using AmbigQA and our curated high-quality version (AmbigQA-HQ), and on executable Text-to-SQL using AMBROSIA. CircleClar achieves the best answer-set F1 in seven of twelve model–dataset settings and outperforms direct-generation baselines across all QA settings. Moreover, its cardinality can predict model-dependent ambiguity and serves as an effective basis for deciding whether to answer, clarify, or abstain. Taken together, these results support a model-dependent view of ambiguity: what matters for a particular LLM is not only which alternatives an input admits, but which of them the model can realize.

A common way to study input ambiguity is to make the possible interpretations of an underspecified input explicit. In open-domain QA, interpretations can be expressed through disambiguated questions, either provided as annotations or generated recursively as part of answering ambiguous questions. In semantic parsing, where natural-language inputs are mapped to executable representations, such as SQL queries or tool calls, different interpretations can be expressed as distinct executable programs, or first stated in natural language before being mapped to logical forms. Related work also makes alternative readings explicit as structured interpretation–answer pairs, while Tomov et al. [20] take a distributional view, representing ambiguity through a ground-truth distribution over semantic answer classes and their relative likelihoods. Beyond such explicit representations, Kirchhof et al. [8] takes a more general view of underspecification, describing it as uncertainty about the intended task or as missing contextual information, modeled via a latent variable model.

Recent work treats input ambiguity as a quantity that can be estimated from model outputs. ICE treats it as a source of aleatoric uncertainty. It generates multiple clarifications of the input, obtains predictions for each, and ensembles them to separate aleatoric uncertainty from epistemic uncertainty. Spectral Uncertainty extends this approach by doing soft clustering via embeddings. CLARA generates multiple clarifications and uses their semantic diversity as an ambiguity signal, while Shi et al. [17] detect ambiguity from sampled-answer distributions. CLUES instead uses a two-stage process from interpretations to answers, separating uncertainty across interpretations from instability in their associated answers.

Beyond estimating ambiguity itself, other work incorporates ambiguity detection or recognition into clarification systems, benchmarks, and policies. Lee et al. [10] formulate open-domain QA as a pipeline that detects ambiguous questions, presents candidate interpretations in a clarification question, and answers based on the user’s response. CLAM similarly classifies whether a question is ambiguous and selectively requests clarification before answering. CLAMBER jointly benchmarks the identification of ambiguous information needs and the generation of clarification questions. INTENT-SIM estimates entropy over simulated user intents to determine when clarification is beneficial. ACT learns multi-turn clarification policies and evaluates implicit ambiguity recognition through models’ clarify-or-answer decisions. Zhang, Knox, and Choi use simulated future conversation turns to train clarify-or-answer behavior and evaluate the resulting decisions against ambiguity labels. Su and Cardie further show that ambiguity recognition capability does not necessarily translate into clarification behavior: models often identify an input as ambiguous when asked explicitly, yet default to answering in ordinary QA. Closely related to our work, BAG uses sampled responses as a belief state to guide whether to answer, clarify, or abstain. Its BAG3 variant groups responses by meaning and proposes interpretations for each group to distinguish alternative readings from factual inconsistencies.

Overall, prior work studied how ambiguity can be represented, estimated, and handled through clarifications. Far less attention has been paid to how ambiguity varies with the responding model’s own knowledge. APA recognizes this, defining perceived ambiguity as a property of a particular model and measuring it through the reduction in the model’s average token entropy from the original question to a self-disambiguated version. While conceptually sharing this perspective, our work goes further by formally distinguishing the two different types of ambiguity and defining not only a quantitative estimator but also actionable estimates of clarifications and their answers.

section: Why Input Ambiguity Should be Model Dependent
text: Ambiguity is typically treated as a property of the input: a question is ambiguous when it admits multiple valid interpretations. As such, most prior work studies ambiguity independently of the used model. Similar to Kim et al. [7], we propose to treat ambiguity as dependent on model knowledge and, therefore, as a model-dependent property. We formalize this distinction below and empirically show that it varies substantially across models (Figure 2), motivating our model-dependent framework for characterizing ambiguity.

LLMs implicitly define a probability distribution p(s) over arbitrary-length strings s\in\mathcal{V}^{<\infty} from a vocabulary \mathcal{V}. Conditioned on an input x\in\mathcal{V}^{<\infty}, the model induces a task-specific predictive distribution p_{T}(y\mid x) over answers y for a task T. We analogously denote by p_{T}^{\star}(y\mid x) the corresponding unknown ground-truth distribution. Importantly, we consider answers in a task-relevant output space \mathcal{Y}_{T}, which abstracts away distinctions that are irrelevant to the task, like surface form or syntax, by aggregating responses with similar semantic meaning into one element. For question answering, for example, semantically equivalent answer strings correspond to the same element of \mathcal{Y}_{T}; for executable outputs, such as SQL queries, syntactically different forms are treated as equivalent when they return the same requested information.

World vs. Model Ambiguity. An ambiguous question x admits multiple interpretations, which may in turn lead to different correct answers. In the running example, the unspecified film yields Sterling Holloway or Scarlett Johansson. We call the set of all such answers the world answer support, \mathcal{W}_{T}(x):=\operatorname{supp}p_{T}^{\star}(\cdot\mid x)=\{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{T}:p_{T}^{\star}(y\mid x)>0\}, where p_{T}^{\star} denotes an oracle or ground-truth mapping. The corresponding world ambiguity is simply |\mathcal{W}_{T}(x)|, the number of correct answers admitted by the question. In particular, x is world ambiguous whenever there is more than one correct answer, i.e. |\mathcal{W}_{T}(x)|>1.

Crucially, however, world ambiguity need not coincide with the ambiguity realized by a particular model. Returning to our example, a model that knows both Jungle Book films can realize that the question admits at least two interpretations and associate each with its corresponding answer. In contrast, another model may only know the 2016 film—due, for instance, to differences in training data, capacity, distillation, or compression—and therefore realize only Scarlett Johansson as a valid answer. The underlying question is equally ambiguous in both cases: its world answer support \mathcal{W}_{T}(x) has not changed. What changes is which parts of this ambiguity are accessible to the model. To capture this distinction, for a model p_{T} we define its model-realizable answer support as \mathcal{M}_{T}(x):=\operatorname{supp}p_{T}(\cdot\mid x)\cap\mathcal{W}_{T}(x)=\{y\in\mathcal{W}_{T}(x):p_{T}(y\mid x)>0\}.

Accordingly, we define the model-realizable ambiguity of x as |\mathcal{M}_{T}(x)|. Unlike world ambiguity, this quantity is inherently model-dependent: Two models facing the same question may realize different subsets of the valid answers. We observe precisely this effect in Figure 2: larger, more capable models tend to realize more of the ambiguity present in the world. Their model-realizable support also tracks the world support more closely across inputs, as shown by a higher input-level Spearman correlation between \lvert\mathcal{M}_{T}(x)\rvert and \lvert\mathcal{W}_{T}(x)\rvert. Nonetheless, even the strongest model remains substantially below the mean world-support size.

This distinction between these two forms of ambiguity matters because, when deciding how a particular model should respond, world ambiguity alone is insufficient. Suppose |\mathcal{W}_{T}(x)|>1, but a model realizes only one of these answers. From an oracle perspective, the question is ambiguous. From the model’s perspective, there is no alternative interpretation on which it can meaningfully act. Conversely, a model that realizes several valid answers should recognize that answering with any single one implicitly commits to a specific interpretation. Thus, the appropriate response—whether to answer, clarify, or abstain—depends not only on which answers exist, but on which of them are realizable by the model. Our goal is therefore not to recover \mathcal{W}_{T}(x), but to estimate the model-specific set \mathcal{M}_{T}(x).

section: A Clarification Framework for Estimating Model-Dependent Ambiguity
text: We now turn to the question of how to estimate the model-realizable answer support \mathcal{M}_{T}(x). To do so, we use clarifications, which provide a natural way to express interpretations as natural-language inputs for the model. While clarifications have been previously used, a precise formal characterization of what constitutes a valid clarification has, to our knowledge, not been provided. This absence is consequential: without a rigorous definition, clarifications may possess undesirable properties that introduce confounds into downstream estimators. To address this gap, we are the first to formally characterize valid clarifications through a set of explicit desiderata (Section 4.1). Crucially, we prove that, under these desiderata, the set of clarifications admits an equivalent representation of the answer space. We then exploit this equivalence to construct CircleClar, a black-box estimator of \mathcal{M}_{T}(x).

We begin with the most basic requirement: a clarification must actually resolve the ambiguity. Consider again the ambiguous question “Who voiced the snake in The Jungle Book?” in which the adaptation is unspecified. A logical clarification would be “Who voiced the snake in the 1967 animated film The Jungle Book?”. This reformulation resolves the ambiguity by selecting a single interpretation and, consequently, a particular answer. This motivates our first desideratum.
Desideratum 1: Uniqueness A clarification shall uniquely determine an answer: \exists y_{c}\in\mathcal{Y}_{T}\quad\text{such that}\quad p_{T}^{\star}(y_{c}\mid c)=1.

Without uniqueness, the clarification itself remains ambiguous and therefore does not isolate one particular unambiguous reading of the original input. Uniqueness alone, however, is not sufficient. For example, “Who voiced Mowgli in the 1967 animated film The Jungle Book?” is also unambiguous, but its answer is not a valid answer to the original question about the snake. A clarification must therefore not only resolve the ambiguity, but also preserve the meaning of the original input.
Desideratum 2: Faithfulness The answer induced by a clarification must also be supported by the original ambiguous input prompt: y_{c}\in\mathcal{W}_{T}(x).

Together, Uniqueness and Faithfulness ensure that a clarification selects exactly one valid answer from \mathcal{W}_{T}(x). In our example, specifying the 1967 film selects Sterling Holloway, while specifying the 2016 film selects Scarlett Johansson; both are valid answers to the original question. Importantly, however, the clarification itself is not unique. The same interpretation can typically be expressed in different ways. For instance, “Who voiced Kaa in Disney’s 1967 animated The Jungle Book?” and “Who is the voice actor for the snake Kaa in the 1967 Jungle Book film?” differ in wording, but both select the same answer, Sterling Holloway. For our purposes, these surface-form differences are irrelevant.

Desideratum 3: Answer Equivalence Let \mathcal{C}_{T}(x) denote the set of valid clarifications of x for task T. Two clarifications are equivalent exactly when they induce the same answer. For two valid clarifications c,c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{T}(x), c\sim_{x}c^{\prime}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y_{c}=y_{c^{\prime}}.

Answer Equivalence therefore groups different surface forms that express the same interpretation into classes. In our example, all valid clarifications that specify the 1967 film belong to one class, since they all induce the answer Sterling Holloway. We denote the class containing a clarification c by [c]_{x}:=\{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{T}(x):c^{\prime}\sim_{x}c\}, and write y_{[c]} for the answer shared by all clarifications in this class, while writing \mathcal{C}_{T}(x)/{\sim_{x}} for the set of all such equivalence classes.

The three desiderata give us a useful structure: Each clarification class identifies exactly one valid answer to the original input. If we additionally assume that every valid answer can be expressed by at least one clarification, then the reverse also holds: every answer in \mathcal{W}_{T}(x) is represented by exactly one clarification class. This gives the following correspondence (Proof in Appendix A):

Suppose clarifications satisfy D1–D3 and every y\in\mathcal{W}_{T}(x) admits at least one valid clarification. Then the map from clarification to response \Phi_{x}:\mathcal{C}_{T}(x)/{\sim_{x}}\longrightarrow\mathcal{W}_{T}(x),\qquad\Phi_{x}([c]_{x})=y_{[c]}, is a bijection.

For each y\in\mathcal{W}_{T}(x), we write [c_{y}]_{x} for the unique clarification class corresponding to y under this bijection. Returning once more to our example, the interpretation referring to the 1967 film can now be represented either by the answer Sterling Holloway or by the entire class of clarifications that uniquely lead to this answer, such as “Who voiced the snake in the 1967 animated film The Jungle Book?”. More generally, Proposition 4.1 gives us two equivalent representations of each interpretation: its answer y and a class [c_{y}]_{x} of natural-language clarifications that induce it. Hence, starting from an answer y, we can move to its corresponding clarification class [c_{y}]_{x}, and any clarification from this class maps back to the same answer y. This yields the cycle y\longrightarrow[c_{y}]_{x}\longrightarrow y, the key consistency relation underlying the estimator introduced next.

The answer–clarification correspondence established under the ideal task distribution p_{T}^{\star} provides a consistency criterion for testing candidate answers using the model distribution p_{T}: if a candidate \widetilde{y} corresponds to an answer of a valid interpretation of x, then expressing that interpretation through a clarification should make \widetilde{y} uniquely correct, and the model should recover it when answering the clarified input. Reliably recovering \widetilde{y} under p_{T} therefore provides evidence that \widetilde{y}\in\mathcal{M}_{T}(x).

As illustrated in Figure 1 c, CircleClar operationalizes this idea in two steps: it first constructs a set of candidate outcomes supported by the model, and then uses the answer–clarification–answer cycle as a consistency test to filter these candidates. Concretely, we first query the model B times with an enumeration prompt that asks for all plausible answers to the original input x, obtaining answer collections Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{B}. We then take the union over these B answer sets and map the resulting responses to semantic answer classes, yielding the candidate set \widetilde{\mathcal{Y}}_{T}(x). This candidate set provides an approximation to the model’s predictive support, \widetilde{\mathcal{Y}}_{T}(x)\approx\operatorname{supp}p_{T}(\cdot\mid x). For each candidate \widetilde{y}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{Y}}_{T}(x), we ask the model to generate a clarification c_{\widetilde{y}} that makes the corresponding interpretation explicit. We then close the cycle by prompting the same LLM to answer this clarification again. If the clarification truly represents the same interpretation, the model should return to the original candidate \widetilde{y}. We capture this through the recovery probability p_{T}(\widetilde{y}\mid c_{\widetilde{y}}), retaining candidates whose recovery probability meets or exceeds a threshold \tau. In practice, we approximate p_{T}(\widetilde{y}\mid c_{\widetilde{y}}) using R Monte Carlo samples from p_{T}(\cdot\mid c_{\widetilde{y}}). The complete algorithm is in Algorithm 1 with prompts in Appendix E.

Our primary evaluation asks how accurately CircleClar recovers the model-realizable answer support. We then evaluate two downstream uses of the recovered support in QA: using its cardinality to detect model-dependent ambiguity and deriving the response action from the estimated support.

We evaluate CircleClar across two domains. For open-domain question answering, we use 1,000 ambiguous questions from AmbigQA, together with AmbigQA-HQ, a manually curated set of 100 questions derived primarily from AmbigQA with more complete and reliable rewrite–answer annotations (see Appendix B). For executable Text-to-SQL, we evaluate on 96 ambiguous requests from AMBROSIA. Since we treat final answers y by their task-relevant semantic meaning rather than as raw strings, we construct the corresponding equivalence classes using an LLM-based semantic grouping procedure tailored to the task (Appendix E).

We construct \mathcal{W}_{T}(x) from the distinct reference answers associated with the dataset-provided resolved inputs. To construct the model-specific reference \mathcal{M}_{T}(x), we test whether the evaluated model reliably recovers each reference answer y from its associated ground-truth clarification c_{y} and if so, include it. (See Appendix E for more details).

Existing methods cannot directly recover a model-realizable answer set. We therefore adapt ICE to recover answer sets by retaining answers with probability above a threshold, which is optimized per model–dataset pair to maximize the mean set F1. We further compare against two direct-generation baselines: Sampling-50, which samples 50 times, and 1-Enumeration, which asks the model once to enumerate all plausible answers. Full details are provided in Appendix E.

Table 1 shows that CircleClar performs strongly across datasets, achieving particularly large gains over baselines on smaller models and on the curated AmbigQA-HQ benchmark. The overall performance gap between AmbigQA and AmbigQA-HQ likely stems from annotation errors in the standard AmbigQA, which introduce noisy estimates of the ground-truth set. Across all methods, performance gaps shrink on larger models. Notably, the simple baseline of enumerating possible answers one-shot achieves remarkably high performance on larger models, indicating that increased scale enables models to surface multiple plausible alternatives directly within a single structured response.

Furthermore, precision and recall breakdowns in Appendix C.1 show that CircleClar ’s gains are most consistent in precision. Moreover, evaluations on unambiguous, single-answer questions in Appendix C.3 confirm that our method largely avoids hallucinating non-existent alternatives in unambiguous cases and, in fact, significantly outperforms other methods on smaller models. Finally, Appendix C.2 examines sensitivity to the enumeration and recovery budgets and the recovery threshold. Increasing the enumeration budget improves performance for the GPT models on AmbigQA-HQ but decreases it for the Qwen models; on AmbigQA, performance is largely stable or decreases. This contrast may indicate that smaller models are primarily constrained by precision, whereas larger models are constrained by recall.

To isolate the effect of the consistency check, we compare the unfiltered candidate set \widetilde{\mathcal{Y}}_{T}(x) which is obtained after the answer enumeration step, with the final estimate \widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{T}(x) obtained after consistency filtering. As shown in Figure 3, the consistency check yields substantial gains in precision across nearly all settings. Because this filtering step can only remove candidates, recall naturally decreases, but the resulting trade-off is generally small compared to the high increase in precision. Notably, the magnitude of the precision gain diminishes with model scale, suggesting that larger models hallucinate fewer invalid initial candidates, and explaining why the simple one-shot enumeration becomes increasingly effective for larger models.

As discussed in Section 3, the same ambiguous input should lead to different behavior from different models, depending on the interpretations they can actually resolve. This motivates using the recovered model-realizable support not only as an object of estimation, but as a basis for deciding whether the model faces unresolved ambiguity and how it should respond. We examine this through model-dependent ambiguity detection and response selection of whether to abstain, answer, or clarify.

Unlike conventional ambiguity evaluation, which asks whether the input itself admits multiple valid answers, i.e., whether |\mathcal{W}_{T}(x)|\geq 2, we label an input as ambiguous for model M when |\mathcal{M}_{T}(x)|\geq 2. As such, the cardinality of the estimated model realizable answer support provides a direct ambiguity score, i.e. |\widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{T}(x)|. We compare against ICE, which uses mutual information between clarifications and answers, CLARA-D, which measures dispersion among generated clarifications, INTENT-SIM, which estimates entropy over simulated intents, and a modified APA version APA^{\dagger}, which computes information gain via semantic entropy of the original vs self-disambiguated question. We evaluate all ambiguity scores using AUROC.

Figure 4a demonstrates that the cardinality of the recovered candidate set effectively identifies whether model-dependent ambiguity is present. CircleClar achieves the highest overall performance, with its most pronounced advantage occurring on AmbigQA-HQ where it consistently outperforms all other methods across all models. This improvement reflects again the higher quality of AmbigQA-HQ’s reference sets: annotations in standard AmbigQA are frequently incomplete or noisy, which artificially distorts the true reference cardinality and degrades the quality of the resulting ambiguity labels (Appendix B). Notably, most baseline methods perform close to random guessing. While prior work shows that these baselines perform well when evaluated against the world ambiguity |\mathcal{W}_{T}(x)|, our findings highlight again the crucial distinction: optimizing for |\mathcal{W}_{T}(x)| does not translate to detecting whether the model itself perceives a question as ambiguous.

The question of whether to abstain, answer, or clarify follows naturally from the model-realizable support. If the support is empty, the model has no valid answer it can provide (Abstain); if it contains a single answer, there is no alternative for the model to resolve (Answer); and if it contains multiple answers, the appropriate choice depends on the intended interpretation (Clarify). The ground-truth label is hence obtained following this logic on \mathcal{M}_{T}(x) while the predictions for CircleClar are based on \widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{T}(x). To assess whether explicitly estimating \widehat{\mathcal{M}}_{T}(x) is beneficial, we compare against methods that prompt an action directly. Direct (Generic) asks the model to clarify when ambiguity prevents answering, and otherwise to answer or abstain based on its knowledge. Direct (Model-Dependent) instead asks it to apply our model-dependent decision rule implicitly without constructing an answer set. Lastly, BAG bases its decision by examining previously sampled responses. We evaluate all methods using balanced accuracy.

Figure 4b shows that CircleClar performs best overall across models and datasets. Directly providing the model-dependent decision rule offers little consistent improvement over Direct (Generic), while BAG remains close to the constant-policy baseline in most settings. This indicates that the recovered answer support provides a stronger basis for response selection. Appendix D complements this analysis by evaluating the set-estimating methods in Table 1 and additionally taking into account whether the produced answers of the sets are correct. We test this across progressively stricter answer-content requirements, with CircleClar generally strongest once the correctness of the recovered answers is taken into account.

CircleClar is a precision-oriented estimator whose recall is limited by the initial candidate set: interpretations that the model can answer when explicitly specified may still be unlikely to arise during candidate generation and therefore remain undiscovered. Relatedly, we focus on the support of model-realizable answers rather than the relative likelihood of interpretations, treating recovered alternatives equally through a set representation and its cardinality. Further, successful recovery through an answer–clarification–answer cycle provides evidence of model realizability but does not guarantee correctness, as a model may consistently reproduce a factual error; under black-box access, such confidently held errors are generally difficult to distinguish from correct knowledge. Similarly, under our desiderata, clarifications are defined by their answers, and, as such, a valid clarification could theoretically have an unrelated meaning. However, in practice, as we create the clarifications based on their answers and the question, this does not happen. Our evaluation is also limited by the quality and coverage of ambiguity annotations, which may omit valid interpretations or introduce unsupported ones. We mitigate this by constructing the curated AmbigQA-HQ benchmark (Appendix B), but cannot guarantee complete coverage.

Finally, \mathcal{M}_{T}(x) captures answerable model-dependent ambiguity and does not include interpretations that a model can recognize but cannot answer, nor purely linguistic ambiguity it may detect without resolving. Explicitly separating interpretation recognition from answerability is an interesting direction for future work.

Our results support a view of ambiguity that distinguishes what an input permits from what a particular model can realize. While the world may admit many valid interpretations, only a subset may be accessible within a model’s knowledge, and it is this model-realizable ambiguity that determines the alternatives on which the model can meaningfully act. This distinction complements the conventional, world-centric view of ambiguity and provides a more model-specific account of how underspecified inputs are represented and handled. Our clarification framework provides a natural way to characterize this object by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between valid answers and equivalence classes of clarifications. CircleClar is one concrete way of exploiting this correspondence under black-box access, but the underlying perspective is more general. We hope this view provides a useful basis for future work on ambiguity-aware language models and their interaction with users.
