Manacá-1B-Instruct-2: Reproducible Safety Alignment for a Native Brazilian-Portuguese LLM. Negative DPO Results, a Controlled Composition Scan, and a Silent Failure Mode of the LLM Judge. Brazilian Portuguese remains underserved by open-source language models, and the few that are safety-aligned rarely document what did not work or validate comparisons with statistical significance. We present Manacá-1B-Instruct-2, the second-generation post-training alignment of Manacá-1B (1.72B parameters, trained from scratch for PT-BR), with an SFT corpus of 291,223 examples. We document three DPO attempts, all negative, including a case where the training reward margin reaches 1.0 while free generation does not change at all, and show that safety came from a dedicated safety-SFT (LLM-jp AnswerCarefully style), refined over three iterations until closing the safety-helpfulness frontier. A controlled scan of the fraction of general data in the safety-SFT mix (10% to 60%) reveals a non-monotonic over-refusal curve with a knee point at 40-50%. The final model is compared against four external PT-BR models on the same items, with Wilson confidence intervals and paired McNemar tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction: the lower bound of its safety interval (94.1%) lies above the upper bound of all four baselines.

We also report a methodological finding for LLM-judge evaluation: on two of six safety items in MT-Bench-PT, the judge categorically refuses to assign a score regardless of the evaluated response, silently reducing the effective N of that category in every prior report of the project. We complement this with an n-gram decontamination check and a Chinchilla-anchored compute-budget table that attributes the gap in general capability to pre-training scale rather than alignment methodology. All code, raw data, logs, and scripts that produce every reported number are publicly released.

Open language models for Brazilian Portuguese have grown in number, but the safety alignment of these models is rarely documented with the same rigor as pre-training: negative results tend to be left out, small N for safety probes rules out any significance test, and evaluation by an LLM judge is treated as a black box trusted by construction. Manacá-1B-Instruct (first generation) had already adopted LLM-jp’s AnswerCarefully method to align safety via dedicated SFT, after on-policy DPO failed to reverse the model’s compliance with harmful requests, but with probes of 16/34 items, insufficient for any paired test.

This report documents the second generation (instruct-2), which closes these methodological gaps rather than simply scaling the model. Our goal is not scale, it is rigor: the same LLM-jp method, but with probes large enough for statistical significance, a controlled scan isolating the composition variable of the training mix, an audit of the evaluation process itself (the LLM judge, corpus decontamination, compute fairness across baselines), and the publication of everything, including three DPO attempts that did not work.

Our contributions are as follows. A reproducible, statistically validated safety alignment. v4 is compared against four external PT-BR baselines on the same 218/184 items, with Wilson intervals and paired McNemar corrected by Holm-Bonferroni, not only against the project’s own history. Three DPO attempts documented as negative results, including the lesson that the DPO training metric (reward margin) can become perfect without changing free generation at all. An empirical finding on how to instantiate the model: prompt template family matters far more than the phrasing within it (generation confidence drops by half outside the trained Alpaca-PT format), and asking the model to admit uncertainty does not make it verbalize doubt, it only swaps one confabulation for another. A controlled composition scan of the safety-SFT mix (10–60% general data), isolating a single variable and revealing a non-monotonic over-refusal curve with a knee point at 40–50%. A methodological finding on LLM-judge evaluation: categorical refusal to score safety items, regardless of the evaluated response, which silently reduces the effective N, corrected retroactively in eight historical project reports. An n-gram decontamination check between the training corpus and the evaluation benchmarks, with manual audit of the findings.
A Chinchilla-anchored compute-budget table, quantifying the pre-training asymmetry across the five compared models.

Figure 1 summarizes the end-to-end path described in this report, from the pre-trained base to the final model. Each box maps to a section of this document; the two red branches are the two negative results that preceded the method that actually worked.

This work builds on three lines of research. The first is the development of open LLMs native to Portuguese: Manacá-1B-Instruct itself, first generation, whose evolution this report documents; the Tucano family, which includes both models trained from scratch in Portuguese (Tucano-1b1, Tucano-2b4) and a continual-pretraining model on Qwen3 (Tucano2-qwen); and TeenyTinyLlama. All four are used as external baselines in Section 4.4. The safety-alignment method followed here, dedicated SFT in AnswerCarefully style, comes from the LLM-jp project, an open-LLM initiative for Japanese whose evaluation practice also informs the design of this report.

The second line is the relationship between pre-training compute budget and final model capacity, formalized by Hoffmann et al. (Chinchilla) and used in Section 4.7 to separate the effect of scale from the effect of alignment methodology when comparing models with vastly different pre-training budgets.

The third is the reliability of LLM judges, relevant to the finding in Section 4.5. The founding MT-Bench paper characterizes positional bias, verbosity bias, self-enhancement bias, and limited reasoning/mathematical ability as the known flaws of the judge-LLM paradigm. More recent work addresses adjacent problems: Eiras et al. show that safety judges are fragile to changes in the style of the evaluated response and to adversarial attacks that trick them into classifying harmful content as safe; Pasch documents that LLM judges score ethics-motivated candidate refusals more favorably than human evaluators (moderation bias); Vishnubhotla et al. document high disagreement across different safety judges, varying by criterion and harm category; and Zhang, using Claude Sonnet 4-6 as the sole judge over 400 HarmBench behaviors, shows that the judge’s prompt choice shifts the measured harmful-response rate by up to 24.2 percentage points. None of these works describes the specific mechanism reported in Section 4.5: the judge itself triggering its API-level safety layer (stop_reason=refusal, officially documented as a normal HTTP 200 response, not an error) when instructed to score a response to a sensitive prompt, silently removing the item from the denominator instead of producing a score.

Manacá-1B-Instruct-2 fully inherits the architecture of the Manacá-1B base model (Table 1): a 24-layer Llama-style decoder-only transformer, model dimension 2048, 8192 SwiGLU FFN, 32 attention heads with 8 key-value groups (GQA), RoPE, RMSNorm, and learned biases in all linear layers. The tokenizer is a 64k-token SentencePiece (nmt_nfkc_cf), which makes the model lowercase by construction. Post-training is a tune on top of these weights: full fine-tuning (SFT) followed by safety-SFT via LoRA.

The instruction corpus is larger and more diverse than the first generation’s: 291,223 examples, confirmed directly in the training log, versus 141 thousand in the previous generation. Table 2 summarizes the main sources, all openly licensed, converted to the Alpaca schema {instruction, input, output}. Counts marked with ∗ are pre-deduplication; the final --dedup step drops duplicates, so the sum does not exactly match the 291,223 in the training log.

Two sources documented in the repository were evaluated and not included in the final corpus: Tucano-SFT and manacá-jaster (ASSIN2/FaQuAD/ENEM/HateBR, used only in the first generation), checked against the table of actual counts before any claim of overlap with the evaluation benchmarks that use these same named datasets. This check is relevant in itself: an earlier version of this repository mistakenly listed manacá-jaster as a source of the instruct-2 corpus, which would have implied direct training \times evaluation overlap with ENEM/FaQuAD/HateBR; the error was found and corrected before publication (§ 4.6 details the systematic check that followed).

SFT uses full fine-tuning on the Manacá-1B base, 291,223 training examples and 3,000 validation examples (split before training, never merged), for 3 epochs with load_best_model_at_end (selects the checkpoint with the lowest eval_loss, not the last one). The actual eval_loss curve, measured every 500 steps, fell monotonically across the 6 recorded points: 1.3474 \to 1.2661 \to 1.2359 \to 1.2119 \to 1.2027 \to 1.1986, with no sign of overfitting within the 3 epochs, which validates the decision to extend beyond the 2 epochs faithful to LLM-jp used in the first generation. train/loss follows the same trend (from 3.14 at step 10 to the 1.05–1.15 range at the end), with no train \times eval divergence. The raw curves (loss, gradient norm, learning rate) are published with the repository, and Figure 3 shows them in full.

During SFT, we tested live (on CPU, over intermediate checkpoints) a practical question: what is the best way to call the model so the answer comes out better, and why (results in Section 4.1). We tested two intermediate checkpoints of manaca-1b-instruct-2-full (steps 2,000 and 2,500 of 3,411, both before safety-SFT), greedy decoding with repetition_penalty=1.3 and no_repeat_ngram_size=3, over a fixed set of factual/enumeration questions (photosynthesis, the founding of Flamengo, Brazil’s last president, Fermat’s theorem, the planets of the solar system, Brazilian states). As a confidence metric we used the average per-token probability under the model’s own softmax distribution, a proxy for how “within the training distribution” the generation is, not a measure of factual correctness.

We compare v4 (the approved safety-SFT checkpoint, results in Section 4.4) against four external PT-BR models that a serious evaluation cannot leave out: TeenyTinyLlama-460m-Chat, Tucano-1b1-Instruct and Tucano-2b4-Instruct, and Tucano2-qwen-1.5B-Instruct, under the same harness, on the same items. Two fairness corrections were applied before running: (i) each baseline uses its own chat template where available, rather than forcing Manacá’s Alpaca-PT format; (ii) we instrumented n_tokens_generated / truncated per response, because Manacá’s 64k vocabulary versus the baselines’ 32–49k means a shared --max_new_tokens is not an equal length budget; truncation was confirmed real (up to 32% at 512 tokens) and fixed by regenerating all 5 models at 1,024 tokens.

The safety (218 held-out items) and over-refusal (184 items) probes were expanded from 16/34 to 218/184 specifically to allow for narrow Wilson intervals and paired McNemar tests; at N{=}16, differences such as “93.8% versus 75%” do not survive non-overlapping confidence intervals. Statistics implemented with no external dependencies: Wilson interval (95%), exact paired McNemar, Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.

No evaluation benchmark is used by name in the training corpus (Section 3.1), but the large-scale web-scrape sources (GigaVerbo-v2, MADLAD-400, FineWeb-2, HPLT2, ClassiCC-PT, LegalPT) may have captured them incidentally. To check this (results in Section 4.6), we compared exact 13-gram textual overlap (the same threshold used by GPT-3/Llama) between the 15,026 items of the 11 evaluation benchmarks (the 7 from the mandatory core via HF plus 4 local ones) and the 294,223 lines of the training corpus on disk.

To quantify the pre-training budget asymmetry across the compared models (results in Section 4.7), we anchor to Chinchilla’s compute-optimal point (D_{\text{optimal}}\approx 20N) and pre-training FLOPs (C\approx 6ND), reconciling N (parameters) and D (processed tokens) from each baseline’s configuration YAML and official model card.

A first test compared five phrasing variants within the same Alpaca-PT family (original preamble, no preamble, requesting precision, requesting detail, few-shot with two correct examples): five different confabulations, zero correct answers. This already signals this section’s central conclusion: rephrasing the instruction within the trained format does not recover missing factual knowledge.

A second, more decisive test compared three templates from the Alpaca-PT family (the training one) against three templates from chat families the Manacá tokenizer never saw as special tokens, ChatML (OpenAI/Qwen standard), Llama-2-chat, and Vicuna. Figure 4 shows the result: average confidence of 0.656 for the Alpaca-PT family versus 0.347 for the chat families, less than half.

And qualitatively it is worse than the number alone suggests: it is not just “a wrong answer”, it is a complete derailment of topic. In ChatML, the question about photosynthesis received an answer about a literal photo (“look at the photo above, it shows a plant…”), the model confused the very subject of the question. The same family, asked about Brazilian states, drifted into computer hardware (“processor, RAM, hard drive, motherboard…”). In Vicuna, the question about Flamengo (a Brazilian football club) ended in a hallucinated entire fan-forum thread, with a player name, “site visitor” comments, and even a made-up URL (flaestatisticas.com/…); the question about states turned into a tourism-chatbot conversation about visiting São Paulo, without ever listing a single state. In Llama-2-chat, one of the answers was nothing but forum formatting tags ([b][color=#0896a5]…) with no content at all. None of the six responses outside the Alpaca-PT family was useful, it is not “answers worse”, it is a complete loss of the thread.

A third test, on checkpoint-2000, isolated a different mechanism: instead of changing the template’s format, we added an explicit instruction asking the model to verbalize doubt instead of making things up (“If you are not sure about specific dates, names, or numbers, clearly say you are not sure instead of making up an answer”), keeping the rest of the Alpaca-PT template identical.

In 4 of 4 cases (Table 3), explicitly instructing the model to admit uncertainty did not produce a single abstention response, the model swapped one confabulation for another different confabulation, with lower confidence in 3 of the 4 cases (the sharpest drop was on Fermat’s theorem, where “Pythagorean theorem, discovered by Euclid” turned into a nonsensical mathematical passage attributed to “Pascal’s theorem”). This confirms, through a mechanism different from the template test, the same boundary: the model cannot introspect and verbalize its own epistemic uncertainty via prompt instruction, missing factual knowledge is a property of what was seen in pre-training (quantified in orders of magnitude in Section 4.7), not something the prompt can work around or make the model recognize it lacks.

The result of the three tests converges on a simple rule already reflected in this repository’s publish/hf-model-card.md: always instantiate v4 with the exact training-time Alpaca-PT template, word for word –

– never a chat template (ChatML, Llama-2-chat, Vicuna, or similar): the tokenizer lacks the special tokens of these formats, and the model treats the text as structural noise, not turn signaling. The model also has no chat_template configured in the tokenizer, anyone calling via apply_chat_template() without adjusting this manually gets the wrong format by default. Paraphrasing the preamble, even with synonyms (“correctly” instead of “adequately”), does not help either: the model learned to associate this fixed text, not a free-form meaning, with the expected response format, deviating from it takes the model out of the distribution it learned, with no accuracy gain (the word “adequately” in the template governs adherence to the genre/format of the request, not factual correctness, the same role “adequately” plays in the original English Alpaca).

This fragility also shapes an architectural decision for any future web search or RAG extension: search must always happen automatically and outside the model’s control (search \to inject the result into the same standard Alpaca-PT template as always \to the model just summarizes/answers using the given context), rather than letting Manacá itself decide when to search and formulate the query, that would be a tool-calling format it has never seen, and it would fall into the same trap ChatML/Vicuna just confirmed here.

Explicit limitation of this section: the three tests were measured on intermediate checkpoints of instruct-2-full, before safety-SFT, not on the final v4. The finding carries over to v4 because safety-SFT (Section 4.3) is a LoRA continuation on these same base weights, with the same Alpaca-PT template (it never introduces a different prompt format), but the specific confidence figures were not re-measured on the final merged checkpoint. There was also no repetition across multiple seeds nor more than 4–6 questions per test, this is strong qualitative/exploratory evidence, not a statistical benchmark like the one in Section 4.4.

Before safety-SFT, DPO was attempted three times across the project: twice in the first generation (results carried over, not re-run here) and once in instruct-2, and none reversed the model’s compliance with harmful requests. We record all three because the pattern that emerges from them is, by itself, the project’s most important methodological lesson.
#1, off-policy, GigaVerbo pairs (1 st generation). Preference pairs extracted from GigaVerbo’s harmful subset, with no generation by the model itself. It did not improve; it over-optimized.

#2, on-policy, faithful to llm-jp-dpo (1 st generation). Pairs generated by the model itself (good refusal vs. the observed harmful compliance), \beta=0.1. The reward curve reached a perfect margin (1.0, accuracy \approx 1.0), and yet free generation did not change at all: the adapter, loaded without merging (DPO’s real, unrounded effect), complied 0/4 even on its own training prompts.

#3, offline, third-party pairs (instruct-2, this report). On manaca-1b-instruct-2-full, using Polygl0t/gigaverbo-v2-preferences (\approx 28.4k harmless/harmful pairs, Apache-2.0) and nicholasKluge/reward-aira-dataset. Same conclusion: this was not what changed the model’s safety.

The general lesson, valid beyond this project: the DPO training metric (margin/probability ratio under teacher-forcing) measures the decision over two specific sequences, not the decision of the first token in free generation (greedy or sampled), which is what actually determines the observed behavior. When the model’s prior (here, “comply”) is strong and the dataset is small, DPO can train perfectly and change behavior by zero, never trust training margin/accuracy as a sign of success without validating against real free generation.

Safety again came from a dedicated safety-SFT, AnswerCarefully style: refusal as a direct cross-entropy target, mixed with examples of helping benign requests (so as not to become a blind refuser) and general data (to preserve broad helpfulness). LoRA r{=}32, \alpha{=}64, 3 epochs, on manaca-1b-instruct-2-full.

It took three actual training rounds to close the safety \times helpfulness frontier (Table 5, small 16/34-item probes used during iteration; v4 ’s final large- N validation comes in Section 4.4). Increasing the harmful seeds (50 \to 465, generating 1,539 refusal examples with k_{\text{refuse}}{=}4) while keeping N_GENERAL fixed in absolute terms (v2) nearly doubled over-refusal: the relative share of general data in the mix fell from \approx 49% to 10.6%, and the model became an over-refuser. Correcting N_GENERAL to keep the proportion (v3) fixed most of the over-refusal, but still left some pro-social cases (“helping a friend in crisis”) mistakenly refused; also scaling the helpfulness side, with oversampling of gold crisis examples (v4), closed the last gap.

The v2 / v3 / v4 points already suggested that mix composition, specifically the fraction of general data, matters more than the absolute volume of any single component, but this clue came from hypothesis-guided trial and error, not a controlled experiment. We therefore decided to isolate the question cleanly: keeping everything else fixed (1,539 deterministic refusal examples, 280 helpful ones, the same training recipe, the same base model), we varied only the fraction of general data in the mix from 10% to 60%, in 10-percentage-point steps, six independent training rounds.

Figure 5 shows the result. Safety saturates at 100% up to 30% general data and only gives way from 40% on (93.8% \to 87.5% at 50% \to 93.8% at 60%, with N{=}16 per point, the oscillation across 40/50/60% is not conclusive on its own). Overall over-refusal drops sharply and monotonically from 10% to 50% (32.4% \to 5.9%), but rises again at 60% (11.8%): the curve is not monotonic. At N{=}34 per point this is also within the range of sampling noise, but it is consistent enough (the same pattern in both over-refusal subgroups, benign and sensitive-legitimate) not to dismiss as pure noise. The 40–50% range dominates the extremes on both axes at once: by a combined metric (harmonic mean of safety and 1{-} over-refusal), the three central points sit close together, 40% (92.5), 30% (92.1), 50% (90.7), within what this sample size can distinguish, with 40% as the recommended point: safety near the ceiling (93.8%) with over-refusal already low (8.8%), without the extra cost seen at 60%.

The uncontrolled v2 / v3 / v4 points used a different helpfulness composition (145 examples, no crisis oversampling) and so are not directly point-by-point comparable to this scan, but the pattern holds: v2 (10.6% general) had 50% over-refusal, consistent with the curve’s left extreme; v3 / v4 (\approx 48.5% general) fall within the knee range identified here, which explains why v4 worked well without having been designed with this curve in hand, the proportion landed near the optimum through hypothesis-guided trial and error, and is now confirmed by controlled experiment.

Explicit limitations of this scan: statistical power (N{=}16 /34 per point, the non-monotonicity at 60% could be a real effect or noise, this sample cannot tell); a single seed/round per point (training variance not measured, may be partly confounded with the composition effect); and the curve was measured only on manaca-1b-instruct-2-full, it is unknown whether the same shape (or the same knee point) holds at another model scale. Probes of 150–300 items per category, with Wilson CIs and paired McNemar, are the next step before claiming the knee point as a robust result rather than merely exploratory.

section: Mandatory Core: Validated Comparison Against 4 Baselines
text: Table 6 carries the main result: v4 compared against the four baselines on the six mandatory-core metrics.

section: Mandatory Core: Validated Comparison Against 4 Baselines
text: On safety, the floor of v4 ’s Wilson confidence interval (94.1%) sits above the ceiling of all four baselines, including Tucano2-qwen; paired McNemar with Holm-Bonferroni correction confirms significance against all four simultaneously (p between 10^{-14} and 10^{-62}). A manual audit of the 6 responses not flagged as refusals by the raw heuristic found 4 false negatives (the model refused with different phrasing than expected) and only 1 real safety failure, the true harmful-compliance rate is 1/218 (0.46%), not the 6/218 (2.8%) the heuristic reported.

section: Mandatory Core: Validated Comparison Against 4 Baselines
text: On general capability, v4 competes evenly with baselines at its own scale, but loses to Tucano2-qwen on anything requiring knowledge/math/code, a pre-training compute-budget effect, quantified in Section 4.7, not an execution error. On over-refusal, only the difference against Tucano-2b4 survives correction (p{=}0.0021); against the other three (including an exact tie in raw rate with Tucano2-qwen, 17/184 for both, but on different items, only {}_{A}{=}17, only {}_{B}{=}17 under McNemar) the difference is not statistically distinguishable at this N.

section: Mandatory Core: Validated Comparison Against 4 Baselines
text: It is worth unpacking the confidence intervals and paired tests in more detail. Table 7 gives the full Wilson confidence interval (95%) per model, and Figure 6 shows the same numbers as a forest plot: each point is the observed rate, each horizontal line the interval. This is where the robustness of the safety result becomes immediately visible, v4 ’s interval never overlaps any baseline’s in the left panel, which already anticipates the paired significance in Table 8.

section: Mandatory Core: Validated Comparison Against 4 Baselines
text: Figure 7 extends the same uncertainty logic to the three multiple-choice exams, using the binomial standard error (95%) over each benchmark’s actual size (ENEM N{=}1{,}432, BLUEX N{=}724, OAB N{=}2{,}210, full sets from the eduagarcia/lm-evaluation-harness-pt harness). It makes directly visible what was already said in text: every model up to 2.4B parameters, v4 included, sits within (or very close to) the chance-level error band (25%, 4 options) on all three exams; only Tucano2-qwen, with its orders-of-magnitude larger pre-training compute budget (Section 4.7), clearly escapes that band.

section: Mandatory Core: Validated Comparison Against 4 Baselines
text: Table 6, however, collapses each benchmark to a single number per model, which hides real variation: v4 is not uniformly better or worse than each baseline, it is better on some dimensions and worse on others, and the overall average masks this pattern. It is worth unpacking the three composite benchmarks (MT-Bench-PT, IFEval-PT, classification) at the granularity they were measured.

section: Mandatory Core: Validated Comparison Against 4 Baselines
text: On MT-Bench-PT, Figure 8 shows the average score (1–10, LLM-as-a-Judge) of the nine MT-Bench-PT categories for the six models. Three patterns stand out. First, on math and code Tucano2-qwen (5.17 on both) isolates itself completely from the rest (1.00 – 1.33 across all other five models, v4 included), directly consistent with Section 4.7: these two categories demand capabilities acquired mostly during pre-training, and Tucano2-qwen inherits Qwen3 pre-training with an orders-of-magnitude larger compute budget. No safety post-training or Portuguese SFT closes that gap. Second, on humanities the order flips: v4 (4.67) and instruct2-full (5.17) lead alongside Tucano-2b4 (4.83), while Tucano2-qwen drops to 2.50, worse than Tucano-1b1 (4.00) and nearly tied with TTL-460m (1.17, by far the weakest in the category). It is the inverse picture of math/code: on tasks that depend on cultural/linguistic domain knowledge in Portuguese, where Manacá’s SFT corpus was designed to help, v4 competes with, and sometimes beats, a model with far more pre-training compute, but inherited from a predominantly English/Chinese-speaking ecosystem.

section: Mandatory Core: Validated Comparison Against 4 Baselines
text: Third, on safety (n{=}4 items per model in this specific MT-Bench category, on the same set of sensitive prompts used in the mandatory core) v4 (9.00) and Tucano2-qwen (9.75) dominate the other four models (1.00 – 4.75), with Tucano2-qwen nominally ahead of v4 on this judged response-quality metric. This does not contradict this section’s main result: held-out safety (N{=}218) measures refusal rate, a binary variable with a narrow Wilson CI, while this MT-Bench category measures the judge’s subjective quality of the refusal, with only 4 items and therefore no statistical power to separate 9.00 from 9.75. It is also worth noting that this is exactly the judge/category pair, safety prompts scored by LLM-as-a-Judge, where Section 4.5 documents a categorical-score-refusal failure mode in the judge itself; the judge’s two refusals per model (the same rate across all six) already reduce this category’s effective n from 6 to 4, which reinforces that this specific number should be read with more caution than the overall MT-Bench-PT average.

section: Mandatory Core: Validated Comparison Against 4 Baselines
text: On IFEval-PT, Figure 9 decomposes Table 6 ’s single line into the benchmark’s four standard metrics (prompt/instruction \times strict/loose). The ranking across the six models is stable across all four: Tucano2-qwen leads (41.7 – 60.0\%), instruct2-full and v4 form the second group (22.2 – 40.0\%), and TTL-460m/Tucano-1b1/Tucano-2b4 sit below (8.3 – 26.0\%). v4 sits systematically a bit below instruct2-full on all four metrics, consistent with the trade-off already discussed in Section 4.3: safety-SFT prioritizes safety over the general capability learned in the prior SFT, and strict format-following is one of the capabilities that suffers.

section: Mandatory Core: Validated Comparison Against 4 Baselines
text: Table 9 goes one level deeper, into the 21 individual instruction types (instr-loose metric). The most striking pattern: on at least six types, comecar_com, min_maiusculas, num_itens_numerados, num_marcadores, num_paragrafos, terminar_com, all five models that do not inherit Qwen pre-training sit at 0\%, and only Tucano2-qwen manages any success (33 – 100\%). These types require precise format control (item counting, positional capitalization, exact delimiters) that does not appear to emerge from Portuguese SFT alone at the volume used in this project (\sim 291 thousand examples), it likely depends on synthetic instruction data specifically designed for format-following, of the kind that fed Qwen3’s pre-/post-training, and that is not present in Manacá’s corpus in the same proportion. Conversely, on types closer to natural content instruction (min_palavras, min_placeholders, max_frases) all five models do reasonably well, some beating Tucano2-qwen point for point (max_palavras: instruct2-full 100\% vs. Tucano2-qwen 0\%).

section: Mandatory Core: Validated Comparison Against 4 Baselines
text: On classification, Figure 10 decomposes Table 6 ’s average into the four tasks (macro-F1, recomputed directly from lm-eval-harness ’s individual items; the harness used does not report a per-task standard error, so the figure has no error bars, unlike the rest of this section). The pattern is the most consistent of the three benchmarks: Tucano2-qwen leads all four tasks by a wide margin (67.6 – 91.5\%), v4 and instruct2-full are essentially tied on all four (difference \leq 0.5 percentage point on three of four tasks, expected, since safety-SFT is a light LoRA on the same base checkpoint and was never meant to change classification), and TTL-460m surprises on assin2_rte_pt (53.61\%), the only task/model outside Tucano2-qwen where a baseline beats v4 (52.96\%), binary textual entailment (RTE) appears to be a capability TTL-460m, despite being weaker overall, acquired well in its own post-training.

section: An LLM-Judge Failure Mode: Categorical Score Refusal
text: While judging the mandatory core’s MT-Bench-PT, we discovered that the LLM judge (Claude) categorically refuses to assign a score on two of the six items in the “safety” category (safety_1, safety_2), via the API’s stop_reason=refusal, regardless of the content of the evaluated candidate’s response. This silently reduces that category’s effective N from 6 to 4: the aggregate keeps being computed over the items that do receive a score, but nothing in the original report flagged that two of the six prompts were never actually judged, for any model.

section: An LLM-Judge Failure Mode: Categorical Score Refusal
text: Through a systematic search (grep) for this signature across every judging report ever published in the project’s history, we verified that this categorical refusal affects the eight historical files of MT-Bench-PT judged up to this work, a systemic finding, not specific to this round. We fixed the presentation (not the underlying data, which was already correctly aggregated) in code (bench/mtbench_pt/report.py, which now shows (n{=}X) per cell and a per-model judge-refusal count section) and in the already-published artifacts. As discussed in Section 2, this specific mechanism, the judge itself categorically refusing, is not described in the related work we reviewed.

section: An LLM-Judge Failure Mode: Categorical Score Refusal
text: The lesson generalizes: when an LLM judge is used to score sensitive items (safety, potentially harmful content), the judge’s own refusal is a possible outcome of the evaluation process, not only of the evaluated model, and must be counted and reported as such, not silently absorbed into the denominator. We recommend that any LLM-judge evaluation protocol over sensitive categories explicitly record the judge’s own refusal rate per item, not only the average score.

We found overlap in 73 items (0.49% of the total evaluated), zero on the benchmarks of the alignment work itself (safety, over-refusal, MT-Bench-PT, IFEval-PT). We manually audited the full text of the 73 cases and classified them into four categories: legal boilerplate (26/73, statute name, court digest, law preamble, identical by definition wherever cited); indirect republication of past ENEM/OAB/BLUEX exams on prep-school websites via web scrape (23/73, several with the exam year explicit in the training text); canonical culture/literature coincidence (5/73); and real dataset overlap at sentence/paragraph level (19/73, FaQuAD-NLI collapses into a single source paragraph shared with ExtraGLUE-QNLI, tested 16 different ways by the benchmark; ASSIN2-RTE reused in extraglue_stsb with a different label). The single most concrete case: one OAB item has the entire hypothetical fact pattern (fictitious names) reproduced almost word for word in a synthetic instruction, a real, if isolated, leak.

The scale is small and mostly non-informative for the benchmark’s multiple-choice task (most synthetic training instructions ask for a summary/explanation, not the correct option). It does not invalidate the mandatory-core results, but it is documented as a transparent limitation, consistent with what any LLM trained on broad Portuguese web crawl and evaluated on ENEM/OAB/BLUEX faces.

The general-capability difference across the five compared models (Section 4.4) is not only an effect of alignment methodology, it is, in large part, an effect of pre-training compute budget, which varies by orders of magnitude. Table 10 quantifies this asymmetry.

Manacá uses \approx 1.2 \times the classic compute-optimal point (close to optimal), TeenyTinyLlama \approx 1.05 \times (also close, smaller scale), the two native Tucano models \approx 10–11 \times (deliberately over-trained, the post-Chinchilla philosophy popularized by LLaMA). Tucano2-qwen is continual-pretraining on Qwen3-1.7B-Base, which alone carries \approx 36 trillion pre-training tokens, \approx 849 \times Manacá’s pre-training FLOPs. This order of magnitude, by itself, explains the greater general capability observed in Section 4.4 without needing any explanation about safety-alignment methodology. The safety/over-refusal comparison remains valid regardless: it is about post-alignment behavior on identical prompts, and does not depend on each baseline’s pre-training budget.

Manacá-1B-Instruct-2 shows that an honest, fully reproducible safety alignment is a useful contribution to natural language processing for Brazilian Portuguese, even at a modest model scale. Measured with paired statistical significance against four external baselines, the final model dominates on safety and competes evenly on general capability with peers of the same compute budget. The methodological findings, the divergence between DPO’s training metric and actual behavior, the fragility to instantiation templates outside the trained format, the non-monotonic composition curve of safety-SFT, and the LLM judge’s categorical score refusal, generalize beyond this specific project. We hope the published model, the reproducible protocol, and the discipline of also documenting what did not work help the community bring safety evaluation in Portuguese, and in small LLMs generally, to a measurable standard.

It is worth stating this work’s scope with the same discipline used in every section above. Safety is not 100%: despite being statistically robust (97.2%, N{=}218), the true measured harmful-compliance rate is 0.46% (1/218), ambiguously phrased requests can still get through. Over-refusal persists on a small fraction of benign requests (9.2%), statistically indistinguishable from three of the four external baselines. In the pro-social case, the model may refuse requests to help someone in crisis, where the right thing is to help and point to a crisis line (in Brazil, CVV 188), mitigated via oversampling of gold examples, not eliminated. General capability sits below PT-BR models with larger-scale pre-training (Section 4.7), a compute effect, not a methodology one. The multiple-choice exams (ENEM/OAB/BLUEX) sit at chance level, a known limit of broad factual knowledge in natively PT-BR \sim 1B models. The composition scan remains at N{=}16 /34 per point and a single round per point, treat the knee point as exploratory, not definitive, until the sample is expanded. Validation by a second judge from a different model family (outside the evaluated LLM) remains blocked by API budget in this work. Research model; not a substitute for professional, legal, or medical advice.

The natural next steps are to expand, not redesign. The composition scan (Section 4.3) needs probes of 150–300 items per point, with paired Wilson/McNemar, before claiming the knee point as a robust result. A second LLM judge from a different family would close this project’s publication checklist’s most serious remaining gap (item 2). A literature review with full-text access (outside this work environment’s network restrictions) would help confirm whether the categorical judge-refusal finding (Section 4.5) is indeed novel before formally claiming so. Finally, the same controlled scan could be repeated at another model scale to test whether the 40–50% knee point is a property of the method or specific to this scale.

As for reproducibility and availability, every number in this report can be recomputed from the public repository. It contains the containerized SFT/DPO/safety-SFT pipeline, the raw training and evaluation logs (including the W&B curves from the main SFT run), the raw responses and judge scores of each benchmark, the scripts that produce every table and figure in this report (including scripts/eval/plot_composition_sweep.py for Figure 5), the decontamination script and its manual audit, and the compute-budget calculations. The code is published at the institutional repository of the Institute of Artificial Intelligence (LNCC), https://github.com/Instituto-IA-LNCC/manaca-1b-instruct-2, under CC BY 4.0; the model weights are published on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/AIInstituteLNCC/manaca-1b-instruct-2, under CC BY-NC 4.0 (§ License), since they inherit non-commercial sources from the first generation (Alpaca-PT, XLSum).

section: Declaration on the Use of AI Tools
text: In the interest of transparency and in line with current scientific publication guidance on the use of generative AI, we declare that an AI assistant (Claude, developed by Anthropic) was used exclusively as spelling and grammar review support for this manuscript. Consistent with COPE and ICMJE guidance, the AI tool is not and cannot be an author, and bears no responsibility for the work. The authors conceived and designed the study, ran the experiments, implemented the evaluation/statistics code, verified every number, table, and figure against its primary source, and take full responsibility for the content and for any remaining errors. The work is original: no text or result was plagiarized, every external source is cited, and every scientific claim reflects the authors’ own analysis and judgment.

The Reliance Hypothesis: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Rises as Language Resource Level Falls. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) faithfulness matters for monitoring, explaining and safely deploying large language models, yet it has been studied mostly in English. Languages differ in level, the amount of text available to learn from, so models know less in lower-resource languages, which may change how much they rely on their reasoning. To our knowledge, we are the first to relate CoT faithfulness to both resource level and task type (knowledge- or reasoning-intensive). On parallel multiple-choice questions from Multilingual Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMMLU) in eight languages, faithfulness rises as resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks but not on reasoning-intensive ones, a gap that points the same way across four models and several faithfulness measures. We propose, and find support for, the Reliance Hypothesis: models rely more on their reasoning when they cannot recall the answer, as in lower-resource languages on knowledge-intensive tasks. Model confidence partly explains the effect of resource level, but not the knowledge-reasoning gap. Languages in which models are less confident rely more on reasoning, yet less confident answers within a language do not, a Simpson's paradox.

In lower-resource languages, models rely on their reasoning for more answers, not more strongly for each. CoT monitoring may therefore be most informative in lower-resource languages, where it is least often validated.

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting elicits intermediate reasoning from large language models (LLMs) before they answer Wei et al. (2022). Beyond improving accuracy, the CoT offers a window into how a model reaches its answer, which makes it valuable for monitoring and safety Korbak et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025) and for explaining their decisions Turpin et al. (2023); Parcalabescu and Frank (2024). This value, however, depends on CoT faithfulness: the CoT must reflect the process by which the model actually reaches its answer Jacovi and Goldberg (2020).

A growing body of work measures CoT faithfulness Lanham et al. (2023); Turpin et al. (2023); Tutek et al. (2025); Zaman and Srivastava (2025), improves it Paul et al. (2024); Sun et al. (2026) and probes its mechanisms Macar et al. (2026); Ye et al. (2026); Chen et al. (2026), but almost entirely in English Ghosh et al. (2025). The few multilingual studies report that faithfulness differs across languages Zhao et al. (2026); Onyame et al. (2026), yet leave open how it relates to a language’s resource level, and why. This matters because models reason differently across languages Zhao et al. (2026); Ghosh et al. (2025) and hold inconsistent factual knowledge across them Qi et al. (2023), so how much a model leans on its CoT may depend on the language it answers in.

Consider the knowledge question in Fig. 1, with one word of the reasoning corrupted. In English, the model can recall the answer and ignores the mistake; in Yoruba, where its knowledge is thinner, it follows the mistake to a different answer. We formalise this intuition as the Reliance Hypothesis: models rely more on their reasoning when they cannot simply recall the answer, as in lower-resource languages on knowledge-intensive tasks.

We test the hypothesis on parallel multiple-choice questions from Multilingual Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMMLU; OpenAI, 2024), which covers both knowledge- and reasoning-intensive subjects, in eight languages whose resource levels span nearly eight orders of magnitude, with four open-weight models and four interventions on the reasoning chain Lanham et al. (2023). We measure faithfulness as reliance on the CoT: how far each intervention shifts the model’s confidence in its original answer, and compare knowledge- and reasoning-intensive subtasks, so that the same languages and models serve as their own control. Our contributions are as follows: To our knowledge, we are the first to relate CoT faithfulness to both resource level and task type. We show that faithfulness rises as resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks, but not on reasoning-intensive ones, a gap that points the same way across models and metrics and largely survives robustness checks. We propose and test the Reliance Hypothesis, finding that model confidence partly mediates the effect of resource level, but that confidence alone cannot explain why the effect is stronger on knowledge-intensive tasks.

We characterise reliance further: models rely more on reasoning in languages where they are less confident, yet within a language, their less confident answers rely on it no more than others (a Simpson’s paradox: a trend across groups that vanishes within them); and lower-resource languages rely on their reasoning more often, not more heavily (4% of answers in English vs. 35% in Yoruba). Faithfulness is thus highest where models know least, suggesting CoT monitoring may be most informative where it is least often validated.

Absent ground truth, how to measure CoT faithfulness remains unsettled. Contextual approaches intervene on the input or on the chain: hint-based tests deem a chain unfaithful if an inserted cue sways the answer without being mentioned Turpin et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2025); Chua and Evans (2025), while other tests truncate the chain, replace it with filler or add mistakes, and check whether the answer or the model’s confidence follows Lanham et al. (2023); Ye et al. (2026). Parametric approaches unlearn the knowledge stated in reasoning steps Tutek et al. (2025); Sun et al. (2026); others compare the chain with input attributions Parcalabescu and Frank (2024) or inspect internal computations Shen et al. (2026); Occhipinti et al. (2026); Wang et al. (2026); Chen et al. (2026). Following Lanham et al. (2023); Zaman and Srivastava (2025), we adopt four interventions, covering both removal and corruption of the CoT, and three metrics (§ 3.1).

Faithfulness across languages has only recently attracted attention Ghosh et al. (2025). In Persian, an LLM judge finds faithfulness driven more by the dataset and model than by the prompting language Yazdani et al. (2026), but such a judge sees only whether a CoT appears to support the answer, not whether the model used it. On maths problems in 11 languages, truncating or corrupting thinking traces instead shows stronger reliance on them outside English Zhao et al. (2026), while adversarial hints go unmentioned in nearly all chains Onyame et al. (2026); the two need not conflict, since a chain can drive the answer without mentioning a hint Zaman and Srivastava (2026). None of these studies relates faithfulness to resource level or contrasts knowledge- and reasoning-intensive tasks. From the pattern we find, we derive the Reliance Hypothesis, which parallels evidence that models gain most from external context on facts they rarely memorise Mallen et al. (2023).

This section examines how CoT faithfulness varies across languages. After describing our setup, we show that faithfulness rises as resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks but not on reasoning-intensive ones, consistently across metrics, models and subtasks.

To measure faithfulness, we intervene on the reasoning chain and observe how the model’s confidence in its original answer changes Lanham et al. (2023). We use four interventions: (i) Early Answering keeps only the first third of the chain; (ii) Filler Tokens replaces every character of the chain with a dot; (iii) Adding Mistakes replaces one word in the chain with its antonym; and (iv) Paraphrasing rewrites the first three quarters of the chain and lets the model complete the rest. The first two remove reasoning; the last two corrupt it. Although Lanham et al. (2023) intend paraphrases to preserve meaning, ours alter the chain substantially and change the answer twice as often as Adding Mistakes, so we treat Paraphrasing as corrupting (App. A).

Let z=P(a\mid x;c) be the probability that the model assigns to its answer a given the input x and its CoT c, and let z^{\prime}=P(a\mid x;c^{\prime}) be the probability after an intervention. We report three metrics: \displaystyle\Delta p \displaystyle=z-z^{\prime}, \displaystyle\Delta\log p \displaystyle=\log z-\log z^{\prime}, \displaystyle\Phi \displaystyle=\mathbbm{1}\left[\arg\max_{v}P(v\mid x;c^{\prime})\neq a\right], where v ranges over the answer options. We mainly use \Delta\log p, the relative drop. Unlike \Delta p, it is not capped by z, which is lower in low-resource languages (App. B), yet it ranks samples almost identically (§ 3.3); unlike \Phi, it also registers drops that leave the answer unchanged.

For English, we use MMLU Hendrycks et al. (2021); for other languages, we use MMMLU OpenAI (2024), its professional human translation, so all languages share the same questions. We select eight of MMMLU’s 15 languages, from five families and five scripts, and eight subtasks, half knowledge-intensive and half reasoning-intensive, with up to 250 questions each (Tab. 1). The languages’ resource levels, measured by token counts in the Common Crawl corpus CulturaX Nguyen et al. (2024), a common proxy for pretraining data Lai et al. (2023); Resck et al. (2025); Resck et al. (2026), span nearly eight orders of magnitude. App. B analyses the model-generated CoTs and answers in each language.

We evaluate four instruction-tuned, multilingual LLMs: Gemma-3-4B-it Gemma Team et al. (2025), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct Qwen et al. (2025), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct Grattafiori et al. (2024) and Aya-Expanse-8B Dang et al. (2024). We use the larger Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct as the perturber to edit the chain for Adding Mistakes and Paraphrasing. All models are open-weight, giving access to the required token log-probabilities.

To quantify how faithfulness varies across languages, we fit a linear regression with fixed effects: \bar{y}_{ms\ell}=\alpha_{m}+\gamma_{s}+\beta\,\mathrm{RL}_{\ell}+\varepsilon_{ms\ell}, where \bar{y}_{ms\ell} is the mean faithfulness (Eqs. (1)–(3)) of model m on subtask s in language \ell, \alpha_{m} and \gamma_{s} are model and subtask fixed effects, and \beta is the change in faithfulness per unit of resource level, that is, per order of magnitude of the language’s token count. We let \beta differ between knowledge- and reasoning-intensive subtasks, giving the slopes \hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{K}} and \hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{R}}. Averaging within each (model, subtask, language) cell weights every model and subtask equally in every language, although the share of valid generations falls from 97% in English to 35% in Yoruba (App. B). Because resource level varies only between languages, the evidence for \beta rests on eight languages, however many generations lie behind each cell. We therefore use a Fisher randomisation test Young (2019): the p -value is the share of all 8!=40{,}320 assignments of resource levels to languages that yield a slope at least as extreme as the observed one.

Fig. 2 shows that, on knowledge-intensive tasks, faithfulness rises as resource level falls under every intervention except Early Answering. Under Adding Mistakes, for instance, \hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{K}}=-0.16 predicts a drop in log-probability 1.3 larger in Yoruba than in English, close to the observed gap of 1.2. On reasoning-intensive tasks, by contrast, no slope is significantly negative, and under Early Answering the trend even reverses. CoT length is a natural suspect for this exception, since the same content takes more tokens in lower-resource languages Ahia et al. (2023), but controlling for it leaves the Early Answering slopes unchanged (Tab. 16). The difference \hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{K}}-\hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{R}} is negative for all four interventions and significant for three: lower resource levels raise faithfulness more on knowledge tasks than on reasoning tasks. The other variation metrics broadly point the same way (§ C.1).

Our conclusions should not hinge on the choice of variation metric, so we check how closely the three metrics agree across individual generations. They agree well: for every intervention, all pairwise Pearson correlations are at least 0.67, and \Delta p and \Delta\log p rank generations almost identically, with Spearman correlations of 0.92–1.00 (Tab. 10). The two continuous metrics thus tell the same story, even though only \Delta p is capped by z (Fig. 7).

We next ask whether our findings hold across models, in two ways (Tab. 2). First, for each pair of models, we correlate their mean faithfulness (\Delta\log p) over languages and subtasks separately by intervention, so that scale differences cannot drive it, and then average the correlations. Every pair agrees positively (0.10–0.52): the models broadly concur on which languages and subtasks elicit more faithful reasoning. This agreement is moderate, however, and weakest for Aya (0.10–0.22).

Second, we check whether the knowledge–reasoning gap appears within each model, averaging the Spearman correlation between faithfulness and resource level across interventions for each subtask type. The correlation is lower on knowledge than on reasoning subtasks for every model, so all four models share the gap’s direction, although its size varies from -0.56 (Aya) to -0.09 (Qwen). The other variation metrics tell the same story, with even stronger agreement between models (0.28–0.66), except that Qwen’s gap vanishes under the answer flip \Phi (Tab. 11).

§§ 3.2 and 3.4 showed cross-lingual faithfulness variation that is stronger on knowledge-intensive tasks and consistent across models. Individual subtasks reveal the same split, motivating the Reliance Hypothesis (§ 4).

Fig. 3 ranks the subtasks by their mean correlation between faithfulness and resource level. The ranking recovers the two families: all four knowledge-intensive subtasks come first. Their correlations are mostly negative (75–94% of model–intervention pairs), so faithfulness rises as resource level falls. Reasoning-intensive subtasks show weaker, less consistent trends, averaging -0.22 to 0.07. We plot \Delta p, which gives the cleanest split; other metrics rank the subtasks similarly (Fig. 8).

The contrast also holds for individual answers. Among items a model answered validly in both English and Yoruba, Adding Mistakes changes the answer in Yoruba alone about nine times as often as in English alone on knowledge subtasks (80 vs. 9), but less than twice as often on reasoning subtasks (73 vs. 40). Every knowledge subtask exceeds every reasoning subtask on this ratio. World Religions, the steepest subtask and a largely culture-bound one, illustrates the mechanism: as accuracy falls towards Yoruba, its answers depend more on the reasoning chain (§ C.3).

We now formalise the common cause behind these findings, the Reliance Hypothesis: a model relies more on its reasoning when it has less, or can access less, relevant parametric knowledge for the queried fact, and this reliance drives cross-lingual variation in CoT faithfulness. We test two consequences: (i) the variation is stronger on knowledge-intensive than on reasoning-intensive tasks, and (ii) it is mediated by the model’s confidence in its answer and reasoning chain.
Let \mathcal{F} be CoT faithfulness under Eqs. (1)–(3), and \beta^{\mathrm{K}},\beta^{\mathrm{R}} its resource-level slopes on knowledge- and reasoning-intensive subtasks (§ 3.2).

When the answer can be recalled, less parametric knowledge forces the model to route it through its reasoning; when it must be computed, reasoning is needed in every language. Hence \beta^{\mathrm{K}}\;=\;\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\mathrm{RL}}\bigg|_{\mathrm{K}}\;<\;\alpha\;\leq\;\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\mathrm{RL}}\bigg|_{\mathrm{R}}\;=\;\beta^{\mathrm{R}}, with \alpha\approx 0; in particular, \beta^{\mathrm{K}}-\beta^{\mathrm{R}}<0.

The knowledge deficit affects faithfulness through model confidence C in its answer or reasoning chain: \mathrm{RL}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{parametric knowledge}\;\longrightarrow\;C\;\longrightarrow\;\mathcal{F}. If \beta_{1} is the slope in Eq. 4 and \beta_{2} the same slope once C enters the regression, this chain predicts \lvert\beta_{2}\rvert<\lvert\beta_{1}\rvert.

We first test the central prediction of Hypothesis 1, \beta^{\mathrm{K}}-\beta^{\mathrm{R}}<0. § 3.2 reported this difference under \Delta\log p; here we derive it from a single regression and test it under all three metrics. We estimate both slopes of Eq. 4 in a single fit, letting the coefficient on \mathrm{RL}_{\ell} depend on whether subtask s is knowledge- (s\in\mathrm{K}) or reasoning-intensive (s\in\mathrm{R}): \displaystyle\bar{y}_{ms\ell} \displaystyle=\alpha_{m}+\gamma_{s}+\varepsilon_{ms\ell} \displaystyle\quad+\big(\beta^{\mathrm{K}}\mathbbm{1}[s\in\mathrm{K}]+\beta^{\mathrm{R}}\mathbbm{1}[s\in\mathrm{R}]\big)\mathrm{RL}_{\ell} \displaystyle=\alpha_{m}+\gamma_{s}+\varepsilon_{ms\ell} \displaystyle\quad+\beta^{\mathrm{K}}\mathrm{RL}_{\ell}+(\beta^{\mathrm{R}}-\beta^{\mathrm{K}})\,\mathbbm{1}[s\in\mathrm{R}]\,\mathrm{RL}_{\ell}. The second form is the familiar interaction model: the coefficient on the interaction term \mathbbm{1}[s\in\mathrm{R}]\mathrm{RL}_{\ell} is \beta^{\mathrm{R}}-\beta^{\mathrm{K}}, the negative of the difference we test and report. Both slopes are re-estimated under the same 8! relabellings of the languages, so the difference receives its own exact p -value.

Tab. 3 reports the difference for each intervention and metric. It is negative in eleven of the twelve combinations and significant in seven, including every metric under Filler Tokens and Adding Mistakes. Under \Delta\log p, it ranges from -0.17 to -0.31 per order of magnitude of token count. The separate slopes (Fig. 2; Tab. 9) show the full ordering \beta^{\mathrm{K}}<\alpha\leq\beta^{\mathrm{R}}, with \alpha\approx 0, most clearly under Adding Mistakes: the knowledge slope is significantly negative under every metric, whereas the reasoning slope stays near zero. Paraphrasing is the exception: under \Delta p and \Phi, faithfulness rises as resource level falls in both families, leaving little difference between them.

The answer to our question is therefore yes: lower resource levels raise faithfulness more on knowledge-intensive than on reasoning-intensive tasks, most clearly under Filler Tokens and Adding Mistakes.

We now test Hypothesis 2: resource level shapes faithfulness through the model’s confidence C, either over the answer tokens (final-answer confidence) or over the whole chain (reasoning-chain confidence). For each subtask family, we compare the resource-level slope with and without C: \beta_{1}:\;\mathcal{F}\sim\mathrm{RL}\quad\text{against}\quad\beta_{2}:\;\mathcal{F}\sim\mathrm{RL}+C, both with model and subtask fixed effects, and report the attenuation (\beta_{1}-\beta_{2})/\beta_{1}, the share of the slope that C accounts for. We standardise all variables, so that slopes are comparable across metrics.

Tab. 4 shows the attenuation for the largest significant slope per family under \Delta\log p: Adding Mistakes for knowledge and Early Answering for reasoning. On knowledge subtasks, final-answer probability and log-probability absorb most of the slope (87% and 70%), whereas no reasoning-chain measure exceeds 5%. On reasoning subtasks, the pattern reverses, if more weakly: reasoning-chain entropy absorbs the most (19%), while the probability of the final answer absorbs none (-13\%). Since confidence and resource level move closely together across only eight languages, the attenuations themselves are imprecise; the robust signal is the contrast between the two kinds of confidence. This contrast holds in 11 of the 13 significant slopes across metrics (Tab. 12).

Can confidence alone explain the gap? It cannot. Final-answer confidence rises with resource level at almost the same rate on knowledge and reasoning subtasks, and reasoning-chain confidence barely changes with it in either family (Tab. 13). A confidence gradient shared by both families cannot produce a faithfulness gradient that differs between them. Hence, confidence partly explains the variation within each family, but not their gap.

Hypothesis 2 posits a chain from resource level to faithfulness through confidence: \mathrm{RL}\;\overset{(1)}{\longrightarrow}\;C\;\overset{(2)}{\longrightarrow}\;\mathcal{F}. § 4.2 examined link (1): confidence rises with resource level at the same rate in both families, and partly mediates its effect on faithfulness. We now examine link (2): is a less confident answer itself more reliant on its reasoning, or does the association exist only between languages?

Fig. 4 shows faithfulness (\Delta\log p) against final-answer log-probability on knowledge-intensive subtasks under Adding Mistakes, the setting where confidence mediates the most (Tab. 4). Between languages, the association is strongly negative (\beta=-10.0, r=-0.97); within each language, it vanishes (mean \beta\approx 0, r=-0.01). This is a structural Simpson’s paradox: a trend that appears across groups disappears, or reverses, within each group, here each language. The pattern is general (Tab. 14): across all 216 combinations of metric, intervention, confidence measure and family, the mean absolute correlation is 0.47 between languages but 0.06 within them, and the within-language correlation stays below 0.1 in absolute value in 76% of cases.

The paradox, however, involves no contradiction. Within languages, the association mostly disappears rather than reverses; and a language-level cause, such as the knowledge deficit that the Reliance Hypothesis posits, should produce exactly this: an association between languages and none between individual items. Hence, the link between confidence and reliance is a property of languages, not of individually uncertain items.

The previous sections established that reliance on the reasoning chain varies across languages, but not how: do models in lower-resource languages rely on it more often, or more heavily? Taking \mathcal{F}=\Delta\log p, reliance separates the two: \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathcal{F}\right]}_{\text{reliance}}=\underbrace{P\!\left(\mathcal{F}>\tau\right)}_{\text{rate}}\times\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathcal{F}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}>\tau\right]}_{\text{magnitude}}, where a small threshold, \tau=0.01, absorbs numerical noise. The rate is the chance that the intervention moves the answer probability at all; the magnitude is the average size of that move.

Fig. 5 plots reliance and its two factors against resource level under Adding Mistakes. On knowledge-intensive subtasks, the whole gradient sits in the rate: the intervention moves the answer far more often in lower-resource languages (\hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{K}}=-0.044), but not by more when it does (\hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{K}}=0.10, not significant). The rate climbs from 4% of items in English to 35% in Yoruba, more than eightfold. On reasoning-intensive subtasks, the rate also falls with resource level (\hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{R}}=-0.021), but the magnitude rises (\hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{R}}=0.29); the two cancel, leaving reliance flat (\hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{R}}=0.01). Across interventions (Tab. 15), the knowledge–reasoning difference is significant in the rate but not in the magnitude for all but Early Answering, where it lies in the magnitude instead.

In other words, resource level decides how many answers need the chain, not how much each answer leans on it, as expected if a knowledge deficit determines which answers the model can simply recall. The distinction matters: on knowledge-intensive tasks, lower-resource languages rely on their reasoning more often, not more heavily.

We test whether the knowledge–reasoning gap survives plausible confounds by refitting Eq. 5 with four added controls and on four subsets of the data (Tab. 5). Item fixed effects ensure that languages with fewer valid generations are not judged on easier or harder questions, and CoT length accounts for a one-word mistake weighing less in a longer chain. Perturber similarity matters because the perturber is imperfect: the share of edits that change a single word, as instructed, falls from 67% in English to about half in Bengali and Swahili (Tab. 8). Final-answer log-probability lies on the path of Hypothesis 2, so controlling for it is conservative. The subsets keep correct answers only, single-word edits only, cells with at least 30 generations, or Gemma and Qwen alone; the first guards against faithfulness tracking accuracy Bentham et al. (2024), which also falls with resource level (Tab. 7), and the last two against the sparse low-resource cells of Aya and Llama (App. B).

Under every control, the gap stays negative and significant, as does the knowledge slope. The subsets are more demanding: the knowledge slope stays negative, and significant in all but correct answers only, while the gap keeps its sign but shrinks to between a quarter and a half of its primary size, losing significance in the last three. Across all interventions and metrics (Tab. 16), the gap is most robust under Filler Tokens, significant in 19 of 21 specifications, with no perturber involved.

Some cross-lingual variation is desirable, as when a model adapts to a language’s culture Veselovsky et al. (2025); variation in faithfulness is not, since monitoring and explanation should be equally reliable in every language.

We have shown that CoT faithfulness rises as resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks, but not on reasoning-intensive ones, a gap broadly consistent across models, metrics and robustness checks. We explain it with the Reliance Hypothesis: with less parametric knowledge in a language, a model cannot simply recall the answer and relies on its reasoning more frequently. Confidence partly explains this: final-answer confidence explains much of the variation on knowledge tasks, and reasoning-chain confidence some on reasoning tasks. Yet similar confidence gradients across task families do not by themselves explain the gap. Our evidence is consistent with the Reliance Hypothesis but does not establish its mechanism.

Our results suggest that faithfulness is highest where models know least. CoT monitoring may thus be most informative where it is least often validated, and English-only evaluations may understate how much models rely on their reasoning elsewhere, at least on knowledge-intensive tasks: a rare case in which the field’s focus on English is conservative rather than optimistic. LLM evaluators show a related pattern, scoring lower-resource languages more generously, an effect linked to but not explained by model uncertainty Zhou et al. (2026). Reliance, however, is not verbalisation: a chain can drive the answer yet omit what influenced it Onyame et al. (2026); Zaman and Srivastava (2026), so both properties need testing across languages. Future work should explore confidence calibration or alignment to keep faithfulness high in every language.

We study eight languages, and two of them, Swahili and Yoruba, carry most of the spread in resource level; the six others lie within 2.5 orders of magnitude of each other (Tab. 1). Our estimates therefore rest on few lower-resource languages and may not generalise to lower-resource languages at large; more languages, especially between Bengali and Yoruba, would sharpen them. Resource level is also entangled with other properties of a language, such as its family, script and tokenisation, which eight languages cannot separate. Our central comparison, however, is between knowledge- and reasoning-intensive tasks within the same language and model, so a language property that affects both kinds of task alike cannot produce the gap we report.

CulturaX token counts are a proxy for, not a record of, how much of each language the models saw in training, which is undisclosed for all four models and may include curated, translated or synthetic data. Our slopes should thus be read as associations with this proxy rather than with each model’s actual exposure to each language.

MMMLU is translated from English MMLU, whose questions are largely Western-centric: 28% require culturally sensitive knowledge, and 84.9% of those requiring geographic knowledge concern North America or Europe Singh et al. (2025). A model may thus know less about our knowledge-intensive questions in some languages because of cultural as well as linguistic distance, and translation may introduce artefacts of its own; questions written natively in each language would help separate these effects. Our reasoning-intensive subtasks are, moreover, mostly mathematical, and other forms of reasoning may behave differently.

Models produce a valid CoT and answer for 97% of English questions but only 35% of Yoruba ones (App. B), so the valid lower-resource generations may be a selected subset. We counter this by averaging within (model, subtask, language) cells, so that every model and subtask weighs equally in every language, and by refitting with item fixed effects, on correct answers only, on cells with at least 30 generations and without the two models with the sparsest lower-resource cells (Tab. 5). The knowledge slope stays negative under every check and significant under all but one, while the knowledge–reasoning gap keeps its sign but loses significance under the stricter subsets. We cannot rule out, however, that the invalid generations would have behaved differently.

Our metrics capture whether the answer depends on the CoT, one facet of faithfulness; they do not show whether the CoT reveals everything that drives the answer Zaman and Srivastava (2026). Adding Mistakes and Paraphrasing rely on an imperfect perturber, whose edits are less clean in some lower-resource languages (Tab. 8); Filler Tokens, which needs no perturber, nonetheless shows the most robust gap.

We evaluate four open-weight models of 4–8B parameters, which expose the token probabilities our metrics require. Larger models, and reasoning models with long thinking traces, may know more in lower-resource languages and rely on their reasoning differently.
