MemDuet: Learning Dual-Process Memory for Long-Context Reasoning. Reasoning over infinitely long documents is becoming a reality with recurrent memory agents. However, increasing context length exacerbates the trade-off between reasoning performance and inference efficiency. Inspired by Kahneman's account of fast and slow thinking, we propose MemDuet, a dual-process memory framework that learns to coordinate a small language model for fast, parallel evidence selection from raw context chunks (System 1) with a large language model for memory-update verification and memory updates in document order (System 2). We train MemDuet in three stages: supervised fine-tuning of System 1 for evidence selection, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) of System 2 for verification and memory rewriting, and joint optimization of both policies to coordinate selection and updating for long-context reasoning. Experiments on diverse long-context reasoning benchmarks (RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA) demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off as context length grows. Averaged across evaluation settings on the three datasets, MemDuet achieves an end-to-end inference speedup of 9.74x and an output-token reduction of 73.91% relative to RL-MemAgent.

Long-context reasoning is essential for large language models (LLMs) to synthesize evidence across documents, understand lengthy reports, and resolve repository-level dependencies in code (Bai et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023). Existing work primarily extends long-context capability through larger context windows, sparse or linear attention, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Chen et al., 2023b; Beltagy et al., 2020; Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2025; Lewis et al., 2020). However, these approaches remain bounded by the amount of context that can be directly represented or retrieved, leaving reasoning over unbounded documents unresolved.

MemAgent instead streams documents through a bounded recurrent memory, enabling reasoning over infinitely long documents with a fixed active context (Yu et al., 2026). Building on this paradigm, InfMem and GRU-Mem learn when to retrieve, update, or stop, while LycheeMemory compresses each chunk and invokes the reasoner only for selected memory blocks (Wang et al., 2026; Sheng et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). These advances make recurrent memory increasingly selective, but expose a common bottleneck: control decisions either remain inside the sequential recurrent loop or operate on representations in which the original evidence has already been compressed. Consequently, as context grows, reasoning performance and inference efficiency remain tightly coupled.

Human reading and memory suggest a different principle: memory formation begins with selective attention. Readers first focus on goal-relevant information and then integrate the attended evidence with prior knowledge into a coherent memory representation (Craik et al., 1996; Kintsch, 1988; Aly and Turk-Browne, 2016). This process naturally maps onto the dual-process account of cognition: System 1 rapidly identifies potentially useful evidence, whereas System 2 deliberately assesses and consolidates it (Kahneman, 2011; Evans and Stanovich, 2013). Based on this insight, we propose MemDuet, a dual-process recurrent memory framework. A small language model (System 1) scans raw context in parallel to select candidate chunks for memory updating. A large language model (System 2) verifies whether each selected chunk warrants a memory update under the current memory, then rewrites memory. By combining small-model selective attention over raw chunks with large-model verification and memory updating, MemDuet balances reasoning performance and inference efficiency as context grows.

A key challenge is how to train the two systems to cooperate. We develop a progressive three-stage training strategy. First, we supervise System 1 to identify context chunks that are likely to trigger useful memory updates. Next, with System 1 fixed, we optimize System 2 using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; Shao et al., 2024), training it to verify memory-update decisions and rewrite memory toward successful downstream reasoning. Finally, we jointly optimize both systems with task-level rewards, allowing evidence selection and memory updating to co-adapt.

We evaluate MemDuet on RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and long-context 2WikiMultihopQA. Results show that MemDuet improves the performance–efficiency trade-off over full-update recurrent memory agents, scaling to 3.5M-token contexts while achieving higher reasoning accuracy with substantially lower inference cost.

Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose MemDuet, a cognitively inspired dual-process memory framework for long-context reasoning, which instantiates System 1 as fast, parallel evidence selection with a small language model and System 2 as memory-update verification and memory rewriting with a large language model. We develop a three-stage training strategy that first establishes the selection and memory-updating capabilities of the two systems through SFT and GRPO, respectively, and then jointly optimizes their cooperation under a shared downstream reasoning objective. Extensive experiments on long-context reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that MemDuet achieves a favorable balance between reasoning performance and inference efficiency.

Recurrent-memory methods process documents incrementally while maintaining a bounded state, allowing language models to handle inputs far beyond their context windows. MemAgent sequentially processes text chunks and repeatedly rewrites a textual memory, using end-to-end reinforcement learning to retain task-relevant information and discard distractors based on downstream rewards (Yu et al., 2026). Building on this paradigm, InfMem and GRU-Mem learn retrieval, memory updating, and early-stopping decisions through SFT-to-RL training or behavior-specific rewards (Wang et al., 2026; Sheng et al., 2026). LycheeMemory compresses individual chunks and selectively invokes the reasoner, jointly optimizing its compressor and reasoner through end-to-end reinforcement learning (Chen et al., 2026). These studies turn memory management from a fixed procedure into a task-driven policy, but their control decisions remain within the sequential loop or operate on already compressed evidence. MemDuet instead scans raw chunks in parallel before recurrent updating and progressively coordinates evidence selection with memory consolidation.

section: Cognitively Inspired Language Models and Memory
text: Cognitive theories have informed both memory design and computational allocation in language-model systems. CoALA organizes language agents around modular memory, decision-making, and action components derived from cognitive architectures (Sumers et al., 2024). MemoryBank adopts an Ebbinghaus-inspired mechanism for dynamically forgetting and reinforcing memories (Zhong et al., 2024), whereas HippoRAG draws on hippocampal indexing theory to support associative knowledge retrieval (Gutiérrez et al., 2024). For reasoning, System 2 Attention deliberately rewrites the context to remove irrelevant information (Weston and Sukhbaatar, 2023), while Dualformer learns switchable fast and slow reasoning modes within a single model (Su et al., 2025). These studies primarily apply cognitive principles to memory organization, retrieval, or the allocation of reasoning effort. MemDuet instead introduces dual-process specialization into recurrent memory: System 1 selects raw candidate chunks in parallel; System 2 verifies whether they warrant memory updates under the current memory and consolidates their evidence.

We consider query-conditioned reasoning over a long document D. Given a query q, the goal is to generate an answer y using evidence from D, whose length may exceed the model’s context window. We divide D into T chunks (c_{1},\ldots,c_{T}) in their original order, with |c_{i}|\leq C, where |\cdot| denotes token length and C is the chunk-size budget. The query is available throughout document processing.

Following MemAgent (Yu et al., 2026), an LLM carries information across chunks through bounded textual memory, using the common interface m^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{mem}}(\cdot\mid q,c_{i},m),\qquad|m^{\prime}|\leq B, Here m and m^{\prime} are the preceding and replacement memories, and B is the memory budget. Under the memory prompt, \pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{mem}} is the autoregressive product of System 2’s next-token policy \pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{gen}}. The same model answers from q and the final memory under the answer prompt. Both C and B are independent of document length.
MemDuet alternates parallel raw-chunk selection by System 1 with verification and memory updates in document order by System 2 (Figure 2).

Here t indexes speculative rounds and i document chunks. At round t, System 1 independently evaluates a window \mathcal{W}_{t} of up to k consecutive chunks in parallel, using the shared query q and memory m_{t} to select candidate chunks for memory updating: \displaystyle a_{t,i} \displaystyle\sim\pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{sel}}\left(\cdot\mid q,c_{i},m_{t}\right), \displaystyle a_{t,i} \displaystyle\in\{\text{Skip}{},\text{Update}{}\}.
The chunks predicted as Update form the candidate set \mathcal{C}_{t}=\{c_{i}\in\mathcal{W}_{t}\mid a_{t,i}=\text{Update}{}\}, which is forwarded to System 2.

section: System 2: Speculative Verification and Memory Consolidation
text: Inspired by speculative decoding’s acceptance rule (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023a), System 2’s binary policy \pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{ver}} assesses whether selected chunks warrant memory updates. For candidate indices \mathcal{I}_{t}=\{i\mid c_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{t}\}, the action-level acceptance probability is \alpha_{t,i}=\min\!\left(1,\,\frac{\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{ver}}(\text{Update}{}\mid q,c_{i},m_{t})}{\pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{sel}}(\text{Update}{}\mid q,c_{i},m_{t})}\right). Independently draw \xi_{t,i}\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) for each candidate and accept it if \xi_{t,i}\leq\alpha_{t,i}.

section: System 2: Speculative Verification and Memory Consolidation
text: If any candidate is accepted, commit the first accepted chunk in document order and generate its replacement memory: m_{t+1}\sim\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{mem}}(\cdot\mid q,c_{i_{t}^{\star}},m_{t}), where i_{t}^{\star}=\min\{i\in\mathcal{I}_{t}\mid\xi_{t,i}\leq\alpha_{t,i}\}. As a special case, if no candidate is accepted, retain the current memory and advance past the window. Otherwise, discard remaining predictions conditioned on m_{t} and resume immediately after the committed chunk with m_{t+1}. Answering uses the query and final memory; Algorithm B.4 in Appendix B.4 gives the complete transitions.

Figure 3 summarizes three-stage training. Stage I trains memory-conditioned evidence selection. Stage II freezes System 1 and trains System 2 to verify candidates, rewrite memory, and generate answers. Stage III jointly optimizes both systems with task rewards, coordinating selection with verification and memory updates.
We initialize System 1 on HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) by aligning gold supporting facts with document chunks. Evidence-containing chunks are labeled Update, and other chunks Skip.

For each Update example (q,c,m), let m^{\prime} be the memory after incorporating the evidence from c. We retain the original example and add a post-update negative: \displaystyle(q,c,m) \displaystyle\longrightarrow\text{Update}{}, \displaystyle(q,c,m^{\prime}) \displaystyle\longrightarrow\text{Skip}{}. We train on the original examples and post-update negatives using the memory-contrastive objective: \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Stage\,I}}(\phi)={} \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{wCE}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{pair}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pair}}, \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pair}}={} \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}}\bigl[\max(0,\gamma-\Delta s_{\phi})\bigr]. Here, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{wCE}} is class-weighted action cross-entropy; \mathcal{P} contains matched memory pairs, with \Delta s_{\phi}=s_{\phi}(q,c,m)-s_{\phi}(q,c,m^{\prime}). The score s_{\phi} is the UPDATE-minus-SKIP logit difference, and \gamma is the margin. Hyperparameters are reported in Appendix B.1.

We freeze System 1 at \phi_{\mathrm{SFT}} and optimize all System 2 parameters \theta by reinforcement learning over complete trajectories. Selections are recomputed online as System 2 updates memory.

For each training instance (q,D,y^{\ast}), sample G complete trajectories using the behavior-policy snapshot \theta_{\mathrm{old}}. From the final-answer rewards R_{g}=R_{\mathrm{task}}(y_{g},y^{\ast}), we compute the group-relative advantage: \widehat{A}_{g}=\frac{R_{g}-\operatorname{mean}(R_{1},\ldots,R_{G})}{\operatorname{std}(R_{1},\ldots,R_{G})+\epsilon_{\mathrm{num}}}.

Here g indexes trajectories and \epsilon_{\mathrm{num}} is a numerical stability term. We use a clipped GRPO loss with generated-token KL regularization (Shao et al., 2024): \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Stage\,II}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{g}\Bigl[\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{E}_{g}|}\sum\nolimits_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{g}} \displaystyle\min\bigl(\rho_{g,e}\widehat{A}_{g},\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{g,e},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\widehat{A}_{g}\bigr)\Bigr] \displaystyle+\beta\mathbb{E}_{g}\Bigl[\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{g}|}\sum\nolimits_{e\in\mathcal{T}_{g}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{gen}}\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}^{\mathrm{gen}}\bigr)\Bigr], where \mathcal{E}_{g} contains verification commitment events for nonempty candidate sets and all generated tokens; \mathcal{T}_{g}\subseteq\mathcal{E}_{g} contains only generated tokens. e is a verification commitment event or generated token, and \rho_{g,e} is its current-to-behavior probability ratio. Verification commitment, token generation, and Stage III selection ratios are denoted by \rho_{g,t}^{\mathrm{ver}}, \rho_{g,t,\ell}^{\mathrm{gen}}, and \rho_{g,t,i}^{\mathrm{sel}}, respectively; \epsilon is the clipping parameter.

For a round- t verification event with a committed chunk, let i_{g,t}^{\star} record its index. The ratio is \displaystyle\rho_{g,e}=\rho_{g,t}^{\mathrm{ver}}= \displaystyle\frac{\Pr_{\phi_{\mathrm{SFT}},\theta}(i_{t}^{\star}=i_{g,t}^{\star}\mid q,\mathcal{W}_{g,t},\mathcal{I}_{g,t},m_{g,t})}{\Pr_{\phi_{\mathrm{SFT}},\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(i_{t}^{\star}=i_{g,t}^{\star}\mid q,\mathcal{W}_{g,t},\mathcal{I}_{g,t},m_{g,t})}, where e is the round- t verification commitment event. \Pr_{\phi,\theta} denotes the distribution of commitment outcomes induced by independent acceptance tests under the given query, window, candidate indices, and memory. For a candidate index j\in\mathcal{I}_{t}, its commitment probability is \alpha_{t,j}\prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{t},\;i<j}(1-\alpha_{t,i}). As a special case, the no-commitment probability is \prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{t}}(1-\alpha_{t,i}); it is one for empty \mathcal{I}_{t}, with no verification-policy loss. The controller’s independent acceptance tests and ordered commitment induce this distribution; selection and verification calls condition on (q,c_{i},m_{t}).

For a committed-chunk memory update, let \ell index tokens and m_{g,t+1,<\ell} denote the generated prefix. Its token-level ratio is \displaystyle\rho_{g,e}=\rho_{g,t,\ell}^{\mathrm{gen}}= \displaystyle\frac{\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{gen}}(m_{g,t+1,\ell}\mid q,c_{i_{g,t}^{\star}},m_{g,t},m_{g,t+1,<\ell})}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}^{\mathrm{gen}}(m_{g,t+1,\ell}\mid q,c_{i_{g,t}^{\star}},m_{g,t},m_{g,t+1,<\ell})}, where e is the generation event for token m_{g,t+1,\ell} and \rho_{g,e}=\rho_{g,t,\ell}^{\mathrm{gen}}. As a special case, first-chunk initialization tokens m_{g,0,\ell} and final-answer tokens y_{g,\ell} use the token-level ratio in Eq. (11), conditioned on (q,c_{1},m_{\mathrm{init}},m_{g,0,<\ell}) and (q,m_{g,\mathrm{fin}},y_{g,<\ell}), respectively. Here, m_{\mathrm{init}} is the fixed initial-memory marker and m_{g,\mathrm{fin}} is the final memory. Both token types contribute to the policy loss and KL regularizer in Eq. (9).
KL uses full token conditions and \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}^{\mathrm{gen}}, a frozen copy of the initial System 2 model. It applies only to generated tokens (Appendix B.2).

Let P_{\phi,\theta}(\tau\mid q,D) denote the complete trajectory distribution induced by selection, verification commitments, and System 2’s memory and answer generation (Appendix B.3). With both backbones frozen, we jointly optimize only their LoRA adapters: \max_{\phi,\theta}\,\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim P_{\phi,\theta}(\cdot\mid q,D)}\left[R_{\mathrm{task}}(y,y^{\ast})\right], using fresh rollout groups under (\phi_{\mathrm{old}},\theta_{\mathrm{old}}) and the Stage-II advantages. The clipped loss adds selection events recording both Skip and Update actions a_{g,t,i}, with ratios \displaystyle\rho_{g,e}=\rho_{g,t,i}^{\mathrm{sel}} \displaystyle=\frac{\pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{sel}}(a_{g,t,i}\mid q,c_{i},m_{g,t})}{\pi_{\phi_{\mathrm{old}}}^{\mathrm{sel}}(a_{g,t,i}\mid q,c_{i},m_{g,t})}, where e is the selection event for chunk i in round t. Commitment ratios follow Eq. (10), replacing \phi_{\mathrm{SFT}} with \phi in the numerator and \phi_{\mathrm{old}} in the denominator, retaining dependence on both systems through Eq. (4). Generation ratios and generation-only KL, including the same frozen reference policy, are retained from Stage II.

We follow MemAgent’s RULER-HQA construction (7K–3.5M tokens) (Yu et al., 2026), reserving its 128-question development set for testing and a disjoint 128-question HotpotQA validation set for checkpoint selection. We further evaluate on LongBench v2 (Bai et al., 2025) and a long-context variant of 2WikiMultihopQA (Ho et al., 2020). We report option accuracy on LongBench v2 and normalized substring exact match (sub-EM) on RULER-HQA and 2WikiMultihopQA. To assess inference efficiency, we additionally report speedup relative to MemAgent and the number of generated output tokens. Dataset construction, sample sizes, and length groupings are detailed in Appendix A.1; evaluation protocols are provided in Appendix A.3.

We compare MemDuet with Search-R1-7B (Jin et al., 2025a), QwenLong-L1-32B (Wan et al., 2025), DS-Distill-32B (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), RL-MemAgent-7B (Yu et al., 2026), LycheeMemory-7B (Chen et al., 2026), and ReMemR1-7B (Shi et al., 2025).

We use Qwen3.5-2B as System 1 for the main results and evaluate Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen3.5-0.8B in the System 1 backbone comparison (Yang et al., 2025a; Qwen Team, 2026). System 2 uses the same Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone as MemAgent (Yang et al., 2025a; Yu et al., 2026). See Appendix B for training and implementation.

Table 1 shows that MemDuet achieves an increasingly favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off as context grows. At 3.5M tokens, it outperforms RL-MemAgent by 3.90 points while achieving a 49.61 \times speedup and generating 99.14% fewer output tokens. At 7K, the limited number of chunks provides little opportunity to offset the fixed cost of System 1 scanning and cross-system coordination. As the context grows, this overhead is amortized and more unnecessary System 2 processing can be avoided, making the efficiency gains increasingly pronounced without sacrificing accuracy.

Table 2 evaluates MemDuet on LongBench v2, which contains realistic long-context tasks, and on length-controlled 2WikiMultihopQA. MemDuet achieves the highest option accuracy on the Long and Ultra groups of LongBench v2, with 3.00 \times and 8.03 \times speedups. Its lower option accuracy on the Short and Medium groups is consistent with selective processing occasionally discarding useful evidence when the full input is still manageable. The same transition appears in sub-EM on 2WikiMultihopQA: MemDuet trails at 14K and 56K, but leads at 224K and 896K, indicating that its advantages are concentrated in the long-context regime for which it is designed.

Figure 4 shows that MemDuet’s latency and output tokens grow more slowly with context length than those of RL-MemAgent. Although MemDuet incurs a small latency overhead at 7K, its runtime advantage becomes increasingly pronounced on longer inputs. The shallower growth in output tokens is consistent with restricting large-model memory updates to selected evidence rather than rewriting memory for every chunk. Latency savings are smaller than token savings, since input processing and System 1 computation remain necessary even when output tokens are substantially reduced.

W/o draft–verify retains System 1 selection but removes System 2 verification and acceptance tests: selected Update actions directly trigger memory rewriting, followed by reevaluation of later chunks. W/o state reevaluation reuses selection and verification/acceptance results computed with the window-start memory even after updates, processing chunks in document order; memory generation still uses the latest memory. W/o parallel execution changes k=4 to k=1, retaining all other decision rules. The k=1 variant preserves accuracy, with speedup changing from 12.16\times to 11.84\times. Removing draft–verify or state reevaluation reduces accuracy by up to 3.90 points; draft–verify removal also lowers speedup to 9.89\times. Verification and state reevaluation thus preserve quality while reducing large-model computation.

The three training stages play complementary roles. Without Stage I, System 1 tends to propose updates for nearly all chunks, maintaining coverage of supporting evidence and limiting the accuracy drop to 3.90–5.47 points relative to the full configuration. More frequent verification and memory rewriting increase computation, reducing speedup from 12.16\times to 2.54\times and roughly tripling the mean output-token ratio. Without Stage II, System 2 lacks dedicated reinforcement learning for memory rewriting, substantially weakening evidence consolidation. The retained Stage III joint training partially restores this capability, keeping accuracy above the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct baseline (112K: 32.81%; 448K: 6.25%; 896K: 1.56%). Stage III aligns the two policies: joint optimization recovers 2.34–6.25 accuracy points over w/o Stage III. The curriculum thus progressively learns when to update, how to update, and how to coordinate the two decisions.

System 1 should favor evidence coverage, since missed evidence cannot be recovered, whereas false positives can still be filtered by System 2. Across both Qwen2.5 and Qwen3.5 backbones, MemDuet consistently turns small models into effective proposers, achieving 80.08–83.36% downstream accuracy with mean speedups of 5.69 – 14.26\times. Qwen3.5-0.8B has the highest selection F1 and lowest output-token ratio, while Qwen3.5-2B, used for the main results, attains the highest final accuracy and mean speedup. Selection quality should be evaluated alongside answer quality and inference cost.

Parallel chunk processing provides only modest gains because MemDuet must preserve the document order of memory updates. System 1 evaluates chunks concurrently, but System 2 rewrites memory from the first accepted chunk in document order and reevaluates later chunks under the updated memory. As k increases, more speculative computation may therefore be discarded, and synchronization overhead can outweigh the benefit of concurrency. The best speedup is 1.111\times at k=8 and 1.75M tokens, whereas k=16 and k=32 slow inference at every evaluated length. Moderate parallelism thus provides the best balance between concurrent evidence discovery and memory consolidation in document order.

MemDuet can be directly applied to proprietary APIs without additional training: a smaller model serves as System 1 to propose candidate chunks, while a stronger model serves as System 2 to accept or reject each proposal before memory rewriting. This plug-and-play setup reduces latency by 70.7–71.8% and cost by 58.2–59.9%, with option accuracy changing by at most 0.60 points.

MemDuet combines memory-conditioned parallel evidence selection by a small language model with large-model verification and document-order memory updates. Three-stage training teaches both systems when to update memory and how to consolidate evidence and coordinate decisions. Experiments on three long-context reasoning benchmarks show a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off, with greater efficiency gains at longer contexts.

Our evaluation is limited to three long-context benchmarks and mainly Qwen-family backbones, so generalization to other domains and model families remains uncertain. MemDuet is also less effective on shorter inputs, where selective processing may discard useful evidence; moreover, evidence missed by System 1 cannot be recovered by System 2. Memory updates in document order further limit the practical benefits of parallel execution.

MemDuet studies efficient reasoning over long documents using existing benchmarks and pretrained language models. These resources can contain inaccurate, biased, or sensitive material. Their use and redistribution should respect the applicable licenses and access conditions. Benchmark performance alone does not establish fairness, privacy protection, or suitability for deployment.

Selective processing can omit relevant evidence or minority viewpoints, while repeated memory updates can preserve unsupported claims and discard qualifications. The verifier evaluates memory-update decisions and should not be treated as an independent guarantee of factual correctness. For consequential applications, users should retain access to original documents, inspect supporting evidence, and require human review of outputs. Additional evaluation across languages, domains, and population groups is needed before such use.

Long documents, intermediate memories, and generated answers may expose personal or confidential information. Deployments should minimize sensitive data, restrict access to stored memories and logs, and define appropriate retention and deletion procedures. Users should confirm authorization before transmitting content to proprietary APIs and consider the providers’ data-handling policies.

Lower inference cost may make document analysis more accessible, but can also facilitate large-scale surveillance or unauthorized profiling. Applications should be limited to authorized, legitimate uses. Finally, reduced latency and output-token counts do not directly quantify energy consumption or carbon emissions; environmental benefits require dedicated measurement that also accounts for training and total usage.

Explaining the Roles of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for Personalization. Personalization of Large Language Models (LLMs) is increasingly important for user-centric applications, yet prior methods mainly adapt dense LLMs, whose polysemantic neurons, each encoding multiple unrelated concepts, hinder localizing the components behind personalization, and thus understanding and controlling it. We propose to personalize Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, which sparsely route each token to a few specialized experts, reducing polysemanticity and enabling such localization. We adapt three open-weight MoE LLMs on a large-scale personalization dataset and train crosscoders on paired activations of the personalized and non-personalized models to learn interpretable personalized latents, from which we identify the experts encoding distinct personalization features. The personalized MoE LLMs perform competitively with dense LLMs while activating only a fraction of their parameters, exhibit lower polysemanticity than dense LLMs with similar active parameters, and, within the same model family, yield personalized latents that are less shared with the non-personalized model. Causal interventions show that these latents suffice to recover the personalized model's behavior and that boosting their associated experts moves the non-personalized model toward it, revealing distinct routing paths for different personalization features.

Personalization of Large Language Models (LLMs) adapts LLMs to user or group preferences (Salemi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b). Due to increasing demand for AI-assisted user-centric applications, Personalization of LLMs has become an important research direction. Most methods use dense LLMs (Zhang et al., 2025b), offering little interpretability of localizing important model components encoding distinct personalized features due to the polysemanticity of encoding multiple orthogonal concepts into a single neuron (Olah et al., 2020). Recent work on developing intrinsically interpretable LLMs suggests that wider, more sparse LLMs enable their neurons to capture more disentangled features and reduce polysemanticity (Yang et al., 2025b). Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs offer a scalable solution for wider and sparser networks by replacing a dense FFN block in the MLP layer with a set of experts of the same size, using a sparse routing mechanism to select a subset of these experts to process each input token (Shazeer et al., 2017). This mechanism enables MoE LLMs to offer better interpretability for downstream tasks by achieving lower polysemanticity (Herbst et al., 2026), where experts encode distinct task-specific features.

Motivated by these observations, we utilize MoE LLMs for personalization and subsequent interpretability analysis, addressing research questions covering polysemamticity of MoE LLMs for personalization (RQ1, § 6.2), identifying distinct personalized features encoded via experts during personalization (RQ2, § 6.3), and localizing unique routing paths for distinct personalized features (RQ3, § 6.4).

Following Bai et al. (2025) on MoE LLMs alignment, we adapt the MoE LLMs towards personalization using a two-stage parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) (§ 4.1), on a large-scale personalization dataset covering diverse preferences for user groups, MULTIFACETED COLLECTION (Lee et al., 2024). We then train a sparse autoencoder-based (Bricken et al., 2023; Huben et al., 2024) architecture crosscoder (Minder et al., 2025) on paired personalized and non-personalized activations to identify interpretable personalization latents. Mapping these latents to experts reveals distinct routing paths associated with personalization. Our proposed method is illustrated in Figure 1.

Extensive experiments on three open-weight instruction-tuned decoder-only MoE LLMs, OLMoE-1B-7B (0125), Qwen3-30B-A3B (2507), and Mixtral-8x7B (v0.1), spanning three personalization benchmarks: MULTIFACETED BENCH (Lee et al., 2024) covering preferences for user groups, and LaMP and LongLaMP benchmarks for per user preference, verifies the scalability of MoE LLMs in personalization by outperforming similar active parameter sized dense LLMs and achieve competitive performance against similar total parameter sized dense LLMs, while utilizing only ~20\% of the total parameters per token (§ 6.1). Furthermore, MoE LLMs enable better learning of crosscoder to identify a high-quality small set of latents (less than 0.25\% of total latents), highly contributing in explaining distinct personalized features encoded during personalization than dense LLMs, verifying lower polysemanticity for personalization (§ 6.2). These personalized latents each capture a distinct personalization feature (§ 6.3) and map onto a small, stable set of specialized experts (§ 6.4), revealing distinct routing paths for personalization in MoE LLMs. Causal interventions further confirm that these latents are sufficient to recover personalized behavior and that the identified experts are necessary for it. Overall, our proposed method offers a principled foundation for understanding and designing more transparent personalized language models.

Methods for aligning LLMs with individual or group preferences (Zhang et al., 2025b) condition on retrieved user history or profile summaries (Salemi et al., 2024; Richardson et al., 2023), encode personas in the prompt (Jiang et al., 2024b), train per-user adapters (Tan et al., 2024), learn personalized reward models or merge preference-specific policies (Cheng et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2024), or steer activations toward a user’s style (Zhang et al., 2025a; Cao et al., 2024). LaMP and LongLaMP (Salemi et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2024) evaluate per-user personalization, while Multifaceted Collection and Bench (Lee et al., 2024) specify group preferences via system messages. These works study dense models as black boxes; we study how sparse MoEs represent personalization.

MoE layers route each token to a few experts, decoupling parameter count from compute (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022; Zoph et al., 2022), and now underlie strong open models such as Mixtral, OLMoE, and Qwen3 (Jiang et al., 2024a; Muennighoff et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a). Analyses of routing report specialization at the level of tokens and syntax rather than domains (Jiang et al., 2024a; Xue et al., 2024), semantic routing in controlled settings (Olson et al., 2025), and language-specific experts identified by contrasting routing frequencies (Bandarkar et al., 2026). Expert-level specialization can be exploited for adaptation and control: Bai et al. (2025) tune routers to identify context-faithful experts, Li et al. (2026) encourage expert divergence during training, and Fayyaz et al. (2026) steer behavior by (de)activating experts. We adopt a two-stage router-then-expert adaptation for personalization and relate the resulting routing changes to interpretable persona features.

Dense-model neurons are polysemantic (Olah et al., 2020); sparse autoencoders recover more monosemantic features (Bricken et al., 2023; Huben et al., 2024), sparse probing measures how few neurons encode a concept (Gurnee et al., 2023), and wider, sparser architectures such as MoEs reduce polysemanticity (Yang et al., 2025b; Herbst et al., 2026). Crosscoders, trained with BatchTopK (Bussmann et al., 2024) and explained automatically (Paulo et al., 2025), isolate latents specific to a fine-tuned model and have been applied to chat tuning (Minder et al., 2025) and to MoE–dense comparisons (Chaudhari et al., 2026). We diff a personalized MoE against its base and map the resulting latents onto the experts that route them.

Given a user query x and a preference P, either the user’s interaction history P=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{|P|} or a set of stated preferences P=\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\}, a personalized LLM M_{\theta} generates \hat{y}_{p}=M_{\theta}\big(x,A_{p}(x,P)\big), where the adapter A_{p} injects P into generation, e.g., via retrieval or learned parameters, and \hat{y}_{p} is scored against a gold response y. We realize A_{p} as PEFT parameters \phi of an MoE LLM (§ 4.1) and decompose what it encodes into a set of interpretable latents \mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{ft}} (§ 4.2).

An MoE layer replaces the dense FFN with N_{E} experts and a router r_{\theta_{r}} that routes each token to its top- k experts (Shazeer et al., 2017; Muennighoff et al., 2025). For token x_{t} with input u_{x_{t}}^{(l)} at layer l, h_{x_{t}}^{(l)}=u_{x_{t}}^{(l)}+\sum_{i\in\text{top-}k\left(r_{\theta_{r}}^{(l)}(u_{x_{t}}^{(l)})\right)}g_{(i,t)}^{(l)}\,E_{i}^{(l)}\big(u_{x_{t}}^{(l)}\big), where g_{(i,t)}^{(l)}=\text{softmax}\big(r_{\theta_{r},i}^{(l)}(u_{x_{t}}^{(l)})\big) is the gate weight of expert E_{i}^{(l)}.

A crosscoder learns a single dictionary of D\gg d latents that jointly reconstructs paired activations h_{x_{t}}^{(l,\mathrm{ft})},h_{x_{t}}^{(l,\mathrm{base})}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} of the personalized and non-personalized models at layer l (Minder et al., 2025): \displaystyle a_{j}(x_{t}) \displaystyle=\text{ReLU}\big(\mathbf{e}_{j}^{\mathrm{ft}}h_{x_{t}}^{(l,\mathrm{ft})}+\mathbf{e}_{j}^{\mathrm{base}}h_{x_{t}}^{(l,\mathrm{base})}+b_{j}^{\mathrm{enc}}\big), \displaystyle\tilde{h}_{x_{t}}^{(l,m)} \displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{j}a_{j}(x_{t})\,\mathbf{d}_{j}^{m}+\mathbf{b}^{\mathrm{dec},m}, where \quad m\in\{\mathrm{ft},\mathrm{base}\}. Each latent j has a separate decoder vector for each model. A latent whose \mathbf{d}_{j}^{\mathrm{ft}} dominates \mathbf{d}_{j}^{\mathrm{base}} contributes mainly to reconstructing the personalized model. We use this property to identify personalized latents (§ 4.2). We train a BatchTopK crosscoder (Bussmann et al., 2024) and the objective and training details are given in Section A.1.

Load balancing during MoE pre-training spreads tokens evenly across experts, which discourages individual experts from specializing in task-specific features. Following Bai et al. (2025), we therefore adapt the model in two stages: we first tune the routers to find the experts relevant to personalization, and then tune only those experts. Let \theta=\{\theta_{r},\theta_{e},\theta_{o}\} denote the router, expert and remaining parameters, and \mathcal{D}_{p} the preference dataset.

We update only the routers with the language-modeling loss: \min_{\theta_{r}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LM}}(M_{\theta},\mathcal{D}_{p})\quad\text{s.t. }\theta_{e},\theta_{o}\text{ frozen}. We then measure how often the tuned router selects each expert E_{i}^{(l)}: f_{i}^{(l)}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{p}|}\sum_{m=1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{p}|}\frac{1}{|x_{m}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|x_{m}|}\frac{\mathbb{I}\big(i\in\mathcal{T}_{m,t}^{(l)}\big)}{k}, where \mathcal{T}_{m,t}^{(l)} is the set of top- k experts selected for token t of sequence x_{m} at layer l. Dividing by k ensures that the frequencies at each layer sum to 1.

We then fine-tune only the k most selected experts per layer, \theta_{e}^{(k)}\subset\theta_{e}: \min_{\theta_{e}^{(k)}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LM}}(M_{\theta},\mathcal{D}_{p})\quad\text{s.t. }\theta_{r},\theta_{o}\text{ frozen}.

We train a crosscoder (§ 3.3) on paired activations of the personalized and non-personalized MoE LLMs over \mathcal{D}_{p}, identify the latents specific to the personalized model, and map each latent to the experts that process it.

Layer selection. Middle layers carry the most informative representations (Skean et al., 2025).Among them, we select the layer whose routing changes most under personalization, measured by the Jensen–Shannon divergence between the routing distributions of personalized vs. non-personalized models (Li et al., 2026; Bandarkar et al., 2026). We require the router to choose experts confidently, as measured by low routing entropy.

Personalized latents. Following Minder et al. (2025), we score each latent by the relative norm difference of its two decoder vectors, \Delta_{j}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\lVert\mathbf{d}_{j}^{\mathrm{ft}}\rVert_{2}-\lVert\mathbf{d}_{j}^{\mathrm{base}}\rVert_{2}}{\max\!\left(\lVert\mathbf{d}_{j}^{\mathrm{ft}}\rVert_{2},\,\lVert\mathbf{d}_{j}^{\mathrm{base}}\rVert_{2}\right)}+1\right)\in[0,1], and assign j to \mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{ft}} if \Delta_{j}\geq 0.9, to \mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{base}} if \Delta_{j}\leq 0.1, and to \mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{shared}} if \Delta_{j}\in[0.4,0.6].

Latent-to-expert mapping. For each j\in\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{ft}}, we take the top- N sequences in \mathcal{D}_{p} by activation a_{j}. Within these sequences, we rank the experts at each layer by how much more often they are selected on tokens where the latent fires than on tokens where they do not (Bandarkar et al., 2026), and keep the top- k^{\prime}: \mathcal{E}_{j}^{(l)}=\mathrm{Top}_{k^{\prime}}\Big(f_{i}^{(l)}\big|_{a_{j}>0}-f_{i}^{(l)}\big|_{a_{j}\leq 0}\Big), where f_{i}^{(l)} is the expert activation frequency (Equation 5) restricted to the given tokens. We choose (N,k^{\prime}) by grid search over two criteria in [0,1]. Distinctiveness (D) is one minus the average overlap of \mathcal{E}_{j}^{(l)} across latents, so different latents should map to different experts. Stability (S) is the agreement of \mathcal{E}_{j}^{(l)} across random subsamples of the N sequences, so the mapping should not depend on which examples are drawn. Larger N improves stability, but if N is too large, the selected sequences overlap across latents and distinctiveness drops.

Data and evaluation. We personalize models and train crosscoders on Multifaceted Collection (Lee et al., 2024). Each example pairs a user query with a system message that encodes a group-level preference across four dimensions (style, background knowledge, informativeness, harmlessness), along with a preference-aligned response generated by GPT-4-Turbo-0125. We evaluate on three benchmarks: (i) Multifaceted Bench (Lee et al., 2024), which uses the same system-message format but has no preferences in common with the training set; (ii) LaMP (Salemi et al., 2024); and (iii) LongLaMP (Kumar et al., 2024). LaMP and LongLaMP instead require inferring per-user preferences from interaction history. Following Zhang et al. (2025a), we use their user splits and omit the email tasks, whose data is not publicly available. We report METEOR and ROUGE-L against the gold responses.

Models and baselines. We study three instruction-tuned MoE LLMs: OLMoE-1B-7B (0125), Qwen3-30B-A3B (2507) and Mixtral-8x7B (v0.1). Each is evaluated without adaptation, after router tuning (RT), and after router and expert tuning (RT+EFT). We compare each MoE model with two dense models, one matching its active and one matching its total parameter count: OLMo-2-1B/7B, Qwen2.5-3B/32B, and Llama-2-13B/70B for Mixtral, following its technical report (Table 1). The dense baselines are evaluated without adaptation and after PEFT on Multifaceted Collection. As a reference, we also report Janus -7B and its ORPO/DPO variants (Lee et al., 2024), which are fully parameter-fine-tuned on the Multifaceted Collection, indicating the upper bound of performance for LLMs with similar parameter counts.

Across model families and evaluation metrics, MoE LLMs outperform dense LLMs with similar active parameters, and for the Qwen and Mixtral families, they match or exceed dense LLMs with similar total parameters (Figure 2). The per-variant results in Table 2 show the same pattern after personalization: personalized MoE LLMs outperform or match personalized dense LLMs with similar active parameters. Router tuning accounts for most of this gain in Qwen3, whereas expert tuning contributes more in Mixtral. Across benchmarks, personalization yields the largest gains on MULTIFACETED BENCH, which shares the training data’s (MULTIFACETED COLLECTION) form of preference (group-level preferences given via system messages), and smaller gains on LaMP and LongLaMP, which require transferring to per-user preferences inferred from interaction history. Overall, MoE LLMs achieve competitive personalization while activating only a fraction of their parameters, motivating a mechanistic analysis of how their experts encode personalization features.

section: RQ1: Do Sparse MoE LLMs offer lower polysemanticity, enabling better disentanglement of personalized features?
text: Polysemanticity. To investigate the polysemanticity behavior of neurons in MoE experts compared to dense LLMs, we use k-sparse probing (Gurnee et al., 2023). Following Herbst et al. (2026), we estimate the mean difference of activations between positive and negative tokens per concept and compute the binary classification of a probe considering only the top- k neurons with the highest activation difference. For our personalization task, we consider the top 5 most frequent sub-dimensions from MULTIFACETED COLLECTION as concepts for each dimension, resulting in 20 independent concepts. For each concept, we take the response tokens (up to 1024 per response, 100 queries) of samples whose system message specifies that sub-dimension as positives, and those of samples specifying a different sub-dimension of the same dimension as negatives (e.g., formal vs. casual under style), giving about 50,000 tokens per class. Following Herbst et al. (2026), we only consider tokens routed to the target expert for MoE LLMs and identify the best layer containing the expert achieving the highest classification accuracy on the test split (25% split). For dense LLMs, the best layer is that with the highest-performing MLP.

section: RQ1: Do Sparse MoE LLMs offer lower polysemanticity, enabling better disentanglement of personalized features?
text: Figure 3 illustrates the variance in k-sparse probe classification accuracy from k=64 to k=1 for the MoE and dense LLMs with similar active parameters. MoE LLMs outperform dense LLMs with similar active parameters in the balanced accuracy metric, and the performance gap is wider for the same model family (Olmo, Qwen). The gap remains wide at k=1, verifying monosemantic behavior of MoE experts for personalization.

section: RQ1: Do Sparse MoE LLMs offer lower polysemanticity, enabling better disentanglement of personalized features?
text: Disentanglement of personalized features. To verify whether lower polysemantic MoE experts enable better disentanglement of personalised features via crosscoder latents, we compare MoE and dense LLMs on how well personalized latents explain activations from non-personalized LLMs. In particular, following Minder et al. (2025), we compute scales \beta^{\text{base}}_{j},\beta^{\text{ft}}_{j} for each personalized latent j\in\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{ft}} in explaining activations from non-personalized and personalized model as: \beta^{\text{base/ft}}_{j}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\beta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\|\beta a_{j}(x_{i})d^{\text{ft}}_{j}-h^{\text{base/ft}}(x_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2}

section: RQ1: Do Sparse MoE LLMs offer lower polysemanticity, enabling better disentanglement of personalized features?
text:
Since,  eta^{	ext{base}}_{j}, eta^{	ext{ft}}_{j} are unbounded, their ratio 
u_{j}= eta^{	ext{base}}_{j}/ eta^{	ext{ft}}_{j} approaching near zero indicate little contribution to reconstructing the non-personalized model relative to the personalized model. Figure 4 compares the 
u_{j} corresponding to personalized latents of MoE and dense LLMs. For the same model family, the MoE LLM has a lower 
u_{j} for personalized latents than dense LLMs, except for Mixtral, which yields a higher

Overall, MoE LLMs offer lower polysemanticity and better disentanglement of personalized features, which justifies the need for interpretability analysis for decoding personalization mechanism.

section: RQ2: What are the different personalized features disentangled into a set of interpretable concepts?
text: Using the routing-divergence and entropy criteria discussed in § 4.2, we identify L25, L15, and L6 as the most distinctive layers for Qwen3-30B-A3B (2507), Mixtral-8x7B (v0.1), and OLMoE-1B-7B (0125) respectively, as illustrated in Figures 5, 12 and 11. As discussed in § 4.2, we identify a very small subset (less than 0.25%) of latents with very high (\geq 0.9) decoder norm to reconstruct activations from the personalized MoE LLMs. In particular, we identify (157/65536), (132/131072), (111/65536) personalized latents for Qwen3-30B-A3B (2507), Mixtral-8x7B (v0.1), and OLMoE-1B-7B (0125) respectively, as illustrated in Figures 6, 14 and 13.

section: RQ2: What are the different personalized features disentangled into a set of interpretable concepts?
text: Interpreting personalized latents. Following Paulo et al. (2025); Minder et al. (2025), we explain each personalized latent with an LLM explainer and evaluate the explanation with an LLM scorer (both Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct). The explainer sees 30 activating examples (the top 20 and 10 weaker ones), each a 40-token window centred on the maximally activating token (32 tokens before, 8 tokens after). The scorer then labels 20 examples as activating and 20 as non-activating, using only the explanation. Figure 8 shows an example: a max-activating latent from Qwen3 is explained as tracking the audience’s level of expertise.

section: RQ2: What are the different personalized features disentangled into a set of interpretable concepts?
text: Most personalized latents encode the requested preference rather than the response: 85% of OLMoE and 82% of Qwen3 latents fire mainly on the system message. Mixtral is the exception, with 41% firing mainly in the response. The models also emphasize different preference dimensions: OLMoE’s latents are dominated by style (52%) and harmlessness (21%), whereas Qwen3’s and Mixtral’s are dominated by background knowledge (45% and 40%). The scorer reaches moderate F1 overall (0.65 OLMoE, 0.63 Qwen3, 0.70 Mixtral; Figure 7), rising monotonically across activation bins to 0.81, 0.83 and 0.88 in the top bin, so the explanations best describe strong activations. Overall, the crosscoder decomposes the features that personalization adds to MoE LLMs into a small set of interpretable concepts.

section: RQ3: How are different experts in MoE uniquely aligned with different personalized features?
text: To test whether distinct personalization features map to different experts, we evaluate the distinctiveness and stability of latent–expert mappings (see § 4.2). As illustrated in Figure 9, for each latent, we select the optimal 400 examples and restrict it to route towards one expert every layer for the Qwen3-30B-A3B (2507). For this setting, we achieve very high stability with S of 0.81, verifying that under repeated sampling over those 400 examples, most of the activating examples are routed towards a specialized expert. To validate whether the routing is heavily influenced by a dominant expert, we measure the distinctiveness and a very high D of 0.94, which verifies that a different set of examples activated by different latents is routed to their respective experts. Overall, experts in MoE LLMs encode distinct personalized features, verifying lower polysemanticity for personalization.

Sufficiency of personalized latents via activation patching. Following Minder et al. (2025) of causally verifying the sufficiency of chat-specific latents for instruction-tuned LLMs, for an input token, we patch the activation of that token at the crosscoder layer of the personalized model with a hybrid activation combining activation from the non-personalized model and personalized latents activations for that token, and continue the generation from the later layer to measure the KL divergence between the next token probability of the personalized and patched personalized model. In particular, for an input token x_{t} with activations from personalized and non-personalized MoE LLMs at the crosscoder layer l as h_{x_{t}}^{l,\text{ft}}, and h_{x_{t}}^{l,\text{base}} respectively, we measure KL divergence \mathrm{KL}\left(p^{\mathrm{ft}}_{h_{x_{t}}^{l,\mathrm{ft}}\leftarrow h_{x_{t}}^{l,\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{ft}}}}\,\middle\|\,p^{\mathrm{ft}}\right), where p^{\text{ft}} is the personalized model’s next token probability, and the hybrid activation h_{x_{t}}^{l,\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{ft}}}=h_{x_{t}}^{l,\mathrm{base}}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{ft}}}a_{j}(x_{t})\,\mathbf{d}_{j}^{\mathrm{ft}}. If we just patch with the non-personalized model, then the KL divergence will be the maximum, and we measure the reduction in KL divergence from the non-personalized patching for our personalized latents. We also randomly select the same number of latents matching the activation frequency of those personalized latents, from the whole and ‘shared’ region of the crosscoder’s latent distribution as baselines.

The top part of Figure 10 verifies that for personalized latents, the KL divergence decrease is the maximum among the baselines across MoE models on the MULTIFACETED BENCH benchmark, causally establishing the sufficiency of personalized latents in explaining personalized features in MoE personalization.

Unique routing paths for distinct personalization features. To causally verify whether a small set of experts encodes distinct personalization features as shown in § 6.4, we steer those experts in the non-personalized MoE LLMs along each dimension from the MULTIFACETED COLLECTION benchmark, and measure the KL divergence from the personalized counterparts. In particular, for each dimension, we collect experts uniquely aligned with the latents (§ 6.3,§ 6.3) and rank them by routing frequency (Equation 5) over the activating examples corresponding to those latents. We steer top- k^{\prime} (Figures 15, 9 and 16) experts for each dimension for all the MoE LLMs as: \tilde{z}^{(l)}_{i}\;=\;z^{(l)}_{i}+\beta^{(l)}\sigma(z^{(l)}_{i}), where i\in\text{top}-k^{\prime}, \sigma(z^{(l)}_{i}) is the standard deviation of the router logits of the non-personalized MoE at layer l (over tokens and experts) and \beta^{(l)} (2 in our experiment) is the boosting strength. We also randomly steer the same number of experts at the crosscoder layer in the non-personalized layer. The bottom panel of fig. 10 shows that, for each dimension, steering the unique top- k^{\prime} experts yields lower KL divergence than random steering, thereby causally verifying unique routing paths for distinct personalization features.

We presented, to our knowledge, the first mechanistic study of personalization in MoE LLMs. Combining a two-stage router-and-expert adaptation for personalization with crosscoder-based interpretability analysis for personalization mechanism shows: (1) MoE LLMs achieve competitive personalization performance than dense LLMs by utilizing only \sim 20\% of total parameters. (2) MoE LLMs exhibit lower polysemanticity than dense LLMs for personalization and they enable better interpretability of encoded personalization features via crosscoder than dense LLMs. (3) MoE encodes distinct personalization features via different routing paths, enabling better localization and subsequent intervention for controlled personalization.

Models and comparisons. We study three open MoE families and analyze one layer per model, selected by routing divergence. Personalization features may also arise at other layers, and our conclusions may not transfer to other MoE designs (e.g., shared experts or fine-grained expert segmentation). The dense counterparts are matched by active or total parameter count, but differ in pre-training data and recipes, so architectural effects cannot be fully separated from training differences.

Data and notion of persona. Multifaceted-Collection describes preferences through synthetic system messages over four dimensions, with categorical, long-tailed subdimension labels. This captures group-level preferences rather than individual users, and our experiments are limited to English. Personalization signals in real user histories may be noisier and more entangled than in this controlled setting.

Crosscoder fidelity. Crosscoders reconstruct activations imperfectly, and reconstruction quality varies across models (with fractions of variance explained of 0.80 for OLMoE, 0.74 for Qwen3-30B-A3B, and 0.65 for Mixtral, whose activations have much larger magnitudes and heavier tails). Information in the reconstruction error is invisible to our latent-level analyses, and the set of personalized latents depends on the decoder-norm threshold. BatchTopK training and latent scaling mitigate known sparsity artifacts (Minder et al., 2025), but do not rule them out entirely.

Probing. Persona concepts are properties of whole responses, whereas sparse probing labels individual tokens, thereby introducing label noise and lowering absolute scores across all models. Selecting the best of many components favors MoE models, which have more candidates (layers \times experts); we mitigate this by selecting on test data and reporting test scores, but selection effects may remain, particularly for k=1. Probes measure whether a concept is decodable, not whether the model uses it.

Expert attribution and causality. Expert sets are derived from routing frequencies at firing tokens and are therefore correlational; they depend on the number of examples, the selection rule, and the background routing rate, and their stability is moderate.

Evaluation of generation. ROUGE-L and METEOR measure overlap with reference responses and are imperfect proxies for personalization: a response can satisfy a preference while diverging from the reference wording, as our steering results illustrate. Sampling-based generation adds variance. Automated explanations rely on an LLM explainer and scorer (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct), whose own biases may shape the descriptions.

Query-aware routing for Cross-lingual performance gains in Encoders. Multilingual encoders can exhibit reduced retrieval effectiveness when queries and relevant documents differ in language, despite strong same-language performance. We investigate whether Finnish and Swedish cross-lingual retrieval can improve while preserving an encoder's existing same-language performance and document index. We combine a query-only low-rank adapter, trained against frozen document embeddings, with deterministic routing based on query and index languages. Cross-language queries use the adapter, while same-language queries use the original encoder. SampoTron, our fine-tuned low-rank (LoRA) adapter alongwith the Nemotron-3-Embed-1B model, improves average retrieval quality across six English, Finnish, and Swedish directions from 0.241 to 0.291 in normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG) at rank ten, a 20.9% relative gain on a sampled financial benchmark. All six cross-lingual directions improve, and routing preserves the original same-language performance, including two full-corpus Finnish evaluations. The approach enables selective cross-language specialization with reusable document embedding vectors.

Multilingual organizations and public information services require access to relevant documents independently of the language used to formulate a query. For example, Finnish or Swedish queries may target English technical documentation, while English queries may target local-language public information. Cross-lingual retrieval addresses this query–document language mismatch by ranking documents according to relevance across language boundaries. In contrast, multi-monolingual retrieval uses a shared model across languages while restricting each query to documents in the same language.

Dense retrievers encode queries and passages as vector representations, or embeddings, and rank passages by their similarity to the query embedding. In retrieval-augmented generation, the retrieved passages provide evidence for response generation. Reranking is restricted to the retrieved candidate set, making initial retrieval quality a constraint on the evidence available downstream. Improved cross-lingual retrieval can support access to organizational and public-service documents without requiring users to reformulate queries in a second language.

Multilingual pretraining and retrieval fine-tuning have substantially expanded language coverage. However, this does not ensure equally effective retrieval across language boundaries. Recent work documents cross-lingual misalignment and develops training objectives that improve it while limiting monolingual regressions. An addtional constraint that arises in deployed systems is that changing the document encoder requires computing the stored corpus vectors again. The practical problem is thus to improve cross-language retrieval while retaining both a useful same-language retriever and its existing document index.

We address this problem through query-only adaptation and language-routed selection at inference. A low-rank adapter introduces trainable parameter updates into the frozen encoder and learns query representations against document embeddings produced by the original model. The proposed query-aware routing policy uses explicit query and index language metadata to activate the adapter when the languages differ. Consequently, a single cross-language adapter is able to serve all evaluated language pairs.

Our principal implementation to achieve this, SampoTron, adapts Nemotron-3-Embed-1B. We evaluate its performance over English, Finnish, and Swedish financial question-answer retrieval and full-corpus Finnish benchmarks. Our contributions can be outlined as follows: A language-routed retrieval architecture that combines a query-only adapter with the original encoder and reuses the original document index. Its same-language score preservation follows directly from retaining the original embedding path. A mathematical analysis of how contrastive learning directs adapted queries toward relevant, fixed document embeddings relative to distractors, together with the conditions under which routing preserves original rankings. A performance evaluation of SampoTron demonstrating 20.9% mean cross-language gain on the sampled FIQA corpus, with all six language pairs improving and same-language scores preserved. Additionally, SampoHarrier applies the same architecture to microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b with a separately trained query adapter and also improves cross-language retrieval. These results support the architecture’s generalizability across encoder models through model-specific query-adapter training.

We write q for a query, d for a document, and \ell_{q},\ell_{D} for query and index languages. Bold letters denote vectors. All retrieval vectors have unit Euclidean norm, so their inner product equals cosine similarity. The upright subscripts \mathrm{base} and \mathrm{adapt} label quantities associated with the original and adapted encoders, respectively. The subscript \mathrm{R} denotes the routed system. Parameter sets are denoted separately by \theta for frozen base parameters and \phi for trainable adapter parameters.

Section 2 positions the proposed approach against the state-of-the-art. Section 3 presents the architecture and geometry. Sections 4 and 5 describe the experiments and results. Section 6 concludes the paper.

Multilingual E5 uses large-scale contrastive pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning. Qwen3 Embedding adapts pretrained Qwen3 language models for embedding and reranking tasks. Its training pipeline also incorporates synthetic multilingual data. Both model families provide representations for multiple tasks and languages.

Beyond multilingual coverage, targeted methods address the balance between monolingual and cross-lingual retrieval. Hybrid batch training combines both types of query–document pairs to improve performance in each setting. Furthermore, Hong et al. combine distributional alignment with contrastive retrieval training. Their evaluation also identifies language bias in mixed-language document pools. CLEAR uses English passages as a bridge between languages. It combines reverse-direction contrastive training with a distribution-matching objective to improve cross-lingual retrieval while limiting English degradation. These methods seek to preserve monolingual performance through training. In contrast, our method preserves the original encoder and document vectors for same-language requests at inference.

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) freezes a pretrained model and learns small matrix updates. Its use in multilingual retrieval is well established in literature. Yang et al. study language and retrieval adapters for zero-shot cross-language transfer. They show that changing language adapters at inference can create alignment problems. Additionally, Jina-embeddings-v3 provides task-specific LoRA adapters, including separate adapters for query and passage encoding.

Query-only adaptation is also an explored area in the state-of-the-art. Specifically, Jain et al. adapt query encoders while keeping document indices fixed. They evaluate this approach on enterprise retrieval and public benchmarks. Moreover, their multi-tenant system selects tenant-specific adapters over a shared base model.

Our contribution combines these components through an explicit language-routing rule. We train one cross-language query adapter against document embeddings from a frozen encoder. The router selects this adapter when the query and index languages differ. Otherwise, it retains the vanilla encoder. Same-language preservation therefore follows from the inference policy, rather than from the adapted model’s ability to retain monolingual performance.

Our evaluation covers Finnish and Swedish with English, including both Finnish–Swedish directions. Consequently, the results demonstrate gains over the selected base models on translated financial retrieval dataset, while maintaining base model performance on monolingual retrieval for Wikipedia dataset in Finnish.

section: A fixed document encoder and an adaptable query path
text: Let F_{\mathrm{base}} denote the original text encoder with frozen parameters \theta. It includes a pooling operation that aggregates token representations into a single embedding. For SampoTron, P_{m} selects the first m=1024 coordinates of its 2048-dimensional output. The normalized representation is E_{\mathrm{base}}(x)=\frac{P_{m}F_{\mathrm{base}}(x)}{\left\lVert P_{m}F_{\mathrm{base}}(x)\right\rVert_{2}},\qquad\mathbf{d}_{\mathrm{base}}(d)=E_{\mathrm{base}}(T_{D}(d)),\qquad\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{base}}(q)=E_{\mathrm{base}}(T_{Q}(q)), where T_{Q} and T_{D} denote query and document preprocessing, respectively. Since, document encoding uses frozen weights, our query adaptation approach does not require rebuilding the inference index.

section: A fixed document encoder and an adaptable query path
text: Concretely, for a frozen weight matrix W\in\mathbb{R}^{a\times b}, LoRA uses W_{\mathrm{adapt}}=W+\frac{\alpha}{r}BA,\qquad A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times b},\quad B\in\mathbb{R}^{a\times r}. Only the parameter matrices A and B receive updates. The parameter set \phi collects these matrices across all adapted projections. The rank r controls each update’s information depth. We apply the updates to the attention and feed-forward projections. The resulting normalized query vector, \mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{adapt}}(q), depends on the frozen parameters \theta and trainable parameters \phi. In contrast, documents always use the original weights \theta. Figure 1 shows how training and inference share the frozen document encoder.

The training objective promotes higher query similarity to relevant documents than to competing documents. For query i, let \mathbf{d}_{i}^{+} denote its positive document vector. The candidate set \mathcal{C}_{i} contains the batch’s positive and hard-negative vectors. Here, hard negatives receive high lexical-ranking scores but are not labeled relevant. For a batch of N queries, inverse temperature \beta=20 controls the concentration of the softmax distribution. The objective function, as defined in, \mathcal{L} is expressed as: \mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{L}_{i},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{i}=-\log\frac{\exp(\beta\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{d}_{i}^{+})}{\sum_{\mathbf{d}_{j}\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\exp(\beta\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{d}_{j})},\quad\mathbf{q}_{i}=\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{adapt}}(q_{i}). A full batch contains 256 positive and 256 explicit negative vectors. Additionally, other rows’ positives serve as negatives for each query. Gradient caching computes this large-batch loss and replays smaller query batches for backpropagation.

For unit vectors, \left\lVert\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{d}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=2-2\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{d}_{j}. Consequently, the same loss can be written as \mathcal{L}_{i}=\log\!\sum_{\mathbf{d}_{j}\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\exp\!\left[\frac{\beta}{2}\left(\left\lVert\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{d}_{i}^{+}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert\mathbf{q}_{i}-\mathbf{d}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\right]. Reducing this objective favors a smaller distance to the relevant document relative to competing documents. Thus, relevance supervision can align a Finnish query with an English answer without requiring literal translations.

The gradient makes the direction of the training signal explicit. Let p_{ij} be the softmax weight assigned to candidate j: p_{ij}=\frac{\exp(\beta\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{d}_{j})}{\sum_{k}\exp(\beta\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{d}_{k})},\qquad-\nabla_{\mathbf{q}_{i}}\mathcal{L}_{i}=\beta\left(\mathbf{d}_{i}^{+}-\sum_{j}p_{ij}\mathbf{d}_{j}\right). The positive vector contributes attraction, partly offset by its own softmax term. Other candidates contribute repulsion, with higher-scoring distractors receiving larger weights. To isolate the attractive component, consider the normalized step \mathbf{q}_{i}(\epsilon)=(\mathbf{q}_{i}+\epsilon\mathbf{d}_{i}^{+})/\left\lVert\mathbf{q}_{i}+\epsilon\mathbf{d}_{i}^{+}\right\rVert_{2}. Its local effect is \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\epsilon}\left\lVert\mathbf{q}_{i}(\epsilon)-\mathbf{d}_{i}^{+}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right|_{\epsilon=0}=-2\left[1-(\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{d}_{i}^{+})^{2}\right]\leq 0. This local result describes the attractive component in embedding space. However, the complete training update also depends on candidate repulsion and the network’s parameterization. Note that, the frozen document vectors provide stationary targets throughout training.

section: Geometrical understanding through the document subspace.
text: For a given candidate set, define \mathcal{S}_{i}=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{d}_{j}:\mathbf{d}_{j}\in\mathcal{C}_{i}\}. This span contains all linear combinations of the candidate document vectors. The gradient in Equation 5 lies in this span. Normalization projects the correction onto the unit sphere’s tangent space at \mathbf{q}_{i} and scales it by the inverse pre-normalization norm. The projected direction changes orientation while preserving unit norm to first order. Let \mathbf{h}_{i} be the unnormalized query vector, with \mathbf{q}_{i}=\mathbf{h}_{i}/\left\lVert\mathbf{h}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}. Then \nabla_{\mathbf{h}_{i}}\mathcal{L}_{i}=\frac{\beta}{\left\lVert\mathbf{h}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}}(I-\mathbf{q}_{i}\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top})\left(\sum_{j}p_{ij}\mathbf{d}_{j}-\mathbf{d}_{i}^{+}\right). The loss therefore induces an angular correction determined by the relevant document and competing candidates. Backpropagation maps this correction to the trainable low-rank parameters. This gradient explains how the objective promotes alignment with document geometry.

section: Geometrical understanding through the document subspace.
text: However, a language’s corpus need not occupy a distinct linear subspace. Its full span can be all of \mathbb{R}^{m}. Moreover, the objective does not guarantee that every update reduces the distance to every positive document. Candidate repulsion, shared parameters, and limited adapter capacity affect the actual update. Subspace alignment, from a training perspective, is indicative of geometric agreement and not an absolute measure of convergence.

The routing policy determines when to use the adapted query representation. It receives explicit query and index language labels and selects g(\ell_{q},\ell_{D})=\mathbf{1}[\ell_{q}\neq\ell_{D}],\qquad\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{R}}=(1-g)\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{base}}+g\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{adapt}},\qquad s_{\mathrm{R}}(q,d)=\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{R}}^{\top}\mathbf{d}_{\mathrm{base}}(d). The binary gate g selects either \mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{base}} or \mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{adapt}} without interpolation. The base scoring function is s_{\mathrm{base}}(q,d)=\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{base}}(q)^{\top}\mathbf{d}_{\mathrm{base}}(d). For same-language requests, \ell_{q}=\ell_{D}\ \Longrightarrow\ s_{\mathrm{R}}(q,d)=s_{\mathrm{base}}(q,d)\quad\text{for every indexed }d. This identity preserves the original ranking when preprocessing, document vectors, search settings, and tie-breaking remain unchanged. Consequently, every metric computed from that ranking is also preserved. The result is independent of the learned adapter parameters. However, it requires correct language metadata and faithful execution of the selected encoder. It does not imply that the original model is equally accurate across languages.

The proposed approach requires one copy of the base model and an unmerged adapter. During serving, the adapter is enabled or disabled for each route. If requests share the adapter state, selection and encoding must form one uninterrupted operation. Furthermore, the evaluated policy assumes one known language per index. Code-switching and mixed-language document pools require a separate routing policy and evaluation, and are beyond the scope of this paper.

section: SampoTron: Query - Routed LoRA Adapted Nemotron-3-1B-BF16 Embedder
text: We disclose in this paper a rank-64 LoRA adapter called SampoTron. It uses NVIDIA’s Nemotron-3-Embed-1B-BF16 embedder as the base model. The model uses average pooling and supports a normalized 1024-dimensional prefix of its native output. We compare the original model, the adapter applied to every query (ungated), and the routed system. All three configurations use the same original document vectors. This comparison also assists in separating the adapter’s effect from the routing policy’s own contribution.

The training mixture contains 113,043 query–positive–negative rows. These comprise 76,377 FIQA rows, 25,674 MIRACL-derived rows, and 10,992 Mr. TyDi-derived rows. The FIQA examples come from its training split. Each row contains one relevant passage and one explicit hard negative. The FIQA portion has 12,729 rows in each of five cross-language directions and 12,732 in Swedish-to-English. However, the full mixture is not balanced across directions. The Finnish datasets add proportionally more English-to-Finnish examples. The final counts are 28,041 (en \to fi), 16,977 (en \to sv), 16,914 (fi \to en), 16,956 (fi \to sv), 17,076 (sv \to en), and 17,079 (sv \to fi).

Cross-language training rows include machine-translated Finnish and Swedish text. For retrieval against English passages, we reused FIQA training examples containing Finnish and Swedish queries translated using NLLB-200. For additional translations a draft-and-refinement pipeline was utilized, wherein the drafting and refinement models were glm-5-3-flash and inferact-glm53-nvfp4, respectively. These models were deployed on an on-premises cluster consisting of NVIDIA B300 GPUs.

Further, we also mine new FIQA hard negatives with BM25 lexical ranking in the document language. A translated query retrieves the top-50 candidates, and deterministic cycling selects eligible negatives. Positive–negative text duplicates are filtered. Additionally, rows sharing a query can contain different relevant passages. During training-data preparation, we exclude any FIQA training example whose query identifier or query text matches a query in the FIQA test set. MIRACL-derived rows originate from the training split. Although evaluation queries are excluded from training, some passages in the evaluation corpus may also appear in the training data as passages that are positives or negatives for a given query in training might be utilized as positive or negative for another query in evaluation phase.

Table 1 presents the training settings utilized for developing the LoRA adapter. The training workload used one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU with 96 GB physical memory. The run imposed an 18 GiB allocator cap. Note that, while the training settings only mention LoRA rank 64, in the actual training runs other LoRA ranks were also used. However, for the sake of brevity, training parameters and results for the most optimal SampoTron settings are reported in this paper. The target projections are the internal linear layers receiving LoRA updates: q, k, v, and o denote the attention query, key, value, and output projections. Additionally, gate, up, and down denote the feed-forward gating, expansion, and contraction projections. Early stopping monitors the trailing 20-step mean training loss from epoch 2.2. Training stops at a checkpoint boundary after 60 optimizer steps without at least a 1% relative decrease from the monitor’s best recorded mean.

We evaluate 194 questions selected from FIQA’s 648 test questions by a random shuffle with a fixed seed, corresponding to approximately 30% of the test set. Each question is available in English, Finnish, and Swedish. Queries in each language search passages in the same language and in each of the other two languages. This gives three same-language and six cross-language tests, each using the same 194 questions.

Each test searches a collection of 14,330 passages drawn from FIQA’s 57,638-passage corpus. The collection contains all 1,706 passages labeled relevant across the full set of 648 test questions, plus 12,624 additional distractor passages. These distractors were selected using BM25 lexical ranking, pooling the top-30 non-relevant passages per test question and removing duplicates. They provide challenging alternatives with lexical similarity to the questions. The same passage identifiers are used for the English, Finnish, and Swedish versions of this collection.

We evaluate Finnish-only retrieval using questions originally written in Finnish from the MIRACL-fi and Mr. TyDi-fi datasets. MIRACL-fi uses 1,271 development questions to search 1,883,509 Finnish passages. Mr. TyDi-fi uses 1,738 development questions to search 1,908,757 Finnish passages. Both evaluations search the complete passage collections rather than sampled subsets.

We rank documents by the dot product of normalized embeddings. The main metric is normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank ten (nDCG@10). It rewards relevant passages near the top of the list and normalizes the score against an ideal ranking. We treat each passage as either relevant or not relevant to a query. For each query-language and document-language pair, we report the average score across all evaluated queries. We then report equal-weight means across the six cross-language or three same-language directions.

section: Cross-language gains in the final system
text: Figure 2 reports the complete language matrix. SampoTron increases the six-direction cross-lingual mean from 0.2406 to 0.2908 nDCG@10. This corresponds to an absolute gain of 0.0502 and a relative gain of 20.9%. Moreover, every cross-language direction improves. Finnish-to-English rises from 0.285 to 0.382, while Finnish-to-Swedish rises from 0.146 to 0.209. Swedish-to-English remains the highest-scoring cross-language direction, increasing from 0.370 to 0.436. English-to-Swedish has the smallest absolute gain, from 0.303 to 0.315.

section: Cross-language gains in the final system
text: These results show improved cross-language ranking of financial passages. Additionally, we evaluated the same query-routed architecture on microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b. This implementation uses a separately trained rank-32 adapter. Its six-direction cross-lingual financial retrieval (FIQA dataset) mean rises from 0.278 to 0.334, approximately 20%. Language routing retains the original same-language FIQA mean of 0.384. It also retains the Finnish monolingual performance scores of 0.723 on MIRACL and 0.709 on Mr. TyDi. Together, the SampoTron and SampoHarrier results support the generalizability of the architecture across encoder models, i.e., separately trained query adapters improve cross-language retrieval for both evaluated models.

Table 2 separates the effects of query adaptation from those of language routing. Applying the adapter to every query slightly increases mean same-language FIQA performance. However, this mean combines an English-to-English decrease with Finnish-to-Finnish and Swedish-to-Swedish improvements. Larger decreases occur on the native Finnish benchmarks. Ungated MIRACL-fi falls from 0.756 to 0.675, and Mr. TyDi-fi falls from 0.728 to 0.665. Thus, query-only training does not by itself preserve native Finnish performance.

In contrast, routing preserves every original diagonal score and both native-Finnish scores. Same-language requests select the original encoder, as established in Equation 9.
