Cross-language requests retain the adapted-query gains. The routed system therefore combines improved cross-language retrieval with unchanged same-language rankings on these benchmarks.

The SampoTron adapter occupies approximately 84 MB. It reuses the original document index, avoiding corpus re-encoding and duplicate storage for the adapted route. The architecture therefore adds a specialized query path without duplicating document representations. The evaluation covers Finnish and Swedish with English, not other Nordic languages. Additionally, native Swedish has no dedicated benchmark in this study. Translated FIQA queries and passages may share systematic translation artifacts. As a result, the gains may not fully represent naturally authored queries. Moreover, in this paper we do not measure the sensitivity to incorrect language labels, downstream answer quality, organizational productivity, or public-service outcomes. The demonstrated benefit is cross-lingual retrieval improvement with preserved same-language behavior and reusable document vectors.

Query-aware routing supports cross-language specialization while preserving the original same-language retrieval path. A query-only low-rank adapter learns relevance against fixed document representations. A deterministic language rule then selects when to use the adapter. On the sampled FIQA benchmark, SampoTron increases mean cross-language nDCG@10 from 0.241 to 0.291. All six English–Finnish–Swedish directions improve, while the original same-language and native-Finnish scores remain unchanged. Additionally, SampoHarrier shows that the architecture can be applied to another base model with a separately trained query adapter to obtain cross-language gains.

The approach also reuses the base model and its document index. The reported cross-language gains are demonstrated on the sampled FIQA financial-retrieval benchmark. Future work should evaluate naturally authored Swedish queries, additional Nordic languages, broader domains, and mixed-language corpora. Future work could combine the proposed routing architecture with other cross-lingual training objectives to assess whether they provide additional retrieval gains while preserving same-language performance.
We acknowledge the contributions of Lucas Björklund, Dan Kozytskyi, Henri Dahl, Nico Roos and Sakari Tanskanen to this work.

Grounding Probes: Generator-Independent Hallucination Detection from Observer Model Hidden States. Detecting responses that retrieval-augmented generation does not ground in its context trades speed against accuracy: surface checks miss paraphrased fabrication, sampling-based methods cost extra generations. Hidden-state probes sit between the two, but every existing one reads the generating model's own activations, so a change of generator invalidates the detector and a closed-weight generator is out of reach. This paper removes that coupling. The Grounding Probe is logistic regression over the mean-pooled middle-layer hidden states of an observer language model that reads the context, question, and response in one forward pass and generates nothing, with the recipe it needs: pool over response tokens, read a middle layer, and control capacity, which closes the train-test AUROC gap from 0.087-0.202 to 0.009-0.013. Asking the observer outright, rather than reading its hidden state, costs at least +0.166 AUROC in every one of four models. Fitted on 15,090 annotated responses it reaches 0.879-0.894 AUROC on RAGTruth test across four observers, and 0.924 AUROC with 0.820 F1@0.5 averaged with a supervised span detector, 0.060 above that detector alone.

One probe holds across six generators, and hold-out controls, including one in which no evaluation prompt appears in training, bound the cost of removing a generator at about 0.02 AUROC. Code, probes, and predictions are released.

Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a language model’s output in retrieved passages, and it does not stop the model from writing things the passages do not support. On RAGTruth, GPT-4 produces unsupported content in 9.3% of its responses (Niu et al., 2024), and weaker generators in the same benchmark exceed 50%. A production system must decide whether each response it is about to return is grounded, and fast enough that the check fits inside the request.

Detection methods split along that latency budget. Supervised token-level classifiers such as LettuceDetect (Kovács and Recski, 2025) annotate unsupported spans in tens of milliseconds, but they work from surface evidence and can miss a fluent paraphrase of something the source never said. Sampling-based methods catch those cases: semantic entropy measures disagreement across several sampled responses (Farquhar et al., 2024) at five to ten times the cost of generating once (Kossen et al., 2024), seconds away from a serving path.

Hidden-state probes occupy the space between. A linear classifier on a transformer’s activations costs one forward pass and detects what those activations already encode (Alain and Bengio, 2017), and applied to hallucination the approach works: semantic entropy probes (Kossen et al., 2024), SAPLMA (Azaria and Mitchell, 2023), HalluRAG (Ridder and Schilling, 2024), ReDeEP (Sun et al., 2025), and LUMINA (Yeh et al., 2026) all report usable detection from model internals. They share an assumption: the activations come from the model that generated the response. Changing the generator invalidates the probe, and a generator behind a closed API cannot be probed at all, which excludes the systems most likely to need the check.

We drop the assumption. A separate model, which we call the observer, reads the finished triple of context, question, and response in one forward pass and generates nothing; a linear probe on its mean-pooled middle-layer hidden states outputs the probability that the response is unsupported (Figure 1). The generator enters only through the text it already produced, so one probe serves any generator, open or closed. Entailment models such as MiniCheck (Tang et al., 2024) and AlignScore (Zha et al., 2023) already evaluate responses with a separate model, but they expose a scalar verdict; we read the representations that produced it.
Three contributions follow.

Observer probing. Hallucination detection from the hidden states of a model that did not generate the response, which decouples the detector from the generator. We evaluate one probe, fitted once, across six generators of the RAGTruth test split. A recipe that generalizes from little data. Mean pooling over response tokens, a middle extraction layer, and a projection to 512 components. Fifteen thousand annotated responses are enough, and without capacity control the probe memorizes them. The projection supplies that control without tuning. Tuning the regularization instead comes out marginally ahead on held-out data, inside the 0.015 AUROC margin we fixed in advance. Complementarity with token-level detection. Averaging the probe score with a supervised span detector’s score improves on the detector on the same test split, in both ranking and threshold behavior, without retraining it. We release the code, the fitted probes, and the per-sample predictions.

RAGTruth (Niu et al., 2024) supplies word-level annotations over close to 18,000 responses from six generators and made supervised response-level detection practical. LettuceDetect (Kovács and Recski, 2025) fine-tunes a long-context encoder on those annotations to predict unsupported spans in one pass, and Luna (Belyi et al., 2025) takes the same supervised route with a different backbone; RAG-HAT (Song et al., 2024) instead fine-tunes a generator to be hallucination-aware. Kovács et al. (2026) extend span-level detection to code and tool output with a 2B generative detector; Section 5.2 says why we blend with an encoder instead. A parallel line treats detection as entailment between source and response, with purpose-built verifiers such as MiniCheck (Tang et al., 2024) or alignment models such as AlignScore (Zha et al., 2023) and SummaC (Laban et al., 2022). Both families read only text, which makes them generator-independent and confines them to what the surface shows.

Linear probes were introduced to ask what a network’s layers encode (Alain and Bengio, 2017), with the caveat that a probe’s success can reflect its own capacity as much as the representation’s content (Belinkov, 2022). Applied to truthfulness the technique has been productive. SAPLMA (Azaria and Mitchell, 2023) classifies statement truth from hidden states; semantic entropy probes (Kossen et al., 2024) predict a sampled uncertainty measure from one pass, extracting at the second-last response token or the last prompt token; HalluRAG (Ridder and Schilling, 2024) trains multi-layer classifiers for RAG and reports a sharp cross-dataset drop. MIND (Su et al., 2024) detects during generation, HaloScope (Du et al., 2024) without labels. ReDeEP (Sun et al., 2025) and LUMINA (Yeh et al., 2026) go further into mechanism, scoring how much a response draws on retrieved context against parametric knowledge, and report the strongest RAGTruth numbers among internals-based methods.

Across that literature the probed model is the generator. Every method above extracts activations from the model that produced the response under evaluation, so a probe is valid for one generator and a closed-weight generator is out of reach entirely. Entailment methods avoid the coupling by giving up internal access. We are not aware of prior work that probes a separate evaluator model which did not generate the response, and that combination is what this paper reports.

Routing inputs by difficulty is old and well understood, from boosted cascades (Viola and Jones, 2001) to transformer early exit (Xin et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020). Hallucination detection has produced several method families that could be combined this way, but they are typically evaluated in isolation, on different splits and generators, so error correlation between families is unmeasured. We report where averaging a response-level probe with a token-level detector helps, and a routing architecture that underperforms that simpler alternative.

A Grounding Probe is a logistic regression classifier over the hidden states of a language model that reads a retrieval-augmented response without having produced it. We call that model the observer. It receives the finished triple of context, question, and response as plain text, in the position of a reviewer reading a document someone else wrote, and never emits a token. Generator independence follows from the setup rather than the training data: the generator appears only through the text it already produced.

The template concatenates the retrieved passages, the question, and a Response: marker followed by the response. Prompt and response are tokenized separately, with a leading space on the response so subword tokenization at the boundary matches training. Inputs over 4096 tokens are truncated from the right. Nothing here is tuned.

The observer then runs one forward pass with hidden-state output enabled and generation disabled. That pass is the entire inference cost. Because the observer is frozen and consumes only text, one probe scores responses from any generator, including one behind a closed API whose internals are unavailable in principle.

Generator coupling is replaced by two narrower couplings. The inference template must match the one used to fit the probe, and the observer must be loaded in the training precision, fp16 here. We did not evaluate the released probes under quantization.

We read the hidden states at one layer \ell, keep only response-token positions, and mean-pool them into \mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, with d from 2048 for Qwen2.5 3B to 5120 for 14B, cast to float32. Dropping the context and question positions is deliberate: responses drawing on the same passage share those tokens whether or not they are faithful, so the signal must live in how the observer represents the response. Section 6.1 settles the layer.

Three fitted transformations turn \mathbf{h} into a probability. Z-score normalization centers and scales each dimension using training-set statistics \boldsymbol{\mu} and \boldsymbol{\sigma}: \tilde{\mathbf{h}}=\frac{\mathbf{h}-\boldsymbol{\mu}}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}} This step matters because L2 regularization penalizes every weight equally, so without it the high-variance dimensions are effectively under-regularized regardless of how useful they are. A principal component projection then reduces the normalized vector to its leading k=512 components: \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{PCA}}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{h}},\qquad\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{PCA}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} Logistic regression maps the result to the hallucination probability: P(\text{hallucinated}\mid\mathbf{x})=\sigma(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+b) The three stages compose into one. Writing \mathbf{S}=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}), the deployed probe is a single affine functional of the raw hidden state, \sigma(\tilde{\mathbf{w}}^{\top}\mathbf{h}+\tilde{b}) with \tilde{\mathbf{w}}=\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{PCA}}\mathbf{w}, so inference is one dot product in \mathbb{R}^{d}, under 0.5 ms, and the observer forward pass dominates. That also locates what the projection does: it adds nothing at inference and confines \tilde{\mathbf{w}} to the span of the leading k components while the probe is fitted, leaving k+1 free parameters rather than d+1. The three stages are fitted together and serialized as one 4 to 11 MB artifact.

Linearity is deliberate. A linear probe recovers only what the hidden states already encode linearly (Alain and Bengio, 2017), whereas a multi-layer probe can compute the target itself and blurs what the representation carries into what the probe invents. Training minimizes binary cross-entropy with L2 regularization at C=1.0 using L-BFGS, with class_weight set to balanced. The projection and C turn out to be substitutes rather than complementary, tuning C at full dimensionality landing marginally ahead, so we deploy the projection at the default C, which needs no search. Section 6.1 sweeps both.

Probes are fitted on the RAGTruth training split, 15,090 responses with human span-level annotations (Niu et al., 2024), collapsed to one binary label per response: y=1 if any span is unsupported. RAGTruth ships the responses, so no generation happens at training time either, and fitting reduces to one forward pass per sample plus a convex optimization, 14 to 50 minutes per observer on an A100. The probe predicts P(\text{hallucinated}) directly, with no score inversion.

A response-level probe and a token-level detector see different things, so we also report their combination. Given the probe score s_{3} and a token-level span score s_{1} max-pooled to the response level, the blend is s=\alpha s_{1}+(1-\alpha)s_{3} with \alpha=0.45 throughout, applied to every sample. We chose blending over confidence routing, which forwards only uncertain samples and replaces the token-level score, because routing costs F1 for structural reasons rather than through a bad threshold choice (Section 6.3).

RAGTruth (Niu et al., 2024) is the primary benchmark. Its training split (15,090 responses) fits the probes and its held-out test split (2700 responses, 34.9% hallucinated) carries every result below unless stated otherwise. The test split is balanced across three task types at 900 responses each, question answering, data-to-text generation, and summarization, and across the six generators named in Table 2 at 450 responses each. HaluEval (Li et al., 2023) supplies 30,000 further samples, used only to measure transfer.

Four observers supply hidden states: Qwen2.5 3B, 7B, and 14B (Yang et al., 2024) and Llama 3.1 8B (AI @ Meta, 2024), read at layers -15, -12, -20, and -16 respectively and projected to 512 components. LettuceDetect (Kovács and Recski, 2025) provides the token-level baseline in both released sizes, base (150M parameters) and large (396M), and is also the codebase our implementation extends. All measurements run on an A100 40 GB. Numeric precision is matched between probe fitting and inference, fp16 in both cases, because mismatching it moves the hidden-state distribution and we measured AUROC drops of 0.02–0.16 when it was mismatched by accident during development.

AUROC is the primary metric, being threshold-free across methods whose scores live on different scales. For threshold-dependent performance we report F1 at the fixed default of 0.5 rather than a threshold tuned on the test split, which would be an upper bound. Intervals are percentile bootstrap over 10,000 resamples, paired on samples where the quantity is a difference.

Three decisions need stating up front, two selections and one reporting population. The blending weight \alpha was selected over a 21-point grid computed on the evaluation split, not on held-out data, and every configuration we report uses that single value. The exposure is small and measurable: at \alpha=0.50, the equal-weight default requiring no selection at all, the headline configuration reaches 0.9236 AUROC against 0.9240 at \alpha=0.45, so selection is worth 0.0004 AUROC, with a paired interval on that difference of [-0.0000, +0.0010]. Section 6.3 has the full sweep. F1@0.5 is the sensitive quantity, 0.820 against 0.804, because shifting \alpha moves the score distribution underneath a fixed threshold. Read 0.016 as an in-sample gain over one particular default rather than as a bound: \alpha=0.50 is not the plateau’s worst point, which sits at 0.30, and the out-of-sample version of the same choice, made on one random half of the split, is worth +0.012 F1 on the other. Fitting \alpha on the training data would not repair any of this, since both components are themselves fitted on RAGTruth train; an honest treatment needs a third split and a fresh extraction run.

The headline is a selected configuration in a wider sense too: the best of 8 detector–observer pairings, on a split that has carried about 944 scored configurations. Choosing among the 84 combinations of \alpha and observer on one random half and scoring the other, over 400 halves, the in-sample maximum overstates held-out performance by 0.002 AUROC and 0.007 F1@0.5. Intervals below are conditional on that selection.

The projection width is the same kind of decision: PCA-512 was chosen on held-out test AUROC and every number we report uses it. Its margin over PCA-256 is at most 0.007 AUROC on paired intervals that overlap zero for three of the four observers, so we present capacity control as necessary and the width as not (Section 6.1). The extraction layer was chosen by cross-validation on training data alone.

The third decision concerns the latency population. Every latency we report is a per-sample mean over the 2700 evaluation rows, drawn from a 12,700-sample benchmark run whose other inputs are shorter HaluEval samples that carry no figure in Table 1. The restriction reorders the cheap pairing: pooled, the smallest observer averages 49 ms against 37 ms for the large detector, and on the evaluation population that ordering reverses, 60 against 81 ms. Section 6.4 derives the blend figures.

A linear probe on observer hidden states reaches 0.879–0.894 AUROC on the RAGTruth test split across the four observers (Table 1). Performance tracks observer size, but the spread over a 4.7-fold parameter range is only 0.015, untested pairwise, so a 3B observer captures most of the signal.

All three task types are detectable: data-to-text at 0.861–0.880, question answering at 0.858–0.870, summarization lowest at 0.770–0.838. Summarization is lowest for every observer; the data-to-text and question-answering gap is within noise and reverses for Qwen2.5 3B. RAGTruth summarization compresses the longest contexts into the shortest responses, but length does not explain the gap: it ranks responses at 0.515 on summarization and at 0.482 on data-to-text, which the probe finds no harder, against 0.712 on question answering.

At the pooled base rate the probe outputs usable probabilities and not only a usable ranking: F1 at the default threshold of 0.5 falls within 0.002–0.006 of the best F1 any threshold achieves here, and expected calibration error stays in 0.073–0.088. That is what makes the score safe to average with another detector’s, and it depends on the supervision (Section 6.1).

Two verdict-style evaluators on the same rows test the central claim directly. MiniCheck (Tang et al., 2024) returns a scalar judgment on the same triple, reaching 0.663 AUROC and 0.577 F1@0.5, which puts the four probes 0.216–0.231 above it, paired interval [+0.194, +0.254]; being a 770M Flan-T5, it changes the model as well as the readout. Prompting the observer removes that confound: asking each of the four in the probe’s fp16, from the same template, whether any part of the response is unsupported by the context and scoring P(\text{Yes}), which points the same way as the probe’s P(\text{hallucinated}), gives 0.418–0.728 AUROC against 0.879–0.894 for the probe read from the same model, a paired +0.166 to +0.470 with every interval excluding zero, narrowest +0.166 [+0.146, +0.186]. Judge quality climbs with observer size across the Qwen family, 0.661 to 0.728, without approaching the probe; on Llama 3.1 8B the same template lands below chance at 0.418. Both readouts cost one forward pass, so this is not a speed argument: the hidden state carries what the decoded verdict does not.

Pooling flatters both, spanning 0.490–0.605 by task for MiniCheck and falling to 0.421 on data-to-text for the 3B judge, whose F1@0.5 of 0.239 appears to follow from an almost complete refusal to answer Yes.

Two qualifications belong with those numbers. The probe’s F1@0.5 of 0.763 is below the detector’s 0.792, so it wins on ranking and loses at the default operating point, which is one reason we combine the two. The calibration holds at the pooled 34.9% hallucination rate and degrades away from it: per-task calibration error reaches 0.121, and on the two generators near a 10% rate the probe’s F1@0.5 falls to 0.404–0.405.

Blending the probe with LettuceDetect-large lifts AUROC from 0.864 to 0.924 and F1@0.5 from 0.792 to 0.820 on the identical split (Table 1). The gain over the detector alone is 0.060 AUROC, and because both methods score the same responses we can put a paired bootstrap interval on the difference itself: [0.050, 0.070]. The F1 gain is the more selection-dependent of the two: at the untuned \alpha=0.50 it is 0.804 rather than 0.820, so 0.016 of the 0.820 figure comes from choosing \alpha. The probe alone contributes 0.030, interval [0.015, 0.045], over the detector, and reaches 0.894, so neither component explains the combination.

Per task the two cover different ground. The detector scores 0.897 on data-to-text, where surface overlap with structured records is informative, 0.855 on question answering and 0.746 on summarization; the probe scores 0.880, 0.858 and 0.838, so its advantage is largest where the detector is weakest, +0.092{} on summarization.

Calibration improves with accuracy: expected calibration error on equal-width bins is 0.101 for the detector, 0.073 for the probe and 0.037 for the blend, so averaging scores that err in different directions moves the result toward observed frequencies. Nor does the gain need a large observer, the same detector with Qwen2.5 3B giving 0.915 AUROC and 0.809 F1@0.5 at the lowest observer latency we measure, 60 ms.

Two published RAGTruth F1 figures sit at or above ours, and we claim to beat neither: RAG-HAT (Song et al., 2024) reports 83.9 against our 82.0, and the 2B generative detector of Kovács et al. (2026) reports 81.8, which our 82.0 matches rather than exceeds. We keep the encoder detector as the blending partner because the blend needs a continuous response-level score, which a token classifier gives directly and a model emitting spans as generated text does not, and because the encoder in that newer family scores below the one we use on RAGTruth.

We break the test split out by the model that produced each response (Table 2). RAGTruth carries six generators at 450 test responses each, four of them open-weight, and the training split carries the same six, so these are in-distribution generators unless a probe is refitted with one held out. The predictions do not record the generator, so we recover it from the positional sample identifiers and accept the join only when label and task type agree on all 2700 rows, which they do; that check is necessary rather than sufficient.

One probe, fitted once and never tuned per generator, scores 0.858–0.934 blended across the six. The weakest is GPT-3.5-turbo at 0.858 and the strongest Llama-2-13B-chat at 0.934, on 450 responses each, so we do not read the spread as an ordering. Grouped by provenance the blend reaches 0.866 pooled over the two proprietary generators and 0.913 pooled over the four open-weight ones, but that grouping tracks hallucination rate rather than provenance. The probe does not win everywhere; on Llama-2-70B-chat it scores 0.865 against the detector’s 0.873.

Comparing this against per-generator numbers in the literature needs care. Our pooled figure, 0.924, is higher than the macro-average over the six generators, 0.896, by 0.028: hallucination rates run from 9.3% to 55.8%, so pooling lets base-rate differences contribute to the ranking and makes the task easier, not harder. The same holds for task type, whose rates span 17.8–64.3%, giving a task macro-average of 0.901 against 0.924 blended and 0.859 against 0.894 for the probe.

Because all six generators appear in probe training, per-generator evaluation alone cannot speak to an unseen one. We refit with one held out under three designs, a positive delta meaning the held-out probe scored higher. Splitting a generator’s rows at matched training size moves macro AUROC by +0.002 to +0.004 across the four observers, and per generator by -0.012 to +0.027, but that leaves two things uncontrolled. RAGTruth pairs each of its 2,514 contexts with all six generators, so a held-out generator’s evaluation prompts stay in training under the other five; splitting on context removes them and gives -0.003, averaged over 5 seeds, with [-0.018, +0.013] across the six generators. Matching training size also displaces other generators’ rows, so a size-only arm keeps the generator in and measures that displacement alone at +0.001 [+0.000, +0.002]; subtracting it within that arm leaves +0.001 [-0.011, +0.013] for generator presence. Read these as bounds. The row and the context design put zero inside intervals of half-width near 0.02 AUROC, and that width is variation between generators rather than between splits. The size-only arm is the exception: its effect is small but detectable, the interval excluding zero below the three decimals shown.

A matched comparison has to name the population. ReDeEP (Sun et al., 2025) reports 0.824 on Llama-2-13B outputs, where our blend scores 0.934, though our blend consumes RAGTruth’s train-split annotations twice over, through the detector and the probe, while ReDeEP’s mechanistic score does not. LUMINA (Yeh et al., 2026) reports 0.857 evaluating GPT-4 and ChatGPT separately, and macro-averaged over exactly those two generators our blend reaches 0.865, a difference of 0.008 that sits well inside the per-generator confidence intervals. Against LUMINA’s protocol, then, we do not claim an improvement. The probe on its own is weaker still on that protocol, 0.818 over LUMINA’s two generators and 0.857 macro-averaged over all six, so what the method offers against LUMINA is not accuracy but a detector that does not need the generator’s weights.
Four choices decide whether an observer probe works at all (Table 3). None of them touches the classifier.

Mean pooling across response-token positions beats reading a single position at every one of the 28 layer and observer combinations we swept. The smallest margin is 0.070 AUROC, and 0.100–0.123 when each method gets its own best layer. Kossen et al. (2024) extract at the second-last response token or the last prompt token and report late layers as best; both are far weaker here. The pre-generation token barely separates the classes at 0.522–0.524, near chance, which is expected since that position precedes the response being judged. The second-last token carries real signal, 0.632–0.703, and pooling still adds a tenth or more on top.

section: Read from the middle, not the end.
text: The best layer sits at 42–50% of the stack counted back from the output, just past the midpoint: -15 of 36 layers for Qwen2.5 3B, -12 of 28 for 7B, -20 of 48 for 14B, -16 of 32 for Llama 3.1 8B. Reading the final layer instead costs 0.054–0.078 under the same protocol. The sweep covered the upper half of each stack in seven steps, so a better layer further down is not ruled out, and for Llama 3.1 8B the selected layer is the deepest tested.

A full-dimensional probe fits its 15,090 training samples almost perfectly, up to 0.9995 training AUROC for Qwen2.5 14B, and reaches only 0.786–0.851 on test. Reducing to 512 components adds 0.028–0.102 test AUROC and collapses the train–test gap from 0.087–0.202 to 0.009–0.013 (Figure 2). Between 256 and 1024 components test AUROC moves by at most 0.007.

Projection is not the only route to that. With the L2 strength swept over 11 values at both widths, C selected on the training split alone and test scored once, a full-dimensional probe reaches 0.886–0.900 against 0.879–0.894 for the deployed PCA-512: +0.006 to +0.010 per observer, every paired interval excluding zero and the four spanning +0.001 to +0.015. The same states at the default C give 0.786–0.851, so regularization alone recovers what the projection was credited with, and PCA-512 barely responds to C. We fixed the decision rule before those states existed: move the deployed recipe only if the held-out margin beat 0.015, the spread across observer sizes (Section 5.1) that this paper already treats as minor. At +0.010 it does not, so PCA-512 stays deployed for needing no search, not for being the better probe. Capacity control rather than dimensionality is what the sweep isolates, now on held-out data. Extraction hardware does not enter: on those test states, taken from a rented A100, the deployed probe agrees with the cluster extraction to 0.0000 AUROC at per-sample r=1.00000{}.

Swapping that probe into the blend would not repay the search either. Through the same blending pipeline at the same \alpha, blended AUROC moves +0.001 to +0.004 across the observers, at most +0.004, and +0.003 [-0.000, +0.006] at the headline pairing, 3 of the four intervals containing zero, so the evidence excludes a blend gain larger than +0.007 AUROC in any observer. Fixed-threshold F1 at 14B moves the other way, -0.011, as strong regularization pulling probabilities toward 0.5 would predict.

section: Match the supervision to the deployment.
text: Holding the classifier and the observers fixed, 15,090 RAGTruth samples with human labels and the retrieved context beat question-answering samples labeled by answer-overlap F1 without context, by 0.162–0.236 AUROC. That comparison is not single-factor: the QA-supervised probes are also full-dimensional, read at their own swept layer, and loaded with 4-bit weights. Against the full-dimensional grounding row, which removes the largest of those differences, the gap narrows to 0.080–0.208 and stays positive for all four observers, and the mismatched set is larger by 6.6 \times to 28 \times. For a specific deployment, labeled examples in its own format beat more of them in another.

Probes fitted only on the RAGTruth training split transfer unevenly to HaluEval (Figure 3), with no HaluEval training data: question answering holds up at 0.837–0.943, above the in-domain figure for three of four observers, while dialogue drops to 0.682–0.804 and summarization to 0.643–0.704. RAGTruth contains no dialogue, the most plausible reason that split is weakest, and that does not extend to summarization, which RAGTruth covers and which still loses 0.10–0.17 AUROC against its RAGTruth counterpart. What transfers is narrower than a shared task label suggests.

section: Blending weight, and why not routing
text: The blend is insensitive to \alpha over a wide interval. Across \alpha\in[0.30,0.50] AUROC varies by at most 0.004 for every configuration, while F1@0.5 traces a hump over 0.802–0.820 that peaks at \alpha=0.45{}, since \alpha slides the score distribution underneath a fixed cut. A deployment can start from equal weights and lose almost nothing in ranking quality; the threshold is what needs attention.

section: Blending weight, and why not routing
text: Confidence routing looks like the natural architecture and performs worse. Routing only uncertain samples to the probe, replacing the token-level score, raises AUROC over the large detector by 0.019–0.029 while costing 0.026–0.042 in F1 at the best threshold (OptF1), because no single cut suits the bimodal mixture routing produces. Averaging every sample removes the problem; Appendix A has the mechanism and the caveat that the two architectures do not consume identical inputs.

Measured per sample on an A100 over the evaluation rows, the token-level detector takes 53 ms in its base size and 81 ms in its large size, and an observer forward pass 60 to 198 ms (Table 1), so observer size moves the total further than detector size does. For the blend we report the per-sample \max(t_{\mathrm{S1}},t_{\mathrm{S3}}), what concurrent execution on separate devices would cost before coordination overhead: the large detector’s 81 ms in the cheap pairing, and the 14B observer’s 198 ms in the accurate one. Sequential execution costs the sum. That substitution is optimistic. Running the two stages at once on two A100s in one machine, each pinned to its own card, over 300 samples, costs 1.33 \times the derived maximum, 33% above what the table reports, with the span detector slowed 1.80 \times and the observer 1.33 \times. Separate cards put the contention on the host, and we did not attribute it further. Table 1 keeps the derived figure, its column coming from one run while the overhead is a ratio from another machine.
All of it stays one to two orders of magnitude below the seconds per query that sampling-based detection costs (Farquhar et al., 2024; Kossen et al., 2024) (Figure 4).

Hallucination detection from hidden states does not require the generator’s. An observer that merely reads a retrieval-augmented response encodes whether it is grounded, linearly enough to reach 0.879–0.894 AUROC, 0.924 blended, and to beat what that model says when asked outright.

We removed the probe’s dependence on the generator and replaced it with a dependence on the observer. Each probe is tied to one observer model, one extraction layer, and one numeric precision, and a probe fitted on one observer’s hidden states cannot be applied to another’s. Swapping observers means re-extracting hidden states, under an hour per model on an A100, plus a one-time layer sweep for an unfamiliar architecture family. Whether a probe transfers across observers is untested. We expect it does not, since the two hidden state spaces are unaligned.

Our evidence rests largely on one benchmark. The probes are fitted on RAGTruth’s training split and evaluated on its disjoint test split, but one annotation convention governs both, so test performance cannot by itself show that a probe tracks groundedness rather than that convention. Transfer to HaluEval question answering at 0.837–0.943 argues against the narrowest version of that concern, and the weaker dialogue and summarization transfer argues for keeping it open. RAGTruth is also public and predates all four observers, so its responses may have appeared in their pretraining data.

Our generator-independence evidence is a per-generator evaluation plus three hold-out controls on the training side (Section 5.3), each run for every observer on the stored train-split hidden states. Those states are too large to release, so the refits are not verifiable from our artifacts, though we do release the per-sample probabilities they produced. The controls bound the cost of removing a generator at roughly 0.02 AUROC rather than showing the cost is zero, they measure the probe alone rather than the blend we headline, and the matched arm trains on only about 46% of a generator’s deployed row count. All six generators date from 2023, and the split contains 450 responses per generator, so the per-generator confidence intervals are wide, spanning up to 0.13 AUROC. On the lowest-prevalence generator only 42 of 450 responses are hallucinated, where a percentile bootstrap may under-cover.

The blend latency we report is derived, a per-sample \max over two separately measured stages, with the sequential figure their sum. That substitution has now been tested and it is optimistic: concurrent execution costs 1.33 \times the derived maximum (Section 6.4). Only the ratio carries over, that run being a different machine, so the blend column is a floor rather than an estimate.

The verdict comparison rests on one prompt. We wrote a single zero-shot template, in the probe’s input format, with no calibration and no tuning per model family, and that is enough to account for a judge below chance: an untuned prompt can collapse the verdict distribution of a model it was not written for, which is what 0.418 on Llama 3.1 8B looks like. We do not know the cause. Every judge figure here is a lower bound on what prompting that observer could reach, and the +0.166 minimum gap is measured against that bound. Nor do we report a probe on a generator’s own hidden states under this protocol, which would measure what dropping generator access costs, or a non-linear probe, which would test the word “linearly”; the former is obstructed for the two closed-weight generators.

Two selection decisions ran on the evaluation split: the blending weight, worth 0.0004 AUROC and 0.016 F1@0.5 over the untuned default, and the projection width, worth at most 0.007 AUROC over the next setting. Both exposures are bounded and neither is zero.

Pooled evaluation flatters every headline number here. RAGTruth’s hallucination rates differ across both generators and task types, so pooling contributes base-rate separation on top of groundedness: the blend’s task macro-average is 0.901 against 0.924 pooled and the probe’s is 0.859 against 0.894. Response length is one correlate we can bound. Length alone ranks responses at 0.664 AUROC, and restricting the probe to compare within deciles of response length moves it from 0.894 to 0.881, so length accounts for little of the probe’s ranking. Other correlates of groundedness we have not isolated.

Threshold behavior is weaker than the pooled figures suggest. The probe’s F1@0.5 of 0.763 is below the detector’s 0.792, per-task calibration error reaches 0.121, and on the two generators with roughly 10% hallucination rates the probe’s F1@0.5 drops to 0.404–0.405 and the blend’s to 0.563–0.579. Under transfer the default threshold is further off still. A deployment whose base rate differs from RAGTruth’s must set its own threshold, and our transfer numbers are reported as AUROC only.

Summarization remains the weakest task type at 0.770–0.838, and it is the task where a detector is most useful, since summarization hallucinations are the least visible to surface checks. The longest RAGTruth test input reaches roughly two thirds of the 4096-token budget and none is truncated, so the long-context regime is untested. Everything reported here is English, and we make no claim about other languages or about specialized domains such as medicine, law, and finance.

The computational results have been achieved using the Austrian Scientific Computing (ASC) infrastructure. The training-split hidden states, the fitted probes, and the layer and pooling sweeps reported here were computed on the Vienna Scientific Cluster (VSC).

"Not" is Not Lost in Translation: A Causal Analysis of Negation Representations in Multilingual LLMs. Negation occurs in every language, yet its surface realization differs drastically. Despite this, multilingual large language models (LLMs) translate negation robustly, raising the question of whether they share an underlying representation of negation across languages. We study this question in six open models across English, French, Vietnamese, and Chinese, using causal interventions on a synthetic contrastive dataset and a negation translation dataset derived from FLORES-200. Across models, we find strong evidence that negation representations are causally controllable and largely shared across languages. In particular, we show that a contrastive activation direction extracted from one language can induce or remove negation in the others, and directions extracted from different languages are substantially aligned. We further find that negation is represented in sparse features: a single sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature per model suffices to control polarity across languages, while responding selectively to negated inputs. Finally, both dense and sparse interventions generalize to four additional languages and FLORES-derived sentences. We release data and code to support future work: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/negation-translation/.

Negation – the reversal of a proposition’s truth value, typically by inserting a word like not – is a universal phenomenon, yet its grammatical realization varies drastically across languages. Where English uses a post-copular not, French splits it into the discontinuous ne…pas, Vietnamese places the particle không before the verb, and Chinese relies on 不/没. Despite these structural differences, large language models (LLMs) translate negation robustly across languages, maintaining near-perfect polarity preservation in our experiments (Appendix D.1). This cross-lingual fluency raises a fundamental question: how do LLMs represent negation in a multilingual setting?

Mechanistic interpretability Olah et al. (2020); Elhage et al. (2021) offers tools to study internal representations, with recent work finding evidence of shared grammatical features and refusal directions across languages (Brinkmann et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). However, whether negation representations are shared during translation remains less clear. Brinkmann et al. (2025) identify features associated with negation in two LLMs, but report weak cross-lingual sharing and do not test their causal role. Meanwhile, Zhou et al. (2026) study negation mechanisms in monolingual English, and Lasnier et al. (2026) analyze translation-related mechanisms without targeting specific semantic phenomena. We instead investigate this question via representation-based causal interventions and cross-lingual intervention transfer, testing whether negation representations extracted from one language can control negation polarity in others.

To this end, we construct two complementary datasets. First, we create Mini-minus-4, a controlled set of minimally contrastive sentence pairs in four languages, to extract and evaluate negation representations. Second, we derive FLORES-minus-4 from FLORES-200 NLLB Team (2024) by introducing negation into naturalistic sentences, to test whether the intervention effects persist on longer, out-of-domain sentences. We release both datasets to facilitate future research.

We first identify candidate negation representations as contrastive activation directions and validate their causal role through interventions that add or remove negation during translation, using Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) Rimsky et al. (2024) (§ 4.1; examples in Figure 1). We then examine whether these directions are shared across languages through cross-language transfer and similarity analysis (§ 4.2). Next, we investigate whether individual sparse autoencoder (SAE) features Huben et al. (2024); Templeton et al. (2024) also capture negation and exhibit causal effects across languages (§ 4.3). Finally, we test whether the intervention effects of both dense directions and sparse features generalize to unseen languages and naturalistic sentences (§ 4.4).

We study six open models from three families — Gemma 3, Llama 3.1, and Qwen3/3.5 Gemma Team (2025); Llama Team (2024); Qwen Team (2025); Qwen Team (2026) — with English, French, Vietnamese, and Chinese as the primary languages. Our findings suggest that negation representations are causally controllable, transfer strongly across languages, and exhibit substantial cross-lingual alignment. Specifically, we show that:

Negation representations are controllable and shared across languages: intervening along a single contrastive direction adds or removes negation, and directions extracted from one language retain strong control in others. Per-language directions are substantially aligned. Negation is represented in sparse features: a single SAE feature can respond selectively to negated contexts and exert strong causal control over polarity across languages. These causal effects generalize: both dense directions and sparse features flip polarity in unseen languages and naturalistic sentences.

We study decoder-only Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017). We denote the residual stream at the output of block l by \mathbf{h}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}}, where d_{\mathrm{model}} is the model’s hidden dimension. We extract activations and apply interventions at this location.

A sparse autoencoder (SAE; Huben et al., 2024; Templeton et al., 2024) decomposes a residual activation \mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}} into a sparse code \mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{SAE}}} and reconstructs it as \hat{\mathbf{h}}=\sum_{f=1}^{F}z_{f}\,\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}[f]+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}, where F=d_{\mathrm{SAE}} is the number of SAE features, z_{f} is the activation of feature f, and \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}[f]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}} is its decoder vector. Sparsity is enforced during training so that only a small number of features are active for any given input. Each decoder vector \mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}}[f] can be interpreted as a direction in residual stream space associated with feature f. We intervene using these decoder vectors in § 2.4.

We construct two complementary datasets. Mini-minus-4 provides controlled minimal pairs for extracting and evaluating negation representations, while FLORES-minus-4 tests whether their intervention effects can generalize to naturalistic sentences. Full construction steps are in Appendix C.

is a synthetic minimally contrastive pair dataset in English (EN), Vietnamese (VI), French (FR), and Chinese (ZH). Using GPT-5.4-mini OpenAI (2026b), we generate single-clause sentences with explicit verbal negation using the primary marker of each language: not (EN), không (VI), ne…pas (FR), and 不 (ZH). Each negative sentence is paired with a positive counterpart identical in lexical content and structure, differing only in polarity. The purpose of this minimally contrastive setup is to isolate the negation signal using the mean difference between positive and negative activations. Examples of Mini-minus-4 pairs are shown in Figure 2.

We construct 350 pairs per language, split into 150 extraction / 100 evaluation / 100 test pairs. The extraction split is used to estimate representation and steering directions, the evaluation split for hyperparameter selection and analysis, and the test split for held-out evaluation. Predicates do not overlap across splits. To test generalization beyond the four languages used for representation extraction and selection, we additionally construct 100 test pairs each in Russian (RU), Hindi (HI), Arabic (AR), and Indonesian (ID).

is a multilingual negation translation dataset, derived from the FLORES-200 devtest split NLLB Team (2024) by inducing negation into the original sentences. We first use GPT-5.6-Luna OpenAI (2026a) to select sentences with a main clause whose predicate can be meaningfully negated, then generate a polarity-flipped counterpart in a separate prompt. Finally, GPT-5.6-Terra verifies that the result is grammatical and preserves the original meaning apart from polarity. Since the dataset supports any-to-any translation, we retain an item only when it is verified in all four languages, yielding 216 items.

At layer l, we extract residual-stream activations at the output of decoder block l. We consider two token positions (Figure 2): the negated predicate (NP), the first token of the negated verb and its corresponding positive counterpart, and the final source token (FST), typically the period.

We first identify candidate negation representations and validate their causal role by intervening on them during generation (i.e. using activation steering). We employ Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA; Rimsky et al., 2024). For each model, layer l, position p\in\{\mathrm{NP},\mathrm{FST}\}, and language L, we compute a negation direction from the N_{\mathrm{extract}}=150 Mini-minus-4 extraction pairs: \mathbf{d}_{\mathrm{CAA}}^{l,p}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\mathbf{h}^{l,p,i}_{\mathrm{neg}}-\mathbf{h}^{l,p,i}_{\mathrm{pos}}\right), where \mathbf{h}^{l,p,i}_{\mathrm{neg}} and \mathbf{h}^{l,p,i}_{\mathrm{pos}} are the activations of the negative and positive members of pair i. We omit the language index L for simplicity unless explicitly needed. We refer to the directions extracted across layers, positions, and languages collectively as negation directions.

During generation, we intervene at a single layer by adding this direction to the activation \mathbf{h}^{\prime}_{t}=\mathbf{h}_{t}+\alpha_{\mathrm{CAA}}\mathbf{d}_{\mathrm{CAA}}. Because \mathbf{d}_{\mathrm{CAA}} points from positive to negative polarity, \alpha>0 adds negation and \alpha<0 removes it; we refer to either operation as a flip. We sweep |\alpha_{\mathrm{CAA}}|\in\{2,4,6\}.

The intervention is applied to all source-sentence tokens, excluding the instruction and generated output. On FLORES-minus-4, we annotate positions of the main clause’s tokens and intervene only on those positions.

We next test whether negation is also represented in SAE features. For each feature f, we compute its mean activation difference between negative and positive examples at the NP position: \delta_{f}=\mu_{\mathrm{neg},f}-\mu_{\mathrm{pos},f}. We rank features by \delta_{f} and retain the top- K features \mathcal{F}_{K}, thereby selecting features that activate more strongly on negative than positive examples.
We construct an SAE steering direction from their decoder vectors: \mathbf{d}_{\mathrm{SAE}}^{l,p,K}=\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{K}}\delta_{f}\,\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}[f].
We intervene using the same sign convention and scope as CAA: \mathbf{h}^{\prime}_{t}=\mathbf{h}_{t}+\alpha_{\mathrm{SAE}}\mathbf{d}_{\mathrm{SAE}}.

Because CAA and SAE directions differ substantially in norm, their steering coefficients are not directly comparable. For an SAE direction at layer l and position p, we use the best CAA coefficient selected on EN at the same (l,p) (Appendix D.5.1), denoted \alpha_{\mathrm{CAA}}^{*}(l,p), and set |\alpha_{\mathrm{SAE}}|=|\alpha_{\mathrm{CAA}}^{*}(l,p)|\frac{\left\|\mathbf{d}_{\mathrm{CAA}}^{l,p,\mathrm{EN}}\right\|}{\left\|\mathbf{d}_{\mathrm{SAE}}^{l,p,\mathrm{EN},K}\right\|}.
We evaluate intervened translations using four criteria. Thresholds and judge prompts are provided in Appendix B.2.

Polarity. The output exhibits the intended polarity change. For Mini-minus-4, we use language-specific negation-marker detection rules. For FLORES-minus-4, GPT-5.6-Terra judges whether the intervened output is negated or affirmative. Target language. fastText language identification Joulin et al. (2016); Joulin et al. (2017) verifies that the output is in the requested target language. Non-degeneracy. The output satisfies minimum token-count and unique-token-ratio thresholds, filtering out degenerate or repetitive generations. Content preservation. For Mini-minus-4, the output must exceed a chrF threshold Popović (2015) against the model’s baseline translation of the opposite-polarity counterpart. For FLORES-minus-4, GPT-5.6-Terra judges whether the baseline and steered translations describe the same underlying content except for the polarity difference.

We compute the Flip Rate as the percentage of eligible examples that satisfy all four criteria. An example is eligible only if the un-intervened baseline translation preserves the source polarity. This prevents attributing incorrect baseline polarity to the intervention. Where necessary, we refer to this metric as the Addition Rate (positive \xrightarrow{} negative) and Removal Rate (negative \xrightarrow{} positive).

We verify our automatic evaluation with human evaluators (details in Appendix B.3). Evaluators independently judged all steered outputs of Gemma-3-4B on both datasets, covering all languages and both flip modes. Over four languages, human evaluations agree with the rule-based evaluator on Mini-minus-4 in 96.5% and with the LLM judge on FLORES-minus-4 in 93.7% of samples. These high agreement rates support the reliability of the automated Flip Rates, which we use throughout our experiments.

We evaluate 6 instruction-tuned models spanning 3 families: Gemma 3 (1B, 4B, 12B) IT, Qwen3 4B, Qwen3.5 9B, and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct Gemma Team (2025); Qwen Team (2025); Qwen Team (2026); Llama Team (2024). We drop the -IT and -Instruct suffixes when referring to the models in text.

For each family, we choose one model for which pretrained SAEs are publicly available to perform SAE-based steering: Gemma-3-4B McDougall et al. (2025), Llama-3.1-8B He et al. (2024), and Qwen3.5-9B Deng et al. (2026). Details of SAEs used in our experiments are in Appendix B.1.
All experiments use a zero-shot translation prompt:
Translate the following sentence into {TargetLanguage}. Only output the translation. Sentence: {sentence}

For the main direction extraction and intervention experiments, we consider four translation settings: EN \xrightarrow{} VI, VI \xrightarrow{} EN, FR \xrightarrow{} EN, ZH \xrightarrow{} EN. For the additional-language generalization test in § 4.4, we evaluate {RU,HI,AR,ID} \xrightarrow{} EN.

We find that varying the target language produces nearly identical negation directions and similar intervention results (Appendix A.2), therefore we only vary the source language in our main experiments. We refer to translation settings by the source languages for brevity.

For each model, we sweep layer-position pairs (l,p) on the EN evaluation set with l ranging from 10-55% of model depth. We select a single (l,p) maximizing addition/removal performance; this pair is then fixed across languages. At the selected (l,p), we compute a direction \mathbf{d}^{l,p} for each language L and separately select |\alpha|\in\{2,4,6\} for addition and removal on that language’s evaluation set. Intervention results of selected (l,p) and \alpha on the test set are reported in Table 1. Full sweeps and selected values are reported in Appendix D.4.1.

Adding or subtracting {\mathbf{d}_{\text{CAA}}} reverses polarity in the translation with high success, providing causal evidence for a negation representation in the model. Negation directions on Gemma-3-(4B, 12B) and Qwen3.5-9B achieve \geq 80\% flip rates on all languages. Addition rates on Qwen3-4B drop to 60.0% on FR, while Gemma-3-1B’s VI addition is 65.0%. Llama-3.1-8B is strong for addition across languages, but its VI removal rate drops to 74.5%. These flip rates are far above those of random directions (typically 0%, Appendix A.3).

The effect also extends beyond explicit negation markers. During manual inspection, we found that 44 ZH negative examples across six models were translated using lexical antonyms or negative prefixes rather than explicit negation (不愿意 \xrightarrow{} unwilling, Figure 5). Subtracting the negation direction reverses the meaning in 68.2% of those cases (unwilling \xrightarrow{} want, Appendix D.2).

section: Negation directions align and transfer across languages
text: To test whether negation directions are shared across languages, we apply the direction and \alpha selected for one language L to test examples in another language L^{\prime} at the same (l,p). Figure 3 reports the resulting test-set transfer matrices, with within-language flip rates on the diagonal and cross-language transfer off the diagonal.

section: Negation directions align and transfer across languages
text: Across all models, a single EN-extracted direction is enough to flip polarity in all four languages. In particular, \mathbf{d}^{\mathrm{EN}} achieves 48–100% addition and 77–99% removal rates across languages. Transfer is particularly strong for Gemma-3-4B, Gemma-3-12B, and Qwen3.5-9B, where \mathbf{d}^{\mathrm{EN}} achieves 93–100% addition and 88–99% removal on non-EN languages.

section: Negation directions align and transfer across languages
text: More broadly, directions extracted from any language transfer to the others. Across models, mean transfer rates range from 80.0–95.1% for addition and 79.7–94.7% for removal. Transfer strength varies by language pair: addition is weakest to VI, especially for \mathbf{d}^{\text{FR}} (45–81%), while Llama-3.1-8B’s \mathbf{d}^{\text{FR}} is also weak for removal on EN, VI, and ZH (43%, 61%, and 49%).

section: Negation directions align and transfer across languages
text: Next, we ask whether cross-language transfer is specific to the selected layer. On the evaluation set, we sweep layers for all models while fixing p=\mathrm{NP} and \alpha=4, and compare the mean within-language flip rate with the mean cross-language flip rate at each layer. Cross- and within-language flip rates track each other closely (Figure 4), suggesting that where negation directions are causally controllable, they also transfer across languages. Furthermore, within and cross-language flip rates remain stably strong in early-to-mid layers of most models except Llama-3.1-8B, indicating this is not an artifact of the chosen layer.

section: Negation directions align and transfer across languages
text: Finally, we analyze the similarity of negation directions extracted from each language at the same (l,p). For Gemma models, we zero out dominant massive-activation dimensions per model before computing similarities; we discuss how they distort similarity in Appendix A.1. In every model, negation directions from all languages are positively aligned, with pairwise cosine similarities ranging from 0.48 to 0.82 (Figure 6). Together, these results provide evidence of cross-lingual alignment in negation representations.

section: Negation is represented in sparse features
text: We next ask whether negation is also captured by individual SAE features. Because exhaustive feature evaluation is costly, we first identify candidate layers using EN. At each layer, we steer with the top- K =10 features (ranked by \delta_{f}) and retain layers with strong addition/removal rates on the EN evaluation set. Within these layers, we evaluate individual features (K =1), select one EN feature per model, and apply it to the test sets of all four languages. Full selection results are in Appendix D.5.

section: Negation is represented in sparse features
text: For every tested model, we find individual SAE features whose decoder directions strongly control polarity across languages (Table 2). Gemma-3-4B’s L4 f331 and Qwen3.5-9B’s L10 f43677 achieve \geq 91\% and \geq 93\% flip rates, respectively, for both addition and removal across all four languages. Llama-3.1-8B’s L13 f12611 is weaker on VI, but still achieves strong control in the other languages.

section: Negation is represented in sparse features
text: We inspect the activation patterns to characterize the three features (examples shown in Figure 7, full details included in Appendix D.5.4). We find that these features respond differently to negation cues: Gemma-3-4B L4 f331 acts as a cross-lingual negation-marker detector, activating strongly on positions of negation markers, while Llama-3.1-8B L13 f12611 activates on tokens in negated contexts. Meanwhile, Qwen3.5-9B L10 f43677 fires on both negation markers and negated contexts. Notably, these features largely separate negated inputs from affirmatives across languages. One exception is Llama’s L13 f12611 firing less frequently on VI, which may explain its weak control.

section: Negation directions and features generalize to unseen languages and naturalistic sentences
text: Finally, we test whether the representations identified on Mini-minus-4 generalize beyond the original four languages and the controlled synthetic setting. For each model, we fix one EN-derived contrast direction \mathbf{d}^{\mathrm{EN}}, and one EN-selected SAE feature from § 4.2 and § 4.3, respectively, without any re-selection. We evaluate these interventions first on RU, HI, AR, and ID test sets, and then on all four original languages in FLORES-minus-4.

section: Negation directions and features generalize to unseen languages and naturalistic sentences
text: We find that both dense and sparse interventions generalize to unseen languages (Table 3). Contrastive directions transfer strongly, with addition/removal rates \geq 85.6/88.0% across all models. Single SAE features likewise maintain \geq 86.9\% across Gemma-3-4B and Qwen3.5-9B, while Llama-3.1-8B remains \geq 77.2%.

section: Negation directions and features generalize to unseen languages and naturalistic sentences
text: Importantly, both dense negation directions and single SAE features generalize to naturalistic sentences (Table 3). Removal is robust: SAE achieves \geq 91.6\% across all models and languages, while CAA is \geq 86.5\% except for Llama-3.1-8B on VI (65.0%). Addition remains strong for Gemma-3-4B and Qwen3.5-9B (\geq 84.2\%), but is weaker for Llama-3.1-8B.

section: Negation in NLP and machine translation.
text: Language models often under-utilize negation cues (Kassner and Schütze, 2020; Ettinger, 2020), and modern LLMs continue to struggle on negation-focused benchmarks (Hossain et al., 2020; Truong et al., 2023; García-Ferrero et al., 2023). Dropped or inverted polarity is also a long-documented failure mode in machine translation (Fancellu and Webber, 2015; Tang et al., 2021). However, this literature is largely behavioral, leaving how multilingual LLMs internally represent negation during translation underexplored.

The linear representation hypothesis posits that high-level concepts correspond to directions in activation space (Park et al., 2024). Causally effective directions have been identified for truth, sentiment, and refusal (Marks and Tegmark, 2024; Tigges et al., 2024; Arditi et al., 2024), and can be manipulated through activation steering (Turner et al., 2024; Rimsky et al., 2024). In this work, we employ activation steering to validate the causal role of identified representations.

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense activations into sparse feature dictionaries (Huben et al., 2024; Templeton et al., 2024), with pretrained SAEs released for several major model families (McDougall et al., 2025; He et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2026). In multilingual settings, Al Ghussin et al. (2026) show that SAEs trained on multilingual data yield more reliable cross-lingual steering, while Nguyen et al. (2026) find that most SAE features do not causally transfer across languages despite recurring activations. Whether SAE features can causally control desired behaviors as effectively as dense directions remains contested (Wu et al., 2025b; Jørgensen and Hansen, 2026; Arad et al., 2025).

Evidence for language-neutral representations in multilingual LLMs is mixed. Some work finds English-centric or dominant-language semantic spaces (Wendler et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025a), while Brinkmann et al. (2025) find shared latent grammatical concepts across typologically diverse languages using SAEs. Causal studies similarly range from a universal refusal direction (Wang et al., 2025) to language-dependent steering effectiveness (Schut et al., 2025).

Zhou et al. (2026) study negation mechanisms in monolingual English, while Lasnier et al. (2026) analyze mechanisms supporting machine translation. The former does not study cross-lingual translation or causal polarity control, and the latter targets whether and in which language translation occurs rather than specific semantic content. Brinkmann et al. (2025) identify SAE features associated with negative polarity, but find weak cross-lingual sharing. They also do not examine dense directions or test the causal role of these features. We instead investigate whether negation representations are causally shared through cross-language interventions on both dense directions and sparse features.

In this work, we investigated how multilingual LLMs represent negation during translation in four main languages. We showed that negation can be causally controlled in multilingual LLMs through both dense activation directions and individual SAE features. Importantly, these representations transfer across languages despite large differences in how negation is expressed, generalizing both to naturalistic sentences and to languages unseen during representation extraction. Similarity analysis revealed negation directions are substantially similar, and activation inspection showed SAE features consistently responding to negation in every language. These findings suggest that multilingual LLMs encode negation in a largely shared and causally controllable representation.

Our extraction and interventions focus on verbal negation marked by explicit lexical cues (e.g., not, không, ne…pas). We also focus only on the translation task. Morphological negation (e.g., un-, im-), implicit negative expressions (e.g., fail, lack) and the role of negation representations in other tasks remain for future work.

Activation addition, like other linear steering methods, depends on the \alpha coefficient (the steering strength), which is a known limitation in the steering literature Vu and Nguyen (2025); You et al. (2026); Aparin and Gaintseva (2026). We select \alpha empirically by sweeping values on the evaluation set rather than a principled selection.
For sparse feature analysis, we rely on pre-trained SAE releases, thus our analysis does not cover all models. Our feature-level interpretation is also limited to one selected feature per model.
