Not One Belief: Answer Payloads, Persistence, and Dissociated Confidence Signals in Conversational Question Answering. Conversational QA systems should fix errors when users push back and signal which answers to trust. We split each follow-up into its speech act (re-ask, agree, or challenge) and its payload (an answer string, correct or not), and measure four confidence signals on the same transcripts: verbalized confidence, length-normalized likelihood, a frozen hidden-state probe, and P(True). Answers change when the user supplies an answer string and almost never under the speech act alone: in every retained full-size cell, the correct answer converts at least four times as many wrong answers as re-asking or agreement. The four signals disagree. On Qwen2.5-7B the frozen probe rises with answer persistence rather than truth; this holds on held-out questions, with Llama-3-8B (cleaned answers) as support, but not on four other models. Among 81 Qwen2.5-7B errors that survive one re-ask, re-asking, a fresh chat, or abstain repair almost none, while a gold answer repairs 75-95%. In two preregistered replications, every repair rate without an answer string stays below 0.15; a larger post-hoc rerun excludes 0.15 except for the empty elicit.

With BM25 TriviaQA evidence, sentences that contain the answer repair 67-76% of persistent errors versus at most 12% when they do not. An end-to-end contain-gate cuts harm on TriviaQA, but a deployable gate that does not know the gold answer repairs few errors.

Chat assistants built on large language models (LLMs) now answer questions in customer support, tutoring, search, and clinical or legal help lines. There, a wrong answer costs something. Two questions follow, both about the reliability of conversational QA and evidence retrieval under user feedback. When a user pushes back, does the system fix its errors or just change its mind? And can the system’s own confidence tell the operator which answers to trust? Recent work on the second question asks whether LLM confidence stays calibrated as a conversation goes on Zhang et al. (2026a); Zhang et al. (2026b). These studies usually score one confidence measure (verbalized confidence, the self-evaluation probability P(\mathrm{True}), or sequence likelihood) against correctness, as if each were an estimate of the same underlying belief.

For that to work, the measures must move together, and every follow-up must count as the same kind of evidence. In our data, neither holds. So we ask a simpler question: when a user sends a follow-up message, which quantity does it change? Figure 1 summarizes the answer. We split each follow-up into two parts. The speech act is what the user does: re-ask, agree, or say the model is wrong. The payload is an optional answer string in the message, either the correct (“gold”) answer or a plausible wrong one (a “foil”). Payloads change the model’s answer. Speech acts alone almost never repair an error. Changes to the answer, whether or not the new answer is true, move a frozen probe readout that, on Qwen2.5-7B, goes with answer persistence. We call it the persistence readout s_{t} and make no psychological or causal claim about it. The other measures respond to other things: verbalized confidence to the number of turns, sequence likelihood to how fluently the model repeats itself, and P(\mathrm{True}) to explicit contradiction. Two papers that calibrate different measures and call both “confidence” are not reporting comparable numbers.

Recent single-turn work already shows that confidence measures can come apart. Kumaran (2026) finds that verbal confidence predicts a model’s later decision to commit to or withhold an answer better than it predicts correctness, while calibrated token log-probabilities track correctness. Zhang et al. (2026a) study multi-turn confidence as hints accumulate and propose InfoECE and P(\mathrm{Sufficient}), but they do not separate what the user does from the answer string the user gives. Kumaran (2026) work in a single turn. Our contribution is to control the user’s turn in multi-turn dialogue, separate the speech act from the answer payload, and measure four signals on the same transcripts.

We write I \to C for an item that is incorrect at turn 1 and correct at turn 2, and C \to I for the reverse. Re-asking (persist) and agreeing with the model (confirm) produce almost no I \to C changes, so the error survives. Stating the gold string produces many, with or without “you are wrong” around it. Stating a plausible foil produces many C \to I changes. An empty challenge (“I think that’s wrong”) makes answers unstable without pointing them anywhere. The string moves the answer. The stance does not. Models differ only in how they take up the string. Qwen2.5 and Llama-3-8B usually copy it verbatim (the fraction of I \to C answers that copy it is 0.70 – 0.91 on NQ and HotpotQA). Mistral-7B-v0.3 restates it inside a longer sentence.

On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, verbalized confidence falls as the user keeps talking, even when accuracy is flat (persist) or rising (correct). Length-normalized sequence likelihood often rises on the same turns. A linear probe on hidden states, fitted once on first-turn answers and then frozen, rises both on items that stay wrong and on items that switch to gold. Kadavath-style P(\mathrm{True}) Kadavath et al. (2022) barely moves, except under foil persuasion, where it collapses on C \to I changes (mean change \approx-0.26 overall and -0.85 on C \to I items). One conversation, four different stories. The same holds for calibrated scores: a single user turn sends the expected calibration error (ECE) down for verbalized confidence, up for likelihood, and nowhere for P(\mathrm{True}) (Section 5).

section: Persistent errors are hard to undo.
text: Asking again or starting a new chat does not fix a persistent error unless the user supplies a string. Among 81 Qwen2.5-7B TriviaQA items that are still wrong after one re-ask, re-asking through turn 5, a fresh chat, and an ABSTAIN option repair two, zero, and zero items. The model abstains on 94\% of these stay-wrong items and on 62\% of stay-correct items. A gold string at turn 3 repairs 0.75 – 0.95 of the same items, depending on phrasing, and an “I don’t know” turn repairs 5/81. Two preregistered replications (230 stay-wrong items from a second Qwen slice, 160 from Llama-3-8B, 139 from Mistral-7B-v0.3, and 61 from Qwen2.5-32B) keep every observed repair rate without an answer string below a 0.15 threshold fixed in advance, under the preregistered answer matcher. A post hoc rerun on about 300 new stay-wrong items per model excludes 0.15 for every such arm except the empty elicit (Section 6.1). With one BM25 sentence per TriviaQA question, retrieval repairs errors only to the extent that the sentence contains the answer string (Section 6.1).

We offer a map of interventions and their effects, not a new method: The answer string, not the speech act, moves the answer. Answers follow a stated gold or foil string. Re-asking and agreement do not repair errors (Section 4). The measures come apart across turns. Single-turn work has shown that verbalized confidence and correctness-tracking signals are not interchangeable Kumaran (2026); Miao and Ungar (2026). We show the same split in dialogue for four measures (verbalized confidence, likelihood, a frozen hidden-state probe, and P(\mathrm{True})), in raw scores and in calibration error, and we show which part of the user turn each one responds to (Section 5). On Qwen2.5-7B the frozen probe goes with answer persistence, and persistent errors are hard to undo. The persistence readout s_{t}=\sigma(v_{\mathrm{acc}}^{\top}\tilde{h}_{t}) is a frozen probe on the current answer state (Section 3.4). On Qwen2.5-7B it rises on stay-wrong items and on I \to C items, also on held-out questions and above a shuffled-label control. Llama-3-8B with cut answers supports this; on the other four models it does not hold on held-out questions. Resetting the chat or offering abstention does not recover these errors; a gold string at turn 3 does (Section 6.1). A retrieval heuristic.

Before relying on evidence to repair an answer, check that it contains the answer string. This is a hypothesis for system design, not a validated rule. Across four models, a retrieved sentence without it repairs at most 0.16 of stay-wrong items under any of our scorers, and it breaks up to 0.70 of correct answers (Section 6.1). The first three points share one argument: if two measures respond to different controlled interventions and disagree on the same transcript, they cannot both estimate a single latent conversational confidence. We do not propose a new uncertainty estimator. Section 8 lists what we do not claim.

Instruction-tuned LLMs tend to adopt a view the user states, even when it is wrong. Perez et al. (2023) documented this with model-written evaluations and found that it grows with model size and with reinforcement learning from human feedback. Sharma et al. (2024) showed that sycophancy is common across production assistants and traced it partly to human preference judgments that reward agreement. Wei et al. (2023) found that scaling and instruction tuning increase sycophancy, that models agree with a user’s clearly false arithmetic claims, and that fine-tuning on simple synthetic data reduces it. These works show that a user’s stated answer is persuasive. They usually bundle the stance (“I think you are wrong”) with the stated string. Our factorial design separates the two. For short factual answers, the string does almost all of the work.

section: Re-asking and answer flipping under pushback.
text: Other work studies what happens when a user challenges an answer, with or without offering a new one. In the FlipFlop experiment, Laban et al. (2023) showed that a simple “Are you sure?” makes models change their answers and lowers accuracy. Xie et al. (2024) found that models waver under skeptical, negating, or misleading follow-ups even when the first answer was correct, and proposed a training method to reduce this. Wang et al. (2023) showed that ChatGPT often cannot defend a correct answer against invalid arguments. Huang et al. (2024) found that models rarely improve their reasoning by intrinsic self-correction without outside feedback, and Laban et al. (2026) showed that performance drops across many tasks in multi-turn conversation. Our results agree on one side and add the other: empty challenges break correct answers (C \to I), but neither challenges nor re-asks repair wrong ones (I \to C). We also test whether a persistent error survives a chat reset.

Asking a model to state its confidence is the cheapest measure in deployed systems. Lin et al. (2022) showed that a fine-tuned GPT-3 can express calibrated uncertainty in words. Without such fine-tuning, the stated confidence of instruction-tuned models is often overconfident or poorly calibrated Xiong et al. (2024), though prompting can help, especially for models trained with human feedback Tian et al. (2023). Geng et al. (2024) survey confidence estimation and calibration for LLMs. Calibration is usually measured with ECE Guo et al. (2017). In our dialogues, the movement of verbalized confidence is mostly a Qwen2.5-7B effect of turn depth, not a response to evidence.

Kadavath et al. (2022) asked a model whether its own proposed answer is true and read the probability of “True”. They found this fairly well calibrated for large models on many single-turn tasks. In our dialogues P(\mathrm{True}) ranks correct answers well at both turns but barely moves under re-asking or agreement. It responds mainly to contradiction by a foil.

Several papers train classifiers on hidden activations to read out whether a statement or answer is true. Azaria and Mitchell (2023) trained such a classifier on true and false statements. Marks and Tegmark (2024) reported linear structure that separates true from false statements. Burns et al. (2023) found latent knowledge without labels. Orgad et al. (2025) showed that truthfulness signals concentrate in the exact answer tokens, generalize poorly across datasets, and that a model may encode the correct answer while generating a wrong one. A probe can learn the task itself rather than reveal what the representation encodes, so probe results need care Hewitt and Liang (2019). We fit a probe at turn 1, freeze it, and follow it after the user speaks again.

Two recent single-turn studies are close to our result on the measures. Kumaran (2026) used a two-stage task: a model answers and reports its confidence, then later decides whether to give the answer to a user or abstain. Across several models, verbal confidence predicted the later commit-or-abstain decision better than it predicted correctness, while calibrated token log-probabilities tracked correctness. In Gemma models, a post-answer hidden state encoded the later decision, and steering along a direction specific to verbal confidence shifted abstention. Miao and Ungar (2026) found that a linear accuracy probe and the direction behind verbalized confidence are nearly orthogonal, and used activation steering to bring verbalized confidence closer to the probe. We do not claim these points as new. Our study differs in three ways. The user turn is controlled, so we can separate the speech act from the answer string. The probe is fitted at turn 1 and frozen, and we follow the same items across turns. And we study the frozen probe readout, not verbalized confidence: in our dialogues, on Qwen2.5-7B, it is the probe that moves with the answer the model keeps. We run no steering, so unlike these two studies our evidence is correlational.

Sarkar et al. (2026) show, in a collaborative dialogue task between two LLMs, that a partner’s assertion can shift a model’s linear representation of whether a proposition is true. Our probe result points the same way for short factual answers.

The closest work studies confidence across turns. Zhang et al. (2026a) evaluate verbalized confidence, P(\mathrm{True}), and a new P(\mathrm{Sufficient}) score as hints accumulate, and propose an information-aware ECE (InfoECE) that requires confidence to rise steadily as gold information arrives. Zhang et al. (2026b) show that persuasion worsens a turn-level ECE (ECE@T) and that sequence likelihood can rise when the answer flips to a wrong one, and they train a calibrator, MTCal, to repair the score. Both ask how well a score tracks correctness. We use their setting (short-answer dialogue under persuasion) and ask an earlier question: which quantity a given user turn moves (Table 1).

Models follow context that contradicts their stored knowledge to varying degrees Longpre et al. (2021); Xie et al. (2024), and whether retrieved context is sufficient to answer the question predicts errors in retrieval-augmented generation Joren et al. (2025). Lathkar (2026) reports that, in multi-hop retrieval-augmented QA, one confirmed intermediate fact can raise the rate of confident wrong answers before complete evidence lowers it. That work is single-turn and measures confidence; we measure whether evidence repairs an error that has already survived a re-ask. In our data, evidence repairs such an error only when it contains the answer string.

Each dialogue starts at turn 1 (T1) with a short-answer question. At turn 2 (T2), and at later turns when used, the user sends one of four core messages, fixed across models: Please answer again, briefly. Do not change your answer unless you are sure you were wrong. Yes, that’s correct. Please answer again, briefly, in one short phrase. One of five challenge templates plus a foil. The same five templates plus a gold alias. Ablations keep the same T1 and change only the T2 message, to separate the speech act from the payload. gold_plain and foil_plain state a string without saying “wrong”. challenge_empty challenges the answer without offering a replacement. confirm_strong repeats the model’s T1 answer and calls it correct. persist_short is Again, briefly. Exact wording is in Online Resource 1, Sect. A.

We compare each item’s correctness at turn t with its correctness at T1. An item is stay-correct (SC) if it is correct at both turns, stay-wrong (SW) if it is wrong at both, I \to C if it changes from incorrect to correct, and C \to I if it changes from correct to incorrect. We report I \to C and C \to I as counts out of the number of items (usually 200) or as rates. For a measure X, \Delta X=X_{\mathrm{T2}}-X_{\mathrm{T1}} is its change from T1 to T2, averaged over the stated items. The copy rate is the fraction of I \to C answers that repeat the payload string exactly. A unit is one model \times dataset combination. Seed copies of the same unit are not counted as independent.

We use the four quantities that current multi-turn papers treat as interchangeable measures of confidence. The list is not exhaustive. Token entropy, logit margin, and semantic entropy Kuhn et al. (2023) read the same next-token distribution as likelihood, so we expect them to behave like it unless an intervention separates them. Verbalized confidence (\Delta verb for its change) is what products elicit Xiong et al. (2024); Tian et al. (2023). The model is asked to state a confidence, which is parsed from a separate CONF field into [0,1]. Sequence likelihood (“ll”) is the quantity scored by ECE@T and MTCal Zhang et al. (2026b): \exp of the mean log-probability of the answer tokens, teacher-forced under the chat template. Frozen probe is the kind of hidden-state readout that the truthfulness-probing literature reads as a signal of truth Azaria and Mitchell (2023); Marks and Tegmark (2024). It is defined in Section 3.4. P(\mathrm{True}) is the Kadavath self-evaluation used alongside P(\mathrm{Sufficient}) Kadavath et al. (2022); Zhang et al. (2026a): a forced choice between A (true) and B (false), scored by the softmax probability of A. We computed it on the Qwen2.5-7B TriviaQA set of 800 rows (200 items \times four core messages).

section: The persistence readout: an operational definition
text: Let h_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be the last-layer hidden state averaged (mean-pooled) over the answer tokens at turn t, and let \tilde{h}_{t} be h_{t} standardized with the training-set mean and variance. We fit a weight vector v_{\mathrm{acc}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} by logistic regression to predict T1 correctness from h_{1}, using only the unique persist T1 items of that model \times dataset. GroupKFold cross-validation is used only as a sanity check. We then freeze v_{\mathrm{acc}} and never refit it after the user speaks. The persistence readout at turn t is s_{t}\;=\;\sigma\!\bigl(v_{\mathrm{acc}}^{\top}\tilde{h}_{t}\bigr), where \sigma(x)=1/(1+e^{-x}) is the logistic function. We use “probe” and s_{t} interchangeably and write \Delta s=s_{2}-s_{1}. Three points make the definition precise: What it is. s_{t} is a frozen readout of the current answer state. The linear map is one choice. Our claims about s_{t} apply to any frozen readout that is fitted only on unique T1 states, is not refitted after the user speaks, and rises on stay-wrong and on I \to C items (Section 6). What the name means. “Persistence” names an observed association with the answer the model keeps. We make no claim about a psychological state, and no claim that s_{t} causes the answer.

section: The persistence readout: an operational definition
text: The main analyses fit the probe on unique T1 items and apply it to rows of the same questions. A post hoc rerun on held-out questions (Section 6) keeps the result on Qwen2.5-7B only. Why it is not truth. If s_{t} measured truth, it would rise only when the answer becomes gold. Instead it rises on stay-wrong and on I \to C items and falls on C \to I items. The behaviour it goes with. An item is stay-wrong if it is wrong at T1 and still wrong after persist at T2. On Qwen2.5-7B TriviaQA there are n{=}81 such items, and \Delta s>0 on 79 of their 80 distinct questions. Reset and abstention fail on this set; a gold string at T3 does not (Section 6.1). We do not read v_{\mathrm{acc}} as a discovered truth direction Marks and Tegmark (2024); Burns et al. (2023). A multilayer perceptron (MLP) probe with one hidden layer matches the T1 discrimination of the linear probe and shows the same pattern, so the result does not depend on linearity.

Answers are normalized (lowercased, articles removed, whitespace collapsed) and counted correct on an exact match or on whole-word containment, in either direction, between the answer and a gold alias Joshi et al. (2017). We call this the contain matcher. It is the primary, preregistered scorer. Where the distinction matters (Qwen3) we also report exact-normalized scores. Containment has a known weakness: it credits an answer that names the gold only to reject it (Norman Rockwell, not Edward Hopper). This matters for Mistral’s long answers, which an LLM therefore read in full. Other models were screened only with a negation regular expression (Online Resource 1, Sect. I). The second preregistration also scored every answer with an LLM judge. The judge missed its preregistered validation bar, so contain stays primary, and judge and model-read rescorings are reported beside it (Online Resource 1, Sect. H). Post hoc, two independent people labelled a blind sample of 300 V2 rows; on the 272 clear ENDORSES/DOES_NOT pairs Cohen’s \kappa was 0.86 (agreement 253/272), with disagreements resolved by discussion. This is a post-hoc reliability check, not a change of the primary scorer (Online Resource 1, Sect. H).

Under our generation settings, Llama-3-8B-Instruct does not stop at its end-of-turn token <|eot_id|> and repeats its answer after a leaked assistant role header. For Llama we score the text before the first leaked role header, because in the raw run-on text the matcher misses answers glued to the header (9 – 19\% of Llama T2 labels change).

The main grid uses instruction-tuned models from 3B to 14B parameters: Qwen2.5-{3,7,14}B Qwen Team (2024), Qwen2-7B, Qwen3-8B Qwen Team (2025), Llama-3-8B-Instruct Grattafiori et al. (2024), Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 Jiang et al. (2023), and Phi-4 Abdin et al. (2024). Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct has one TriviaQA T1/T2 cell. We use it only to find stay-wrong items for the turn-3 battery and the retrieval study (Section 6.1), and it is not one of the 24 units below. We had no access to the gated Llama-3.1 and Gemma checkpoints.

Datasets are TriviaQA rc.nocontext Joshi et al. (2017), NQ-open Kwiatkowski et al. (2019), HotpotQA questions without passages Yang et al. (2018), TruthfulQA Lin et al. (2022), and WebQuestions Berant et al. (2013). For TriviaQA we use a main slice [0,200), fixed after shuffling with seed 42, plus a disjoint slice [200,400) and an extra slice of n=500. GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021) uses the same short-answer protocol on grade-school mathematics (matching the last number); we make no claim about long-form reasoning. We exclude PopQA because several models fall to accuracy 0, a matcher and format failure. Unless stated otherwise, n=200, seed 42, and decoding is greedy.

To check whether each pattern generalizes, we evaluate five yes/no predicates on every independent unit: \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{err}}: on stay-wrong items, \Delta probe >0 under both persist and confirm. \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{gold}}: I \to C under correct is at least 0.15, and I \to C is at most 0.03, 0.05, and 0.05 under persist, confirm, and persuade. \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{verb}}: mean \Delta verb <0 on all four core messages (models whose verbalized confidence is flagged VERB_UNTRUSTED are skipped). \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ll}}: under persist, the most common sign combination is verbalized confidence not up and likelihood up, or mean \Delta ll >0 with mean \Delta verb <0. \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{artifact}}: at least 80\% of C \to I changes under correct are items whose T1 answer was already gold under a loose alias check, that is, a matcher artifact rather than a real loss. On 24 independent units, \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{err}}=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{ll}}=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{artifact}}=24/24. \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{gold}} holds on 19/24. The five failures are the three Qwen3 units, which we keep in the denominator although their cells are truncated “self-repair” cells that we withdrew after extracting answers past </think> (Online Resource 1, Sect. C), and Llama-3-8B on TriviaQA and NQ (Section 4). \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{verb}} holds on all six Qwen2.5-7B dataset units and on no other model family.

Before any generation, a frozen pilot preregistration Tran (2026a) fixed two hypotheses and a stopping rule. H1 stated that the frozen v_{\mathrm{acc}} predicts T2 correctness after misleading persuasion better than verbalized confidence does. H2 stated that verbalized confidence rises from T1 to T2 under persuasion while the probe’s predicted probability of correctness does not. H2 failed its gate: verbalized confidence fell (-0.17). H1 met neither preregistered bar: the advantage was +0.06 with a bootstrap interval covering zero. The verdict fixed in advance was to continue with no surviving hypothesis. We report H2 as failed rather than dropping it. What replaced the hypotheses was an observation: the measures were responding to different parts of the user’s turn.

Apart from two later preregistered studies of persistent errors and retrieval Tran (2026b); Tran (2026c) (Section 6.1), nothing in this paper is confirmatory. Every other result is exploratory measurement, and we label it as such. All three preregistration documents are in the supplementary material (Online Resource 2).

section: The answer string, not the speech act
text: Table 2 and Figure 2 are the controlled core of the study: T1 is identical and only the T2 message changes. On the 200 main TriviaQA items, the accusation does almost none of the work. Removing it leaves gold uptake nearly intact (gold_plain converts 57 items against 65 for correct), and a bare foil pulls more answers away from gold than the templated persuade message (77 vs. 30). Removing the string instead removes the direction. challenge_empty scatters answers both ways (71 C \to I, 12 I \to C), which looks like added randomness rather than an update. Agreement, bare or emphatic, behaves like re-asking, and dropping “briefly” does not loosen uptake.

section: The answer string, not the speech act
text: The split does not depend on our exact T2 wording. Twenty-seven everyday paraphrases of the four T2 messages, applied to the same T1 histories, keep mean I \to C at 0.026 when no string is named and 0.275 when gold is named (foil C \to I 0.325; Online Resource 1, Table D1). Hedged, assistant-like phrasing does not replace the payload either. I think it’s { gold } still converts (0.295), while I think you might be off does not (0.045). The same three ablations meet the same gates on NQ, HotpotQA, and WebQuestions. The pattern also holds on GSM8K under the short-answer protocol: persist converts 14/188 T1-wrong items, and on the 174 items still wrong, gold converts 0.437 against 0.103 for Try again.

In every retained full-size cell (all except PopQA, the 64-token Qwen3 cells, and the n{\approx}20 turn-depth subsamples), I \to C under correct is at least four times that under persist or confirm (Table 3). The closest cases are Llama-3-8B TriviaQA (48 vs. 11) and GSM8K (76 vs. 18 for Try again). Across cells, I \to C under persist has a median of 2/200 (minimum 0). An earlier persist I \to C of 40 came from the truncated Qwen3 cell that we withdraw in Online Resource 1, Sect. C. Llama-3-8B misses \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{gold}} on TriviaQA and NQ because re-asking and agreement convert slightly more than the gates allow (persist I \to C 8 and 11/200; confirm 11 and 10/200). This is still far below gold’s 48 and 107. Phi-4 barely moves under persuade (accuracy 0.70\to 0.71 on TriviaQA) but still adopts gold (I \to C =50, C \to I =0). Qwen2.5 and Llama-3-8B mostly copy the payload; Mistral-7B restates it inside a longer sentence, sometimes only to reject it. Copy rates and the model-read audit are in Online Resource 1, Sect. I.

The four measures disagree in sign in every row of Table 4 and Figure 3. Under correct, verbalized confidence falls while accuracy climbs to 0.845. The disagreement remains when we split items by what the answer did. Under persist, P(\mathrm{True}) barely moves on items that stayed wrong (+0.012), while the probe rises by +0.38 on the same items. Under persuade, P(\mathrm{True}) falls most where the answer flipped (C \to I -0.845, stay-wrong -0.171), yet the probe on stay-wrong items still rises (+0.27). Under correct, P(\mathrm{True}) moves both ways at once (I \to C +0.148, C \to I -0.411) around a mean of \approx 0, while the probe rises by +0.64 on I \to C items and +0.27 on the 16 stay-wrong items. No single ECE curve can capture that.

section: The drop in verbalized confidence is model-specific.
text: The drop survives two obvious explanations. Residualizing on answer length leaves a mean \Delta of -0.13, and the word “briefly” is not responsible, since correct_long still converts. It does not survive a change of model. \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{verb}} holds on 6/6 Qwen2.5-7B dataset units and on no other family once untrusted parses are dropped. Phi-4 moves the other way on all four core messages. Qwen2.5-3B and 14B fail on confirm (+0.013, +0.044). Llama-3’s -0.537 is flagged VERB_UNTRUSTED because its values pile up at 0. Qwen3 fails to parse on 96% of truncated rows because the CONF field sits inside <think>.

section: The drop in verbalized confidence is model-specific.
text: Under persist on Qwen2.5-7B TriviaQA, the most common sign pattern is likelihood rising while verbalized confidence does not rise (172/200 in the pilot cell; 51 with a strict drop). In that cell, likelihood (the quantity MTCal calibrates) and verbalized confidence point in opposite directions on the same tokens.

On Qwen2.5-14B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Phi-4, and Qwen2-7B (not preregistered; Online Resource 1, Sect. J), likelihood still rises under persist except on Mistral, P(\mathrm{True}) stays within 0.03, and the all-item \Delta probe is negative on three of the four. The exact pattern in Table 4 is a Qwen2.5-7B result; what holds across models is the disagreement.

section: The same split appears in ECE.
text: Table 5 scores all four measures against T1 and T2 correctness on one transcript. Under persuade, verbalized ECE falls (0.50\to 0.38), likelihood ECE nearly doubles (0.23\to 0.41), and P(\mathrm{True}) ECE is flat (0.22\to 0.20). The split in Figure 1 therefore also appears in the field’s standard metric. A study has to say which measure it calibrates.

section: The same split appears in ECE.
text: The drop in verbalized ECE is not better calibration. Stated confidence stays about 0.3 below accuracy at both turns (0.28 vs. 0.59, then 0.10 vs. 0.44). AUROC (how well a score ranks correct above wrong answers) shows the same. At T1, verbalized confidence is close to uninformative (0.564), while likelihood, the probe, and P(\mathrm{True}) all sit near 0.85. At T2 the order changes: verbalized confidence rises to 0.729 and likelihood drops to 0.630. Which measure a study happens to elicit decides how calibrated the result looks, and also whether it ranks correct answers at all. A post hoc rerun reproduces every cell of Tables 4 and 5 within \pm 0.002. An older output file listed verbalized ECE as 0.582\to 0.435; it divided confidences that were already in [0,1] by 100 again, and the values above are the corrected ones (Online Resource 1, Sect. J).

section: The same split appears in ECE.
text: The probe’s own drop in AUROC (0.848\to 0.649) is not noise. It is the persistence effect of Section 6 seen in calibration terms. A readout that rises on items that stay wrong (Table 4) must lose discrimination against correctness once the user has spoken, because it now follows the answer the model keeps rather than what is true. In the same turn, the probe becomes a worse readout of truth and a better readout of answer persistence, and a single “confidence” number hides this.

On Qwen2.5-7B, the frozen v_{\mathrm{acc}} is a weak readout of truth and a consistent correlate of answer persistence. The post hoc controls below, including a rerun on held-out questions, limit the strong form of this result to Qwen2.5-7B, with Llama-3-8B on cut answers as support.

On all 24 independent units, stay-wrong \Delta probe is positive under both persist and confirm (\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{err}}=24/24). These are in-sample numbers: the probe scores questions it was fitted on. On held-out questions the sign survives on Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3-8B and fails on Qwen2.5-14B, Mistral, and Phi-4 (see Held-out questions below). A sign count is the weakest form of this result, so we also report magnitudes. Across the 32 unit \times message cells with item-level states, the median of the mean \Delta probe is 0.264 (interquartile range [0.127,0.384], range [0.025,0.758]), and each cell’s own bootstrap 95\% interval excludes zero (32/32). These cells are TriviaQA for seven models (Qwen3 in its truncated cell) and Qwen2.5-7B on five further slices. Six of the 32 are seed or configuration copies of the main Qwen2.5-7B cell. Sign counts over all 113 cells are in Online Resource 1, Sect. J. An MLP probe, a probe refitted on persist T2, and layer and token ablations keep the sign (Online Resource 1, Sect. J).

So the probe rises when the model keeps a wrong answer and when it adopts gold, and it falls when a correct T1 answer is pulled away (persuade C \to I \Delta probe -0.35 in the unique-fit follow-up). It goes with the current answer, not with a latent true/false feature Marks and Tegmark (2024).

Four checks were defined in a note written before the numbers and were not preregistered (Online Resource 1, Sect. J). (a) A probe fitted on shuffled T1 labels (100 seeds) stays near 0 on Qwen2.5-7B, against 0.383 for the real probe; on Qwen2.5-14B persist, Mistral, and Phi-4, 29 – 59\% of shuffles reach the real value. (b) On Qwen2.5-7B the rise does not need a changed answer (identical answers 0.397, n=67; changed 0.318, n=14). (c) Within stay-wrong items, \Delta probe and \Delta likelihood are only weakly related (Spearman -0.09 to 0.27). (d) A planned re-read without dialogue history is not interpretable: re-scoring the T1 answer did not reproduce the stored states (cosine 0.81, below the required 0.95, even after reusing the generated token ids), so we draw no conclusion from it (Online Resource 1, Sect. J).

We refitted the probe in five folds grouped by question, so it never saw a test question at any turn, and scored stay-wrong items on the held-out folds only (Online Resource 1, Table J10). On Qwen2.5-7B, \Delta s is 0.321 [0.255, 0.389] under persist and 0.324 [0.252, 0.395] under confirm (in sample 0.383, 0.384), and no shuffled-label probe reaches it. Llama-3-8B, with states recomputed on cut answers, gives 0.201 [0.131, 0.275] and 0.119 [0.051, 0.192], also above every shuffle. On the other models the result does not hold. Qwen2-7B drops to 0.067 [-0.003, 0.136] and 0.019 [-0.058, 0.090]. Mistral and Phi-4 turn negative. Qwen2.5-14B is negative under persist (-0.100) and positive under confirm (0.117 [0.019, 0.212]). The held-out probe still ranks T1 correctness on every model (AUROC 0.69 – 0.85).

section: Stay-wrong errors are hard to fix
text: Take the 81 Qwen2.5-7B TriviaQA items that are wrong at T1 and still wrong after persist at T2 (80 distinct questions; one appears twice in the slice). Further persist turns convert one of them by T3 (accuracy on stay-wrong items =0.012), two by T5 (0.025), and three by T10 (0.037). A reset at T3 (a fresh chat with only the original question) converts none. A T3 that continues the chat and offers abstention (If you are not confident … reply ABSTAIN) draws abstention on 94\% of stay-wrong and 62\% of stay-correct items. Every stay-wrong item that still answers is wrong, so coverage on stay-wrong items is 0.06. Gating on the probe (\mathrm{probe}_{T2}>\mathrm{probe}_{T1}, true for 79 of the 80 distinct stay-wrong questions) does not change these accuracies. Re-asking, wiping the transcript, and offering abstention do not repair these errors.

section: Stay-wrong errors are hard to fix
text: A gold string at T3 does (Table 6). Every gold phrasing recovers 0.75 – 0.95 of the 81 items. Hedging does not lower it (0.79). A different gold alias recovers 0.77 (n_{\mathrm{SW}}=69), with a copy rate of only 0.49 for that surface form (main gold messages 0.61 – 0.71), so the repair is not only echoing. The gold retrieved-note phrasing leaves stay-correct items intact (accuracy 0.965, C \to I 4/114).

Two preregistrations fixed models, items, messages, metrics, and a decision rule before any generation: a message without an answer string that reaches \geq 0.15 repair on stay-wrong items breaks the null for that model Tran (2026c); Tran (2026b). The first ran the turn-3 battery on Qwen’s n{=}500 slice (230 stay-wrong items) and on the original Llama and Mistral items (61 and 58; Online Resource 1, Sect. E). The second regenerated Llama-3-8B and Mistral-7B-v0.3 on the same 500 items with correct stop tokens (160 and 139 stay-wrong items) and added Qwen2.5-32B (61), all on GPU (Online Resource 1, Sect. F).

Under the preregistered matcher, every observed rate without an answer string is below 0.15 on every unit, so the decision rule never fires (Table 6). That is weaker than excluding 0.15, and several small cells did not (Wilson upper bounds up to 0.26). A post hoc rerun on 298 (Llama) and 269 (32B) new stay-wrong items (Online Resource 1, Table J11) now excludes it for re-asking, fresh chat, and ABSTAIN (at most 6/269, upper bounds \leq 0.048). The empty elicit does not: 35/298 [0.086, 0.159] and 32/269 [0.086, 0.163]; pooled with earlier rows, Llama excludes 0.15 (50/458, upper 0.141) and 32B does not (38/330, upper 0.154). Llama’s highest arms in the first replication (up to 9/61=0.148) come mostly from the leaked role header. In a post hoc check on the 54 rows that are still stay-wrong after cutting answers at the header, fresh chat recovers 2/54 (0.04) and the other arms without an answer string recover none (Online Resource 1, Table E2). In the second replication the highest such arm is the empty elicit, at 6/61=0.098 on 32B and 15/160=0.094 on Llama (Wilson upper bounds 0.198 and 0.149; the 32B interval includes 0.15).
Mistral’s gold rates (0.72 / 0.71) overstate uptake; read by a model, they are 0.55 / 0.25.

One result goes against the null. With judge labels, and model-read labels for the rows where the matcher and judge disagree, Llama’s empty elicit is 24/160=0.150 [0.103, 0.213], so the decision rule applied to those labels does not replicate for Llama. But 9 of the 24 repairs were already correct at T1 and T2 under those labels; with stay-wrong defined by them (post hoc), the arm is 15/149=0.101 [0.062, 0.159] (Online Resource 1, Sect. H).
Frozen s_{2} does not predict which stay-wrong items gold leaves unrepaired (AUROC 0.39, 0.49, 0.62 on Llama, Mistral, 32B; every interval contains 0.5; Online Resource 1, Tables E2 and F3).

section: Retrieval repairs only when it contains the answer
text: Every gold arm above is an oracle: the user hands the model the right answer. The second preregistration therefore tested real evidence on the same stay-wrong items and on up to 150 stay-correct items per model. BM25 Robertson and Zaragoza (2009) ranks the sentences of each question’s TriviaQA evidence documents, and T3 inserts one sentence into the retrieved-note message. The top-ranked sentence repairs 0.22 – 0.27 of stay-wrong items, and how often it contains the answer explains that rate. Pooled over four models, 90/111 items recover when it contains a gold alias and 20/330 when it does not. Holding the ranking fixed, the best sentence that contains the answer repairs 0.67 – 0.76, and the best sentence that lacks it repairs 0.02 – 0.12. The difference is 0.56 – 0.73, with every interval above 0, and 0.55 – 0.61 with model-read labels, under which Llama’s no-answer sentence reaches 26/160=0.16. Sentences without the answer are not neutral. They cut stay-correct accuracy from 1 to 0.65, 0.78, 0.30, and 0.78.

You have to split conversational confidence into its parts before you can calibrate it. ECE@T on likelihood Zhang et al. (2026b) scores fluency, and P(\mathrm{Sufficient}) Zhang et al. (2026a) scores evidence. Neither measures uptake of the user’s string or the persistence readout s_{t}. On one transcript, I \to C and C \to I counts show whether a user string overwrote the answer, s_{t} (on Qwen2.5-7B) follows the answer the model keeps, P(\mathrm{True}) shows whether a contradiction landed, and likelihood shows fluency. Table 7 lists what this means in practice.

Studies of multi-turn confidence should state which measure they use, separate the speech act from the answer string in their user turns, and use an answer matcher that rejects negated mentions of the gold answer. A calibration result for one measure is not evidence about another.

A re-ask, a chat reset, or an abstain option will not undo a persistent error, and a drop in verbalized confidence will not flag one. In our data, the only reliable repair was new content that contained the answer. For retrieval-augmented assistants this suggests a heuristic: before presenting retrieved evidence as a correction, check whether it contains a candidate answer string. In our data, evidence without one rarely repairs an error and can break up to 0.70 of answers that were correct. In a post hoc end-to-end test (BM25 passages, TriviaQA and HotpotQA, three models; Online Resource 1, Table J12), the gold-based gate cut harm on TriviaQA while keeping most repairs (Llama, k=1: harm 0.179\to 0.038, net per 100 items 15.9\to 27.4); on HotpotQA the gain was mixed. A gate that checks the model’s own answer instead of the gold repaired only 0.02 – 0.12 of errors, and dense retrieval and a judge check were not run. So the check is a heuristic for systems that can verify answers, not a validated rule.

We do not claim that verbalized confidence always falls over turns (we observe this for Qwen2.5-7B only), that hidden states contain a truth direction, or that we outperform MTCal Zhang et al. (2026b) or P(\mathrm{Sufficient}) Zhang et al. (2026a) on ECE. We do not claim to be first to show that verbalized confidence and correctness-tracking signals come apart, or that confidence can track commitment; single-turn studies showed both Kumaran (2026); Miao and Ungar (2026). We make no psychological or causal claim about the persistence readout. We propose no new uncertainty estimator.

All experiments use English short-answer question answering, with GSM8K run under the same short-answer protocol. We did not study naturalistic or multi-party dialogue, long-form reasoning, coding, or agents, and we did not run closed APIs or logged user conversations. Our evidence is about controlled interventions, not open-ended human conversation. The turn-3 battery contains no reasoning prompt, so we do not claim that step-by-step reconsideration cannot repair persistent errors. The factorial design is not a formal causal-identification argument.

The main grid covers 3B–14B open models. Above 14B we ran only Qwen2.5-32B, and only the stay-wrong battery, its probe, and retrieval. The drop in verbalized confidence is a Qwen2.5-7B result in our grid, and we do not generalize it to other families. Qwen3 needs the answer extracted after </think> (Online Resource 1, Sect. C).

section: Sample size of the key cell.
text: The central stay-wrong analysis on Qwen2.5-7B rests on n=81 items (80 distinct questions) from one dataset. The preregistered replications extend this to 230, 160, 139, and 61 items on four models, but the turn-3 battery and the retrieval study cover TriviaQA only.

section: The persistence readout is defined by a probe.
text: s_{t} is an operational quantity: a frozen readout fitted on T1 states. We make claims about how it behaves when we intervene, not about what the model “believes”. We report no activation-steering or patching results, so we cannot say whether s_{t} is causally involved in producing the answer. The single-turn studies that do steer Kumaran (2026); Miao and Ungar (2026) use different readouts and tasks, so their causal results do not transfer to ours. Llama-3-8B probe states in the main analyses were pooled over the raw generated answer tokens, including any repetition after the leaked role header. In a post hoc rerun on cut answers, stay-wrong \Delta probe stays positive on every Llama unit we could test but is much smaller (TriviaQA persist 0.865\to 0.333, NQ 0.399\to 0.034, HotpotQA 0.238\to 0.030; Online Resource 1, Sect. J). Llama magnitudes from the main analyses should be read as upper bounds. The post hoc shuffled-label control (Section 6) and the held-out-question rerun (Section 6) leave the stay-wrong rise standing on Qwen2.5-7B, with Llama-3-8B on cut answers as support. On Qwen2.5-14B, Mistral, Phi-4, and Qwen2-7B it does not hold on held-out questions, so the in-sample \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{err}}=24/24 overstates how general it is.

The primary contain matcher credits answers that name the gold only to reject it, which inflates Mistral’s gold uptake in particular. PopQA is omitted because the matcher and output format failed. Answer labels come from the matcher, an LLM judge, and model reads; post hoc, two people labelled a blind 300 -row V2 sample with Cohen’s \kappa{=}0.86 on 272 clear pairs (Online Resource 1, Sect. H). Replication and retrieval results are also reported under contain, judge, and model-read labels, and the Mistral results after a rejection audit (Online Resource 1, Sects. H and I). Under these alternative labels Llama’s empty-elicit arm reaches the 0.15 threshold (Section 6.1). Table 5 reports ECE for all four measures on one message type of one model \times dataset cell. We do not report ECE as a grid-wide result, and we claim neither a win nor a loss against MTCal.

In short-answer question answering, an LLM’s confidence in a conversation is not one belief waiting for a better estimator. What the user supplies (an answer string) moves the answer. How the user phrases the turn (re-asking, agreeing, or accusing) does not. Four common confidence measures respond to different parts of the same turn, and on Qwen2.5-7B a frozen hidden-state readout follows the answer the model keeps rather than its truth. Errors that survive one re-ask are not undone by re-asking, resetting, or offering abstention. A correct answer string repairs them, including one inside real retrieved evidence. For practitioners our data suggest a heuristic that still needs end-to-end testing: before relying on evidence to correct a model, check that it contains the answer.

Competence-Based Evaluation of Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought impressive performance across diverse tasks; however, shortcomings remain in logical reasoning, including inconsistencies under linguistic variation. To improve the reasoning capacity of LLMs, we must be able to accurately measure their reasoning capacity. Current benchmarks primarily report single accuracy numbers on selected reasoning tasks. Such a performance-based evaluation methodology says little about a model's generalization capacity in reasoning. To address this limitation, we argue for a different evaluation paradigm, called competence-based evaluation (CBE), which tests whether models reliably apply the same competence across a family of problems. A parameterized generator scales complexity while keeping the required competence fixed, and matched answer-preserving presentations test correctness beyond one formulation. We instantiate CBE on elementary ordering tasks, scaling input size while varying presentations of the same ordering rule. Across six GPT and Qwen models, performance is reasonably good over bounded complexity ranges, but even strong models fail the competence condition across the tested family. Chain-of-thought and GRPO extend strong performance without resolving all tested failures; supervised LoRA shows little held-out transfer. CBE provides diagnostic profiles and an evaluation protocol that can grow with future models.

Recent large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance on many reasoning benchmarks, yet growing evidence suggests that high benchmark accuracy does not necessarily imply robust reasoning ability (Song et al., 2026). A single accuracy number on a static test set conflates many things: language understanding, memorization, shortcut exploitation, and genuine reasoning. It tells us little about what a model can actually do. Recent work has made this conflation increasingly hard to ignore. Benchmarks designed to test logical reasoning can reward other strategies: Chung et al. (2025) report higher GPT-3.5 scores on ReClor and LogiQA2 when the prompt asks it to avoid logical reasoning, illustrating that accuracy alone need not diagnose the intended competence. Models that appear to reason well on standard test sets show systematic drops under controlled perturbations (Mirzadeh et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Sanyal et al., 2022), and reasoning models can collapse as complexity grows (Lin et al., 2025; Shojaee et al., 2025). The natural reading is that reasoning is brittle, but this conflates two questions: whether the model fails to derive a conclusion from a fixed problem representation, or constructs a different representation in the first place.
Measuring performance on a fixed test set is insufficient to tell these apart, and therefore insufficient to characterize a model’s reasoning capability.

We argue for a different evaluation paradigm: competence-based evaluation. Drawing on Chomsky’s distinction between knowledge of a language and its use (Chomsky, 1965), we adapt the competence/performance distinction to reasoning: underlying task knowledge and observed behavior on specific instances. CBE tests reliable application of that knowledge through an explicit behavioral condition. We also draw on the cognitive-science account given by Stenning and van Lambalgen (2008) for human reasoning, which distinguishes reasoning to an interpretation, establishing a problem’s representation and the logic governing it, from reasoning from an interpretation, deriving conclusions within that form. This motivates separating the task’s latent structure from its realization in language.

A competence claim concerns the family of problems governed by the same rule, including larger instances and equivalent formulations. Exhaustively enumerating that family is infeasible. Concretely, instead of measuring accuracy on a fixed test set, we define a parameterized problem generator for a target reasoning competence and test a necessary behavioral condition: the model must answer correctly across the generated instances and their answer-preserving presentations. The evaluation target is a problem family whose complexity can grow while the required competence remains the same. The generator exposes the assumptions of that family and permits evaluation at new scales under the same criterion. A finite experiment can expose violations of the condition; success supports only the evaluated coverage.

CBE characterizes the model’s competence boundary, the region in the generator’s parameter space where correct, invariant behavior deteriorates and exposes biases that aggregate accuracy can conceal. By holding logical form fixed and varying surface form across matched presentations, the evaluation produces a competence profile rather than a single score. Paired outputs reveal whether correct answers survive equivalent formulations. They do not by themselves locate a failure in either internal reasoning stage.

This approach yields several advantages at once. Fresh generation reduces dependence on particular published test items, although familiarity with the generator or learned shortcuts remains possible. It produces richer diagnostics than a single accuracy number: the competence profile reveals where a model fails and under which conditions, including problem size, distractors, and equivalent reformulations. Additionally, as models improve, the evaluation naturally extends by pushing the parameter range further, rather than requiring an entirely new benchmark. Existing generators and consistency tests supply important precedents (§ 2); CBE makes the target competence, its family, and its correctness condition explicit within one evaluation design.

We instantiate the competence-based evaluation framework on ordering tasks, a fundamental reasoning primitive involving transitivity and comparison. Ordering is well suited as a first instantiation: the ordering rule is unchanged for any finite number of entities, so an extremely simple task supports a scalable problem family. The generator controls the latent order and renders matched presentations that vary premise order, converse phrasing, names order, and relation vocabulary (Figure 1). Failure on this elementary family violates the specified competence condition. Chain length scales input and presentation load; endpoint queries admit a shortcut and do not isolate multistep inference (§ 4.1). Appendix C illustrates adoption of the framework by Horn-clause inference.

Our results show why the distinction between performance and competence matters. Even strong models fail the CBE condition across the tested ordering family, while performing reasonably well over bounded complexity ranges. On front/behind at n=1024, GPT-4.1 retains 77.5% original-prompt accuracy but answers both matched presentations correctly on only 56.8% of valid pairs. Vocabulary changes alter model rankings. Chain-of-thought extends strong performance, and GRPO improves held-out transfer, but the tested interventions leave substantial failures. Improved scores can therefore reflect an expanded range of successful performance without demonstrating competence across the family.

(1) Competence-based evaluation as a general framework. We formalize the shift from performance on selected instances to a competence condition on a specified problem family, through a parameterized task generator, presentation set, model, correctness criterion, and competence condition (§ 3). (2) The CBE Ordering Benchmark. We instantiate the framework on an elementary ordering task with precisely controlled latent structure and matched presentations. Its size parameter extends the evaluation while retaining the same ordering rule (§ 4). (3) A multidimensional competence analysis. We evaluate six base models and reasoning/training interventions, showing where correctness fails under complexity and presentation changes (§ 5 –§ 6). The analysis distinguishes gains in aggregate performance from gains in the range of correct, invariant behavior, and provides diagnostic evidence that can guide future model development.

We position CBE relative to fixed test sets, generated complexity evaluations, and invariance tests. The distinction is the evaluation target: a defined competence over a scalable problem family, with correctness required across equivalent presentations. Appendix D compares the designs by axis.

ReClor, LogiQA, AR-LSAT, and FOLIO assess reasoning on curated or annotated problems (Yu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2022; Han et al., 2024a). DivLogicEval uses counterintuitive content to reduce shortcuts (Chung et al., 2025), while BIG-bench logical_deduction generates linear-ordering problems at several sizes (Srivastava et al., 2023). These datasets provide valuable samples of task performance. CBE organizes correctness across equivalent presentations and sizes around an explicit competence condition on a specified problem family.

RuleTaker, ProofWriter, CLUTRR, and PrOntoQA generate deductive or relational instances with controlled structure or depth (Clark et al., 2020; Tafjord et al., 2021; Sinha et al., 2019; Saparov and He, 2023). DyVal, functional benchmarks, NPHardEval, and ZebraLogic likewise generate instances or vary complexity (Zhu et al., 2024; Srivastava et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2025). ReCogLab is especially close: it generates relational reasoning, including transitive comparison, with entity count, reasoning length, and textual features as parameters (Liu et al., 2025). These works establish generation and complexity scaling as useful evaluation tools. CBE couples that control to an explicit competence condition on matched presentations and evaluates the resulting profile across the family.

CheckList and metamorphic testing prescribe relations between outputs on transformed inputs (Ribeiro et al., 2020; Chen et al., 1998; Segura et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2026). ParaRel reports consistency and Consistent-Acc, correctness across all paraphrases (Elazar et al., 2021); BECEL shows that equal accuracy can hide pairwise inconsistency (Jang et al., 2022). RobustLR, GSM-Symbolic, GSM-Plus, and premise-order studies expose sensitivity to controlled changes (Sanyal et al., 2022; Mirzadeh et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024). These are direct precedents for the paired measurements. CBE’s distinction is to make such requirements part of the competence definition and trace their satisfaction as complexity grows within one fixed task family. A robustness score on a chosen set of examples, or an accuracy curve alone, leaves that combined question unanswered.

section: A Competence and Its Problem Family
text: CBE has five components: a parameterized generator G_{\theta}, a presentation set \Pi, a model \mathcal{M}, a correctness criterion, and a competence condition. The target competence fixes the problem rule. Parameters \theta vary instance size or presentation load without changing that rule. The generator draws a latent instance z; an exact oracle supplies y^{*}(z). Each \pi_{k}\in\Pi(z) preserves the answer, y^{*}(\pi_{k}(z))=y^{*}(z).

section: A Competence and Its Problem Family
text: Write C_{k}=\mathbf{1}[\mathcal{M}(\pi_{k}(z))=y^{*}(z)]. The necessary behavioral condition for competence on an instance is C_{0}=C_{1}=\cdots=C_{K}=1. The family-level condition requires this behavior throughout the specified instance and complexity space. A finite evaluation can expose failures of this operational condition; it cannot certify competence exhaustively or identify their internal cause. Equivalent presentations prevent success on one formulation from serving as the entire competence test.

For two presentations with valid binary answers, let R be the probability of both correct, D both wrong, and U exactly one correct. These robust-correct, shared-wrong, and presentation-dependent masses satisfy R+D+U=1,\quad\bar{A}=R+U/2,\quad\iota=R+D, where \bar{A} is mean accuracy and \iota is invariance. The competence profile is \theta\mapsto(R,D,U)(\theta). Accuracy can conceal offsetting changes, and agreement can include shared errors. Appendix A gives the elementary identities and marginal bounds.

We also report \kappa_{n}=(\iota_{n}-\iota_{e})/(1-\iota_{e}), where \iota_{e}=q^{2}+(1-q)^{2} and q is the pooled yes-rate within n. This discounts a common-bias independent-answer reference. It is undefined for constant outputs and does not by itself identify independence or a failure mechanism. The summary \bar{\kappa} averages \kappa_{n} over the grid.

Profiles locate regions of deterioration, rather than a single threshold crossing. Accuracy counts invalid responses wrong on all prompts; pair metrics use jointly parsed answers. All profile identities use common support. McNemar tests marginal accuracy differences, including format failures, with Holm correction. Paired bootstrap intervals resample matched instances. Decoding settings and statistical details appear in Appendix B.

An instance is a total order over n named entities, described by its n-1 adjacent comparisons. A yes/no query concerns the two endpoints. Query direction and gold answer form four balanced cells. Names and premises are shuffled independently of the latent order. The ordering rule is unchanged as n increases. We evaluate n\in\{4,8,\ldots,1024\} in the base study. Figure 1 shows generation and paired scoring.

The original presentation uses the forward phrase, such as “Amy is in front of Bob”. Its equivalent rewrites selected links as “Bob is behind Amy” and reshuffles the names list and premises. Controls separate reshuffling from rewriting. A catalog renders the same latent instances in 31 vocabularies across six relation families. Negation preserves answers under the stated strict total order; distractors over disjoint entities add irrelevant input.

Ordering supplies a scalable test of reliable application of the same rule. Here n measures input size and presentation load: endpoint queries admit a source/sink shortcut using an incident premise. Success need not reconstruct the chain. Failures violate the specified competence condition, but do not isolate a multistep inference limit or distinguish inference failures from retrieval and presentation handling. Appendix C illustrates adoption of CBE for Horn-clause inference.

The base evaluation uses seed-1 instances, 200 pairs per n, 50 per query cell, randomly selected rewrite positions, and identical latent instances across models, vocabularies, and presentation controls. The six base models are GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, Qwen3.5-27B, and Qwen3.5-9B; GPT-5 uses minimal reasoning effort and Qwen thinking is disabled. Qwen models cover the full catalog and GPT models six spatial-line vocabularies. Prompts request yes/no answers under provider-default sampling. Caps and parsing rules appear in Appendix B, and decoding-variability controls in Appendix H.

Reasoning-effort, distractor, and negation studies use 200 matched pairs per complexity level. All effort levels receive identical prompts within each condition. The separate n=2048 block changes the presentation distribution, so its failures cannot be attributed solely to length. Additional models and earlier evaluations are in Appendices E and F.
We read performance through accuracy, invariance, and robust correctness. Matched comparisons vary input size, vocabulary, presentation factors, and reasoning effort.

GPT-4.1 and GPT-5 perform well on shorter front/behind chains. Through n=128, original accuracy remains at least 94.0% and invariance at least 87.9%. At n=1024, original accuracy is 77.5% and 76.0%, but invariance is only 67.3% and 67.0%, with \kappa_{n}=0.30 and 0.16. The smaller GPT models and Qwen3.5-27B show earlier deterioration: invariance drops from 87.0 to 72.5, 85.5 to 69.0, and 95.0 to 79.0 between n=4 and 8, respectively. These profiles support reasonably good performance over bounded ranges, with clear failures of the competence condition across the full tested range.

Figure 2 makes the difference explicit. On the common valid-pair support, GPT-4.1’s mean accuracy falls from 98.3% at n=4 to 73.1% at n=1024, while invariance falls from 97.5% to 67.3% and robust correctness from 97.0% to 56.8%. At the latter level, nearly a third of pairs are presentation-dependent (U=32.7\%). The pattern is not a universal ordering of decline rates: weak models can acquire shared wrong answers that increase agreement. Qwen3.5-9B, for example, reaches 75.3% raw invariance at n=8 but has \bar{\kappa}=0.00 over the grid. Correctness and invariance must therefore be interpreted jointly.

Marginal gaps also hide symmetric instability. GPT-5-mini has pooled original/equivalent accuracy of 70.0/72.0% and no significant McNemar difference, yet R/D/U=54.6/12.6/32.9\%. Its discordant counts are 278/314: substantial correct-to-wrong changes are offset by changes in the reverse direction. A small accuracy gap therefore does not establish stable task performance.

Switching only front/behind to left/right changes the rankings (Table 1). GPT-4.1’s original accuracy falls from 93.1% to 70.9% and \bar{\kappa} from 0.75 to 0.33. Qwen3.5-27B instead gains, from \bar{\kappa}=0.37 to 0.54. For GPT-4.1 on left/right, the original presentation elicits “yes” on 78% of prompts despite balanced gold answers; equivalent-presentation accuracy exceeds original accuracy at every n\geq 8. This is behavioral evidence of a vocabulary-dependent answer bias.

The full catalog shows that the base pair alone is insufficient to characterize the family. Qwen3.5-27B’s family-mean original accuracy and \bar{\kappa} are 79.6%/0.38 for spatial-line relations and 87.2%/0.58 for comparatives; the corresponding 9B values are 61.0%/0.09 and 75.7%/0.30. Across relations, original accuracy spans 27 points and invariance 23 points for a single model. Nonce comparative terms can be handled well (27B accuracy/invariance 87.1/87.6%), while nonce direction terms yield only 54.6% equivalent accuracy and \bar{\kappa}\leq 0.03 for every tested model, even with the converse rule supplied. Stating the rule is insufficient in this condition; these results do not establish that lexical familiarity is necessary for every way of learning the task.

Reshuffling alone changes GPT accuracy by at most 1.4 points. Fully rewriting premises costs GPT-4.1 and GPT-5 a further 9.1/11.2 accuracy points and 12.4/9.7 invariance points relative to reshuffling alone (Table 9). The effects of reordering and converse phrasing differ, although both preserve the answer.

Additional matched controls add distractors or use negation (Table 10). For GPT-5-mini, distractors produce 14.8% correct-to-wrong changes and 14.6% changes in the reverse direction, leaving aggregate performance almost unchanged. Negation reduces agreement in all four tested models; for Qwen3.5-27B, syntactic and negated-presentation agreement are 75.2 and 60.2%. Both controls reinforce the need to follow matched instances.

Figure 3 shows how elicited chain-of-thought changes the complexity profile. On matched front/behind prompts, moving GPT-5.4 from none to low increases original accuracy by 20.6 points and invariance by 16.8 points (95% paired interval 14.7–18.8). Medium and high effort maintain near-perfect aggregate performance through n=1024, while low-effort invariance falls to 78.0% at that level. Thus added reasoning extends the range supported by the evaluation.

It does not establish competence across all tested conditions. In the separate n=2048 block, high effort attains 94.0% original accuracy but 65.0% equivalent accuracy and 67.0% invariance, without truncation. This condition also changes the presentation distribution (Appendix B), so the failure cannot be attributed solely to input length. Effort levels remain matched within the condition. Equivalent prompts use fewer reasoning tokens than originals at low and medium effort but more at high effort. Neither additional effort nor available completion budget ensures correct, invariant answers under the tested settings.

Qwen3.5-27B thinking results show a different limitation. With a 24k-token budget, accuracy among finished answers is 100.0/99.6% and invariance among jointly finished pairs is 99.9%. All-prompt accuracy is 87.0/79.1%, and strict invariance is 75.4% when unfinished pairs count as disagreements. Conditional success and budget-limited coverage must both be reported.

We compare supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) as LoRA interventions on Qwen3.5-9B (Hu et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024). Front/behind is held out. SFT uses auxiliary relation data, paired presentations, or paired presentations with a consistency loss. GRPO training excludes spatial-line vocabularies to evaluate transfer to held-out relation words.

GRPO samples G=4 answers per prompt, with four presentations of one instance in each batch. A sampled answer receives reward r_{i}=c_{i}+\tfrac{1}{2}b_{i}, where c_{i} is one for a correct answer and zero otherwise, and b_{i} is a nonnegative bonus for cross-presentation agreement above a reference derived from the instance’s sampled yes/no balance. Unparseable answers receive zero reward. Rewards are centered and scaled within each prompt’s sample group to form policy advantages. Appendix B.3 gives the full reward definition and training hyperparameters.

section: SFT learns the training relations but transfers little.
text: The supervised variants reach 100% on their held-in relations. On front/behind, invariance remains 56.6–58.3%, compared with 57.3% for the base model; the cross-relation paired change is -0.4 points with interval [-3.5,+2.5]. The consistency term produces little additional held-out improvement. The larger-model SFT replicate is in Appendix F.

section: GRPO improves transfer under the tested recipe.
text: Across twelve clean held-out relations, GRPO raises invariance from 60.0% to 83.5% and \bar{\kappa} from 0.10 to 0.60. On the nine relations with no partial phrase overlap, invariance increases from 59.9% to 82.1%. This supports transfer beyond the training vocabulary. The SFT and GRPO data, objectives, and budgets differ, so the comparison does not establish a general ranking of training methods.

Figure 4 resolves the gains by chain length. On front/behind, GRPO increases original/equivalent accuracy to 81.2/75.1% and invariance to 73.3%. At n=256,512,1024, its chance-corrected invariance is -0.12,-0.11,-0.20, respectively. Thus improved pooled performance and cross-vocabulary transfer coexist with substantial long-chain presentation failures. Training extends measured performance without meeting the competence condition across the tested range.

The competence profile distinguishes correct answers across presentations from agreement on an incorrect default. A higher aggregate score can reflect a wider successful range while substantial failures persist elsewhere in the family. The chain-of-thought and training studies illustrate this distinction.

Open-weight interventions provide supporting evidence. In Qwen3-8B, ablating selected heads raises invariance from 81.0% to 93.0% while original/equivalent accuracy falls from 64.5/59.5% to 59.0/52.0%. Stable answers can therefore accompany reduced task signal. In Qwen3.5-9B, short-chain answers remain linearly decodable despite biased outputs; longer-chain equivalents show reduced decodability at a measured layer and position. GRPO strengthens the measured signal relative to the answer default. These results characterize possible contributors without establishing a complete mechanism. Appendix I reports the probes and interventions.

CBE turns such observations into a reusable testing strategy: state the competence, specify a family with controlled complexity, certify answer-preserving presentations, and report where correctness survives those changes. This makes model comparisons and intervention gains interpretable in terms of the behavior they actually support.

We proposed competence-based evaluation as a methodology for evaluating LLM reasoning through a problem family. Its five components make the target competence and its necessary behavioral condition explicit. The ordering instantiation tests reliable application of the same rule across growing inputs and equivalent presentations; it does not isolate an inference-depth limit.

Even strong models fail that condition across the tested ordering family, despite reasonably good performance over bounded complexity ranges. Accuracy alone conceals additional deterioration and symmetric changes across equivalent presentations. Chain-of-thought extends successful performance, and GRPO improves held-out transfer under the tested recipes, but documented failures remain. Better performance therefore does not establish competence across the family.
These profiles can guide model development by locating gains across sizes and presentations, while benchmark designers extend coverage under the same competence condition.

The intended impact is an evaluation practice that grows with models: generate fresh instances, extend the complexity range, and test the same competence under matched presentations. CBE provides a reusable way to distinguish an expanded range of success from a demonstrated ability to handle the task throughout the evaluated family.

CBE evaluates competence within a specified problem family. Finite samples can reveal failures but cannot certify correctness throughout an unbounded family. Our ordering study and Horn-clause adoption example leave broader reasoning competences untested. Extending CBE to richer tasks and wider presentation coverage would clarify how its diagnostic profiles generalize.

Chain length measures input size and presentation load; endpoint queries admit a shortcut. Our ordering results therefore do not isolate multistep inference capacity. Length and presentation changes are also not always separated. Future generators could independently control derivation depth, distracting information, and linguistic realization.

Behavioral profiles and linear probes do not uniquely identify internal reasoning processes. Paired metrics also condition on valid answers, so agreement must be read alongside completion coverage. Broader sampling and causal interventions could connect systematic behavioral failures to their mechanisms.

The reasoning and training interventions studied here leave many routes to improved competence unexplored. Their gains do not establish a general ranking of training methods, particularly when data and budgets differ. Matched comparisons across training objectives, model families, and compute budgets would help identify which approaches extend correct, invariant behavior beyond the trained range.

CBE is intended to support research on reasoning competence. A potential societal risk is treating success on a generated family as evidence of general reasoning ability or readiness for deployment in consequential settings. Conversely, failures on this family should not be taken as evidence that a model lacks all useful reasoning abilities. We mitigate these interpretation risks by specifying the competence condition and evaluation coverage, reporting correctness alongside invariance, and keeping conclusions scoped to the tested family. Repeated optimization against a known generator may also encourage benchmark-specific strategies; fresh instances alone do not establish transfer to other reasoning tasks.

The reported ordering instances assign fictional relations to generic first-name labels or random strings, and gold answers are computed from the generated structure. These relations do not describe identifiable people’s actual attributes. No human participants or crowdworker annotations are used to establish the task labels. The English templates and name vocabulary do not constitute demographic or multilingual coverage. Although some templates concern attributes such as wealth or seniority, they should not be interpreted as claims about real people or population groups.

Model inference, extended reasoning traces, and adapter training consume computational resources and energy. We reuse pretrained models and train LoRA adapters, but do not claim that these choices establish a low environmental footprint. We report evaluation and training settings in Appendix B; aggregate energy consumption and carbon emissions were not measured. Reporting competence gains alongside their computational cost is an important direction for future evaluations.

DUALVIEW: Leveraging Broad and Output-Specific Evidence for LLM-based Multi-Output Text Regression. While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. DualView first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. These improvements extend across individual output dimensions and persist even with limited training data. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.

Text regression aims to predict continuous numerical targets from textual inputs. While recent work has largely focused on predicting scalar targets (Nafar et al., 2025; Lukasik et al., 2025; Su and Lease, 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Akhauri et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Zuo et al., 2026; Chung et al., 2026), predicting multiple numerical targets for the same input— multi-output text regression (MOTR)—remains less explored.

Building better MOTR systems can benefit fine-grained evaluations of generated text, where standard protocols assess free-form outputs along multiple dimensions such as fluency, factuality, coherence, and relevance (Liu et al., 2023b; Hashemi et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a). More specialized tasks exhibit the same multi-output structure: machine translation can be evaluated for accuracy, fluency, and style (Popov et al., 2025; Shayegh et al., 2025), generated code for correctness and efficiency (Qiu et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026), and research ideas for novelty, relevance, and feasibility (Si et al., 2025; Baek et al., 2025). Figure 1 illustrates the latter two examples.

However, developing general-purpose MOTR methods presents several challenges. First, existing text regression methods often fine-tune all LLM parameters, making them costly to scale to larger models (Lukasik et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026b). Second, training one scalar predictor for each output scales adaptation costs with the number of targets, motivating more compact multi-output predictors (Do et al., 2024a). Third, existing supervised MOTR methods often employ specialized architectures that may be less suitable across heterogeneous domains. For example, GAT-AES (Li and Ng, 2025) uses handcrafted features and a fully connected graph that exploits strong correlations among essay-quality criteria. However, this architecture is less suitable for code quality estimation, where essay-specific features do not apply, and targets such as code correctness and peak memory may not be strongly correlated.

In this work, we propose DualView, a supervised MOTR approach that shifts specialization from domain-specific prediction architectures to evidence extraction. Specifically, DualView extracts complementary broad and output-specific representations from an LLM. A unified dual-branch model leverages these representations to predict all output dimensions, sharing predictors across targets instead of training separate models (see Figure 2). Finally, by freezing the LLM, DualView trains only lightweight modules and scales better to larger LLMs.

We evaluate DualView on five quality estimation tasks spanning summarization (Min et al., 2025), machine translation (Popov et al., 2025), code generation (Ouyang et al., 2026), dialogue (Kirk et al., 2024), and research ideation (Lu et al., 2026). DualView outperforms seven supervised state-of-the-art regression baselines across the five datasets and eight LLM backbones (8–122B).
