Relative to the second-best method, GAT-AES (Li and Ng, 2025), DualView improves aggregate Pearson correlation by 18.4% and NRMSE by 2.8% (Table 1). Output-level results further show that DualView outperforms the strongest supervised baselines on nearly all targets (Figure 3).

By freezing the LLM and sharing predictors across targets, DualView requires only 5.1K–57.4K fitted parameters, compared with 82–1842 \times more for the strongest supervised baselines (Table 2). Training-data efficiency experiments show that DualView continues to outperform the strongest baselines even with limited supervision (Figure 4). DualView outperforms Gemini 3.1 Pro under zero- and few-shot LLMaaJ (Table 3).

Existing supervised, LLM-based text regression methods broadly fall into three families. i) Autoregressive decoding generates numerical values as text (Vacareanu et al., 2024; Song and Bahri, 2025; Chen et al., 2026b). ii) Regression-aware inference derives point estimates from the model’s output distribution under a regression objective (Lukasik et al., 2024; Lukasik et al., 2025). iii) Predictive heads map LLM hidden representations directly to continuous values (Tang et al., 2025; Su and Lease, 2026).

Our work differs in three key respects. 1) While most supervised methods focus on scalar prediction, we study the joint prediction of multiple numerical targets. 2) Existing multi-output methods often introduce specialized prediction architectures such as target-specific experts and graph-based interactions (Wang and Liu, 2025; Li and Ng, 2025). In contrast, DualView shifts specialization to evidence extraction, using simple predictors over complementary representations from a frozen LLM. 3) Recent supervised methods only evaluate LLMs with up to 32B parameters (Su and Lease, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a), whereas we experiment with LLMs up to 122B parameters.

Fine-grained text evaluation (also known as multi-dimensional, multi-criteria, or multi-trait evaluation) assesses the same text input along multiple numerical axes (Fabbri et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023b). By assessing distinct aspects of quality, fine-grained evaluation helps identify specific weaknesses, reveal performance trade-offs, and guide targeted revisions (Hashemi et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025; Kola et al., 2026). However, obtaining human annotations or execution-based metrics (e.g., code correctness and peak memory) across multiple dimensions can be expensive, motivating automated evaluation methods that learn from limited supervision. We show that DualView consistently outperforms supervised baselines even with as few as 64 training examples (\lx@sectionsign E.3).

Multi-task learning (MTL) trains a single model to perform multiple related tasks simultaneously (Ding et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026). Multi-output text regression is closely related but imposes a more structured prediction problem. Whereas MTL may combine tasks with different inputs, outputs, or objectives, MOTR predicts the same set of continuous targets from the same text input. This shifts the focus from knowledge transfer across heterogeneous tasks to balancing shared and target-specific information within the same prediction problem. Regression-capable MTL methods such as UniSO-N (Tan et al., 2025) and MT-ICL (Zhu et al., 2026a) provide general mechanisms for sharing across tasks, but do not specifically exploit this same-input, fixed-target structure. In contrast, DualView exploits this structure directly through a dual-branch architecture that leverages complementary evidence extracted from frozen LLMs. \lx@sectionsign B details additional comparisons.

Let \mathcal{S}=\{(x_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} denote a training set of textual inputs x_{i}\in\mathcal{X} paired with target vectors \mathbf{y}_{i}=(y_{i1},\ldots,y_{iD})\in\mathbb{R}^{D}. Let \mathcal{Q}=(d_{1},\ldots,d_{D}) denote an ordered set of target descriptions, where d_{j} specifies the meaning and numerical scale of target j. Given \mathcal{Q}, multi-output text regression aims to learn a predictor f_{\mathrm{REG}}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{D} that jointly predicts all D targets for each input.

Following Tang et al. (2025) and Su and Lease (2026), we standardize each target using its training-set mean \mu_{j} and standard deviation \sigma_{j}: z_{ij}=\frac{y_{ij}-\mu_{j}}{\sigma_{j}},\qquad\widehat{y}_{ij}=\mu_{j}+\sigma_{j}\widehat{z}_{ij}. All predictors are trained on standardized targets. At inference, predictions are rescaled by \sigma_{j} and shifted by \mu_{j} to restore their original scales.

Rather than tailoring architectures to each domain, DualView applies simple predictors to complementary evidence extracted from a frozen LLM. We first extract a broad representation to capture evidence relevant to all targets. Since different targets may depend on different aspects of the input, we also extract output-specific representations to identify cues particularly relevant to each target.

Let s(\mathcal{Q}) denote a shared task instruction specifying all prediction targets, and let q(d_{j}) denote a short instruction requesting only an assessment of target j. For each input x_{i}, we construct a broad prompt and D focused prompts: \displaystyle P_{i}^{b} \displaystyle=[s(\mathcal{Q});x_{i}], \displaystyle P_{ij}^{f} \displaystyle=[s(\mathcal{Q});x_{i};q(d_{j})].
For the broad view, we mean-pool model hidden states across all tokens of the broad prompt: \mathbf{J}_{i}=\frac{1}{|P_{i}^{b}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|P_{i}^{b}|}\mathbf{h}_{t}(P_{i}^{b})\in\mathbb{R}^{H}.

For the focused view, we extract the hidden state at the last token of each focused prompt, immediately before generation: \mathbf{C}_{ij}=\mathbf{h}_{|P_{ij}^{f}|}(P_{ij}^{f})\in\mathbb{R}^{H}. Here, we use the final hidden state rather than mean pooling because most tokens precede the target-specific instruction and are shared across targets. Averaging their representations thus could dilute the effect of the focused instruction.

The broad and focused prompts share the task instructions, target descriptions, and input. We therefore cache the shared prefix’s model states (e.g., attention KV pairs) and reuse them across prompts. Rather than independently evaluating D+1 complete prompts, we process the shared prefix once and evaluate only the remaining suffix of each prompt. See \lx@sectionsign C for details on extraction and normalization.

The broad branch predicts all D targets jointly from \mathbf{J}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{H} using a linear predictor: \widehat{\mathbf{z}}^{\,\mathrm{b}}_{i}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{b}}^{\top}\mathbf{J}_{i}. An unconstrained \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{b}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times D} effectively fits a separate linear predictor for each target. To obtain a compact multivariate predictor, we adopt reduced-rank regression (Izenman, 1975), factorizing \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{b}}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}, where \mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times k} and \mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times D}, with k<D. Each target j uses a coefficient vector \mathbf{A}\mathbf{b}_{j}, where \mathbf{b}_{j} is the j -th column of \mathbf{B}. Thus, all targets are predicted from the same k linear projections of \mathbf{J}_{i}, but each target assigns different weights to these projections. This factorization provides a compact multivariate predictor by sharing k linear projections across outputs.

The focused branch uses a shared linear predictor to estimate target j from \mathbf{C}_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{H}: \widehat{z}^{\,\mathrm{f}}_{ij}=\mathbf{v}^{\top}\mathbf{C}_{ij}. Because \mathbf{C}_{ij} captures evidence specific to target j, a shared coefficient vector \mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{H} can produce distinct predictions for different output targets. Sharing one predictor also allows supervision from all targets to inform a common scoring function, while requiring fewer parameters than fitting separate predictors for each target.

Notably, the two branches serve complementary purposes: the broad branch learns common predictive directions across different targets, while the focused branch pools supervision across targets to score their specialized evidence.

We jointly train the broad and focused predictors to exploit their complementary evidence. The final prediction for target j combines both branches: \widehat{z}_{ij}=\mathbf{J}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{b}_{j}+\mathbf{v}^{\top}\mathbf{C}_{ij}+a_{j}, where a_{j} is a target-specific intercept. We minimize regularized squared error on the combined predictions, subject to \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{b}})\leq k: \displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{b}},\,\mathbf{v},\,\mathbf{a}} \displaystyle\frac{1}{ND}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{D}(z_{ij}-\widehat{z}_{ij})^{2} \displaystyle+\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}\|\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{b}}\|_{F}^{2}+\lambda_{\mathrm{f}}\|\mathbf{v}\|_{2}^{2}, where \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{b}}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}, \mathbf{a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{D}), and \lambda_{\mathrm{b}},\lambda_{\mathrm{f}} control regularization. We optimize this objective through alternating minimization. Starting from a reduced-rank ridge solution with \mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}, we alternate between fitting the shared predictor to the broad predictor’s residuals and refitting the broad predictor to the focused predictor’s residuals. We repeat until convergence and select the rank and regularization parameters using the validation split.

We assess DualView over eight LLM backbones: Gemma 4 E4B and 31B (Gemma Team, 2026), Qwen3.5 9B and 122B-A10B (Qwen Team, 2026), Qwen3.6 27B, Llama 3.3 70B Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen2.5 72B Instruct (Qwen Team, 2025), and GPT OSS 120B (OpenAI, 2025). We freeze all LLM backbones and fit only lightweight regression predictors. We further compare against Gemini 3.1 Pro in \lx@sectionsign 5.4.

We evaluate DualView on five fine-grained quality estimation tasks: MSumBench for summarization (Min et al., 2025), RATE for translation (Popov et al., 2025), CreativeEval for research ideation (Lu et al., 2026), DSCodeBench for code generation (Ouyang et al., 2026), and PRISM for dialogue (Kirk et al., 2024). \lx@sectionsign D.2 reports dataset split sizes and target ranges (Table 8).

We evaluate against seven supervised baselines: RELISH (Su and Lease, 2026), GenRe2 (Chen et al., 2026b), T-MES (Wang and Liu, 2025), GAT-AES (Li and Ng, 2025), SAJA (Kola et al., 2026), UniSO-N (Tan et al., 2025), and MT-ICL (Zhu et al., 2026a). We use frozen LLMs for all supervised methods and adapt their prediction modules to the multi-output setting where necessary (§ D.3). We also report zero- and four-shot LLM-as-a-judge prompting baselines.

We report Pearson correlation and normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE). Following prior work (Lin et al., 2023; Allison et al., 2023; Holzmüller et al., 2024), we normalize RMSE by the training-set standard deviation to fairly compare across datasets and targets with different scales. We additionally report Spearman correlation in the appendix to assess rank-order agreement. \lx@sectionsign D.4 provides further details.

Table 1 shows that DualView achieves the strongest aggregate performance across five datasets and eight LLM backbones. Compared with GAT-AES, the strongest supervised baseline, DualView improves Pearson correlation by 18.4% and NRMSE by 2.8%. The substantially higher NRMSE of zero- and few-shot prompting reflects large out-of-range predictions.

Since our MOTR setting emphasizes predicting multiple targets per dataset, a robust method should ideally perform well on all targets. While Table 1 ’s results usefully summarize predictive performance on average, simple arithmetic averaging across target dimensions risks strong performance on some dimensions masking weak performance on others. Thus, Figure 3 compares DualView with the three strongest supervised baselines across all 21 output targets and reports Pearson correlations macro-averaged over eight LLMs. DualView achieves the strongest performance on 20 of 21 targets, with MSumBench faithfulness effectively tied at 0.675.

Figure 3 still averages performance across LLMs, which can hide inconsistent results for individual LLM–target pairs. Table 14 in \lx@sectionsign E.1.1 reports two additional fine-grained measures against the three strongest supervised baselines. The strict win rate is the percentage of LLM–target pairs on which a method outperforms all competitors. The worst-output gap is the largest performance difference from the best method across targets within each dataset–LLM setting, averaged across settings. DualView achieves the highest win rates of 65.9% for Pearson and 71.4% for NRMSE, compared with 8.9% and 7.7% for GAT-AES. Our mean worst-output gaps are also smaller: 0.039 versus 0.149 for Pearson and 0.016 versus 0.055 for NRMSE. These results show that DualView wins more consistently with smaller target-level gaps.

DualView also outperforms all supervised baselines under aggregation schemes that place greater weight on poorly predicted targets (Table 15). Detailed results for every dataset–LLM combination are reported in Tables 11, 12, and 13 (\lx@sectionsign E.1), with complete breakdowns in \lx@sectionsign I.

Table 2 shows that DualView requires only 5.1K–57.4K fitted parameters, compared with 1.84M–20.98M for the three strongest supervised baselines (82–1842 \times more). Reduced-rank and shared predictors avoid fitting separate high-dimensional models for each target. Notably, the trainable footprint scales with representation width rather than backbone parameter count, facilitating adaptation to larger LLMs. Table 17 in \lx@sectionsign E.2 provides detailed counts for all baselines across datasets and LLMs.

We also investigate training-data efficiency by examining how predictive performance varies as the number of training examples increases. We compare DualView against the three strongest supervised baselines and report Pearson correlation macro-averaged across all 8 LLM backbones and 3 seeds for each dataset. We refit methods on nested training subsets (e.g., larger subsets must contain all examples from smaller ones), starting at 64 instances and doubling the budget up to each dataset’s full training split. We hold the validation and test splits fixed across budgets.

Figure 4 shows that DualView consistently outperforms the three strongest baselines at every evaluated training budget. DualView ’s lead on MSumBench narrows but remains stable or widens on the other four datasets. Figures 7, 8, and 9 (\lx@sectionsign E.3) compare DualView against all seven supervised baselines for the three metrics.

Table 3 compares DualView using Gemma 4 31B with Gemini 3.1 Pro under zero-shot and few-shot prompting. Relative to the stronger few-shot condition, DualView improves Pearson correlation and NRMSE by 30.7% and 19.8%, respectively. This result shows that supervised prediction with a smaller open LLM can outperform unsupervised prompting using a frontier proprietary LLM.

\lx@sectionsign 6.1 examines the complementarity of broad and focused evidence. \lx@sectionsign 6.2 ablates other training strategies. \lx@sectionsign 6.3 investigates the importance of target-specific evidence alignment. Finally, \lx@sectionsign 6.4 assesses parameter sharing across outputs. Unless otherwise stated, ablation results are macro-averaged across five datasets and eight LLM backbones with standard deviations across three training seeds (\pm).

We first investigate whether broad and focused representations provide complementary predictive information. We compare the reduced-rank broad and shared focused predictors individually against their combination, using the same regularized squared-error objective. To assess whether single-view performance is limited by predictor capacity, we also evaluate full-rank broad regression and independent focused predictors for each target. All variants are refitted using their respective features.

Table 4 shows that combining both evidence outperforms either alone, even with more capacity. Compared with the strongest single-view configuration (full-rank broad ridge), DualView improves Pearson correlation by 11.3% and reduces NRMSE by 2.1%. These results support the complementarity of the two evidence views, suggesting that target-focused representations capture predictive information not fully captured by the broad view.

We also examine whether our alternating optimization improves over two simpler training strategies. Separate fitting + fusion trains the broad and focused predictors independently, then combines their predictions using a validation-tuned weight \alpha. Fixed-basis joint fitting first trains the broad predictor alone, then fixes its learned basis \mathbf{A} while jointly fitting the target-specific weights \mathbf{B} and focused predictor \mathbf{v}. All strategies use the same extracted representations and rank constraints.

Table 5 shows that alternating joint fitting achieves the strongest performance, improving Pearson correlation by 3.1% and 4.3% over separate fitting and fixed-basis joint fitting, respectively, while reducing NRMSE by 0.8% and 0.9%. Notably, fixed-basis joint fitting does not improve over separate fitting, suggesting that joint optimization alone is insufficient. Instead, the results suggest that adapting the broad predictive directions to focused evidence helps the two branches make more complementary contributions.

The focused view assumes that target-specific prompting extracts evidence particularly useful for the corresponding output. To test this, we introduce a “mismatched” control that assigns each target to another target’s focused representation through cyclic permutation. We refit focused predictors using their permuted features with and without the broad predictor, applying the permutation consistently during training and evaluation.

Table 6 shows that mismatched focused representations degrade predictive performance in both the focused-only and the dual-branch configurations. The performance loss is more pronounced in the combined setting: Pearson drops by 10.0% versus 5.3%, and NRMSE increases by 1.8% versus 1.2%, respectively.

Finally, we assess the accuracy–parameter trade-off introduced by the two forms of sharing in DualView. We compare reduced-rank and full-rank broad predictors, crossed with shared and target-specific focused predictors. All configurations use the same extracted evidence and are fitted jointly using the L_{2} -regularized objective in \lx@sectionsign 3.5. Table 7 shows that DualView achieves comparable predictive performance to less constrained alternatives while fitting the fewest parameters.

Parameter sharing reduces the trainable footprint in two ways. First, the reduced-rank broad predictor uses k(H+D) rather than HD coefficients for an unrestricted predictor, with k(H+D)<HD in all evaluated configurations. Second, sharing the focused predictor reduces its coefficients from HD to H. Including D target-specific intercepts, DualView requires only (k+1)(H+D) parameters, compared with 2HD+D for full-rank broad and independent focused predictors.

section: When does supervised adaptation pay off?
text: Comparisons with Gemini raise a practical cost question beyond predictive performance. Direct prompting requires no task-specific training, whereas DualView incurs an upfront fitting cost but can use a smaller open-weight LLM for repeated inference. In principle, if the supervised system has lower marginal inference cost, this upfront cost can be amortized over sufficient requests. For DualView, however, the trade-off also depends on the number of outputs: processing N inputs requires N broad and ND focused representations, although shared-prefix reuse avoids redundant backbone computation. The preferred configuration, potentially including hybrid strategies that balance latency and predictive performance, therefore depends on the practical deployment context.

Our multi-output formulation may extend from predicting multiple semantic targets to predicting multiple points of a conditional distribution. Vedula et al. (2025) explored LLM-based quantile regression for text-based price prediction, and Zhu et al. (2026b) extend it to general text-to-distribution settings using dense quantile grids. Specifically, for quantiles {\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{N}}, a text input maps to a vector of quantile estimates [q_{\tau_{1}}(x),\ldots,q_{\tau_{N}}(x)]. To leverage DualView, we can treat each quantile level as a separate target and extract broad and quantile-specific representations from the LLM. Downstream ridge predictors can be applied as-is since they are domain-agnostic. Training could use pinball loss with a monotonicity constraint to prevent quantile crossing. We leave text-to-distribution extensions to future work.

Multi-output regression can also be viewed through a multi-objective lens: DualView uses the same L_{2} -regularized objectives across targets, but each target contributes separate loss terms that can induce conflicting updates to shared parameters. Multi-objective optimization (MOO) methods offer a natural way to address such conflicts by reweighting or modifying output-wise gradients during shared-parameter training (Sener and Koltun, 2018; Efroni et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). MOO methods are thus complementary to DualView, modifying how supervision is balanced across outputs without affecting how to extract features from the LLM backbone. Integrating MOO strategies is left for future work.

The shared focused predictor may generalize to unseen target descriptions without retraining. However, the broad predictor uses coefficients learned for a fixed output set, so extending the full DualView model to new targets would require additional adaptation. This would be another interesting direction to pursue.

We proposed DualView, a lightweight approach to multi-output text regression that leverages broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM. A rank-constrained multivariate predictor captures shared structure across outputs, while a shared scalar predictor uses evidence specialized to each target. Across five tasks and eight LLM backbones, DualView outperforms seven supervised baselines while fitting substantially fewer parameters. These advantages extend across nearly all output dimensions and persist even with limited supervision. Ablations show that the two evidence views are complementary and that parameter sharing preserves performance with fewer parameters.

Because DualView extracts representations from LLMs, the extracted vectors may be sensitive to changes in prompt formatting, which can affect predictions. We use fixed prompt templates for each dataset and do not evaluate alternative formulations.

DualView requires access to model internals to extract representations and thus may not work with black-box models. Because the LLM backbone is frozen, DualView ’s predictive performance also depends on the quality of its pretrained representations and may degrade on unfamiliar domains.

The rank-constrained joint objective specified in \lx@sectionsign 3.5 is nonconvex. Although each alternating update optimally fits one predictor while holding the other fixed, our optimization strategy does not guarantee a globally optimal joint solution.

While DualView fits fewer parameters (\lx@sectionsign 5.2) versus supervised baselines, actual computational costs depend on the practical deployment environment. Specifically, DualView requires one broad representation and D focused representations per input. Although shared-prefix reuse avoids redundant computation, the D focused suffixes still require separate processing. Thus, inference computation grows approximately linearly with the number of targets, and fewer fitted parameters do not necessarily translate into lower inference latency or memory use.

How Depth Growth and Looping Shape In-Context Learning in Language Models. Looped and depth-grown language models reuse computations across depth and have attracted interest for their reasoning capabilities. Building on prior suggestive evidence of improved in-context-learning (ICL), we investigate how such reuse favors ICL, including how it shapes the acquisition, retention, and mechanisms of this ability. Our analysis spans pretrained language models up to 3B parameters and controlled tasks. The experiments provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context: grown and looped models rely more on information in context and, compared with a full-depth dense reference, acquire ICL earlier in controlled tasks and retain it more strongly when learning fixed associations in the weights is also possible. Tracing attention heads through training reveals that depth growth propagates early induction heads across layers. Ablations show that grown and looped models rely more strongly on induction-ranked heads for both few-shot performance and later-token prediction. Together, these findings provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context and suggest that (soft) parameter reuse shapes how this ability develops and which attention mechanisms support it.

How a language model acquires its depth can shape the computations it learns. Depth growing trains an initially shallow network and progressively duplicates blocks of layers, allowing later training stages to reuse computations learned earlier. Looping instead repeatedly applies a shared block within each forward pass. Originally motivated by training efficiency (Fahlman and Lebiere, 1989) and parameter efficiency, respectively, both approaches have attracted renewed interest for their reasoning capabilities (Saunshi et al., 2024; Saunshi et al., 2025; Geiping et al., 2025). Although grown layers become independent after duplication, whereas looped layers remain tied, the two approaches can produce related patterns of iterative computation across depth (Kapl et al., 2026a; Kapl et al., 2026b).

This reuse of computation may also favor in-context learning (ICL), as suggested by initial evidence in both grown and looped models (Kapl et al., 2026b). ICL is the ability to use information supplied in a prompt or sequence without updating the model’s parameters (Brown et al., 2020). A model that repeatedly refines its representations might also be better equipped to extract and apply patterns from context. Yet, improved reasoning performance alone does not establish this ability. Predictions can rely on associations stored in the weights, on information inferred from the current sequence, or on both. Moreover, a model’s improvement in predicting later tokens and its ability to learn a task from demonstrations are related but distinct measurements, with potentially different underlying mechanisms (Olsson et al., 2022; Yin and Steinhardt, 2025).

Prior work provides promising evidence for a connection between depth reuse and ICL. Looped Transformers can learn synthetic regression and other data-fitting tasks with substantially fewer parameters than standard Transformers (Yang et al., 2024; Von Oswald et al., 2023). Studies of pretrained language models also report improved adaptation from demonstrations in grown and looped models for synthetic reasoning tasks (Kapl et al., 2026b). Concurrently, Wang et al. (2026) report stronger gains with increasing context length and demonstration count in compute-matched looped mixture-of-experts models. What remains less understood is how these behavioral differences arise during training: whether growing and looping favor a context-based solution when memorization is also possible, how they affect the persistence of that solution, and how changes in attention-head mechanisms relate to the different measures of ICL.

In this work, we investigate these questions through complementary experiments on natural language and controlled tasks. We compare dense baselines with depth-grown and looped models on language-model configurations with dense reference sizes from 360M to 3B parameters. We measure position-dependent token loss and scaling with the number of demonstrations for few-shot learning. We then use RegBench (Akyürek et al., 2024) to study learning previously unseen formal languages, and Omniglot-based tasks (Chan et al., 2022; Singh et al., 2023) to separate learning from context from learning fixed associations in the weights. Finally, we track induction and function-vector heads through training and intervene on them in the final models. Our contributions are the following:

Grown and looped language models benefit more from context. In the main 3B language-model comparison, both achieve larger early-to-late token-loss reductions than the dense baseline, with the grown model also attaining lower absolute late-token loss. Both models also achieve higher GSM8K accuracy across all demonstration counts. On RegBench, grown and looped models predict unseen formal languages more accurately, with their advantage emerging within the first string (Figures 1 and 2). Growing and looping favor earlier acquisition and stronger retention of ICL. In controlled Omniglot tasks where both context and fixed class–label associations can solve training queries, grown and looped models retain higher ICL accuracy and exhibit lower in-weights learning (IWL) accuracy than the full-depth dense reference. When labels are reassigned in every sequence, removing a fixed class–label solution, both acquire ICL earlier than the same reference (Figure 3). Depth growth propagates early induction heads across layers. Tracing final induction heads backward through training shows that strong heads in the grown model predominantly descend from heads already exhibiting strong induction behavior in early growing stages.

Layer duplication produces repeated patterns of this behavior across depth, while looped models exhibit analogous patterns across successive applications of their shared looped block (Figures 4 and 5). Grown and looped models rely more strongly on induction heads for ICL. In the main language-model comparison, ablating induction-ranked heads causes larger drops in few-shot performance and larger increases in late-token loss than in the dense baseline. These interventions establish a greater contribution from induction-ranked heads to both behaviors, while function-vector heads remain important (Figure 6).
Together, these experiments show that constructing depth through (soft) parameter reuse shapes both the development of context use and the attention mechanisms supporting it.

Model growth reduces training cost by starting with a smaller network (Fahlman and Lebiere, 1989). Language-model approaches use layer copying and progressive stacking (Gong et al., 2019; Reddi et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024), learned transformations between model sizes (Wang et al., 2023), or masked and function-preserving expansions (Yao et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2015; Gesmundo and Maile, 2023). Growth operators also shape model capabilities: MIDAS duplicates a central block of layers and improves reasoning at comparable language-model capabilities (Saunshi et al., 2024). Kapl et al. (2026a) find stronger reliance on later layers in grown models and propose LIDAS, which duplicates layers around the network’s center independently of existing block boundaries.

Cross-layer parameter sharing provides computational depth with fewer weights, as in Universal Transformers (Dehghani et al., 2019), recurrent stacking for translation (Dabre and Fujita, 2019), and ALBERT (Lan et al., 2020), while Takase and Kiyono (2023) study its design choices. Extensions add layer-specific low-rank adapters (Bae et al., 2025) or mixture-of-experts capacity (Csordás et al., 2024). Recurrence has also been studied for algorithmic length generalization (Fan et al., 2025), latent reasoning (Saunshi et al., 2025), and inference-time computation scaling (Geiping et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025). Other work retrofits recurrence into pretrained models (McLeish et al., 2025; Koishekenov et al., 2025) or explores hierarchical and compact recursive architectures for iterative refinement (Wang et al., 2025; Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025).

ICL enables adaptation from demonstrations without parameter updates (Brown et al., 2020). Studies show that Transformers infer unseen functions from examples (Garg et al., 2022), learn gradient-descent-like computations in restricted regression settings (Von Oswald et al., 2023; Gatmiry et al., 2024), and can be programmed to execute learning algorithms in context (Giannou et al., 2023). Data properties such as burstiness and dynamic meanings encourage ICL (Chan et al., 2022), which can decline as persistent associations are learned in the weights (Singh et al., 2023). Other work connects regular-language learning to in-context n -gram heads on RegBench (Akyürek et al., 2024) and studies context-dependent representations and their competition with pretrained semantics through graph tracing (Park et al., 2025). These settings let us probe context use with and without competing in-weights solutions.

Induction heads support pattern copying and are associated with improved later-token prediction (Elhage et al., 2021; Olsson et al., 2022). Their formation has been studied in controlled synthetic tasks (Singh et al., 2024) and language-model pretraining (Aoyama et al., 2026). Function-vector heads transmit task representations from demonstrations (Todd et al., 2024). Yin and Steinhardt (2025) find that few-shot performance depends primarily on these heads, many of which first exhibit induction behavior.

Looped Transformers can match standard Transformers on synthetic data-fitting tasks with substantially fewer parameters (Yang et al., 2024). Concurrent work (Wang et al., 2026) reports gains that increase with sequence length and demonstration count in looped mixture-of-experts language models under matched compute, parameter, and KV-cache budgets.

Most closely related, Kapl et al. (2026b) identify shared depth-wise computational patterns in grown and looped models, show that grown models can benefit from inference-time repetition, and report improved adaptation from demonstrations on reasoning primitives. We extend this evidence to ICL acquisition, retention, and mechanisms across pretrained language models and controlled tasks. We test whether growing and looping favor context use when memorization is possible, trace induction heads through layer duplication, and ablate induction and function-vector heads to assess their contributions to few-shot learning and token prediction.

section: In-Context Learning of Depth-Grown and Looped Models
text: We first examine how growing and looping affect learning from context. After introducing the models and measures (Section 3.1), we evaluate context use in language models (Section 3.2), adaptation to unseen formal languages on RegBench (Section 3.3), and ICL with and without an in-weights solution on Omniglot (Section 3.4).

A dense model trains L independently parameterized Transformer layers from scratch. A depth-grown model instead begins with a shallower model and periodically duplicates a block of layers, after which the copies train independently. The main paper focuses on LIDAS (Kapl et al., 2026a), which selects the central layers without respecting earlier block boundaries. Comparisons with MIDAS (Saunshi et al., 2024) and at other model sizes (360M and 1.7B) appear in Section A.3. The language models start with block size b=4 layers and add b layers at each growth event, copying both weights and optimizer moments while retaining the training schedule.

A looped model reuses the same block of layers several times within each forward pass, with parameters remaining tied throughout training. We write \LoopOp\,p{\mkern 2.0mu\text{-}\mkern 2.0mu}b{\mkern-1.5mu\times\mkern-1.5mu}r{\mkern 2.0mu\text{-}\mkern 2.0mu}c for p prelude layers, a block of b layers applied r times, and c coda layers, borrowing the naming conventions by Geiping et al. (2025). Its effective depth is p+br+c, with p+b+c unique layers. Our main 3B comparison uses a 36-layer dense reference (Bakouch et al., 2025), a LIDAS -grown model reaching that depth, and the \LoopOp\,10{\mkern 2.0mu\text{-}\mkern 2.0mu}8{\mkern-1.5mu\times\mkern-1.5mu}2{\mkern 2.0mu\text{-}\mkern 2.0mu}10 model, which has 36 layer applications and 28 unique layers. All three models are trained on the same 100B tokens in the same order. Within each size, all models share the data and optimizer-step budget and have matched final inference FLOPs. Growing uses shallower networks during part of training, saving an estimated 26% of training FLOPs at 3B and 22% at both 360M and 1.7B. Looping reduces unique parameters while retaining the same effective depth. Appendix A reports the configurations and training schedules.

In-Context Learning Measures. We evaluate language models using next-token negative log-likelihood (NLL, lower is better), a token-loss ICL-Score (Olsson et al., 2022), and few-shot task performance. The ICL-Score measures the reduction in mean NLL from early positions 40–60 ("50") to later positions 490–510 ("500"), with higher values indicating greater early-to-late improvement. We use these token-loss windows to smooth potential single token position spikes and refer to the positions in the following by a single position for simplicity. In Figure 1 (b), we instead average later losses over power-of-two bins ending at x, keeping the early reference fixed. This measures improvement within each model, while we report individual token loss separately. Few-shot performance is measured through benchmark accuracy or token-overlap F1. Full protocols are given in Appendix B.

We first compare how the different models use additional context in sequence modeling and few-shot tasks. These evaluations distinguish improvement with more context from absolute performance relative to the dense baseline. For sequence modeling, the depth-grown and looped models are worse at predicting early tokens compared to the baseline (Figure 1 (a)), with the biggest gap for very early tokens (token index \leq 8). After this peak, both models improve the prediction of tokens by lowering their NLL more, making better use of more tokens in the context. This is especially apparent when measuring the improvement of later tokens versus a fixed early position (50) and comparing it to the improvement of the baseline (Figure 1 (b)). The looped model, which uses significantly fewer unique parameters, retains higher NLL than the baseline even at the end of the sequence. LIDAS matches the baseline around position 1000 and achieves lower NLL thereafter (solid line) and on average across positions (dashed line).

On GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) few-shot accuracy in Figure 1 (c), the looped model, again using fewer parameters, keeps its advantage over the baseline across demonstration counts, but the baseline almost closes the gap at eight shots. The depth-grown model instead widens its performance improvement gap with additional examples, ending up around +7\% above the baseline. GSM8K evaluates final answers extracted from generated solutions to new questions, so these gains reflect improved answer generation from in-context demonstrations, a setting relevant to practical few-shot prompting. As an additional comparison, Appendix Figure 9 reports separate averages over five multiple-choice and three generation tasks. At 3B, LIDAS improves on the baseline in both subsets, while the looped model’s advantage is concentrated in generation.

RegBench (Akyürek et al., 2024) tests adaptation to an unseen formal language. Each input concatenates strings sampled from one deterministic finite automaton (DFA), with held-out automata used for testing. We measure total variation distance (TVD) between the predicted next-symbol distribution and the uniform distribution over legal continuations. All models apply twelve layers per forward pass, with two unique layers for the looped model.

In Figure 2 (a), the grown and looped models achieve lower TVD than the dense baseline on novel languages. Their advantage increases over the first few strings, peaking around the fourth (Figure 2 (b)). When zooming in on the test sequences in Figure 2 (c), both alternative training variants adapt faster to the new language by predicting symbols (akin to characters or tokens) within the first string better after roughly 15 symbols. Additionally, on average, after the first string the grown and looped model do not continue to increase their advantage with more symbols but keep a constant improvement. Appendix Figure 12 extends the comparison including DFA accuracy and additional grown models also evaluated with four training seeds, with the precise setup in Appendix C.

We next examine learning from context when fixed associations can also be stored in the weights, or when labels vary between sequences, removing the in-weights learning (IWL) solution. For that purpose, we use the Omniglot image-classification setup of Chan et al. (2022). Each sequence contains eight image–label pairs followed by a query image. In the fixed-label setting, every training class has a persistent label and the query class always appears among the context examples, with P(\mathrm{bursty})=1, meaning that every training sequence contains multiple demonstrations of the same classes. The training query can therefore be answered either by matching it to the current examples in context or by learning its class–label association in the weights. We distinguish these capabilities with two probes: ICL accuracy on held-out classes with labels reassigned in each sequence, and IWL accuracy on training classes whose query class is absent from context. We compare dense models with 4 and 12 layers, a \LoopOp\,4{\mkern-1.5mu\times\mkern-1.5mu}3 model, and a LIDAS -grown model that expands from 4 to 8 layers at 50k steps and to 12 layers at 100k steps. All models have the same hidden width and use the same optimizer and batch size.
We average over four training seeds for the fixed-label setting and eight for the ICL-only setting below. Appendix D gives the full setup.

Figure 3 (a) shows an early rise in ICL followed by a gradual decline as IWL improves, reflecting the transience of ICL observed by Singh et al. (2023). Over the shared training horizon, the grown and looped models retain higher mean ICL accuracy but lower IWL accuracy than the dense 12-layer model. The grown model has similar ICL and IWL accuracies to its four-layer reference, from which it first grows at 50k steps. The looped model attains similar ICL accuracy to the grown model but significantly lower IWL accuracy. These trajectories are consistent with growing and looping favoring learning from context relative to the full-depth dense model at the same effective depth. For looped models, this can come at the cost of weaker in-weights learning, while the grown model appears to inherit both capabilities from its shallow starting model.

To test acquisition when a fixed class–label solution is unavailable (ICL-only), we train a different set of models with labels 0 and 1 reassigned independently in every sequence, mirroring the ICL probing setup on training images. Each sequence contains two classes with four examples each, followed by a query from one of them. In Figure 3 (b), ICL accuracy emerges earlier for the looped, grown, and four-layer dense models than for the dense 12-layer model. By 1M steps, all four tested configurations almost reach 100%. Thus, this setting does not differentiate how much ICL is attained but rather the timing and consistency of ICL emergence, given that ICL is the only correct solution to the training problem.

section: Growing and Looping Increase Reliance on Induction Heads
text: The behavioral results suggest that growing and looping favor learning from context. Returning to language models, we examine the attention mechanisms supporting this behavior. We first track induction behavior during training and across layers (Section 4.1), then ablate heads to test their contribution to context use (Section 4.2).

section: Depth Growth Propagates Early Induction Heads
text: Attention-Head Measures. We characterize attention heads using prefix-matching (PS) and function-vector (FV) scores. PS measures attention to the token following an earlier occurrence in repeated random-token sequences (Olsson et al., 2022). FV scores measure how much replacing a head’s output with its clean task mean restores correct-answer prediction when demonstration labels are shuffled (Todd et al., 2024). We use these scores to select heads for ablation. Full evaluation protocols are given in Section E.1. We first compare induction behavior during language-model pretraining by averaging PS over the top 2% of heads at each checkpoint, reselecting them as training progresses. Checkpoint and aggregation details are given in Sections A.3 and E.1.

section: Depth Growth Propagates Early Induction Heads
text: In Figure 4, LIDAS develops higher PS than the dense baseline and finishes training with a higher score, while the looped model finishes close to the baseline. Early growth events temporarily disrupt prefix matching, followed by quick recovery during further training. These aggregate scores motivate tracing the heads responsible for the grown model’s strong induction behavior. Full trajectories of PS, function-vector scores, few-shot performance, and the token-loss ICL-Score appear in Appendix Figure 13.

section: Depth Growth Propagates Early Induction Heads
text: We next follow the twelve final top-2% PS heads in each 3B model through training (Figure 5, top). These identities remain fixed, unlike the checkpoint-wise selection for the average in Figure 4. For LIDAS, we trace the heads backward through layer duplication to the starting four-layer model. Copies share an ancestral trajectory until duplication, so we draw that shared path once.

section: Depth Growth Propagates Early Induction Heads
text: The twelve final LIDAS heads trace back to just four ancestors. Two of these, L2H9 and L2H10 (zero-based indices), already have high PS before the first growth event and account for ten of the twelve final heads, highlighted in orange. The remaining two originate from initially low-scoring heads whose induction behavior develops later. Thus, most of the strongest final induction heads arise from copying and further training early induction heads. The original L2H10 retains high PS but is outside the final top-2% heads, while three of its copies are included.

section: Depth Growth Propagates Early Induction Heads
text: The final locations in Figure 5 (bottom) connect these lineages to repeated patterns across depth. In LIDAS, strong heads recur at the same head index in layers separated by multiples of the four-layer growth block, extending from early layers (L<8) into later layers. In \LoopOp\,10{\mkern 2.0mu\text{-}\mkern 2.0mu}8{\mkern-1.5mu\times\mkern-1.5mu}2{\mkern 2.0mu\text{-}\mkern 2.0mu}10, high-PS heads likewise recur across the two applications of the eight-layer shared block, highlighted in orange. These are separate applications of tied heads, whereas the grown model’s copies train independently. The dense baseline shows no comparable pattern of repetition by block size.

section: Depth Growth Propagates Early Induction Heads
text: FV heads likewise recur at the grown or looped block size, but emerge later than induction heads (Appendix Figure 14). In LIDAS, two ancestors give rise to six of the twelve final top-2% FV heads.

section: Induction Heads Contribute More to Context Use
text: The trajectories and locations reveal how induction behavior develops and repeats across depth. A high prefix-matching score alone does not establish a head’s importance for ICL. We therefore ablate heads in the final models to test their contributions to few-shot performance and token loss.

section: Induction Heads Contribute More to Context Use
text: Following the mean-ablation protocol of Yin and Steinhardt (2025), we rank final-checkpoint heads by PS or FV score and replace the outputs of the selected 1–20% with mean activations. For looped models, each head application is counted and ablated separately. Here we focus on exclusive induction rankings, which first exclude the top 2% of FV heads, and exclusive FV rankings, which first exclude the top 2% of induction heads. We evaluate changes from each model’s unablated few-shot ICL (F1) and ICL-Score. Appendix F specifies the replacement means, indexing, and additional random controls.

section: Induction Heads Contribute More to Context Use
text: Consistent with observations by Yin and Steinhardt (2025), all three models in Figure 6 (a,b) show greater few-shot ICL degradation from FV-head ablation and greater ICL-Score (token-loss difference) reduction from induction-head ablation. At larger ablation fractions, exclusive induction-head ablation reduces few-shot performance and ICL-Score more in grown and looped models than in the baseline, indicating greater reliance on these heads. FV heads remain important in all models, but their ablation effects relative to the baseline vary across models and sizes for this comparison (Appendix Figure 20).

section: Induction Heads Contribute More to Context Use
text: Figure 6 (c) shows the NLL increase by token position at 9% ablation. Beyond the first few tokens, FV-head ablation hurts early-token prediction more than induction-head ablation. The FV-ablation effect then largely plateaus, while the induction-ablation effect grows with position. Compared with the baseline, LIDAS and \LoopOp\,10{\mkern 2.0mu\text{-}\mkern 2.0mu}8{\mkern-1.5mu\times\mkern-1.5mu}2{\mkern 2.0mu\text{-}\mkern 2.0mu}10 show smaller FV-ablation effects across most positions and larger induction-ablation effects at later positions. Within both models, induction heads eventually become more important than FV heads for later-token prediction, whereas FV heads remain more important in the baseline. Together, these results indicate that both head types support context use, with greater reliance on induction heads in grown and looped models.

Our experiments provide evidence that depth growing and looping favor learning from context. In the main language-model comparison, both achieve larger early-to-late token-loss reductions and higher GSM8K accuracy than the dense baseline. Grown and looped models also predict unseen formal languages more accurately. In controlled classification tasks, both acquire ICL earlier than a full-depth dense reference when labels are reassigned between sequences, and retain higher ICL accuracy when fixed associations can also be learned in the weights. Mechanistically, depth growth propagates early induction heads through layer duplication, with most of the strongest final heads descending from a small set of early ancestors. This produces repeated patterns across depth analogous to those in looped models, even though grown layers train independently after copying. Ablations in the main language-model comparison show that grown and looped models rely more on induction-ranked heads for few-shot performance and later-token prediction. Function-vector heads remain more important for few-shot performance in all models, suggesting that depth reuse shifts the relative contributions of these mechanisms. Together, these findings suggest that reusing computations across depth shapes how models acquire and retain ICL, as well as the attention mechanisms supporting it.

The controlled tasks suggest that depth reuse shifts the competition between in-context and in-weights learning: grown and looped models retain higher ICL accuracy while attaining lower IWL accuracy than the full-depth dense reference. One possible explanation is that copying early context-dependent computations through growth, or repeatedly applying them through shared layers, makes a context-based solution less susceptible to being displaced as fixed associations are learned in the weights.

When Does a Second Model Help? Cross-Model Review in LLM Verification. Large language models now generate code, documentation, and analyses, and are increasingly used to review such output. We ask when a second review by a different model helps. Building on the author's earlier preprints, which varied context, repetition, and role structure within one model, we test model independence in a controlled experiment: 30 artifacts with 150 planted errors, 10 review conditions, and 900 review sessions with three reviewer models from two developers. In this experiment, (1) a top-tier cross-model reviewer is not significantly different in F1 from same-model review in a fresh session (CCR), which does not establish equivalence; (2) the two find partly different errors (Jaccard 41.2%); and (3) at two review calls, one CCR plus one cross-model review matches more planted errors than two CCR reviews (56.7% vs. 42.7%; Holm-adjusted p=.006), but not significantly more than two reviews by the top-tier cross-model reviewer, so model difference and reviewer capability are not separated. A lightweight cross-model reviewer scores no higher than same-model review.

Withholding requirements from the reviewer raises F1 for the two lower tiers but not the top tier, in untested point estimates whose pattern depends on how failed sessions are scored. Before analysis we audited all session records, excluding one baseline run of uncertain provenance and 14 failed calls; results with all sessions are also reported. A partial check on public detector outputs from another benchmark neither replicates nor contradicts the main comparison. Records, artifacts, and scripts are available from the author on request.

Large language models (LLMs) now generate code, documentation, data analyses, and research artifacts faster than people can review them. This has motivated the use of LLMs themselves as reviewers, an approach that is already gaining industrial traction, as evidenced by the recent release of cross-model review tooling integrated directly into AI coding assistants (OpenAI, 2026). Two questions are open: what makes AI review of AI output independent, and does cross-model review improve defect detection?

Verification is only as useful as it is independent of what produced the output. In human contexts, peer review, double-blind evaluation, and independent auditing all derive their value from ensuring that the verifier’s judgment is not contaminated by the same biases that produced the original output. When the same LLM reviews its own generation within the same conversational context, it shares its training data, parameters, and conversational context, and in-context self-correction without external feedback has been found to degrade accuracy (Huang et al., 2024).

A series of earlier studies by the author explored individual dimensions of independence within one model. Cross-Context Review (Song, 2026a, CCR;) reported that context independence (removing the generation conversation before review) improves defect detection; in the data reused here, after excluding one baseline run of uncertain provenance, CCR exceeds same-context self-review by only 1.5pp in F1, which is not significant (Section 5.1); the two also differ in whether the reviewer sees the original request. Diachronic CCR (Song, 2026c, D-CCR;) reported that adding repeated review rounds, which removes temporal independence in our terms, is counterproductive, increasing false positives by 62% without improving recall. In a study whose main subject is benchmark-contamination detection, the Hierarchical Cross-Context Architecture report (Song, 2026b, HCCA;) also describes a pilot in which a multi-stage pipeline (worker, verifier, director) whose later stages could see earlier conclusions produced only sycophantic confirmation, and identify information restriction rather than structural complexity as the key mechanism.

These three reports are the author’s own single-author preprints that have not been peer reviewed, so we do not rely on their conclusions: every baseline number below is recomputed from the per-session data, the benchmark and matching procedure are specified in Appendix A, and where our test disagrees with an earlier report we say so.
All three studies stayed within one model. The most intuitive form of independence, using a different model, remained untested. This paper addresses that gap.

We introduce a four-dimensional framework for independence in LLM verification, encompassing context, temporal, structural, and model independence. Through a controlled experiment with 900 review sessions across 10 conditions, we systematically evaluate model independence and its interaction with other dimensions. Our key findings are:

We use complementary to mean partially non-overlapping detection, not super-additive coverage. (1) Complementary detection: cross-model review (XMR) and CCR find partly different defects (Jaccard 41.2%), with CCR ahead on code (F1 40.7%) and XMR on documents (F1 up to 42.1%); (2) call-matched coverage: one CCR plus one XMR review matches 56.7% of planted errors against 42.7% for two CCR reviews, while the gain over two top-tier XMR reviews is not significant; (3) reviewer capability appears to shape the effect —a top-tier reviewer shows no significant difference from CCR, but a lightweight model scores numerically below even baseline same-context review, so the value of model independence appears to depend on reviewer quality; and (4) information restriction raises cross-model F1 for the two lower tiers (+2.2 and +3.0pp) but not the top tier (-0.2 pp; untested point estimates).

These results suggest tentative guidance: pairing a same-model review with a cross-model one gave more coverage than two same-model reviews, though not significantly more than two top-tier cross-model reviews; for resource-constrained settings, a single cross-model review with a top-tier reviewer had the highest F1 of any single condition in our data (not significantly above CCR); and lightweight cross-model reviewers offered no advantage over same-model review.

Cross-Context Review (Song, 2026a, CCR;) conducts review in a fresh session, so the reviewer receives only the artifact, not the conversation that produced it. Across 360 sessions over 30 artifacts with 150 ground truth errors, the original report found CCR ahead of same-context review, testing run 1 alone (paired t, p=0.008); among the four same-model conditions, CCR ranks first in that run only (run-level F1 in Appendix F). In the data used here, after excluding one same-context run of uncertain provenance (Section 4.1), CCR’s F1 is 28.6% versus 27.1% (a comparison that changes both the context and whether the request is visible; Section 3.2), and the artifact-level test finds no significant difference (unadjusted p=0.26; Table 2). The original report attributed the gap to removing the conversational anchoring that biases a model toward defending its own output.

Diachronic CCR (Song, 2026c, D-CCR;) tested repeated review rounds: counter-intuitively, a second round decreased performance, with false positives increasing by 62%. The report attributes this to the same model amplifying its existing false-confidence patterns rather than gaining new perspectives, which would suggest that repeating review in the same session is not a path to independence.

The HCCA report (Song, 2026b) assigns specialized analytical roles under intentional information restriction. In a pilot extending this to a multi-stage pipeline (worker, verifier, director) in which later stages could see earlier conclusions, the report observes only sycophantic confirmation and attributes the benefit of its main design to information restriction rather than to structural complexity.

The three prior studies explored three ways of varying review within a single model: context can be reset, timing varied, and roles restructured, but the model’s training data, weights, and systematic biases remain constant. The natural next question is whether a different model, trained on different data with different objectives, provides a fundamentally different form of independence.

Indirect evidence suggests it should. LLMs differ in measured capability across tasks (Zheng et al., 2023; Chiang et al., 2024), and cross-model review has already been integrated into production developer tools (OpenAI, 2026). However, we are not aware of prior work that systematically measures whether these differences translate into complementary defect detection.

LLM self-correction and self-preference. In-context self-correction without external feedback degrades accuracy (Huang et al., 2024); Kamoi et al. (2024b) attribute the failure to the feedback (error-detection) stage and recommend analysing the quality of generated feedback directly. They also note that cross-model correction is unsuitable for testing whether a model can improve its own responses, and recommend comparisons against baselines of comparable computational cost; our two-review-call analysis matches the number of review calls, not compute. LLMs also favor their own generations (Panickssery et al., 2024). Neither line compares a same-conversation reviewer against a fresh-context or different-model reviewer: the axis we vary.

Sycophancy and evaluation bias. LLMs adjust outputs to match perceived user preferences (Sharma et al., 2024) and, as judges, exhibit positional and other judgement biases (Wang et al., 2024b; Chen et al., 2024).

Multi-agent systems and LLM-as-judge. Multi-agent frameworks structure multiple LLM instances to debate answers or assume specialized roles (Du et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024), while LLM-as-judge approaches use LLMs to score or rank outputs (Zheng et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024). These systems primarily manipulate structural and context independence but typically use a single underlying model, leaving model independence unexplored. Error-detection benchmarks: ReaLMistake (Kamoi et al., 2024a) and BIG-Bench Mistake (Tyen et al., 2024) report low detection rates even for strong models, and CriticBench (Lin et al., 2024) finds that stronger models critique weaker ones better while weaker models can sometimes surpass stronger ones in self-critique; but none of these analyses is organised around a model inspecting its own output versus another model’s.

Software review and blind spots. LLMs are increasingly applied to code review (Li et al., 2022; Pornprasit and Tantithamthavorn, 2024; Cihan et al., 2025); in a related setting, Shin et al. (2025) find that LLM-generated reviews of research papers over-focus on technical validity and overlook novelty compared with human experts. Doddapaneni et al. (2024) probe five evaluator LLMs with 2,400 perturbed answers and report that they miss quality drops in over 50% of cases on average. We use “blind spot” in a narrower sense (defects one reviewer model misses and another catches) and quantify it through Jaccard overlap.

Hallucination detection, ensembles, and N-version. Consistency-based methods exploit the intuition that disagreement across independent samples signals unreliability, via semantic entropy (Farquhar et al., 2024) or reference checking (Manakul et al., 2023). Ensemble and mixture-of-agents methods show that model diversity improves aggregate performance (Dietterich, 2000; Wang et al., 2024a; Tekin et al., 2024), echoing N-version programming (Chen and Avizienis, 1978); we extend these principles to across-model defect detection.

Correlated errors and frontier blind spots. Kim et al. (2025) analyze over 350 LLMs, largely on multiple-choice benchmarks; on one leaderboard (HELM), pairs of models that both err choose the same wrong answer about 60% of the time, and larger, more accurate models have more highly correlated errors. This result raises concerns about naive multi-model ensembles and motivates our measurement of pairwise finding overlap (52.2% within the same model vs. 37–46% across models; Section 5.3), a descriptive comparison rather than a test of error correlation.
We define four binary dimensions characterizing the relationship between a generator LLM (which produces the artifact) and a reviewer LLM (which verifies it):

Context independence (C): the reviewer has no access to the generation conversation, operating with P(\text{findings}\mid\text{artifact}) rather than P(\text{findings}\mid\text{artifact},G), where G is the generation transcript.
Temporal independence (T): the review occurs in a single pass, with no memory of prior review rounds on the same artifact.
Structural independence (S): the reviewer operates without hierarchical subordination to the generator, avoiding deference or sycophancy.

Model independence (M): the reviewer is a different model, typically from a different developer. This does not guarantee different training data or uncorrelated errors; whether cross-model errors are less correlated is an empirical question (Section 5.3).

We additionally define information restriction (R) as a cross-cutting modifier: the reviewer receives only the artifact, without the original prompt or requirements, forcing assessment on intrinsic merits rather than compliance with stated goals.

Our 10 conditions map onto the framework as shown in Table 1. All XMR conditions inherently include context independence, because in our design the cross-model reviewer never receives the generation conversation. In the experiment code, CCR is specified with the same user-prompt string as the information-restricted XMR conditions (the artifact only), and SA with the same structure as the unrestricted ones (the original request and the artifact). In terms of the specified prompt, the comparisons closest to changing only the reviewer model are therefore CCR versus the -R conditions and SA versus the unrestricted XMR conditions (the latter also changes structure if SA’s sub-agent role matters); comparing CCR with an unrestricted XMR condition changes both the reviewer model and the information given, and comparing CCR with SR changes both the context and the information given. The reviewers also run under different system instructions (the Claude Code agent tool, the Codex CLI agent, or none for the Gemini API), and replacing the reviewer model changes reviewer capability and other model characteristics, so none of these comparisons isolates model independence.
Based on our framework, we test the following hypotheses:

H1 (Unique Finding). Cross-model review discovers defects that cross-context review misses, and vice versa. Formally: \text{UFR}(\text{XMR}\to\text{CCR})>0 and \text{UFR}(\text{CCR}\to\text{XMR})>0, where \text{UFR}(A\to B) is the proportion of A ’s true positives not found by B.

H2 (Union Superiority). The union of CCR and XMR findings achieves higher recall than either alone (implied by H1 under a fixed matcher; we report it for its magnitude). Formally: \text{Recall}(\text{CCR}\cup\text{XMR})>\max(\text{Recall}(\text{CCR}),\text{Recall}(\text{XMR})).

H3 (Bias Orthogonality). The overlap between CCR and XMR findings is lower than the overlap between independent sessions within the same model, which would be consistent with systematically different blind spots. Formally: \text{Jaccard}(\text{CCR},\text{XMR})<\text{Jaccard}(\text{CCR}_{A},\text{CCR}_{B}).
We additionally explore two non-directional hypotheses:

H4 (Dimension Interaction). The combination of context and model independence exhibits interaction effects (synergistic or antagonistic) beyond the sum of individual effects. This hypothesis is not identifiable in our design, which has no condition with model independence but no context independence; we state it for completeness.
H5 (Error-Type Specialization). Different independence dimensions are differentially effective across error types (FACT, CONS, CTXT, RCVR, MISS) and artifact categories (code, document, script).

Artifacts. We reuse the 30 software artifacts and 150 ground truth errors from Song (2026a). The artifacts span three categories: code modules (C1–C10), technical tutorials (D1–D10), and presentation scripts (S1–S10). Each artifact contains 5 planted defects across 5 error types: factual errors (FACT), internal consistency violations (CONS), missing context handling (CTXT), recoverability gaps (RCVR), and missing functionality (MISS). Error severities range from Critical to Minor. Reusing identical artifacts enables direct comparison with prior results.

Generator model. All 30 artifacts were generated by a single frontier-class LLM, Claude Opus 4.6 according to our run logs; the artifact files themselves do not record the generating model. The same-model baselines (SR, SR2, SA, CCR) were run with that model, subject to the same caveat. Reviewer model identifiers denote the requested model setting (an API parameter for Gemini, a Codex CLI setting for GPT-5.4) rather than a confirmed served checkpoint; we did not record a served model identifier. Using a single generator ensures that all reviewer conditions evaluate identical artifacts, removing generator variation; it does not separate reviewer independence from other reviewer characteristics such as capability.

Dependence on prior work. The four baseline conditions (SR, SR2, SA, CCR), the C/T/S dimensions, and the artifacts with their ground truth come from the earlier preprints; only the XMR conditions and the unifying taxonomy are new. Appendix A specifies the artifacts, error injection, and matching so that the claims here can be checked without those reports. The baselines were collected before the XMR conditions under the same protocol, a temporal asymmetry noted in Limitations.

Data provenance and exclusions. We audited all 900 session records against the raw files before the analysis reported here. The 540 cross-model records carry the reviewer model identifier, call duration, and a per-session timestamp. The 360 same-model baseline sessions were run through the Claude Code agent tool and transcribed into structured files by the host session; they carry no raw model output, and in several runs all 30 files share one timestamp. For one run (SR, run 3), 92% of the finding descriptions appear verbatim inside the script that wrote the files, so we cannot confirm that they are unedited model output, and we exclude this run from all analyses. Fourteen cross-model sessions failed (five timeouts or crashes and nine unparseable outputs; eight of the fourteen were XMR-Ge-R sessions) and had been scored as reviews with no findings; because a failed call is not a review, we exclude them as well. The analyses therefore describe cross-model review when the call succeeds; Appendix F reports the main values with failures scored as zero.

The exclusion rules followed from the audit and were fixed before the full recomputation, although a partial check of their effect on cross-model F1 was run during the audit. The remaining baseline records are unverified rather than known to be clean.
Conditions and scale. We evaluate 10 conditions (Table 1), each with 90 sessions (3 runs per artifact \times 30 artifacts), yielding 900 sessions total.

Reviewer models. We employ three external reviewer models from two developers at different capability tiers. The tiers reflect the vendors’ positioning at the time of the experiment, not a capability we measured, and GPT-5.4 is also a later model generation than Gemini 2.5: GPT-5.4 (top-tier): a model from a different developer than the generator, run through the Codex CLI agent (see Limitations on its working directory). Gemini 2.5 Pro (capable): a strong model from a developer other than those of the generator and GPT-5.4. Gemini 2.5 Flash (lightweight): a cost-optimized model from the same developer as Gemini 2.5 Pro, testing whether model independence helps even with reduced capability.
For each family, we test both unrestricted (full artifact + requirements) and information-restricted (artifact only) conditions.

Procedure. Each session proceeds identically: the reviewer receives the artifact (in SA and the unrestricted XMR conditions, also the original request, i.e., the requirements; SR and SR2 review in the generation session; prompts in Appendix B) and produces a structured list of findings (location, description, severity, error type). Findings are matched against the ground truth by location- and keyword-overlap scoring, each finding assigned to at most one ground-truth error and each ground-truth error credited at most once per review (Appendix A).

Statistical testing. We use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired comparisons at the artifact level (averaging the available runs per artifact per condition after the exclusions of Section 4.1; every artifact keeps at least one run in every condition, so each test uses 30 paired observations), with Holm-Bonferroni correction over the nine comparisons against CCR. For comparison with the original CCR report, Table 2 also gives paired t -tests on run 1 alone without correction; our conclusions use the former. Union analysis computes the unique ground truth errors detected by at least one session per condition, yielding Union Recall, Unique Finding Rate (UFR), and Jaccard similarity.

The artifacts, ground-truth annotations, review prompts, per-session review records, and analysis scripts are available from the author on request. Raw reviewer outputs and per-session model identifiers exist only for the cross-model conditions; the same-model baseline records were transcribed into structured files by the host session and do not include raw model output (Section 4.1). We note that exact reproduction is limited by the non-deterministic nature of LLM outputs, and the 90 sessions per condition are repeated measurements on 30 artifacts, so our tests use 30 artifact-level pairs.
Table 2 presents the main results across all 10 conditions, ranked by F1 score, and Figure 2 (Appendix) visualizes this ranking.

The top three conditions are all cross-model configurations, and the bottom three are the lightweight cross-model condition (XMR-Ge), the sub-agent baseline (SA), and the repeated baseline (SR2). XMR-Ge-R (27.0%) is level with SR (27.1%), so model independence with a lightweight reviewer shows no clear advantage over baseline self-review.

The difference between the best XMR condition (XMR-GPT, 32.3%) and CCR (28.6%) is not statistically significant (adjusted p_{\mathrm{W}}=1.00; run-1 p_{t}=0.478). We therefore detect no F1 difference between these two conditions; without an equivalence test, this is not evidence that the two are equal. XMR-GPT also receives the original request, which CCR does not; the comparison with the same prompt as CCR, XMR-GPT-R (32.1%), is likewise not significant (adjusted p_{\mathrm{W}}=1.00).

The spread across reviewer models is larger. XMR-GPT (32.3%) exceeds XMR-Ge (24.0%) by 8.3 percentage points, more than the gap between CCR and SR (1.5pp). This single comparison is outside the nine-comparison family; its unadjusted Wilcoxon p is 0.020 with failed sessions excluded and 0.071 with them scored as zero, and it would not survive correction if added to the family. The data are consistent with reviewer capability mattering more than independence per se, but do not establish it.
While individual F1 scores are similar between CCR and top XMR conditions, their coverage patterns differ meaningfully.

Union Recall (Figure 1): under the existing automated matcher, a two-review-call comparison yields 85/150 (56.7%) matched ground-truth errors for one CCR plus one XMR-GPT-R review versus 64/150 (42.7%) for two CCR reviews (all four reviews are specified with the same artifact-only prompt), a 14.0pp gain (artifact-level bootstrap 95% CI [6.7, 22.0]; signed-rank p=.006, Holm-adjusted over the three union comparisons). These are set-level recalls over run 1 (singles 56 and 64; 56+64-35=85), not the per-session means of Table 2. Across the three runs per condition, mixed unions cover 44.7–56.7% and CCR-only unions 30.0–42.7% (reused runs, not independent replications). Against two XMR-GPT-R reviews, on the 29 artifacts without a failed session (76/145 vs. 82/145 for the mixed pair), the gain is 4.1pp (95% CI [-2.1, 10.3]; adjusted p=.184). The third comparison in the family uses self-review as the same-model partner: SR plus XMR-GPT-R matches 77/150 against 53/150 for SR plus SR2 in run 1 (+16.0pp, 95% CI [6.7, 26.0]; adjusted p=.008). These retrospective results are conditional on the matcher; condition-specific matching bias remains unmeasured.

The Jaccard similarity between CCR and XMR-GPT-R is 41.2% (35 of 85 unique errors found by either), indicating moderate overlap: the approaches share a substantial core, but \sim 59% of unique findings come from only one approach, supporting H1 (each finds defects the other misses). The 14.0pp union gain is consistent with H2 (union superiority) in the narrow sense that the union covers more than either review alone. Any two imperfect, non-identical detectors raise union recall mechanically; the observed unions in fact fall below both pooled and within-artifact independence reference values (r_{A}+r_{B}-r_{A}r_{B}). These descriptive comparisons do not establish synergy or its absence; we do not claim synergy (super-additive coverage beyond independent expectation)—complementarity here refers to non-overlap (Jaccard 41.2%).

To test whether cross-model overlap is lower than within-model overlap (which would be consistent with systematically different blind spots), we computed pairwise Jaccard similarity at the finding level across all run pairs.

Within-condition overlap (same model, different sessions): CCR 52.2% (90 run pairs), SR 61.8% (30 pairs, runs 1–2 only), XMR-GPT 59.3% (84), XMR-Ge 55.1% (88). Cross-condition overlap (all run combinations): CCR vs. XMR-GPT 46.1% (258 pairs), CCR vs. XMR-Ge 36.5% (267), and CCR vs. SR 59.9% (180; same model, different context and information). Pairs involving an excluded session are dropped, so the pair counts differ.

Within-model session pairs share 52–62% of findings, while cross-model pairs share 37–46%. The difference between CCR intra-condition overlap (52.2%) and CCR-vs-XMR cross-model overlap (average 41.3%) is 10.9 percentage points, consistent with H3. Lower overlap can also arise from differences in detection rates or finding counts, and the run pairs share artifacts, so this is descriptive support rather than a test.

CCR vs. SR overlap (59.9%) is comparable to within-condition overlaps: we see no clear sign that changing the context (together with withholding the request) changes which errors the model finds, whereas changing the model is accompanied by lower overlap, which matters given that high-capability LLMs exhibit strongly correlated errors (Kim et al., 2025).
The aggregate F1 scores mask a reversal at the category level (Table 3).

For code artifacts, CCR outperforms all XMR conditions; one possible explanation is that the generating model shares an understanding of programming patterns and code structure that an external model lacks. For documents, the pattern reverses, and it holds for every condition, not only those in the table: all six cross-model conditions (F1 30.1–42.1%) score above all four same-model conditions (17.4–24.5%). XMR conditions perform better, suggesting a different model brings different expectations about consistency and completeness, shaped by different training corpora.
