This category reversal is our clearest descriptive support for H5, although the category estimates carry no uncertainty intervals and the explanations above are conjectures; it suggests that the choice between CCR and XMR should depend on artifact type.
Breaking down results by error type reveals further specialization (Table 4). Detection rates are per-session recall for each error type, averaged over the analysed sessions (n as in Table 2).

Several patterns emerge. The top-tier cross-model reviewer is higher than CCR on FACT (58% vs. 48%) and CONS (53% vs. 37%). On CTXT, where operational context matters, the two top-tier conditions reach 26–31%, against 9–18% for every other condition (XMR-GPT-R and SR are not shown in the table). Across all six cross-model conditions (including three not shown in Table 4), RCVR varies most (7–38%), followed by FACT (35–58%) and CTXT (9–31%), consistent with these types being sensitive to reviewer capability.

The apparent tension between Tables 3 and 4, namely CCR’s higher F1 on code (40.7% vs. 37.2%) despite XMR-GPT’s comparable or higher per-type recall, is consistent with precision: on code, CCR’s precision is 46.9% versus 35.6% for XMR-GPT, while its recall is 36.7% versus 40.0%. The analyses also operate at different granularities, so dominance at one level need not imply it at the other.

Restricting the information available to the reviewer, by providing only the artifact without the original requirements, changes cross-model F1 by tier as follows: top-tier 32.3 \to 32.1 (-0.2), capable 26.8 \to 29.0 (+2.2), and lightweight 24.0 \to 27.0 (+3.0). The two sides of each comparison are not the same session sets after exclusions, and with failed sessions scored as zero the changes are +0.9, +2.2, and +0.9 (Appendix F).

This pattern is consistent with the earlier HCCA report (Song, 2026b) that less information promotes more independent judgment; the per-tier gains are untested point estimates, and the account that follows is a hypothesis. When the reviewer cannot simply check the artifact against stated requirements, it must assess the artifact on its intrinsic quality, detecting inconsistencies, logical gaps, and errors that requirement-checking might overlook. After the exclusions the top-tier reviewer shows no gain (+0.9 with failures scored as zero), and the size of the lightweight tier’s gain depends on how failed sessions are handled, so the relationship between reviewer capability and the benefit of restriction is unclear.

Within each restriction setting, F1 increases with reviewer tier: top-tier 32.1–32.3% (above CCR’s 28.6%, not significantly), capable 26.8–29.0% (approaching CCR with restriction), and lightweight 24.0–27.0% (at or below the SR baseline of 27.1%). The spread between the best and worst XMR conditions (8.3pp) is larger than the total spread among all same-model conditions (6.9pp), although ranges over different sets of conditions are not directly comparable effect sizes.

Cross-model review introduces a new category of false positive: model bias errors, where the reviewer flags issues based on its own training data rather than actual defects. Classifying all XMR false positives via keyword-based analysis, 187 of 1,995 (9.4%) were model bias; the most common subcategory (72.7%, 136/187) involved flagging generator-specific features or tools as non-existent, which may reflect differences in training data between model families (the classification is keyword-based and was not validated). Information restriction partially mitigates this (lightweight 13% \to 10%, capable 10% \to 8%), and the top-tier model shows the lowest rate (9% unrestricted, 8% restricted).

The severity label a reviewer attaches is a weak guide to which findings to check first. Major or Critical labels were attached to 70.0% of cross-model true positives and to 54.7% of cross-model false positives (same-model: 54.5% and 28.2%; Appendix C). Because a correct finding of a pre-existing defect counts as a false positive (Appendix A), some of these false positives may be real defects; we have not checked them by hand.

We ran five case studies outside software review—agricultural anomaly detection (B1), recession identification (B2), news fact-checking (B3), a meta-review of this paper’s own analysis code (B4), and a security audit (B5). Because their evidential value varies sharply, we summarize them here and report them in full in Appendix H.

Only B3 (news fact-checking) is informative for our hypotheses: the top-tier cross-model reviewer again has the highest F1, and the union of CCR and XMR-GPT findings reaches 86.0% recall against 76.7% for XMR-GPT alone (CCR 55.8%), with a Jaccard of 54.1%; each condition’s recall here pools its three runs, so the union pools six reviews against three and is descriptive, not a matched comparison. B1 and B2 reached 100% accuracy under every condition; a ceiling leaves no room to discriminate between conditions, so we draw no comparative conclusion from them and report them only as evidence that the task framing transfers. B4 and B5 lack independent ground truth and are qualitative demonstrations, not tests. We therefore rest the cross-domain claim on B3 alone, with the caveat that 12 articles from a single source is a small sample.

section: Why Different Models Find Different Things
text: The partial non-overlap is consistent with several explanations, though our design does not establish causal mechanisms: training-data divergence (different corpora, different standards), different capability profiles (the category reversal is consistent with code review benefiting from the generator model’s own programming knowledge, document review from diverse perspectives), and model-specific knowledge gaps (cross-model reviewers also flag non-errors from their own gaps; Section 5.8).

section: Why Different Models Find Different Things
text: Kim et al. (2025) find strongly correlated errors on closed-ended benchmarks; our unions also fall below the independence reference (Section 5.2), so the partial non-overlap we observe should not be read as independent errors. Perspective diversification (B5) and three-model unions are discussed in Appendix G.1.

Based on our findings, we offer the following tentative guidance, limited to this sample of artifacts and reviewers. For maximum coverage, combine same-model and cross-model review (56.7% vs. 42.7% for two same-model reviews at the same number of review calls; not significantly above two top-tier cross-model reviews). For a single review, top-tier cross-model review scored highest (F1 32.1–32.3%), but not significantly above CCR (28.6%). Prioritize same-model review for code-heavy projects (F1 40.7% vs. 37.2% on code) and cross-model review for documentation/consistency (F1 42.1% vs. 24.5% on documents); avoid cross-model review with lightweight models (F1 24.0–27.0% vs. CCR 28.6%).

We presented a four-dimensional framework for independence in LLM verification and new experiments on model independence. Across 900 sessions, CCR leads on code and XMR on documents, and one CCR plus one XMR review covers more ground-truth errors than two CCR reviews (56.7% vs. 42.7%). Most other comparisons are descriptive; in our primary test, only SR2 differs significantly from CCR. A factorial design that varies generator, reviewer model, and context independently, and evaluation on established benchmarks such as FEVER (Thorne et al., 2018), AVeriTeC (Schlichtkrull et al., 2023), CUAD (Hendrycks et al., 2021), or LegalBench (Guha et al., 2023), would test these patterns more directly.

Design. All artifacts came from a single generator, and each capability tier is represented by one reviewer model (three models from two developers), so reviewer capability and model identity are confounded. All cross-model conditions also include context independence, so H4 (an interaction between context and model independence) cannot be identified; a factorial design is left to future work. CCR and SR differ both in context and in whether the reviewer sees the original request, so their comparison does not isolate context independence. The GPT-5.4 reviews ran through the Codex CLI agent, which can read files in its working directory; we have no record of which directory that was. No GPT-5.4 finding mentions a ground-truth identifier or file, but that absence does not rule out access.

Data and measurement. The ground truth consists of planted errors written at injection time and was not independently annotated, and the matcher was not audited by hand. The same-model baselines reuse data collected before the cross-model conditions; their records cannot be checked against raw model output, and we treat them as unverified rather than clean (Section 4.1). The union comparison is retrospective: CCR runs differ widely (56, 37, and 29 matched errors), the headline pairing is among the higher of the reused run combinations, and whether the matcher treats the reviewers’ output styles equally is unmeasured. The per-error-type and per-category comparisons are descriptive and were not tested for significance. Token counts were recorded only for the four Gemini conditions, so we cannot report cost per review or per detected error across conditions; the two-review-call comparison matches calls, not compute.

Language. All artifacts and ground-truth annotations are in Korean, and review output language was not fixed across conditions: in run 1, 20 of 30 CCR reviews are in English while the other conditions’ reviews are mostly in Korean. Because the matcher’s keyword component compares findings with Korean ground-truth text (Appendix A), it may under-credit English-language reviews. Other languages are untested.

Generalization. The case studies are small: B1 and B2 showed ceiling effects, B3 has 12 articles from a single source, and in B5 one model returned no findings for one target. Our results are a snapshot of early-2026 models. A partial external-data check on ReaLMistake detector outputs (Appendix D) neither replicates nor contradicts our main comparison.

Improved verification can catch errors in AI-generated code and analysis before they cause harm, but over-reliance is a risk: even our union approach matches only 56.7% of the planted errors under our automated matcher. We emphasize that our framework is intended to augment, not replace, human review; the undetected planted errors and the model-bias false positives (Section 5.8) underscore the continued importance of human judgment for high-stakes applications.

AI tools were used throughout this work, and we report their use as part of the method. The artifacts, the injected errors, and the same-model baseline reviews were produced by Claude Opus 4.6 through the Claude Code agent tool; the cross-model reviews were produced by the listed reviewer models, Gemini through its API and GPT-5.4 through the Codex CLI agent. Claude Code was also used to write the analysis and audit scripts, to recompute every reported number from the per-session records, to check the manuscript against the raw data (which led to the corrections described in Section 4.1), and to draft and revise substantial parts of the text under the author’s direction. Every reference was checked for existence against bibliographic databases, and unresolved entries were checked by hand. The author reviewed the final text and takes full responsibility for all of its content.
We thank Evgenii Arsentev for a public review of version 1 (PREreview, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23132634), which prompted the additions in version 2.

The per-session review records, the 30 artifacts with their 150 ground-truth defect annotations, and the matching, aggregation, and audit scripts are available from the author on request. They include the per-session sets of detected ground-truth identifiers, which are what the union and Jaccard figures in Section 5.2 are computed from, so every set-level number in this paper can be recomputed independently.

Old Ideas, Novel Problems: The Instability of LLM-Based Novelty Evaluation. AI-based ideation systems are often evaluated on the novelty of their ideas, and that judgment is increasingly delegated to large language models. Such judges are typically built ad hoc and validated, if at all, on human-authored papers rather than on the generated ideas they are meant to score. So, how do novelty judges perform? Not well. We present a systematic controlled study of novelty evaluation design choices. We build an evaluation set automatically, mining OpenReview for passages where reviewers explicitly affirm or dispute a paper's originality and keeping only submissions with unanimous agreement at the extremes of their research area; we pair these with ideas from a vanilla LLM generator. Across six judges, we find that seemingly small prompt design choices have large consequences; e.g., simply telling the judge that reviewers found one idea novel and the other not can change its verdict on more than half of the identical idea pairs it is shown, shifting pairwise accuracy by over 50 points and occasionally pushing it below chance. The same change helps one judge and hurts another.

Retrieval and larger reasoning budgets help little, and two purpose-built novelty evaluators are outperformed by our cheapest prompted baseline. These results raise questions about reported novelty gains of automated ideation systems, and call for robust novelty evaluation methods.

Recent years have seen a proliferation of systems that generate research ideas and propose new directions. A central criterion for judging such systems is novelty: whether the ideas they produce contribute a meaningful conceptual advance. Many works therefore automate this assessment, using it both to evaluate the ideas a system outputs and as an internal component of the ideation pipeline, letting agents filter and refine a pool of candidate ideas Wang et al. (2024); Yamada et al. (2025).

To date, there is no standard approach for novelty assessment, and papers suggesting a new ideation system typically ship their own ad hoc LLM judge Radensky et al. (2026); Gottweis et al. (2025). Such judges are built around the system at hand, and might assume certain priors (e.g., a particular idea format). Their robustness, and the design choices behind them (such as their instructions, or whether they are allowed to access prior work), are rarely tested or justified. Validation rests on small annotated sets Radensky et al. (2026), outdated data that predates LLMs’ knowledge cutoffs Shen et al. (2026), or human-authored papers Si et al. (2024), a different distribution from the generated ideas the judge is actually applied to Chen et al. (2026).

We present a systematic, extensive study of LLM-based novelty evaluation. Through controlled experiments, we vary the design choices practitioners make: which LLM is used as a judge and how the judge is prompted, whether evaluation is pointwise (is this idea novel?) or pairwise (which of these two is more novel?), its reasoning budget, whether it may retrieve related work, and the format of the judged ideas. We evaluate judges on human-authored ideas, and explore how their behavior changes when LLM-generated ideas are judged alongside them. We also benchmark off-the-shelf LLMs against specialized novelty judges Yamada et al. (2025); Shahid et al. (2025).

To this end, we build a benchmark using an automated pipeline that mines high-precision novelty labels from peer reviews (Figure 2). Unlike prior work relying on coarse proxies like paper acceptance Qiao et al. (2026) or outdated novelty scores that venues no longer publish Schopf and Färber (2026), we derive labels from the review itself. We isolate passages where reviewers explicitly affirm or dispute the originality of a contribution, retaining only submissions with unanimous consensus in the top or bottom decile of their venue. We complement these with LLM-generated ideas, sampled under settings very likely to yield lower novelty.

Using this benchmark, we find that novelty judges are strikingly brittle. Changes to the evaluation setup, such as telling the judge that reviewers found one of two ideas novel, change a judge’s verdict on more than half of the identical pairs it is shown and swing its accuracy by more than 50 points (Figure 1). Judges also behave differently on generated ideas than on human-authored ones, exposing a systematic gap in current evaluation practice: pairwise judges degrade once the comparison involves generated ideas, and grow markedly more brittle there. How brittle also depends on the judge, in ways that are hard to anticipate: in Figure 1, the steadier judge on human-authored ideas is the one that collapses on generated ones. The usual remedies, such as more reasoning or retrieval, help little and can even hurt. We further show that costlier, more complex dedicated novelty evaluators do not necessarily give better verdicts. Overall, LLM novelty judges are highly unstable, calling into question the robustness of a large body of prior work that uses LLM judges to evaluate the novelty of generated scientific ideas.

Our contributions are as follows: A controlled study of novelty judges, spanning six judge backbones, pointwise and pairwise judgments, and design choices like prompt design, retrieval, reasoning effort, and idea format, on human-written and LLM-generated ideas. An automated, reusable pipeline that mines explicit novelty signals from peer reviews, yielding two evaluation setups: Human-Only (strongest high-novelty vs. weakest low-novelty human papers) and Human+Generated (strongest high-novelty vs. ideas from a deliberately simple LLM generator). The pipeline can be rerun on new conference data, and we release all data and code. An empirical finding that the same judge flips its verdicts on the same instances across plausible configurations. The effect can be stronger on generated ideas, where judges are actually used, and common fixes (retrieval, more reasoning, costlier dedicated judges) offer limited help.

Ideation systems span end-to-end agentic scientists Lu et al. (2026); Yamada et al. (2025), multi-agent pipelines that debate and refine hypotheses Gottweis et al. (2025); Su et al. (2025), and literature-grounded ideators that search over or recombine prior work Wang et al. (2024); Hu et al. (2024); Li et al. (2024); Baek et al. (2025); Radensky et al. (2026). Novelty is central to all of them, and its assessment is often delegated to LLM-based judges.

Large-scale evaluations of such novelty judges have so far used human-authored ideas. Examples are Moussa et al. (2026); Wu et al. (2026), who align judges with peer-review content, Schopf and Färber (2026); Qiao et al. (2026), who extract novelty labels from review scores, and Lin et al. (2024), who use a temporal proxy, treating the later of two arXiv papers published years apart as more novel. Liu and Zhai (2026) forgo labels altogether, testing whether a novelty metric’s score moves as expected when the pool of prior work is perturbed, e.g., by inserting the paper itself or removing the papers it cites. Work that does examine generated ideas rests on human annotation and is thus small and specific. Si et al. (2024) present a small dataset of mostly student-annotated ideas, focusing on a single generation system and 7 LLM-related research topics. Shahid et al. (2025) evaluate a literature-grounded novelty checker on a small set of ideas produced by one system Radensky et al. (2026), Sinhahajari et al. (2026) validate LLM judgments of generated research questions against expert annotation, and Gupta and Pruthi (2025) have annotators trace generated research documents back to prior work, targeting plagiarism rather than novelty.
To our knowledge, no prior work systematically studies automatic novelty evaluation of generated ideas.

LLM judges are sensitive to design choices such as presentation order Wang et al. (2023), pointwise versus pairwise formats Liusie et al. (2024); Tripathi et al. (2025), and authority cues Ye et al. (2025). LLMs more broadly are swayed by external context Xie et al. (2024). Such brittleness has seen little examination in novelty judgment, which we study here.

Our goal is to evaluate novelty judges on ideas spanning higher and lower levels of novelty, authored both by humans and by automated ideation systems. We collect ideas into two pools, such that ideas in one are expected to be more novel than those in the other (Figure 2). The described data collection pipeline scales to larger idea pools and can be rerun on future review cycles, keeping the benchmark evergreen. It is also not tied to ICLR: it applies to any venue that publishes free-text reviews, such as NeurIPS or ACL Rolling Review.

We extract novelty labels from ICLR 2026 submissions and their reviews. Unlike prior review-based datasets (§ 2), which rely on acceptance decisions Qiao et al. (2026), a coarse proxy that folds in other quality dimensions, or on novelty scores that venues no longer publish Schopf and Färber (2026), we derive labels from the review text. Reviewers state verdicts on originality in prose, scattered across the strengths and weaknesses sections. We therefore prompt claude-opus-4-6 to extract novelty signals: snippets where reviewers affirm or dispute the novelty of the contribution itself. We validate extraction on 50 samples: an expert annotator agreed with the extracted polarity (positive/negative) 94 % of the time, and no disagreement would flip a reviewer’s polarity. Appendix A.1 lists additional details on mining novelty labels from human reviews.

We label a submission novel when most reviewers praise its originality and none dispute it. It must also score at the top of the venue: accepted, in the top decile of its ICLR primary area by average rating, and above a fixed floor on average contribution score. We use its abstract as the idea.

The complementary pool inverts every criterion. Its reviewers must dispute the contribution’s originality: a majority give negative novelty signals, and no reviewer gives a positive one. Its submission must sit at the bottom of the venue: rejected, with an average rating in the bottom decile of its ICLR primary area and an average contribution score below a fixed ceiling.

As discussed in § 2, novelty judges have been evaluated at scale only on human-authored papers, while work on generated ideas, the target distribution when evaluating ideation systems, relies on small expert-annotated sets. Such annotations are slow and expensive to collect, and, once released, liable to leak into the training data of the very models later used as novelty judges. We therefore build the generated pool under an explicit weak-labeling assumption: every idea in the generated pool is less novel than every validated novel idea. We design the pool to keep this assumption conservative. Its human side is the validated novel pool described above: top-decile accepted ICLR papers whose reviewers, having read the full paper, unanimously affirmed the novelty of the contribution. Its generated side comes from claude-sonnet-4-5, a deliberately non-frontier model released over a year ago, which is given only the ICLR primary area of its human counterpart and asked to “generate a novel idea” in a single pass, with no literature access, tools, scaffold, or feedback.

For the pairwise format, we consider each generated idea less novel than the top-decile human idea it is paired with, and for the pointwise format we treat generated ideas simply as not scientifically novel. We argue this is highly plausible given the state of technology in 2025 (see Appendix on newer generators).

As a check that the assumption is not obviously violated, a computer science professor with broad expertise across AI areas annotated 30 Human+Generated pairs blind to source and with idea order shuffled, following the same instructions as our judge prompts. For each pair, the expert (1) chose the more novel idea and (2) decided whether the idea they ranked lower is novel, giving written justifications and citing prior work where relevant. We concentrated the sample where the assumption is most likely to fail. It included 25 pairs our strongest pairwise judge (claude-opus-4-6) got wrong, and five controls it got right. The expert sided with the human idea in all 30 pairs, with no ties, and judged none of the 30 generated ideas novel, over roughly five hours of annotation. We present this as a sanity check on the hardest cases rather than a validation of every label (see Appendix for details and examples).
Finally, this labeling assumption has no bearing on our evaluation of instability: two configurations that return different verdicts on the same pair cannot both be right, whatever its label.

We consider the two common formats of novelty evaluation: (1) Pointwise Shahid et al. (2025); Yamada et al. (2025), where the judge is given a single idea and decides whether it is novel enough to clear the bar of a top AI venue (binary classification), and (2) Pairwise Qiao et al. (2026), where the judge is given two ideas and decides which of the two is more novel (ranking). The pointwise verdict is thus a thresholded judgment: an idea can be original in some respect and still be not-novel in this sense, as with a straightforward composition of known methods. Our judge prompt sets this bar by casting the judge as a senior reviewer at a venue such as ICLR and instructing it not to credit trivial innovation (Appendix). Beyond their prevalence, pointwise and pairwise evaluations are the atomic components underlying more complex protocols, such as majority voting and tournament-style ranking Si et al. (2024); Gottweis et al. (2025).

We assemble the collected ideas into two setups, each a pair of pools: \boldsymbol{D_{+}} (novel ideas) and \boldsymbol{D_{-}} (lower-novelty ideas), populated so that an idea drawn from D_{+} can be assumed more novel than one drawn from D_{-}. In Human-Only, D_{+} holds the validated novel ideas and D_{-} the validated lower-novelty ideas, so both sides are human-authored. In Human+Generated, D_{+} is unchanged and D_{-} holds the weakly labeled generated ideas. The two setups thus share D_{+} and differ only in the source of D_{-}. Accordingly, D_{-} does not denote a fixed set of ideas, but whichever pool fills the lower-novelty side of the setup at hand. Each data setup supports both pointwise and pairwise judgment. In pointwise, every idea is one instance, labeled by its pool: D_{+} ideas are novel and D_{-} ideas not-novel, i.e., below the novelty bar of a top venue. In pairwise, each idea in D_{+} is matched with one from D_{-} in the same ICLR primary area (e.g., generative models), so the two sides are topically comparable. In Human-Only, where D_{-} is the smaller pool, an idea may be matched more than once (Table, Appendix).

An idea in our benchmark is a single abstract, human-authored or generated. A submission’s own abstract advertises experimental outcomes that an LLM ideator, with no execution, cannot produce without hallucinating results. We therefore apply opus-4-6 to every human abstract to remove evaluation artifacts (e.g., numerical results, claims of superiority to specific baselines; see Prompt, Appendix A.1). Generated ideas are emitted in this format directly.

We perform a systematic study of novelty judges, spanning both judgment formats, a range of judge backbones, and several evaluation dimensions, on both data setups (Figure 3). Each run modifies a single design choice relative to a reference configuration, holding the rest of the evaluation process fixed. In the reference configuration, the judge receives a single idea (pointwise) or a pair of ideas (pairwise) and returns a novelty verdict with its reasoning, using high reasoning effort (where exposed) and no literature search. To stabilize predictions, we aggregate multiple calls. Pointwise judges take the majority vote of three calls. Pairwise judges are called three times per presentation order (A vs. B and B vs. A) to mitigate position bias (Wang et al., 2023), and the idea selected in more of the six calls wins. An even split is recorded as a tie, i.e., the judge cannot distinguish the two ideas. In Human+Generated, the reference D_{-} is generated by claude-sonnet-4-5 (§ 3.1); since this generator fixes the lower-novelty side of the benchmark, we also treat it as a study parameter. Appendix summarizes the reference and its controlled changes (Table), and Appendix gives the judge prompts and implementation details.

The instructions given to the judge. We explore six prompts: the reference, which casts the judge as a reviewer and gives explicit novelty criteria with guardrails against trivial contributions (Prompt), and five alternatives (P1–P5, Table, Appendix). P1 and P2 weaken the novelty definition given in the reference prompt: P1 drops the warning against trivial or incremental contributions, and P2 removes the definition of novelty altogether. P3–P5 (a family of pairwise prompts inspired by Si et al. (2024)) ask the judge to choose between two ideas: P3 tells the judge that reviewers at a top AI conference found one idea novel and the other not, P4 omits this reviewer framing and asks which idea is novel, and P5 retains the reviewer framing but asks which idea was judged more novel. The prompts are not equivalent, but each is a formulation a practitioner could reasonably choose for the same evaluation goal.

Whether the judge sees related work alongside the idea. In the retrieval condition the judge additionally receives 5 abstracts of related work, found by queries probing the novelty of the idea’s main contributions and restricted to papers published before the submission deadline (Appendix). We also adjust the prompt, asking the judge to assess novelty against the retrieved work.

The inference-time reasoning budget given to the judge. Assessing novelty requires comparing an idea against the judge’s knowledge and deciding whether the overlap with prior work is substantial, which we expect to be reasoning-intensive. We test that expectation by lowering reasoning_effort from high to low for the backbones that expose the parameter.

The surface form in which ideas are presented to the judge. Prior work presents ideas in different formats, from free-form abstracts Wang et al. (2024) to structured research plans Shahid et al. (2025); Si et al. (2024), typically without justifying the choice. We therefore test the effect of converting every idea into a two-field purpose / mechanism plan, which holds the content of the idea fixed and changes only its presentation.

The number of judge calls we pool into one decision. Aggregation is a simple but costly way to stabilize verdicts Wang et al. (2023). We test whether dividing the aggregated calls by 3 (calling pointwise judges once, pairwise judges once per presentation order) degrades them.

We run our controlled study with a range of judge backbone models (gpt-5.{1,2,4}, claude-sonnet-4-5, claude-opus-4-{5,6}), all with training cutoffs predating the ICLR 2026 submission deadline so that the evaluated ideas fall outside their training data. The novelty labels are further still out of reach: they are derived from reviews that were only released on OpenReview on 2025-11-12, roughly two months after the deadline. Thus, even if an idea reached a judge’s training data through an earlier preprint, the reviewers’ verdict on its novelty could not have.

For pointwise evaluation we report F1 per class (novel / not-novel) and a macro average. For pairwise, we report two accuracy variants that differ in tie handling: (1) soft-accuracy: ties count as 0.5; (2) strict-accuracy: ties receive no credit. We mark with * changes that differ significantly from the reference configuration (p<0.05, two-sided non-parametric paired bootstrap; Appendix).

Figure 4 reports the controlled-study results. The first thing to note is that judges generally underperform, and rarely approach perfect results on this task. This happens even in the Human-Only setup, where D_{+} and D_{-} are drawn from opposite ends of the ICLR rating distribution and should be maximally separable. Performance is also highly unstable under configuration changes. Removing the guardrails from the novelty criteria, or dropping the criteria entirely (P1–P2), generally degrades pairwise judges while helping some pointwise ones. On pairwise Human+Generated, replacing the reference prompt with one that asks which idea human reviewers judged novel (P3) improves every judge (by over 20 points in some cases). Yet deleting the sentence about reviewers (P4) makes gpt-5.4 collapse below 50\%. Because both prompts judge the same pairs, the 52.6 -point gap means they disagree on at least 52.6 % of pairs (55.8% in practice), so this instability is independent of our labels.

To rule out the possibility that judges are reacting to stylistic differences between human-written and LLM-generated ideas rather than to their novelty, we rewrite all ideas into a shared plan format and rerun a subset of the changes that produced the largest shifts. The direction of the shifts is unchanged, and instability even grows: some changes flip the verdicts on more than two thirds of the examples, and P4 now costs gpt-5.4 24 points even on Human-Only (Figure, Appendix).

These shifts also do not move models together. The same change can be neutral or beneficial for one judge but destructive for another. This is clearest in pointwise judging (e.g., P1–P2), but also holds pairwise: retrieval is a large gain for claude-opus-4-5 on Human+Generated while neutral for others. A configuration validated on one judge thus carries no guarantee for another.

Design choices that prior work commonly reaches for, like increased reasoning Saha et al. (2025) or retrieval Shahid et al. (2025); Lin et al. (2024), have a limited and unexpected effect. Lowering the reasoning effort from "high" to "low" costs at most 7 points, and is usually neutral. Surprisingly, some models even benefit from a smaller reasoning budget. Retrieval is similarly underwhelming: it yields a statistically significant gain of at most 16 points (less than replacing the reference prompt with P3), only for some models, and never brings the absolute numbers near 100. This remains true when D_{-} is generated by other backbones, where retrieval even significantly degrades performance in some cases (Figure).

The effect of the same prompt change also depends on the judge and the data. Switching from P3 to P4 already shifts strict-accuracy on Human-Only by 21 points for claude-opus-4-6, but only about 7 for gpt-5.4. On Human+Generated, the shift grows for both judges, and gpt-5.4 becomes the more sensitive one (52.6 points). Which judge looks robust thus depends on the data, and validating on human-authored ideas can understate how much a prompt matters on generated ones.

Interestingly, removing instructions against trivial or additive novelty from the prompt (P1) harms every judge once AI-generated ideas are involved, while being mostly neutral on human-authored pairs. This might indicate that LLM-generated ideas lean more towards this style of ideation.

Across ideation models generating D_{-}, judges generally degrade once the lower-novelty ideas are LLM-generated rather than human-authored, with performance below chance for some backbones (Figure, Appendix). Older generators are no easier to judge: ideas from gpt-5 hurt judges about as much as those from gpt-5.4.

Another concern is the judges’ tie rate: how often a pairwise judge gives an uncertain verdict (§ 4). Depending on the configuration, even strong judges like claude-opus-4-6 can tie on 35\% of pairs, and weaker ones like claude-sonnet-4-5 on more than half. Ignoring ties or counting them as half-correct can substantially change how evaluation systems are ranked (soft-accuracy results in Figure, Appendix). Judges tie more often on Human+Generated than on Human-Only, roughly twice as often for claude-opus-4-5 and claude-sonnet-4-5, indicating higher uncertainty there. Turning off verdict aggregation adds further uncertain predictions, more than doubling tie rates in certain cases (Table, Appendix). Together with the tendency to tie more on generated data, this explains the drop it causes on Human+Generated.

We also observe that, in line with prior work Raina et al. (2024); Liusie et al. (2024), pairwise judging is more stable than pointwise judging, but only on Human-Only. On the same data, pointwise judges are as unstable as on Human+Generated.

A common use of a novelty judge is to compare two ideation systems, a setting with no gold label. To test it, we pit the ideas of a stronger backbone against those of a weaker one from the same family (Appendix), and count the number of verdicts changed. Changing the prompt alone flips a quarter to a third of the verdicts on average, and moves the share of pairs awarded to the stronger system by up to 29 points.

Surprisingly, retrieval yields limited gains, if any (Figure 4). To understand why, we inspect 10 cases where retrieval flips a correct pointwise verdict to a wrong one, keeping only flips where all three aggregated calls agree on each side, ruling out noise (Appendix). We find that retrieved papers can lead the judge to dismiss contributions it had considered novel, even when nothing contradicts their novelty. In one case, the judge without retrieval deemed an idea combining two concepts novel, agreeing with the reviewers. Given papers presenting each concept separately, it dismissed the same idea as “a direct combination of existing ingredients…”. Retrieval can also mislead the other way, overriding the judge’s knowledge. Without retrieval, the judge correctly described an idea from D_{-} as “a broad composition of known components”, but with retrieval it concluded the idea “…does appear novel in its overall problem formulation and synthesis relative to the provided related work …”. This matters, as many pipelines ask novelty judges to assess ideas against retrieved work Shahid et al. (2025); Moussa et al. (2026).

A possible explanation is that our retrieval pipeline is too weak, and a stronger retriever would let judges ground their verdicts in the right prior work. We test this by exploring a much stronger retrieval-augmented judge. We instantiate a strong agentic RAG judge on top of gpt-5.6-sol, a newer and stronger backbone than any judge so far, run at reasoning_effort=xhigh and equipped with a web-search tool. Unlike the standard pipeline, which hands judges five pre-retrieved abstracts, this judge searches the literature iteratively, with no cap on searches or inspected results. As in our standard pipeline, search is restricted to papers published before the submission deadline (Appendix).

We compare it on Human+Generated to judges using the standard pipeline, all called once per idea for parity (Figure in the appendix). The agentic judge reaches 0.78 macro-F1, 11 points behind claude-opus-4-6 and within noise of claude-opus-4-5 and gpt-5.4, at 10\times the cost. The modest retrieval gains in Figure 4 are thus not an artifact of our pipeline.

Our study focuses on prompted novelty judges, off-the-shelf LLMs instructed to return a novelty verdict, since this is how most ideation systems assess novelty Li et al. (2024); Hu et al. (2024); Shen et al. (2026). Prior work also proposes dedicated novelty judges, which spend far more compute per decision. We test whether this pays off for two of them: Idea Novelty Checker Shahid et al. (2025), a literature-grounded pipeline that retrieves, filters, and re-ranks candidate papers before judging the idea against them, and AI-Scientist Yamada et al. (2025), a ReAct-style agent that iteratively searches Semantic Scholar until it reaches a verdict. We run each with claude-opus-4-6 and gpt-5.4 under its original settings (one call per decision, without verdict aggregation). Since both are pointwise, we compare them to prompted judges in the pointwise format only, measuring cost in USD over the full evaluation set (details in Appendix, per-evaluator results in Appendix).

Figure 5 plots the cost-quality tradeoff for claude-opus-4-6 (see Figure for gpt-5.4). The extra machinery does not pay off: in every setup and backbone, our cheapest prompted configuration outscores both dedicated judges by 8 to 29 macro-F1 points, while costing up to 32\times less.

We ran a controlled study of LLM novelty judges, using an automatic pipeline that mines novelty labels from peer-review text and pairs human-authored with LLM-generated ideas. Judges are brittle: plausible prompt edits swing pairwise accuracy by over 50 points, and the same edit that helps one backbone sinks another below chance. Even on human-authored ideas, where judges are usually validated, a single edit moves a strong judge by over 20 points, and which judge looks most robust can flip once generated ideas are involved. The usual remedies (retrieval, more reasoning, costlier dedicated judges) help little. Pairwise judges are least stable in the setting they are built for: large shifts are far more common on Human+Generated than on Human-Only, and judges grow less certain on generated data. Validating a judge on human-authored papers, or against a single ideation system, says little about how it will behave on the generated ideas it is asked to score. Until evaluation protocols account for these sensitivities, automated novelty assessments should be interpreted with caution.

The lower-novelty side of Human+Generated carries no observed novelty label. Its labels rest instead on a weak-labeling assumption: a top-decile ICLR submission whose reviewers agree is original is more novel than an idea produced in a single scaffold-free, tool-free pass of a deliberately non-frontier model. We argue for this ordering in § 3.1, but cannot verify it for the entire dataset, and a generated idea that occasionally clears the bar would add label noise. Such noise could blur which configuration is more accurate, but not our instability findings. If two configurations score differently on the same examples, they disagree on some of them, and at most one can be right on each, whatever the true label. To check that the assumption is not obviously violated, we ran a blind expert study. Because our pairs span many ICLR areas, judging them requires broad expertise in AI, so we recruited a single computer science professor with that breadth. They annotated 30 pairs in roughly five hours, most of them pairs our strongest judge got wrong, and agreed with our labels on every one (Appendix). This makes a systematic violation of the assumption improbable.

The assumption is strongest for the non-frontier generator used in most of our experiments (claude-sonnet-4-5). Stronger generators are more likely to produce ideas that clear the bar, so results that regenerate the lower-novelty pool with them warrant more caution.

section: Partial coverage of the design space.
text: Our controlled study varies one design dimension at a time relative to a fixed reference configuration. We do probe interactions between design choices, but only in a few places: the retrieval experiment across ideation backbones, for instance, uses a single judge per model family (Appendix, Figure). The full cross-product of judges, ideation backbones, and design choices grows quickly, so we intentionally picked only a few cross-interaction experiments in order to keep costs manageable. For reference, the experiments described here cost roughly $15,000 in API spend at 2026 list prices, including preliminary and discarded runs.

We focus on novelty because it is a widely used and thoroughly studied evaluation criterion. However, novelty is only one of several important criteria for evaluating ideas. Others include estimated impact Li and Jacobson (2026) and surprisal Agarwal et al. (2026). We believe many of these attributes are intertwined, and future work should study them as well.

Our benchmark is built from ICLR 2026 submissions and reviews obtained through the public OpenReview API, and used in accordance with its terms. Both annotators in our validation studies (§ A.1.1, §) are volunteers. Part of our data consists of LLM-generated ideas, which we release clearly marked as synthetic and unvalidated. Given that our findings show current novelty judges to be brittle, we caution against deploying them in consequential settings, and in particular as a substitute for human peer review. To support transparency and reproducibility, we release our data, prompts, and code under an open license. We used LLM-based tools for parts of our data collection pipeline (§ A.1) and for minor writing and coding assistance.

Steering Follows Geometry, Not Labels: Emotion Directions in a Full-Duplex Speech Model. Full-duplex voice agents need to modulate emotion and delivery during real-time conversations, when de-escalating a complaint, carrying urgency in dispatch, softening a clinical result. Emotion and delivery control is well studied for TTS and turn based models through prompt-conditioned synthesis, reference-conditioned synthesis and activation steering; PersonaPlex controls identity in a duplex model but not affect. We study emotion steering in Moshi, a fully open sourced full-duplex speech language model, across four emotions, using mean-difference activation steering, which costs only a few vector additions per frame and no retraining. We show that emotion is linearly decodable from Moshi's residual stream, but activation steering is only partially achievable, and unevenly so; as happy, angry and surprise steer towards a shared direction while sad is distinctly steerable. We also show that the shared component across the three emotions cannot simply be projected away from all the emotions equally.

Emotion and delivery control is a well understood problem statement for voice agents with use-cases spanning across various real time voice interactions involving de-escalating a complaint by modulating delivery, carrying urgency in dispatch, or softening clinical results. Different scenarios require varying degrees of emotion control in voice agents which humans are able to gauge and dictate quite effectively.

Mechanisms such as prompt-conditioned and reference-audio-conditioned audio synthesis have been studied extensively [1,2], which suits turn based or Text-to-Speech (TTS) synthesizers. Activation steering [3,4] is another effective and efficient methodology to control emotion or delivery, as shown in EmoSteer-TTS [5]. Full-duplex speech models are superseding turn-based voice agents due to improved natural communication with humans.

With Full duplex models becoming more powerful and feasible in the modern world, the effect of activation steering becomes more relevant in the context of emotion and delivery control. At the same time prior work understudies its impact on newer full-duplex speech language models such as Moshi [6], which listens and speaks at once, emits audio frame by frame at 12.5 Hz through a neural codec, and carries its own dialogue state. Recent full duplex models, such as PersonaPlex [10], which is an extension to Moshi, focus primarily on identity control via prompt conditioning, instead of dynamic delivery or emotion control.

Whether a mean-difference vector direction still controls emotion effectively, under those conditions is untested. In this paper we analyze Moshi’s[6] capability to steer towards four emotions; angry, sad, happy and surprise.
Our contributions include:
(i) A linear probe that is able to read the emotions accurately off the residual stream (§ 5.1).
(ii) A diagnosis about the effectiveness of mean-difference activation steering for all the four emotions (§ 5.4)

(iii) A demonstration of shared common axis across happy, angry and surprise emotions that explain the gaps, with their cosine similarity being very high compared to a cross-speaker variance of the residual stream.
(iv) A method to project out the shared component to fix angry, but not as effectively for surprise. (§ 5.5)
(v) An analysis of the model’s own generative limitations to produce emotions in audio (§ 5.6).

Activation steering for emotion in full duplex models. Adding a direction to hidden states controls behaviour in text language models [3,4]. EmoSteer-TTS [5] brings this to speech, applying difference vectors to a searched subset of activations in flow-matching synthesisers, training-free. Two recent studies question whether a single direction is the right instrument at all. Du et al. [15] find with sparse autoencoders that emotional variation in an LLM-based TTS model is distributed over several latent features rather than one global shift, and that intervening on a chosen subset outperforms global steering. Wang et al. [16] compare steering sites geometrically and report that a flow-matching module generalises poorly across speakers because speaker and emotion are entangled there, while the speech-LM module offers a cleaner low-dimensional emotion subspace. Braun et al. [17,18] make the same kind of geometric argument in text language models, predicting steering reliability from the cosine structure of the activation differences a vector is built from - measured within one behaviour, where ours is measured between emotions.
Our result is the duplex counterpart of both observations.

Steering has reached full-duplex models, though not for delivery: Chang et al. [12] add a perception vector to reduce the state inertia that makes a model miss the opening of an interruption, training-free, on Moshi among others. Duplex systems that do control delivery train for it - F-Actor [13] conditions on voice, topic and conversational behaviour, and JoyAI-Talker [14] takes delivery instructions at inference after fine-tuning on expressive speech. We are not aware of prior work controlling emotion in a streaming duplex model by editing activations.

We write real ESD [7] recordings into Moshi’s output codebooks, with their transcripts forced through Moshi’s inner monologue, and let it run a forward pass. Moshi’s audio output is a stream of Mimi codebook tokens that can be overridden. For those frames the model is producing that recording.

We read the residual stream over the last few frames before the override ends, by which point the model has been carried through the whole utterance rather than its opening. Averaging over frames and clips and subtracting the same quantity on neutral recordings gives one direction per layer, v_{l}=\mathrm{mean}(h_{l}\mid e)-\mathrm{mean}(h_{l}\mid\mathrm{neutral}), which we unit-normalise. Whether that state is genuinely emotional is measured at § 5.6.

section: Injecting direction vectors to steer emotion
text: At the injection stage, we interpolate the output of layers 0, 8 and 24, at every frame (Figure 1) towards the desired emotion, by adding \alpha\cdot w(l)\cdot r_{l}\cdot\hat{v}_{l}. Here r_{l} is that layer’s median residual norm, so \alpha is relative to the activations it is added to, and w(l)=1-l/31 weights deeper layers down. The depformer that predicts the audio codebooks, the codec and the other 29 layers are left untouched.

section: Injecting direction vectors to steer emotion
text: We use \alpha=0.30 and this three-layer schedule throughout the experiments. Both were chosen in preliminary work on held-out sentences: strength peaks at 0.30 and falls away past it as intelligibility degrades faster than the emotion improves, and spreading the push across layers 0, 8 and 24 beat concentrating it at specific layers.
To determine whether Moshi is able to distinguish the emotions accurately, we fit one multinomial logistic regression per layer to 60 clips per emotion drawn from the same states.

Inputs are standardised and reduced to 30 principal components inside each split, since 4096 features against 240 rows is ill-conditioned. Accuracy is cross-validated over five splits, each holding out two of the ten speakers, so no speaker appears in both training and test.

Model. All experiments use kyutai/moshika-pytorch-q8, the int8 release of Moshi [6], with its Mimi codec at 12.5 Hz, on a single 16 GB RTX 4090 laptop GPU, which the int8 checkpoint is chosen to fit. Quantization raises word error rate across all unsteered and steered generated audio, so we report word error as a difference from the unsteered baseline on the same sentence and seed rather than as an absolute measure.

Vectors. For emotion direction vector construction we use 800 clips per emotion from the English half of ESD [7], which covers angry, happy, sad, surprise and neutral over ten speakers, across all ten speakers.
Audio Generation. We use two different modes for audio generation in Moshi.

Forced text mode fixes what is said so that only delivery can vary: all 720 Harvard sentences [11] - the 72 phonetically balanced lists of ten from the IEEE speech-quality standard, whose content is emotionally neutral - are forced through the inner monologue, and the model renders each one. Any change in the emotion score is then attributable to delivery, since the words are identical across conditions.

Free duplex mode is the setting the model is built for and gives up that control: Moshi hears an emotional ESD utterance on its input stream and answers in its own words, with nothing forced, 50 clips for each of five input emotions. Content is free to vary, so an emotion score there reflects delivery and wording together, and replies are short - the model often says little. Vectors, injection schedule and \alpha are identical in both.

Metrics and Evaluation. emotion2vec+ large [8] (iic/emotion2vec_plus_large) is used for emotion probability labels and emotion embeddings. Emotion is scored only on clips with at least 1.5 s of voiced audio, since emotion2vec reads silence as sad and averaging over near-silent clips invents a sad result that is not there. Every emotion number is reported against the score real ESD speech of that emotion receives from the same classifier, which we call its ceiling: held out from the clips building the similarity centroids, referring to the mean classifier score and not a theoretical bound from human level speech. Similarity to real speech is reported as a mean-centred cosine: raw cosine between two unrelated real recordings is already 0.713, so uncentred values compress into the top quarter of their range.

Whisper large-v3 [9] (openai/whisper-large-v3) is used for word error rate (WER), against the imposed sentence under the forced text mode and against the model’s own inner monologue in free duplex mode where no reference sentence exists. The two therefore measure different things - fidelity to a script, and agreement between what the model planned to say and what its codec produced - and are not directly comparable across settings, only across conditions within one.

The probe successfully reads emotion out of the residual stream at every layer (Table 1). We report accuracy at layers 0, 8 and 24, the three the directions are injected into, with the best of all 32 alongside. Layer 0 is weaker throughout, which is consistent with the emotion being progressively linearly separable with depth rather than present at the input.

The contrast that will be apparent in following sections is the three-way accuracy over angry, happy and surprise - the emotions found to share highly similar steering directions (§ 5.4) reaches reasonably high accuracy of 0.661 at layer 8 and 0.678 at layer 24, against a chance rate of 0.333.

The information distinguishing these emotions is therefore present in the residual stream, and the limitations in steering highlights the shortcoming to be present in the steering vectors instead of the representation.

Table 2 displays steering accuracy for both audio generation modes together. Only sad reaches its own target, and it overshoots: 0.650 against the 0.448 genuine ESD sad scores. Angry reaches a quarter of its ceiling and surprise under a third, and in both the strongest rival is happy rather than the emotion asked for.

The two settings agree closely. Angry reaches 25% of ceiling with the forced text mode and 26% when the model chooses its own words; surprise 30% and 31%. Sad is steered exceptionally well. Word error is lower in duplex - 13.5% for angry against 32.2% - but reasonably so as explained in WER experimental setup section.

We notice that for angry, surprise and happy, where the probability goes is systematic rather than diffuse. Table 4 demonstrates the full distribution under both modes against the unsteered baseline. In both modes, we observe the audio being steered towards happy for all these three emotions.

We, additionally, provide results of steering against arbitrarily chosen random vectors as control to reinforce the observations above. (Table 3) compares the probability scores of Neutral and Happy across four arbitrary vectors against the steered counterparts. Injecting the four arbitrary vectors leaves emotion distribution virtually unaltered while the ESD constructed steering vectors differ significantly in terms of P(emotion), and WER.
The ordering is not an end-of-clip effect. Scoring only the first 1.2 s of each forced-text clip (Table 5) already gives 0.241 happy against 0.122 angry, and 0.376 happy against 0.125 surprise.
Intelligibility degrades under both conditions, especially under forced text mode with 71.5% for surprise being the worst.

Table 6 measures the same clips a second way: mean-centred cosine to the centroid of real ESD speech of each emotion, built from recordings disjoint from the clips scored against them. The pattern is the same, though both readings come from emotion2vec and are therefore not independent of one another.

The steering result is reasonably explained when the steering vectors themselves are analysed against each other. A cosine between two directions needs a scale to be read against, so we build every direction from one half of the ten speakers and compare it with the other half’s (Figure 2, right).

Angry agrees with itself at 0.65 and with surprise at 0.60; happy with itself at 0.60 and with surprise at 0.59, the margins beside each row. For these high-arousal emotions a different emotion is nearly as close as the same emotion recorded by different speakers. Sad’s nearest neighbour is 0.58 away.

Cosine across the entire corpus of speakers varies from the similarity scores on disjoint halves (Figure 2, left). Roughly a third of the apparent similarity between two emotion directions is shared speaker identity rather than shared emotion - the entanglement Wang et al. [16] report for flow-matching modules, measured here directly.

The contrast in the margins of 0.01 to 0.05 against 0.58, for self versus cross emotion similarity, separates the emotions that reach their own target from those that do not, and it is apparent in the direction vectors themselves prior to any audio generation.

section: Removing the shared direction does not fix it completely
text: We may assume that if the mean difference is dominated by what these emotions share, projecting that component out should separate them. To test this, we take the shared direction s_{l} at layer l to be the first right singular vector of the four unit-normalised directions stacked as a 4\times 4096 matrix - their leading principal component, about the origin rather than their mean since there are only four. It carries 61–64% of the total squared singular value at layers 0, 8 and 24. Subtracting a fraction of each unnormalised mean difference’s component along it, v_{e,l}(\beta)=v_{e,l}-(1-\beta)\,(v_{e,l}^{\top}s_{l})\,s_{l}, leaves the plain vector at \beta=1 and removes the shared component entirely at \beta=0, where angry and happy move from +0.69 to -0.56 at layer 24. Each is unit-normalised before injection (§ 3.2), so every setting enters at the same magnitude. 240 sentences each.

section: Removing the shared direction does not fix it completely
text: Removing the shared direction entirely leaves nothing to steer with - angry falls to 0.016, below the unsteered rate - implying it carries the direction that makes angry sound angry.

section: Removing the shared direction does not fix it completely
text: Removing half separates angry from happy for the first time here: P(angry) rises from 0.184 to 0.288, 26% to 40% of ceiling, the happy rival falls from 0.334 to 0.162, and word error falls from 32.2% to 22.6%, marginally under the 24.7% unsteered baseline.

section: Removing the shared direction does not fix it completely
text: The sweep leaves sad almost untouched, at 0.647 to 0.701 across all four settings. That is the control the construction provides: sad is the one direction not aligned with the shared component (|\cos|=0.245 at layer 24 against 0.89 – 0.94 for the others), so the manipulation barely changes it, and the movement in angry cannot be a generic effect of perturbing the vectors.

section: Removing the shared direction does not fix it completely
text: Surprise is not recovered at any setting, and removal makes it worse rather than better: it falls from 0.139 to 0.031 as \beta goes to zero, and never beats its strongest rival - happy at \beta\geq 0.5, sad below that. Partial removal resolves one of the three merged emotions, not all of them.

section: Analyzing Moshi’s limitations in rendering emotions
text: § 5.2 scored steered speech against real speech, which may be a harsher baseline to compare against. Some of that loss is the model’s own limitation as the model tries to propagate the stream via one forward pass. Driving a real recording through its output codebooks and scoring the model’s re-rendering of it — the prime condition — bounds how much of an emotion can reach the waveform at all through Moshi (Table 8).

section: Analyzing Moshi’s limitations in rendering emotions
text: The bound is non uniform. The re-rendering keeps 85% of the recording’s happy score but only 40% of its angry, and the lost probability moves to neutral instead of another emotion, implying that the codec may be discarding the prosodic extremes to keep what it needs for intelligible reconstruction. Angry loses most. Surprise is the only exception with a good re-render capacity of 0.459 compared to 0.593 for real recordings but a sharp drop in the continuation audio to 0.151; as it loses emotions partially towards happy.

section: Analyzing Moshi’s limitations in rendering emotions
text: Scored against that bound instead (Table 9), angry rises from 25% to 56% of ceiling and happy from 76% to 85%: about half of angry’s shortfall is the codec rather than the direction. Surprise does not recover at all. Its bound is 0.459 against the 0.458 real surprised speech scores, though those are different clip sets (Appendix A); on the same clips the re-rendering retains 77% of the recording’s surprise. Either way the codec carries most of it, so most of the gap between 0.136 and its ceiling belongs to the direction we inject.

section: Analyzing Moshi’s limitations in rendering emotions
text: But much of the confusion the steering vectors produce is already present in the shared direction and Moshi’s internal incapabilities in rendering emotions, before any direction is added, leaving aside surprise which remains unexplained after above analyses.
We test one model, one corpus, one extraction point and one injection schedule; we do not establish that other duplex speech models behave the same way.

The int8 checkpoint puts unsteered word error at 24.3% before any intervention, and we cannot rule out that a bf16 model carries emotion differently. The WER is high for many steered audio samples, hence we offer a diagnosis rather than a comprehensive method of delivery control. Every measurement comes from emotion2vec with no human listening test. The four emotions are ESD’s, and we make no claim about how emotion is organised in general.
Modern steering algorithms such as Sparse Auto Encoders (SAEs), LoRA or full retraining/fine-tuning remain unexplored in the paper.

We study whether activation steering controls emotion in a full-duplex speech model, where fast and dynamic controls to delivery control is highly beneficial. We derive steering directions from the residual stream and find that a linear probe separates the emotions in the activations while the mean-difference directions built from them barely do. For the high-arousal emotions, two different directions agree to within a few hundredths of what a single emotion’s direction agrees with itself across a change of speaker. Steering follows that geometry rather than the requested label, and only the emotion whose direction stands apart is controlled as its label implies. The result holds with the text forced as well as in a full duplex dialogue. We propose a generation-free check that explains it from the vectors alone, and show that the shared component is necessary rather than incidental: removing it entirely leaves a direction that steers nothing, while retaining half of it restores one of the merged emotions. Modern estimators built to discriminate smartly rather than to average, and the same comparison applied to a model finetuned for controllability, fall under further extensions to this work.

Thinking Inertia: LLMs Keep Thinking When Told Not To. Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly ship with explicit "thinking modes", yet their counterpart, "no-thinking", has received far less attention. We study LLMs' no-thinking behavior along two axes. a. How to measure no-thinking? Prior work typically defines no-thinking through proxies such as a disabled thinking mode or the absence of long traces. These proxies are unreliable: disabled thinking modes may still emit reasoning, while long traces may contain filler rather than genuine inference. We instead normalize each response into a pre-answer trace and final answer, and evaluate it at three levels: (i) Empty-Thinking Rate for strict answer-only compliance; (ii) instruction-aware Question-Pre-answer Relevance for similarity between the question and pre-answer trace; and (iii) LLM-as-judge Explicit Inference Rate for visible explicit inference. Together, these metrics distinguish answer-only output, relevant but non-inferential text, and explicit inference. b. How does no-thinking vary across tasks and models? We evaluate six prompting interventions on six LLMs across Boolean, multiple-choice, and open-ended questions. We find that explicit no-think controls cannot reliably eliminate visible inference. Models instead exhibit "Thinking Inertia": explicit inference persists even under strict controls and becomes more prevalent as the answer space opens.

Accuracy remains stable on Boolean and multiple-choice tasks, whereas open-ended tasks reveal a trade-off between answer-only compliance and task accuracy. Rewriting the same questions across answer spaces shows that supplying candidate answers makes answer-only responses easier to produce. These findings establish no-thinking as a non-trivial capability: stopping explicit reasoning cannot be assumed from model settings or instructions alone and deserves systematic evaluation alongside reasoning ability.

LLMs have benefited substantially from extended reasoning. From early chain-of-thought prompting to more recent test-time scaling, allocating additional tokens to intermediate computation before returning an answer has significantly improved performance across a wide range of tasks. The same mechanism, however, raises inference cost in both latency and token consumption, motivating a line of work on shortening, budgeting, or compressing reasoning traces. Beyond efficiency, knowing when to answer directly without extended reasoning is also important for human-like adaptive reasoning: humans often respond from intuition and deliberate only when needed. Together, these efficiency and adaptivity considerations motivate explicit control over reasoning behavior. As illustrated in Figure 2 (a), current frontier systems expose native thinking switches and reasoning-effort settings, while users can request direct answers through prompting.

Despite these explicit controls, as Figure 2 (b) illustrates, a frontier model with its reasoning channel disabled can still emit question-conditioned content in the ordinary answer channel or produce a short response that nonetheless contains a compact, task-specific reasoning step. Moreover, the community still lacks a clear definition of what a “no-thinking” response should look like. In practice, no-thinking is typically inferred from surface proxies: the prompt is placed in a no-think regime; the response does not return a separate reasoning trace, or the <think> block is absent; or the output is simply short. These proxies conflate instruction control with the suppression of visible reasoning. For example, a generic lead-in such as “Let me think about this. The answer should be <ans> ” carries no task-specific content, yet would be counted as reasoning by surface proxies. Conversely, a single compact equation may expose an explicit inferential step even when the response is short or contains no special reasoning tokens.

Motivated by this conflation, we study no-thinking as an observable response behavior and inspect the pre-answer text exposed before the final answer. In general question answering, pre-answer text may reflect reasoning, paraphrasing, fact restatement, or simple assertion. We therefore define three progressively more specific criteria for characterizing such text. (a) a discrete view of whether the complete visible output reaches the strict answer-only boundary, measured by the Empty-Thinking Rate (ETR); (b) a continuous view of whether any remaining pre-answer text T is relevant to the question Q, measured by instruction-aware Qwen3-Embedding-4B via Question–Pre-answer Relevance (QRel.); and (c) a reasoning view of whether T contains an explicit inferential step that addresses Q, measured by a blinded GPT-5.5 judge through the Explicit Inference Rate (EIR). The judge separates explicit inference from paraphrases and relevant non-inferential text, while task accuracy independently evaluates the final answer A. Thus, QRel. provides a relevance signal rather than final evidence of reasoning; conclusions about visible reasoning and thinking inertia rely on EIR together with ETR. This view defines a testable behavioral framework for comparing interventions, benchmarks, model families, and model scales.

Based on these metrics, our experiments further examine whether no-thinking can be controlled, regularized, and generalized. We first ask Q1. whether enabling or disabling the thinking mode actually suppresses visible pre-answer content. We then Q2. compare several interventions to test whether stronger answer-only constraints can make responses more answer-only without damaging task accuracy. Finally, we evaluate Q3. how this behavior changes across answer spaces, benchmark domains, and LLMs of different families and scales. The detailed intervention spectrum is introduced in Section 2.4; at a high level, it separates native no-think behavior, reasoning re-elicitation, semantic suppression, and structural prefix forcing. Our human validation supports all three metrics: a manual boundary audit corroborates ETR, the five annotators’ relevance judgments align closely with QRel., and their explicit-inference labels achieve 98.8% mean binary agreement with the primary GPT-5.5 judge used to compute EIR. The human annotations also reproduce the main answer-space and intervention trends, further supporting our central conclusions. The EIR results also remain robust when evaluated by an independent judge from a different model family.

Our results highlight four findings. (i) Explicit no-think controls are not reliable no-thinking controls: even a frontier LLM such as DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B) retains visible explicit inference in 99.9% of open-ended responses under its disabled-thinking setting. (ii) LLMs exhibit “thinking inertia”: visible inference is organized more by the task’s answer space than by the switch itself. Under both native and strict no-thinking settings, it remains lowest on Boolean tasks, intermediate on multiple-choice tasks, and highest on open-ended tasks. (iii) On open-ended tasks, stronger answer-only instructions reveal what we call a no-thinking–performance trade-off: stronger suppression improves answer-only compliance and reduces visible inference, but can also reduce task accuracy. Specifically, across the five LLMs with fully disabled thinking, strict answer-only prompting raises mean ETR from near zero to roughly 40% while reducing mean accuracy by about 15 percentage points. (iv) Answer space matters: for the same question, fact-like and candidate-visible formats make answer-only responses easier to produce than open-generation formats, showing that the pattern is not explained by benchmark difficulty or answer length alone.

In summary, our work makes two contributions. First, we define no-thinking as a measurable response-level behavior and provide a framework for evaluating it. Second, through comprehensive experiments across task families and diverse LLMs, we identify systematic behaviors including thinking inertia, the no-thinking–performance trade-off, and answer-space dependence. Together, these contributions support the broader goal of developing LLMs that, like humans, can adaptively determine when to reason and when to answer directly.

No-thinking in LLMs does not have a concrete definition. In practice, existing work often identifies it through three surface proxies, as summarized on the left side of Figure 2: (i) prompt-side control, where the model is run in a no-think setting or is not prompted to think step by step; (ii) visible-format control, where no-thinking is inferred from the absence of an explicit <think> block or a separate reasoning trace; and (iii) length-based control, where shorter generations produced by length control or chain-of-thought compression are treated as reduced reasoning. These proxies are convenient and easy to monitor, but they characterize the response by its surface prompting condition, visible format, or length, rather than by the actual content of the LLM response (such as the question-conditioned information it actually exposes).

Each of these formulations, however, has a simple failure case, illustrated on the right side of Figure 2. (i) A no-think instruction can still yield explanatory, question-dependent text before the final answer; disabling a thinking mode therefore does not by itself remove visible reasoning. (ii) Removing explicit <think> tags only removes a particular format; reasoning may still appear as ordinary language in the answer channel. (iii) Making an output short does not make it no-thinking, since a compact response can still encode the essential intermediate step needed to answer the question. Thus, the problem is not that these proxies are useless, but that none of them defines the behavioral object we want to study. We therefore operationalize no-thinking at the response level and progressively distinguish strict answer-only compliance, question relevance, and visible explicit inference. This observable definition does not make claims about latent computation inside the model, because extending the analysis to latent reasoning would substantially broaden the scope and make the boundary of no-thinking difficult to define clearly.

The observations above suggest that prompt-side heuristics alone are insufficient for studying no-thinking in a controlled way. We therefore ground our analysis in the response-centric framework shown in Figure 3.

Formally, let \pi denote a language model and Q a task sample. The query is wrapped by an intervention S(\cdot) (e.g., a system prompt such as “please answer <Question> directly”) before being passed to the model, which produces an observable response \pi\bigl(S(Q)\bigr)=\left(T,A\right) where A is the last parseable final answer and T comprises all readable visible text preceding it. We use (T,A) only as a decomposition of the observable response, without making claims about task-relevant computation in unobserved model states. The strict compliance check additionally scans the complete output, so substantive text after A is not treated as answer-only. Appendix E audits question restatement and answer-first edge cases.

Visible pre-answer text T. T contains all readable visible content before the final answer A, whether it appears in a special reasoning block, the ordinary answer channel, or a short lead-in. It may include an explicit derivation, a compact reasoning step, a paraphrase, a relevant assertion, or a generic template such as “The answer is”. These cases motivate evaluating the content of T rather than equating every non-empty T with reasoning.

Question type and answer space (Q,A). We write each task sample as Q=(q,c,\mathcal{A}), where q is the question, c is optional context, and \mathcal{A} is the admissible answer space, with A\in\mathcal{A}. For example, \mathcal{A}=\{\texttt{yes},\texttt{no}\} for Boolean verification, \mathcal{A}=\{\texttt{A},\texttt{B},\texttt{C},\texttt{D}\} for multiple-choice, and \mathcal{A} permits free-form generation for open-ended tasks. This lets us test whether no-thinking behavior changes under different answer interfaces.

Intervention S(\cdot). S(\cdot) denotes an external intervention applied to Q before generation, producing the model input S(Q). We consider two broad classes: (i) question-irrelevant interventions, which change the instruction, output constraint, or explicit thinking configuration while keeping Q fixed (e.g., prepending “Answer directly without thinking”); and (ii) question-relevant interventions, which modify the task instance itself, such as its surface form or answer space \mathcal{A} (e.g., converting an open-ended question into a multiple-choice one).
Together, this unified framework allows us to study no-thinking through strict compliance, relevance, and explicit inference rather than through surface proxies alone.

Under our formulation, T serves as the primary observable target, while task accuracy separately evaluates the final answer A. We therefore organize the T measurement into three progressively more specific levels (as depicted in Figure 3): strict answer-only compliance, pre-answer relevance, and visible explicit inference. At the response level, Levels 1 and 3 yield binary scores, whereas Level 2 yields a continuous score; their benchmark-level aggregates are defined below.

Level 1: Empty-Thinking Rate. We first ask whether each output is strictly answer-only. For output i, let e_{i} denote the response-level empty-thinking indicator. For a benchmark with N outputs under a fixed model and intervention, we define the response-level score and the Empty-Thinking Rate (ETR) as e_{i}=\mathbf{1}\!\left\{|T_{i}|=0\right\},\qquad\mathrm{ETR}=100\%\times\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}e_{i}. Here, e_{i} is the response-level score, whereas ETR is its benchmark-level rate. Operationally, e_{i}=1 only when A_{i} is parseable and the complete visible output contains no substantive text outside its permitted answer wrapper; otherwise, e_{i}=0. Thus, empty T_{i} does not override a malformed final-answer format, and substantive text following A_{i} also violates strict compliance. ETR gives the cleanest operational limit, but cannot distinguish a generic template, a paraphrase, and a question-specific inference once T_{i} is non-empty.
