Sequential Functional Structured Tucker Compression for Large Language Model Attentions. Post-training compression of LLM attention is often formulated as independent matrix approximation, ignoring both the shared structure among attention projections and the representation shift introduced by earlier compression. We propose FTC, a sequential structured compression framework that adapts the approximation to the current compressed model while jointly exploiting the native Q/K/V head structure under a fixed storage budget. The output projection is handled separately to account for the changed post-attention representation. FTC requires neither fine-tuning nor gradient-based recovery. Across seven decoder-only LLMs from 6B to 32B parameters, FTC achieves the lowest WikiText-2 perplexity among the compared methods at every tested keep ratio on five modern GQA models, with the largest gains under aggressive compression. The improvements transfer to downstream tasks and remain substantial at the 32B scale.

Large language models (LLMs) remain costly at inference time because Transformer blocks repeatedly apply large dense projection matrices, creating substantial memory and computational overhead on resource-constrained hardware. A common approach is to approximate each projection independently with low-rank factors (Yuan et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025c). This can miss redundancy between projections: the query, key, and value projections read the same hidden input and may use overlapping feature directions. Although independent low-rank factorizations reduce the cost of each projection, they may still spend a fixed budget repeatedly representing feature directions shared across Q/K/V. A joint tensor representation can instead represent these common directions through shared factors, leaving more of the budget to capture the differences across projections and heads. Previous methods like TensorLLM and LeSTD exploit shared structure through Tucker representations (Gu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). The remaining challenge is to share useful feature structure without overly restricting the representation available to individual heads.

Sharing structure across Q/K/V is not sufficient by itself, since the features worth preserving depend on how approximation error is evaluated.Activation-aware low-rank methods use calibration activations for this purpose (Yuan et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025c), yet the representations seen by later layers change as compression proceeds. A shared subspace fitted to the original activations may therefore become misaligned with the current compressed model. Moreover, the output projection operates on the post-attention representation, so it requires a separate approximation metric. These observations motivate a sequential framework that adapts the Q/K/V representation to the current compressed model while treating the output projection separately.

We propose FTC, a sequential F unctional structured T ucker C ompression framework for attention projections. At each layer, FTC constructs an activation-induced metric from the current compressed model and uses it to fit the query, key, and value projections jointly. The factors along the model and within-head feature dimensions are shared across projections, while each head slice retains its own core coefficients. Leaving the head-slice mode uncompressed preserves head-specific coefficients and naturally supports both multi-head attention (MHA) and grouped-query attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., 2023). We also balance the head slices during factor estimation to keep differences in projection magnitude from dominating the shared fit.

Sharing feature directions does not require each head to use every possible combination of them. A dense Tucker core nevertheless stores a coefficient for every pair of retained input and within-head directions. We instead allow each head slice to retain a subset of these interactions. The Tucker ranks and the total number of retained coefficients are chosen together, counting the factors, core values, and support metadata in the budget. This provides a choice between fewer shared directions with a denser core and more directions with a sparser core. We then prune the core gradually, refitting the factors and surviving coefficients between stages.

The output projection requires a different treatment because it acts on the attention representation rather than on the common input to the query, key, and value projections. After compressing these projections, we recompute the attention features. Using these updated features, we construct a calibrated target for the output projection by matching the original model’s attention-branch outputs with regularization toward the pretrained weights, yielding a closed-form linear solution.. The calibrated target is then compressed under a separate activation-induced metric, and the updated block provides the inputs for compressing the next layer.

We evaluate FTC across seven decoder-only LLMs spanning MHA and GQA architectures, with the largest gains appearing under aggressive compression. A matched per-matrix baseline helps separate the effect of the joint structured representation from that of the activation-induced metric and sequential calibration.

Our contributions are as follows: We develop FTC, which jointly fits shared Q/K/V Tucker factors under an activation-induced metric from the current compressed model, while preserving the native MHA/GQA head structure. The output projection is calibrated separately in closed form using updated attention features and teacher branch outputs. We jointly allocate Tucker ranks and sparse-core capacity under a storage budget accounting for factors, retained coefficients, and support metadata. The resulting allocation balances subspace and sparsification errors, followed by gradual core pruning with intermediate refitting. Across seven decoder-only LLMs from 6B to 32B, FTC achieves lower WikiText-2 perplexity and higher aggregate downstream accuracy under aggressive compression on all five GQA models, without fine-tuning or gradient-based recovery. A matched per-matrix control further supports the benefit of the structured representation.

Recent low-rank compression methods extend beyond weight-space reconstruction by incorporating model inputs or parameter importance into the approximation objective. Fisher-weighted SVD uses parameter sensitivity (Hsu et al., 2022), while ASVD and SVD-LLM exploit activation information to improve low-rank approximation (Yuan et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025c). Later work further considers rank allocation, truncation-error compensation, and numerical stability (Wang et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2025; Parkina and Rakhuba, 2025). Ftc differs by constructing its activation-induced metric from the current compressed model and using it to fit a joint head-wise Q/K/V representation rather than independent projection matrices.

Shared and tensorized compression methods seek to exploit redundancy across projections or layers through common low-dimensional structure. Basis Sharing uses shared low-rank bases with layer-specific coefficients (Wang et al., 2025a), while TensorLLM and LeSTD model attention projections with Tucker-based shared factors (Gu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). Other work explores tensor-train and sparse tensor representations for model compression (Xu et al., 2023; Solgi et al., 2025), as well as joint Q/K/V factorization (Wang et al., 2025d). Recent studies also indicate that overly restrictive shared subspaces may not capture the heterogeneous structure of modern LLM representations (Zagitov et al., 2026). FTC addresses this issue by sharing Tucker factors across Q/K/V and retaining head-specific core coefficients, balancing common structure with head-specific flexibility.

Sequential compression and error correction have been explored in prior work. SparseGPT performs layerwise activation-aware pruning (Frantar and Alistarh, 2023), while MPIFA and AA-SVD introduce reconstruction or refinement steps to reduce accumulated compression error (Zhao et al., 2025; Sinha and Fleuret, 2026). FTC instead uses the current student activations to define the activation-induced metric for the joint Q/K/V tensor approximation, and compresses the output projection separately using the updated attention representation.

Pruning methods such as Wanda and SliceGPT remove individual weights or structured hidden dimensions (Sun et al., 2024; Ashkboos et al., 2024), while LoRAP assigns low-rank approximation and structured pruning to different Transformer sublayers (Li et al., 2024). Global low-rank-plus-sparse allocation has also been studied across layers (Zhou et al., 2026). In contrast, FTC couples the Tucker factor ranks and the number of retained latent-core coefficients within each attention layer. Core sparsity selects rank-one interactions between shared directions rather than producing zeros in the reconstructed weight matrices; practical acceleration therefore requires a kernel that exploits the latent representation. Hardware-supported patterns such as 2:4 provide one possible deployment route (Mishra et al., 2021).

We compress the attention blocks sequentially using representations generated by the current compressed model. Figure 1 summarizes the overall framework, and the following subsections develop its activation-induced metric, structured Q/K/V approximation, and output-projection calibration.

Consider the l -th Transformer block and let X_{l}^{\mathrm{S}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} denote the hidden representations produced by the current compressed student model, where the superscript \mathrm{S} denotes the student stream and N is the number of tokens. Since the preceding layers have already been compressed, X_{l}^{\mathrm{S}} reflects the representation encountered by the current student at layer l.

Let h_{q,l} and h_{kv,l} denote the numbers of query and key/value heads, respectively. We stack the corresponding head-wise Q/K/V projection matrices along the third mode to form the joint tensor \mathcal{W}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_{\mathrm{head}}\times m_{l}},\qquad m_{l}=h_{q,l}+2h_{kv,l}. The third mode contains all query-head slices together with the native key- and value-head slices. Hence, in GQA and MQA, shared K/V heads are included only once rather than being replicated to match the number of query heads. This joint representation exposes the shared feature structure across the Q/K/V projections while retaining their native head organization.

Since all Q/K/V projections operate on the same hidden representation, we compress them jointly while sharing the first two Tucker factors (Kolda and Bader, 2009): \widehat{\mathcal{W}}_{l}=\mathcal{G}_{l}\times_{1}U_{1,l}\times_{2}U_{2,l}, where U_{1,l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times R_{1,l}}, U_{2,l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{head}}\times R_{2,l}}, and \mathcal{G}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{R_{1,l}\times R_{2,l}\times m_{l}} is a latent core tensor. Sharing U_{1,l} and U_{2,l} exploits common feature subspaces across Q/K/V, while leaving the third mode uncompressed. Moreover, the output projection W_{O,l} is compressed separately due to its distinct input representation; implementation details are provided in Appendix B.

For Q/K/V, we do not directly regress to teacher outputs. Instead, we measure the effect of a weight perturbation on the current student activation stream. For a projection perturbation \Delta W_{l}, \frac{1}{N}\left\|X_{l}^{\mathrm{S}}\Delta W_{l}\right\|_{F}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}\left(\Delta W_{l}^{\top}C_{s,l}\Delta W_{l}\right),\qquad C_{s,l}=\frac{1}{N}(X_{l}^{\mathrm{S}})^{\top}X_{l}^{\mathrm{S}}, where C_{s,l} is the empirical second-moment matrix of the current student representations. We therefore define the regularized activation-induced metric H_{\varepsilon,l}=C_{s,l}+\varepsilon_{l}\bar{t}_{l}I,\qquad\varepsilon_{l}>0,\qquad\bar{t}_{l}=\operatorname{tr}(C_{s,l})/d_{\mathrm{model}}, where \bar{t}_{l} is the mean diagonal value of C_{s,l}, which normalizes the damping scale across layers, and \varepsilon_{l} controls the regularization strength.

For the joint Q/K/V tensor, the resulting structured approximation problem takes the form \min_{\widehat{\mathcal{W}}_{l}\in\mathcal{M}_{l}(B_{l})}\left\|\widehat{\mathcal{W}}_{l}-\mathcal{W}_{l}\right\|_{H_{\varepsilon,l}}^{2}, where \mathcal{M}_{l}(B_{l}) is the family of such structured representations whose total storage cost satisfies a layerwise compression budget B_{l}, including the shared factors, retained core values, and associated index metadata. Since H_{\varepsilon,l} is constructed from the current student representations, the approximation metric is updated sequentially as compression proceeds. Equation (1) defines the activation-induced approximation objective. We first convert this objective exactly into a Euclidean reconstruction problem by metric whitening. We then introduce slice balancing to prevent high-energy Q/K/V head projections from dominating the shared Tucker factors.

We now transform the activation-metric problem in Eq. (1) into a standard Euclidean tensor approximation. Since H_{\varepsilon,l}\succ 0, let H_{\varepsilon,l}=L_{l}^{\top}L_{l} be its Cholesky factorization. For any tensor \mathcal{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_{\mathrm{head}}\times m_{l}}, the weighted norm satisfies \|\mathcal{A}\|_{H_{\varepsilon,l}}^{2}=\|\mathcal{A}\times_{1}L_{l}\|_{F}^{2}. We therefore define the metric-whitened tensor \widetilde{\mathcal{W}}_{l}=\mathcal{W}_{l}\times_{1}L_{l}. For the Tucker representation \widehat{\mathcal{W}}_{l}=\mathcal{G}_{l}\times_{1}U_{1,l}\times_{2}U_{2,l}, setting \widetilde{U}_{1,l}=L_{l}U_{1,l} gives \widehat{\mathcal{W}}_{l}\times_{1}L_{l}=\mathcal{G}_{l}\times_{1}\widetilde{U}_{1,l}\times_{2}U_{2,l}.

Hence, Eq. (1) is equivalently written as \min\left\|\widetilde{\mathcal{W}}_{l}-\mathcal{G}_{l}\times_{1}\widetilde{U}_{1,l}\times_{2}U_{2,l}\right\|_{F}^{2}, with the layerwise storage budget B_{l}. After compression, the mode-1 factor is mapped back by U_{1,l}=L_{l}^{-1}\widetilde{U}_{1,l}. Thus, metric whitening exactly converts the activation-induced objective into a Euclidean tensor approximation problem. The following subsection introduces a separate slice-level reweighting to balance the contributions of Q/K/V head projections with different magnitudes.

section: Shared Tucker Representation with Slice Balancing
text: After metric whitening, the activation-induced objective becomes a Euclidean reconstruction problem. We further balance the Q/K/V head slices when estimating the shared Tucker factors, so that high-energy slices do not dominate the shared subspaces. Specifically, let \widetilde{W}_{l,j}:=\widetilde{\mathcal{W}}_{l}(:,:,j),\qquad s_{j,l}:=\|\widetilde{W}_{l,j}\|_{F},\qquad w_{j,l}:=s_{j,l}^{-2}, for j=1,\ldots,m_{l}. We therefore consider \min_{\mathcal{G}_{l},\widetilde{U}_{1,l},U_{2,l}}\sum_{j=1}^{m_{l}}w_{j,l}\left\|\widetilde{W}_{l,j}-\widetilde{U}_{1,l}\mathcal{G}_{l}(:,:,j)U_{2,l}^{\top}\right\|_{F}^{2},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\widetilde{U}_{1,l}^{\top}\widetilde{U}_{1,l}=I,\qquad U_{2,l}^{\top}U_{2,l}=I. Since w_{j,l}=\|\widetilde{W}_{l,j}\|_{F}^{-2}, each term measures the reconstruction error relative to the energy of the corresponding slice. Thus, each Q/K/V slice contributes according to its relative approximation error rather than its absolute magnitude.

section: Shared Tucker Representation with Slice Balancing
text: To characterize the shared model-dimension subspace, we temporarily omit the mode- 2 compression and consider the reduced problem \min_{\begin{subarray}{c}B_{1,l},\ldots,B_{m_{l},l}\end{subarray}}\sum_{j=1}^{m_{l}}w_{j,l}\left\|\widetilde{W}_{l,j}-\widetilde{U}_{l}B_{j,l}\right\|_{F}^{2},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\widetilde{U}_{l}^{\top}\widetilde{U}_{l}=I. For fixed \widetilde{U}_{l}, the optimal coefficient matrices are B_{j,l}^{\star}=\widetilde{U}_{l}^{\top}\widetilde{W}_{l,j}. Consequently, the optimal rank- R_{1,l} shared column subspace is spanned by the leading left singular vectors of \widetilde{W}_{\mathrm{cat},l}=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{w_{1,l}}\widetilde{W}_{l,1}&\cdots&\sqrt{w_{m_{l},l}}\widetilde{W}_{l,m_{l}}\end{bmatrix}. Hence, the shared mode- 1 factor captures the dominant directions jointly supported by the normalized Q/K/V head projections. A formal proof is given in Appendix D.

section: Shared Tucker Representation with Slice Balancing
text: We extend this shared-subspace principle to the first two modes through the Tucker representation \widehat{\widetilde{\mathcal{W}}}_{l}=\mathcal{G}_{l}\times_{1}\widetilde{U}_{1,l}\times_{2}U_{2,l}, while leaving the third mode uncompressed. Thus, the first two factors are shared across Q/K/V head slices, whereas each core slice retains its own coefficients. The next subsection jointly allocates the layerwise storage budget between the Tucker ranks and the retained sparse-core coefficients.

We allocate the layerwise storage budget among the shared Tucker factors, the retained latent-core coefficients, and their support metadata. For a candidate rank pair \mathbf{R}_{l}=(R_{1,l},R_{2,l}), define P_{\mathrm{fac}}(\mathbf{R}_{l})=d_{\mathrm{model}}R_{1,l}+d_{\mathrm{head}}R_{2,l},\qquad N_{l}(\mathbf{R}_{l})=R_{1,l}R_{2,l}m_{l}. The sparse-core support is stored as a bit-packed binary mask \mathcal{M}_{l}\in\{0,1\}^{R_{1,l}\times R_{2,l}\times m_{l}} with \|\mathcal{M}_{l}\|_{0}=K_{l}, requiring one bit per latent-core location. Only the K_{l} surviving core coefficients are stored, in packed form. If each stored value uses b_{v} bits, the total storage cost is S^{\mathrm{bit}}_{l}(\mathbf{R}_{l},K_{l})=b_{v}\left[P_{\mathrm{fac}}(\mathbf{R}_{l})+K_{l}\right]+N_{l}(\mathbf{R}_{l}). Let B_{l}=B_{l}^{\mathrm{bit}}/b_{v} denote the layer budget in b_{v} -bit scalar equivalents. The largest admissible core cardinality is K_{l}(\mathbf{R}_{l})=\min\left\{N_{l}(\mathbf{R}_{l}),\left\lfloor B_{l}-P_{\mathrm{fac}}(\mathbf{R}_{l})-\frac{N_{l}(\mathbf{R}_{l})}{b_{v}}\right\rfloor\right\},\qquad P_{\mathrm{fac}}(\mathbf{R}_{l})+\frac{N_{l}(\mathbf{R}_{l})}{b_{v}}\leq B_{l}.

To evaluate candidate rank pairs, we absorb the slice-balancing weights into the whitened tensor, \overline{\mathcal{W}}_{l}(:,:,j)=\sqrt{w_{j,l}}\,\widetilde{\mathcal{W}}_{l}(:,:,j),\qquad j=1,\ldots,m_{l}.

For fixed orthonormal Tucker factors, the projection core is \overline{\mathcal{G}}_{l}^{\star}=\overline{\mathcal{W}}_{l}\times_{1}\widetilde{U}_{1,l}^{\top}\times_{2}U_{2,l}^{\top}, with corresponding subspace approximation error E_{\mathrm{sub}}(\mathbf{R}_{l})=\left\|\overline{\mathcal{W}}_{l}-\overline{\mathcal{G}}_{l}^{\star}\times_{1}\widetilde{U}_{1,l}\times_{2}U_{2,l}\right\|_{F}^{2}.

Given a core cardinality K_{l}, let \mathcal{P}_{K_{l}}(\overline{\mathcal{G}}_{l}^{\star}) retain the K_{l} largest-magnitude coefficients of the projection core. The corresponding one-step sparsification error is D_{\mathrm{sp}}(\mathbf{R}_{l},K_{l})=\left\|\overline{\mathcal{G}}_{l}^{\star}-\mathcal{P}_{K_{l}}\left(\overline{\mathcal{G}}_{l}^{\star}\right)\right\|_{F}^{2}.

For fixed orthonormal Tucker factors and their projection core, the subspace residual is orthogonal to the represented Tucker subspace. Consequently, the error further decomposes exactly as E_{\mathrm{struct}}(\mathbf{R}_{l},K_{l})=E_{\mathrm{sub}}(\mathbf{R}_{l})+D_{\mathrm{sp}}(\mathbf{R}_{l},K_{l}). This decomposition exposes the budget trade-off: increasing the Tucker ranks reduces the subspace approximation error, but consumes more storage in the shared factors and support mask, potentially leaving fewer coefficients for the core. We therefore optimize the Tucker ranks and core cardinality jointly under the layerwise storage budget. The resulting problem admits the following reduction:

For each feasible rank pair \mathbf{R}_{l}\in\mathcal{R}_{l}, let K_{l}(\mathbf{R}_{l}) be the largest core cardinality allowed by the storage budget. Since D_{\mathrm{sp}}(\mathbf{R}_{l},K_{l}) is non-increasing in K_{l}, the joint surrogate problem \min_{\mathbf{R}_{l},K_{l}}\;E_{\mathrm{sub}}(\mathbf{R}_{l})+\beta D_{\mathrm{sp}}(\mathbf{R}_{l},K_{l}),\qquad\beta\in(0,1], subject to the layerwise storage budget, reduces to \mathbf{R}_{l}^{\star}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{R}_{l}\in\mathcal{R}_{l}}E_{\mathrm{sub}}(\mathbf{R}_{l})+\beta D_{\mathrm{sp}}\left(\mathbf{R}_{l},K_{l}(\mathbf{R}_{l})\right),\qquad K_{l}^{\star}=K_{l}(\mathbf{R}_{l}^{\star}).

Here, \beta discounts the one-step sparsification cost to account for the subsequent prune–refit refinement. After allocation, the selected core is gradually pruned to K_{l}^{\star} with support-constrained refitting; details are given in Appendix E.

section: Separate Compression of the Output Projection
text: The output projection is treated separately since it operates on the post-attention representation rather than on the block input X_{l}^{\mathrm{S}} shared by Q/K/V. After compressing Q/K/V, we recompute the student attention representation Z_{l}^{\mathrm{S}} and use it to construct a dedicated activation-induced metric for W_{O}.

section: Separate Compression of the Output Projection
text: When output-projection calibration is enabled, we additionally use the corresponding teacher representation Z_{l}^{\mathrm{T}} to define a target adapted to the compressed attention features. Specifically, we solve \min_{W}\frac{1}{N}\left\|Z_{l}^{\mathrm{S}}W-Z_{l}^{\mathrm{T}}W_{O,l}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\mu_{o}\left\|W-W_{O,l}\right\|_{F}^{2}, which balances recovery of the teacher attention-branch output against deviation from the pretrained output projection. This quadratic problem has a closed-form solution, denoted by W_{O,l}^{\mathrm{cal}}. When calibration is disabled, we simply use the original W_{O,l} as the compression target.

section: Separate Compression of the Output Projection
text: After replacing W_{O,l} with its compressed counterpart, the updated block produces X_{l+1}^{\mathrm{S}}, which is used to construct the metric for the next layer. The procedure therefore continues sequentially through the model. Full calibration and implementation details are provided in Appendix B.

We evaluate our Ftc across decoder-only LLMs of different scales and attention architectures. We report perplexity and downstream performance, followed by ablations and analyses of the main components. Below we first introduce the models, baselines and protocol of our experiments:

Models. We evaluate on two MHA models (GPT-J-6B, Llama-2-13B) and five modern GQA models (Mistral-7B-v0.3, Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B-Base with QK-norm, and Qwen3-32B). Among them, Qwen3-32B is further used to test scale and architectural generalization.

Baselines. We compare Ftc with five published baselines: enh-LeSTD, our GQA-capable port of LeSTD using the same head-concat tensorization (Li et al., 2026); TLLM-gen, a TensorLLM-style data-free dense Tucker baseline (Gu et al., 2025); MPIFA (Zhao et al., 2025); SVD-LLM (Wang et al., 2025c); and Basis Sharing (Wang et al., 2025a). Seq-SVD is our per-matrix control under the same functional metric and sequential calibration as Ftc, rather than a published baseline.

Protocol. Ftc uses 256 WikiText-2 calibration sequences of 2,048 tokens (seed 42), while data-dependent baselines follow their published 128-sequence configurations; Table 17 quantifies this difference. All methods use the same evaluation windows and parameter-count accounting. Following LeSTD, \rho denotes the retained storage ratio; smaller \rho means stronger compression. The detailed storage accounting is provided in Appendix A.1.

All main-table Ftc results use one fixed recipe across models and ratios: the budget-allocation parameter \beta=0.5, the teacher-Gram anchoring parameter a=0.5, no QKV teacher map, a closed-form teacher map for W_{O} with regularization parameter \mu=1, the gradual core-pruning rate \alpha=0.02, two refits, 256 calibration windows, and slice-wise normalization. No fine-tuning or gradient-based recovery is used.

We first evaluate model-level degradation using WikiText-2 perplexity across all seven models and compression ratios. Table 1 reports two representative operating points, while Figure 2 shows the full compression sweep.
The results reveal three consistent trends across model families and compression levels.

(1) Aggressive compression magnifies the performance gap. The gap widens sharply as compression becomes more aggressive. At \rho=0.2, with WikiText-2 calibration, Ftc achieves the best perplexity on all five modern GQA models and remains within 1.21 – 1.83\times dense WikiText-2 perplexity. In contrast, SVD-LLM reaches 4.8 – 37.3\times dense perplexity. At \rho=0.2, Ftc reduces perplexity by 39 – 88\% relative to the best competing baseline on each GQA model.

(2) Joint tensorization provides substantial gains beyond the metric and sequential calibration. Seq-SVD serves as a controlled per-matrix counterpart to Ftc, sharing the same activation-induced metric and sequential calibration while factorizing each projection independently. At \rho=0.2, Ftc achieves 39 – 92\% lower perplexity across the five GQA models, highlighting the substantial contribution of joint tensorization beyond the activation-induced metric and calibration alone.

(3) The advantage persists at 32B scale. On Qwen3-32B, FTC reaches 9.22 perplexity at \rho=0.2, or 1.21\times the dense perplexity, compared with 15.23 for the strongest competing baseline (39.5\% lower). On Qwen3-8B, the corresponding reduction is 51.9\% (10.70 vs. 22.23). Thus, FTC retains the lowest perplexity at both scales, although the relative margin is smaller on the 32B model.

We next examine whether the perplexity improvements translate to downstream performance. Table 2 reports avg6 and 5-shot GSM8K accuracy at representative storage ratios, while Figure 3 shows performance retention across the full compression sweep.
The downstream results reveal two main patterns across tasks, model scales, and compression levels.

(1) Generative reasoning is more sensitive to compression than multiple-choice performance. At \rho=0.4, Ftc retains 86 – 93\% of the dense avg6 on the four 7–8B models, whereas its GSM8K retention ranges from only 12 – 55\%. This gap is substantially smaller at larger scale: Qwen3-32B retains 98.7\% of its dense avg6 and 84.7\% of its dense GSM8K accuracy at the same compression ratio. These results indicate that reasoning-intensive generation degrades earlier under compression, while increased model scale provides considerably greater robustness.

(2) Performance differences become more pronounced under aggressive compression. At \rho=0.2, Ftc exceeds the best published baseline by 10.7 – 17.0 percentage points in avg6 across the four 7–8B models, and by 21.1 points on Qwen3-32B. Thus, even when GSM8K has collapsed to near-zero accuracy on smaller models, the multiple-choice aggregate continues to reveal substantial differences in the quality retained by different compression schemes.

We next isolate the contribution of the main components of FTC through controlled ablations under the same realized compression budget. Table 3 reports the resulting WikiText-2 perplexity after removing or replacing one component at a time.
The ablation results reveal three main patterns in how the individual components contribute across compression levels and model architectures.

(1) Metric whitening, sequential calibration, and joint tensorization become increasingly important as the compression budget tightens. At \rho=0.6, removing whitening, sequential calibration, or joint tensorization increases perplexity by at most 11.7\%. At \rho=0.2, the corresponding penalties rise to 79.8 – 1662.4\%, 70.2 – 457.7\%, and 65.0 – 1102.8\%, respectively. These results show that activation-induced metric, adaptation to the evolving student stream, and joint Q/K/V modeling become increasingly important as the compression budget tightens.

(2) The contributions of the remaining components vary more substantially across models. At \rho=0.2, removing anchoring changes perplexity by only 1.5 – 14.5\%, whereas removing slice-wise normalization costs 11.8 – 492.4\%. Replacing the sparse core with its matched-budget dense counterpart incurs only 4.3 – 8.7\% on three models but 114.3\% on Qwen2.5-7B. The W_{O} teacher target is beneficial on all four models, with its removal increasing perplexity by 2.6 – 182.6\%.

(3) Fixed head-concat is consistently preferred to K/V repeat-expansion. At \rho=0.2, replacing head-concat with K/V repeat-expansion increases perplexity by 41.9\% on Mistral-7B, 64.6\% on Llama-3-8B, 2.6\% on Qwen2.5-7B, and 35.8\% on Qwen3-8B. The magnitude varies substantially across architectures, but the native head-concat construction is preferred on all four GQA models. Additional teacher-map and hyperparameter studies are reported in Appendix A.4.

We proposed Ftc, a structured attention-compression framework combining an activation-induced metric, sequential calibration, joint Q/K/V tensorization, and budget-coupled rank–sparsity allocation. Across MHA and GQA models from 6B to 32B, Ftc achieves consistently lower perplexity and stronger downstream retention than the compared methods, without fine-tuning or gradient-based recovery. Ablations further show that metric whitening, sequential calibration, and joint tensorization become increasingly important as the compression budget tightens.

Easy to anticipate, hard to compute: boundary dependence finds the computed outputs that entropy patching misses. Byte-level language models such as the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) group bytes into patches and run their large global model once per patch. BLT starts a patch where a small model's next-byte entropy is high, so global compute goes where the next byte is hard to predict. We show that this rule has a systematic blind spot: positions whose type is predictable but whose value must be computed, such as the number after "=" in a worked math solution. Under tight patch budgets, entropy-triggered layouts skip these positions, and accuracy on them collapses. In Meta's BLT-1B with patch starts on 10% of bytes, the entropy rule puts a patch start at 16% of the computed results in GSM8K solutions and gets 19.0% of them exactly right; a boundary after each "=" at the same patch count gets 51.8%, and entropy combined with a label-free boundary-dependence signal gets 67.1% (default layout at 26% of bytes: 76.8%).

The gap survives adapting BLT-1B to the budget with low-rank fine-tuning (32.9% vs 72.7%, three runs per rule, paired p < 1e-200) and grows with model size in byte models trained from scratch at a 10% budget: at 1M, 12M and 50M parameters, boundary dependence beats entropy on final answers by -1.6, +10.1 and +19.8 points, and at 50M it gets 35.9% of computed results against 13.9% (3 seeds each). BLT's entropy-jump rule helps neither target at 50M. The entropy trigger of Scratchpad Patching is likewise indistinguishable from random scratchpads on final answers (5.6% vs 5.9%, 5 seeds), while answer-start scratchpads give 38.1%. The effect is specific to computed values: copies and lookups gain little, and values the model cannot compute gain nothing. Boundary dependence, the rise in the model's own loss when a patch start is removed, measured per two-byte context, finds these positions without labels: combined with entropy it beats the hand-written rule on computed results.

Byte-level models avoid a fixed tokenizer by working on raw bytes, and recover efficiency by grouping bytes into variable-length patches [Pagnoni et al., 2025, Slagle, 2024, Hwang et al., 2026]. In BLT, a small byte-level language model estimates the entropy of each next byte; a patch starts where that entropy crosses a threshold, and the large global transformer runs once per patch. The intuition is that compute should go where prediction is hard.

Entropy measures uncertainty about the next byte. What a patch start actually provides is different: a fresh global state for the bytes that follow. These coincide in prose, where a surprising byte often begins a new word. They come apart at a computed result. After 16 - 3 - 4 =, the next byte is certainly a digit, so the entropy model may be confident about its type, while its value requires computation over context the local model cannot see. When patch budgets are tight, an entropy threshold spends patches on hard-to-predict prose and skips exactly these positions.
We make four contributions:

A blind spot in a trained 1B model. At 10–15% patch budgets, BLT-1B’s own entropy rule skips most computed results in GSM8K solutions; forcing a boundary after each = at the same patch count raises exact accuracy on them by 19–33 points (§4). The gap survives training and adaptation, and grows with scale. BLT-style models trained from scratch at 10–20% budgets show the same ordering across 3 seeds; trained at 1M, 12M and 50M parameters on a 1.9 GB math corpus, the advantage of the label-free trigger over entropy grows from none to 20 points on final answers and to 22 points on computed results (§5). BLT-1B adapted to a 10% budget with low-rank adapters keeps a 40-point gap (§7). A label-free trigger. Boundary dependence, the increase in the model’s own loss when a patch start is removed, averaged per preceding two-byte context, finds computed results without hand-written rules (§6). Scope. The effect needs a computed value and a model able to compute it: copies and lookups gain 1–3 points from a patch start, and values the model cannot compute gain nothing (§8). Scratchpad Patching’s entropy trigger shows the same blind spot (§9).

Patching rules. BLT [Pagnoni et al., 2025] describes two entropy rules: a global threshold, H(x_{t})>\theta_{g}, and an approximate monotonic rule that starts a patch where entropy rises, H(x_{t})-H(x_{t-1})>\theta_{r}. Its final version compares both at 8B scale and defaults to the global threshold when not specified, as do the released BLT-1B checkpoint and the official code (monotonicity: false, threshold 1.335); we call that rule entropy and the monotonic rule jump. Entropy spikes as boundaries go back to dynamic pooling [Nawrot et al., 2023]. SpaceByte [Slagle, 2024] starts patches at word boundaries; H-Net [Hwang et al., 2026], AU-Net [Videau et al., 2025], MrT5 [Kallini et al., 2024] and ByteSpan [Goriely et al., 2025] learn or derive boundaries in other ways. AU-Net reports GSM8K accuracy as a benchmark, rising with the number of hierarchy stages; none of these papers examines where boundaries fall on computed outputs or measures answer accuracy as a function of where boundaries are placed.

Compute between patches. Scratchpad Patching [Zheng et al., 2026] decouples compute from patch size by inserting transient global steps (“scratchpads”) inside patches, triggered by an absolute next-byte entropy threshold, and names the stale-context problem patch lag. Its trigger ablation compares strategies on validation bits per byte (code, natural-language and math splits) and finds the entropy trigger best; its downstream evaluation (code pass@1, multiple-choice understanding) includes no math answer accuracy. Fast BLT [Kallini et al., 2026] speeds up decoding without changing where boundaries go. EntropyMoE [Liu et al., 2026] uses patch entropy to route each patch of a BLT-style model to feed-forward experts; it is evaluated on bits per byte and downstream accuracy, not on math.

Tokenization and arithmetic. For static tokenizers, how numbers are segmented affects arithmetic [Singh and Strouse, 2024, Meister, 2026]. Our setting differs: boundaries are decided online by a model, and the question is which positions receive a fresh global step.

Selection signals. Rho-1 [Lin et al., 2024] selects training tokens by excess loss against a reference model; we test a patch rule built on the same signal as a baseline (§11). Mixture-of-Depths [Raposo et al., 2024] routes compute per token by a learned router.

BLT-1B. We use the released BLT-1B (the HF conversion of facebook/blt-1b), which accepts explicit patch lengths, so layouts can be changed at inference without retraining. The released conversion drops BLT’s 512-byte sliding window in the entropy patcher and in the local encoder and decoder (Hugging Face transformers issue 49185, open as of 7 October 2026). We restore it with the fix proposed upstream (pull request 49188, applied to transformers 5.18; the patch is in our repository) and use the corrected model throughout. Positions before byte 512 are unchanged by the fix, since the window covers every earlier byte; past it the released conversion over-segments, and 121 of our 294 test problems are longer than 512 bytes. With the window, the default layout starts a patch on 25.5% of bytes on GSM8K, against 28.4% without it. We build tight-budget layouts at R = 10% and 15% of bytes. Thresholds are fitted once on 300 GSM8K training problems so that the mean patch rate there is R, then applied position by position at test time; whether a byte starts a patch never depends on later bytes. (Choosing the top R% within each test problem instead gives the same conclusions; §12.)

Layouts. entropy: BLT-1B’s next-byte entropy. results (hand-written): a boundary right after every =, the rest filled by entropy. dep: boundary dependence (§6). entdep: the sum of standardized entropy and dependence.

Evaluation. 294 GSM8K test problems (question, worked solution with calculator annotations removed, and “The final answer is N”), containing 796 in-line computed results: the number right after =. A target counts as exactly right when every byte is the model’s top prediction given the true preceding text (teacher forcing). We report final answers as well, and test paired differences with exact McNemar tests and 95% intervals that resample whole problems.

Small models trained from scratch. A BLT-style model in MLX: a local encoder (byte embedding plus in-patch offset embedding), cross-attention pooling with the patch mean as query, a global transformer (D = 128, 4 layers unless noted; 1.1M parameters in all, 0.8M of them global), and a local decoder layer that attends to the previous 32 bytes across patch boundaries. Patch starts come from a fixed rule applied to the bytes and to a small entropy model (one layer, 32 dimensions) trained on the same corpus. Training: GSM8K and MATH training solutions [Cobbe et al., 2021, Hendrycks et al., 2021] (9.7 MB), 32,000 steps of 32 windows of 128 bytes, AdamW with warmup and cosine decay. Evaluation: 660 GSM8K and 700 MATH test problems held out from training, with greedy exact match given the true prefix on 1,000 computed results, 660 final answers and 700 MATH \boxed{} answers; patch boundaries during decoding are decided online by the same rule. Three seeds per configuration.

At BLT-1B’s default budget its patcher covers computed results well (79% of them start a patch), and removing the patch start at the final answer costs 19 points of exact match (97.0% \rightarrow 78.3%), confirming that the boundary matters. (That test scores the final answer as the solution last wrote it, with any $ and thousands separators, on 300 problems; Table 1 scores the plain number after “The final answer is” on the 294 problems that fit the context, which gives 73.5% for the default layout.) Under a tight budget, entropy drops computed results faster than other positions: at 15% it covers 48% of them, at 10% only 16%.
Table 1. BLT-1B, patch layouts changed at inference (train-fitted thresholds). Exact match on 796 in-line computed results and 294 final answers.

At equal patch counts, a boundary after each = beats entropy on computed results by +19.1 points at 15% (95% interval +15.8 to +22.4; 172 results right only under results vs 20 only under entropy; McNemar p=3\times 10^{-31}) and +32.8 at 10% (p=7\times 10^{-69}). All layouts run slightly above budget on the test problems (patch rates 0.157 and 0.106 for entropy and the result-aware layouts at 15% and 10%). Figure 1 shows a single solution (425 bytes) with the top 10% of its positions by each score: entropy places its patch starts at word beginnings and misses all six computed results; entropy plus dependence starts a patch right before each of them.

Changing layouts at inference puts BLT-1B out of distribution. To test whether the blind spot survives a model that learned with the tight layout, we train small byte models from scratch with each rule.

Table 2. Trained at a fixed budget (D = 128, 4 global layers, 1.1M parameters, 3 seeds). Computed results / final answers / bits per byte. Every entropy seed is below every seed of the other two rules on both accuracies; the hand-written and dependence seeds overlap on computed results at 20%.

The ordering hand-written > dependence > entropy holds at every budget. BLT’s own monotonic rule (jump) separates the two targets: at 10% it recovers final answers (64.1% against 10.4% for entropy) but not computed results (7.0% against 7.1%). An entropy rise marks the answer that follows the long, predictable phrase “The final answer is”, but not a computed result, whose position is as predictable as its type. (In larger models on a larger corpus this recovery disappears; see below.) Placement matters more than budget: dependence at 10% beats entropy at 20% on final answers by 23.4 points (pooled 95% interval +20.4 to +26.6) with half the patches. Entropy needs budget to reach the answers (final-answer accuracy 10% \rightarrow 33% \rightarrow 44%); the result-aware rules are flat from 10% up. Computed-result accuracy does not improve with budget for any rule, and MATH answers stay near 3% for every rule: at this size, arithmetic capacity, not placement, caps them. The hand-written rule also has the lowest bits per byte at every budget, so its gain is not bought elsewhere; dependence costs 1.5–7% in bits per byte against entropy.

The same pattern holds at entropy’s usual 25% budget. At D = 128, word starts plus math syntax (18.5% of bytes) gets 30.4% of computed results against 11.0% for entropy (+19.4 points, 3 seeds); word starts alone get 15.5% and a 6-byte stride plus math syntax 16.6%, so word alignment and the result boundary each reach only about half the combined accuracy. At D = 64 (0.2M parameters), BLT’s entropy rule gets 9.8% of final answers, its jump variant 67.5%, and word starts plus math syntax 77.1% (3 seeds each).

Scaling to 50M parameters. The models above are small (1.1M parameters) and trained only on GSM8K and MATH solutions. To test whether the gap shrinks as models grow, we trained the same architecture from scratch at 1.1M, 11.7M and 53.7M parameters on a larger corpus: the first four shards of OpenWebMath [Paster et al., 2024] (221,264 documents, 1.71 GB, after dropping 324 that share a 13-word sequence with a test problem), plus the GSM8K and MATH training solutions repeated to 10% of the bytes (1.90 GB in total). Each rule is applied at 10% of bytes with thresholds fitted on this corpus; the dependence rule uses the table of §6, because a table refitted on this corpus is dominated by web-text contexts and covers none of the computed-result starts. The models see 0.13, 0.5 and 1.5 billion bytes. The code is a PyTorch port of our MLX harness, checked against it (logits agree to 3e-6; masks are identical), and the whole study ran on one rented A40 GPU for about $19.

Table 3. Models trained from scratch at a 10% patch budget on the scaling corpus. Exact match on 660 final answers and 1,000 computed results; patch rates are measured on the evaluation text (thresholds are fitted on the training corpus, so entropy spends slightly more than 10% there).

The advantage of dependence over entropy grows with size (Figure 2). On final answers it is - 1.6 points at 1.1M (seeds overlap), +10.1 at 11.7M and +19.8 at 53.7M (78.9% against 59.0%), with every dependence seed above every entropy seed at the two larger sizes. Computed results show the blind spot once the models can compute: at 53.7M dependence gets 35.9% of them against 13.9% for entropy, again with every seed above every entropy seed, and the hand-written rule 43.4% (85.5% of final answers; two seeds). Bits per byte are about equal at 53.7M (1.420 against 1.439), so the gain is not bought elsewhere. BLT’s jump rule does not help at this scale: one seed gets 53.8% of final answers and 6.3% of computed results, below every entropy seed, although it has the lowest bits per byte of the rules at a 10% budget (1.410). Given twice the budget (20%, which is 22.8% of the evaluation text), entropy matches dependence at 10% on final answers (80.2%, one seed) but still trails it on computed results (23.1% against 35.9%): at this size extra patches reach the answer that follows a predictable phrase, but placement, not budget, limits the computed results.

(In the 1.1M models of Table 2, dependence at 10% also beat entropy at 20% on final answers.) At 1.1M on this corpus only the hand-written rule rises above the floor on final answers: these models see the GSM8K and MATH solutions about once, against about 13 times for the models of Table 2, which is why the two 1.1M results differ. One of the 28 training runs (1.1M, dependence, seed 0) never learned (bits per byte 4.72 against 2.08–2.26 for the other 1.1M runs) and is excluded.
The hand-written rule uses domain knowledge (=). We look for a signal that finds the same positions from the model alone.

Definition. For BLT-1B: on 400 GSM8K training problems, compute the per-byte loss under the default layout and under a 10% entropy layout. For each position t, take the mean rise in loss over bytes t…t+3, and average it per preceding two-byte context (b_{t-2},b_{t-1}). At inference the score is a causal table lookup. The top contexts are arithmetic (=$, 0*, 5=, 3=); after = the mean rise is 0.88 nats against 0.13 on average.

For the small trained models the same recipe fails: a reference model trained with entropy patches rarely had a boundary at a result, so it never learned to use one, and removing one costs little. Training the reference model with random patch starts (25%) and measuring the drop in loss from adding one patch start at t to a random 10% layout fixes this; the top contexts then include <<, =6, x= and >>.

Results. On BLT-1B (Table 1), entropy plus dependence beats entropy on computed results by +29.5 points at 15% (+25.6 to +33.4) and +48.1 at 10%, and beats even the hand-written rule by +10.4 (+7.7 to +13.2): the table also places boundaries at operands and operators, not only after =. On final answers it beats entropy by +11.6 points at 10% (p=3\times 10^{-5}) but not at 15% (+2.4, p = 0.26), where entropy alone already reaches most final answers, and it does not differ significantly from the hand-written rule. Dependence alone fails on final answers on BLT-1B (40.8% and 4.8%), because “The final answer is” is not an arithmetic context; in the trained models dependence alone is the better variant (Table 2; entropy plus dependence is dominated by entropy there: 9.7% / 22.5%, 2 seeds).

To test whether BLT-1B can learn its way around the blind spot, we train low-rank adapters (rank 16, 16.9M parameters, on the global transformer and the decoder’s cross-attention) for 1,500 steps on GSM8K training solutions under each 10% layout, three runs per rule. Each model is tested on the same 796 results under its own training layout.
Table 4. BLT-1B adapted to a 10% budget, computed results exact.

Adaptation helps every layout but closes none of the gap: entdep - entropy is +39.8 points (pooled over runs, +36.3 to +43.2; p=6\times 10^{-217}), hand-written - entropy +29.8, and entdep - hand-written +10.0. The models trained under entropy do better under entdep (66.2% on average), a layout they never trained on, than under their own (32.9%). Final answers saturate near 97% after fine-tuning, because the final answer repeats the last computed result and fine-tuning teaches the copy; they no longer separate the layouts.
If the blind spot is about computed values, copies and lookups should gain little from a patch start. We repeat the BLT-1B test on four other target types at 10% (train-fitted thresholds).
Table 5. BLT-1B at 10%, exact match. Forced: a patch start at every target, the rest by entropy.

Copies and lookups gain 1–3 points from a patch start (code: +1.4, p=4\times 10^{-5}), against 32.8 for computed results. Where BLT-1B cannot compute the value (program-trace arithmetic, 20.5% even with default patches) or answer at all (logic Yes/No answers at chance under every layout), placement has nothing to act on. Small models trained on the logic and trace tasks give the same picture: logic is not learned (answers at chance), and on traces, where each value’s operands sit inside the local decoder’s 32-byte window, the hand-written rule matches entropy (21.8% vs 20.6%, 2 seeds). With the window cut to 8 bytes the hand-written rule leads by 4 points (24.2% vs 20.1%, 3 seeds), but the seeds overlap. Our reading is that the blind spot needs a value that is computed from context beyond the local model’s reach, by a model able to compute it.

We reimplemented Scratchpad Patching in the small-model harness (16-byte fixed patches, scratchpads on 6% of bytes, pooled by cross-attention over the partial patch with the mean as query) and compared triggers at equal scratchpad counts (D = 64, 2 global layers, 0.2M parameters).
Table 6. Final-answer exact match on GSM8K by scratchpad trigger, with the accuracy of each seed.

The entropy trigger is indistinguishable from random scratchpads (- 0.3 points, Welch 95% interval - 2.2 to +1.6). Answer-start scratchpads give about six times the accuracy on average, with one of five seeds failing to train (8.3%). This does not contradict the paper’s ablation, which found entropy best on bits per byte: averaged bits per byte can hide a failure at a few positions that decide answer accuracy.

Fewer patches save global compute, but local layers run on every byte. For BLT-1B, counting matrix-multiply FLOPs, the local layers cost 299 MFLOPs per byte, the global model 2,653 MFLOPs per patch, and the entropy model 199 MFLOPs per byte. A 10% budget then costs 65% of the default’s forward compute and 15% costs 76%. A dependence-table rule is a lookup and needs no entropy model: 48% at 10% and 59% at 15%. On computed results, dependence alone reaches 77.3% at 59% of default compute, against 76.8% for the default (Figure 3), though it fails on final answers (§6). In our small models the local layers dominate, so a 10% budget saves only 24% of compute.

Spending patches on hard or learnable bytes does not help. A Rho-1-style rule (patches where a small model’s loss exceeds a reference model’s) and simplified learned chunking lost to hand-placed boundaries in every setting tried.
Finer arithmetic boundaries do not help. Per-digit patches after = and operand-aligned patches looked promising at two seeds and vanished at five seeds against matched random controls.

A learned patcher does not beat the table. A small network that predicts the dependence gain from the last 8 bytes, trained on math and on logic/trace data together, matches each domain’s own table on held-out correlation and covers 83% of computed-result starts (table: 37%), but trained into a model at 10% it gets 14.3% / 57.4% against the table’s 17.1% / 67.4%.

Token models are partly protected. With a Qwen2.5-0.5B draft and a 1.5B target on generated program traces, the draft agrees with the target on only 53% of computed-value tokens (86% on text), so speculative decoding loses speed there; but the draft is rarely confident on them (6.5%), so a confidence-based early exit would let few errors through. On GSM8K, computed results are the easiest tokens for these models; we did not test why (overlap with their training data is one possibility). In token models a computed value’s uncertainty shows in the model’s own confidence; in byte patching, the decision to start a patch before a result is made from bytes whose type is predictable.

The original synthetic result was mostly architectural. In an earlier synthetic benchmark with sum pooling and a patch-local decoder, splitting a computation across patches cost up to a full bit; with cross-attention pooling and a decoder that sees across patch boundaries, most of that penalty disappeared. All results above use the cross-attention model.

Scale. Models trained from scratch reach 53.7M parameters, on 1.5 billion bytes (the models of Table 2 have 1.1M; D = 64 is 0.2M); the gap grows over that range, but three sizes on one corpus show a trend, not a law. BLT-1B results come from inference-time layout changes and low-rank adaptation, not from full training at a tight budget. At 50M the hand-written rule has two seeds and the jump and double-budget results one each.

Teacher forcing. All accuracies score each target given the true preceding text. End to end, BLT-1B cannot solve GSM8K by itself: even after adaptation it gets about 2% of final answers under every layout (measured with the released conversion), so the gaps above could not be measured end to end. The models trained from scratch also solve essentially no GSM8K problems end to end at any size (at most 1 of 100 for any run).

Domain. The effect is established for arithmetic in worked math solutions. Code shows a small, significant effect; logic and program traces were inconclusive because the models lacked the skill or the local model already saw the operands.

Label-free trigger. The dependence table is fitted on the same domain it is tested on and does not transfer across formats (the GSM8K table covers 0% of program-trace values). On BLT-1B, the best variant (entropy plus dependence) differs from the best variant in trained models (dependence alone).

Checkpoint conversion. The public BLT-1B conversion lacks the 512-byte sliding window (§3); our BLT-1B results use it with the window restored by the upstream fix, which is not yet merged. With the released conversion the conclusions are the same, with different magnitudes (results - entropy at 15% and 10%: +25.0 and +26.6 points).

Thresholds. Our original BLT-1B layouts chose the top R% of positions within each test problem, so a position’s selection could depend on later bytes. Train-fitted, position-by-position thresholds reproduce every conclusion, with gaps as large or larger (released conversion, results - entropy at 15%: +25.0 vs +21.5 points).

Entropy tells a byte-level model where the next byte is surprising, not where its decoder needs the global model. The two diverge at computed outputs: positions whose type is predictable and whose value must be computed. Under tight budgets, entropy-triggered patching and scratchpad triggering skip these positions, and accuracy on them collapses, in a trained 1B model, in models trained at the budget, where the gap grows from 1M to 50M parameters, and after adaptation. Measuring the dependence directly, as the loss the model loses when a patch start is removed, finds these positions without labels. Compute allocation in byte models should follow what the decoder needs from the global model, not how surprising the next byte is.
