The project ran as a partly autonomous research loop, and several early conclusions were wrong. The standards in program.md exist because breaking each produced a wrong result: a word-start rule that read the byte it was predicting (caught by an automatic causality test, test_causal.py); effects at two seeds that vanished at five; a synthetic generator that placed dependencies outside the model’s context; an effect that was mostly architectural; undertrained models hiding the effect; and a rule that exploited the generator’s fixed number of variable names. Every trained-model comparison in the tables uses three or more seeds (the two two-seed comparisons in the text are marked), BLT-1B comparisons use paired tests, and every rule is checked for causality.

On the Fragility of Tasks under Composition: Implicit Budgeting in Language Models. Modern language models are increasingly asked to handle several tasks within a single prompt. Doing so requires solving each task correctly while integrating the resulting answers into a coherent response. In this paper, we identify a fundamental limitation in this process, where models make substantially more errors when tasks are composed, even when they can solve every constituent task reliably in isolation. This degradation cannot be fully explained by the accumulation of independent errors. Across both open-weight models and the frontier model Claude Opus 5, our findings instead point to an implicit thinking budget underlying this effect. In particular, under composition, models use substantially fewer tokens per task than in isolation, even when the full sequence remains well within the context window. Tasks that require longer solution traces in isolation are consequently more $\textit{fragile}$ under composition, i.e., models make more errors on prompts containing these tasks. In isolation, non-fragile tasks receive more reasoning than they need and waste compute.

However, by grouping tasks according to their fragility, the implicit budgeting can be manipulated to reduce token usage by $43$\% across a range of math and linguistic tasks while also preserving accuracy.

A single prompt often asks a language model to do several things at once, such as answering a handful of questions, solving a set of math problems, or following a list of instructions before writing one response. Common benchmarks, however, still test models one task at a time (Rein et al., 2023; Hendrycks et al., 2021; Gema et al., 2025). As scores on these benchmarks saturate, they may overstate how robust the underlying capabilities are. We ask whether a model that reliably solves a task on its own can still solve it when other tasks share the prompt.

One natural explanation is error accumulation. If each task fails with nonzero probability, solving many at once fails more often. Prior work has found this phenomenon when models are tasked to do familiar reasoning steps (Press et al., 2023; Dziri et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2026) or follow several instructions at once (Harada et al., 2025; Vasileva, 2026). However, accumulation is only half of the story. Because composition in these settings also changes the structure and token demands of the task, it remains unclear whether the model’s ability to solve each constituent task degrades as well, and what mechanism drives that degradation.

To investigate the question, we analyze the effect of composition on each constituent task of a composition. We start by establishing that this per-task degradation exists at all. For that, we select tasks the model solves correctly in isolation, which establishes that the requisite capability is present. We then leave those tasks unchanged and simply concatenate them within a single prompt. This design separates degradation under increased task load from baseline solvability on the constituent tasks.

Across state-of-the-art open models, as well as the frontier model Claude Opus 5, we find substantial performance degradation when more previously solved tasks are concatenated within the same prompt. The drop in accuracy is substantially larger than what the constituent tasks’ isolated error rates would predict, and is consistent across both mathematical and linguistic domains. We characterize this degradation along two dimensions. 1) Failures concentrate on a subset of fragile tasks that, for a given model, remains stable across sampling noise and composition sizes. These tasks also have longer reasoning traces in isolation. 2) As more tasks are presented together, models systematically reduce the reasoning tokens devoted to each task, even though no explicit per-task token constraint is imposed. This reduction follows a clear scaling pattern, with reasoning per task decreasing approximately as a power law with composition size. Together, these findings reveal an implicit thinking budget under composition, under which fragile tasks disproportionately lose accuracy as per-task reasoning decreases.

This mechanism also creates an opportunity for more efficient inference than solving every task separately. Non-fragile tasks can be grouped into larger batches, where the implicit thinking budget reduces per-task reasoning and token usage without impacting accuracy. Fragile tasks, in contrast, are placed in smaller batches so that each receives more reasoning and remains accurate. We demonstrate this with fragility-aware batching, a strategy that composes each task based on its fragility. By using empirical measurements of the fragility of tasks, it reduces token usage by 43 % on average with no drop in performance compared to solving each task individually. Because it is entirely black-box, it also applies directly to proprietary models, reducing generated tokens by 24\% on GPQA-Diamond with Claude Opus 5 without degrading performance.

Taken together, these results show that the failure of LLMs to generalize their reasoning budget management is a double-edged sword. Under composition, it causes fragile tasks to fail, whereas in isolation, it makes models overspend reasoning on non-fragile tasks, thus wasting compute during inference. Our key contributions and findings are:

We show that simply concatenating tasks that are already solved correctly in isolation causes substantial accuracy degradation across both frontier and open models (Section 3). We identify an implicit per-task thinking budget that shrinks as a power law in the number of composed tasks (Section 3.1). We show that this uniform reduction concentrates degradation on tasks with long isolated reasoning, a set that is stable within each model but differs between models (Sections 3.1 and 3.2). We refer to this set of tasks as fragile. We turn these findings into fragility-aware batching, a strategy that groups tasks according to their measured fragility. It reduces generated tokens by \sim 43% across all datasets while preserving accuracy on both state-of-the-art open-weight models and proprietary frontier models (Section 4).

Our central goal is to investigate whether an LLM that can solve a task in isolation keeps this ability when several such tasks are presented together. To answer this, we use a controlled setting in which the constituent tasks are unchanged and only the number of tasks in the prompt varies. We then measure how each task’s accuracy changes relative to its performance in isolation. All experiments share the setup described below.

Compositions. We compose independent tasks drawn from the same dataset \mathcal{D}. A composition of size k is a tuple C=(t_{1},\dots,t_{k}) with t_{i}\in\mathcal{D}, rendered into a single prompt by a fixed per-dataset template that asks the model to answer all k tasks in order. We split the model’s single response into k answers and grade each for correctness (further details in Appendix A.2.6).

Accuracy drop. For a model m, the accuracy drop of each individual task t_{i} at composition size k is \Delta^{m}_{i}(k)=\mathrm{acc}^{m}_{i}(k)-\mathrm{acc}^{m}_{i}(1), where negative values indicate degradation. Unless stated otherwise, accuracy is estimated from 5 independent trials.

Datasets. We use eight datasets whose tasks vary widely in the reasoning they require. We build two datasets ourselves: 1,000 indefinite integrals with randomized coefficients across diverse function classes, verified symbolically, and OneWordQA, a set of factual questions with single-word or numeric answers that require minimal reasoning. The remaining six are established benchmarks: GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2023), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2023), MMLU-Redux (Gema et al., 2025), StrategyQA (Geva et al., 2021) and AIME (further details in Appendix A.2.6).

Models. We evaluate three Qwen3 models (4B Thinking, 8B, 14B) (Yang et al., 2025a), trained by strong-to-weak distillation from larger RL-trained Qwen3 models, and Qwen3.8 27B (Qwen Team, 2026). We also evaluate three DeepSeek-R1-distilled models (Qwen 7B, Llama 8B, Qwen3 8B) (Guo et al., 2025), obtained by supervised fine-tuning on R1 reasoning traces, and the frontier model Claude Opus 5 with medium reasoning effort. The first two groups let us compare two different post-training recipes at similar scale. Open-weight models are sampled at temperature 0.6 and use a context limit of at least 131{,}072 tokens (further details in Appendix A.2.2).

Prior work has repeatedly reported that accuracy falls when several tasks share a single prompt. However, these evaluations do not isolate whether a model fails because it cannot solve a task reliably or purely because the task is composed with others, which leaves the underlying mechanism unclear.

Building on these observations, we ask whether degradation can arise from composition alone. Answering this requires separating a model’s ability to solve a task from its ability to solve the same task in composition. For that, we restrict each model M to a subset \mathcal{D}_{M}\subseteq\mathcal{D} of confidently solved tasks: a task enters \mathcal{D}_{M} only if M solves it in isolation in three out of three independent attempts. We then build compositions C of size k\in\{3,6,10,20\} exclusively from \mathcal{D}_{M}, sampling task categories uniformly within each dataset, and evaluate the accuracy of each task within them. The accuracies at k=1 come from runs independent of those used for selection.

As Figure 2 shows, simply concatenating tasks that are solvable in isolation causes substantial accuracy degradation across all models on GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2023). This observation also holds for all other datasets we tested, except OneWordQA and StrategyQA, whose tasks require little reasoning. Furthermore, this degradation cannot be explained by context-length issues, since nearly all responses stay within the context limit (see Figure 3 and Appendix A.1.1). Compositional degradation is therefore driven by effects inherent to composition and cannot be predicted from the solvability of tasks in isolation alone.

The extent of this degradation varies strongly across models. The R1-distilled models degrade the most, while the Qwen3 models degrade moderately less. Frontier models are not immune either: Claude Opus 5, despite its leading benchmark results, loses about 7 pp at k=10 on GPQA-Diamond, on tasks it solved in all three runs individually.

Contrary to explanations for compositions with dependent tasks, where models either match solution patterns seen in training instead of learning systematic procedures (Dziri et al., 2023) or fail to combine facts they know individually (Press et al., 2023), we propose that compositional degradation arises from a misallocation of the implicit thinking budget.

section: Degradation as a misallocation of the implicit thinking budget
text: Reasoning models solve tasks by thinking stepwise, a process shown to be crucial for task success (Wei et al., 2023). We therefore ask whether the accuracy degradation under composition can be explained by changes in thinking behavior. A central property of this behavior is the number of thinking tokens the model spends on a task, i.e., how much effort it invests in it. This effort can strongly affect whether a task is solved (Snell et al., 2024), and prior work has shown that overall reasoning shortens when batching tasks (Srivastava et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2026; Cheng et al., 2023). What remains unclear is how each constituent task is affected, that is, how its thinking length under composition compares to its thinking length in isolation and how that change affects the task’s success.

section: Degradation as a misallocation of the implicit thinking budget
text: Thinking traces shrink under composition. We close this gap by measuring the thinking tokens spent on each task within a composition of k tasks, denoted T_{i}(k). To this end, we prefix each task with a unique tag (Q01, Q02, …) in the prompt that does not appear in the task description itself. These tags let us attribute each segment of the reasoning trace to the task it addresses (details in Appendix A.2.1). We quantify the reduction for each task by the token ratio r_{i}(k)=T_{i}(k)/T_{i}(1) between its thinking tokens under composition and in isolation. Figure 4 shows how this token ratio evolves with composition size. With one exception (R1 Qwen 7B on MATH-500), the thinking tokens of almost all tasks decrease monotonically as compositions grow (further models and datasets in Appendix A.1.2); a weak positional bias is discussed in Appendix A.1.4.

section: Degradation as a misallocation of the implicit thinking budget
text: Long-reasoning tasks degrade more. This reduction has important implications, since prior work has established that the number of thinking tokens spent on a task can influence its accuracy. In particular, interrupting the thinking process externally at earlier stages causes a larger degradation (Muennighoff et al., 2025). Composing tasks has an analogous effect on thinking length, as it implicitly constrains the per-task thinking tokens but without any external enforcement. This naturally raises the question of whether the implicit token reduction under composition is related to the accuracy degradation. Figure 5 shows how the reduction affects tasks with different isolated thinking lengths. Tasks with longer isolated traces degrade substantially more when thinking tokens are reduced, whereas tasks with shorter traces are largely unaffected. We refer to tasks that break under composition in this way as fragile.

section: Degradation as a misallocation of the implicit thinking budget
text: Thinking length follows a power law. One possible source of the uneven degradation in Figure 5 could be that long-reasoning tasks lose a larger share of their thinking tokens. The token ratio approximately follows a power law in k, \log r_{i}(k)\approx m\log k\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r_{i}(k)=\frac{T_{i}(k)}{T_{i}(1)}\approx k^{m}. Since r_{i}(1)=1 by definition, we fit a line through the origin on log-log axes for each model and dataset. The fitted slopes have a median of m=-0.54 (m\in[-0.88,-0.04]), with a median R^{2} of 0.91; averaged per model, R^{2} ranges from 0.55 to 0.94 (Appendix A.1.2). Under composition, the reasoning trace of each task thus shrinks by approximately the same factor k^{m}, without systematic dependence on its isolated length T_{i}(1), so long-reasoning tasks do not systematically lose a larger share of their reasoning than short ones. The model preserves the relative allocation across tasks, assigning more reasoning to tasks that required more in isolation, but applies roughly the same proportional reduction to all of them. Considering that every task loses roughly the same fraction of its reasoning, the uneven degradation is best explained by how much reasoning each task can afford to lose.

section: Degradation as a misallocation of the implicit thinking budget
text: Short isolated traces seem to contain redundancy in reasoning beyond what the task requires, whereas long traces lie closer to the minimum reasoning needed to solve the task reliably. Hence, the same relative reduction pushes long-reasoning tasks below their minimal requirement while leaving short ones above it, concentrating degradation on tasks with long isolated traces. Since k^{m} decreases with k (m<0), the implicit thinking budget shrinks as more tasks are composed, and degradation grows accordingly. This reveals a systematic failure of implicit thinking budget allocation under composition. The way models allocate their implicit thinking budget does not generalize well to composed tasks.

section: Fragile tasks are stable within a model
text: It remains to establish whether the implicit thinking budget estimation fails consistently on the same tasks across models and composition sizes. This tells us how the proposed misallocation changes as the conditions, i.e., model and composition size, vary. Since a failure in implicit thinking budget estimation manifests as accuracy degradation, we can test this consistency directly on the accuracy drops. For two conditions A and B, we obtain the accuracy drops across tasks, \Delta_{A} and \Delta_{B}, and measure their Pearson correlation, applying Spearman’s correction for attenuation to reduce the impact of noisy accuracy estimates (details in Appendix A.2.3).

section: Fragile tasks are stable within a model
text: At a fixed composition size, the mean correlation across models is only 0.24\pm 0.03. Different models thus largely disagree on which tasks degrade, even when evaluated under identical conditions. The exception is models trained with the same recipe, such as Qwen3 8B and 14B, which correlate at 0.56\pm 0.09. Within a single model, the correlation across composition sizes reaches 0.81\pm 0.04. When the same model faces compositions of different sizes, groupings and orderings, the same set of fragile tasks tends to break. Fragility is therefore a stable property of a task for a given model. Measuring a task’s accuracy drop at some composition sizes lets us anticipate how it will degrade in new compositions presented to the same model, which makes fragility predictable.

section: Exploiting implicit budgeting for efficient inference
text: So far, our results suggest that LLMs fail on compositions mainly because their estimate of the implicit thinking budget does not generalize, rather than because they cannot transfer their problem-solving skills. If so, controlling how much reasoning each task receives should prevent the drop. The composition size k offers a practical control mechanism on implicit budgeting, since the token reduction ratio follows a power law in k. Hence, assigning robust tasks to larger compositions and fragile tasks to smaller ones could save tokens while limiting accuracy degradation.

To test whether this idea is viable, we first ask how many tokens could be saved if each task’s fragility were known. We estimate fragility from the measured accuracy drops and compose tasks accordingly, which gives a sense of what fragility-aware batching can achieve. In Section 4.2, we replace these measurements with a linear predictor that predicts fragility, turning the approach into a method that can be deployed. Formally, we seek to assign each task a composition size k_{i} that maximizes the expected token savings while bounding the expected accuracy degradation by B. We express this trade-off as a Lagrangian relaxation, k_{i}(\lambda)=\argmax_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\Big[\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{i}(k)]+\lambda\big(1-\mathrm{cost}_{k}\big)\Big], where \mathcal{K} is the set of available composition sizes, \mathbb{E}[\Delta_{i}(k)] is the expected accuracy drop of task t_{i} at composition size k, and \mathrm{cost}_{k}\in(0,1] is the model-specific token cost of solving a task within a composition of size k, relative to solving it in isolation. The parameter \lambda\geq 0 acts as an exchange rate between saved tokens and accuracy. We then choose \lambda such that the mean expected accuracy drop over the dataset, \bar{\Delta}(\lambda)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\big[\Delta_{i}(k_{i}(\lambda))\big], conservatively stays within the budget B, \lambda^{*}=\max\Big\{\lambda\geq 0\;:\;\bar{\Delta}(\lambda)-\mathrm{SE}\big(\bar{\Delta}(\lambda)\big)\geq-B\Big\}.

We find \lambda^{*} by a grid search on held-out splits, using repeated nested 5 -fold cross-validation (Cawley and Talbot, 2010) to reduce the effect of noise in the empirical accuracy estimates. Given the assignments k_{i}(\lambda^{*}), we greedily group tasks into as few compositions as possible such that every task t_{i} lands in a composition C with |C|\leq k_{i}(\lambda^{*}) (details in Appendix A.2.4). Throughout our experiments, we use the composition sizes \mathcal{K}=\{1,3,6,10,20\}, where k=1 solves a task alone, and an accuracy drop budget of B=0.5\%.

Table 1 compares the accuracy degradation and token savings of different batching strategies relative to solving tasks in isolation. The common practice of batching tasks randomly into fixed-size compositions (Cheng et al., 2023), here of six tasks, saves the most tokens on average but degrades accuracy strongly, particularly on GPQA-Diamond, whose tasks require many reasoning steps. Fragility-aware batching almost entirely avoids this degradation while still achieving substantial token savings. Averaged over all models and over every dataset but AIME, where fragility-aware batching leaves nearly every task in isolation (Appendix A.1.6), it saves 43\% of tokens while keeping accuracy constant (+0.6 pp). How these savings arise depends on the dataset. On OneWordQA and StrategyQA, fragility-aware batching matches random batching, saving 68 – 74\% of output tokens without losing accuracy relative to solving each task individually. On the remaining five datasets, where random batching degrades accuracy, fragility-aware batching preserves it while still saving roughly 32\%.

These results show that much of the thinking an LLM spends on a task in isolation is not needed to solve it. Specifically, on GPQA-Diamond, GSM8K and MMLU-Redux, grouping tasks by fragility saves a substantial share of tokens at no cost in accuracy.

Our results show that the set of fragile tasks is stable for a given model, which hints at the existence of steady properties that define fragility. If such properties exist, fragility should be predictable for tasks the model has never seen under composition. Hence, we extend the intervention to unseen tasks by predicting their fragility with a simple linear predictor. We encode each task description with Qwen3 Embedding 8B (Zhang et al., 2025), keep the embeddings fixed, and train a separate linear predictor for each evaluated language model. To generate labels, we evaluate each task in the training split with 10 trials at every composition size k\in\{3,6,10,20\}, placing it in a different composition each time. Then, for each composition size k the predictor outputs the probability that the task performs at least as well in composition as in isolation. To obtain predictions on unseen tasks, we use 5 -fold cross-fitting (Chernozhukov et al., 2024), so that the held-out folds together cover the entire dataset (details in Appendix A.2.5). Finally, we feed the predicted accuracy drops into the same batching algorithm as in Section 4.1.

Table 1 reports the results of the linear predictor. Guided by the predictor, fragility-aware batching limits the accuracy loss to at most 0.5 pp on every dataset and saves 31.0\% of tokens on average. Because few training examples are available, the predictor is simple, and it works best on tasks with short, plain descriptions such as Integrals, GSM8K and OneWordQA. This simple demonstration thus shows that fragility is partly predictable from task properties encoded in the embeddings. Scaling such predictors further could enable saving tokens on real-world unseen tasks, just by batching them well.

Fragility-aware batching on a frontier model. We further test whether fragility-aware batching carries over to flagship frontier LLMs. Since the intervention requires neither fine-tuning nor access to internal states and works purely by restructuring compositions, we can apply it directly to Claude Opus 5 on GPQA-Diamond (Table 1). In isolation, Claude Opus 5 reaches an accuracy of 89.5\% with 689 output tokens per task. Random composition with k{=}6 lowers accuracy by 0.9 pp and saves 18\% of output tokens. Batching by measured fragility does better on both metrics, losing just 0.4 pp while saving 24\% of generated tokens. The linear predictor, trained on fewer trials for Opus than for the open-weight models, transfers less well: it saves almost no tokens and loses 2.0 pp. At least in its consequences, the mechanism we found in open-weight models carries over to a frontier model.

section: Effects of post-training on compositional degradation
text: The models in our analysis degrade very differently under composition, most clearly between the two model families, which differ in their post-training strategy. This hints that post-training strongly influences how well a model handles compositions. To investigate this, we repeat our analysis on OLMo 3 7B (Olmo et al., 2026) at three stages of its training curriculum: SFT (Ouyang et al., 2022), DPO (Rafailov et al., 2024) and RLVR (Lambert et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025).

section: Effects of post-training on compositional degradation
text: Figure 6 summarizes the results on OLMo 3 7B. All three stages show very similar implicit budgeting under composition, and their token counts shrink at similar rates. Nevertheless, the same reduction affects accuracy differently. At similar token ratios, the final RLVR stage loses substantially less accuracy than the SFT and DPO stages. These degrade by similar amounts and also tend to fail on the same fragile tasks. Correlating their accuracy degradation on GPQA-Diamond, MATH-500 and MMLU-Redux as in Section 3.2 gives a disattenuated Pearson \rho of 1.03\pm 0.35. RLVR’s fragile set tends to overlap less with theirs, with \rho=0.69\pm 0.23 against SFT and \rho=0.89\pm 0.26 against DPO.

section: Effects of post-training on compositional degradation
text: We conclude that RLVR post-training mitigates the accuracy drop incurred by implicit budgeting under composition, but it does not eliminate the misallocation of the thinking budget in the first place, which remained similar across the stages.

Previous work has examined both how task composition affects accuracy and reasoning length and how batching can improve efficiency or reliability. Several studies ask whether models can solve tasks as reliably together as they do separately (Pan et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). Related studies examine whether failures to meet multiple response requirements can be explained by independent errors (Harada et al., 2025; Vasileva, 2026). These studies document accuracy losses under composition, although their causes are not yet fully understood. At the same time, batching methods have shown promise for improving efficiency and reliability (Xu et al., 2026a; Ji et al., 2025), with accuracy gains reported in some settings (Srivastava et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b; Lin et al., 2024) (consistent with our observations on light-reasoning datasets OneWordQA and StrategyQA, see Appendix A.1.6). Batching has also been observed to reduce the number of reasoning tokens used per task (Srivastava et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2026). The effects of added context also vary across questions.

For factual questions, models tend to resist misleading information more successfully when they can also answer related questions correctly, suggesting that accuracy in isolation does not fully capture robustness (Xu et al., 2026b). The number of steps needed to solve a task also matters. Tasks requiring more steps show larger accuracy drops when irrelevant information is added (Yang et al., 2025b). More broadly, researchers distinguish task difficulty from sensitivity to prompt changes (Romanou et al., 2026) and examine how that sensitivity varies with model size, training and architecture (Qin et al., 2026). Overall accuracy can remain largely unchanged even when irrelevant context changes which questions a model answers correctly (Zhang et al., 2026). Estimates of this sensitivity also depend on how answers are graded. Rigid matching rules can treat differently worded correct answers as errors, exaggerating the apparent sensitivity (Hua et al., 2025). Alongside these studies, work on reasoning allocation has shown that adding other tasks or irrelevant text can shorten reasoning traces and reduce self-checking (Rodionov et al., 2026). Researchers have also trained models to solve groups of tasks more efficiently under a shared token limit (Yang et al., 2026a).

However, studies of budget allocation find that models often devote more reasoning to earlier questions than to those worth more points (Fan et al., 2026). In a single-task setting, model confidence has also been used to guide a search for shorter reasoning paths (Huang et al., 2026).

These findings can be difficult to reconcile within a common explanation, given the differences in experimental settings, interventions and datasets. Our work offers a unifying perspective on several of these observations. Budget misallocation is consistent with the greater sensitivity of deeper reasoning tasks to irrelevant context (Yang et al., 2025b), self-compression (Deng et al., 2026), composition errors that cannot be explained by independent error rates alone (Harada et al., 2025), and the token savings achieved through batching (Srivastava et al., 2026; Cheng et al., 2023). We identify reasoning trace length in isolation as a key variable that helps connect these findings and informs simple, effective interventions. Using this information, we are able to show how to mitigate degradation under composition, even in frontier models.

In this work, we show that language models fail on tasks they solve reliably in isolation once those tasks are combined in a single prompt. The resulting accuracy drop is larger than expected from isolated error rates alone. As more tasks are combined, models use fewer reasoning tokens per task, following an approximate power-law decay with composition size, and the largest failures occur on tasks that require longer reasoning in isolation. This reveals an implicit per-task budget that acts as a double-edged sword. Under composition, fragile tasks receive too little reasoning and fail. In isolation, non-fragile tasks receive more reasoning than they need and waste compute. By batching tasks according to their fragility, however, the implicit budgeting can be manipulated to reduce token usage by about 43% on average while preserving accuracy, and since it does not require internal states of the model, it also applies to proprietary models such as Claude Opus 5.

Previous context can cause degradation too. We deliberately compose independent tasks of the same type, isolating the budget effect in its simplest form. An important question is how this effect extends to richer contexts. Prior work finds that reasoning traces also shorten when the same task is embedded in irrelevant context, conversation history, or a larger task (Rodionov et al., 2026), suggesting that implicit thinking budgeting may extend beyond same-type composition.

Long-running agents in production. This is particularly relevant to agentic workflows, where tool outputs, interaction histories, and intermediate results continually accumulate. Agents are widely observed to degrade as their context grows, a phenomenon known as context rot (Hong et al., 2025). Our results point to a degradation that sets in long before the context fills up. In an agentic workflow, this means a high-effort step can be unknowingly misbudgeted, thus possibly leading to error propagation in subsequent tasks. As a direct practical intervention, agents can keep their context lean and hand reasoning-intensive steps to subagents that start from a fresh context.

Post-training as a potential mitigation. Our results suggest that reasoning allocation contributes to the difficulty of composed tasks, even when the constituent tasks are solvable in isolation. Post-training may therefore help mitigate degradation under composition. For instance, integrating budget management into RL pipelines through explicit training on composed tasks could help models allocate reasoning more effectively across a shared prompt.

Limitations. While we show that composition systematically reduces per-task reasoning and disproportionately harms fragile tasks, we do not yet know what drives this reduction. Our study is limited to independent, same-dataset compositions, and detailed reasoning-length analysis is restricted to open-weight models. Extending these results to mixed-domain, dependent, and proprietary-model settings remains important future work.

COFFEQA: Counterfactual-Guided Few-Shot Distillation for LLM Question Answering. Knowledge distillation aims to train a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher model for resource-constrained environments. However, the process of distillation is typically data-intensive and computationally expensive, particularly for generative tasks. Few-shot distillation offers an alternative by transferring teacher knowledge using limited training samples. However, we observe that few-shot distillation performance is heavily dependent on the choice of these training samples. In fact, we demonstrate that using more uncertain samples near the teacher's decision boundary can significantly deteriorate distillation performance. Motivated by this observation, we propose Counterfactual-guided Few-shot Distillation in Open-book Question Answering (COFFEQA), a novel strategy that aptly uses counterfactuals to provide additional supervision around challenging factual samples. In the generative QA setting, we define a counterfactual as a minimally modified context that induces the teacher to change its response to an alternative answer. We provide geometric insights on how factual-counterfactual pairs can constrain the deviation between the teacher's and student's decision boundaries. We further introduce a new metric, Context Following Difficulty (CFD) that further validates counterfactuals prior to distillation based on agreement with the intended alternative answer and dependence on the modified context.

COFFEQA uses CFD-validated factual-counterfactual pairs for few-shot distillation. Experiments across five in-domain and three out-of-domain QA benchmarks using T5 and Qwen2.5 families show that COFFEQA outperforms factual-only distillation baselines under the same few-shot budget. For instance, on TriviaQA, COFFEQA improves over the factual-only baseline by 8.77 average EM points and 9.98 average F1 points under the T5 setting with 32 few-shot pairs.

Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of natural language processing tasks (Achiam et al., 2023; Chung et al., 2024; Gou et al., 2021; Raffel et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2026). However, their increasing size and computational requirements make deployment in resource-constrained environments particularly challenging (Kaplan et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2020; Strubell et al., 2019; Hoffmann et al., 2022). This motivates the need for compact models with low training and inference costs that preserve task-relevant capabilities of larger models (Liang et al., 2023; Saadi and Wang, 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Dissanayake et al., 2024). Knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015) (see surveys Gou et al. (2021); Sanh et al. (2019); Xu et al. (2024b)) seeks to address this challenge by transferring knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. However, most distillation approaches typically rely on large-scale datasets or extensive supervision from the teacher, thus incurring prohibitive training costs for already resource-intensive language models (Sanh et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Dissanayake and Dutta, 2025; Hamman et al., 2025).
This leads to our primary question: How can we perform data-efficient distillation in LLMs?

Towards addressing this question, our work studies few-shot distillation for generative tasks, with a focus on open-book question answering. We find that the performance of few-shot distillation is heavily dependent on the choice of the distillation dataset, consistent with the broader importance of data selection for efficient LLM training (Fu et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2023). In particular, samples near the teacher’s decision boundary can significantly deteriorate distillation performance (see Fig. 6 in Section C), also consistent with prior findings on knowledge transfer around decision boundaries (Chen et al., 2025). This motivates us to provide additional supervision around these challenging regions while maintaining a limited few-shot budget. To achieve this, we leverage counterfactual examples. Counterfactual-based data augmentation has improved classification performance (Kaushik et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2021; Ross et al., 2021; Gardner et al., 2020; McAleese and Keane, 2024; Bhattacharjee et al., 2024; Egea et al., 2025) by encouraging models to capture causal dependencies and avoid shortcut learning (Guo et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023b). However, its applicability to few-shot distillation for generative tasks remains largely unexplored. Unlike classification, generative tasks produce free-form outputs, making counterfactuals non-trivial to define.

In generative tasks, we define a counterfactual to be a minimally modified input that changes the expected output while preserving overall semantic consistency, such as modifying supporting context in a question to induce a different answer (Guo et al., 2023; Longpre et al., 2021; Paranjape et al., 2022; Köksal et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2023).

In this work, we propose Co unter f actual-guided Fe w-shot distillation in open-book Q uestion A nswering (CofFeQA), a novel strategy for few-shot distillation that aptly uses counterfactuals to provide additional supervision around challenging factual samples near the teacher’s decision boundary. We demonstrate how selecting high-quality counterfactuals can guide knowledge transfer more effectively using extremely limited few-shot budget. Our main contributions are as follows:

Counterfactual-guided few-shot distillation for generative tasks. We show that few-shot distillation becomes particularly challenging for factuals near the teacher’s decision boundary, where the teacher has a smaller margin between its preferred answer and competing alternatives. Motivated by this observation, we propose CofFeQA, a novel framework which leverages counterfactuals for few-shot distillation in open-book QA. Rather than relying solely on factual supervision, CofFeQA pairs challenging factuals with their counterfactuals that expose changes in the teacher’s response under minimal modifications to the input context, providing additional supervision around the teacher’s decision boundary. This reduces dependence on large factual training corpora and improves training efficiency under limited supervision (see Figure 1 for an overview).

Geometric analysis of counterfactual-guided knowledge transfer. We first introduce a notion of decision boundaries for the teacher and student in the context-embedding space, motivated by the fact that variations in the input context can lead to different answers. Our formulation enables us to analyze distillation in open-book QA from a geometric perspective. Specifically, we show that factual-counterfactual pairs can act as probes for the student to approximate the local geometry of the teacher’s decision boundary. To quantify the deviation between the teacher and student, we use the Hausdorff distance (Rockafellar and Wets, 1998), which measures the worst-case deviation between their decision boundaries. We show in Proposition 1 that this deviation is bounded by the magnitude of the counterfactual perturbations and their coverage of the teacher’s decision boundary. Importantly, factuals near the teacher’s decision boundary can require smaller perturbations to induce a change in the teacher’s response, which can lead to tighter teacher-student boundary alignment.

Context Following Difficulty (CFD) for counterfactual validation. Although we generate counterfactuals by perturbing the original input context to induce a targeted alternative answer, not all generated examples are truly valid with respect to the teacher. The teacher may not produce same target answers using the modified context or may still be able to infer them without actually relying on the context. Such cases weaken the intended causal relationship that the student was intended to learn from the teacher and may encourage shortcut learning. To address this issue, we introduce a new metric Context Following Difficulty (CFD) to evaluate generated counterfactuals before distillation. CFD jointly considers whether the teacher produces the intended alternative answer and whether that answer becomes more predictable when conditioned on the modified context. CofFeQA uses CFD-validated counterfactuals, ensuring that the resulting supervision better captures the teacher’s context-dependent behavior.

Empirical evaluation. We conduct comprehensive experiments across five in-domain and three out-of-domain benchmarks using the T5 (Raffel et al., 2020) and Qwen2.5 (Bai et al., 2023) model families. The in-domain benchmarks include NaturalQuestions, SQuAD, NewsQA, TriviaQA, and HotpotQA, while the out-of-domain benchmarks include DROP, DuoRC, and RelationExtraction (Fisch et al., 2019). We evaluate CofFeQA with standard knowledge distillation (KD), sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD), and layer-wise distillation (LWD) baselines, under the same few-shot training budget. Across these settings, CofFeQA outperforms factual-only baselines. For instance, on TriviaQA, CofFeQA improves over the KD baseline by 8.77 average EM points and 9.98 average F1 points under the T5 setting with 32 few-shot pairs.

Counterfactual Data Augmentation. Counterfactual data augmentation has been widely studied for improving robustness in neural networks (Kaushik et al., 2020; Sachdeva et al., 2024; Calderon et al., 2022; Egea et al., 2025; Mishra et al., 2021). Early approaches relied on human-generated counterfactuals (Kaushik et al., 2019; Gardner et al., 2020), while later works automated counterfactual generation through trained generators and editors (Wu et al., 2021; Ross et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021; Tokpo and Calders, 2024) and more recently through prompting LLMs (Bhattacharjee et al., 2024), alongside efforts to evaluate the quality of generated counterfactuals (Youssef et al., 2024; McAleese and Keane, 2024). For example, VISION (Egea et al., 2025) uses LLM-generated counterfactuals to train graph neural networks for vulnerability classification. Other works study counterfactual augmentation through active learning (Balashankar et al., 2023) and fairness-aware pipelines (Tokpo and Calders, 2024). Counterfactual explanations have been studied for model extraction with theoretical guarantees (Dissanayake and Dutta, 2024; Dissanayake and Dutta, 2026) and for robustness to model changes (Noorani et al., 2025; Hamman et al., 2024). Counterfactual applications also extend to generative tasks, including machine translation (Liu et al., 2021) and dialogue (Ou et al., 2022).

However, most of these works focus on neural network models. Counterfactual augmentation to fine-tune LLMs has received limited attention. CATfOOD (Sachdeva et al., 2024) uses LLM-generated counterfactuals to train smaller language models, while Rajagopal et al. (2022) use counterfactually augmented training data for pretrained summarization models. In contrast, we use factual-counterfactual pairs as structured supervision for few-shot distillation in generative open-book QA, where the teacher produces free-form answers rather than predictions over a predefined labels.

Counterfactual Question Answering. Counterfactual reasoning has recently gained traction in question answering (QA) (Ross et al., 2022; Khashabi et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2025). DisentQA (Neeman et al., 2023) uses counterfactual supervision to separate parametric and contextual knowledge (Xu et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2023a), while IfQA (Yu et al., 2023) provides a benchmark for QA under hypothetical scenarios that require reasoning beyond factual retrieval. Counterfactual reasoning has also been studied in multi-hop QA (Guo et al., 2023) and CofCA (Wu et al., 2024), where counterfactual inference is used to mitigate shortcut reasoning. Retrieval-guided approaches further construct counterfactuals through context and answer modifications (Paranjape et al., 2022; Dixit et al., 2022). While these works demonstrate the value of counterfactuals for improving robustness and reasoning in QA, they do not study how they can facilitate knowledge distillation.

Distillation in LLMs. Knowledge Distillation (Hinton et al., 2015) aims to train smaller student models to mimic larger teacher models, with extensions to sequence-level distillation (Xu et al., 2024b; Kim and Rush, 2016; Gu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025), task-specific distillation (Dissanayake et al., 2024; Sanh et al., 2019; Team et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025), and layer-wise distillation (Jiao et al., 2020). Few-shot distillation has been studied for transferring pretrained transformer knowledge in tabular classification (Dissanayake and Dutta, 2025) and multiple-choice question answering (Sutanto et al., 2025). In particular, Sutanto et al. (2025) use an LLM to generate multiple-choice questions and answer options, together with probability scores that are distilled into an encoder-only student model. However, their approach relies on a predefined answer-choice space, making it less directly applicable to generative open-book QA, where the student produces free-form answers. While generative and instruction-level distillation often rely on direct supervision or synthetic data (Hsieh et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023b; Gu et al., 2024), only a few recent works have investigated counterfactuals for knowledge transfer.

DISCO (Chen et al., 2023a) generates counterfactual examples using an LLM and employs a task-specific teacher to filter the generated examples, which are then used as an augmented dataset to train a smaller student model. Notably, DISCO is different from standard distillation via aligning representations since the teacher primarily serves as a data-filtering mechanism rather than directly transferring its predictive behavior to the student through a distillation loss. Moreover, its empirical evaluation focuses on natural language inference, a classification task with a predefined label space. Another related work Hamman et al. (2025) study counterfactual supervision for few-shot distillation, but also focus on classification settings. These approaches do not address generative tasks, where the outputs are open-ended. In contrast, we specifically focus on few-shot knowledge distillation for generative open-book QA. Our approach is motivated by the difficulty of distilling with factuals near the teacher’s decision boundary and uses counterfactuals to provide additional supervision around these challenging regions. We also provide new geometric insights on counterfactual-guided knowledge transfer and a new metric CFD to further check counterfactual validity in open-book QA.

Our strategy is motivated by the observation that factual samples near the teacher’s decision boundary are particularly challenging to distill under limited supervision. We use margin sampling (Scheffer et al., 2001) as an operational proxy for boundary proximity, where smaller teacher prediction margins indicate boundary near samples. Empirically, we observe that distillation performance degrades as this margin decreases; a detailed analysis is provided in Section C. Motivated by this observation, CofFeQA pairs boundary-near factuals with their counterfactuals that expose how the teacher’s response changes under minimal variations of the input context. We first define and describe the counterfactual generation process, and then geometrically analyze how factual-counterfactual pairs facilitate teacher-student boundary alignment. Finally, we introduce Context Following Difficulty (CFD) to validate generated counterfactuals and present the overall CofFeQA distillation framework.

We define counterfactual generation for open-book QA as constructing minimally modified training examples that preserve the original question while changing the evidence to support a different answer. Given a triplet (Q,C,A), where Q is the question, C is the context, and A is the answer, the counterfactual generation framework constructs a counterfactual by modifying the context using an alternative answer. The resulting counterfactual triplet is denoted as (Q,C^{\prime},A^{\prime}). We generate counterfactuals using GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI, 2024) in three stages. First, the answer A is classified into one of five entity types: person, location, organization, date, or numeric; samples outside these categories are excluded. Second, GPT-4o-mini generates an alternative answer A^{\prime} of the same entity type that is similar in category but distinct from A. Previously generated alternatives are excluded to encourage diversity across generation attempts. Finally, GPT-4o-mini is provided with the original triplet (Q,C,A) and A^{\prime} to generate the counterfactual context C^{\prime} by minimally editing C. Specifically, occurrences of A are replaced with A^{\prime}, together with any related references that must be changed to keep the passage grammatically consistent. As a result, the modified context C^{\prime} supports A^{\prime} as the answer to the same question Q, yielding the counterfactual triplet (Q,C^{\prime},A^{\prime}).
The system and user prompts used are shown in Figure 2. Additional prompt details are provided in Appendix D.

section: Geometric analysis of counterfactual-guided knowledge transfer
text: We provide a geometric perspective on how factual-counterfactual pairs can facilitate knowledge transfer. We first introduce a notion of a decision boundary for open-book QA. While classification tasks typically consider a label-flipping boundary, we define a context-response boundary in the context-embedding space. In classification, the boundary separates regions where two classes have equal probabilities. In contrast, in open-book QA, it represents the transition region in context embedding space where the model shifts from generating one answer to another answer. In open-book QA, the context space may contain regions corresponding to the factual answer A, the intended counterfactual answer A^{\prime}, and other answer (A^{\prime\prime}) regions, different from both A and A^{\prime} corresponding to out-of-context or unrelated outputs. Our analysis focuses specifically on the boundary between the A and A^{\prime} response regions, as this is the boundary relevant to factual-counterfactual supervision. Our CFD-based validation helps identify and reject counterfactual candidates that induce responses corresponding to the other answer (A^{\prime\prime}) regions before distillation. We therefore restrict the geometric analysis to the boundary between factual answer space (A) and intended counterfactual answer (A^{\prime}) space.

Consider a teacher and a student with response functions G_{t}(Q,c)=\arg\max_{A}P_{t}(A|Q,c) and G_{s}(Q,c)=\arg\max_{A}P_{s}(A|Q,c). The respective context-flipping boundaries can be defined as the sets: \mathcal{M}_{t}=\{c\in\mathcal{C}\mid P_{t}(A|Q,c)=P_{t}(A^{\prime}|Q,c)\},\quad\mathcal{M}_{s}=\{c\in\mathcal{C}\mid P_{s}(A|Q,c)=P_{s}(A^{\prime}|Q,c)\}.
