section: Geometric analysis of counterfactual-guided knowledge transfer
text: Intuition behind proposition and assumptions. Proposition 1 highlights two properties of factual-counterfactual supervision that govern teacher-student boundary alignment: the magnitude of the counterfactual perturbations (\alpha) and the coverage of the context-response boundary (\epsilon). First, each factual-counterfactual pair provides supervision across a local change in the teacher’s response. Importantly, when the factual sample is already close to the teacher’s decision boundary, a smaller contextual perturbation is sufficient to cross the boundary and induce the alternative response A^{\prime}. Therefore, starting from boundary-near factual samples leads to a smaller upper bound on the perturbation \alpha, tightening the bound. Although those samples are difficult under factual-only supervision, their proximity to the boundary makes them useful starting points for constructing local counterfactual supervision. Second, the boundary coverage condition captures how well the induced crossing points cover both the context-response boundaries. Better coverage corresponds to a smaller \epsilon, tightening the bound. Thus, we provide a geometric characterization of how local counterfactual perturbations and boundary coverage relate to teacher-student boundary deviation.

section: Geometric analysis of counterfactual-guided knowledge transfer
text: The analysis above also assumes that the student model agrees with the teacher model on the paired factual and counterfactual samples (Assumption (2) Exact answer generation). This idealized condition captures the objective of distillation, where the student is trained to reproduce the teacher’s behavior on the available supervision. More importantly, the analysis also relies on the generated counterfactual context C^{\prime} to induce the intended alternative answer A^{\prime}. In practice, this may not be guaranteed due to inherently stochastic and unpredictable generative behavior of LLMs Holtzman et al. (2019). The teacher may fail to produce A^{\prime}, or conditioning on C^{\prime} may provide only limited additional predictive benefit for A^{\prime}. For realization of this objective in our implementation, we therefore introduce a new metric Context Following Difficulty (CFD) in the following section to validate generated counterfactuals before they are used for knowledge distillation.

section: Context Following Difficulty (CFD) for counterfactual validation
text: Generated counterfactual samples should be evaluated using the teacher to determine whether they induce the intended alternative answer A^{\prime} rather than another response. Since exact matching can be unreliable for generative tasks (Holtzman et al., 2019), we use token-level F1 (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) to measure agreement between the teacher output and A^{\prime}. However, answer agreement alone is insufficient, as generating the intended answer does not necessarily indicate that the C^{\prime} provides strong evidence for that prediction. A high-quality counterfactual should therefore not only induce the intended answer A^{\prime}, but also make A^{\prime} substantially more predictable when conditioned on C^{\prime} than from the Q alone. To capture these two properties, we introduce a new metric Context Following Difficulty (CFD), which combines Answer Agreement (AA) with the Contextual Loss Ratio (CLR). First, \mathrm{AA}_{\theta} measures whether the teacher generates the intended alternative answer A^{\prime} under the counterfactual context C^{\prime}: \mathrm{AA}_{\theta}(Q,C^{\prime},A^{\prime})=\mathrm{F1}\big(\hat{A}_{\theta}(Q,C^{\prime}),A^{\prime}\big), where \hat{A}_{\theta}(Q,C^{\prime}) is the answer generated by the teacher given Q and C^{\prime}. A higher \mathrm{AA}_{\theta} indicates stronger agreement with the intended answer A^{\prime}. However, high answer agreement alone does not establish that the counterfactual context plays a role in predicting A^{\prime}.

section: Context Following Difficulty (CFD) for counterfactual validation
text: Inspired by the Instruction Following Difficulty (IFD) metric (Li et al., 2024), we define the Contextual Loss Ratio (CLR) as: \mathrm{CLR}_{\theta}(Q,C^{\prime},A^{\prime})=\frac{L_{\theta}(A^{\prime}\mid Q,C^{\prime})}{L_{\theta}(A^{\prime}\mid Q)}. A low \mathrm{CLR}_{\theta} indicates that conditioning on C^{\prime} substantially reduces the teacher’s loss for A^{\prime} relative to conditioning on Q alone, i.e., C^{\prime} plays a strong role in predicting the intended alternative answer. Conversely, a higher \mathrm{CLR}_{\theta} indicates that providing C^{\prime} yields only a limited reduction in the loss of A^{\prime}, suggesting weaker dependence of the target prediction on C^{\prime}. Thus, \mathrm{CLR}_{\theta} measures how strongly C^{\prime} contributes to the prediction of the teacher model A^{\prime}.

section: Context Following Difficulty (CFD) for counterfactual validation
text: Combining these two measures, we finally define our Context Following Difficulty (CFD) score as: \mathrm{CFD}_{\theta}(Q,C^{\prime},A^{\prime})=\frac{\mathrm{CLR}_{\theta}(Q,C^{\prime},A^{\prime})}{\mathrm{AA}_{\theta}(Q,C^{\prime},A^{\prime}){+}\delta},

section: Context Following Difficulty (CFD) for counterfactual validation
text: where \delta>0 is a small constant for numerical stability. We prefer low \mathrm{CLR}_{\theta} and high \mathrm{AA}_{\theta}. A lower \mathrm{CFD}_{\theta} score favors counterfactuals for which the teacher both generates an answer close to the intended target A^{\prime} and relies more strongly on the counterfactual context when predicting A^{\prime}. Figure 4 illustrates the complementary roles of \mathrm{AA}_{\theta} and \mathrm{CLR}_{\theta} in four representative cases. Cases (a) and (b) show that a counterfactual may fail to induce the intended answer even when the modified context contains or supports it. Case (c) has high \mathrm{AA}_{\theta} but high \mathrm{CLR}_{\theta}, indicating limited additional predictive benefit from C^{\prime}. In contrast, case (c) represents a valid counterfactual with a low \mathrm{CFD}_{\theta}. Together, these examples show why both \mathrm{AA}_{\theta} and \mathrm{CLR}_{\theta} are necessary for validation. The two components of \mathrm{CFD}_{\theta} therefore capture complementary properties of a valid and informative counterfactual. \mathrm{AA}_{\theta} verifies the intended answer A^{\prime}, while \mathrm{CLR}_{\theta} measures how strongly the modified context contributes to predicting A^{\prime}. Our algorithm is provided in Algorithm 1 (also in Figure 1).

Datasets. We evaluate CofFeQA on eight open-domain question answering benchmarks. The five in-domain benchmarks are Natural Questions (NQ) (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019), SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), NewsQA (Trischler et al., 2017), TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), and HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018). The three out-of-domain benchmarks are DROP (Dua et al., 2019), DuoRC (Saha et al., 2018), and RelationExtraction (Levy et al., 2017). Additional details about the datasets used in our experimental evaluations are provided in Appendix F.1

Models. We evaluate our method using two model families with different architectures: the encoder-decoder model T5 (Raffel et al., 2020) and the decoder-only model Qwen2.5 (Bai et al., 2023). In the T5 setting, T5-Large (770M parameters) serves as the teacher, while T5-Base (220M parameters) serves as the student. In the Qwen2.5 setting, Qwen2.5-7B-IT serves as the teacher, while Qwen2.5-1.5B-IT serves as the student. Full-training details are in Appendix F.2.

Baselines. We compare CofFeQA against three distillation baselines: (i) Standard Knowledge Distillation (KD) (Hinton et al., 2015), (ii) Sequence-Level Knowledge Distillation (seqKD) (Kim and Rush, 2016), and (iii) Layer-Wise Distillation (LWD) (Jiao et al., 2020). All methods use the same few-shot splits for fair comparison. Additional details of the baselines and implementation details are provided in Appendix F.3.

Setup. Following prior work (Hamman et al., 2025), we first fine-tune the teacher model on the full training dataset. For each few-shot budget k\in\{16,32,64,128,256\}, we rank factual samples by their teacher prediction margins, using margin sampling (Scheffer et al., 2001). The factual-only distillation baseline uses the k samples with the smallest margins. CofFeQA instead uses the k/2 factual samples with the smallest margins together with their corresponding k/2 counterfactuals, maintaining the same total few-shot budget k. We evaluate accuracy using EM and F1 against the gold answers and teacher-student agreement using EM and F1 between their generated answers. All results are reported as the mean and standard deviation over five random seeds.

CofFeQA outperforms the baselines. As shown in Table 1, CofFeQA improves performance across all three distillation baselines under the T5 setting. When averaged across all datasets and k -shot settings, CofFeQA improves the F1 score from 66.42 to 69.27 with standard KD, from 66.37 to 69.28 with LWD, and from 68.63 to 70.52 with SeqKD. Moreover, CofFeQA exhibits lower standard deviations than the corresponding baselines in many settings, indicating more stable performance across seeds. These results demonstrate that counterfactual supervision provides consistent benefits over the baselines. Detailed EM scores are provided in Table 8 in Appendix H.1.

CofFeQA generalizes across different model families. CofFeQA improves standard KD across both the encoder-decoder T5 and decoder-only Qwen2.5 model families, where the teachers are approximately 3.5\times and 4.7\times larger than their respective students. Under Qwen2.5, CofFeQA improves the average F1 score from 66.21 to 67.72 with standard KD, from 66.77 to 68.00 with LWD, and from 67.16 to 67.88 with SeqKD. These results indicate that the benefits of CofFeQA extend across different model architectures and scales.

Students mimic the teacher more closely under CofFeQA. To examine how closely the student follows the teacher, we measure teacher-student agreement using EM and F1. As shown in Figure 5, CofFeQA generally achieves higher teacher-student agreement than standard KD across datasets and k -shot settings. Averaged across all benchmarks and settings, CofFeQA improves F1 agreement under standard KD from 68.51 to 71.50 under T5, with a similar trend for Qwen2.5. These results suggest that counterfactual supervision helps the student more closely reproduce the teacher’s output behavior. Detailed results and additional radar plots are provided in Appendix H.2.

CofFeQA generalizes well to out-of-domain datasets. To evaluate out-of-domain generalization, we use Natural Questions for distillation and evaluate the resulting students on three out-of-domain test sets: DROP, DuoRC, and RelationExtraction. As shown in Table 2, CofFeQA improves over standard KD when averaged across datasets and k -shot settings for both model families. For T5 and Qwen2.5, CofFeQA improves the overall F1 score over standard KD from 53.35 to 54.52 and from 57.09 to 57.77, respectively. These results indicate that the benefits of counterfactual supervision extend beyond the in-domain datasets used for distillation. Detailed EM scores are in Appendix H.3.

CofFeQA improves performance under modified contextual evidence. Following Longpre et al. (2021), we replace each test answer in the context with a randomly selected answer of the same entity type and evaluate against the modified target. As shown in Table 13, CofFeQA improves average F1 agreement over standard KD from 66.72 to 69.55 for T5 and from 49.23 to 53.55 for Qwen2.5. This suggests that CofFeQA better adapts predictions to modified contextual evidence when it differs from pre-trained knowledge. Corresponding EM results are provided in Appendix H.4.

We conduct three ablation studies to examine different components of CofFeQA: (i) We compare CofFeQA with a variant that uses generated counterfactuals without CFD verification to isolate the contribution of CFD; (ii) We vary the CFD threshold \tau to analyze its effect on downstream performance and teacher-student agreement; and (iii) We measure counterfactual generation costs, training time and energy consumption across baselines to analyze the computational cost of CofFeQA. Full ablation results and experimental details are in Appendix G.

In this paper, we present a counterfactual-guided knowledge distillation method for few-shot open-book question answering. Motivated by the difficulty of distilling with factual samples near the teacher’s decision boundary, our approach uses factual-counterfactual pairs to provide additional supervision around these challenging regions. We further introduce CFD to validate counterfactuals before distillation. Experiments across multiple datasets and LLM architectures demonstrate improved knowledge transfer under limited supervision. Limitations and future directions are discussed in Appendix B. Overall, our findings highlight the potential of counterfactual supervision for improving knowledge transfer in generative QA under limited supervision in the few-shot setting.

To support reproducibility, we provide detailed descriptions of the datasets, training procedures, evaluation settings, and baseline implementations in Appendix F. Specifically, Appendix F.1 describes the datasets and experimental splits, Appendix F.2 provides details of teacher model fine-tuning and evaluation, and Appendix F.3 describes the baseline formulations and implementation details. We also provide the assumptions and complete proof of our geometric analysis in Appendix E.

Reading Between the Layers: Cross-Modal Alignment and Representational Hierarchy in Vision Transformers. While large vision-language models excel at optical character recognition, it remains unclear how their underlying vision encoders process text and its meaning, and whether they support anything resembling reading comprehension. We systematically study transformer-based vision encoders, using cross-modal alignment between rendered text and visual concepts together with probing and retrieval-based analyses as a controlled window into these broader capabilities. Our layer-wise analyses span orthographic, grammatical, and semantic organization, and reveal that strong cross-modal mapping emerges only in the deepest layers, after unimodal object and text recognition have already developed, coinciding with a progression from surface-level to semantic representations. Although this hierarchy is strongest in contrastively trained models, larger self-supervised models and text-rich training data partially support similar behaviors without explicit language supervision. Together, our results suggest that increasing model and training-data scale, as well as text-rich training data, can partially compensate for the absence of language supervision.

In human literacy research, a distinction is often drawn between decoding, the ability to recognize written symbols, and reading comprehension, the ability to connect those symbols to semantic meaning Gough and Tunmer (1986); Hoover and Gough (1990). Much like novice learners of English who recognize “horse” across contexts without grounding it in the concept of the animal itself, modern vision encoders exhibit decoding (a.k.a. OCR) capabilities in their processing of in-image text (Lin et al., 2024). While some studies suggest that transformer-based vision encoders (ViT) develop representations supporting cross-modal semantic alignment between text and visual concepts (Wang and Ma, 2025; Materzyńska et al., 2022), the scope of these capabilities and their underlying representational dynamics have not been systematically studied. In this work, we use cross-modal alignment between rendered text and visual concepts, together with probing and retrieval-based analyses, as a controlled window into these broader reading comprehension capabilities.

Motivated by the distinction between surface decoding and broader reading capabilities, we study whether cross-modal semantic alignment builds upon visual object recognition or develops independently across network depth. As shown in Figure 1, we extend standard probing methodologies (Rogers et al., 2020; Conneau and Kiela, 2018) to ViT encoders by rendering textual stimuli as images with diverse visual augmentations. Using these stimuli, we conduct layer-wise probing to examine whether linguistic representations in vision encoders are organized hierarchically across layers, progressing from surface form to grammatical regularities and finally semantic understanding, analogous to hierarchies observed in humans Friederici (2002) and language models Jawahar et al. (2019); Tenney et al. (2019). To support these probe-based findings, we also evaluate cross-modal alignment and retrieval between rendered text and images, allowing us to compare when shared cross-modal structure emerges relative to unimodal object and text recognition. Finally, we address the role of training signals: while language supervision and data composition are known to shape surface-level reading (Lin et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025), we study if they similarly govern the development of deeper grammatical and semantic organization.

Through a systematic study via layer-wise probing, supported by controlled cross-modal alignment experiments, spanning surface-level character recognition, grammatical regularities, and semantic alignment, we address these questions across three training paradigms — contrastive (CLIP) Radford et al. (2021), self-supervised (DINO) Caron et al. (2021), and masked autoencoding (MAE) He et al. (2022) — to understand how training objective modulates each:
RQ1. How and when does cross-modal semantic alignment emerge in vision encoders?
RQ2. What representational structure underlies this alignment?
RQ3. How do scale and data composition shape its development?

Our results reveal three main findings. First, strong cross-modal semantic alignment between rendered text and visual concepts emerges only in the deepest layers, after unimodal object and text recognition have already developed. Second, this alignment coincides with a representational hierarchy, clearest in CLIP, in which orthographic information emerges early, grammatical regularities peak at intermediate depths, and semantic organization consolidates in the deepest layers. Third, in self-supervised encoders, increasing model capacity from 300M to 2B mainly strengthens surface-level representations, whereas the 7B model, which is also trained on more data, develops a clearer hierarchy and measurable cross-modal transfer; enriching training data with text produces more modest improvements.

section: From Decoding to Cross-Modal Semantic Alignment in Vision Encoders
text: Vision-language models trained using contrastive learning can align natural-language descriptions with visual concepts at the level of whole images (Radford et al., 2021). Yet compositional image-text evaluations reveal limited sensitivity to word order, relations, and other fine-grained linguistic distinctions (Thrush et al., 2022; Yuksekgonul et al., 2022). Because these studies assess the final cross-modal embedding space, they do not isolate how an image encoder processes written language presented as pixels.

section: From Decoding to Cross-Modal Semantic Alignment in Vision Encoders
text: Whether ViTs go beyond decoding to develop cross-modal semantic alignment between written words and visual concepts has received less attention than surface-level character recognition. Materzyńska et al. (2022) provide evidence that they can, showing that CLIP’s image encoder matches rendered images of words to natural images of the concepts those words describe. Wang and Ma (2025) extend this picture with a layer-wise analysis, finding that the early layers process text as visual texture while semantic differentiation appears only in the final layers, though they argue that improvements are largely driven by orthographic disambiguation rather than abstract meaning, casting doubt on whether these representations reflect semantic grounding beyond orthographic disambiguation, even in the deepest layers.

section: From Decoding to Cross-Modal Semantic Alignment in Vision Encoders
text: Consistent with this, Lemesle et al. (2022) find that semantic word representations in CLIP’s visual processing are not shared with image representations, with word form dominating over visual meaning for word-embedded images. Park et al. (2025) further show that surface text reading ability develops abruptly during training while semantic alignment develops more gradually, suggesting that the two capabilities are not only functionally distinct but follow different developmental trajectories. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, prior studies have left questions about the emergence of language-relevant representations in image encoders unanswered. Specifically, it remains unclear whether image encoders develop these representations, whether the representations underlying cross-modal semantic alignment follow a principled surface-to-semantic hierarchy, and how these representations relate to the encoder’s broader visual capabilities. We address these gaps through controlled layer-wise probing and cross-modal alignment experiments.

Prior work on probing pretrained language models reveals a consistent hierarchical organization across layers, from surface features to grammatical structure to semantics (Rogers et al., 2020; Jawahar et al., 2019; Tenney et al., 2019). Tatariya et al. (2024) extend this to PIXEL (Rust et al., 2023), a ViT-based language model trained on rendered text, finding a similar surface-to-semantic progression, although notably absent in ViT-MAE, which lacks language supervision. Dumpala et al. (2024) further show that VLM text encoders exhibit weaker syntactic organization than unimodal language models, with pre-training objective as the primary driver. Our work extends this line of inquiry to vision encoders processing rendered text through their image encoder, asking whether hierarchically organized language-relevant structure arises in models never trained on language.

section: Role of Training Paradigm, Data, and Scale
text: Learned model behavior is shaped not only by architecture and training objective, but also by the composition and scale of pretraining data. Visual datasets can contain incidental correlations that models exploit as shortcuts (Torralba and Efros, 2011; Geirhos et al., 2020); in self-supervised learning, data curation likewise affects the invariances and semantic distinctions captured by learned representations (Purushwalkam and Gupta, 2020; Van Gansbeke et al., 2021). These findings motivate studying which statistical regularities support visual text processing.

section: Role of Training Paradigm, Data, and Scale
text: This question is particularly salient for reading-related behavior in vision encoders. Lin et al. (2024) show that CLIP’s text recognition arises largely from a shortcut: roughly half of training images contain embedded text, and the majority of these have captions that repeat the same text, leading the model to associate visual character patterns with their transcriptions rather than principled reading. Liu et al. (2025) disentangle the contributions of data composition and language supervision more directly, finding that text-rich training data accounts for a substantial portion of the OCR gap between CLIP and DINO, with language supervision providing an additional benefit. Building on this, Fan et al. (2025) show that the remaining advantage of language supervision on surface-level reading can be further offset by increasing model scale. Whether these factors—supervision, data composition, and scale—similarly govern the emergence of cross-modal semantic alignment, as measured through cross-modal alignment between written words and their visual referents, remains an open question and the primary motivation for RQ3.

A central challenge in studying visual text processing in vision encoders is isolating textual representations from broader visual context, since vision encoders operate directly on pixels and do not accept discrete text tokens as input. Moreover, real images containing text introduce uncontrolled variation in layout, context, and background, making it difficult to isolate the mechanisms underlying visual text processing. We adopt a controlled evaluation strategy in which textual inputs are rendered as images (Figure 2, top row). This allows us to present identical linguistic content in diverse visual forms by changing typographic features such as font, size, and layout. These variations reduce reliance on fixed low-level visual cues, allowing us to assess whether representations capture more generalizable textual structure. An additional advantage of this strategy is that rendered text images naturally serve as a cross-modal bridge between visual and textual representations. We leverage this in our cross-modal experiments by pairing natural images with rendered text images of their corresponding class labels, allowing us to compare how shared concepts are represented across modalities while controlling for visual form.

We analyze frozen representations across network depth, extracting the post-LayerNorm residual stream from every transformer block. At each layer, we consider both the CLS token and mean-pooled patch tokens (AVG). For MAE models, we set the mask ratio to zero at inference so that all patch tokens are present. These representations form the basis of the task-specific analyses introduced below, where we define the inputs, prediction targets, and datasets for each research question.

We study vision encoders representing three distinct pre-training paradigms: contrastive learning (CLIP; Radford et al. 2021), self-supervised learning (DINO; Oquab et al. 2023), and masked autoencoding (ViT-MAE; He et al. 2022). To ensure a fair comparison, we follow Fan et al. (2025) and use models of comparable scale (\approx 1B parameters) trained on the same data. We additionally examine scaling effects using 300M, 2B, and 7B DINO models. All models use the ViT architecture. During probe training, the model weights are kept frozen and the weights of the respective classifiers are adjusted. Freezing the weights helps to ensure that the probing measures properties of the pretrained representations without altering them via task adaptation (Hewitt and Liang, 2019). Appendix B lists full model details.

Cross-modal classification tests whether object categories can be decoded across modalities from a shared representation space. The input is a frozen layer representation of either a natural image or a rendered class label, and the prediction target is the corresponding object category. We pair natural images from Caltech-256 (Griffin et al., 2007) (143 classes, 50 images per class) and ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009) (1,000 classes, 50 validation images per class) with rendered text images of their class labels, generated across diverse fonts, sizes, and backgrounds. At each layer, we train a logistic regression classifier on representations from one modality and evaluate it on representations from the other, averaging accuracy across the two transfer directions. We also evaluate within-modality classification to compare cross-modal transfer with unimodal object and text recognition.

Because probing tasks vary substantially in label cardinality, raw accuracy is not directly comparable across tasks, layers, and models. We normalize using Percentage Accuracy Gain (PAG) (Goodfellow et al., 2016, e.g.): \text{PAG}=\frac{\text{Acc}-\text{Acc}_{\text{base}}}{100-\text{Acc}_{\text{base}}}, where \text{Acc}_{\text{base}} denotes the task-specific chance baseline. We use the same normalization for the linguistic classification tasks in Section 5.
To complement probe-based analyses, we evaluate zero-shot cross-modal retrieval on the same datasets using cosine similarity without training additional classifiers, reporting layer-wise Recall@K.

While cross-modal classification tests whether models map isolated words to their visual referents, it leaves open whether this alignment extends to compositional, attribute-level meaning. We introduce controlled relational retrieval tasks using synthetically generated scenes composed of fruit objects Oltean (2017) targeting three attributes: cardinality (e.g., “3 apples”), spatial direction (e.g., “apple right of banana”), and relative size (e.g., “tiny orange”). This dataset consists of isolated fruit images against clean backgrounds, making it straightforward to compose controlled scenes by combining and manipulating individual objects to express target relations. These tasks pair natural images with rendered text-image descriptions of the target relation, enabling us to test whether cross-modal alignment extends beyond simple object-label correspondence to relational and attribute-level structure. We evaluate retrieval in both image-to-text and text-to-image directions and report average Recall@K.

Cross-modal alignment could in principle reflect orthographic co-occurrence rather than semantic grounding. That is, a model might associate an image of a horse with “horse” simply because they co-occur in training, not because it understands the concept. We therefore curate 90 orthographic neighbor pairs corresponding to a subset of the 143 Caltech-256 classes, each pairing a class name with a semantically unrelated distractor at edit distance 1 (e.g., “horse” vs. “house”). For each natural image, we report the cosine similarity gap between the correct and distractor rendered texts:
\Delta_{\cos}=\cos(E_{\text{text}},E_{\text{img}})-\cos(E_{\text{ortho}},E_{\text{img}}),

where E_{\text{img}}, E_{\text{text}}, and E_{\text{ortho}} are the embeddings of the image, correct text, and orthographic distractor, respectively. Positive values indicate that the model favors the semantically correct match over the orthographically similar one.

Across all models, image recognition (img-img) develops before text recognition (txt-txt), and cross-modal transfer, when present, emerges only after both, in the deepest layers (Figure 3). In CLIP, cross-modal transfer increases sharply in the final layers, whereas in DINO and MAE it remains near baseline throughout depth. In CLIP specifically, img-img scores rise steeply from depth 0.4, txt-txt scores follow from depth 0.6, and cross-modal transfer only begins to noticeably increase after depth 0.9. This suggests that shared cross-modal structure is not reducible to unimodal competence alone, but instead emerges only once image and text representations become sufficiently expressive. In DINO and MAE, both unimodal settings reach high PAG by depth 0.6–0.7, yet cross-modal transfer remains near baseline across all layers, indicating that strong unimodal representations alone are insufficient for robust cross-modal alignment. Results on ImageNet-1K (Appendix C.1) show the same pattern. Supporting zero-shot retrieval experiments exhibit the same late-layer trend, with CLIP developing strong retrieval alignment while DINO and MAE (1B) remain near chance across depth (Appendix C.2).

Taken together, these results point to a consistent ordering: cross-modal alignment does not develop in parallel with unimodal recognition, but emerges only after both image and text representations have individually matured — suggesting it depends on the prior consolidation of unimodal competence rather than developing alongside it.

Relational retrieval experiments further show that this alignment extends beyond isolated object-label correspondence to attributes such as direction, size, and cardinality (Figure 4, first 3 subplots). While absolute Recall@1 scores remain low across all tasks, CLIP consistently rises well above chance in the deepest layers, confirming that late-layer representations carry meaningful relational structure despite the overall difficulty of these tasks. Among the three attributes, cardinality shows the strongest alignment, followed by size, while spatial direction remains substantially weaker — suggesting that fine-grained relational correspondence is more difficult to recover than object-level semantic alignment. This is consistent with prior work showing that CLIP struggles broadly with spatial direction (Liu et al., 2023), likely because directional prepositions are systematically underspecified in the web-scraped image-caption pairs used for contrastive pretraining.

Orthographic control experiments (Figure 4, last subplot) further show that in early and middle layers, all three models assign similarly high cosine similarity to both the correct text and the orthographic distractor, indicating that representations at these depths are not yet semantically discriminative. In the deepest layers, however, CLIP shows a clear divergence: similarity to the correct text drops less sharply than similarity to the distractor, opening a growing gap that favors the semantically corresponding match. DINO and MAE show no such separation, with correct and distractor similarities tracking each other closely throughout depth.

Across all three evaluations — cross-modal classification, relational retrieval, and orthographic control — CLIP consistently outperforms DINO and MAE, and in each case the advantage is concentrated in the deepest layers. This pattern is consistent with a role for contrastive language supervision: CLIP is explicitly trained to align image and text representations through contrastive language supervision, whereas DINO and MAE receive no such signal, suggesting that, at the 1B scale, robust cross-modal transfer, relational alignment, and semantic disambiguation beyond orthographic similarity depend strongly on language-aligned training signals; Section 6 examines whether scale and data composition can compensate.

We examine which linguistic properties are recoverable from frozen representations at different network depths. Each example consists of a rendered word or phrase paired with a task-specific label. Given its representation at a particular layer, a probe predicts an orthographic, grammatical, or semantic property, as defined below.

We assess character identity via 26 binary classifiers (one per letter) and word length via length bin prediction. For character presence, each classifier is trained on 100 positive examples (words containing the target letter) and 100 negative examples (words not containing it), balanced by selecting the most frequent words from SUBTLEX-US (Brysbaert and New, 2009); each word is rendered as a single 224\times 224 image. For letter count, we define four word-length bins ([3–5], [6–8], [9–11], [12–14] characters) with 300 words per bin (100 per individual length), again frequency-ordered from SUBTLEX-US, giving a 4-class problem with a chance level of 25%. These tasks establish whether the encoder captures the most basic orthographic properties of rendered text, which are the building blocks of any deeper linguistic organization. For Letter Count, word length is directly recoverable from image width, introducing a visual confound that could inflate probe performance independently of any orthographic content.

To discount this, we apply rectangle input controls, which are blank rectangles rendered in the same style and position as the original word, with width proportional to character count at the rendered font size and height equal to the text bounding box but containing no linguistic content (Figure 2, bottom row), and compute a confound PAG from their performance. The final adjusted score \text{PAG}_{\text{adj}} subtracts this confound, ensuring that reported performance reflects orthographic encoding rather than incidental visual cues.

We use part-of-speech (POS) prediction as a proxy for grammatical organization beyond surface form. If representations encode not just what a word looks like but what syntactic role it plays, this would suggest that the encoder has internalized structure that goes beyond orthographic pattern matching. For isolated-word POS tagging, we build a 4-class dataset (NOUN, VERB, ADJ, ADV) of up to 200 words per class drawn from five Universal Dependencies English treebanks (Nivre et al., 2020) (EWT, GUM, LinES, ParTUT, PUD), retaining only unambiguously tagged lemma; each word is rendered as a single image. For contextual POS, we target 4 classes (NOUN, VERB, ADJ, ADV) using words that appear under multiple POS tags across the same treebanks, collecting up to 500 instances per class; each image shows a 5-word context window with the target word circled, which is intended to reduce reliance on lexical priors.

We assess whether representations capture higher-level conceptual structure through two tasks: supersense categorization, which tests whether words are grouped by broad semantic category, and concreteness prediction, which tests whether the encoder distinguishes between abstract and concrete concepts. For supersense, we define 10 WordNet-derived categories (animal, fruit, vegetable, furniture, vehicle, clothing, instrument, building, tool, tree) with up to 50 words per class, filtered by SUBTLEX-US frequency; each word is rendered as a single image. For concreteness, words are drawn from SUBTLEX-US and labeled as abstract (concreteness rating \leq 2.0) or concrete (\geq 3.0) based on the concreteness ratings from Brysbaert et al. (2014), with the ambiguous mid-range dropped; 500 words per class are selected with word-length distributions matched across classes to remove length as a confound. Together, these probe whether the encoder has moved beyond surface and grammatical organization toward something closer to meaning. Rectangle input controls are applied to concreteness prediction, where word length is a known correlate of abstractness (Lewis and Frank, 2016).

For each task, an example consists of a frozen representation of a rendered word or phrase paired with its task-specific label. We evaluate independent L2-regularized logistic regression probes for each vision encoder, layer, and pooling method using stratified five-fold cross-validation with random shuffling. We standardize features using the mean and variance estimated from the training split. We select the regularization strength C\in\{10^{-3},10^{-2},10^{-1},1,10,100\} by maximizing accuracy on a held-out validation subset comprising 10% of the training split, then refit the classifier on the entire training split. We report mean test accuracy and standard deviation across the five folds and normalize accuracy using PAG (see § 4.1). For tasks with rectangle input controls, we report \text{PAG}_{\text{adj}}=\text{PAG}-\text{PAG}_{\text{confound}}, where \text{PAG}_{\text{confound}} denotes probe performance on rectangle controls.

To ensure probe performance reflects structured information rather than superficial cues, we apply label controls (shuffled labels, fixed inputs) to all tasks (Hewitt and Liang, 2019); as control performance remained consistently near chance level, we exclude them from further analysis. To reduce task-specific variance in reporting, we aggregate probing performance within each linguistic level into a single composite PAG. Full dataset construction details are in Appendix A.

Figure 5 shows layer-wise PAG for surface, grammatical, and semantic probing tasks across 1B models. CLIP develops a clear surface-to-semantic hierarchy across layers: surface information emerges early, grammatical regularities peak at intermediate depth, and semantic organization consolidates only in the deepest layers (depth \approx 0.9). Similar trends are observed in the contextual POS setting (Appendix C.4), confirming that these grammatical signals are not limited to isolated lexical priors. In contrast, DINO and MAE exhibit strong surface signals but substantially weaker grammatical and semantic structure.

Importantly, the emergence of semantic probe performance in CLIP coincides with the onset of strong cross-modal transfer and retrieval alignment from RQ1. Orthographic control experiments further show that late-layer image-text similarity increasingly favors correct semantic matches over orthographically similar distractors, indicating that late-layer alignment in CLIP corresponds to increasingly structured semantic organization rather than purely orthographic matching. These findings corroborate Materzyńska et al. (2022) while extending their results by localizing strong cross-modal alignment to the deepest layers and relating it to a progressively organized representational hierarchy. They also partially support the concerns of Wang and Ma (2025): orthographic similarity contributes substantially in earlier layers, but later CLIP representations increasingly reflect semantic correspondence beyond surface form.

The contrast with DINO and MAE is informative: both models develop strong surface representations from visual form alone, but, at this scale, the absence of language supervision limits the emergence of the deeper grammatical and semantic structures that support cross-modal alignment in CLIP.

Having established that cross-modal alignment and its underlying representational hierarchy depend strongly on training objective, we examine whether scale and data composition can compensate for the absence of language supervision. We study a family of self-supervised DINO variants that differ either in model size or training data composition. To examine how model scale and training-data composition affect alignment and representational structure, we apply the tasks and evaluation protocols introduced in Sections 4 and 5 to the DINO variants described below.

We compare DINO models with 300M, 2B, and 7B parameters to examine how scaling is associated with cross-modal transfer and representational organization. The 300M and 2B models are trained on the same 2B-image dataset, whereas the 7B model is trained on a larger 8B-image dataset. Thus, comparisons between the 300M and 2B models isolate the effect of model capacity, while differences involving the 7B model reflect the combined effects of increased capacity and training-data scale.

We examine DINO-2B models trained on subsets of the MC dataset Xu et al. (2024) enriched for text-heavy content. The “light” variant retains 50.3% of images in total through mild OCR-based filtering, while the “heavy” variant retains only 1.3%, primarily documents, charts, and tables.

Figure 6 shows that scale improves both cross-modal transfer and representational organization, with the largest gains at 7B. While image-to-image alignment improves steadily across depth for all models, text-to-text recognition is less stable in smaller models, showing gains in intermediate layers but degrading in deeper layers for the 300M and 2B variants. In contrast, the 7B model maintains strong text representations in later layers and first exhibits clear cross-modal transfer in deep layers among self-supervised models.

Surface-level information is learned early across all scales, with larger models consistently performing better. Increasing scale also produces a clearer separation between surface, grammatical, and semantic representations across depth, with semantic probe performance strengthening substantially in the deepest layers. This hierarchical organization remains weak in smaller models, where semantic probe performance stays near baseline. Zero-shot retrieval, relational retrieval, and orthographic control experiments exhibit the same trend (Appendix C.2, C.3), with DINOv2 7B showing substantially stronger late-layer alignment and semantic separation than smaller self-supervised models.

Prior work by Fan et al. (2025) showed that scale and text-rich data can partially offset the OCR advantage provided by language supervision. Figure 7 shows that this effect extends beyond surface-level recognition into cross-modal transfer and representational organization. Filtering toward text-rich data stabilizes text-to-text representations in deeper layers. The baseline model exhibits a noticeable degradation in late-layer text recognition that text-rich filtering corrects. Filtering also produces modest improvements in late-layer cross-modal transfer and semantic probe performance. However, these gains remain substantially weaker than those observed in DINOv2 7B and CLIP. Supporting retrieval and orthographic control experiments show the same qualitative trend (Appendix C.2, C.3), suggesting that data composition alone is insufficient to fully recover the stronger cross-modal alignment observed in contrastively trained or large-scale models.

Overall, both increased model capacity and training-data scale are associated with stronger hierarchical linguistic organization and cross-modal alignment in self-supervised vision encoders. The controlled 300M-to-2B comparison shows that capacity alone mainly improves surface-level representations, with little effect on cross-modal transfer or semantic organization, while the stronger performance of DINOv2 7B reflects the combined effects of increased capacity and a larger training dataset. Optimized data composition improves text recognition and reduces modality gaps, but, in our experiments, does not match the transfer or semantic organization observed in the 7B model.

In this work, we studied how vision encoders process and organize textual information across network depth, using cross-modal alignment between rendered text and visual concepts as a controlled lens into broader reading comprehension capabilities. Through controlled cross-modal transfer experiments and supporting layer-wise probing analyses, we showed that strong cross-modal alignment between rendered text and natural images emerges only in the deepest layers, after unimodal object and text recognition have already developed. Zero-shot retrieval and relational retrieval experiments corroborate this picture, showing that late-layer CLIP representations support not only object-label correspondence but also attribute-level structure such as cardinality and size, while spatial direction remains consistently the most difficult relational attribute to recover. Our analyses further revealed that this transition coincides with a progressively organized hierarchy of representations spanning surface-level orthographic information, grammatical regularities, and semantic organization. Our findings suggest that strong cross-modal semantic alignment in vision encoders emerges jointly from sufficient model capacity and exposure to language-aligned visual signals. Among the models studied, increasing model size and training-data scale yield larger gains in cross-modal transfer and hierarchical linguistic organization than enriching training data with text does.
Text-rich data stabilizes late-layer text recognition and modestly improves semantic alignment, but does not match the stronger transfer and semantic organization observed in the 7B model.

Our work studies language-relevant representations in vision encoders primarily through cross-modal semantic alignment between rendered text and visual concepts. While this provides a measurable operational proxy, reading comprehension is substantially broader and more complex than the behaviors evaluated here, involving compositional reasoning, discourse understanding, world knowledge integration, long-range dependency processing, and pragmatic interpretation. As a result, our findings should be interpreted as evidence of language-relevant representational organization and cross-modal alignment rather than full human-like reading comprehension.

Our analyses also rely heavily on probing methods, which measure information accessible within intermediate representations rather than the causal mechanisms used during inference. Although we complement probing with cross-modal transfer, retrieval, and orthographic control experiments, these methods cannot fully determine how models internally compute or use linguistic representations. Moreover, many of our probing tasks operate primarily on isolated words. While this enables controlled analysis of orthographic, grammatical, and semantic structure, natural language understanding depends heavily on broader contextual and compositional information. We partially address this through contextual POS experiments, but more complex sentence-level and discourse-level evaluations remain outside the scope of this work.

Finally, our study focuses exclusively on standalone vision encoders rather than full large vision-language models (LVLMs) that integrate these encoders within larger multimodal systems. Since downstream language models may substantially alter or amplify the language-relevant representations present in the visual backbone, it remains unclear how these findings transfer to instruction-tuned or generative multimodal systems, which we leave for future work.

Scaling and Distilling Text Embeddings for Better Diffusibility. Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a promising alternative to autoregressive (AR) language generation. Recent advances in continuous DLMs, which apply latent diffusion to continuous text embeddings, raise a practical question: which embedding makes the best latent space, i.e., the most diffusible? To answer this, we search through different embeddings and find that scaling the embedding model to stronger ones within the same family (T5 to T5Gemma-1 to T5Gemma-2) greatly improves generative performance. But the raw T5Gemma-2 embeddings are still not optimal. They are so discriminative that even the embeddings of plausible alternative words are separated, which makes the generation vulnerable to imperfect sampling. Consequently, continuous diffusion often fails to reach any of them and ends up at an invalid embedding instead. To address this, we distill T5Gemma-2 into a student encoder that learns the teacher's decoded probabilities as soft labels. Learning from such soft labels makes the student pull the alternative embeddings closer while maintaining the encoding-decoding mechanism. The distilled embeddings form a more connected and diffusible latent space, improving over the vanilla T5Gemma-2 embeddings. As a result, our medium-sized DLM achieves Gen.
PPL 17.8 (against real-text PPL 15.4) at real-text entropy on OpenWebText, outperforming GPT-2-M on Gen. PPL.

Diffusion models (Ho et al., 2020) have achieved huge success in continuous modalities such as image (Black Forest Labs, 2025b) and video (ByteDance Seed, 2026). A natural question is whether their strong modeling transfers to language generation, and whether Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) can serve as a more parallelizable and efficient paradigm beyond autoregressive (AR) generation. There are two families of DLMs: the first is discrete DLMs (Austin et al., 2021; Nie et al., 2025), which apply a discretized diffusion process directly on tokens, and use likelihood training (Lou et al., 2023). They have drawn the most attention since they can be adapted from foundation models and scale with them (Ye et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026). The second is continuous DLMs (Li et al., 2022) which we study in this paper. They apply latent diffusion on text embeddings and decode generated embeddings back to tokens, and are trained with MSE loss.

Interestingly, though introduced as early as discrete DLMs, continuous DLMs remain less studied until their recent revival (Hu et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026), partly due to the incorporation of new techniques including self-conditioning (Chen et al., 2022), diffusion transformers (Peebles & Xie, 2023; Li & He, 2026), and the adoption of pretrained embeddings (Meshchaninov et al., 2026a).

A central question for continuous DLMs is which text embedding to use as the latent space. The same question is already a major topic in image diffusion (Yao et al., 2025; Black Forest Labs, 2025a), where the recent Representation Autoencoder (RAE) (Zheng et al., 2026) finds that replacing the VAE latents (Rombach et al., 2022) with pretrained image embeddings improves diffusibility. For text, earlier work finds that pretrained embeddings improve continuous DLMs over simple embeddings from lookup tables (Lovelace et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023). However, existing approaches either modify the embeddings and the diffusion model jointly (Lemercier et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a) or rely on relatively older embedding models (Hu et al., 2026), making it difficult to isolate the contribution of the embedding space or fully realize its potential.

In this paper, we study the embedding space for continuous DLMs in isolation. We fix the diffusion side as the recent Embedded Language Flow (ELF) (Hu et al., 2026) framework for its minimalist design, and change only the embedding. We find two things. (i) Scaling the embeddings leads to a more diffusible latent space. By scaling, we mean moving to stronger embedding models of the same family, which are pretrained with more data and better recipes, and not only adding parameters. We find that along with the scaling of T5-small/base (Raffel et al., 2020) \to T5Gemma-1 \to T5Gemma-2 (Zhang et al., 2025b), diffusibility also increases, and replacing the default T5-small embedding in ELF with T5Gemma-2-270M reduces generative perplexity by about 40% at the same entropy. (ii) Scaled embeddings can be further enhanced via distillation. A student encoder trained to match the probabilities from the T5Gemma-2 decoder is more diffusible than the teacher. As a result, the same DLMs trained on the distilled embeddings improve over the teacher on perplexity and MAUVE and sample more stably, as illustrated in Fig. 1.

Distillation helps because it fixes a problem of the raw T5Gemma-2 embeddings, which is that they are hard to generate perfectly. When sampling is insufficient or imperfect, the trajectories end at invalid embeddings that deviate from the real ones and decode to an uncertain or even wrong word (Shabalin et al., 2026). We relate this to the strong representation learning of T5Gemma-2, which makes its embeddings information-dense and distinct, so even the words that could fill the same position are kept apart (Yu et al., 2020). That helps discriminative tasks but hurts generation, since a continuous trajectory has to settle on one of several separate candidates and can end at none of them. The soft labels in distillation mitigate such separation, since the student learns to predict the plausible candidates so the alternative embeddings are placed near each other, and the generated embedding lies in the region they form.

Our results also shed light on new understandings of language representation learning and generation. Although text embeddings are considered contextualized and continuous, they inherit discreteness from text and do not fill the entire embedding space, so continuous DLMs can still generate embeddings that do not represent any word. This, in turn, is the other side of continuous language generation. Though more flexible than predicting tokens, they also risk deviating and generating invalid embeddings. Whether continuous DLMs will become a fully workable route still needs to be tested on even larger and practical scales, and the scaling and distillation here provide a basis for that. In all, our contribution can be summarized as follows: We show that scaled embeddings make good latent spaces for continuous DLMs, providing a strong baseline and starting point for continuous DLMs with T5Gemma-2 embeddings. We study the diffusibility of text embeddings from the perspective of generating valid, decodable embeddings. We enhance T5Gemma-2’s diffusibility by distilling its decoder probabilities, providing insights for taming and incorporating foundation models for continuous DLMs.

Continuous DLMs are latent diffusion on text embeddings. We follow the ELF (Hu et al., 2026) setup and first map the input token sequences \bm{s}\in\mathcal{V}^{L} to the sequences of embeddings with a (frozen) embedding model: \displaystyle\bm{x}=\text{Emb}(\bm{s})\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} This is also the only part we change throughout the paper. Training and sampling are standard diffusion, where we train a denoiser \bm{x}_{\theta}(\bm{z}_{t},t) on embedding sequences corrupted by sequence-wise Gaussian noise \bm{\epsilon}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}, \displaystyle\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}_{t,\bm{x},\bm{\epsilon}}\Big[\frac{1}{(1-t)^{2}}\|\bm{x}_{\theta}(\bm{z}_{t},t)-\bm{x}\|^{2}\Big],\quad\bm{z}_{t}:=t\bm{x}+(1-t)\bm{\epsilon}, and the optimal denoiser is the posterior mean: \displaystyle\bm{x}^{\star}(\bm{z}_{t},t)=\mathbb{E}[\bm{x}\mid\bm{z}_{t}]=\sum_{i}p(\bm{x}_{i}\mid\bm{z}_{t})\,\bm{x}_{i}, where \{\bm{x}_{i}\} are the embeddings of the training data, and weights p(\bm{x}_{i}\mid\bm{z}_{t}) decrease with \|\bm{z}_{t}-t\,\bm{x}_{i}\|.

We also train a decoder that maps the generated embeddings back to tokens. It shares weights with the denoiser \bm{x}_{\theta} plus a trainable head, and is trained on embedding sequences with token-wise corruption, where \bm{\lambda}\in[0,1]^{L} is a per-token noise level \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}=\text{CE}(\text{Head}_{\theta^{\prime}}(\bm{x}_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{z}},t=1)),\bm{s}),\quad\tilde{\bm{z}}=\bm{\lambda}\,\bm{x}+(\bm{1}-\bm{\lambda})\,\bm{\epsilon} This improves robustness for decoding imperfect embeddings. We also keep specific design choices of ELF (noise scheduling, self-conditioning, SDE sampling, etc.) unchanged; see App. B.1.

Earliest continuous DLMs adopt simple and co-trained embeddings (Li et al., 2022). However, co-training collapses the embeddings, since one point for all is the easiest way to reduce the MSE loss (Dieleman et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2024). Recent work finds that pretrained text embeddings perform better (Meshchaninov et al., 2026a; Hu et al., 2026); this paper follows this line and tests their full potential.

Discrete DLMs use a generalized diffusion process with categorical corruption on the tokens (Lou et al., 2023; Ou et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2024). Importantly, they can be adapted from AR foundation models and benefit from their progress (Gong et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026). We show that continuous DLMs can co-evolve with them too (Yang et al., 2026, see also), by using embedding models that are adapted from such foundation models. There are also papers showing discrete DLMs can be enhanced via continuous text embeddings (Zhou et al., 2025; Lemercier et al., 2026), or continuous relaxations (Deschenaux et al., 2026).

Which latent is easy to diffuse is a central question in image diffusion (Chen et al., 2025; Skorokhodov et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026), and replacing VAE latents with pretrained representations such as DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2023) improves diffusibility (Zheng et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026b). We find the text counterpart, where the scaled T5Gemma-2 provides a strong latent space, and instead of explicitly redesigning (Zhang et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2026) the latent, we distill the scaled encoder for diffusibility.

section: 3 Scaling Text Embedding for Continuous DLMs
text: (1) Scaled embeddings are high-potential latents. Embeddings trained with richer data and a better recipe can expose more information for the diffusion to learn, and scaling from T5-small to T5Gemma-2 cuts Gen. PPL by about 40\% at matched entropy. (2) Scaled embeddings can still be hard to generate. Generated embeddings can be invalid and far from real ones. This is because T5Gemma-2 keeps the plausible words for a position apart, so a generated embedding can miss all of them and decodes problematically.

section: 3.1 Scaling improves the diffusibility of embeddings
text: We start with off-the-shelf embedding models, on which we train the same ELF-B on a 25% subset of OpenWebText (Gokaslan et al., 2019) (512 tokens per sequence, denoted as ‘OWT-512’) for faster comparison. We mainly study the family of encoder-decoder (Sutskever et al., 2014) models, including T5-small (Raffel et al., 2020) used in ELF, T5-base, T5Gemma-1-S/B (Zhang et al., 2025a), T5Gemma-2-270M (Zhang et al., 2025b) (denoted as T5Gemma-2 throughout the paper); and we also include a strong modern encoder-only model, ModernBERT (Warner et al., 2025). The embeddings are normalized by their global mean and variance, as in ELF.

section: 3.1 Scaling improves the diffusibility of embeddings
text: We find that as the embedding models scale from T5-small through T5Gemma-1 to T5Gemma-2, their diffusion performance (shown in the PPL-entropy curves in Fig. 2) also improves. T5Gemma-1-B can outperform T5-small, while T5Gemma-2 further improves over T5Gemma-1-B. This suggests that stronger representation learning exposes richer information from the training data for the diffusion to learn. While the encoder-only ModernBERT also performs well on downstream tasks, it is less suitable for diffusion and generates repetitive sentences. So an embedding that is strong on discriminative tasks is not necessarily a diffusible one.

section: 3.1 Scaling improves the diffusibility of embeddings
text: Here, T5Gemma-2 is the only embedding space that reaches real-text entropy, and it cuts Gen. PPL by about 40% at the same entropy as T5-small. We therefore pick T5Gemma-2 as the baseline for the rest of the paper. Here we focus on smaller-sized embedding models for a controllable experiment size, so further scaling to bulky encoders (e.g., T5Gemma-2-1B/4B) is left for future work.

section: 3.2 Scaled embeddings are hard to generate perfectly
text: However, when we inspect the generated embeddings, we find a failure mode: a generated embedding can be far from every candidate word. We take the candidates of a position from the deployed decoding head in equation 2, since its top- k are the words it would decode to, usually plausible alternatives for this position. To get the embedding of a candidate, we put it at this position of the decoded sequence and encode the sequence again. Embeddings that deviate from their candidates can still be decoded, but often with low confidence or to a wrong word.

section: 3.2 Scaled embeddings are hard to generate perfectly
text: To quantify this, we count how often such embedding errors occur over 64 generated sequences (Fig. 3). We call a generated embedding invalid when no candidate lies within reach. Formally, with \bm{x}_{1},\dots,\bm{x}_{k} the embeddings of the top- k candidates, \hat{\bm{x}} is invalid iff \min_{i}\|\hat{\bm{x}}-\bm{x}_{i}\|>0.91\,\mathrm{nn}, where nn is the median nearest-neighbor distance between real embeddings; we also flag positions with top-1 below 0.6 as uncertain. Both thresholds (0.91 -nn, 0.6) are derived from real text references, where the top-1 decoded probabilities from real embeddings are \geq 0.98, and the nearest neighbor distance is 1 nn by definition. So an embedding within 0.91 nn of a candidate is closer than the nn distance between real embeddings, and a top-1 below 0.6 means the decoder does not produce a clear majority word. The exact threshold is not critical, as long as it divides the teacher’s bimodal distances. On average, a generated sequence of 1024 tokens has 142 uncertain positions, and 109 of them are invalid. For each uncertain position, we collect the distance from the generated embedding to its nearest candidate and the decoder’s top-1 probability, and Fig. 4 further shows one generated sequence in 2D.

section: 3.2 Scaled embeddings are hard to generate perfectly
text: We analyze at NFE 32 for Sec. 3.2 and Sec. 4.2, as it is where the failure is most obvious. Our distillation is designed to fix this failure, and it also improves the generation at every NFE we test, from 64 to 512 in Sec. 5.

section: 3.2 Scaled embeddings are hard to generate perfectly
text: Previous works have studied such embedding errors as interpolation effects (Chen, 2026; Ashiq et al., 2026; He et al., 2026) or mode-averaging (Aithal et al., 2024), and a common finding is that discrete and separated targets are hard for continuous diffusion to generate (Shabalin et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). We reiterate here that (ideally) sampling is guided by the optimal denoiser Equation 1, which is a weighted mean of candidate embeddings. If candidates are separated, the mean falls between them and provides an ambiguous direction, and an imperfect sampling trajectory can end at an invalid location far from any of them. The decoder is then forced to predict with such embeddings, causing errors in the final generation.

(3) Distilling with soft labels makes the embeddings easier to generate. A student that learns the teacher’s decoded probabilities can place the plausible words closer to each other; the diffusion then lands on concrete words more often and generates better.

Why do T5Gemma-2 embeddings have the aforementioned separation problem? We relate it to how T5Gemma-2 is trained. As an encoder-decoder model, it mostly predicts and reconstructs its input as one-hot labels. This maximizes the likelihood of the input token against every alternative, pushing its embeddings away from semantically similar candidates that could fill its place (Wu & Papyan, 2024). This helps with learning rich and distinctive representations (Yu et al., 2020), but hinders similar embeddings from forming a region and leads to invalid embeddings, as a trade-off between discrimination and generation.

Therefore, we distill the T5Gemma-2 encoder into a student encoder that learns the teacher decoder’s probabilities as soft labels (Fig. 5). The soft labels spread over the plausible candidates of a position, so the student places these candidates closer (Hinton et al., 2015; Müller et al., 2019). For a training sequence \bm{s}\in\mathcal{V}^{L}, we minimize \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}}(\theta)=\sum_{j=1}^{L}\mathrm{KL}\big(p^{\mathrm{T}}_{j}\,\|\,p^{\mathrm{S}}_{j}\big),\quad p^{\mathrm{T}}=\text{Dec}^{\mathrm{T}}(\text{Enc}^{\mathrm{T}}(\bm{s})),\quad p^{\mathrm{S}}=\text{Dec}^{\mathrm{T}}(\text{Enc}^{\mathrm{S}}_{\theta}(\bm{s})) where p^{\mathrm{T}}_{j} and p^{\mathrm{S}}_{j} are the frozen teacher decoder’s distributions at position j. We distill on the full OWT, initialize the student with 9 evenly spaced layers from the teacher’s 18 layers (Sanh et al., 2019), and keep the top- 256 candidates of the 262 k vocabulary with renormalized probabilities; see App. B.2.

For the objective, replacing the KL on soft labels with CE on the one-hot input or MSE on the teacher’s embeddings leads to students that never reach real-text entropy 5.43 (CE \leq 4.18, MSE \leq 5.26, see Fig. 10 in Appendix). For the layer choice, we find that students initialized from the full 18 layers to the 9 we use consistently match or outperform the teacher, so the improvement is not due to reduced capacity. A randomly initialized student cannot converge. See App. A.3 for details.

Though we only distill on OWT, the student does not collapse to it. It is still able to encode and decode other text sources, e.g., WikiText (Merity et al., 2016), as shown in App. A.4. As expected, the distillation costs some discriminative power and degrades downstream classification performance (89.4 to 78.1 on SST-2 (Wang et al., 2018)), but it increases the diffusibility as we show in the following section.

section: 4.2 Distilled embeddings are easier to generate
text: To verify that the distilled student is more diffusible, we compare the embeddings generated by ELF-B trained on the teacher and student embeddings in Fig. 6. By inspecting the generated samples at NFE 32, we find that the teacher sample contains more invalid and uncertain embeddings than the student, along with more grammatical mistakes.

section: 4.2 Distilled embeddings are easier to generate
text: We also test the denoising behavior of the diffusion trained on T5Gemma-2 vs. the student embeddings via round-trip denoising (Meng et al., 2021), as in Fig. 7. Given the same sentence and the same added noise, we see that the teacher has a much larger embedding error after denoising and changes the sentence, while the student returns valid embeddings closer to the original sentence, with meaningful fluctuations.

We evaluate the diffusibility of our embeddings by training the same ELF-B and ELF-M models on OWT-1024 (the full OWT partitioned into 1024-token sequences) and on LM1B (Chelba et al., 2013) (128-token sequences). For each embedding+diffusion, we sweep the self-conditioning scale and NFE, re-tokenize the samples with the GPT-2 tokenizer and report the best Gen. PPL under GPT-2-Large at or above real-text entropy, and the mean and std are calculated over 3\times 1024 samples from 3 seeds.

We compare our performance against previous state-of-the-art continuous DLMs. We include GPT-2-S/M as AR baselines, and also Duo (Sahoo et al., 2025) as a uniform-state discrete DLM representative. We find that ELF models trained on the T5Gemma-2 embeddings are already competitive, and our distilled embeddings further improve over the teacher, outperforming previous methods on Gen. PPL at real-text entropy. Note that the pretrained encoders have seen far more text than the OWT-trained baselines and the original T5-small, so rows with different encoders are not fully controlled; the controlled comparison in Table 1 is T5Gemma-2 against the student.

We visualize the sampling sweeps in Fig. 8 that lead to Table 1. Across different sampling configurations, the student consistently reaches lower Gen. PPL at higher entropy than the T5Gemma-2 teacher. Notably, T5Gemma-2 collapses at extremely low NFEs such as 16–32, due to under-integration (not shown in Fig. 8), while our distilled embeddings are more stable.

We report the performance on LM1B (128 -token sequences) in Table 2 to show that the improvement is not due to overfitting or familiarity with OWT data, but a better geometry. The distilled student again performs well and surpasses the raw T5Gemma-2 embeddings on PPL. LM1B is a problematic corpus (Pynadath et al., 2026) and serves as a check rather than a comparison, as we can see the re-trained AR model even has a lower PPL than real text.

Scaling the embeddings is cheap for both training and sampling, as decomposed in Table 3. For training, the embeddings are frozen and take up a small part of the FLOPs and latency, and can also be cached; our distilled student halves the encoding cost of T5Gemma-2. For sampling, they affect only the final decoding step by the LM head, which is fast and performed once per sample. This is why LM head parameters are less important and are put in a subscript in Table 1. End-to-end, ELF-M produces a 1024 -token sequence in 1.5 s at NFE 64 and 11.8 s at NFE 512; GPT-2-M takes 10.7 s with 1024 serial steps.

In this paper, we explore scaling the text embeddings that continuous DLMs operate on, and find that scaling improves diffusibility. We further find that scaling itself is not enough, as strong embeddings can be hard for continuous diffusion to generate perfectly. We view diffusibility as generating valid and decodable embeddings from the same DLM, and propose a distillation that further enhances the scaled embeddings. Perhaps counterintuitively, we find that such distillation trades discriminative power of the embeddings for generation, and an embedding space where similar embeddings are more connected is better for diffusion.

Our results serve as a starting point for what this paper leaves open: few/one-step generation (given ELF trained on raw T5Gemma-2 under-integrates at low NFE), practical-scale models for real-world tasks such as QA, and adapting existing AR models directly into embeddings for DLMs (T5Gemma-2 is adapted from Gemma-3 (Team et al., 2025), and one would want to skip that step). In all, our findings suggest that designing a suitable embedding space of DLMs is as important as designing the diffusion, and also provide a promising and reliable way to scale continuous DLMs from their embeddings.

We use fully public corpora (OpenWebText, LM1B, WikiText-103) and models (T5Gemma-2, T5-small, ModernBERT). No human subjects or private data are involved. Our models generate unfiltered web-style text that can be false or biased; we use the samples only for evaluation.

Our continuous DLM code is adapted from the public ELF-pytorch implementation. We change only the embedding model and keep the training and sampling recipe (App. B.1). Distillation details are in App. B.2; App. B.3 gives the evaluation protocol, the sampling grid, and how each table row is chosen. Baselines are re-run with their authors’ code and checkpoints, or cited where no checkpoint is public. Generated samples are in App. C.
