A Strong MoE Is All You Need for Process Supervision. Process reward models (PRMs) provide fine-grained supervision for multi-step reasoning, yet obtaining reliable process labels remains a central bottleneck. Existing approaches typically rely on human annotation, rollout-based estimation, or auxiliary verification. In this work, we explore a different source of process supervision natively exposed by Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models: expert routing. We show that simple routing statistics provide an intrinsic process-confidence signal that is competitive with conventional output-logit confidence. Building on this observation, we construct routing confidence by combining overall routing mass, head routing mass, and within-step routing variation, and introduce RoCo-Rethink, which identifies the least confident reasoning step and selectively regenerates the subsequent trajectory. We further introduce RoCo-PRM, which uses a strong MoE to automatically annotate reasoning trajectories with routing-derived step scores and distills them into a standalone PRM. Across multiple MoE architectures and diverse reasoning tasks, both RoCo-Rethink and RoCo-PRM consistently outperform strong baselines, while RoCo-PRM transfers effectively across both model architectures and tasks. Our findings suggest that expert routing is more than a computational dispatch mechanism: it provides an architecture-native source of process supervision for reasoning.

Large language models (LLMs) have made rapid progress on multi-step reasoning tasks, yet their reasoning trajectories remain highly fallible. A model may proceed correctly for several steps before making an error that propagates through the rest of the solution. This has motivated increasing interest in process supervision, where intermediate reasoning states are evaluated rather than assigning feedback only to the final outcome. Process reward models (PRMs) have consequently become an important component of reasoning verification, test-time search, self-correction, and reinforcement learning (Lightman et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Setlur et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026).

A fundamental challenge is where such process supervision should come from. Existing approaches obtain process supervision from human annotations, rollout-based estimation, automated verification, outcome-derived supervision, or model-internal uncertainty signals (Lightman et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025b; Tan et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025a; Cao et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026a). While recent automated methods substantially reduce dependence on manual annotation, they often require additional evaluation computation, outcome signals, or auxiliary evaluators. Comparatively little attention has been paid to architecture-native computation signals that arise naturally during a single forward pass. This is particularly relevant for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, where routers continuously map hidden representations to sparse expert allocations. These routing decisions are produced intrinsically during ordinary inference, raising the central question of this work:
Can native MoE routing serve as intrinsic process supervision for reasoning?

There are both architectural and empirical reasons to believe that it can. Given a hidden state h_{t}, token prediction and expert routing can be viewed as two distinct projections of the same latent representation: h_{t}\xrightarrow{W_{\mathrm{LM}}}p(v\mid h_{t}),\qquad h_{t}\xrightarrow{W_{\mathrm{router}}}p(e\mid h_{t}). The former reflects uncertainty over what token to generate next, whereas the latter reflects how computation is allocated across experts. Recent work further shows that native MoE routing preserves structured information about latent reasoning states beyond the emitted trace (Chen et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026b). This motivates us to ask whether routing behavior can be compressed into a lightweight process-confidence signal and further converted into reusable process supervision.

We investigate this through routing confidence, which combines three complementary routing statistics at each reasoning step: overall routing mass, head routing mass, and within-step routing variation. Across multiple MoE architectures and reasoning domains, these statistics exhibit systematic relationships with step-level reliability, and routing-based predictors often outperform conventional output-side confidence signals.

Building on this signal, we introduce RoCo (Ro uting Co nfidence), with two instantiations. RoCo-Rethink directly uses routing confidence at test time to identify the least confident reasoning step, preserve the preceding prefix, and regenerate the subsequent trajectory. RoCo-PRM uses a strong MoE teacher to annotate reasoning trajectories with routing-derived step scores and distills them into a standalone PRM that scores reasoning steps without access to routing information.

Empirically, RoCo-Rethink consistently outperforms strong test-time reasoning baselines, while RoCo-PRM consistently surpasses automatic PRM baselines, including when applied to dense target models. Further analyses show that composite routing confidence more reliably identifies revision points with high corrective value and that RoCo-PRM benefits more from stronger routing teachers than from larger PRM backbones.

Our main contributions are fourfold. (1) We introduce a lightweight step-level routing-confidence formulation that combines three complementary statistics from native MoE routing. (2) We develop RoCo-Rethink, which uses routing confidence to identify error-prone reasoning steps and selectively regenerate the subsequent trajectory. (3) We introduce RoCo-PRM, which uses a strong MoE to automatically annotate reasoning trajectories with routing-derived step scores and distills them into a standalone PRM that can guide both MoE and dense target models. (4) RoCo-Rethink outperforms the strongest test-time baseline in all 18 evaluated settings, while RoCo-PRM achieves the best or tied-best performance in all 30 settings.

section: Process Supervision and Process Reward Models
text: Process supervision provides fine-grained feedback on intermediate reasoning steps and has become an important paradigm for improving multi-step reasoning. Early work demonstrates the effectiveness of human-annotated process supervision (Lightman et al., 2024), while subsequent studies construct process supervision automatically through rollouts, outcome-derived signals, automated verification, or model-internal uncertainty (Wang et al., 2024; Setlur et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025b; Yuan et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025a; Tan et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026; Cao et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026a). Many of these approaches nevertheless require additional evaluation computation, outcome information, or auxiliary evaluators. In contrast, we investigate whether process supervision can be derived directly from architecture-native routing dynamics arising during ordinary MoE inference.

section: MoE Routing as a Reasoning-State Signal
text: Mixture-of-Experts models dynamically route tokens to sparse subsets of experts, with prior work largely focusing on routing efficiency, load balancing, and expert specialization (Fedus et al., 2022; Dai et al., 2024; Muennighoff et al., 2025). More recent studies suggest that routing also reflects latent reasoning dynamics. Chen et al. (2026a) show that routing retains information about task context and trajectory state even when emitted tokens are controlled, while Chen et al. (2026b) demonstrate that native routing can recover structured representations of latent reasoning states. Complementary studies further connect routing behavior with reasoning reliability and the consequences of routing interventions (Yoon et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). Building on this emerging view, we ask whether routing information can be compressed into a lightweight step-level confidence signal and further converted into reusable process supervision.

Test-time reasoning methods improve model performance by allocating additional computation to uncertain or difficult parts of a reasoning trajectory. General self-correction frameworks iteratively critique, revise, or regenerate model outputs (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Gou et al., 2024), while more recent work uses localized confidence or process verification to determine when and where additional reasoning is needed (Yao et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026b; Jin et al., 2026). These approaches demonstrate the value of fine-grained reliability signals for adaptive reasoning guidance, but typically rely on output-side confidence or separately trained evaluators. In contrast, RoCo-Rethink derives its guidance signal directly from native MoE routing and uses it to identify low-confidence reasoning steps for targeted regeneration.

section: Understanding MoE Routing as a Process Signal
text: We first examine whether native MoE routing tracks step-level reasoning reliability and provides a competitive alternative to conventional output-side confidence. Based on these observations, we construct a lightweight routing-confidence signal for reasoning guidance and process supervision.

Inspired by the step-confidence decomposition of Yao et al. (2024), we examine three complementary dimensions of routing behavior: overall routing mass (M), head routing mass (H), and within-step routing variation (D).

For token t at MoE layer \ell, let r_{t,\ell}=\sum_{e\in\mathrm{TopK}_{t,\ell}}p_{t,\ell}(e) denote the routing probability mass assigned to the selected top- k experts. To account for scale differences across layers, we min–max normalize r_{t,\ell} within each MoE layer over the current reasoning trajectory and then average across the L MoE layers, yielding a token-level routing signal r_{t}.

For reasoning step s_{i} with token set \mathcal{T}_{i} and head-token subset \mathcal{H}_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{i}, we define M_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{i}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{i}}r_{t},\qquad H_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{H}_{i}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{H}_{i}}r_{t},\qquad D_{i}=\operatorname{Std}_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{i}}(r_{t}). Thus, M_{i} captures the overall routing mass of the step, H_{i} emphasizes routing behavior near the beginning of the step, and D_{i} measures within-step routing variation.

We first ask whether these routing statistics systematically track intermediate reasoning quality. Using within-trajectory Spearman correlation, we compare their relative ordering with scores from external process verifiers across three MoE architectures and multiple reasoning domains. For mathematical tasks, we use two independently trained math PRMs as references (Zhang et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2024); for MMLU and code reasoning, we use VersaPRM and CodePRM, respectively (Zeng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). As shown in Figure 1 (a), higher M and H are associated with higher step quality in nearly all settings, whereas greater D exhibits the opposite relationship. The same directional pattern persists across independent verifiers and reasoning domains, indicating that native routing statistics preserve information about step-level reliability.

We then examine whether this routing information is competitive with conventional output-side confidence. We train lightweight bad-step predictors using either routing features or logit features and evaluate them with grouped cross-validation at the reasoning-trajectory level. Figure 1 (b) shows that routing-based predictors outperform their logit-based counterparts in 13 of 18 model–task–verifier settings. Together, the two analyses show that native routing not only tracks intermediate reasoning quality, but also provides a reliability signal that is often stronger than conventional output-side confidence.

section: From Routing Statistics to Routing Confidence
text: Given that M and H consistently correlate positively with step reliability while D shows the opposite trend, we combine them into a lightweight step-level confidence score. We min–max normalize each statistic across reasoning steps within the current trajectory, yielding \widetilde{M}_{i}, \widetilde{H}_{i}, and \widetilde{D}_{i} for step s_{i}, and define C_{i}=\widetilde{M}_{i}+\widetilde{H}_{i}-\widetilde{D}_{i}.

section: From Routing Statistics to Routing Confidence
text: The signs follow the empirical pattern in Figure 1 (a): greater overall and head routing mass indicate higher reliability, whereas greater within-step routing variation indicates lower reliability. Importantly, routing confidence is computed entirely from quantities already produced during ordinary MoE inference, requiring neither additional rollouts nor an auxiliary verifier.

Building on the routing-confidence signal defined in Section 3.2, we introduce RoCo (Ro uting Co nfidence; Figure 2), a framework that turns native MoE routing into step-level reasoning guidance and process supervision. RoCo has two instantiations: RoCo-Rethink directly uses routing confidence for test-time reasoning guidance, while RoCo-PRM distills routing-derived supervision into a standalone process evaluator.

Given a reasoning trajectory S=(s_{1},s_{2},\ldots,s_{T}) with routing-confidence scores \{C_{i}\}_{i=1}^{T}, RoCo-Rethink selects the least confident reasoning step as i^{*}=\arg\min_{i}C_{i}. Rather than regenerating the entire response, we preserve the reasoning prefix before s_{i^{*}} and regenerate the trajectory from that point onward. Specifically, the model receives the original input together with the preserved prefix (s_{1},\ldots,s_{i^{*}-1}) and generates a new continuation beginning from step s_{i^{*}}. In this way, additional test-time computation is selectively allocated to the portion of the trajectory indicated as least reliable by routing confidence.

The procedure is applied iteratively. After each regeneration, we recompute routing confidence over the updated trajectory and select the currently least confident step for the next rethink round. We terminate when the prediction stabilizes across successive rounds or when a predefined maximum number of rethink rounds is reached. The final output is determined using task-appropriate aggregation or convergence criteria, detailed in Appendix C. In this way, RoCo-Rethink turns native routing information into a direct step-selection signal for targeted reasoning revision without requiring a separately trained process evaluator.

RoCo-PRM uses routing confidence as an automatic source of process supervision. Given a sufficiently capable MoE teacher, we generate reasoning trajectories and assign each intermediate step s_{i} its routing-confidence score C_{i}. This produces automatically labeled training examples of the form (x,s_{\leq i},C_{i}), where x denotes the original problem and s_{\leq i} denotes the reasoning prefix up to step i.

We then train a standalone PRM to predict the routing-derived confidence score from the problem and reasoning prefix. Let f_{\theta}(x,s_{\leq i}) denote the predicted score for step i, and let i_{n} denote the step index associated with the n -th training example. We optimize the PRM by regression toward the routing-derived target: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PRM}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(f_{\theta}\left(x^{(n)},s^{(n)}_{\leq i_{n}}\right)-C_{i_{n}}^{(n)}\right)^{2}. Because routing information is used only by the MoE teacher to construct supervision labels, the resulting PRM need not itself be an MoE and does not require routing access from the target model.

At test time, RoCo-PRM follows the same step-level reasoning-guidance principle as RoCo-Rethink, but replaces direct routing confidence with the learned PRM score. Given a target-model trajectory, the PRM scores each reasoning prefix, the lowest-scoring step is selected as the revision point, and the target model regenerates the subsequent trajectory conditioned on the preserved prefix. This allows the same PRM to guide both MoE and dense target models, converting architecture-native routing information into reusable process supervision that is decoupled from routing access.

Models and Benchmarks. For RoCo-Rethink, we evaluate three MoE models: DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat (Liu et al., 2024, hereafter DeepSeek), OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-SFT (Muennighoff et al., 2025, OLMoE), and Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B-Chat (Qwen Team, 2024, Qwen1.5). Each model derives routing confidence from its native expert-routing behavior for selective reasoning revision. For RoCo-PRM, we evaluate the resulting PRM on these three MoE models and two dense models, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2025, Qwen2.5) and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Dubey et al., 2024, Llama), allowing us to assess whether routing-derived supervision transfers beyond MoE architectures.

We evaluate six benchmarks covering mathematical reasoning, knowledge reasoning, code generation, instruction following, and logical reasoning: GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021b), MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023), and LogicBench (Parmar et al., 2024). For PRM training, supervision data are constructed from training datasets that are disjoint from the corresponding evaluation sets, with dataset-specific sources detailed in Appendix B.

Baselines. For test-time reasoning guidance, we compare RoCo-Rethink with Vanilla decoding, Self-Consistency (Wang et al., 2023), and LECO (Yao et al., 2024). Self-Consistency aggregates multiple sampled reasoning trajectories, while LECO uses generation-logit-based confidence to identify low-confidence steps for selective regeneration. For process supervision, we compare RoCo-PRM with MC-PRM (Wang et al., 2024), which estimates step quality through Monte Carlo rollouts, and CPMI-PRM (Lee et al., 2026a), which derives process rewards from contrastive mutual information between reasoning steps and target answers.

Implementation Details. All experiments are repeated with five random seeds, and we report the mean and standard deviation. For RoCo-Rethink, the initial response is generated greedily and subsequent rethink rounds regenerate from the least confident reasoning step. For RoCo-PRM, we use Qwen3-30B-A3B (Yang et al., 2025) as the routing teacher and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the PRM backbone. At evaluation time, all learned PRMs use the same step-level rethink protocol: the lowest-scoring step is selected as the revision point, and the target model regenerates the suffix from the preserved prefix. Detailed implementation settings are provided in Appendix B.
Table 1 summarizes the main results.

section: RoCo-Rethink consistently improves test-time reasoning guidance.
text: RoCo-Rethink achieves the best performance in all 18 model–task settings across the three MoE models. On average, it improves over the strongest test-time baseline by 1.2, 1.9, and 1.5 points on OLMoE, DeepSeek, and Qwen1.5, respectively. Compared with Vanilla decoding, the corresponding average gains are 4.5, 4.8, and 4.5 points. The improvements span mathematical reasoning, code generation, knowledge reasoning, instruction following, and logical reasoning, showing that routing confidence provides a broadly effective signal for selective reasoning revision.

section: RoCo-PRM provides strong and transferable process supervision.
text: RoCo-PRM achieves the best or tied-best performance in all 30 model–task settings across the five evaluation models, with 29 strict wins and one tie. Compared with the strongest PRM baseline, it improves average performance by 1.7, 1.5, and 1.5 points on OLMoE, DeepSeek, and Qwen1.5, respectively. The gains also transfer to dense models: RoCo-PRM improves over the strongest baseline by 1.4 points on Qwen2.5 and 1.6 points on Llama. These results demonstrate that routing-derived supervision remains effective across both MoE and dense target models.

section: Composite Routing Confidence Enables Better Revision-Point Selection
text: We examine why combining the three routing statistics yields a stronger reasoning-guidance signal. We first ablate the components of routing confidence and then evaluate whether different formulations identify revision points with higher counterfactual corrective value.

Figure 3 compares RoCo-Rethink with variants using only overall routing mass (M), head routing mass (H), or negative routing variation (-D), as well as their partial combination M+H. Random rethink is included as a reference to separate the effect of routing-guided revision from that of additional test-time computation alone.

Across the three MoE models, each individual routing statistic generally improves over random rethink, indicating that all three components provide useful signals for reasoning revision. Combining overall and head routing mass further strengthens performance: M+H outperforms all single-component variants in 17 of 18 model–task settings, suggesting that global routing behavior and early-step routing provide complementary information. Adding negative routing variation yields the complete confidence score M+H-D, which achieves the best performance in 17 of 18 settings.

To understand why the composite score leads to better rethink performance, we construct a Monte Carlo revision oracle on initially incorrect trajectories. For each candidate step i, we preserve the preceding prefix and sample K regenerated suffixes using the same rethink policy. We define V_{i}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{I}[\hat{y}_{i}^{(k)}=y^{\star}],\qquad V^{\star}=\max_{i}V_{i},\qquad R_{g}=V^{\star}-V_{i_{g}}, where V_{i} estimates the corrective value of revising from step i, V^{\star} is the oracle revision value, and R_{g} is the regret of a selector g choosing step i_{g}. Lower regret indicates a higher-value revision point.
We also report oracle hit rate, the fraction of trajectories for which the selector chooses an oracle-optimal step. We evaluate GSM8K, HumanEval, and LogicBench across all three MoE models.

Figure 4 shows a consistent advantage for composite routing confidence. The full M{+}H{-}D selector achieves the lowest oracle regret and the highest oracle hit rate in all nine model–task settings. Averaged across settings, its oracle regret is 0.140, compared with 0.183 for random selection and 0.152 for the partial M{+}H formulation, corresponding to a 23.5\% reduction relative to random selection. Its average oracle hit rate increases from 0.511 under random selection to 0.583, exceeding M{+}H at 0.549. While the strongest individual routing statistic varies across models and tasks, their full combination remains consistently strongest. These results suggest that the gains of composite routing confidence arise from its ability to identify revision points with higher counterfactual corrective value.

section: RoCo-Rethink Uses Test-Time Rethink Budget More Effectively
text: We analyze how effectively different rethink methods convert additional test-time budget into performance gains. We vary the maximum number of rethink rounds from 0 to 3 and report the mean gain over Vanilla on four benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH500, MMLU, and LogicBench. For each model–task pair, we compute the gain relative to Vanilla and average these gains across tasks.

section: RoCo-Rethink Uses Test-Time Rethink Budget More Effectively
text: Figure 5 shows that RoCo-Rethink consistently delivers larger gains than both LECO and random rethink under the same rethink-round budget. On OLMoE, the average gain of RoCo-Rethink increases from 2.9 at one rethink round to 4.7 at three rounds, compared with 1.9 to 3.7 for LECO. On DeepSeek, the corresponding gains are 3.2 to 5.6 for RoCo-Rethink and 1.4 to 3.4 for LECO. On Qwen1.5, RoCo-Rethink improves from 2.5 to 4.4, whereas LECO improves from 1.3 to 2.8. Random rethink yields only small and less stable gains across all models.

section: RoCo-Rethink Uses Test-Time Rethink Budget More Effectively
text: These results show that RoCo-Rethink not only achieves stronger final performance, but also converts additional rethink rounds into performance gains more effectively. Substantial improvements already emerge at low rethink budgets, indicating that routing confidence allocates extra test-time reasoning more effectively than logit-based confidence.

section: RoCo-PRM Is More Sensitive to Teacher Quality than Backbone Scale
text: We next examine whether RoCo-PRM is more strongly affected by the routing teacher or by the capacity of the standalone PRM. We vary the routing teacher while fixing the PRM backbone, and separately vary the PRM backbone while fixing the routing teacher.

section: RoCo-PRM Is More Sensitive to Teacher Quality than Backbone Scale
text: We first fix the PRM backbone to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and compare routing supervision generated by DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat and Qwen3-30B-A3B. Using Qwen3 as the routing teacher yields an average improvement of 2.0 points over DeepSeek across the 30 model–task settings. The gain is consistent across all five target models, ranging from 1.4 to 2.7 points in average score. These results indicate that the quality of routing-derived supervision has a substantial influence on the effectiveness of the resulting process evaluator.

section: RoCo-PRM Is More Sensitive to Teacher Quality than Backbone Scale
text: Setting Avg. Gain DeepSeek teacher 49.5 – Qwen3 teacher 51.5 +2.0 Qwen2.5-1.5B backbone 50.6 – Qwen2.5-7B backbone 51.5 +0.9

section: RoCo-PRM Is More Sensitive to Teacher Quality than Backbone Scale
text: We then fix Qwen3-30B-A3B as the routing teacher and compare Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as PRM backbones. Scaling the backbone from 1.5B to 7B improves the average score by 0.9 points across the same 30 settings, with per-model gains ranging from 0.6 to 1.5 points. Notably, the 1.5B backbone already retains most of the performance achieved by the 7B model. Overall, RoCo-PRM is more sensitive to the quality of routing-derived supervision than to PRM backbone scale, suggesting that improving the routing teacher is more valuable than simply increasing the capacity of the downstream process evaluator.

section: Routing-Derived Process Supervision Transfers Across Tasks
text: Finally, we examine whether RoCo-PRM learns task-specific routing patterns or a more transferable notion of process quality. For each of four evaluation tasks (GSM8K, MATH500, MMLU, and HumanEval), we train a leave-one-task-out RoCo-PRM while excluding task-aligned routing supervision from the corresponding evaluation task. We then use the resulting PRM to guide three target models spanning both MoE and dense architectures.

section: Routing-Derived Process Supervision Transfers Across Tasks
text: Figure 6 shows consistent cross-task transfer. Despite excluding task-aligned routing supervision for the evaluation task, the leave-one-task-out RoCo-PRMs improve performance in all 12 target-model–task settings, with an average gain of 1.98 points. The average gains reach 2.53 points on both MATH500 and GSM8K and 1.97 points on HumanEval. Transfer to MMLU is smaller, with an average gain of 0.87 points, but remains positive across all three target models. These results indicate that routing-derived process supervision captures signals that generalize beyond the task from which the supervision is collected.

We introduced RoCo, a framework that turns native MoE routing into reasoning guidance and automatic process supervision. RoCo-Rethink uses routing confidence for targeted test-time revision, while RoCo-PRM distills routing-derived step scores into a standalone process evaluator that transfers across both MoE and dense models. Extensive experiments show consistent gains over strong test-time and PRM baselines, while further analyses link these gains to better revision-point selection, stronger routing teachers, and cross-task transfer of routing-derived supervision. Overall, our results establish expert routing as a practical, architecture-native source of process supervision and motivate broader exploration of internal computation signals for reasoning and learning.

Precision over Scale: A Polish-Silesian Benchmark and a Translation System Outperforming Open-Source and Commercial Models. Dialectal machine translation remains challenging due to limited data and strong linguistic variation not captured by standard benchmarks, which often assume standardized and well-edited text. We study Polish-Silesian MT using neural and rule-based systems, evaluating on SiLTT - a new Pol-Szl testset, alongside established BOUQuET and FLORES benchmarks. Results show our rule-based system is consistently strongest on SiLTT and BOUQuET datasets and that TranslateGemma fine-tuned on a curated dataset improves over strong neural baselines but does not surpass the rule-based system in dialectal settings. We release SiLTT and our best neural model to support further research.

Silesian (ISO 639-3: szl) is a West Slavic regional language of Poland with limited NLP resources and an ongoing debate about its linguistic status. According to the National Population and Housing Census 2021, 467,145 residents of Poland declared Silesian as a language used in home contacts Statistics Poland (2022). Despite growing interest in low-resource machine translation, Silesian remains largely absent from dedicated MT benchmarks and system comparisons.

A key challenge in developing Silesian language technologies is not only the scarcity of parallel data, but also its uneven quality. While Silesian text is present in online sources, much of it is inconsistent in orthography, heavily influenced by Polish, or shaped by ad-hoc writing conventions rather than stable linguistic norms. As a result, large-scale corpora derived from web data or generic multilingual resources often mix heterogeneous and noisy forms of Silesian, limiting their usefulness for training robust translation systems.

Existing multilingual benchmarks such as FLORES-101/200 Guzmán et al. (2019); Goyal et al. (2022) include Silesian as part of broad evaluation coverage. However, they primarily reflect formal, edited text and do not capture the variability and informal usage found in real-world Polish–Silesian communication. This mismatch becomes more pronounced when models are trained on large but noisy corpora (e.g., OPUS and other web-mined datasets), where Silesian-like data often lacks linguistic consistency and contains substantial cross-lingual contamination.

In this paper, we investigate Polish–Silesian machine translation under realistic, data-constrained conditions. Rather than relying on large, noisy corpora, we construct a compact but curated parallel dataset of approximately 22k sentence pairs designed to better reflect usable Silesian. We compare neural and rule-based with commercial and other state of the art multilingual translation systems.

Our results show that systems trained on large, heterogeneous corpora do not necessarily generalize well to cleaner dialectal evaluation settings. In contrast, our rule-based system remains consistently strong, while neural models trained on the curated dataset outperform strong baselines but still fall short of rule-based performance in dialect-sensitive evaluation.

Our contributions are the following: SiLTT: a new Polish–Silesian translation evaluation dataset; a systematic comparison of neural and rule-based MT systems across three benchmarks; a publicly released evaluation dataset and fine-tuned neural model.

Machine translation for low-resource and dialectal language varieties remains challenging due to limited parallel data and high linguistic variation Haddow et al. (2022); Ranathunga et al. (2023). Recent multilingual systems such as mT5 Xue et al. (2021), NLLB Team et al. (2022), and OPUS-MT Tiedemann et al. (2024) showed that transfer learning and massively multilingual training can improve translation quality for under-resourced languages. Several studies further demonstrated that transfer between related languages is particularly effective in low-resource and zero-shot MT settings Zoph et al. (2016); Dabre et al. (2017); Lakew et al. (2019).

Silesian is included in two multilingual evaluation benchmarks: FLORES-101/200 Guzmán et al. (2019); Goyal et al. (2022) and BOUQuET Team et al. (2025), enabling evaluation of multilingual MT systems on this language. However, FLORES has seen extensive and repeated use in multilingual MT evaluation, which can lead to benchmark saturation effects.

The closest work to ours is Signoroni (2023), who studied zero-shot Silesian–English translation using mT5 and ByT5 models fine-tuned on related Slavic languages. They found that cross-lingual transfer from related languages can improve performance, though the effect depends on model architecture and language similarity. Their evaluation relied on FLORES due to the lack of dedicated resources for Silesian.

Silesian’s orthography was standardized only in 2009 with the ślabikŏrz system, following centuries of ad hoc adaptations of Polish orthography or phonetic scripts Bandtkie (1821); Steuer (1935). Its status as a distinct language or Polish dialect remains debated: some classify it as an Abstand language, isolated from Polish and neighboring dialects Hentschel (2018), while others argue for mutual intelligibility and shared features with Polish dialects Dubisz (2024); Siuciak (2025). Lack of official recognition limits its use in education, and most speakers rely on Polish orthography, reinforced by the absence of default Silesian keyboard support. Silesian exhibits variation across orthography, regional morphology, and lexical borrowings from neighboring languages (Polish, Czech, German). These properties make direct sentence-level translation challenging for purely data-driven systems, especially in low-resource regimes For more details, see the Appendix A.

We implement a rule-based Polish–Silesian translator built on the Apertium platform Forcada et al. (2011); Khanna et al. (2021). The system follows a shallow-transfer architecture and includes: (1) finite-state transducers for lexical transformations, (2) morphological analysis and generation, (3) Hidden Markov Models for POS tagging and ambiguity resolution, and (4) handcrafted transfer rules encoding systematic correspondences.

Our system contains 31,757 lexical translation pairs and 2,349 grammatical rules derived from dictionaries Przywara (1904); Olesch (); Zaręba (1960); Pluta (1973); Cząstka-Szymon et al. (2000), as well as theses and articles on Silesian vocabulary (e.g., Spectator (1908); Nikel (1908); Koszyk (1957); Iżykowska and Starczewska–Wojnar (2017)). We have included a detailed illustrated system pipeline in Appendix B.

To evaluate the performance of various neural machine translation architectures on the Silesian language, we selected a representative suite of models ranging from specialized multilingual systems to large-scale commercial language models (details in Appendix C):

PLLuM-12B-nc-chat: Polish general-purpose LLM Kocoń et al. (2025) Bielik-PL-11B-v3.0-IT: Polish-focused multilingual model with claimed Silesian support Ociepa et al. (2025) NLLB-200-3.3B, NLLB-54B MoE: Silesian-capable MT models Team et al. (2022) MADLAD-400-10B-MT: multilingual MT model based on the T5 architecture Kudugunta et al. (2023) GPT-5.4: frontier zero-shot LLM Singh et al. (2026) Google Translate: a production-grade MT system Wu et al. (2016) TranslateGemma-4B-IT (base, fine-tuned): instruction-tuned and custom finetuned MT variants Finkelstein et al. (2026)

Our Polish-Silesian training data consists of three complementary sources. In particular, we combine manually curated and post-edited data with automatically generated resources obtained via pivoting through English and backtranslation. All data was filtered using a maximum length ratio threshold of 1.3.

22,783 sentences — Custom backtranslated dataset of Silesian sentences (CBT-22k): We used articles provided to us by the websites Wachtyrz.eu and Slazag.pl as well as several older dialect texts, the largest being the collection gathered by Malinowski (1899). The older texts were transliterated to the current alphabet. The Silesian sentences were translated into Polish using the rule-based system described in Section 4.1, and subsequently post-edited by a professional translator to ensure high-quality references. 50,000 sentences — NLLB corpora (pivoting via English): Sampled from the OPUS corpora Tiedemann and Nygaard (2004), specifically the NLLB dataset Schwenk et al. (2020); Fan et al. (2020), which contains approximately 1.7 million English–Silesian pairs. The English side was translated into Polish using a quantized version of EuroLLM-9B-Instruct Martins et al. (2025) model. We decided to sample only 50,000 sentences to avoid overflowing our custom high-quality dataset (CBT-22k). 28,107 sentences — HPLT backtranslation Extracted from the monolingual Silesian HPLT v3.0 corpus Oepen et al. (2026). Silesian sentences were translated into Polish using the NLLB-3.3B model to obtain a back-translated dataset.
We use three evaluation datasets:

BOUQuET: Team et al. (2025) a multilingual, multicentric benchmark consisting of 854 Polish–Silesian sentence pairs translated by community contributors. We additionally conducted a manual evaluation with native Silesian and Polish speaker to verify overall quality of the translations.

SiLTT (Si lesian L iterary T ranslation T estset): 1,237 Polish–Silesian sentence pairs derived from human translations and automatically aligned using LaBSE Feng et al. (2022). The dataset was compiled from literary and cultural corpora, including “ Cinderella ”, “ Rapunzel ”, “ Janko the Musician ” and “ A Christmas Carol ”. We applied automatic alignment filtering based on cosine similarity of sentence embeddings, retaining only pairs with similarity above 0.6. Sentence pairs below this threshold were excluded from the final dataset. Dataset statistics are shown at Table 1. The resulting test set is released under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license.
FLORES-200: Guzmán et al. (2019) A multilingual evaluation benchmark consisting of 1,012 high-quality sentence pairs for each language pair.

We primarily focus on the Polish-to-Silesian translation direction, as it represents the more challenging task. Compared to Silesian, Polish is a high-resource language, making text generation substantially easier for modern models.

We fine-tuned the 4-billion-parameter instruction-tuned version of TranslateGemma using QLoRA Dettmers et al. (2023). We performed two fine-tuning experiments with different training data configurations: (1) using only the custom dataset of Silesian sentences (CBT-22k), and (2) using all corpora described in Section 5.1. This setup was motivated by concerns, based on manual inspection, that the Silesian side of the NLLB- and HPLT-derived data may contain noise and low-quality texts. Due to the low-resource nature of Silesian, reliable automatic filtering methods are not available.

We use sacreBLEU Post (2018) to calculate the BLEU Papineni et al. (2002) and chrF Popović (2015) scores. We do not use neural-based evaluation metrics such as COMET Rei et al. (2020) or LLM-as-a-Judge approaches, as the low-resource setting may lead to unreliable and potentially misleading results in this context.

The evaluation results on SiLTT, the BOUQuET POL \rightarrow SZL task, and FLORES are presented in Tables 2 and 3, while results for the reverse direction (SZL \rightarrow POL) are provided in Appendix D.

The rule-based system achieves the best results on SiLTT and BOUQuET, maintaining a clear advantage on both benchmarks, while remaining competitive with the strongest systems on FLORES. The base TranslateGemma model performs poorly on all evaluation sets, indicating limited zero-shot capability for this low-resource language pair. However, fine-tuning on the CBT-22k corpus yields substantial improvements, producing the strongest neural system and surpassing both GPT-5.4 and Google Translate. These results highlight the importance of high-quality parallel data for effective adaptation in low-resource MT. In contrast, augmenting the training data with additional NLLB and HPLT corpora consistently degrades performance compared to the CBT-22k-only setup, likely due to noise.

The Polish models Bielik and PLLuM also achieve relatively weak results across all evaluation settings. Although Bielik was pretrained on Silesian text, its performance remains limited, only slightly better than that of the base TranslateGemma model. PLLuM performs poorly, failing to generate usable translations. Overall, strong Polish language ability or incidental exposure to Silesian is insufficient for effective Polish–Silesian MT without dedicated bilingual supervision.

As shown in Table 3, Google Translate achieves the best performance on the FLORES benchmark. This unusually strong performance may indicate that the model was exposed to FLORES sentences during training, particularly given that the benchmark has been publicly available for a long time. However, this advantage does not transfer to the SiLTT and BOUQuET datasets.

We conduct an qualitative analysis of selected best models on the BOUQuET dataset (see Table 4). Key observation: explicit linguistic rules provide robustness in low-resource dialect translation. The rule-based system provides the best results in the context of closely related languages. Its weaknesses usually have their origins in homographs. This could be remedied by creating more rules but we have not estimated neither the count of the remaining homographs, nor the time needed to create rules for them. Google Translate seems to create plausible but hallucinated phrases. Many mistakes made by that tool stem from its translating through English. The resulting text often has pronouns usually redundant in Slavic languages. At the same time the lack of person markers in English verbs leads to incorrect verb forms in output sentences. Fine-tuned TransGemma high-quality CBT-22k dataset provides promising results despite minor mistakes. The frequency of its hallucinations is low. Mistakes are usually made by keeping original words in the output text.

All systems lack the ability to rephrase sentences to a more probable word order and style, eg. "Rzeczy, kere chcioł bych wiedzieć wczaśnij" seen in the last example in the Table 4 is a grammatically correct sentence, however "Rzeczy, co bych je chcioł wiedzieć wczaśnij" would be a more often used one in live speech.

We presented a new benchmark and evaluation of Polish–Silesian machine translation systems. Our findings suggest that rule-based systems remain highly competitive in dialectal and low-resource settings, particularly when evaluated on newer datasets. We open-source the SiLTT testset and the best performing neural model.

This study is limited by the size and scope of the available evaluation and training data. Although the CBT-22k corpus is carefully curated, it remains relatively small compared to large-scale multilingual MT datasets, which may constrain the generalization of the neural models.

Our evaluation focuses on Polish–Silesian translation and three benchmark datasets; while these cover both curated and existing benchmark settings, they do not fully capture the breadth of real-world Silesian usage across domains, speakers, and registers. In particular, spoken language and highly informal communication styles are underrepresented.

The rule-based system relies on manually designed correspondences and linguistic assumptions, which may not scale to broader coverage or other dialectal language pairs without significant adaptation effort. While it performs strongly in the evaluated setting, its portability and maintenance cost remain open questions.

Residual Advantage: Student-Relative Teacher Guidance for RL with Verifiable Rewards. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and on-policy distillation (OPD) have become two main paradigms for post-training reasoning models. RLVR gives each response a single outcome label, leaving the steps inside it without separate credit. OPD provides token-level guidance at student-visited prefixes, but its pointwise signal does not directly reflect the pattern of teacher--student disagreement across the vocabulary. Dense, unbounded log-ratio supervision can amplify the teacher's influence, yet a strong solver is not necessarily a suitable guide when the student's solution paths depart from the teacher's. We propose Residual Advantage (\RA{}), which treats the teacher--student probability residual as a bounded one-step reward, subtracts the corresponding state value under the student policy to form a standard advantage, and centers the result within each response before adding it to the verifier advantage. The guidance term has zero mean within each response, so the verifier advantage remains the response's mean label and the teacher only redistributes credit among the steps within it. \CoRA{} further updates a teacher LoRA with verifier advantages on the same scored student batch and uses the updated teacher in the next iteration's residual, adapting guidance to the student's attempts.

With Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base students and a Qwen3-8B teacher, \RA{} combined with GRPO or REINFORCE++ improves the underlying sequence-advantage algorithm in all 24 comparisons on three mathematical benchmarks, raising macro Avg@8 by 1.7--3.6 points and Pass@8 by 3.9--6.3 points. Both combinations surpass teacher-only OPD, and \CoRA{} adds a further 1.0--1.5 Avg@8 points.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains a language model on its own sampled solutions, scored by a checker of the final answer (Shao et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025). GRPO and REINFORCE++ turn this terminal reward into one advantage per response (Shao et al., 2024; Hu, 2025), so every step receives the same label even when the response mixes useful and mistaken steps. Learning is also confined to the successful paths the student can sample, and under practical budgets much of the gain reflects sharpening of what the model can already do (Yue et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025).

On-policy distillation (OPD) instead supplies a teacher’s next-token distribution at every prefix the student visits (Agarwal et al., 2024; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Its label, the log ratio \log(q(a)/p(a)) or one coordinate of a top- k or full-vocabulary divergence, says how far apart teacher and student are at that token but does not directly reflect where the teacher’s extra mass sits; a full-vocabulary objective sees this only implicitly, through the softmax coupling of the coordinates. The log-ratio label is moreover unbounded, growing as \log(1/q(a)) at a token the teacher assigns little probability, so on such tokens the teacher’s signal can become disproportionately strong. At the same time, a strong solver is not necessarily a good teacher for the current student, least of all on prefixes where the student has left the teacher’s solution paths (Li et al., 2025; Tiapkin et al., 2025). The question is how teacher guidance should enter RLVR so that the student draws on the teacher’s knowledge while the response-level label stays tied to outcome feedback and room for exploration remains.

To this end, we propose Residual Advantage (RA). RA treats the probability difference d=q-p as a bounded one-step reward. At each visited prefix it subtracts the reward’s expectation under the student’s own policy, that is, the policy’s value under this reward, A^{d}(a)=d(a)-\langle p,d\rangle=\mathbb{E}_{v\sim p}\big[(q(a)-q(v))-(p(a)-p(v))\big], This design reflects how the teacher’s disagreement with the student is distributed. It asks whether, relative to the student, the teacher favors the sampled token over the other candidates the student would consider, each weighted by the student’s probability of choosing it. Even with the same residual at the sampled token, teachers that distribute the rest of the vocabulary differently can therefore give local advantages of opposite signs (Appendix A.4). RA then centers the local advantages within the response and adds them to the verifier advantage, A_{t}=A^{V}+\lambda(A_{t}^{d}-\overline{A}^{d}), where \overline{A}^{d} is the response mean and \lambda the guidance weight. This gives the guidance term zero mean within every response, so the verifier advantage remains the response’s mean label and the teacher only redistributes credit among the steps within it. The guidance is thus student-relative twice over, as an advantage under the student’s own next-token distribution and as a deviation within the student’s own response.

The appeal of the construction is that it is both elegant and natural. The local advantage is a single inner product, A^{d}(a)=\langle e_{a}-p,\,q-p\rangle, and three properties follow from it. It is the rate at which the squared distance \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert p-q\rVert_{2}^{2} falls when the student moves probability toward a. Its expected update at a prefix is the exact logit gradient of that distance, so the student’s own probability of a token scales how strongly the teacher can move it. And it is bounded by the student–teacher distance times the probability the student leaves to other tokens, so guidance fades on its own as the two converge. Scaled in this way by the student’s own probability, it also stays small wherever the student is already sure, so the teacher mainly adjusts the choices the student is still weighing instead of imposing its preference on those the student has settled, and it does not inflate small disagreements into large labels. The construction requires no schedule, threshold, or learned component.

Co- RA extends the construction to a teacher that learns from the student’s attempts. Each iteration scores a student batch, fixes its labels, and updates a teacher LoRA with the base estimator’s verifier advantages while the student receives the guided label, much as actor and critic share a rollout batch in PPO (Schulman et al., 2017). The updated teacher supplies the distribution in the next iteration’s residual, with the same advantage construction and weight as RA. Training on the student’s own rollouts with the verifier’s advantages lets the teacher adapt to the reasoning along the student’s solution paths, with the aim of reducing the bias a frozen teacher carries on trajectories it would not have generated itself. Across two students, two estimators, and three mathematical benchmarks, RA improves all 24 three-seed benchmark means of its base estimator, both combinations surpass teacher-only OPD, and Co- RA raises accuracy further with mixed changes in coverage.

A student p_{\theta} generates a response a_{i,1:L_{i}} to prompt x_{i}. At the visited prefix \xi_{it}=(x_{i},a_{i,<t}), let p_{it} be the rollout student’s next-token distribution and q_{it} the teacher’s distribution at the same prefix over the same aligned vocabulary. We write \langle p,f\rangle=\sum_{v}p(v)f(v), let e_{a} be the one-hot vector of token a, and drop the index i when a single response is meant. The base estimator converts a terminal verifier reward into one advantage A_{i}^{V} per response, by GRPO’s within-group normalization (Shao et al., 2024) or by REINFORCE++’s batch statistics (Hu, 2025), and the actor maximizes the clipped PPO surrogate (Schulman et al., 2017) with importance ratio \pi_{\theta}(a\mid\xi)/p(a\mid\xi), the actor’s own ratio, distinct from the teacher–student ratio q/p. RA changes only the per-token label that enters this surrogate. Every teacher-derived quantity is computed at the rollout policy and held fixed, so no gradient flows through it.

At prefix s, we define the one-step reward of token v as the teacher–student probability residual, R_{s}(v)=d_{s}(v)=q(v\mid s)-p(v\mid s). Under the student policy, the state value of this reward is V_{d}^{p}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{v\sim p}R_{s}(v)=\langle p_{s},d_{s}\rangle, its action value is the immediate reward Q_{d}(s,a)=d_{s}(a), and the token advantage is \boxed{\,A_{s}^{d}(a)=Q_{d}(s,a)-V_{d}^{p}(s)=d_{s}(a)-\langle p_{s},d_{s}\rangle=\langle e_{a}-p_{s},\,d_{s}\rangle.\,} The reward is immediate, so nothing is propagated to earlier positions; credit across positions comes from the verifier advantage. Subtracting V_{d}^{p} is the REINFORCE baseline for this reward, computed exactly (Williams, 1992; Sutton et al., 2000; Foerster et al., 2018), and we call it the student value baseline. The gap d_{s}(a) at the sampled token alone does not determine the sign (Appendix A.4).

At a fixed prefix, whose index we drop, let L(p,q)=\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert p-q\rVert_{2}^{2}, let p=\operatorname{softmax}(z), and let \psi_{a}=e_{a}-p=\nabla_{z}\log p(a) be the score of token a in logit coordinates. (i) A^{d}(a)=\langle\psi_{a},d\rangle is the first-order decrease of L along the feasible move p\mapsto(1-\eta)p+\eta e_{a}; the exact change is -\eta A^{d}(a)+\tfrac{\eta^{2}}{2}\lVert\psi_{a}\rVert_{2}^{2}. (ii) \mathbb{E}_{a\sim p}\psi_{a}=0 and \mathbb{E}_{a\sim p}\psi_{a}\psi_{a}^{\top}=J_{p}=\operatorname{Diag}(p)-pp^{\top}, the Jacobian of the softmax. Hence, with d held fixed, \mathbb{E}_{a\sim p}A^{d}(a)=0 and \mathbb{E}_{a\sim p}\big[A^{d}(a)\,\psi_{a}\big]=J_{p}d=-\nabla_{z}L(p,q),\qquad-\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_{b}}=p(b)\,A^{d}(b). (iii) |A^{d}(a)|\leq\lVert\psi_{a}\rVert_{2}\lVert d\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{2}\,(1-p(a))\lVert d\rVert_{2}, and -\tfrac{1}{2}\leq A^{d}(a)\leq 2.

Part (i) says what the local advantage measures. Part (ii) says what it does on average. The update descends the squared distance to the teacher, and logit b moves by p(b)A^{d}(b), so the student’s own probability of a token scales how far the teacher can move it. Since \mathbb{E}_{a\sim p}\psi_{a}=0, the student value baseline is applied automatically in expectation at a single prefix; its role appears only when local advantages are compared across prefixes (Appendix A.7). Part (iii) is where the residual parts from the log ratio, which estimates reverse-KL descent without bias but has no bound. The residual’s bound gives the guidance bounds of Section 2.2.

Separating the sampled token makes this scaling explicit, A^{d}(a)=\big(1-p(a)\big)\Big[d(a)-\mathbb{E}_{v\sim p(\cdot\mid v\neq a)}d(v)\Big], the teacher’s preference for a over the student’s other choices, weighted by the probability the student still gives them. The local advantage vanishes on a token the student has settled, whatever the teacher says, and by part (ii) logit b moves in expectation by p(b)(1-p(b)) times a bounded contrast, so the teacher acts most where the student is undecided. None of this is imposed by hand. The relative comparison, the confidence scaling, the zero mean, and the bound are all read off one inner product.

Let c_{t}\geq 0 be the actor’s relative weights on the response’s positions, summing to one (c_{t}=1/M for token-mean reduction over M positions), and let \overline{A}^{d}=\sum_{t}c_{t}A_{t}^{d} be the response mean of the local advantages. RA adds the centered local advantage, scaled by the guidance weight \lambda, to the verifier advantage, \boxed{\,\delta_{t}=\lambda\,(A_{t}^{d}-\overline{A}^{d}),\qquad A_{t}=A^{V}+\delta_{t},\qquad\lambda\geq 0.\,} For every response, \sum_{t}c_{t}A_{t}=A^{V},\qquad\delta_{t}-\delta_{u}=\lambda\,(A_{t}^{d}-A_{u}^{d}), so the verifier advantage is exactly the response’s mean label and every difference between two decisions is preserved. Under the weighted inner product \langle u,v\rangle_{c}=\sum_{t}c_{t}u_{t}v_{t}, the constant verifier label and the centered guidance term are orthogonal, and the label splits as \lVert\mathbf{A}\rVert_{2,c}^{2}=(A^{V})^{2}+\lambda^{2}\operatorname{Var}_{t\sim c}(A_{t}^{d}). The verifier decides how good the response is as a whole, and the teacher decides how that credit is shared among its steps. This division concerns the label. Multiplied by different score vectors, a zero-mean guidance term need not give a gradient orthogonal to the verifier’s, and on a single token it can outweigh it (Appendices A.3 and A.7). Centering is the orthogonal projection onto zero-mean labels. Without it, a nonzero response mean in the teacher label would be indistinguishable from a change of A^{V}, since both multiply the same mean score direction \sum_{t}c_{t}\psi_{t}.

section: Bounded by the distance, fading on its own.
text: By Proposition 1 (iii), |\delta_{t}|\leq\tfrac{5}{2}\lambda(1-c_{t}),\qquad\sum_{t}c_{t}|\delta_{t}|\leq\lVert\delta\rVert_{2,c}\leq\sqrt{2}\lambda\Big(\sum_{t}c_{t}\lVert p_{t}-q_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}\Big)^{1/2}. The first bound limits each guidance term. The second bounds the guidance amplitude by the student–teacher distance on the visited prefixes (Appendix A.6), so teacher guidance fades as the two converge, at a fixed weight and without a schedule; Appendix C.1 shows the mean absolute guidance declining over a training run. The log ratio also vanishes at exact agreement but admits no such bound, since it diverges at a token of vanishing student probability while \lVert p-q\rVert_{2}\to 0.

section: Co- RA teaches the teacher on the student’s attempts
text: Co- RA follows a score-then-update cycle. In every iteration the student generates a batch, the verifier scores it, and the current student and teacher produce the actor labels. These labels are fixed before the student and a LoRA adapter q_{\phi} (Hu et al., 2022) on the frozen teacher q_{0} are updated on the same batch. Both updates use the run’s own GRPO or REINFORCE++ advantages, the adapter receiving A_{i}^{V} and the student the combined label, so the teacher is adapted at the prefixes this student visits according to how its continuations turned out. The aim is for the teacher to become familiar with the reasoning along the student’s solution paths and to take in the verifier’s signal there, reducing its bias on the student’s trajectories so that its guidance becomes more accurate for this student. With batch token-mean reduction (Appendix B.8), the adapter’s gradient at the start of each update is \left.\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{J}_{T}\right|_{\phi_{k}}=\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{i}A_{i}^{V}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{i}}\left.\nabla_{\phi}\log q_{\phi,it}(a_{it})\right|_{\phi_{k}},\qquad Z=\sum_{i}|\mathcal{T}_{i}|, where \mathcal{T}_{i} is the set of token positions of response i. This is the base estimator’s clipped update applied to the teacher LoRA on student-generated data.

section: Co- RA teaches the teacher on the student’s attempts
text: At iteration k the adapted teacher q_{\phi_{k}} supplies the residual d_{t}^{(k)}=q_{\phi_{k},t}-p_{k,t} against the rollout student p_{k}, and the student uses the same construction and weight \lambda=10 as RA, A_{t}^{\text{Co-{RA}}}=A^{V}+\lambda\bigl(A_{t}^{d,(k)}-\overline{A}^{d,(k)}\bigr),\qquad A_{t}^{d,(k)}=d_{t}^{(k)}(a_{t})-\langle p_{k,t},d_{t}^{(k)}\rangle, where \overline{A}^{d,(k)}=\sum_{t}c_{t}A_{t}^{d,(k)}. After the updates, q_{\phi_{k+1}} supplies the residual in the next iteration. The adapter starts at zero, so the first student update coincides with RA. At each scored batch the response-mean identity and the distance bound hold with the current teacher q_{\phi_{k}} (Appendix A.9).

Students are Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base; the teacher is the post-trained Qwen3-8B model in non-thinking mode, which shares their vocabulary (Yang et al., 2025). Training uses DAPO-Math-17K (Yu et al., 2025) for two epochs with 128 prompts per rollout batch, eight responses per prompt for GRPO runs and one for OPD and REINFORCE++ runs, temperature 1.0, and a 12,000-token cap. Verifier runs reward answer correctness, linearly discounted for correct responses beyond 8,000 tokens (Appendix B.3), and RA is added to the base estimator at the reference weight \lambda=10, chosen on a validation split of training prompts (Appendix B.5). Teacher-only OPD minimizes the reverse KL divergence \operatorname{KL}(p_{t}\|q_{t}) over the full vocabulary at every visited prefix (Agarwal et al., 2024; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), the same teacher information RA uses. Evaluation samples eight completions per problem at temperature 0.8 with the same cap on MATH-500 (Lightman et al., 2024), AIME24, and AIME25 and reports Avg@8 and Pass@8 (Table 1) from unshaped answer correctness; macro scores weight the three benchmarks equally. Each RA run adds one teacher forward pass per rollout, and Co- RA also trains the adapter (Appendix B.8).

Table 1 contains 24 comparisons of RA with its base estimator (two students, two estimators, three benchmarks, two metrics), and RA improves all 24 three-seed means. The macro gains are 1.74 – 3.58 Avg@8 and 3.89 – 6.33 Pass@8 points (Table 10).

The gains are larger for REINFORCE++, narrowing its macro Avg@8 deficit to GRPO at both sizes. GRPO keeps the higher completion accuracy after guidance, but REINFORCE++ with RA has the higher macro Pass@8 at both sizes, a trade between accuracy and coverage that a single score would hide.

section: Verifier plus teacher improves on teacher-only distillation.
text: Both RA combinations exceed teacher-only OPD in macro Avg@8 and Pass@8 at both sizes, by 1.80 – 2.96 and 2.73 – 3.90 points (Table 10). The one exception is AIME25 Avg@8 at 1.7B, where OPD’s 5.97 exceeds the 5.00 of RA +REINFORCE++, although both RA runs have the higher Pass@8 there. In training, OPD also starts more slowly than REINFORCE++ and stays below RA +REINFORCE++ over most of the shared budget (Appendix C). At the same budget, OPD followed by REINFORCE++ reaches 28.39 and REINFORCE++ with an added reverse-KL loss 26.14, both below RA +REINFORCE++ (Appendix D.5), and sampling the log ratio at the generated token, with the same expected update at each prefix, drops OPD to 24.80 at 1.7B, below verifier-only training (Appendix D.6).

section: Teaching the teacher on student rollouts raises accuracy in every tested setting.
text: Co- RA adds 1.03 – 1.45 macro Avg@8 points to the four RA runs, and Avg@8 rises in all twelve benchmark means. Coverage changes are mixed: Pass@8 rises in four benchmark means, is unchanged in two, and falls in six (Table 10). Co- RA +GRPO is the most accurate run for both students. Yet each adapted teacher scores 0.8 – 2.3 macro Avg@8 and 0.7 – 3.5 Pass@8 points below the frozen teacher (Appendix D.9), while the students it guides improve: it is a better guide, not a better solver.

section: The margin over the untrained student persists up to Pass@512.
text: From K=8 to K=512 for the 1.7B REINFORCE++ runs (Appendix D.7), the macro margin of RA over the untrained student grows from 13.4 to 16.9 points, and its margins over REINFORCE++ and OPD from 5.8 to 10.4 and from 3.9 to 6.8, while that of verifier-only training narrows from 7.6 to 6.6, as Yue et al. (2025) report for RLVR. Within the tested budget RA thus raises the coverage the student can reach.

We remove the student value baseline and response centering in turn on Qwen3-1.7B-Base with REINFORCE++ at the unchanged weight \lambda=10 and compare every control with full RA. Since removing either operation also changes the guidance amplitude, every control is also run at weights 5 and 20 (Table 2, Appendix D.4), so that no conclusion rests on a single amplitude.

Removing the student value baseline lowers both macro scores, by 2.09 Avg@8 and 3.58 Pass@8 points at the reference weight and similarly at weights 5 and 20 (Table 2). The label then carries the sampled residual d_{t}(a_{t}), which still contains the state value \langle p_{t},d_{t}\rangle. This value is fixed before the token is chosen, so it rewards whatever token is sampled at a prefix where the teacher concentrates on the student’s likely tokens, and response centering then spreads this prefix-level effect over the other positions (Proposition 4). Removing both operations costs 1.73 Avg@8 and 2.77 Pass@8 points; the state value then also enters the response mean, shifting it by -0.32 on average and beyond 0.5 on a quarter of the offline responses (Table 16).

Restoring response centering at the same weight adds 0.54 Avg@8 and 0.46 Pass@8 points, a smaller gain that holds at all three weights (Table 2). Without centering, the response’s mean label is A^{V}+\lambda\overline{A}^{d}. On the 256 offline responses of Appendix C.2, the local advantages average to 3\times 10^{-4} per token, so the student value baseline leaves no systematic part, and on responses longer than 1{,}000 tokens the shift has an SD below 0.03, where centering changes almost nothing (Proposition 4). On shorter responses, where few tokens set the average, the SD is 0.32, and 8\% of all responses carry a shift beyond 0.5, the scale of a verifier advantage (Table 16). Without centering these responses receive a response-level label the verifier did not assign, which can even reverse the sign of the verifier’s judgment; centering removes this shift deterministically for every response (Equation 6), so the response-level label no longer depends on how the guidance happens to average along a response. Across seeds, full RA also varies less than the uncentered control in macro Avg@8 at every weight (Table 23).

All tested weights improve both macro scores over verifier-only training (Table 2). Halving the reference weight lowers both means; doubling it leaves them nearly unchanged (29.29 vs. 29.25 Avg@8) but widens the seed SD from 0.25 to 1.68, as in every variant (Table 23).

Table 3 replaces the residual by the log ratio at the sampled token, raw or with both operations. The raw log ratio helps only at small weights, peaking at \beta=0.2, and falls below verifier-only training from \beta=1.2 on; its conditional mean at a prefix is -\operatorname{KL}(p_{t}\|q_{t}) (Appendix A.7), so it shifts the mean label in proportion to \beta. With both operations, clipped to [-5,5] or not, the log ratio stays above verifier-only training at every swept weight, and the probability residual is better still, by 1.21 Avg@8 and 1.70 Pass@8 points over the best log variant.

A full-vocabulary squared-distance loss, whose gradient at each visited prefix equals the expected update of the uncentered residual label (Appendix A.2), beats verifier-only training but stays below RA and the uncentered control at every weight (Table 2). The gap lies not in the expected teacher gradient, which the sampled label matches (cosine 0.99 with its analytic value), but in how the update is shared with the verifier (Appendix C.3). Because RA ’s teacher term acts on the tokens the verifier scores, 64\% of its gradient mass raises correct or lowers incorrect responses, against 49\% for the direct loss, and after clipping and Adam the teacher takes 0.28 of the update against 0.44, keeping RA ’s update closer to the verifier’s direction (cosine 0.93 against 0.80).

By Equation 4 and Proposition 1 (ii), the teacher moves logit b in expectation by p(b)(1-p(b)) times a bounded contrast. The student-centered log ratio factorizes the same way, but its contrast is unbounded in both directions (Appendix A.3). Table 15 (Appendix C.2) describes the start of training, bucketing the tokens of 256 offline responses of the untrained 1.7B student by the student’s probability of the sampled token. Confident tokens, with p(a_{t})\geq 0.9, are 61% of all tokens and receive under 1% of either label, as the factor 1-p(a) predicts. The residual puts 59% of its guidance on the 12% of tokens with 0.1\leq p(a_{t})<0.5, five times their share, where the student is choosing among live alternatives. The centered log ratio puts 50% of its total on the 4% of tokens the teacher assigns less than 10^{-4}, where its label diverges. The residual thus weights the forks of the student’s own reasoning, consistent with the finding that a few high-entropy tokens carry most of the useful RL signal (Wang et al., 2025), whereas the log ratio puts it on tokens that one side considers nearly impossible.

section: More guidance is not always better
text: RA assigns the teacher a restrained role. It labels only the tokens the student samples, so where the teacher clearly disagrees, its preferred token receives no supervision of its own unless the student samples it. A natural alternative is denser, more direct supervision that prescribes the student’s actions rather than only evaluating them; we examine it through a minimal extension of the sampled route, a teacher-peak branch. At each position where the teacher’s top token v_{t}^{\star}=\arg\max_{v}q_{t}(v) differs from the student’s top token and from the sampled token, which may itself be the student’s top token, the branch adds v_{t}^{\star} as a pseudo-sample. The added token receives the label a sampled token there would receive, with the verifier part clipped at zero, \big([A^{V}]_{+}+\lambda(h_{t}(v_{t}^{\star})-\bar{h})\big)\log\pi_{\theta}(v_{t}^{\star}), where h_{t}(v)=A_{t}^{d}(v) and \bar{h} is the response mean of the sampled route. The sampled route and its centering are unchanged; the branch supervises the teacher’s top token as if the student had also sampled it, and its verifier part can only raise a response’s total label (Appendix A.8).

section: More guidance is not always better
text: Since the value of additional guidance may depend on the training objective, we add the same branch to three base methods. Sampled OPD (Appendix D.6) learns from the teacher alone; there the added token receives the sampled-OPD label \log q_{t}(v_{t}^{\star})-\log p_{t}(v_{t}^{\star}), which makes sampled OPD a top- k variant. REINFORCE++ learns from the verifier alone, so the branch is its only source of teacher signal. RA +REINFORCE++ already receives a teacher label at every sampled token.

section: More guidance is not always better
text: Under sampled OPD (Table 4) the branch raises macro Avg@8 from 24.80 to 25.10 and the Avg@8 of every seed. Under REINFORCE++, where \lambda scales only the branch, it lowers macro Avg@8 by 0.38 – 1.76 points and Pass@8 by 0.46 – 2.11 points, a loss that grows with the branch weight. Added to RA, it lowers macro Avg@8 by 2.05 – 2.16 points and Pass@8 by 3.41 – 3.91 points, and at every weight each seed falls below the same seed of RA, whereas doubling RA ’s own weight does not (Table 2).

section: More guidance is not always better
text: Because the branch alters several factors at once, it does not isolate a mechanism, and we do not pursue one here. It does answer the question it was designed for: stronger and denser teacher supervision does not by itself yield better performance. A student trained only to imitate the teacher benefits slightly from the teacher’s top token, whereas both students trained with the verifier degrade, increasingly so with the branch weight under REINFORCE++. One conjecture is that steering the student directly toward the teacher’s choice crowds out the exploration on which RL relies. RA instead scales its expected update on each token by the student’s probability of that token and leaves the choice to the student’s interaction with the verifier; amplifying this gated signal is harmless. This restraint may be part of what makes its guidance effective, and it leaves an open question for RLVR: how a dense, critic-like signal such as a teacher’s should be shaped and enter RL training.

section: Distilling on the student’s own samples.
text: GKD studies divergence choices on student-generated sequences (Agarwal et al., 2024), MiniLLM optimizes reverse KL with log-ratio returns (Gu et al., 2024), sampled OPD uses the log ratio at the generated token as a dense reward (Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), and OPD+ derives divergence-dependent corrections (Zhao et al., 2026). RA replaces the log ratio by the bounded residual, judges the chosen token against the student’s own alternatives, and removes the teacher’s response mean. What distinguishes RA is its restraint: the teacher acts not as a distillation target, as in these works, but as a critic-like signal within RL.

LUFFY mixes off-policy teacher traces into RLVR (Yan et al., 2025). OPDVR gates the sampled log ratio so that token reward signs agree with the verifier (Lin et al., 2026), whereas RA keeps the verifier advantage as the response mean and allows local sign changes. Li et al. (2026a) favor OPD followed by RL over joint combinations; at our matched budget both schedules stay below RA (Appendix D.5).

A state-value baseline leaves the expected policy gradient unchanged (Williams, 1992; Sutton et al., 2000), and the variance-optimal baseline also accounts for the score norm (Greensmith et al., 2004). GRPO, REINFORCE++, RLOO, and ReMax use group, batch, leave-one-out, and greedy baselines (Shao et al., 2024; Hu, 2025; Ahmadian et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024), and COMA marginalizes an action under the policy (Foerster et al., 2018); RA uses an exact policy expectation as the baseline of its local reward. Process supervision uses finer labels (Lightman et al., 2024), VinePPO extra sampling (Kazemnejad et al., 2025), and implicit PRMs and PRIME the log ratio of an outcome-trained model to a reference (Yuan et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2025). VPD refines a feedback-conditioned teacher with outcome supervision and distills it on student rollouts (Li et al., 2026b); Co- RA instead trains a teacher LoRA with the base estimator’s clipped update on the same scored student batch.

Residual Advantage judges the teacher–student probability difference against the student’s own alternatives and centers it within each response, so the verifier sets a response’s mean label and the teacher allocates credit among its steps. The guidance term decreases both as the student approaches the teacher and as the student becomes confident in its own choice, an elegant property that helps RA preserve exploration in RL. Across two students, two estimators, and three benchmarks, RA improves every matched three-seed mean, both combinations surpass teacher-only OPD, and Co- RA improves accuracy further while its adapted teacher becomes a worse solver than the frozen one. Up to Pass@512 the margin of RA over the untrained student grows while that of verifier-only training narrows. Removing either baseline, replacing the residual by the log ratio, or adding direct supervision of the teacher’s top token lowers performance.
