System One models Are Not Better Rerankers. System One models, or decision models, answer a question about an input with a calibrated probability instead of generated text. Within weeks of the first release, in September 2026, they were used as rerankers. We test whether the decision fine-tuning behind them makes a better reranker than plain reranker fine-tuning of the same model. For six Qwen backbones from 0.6B to 27B parameters and ten TREC DL and BEIR collections, we compare the untuned model, asked zero-shot, with its decision fine-tunes and its reranker fine-tunes, two of which we train ourselves. In our work, we draw the conclusion that decision fine-tuning never makes the better reranker. From 0.6B to 9B, reranker fine-tuning wins on every backbone by 5 to 29 points nDCG@10, also on zero-shot collections, and at 27B the two tie. Up to 9B, decision fine-tuning adds nothing over simply asking the untuned model. Moreover, we find that the calibration advantage of decision models depends on the question. Asked whether a passage answers the query, they are better calibrated than the published reranker fine-tunes from 4B on. Asked a slightly different question from prior work, they lose this advantage.
Lastly, calibration does not make up for a worse ranking: up to 9B, a reranker fine-tune keeps the better passages at a fixed threshold. If you need a reranker, fine-tune a reranker.

Cross-encoders are a well-established way to rerank the candidates of a first-stage retriever (Nogueira and Cho, 2019; Nogueira et al., 2020), and open large language models fine-tuned for ranking are the current state of the art (Ma et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhang, 2026). System One models, which we call decision models, promise something else. They answer a question about an input with a calibrated probability instead of generated text. The name refers to fast, intuitive thinking, Kahneman’s “System 1” (Kahneman, 2011; TypeSafe AI, 2026). TypeSafe AI released the first of them, Jev, on 15 September 2026, trained with an unpublished method called RLCD (reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions) (TypeSafe AI, 2026). Within weeks, Jev was reported to be a competitive reranker (S1Rank, 2026; jev-rerank, 2026) and was evaluated or integrated in retrieval systems (Elastic Search Labs, 2026; LanceDB, 2026; Vectorize, 2026). Open decision models followed: Kev (Palmer, 2026b) and Cloudflare’s Clef (Cloudflare, 2026). They are fine-tuned from Qwen backbones, the same backbones that dedicated rerankers such as Qwen3-Reranker (Zhang et al., 2025) and Prism (Zhang, 2026) are built on.

This makes a clean test possible, and the reports so far have not run it. They compare Jev with rerankers built on other, mostly smaller models, so they cannot tell how much of its effectiveness comes from decision fine-tuning and how much from the underlying language model. We therefore compare decision fine-tuning with plain reranker fine-tuning of the same backbone. Calibration needs a test of its own. A ranking uses only the order of the scores, so a model can rank well with badly calibrated probabilities, and the other way round. Calibration matters when a score is read on an absolute scale: to decide how many passages to pass on to a language model, to drop passages that do not answer the query, or to estimate how many relevant passages there are. We therefore also test whether the advertised calibration holds for relevance and whether it helps in such use cases:
\rq@badge 1RQ1 Do decision models rerank better than the untuned model or a reranker fine-tune of the same backbone?
\rq@badge 2RQ2 Are their relevance probabilities better calibrated than those of the untuned model and the reranker fine-tune, and is that calibration of any use?

Figure 1 shows how a decision model reranks and what we compare. For six Qwen backbones from 0.6B to 27B parameters, we evaluate the untuned model, asked zero-shot, its decision fine-tunes (Kev and Clef) and its reranker fine-tunes, including two we train ourselves on MS MARCO alone (at 9B as a control, at 27B where none has been released). All of them rerank the same BM25 candidates of TREC DL 2019–2023 and five BEIR collections, and all return a probability of relevance per passage. Decision and untuned models are asked whether the passage answers the query. For comparison, we repeat all their runs with the looser question of S1Rank (S1Rank, 2026), an earlier report on Jev as a reranker. We find: Reranker fine-tuning beats decision fine-tuning. From 0.6B to 9B, the reranker fine-tune ranks better on every backbone, by 5 to 29 points nDCG@10. The difference is significant on 48 of the 60 pairs of reranker fine-tune and collection, never significantly in favour of the decision fine-tune, and it holds on collections that no fine-tune was trained on. At 27B, the two tie. On no backbone does decision fine-tuning make the better reranker.

Up to 9B, decision fine-tuning adds nothing over the untuned model. It stays within -2.5 and +0.7 points of simply asking the untuned model the same question, while reranker fine-tuning adds 6 to 30 points. The calibration advantage depends on the question. Asked whether a passage answers the query, decision models from 4B on are better calibrated than the published reranker fine-tunes. Asked S1Rank’s question, they lose this advantage while their ranking hardly moves, and the untuned models gain as much from the wording. Calibration also does not make up for a worse ranking: up to 9B, a reranker fine-tune keeps the better passages at a fixed threshold. Our position is straightforward and runs counter to the recent trend: System One models are not better rerankers.

Neural rerankers are trained to score query–passage pairs from relevance labels, first with encoder or sequence-to-sequence models (Nogueira and Cho, 2019; Nogueira et al., 2020) and more recently with open large language models (Ma et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhang, 2026). Qwen3-Reranker and Prism read relevance from the probability of “yes” against “no” after a prompt that asks whether the document meets the query, which makes their output directly comparable to that of a decision model. Other approaches rerank the candidates jointly, either by generating a ranked list (Sun et al., 2023; Pradeep et al., 2023) or by letting passages attend to each other, as in the Set-Encoder (Schlatt et al., 2025). Large language models can also rank without any reranking-specific fine-tuning, through relevance prompting (Qin et al., 2024; Zhuang et al., 2024), but their effectiveness is sensitive to how the prompt is worded (Sun et al., 2025). Abdallah et al. (Abdallah et al., 2025) compare many of these rerankers on the candidates we use.

Besides Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026), Kev (Palmer, 2026b; Palmer, 2026a), Clef (Cloudflare, 2026) and Laya (ConvAI Innovations, 2026) are open decision models. The evidence on decision models for retrieval is so far limited to reports that are not peer-reviewed: Jev reranking BM25 candidates (S1Rank, 2026; jev-rerank, 2026; LanceDB, 2026), as a reranker in production search (Elastic Search Labs, 2026; Vectorize, 2026), and the open Laya as a relevance gate before recall (ConvAI Innovations, 2026; smriti, 2026). These reports compare Jev with existing rerankers, which are built on other models. None compares decision fine-tuning with reranker fine-tuning of the same backbone, and none asks whether the calibration of the probabilities pays off.

Neural networks tend to be overconfident, and temperature scaling after training is a simple remedy (Guo et al., 2017). Neural rankers are no exception (Penha and Hauff, 2021). Common ranking losses are invariant to shifting the scores of a query, so rankers trained with them can order passages well without being calibrated (Penha and Hauff, 2021; Yan et al., 2022); scores can be calibrated during or after training (Guo et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2025). Calibrated probabilities matter wherever a score is read on an absolute scale, for example to cut off a ranked list (Bahri et al., 2020). This is the use we test in RQ2.

A decision model takes an input, the state, together with one or more questions about it, and returns a probability for each possible answer. We use binary questions only, so every question yields one number, the probability of “yes”. Reranking follows directly: for a query q with candidates d_{1},\dots,d_{k} from a first-stage retriever, we ask about each passage d_{i} whether it answers q and order the passages by the returned probabilities p_{i}.

For the state, we consider two modes, the same as S1Rank (S1Rank, 2026). In isolated mode, the state holds the query and a single passage, so that p_{i}=P(\textit{yes}\mid q,d_{i}), as in a cross-encoder. In joint mode, the state holds the query and all k candidates in first-stage order, and the k questions are asked about this one state, so that p_{i}=P(\textit{yes}\mid q,d_{1},\dots,d_{k}) can depend on the other candidates. Joint mode sees the same input as a listwise reranker such as RankGPT, but it returns a score per passage instead of an order, like the Set-Encoder (Schlatt et al., 2025). In both modes the model scores each passage on its own scale, so both are pointwise rerankers.

A backbone is one pretrained Qwen model of a given size. For every backbone we compare three variants, all of which return a probability of relevance per query and passage: The untuned model is the released chat model of the backbone, not fine-tuned by anyone for ranking or for decisions. We ask it the decision models’ question in its chat format and take p_{i} as the probability of “yes” as its first answer token. A decision fine-tune (Kev, Clef) is the backbone fine-tuned to act as a decision model. A reranker fine-tune (Qwen3-Reranker, Prism, ours) is the backbone fine-tuned on relevance labels. It keeps its own prompt with q and d_{i} and gives p_{i} as the probability of “yes” against “no”. We can therefore rank by p_{i} (RQ1) and read it on an absolute scale (RQ2) for every variant. Decision models are all models of this kind, including Jev (closed) and Laya, which we report for context only.

We study six Qwen backbones: Qwen3-0.6B and 8B, Qwen3.5-0.8B, 4B and 9B, and Qwen3.8-27B, each in the three variants of Sect. 3 (Figure 1). The untuned model is asked with thinking off. The decision fine-tunes are Kev (Palmer, 2026b; Palmer, 2026a) on every backbone, Clef-Flash on the 9B and Clef on the 27B backbone (Cloudflare, 2026), each run in isolated and in joint mode. Kev up to 9B is a LoRA fine-tune of the pretrained checkpoint; Kev-27B is a full fine-tune of the released chat model. The decision fine-tunes are trained to give Jev’s kind of output; they are not reproductions of RLCD, which is unpublished (Palmer, 2026a). The reranker fine-tunes are Qwen3-Reranker (Zhang et al., 2025) (0.6B, 8B), built on the same pretrained checkpoints as Kev, and Prism (Zhang, 2026) (0.8B, 4B, 9B).

No reranker fine-tune of Qwen3.8-27B has been released, so we train one ourselves (Ours-27B), from exactly the checkpoint that Kev-27B and Clef start from. As a control, we train a second one with the same recipe on Qwen3.5-9B (Ours-9B), where it can be compared with Prism-9B. The recipe is public and deliberately plain: LoRA (r=32) in Qwen3-Reranker’s prompt format, one epoch over 100k MS MARCO training queries (Nguyen et al., 2016), each with one relevant passage and 15 hard negatives (eight from a dense retriever, seven from BM25), and a ranking loss (InfoNCE over the group) plus a yes/no classification loss (binary cross-entropy of every passage’s score). The second term gives the model a meaningful P(\textit{yes}). We removed training queries that match a test or development topic and chose the checkpoint on 200 MS MARCO dev queries by a rule fixed in advance. No decision data and no hyperparameter search are involved. Qwen3-Reranker, Prism and our fine-tunes saw MS MARCO in training; Kev’s training data contain neither MS MARCO nor BEIR (Palmer, 2026a).

Every decision and untuned model is asked one question per passage: “Does document {doc} answer the query?” It matches the relevance labels we evaluate against (on TREC DL, a passage counts as relevant if it answers the query, from grade 2). We fixed this question before running the experiments, but did not choose it on development data, and we report every result with it. The only other wording we ran is the question of S1Rank (S1Rank, 2026): “Is document {doc} relevant to the query? Relevant means it answers the query or contains information that directly addresses it.” Section 6 compares the two. Reranker fine-tunes ask no question of this kind; they keep their own prompt.

We use TREC DL 2019–2023 (Craswell et al., 2020; Craswell et al., 2021b; Craswell et al., 2021a; Craswell et al., 2022; Craswell et al., 2023) on the MS MARCO v1 and v2 passages (Nguyen et al., 2016) and five BEIR collections (Thakur et al., 2021): TREC-COVID, NFCorpus, SciFact, Touché and DBPedia. None of the fine-tunes was trained on TREC-COVID, Touché or DBPedia, which form the zero-shot subset (ZS). Every system reranks the BM25 top-100 of Pyserini (Lin et al., 2021); these are the candidates of S1Rank (S1Rank, 2026) and of earlier comparisons (Sun et al., 2023; Pradeep et al., 2023; Abdallah et al., 2025), whose published numbers we use where we did not rerun a system.

For context, we report BM25, Jev 1.13.0 (closed, in both modes), Laya (ConvAI Innovations, 2026) (isolated only, as its context is too short for a joint state), monoT5-3B (Nogueira et al., 2020), bge-reranker-v2-m3 (Chen et al., 2024), the Set-Encoder (Schlatt et al., 2025), RankZephyr (Pradeep et al., 2023) (run by us on TREC DL) and RankGPT-4 (Sun et al., 2023) (published numbers only).

We measure nDCG@10 and test differences with paired t -tests over queries, Holm-corrected across the ten collections (p<0.05). Per backbone, we test three differences: the reranker fine-tune against the strongest decision fine-tune (the decision fine-tune and mode with the best average), that decision fine-tune against the untuned model, and joint against isolated mode.

We compute the expected calibration error (ECE, 15 equal-width bins) (Guo et al., 2017) and the Brier score (the mean squared error of the probability against the binary label, which also rewards separating relevant from non-relevant passages) on the judged query–passage pairs of TREC DL 2019–2023, the only collections that also judge many non-relevant passages; a passage counts as relevant from grade 2. We test two uses of the probabilities. The fixed cutoff keeps every candidate with p\geq 0.5; we report the F_{1} of this set (unjudged passages count as non-relevant) and its size. Its regret is what a better threshold would gain: the F_{1} at the best threshold of each collection, chosen afterwards, minus the F_{1} at 0.5. The count test adds up a query’s probabilities over its judged passages. If the probabilities are calibrated, this sum estimates how many of the passages are relevant. We report the mean absolute error of this estimate, in passages. As a reference, always guessing the median number of relevant passages of the collection is off by 8.6 passages.
Reranker fine-tunes are also calibrated after the fact, with temperature and Platt scaling of their logit fitted on 1,000 MS MARCO dev queries, never on a test collection.

Our BM25, monoT5-3B and RankZephyr runs reproduce published numbers (Pyserini, 2026; Abdallah et al., 2025) within 0.2 points nDCG@10. Jev in joint mode, asked S1Rank’s question, reproduces S1Rank’s numbers (S1Rank, 2026) within 0.5 points on four of five collections (1.5 below on TREC-COVID).

On every backbone from 0.6B to 9B, the reranker fine-tune ranks better than the decision fine-tune in either mode (Table 1). Averaged over the ten collections, its margin over the better decision mode ranges from 5.2 points nDCG@10 at Qwen3.5-9B (Prism-9B 59.0 vs. Clef-Flash 53.8) to 28.8 points at Qwen3-0.6B (56.1 vs. 27.3). The difference is significant on 48 of the 60 pairs of reranker fine-tune and collection, and the decision fine-tune is never significantly better (∗). The margin does not come from training on MS MARCO: on the zero-shot subset, which no fine-tune was trained on, it ranges from 5.4 to 23.9 points. Nor does it come from the undisclosed recipes of the published rerankers: Ours-9B, trained on MS MARCO alone with standard losses, matches Prism-9B (59.4 vs. 59.0 on average, 56.1 vs. 53.7 on the zero-shot subset). At 27B, the two kinds of fine-tuning tie. Our reranker fine-tune of the checkpoint that Kev-27B starts from reaches 59.6 against Kev-27B’s 60.1, and 54.9 against 55.0 on the zero-shot subset; they differ significantly on one collection only, DBPedia, where ours is better. On no backbone does decision fine-tuning make the better reranker.

section: Up to 9B, decision fine-tuning adds nothing over the untuned model.
text: Up to 9B, the better mode of a decision fine-tune stays within -2.5 and +0.7 points of its untuned model, asked the same question, with significant gains on at most three of ten collections (†). Reranker fine-tuning of the same backbones adds 5.9 (Prism-9B) to 29.5 points (Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B). A user who takes the released Qwen3.5-4B or Qwen3.5-9B and asks it whether a passage answers the query gets the same ranking as from the decision fine-tunes built on it, at no training cost. At 27B, both kinds of fine-tuning add about the same to the untuned model (56.4): Kev-27B 3.7 points, significantly on eight collections, and our reranker fine-tune 3.2. Clef, the other 27B decision fine-tune, adds nothing (54.8 joint, 53.9 isolated).

Table 2 places the triplets among other rerankers on the same candidates. Jev (59.1) ranks as well as the reranker fine-tunes of 8B and 9B (59.0 to 59.4) and the Set-Encoder (59.0). The open Kev-27B (60.1) matches the closed model it imitates, and so does our 27B reranker fine-tune (59.6). A fine-tune of a strong open backbone reaches Jev, with or without decision data. Laya (43.5) does not improve on its BM25 candidates (43.2).

section: Joint scoring helps only the largest models.
text: Scoring all candidates in one state gains about one point for Kev-27B (60.1 vs. 59.0) and Clef (54.8 vs. 53.9), but costs Kev-0.6B 12.2 points and Kev-8B 13.0 (‡; significant on all ten and on five collections). A likely reason is the length of the state. A joint state of 100 passages has about 13k tokens on TREC DL and 40k or more on BEIR, whereas the model cards of the small Kevs report training states of at most 7,552 tokens (Kev-0.8B and Kev-4B), and that of Kev-27B states of up to 32,768 (Palmer, 2026a).

section: RQ2: Are Decision Models Better Calibrated?
text: Calibration is the main promise of decision models. Table 3 reports it on the judged pairs of TREC DL 2019–2023, together with the two uses we test. Table 4 repeats every run of a decision or untuned model with S1Rank’s question.

section: Asked our question, decision models are well calibrated.
text: The untuned models of 0.6B and 0.8B parameters say “yes” to almost everything (ECE 0.750 and 0.617); from 4B on, they are reasonably calibrated already (0.117 to 0.231). Decision fine-tuning improves on the untuned model on every backbone, for example from 0.231 to 0.113 on Qwen3-8B. From 4B on, the decision fine-tunes are also better calibrated than the published reranker fine-tunes (Kev-8B 0.113 vs. Qwen3-Reranker-8B 0.257); on the two smallest backbones they are not. The best calibrated systems in the study are Jev (0.075) and Kev-27B (0.076). Decision fine-tuning is not the only way there: our 9B reranker fine-tune, trained with a plain yes/no loss, is as well calibrated as Clef-Flash (0.111 vs. 0.112). Our 27B reranker fine-tune is less well calibrated than Kev-27B (0.110).

section: The advantage depends on the question.
text: S1Rank’s question asks whether the passage is relevant and defines relevance more loosely: the passage “answers the query or contains information that directly addresses it”. Both wordings are reasonable, and S1Rank’s is the one under which Jev was first shown to be a good reranker. The ranking hardly moves between the two: the mean nDCG@10 of the decision fine-tunes changes by -2.5 to +2.6 points, and with S1Rank’s question, too, the best decision fine-tune of every backbone up to 9B is 4 points or more behind the reranker fine-tune. The answer to RQ1 does not depend on the wording. Calibration moves a lot. With S1Rank’s question, almost every model is worse calibrated, often by a factor of two or three (Jev joint: ECE 0.224 instead of 0.075). The decision fine-tunes are then at best as well calibrated as the best reranker fine-tune of their backbone (Kev-8B 0.243 vs. Qwen3-Reranker-8B 0.257, Kev-27B 0.156 vs. Ours-27B 0.110). One sentence of the prompt decides whether decision models are better calibrated than reranker fine-tunes.

section: The advantage depends on the question.
text: The untuned models gain as much from our wording as the decision fine-tunes (Qwen3-8B: 0.383 with S1Rank’s question, 0.231 with ours). A question that matches the definition of relevance in the labels makes the probabilities better calibrated, with or without decision fine-tuning. The user of a decision model has to put that definition into words, and a small change in the words changes the calibration severalfold. A reranker fine-tune has no such knob: its notion of relevance is fixed by its training labels.

section: Calibration does not make up for a worse ranking.
text: If every passage with p\geq 0.5 is kept, a reranker fine-tune keeps the better set on every backbone up to 9B (e.g. F_{1} @.5 of 51.0 for Prism-4B vs. 42.6 for Kev-4B), although it is the worse calibrated model on most of them. The threshold is not the problem: for the decision models, 0.5 is close to the best threshold of each collection (regret of 0.9 to 3.1 points). A well-placed threshold on a worse ranking still yields the worse set. Where the rankings are equally good, calibration does pay off: at 27B, the better calibrated Kev-27B keeps the better set (57.2 vs. 48.3), while our fine-tune is underconfident and keeps only 7.9 passages per query.

A ranking cannot tell how many passages are relevant; the sum of calibrated probabilities can. Asked our question, most decision models from 4B on count better than the median guess (8.6 passages off) and better than the published reranker fine-tunes of their backbone (Kev-8B 7.6 vs. Qwen3-Reranker-8B 12.9). Decision fine-tuning is not what makes this work: the untuned Qwen3.8-27B counts most accurately of all (5.8), and Ours-9B counts better than Clef-Flash (7.3 vs. 8.1). With S1Rank’s question, no decision model beats the median guess by more than a fraction of a passage (best: Clef joint, 8.4).

Rerankers can also be calibrated after training. Temperature scaling fitted on MS MARCO dev lowers the ECE of the worst calibrated rerankers (Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B from 0.511 to 0.326) and changes the others little. Platt scaling backfires at the fixed cutoff (F_{1} @.5 of 8.1 or less): MS MARCO dev has about one relevant passage per query, so the fitted probabilities are far too low for TREC DL, where queries have many more. A calibration holds only for the notion of relevance and the base rate it was fitted on (Sect. 7).

section: Why decision fine-tuning does not make a reranker.
text: A reranker fine-tune is trained on the very task it is tested on: telling relevant from non-relevant passages of a query, with a ranking loss over hard negatives. The decision fine-tunes we tested learned to answer many kinds of questions about many kinds of states, and Kev’s training data contain no MS MARCO and no BEIR (Palmer, 2026a). That general skill transfers to relevance about as well as the untuned model’s own instruction following, which is what we observe up to 9B. The zero-shot subset shows that the gap is not about having seen the test domain: it persists on collections that neither kind of fine-tune was trained on.

Kev-27B is the only decision fine-tune that adds to its untuned model. It differs from the smaller Kevs in more than size: it is a full fine-tune of the released chat model, whereas the smaller Kevs are LoRA fine-tunes of pretrained checkpoints, and it was trained on longer states (Sect. 5). We cannot tell which of these matters. Size alone is not enough: Clef, a decision fine-tune of the same 27B model, adds nothing. Reranker fine-tuning also adds less at 27B than on the smaller backbones, because the untuned 27B model already ranks well.

A probability of relevance is calibrated only with respect to a definition of relevance and its base rate. Our results show three ways to move it: the wording of the question, the labels of the training data (our reranker fine-tunes) and the labels a scaling is fitted on (Platt scaling on MS MARCO dev, Sect. 6). A model that is “calibrated out of the box” is calibrated against a notion of relevance that someone chose, and the user of a decision model has to put that notion into words. For ranking none of this matters; for a threshold or a count it matters a lot.

We compare released models, and the fine-tunes of a backbone differ in their training data as well as in their objective. Our results therefore describe decision fine-tuning as it is available today, not RLCD as such, which is unpublished and may be done better. The controlled comparison rests on our own reranker fine-tunes at 9B and 27B, which were trained once, with one recipe and without any hyperparameter search. We measured calibration only on TREC DL, where non-relevant passages are judged, and at a single relevance grade and a single threshold. Our question was fixed before the runs but not chosen on development data, and we tried only one other wording. All decision models are at most a month old, and newer versions may change the picture; we release all raw outputs so that the comparison can be repeated.

System One models are not better rerankers. On the same backbone, decision fine-tuning never makes the better reranker: plain reranker fine-tuning wins by 5 to 29 points nDCG@10 from 0.6B to 9B, and the two tie at 27B. Up to 9B, decision fine-tuning adds nothing over simply asking the untuned model. The calibration advantage of decision models depends on the question. A question that matches the relevance labels makes decision and untuned models alike much better calibrated; with a looser one, decision models lose their advantage over reranker fine-tunes. Up to 9B, calibration also does not make up for a worse ranking when passages are kept at a fixed threshold. If you need a reranker, fine-tune a reranker.

Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox. Personal email agents decide, for every message, what it is, whether it is urgent, whether to draft a reply, create a task, or ignore it. Their error rate is rarely measured: the stored labels were written by the system itself. We present Foyer, a self-hosted personal inbox agent in daily use, and a measurement protocol (stratified sampling, frozen snapshots, thread-grouped splits, pre-registered hypotheses, human labels in the agent's review loop) that yields ground truth before any training. On 739 real Italian/English emails labelled by the owner (231 unbiased, 500 adversarially sampled), we compare nine systems under thread-grouped cross-validation: the production keyword rules, a TF-IDF + logistic-regression baseline, local typed decision models (Tev1, Nimble), a hosted decision model (Nimble v4-max), and hosted generative LLMs (Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma 4 26B/31B). Four results. The production rules score 28% on message type against a 58% majority class: the field shown most prominently carried no information.

With ~200 labels, logistic regression has the highest accuracy on every field (type 0.79, urgency 0.74, needs-reply 0.83, is-noise 0.90), though it never predicts the two rarest classes and is statistically tied with Gemma 4 on type; few-shot prompting does not close the gap. The sender's relationship (client, supplier, service) is recovered from other emails of the same contact with 98.6% accuracy where the contact has been seen, and is not inferable from a single message by any model: it belongs in the contact graph, not the prompt. Finally, accuracy is not the product metric: composed into actions, the most accurate system most often ignores emails needing action (18% vs 4% for the best LLM); a cost-chosen threshold on its noise probability halves that rate and makes it the cheapest system.

A growing share of what personal AI agents do is not generation but decision: which project does this email belong to, is it urgent, does it need a reply, is it noise. Generative LLMs answer these questions by producing text that is then parsed; typed decision models, introduced with TypeSafe’s Jev in September 2026 and followed within weeks by open models (Nimble, Tev1, Clef, Strands Decider) and a local endpoint in Ollama, answer them directly with a probability distribution over caller-defined options, in one forward pass and without free text.

Whether this new class of models is good enough to replace the generative step in a personal agent is an empirical question, and it cannot be answered with the data such agents typically keep: the stored labels are the model’s own output. Early evidence is mixed. Classical classifiers trained on a few thousand records outperform Jev on network-traffic classification; a community benchmark reports a plain 9B instruct model ahead of every decision model on triage tasks; the vendor’s own benchmark places the open models within three points of Jev. None of it concerns personal, multilingual correspondence.

This paper makes three contributions. A measurement protocol for a production email agent that yields human ground truth without changing the system: stratified sampling by predicted class, a frozen snapshot of the exact model input, deterministic splits keyed on record ids, and labelling in the agent’s own interface. A comparison of nine systems on that ground truth—production rules, a classical baseline, local and hosted typed decision models, hosted generative LLMs—on message type, urgency, three agent switches (draft a reply, create a task, ignore) and project assignment, with calibration, latency and cost. A decomposition of the agent’s labels into what is learnable from the text of one message (type, urgency, the three switches) and what is not (the sender’s relationship to the owner), with a measured alternative for the latter: inheritance from the contact graph.

Jev defined the interface: a state, a set of typed questions (choice, yes/no, score), and a distribution per question. Open models followed: Bespoke Nimble 9B, fine-tuned from Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA on answer tokens only and released with its contrastively curated data and recipe —its held-out comparison places the untuned 9B base at 66% against 90% for Nimble and 93% for Jev, and its evaluation notes insist that models be compared only on the same examples under the same procedure, which we adopt; Together’s Tev1 4B/0.8B, Cloudflare’s Clef, Amazon’s Strands Decider and Perplexity’s pplx-decider; Ollama 0.35 exposed them locally through /v1/systemone. The LLM-as-Jev framework shows that any causal LLM can be scored under the same convention. An early evidence audit found 29 arXiv papers mentioning typed decision models within nine days of the Jev release and proposes an evaluation checklist, which we follow; a broader benchmark places Jev against nineteen general-purpose LLMs.

On network-flow classification, Random Forest and Extra Trees trained on 8,000 records beat Jev in every test week; a community test of 14 decision models on 56 triage tasks found a plain Qwen3.5-9B ahead of all of them. We take the classical baseline as the cost floor every neural option must beat.

Email classification predates LLMs by three decades: rule learning for mail filing, folder prediction on the Enron corpus, reply prediction—“does this message need a reply”—and attachment prediction as the first “intelligent email” tasks, the former being exactly our needs-reply switch, and the observation that users need a handful of broad categories rather than many folders, which is what our six types and three switches are. That work trained per-user classifiers on a few hundred labelled messages, which is also where our baseline sits. What is new is the alternative: zero-shot decisions from a language model, generative or typed, without any per-user data—and the question of whether, for one inbox, that alternative beats a classifier trained on labels the user can produce in an afternoon. Privacy motivates the local setting: keeping the model where the data are is the premise of federated and on-device learning, and personal correspondence is the canonical example of data that should not leave the device.

Foyer (formerly SecondBrain) is a self-hosted personal dashboard (React + Django) that ingests Gmail and IMAP accounts, assigns each email to a project, extracts tasks and timeline events, and runs background agents. The classification pipeline (classify_emails) proceeds in stages: Noise rules. Domain and pattern lists for newsletters and bot senders, with a separate robot test that a contact in the address book cannot override—a rule added after a notification address entered the address book and became permanently exempt. Self-mail to a dedicated project. Grouping by sender: by domain for organisations, by full address for consumer providers; groups above five messages are split by normalised subject. Type and urgency by rules. At ingest (sync_gmail), each message receives a type and an urgency from a keyword heuristic (Appendix B.4): type is offerta, richiesta or aggiornamento if one of a handful of Italian/English keywords appears in subject or snippet, else altro; urgency is alta or media on a list of urgency words, else bassa. The heuristic can never produce cliente, spam or newsletter; messages later attached to a spam or newsletter project inherit that type. No model is involved in these two fields.

LLM pass 1 per group: a prompt with up to 8,000 characters of messages and the list of existing projects (up to 80, with human contacts), returning project name, project type, description, contacts, tasks and timeline as JSON. The LLM therefore decides project assignment, not the per-email type or urgency. LLM pass 2: cross-group merge. Upsert with three matching rules: exact name; same name root plus at least one shared contact; at least three shared contacts. Attachments, mail labels, drafts, suggested tasks, structured contacts. Every decision is logged through a structured decision(kind, outcome, context) call with a flow id, which gives provenance for the error analysis. At the time of the study the LLM backend was a hosted gateway (OpenRouter) with a local Ollama model as fallback; the local 3B model had been demoted after timing out on CPU. The study therefore measures the production system as it actually ran, not as its documentation describes it: reading the code rather than the README revealed both that the local model was no longer primary and that type and urgency were never produced by a model at all.
The stored classification field is written by the model; counting it says nothing about error.

We added a dataset_email command that: samples stratified by predicted type (seven classes: richiesta, aggiornamento, offerta, cliente, altro, spam, newsletter), because 39% of stored labels are altro and 94% of urgencies bassa; uniform sampling would teach the prior, not the content; freezes a snapshot of exactly what the model sees (sender, subject, body truncated to 1,500 characters, date, channel) next to the model’s prediction, so later re-runs cannot change the example; assigns splits deterministically by thread, stratified by type: a first version keyed on sha1(id) put 11 threads across splits and gave 4 test emails a near-duplicate in train, so the unit is the thread (normalised subject + sender key), and, while the test split is below 60 emails, the primary protocol is 5-fold thread-grouped cross-validation with the baseline trained out-of-fold; redacts secrets in the frozen body (passwords, tokens, card and account numbers) before storage—a pilot export contained a VPN password in clear text; collects human labels in the interface: type, area, project, urgency, needs-reply, action-within-48h, is-noise; reports, before any training, the only number that matters: how often the production model was right; pre-registers the hypotheses of each new labelling round: for the third round, eleven hypotheses with thresholds and a verification script were committed before the labelled file was opened (one post-hoc change: a format fix in the script, not a threshold).

In the first round the id-keyed split placed 11 of 92 threads across splits and gave 4 test emails a near-duplicate in train; the second round was split by thread and stratified by type (train 159 / validation 39 / test 33), with one inherited thread still crossing. Because the fixed test split holds no alta and one offerta, every number in this paper comes from thread-grouped cross-validation (trained baseline) or from all 231 rows (zero-shot systems); the fixed split is kept in the repository for future rounds.

Three labelling rounds on the owner’s production database. Rounds 1–2 were sampled stratified by the type predicted by the production rules: 119 emails on 20 October 2026 (4 skipped as ambiguous) and 120 on 21 October; eight rows marked ignore (private family mail, empty bodies) are excluded, leaving the v2 corpus: 231 emails in 207 threads, our unbiased reference. Round 3 (500 emails, 491 kept) was sampled adversarially: all 118 emails of the unlabelled pool in which Nimble or Gemma 4 saw offerta or spam (G1), 125 on which the models disagreed on action-48h (G2), and 257 at random stratified on the baseline’s prediction (G3). The v3 corpus (722 emails, 698 threads) is therefore a stress test built on the LLMs’ presumed errors, not a sample of the natural inbox; system comparisons are reported on v2, and v3 is used for the pre-registered hypotheses, the contact-graph result and the action analysis.

In the first round two model annotators proposed type and urgency and the owner confirmed or corrected each row in a spreadsheet that showed sender, subject, 700 characters of body and both proposals but not the production prediction (110/115 types and 104/115 urgencies survived review); in the second round the owner labelled from the model proposal with the same interface, then the full set was revised jointly with an assistant to apply the final label definitions below. The ground truth is therefore a single human reviewer anchored on model proposals. Class distribution in Table 1.

Two axes were separated after the first round, because the stored type mixed what a message says with who sent it. Type (six classes: richiesta, aggiornamento, offerta, newsletter, spam, altro) describes the message. Relationship (cliente, fornitore, socio, famiglia, istituzione, servizio, monitoraggio, me) describes the sender and is assigned per contact; cliente covers every interaction that can lead to a deal, before or after a signature. Urgency has three levels. Three booleans are the agent’s switches: needs-reply (the agent drafts an answer), action-48h (the agent creates a task) and is-noise (the agents ignore the message; it is kept only as context). Project is the project the email belongs to as of October 2026; 26 rows are deliberately empty (“none”) because the project-manager agent has not proposed one yet.

Production rules: the keyword heuristic of Appendix B.5 (type, urgency); it has no output for the booleans and still emits cliente for 32 rows, wrong by construction after the label change. Classical baseline: TF-IDF word 1–2-grams and character 3–5-grams, logistic regression with balanced class weights, 5-fold cross-validation grouped by thread (207 threads), the only trained system. Typed decision models: Tev1 0.8B on CPU (i5-1245UE), Tev1 4B and Nimble 9B (Q8) on a Kaggle T4 via Ollama /v1/systemone, and Bespoke Nimble v4-max through its API. Generative LLMs: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma 4 26B-A4B and Gemma 4 31B through OpenRouter, JSON mode, temperature 0. All systems received the same Italian question and one-line class definitions (Appendix B); the body was stripped of markup and URLs and truncated to 1,500 characters. Zero-shot systems were run once on all 231 rows. The hosted Gemma 4 26B is not deterministic at temperature 0 (0.774, 0.800, 0.791 on the first-round corpus); hosted figures are single-run estimates.

Accuracy and macro-F1 against the majority class; for systems that return probabilities, mean confidence on correct vs. incorrect decisions; latency as median per decision; cost per 1,000 emails from provider usage. With 231 rows one email is 0.43 accuracy points; offerta (5) and spam (3) make macro-F1 on type unstable, so for type we read accuracy and the F1 of the four large classes.

The production rules are worse than no classifier. The keyword heuristic that populated the type field of every email in the system reaches 0.28 accuracy against a 0.57 majority class; on urgency it sits just below the majority (0.68 vs 0.70). Because the sample was stratified on the heuristic’s own prediction, this is not an unbiased estimate of its production accuracy, but a field that performs below “always say the most common class” on a sample built to be favourable to it had never carried information. This is the paper’s first result, and it was invisible until someone counted.

Two hundred labels and a logistic regression have the highest accuracy on every field—while never predicting the two rarest classes. Out-of-fold TF-IDF + logistic regression leads on type (0.79), urgency (0.74), needs-reply (0.83), action-48h (0.93), is-noise (0.90) and project assignment (0.71 on rows with a project), in under a millisecond. The claim is about accuracy: on type its macro-F1 (0.47) is below Gemma 4’s (0.54) because it never predicts offerta or spam, which have fewer threads than folds. Two ablations qualify the win (Table 4). Removing the sender from the baseline’s input costs four points on type (0.74 to 0.70 in the ablation harness, whose folds differ slightly from the main run), one to two on the switches and none on urgency: most of the advantage is textual, and the sender matters chiefly for altro, which is almost entirely the owner’s own mail (16/18 rows; no zero-shot system reaches F1 0.3 on it, B gets 0.83).

Replacing TF-IDF with a sentence-embedding model (MiniLM) and the same classifier does not help: the English all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is below the majority class on type (0.55) and the multilingual paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 reaches 0.69, still below the n-gram baseline, which on this corpus benefits from character n-grams over Italian/English morphology and sender tokens. Aggregating the three rare types into one class (altro + offerta + spam, 26 rows) gives a four-class view in which macro-F1 is stable: B 0.57, Tev1 4B 0.58, Nimble 9B 0.50, against 0.57 majority accuracy.

Which differences are real. McNemar’s test on paired per-email correctness (Table 2) separates the comparisons that matter from those that do not. On type, B is significantly better than the production rules (\chi^{2}=92, p<0.01) and than Nimble (\chi^{2}=4.1, p<0.05), but not than Gemma 4 26B or 31B (\chi^{2}=1.2, 1.8, n.s.): the trained baseline and the best generative model are tied on type. Gemma 4 26B is significantly better than Qwen2.5-7B (\chi^{2}=27) and Nimble than Tev1 0.8B (\chi^{2}=4.4). On urgency, B and Nimble are tied (\chi^{2}=0.2) and both beat the Gemmas (p<0.05); B’s lead over the production rules on urgency is not significant (\chi^{2}=2.6). Bootstrap intervals are \pm 5 – 6 points throughout.

Among zero-shot systems the ranking depends on the field. On type the generative Gemma 4 26B-A4B is best (0.74, and the best F1 on the four large classes), the hosted decision model Nimble v4-max second (0.70); on urgency and is-noise Nimble is best (0.71, 0.86) and the Gemmas fall to 0.63 and 0.81; on needs-reply Nimble and Gemma 31B tie (0.81). Nimble answers in 0.5 s at about $0.02 per 1,000 emails, Gemma 26B in 0.76 s at $0.03. Qwen2.5-7B—the same open weights a user could run locally—is at or below the majority class on both type and urgency. Giving the generative models examples does not close the gap: with three labelled examples per class in the prompt (drawn from each fold’s training part), Qwen gains one accuracy point and nine macro-F1 points on type, neither significant (p=0.77, 0.10), and Gemma 4 26B is unchanged (0.74 to 0.73), at six to eight times the cost per email.

Local decision models: size matters more than quantised depth. On a T4, Tev1 4B reaches 0.69 on type at 0.35 s per decision, above both Tev1 0.8B (0.62) and the locally served Nimble 9B in Q8 (0.62); the hosted Nimble v4-max does better (0.70), so either the Q8 quantisation or the serving stack costs roughly eight points. All local decision models fail on urgency (0.25–0.45): they assign media or alta to most messages (Tev1 0.8B: 151 and 66 of 231), where bassa is 70% of the labels. A three-level scale phrased as “how urgent” is part of the problem: rephrasing it as “what should the recipient do with this email” lifts Tev1 4B from 0.45 to 0.56 and Nimble 9B from 0.41 to 0.46, still below the majority class; the switches, phrased as actions, fare better (Table 3: Tev1 4B on a T4 reaches 0.79 / macro-F1 0.74 on needs-reply). Asking the type question in English instead of Italian does not help either model (Tev1 4B 0.69 to 0.64, Nimble 0.62 to 0.64).

action-48h is the hard switch. With 20 positives in 231, no zero-shot model beats the majority class in accuracy (0.91); all beat it in macro-F1 (0.54–0.58 vs 0.48), B reaches 0.73. This is the switch with the highest cost of error—a task created or not—and the one where a classifier needs the most examples.

The relationship belongs in the contact graph. Where a contact has at least one other labelled email (146 of 231, 63%), inheriting the relationship from the same address is right 98.6% of the time; the remaining 37% of emails come from senders seen once, for whom a majority fallback gives 0.857 overall against 0.498 for the majority class (Table 5). In production the covered fraction grows with every labelled contact, and a new sender is exactly the case where the agent should ask rather than guess. Matching on domain covers more (75%) but errs more (0.890): gmail.com mixes the owner, clients and partners. As a negative control we did ask two local decision models to infer the relationship from the text of one message: Tev1 4B reaches 0.52 and Nimble 9B 0.55 against a 0.50 majority class—no better than guessing—where inheritance from the contact gives 0.86. The agent’s production logic is being changed to inherit it from the contact (Section 3).

Project assignment needs descriptions, not names. Given only the sixteen project names, zero-shot models score 0.26–0.47 and over-use none (precision 0.13–0.22); the baseline, which learns from the other emails of a thread’s neighbours, reaches 0.70. A fair zero-shot comparison requires a description per project written by the owner rather than derived from the labels; it is left for the next round.

Accuracy is not the product metric. The labels compose into one of four actions per email: draft a reply, create a task, ignore, or nothing, with the rule that is-noise wins. Scored that way (Table 6), the error that costs most— false noise, an email that needed a reply or a task and was ignored—inverts the ranking. On v2, of 68 emails that needed action, the trained baseline ignores 12 (18%), Nimble 8 (12%), Gemma 4 26B 3 (4%), Tev1 0.8B 25 (37%); on v3, B 23% against Nimble 9%. The baseline is precise and conservative (drafts: precision 0.80, recall 0.47; tasks: 0.71 / 0.25), the LLMs recall more and over-act (Nimble creates 28 useless tasks in 33, Gemma 19 in 24; the baseline 2 in 7). Inheriting the relationship from the contact and applying the monitoring rule raises task recall for every system (B 0.25 to 0.40, Gemma 0.25 to 0.65) at no cost in false noise; the oracle relationship adds nothing more, so the relationship is not the bottleneck. Which system is right depends on the price of a missed email versus a useless task.

Making that price explicit settles it: with a useless task costing 1, a useless draft 0.5 and a missed email c, the baseline has the lowest total cost only while c<3; from c\approx 3 upward Gemma 4 26B is cheapest at every price, and at c=10 its cost is less than half the baseline’s (60 vs 126 on v2). For a personal agent, where a missed client email is worth far more than a task to dismiss, that favours the generative model out of the box. But the baseline’s false-noise rate is a threshold, not a ceiling: choosing the is-noise threshold inside the cross-validation to minimise the same cost (missed email 10, email handled needlessly 1) halves it—on v3 from 28/120 to 13/120, on v2 from 12/68 to 7/68, and to 4/68 with Platt scaling—at the price of handling two to three times more noise. With that threshold the baseline’s false noise is no longer distinguishable from Nimble’s (v3: 0.108 vs 0.092, p=0.72; v2: 0.059 vs 0.118, p=0.34) and its total cost is lower (v3: 225 vs 250; v2: 79 vs 99), while it keeps its accuracy lead.
Calibration itself is not what does the work—a cost-chosen threshold depends only on the ranking of probabilities—but it is what makes the probabilities safe to display or combine.

Calibration. The hosted decision model is the best-calibrated system on every field (ECE 0.04–0.11 on v2, 0.04–0.09 on v3), and it is deterministic (491/491 identical answers on a repeated run). The trained baseline is strongly under -confident: on type its mean confidence is 0.32 for an accuracy of 0.79 (ECE 0.47), an artefact of balanced class weights on few rows; recalibrating it inside the cross-validation (Platt or isotonic, fitted on each outer fold’s training part) cuts its ECE by a factor of 4–17 (type: 0.47 to 0.11 on v2, 0.37 to 0.05 on v3; is-noise: 0.29 to 0.03), to the same range as the hosted decision model, at a cost of five accuracy points on type when the corpus is small (231 rows) and none when it is larger (722). The local decision models are over-confident on errors (Tev1 4B 0.81 right vs 0.70 wrong on type; Nimble 9B Q8 0.88 vs 0.76).

The adversarial corpus is a stress test, not a second sample. On v3 (722 emails) the baseline’s lead over Gemma 4 26B on type becomes significant (+0.136, p<0.001), as does its lead over Nimble on every switch; the contact-graph relationship reaches 0.927 on the 73% of covered emails and 0.898 overall (coverage is inflated on v3, where G3 was drawn by sender strata and many senders recur: the v2 figures, 63% covered and 0.857 overall, are the ones to carry to production); the production rules fall to 0.17 on type; the local decision models on a T4 fall below the majority class on every field (Tev1 4B 0.52 on type, Nimble 9B Q8 0.50; 0.40 and 0.34 on urgency), as do their hosted and generative counterparts on type (Nimble v4-max 0.56, Gemma 4 26B 0.65 against 0.58). But v3 was sampled on the LLMs’ presumed errors, and the baseline was the first proposal shown to the reviewer, so these gaps are upper bounds, not estimates.

The pre-registered hypotheses give the honest summary: seven of eleven confirmed, four refuted—among the refuted, that rare commercial classes could be found by sampling where the LLMs see them (all 118 such emails yielded 3 offerta and 7 spam: the models over-predict commercial mail, the inbox simply has little of it after Gmail’s own filtering), and that the baseline would learn offerta with eight examples (its F1 stays 0).
Jev was not run for lack of an API key; Nimble’s public demo was offline and the paid API was used; GPU runs were made on Kaggle’s free T4 with the same script and data.

From the divergences between the six systems we counted, per cause, the emails on which at least three systems err in the direction of that cause (ERRORI.md). Relational classes. In the first round all 5 cliente emails were misread as richiesta or aggiornamento by at least three systems; after the label change, altro (mostly the owner’s own mail) plays the same role: no zero-shot system reaches F1 0.3 on it. Who the sender is to the owner is not in the text of one message; it lives in the contact graph (Table 5). Automated senders are not the problem. We expected deploy, CI and console notifications to be misfiled; on the reviewed labels no email with an automated sender is misclassified by any system. The rule-based robot filter in front of the models already removes the hard cases, and the models handle the rest. Thin text. Bodies under 20 characters are now excluded as ignore; in the first round every system failed on them on both fields. Debatable labels. On 9 type labels and 5 urgency labels at least four of the six systems agree with each other against the reviewer.

These are candidates for a second annotator rather than evidence of model error; at 8–12% of the corpus they bound the achievable accuracy. Rare commercial classes are rare. Sampling every email in which two LLMs saw offerta or spam (118 of a 1,322-email pool) produced 3 and 7 true cases: Nimble’s precision on spam is 0.10. The models over-predict commercial mail; the inbox, filtered upstream by Gmail, has little of it. Taxonomy drift. The stored type mixes message kind (request, update, offer) with relationship (client, spam), which is the root of cause 1.

Single user, single inbox, two languages. What would not transfer to another user is clear from the components: the baseline’s weights (they encode this owner’s senders and vocabulary and must be retrained from that user’s labels), the contact graph (empty for a new user until contacts recur, which is why coverage, not accuracy, is the quantity to watch), the class priors (70–82% bassa here) and any confidence threshold. What should transfer is the protocol itself, the zero-shot behaviour of the decision models, and the finding that the sender’s relationship is a graph property; the second inbox needed to test this is the obvious next study; the owner reviewed labels proposed by model annotators rather than labelling from scratch (110/115 first-round type proposals survived review), and the final label definitions were applied in a joint revision with an assistant, which may reflect anchoring as much as agreement (no independent second annotator). 231 labels give 95% confidence intervals of roughly \pm 6 points on accuracy, so differences below eight points between systems are not significant; the gap between the production heuristic and every other system, and between the trained baseline and the zero-shot models on is-noise, are.

The sample was stratified on the production heuristic’s prediction, so its accuracy is not a production estimate. The data cannot be released; the protocol, the harness and aggregate statistics can. Round 3 was sampled on the LLMs’ presumed errors and shown with the baseline’s proposal first; v3 comparisons inherit both biases. Three gaps are known and scheduled for the next round: a second annotator blind to model proposals on a 60-email subset, with Cohen’s \kappa; a reweighting of the zero-shot accuracies by the production distribution of the heuristic’s predictions, to correct the stratified sample; and a project-assignment run with a one-line description per project written by the owner, since names alone are not a fair zero-shot input (Table 7). Few-shot prompting and recalibration of the baseline, raised by early reviewers, have been run and are reported above. The generative naming step for new projects was run through a hosted endpoint serving open weights (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) that are deployable locally; local latency for that step is reported on a -email subsample only. Local GPU results come from Kaggle’s free T4, not from the owner’s hardware; the locally served Nimble is the Q8 build.
The hosted generative model was not deterministic across runs at temperature 0 (0.774–0.800 on type), so hosted figures should be read as single-run estimates.

Two days of measurement on 231 emails showed that the field a personal agent displayed most confidently had never carried information; that two hundred human labels and a logistic regression beat every zero-shot model—decision models and generative LLMs, local and hosted—on every one of the agent’s decisions, at negligible cost; that among zero-shot options a hosted typed decision model is the best choice for the agent’s switches and a mid-size generative model for message type, with a 4B local decision model on a consumer GPU close behind; that the one label no model should be asked for, the sender’s relationship, is recovered almost perfectly from the contact graph; and that the most accurate system is also the one that most often ignores an email that needed action, so the choice between a classifier and a model is a choice about the price of errors, not about accuracy—and once that price is written down, a threshold chosen for it makes the classifier the cheapest option again. The protocol—stratified sampling, frozen snapshots, thread-grouped splits, secret redaction, counting before training—cost less than the labelling and is reusable for any personal agent.

The production system is being changed accordingly: type and urgency will no longer be rule-based, the relationship will be inherited from the contact, and the three switches will drive the agent’s actions directly; the change is in progress at the time of writing and will be reported with the next labelling round.

GPU runs: a single-cell Kaggle notebook (T4) with the same questions. Models: tev1:0.8b, tev1, nimble on Ollama 0.40; scikit-learn 1.9.

ANCHOR: Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding. For repository-grounded coding agents, a functionally correct patch is not necessarily an acceptable one: developers also constrain how the task must be carried out-modification scope, workflow order, validation, tool use, and reporting. This capability, which we call engineering constraint following, remains largely invisible to current evaluations. We introduce ANCHOR (Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding), a benchmark built on naturalistic, multilingual repository tasks spanning eight language groups. ANCHOR combines (i) a hierarchical taxonomy of 10 categories and 78 leaf types distilled from real developer interactions, (ii) an automated pipeline that instantiates task-grounded atomic constraints and composes them into typed AND/THEN/PRIORITY relations, and (iii) a trajectory-grounded evaluation framework that checks both the code diff and the execution trajectory with rule-based and LLM judges. Across 19 agent configurations spanning 2 scaffolds and 10 foundation models on 358 tasks, the strongest measured system, Claude Opus 4.8 under Cline, reaches 70.1% atomic compliance and 63.7% relation compliance, while 19.0% of tasks pass every scored checklist item under the strict all-item FCCR criterion. A five-engineer audit of constraints from 50 instances reports 94% feasibility, 94% repository consistency, and 96% realism.

In the primary paired set (14 configurations), the mean signed change in task completion after adding constraints is +0.7 percentage points; individual changes vary in both directions. These results distinguish functional success from constraint compliance, with failures concentrated in workflow ordering, tool-use discipline, and reporting, and substantial interactions between models and scaffolds.

Software engineering tasks are rarely unconstrained objectives. Developers ask agents not only to fix the bug, but also to preserve APIs, reproduce before patching, run specific tests, avoid prohibited tools, and report what was actually executed. For coding agents, success is therefore not merely to solve the task, but to solve it under explicit engineering constraints.

We argue that this is not simply generic instruction following with code context. In repository-grounded agentic coding, many requirements are trajectory-grounded: they constrain tool use, workflow order, validation, and reporting over the course of execution rather than only the final artifact. They are also often structured, because multiple requirements must be satisfied jointly, in order, or under explicit priority. Engineering constraint following is thus a distinct capability dimension, complementary to both task completion and scaffold-level policy compliance. Figure 1 illustrates this distinction: two trajectories may solve the same issue, yet only one is acceptable under the stated engineering requirements.

This gap has become important because modern coding agents can already solve a substantial fraction of real repository issues on SWE-bench-style benchmarks. Yet these benchmarks largely evaluate whether the final artifact is correct, not whether the agent obeyed the task-level requirements that governed its execution. General instruction-following benchmarks do not capture repository-grounded, multi-step engineering workflows, while recent agentic instruction-following benchmarks still emphasize generic agentic instructions or scaffold-level policies rather than task-level engineering requirements. Current evaluations may therefore overestimate real-world readiness. Table 1 situates ANCHOR within this landscape.

To address this gap, we introduce ANCHOR (A ssessing N aturalistic C onstraint H ierarchies and O rdering in R epository-Grounded Agentic Coding), a benchmark for evaluating engineering constraint following in repository-grounded coding tasks. ANCHOR combines a 10-category, 78-leaf taxonomy, an automated pipeline that instantiates atomic constraints and composes them into structured and / then / priority relations, and a trajectory-grounded evaluation framework with rule-based and LLM judges. Across 19 constrained configurations, including a full-benchmark Claude Opus 4.8 evaluation under Cline, the highest strict all-item FCCR is 19.0%. The primary paired set (14 configurations) shows a mean signed completion change of +0.7 percentage points after adding constraints, with gains and losses across systems. This calibration does not establish joint satisfiability or equal task difficulty; the direct evidence is that functional completion and checklist compliance differ within each evaluated configuration. Our contributions are to define engineering constraint following, operationalize it in a benchmark, and characterize the resulting failures, supported by human audits of both generated constraints and judge decisions.
Benchmark instances are available on Hugging Face; the construction/evaluation prompts and taxonomy are available in the public repository.

Repository-grounded coding benchmarks such as SWE-bench, SWE-Compass, and SWE-Rebench V2 measure whether an agent can resolve real software engineering tasks in real repositories, typically through final-patch correctness under an executable test harness. These benchmarks have driven rapid progress in coding agents, but they primarily measure task completion. They therefore provide limited visibility into whether an agent respected task-specific engineering requirements on scope, workflow, validation, or reporting during execution.

Constraint-aware instruction-following benchmarks establish the importance of explicitly verifiable requirements, both in natural language and in code generation. However, they mostly evaluate single-turn settings, final artifacts, or flat constraint sets. Recent work such as Inverse IFEval further shows that even strong LLMs can fail to override entrenched training conventions in order to follow explicit user instructions. ANCHOR instead targets repository-grounded agentic coding, where many requirements are trajectory-level and many must be interpreted jointly through ordering or priority relations.

The closest concurrent work is OctoBench, which studies scaffold-aware instruction following in repository-grounded coding. We view the two benchmarks as complementary rather than competing. OctoBench targets scaffold- and platform-level policies, whereas ANCHOR targets task-level engineering constraints specified by the developer instruction itself. ANCHOR further contributes an explicit engineering constraint taxonomy and structured composite relations, enabling direct evaluation of hierarchy, ordering, and precedence. Table 1 summarises this positioning against prior instruction-following and coding benchmarks.

The ANCHOR taxonomy is constructed bottom-up from real developer interactions with coding agents rather than from an a priori schema. We first collected a corpus of agentic coding interactions—task instructions, inline review comments, and post-hoc feedback on agent trajectories—and performed grounded open-label annotation to extract the engineering constraints that developers impose on coding agents in practice. A panel of senior software engineers then iteratively refined this raw label space by clustering near-duplicate labels, resolving boundary cases, and stress-testing the emerging hierarchy against held-out trajectories. The resulting hierarchy contains 10 top-level categories, 34 mid-level subcategories, and 78 leaf categories; in the current release, these leaves account for 2,836 instantiated atomic constraints. Full annotation guidelines, boundary cases, and the complete taxonomy are provided in Appendix A and Appendix B.

Throughout this refinement, the taxonomy is treated as an evaluation substrate rather than a descriptive catalog, guided by five design principles. Coverage: the taxonomy should span the major constraint types observed in real developer data, so that practical instructions map into it with minimal residue. Semantic exclusivity: leaf categories should be as disjoint as possible, reducing ambiguity during annotation and automatic mapping. Operationalisability: each leaf should admit concrete, testable instantiations with stable pass conditions under either rule-based or LLM-based judging. Hierarchical organisation: the structure should support both fine-grained diagnosis at the leaf level and coarse-grained reporting at the category level. Language neutrality: the same conceptual categories should transfer across the multilingual repository settings covered by ANCHOR.

At the top level, the ten categories capture complementary dimensions of agentic coding. C1 (Tool Execution Protocol) governs how tools are invoked, including tool selection, invocation parameters, failure handling, and result verification, and C2 (Workflow & Behaviour) governs how the agent conducts the task over time, including execution order, user confirmation, information disclosure, and commit discipline. C3 (Modification Scope & Change Budget) bounds the spatial, quantitative, and semantic extent of changes, C4 (Code Style & Engineering Standards) covers formatting, naming, type-system usage, and documentation, and C5 (Code Implementation) constrains implementation choices such as algorithms, error handling, side-effect control, and technology selection. C6–C8 specify environment compatibility and isolation, dependency and build policy, and prohibitions on dangerous or privileged operations, while C9 (Testing) and C10 (Output Format & Reporting) impose validation and reporting requirements. Leaf categories are the smallest operational unit: each captures a semantically coherent developer requirement that can be instantiated into task-grounded constraints and verified with relatively stable logic. The categories are complementary rather than alternative—a single instruction such as “only modify files under common/crypto/, reproduce the bug before applying the fix, and add a regression test before reporting completion” simultaneously invokes C3 (scope), C2 (workflow), and C9 (testing).

Figure 2 summarizes the source-query corpus, while Figure 3 and Table 2 describe the instantiated benchmark. As a lightweight sanity check against template collapse, we mask repository names, file paths, function names, and other task-specific identifiers, then measure pairwise similarity among constraints instantiated from the same leaf. Across 130,049 within-leaf pairs drawn from 70 multi-instance leaves, the mean masked cosine similarity is 0.565, indicating shared semantics within a leaf without near-duplicate templating.

ANCHOR draws repository-level coding environments from the multilingual benchmark SWE-Compass, which is built from real GitHub issues and provides gold-standard patches with executable test environments across Python, Go, Java, TypeScript, Rust, C, C++, and C#. We retain instances that satisfy four properties: (i) a usable execution environment, enabling trajectory-grounded evaluation in a unified sandbox; (ii) sufficient task and repository context to support downstream constraint selection; (iii) moderate patch complexity, excluding both trivial micro-edits and long-horizon changes that are difficult to evaluate consistently; and (iv) broad coverage across programming languages and repository types. The purpose of this filtering is not to favour easier tasks, but to ensure that each retained instance can support realistic, task-grounded, and verifiable engineering constraints. Figure 4 summarizes how ANCHOR converts a raw repository task into both a natural developer instruction and a structured constraint object that can be evaluated after agent execution, through five explicit steps.

For each retained task, we gather the repository identifier, target language, original problem statement, gold patch, and repository-level documentation from DeepWiki. Raw documentation is often too long and noisy to include directly in downstream prompts, so we compress it into a compact project-context card that preserves repository purpose, technology stack, directory structure, engineering conventions, testing practices, and version information, while discarding diagrams, verbose API documentation, illustrative code examples, and marketing language. This is a targeted information-distillation step rather than mere length reduction: the card supplies repository-level evidence for later decisions, such as whether linting, testing, or dependency-policy constraints are meaningful for a given project.

Given the 78 leaf categories, this stage retrieves a high-recall subset of potentially relevant leaves for the task, based on three complementary evidence sources: task-type evidence (e.g., testing and interface-compatibility constraints are natural in bug-fixing tasks), repository-context evidence (e.g., explicit formatter, linter, or type-checking conventions make the corresponding categories meaningful), and modification-scope evidence (e.g., tasks touching public interfaces, filesystem logic, or security-sensitive code raise different constraint families). The selector deliberately avoids categories that are only theoretically applicable to almost any coding task, since these tend to yield generic and weakly discriminative constraints later on.

section: Step 3: Atomic constraint instantiation and filtering.
text: Each selected leaf is instantiated into zero or more atomic constraints —concrete, task-specific constraint statements grounded in the actual files, tools, and technologies involved. The selection and instantiation prompts receive the gold patch as context, including affected modules and plausible implementation concerns. They explicitly prohibit copying its exact file/line counts or restating its implementation as a constraint; an engineering requirement should admit valid implementations beyond the reference patch. Because instantiation and composition share a prompt, the patch is also visible at composition time. These safeguards reduce, but do not rule out, indirect solution leakage. Every retained constraint must be naturalistic (plausibly stated by a senior engineer assigning the task), non-blocking (constraining how the task is done without making it infeasible), specific and verifiable (admitting an objective pass/fail judgement), task-grounded (referencing concrete task details), and independent in content from the gold solution: the generator may inspect the patch for task context, but the final constraint should not encode patch-specific file/line counts or implementation details.

section: Step 3: Atomic constraint instantiation and filtering.
text: The generator is instructed to discard candidates that fail these criteria, so Steps 2 and 3 jointly form a recall–precision cascade: coarse selection avoids prematurely missing meaningful categories, while instantiation enforces quality control over what enters the benchmark.

Real developer instructions are often not flat lists of independent requirements; they specify joint satisfaction, required execution order, or precedence among competing requirements. ANCHOR captures this structure by composing task-grounded atomics into connected composite graphs whose edges carry one of three typed relations: AND requires joint satisfaction; THEN requires both satisfaction and correct temporal order—reaching the right end state in the wrong order is scored as a failure; and PRIORITY places two constraints intentionally in tension, and a PRIORITY edge passes if and only if the higher-priority source constraint is upheld, regardless of whether the lower-priority target is sacrificed to it. This edge-level rule does not waive other requirements in a mixed-relation composite. Edge types may be mixed within a single composite, so multi-step and prioritised workflows can be expressed in one graph. Composites are introduced only when the underlying relations are semantically natural and task-meaningful, and atomics that do not admit such structure remain standalone instruction items. Each atomic constraint participates in at most one composite, and the connected-subgraph formulation keeps each composite interpretable as a single instruction unit rather than an arbitrary bundle of clauses.

The non-blocking criterion is a construction safeguard for individual constraints, not a formal proof that all constraints can be jointly satisfied. AND and THEN require compatible requirements; PRIORITY intentionally introduces a conflict together with an explicit precedence rule. Assigning an atomic constraint to at most one composite limits graph overlap, but does not eliminate semantic interactions between distinct composites. Small completion-rate changes likewise cannot establish satisfiability, since an agent can solve the task while ignoring a constraint. We therefore complement these safeguards with a separate human audit: five senior engineers independently assessed the atomic constraints in 50 instances for feasibility, repository consistency, and realism, with reported validity rates of 94%, 94%, and 96%, respectively. Section 4.1 provides the rubric and agreement statistics; these results characterize sampled constraint quality rather than certify every full constraint set.

The final stage renders the structured representation as a natural developer instruction in two parts: a short task description rewritten in the voice of a developer assigning work, followed by a constraint list of separable instruction items. Independent atomics become individual items, while each composite is rendered as a single natural-language item that preserves the relation semantics among its members. Synthesis must preserve specificity: exact file paths, command names, flags, module references, and behavioural conditions from the instantiated constraints remain intact. It must also neither introduce new constraints nor leak gold-solution details—the query expresses requirements, not answers.

This five-stage design preserves the natural surface form of developer instructions while grounding evaluation in an explicit, machine-checkable representation of what the agent was required to do and in what relational structure. Detailed filtering criteria, design rationales, prompt templates, and stage-specific schemas are provided in Appendix B and Appendix C.1 – C.4. Section 5 then operationalizes this structured representation into executable checklist items for code- and trajectory-grounded evaluation.

This audit examines the generated requirements themselves, separately from the 480-item judge–human study in Section 5.1. We sampled 50 benchmark instances. All five engineers independently labelled every atomic constraint in these instances on three binary dimensions, without seeing one another’s labels. They were the same senior engineers used in the judge study, with 6–12 years of experience: two Python/Go backend engineers, one infrastructure engineer with Java/Bash and CI/CD expertise, one TypeScript/Rust full-stack engineer, and one research engineer with broad open-source code-review experience.

The rubric was as follows. Feasibility: PASS if the requirement can be met in the given repository and task without preventing completion; FAIL for an unsatisfiable or task-blocking requirement, such as restricting edits to a directory that excludes the relevant files. Repository consistency: PASS if referenced paths, symbols, tools, dependencies, and conventions agree with the repository; FAIL for hallucinated referents or an inapplicable toolchain. Realism: PASS if a senior engineer could plausibly impose the requirement here; FAIL if it is artificial, trivially satisfied, or merely restates the task or reference solution.

Table 3 summarizes the five-annotator audit. Raw agreement ranges from 92.0% to 97.6%, and Gwet’s AC1 ranges from 0.91 to 0.97. These results support consistency of the sampled quality judgments, while the audit covers atomic constraints from 50 instances rather than every composite or complete task-level constraint set. The validity rates do not estimate how much FCCR would change after repairing ambiguous items.

Section 4 produces, for each task, a natural developer instruction paired with a structured constraint representation. We now describe how that representation is operationalized into executable checks over the agent’s code diff and trajectory. Figure 5 summarizes this process.

For each task instance, we generate a checklist: a structured set of evaluation items generated from the constraint representation and checked against the final developer instruction, which is authoritative if the two differ. This intermediate checklist layer is necessary because the construction-time representation is convenient for instantiation and composition, but evaluation requires item-level pass conditions, judge assignments, and explicit evidence targets. Only constraints preserved in the final instruction are retained. Verified atomic constraints yield atomic items one-to-one, including atomics that participate in composites; each composite constraint additionally yields a relation item that references its member atomic items as dependent checks and evaluates the higher-order property—joint satisfaction, temporal ordering, or priority handling—on top of them.
