Table 1 additionally separates a subgroup of the dissociation regime, labelled IIb: artifacts whose surface inclusion also falls substantially while definitions degrade even more strongly. Two of its members (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B) remain significantly definition-selective under the interaction test and are therefore classified with Regime II; the third member (Phi-4-mini, 3.8B) is included because of the severity of its losses even though its damage is symmetric. IIb is the severe end of the dissociation regime, rather than a separate fourth regime.

Figure 4 shows one exemplar ladder for each regime. Surface inclusion is unchanged through Q3 for all three examples (K_M files). The regimes are separated only by the definitional probe. And the collapse is like a cliff at Q2, instead of a gradual slope.

Zhou et al. (2026a) give a mechanistic account of this kind of failure, separating it into two modes: signal degradation, where the computational pattern remains intact and quantization error accumulates as noise; and computation collapse, where components stop functioning and the knowledge signal is destroyed in the early layers. In that mode, even patching clean full-precision activations into the build failed to restore the correct answer. Their collapsed 2-bit builds produced chaotic content such as meaningless numbers and repetitive loops. Our Regime I shows the same behaviour, including the non-linguistic digit runs we recover from the Qwen2.5-3B Q2 build, while Regimes II and III are consistent with their signal degradation mode. They also reported that the two modes are not strictly tied to a particular bit-width but reflect the nature of the damage, which matches our finding that regime membership is a property of the individual artifact rather than of its quantization level.

section: Regime I: collapse is an artifact property
text: Three artifacts meet the unusable-build criterion of Sec. 3.4 at Q2: Phi-3, Phi-3.5, and Qwen2.5-3B. Each loses over 97\% on both probes against their own FP16 baselines (Table 1). Two further observations support the classification on individual members: 1. Manual inspection of all 1,287 Qwen2.5-3B Q2 generations finds only non-linguistic output (digit runs, mixed-script fragments; mean length 412 {\to} 133 characters), and 2. for Phi-3.5, the common-word control collapses alongside the rare-word probes (0.95{\to}0.03 inclusion, 0.87{\to}0.03 definition; Sec. 4.5), indicating that its failure is not limited to just the rare-word vocabulary. The classification is based only on the paired probe results; the above two observations only provided the corroborating evidence.

section: Regime I: collapse is an artifact property
text: A third, instrument-based check provided the final confirmatory evidence for the classification: WikiText-2 perplexity for the Qwen2.5-3B Q2 build measures 21,797 against a 9.04 full-precision baseline ({\sim}2{,}400{\times}; Sec. 4.8), against 11–46 for every functional artifact in our perplexity sweep at Q2. Thus, the build is unusable by measurement using a staple instrument (perplexity score), not just by our two probes.

section: Regime I: collapse is an artifact property
text: All three are official registry builds that users can pull without any warning on the download page. We therefore report these separately from the selective semantic effects, where the artifacts can retain useful output while losing definitional performance.

section: Regime I: collapse is an artifact property
text: Our experiments provide no explanation for the cause of this collapse. We cannot say whether the quantization of these specific files went wrong, or whether these models are intrinsically not compressible to {\sim}2.6 bits per weight. The two possibilities are indistinguishable by their probe outputs alone.

section: Regime I: collapse is an artifact property
text: The three models also reach the Q2 failure differently. For the Phi pair (Q3_K_M variant) the drop is abrupt: definitional loss is {\leq}4\% at Q3. Qwen2.5-3B instead fails through an intermediary stage. Its Q3 outputs are still fluent English (manual inspection; non-ASCII rate 0.03%) with inclusion only moderately reduced (0.92{\to}0.83 at Q3_K_M) while definitions fall 47\% (0.89{\to}0.47; McNemar p{=}4{\times}10^{-34}; interaction p{=}5{\times}10^{-8}, odds ratio 0.27).

section: Regime I: collapse is an artifact property
text: Notably, for Qwen2.5-3B, this stage is also visible in the chosen staple instrument: its WikiText-2 perplexity rises +70.1\% at Q3, the largest Q3 penalty in our sweep. So, perplexity does register that this artifact is damaged, but not what exact capability is actually increasing the perplexity score. The following section sheds more light on this shortcoming: perplexity alone cannot reveal that the damage is definitional.

section: Regime I: collapse is an artifact property
text: This is a genuine selective dissociation at 3.1B, the largest we observed outside the sub-2B cohort, before becoming unusable at Q2. This provides another example of the continuum described below and suggests that the Qwen2.5 lineage is particularly fragile under this format.

section: Regime II: selective dissociation below {\sim}2 B
text: Every sub-2B artifact (\ddagger) shows a larger loss in definitional accuracy at Q2 compared to its corresponding surface inclusion. This holds across dense (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B), hybrid-SSM (Granite-4.0-H-1B), and hybrid-convolution (LFM2/LFM2.5) architectures.

section: Regime II: selective dissociation below {\sim}2 B
text: Two of these, Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen2.5-1.5B, are placed in stratum IIb of Table 1 because their surface inclusion also drops by roughly a third. Their probe \times quantization interactions nonetheless remain strongly definition-selective. We therefore treat IIb as the severe end of Regime II rather than a separate regime.

section: Regime II: selective dissociation below {\sim}2 B
text: Phi-4-mini (3.8B) degrades severely but symmetrically (p{=}.68): severe, not selective.

section: Regime II: selective dissociation below {\sim}2 B
text: The clearest example is Granite-4.0-H-1B: surface inclusion barely moves (-2.1\%, word-level Wilcoxon p{=}.046) while definitional accuracy falls 43.6\% (McNemar p{=}1.2{\times}10^{-28}; 179 vs. 21 discordant words). The probe \times quantization interaction is significant in six of the seven sub-2B artifacts whose Q2 build is used in the study (Table 1). LFM2-700M is the exception among these seven, with a marginal interaction (p{=}.084) because its Probe A also declines. The eighth sub-2B model, Granite-4.0-H-350M, has no Q2 build. Its Q3 endpoint appears in Table 1 (\ddagger) and is discussed below.

section: Regime II: selective dissociation below {\sim}2 B
text: The probe \times quantization interaction (Sec. 3.5) applies a logistic regression to predict probe success based on probe identity (A or B), quantization level (baseline or Q2), and their interaction. The interaction coefficient evaluates whether quantization alters the odds of success for Probe B by a distinctly different multiplicative factor than for Probe A, controlling for any shared, proportional performance decline. This relationship is quantified by the Odds Ratio (e^{\text{coefficient}}), which expresses the relative magnitude of quantization’s multiplicative effect on Probe B’s odds compared to Probe A’s. An odds ratio of 1 indicates the absence of a differential effect, signifying both Probe A and Probe B move proportionally, in either direction, or not move at all.

section: Regime II: selective dissociation below {\sim}2 B
text: For Granite-4.0-H-1B, the odds ratio is 0.21 (Wald 95% CI: 0.14–0.31). This shows that the impact of quantization on the odds of a correct definition is approximately one-fifth of its impact on the odds of surface inclusion, demonstrating a selectively differential impairment rather than a uniform decline. We report Odds Ratio in this study instead of raw percentage-point differences to systematically account for baseline performance disparities. Since Probe A is above 0.90 for twenty of the twenty-four artifacts that have a full-precision baseline, its potential for absolute percentage-point decline is constrained on an absolute percentage scale. The log-odds scale inherently corrects for this ceiling effect to provide a more robust scale to measure the degradation.

section: Regime II: selective dissociation below {\sim}2 B
text: The same pattern holds across the cohort: the six significant interactions correspond to odds ratios between 0.19 and 0.58. At Q2, the multiplicative change in the odds of producing a correct definition is between roughly one fifth and one half (\sim\times 3) of the corresponding change in surface-inclusion odds.

section: Regime II: selective dissociation below {\sim}2 B
text: Every individually significant interaction in this cohort survives the pre-specified nine-member family-wise Holm–Bonferroni correction. This includes the six sub-2B interactions at Q2, Granite-4.0-H-350M’s interaction at Q3, and Qwen2.5-3B’s interaction at Q3. The interaction for LFM2-700M is excluded from this surviving group, as it was only marginally significant prior to the correction.

section: Regime II: selective dissociation below {\sim}2 B
text: The regimes are descriptive strata over what is plausibly a continuum, and the full interaction column supports this interpretation. Qwen2.5-3B, which sits at the regime boundary, demonstrates this directly. It shows selective dissociation at Q3, then collapses at Q2: the same artifact is moving along the continuum as compression increases. Selective decline remains statistically detectable in some models in the 3–4B range, although the effect is milder compared to smaller models. Granite-4.0-H-3B (p{=}8{\times}10^{-4}) and Qwen3-4B (p{=}.007) show significant interactions, while Gemma-2-2B is marginal at p{=}.0502. Llama-3.2-3B provides a related, but distinct case. Its rare-word-selective definitional decline (\Delta_{\mathrm{B}}{=}{-}14.1\%, p_{B}{=}9{\times}10^{-8}) is statistically significant, but its probe interaction is not individually significant at this model size (p{=}.59).

section: Regime II: selective dissociation below {\sim}2 B
text: No artifact at 7B or above shows a significant definition-selective interaction. The only significant 7B+ interactions are positive, indicating that definitions are better preserved than inclusion. The effect therefore concentrates in the smaller artifacts of our sweep. The largest artifact with a significant definition-selective interaction is Qwen3-4B; among the 7B–14B artifacts, no definition-selective interaction is detected. It is not a universal law, and our roster cannot speak to sizes above 14B.

The smallest evaluated artifact provides the sharpest illustration of scale-dependence in quantization-induced definitional damage. Granite-4.0-H-350M shows a first, modest definitional dip already at Q4 (-12.5\%, McNemar p{=}.001), well before quantization becomes aggressive. By Q3 that dip has become severe semantic dissociation: definitions fall 47.3\% at Q3_K_M (0.615{\to}0.324, McNemar p{=}5{\times}10^{-22}) and 60.2\% at the more aggressive Q3_K_S, while surface inclusion moves only +0.9\%. The probe \times quantization interaction at Q3 is significant (-1.24, p{=}8{\times}10^{-16}, odds ratio 0.29), confirming the measured gap between the two probes is not there by chance.

Its common-word control for the same artifact confirms the loss is, indeed, rare-selective. Common-word definitions are unchanged at Q3 (-2.9\%, McNemar p{=}.82) while rare-word definitions fall 47.3\% (word-type \times quantization interaction -1.11, p{=}3.5{\times}10^{-6}).

We present the full analysis in the grid in Fig. 5, which shows this selective dissociation is a general pattern in small models at aggressive quantization levels. It first shows up in Granite-4.0-H-350M as it’s the smallest model (by number of parameters, not disk space) in our study. The smaller the model, the earlier in the quantization ladder definitional loss begins. While the entire sub-2B cohort shows severe degradation at Q2, the degradation starts at higher precision levels.

The Q4 is the empirically safe boundary against this degradation for larger models. The standard Q4_K_M file maintains lexical competence for every primary artifact of 1B or larger size, while the aggressive Q4_K_S already causes small significant losses (3–6%) in three of the artifacts: LFM2.5-1.2B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen3-4B. Below 1B the picture diverges: the two smallest artifacts lose 8–19% at either Q4 variant (Granite-4.0-H-350M -12.5\% / -18.9\%, Qwen2.5-0.5B -7.6\% / -10.0\%, all four significant), while LFM2-700M shows no significant loss at either.

At Q3, 22 of the 51 studied 3-bit files show significant loss. While the loss is generally minor (4–8%) in most models and concentrated in the Q3_K_S sub-variant, it’s already large in LFM2.5-1.2B (-22\%) and Granite-4.0-H-350M (-60\%) at Q3_K_S level. (Note: The 51-file count includes control-ladder files; restricting to the 27 primary artifacts returns 50 files, 21 of which show significant loss).

The selection of a sub-variant (K_L, K_M, K_S) at a particular quantization level matters as well. At 3-bit precision the damage is concentrated in the S sub-variant, which accounts for 12 of the 22 significant files. Although the trend is dominant, it is not universal. Among the thirteen artifacts with a significant 3-bit file and both sub-variants studied, S is the more damaging file in eleven, while the two exceptions, LFM2-700M and Phi-3.5-3.8B, degrade more at K_M and K_L respectively. Which sub-variant degrades more is therefore a property of the individual builds being used, rather than of their bit-class. The results are consistent with the artifact-source sensitivity of Sec. 4.9.

Fig. 5 summarizes the change from the baseline of an artifact, and Fig. 6 plots the absolute trajectory of both probes for every one of the 27 artifacts across its evaluated ladder. The K_M ladder remains essentially flat until the final precision rungs of the small models, where it falls steeply. It collapses to the floor in the three Regime-I builds and falls 43.3\% in Phi-4-mini-3.8B, the one Regime-IIb artifact at this size. Across the remaining artifacts it declines only gradually from {\sim}3 B up, the largest such loss being Llama-3.2-3B’s -14.1\% at Q2.

section: Rare-word selectivity: common-word control and frequency gradient
text: It is intuitive to ask whether defining a word is simply harder than including it in a sentence; so, any compression should damage our Probe B more. We proactively controlled for this variable of task-difficulty through two independent analyses.

section: Rare-word selectivity: common-word control and frequency gradient
text: Common-word control. Eleven artifacts, comprising every sub-2B model in the sweep plus the robust and collapse exemplars, were re-evaluated on the 100 common words with an identical pipeline (Fig. 7).

section: Rare-word selectivity: common-word control and frequency gradient
text: Regime-II (rare-selective damage): under Tier 2, the change in common-word definitions at Q2 is not significant in three Regime-II artifacts, while rare-word definitions decline sharply; the word-type \times quantization interaction tests the difference directly.

section: Rare-word selectivity: common-word control and frequency gradient
text: Granite-4.0-H-1B: common -12.0\% (McNemar p{=}.076) vs. rare -43.6\% (word-type \times quantization interaction -1.19, p{=}4{\times}10^{-4}). LFM2.5-1.2B: common -7.6\% (p{=}.33) vs. rare -49.0\% (interaction -1.17, p{=}2{\times}10^{-4}). LFM2-700M: common +3.9\% (p{=}.65) vs. rare -41.8\% (interaction -1.38, p{=}1.4{\times}10^{-6}). (Note: interactions are word-clustered, with negative values indicating rare-selective damage. Granite-4.0-H-350M, which has no Q2 build, shows the same signature at Q3; it is the sixth significant interaction counted below.)

section: Rare-word selectivity: common-word control and frequency gradient
text: The two Regime-IIb artifacts in this cohort lose common-word definitions as well: Llama-3.2-1B -29.6\% (p{=}4{\times}10^{-5}), and Qwen2.5-1.5B -36.7\% (p{=}2{\times}10^{-6}), which is consistent with their severe-on-both-probes classification. Yet their rare-word loss remains significantly larger (interactions -1.11, p{=}4{\times}10^{-4}; -1.48, p{=}5{\times}10^{-6}).

section: Rare-word selectivity: common-word control and frequency gradient
text: In the remaining two sub-2B artifacts the interaction is directionally consistent but not individually significant. Qwen2.5-0.5B -0.39, p{=}.12, and LFM2-1.2B -0.30, p{=}.32. The latter does have a significant common-word dip of -13.4\%, p{=}.043. The broader pattern of word-type interaction is significant in six of the eight sub-2B artifacts, and no sub-2B artifact shows the reverse pattern. For larger models and Regime I artifacts: at Q2, Llama-3.2-3B’s rare-word definitions drop 14.1\% (p{=}9{\times}10^{-8}) while common-word definitions are unchanged (+3.7\%, McNemar p{=}.55); Gemma-2-9B shows no degradation on either word class at any level; and Phi-3.5 collapses on both.

section: Rare-word selectivity: common-word control and frequency gradient
text: Task difficulty alone cannot explain this effect: within the same task and the same artifact, damage is concentrated on low-frequency vocabulary.

section: Rare-word selectivity: common-word control and frequency gradient
text: Frequency gradient within the rare set. The same conclusion is further validated from frequency selectivity inside the 429-word set itself, using its Zipf range (0–3.81). Conditioning strictly on words defined correctly at baseline, the probability that a definition is lost at Q2 rises significantly with rarity in six of the seven sub-2B artifacts with a Q2 build (Fig. 8). Rarest vs. least-rare tercile loss rates: Granite-4.0-H-1B 0.57 vs. 0.37 (logistic Zipf coefficient -0.59, p{=}.002); LFM2-700M 0.58 vs. 0.34 (-0.83, p{<}.001); LFM2-1.2B 0.51 vs. 0.21 (-0.96, p{<}.001); LFM2.5-1.2B 0.67 vs. 0.48 (-0.60, p{=}.003); Qwen2.5-1.5B 0.80 vs. 0.53 (-1.10, p{<}.001); Llama-3.2-1B 0.73 vs. 0.58 (-0.51, p{=}.013). The exception is Qwen2.5-0.5B, whose losses are frequency-flat (+0.01, p{=}.97), consistent with its lowest baseline competence (0.68) and unreliable inclusion metric. Without that conditioning, a Zipf \times quantization term over all 429 words (word-clustered) points the same way in five of these seven artifacts and is significant in two (Qwen2.5-1.5B and LFM2-1.2B), since it also counts words the model never knew, which cannot be lost.

section: Vocabulary size does not predict fragility; scale does
text: The fragmentation hypothesis predicts that models with relatively smaller vocabulary (32k vs. 131k), which split rare words into more subword tokens, should degrade more. It follows from how subword tokenizers are built (Sennrich et al., 2016; Kudo & Richardson, 2018): algorithms such as Byte-Pair Encoding start from individual characters and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent symbol pair in the training corpus into a new token, until the vocabulary reaches its target size. Since rare words are made of character sequences that co-occur infrequently, the merges needed to assemble them into a single token are lower priority and often do not survive the fixed vocabulary budget, leaving rare words split across more, shorter subword tokens. Common words, built from frequently co-occurring sequences, get merged early and typically end up as a single token, or at least fewer tokens than a rare word of comparable length.

section: Vocabulary size does not predict fragility; scale does
text: Our data do not support the fragmentation hypothesis, in three ways (Figs. 9 and 10).

section: Vocabulary size does not predict fragility; scale does
text: 1. Two dense Mistral-lineage artifacts whose vocabularies differ fourfold, Mistral-7B (32k) and Mistral-Nemo-12B (131k), are both robust (-5.7\% vs. -8.2\% definitional), though they also differ in parameter count and in baseline precision, the 12B being measured from a Q8 file rather than FP16.

section: Vocabulary size does not predict fragility; scale does
text: 2. Across the 32k vocabulary cohort, Mistral-7B is robust while Phi-3/3.5 collapse entirely, signalling failure at the artifact level rather than vocabulary level; and

section: Vocabulary size does not predict fragility; scale does
text: 3. Across all 23 non-collapse primary artifacts with a Q2 build, the Spearman correlation between vocabulary size and definitional drop is \rho{=}0.12 (p{=}.59). Conversely, the correlation for parameter count is very strong: \rho{=}0.72 (p{=}1{\times}10^{-4}).

section: Vocabulary size does not predict fragility; scale does
text: The scale correlation is not an effect of pooling two build providers: it holds independently within each build-provider subset of the 23 non-collapse artifacts (Ollama-native \rho{=}0.75, n{=}10, p{=}.013; Unsloth \rho{=}0.66, n{=}13, p{=}.015). The same-tokenizer Qwen2.5 ladder (0.5B/1.5B/7B, all sharing the same 152k tokenizer) shows severe definitional damage at small scale that vanishes by 7B (-66.6\% at 1.5B vs. -3.6\% at 7B). (Note: We do not interpret the ladder as strictly monotonic. The 0.5B model’s losses are frequency-flat and its inclusion metric is unreliable, so that artifact is not showing the rare-selective damage the ladder tracks. The 3B artifact is the collapsed build discussed earlier.)

section: Vocabulary size does not predict fragility; scale does
text: So we could claim that it is the parameter count, not tokenizer vocabulary, that predicts definitional robustness under quantization.

section: Vocabulary size does not predict fragility; scale does
text: This is not a surprising pattern for us. A systematic on-device evaluation of GGUF-quantized models had already reported the same scale-dependence for reasoning and code generation (Song et al., 2025): from Q5_K to Q3_K, a 14B model holds its GSM8K accuracy at 89\% while a 1.5B model falls from 59.1\% to 46.5\% over the identical precision range, with code generation degrading even more sharply. While their results are measured on mathematical reasoning or code correctness, our result extends the scale-dependence to lexical-semantic knowledge. Zhou et al. (2026b) found a similar threshold when fitting a scaling law to 293 post-training quantization configurations across the Qwen3 and Llama-3 families. They found a phase transition on entry to 2-bit. Below roughly 2B parameters, performance collapsed across every task type and the scaling fits stopped converging, while models of 4B and above maintained their memorization and application scores, provided group size and calibration data were chosen well. Their group-size term is the nearest analogue to the K_S/K_M distinction we observe at Q4.

section: Vocabulary size does not predict fragility; scale does
text: The same relationship holds in all three studies: larger models are disproportionately more resilient to quantization damage. The fact that this relationship reappears across such different tasks, metrics and quantization severities makes it unlikely to be specific only to reasoning benchmarks, or to our own probes.

section: Vocabulary size does not predict fragility; scale does
text: This scale effect is independently corroborated by Dutta et al. (2024). They find that across different model families (Llama-2, Yi) and different tasks (MMLU, PIQA, HellaSwag, ARC), larger models flip fewer individual answers under quantization than smaller ones, while noting that the residual rate stays non-negligible: Llama-2-70B still flips 3 – 8\% of answers at 4-bit. They attribute it, tentatively, to larger models being more resistant to the perturbation introduced by quantization. None of the four studies varied scale while holding the other factors fixed, so the convergence is consistent with a general effect, but does not establish one.

The correlation in the previous subsection is computed across model families, so parameter count as a variable is confounded there with difference in the training data, instruction-tuning recipe, build provider, and their tokenizers. The presented results might raise the question of whether the results we show are because the model families themselves are weaker. Our experimental sweep is large enough to answer that directly. We have six model families which provide multiple parameter sizes on a fixed tokenizer (for that family), covering 18 of the 27 artifacts and 129 file-level evaluations: Granite-4.0-H (350M/1B/3B/7B, 100k vocabulary size), Qwen2.5 (0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B, 152k), LFM2 (700M/1.2B/8B, 65k), Ministral-3 (3B/8B/14B, 131k), Llama-3.2 (1B/3B, 128k), and Gemma-2 (2B/9B, 256k).
Within each of these families, the tokenizer, the build provider and the evaluation protocol are held fixed.

Fig. 11 compares the members of each family at their most aggressive shared precision level used in the study, using the worst published sub-variant at that level (out of K_L, K_M and K_S). Meaning, across a family of models, such as Ministral-3, we take the most aggressive quantized variant from each of the 3 models we studied. For example, for Ministral-3 3B/8B/14B we analyse the effect of changing just the parameter size at that quantization level. Every other result in this paper uses the K_M file by default. We depart from that default here to capture the broadest available evidence across all 129 files, without restricting six ladders to a single sub-variant.

Within each family we compare its smallest member against its largest at that matched level (e.g., Gemma2:9B-q2 vs Gemma2:2B-q2). This gives one comparison per family and six in total, across the changing parameter count. The cross-family correlation predicts that the larger member should be less damaged in definitional degradation, which we directly check here within-family.

In five of the six families the larger member is the less damaged one. The single exception is Ministral-3, by less than half a percentage point. The same five of six hold under each of the three sub-variant conventions: 1. the K_M file alone, 2. the worst published sub-variant, and 3. the mean over every published sub-variant. Changing the sub-variant used for analysis does not affect the overall inference we are claiming.

Granite-4.0-H is the clearest instance we show, which has the widest parameter span we studied, across a twentyfold range on a single 100k tokenizer. Its three dense models show a clear size gradient: the 350M member already loses 60.2\% of its definitional capability by Q3, its 1B member is intact until Q2, and the 3B member loses 8.1\% at Q2. Its 7B member is not significantly damaged at any level, but it changes its architecture to hybrid-MoE. We cannot claim that last step as parameter count alone, as we cannot separate the change in architecture as a confound for it, but the pattern holds for the remaining three 350M, 1B and 3B members, across a single dense (hyb-SSM) architecture.

Fig. 12 plots every level for every member of all the 6 families in this section. Within a family the larger member’s trajectory sits at or above the smaller member’s trajectory at nearly every level, from which we infer that increasing scale raises the endpoint (across family members at the same level), as well as provides a later, and shallower descent into semantic degradation. The two families producing dissimilar curves in Fig. 12 are explained here:

1. Ministral-3’s whole curve is almost flat, as none of its members shows meaningful semantic damage at all, its three artifacts moving by -2.3\%, +0.8\% and -2.7\% at Q2. And the -0.4\% gap between its 3B and 14B members is negligible.

2. Qwen2.5 does conform to our claim, at its endpoints. Its 7B member loses 3.6\% against the 0.5B member’s 20.3\%, but it is not monotonic in between, as the 1.5B member loses 66.6\%. We have already shown that the 0.5B artifact’s losses are frequency-flat and its inclusion metric is not reliable, so it does not show the rare-selective signature the ladder is following, even though its definitional loss is real. Its 3B member is the collapsed build.

We do not claim that these ladders hold everything except parameter count fixed. Training data and compute per size are not observable from the released artifacts, since even open-source releases publish only weights and architectures. Two families also change architecture class at their largest member: Granite-4.0-H at 7B and LFM2 at 8B are both mixture-of-experts builds activating a fraction of their stored parameters per token ({\sim}1 B and {\sim}1.5 B respectively), where every smaller member of both families is dense.

Two members are also measured from a baseline below full precision, because no higher-precision build fits within our 16GB VRAM budget: Ministral-3’s 14B member from a Q6 file, and Granite-4.0-H’s 7B member from a Q8 file. Using an already-quantized baseline instead of FP16 understates an artifact’s true degradation, since the quality lost between FP16 and that baseline never enters the measured delta. For Granite-4.0-H-7B this makes the reported robustness look somewhat stronger than a full-precision comparison would. For Ministral-3 the direction is reversed: it is already the flatter of the two exception families, so the below-FP baseline does not explain its flatness. Neither caveat is load-bearing on its own.

The narrower conclusion we claim here, which the cross-family correlation could not establish, is that the association between scale and definitional robustness survives when family, provider and tokenizer are held constant, in five of the six families we can test it in.

section: Perplexity tracks the damage but cannot calibrate it
text: We tested nine artifact-matched ladders (8 models spanning 0.5–7B in parameter size, including two robust artifacts, one unusable build, and two available builds of the same model) to test whether a standard aggregate metric can calibrate rare-word semantic degradation.

section: Perplexity tracks the damage but cannot calibrate it
text: WikiText-2 (Merity et al., 2017) perplexity (llama-perplexity, 100 chunks of 512 tokens, identical text at every level of a ladder, K_M files) rises along the same familiar accelerating curve documented in published quantization-quality tables over the 3–8 bit range they cover (Kurt, 2026), continuing unbroken into Q2 in every functional ladder, across dissociating as well as robust artifacts (Figs. 4 c, 13, and 14).

section: Perplexity tracks the damage but cannot calibrate it
text: At Q2 the penalty is +47.6\% for Granite-4.0-H-1B (11.80{\to}17.42), +137.9\% for LFM2.5-1.2B, +145.3\% for Qwen2.5-1.5B, +25.9\% for Qwen2.5-0.5B. Crucially, the penalty is noticeable for the robust models as well: +44.7\% for the robust Qwen2.5-7B (7.71{\to}11.16) and +18.0\% for the robust Granite-4.0-H-7B MoE (from its Q8 baseline).

section: Perplexity tracks the damage but cannot calibrate it
text: The perplexity curve is not flat, but it cannot be read as a measure of definitional damage, in three specific ways.

section: Perplexity tracks the damage but cannot calibrate it
text: 1. Matched Penalties, Opposite Outcomes: Qwen2.5-7B and Granite-4.0-H-1B suffer nearly identical Q2 perplexity penalties (+44.7\% vs. +47.6\%) while losing 3.6\% vs. 43.6\% of their definitions, respectively: a twelvefold difference in lexical damage from the same perplexity signal (Fig. 14 b). On the odds scale each artifact is measured against its own Probe B baseline (0.897 vs. 0.844), not against Probe A as in the probe \times quantization interaction odds ratio. Qwen2.5-7B’s odds fall from 8.71 to 6.41, a ratio of 0.74, against Granite-4.0-H-1B’s 5.41 to 0.91, a ratio of 0.17: a 4.4 -fold gap. The direction and the qualitative result are the same on both scales.

section: Perplexity tracks the damage but cannot calibrate it
text: 2. Matched Damage, Unmatched Penalties: In contrast, Granite-4.0-H-1B and the Unsloth build of Llama-3.2-1B lose the same 43.6\% of definitions (both define 362 of 429 words at FP16 and 204 at Q2, though not the same words) at +47.6\% vs. +93.7\% perplexity, a twofold divergence in penalty for the same lexical outcome. The \Delta PPL {\to}\Delta definition trade-off at Q3 spans wildly, from +9.2\%{\to}{-}1.6\% (Qwen2.5-7B) to +70.1\%{\to}{-}47.1\% (Qwen2.5-3B).

section: Perplexity tracks the damage but cannot calibrate it
text: 3. No Usable Absolute Threshold: Absolute perplexity doesn’t provide any baseline for semantic retention. LFM2.5-1.2B at Q3 (PPL 24.8) defines 60.4\% of the rare words while Qwen2.5-1.5B at Q2 (PPL 25.0) defines just 29.1\%. Within a single tokenizer, where absolute perplexities are directly comparable, Qwen2.5-3B at Q3 (PPL 15.38) defines 47.1\% while Qwen2.5-0.5B at FP16 (PPL 15.29) defines 67.8\%: the almost same aggregate metric describing a quantization-damaged artifact as well as a merely small healthy one.

section: Perplexity tracks the damage but cannot calibrate it
text: Across the nine Q2 endpoints, perplexity change and definitional loss show strong rank-correlation (Spearman \rho{=}0.96; 0.95 excluding the collapsed build): both worsen together as overall damage grows more severe. This correlation however does not provide a useful threshold to detect the definitional damage. Neither the absolute perplexity nor its change tells a practitioner how much definitional knowledge a given build has lost. However, perplexity does flag the unusable quantized builds clearly. The collapsed Qwen2.5-3B Q2 build scores PPL 21,797 against a 9.04 baseline. Beyond flagging unusable builds, perplexity cannot tell a practitioner that the ability to define rare words is what was lost.

section: Perplexity tracks the damage but cannot calibrate it
text: Perplexity, as an aggregate likelihood over ordinary text, is dominated by common tokens; it tracks generic degradation, but is not designed to isolate the selective loss of a narrow, low-frequency capability. This limitation is partly inherent to the metric itself: perplexity is computed as the inverse of the geometric mean of per-token probabilities, so a handful of catastrophically low-probability tokens making up a lost rare-word definition in our study can be mathematically cancelled by higher probabilities elsewhere in the same pass (Dutta et al., 2024).

section: Perplexity tracks the damage but cannot calibrate it
text: A practitioner selecting a quantization level based on standard perplexity tables will see Q2 as generically worse, but they cannot infer why it is worse, specifically if they want to use the model for tasks which require rare-word knowledge and capabilities. Perplexity cannot reveal the exact threshold where a model forgets the meaning of rare words, nor can it signal which model has relatively better semantic capabilities compared to another model with the same score.

Quantized builds of the same model from different providers are not equivalent (Fig. 15). Llama-3.2-1B in Ollama’s build loses 34.3\% / 61.1\% (inclusion/definition) at Q2; the independent Unsloth build loses 11.1\% / 43.6\%. On the odds scale, which we are using since the two builds’ baselines differ (0.821 vs. 0.844), the same asymmetry holds: Ollama’s odds fall from 4.59 to 0.47, a ratio of 0.10, against Unsloth’s 5.41 to 0.91, a ratio of 0.17 (identical to Granite-4.0-H-1B’s by coincidence). The build sensitivity is therefore not merely a result of using a percentage-change scale. Nor does it begin at Q2. At FP16 only 63 of the 429 definitions are identical across the two builds, so part of what separates them is present before quantization, and our design cannot separate it from the quantization pipeline. The builds also diverge at Q4_K_M, where Unsloth’s loses 5.0\% (p{=}.010) and Ollama’s gains 1.7\%.
The larger loss in the definitions than inclusion is replicated across both builds, but the magnitude of the loss is different.

Our regime classification of a file under study is based on the artifact, not models. The strata of Table 1 classify artifacts as well. This difference between build providers affects how a model is classified. For example, Llama-3.2-1B’s Ollama build falls in Regime IIb, while its Unsloth build falls in Regime II proper, its inclusion falling 11.1\% against 43.6\% on definitions.

We found that the dissociation is not specific to a single provider’s quantization pipeline. Our sweep itself spans both providers: the sub-2B cohort contains Ollama-native artifacts (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B) and Unsloth artifacts (Granite-4.0-H-1B, the LFM2 family).

Build sensitivity also replicates on the aggregate metric for Llama-3.2-1B: the two builds’ FP16 files score identical WikiText-2 perplexity (15.14), yet at Q2 Ollama’s build costs +158.0\% (15.14{\to}39.07) against Unsloth’s +93.7\% (15.14{\to}29.34), which is directionally aligned with their definitional losses (-61.1\% vs. -43.6\%). So perplexity does pick up the difference between the two builds. Although this evaluation rests on a single model we used for calibration across two build providers, we can only infer about directionality, not magnitude of definitional loss. Our data do not support the use of one provider’s perplexity loss to quantitatively predict or proxy for definitional loss of an alternate provider’s build of the same model.
The behaviour of a quantized model therefore must be validated at the artifact level, not the architecture level.

section: Why saying survives while knowing fails
text: GGUF K-quants (Gerganov et al., 2023–2026) use different effective precisions for different tensors: they preserve token-embedding and output matrices at higher effective bit-widths while compressing interior FFN, attention, or state-space blocks. Producing a word supplied in the prompt (surface inclusion) depends mostly on embedding and output-matrix precision, which GGUF’s scheme protects, plus the local context. A definition, however, is not retrieved directly as a stored string; it must be constructed at inference time by composing semantic associations encoded as distributed representations across the model’s interior weights. If that information is more vulnerable to quantization, definitional performance could fall while surface inclusion remains relatively intact.

section: Why saying survives while knowing fails
text: The frequency results fit this interpretation. Low-frequency words receive relatively less exposure during pre-training, so their semantic representation plausibly contains less redundancy and would therefore be more vulnerable to weight perturbations. Quantization noise could then disrupt their semantic reconstruction first, while the common-word control, whose associations are reinforced by far more training exposure, survives the same noise.

section: Why saying survives while knowing fails
text: An independent, similar result points the same way from a different task. Hua et al. (2026) found that quantization changed answers selectively based on how confident the model was about them. Items the full-precision model was least confident about flipped three to eleven times more often after quantization than items it was confident about. Rare words are also likely to be low-confidence items, so a process that preferentially damages low-confidence items would reach rare words first, without needing any lexically specific mechanism. Their probe is a bias benchmark and ours is a lexical task, so this is corroborating evidence about which items are fragile. Sec. 6 considers the same selectivity at the decision level, where confidence becomes decision margin.

section: Why saying survives while knowing fails
text: Under the precision-allocation interpretation, our two probes benchmark opposite ends of the lexical pipeline: Probe A measures surface-form production (which is protected), while Probe B measures the integrity of meaning construction (which is not protected). This structural reason might explain why the dissociation runs in the direction it does and not the reverse. The dissociation appears across architectures with very different interior blocks: attention, Mamba-2 SSM, hybrid-convolution. GGUF uses the same weight-block quantization scheme for all three, while state-space models have needed separate, architecture-specific quantization methods (Chiang et al., 2025). A generic effect of low-precision weight perturbation on the distributed semantic associations is therefore a more plausible explanation than a failure tied to one particular architecture.

section: Why saying survives while knowing fails
text: We did not inspect the affected weights directly, however, so this remains an interpretation of the behavioural results rather than a mechanistic finding.

Duan (2026) finds that sparse-autoencoder features of a full-precision model survive RTN quantization in a graded rather than cliff-like fashion. Most features that do not survive RTN quantization are degraded (blurred) rather than damaged (destroyed); which features survive can be predicted from their full-precision activation statistics; and perplexity can miss the feature damage entirely. Superficially, this differs from our finding that quantization can substantially reduce rare-word definition performance. The possible explanation we propose, as a hypothesis, is compositional: individual features can remain usable even when their combination becomes less reliable. A definition, however, requires several pieces of semantic information to be combined during generation. Retrieval of a single feature survives blurring; reconstruction of a precise meaning from many simultaneously blurred, thinly-reinforced features fails first. This interpretation would also explain why the definitional failure concentrates on rare words, which have the fewest redundant supports, and why surface inclusion is spared, since it leans on protected tensors and local context rather than deep composition. Perplexity can also miss the effect, since common tokens contribute much more to its aggregate value.
Testing whether quantization actually disrupts feature combinations would require analysis of the model’s internal representations, which we leave for future work (Sec. 7).

At the representational level, Wang et al. (2026) traced quantization-induced loss of factual recall to the last layers of the network, using attribution at both the neuron and layer level. They found that the relations most affected were those where full-precision performance had not saturated. We interpret low-saturation knowledge as thinly encoded, the same property we attribute to rare words, argued from the representational side rather than the behavioural one. Their measured losses are modest and they conclude that quantization is still worth doing. Our results are compatible with theirs. They evaluated 4-bit and 8-bit builds from GPTQ, AWQ and integer quantization, and state that 1-bit and 2-bit quantization is outside their scope. Our sharpest dissociations occur at Q2 and Q3, below that range. Even at the bit-widths they tested, five of our artifacts show significant definition loss at Q4, all at or below 4B, smaller than any model they tested. This is consistent with their finding that smaller models within a family lose more.

section: Stored capacity may matter more than active compute
text: A parameter-count only interpretation of the scale effect is complicated by our two Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) artifacts. MoE architectures by design contain a large number of total parameters, but a single token activates only a small subset of those during auto-regressive inference.

section: Stored capacity may matter more than active compute
text: The two MoE artifacts in our sweep are both robust through Q2, despite active compute comparable to the dense sub-2B models that show severe dissociation. LFM2-8B-A1B (8.3B stored, {\sim}1.5 B active per token) loses only \Delta_{\mathrm{B}}{=}{-}9.0\% (interaction p{=}.46), and Granite-4.0-H-7B (7.0B stored, {\sim}1 B active) gains \Delta_{\mathrm{B}}{=}{+}1.3\% (interaction p{=}.006) from a Q8 baseline, which understates its degradation relative to a full-precision comparison (Sec. 4.7). In both models the interaction coefficient is positive on the log-odds scale (Table 1): definitional accuracy holds up at least as well as surface inclusion once Probe A’s near-ceiling baseline is accounted for, though only Granite-4.0-H-7B’s coefficient is individually significant.

section: Stored capacity may matter more than active compute
text: This resilience suggests that stored capacity protects semantic knowledge independent of active compute, the two quantities which normally get confounded in dense architectures. It aligns with the redundancy hypothesis above as well, that a rare-word association must survive the destruction of its redundant copies, whose number scales with total stored parameters rather than with the parameters active in a single forward pass.

section: Stored capacity may matter more than active compute
text: Allen-Zhu & Li (2025) provide a quantitative baseline for our qualitative hypothesis: transformer language models are estimated to have a knowledge capacity of 2 bits per parameter; quantization to int8 shows negligible impact on this capacity, while int4 reduces it to roughly 0.7 bits per parameter.

section: Stored capacity may matter more than active compute
text: Two further results from their study support our behavioural observation:

section: Stored capacity may matter more than active compute
text: 1. Mixture-of-experts models retain nearly all of their theoretical capacity despite activating only a small fraction of their parameters per token (activation sparsity). With 32 experts, capacity falls only 1.3-fold relative to the base dense scaling law in their 1,000-exposure setting, and 1.5-fold at 100 exposures, even though just 8.8% of total parameters are active during inference. If capacity were dependent only on active parameters, that 8.8% figure would imply a much larger reduction, roughly eleven-fold. The observed reduction therefore supports the premise that knowledge capacity tracks stored rather than active parameters. They do not quantize any mixture-of-experts model, so whether that stored capacity is what protects our own MoE artifacts under quantization remains our inference, not their result.

section: Stored capacity may matter more than active compute
text: 2. Separately, they find that knowledge seen only 100 times during training, what they term “ 100-exposure ”, is stored at half the bit-per-parameter density of knowledge encountered 1,000 times: 1 bit per parameter rather than the 2 bits their sufficiently-trained models reach. Less-exposed knowledge occupies less capacity independent of quantization, the same low-exposure, low-redundancy logic proposed above for rare words.

section: Stored capacity may matter more than active compute
text: The perplexity ladder of Granite-4.0-H-7B completes this picture. Its Q2 perplexity rises only 18.0\% (9.09{\to}10.73 from its Q8 baseline), the smallest penalty among our nine ladders, and its definition score changes minimally by +1.3\% as well. This is despite having active compute of just {\sim}1 B, the scale at which the 1–1.5B artifacts in the same ladder set all dissociate and pay perplexity penalties of +47.6\% to +158.0\% (Sec. 4.8, Fig. 14 a). On both metrics, definitional degradation and aggregate perplexity, this MoE artifact’s behaviour is more consistent with its larger stored capacity (total parameters), rather than being limited by the vulnerabilities of small active compute.

section: Stored capacity may matter more than active compute
text: This should not be read as a general claim that larger models are more robust. Hua et al. (2026) evaluated Qwen2.5 from 0.5B to 14B and found no consistent scaling advantage for bias stability: the 14B artifacts were no more stable than the 0.5B ones, and the within-family pattern was erratic. Their measurements stop at 4-bit and concern alignment behaviour rather than stored knowledge, so the two findings do not conflict. Taken together, these findings show that scale protection is capability-specific: our evidence is strictly constrained to the preservation of lexical-semantic knowledge at the K-quant floor.
For practitioners deploying GGUF artifacts on consumer hardware, we recommend the following four guidelines:

1. Q4_K_M is lexically stable for every artifact of 1B or larger in our sweep except one, Unsloth’s build of Llama-3.2-1B, which loses 5\%. The more aggressive Q4_K_S variant already starts to show small losses in some artifacts, and below 1B two of the three artifacts already lose material definitional accuracy at Q4.

2. At precisions below Q4, small (\lesssim 2B) models should be assumed to lose definitional knowledge even when output remains fluent. Applications depending on lexical precision, such as technical writing, education, translation, or domain-specific assistants, should validate the models at the artifact level. This is particularly relevant for on-device or edge deployments, which are more likely to run smaller models on consumer hardware.

3. Unusable Q2 builds can ship without any warning. To screen for this before deployment, we recommend using either a 100-word common-word probe or a single WikiText-2 perplexity check. Both are cheap and catch unusable build failure. Unusable builds fail even on common words (as confirmed directly in one case, Phi-3.5), and perplexity rises far beyond any functional build in the one Regime-I artifact we measured a ladder for ({\sim}2{,}400{\times} baseline), while every Regime-II artifact in our nine-ladder sweep remained within functional range.

4. Perplexity catches unusable builds, but it is not a substitute for capability-specific validation. In our nine perplexity ladders, we observed that nearly identical Q2 perplexity penalties (+44.7\% / +47.6\%) correspond to both intact (-3.6\%) and severely dissociated (-43.6\%) definitional outcomes. No perplexity threshold, on either its absolute value or its change, identifies the selective definitional damage. This blindness is not specific to perplexity or to our probes; for instance, aggregate bias scores conceal response-level flips by averaging them out (Hua et al., 2026). Hua et al. recommend a stratified, task-specific post-quantization evaluation in place of benchmark averages, and our results support the same for lexical semantics.

Scorer and metric. Our scorer is a string matcher, not an LLM judge; we bound the matcher’s error with an LLM-judge census of every definition (primary judge gpt-oss-20b, replicated by Gemma 4; its misses are quantization-asymmetric) and release the word lists, synonym key, evaluation code, every definition with both judges’ verdicts, both human-verification samples (for the synonym key and the judges), and all {\sim}100 k word-level scored definition outcomes at https://github.com/NietzscheDostoevsky/snk-release. The word list (Gemini 3.1 Pro, Google), the synonym key (Claude Fable 5, Anthropic) and the scorer’s validation (gpt-oss-20b, OpenAI; Gemma 4, Google) all involve LLMs, which we disclose as a potential source of circularity. The primary judge’s developer has no other role in the pipeline, and each judge agrees with a human author on 62 of 65 items; the human verification of 65 definitions and of 20 synonym-key entries is released with the reviewer’s per-item verdicts, and both checks can be re-read from released data. The rare-word set’s rarity claim rests on corpus statistics (Zipf frequency) alone. The binary inclusion metric is insensitive to overuse (Qwen2.5-0.5B inflates its Q2 score by repetition, which we flag).

Probe A is deliberately the lighter task, and at full precision it scores above Probe B in all but two of the 27 artifacts (both Qwen2.5; Fig. 6). Our conclusions rest on the probe contrast and the controls, and do not require the two probes to be equally hard.

Decision margins and selectivity. The probe asymmetry can also be viewed in terms of decision margin. Dutta et al. (2024) show that quantization disproportionately flips low-margin decisions and that harder tasks flip more than easier ones; Hua et al. (2026) find the same item-level selectivity from a different confidence statistic. Both our probes supply the target word; what differs is what we are asking the model to generate in response to those probes. Probe A scores the surface inclusion of a token already in the context, which can be argued as a relatively high-margin operation, whereas Probe B requires the model to construct and produce that word’s stored meaning unaided, a comparatively lower-margin task. Margin offers a plausible candidate mechanism for the inclusion/definitional dissociation, i.e., “rare-word meaning is thinly encoded” and “rare-word definitions are low-margin decisions” describe the same phenomenon at two levels of description, and margin might be how thin encoding shows up at the decision boundary. Our behavioural finding that fluent production of words the artifact can no longer define holds under either reading, and the common-word control already rules out the pure task-difficulty version of the account.

Our result establishes the behavioural dissociation, but this design cannot tell us whether the underlying explanation should be described at the representation level (“thin encoding”) or decision level (“low margin”). The distinguishing test is a per-token log-probability analysis, with margins measured directly on both probes across the ladder, which our pipeline did not capture and which we leave to future work (Sec. 7).

Evaluation ecosystem and corpora. Scope varies across controls and comparisons: the common-word control covers 11 of the 27 artifacts (including all eight sub-2B models), while perplexity comparisons span nine ladders across eight models (0.5B–7B), encompassing two robust artifacts and one unusable build. Each probe uses a single prompt template, and perplexity evaluations rely on a single corpus (WikiText-2) and a single measurement protocol (llama-perplexity, 512-token chunks). Prompt sensitivity evaluation and multi-corpus generalization, alongside perplexity protocol sensitivity control, remain future work.

All artifacts were served through the Ollama/llama.cpp inference ecosystem, and originate from two quantization providers (Ollama-native and Unsloth). One model in the sweep was evaluated in both providers’ builds. Degradation direction was consistent across the two builds, but magnitude differed. From this single comparison we can infer the effect’s directionality but not its magnitude across build providers.

To address mutable registry tags and potential upstream re-quantization, exact registry tags for all evaluated artifacts are logged in the released package. Cryptographic digests were not captured during initial probe sweeps due to local storage retention constraints; however, the released package includes SHA-256 digests for 46 of the 51 perplexity files, covering eight of the nine ladders (excluding Qwen2.5-1.5B).

Linguistic scope. The study is English-only. Several sweep families (Qwen2.5, Mistral-Nemo, Gemma-3n) are explicitly multilingual, so part of their trained capacity also serves languages that our probes do not test. Also, whether the rare-word dissociation observed in English extends to other languages, particularly lower-resource languages, remains untested.

Scale-severity anomalies. The relationship between model scale and quantization severity is not strictly monotonic within a family (Sec. 4.7). On the shared Qwen2.5 tokenizer the 1.5B member loses more of its definitions at Q2 than the smaller 0.5B member does. The same lineage’s 3.1B member is unusable at Q2 and is excluded from the scale trend for that reason (Sec. 4.2). As with the other Regime-I artifacts, we cannot distinguish a quantizer error in that build from a capacity threshold specific to that model at this compression ratio. The probe outputs alone do not favour either explanation.

The behavioural evidence localizes the damage to meaning construction rather than surface inclusion. The natural next step is to identify which internal structures fail, and the present results specify what these experiments should test, beginning with three directions of increasing evidential strength.

First, embedding-geometry tracking: measure the geometry of rare-word representations across the quantization ladder in the models already studied, requiring instrumentation rather than new sweeps. It would establish whether the artifacts that lose definitions are the ones whose rare-word geometry moves, and whether the words lost are those that move furthest.

Second, a predictive signature: link a representational statistic computed on the FP16 model to which specific words lose their definitions after quantization, in the spirit of the survival predictors of Duan (2026). It could provide a word-level prediction of which words would survive quantization, and up to what level of aggressive compression.

Third, the causal step: protect candidate fragile directions during quantization and show definitions recover, or inject selective perturbations and show definitions break while surface production is untouched. Qwen2.5-3B at Q3 could be used as a natural testbed: a dense, HF-loadable artifact with a large, clean behavioural dissociation on fluent output (0.92{\to}0.83 inclusion vs. 0.89{\to}0.47 definition) and a same-tokenizer family ladder for scale contrasts. Before such internal measurements, however, the dequantized model should first be verified to reproduce the behavioural dissociation observed in the present evaluation.

A fourth direction addresses the decision-margin question: re-running both probes through an inference pipeline that logs per-token output probabilities would let us compute decision margins and quantization-induced flips in the spirit of Dutta et al. (2024). This would test whether the definitions lost under quantization are disproportionately low-margin decisions, and could provide a mechanistic account of the dissociation that the current log-probability-free Ollama runs cannot establish. Existing margin and uncertainty results (Dutta et al., 2024; Hua et al., 2026) are computed by ranking a supplied set of answer options. Probe B has no option set, so the test proposed here is per-token margins over free generation, scored against a reference definition rather than against a chosen option.

A fifth direction would extend Probe A from production to usage. Verbatim inclusion establishes that the word form is produced, but does not establish whether it is deployed with its intended sense. Separating the two requires a usage-quality assessment on the generated sentences. Since appropriate use and grammatical correctness are subject to expert judgement rather than deterministic scoring, a rigorous usage-quality evaluation requires qualified annotators, an agreement statistic across at least two of them, and a word-paired sample large enough to support the comparison. A narrower, deterministic proxy is available for one part of it: malformed morphological variants of the target word (ephemerous for ephemeral, idiosyncracy for idiosyncrasy) can be detected by dictionary lookup against WordNet and the web2 word list, which were used as independent sources to validate the stimulus set used here as well. This would provide a reproducible measure of word-form corruption without requiring judgement about semantic appropriateness.

Finally, the evaluation itself can be broadened naturally to multilingual lexicons, additional GGUF sources, prompt-template robustness, and perplexity generalization across additional corpora and measurement protocols.

Across 27 quantized artifacts spanning four architecture backbones, aggressive GGUF quantization does not degrade lexical competence uniformly. Below {\sim}2 B parameters, it can split definitional knowledge from fluent surface production, leaving models that continue to produce rare words in their output, usually at near-baseline rates, after losing the ability to define them. The damage is rare-word-selective and frequency-graded, begins earlier in the quantization ladder as the model size decreases, is not calibrated by perplexity, and varies between different provider builds of the same model. Total collapse, where it occurs, is a property of individual quantized builds rather than an intrinsic property of rare-word semantics. Tokenizer vocabulary size does not predict it (Spearman \rho{=}0.12). Model capacity and training exposure, not the token inventory, are the probable constraints on the retention of meaning. The validation burden for an AI practitioner shifts from architectures to artifacts, and the central lesson is fluency is not evidence of meaning.

The word lists (with Zipf validation), the multi-synonym answer key, all {\sim}100 k word-level scored definition outcomes with per-configuration inclusion metrics, per-level statistics (McNemar, interaction, onset grid, within-family scale ladders), every definition with both judges’ verdicts, the human-verification samples, and the perplexity ladders (nine ladders over eight models, including a dual-build pair) are available at https://github.com/NietzscheDostoevsky/snk-release.

The tiered scorer, the judge rubric and runner, a script that reproduces the scorer-validation numbers of Sec. 3.3, and the word-list validation script are included in the same repository. The inference notebooks that produced the generations are not released; the prompts, decoding parameters and procedures they implement are specified in the Methods section.

Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts. Sparse Mixture-of-Experts models scale parameter capacity efficiently while maintaining a fixed compute budget per token. However, traditional training paradigms enforce a static choice of top-$k$ experts, which converts a continuous routing distribution into a rigid step function. This constraint introduces a brittle boundary where highly competitive experts are arbitrarily separated into full-supervision and zero-feedback zones based on minor score fluctuations. To address this issue, we propose Elastic Expert Routing, which stochastically samples the active expert budget from a localized discrete distribution centered at $k$. Over multiple training iterations, this mechanism softens the sharp threshold into a gradual probability distribution. Because the sampling neighborhood remains symmetric, this approach matches the expected computational cost of deterministic training, while preserving the inference budget. During supervised fine-tuning, elastic routing improves downstream macro-averages on OLMoE-1B-7B and Qwen3-30B-A3B by $+0.84$ and $+2.02$ points, respectively. In addition, in from-scratch pretraining, it reduces validation LM loss by up to $0.04$ and outperforms the static top-$k$ baseline by $1.6$ points on average across downstream tasks. Comparisons on Qwen3 fine-tuning and from-scratch pretraining further show higher average scores than Noisy top-$k$, expert FFN dropout, and DefaultMoE.

Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) could scale model capacity efficiently by enlarging the number of total experts while conditionally activating a restricted subset of parameters per token (Jiang et al., 2024; Dai et al., 2024; Du et al., 2022). In the common top- k architecture, a routing network ranks the experts for each incoming token and dispatches that token to the first k candidates Shazeer et al. (2017); Fedus et al. (2022). Since the choice of k directly serves as a static computational hyperparameter that dictates per-token costs, this design provides an intuitive mechanism for controlling computational requirements, where the compute would stay almost the same while the total model capacity scales Tian et al. (2025); Krajewski et al. (2024). Consequently, a common practice would enforce a uniform value of k throughout both the training and deployment phases.

However, this fixed threshold converts a continuous routing distribution into a rigid step function at the selection threshold Wang et al. (2025b). This constraint introduces a harsh boundary that restricts model optimization. As shown in Figure 1, highly competitive experts with virtually identical routing scores are arbitrarily separated into full-supervision and zero-feedback zones based on minor score fluctuations. Consequently, an expert ranked precisely inside the cutoff receives full gradient supervision, whereas an adjacent competitor ranked just outside receives zero task-loss feedback. Because traditional top- k training repeatedly presents the routing network with this rigid boundary, optimization near the cutoff becomes highly brittle.

One intuitive approach to mitigate boundary rigidity is dynamic routing. Existing adaptive methods vary the number of activated experts dynamically by allocating more capacity to difficult inputs Guo et al. (2025) or sampling token-specific budgets from routing signals (Yue et al., 2024). While this strategy removes the top- k threshold, it may change the deployment budget Wang et al. (2025b); Huang et al. (2024), alter the model structure Zeng et al. (2024); Jin et al. (2025); Team et al. (2025), or lead to suboptimal task performance for extreme efficiency Lv et al. (2026), which is hard to be applied on model serving infrastructures.

To address this issue, we propose Elastic Expert Routing. Our framework preserves the standard fixed-budget inference constraints but softens the sharp threshold during training. Specifically, our method stochastically samples the active expert budget from a localized discrete distribution centered at k. As illustrated in Figure 1 (right), over multiple training iterations, this mechanism statistically transforms the sharp selection threshold into a smooth selection probability distribution. Consequently, competitive near-boundary experts can be optimized during training. Because the sampling neighborhood remains symmetric around k, this approach matches the expected computational cost of vanilla static top- k training. Furthermore, the model preserves the standard static top- k routing rule at inference time with zero structural modification or latency overhead.

We evaluate the efficacy of elastic routing across fine-tuning and pretraining settings. In supervised fine-tuning experiments, we test our method using OLMoE-1B-7B Muennighoff et al. (2025) and Qwen3-30B-A3B backbones (Yang et al., 2025). Our approach consistently improves downstream task performance over static top- k baselines, yielding improvements of +0.84 and +2.02 points, respectively. We further validate the foundational utility of budget elasticity during from-scratch pretraining under strict compute-matched and token-matched conditions. In this setting, elastic routing reduces validation LM loss by up to 0.04 and outperforms the static top- k baseline by 1.6 points on average across downstream tasks. On Qwen3 fine-tuning and from-scratch pretraining, elastic routing also outperforms Noisy top- k, expert FFN dropout, and DefaultMoE in average downstream performance under the same static top-8 inference rule. Subsequent internal diagnostics confirm that boundary smoothing refines expert prioritization rankings and alters routing distribution behaviors within the foundational middle layers of the network.

Our contributions are summarized below: We formulate static top- k MoE training as a hard rank-exposure boundary and introduce Elastic Expert Routing to soften it into a gradual selection probability distribution without modifying inference mechanics. We demonstrate consistent performance gains during supervised fine-tuning on OLMoE-1B-7B and Qwen3-30B-A3B backbones, as well as during from-scratch pretraining under fair settings. We provide routing diagnostics and router-swap interventions showing that the gains are associated with middle-layer routing changes and improved expert prioritization.

Sparse MoE models replace dense feed-forward blocks with sparsely activated expert modules (Shazeer et al., 2017; Lepikhin et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2022; Du et al., 2022; Zoph et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2024). For a token state h_{i}, the router computes routing logits z_{i}=W_{\mathrm{gate}}h_{i},\qquad p_{i}=\mathrm{softmax}(z_{i}), and under static top- k routing selects S_{i}^{(k)}=\mathrm{TopK}(p_{i},k),\qquad y_{i}=\sum_{e\in S_{i}^{(k)}}\alpha_{i,e}E_{e}(h_{i}). Fixing k during training and inference creates a hard exposure boundary: only selected experts participate in each token’s task-loss computation. The budget therefore shapes both per-token computation and the training exposure distribution.

MoE training commonly relies on auxiliary objectives, capacity constraints, and routing regularization to prevent expert collapse and improve expert utilization (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022; Zoph et al., 2022). Other work revisits token–expert assignment by changing the assignment rule itself, for example allowing experts to select tokens rather than assigning a fixed number of experts per token (Zhou et al., 2022), or introducing alternative selection mechanisms based on BASE layers Lewis et al. (2021) and differentiable sorting and ranking Wang et al. (2025b); Hazimeh et al. (2021) strategies. In contrast, our approach preserves the routing architecture and assignment mechanism, and instead changes the training distribution over the active expert budget. Noisy top- k perturbs routing scores while retaining a fixed expert count (Shazeer et al., 2017); our FFN dropout baseline instead perturbs expert activations. DefaultMoE approximates uncomputed expert outputs with exponential moving averages to provide dense router feedback (Panda et al., 2025), whereas elastic routing changes the active expert count and near-boundary exposure.

Recent work relaxes static top- k routing by allowing the number of activated experts to vary across tokens. Existing approaches mainly differ in how dynamic budgets are determined, including threshold-based routing such as cumulative, trainable, and non-linear thresholding (Huang et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b), auxiliary proposer modules for predicting token-specific budgets (Yue et al., 2024), and architectural designs based on low- or zero-computation experts (Zeng et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025). Matryoshka MoE varies the number of active experts during training to support elastic inference across different budgets (Wang et al., 2025a). Our method instead samples a local, centered budget distribution to improve fixed top- k inference, smoothing rank exposure while preserving the expected active-expert count.

We first describe elastic routing as a change to the training objective. Let \mathcal{D} denote the training distribution and g(\hat{y},y) denote the task loss. For an input x, let f_{\theta}(x;\boldsymbol{\kappa}) denote the MoE forward pass under a budget schedule \boldsymbol{\kappa}, where \kappa_{i,\ell} denotes the number of experts used by token i in MoE layer \ell. The fixed-budget baseline uses the constant schedule \boldsymbol{k}_{0}, with every entry equal to the target budget k_{0}, and optimizes \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fixed}}(\theta) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[g(f_{\theta}(x;\boldsymbol{k}_{0}),y)\right], \displaystyle\boldsymbol{k}_{0} \displaystyle\equiv(k_{0},\ldots,k_{0}). This objective trains at a single budget configuration. Elastic routing instead samples a schedule \boldsymbol{\kappa} from a distribution Q centered at the target budget and optimizes \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{elastic}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}\sim Q}\left[g(f_{\theta}(x;\boldsymbol{\kappa}),y)\right]. The fixed-budget objective is recovered when Q degenerates to a point mass at \boldsymbol{k}_{0}. In the remainder of this section, Q is local around k_{0} and centered in expectation, \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}\sim Q}[\kappa_{i,\ell}]=k_{0} for each token and layer, so elastic routing changes the training-time budget distribution while preserving the expected active-expert count. Section 3.3 formalizes the resulting rank-neighborhood smoothing.

We now specify the budget distribution used for elastic routing. An a – b schedule restricts the sampled budget to \mathcal{K}_{a:b}=\{a,\ldots,b\} and assigns probability \displaystyle q_{a:b}(r) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z_{a:b}}\exp\left(-\frac{(r-k_{0})^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right),\quad r\in\mathcal{K}_{a:b}, \displaystyle Z_{a:b} \displaystyle=\sum_{s=a}^{b}\exp\left(-\frac{(s-k_{0})^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right). Here r denotes a candidate active-expert budget, k_{0} is the center, and \sigma controls the neighborhood width. Unless otherwise stated, all elastic schedules in our experiments use \sigma=1.5. For each token i and MoE layer \ell, we sample \kappa_{i,\ell}\sim q_{a:b} and dispatch the token to the top- \kappa_{i,\ell} experts under the current router ranking. Experts outside the sampled prefix are masked out, and load-balancing statistics are computed over the realized dispatched assignments.

We formalize boundary smoothing through rank-exposure accounting. Conditioned on the current router order for representation h, let \pi_{j}(h) denote the expert at rank j and define the top- r prefix mask m_{j}^{(r)}=\mathbf{1}[j\leq r]. For a scalar budget distribution q, the task-loss exposure probability of rank j is \displaystyle a_{q}(j) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{K\sim q}\!\left[m_{j}^{(K)}\right] \displaystyle=\Pr(K\geq j)=\sum_{r=j}^{K_{\max}}q(r). Static top- k_{0} training corresponds to the point-mass case a_{\delta_{k_{0}}}(j)=\mathbf{1}[j\leq k_{0}], whereas elastic routing replaces this step mask with the survival function of q.

The budget distribution is the discrete derivative of the exposure curve: a_{q}(j)-a_{q}(j+1)=q(j),\qquad a_{q}(M+1)=0. Thus the smoothing effect is local in router rank space, not a differentiable relaxation of top- K selection. If \mathrm{supp}(q)=[K_{\min},K_{\max}], then ranks j\leq K_{\min} are always exposed, ranks K_{\min}<j\leq K_{\max} have fractional exposure, and ranks j>K_{\max} are never exposed.

The same accounting yields expected exposure conservation: \sum_{j=1}^{M}a_{q}(j)=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\Pr(K\geq j)=\mathbb{E}[K]. When q is exactly centered at the deployment budget, \mathbb{E}[K]=k_{0}, elastic routing preserves the expected active-expert count while changing which boundary ranks enter the task-loss path. Moreover, \sum_{j>k_{0}}a_{q}(j)=\sum_{j\leq k_{0}}\bigl(1-a_{q}(j)\bigr)=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}|K-k_{0}|, so the exposure above the cutoff is balanced by exposure from ranks at or below it.

The schedule width controls how much conserved exposure shifts across the deployment cutoff: narrow neighborhoods transfer little exposure, while wider neighborhoods shrink the always-on core and include lower-ranked candidates.

We evaluate elastic routing in two supervised fine-tuning (SFT) settings and one from-scratch pretraining setting. For SFT, we fine-tune OLMoE-1B-7B-0924 on Dolci-Instruct-SFT (Olmo et al., 2026) and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base on Infinity-Instruct 7M Core (Li et al., 2025). For pretraining experiments, we train 1.42B-A365M MoE models with 6e19 FLOPs budget. The model structure, optimal learning rate, and global batch size are guided by the scaling laws of Tian et al. (2025) and Hoffmann et al. (2022). The model has 128 experts per layer and is trained on FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024) for 26.25B tokens.

Each setting compares static top-8 training with token-level elastic schedules 7--9, 6--10, and 5--11. Elastic budgets are sampled from the discrete Gaussian neighborhood in Section 3.2, with \sigma=1.5 and center k_{0}=8. Since the schedules are centered at top-8, they match the baseline in expected active-expert count and expected expert-side training FLOPs. All main evaluations use static top-8 inference; training cost and system profiling results are reported in Appendix A.2 (Tables A.2 and A.3).

For SFT, we report Avg(9) over a nine-task suite covering Knowledge: MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a), AGIEval (En) (Zhong et al., 2023), GPQA (Main) (Rein et al., 2023), Reasoning: BBH (Suzgun et al., 2022), Mathematics: GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021b), Coding: MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), and Instruction Following & Alignment: IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023), TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2022). For pretraining, we report averaged results on LAMBADA (Paperno et al., 2016); HellaSwag Zellers et al. (2019), PIQA Bisk et al. (2019), WinoGrande Sakaguchi et al. (2019),CommonsenseQA Talmor et al. (2019), SciQ Welbl et al. (2017), OpenBookQA Mihaylov et al. (2018), ARC Clark et al. (2018), MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a), and LogiQA (Liu et al., 2020). We use standard task metrics through lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2024). See Appendix A for details.

Table 1 reports the SFT results under static top-8 inference. Comparisons are made within each backbone: every elastic checkpoint shares the same data, optimizer, evaluation protocol, and decoding setup as its static top-8 counterpart, and differs only in the training-time routing schedule.

section: Elastic routing improves static top-8 SFT.
text: On OLMoE, all three elastic schedules outperform the static top-8 baseline, with 6--10 increasing Avg(9) from 30.57 to 31.41. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, 6--10 raises Avg(9) from 56.42 to 58.44, and the other elastic schedules also remain above the baseline. The improvement is broad: an elastic schedule obtains the best score on all nine OLMoE tasks and on eight of nine Qwen3 tasks.

section: Moderate interval gives the strongest aggregate result.
text: The 6--10 schedule gives the best Avg(9) for both backbones, whereas the narrower 7--9 and wider 5--11 schedules are beneficial but not consistently strongest. This pattern agrees with the rank-exposure view in Section 3.3 that useful smoothing should expose experts near the cutoff threshold without allocating excessive routing probability to low-ranked, irrelevant candidates.
To test whether the effect could be generalized to pretraining, we conduct experiments to train four MoE baselines from scratch. The downstream task results are listed in Table 2.

section: Elastic routing improves from-scratch pretraining under matched compute.
text: All three elastic schedules improve the average validation score over static top-8: 6--10 raises the average from 41.3 to 42.9, while 7--9 and 5--11 reach 42.8 and 42.4, also significantly beyond baseline.

section: Moderate interval remains strongest in pretraining.
text: The 6--10 schedule gives both the best average score and the lowest LAMBADA perplexity, reducing perplexity from 54.2 to 42.7. Elastic 6--10 also achieves the lowest validation LM loss, reducing it from 2.6465 to 2.6085 under static top-8 evaluation. This is consistent with the SFT results, supporting elastic routing as a training-time improvement for static top-8 MoE models. Its repeated advantage across SFT and pretraining suggests that this neighborhood size captures a robust local smoothing regime rather than a setting-specific fluctuation.

section: Comparison with Other MoE Training Methods
