text: We compare elastic routing with three alternative MoE training methods under matched settings. The baselines are Noisy top- k (Shazeer et al., 2017), expert FFN dropout, and DefaultMoE (Panda et al., 2025). Within each Qwen3-30B-A3B SFT or 1.42B MoE pretraining setting, all methods use the same backbone, training data, and optimization budget, and are evaluated with static top-8 routing.

section: Comparison with Other MoE Training Methods
text: Elastic 6--10 achieves the highest average in both settings. It reaches 58.44 on the nine-task SFT suite and 42.9 on the eleven-task pretraining suite, while also achieving the lowest pretraining validation LM loss of 2.6085 (Table 3). Appendix A.5 provides the baseline configurations and full task-level results in Tables A.5 and A.6.
We examine where elastic training changes the router across depth and whether restricting elasticity to these layers improves static top-8 inference.

section: Elastic routing changes the router most strongly in the middle layers.
text: We compare 6--10 and static top-8 under the same static top-8 evaluation rule. For each task and layer, we compute the Jensen–Shannon (JS) divergence between the two routers’ per-token expert probability distributions. Figure 2 shows the mean divergence across tasks. The largest non-boundary divergence forms a contiguous L3–L7 block. Although L0 and L15 also exhibit elevated divergence, we exclude these boundary layers from the diagnostic block to separate the internal routing changes from input adaptation and final representation readout.

section: The depth-restricted diagnostic supports the middle-layer interpretation.
text: We apply the 6--10 rule only to L3–L7, keeping all other layers at static top-8, and use L8–L12 as a later-layer control. Table 4 reports the task-level results. Restricting elasticity to L3–L7 reaches Avg(9) 31.50, compared with 31.41 for all-layer 6--10 and 30.57 for static top-8. The L8–L12 variant also improves over the static baseline, but reaches only 30.94. These results identify L3–L7 as a beneficial diagnostic region, without establishing it as the optimal layer subset.

We examine how elastic training changes discrete expert selection, and whether the learned routing policy contributes to the observed gain. The first diagnostic experiment compares selected experts under static top-8 evaluation, and the second one uses an evaluation-time router swap to intervene on the routing policy while holding the target model otherwise fixed.

We sample 100 evaluation instances from each of our 9 downstream benchmarks to form a representative validation token set t\in\{1,2,\dots,T\}. For a given layer \ell and token t, let e^{\text{elastic}}_{\ell,t} and e^{\text{static}}_{\ell,t} denote the top-1 expert chosen by each configuration, respectively. Similarly, let S^{\text{elastic}}_{\ell,t} and S^{\text{static}}_{\ell,t} represent their respective active top-8 expert sets. We define two layer-averaged disagreement ratios, D_{1} and D_{8}:

D_{1}=\frac{1}{L\cdot T}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf{1}\left[e^{\text{elastic}}_{\ell,t}\neq e^{\text{static}}_{\ell,t}\right], D_{8}=\frac{1}{L\cdot T}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(1-\frac{\left|S^{\text{elastic}}_{\ell,t}\cap S^{\text{static}}_{\ell,t}\right|}{8}\right), where L denotes the total number of layers. D_{1}\in[0,1] measures the fraction of top-1 assignments that change, while D_{8}\in[0,1] measures the average fraction of differing experts in the top-8 sets.

Figure 3 shows that elastic routing primarily refines expert rankings rather than altering the global composition of the active expert pool. Aggregated across the nine benchmark tasks, Figure 3 shows that 6--10 changes the top-1 routed expert for 13.62% of tokens on average, while only 7.08% of the selected top- 8 set differs, about 0.57 experts out of 8.
We swap routers at inference to test their contribution to the gain, keeping all other target parameters fixed.

Table 5 shows that optimal performance gains require the mutual alignment through joint router–expert co-adaptation. Replacing the static top-8 router with the 6--10 router improves the static checkpoint, while replacing the elastic router with the static router reduces the elastic checkpoint. Neither swap recovers the full 6--10 performance.

section: Performance Under Different Top- k Values
text: Since the main results focus on eight active experts, we further examine whether the gains persist when the number of active experts changes. Elastic routing is designed to expose training to a local range of expert-count configurations, allowing the model to learn multiple nearby patterns of expert cooperation instead of only one static top-8 composition. If this diversity is useful, its effect should not be limited to the exact eight-expert setting used in the main evaluation; it should also appear when inference uses other expert counts.

section: Performance Under Different Top- k Values
text: Elastic routing improves performance beyond the eight-expert inference setting. Figure 4 shows that 6--10 is the strongest schedule at the default k=8 point and remains above the static top-8 baseline throughout the scanned range. The narrower 7--9 and wider 5--11 schedules also improve some parts of the curve, but neither gives the same consistently strong profile. This supports the view that training over a moderate range of expert counts helps the model learn more robust expert cooperation patterns under several nearby settings, rather than only optimizing the single eight-expert setting.

The preceding analyses characterize where elastic routing changes routing and how the learned ordering behaves around the deployment cutoff. We further isolate the effect of budget design by varying the probability shape within a fixed local neighborhood and comparing against simpler alternatives that increase active experts without smoothing the top-8 boundary.

The main experiments use \sigma=1.5 for all elastic schedules. We fix the 6--10 support and vary only \sigma: smaller values concentrate probability around the target cutoff, while larger values flatten the distribution. The default \sigma=1.5 outperforms both \sigma=1.0 and \sigma=3.0 (Table 6), suggesting that the smoothing distribution should be neither too concentrated nor too flat.

We also compare uniform sampling over \{6,7,8,9,10\}, with \mathbb{E}[K]=8 and static top-8 inference. Uniform sampling reaches an Avg(9) score of 30.93, compared with 30.57 for static training and 31.41 for Gaussian 6–10 with \sigma=1.5.

We compare with controls that increase expert-side computation without smoothing the top-8 boundary. Fixed top-9 and top-10 activate more experts per token during training. The top- p control uses a routing probability threshold of p=0.4 and activates 13 experts per token on average, making it the most computationally expensive control. All checkpoints use static top-8 inference unless explicitly stated.

Table 7 shows that static top-9, static top-10, and top- p all remain below 6--10, despite using more expert computation. This suggests that the gain cannot be explained solely by activating more experts, but by smoothing task-loss exposure across ranks that straddle the deployment cutoff. Full task-level results appear in Tables A.7 (Gaussian shape) and A.8 (budget controls).

In this work, we address the rigid rank-exposure boundary that severely restricts model optimization near the selection threshold under traditional static top- k routing. We introduce Elastic Expert Routing, which smooths this selection boundary by stochastically sampling from a discrete budget distribution during training while preserving the static top- k inference rule. We conduct experiments on both supervised fine-tuning and from-scratch pretraining, and the results demonstrate that this simple training-time modification consistently improves MoE performance without increasing inference cost. Empirical analyses show that elastic training primarily alters the learned routing policy within the foundational middle layers of the network while simultaneously refining expert prioritization rankings near the deployment cutoff.

The main limitation of this study is the scale of from-scratch pretraining. Our supervised fine-tuning experiments are conducted on established sparse MoE backbones with substantially larger parameter budgets: OLMoE-1B-7B has 7B total parameters with 1B active per token, and Qwen3-30B-A3B has 30.5B total parameters with 3.3B activated. In contrast, our from-scratch pretraining experiments use a 1.427B-parameter MoE with 0.365B active parameters, reflecting the computational cost of training larger MoE models from initialization under available GPU resources. Therefore, the pretraining results should be interpreted as a controlled validation of the proposed training objective at a moderate scale, while validating the approach under large-scale from-scratch pretraining remains an important direction for future work.

Evaluating Tibetan Speech Recognition Across Dialects and Adaptation Regimes: A Multi-Granularity Analysis. Tibetan speech recognition is usually evaluated with character or syllable error rates because the writing system does not mark word boundaries. These metrics can rank systems differently and respond differently to adaptation failures. We combine character error rate, syllable error rate, and segmented word error rate in one evaluation framework. We use dictionary-based, neural, and language-model-based segmentation and compare their boundaries with expert annotations. We evaluate five ASR architectures on Lhasa Tibetan, then test zero-shot transfer and target-corpus adaptation on five additional corpus subsets. We also vary LoRA rank and training-data size to examine adaptation failure. The results show that a lower character error does not always lead to a lower syllable or segmented-word error. These ranking differences persist across corpora. Metric correlations also weaken in some unsuccessful adaptation settings. Higher LoRA ranks improve syllable and segmented-word scores but remain worse than full fine-tuning in the tested range. A standardized phonological representation provides another view of spelling errors. These findings support evaluation at several linguistic levels and motivate better segmentation and adaptation methods for low-resource ASR.

Automatic speech recognition (ASR) converts speech into text. Evaluation should measure both spelling accuracy and accuracy at larger linguistic units. Tibetan marks syllable boundaries with the tsek, but does not consistently separate words with spaces. A word may contain one or several syllables. Computing word error rate (WER) therefore requires word segmentation.

Most Tibetan ASR studies report character error rate (CER). Some also report syllable error rate (SER). CER is easy to calculate because it requires no word segmentation. However, a small character error can affect a whole syllable or multi-syllable word. Metrics at different levels can therefore favor models with different error patterns.

Our earlier IEEE Access study evaluated Tibetan ASR with segmented word error rate (SWER). It applied Botok, BERT-UPOS, and Gemini segmentation before computing WER. Character-level and higher-level scores ranked models differently on NICT-Tib1. LoRA and quantized LoRA also performed poorly. That study used one Lhasa read-speech corpus and one adapter rank. It left two questions open. Do these metric differences occur in other corpora and dialects? Can larger adapters or more training data improve the poor adaptation results?

We address both questions in a common experimental design. We use the updated Lhasa reference and evaluate its five checkpoints on five additional corpus subsets. We also fine-tune each architecture on each target subset. The target data cover Amdo, Kham, Lhasa, and Shigatse speech. On NICT-Tib1, we test four LoRA ranks at four training-data fractions. A standardized phonological representation provides a separate view of spelling differences.

We study three sources of variation: architecture, corpus and dialect shift, and adapter capacity. Metric behavior changes across these settings. Syllable and segmented-word scores can reverse CER rankings. Their correlations with CER can also weaken after unsuccessful adaptation. Each SWER variant uses its own segmentation procedure, so its scores depend on the resulting token sequences.

The contributions are as follows. We combine character-, syllable-, and segmented-word evaluation. We distinguish tokenization, score aggregation, and utterance-level correlation. We extend a five-architecture Lhasa benchmark with 25 zero-shot transfer evaluations and 25 target-corpus adaptation runs across five additional corpus subsets. We test 16 LoRA rank-by-data configurations and three new full-fine-tuning baselines under a fixed epoch budget. We analyze model rankings, failure modes, and metric correlations. We use these findings to guide Tibetan ASR evaluation. The transfer experiments and rank ablation extend our published SWER study. Cross-corpus differences include recording conditions, speakers, text domains, and dialect.

Tibetan syllables can contain several orthographic components, including prefixes, superscripts, subscripts, vowel marks, and suffixes. Written forms can preserve distinctions that pronunciation reduces. Short grammatical particles also carry important information. Evaluation at the character, syllable, and word levels, therefore, describes different aspects of the transcript.

Dictionary segmentation finds lexical entries in a sequence of syllables. Botok provides a public implementation. It keeps an unrecognized syllable as a separate token. An ASR error can therefore break a dictionary match and split one word into several tokens. BoTok-SWER reflects both transcription errors and their effects on dictionary segmentation.

Statistical and neural segmenters use context to predict boundaries. Earlier methods include conditional random fields and CNN-BiLSTM-CRF models. Tibetan transformer models also support contextual analysis. BERT-UPOS uses Tibetan BERT in a part-of-speech pipeline. We use its returned entities as evaluation units. These units may differ from linguistic word boundaries.

Segmentation also affects ASR evaluation in other writing systems. Ni and Leung showed that Chinese segmentation standards and algorithms change the reported WER. A segmented-word score should therefore specify its segmenter and tokenization standard.

Wav2Vec 2.0 and HuBERT learn speech representations through self-supervised pretraining. Their ASR models use connectionist temporal classification (CTC). CTC converts acoustic outputs into token sequences by collapsing repeats and removing blanks. Whisper uses an acoustic encoder and an autoregressive decoder trained on multilingual speech-text data. These systems differ in pretraining data, decoding objectives, and output representations. Their comparison, therefore, reflects complete systems, not decoder architecture alone.

LoRA introduces a low-rank update to a frozen weight matrix. For a matrix W_{0}, the adapted weight is W=W_{0}+\frac{\alpha}{r}BA, where A and B are trainable factors, and r is the adapter rank. Quantized LoRA trains adapters on a quantized base model. QLoRA is a prominent implementation. Rank controls the available update space. Training data and optimization determine how the model uses that space. We test several ranks and data fractions to examine these factors.

section: A. Error rates at three granularities
text: Let R_{i} and H_{i} denote the normalized reference and hypothesis for utterance i. For a tokenization function T, the normalized edit error is E_{i}(T)=\frac{d(T(R_{i}),T(H_{i}))}{|T(R_{i})|}, where d is the Levenshtein edit distance. CER uses character units; SER uses tsek-delimited syllables. For an automatic word segmenter s, we define \mathrm{SWER}_{s}=\frac{S_{s}+D_{s}+I_{s}}{N_{s}}, where the edits align s(R) and s(H), and N_{s} is the reference-token count. Insertions can cause an error rate to exceed one, meaning that the edit count exceeds the reference length.

section: A. Error rates at three granularities
text: Botok produces BoTok-SWER, BERT-UPOS produces BERT-SWER, and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite produces Gem-SWER. Both reference and hypothesis are segmented independently using the same method. BoTok-SWER and BERT-SWER cover the full test sets. Gem-SWER is available only for the original 500-utterance NICT-Tib1 subset; it was not computed for the cross-corpus or rank-ablation extensions.

section: A. Error rates at three granularities
text: The Gemini prompt requests pipe-delimited words and preserves the original Tibetan characters and tsek marks. Temperature is zero. The original study excluded per-utterance Gem-SWER values above 3.0 as segmentation failures. This threshold can also remove genuine ASR errors. Character-preservation checks provide a more direct way to detect invalid segmentation.

The original boundary study sampled 100 NICT-Tib1 test utterances, stratified by speaker. One expert annotated 2,634 inter-syllable positions. Each position received a binary label indicating whether a word boundary followed that syllable. Botok, Gemini, BERT-UPOS, and Claude Haiku segmented the same reference transcriptions independently. Claude served as an additional comparison and was not used to produce an ASR score.

We measure agreement with boundary F1 and Cohen’s \kappa. Boundary rate is the fraction of inter-syllable positions marked as word boundaries. Gemini has the highest agreement with the expert (Table 1). Botok marks more boundaries and produces units closer to syllables. This study uses one annotator and clean Lhasa references. Boundary accuracy on ASR hypotheses and other dialects remains untested.

BoTok-SWER measures errors under dictionary segmentation. Gem-SWER measures errors under LLM segmentation. Both depend on their tokenization rules. Neither directly measures listener comprehension or downstream task accuracy.

For n utterances, let e_{i} be the edit count and N_{i} the reference-token count. We distinguish \displaystyle E_{\mathrm{micro}} \displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i}e_{i}}{\sum_{i}N_{i}}, \displaystyle E_{\mathrm{macro}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\frac{e_{i}}{N_{i}}. Micro-averaging weights reference tokens equally. Macro-averaging weights utterances equally. Both can use utterance bootstrap sampling. Each micro bootstrap sample recomputes the ratio of total edits to total reference tokens. Each macro sample recomputes the mean utterance error.

We retain the reported macro-averaged confidence intervals (CIs), based on 10,000 utterance bootstrap samples. Primary corpus-level tables are labeled separately. Pearson correlations use per-utterance scores within each model-corpus cell unless stated otherwise. They describe how errors vary across utterances rather than how metrics rank different models.

Paired bootstrap differences assess model comparisons directly. Overlap between separate CIs does not establish equivalence. We report the extension’s model differences descriptively because its reports do not include the raw predictions needed for new paired tests. With few test speakers, utterance-level CIs mainly describe uncertainty over the sampled utterances.

We compute the standardized phonological error rate (PER) by mapping both transcripts through bophono’s implementation of Tournadre’s Manual of Standard Tibetan scheme, then calculating character edit errors. All corpora use the same mapping. This score shows how spelling differences change under a standard pronunciation representation. It does not measure dialect-specific pronunciations against manually annotated phones.

Table 2 summarizes the six corpus subsets. NICT-Tib1 provides the original Lhasa benchmark. Its 20 speakers are split into 17 training speakers and three test speakers. The test set contains 1,547 utterances.

We use the official XBMU-AMDO31 split and custom speaker-disjoint splits for four TIBMD@MUC subsets. The subsets cover Amdo, Kham, Lhasa, and Shigatse. Their transcripts originally separate syllables with spaces. We replace these spaces with tsek marks to match the NICT-Tib1 evaluation convention.
MUC Shigatse has one test speaker, and Kham has two. The results therefore describe these corpus subsets, with limited coverage of speaker variation within each dialect.
We compare Whisper Tiny, Base, and Small with Wav2Vec 2.0 Base and HuBERT Base. All target-corpus runs start from pretrained models.

The cross-corpus adaptation runs use 4,000 optimizer steps, 500 warmup steps, a per-device batch size of two, and eight gradient accumulation steps. The effective batch size is 16. Training uses fp16 and gradient checkpointing. Learning rates are 3.75\times 10^{-5}, 2.5\times 10^{-5}, and 1.25\times 10^{-5} for Whisper Tiny, Base, and Small, respectively, and 10^{-4} for both CTC systems. CTC models use corpus-specific vocabularies with matching training and decoding blank/pad identifiers.

A fixed step budget gives different epoch counts across training sets. HuBERT completes 2.39 epochs on MUC Lhasa and 15.94 on MUC Kham. The protocol fixes optimizer updates, while data exposure varies with corpus size.

Experiment 1: original Lhasa benchmark. The earlier study compared five architectures. It also tested six settings for each Whisper size: standard fine-tuning, 8-bit and 4-bit post-training quantization, unquantized LoRA, and LoRA with 8-bit or 4-bit base weights. Adapters used rank eight, \alpha=16, and dropout 0.1. They targeted the key, query, value, and output projections, plus both feed-forward layers in every Whisper block. We retain the reported bit-width labels for these earlier quantized settings.

Experiment 2: zero-shot transfer. We evaluate the five NICT-Tib1 checkpoints on each of the five additional test subsets. This gives 25 evaluations. The models have Tibetan training but no target-corpus adaptation.

Experiment 3: target-corpus adaptation. We fine-tune each architecture on each target training subset using the fixed-step protocol. This gives 25 runs. Each transfer-adaptation comparison uses the same target test set.

Experiment 4: rank-by-data ablation. We adapt Whisper Small on NICT-Tib1 with ranks r\in\{4,8,16,32\} and data fractions f\in\{25,50,75,100\}\%. We sample utterances from the same 17 training speakers to preserve speaker diversity. Setting \alpha=2r keeps \alpha/r constant. Learned update norms can still differ across ranks.

Each of the 16 LoRA runs uses 4.24 epochs. This fixes the number of data passes, so smaller subsets receive fewer optimizer updates. Three full-fine-tuning runs use 25%, 50%, and 75% of the data. The 100% reference CER is 0.086; this condition was not rerun in the grid. We merge each trained adapter into the shared pretrained Whisper Small model before decoding. The grid tests unquantized LoRA.

For each LoRA cell, we define the descriptive gap G=\mathrm{BoTok\mbox{-}SWER}-\mathrm{CER}. The technical report fits G to rank, data percentage, and their interaction using ordinary least squares: G=\beta_{0}+\beta_{r}r+\beta_{f}f+\beta_{rf}rf+\epsilon, Here, f is measured in percentage points. The gap compares errors with different token denominators, so we use it as a diagnostic measure. The regression uses 16 runs without repeated seeds. Its coefficient tests are exploratory.

Table 3 lists the updated NICT-Tib1 reference results. Wav2Vec2 has the lowest CER at 0.075, followed by Whisper Small at 0.086. CER and SER are strongly correlated within each model. The cross-corpus results below show whether they also favor the same models.

Whisper Small’s full-data full-fine-tuning reference CER is 0.086. At rank eight with full data, LoRA gives CER 0.714, SER 0.960, BoTok-SWER 0.978, BERT-SWER 0.951, and standardized PER 0.667. These values follow the updated cross-corpus and LoRA reports.
Table 4 reports the 25 transfer evaluations. Error rates are high on the additional corpora, including MUC Lhasa. Transfer loss therefore includes corpus differences as well as dialect differences.

The ranking reversal remains clear on the Amdo subsets. On XBMU-AMDO31, Wav2Vec2 has the lowest CER at 0.472, while Whisper Small has lower SER (0.762 versus 0.869) and BoTok-SWER (1.014 versus 1.157). On MUC Amdo, Wav2Vec2 again has the lowest CER at 0.552, but Whisper Small performs better on SER, BoTok-SWER, and BERT-SWER. Character-level preservation therefore does not identify the best higher-granularity output in these transfer settings.

The same pattern appears within Central Tibetan. On MUC Lhasa, Wav2Vec2 has CER 0.382 versus Whisper Small’s 0.520, but Whisper Small has lower SER and both segmented-word scores. On Shigatse, the corresponding CER values are 0.343 and 0.427, whereas BoTok-SWER favors Whisper Small at 0.797 versus 0.917. These comparisons show that the evaluation issue extends beyond the original test corpus.

Table 5 reports the 25 target-corpus training runs. Adaptation improves the four scores for every model on both Amdo subsets. For example, Whisper Small on XBMU-AMDO31 improves from CER 0.491 to 0.144 and from BoTok-SWER 1.014 to 0.295. On MUC Amdo, its BoTok-SWER falls from 1.173 to 0.292.

After adaptation, Wav2Vec2 still has the lowest CER on both Amdo subsets, while Whisper Small has the lowest SER and segmented-word scores. On XBMU-AMDO31, Wav2Vec2 achieves CER 0.105 compared with Whisper Small’s 0.144; BoTok-SWER instead favors Whisper Small, 0.295 versus 0.353. On MUC Amdo, the difference is larger at the syllable and word levels: Whisper Small has SER 0.222 and BoTok-SWER 0.292, compared with 0.319 and 0.466 for Wav2Vec2.

Kham is more difficult under this protocol. All five models have higher CER after target-corpus adaptation than under transfer. However, the Whisper models and Wav2Vec2 have lower BoTok-SWER after adaptation. For Whisper Small, CER rises from 0.596 to 0.679, while BoTok-SWER falls from 1.181 to 1.078. The metrics therefore move in opposite directions on the same model and test set. Corpus size and training exposure vary together, which limits the interpretation of this result.

HuBERT produces empty predictions on MUC Kham and MUC Lhasa after adaptation. All four micro error rates equal one because every reference token is deleted. The lack of score variation also limits correlation analysis. These failures occur at both ends of the reported epoch range, so epoch exposure alone does not explain them.

We compute correlations within each model-corpus cell. On the NICT-Tib reference predictions, CER-SER correlations range from 0.874 to 0.929. For Whisper Small, CER-SER is 0.929, and SER-BoTok-SWER is 0.921. Utterances with more errors at one level generally have more errors at the other levels, even when the metrics favor different architectures.

CTC correlations weaken on Kham. Wav2Vec2’s CER-BoTok-SWER correlation falls from 0.797 on XBMU-AMDO31 to 0.151 on Kham. CER-SER falls from 0.909 to 0.695, and BoTok-BERT falls from 0.804 to 0.044. The relation between metrics thus changes with the corpus and adaptation setting.

For Whisper, CER-SER correlations are at least 0.86 across transfer and target-adaptation cells. They are lower in the LoRA grid. Strong within-model correlations can therefore coexist with different architecture rankings. Poor adapter training can also weaken these correlations.

Table 6 reports the 19 new training configurations. Every LoRA cell remains far worse than the full-fine-tuning baselines. Increasing rank helps, especially at full data. From rank four to rank 32, SER falls from 0.958 to 0.919 and BoTok-SWER falls from 0.987 to 0.929. CER changes from 0.725 to 0.707. Greater capacity therefore improves all three measures, but the absolute error remains high.

More data also tends to improve performance. At rank 32, increasing the fraction from 25% to 100% reduces CER from 0.744 to 0.707 and BoTok-SWER from 0.972 to 0.929. At rank eight, CER improves with data while BoTok-SWER is lowest at 50%, so the changes are not strictly monotonic across every metric and rank.

Full fine-tuning with 25% of the data gives CER 0.455 and BoTok-SWER 0.641. Both are below the best LoRA values of 0.707 and 0.929. Full fine-tuning improves further at 50% and 75% data. Its full-data reference CER is 0.086. Thus, increasing rank and data within the tested LoRA grid does not recover full-fine-tuning performance.

The gap regression gives a rank coefficient of -0.00207 (p=0.0375), a data coefficient of -0.00040 (p=0.1223), and an interaction coefficient of 0.000011 (p=0.3996). The model has R^{2}=0.596. Because it includes an uncentered interaction, the rank coefficient applies at zero data. Within the tested range, the fitted rank slope is -0.00207+0.000011f. We interpret these estimates with the observed grid. The data coefficient’s p value does not rule out a data effect.

Mean per-cell CER-SER correlation increases from 0.489 at rank four to 0.663 at rank 32 (Table 7). Mean CER-BoTok-SWER correlation rises from 0.233 to 0.336, with a non-monotonic intermediate value at rank eight. The full-fine-tuning subset models have much higher correlations. Increasing rank thus improves part of the correlation structure, but does not restore the full-fine-tuning behavior within this grid.

Standardized PER is often lower than orthographic CER in the macro results. The mean relative reduction is 19.1% across 25 transfer cells and 13.4% across 23 non-collapsed adaptation cells. These aggregate values follow the cross-corpus report.

For in-domain XBMU-AMDO31 Whisper Small, macro CER is 0.127 and standardized PER is 0.106. On Kham, the values are 0.699 and 0.616. The standard mapping removes some orthographic distinctions, but substantial error remains on Kham. Since all varieties use a Lhasa-based mapping, the scores describe standardized representations rather than actual dialect-specific pronunciation.

Two patterns emerge. First, the lowest CER often does not identify the lowest SER or SWER. This occurs on the original corpus and on additional Amdo and Central Tibetan subsets. Second, within-model correlations weaken in some difficult adaptation settings, especially the LoRA grid and Wav2Vec2 on Kham.

SER uses explicit syllable boundaries, so it requires no inferred word boundaries. In several comparisons, it selects the same model as SWER. SWER adds information about errors under a specific word segmentation procedure. Its value should therefore be assessed alongside SER as well as CER.

Botok can split a corrupted multi-syllable word into shorter tokens. This can increase the error count after segmentation. BERT-UPOS and Gemini use different boundaries and produce different score scales. Segment length, reference-token count, and hypothesis boundaries all affect SWER.

Gemini agrees best with the expert in the original Lhasa boundary study. The cross-corpus experiments use Botok and BERT-UPOS, whose boundaries were not validated on Amdo or Kham. Dialect-specific boundary annotations would help interpret their scores.

Higher rank improves several LoRA scores, but all tested configurations remain worse than the new full-fine-tuning baselines. The tested increases in capacity and data therefore reduce errors without resolving the adaptation failure.

Several training choices may affect the remaining gap, including adapter placement, learning rate, update count, checkpoint selection, and decoding. The design fixes \alpha/r and epoch count. It still allows learned update norms and optimizer update counts to vary. Repeated seeds and further optimization tests would help separate these effects.
The grid tests unquantized adapters merged into the base model before decoding. Extending its capacity findings to quantized LoRA requires a separate controlled comparison.

section: C. Aggregation as part of the evaluation
text: For a fixed tokenization and nonempty reference, micro error is a reference-length-weighted average of per-utterance error. The difference from macro error is E_{\mathrm{micro}}-E_{\mathrm{macro}}=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(N_{i},E_{i})}{\overline{N}}. A positive difference means that longer references tend to have higher utterance error rates. Short-reference errors receive more relative weight in the macro average.

section: C. Aggregation as part of the evaluation
text: For Whisper Tiny transferred to XBMU-AMDO31, micro BERT-SWER is 1.060 and macro BERT-SWER is 0.493. The gap shows how reference-length weighting changes the score. Repetition loops also occur in some predictions. Their contribution to the two aggregates requires per-utterance counts.

Tibetan ASR evaluation should report CER and SER together. A named segmented-word score is also useful when word-level processing matters. Every table should state its aggregation. Micro and macro scores should use the same per-utterance edit counts.

SWER reporting should specify the segmenter version, configuration, normalization, and handling of malformed output. LLM segmentation also needs a fixed prompt and character-preservation checks. Boundary agreement should be assessed on both clean references and ASR hypotheses.

Model comparisons should use paired differences on the same test utterances. Correlation analyses should state whether they use individual cells, cell averages, or pooled predictions. Empty predictions and repetition loops should be counted separately to identify failure types.

The original study provides a public evaluation package and a 100-utterance boundary dataset. This study uses the updated cross-corpus and LoRA reference scores, correlations, and regression results. Raw per-utterance counts would allow further paired analyses.

Reproduction requires model identifiers and revisions, speaker splits, random seeds, and data-sampling lists. It also requires optimizer settings, adapter targets, checkpoint selection, decoding arguments, and segmenter versions. Released scoring records should include per-utterance edit counts and separate micro and macro aggregates. Quantization experiments should specify the bit-width implementation.

The experiments cover read speech with limited test-speaker diversity. Future work should evaluate conversational speech, listener comprehension, and downstream translation or retrieval. Multiple boundary annotators and dialect-specific phonological mappings would also improve the evaluation.

We evaluated Tibetan ASR across architectures, corpora, and adaptation settings. Lower character error did not consistently lead to lower syllable or segmented-word error. Several ranking reversals persisted across corpora. Metric correlations also changed under difficult adaptation conditions. Higher LoRA ranks improved some scores but remained worse than full fine-tuning within the tested grid. Standardized phonological scores provided another view of spelling errors. These results support evaluation at several linguistic levels, with explicit choices for segmentation and aggregation. Future work should link these scores to dialect-aware human judgments and downstream performance and improve adaptation under limited supervision.

Knowing When Not to Answer: Cross-Domain and Multi-Turn Generalization of Latent Underspecification Signals. Large language models routinely answer questions that cannot be answered from the information given, and in dialogue they answer before enough has been said. Unanswerability is linearly decodable from hidden states, but it is unclear which of its forms share a representation and whether the signal is useful in dialogue. We contribute a turn-labeled multi-turn benchmark (423 conversations, 1,661 labeled turn-states) and an evaluation harness with a simulated user who answers clarifying questions, and use them with six datasets and six open-weight LLMs to test how far probes for unanswerability carry. Probes transfer robustly between datasets that share a ground of unanswerability: missing information in math (AUROC 0.77-0.97) and in a passage (SQuAD 2.0<->MuSiQue, 0.77-0.90). Probes for epistemic "known-unknowns" transfer poorly to math, but this separation weakens under lexical controls and changes with layer and coordinate system, so it remains unresolved. Single-turn probes fail zero-shot to detect when a conversation becomes answerable; in-structure probes recover it, but no better than a bag-of-words classifier.

A gate on the calibrated probe, with no model fine-tuning, fires on underspecified turns far more precisely than chance, and its end-task success comes within 0.08 of a gate given the true labels. Yet across four models it does not reliably beat vanilla generation or prompted consolidation. The remaining gap lies mostly in how models use a clarification, not in detection.

Recent work shows that whether a question is answerable is linearly decodable from a language model’s hidden states, and uses this to mitigate abstention failures in reasoning models (Liu et al., 2026). That work is, however, demonstrated within a single domain (unanswerable math), and its outlook is training-centric: “Future work aims to explore training-time alignment strategies to improve abstention fidelity” (Liu et al., 2026). Transfer beyond the training data has been examined before: answerability probes carry across extractive QA benchmarks (Slobodkin et al., 2023), while hidden-state error and truthfulness detectors generalize only partially across tasks and domains (Orgad et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024). What remains open is which forms of unanswerability share a representation. A question can be unanswerable because the question omits information (a math problem missing a quantity), because the supplied context omits it (a passage without the answer), or because no one knows the answer. All three call for the same behavior, abstention, but need not share a latent direction usable as a read-out without fine-tuning the model.

Independently, LLMs degrade sharply when instructions are revealed incrementally across an under-specified conversation rather than stated all at once (Laban et al., 2025). That work maps the degradation and its workarounds but leaves its scope open (“Establishing whether models get lost in conversation in other languages, or in tasks that involve multiple modalities […] could help establish the scope of the degradation observed in LLM multi-turn capabilities” (Laban et al., 2025)), and it does not provide a mechanism that detects, turn by turn, when a conversation is still under-specified.

These two open problems share a premise: if the latent unanswerability signal were domain- and structure-general, it could gate generation without any fine-tuning of the model: read the probe, then abstain on unanswerable inputs and ask a clarifying question in under-specified dialogue. We evaluate RQ1 on six open-weight models from four families and test the full premise end-to-end on the four 8–12B models. It holds only in parts: RQ1, across datasets. The signal transfers robustly between datasets that share a ground of unanswerability. Whether epistemic unknowability is represented separately remains unresolved: its apparent separation depends on layer, lexical controls and coordinate system. RQ2, across structure. Single-turn probes do not transfer zero-shot to turn-level dialogue states at the layers where they are strongest. Turn-level answerability is recoverable in-structure, but no better than a TF-IDF classifier on the user turns recovers it. RQ3, at deployment. A leakage-free gate fires on underspecified turns far more precisely than chance, and its end-task success comes close to that of a gate given the true labels. It still does not beat prompting workarounds.

A turn-labeled multi-turn underspecification benchmark. The benchmark has 423 conversations and 1,661 turn-states, with constraints revealed one per turn and labels fixed by construction. It was audited by eight annotators and repaired by a judge from a model family other than the generator’s, under rules fixed before the repair ran. An answering-user evaluation harness for clarification policies. The simulated user answers from the not-yet-revealed constraints but cannot leak anything beyond them. Oracle, position and rate-matched random gates separate detector error from intervention cost. Careful transfer and deployment results, mostly negative. RQ1: probes transfer robustly within a ground of unanswerability: math 0.77–0.97, and extractive QA 0.77–0.90, replicating Slobodkin et al., 2023. The known-unknowns separation is fragile under lexical, layer and coordinate controls (Tables 1 and 2). RQ2: single-turn probes fail zero-shot on turn-states, and in-structure probes only match TF-IDF (Table 3). RQ3: the probe gate beats vanilla on single-turn abstention but trails a one-line prompt. In dialogue, its firing precision is 0.74–0.88, against 0.54–0.58 for a random gate, and its success is within 0.08 of the oracle gate. Its end-task endpoint, fixed in advance, is still negative (Table 4).

For every (model, dataset) pair we run a single prompt-only forward pass per example (the model’s own chat template, no generation), cache all layers’ hidden states in fp16, and read out at the last prompt token (a mean-pooled read-out is cached alongside; last-token is used throughout). Probes are \ell_{2} -regularized logistic regressions on the read-out at one layer: features are standardized by a scaler fit on the training data only; the regularization strength is chosen from a log-grid (10^{-4} – 10^{2}) by inner cross-validation on the training fold; within-domain numbers are 5-fold stratified CV over seeds \{13,42,77\} and reported as mean \pm sd. Cross-domain and cross-structure evaluations apply the frozen probe with its frozen train-domain scaler to the entire test set: no test-side fitting of any kind. Layer indices are model-specific. For the transfer matrix, the common layer maximizes mean within-domain cross-validation AUROC. For LODO, we evaluate the full layer sweep and report the best held-out-domain layer as an explicitly optimistic, descriptive upper bound; it is not used to fit or tune the probe.

We use six open-weight instruction models from four families (Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.6-27B, gemma-4-12B-it, gemma-4-31B-it, Ministral-3-8B-Instruct, and granite-4.1-8b), plus DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B as the anchor for reproducing the single-domain result of Liu et al. (2026) (reproduced at AUROC 0.871/0.948 on SUM/UMWP, within the published range). The two 27–31B models enter RQ1 only: RQ2 and RQ3 require multi-turn roll-outs and many generation runs per model, which our compute budget allowed for the four 8–12B base models. Label-shuffle nulls and TF-IDF baselines on identical splits are run for all six models and reported inline with the results. Nulls are at chance throughout. On the math and extractive sets the probe beats TF-IDF by a wide margin; the known-unknowns sets are lexically separable, which we analyze separately.

Six frozen single-turn datasets (600 balanced items each; SUM 568), two per ground of unanswerability: information missing from the question (math): SUM (Song et al., 2025), minimally edited answerable/unanswerable pairs of math problems, and UMWP (Sun et al., 2024), unanswerable math word problems; information missing from the context (extractive): SQuAD 2.0 (Rajpurkar et al., 2018), and MuSiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022) built as minimal pairs in the setting of Slobodkin et al. (2023). Each MuSiQue question appears in both classes; its unanswerable context replaces the missing hop’s supporting paragraph with the most similar paragraph that contains no hop answer; epistemic unknowability (known-unknowns): SelfAware (Yin et al., 2023) (e.g. “Did we invent math or discover it?”), and KUQ (Amayuelas et al., 2024), restricted to its epistemic categories (future, unsolved, controversial, counterfactual). Labels follow each source. Every frozen set is versioned with a content hash and deduplicated against the others.

RQ1 measures the full train \times test matrix: for each ordered domain pair, the frozen probe (with its train-domain scaler) is evaluated on the full test domain; the diagonal is within-domain CV. A leave-one-domain-out (LODO) variant trains one pooled probe on all-but-one domain and tests on the held-out domain. Geometry compares class-separation directions \Delta\mu=\overline{x}_{y=1}-\overline{x}_{y=0} per (domain, seed, fold) at the common best layer: pairwise cosines, the participation-ratio effective rank of the stacked directions, and the principal angle between the {math, extractive} subspace and the known-unknowns axis, all mean \pm sd over the 15 seed \times fold splits. The robustness analyses add three things: bootstrap-over-items 95% CIs with within-dataset split-half null angles, plus a whitened (shrinkage-LDA) variant in a common pooled coordinate system; a lexical residualization, which removes the component of the hidden state predicted from TF-IDF features, with the map fit on training folds only; layer selection from the training dataset alone. Each analysis has a decision rule committed before it ran (Appendix A).

Following the sharded-instruction setting of Laban et al. (2025), each conversation reveals the atomic constraints of a task one per user turn in a randomized order; a deterministic rule labels every turn-state (the conversation up to and including user turn t, before the model’s reply) as underspecified (1) until the predefined sufficiency set of constraints has been revealed, then answerable (0). Sources: grade-school math (numeric answer), small Python functions (reference implementation), and data-to-text (slot-value sentence); 21% of conversations are early-fully-specified distractors so that position alone does not determine the label. The generated pool (504 conversations) was audited by eight human annotators (728 verdicts, disjoint shards plus a shared calibration set), which surfaced a systematic defect: default-confirming constraints padded into sufficiency sets. A shrink-only repair by a judge model from a family other than the generator’s, with rules fixed in advance and validated against the annotators’ calibration set, plus a rule-based drop pass, froze the benchmark at 423 conversations / 1,661 turn-states (drops: 58 question-arrives-last math items, 19 unexplained flags, 4 judge conflicts).

For RQ2, each model first replies to every turn of every conversation (greedy roll-out), so turn-state read-outs contain the model’s own intermediate replies in context; an excluded-replies variant is the control.

RQ3 turns the probe into a gate that requires no fine-tuning of the model (a worked example of one conversation, from constraints to gate decisions, is in Appendix F). The raw probe score at the last prompt token is mapped to a calibrated probability by Platt scaling (Platt, 1999) fit on held-out training-side validation data, and thresholded at \tau=0.5 (\tau swept in the appendix). Gate probes never see gated items: single-turn items of domain D are gated by the LODO probe trained on the other domains (transfer is the mechanism); multi-turn conversations are gated out-of-fold: probes trained on grouped conversation folds that never contained the gated conversation, since single-turn probes do not transfer across structure (see the RQ2 results). When the gate fires, the model does not answer: single-turn, it emits the same fixed abstention string as the prompted abstain baseline; multi-turn, a fixed prompt appended to the flagged turn makes the same model ask one clarifying question about the most important missing constraint. Baselines on identical, N-matched items: vanilla generation, prompted ask-when-unsure, prompted abstain, and RECAP-style consolidation (a recap turn restating all user turns before the final answer) (Laban et al., 2025).

All decoding is greedy with a 384-token cap. In multi-turn runs the user answers clarifying questions. An LLM (gpt-5.6-terra, T=0, from a family distinct from the generator and the evaluated models) only selects which not-yet-revealed constraint answers the model’s question. The user then sends that constraint verbatim; the math goal sentence is also selectable. A generic question receives the next scripted constraint, and an unanswerable question receives a fixed “no further details” reply. Scripted turns already revealed are skipped, and the same user serves every condition.

To separate detector error from intervention cost, three reference gates use the same clarify prompt: an oracle gate (fires iff the sufficiency set is unrevealed), a position gate (fires while any scripted constraint is unrevealed), and a random gate that matches the probe gate’s per-conversation firing rate (seeds 13/42/77). End-of-conversation success is objective per source: numeric match (math), differential execution against the reference implementation on a typed input battery (code), and slot-value coverage (data-to-text); single-turn correct behavior is refusal on unanswerable items and a normalized gold match on answerable ones. Paired comparisons use exact McNemar tests and paired bootstrap CIs on matched items.

Before each analysis we committed its decision rule to version control, then ran it. Appendix A lists the commits and timestamps, and the code release will include each report as it stood at its commit. This is a timestamped record kept by the authors, not registration with a third party, and one rule was amended before its run; we flag both where relevant.

Within-dataset probes are strong everywhere (mean diagonal 0.94–0.98; Table 1). The robust transfer result concerns datasets that share a ground of unanswerability. The two math sets transfer at 0.77–0.97 in all six models, in both directions. The two extractive sets also transfer in both directions in every model: SQuAD 2.0 and MuSiQue, the latter built as minimal pairs in the setting of Slobodkin et al. (2023), transfer at 0.77–0.90 at the six-dataset common layer. This replicates Slobodkin et al. ’s cross-dataset result on current models.

Transfer across grounds depends on model and layer. At the layer that maximizes within-domain AUROC over the four core datasets, math and extractive QA transfer at 0.66–0.94 (Figure 1). Adding the two new datasets moves the common layer in three of six models (Qwen3.5 20 \rightarrow 29, Granite 26 \rightarrow 31, Gemma4-12B 32 \rightarrow 31). At that layer the same math \leftrightarrow SQuAD cells span 0.38–0.94, and math \leftrightarrow MuSiQue spans 0.17–0.90 (Appendix Figure 3). Known-unknowns probes are at or near chance on SUM (SelfAware \rightarrow SUM 0.46–0.57) despite \approx 0.995 within-dataset AUROC.

By the decision rule we fixed before the first transfer run (cross-dataset mean \leq 0.65 or drop \geq 0.20 \Rightarrow dissociation), four of six models land on dissociation. Two of these verdicts sit on the boundary under seed-and-sampling bootstrap (Qwen3.5 0.93, Ministral 0.87 of replicates; Table 1). If the layer is instead chosen per training dataset, so that no target label touches selection, all six models are classified as dissociation. These verdicts concern the four-dataset matrix as a whole; the next paragraph asks which part of it is robust.

SelfAware is lexically separable (TF-IDF 0.94), and so is the second known-unknowns benchmark we add, KUQ (0.94). Both build the answerable class from factoid QA sets and write the unanswerable class separately, so the label coincides with the source genre. A TF-IDF classifier trained on either set transfers to the other at 0.89–0.91. KUQ therefore replicates SelfAware rather than controlling for its confound. We tested the separation three ways, each with a decision rule committed before the run (Table 2).

Replication on KUQ. At the six-dataset layer, KUQ’s probe also transfers poorly to SUM (\leq 0.65 in 5/6 models). At the four-dataset layer, KUQ \rightarrow SUM exceeds 0.65 in 3/6. Lexical residualization. We remove the component of the hidden state that TF-IDF features predict, fitting the projection on training folds only. A known-unknowns signal survives: within-dataset AUROC is 0.81–0.92 for SelfAware, and items that TF-IDF misclassifies are separated at 0.98–0.99. Its non-transfer to math does not survive: SelfAware \rightarrow SUM rises above 0.65 in 3/6 models, which our decision rule classifies as negative. Our committed rule compared residualized SelfAware \leftrightarrow KUQ transfer with raw known-unknowns \rightarrow math transfer and held in 6/6. Compared like for like, both residualized, it holds in only 4/6: it fails for both Gemma models, and Qwen3.5 passes by 0.02. Geometry with uncertainty. In \Delta\mu space the {math, extractive} subspace is further from the known-unknowns direction than math is from extractive in 6/6 models (CI >0), well above the within-dataset split-half floor (14–29 ∘). After whitening by the pooled covariance (shrinkage LDA), the gap is positive in no model and significantly negative in 3/6.
With MuSiQue as the extractive set, the raw gap reverses for both Gemma models.

The known-unknowns separation is therefore unresolved. Raw probes and raw \Delta\mu geometry suggest a separate direction in every model, but removing lexical cues, whitening the coordinates, or changing the layer or the extractive dataset each removes it in some models. We read RQ1 as robust transfer within a ground of unanswerability, and make no claim about separation between grounds.

Controls: label-shuffle nulls are 0.47–0.52 for all six models and six datasets. The model-independent TF-IDF baseline trails the probe by 44–72 AUROC points on the math and extractive sets; SUM’s and MuSiQue’s minimal pairs defeat it outright (0.24, 0.48). Best-layer selection cannot create the weak cross-ground transfer: the weakest headline AUROC survives Bonferroni correction across layers (appendix).

Can the single-turn probe detect, zero-shot, the moment a conversation becomes answerable? No – and the failure is itself structured (Table 3). Applied to turn-states, frozen single-turn probes are at or below chance at the mid/late layers where they live (0.20–0.55 for three of four models): the single-turn underspecification direction anti-correlates with turn-level underspecification. What zero-shot signal exists sits in the first one or two layers (0.77–0.85) and is partially surface-driven. Behaviorally, the frozen probe declares “sufficient” one to two turns prematurely in 74–98% of conversations (mean lag -1.3 to -2.3 turns): it would stop asking clarifying questions too early.

Turn-level underspecification is nonetheless strongly decodable in-structure: probes trained on turn-states (grouped by conversation so no conversation straddles train/test) reach 0.925–0.935 AUROC. Because turn-level labels are position-correlated by construction (relative position alone scores 0.934), we also evaluate within fixed turn indices, where absolute position is constant: the ceiling stays at 0.76–0.86 (min–max over turns 2–4 and models; Table 3), while zero-shot retains only a weak trace (0.51–0.79). Within a turn index, however, the label remains partly predictable from the text of the user turns alone: a TF-IDF classifier on them, trained with the same conversation-grouped splits, reaches 0.79 within-turn (0.91 overall), on par with the ceiling averaged over turns 2–4 (0.79–0.81 across models). We therefore read the in-structure result as showing that the information is present and linearly available, not that the probe captures more than the surface text does. Labels also remain largely predictable from the conversation’s design within a turn index. Position relative to the total number of turns, which a turn-state prefix does not reveal, matches the probe within 0.02. A logistic model on design features (turn index, total turns, source task, context length) exceeds it by 0.07–0.10.

The probe’s within-turn signal is therefore consistent with, but not proof of, the model inferring task size from content. This makes the zero-shot failure starker: a signal that a bag-of-words classifier recovers is not picked up by the single-turn direction. Label-shuffle nulls for the ceiling are clean (0.486–0.496). Geometrically, the multi-turn direction is rotated 57–81 ∘ from the entire single-turn subspace (raw \Delta\mu coordinates), and its cosine to the known-unknowns direction is negative in all four models. Two further controls: per-domain zero-shot transfer follows the RQ1 ordering (math probes transfer best, known-unknowns worst); and removing the model’s own replies from the context improves zero-shot transfer for granite (0.829 vs 0.789) while slightly shrinking the rotation: the model’s own reply tokens are part of what rotates the direction. Replies truncated at the 384-token cap (17–63% of replies, depending on the model) shift within-turn AUROC by up to 0.10 for the ceiling and 0.15 for zero-shot, in opposite directions across models (Appendix J). These shifts are far smaller than the zero-shot failure itself.
RQ3 asks whether the signal, deployed as a leakage-free calibrated gate, improves end-task performance. We test it on all four 8–12B models (Table 4).

In all four models the gate beats vanilla by +0.15 to +0.21 (McNemar p\leq 10^{-24}), but it trails the one-line abstain prompt by 0.05–0.09. The cause is threshold transfer, which RQ1 predicts. For Qwen and Granite, which our offline risk–coverage analysis covers, the leave-one-domain-out gate’s calibrated threshold fires on 94–99% of math items and on none of SQuAD. Yet its ranking within each dataset beats chance in 7 of 8 model–dataset pairs, and at the same abstention budget an oracle detector would beat the prompt. A full \tau -sweep (appendix) rescues neither model, and a cost-sensitive threshold fixed in advance does not help either.

section: Multi-turn, with a user who answers.
text: A scripted user who cannot answer clarifying questions makes asking pure cost. We therefore evaluate with a simulated user in the style of CLAM (Kuhn et al., 2022), who knows the not-yet-revealed constraints. An LLM only selects which hidden constraint answers the model’s question, and the user then replies with that constraint verbatim, so nothing beyond the scripted information can leak. The simulator was validated before use: on 60 real exchanges it was judged correct in 56 by a human, with no over-reveals.

section: Multi-turn, with a user who answers.
text: The endpoint, fixed before any gated run was scored, is negative. The probe gate beats vanilla significantly in two of four models (Granite +0.083, Gemma +0.078; Holm-adjusted p<0.02). It is significantly worse for Qwen (-0.071) and indistinguishable for Ministral. It loses to RECAP-style consolidation in two of four (-0.144 for Qwen and Granite). The reference gates locate the gap: Detection. Against the turn labels, the probe gate fires with precision 0.74–0.88, against 0.54–0.58 for a random gate. It misses 10–32% of underspecified turns (recall 0.68–0.90; the oracle is exact by construction), and these misses account for 68–100% of its premature answers. These premature answers cost little: conversations with one end correct as often as those without, within 0.04 in every model, because the model revises its answer once the remaining constraints arrive (Appendix F). This is why better detection would add little: the true-label gate’s success is at most 0.08 higher. Asking at the right moment matters. At the same firing rate, the probe gate beats randomly timed asking by +0.14 to +0.28 in every model, and random asking is strongly harmful. The remaining limit is how the model uses a clarification.

section: Multi-turn, with a user who answers.
text: For Qwen, even the true-label gate does not beat vanilla. The non-deployable position gate keeps asking until the script is exhausted, and it is the best gate in every model. This suggests that more persistent asking can pay off. Letting the user answer raises the probe gate by +0.10 (Qwen) and +0.19 (Granite) over the scripted-user setting, so a user who cannot answer gives a loose lower bound. In short, the probe gate asks at better-than-chance moments and nearly matches a true-label gate, but neither turns asking into end-task gains over consolidation. Firing precision and recall are a descriptive analysis added after the endpoint was scored.

section: Probing internal states for answerability and truthfulness.
text: Linear structure in the residual stream has been reported for truthfulness: supervised probes separate true from false statements (Azaria and Mitchell, 2023), unsupervised consistency objectives recover latent truth directions (Burns et al., 2023), and true/false datasets exhibit emergent linear geometry that supports steering (Marks and Tegmark, 2023). Closest to us, Liu et al. (2026) show that answerability is linearly decodable from hidden states of reasoning models and use it to analyze abstention failures – within a single (math) domain. Slobodkin et al. (2023) probe answerability on SQuAD 2.0, Natural Questions and MuSiQue and find that the learned subspace transfers across these extractive benchmarks; Orgad et al. (2025) show that hidden-state error detectors do not transfer universally across ten tasks, and Liu et al. (2024) search for a single truthfulness hyperplane shared across tasks and domains. We build on this line but vary the ground of unanswerability rather than the benchmark: information missing from the question, information missing from the context, and epistemic unknowability. We then follow the same signal across conversational structure (RQ2) and into a deployed gate (RQ3). Transfer is robust within a ground, while the separation between grounds remains unresolved.

Abstention in LLMs is typically elicited by prompting, fine-tuning, or confidence heuristics; Wen et al. (2024) survey the space and explicitly pose whether abstention can be “a meta-capability that transcends specific tasks or domains.” Our unanswerable sets instantiate distinct abstention grounds: information missing from the question (SUM (Song et al., 2025), UMWP (Sun et al., 2024)), information missing from a passage (SQuAD 2.0 (Rajpurkar et al., 2018)), and questions unanswerable for anyone (SelfAware (Yin et al., 2023), KUQ (Amayuelas et al., 2024)). Our RQ1 results give a partial answer to the survey’s question. Missing-information abstention transfers across datasets that share a ground. Whether epistemic unknowability shares that representation is not settled by our data: its apparent separation weakens under lexical controls and changes with layer and coordinate system.

Laban et al. (2025) document that models “get lost” in sharded, underspecified conversations and evaluate prompt-level workarounds (recap and snowball-style consolidation), which we adopt as baselines. We add what that line lacks: a benchmark whose turn-states are labeled for answerability by construction (with human audit and rule-based repair), a latent detector evaluated turn-by-turn against those labels, and a gate that asks a clarifying question exactly when the detector fires. Our RQ3 result sharpens the workaround comparison: consolidation attacks context loss and wins. Detection-gated asking fires far more precisely than chance and nearly matches a true-label gate, yet does not convert this into end-task gains, even with a user who answers. Selective clarification has also been studied with simulated users who hold the missing information: CLAM (Kuhn et al., 2022) asks only for ambiguous inputs and answers from such a simulator, and Zhang and Choi (2025) decide when a clarification is worth its cost from its expected benefit. Our gate makes this decision from a hidden-state probe rather than from the model’s own outputs.

Our gate reads a single scalar through Platt scaling (Platt, 1999) fit on training-side validation data only, a monotone recalibration that leaves probe ranking untouched; the model itself is never fine-tuned. Throughout, we control the classic confound of confidence read-outs: label-shuffle nulls and TF-IDF baselines on identical splits separate representation content from lexical surface, and a position-only baseline plus within-turn evaluation do the same for conversational position (RQ2 results).

We asked how far the latent unanswerability signal in LLM hidden states carries, using a new turn-labeled benchmark and an answering-user harness. Across datasets. Probes transfer robustly when two datasets share a ground of unanswerability. Whether epistemic unknowability is represented separately remains open: the evidence changes with layer, lexical controls and coordinate system. Across structure. Single-turn probes fail zero-shot on turn-level dialogue states. In-structure probes recover turn-level answerability, but no better than a classifier on the user turns. At deployment. A leakage-free gate fires on underspecified turns far more precisely than chance, and comes within 0.08 of a true-label gate in end-task success. It still does not beat consolidation. These are mostly negative results, reported with their controls. The benchmark, the simulator and the result tables are the parts we expect to be most useful, and we release all of them.

Scale and architecture coverage. Four model families and two size tiers (8–12B and 27–31B), but only Qwen and Gemma are represented in both; the Qwen pair also changes model generation (3.5 to 3.6), so it is not a controlled scaling comparison. granite-4.1-8b is a hybrid Mamba-2/transformer, so layer indices are not comparable across architectures; all layer selections are per-model. Synthetic multi-turn data. The benchmark’s conversations are generated, then human-audited and repaired under a fixed protocol (728 verdicts surfaced a systematic sufficiency-set defect; the repaired, frozen set drops 81 of 504 conversations); labels are deterministic given sufficiency sets, but the conversations are not naturally occurring dialogue. Correlational probes. All probe results are decoding claims, not causal ones: we did not run the planned activation-steering ablation, so nothing here shows the probed direction causally mediates abstention. Layer selection and multiple comparisons. Best layers come from full layer sweeps; the appendix quantifies the exposure: the weakest headline AUROC survives Bonferroni correction across all layers (p\approx 2\times 10^{-13} vs \alpha\approx 10^{-3}), the RQ2 ceiling is layer-insensitive (0.885–0.934 across all layers), and held-out LODO layer selection biases transfer upward, so it cannot create the weak transfer we report. Annotators are authors.

The eight benchmark annotators are authors of this paper, so the audit is not independent. Its role was to find defects, which it did; the labels themselves follow from the sufficiency sets by rule. Simulated user. The answering user replies only with scripted constraints, selected by an LLM, and never improvises or misunderstands. It was validated on 60 exchanges by a single annotator. Real users would answer less cleanly, which affects every ask-based condition alike. Known-unknowns datasets. Both known-unknowns benchmarks build their answerable class from a different source than their unanswerable class, so label and genre coincide. Lexical residualization reduces this confound but cannot remove it; a lexically matched known-unknowns set would be needed. Run recovery. Some RQ3 generation runs were resumed from checkpoints after infrastructure failures, and one run spans two GPU types; all are listed in a run log released with the code. Judge-scored clarify quality was declared in advance as secondary-only evidence and is not reported; all multi-turn success metrics are objective (numeric match, differential code execution, slot coverage). Token accounting uses whitespace tokens, identical across conditions, so only deltas are meaningful.

Potential risks. A probe gate that fires too often withholds answers users need. One that fires too rarely gives false assurance that a model “knows” when it cannot answer. Our gates do not beat simple prompting baselines, so we do not recommend deploying them as a safeguard. The probes read hidden states of open-weight models and offer no defense against adversarial inputs.

Data and annotation. All data are public research datasets, used under their licenses, or synthetic conversations without personal information. The eight benchmark annotators are authors of this paper and took part voluntarily; no data about them were collected.

Use of AI assistants. Beyond the LLMs that are part of our method (benchmark generation, benchmark repair, and the user simulator; Section 2), we used AI assistants to help write code, to draft parts of the text, and to fix grammar. The authors designed the study, fixed the decision rules before each run, checked the results, and take responsibility for all content.

A Reality Check of Inference-Time Context Augmentation Methods. Large language models (LLMs) often fail to utilise the context given in the input, resulting in hallucinations or a fallback to parametric knowledge. Context augmentation methods aim to improve model performance by modifying the input, from inserting filler tokens that add computational time to adding relevant content such as elaboration of a context during inference. However, these methods have been evaluated in isolation and only by their performance gains, leaving it unclear how they compare and whether they reliably improve performance. In this paper, we present an evaluation framework spanning five methods that differ in how informative the inserted content is and apply them at the sentence level across seven models spanning multiple sizes on three datasets. We find that accuracy gains are not always genuine improvements but undirected perturbations: the methods correct some predictions while breaking others, particularly when the inserted text allows only for more computational time. Our analysis reveals that methods that bring no additional content primarily change model predictions near the decision boundary. Our findings highlight the need to evaluate the reliability of the accuracy gains before adopting them in practice.

Providing contextual knowledge during inference time allows large language models (LLMs) to better ground their answers in information, especially recent, domain-specific knowledge, without additional training. Despite the contextual knowledge being explicitly provided in the input, LLMs often fail to utilise it, resulting in hallucinations or defaulting to parametric knowledge Wang et al. (2024); Xie et al. (2024); Sun et al. (2025). To address this, a growing body of work proposes methods that insert additional content into the context at inference time, ranging from inserting filler tokens to augmenting the input with additional knowledge Xu et al. (2024); Pfau et al. (2024); Zhu et al. (2022); Chen et al. (2023). We refer to these as context augmentation methods, a subset of the broader family of context engineering methods.

However, these methods have been developed and evaluated in isolation and only by their performance gains. Performance gains alone do not explain whether the methods affect the model predictions in a reliable way. Furthermore, existing methods insert content at a limited, single, predetermined location, which differs across methods. To compare these methods systematically and understand their effects, we propose an evaluation framework that investigates the reliability of the accuracy gains across seven models and three datasets covering multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) and fact-checking.

Our evaluation framework covers five methods, each representing a family of context augmentation methods from prior work, as shown in Figure 1. We choose them to vary in how much information the inserted content carries, which allows us to compare how different amounts of information affect the model’s predictions. We further investigate how the intervention’s position within the context affects its effectiveness. We therefore apply each method after every sentence of the context, one position at a time (Table 1). This provides a consistent set of intervention positions across methods and enables a systematic analysis of position-dependent effects.

Our framework evaluates each method in two ways: by its accuracy, and by a sign-randomisation test that assesses how reliably an accuracy gain reflects improvement. The test examines whether a gain stems from moving the model toward the correct answer given the context, or from perturbing its predictions without a consistent direction (§ 3.2.2). This distinction is necessary because such undirected perturbation can itself raise accuracy, reproducibly. We further analyse individual sentence-level interventions to understand which predictions each method changes (§ 6.1), at how many positions in a context (§ 6.2), and whether successful positions can be identified in advance (§ 6.3).

Our findings are: Perturbations are undirected. Accuracy gains from context augmentation methods do not always reflect a directed improvement (§ 5). Particularly for methods with less information, they often arise from random changes, which we refer to as undirected perturbation. The effect of a method also varies considerably across models and datasets. Interventions act near the decision boundary. Context augmentation methods with less information mainly change predictions that lie close to the decision boundary (§ 6.1). Whether they flip a prediction toward or away from the correct answer, they shift the prediction by similar amounts. Intervention position is important. Incorrect and correct predictions can be flipped from half of the positions in context (§ 6.2). Successful positions, however, cannot be predicted in advance, neither from lexical characteristics of a sentence nor by using the last position, where content is commonly added (§ 6.3). Identifying successful positions remains an open problem for future work.

Context augmentation methods modify the input to enhance model capability. For example, inserting filler tokens expands the computational space before answer generation, providing the model with additional computation to better process the input text Pfau et al. (2024); Goyal et al. (2024); Jang et al. (2025). Input repetition, on the other hand, enriches the model’s internal representations by enabling bidirectional-like computation Springer et al. (2025), and has been shown to improve performance on downstream language understanding tasks Xu et al. (2024); Leviathan et al. (2025).

Another line of work augments the context with additional knowledge rather than restructuring it. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) prepends retrieved passages to the input and has become a dominant paradigm for knowledge-intensive tasks Lewis et al. (2020); Zeng et al. (2025). Beyond retrieval from external corpora, several studies leverage the model itself or a better-performing model as a knowledge source, generating explanations or elaborations first and then incorporating them back into the input text Liu et al. (2022); Chen et al. (2023); Li et al. (2025). These methods also differ in where they intervene in the input: over the whole input Xu et al. (2024); Leviathan et al. (2025), between the context and the question Liu et al. (2022); Li et al. (2025), or at the end of the input Pfau et al. (2024); Greenblatt (2025).

Zhang et al. (2026) examine how robust models are to task-irrelevant context by prepending it to benchmark questions, including semantically meaningless pseudo-words. They find that aggregate accuracy remains nearly unchanged while individual predictions flip in both directions, and call for per-example evaluation. Their study covers only the least informative kind of intervention; we compare it with methods that add increasing amounts of information and examine how their effects differ.

Overall, existing methods have been developed and evaluated in isolation and only by their performance gains. Because they intervene at different positions, practitioners have little guidance on when to apply which method and where. We address this gap with an evaluation framework that compares methods under the same conditions and analyses.

Context augmentation methods intervene on the input text at inference time. We focus on methods that insert additional content into the input to improve context utilisation. These methods differ in how informative the inserted content is. Some add no new information and merely increase the amount of computation the model performs before answering, for example by inserting semantically irrelevant filler tokens Pfau et al. (2024); Greenblatt (2025). Others supply knowledge relevant to the question.

Existing methods have been proposed and evaluated in isolation, without systematic comparison. To compare them under the same conditions, we apply each method at the sentence level, standardising the intervention position across methods and allowing us to examine whether position matters. Our evaluation framework covers five methods, chosen to vary in how much information the inserted content carries, allowing us to compare how different amounts of information affect the model.

For a context c=[s_{1},...,s_{n},...,s_{N_{c}}] containing N_{c} sentences, an intervention function \mathcal{I} targets a sentence s_{n} by appending an intervention i_{n} after it. Formally, \mathcal{I}(c,s_{n})=[s_{1},...,s_{n},i_{n},...,s_{N_{c}}]. Each context is followed by a question, and the model outputs a token distribution over the vocabulary. Specifically, we compute the log probability of all possible answers and select the one with the highest log probability as the model answer. Our intervention approaches include five types: Blank, Repeat, Paraphrase, Self-explanation, and Teacher-explanation, which are described below.
We append semantically irrelevant filler tokens after s_{n}, increasing the amount of computation the model performs over the context without adding any information.

A verbatim copy of s_{n} is added. Beyond adding computation, repetition reinforces the original contextual information without introducing additional knowledge. This follows work showing that re-reading or repeating the input improves performance Xu et al. (2024); Leviathan et al. (2025).

We insert a paraphrase of s_{n} that preserves its meaning but uses different wording. Compared with Repeat, the content is the same, but the surface form differs, allowing us to test whether restating information in different words affects the model beyond repetition.

We insert an explanation of s_{n} generated by the evaluated model itself. Since the relevant knowledge the model holds in its parameters is only implicit, generating it as text enables us to place it in the context, where the model can attend to it when answering Yu et al. (2023); Sun et al. (2023); Li et al. (2025). Unlike Paraphrase, this adds information beyond the context, but only information the model already has.

We insert an explanation of s_{n} generated by a larger teacher model. It adds computation and information in the same way as Self-explanation, but from a more capable model, and can therefore supply knowledge the evaluated model lacks.

Each intervened input contains a single intervention applied after one of the original sentences. A context c with N_{c} sentences thus yields N_{c} separate intervened inputs per method, all paired with the same question.
