AccentCL: Robust Accent Classification with Incremental Expansion. Accent classifiers are typically trained with a fixed label inventory and cannot accommodate new accent categories as new data becomes available. Moreover, accented speech corpora often exhibit substantial class imbalance and/or domain shift due to differences in recording conditions across corpora. We present AccentCL, a class-incremental learning framework for English accent classification that is robust to class imbalance and cross-corpus domain shift. AccentCL extracts multi-layer representations from a frozen Whisper-Large-v3 encoder, optimized with an imbalance-aware cross-entropy loss to reduce bias toward the majority accent classes and a domain mean alignment loss that minimizes distributional mean shift across training corpora. The label space is then expanded via replay-based continual learning, using the frozen base model for knowledge retention and an old-to-new margin loss to reduce overprediction on newly added classes. On a five-class accent classification task, AccentCL achieves 77.1% balanced accuracy and a 76.9% macro-averaged F1 score. We further evaluate the model's ability to incrementally incorporate two new accent categories: Spanish-accented and Chinese-accented English. When adding Spanish-accented English to the pretrained model, AccentCL attains an F1 of 83.3% on the new class while retaining 77.3% balanced accuracy on the base classes.

When subsequently adding Chinese-accented English, it achieves 61.8% F1 on the new class while preserving 77.6% balanced accuracy on the previously learned classes. These results show that AccentCL enables robust regional accent classification while allowing new accent categories to be added without full retraining.

The ability to identify regional or non-native varieties of speech enables a range of applications, including speaker population analysis, evaluation of accented speech synthesis/conversion systems, and measurement of performance disparities in downstream speech models. Further, accent-related variation carries acoustic and phonetic cues (e.g., in pronunciation, rhythm, and prosody) that can affect the performance of automatic speech recognition, voice conversion, and spoken language understanding systems. As speech technologies are increasingly deployed across diverse speaker populations, developing accent classifiers that are both robust and extensible has become an important research direction.

Recent accent classifiers benefit from large pretrained speech encoders and public speech corpora, but often rely on strong assumptions about the underlying data. First, accent labels are typically defined along political or national boundaries (e.g., American vs. Canadian English) rather than geographic or cultural lines, even though intra-national accent variation can be substantial — differences between Southern and Northeastern US accents, for instance, are often more pronounced than those between American and Canadian English. Second, accent label distributions tend to be long-tailed, with some categories represented by substantially fewer samples than others. Third, training samples are frequently pooled across multiple corpora that differ in recording conditions, speaker demographics, and collection protocols, introducing corpus-level domain shift. Finally, these models do not allow new accent categories to be added after a classifier has already been deployed. Retraining from scratch to accommodate new classes is computationally costly and often impractical when the original training data are no longer available or when only limited replay of old-class samples can be retained.

We propose AccentCL, a framework for robust, class-incremental English accent classification. AccentCL first trains an accent classifier by merging closely related fine-grained accent labels into broader regional groups that reflect geographic influences, reducing ambiguity arising from acoustically similar or inconsistently annotated labels. The classifier operates on multi-layer representations extracted from a frozen Whisper-Large-v3 encoder and is trained with class-prior adjustment and corpus-mean alignment to improve robustness to class imbalance and cross-corpus domain shift, respectively. AccentCL then expands the label space by incorporating new accent classes, using a small replay memory of previously learned accents stratified across corpora. During continual training, the updated model is regularized against the frozen base classifier for knowledge retention and uses an old-to-new margin loss to reduce overprediction of newly added classes on samples from previously learned accents. Together, these components allow the classifier to learn new accent categories while preserving performance on previously learned ones.

Our main contributions are: We formulate English accent classification as a robust class-incremental learning problem, one that must contend with ambiguous accent boundaries, class imbalance, domain heterogeneity, and limited replay. We show that multi-layer representations from a frozen speech foundation model can be adapted for robust regional accent classification through imbalance-aware training and class-conditional domain mean alignment. We introduce a replay-based continual training objective that combines domain-stratified memory, frozen-model retention, and an old-to-new margin loss, enabling new accent classes to be added while preserving performance on old ones.

section: Accent classification with speech foundation models
text: Accent classification aims to identify a speaker’s regional or non-native accent from speech. Recent systems commonly build on pretrained speech representations, including wav2vec 2.0, XLS-R, WavLM, and Whisper. These models yield contextual frame-level representations that capture acoustic, phonetic, and speaker-related information, which can then be aggregated via utterance-level pooling and passed to a classification head.

section: Accent classification with speech foundation models
text: CommonAccent is a pretrained English accent classifier trained on CommonVoice with a fixed 16-class accent inventory, but its single-domain training data and fine-grained label space may limit how well it generalizes to other domains. In our evaluation, many low-resource and out-of-domain accents are confused with related labels or absorbed into dominant classes, which motivates our use of a regional label mapping together with domain-aware training. Voxlect introduces a larger mixed-corpus benchmark for English dialect and regional language classification, evaluating several speech foundation models with LoRA fine-tuning; its strongest configuration, based on Whisper-Large-v3, serves as a strong reference model for accent-related classification. However, Voxlect remains a fixed-label classifier and is not built to accommodate new accent categories after training.

section: Accent classification with speech foundation models
text: AccentCL addresses this limitation by first training a robust regional accent classifier and then extending it through class-incremental learning. Our model also draws on the layer-wise structure of speech foundation models: prior work shows that different encoder layers capture different types of information, including acoustic, phonetic, speaker, and linguistic properties. Since accent cues span pronunciation, phoneme realization, rhythm, and prosody, AccentCL aggregates representations across multiple Whisper encoder layers rather than relying on the final layer alone.

Class-incremental learning addresses the problem of extending a model with new classes while preserving performance on previously learned ones. Unlike task-incremental learning, the model must predict over a unified label space at test time, which makes this setting especially prone to catastrophic forgetting and bias toward recently added classes.

Existing methods typically reduce forgetting through replay, which mixes stored old-class examples with new-class data, or through regularization and distillation, which encourage the updated model to stay close to the previous model. This line of work is directly relevant to accent classification, since new accent categories may need to be introduced after a classifier has already been trained. However, fine-tuning directly on the new accent can bias the classifier toward that class and degrade previously learned accents.

AccentCL supports incremental accent-class expansion by combining new-accent data with memory of previous accents drawn from multiple corpora. During training, it preserves the earlier model’s behavior on old-accent examples and suppresses the tendency to misclassify old accents as the newly added class, limiting degradation on earlier learned accents.

We study accent classification as a robust class-incremental learning problem. Given an accent classifier trained on a set of “old” accent classes \mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{old}}, the goal is to add a “new” accent class y_{\mathrm{new}} while preserving performance on the old classes. Before each incremental step, we construct a replay memory \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{mem}} from the previously learned classes. During incremental training, the updated classifier f_{\theta} is trained on \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{new}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{mem}}, where \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{new}} contains training utterances from the newly added accent class. Each training example is represented as (x_{i},y_{i},d_{i}), where x_{i} is an utterance, y_{i}\in\mathcal{Y} is the accent label, and d_{i} is the domain/corpus label. The objective is to learn a function f_{\theta} that recognizes the new accent class, retains performance on old classes, and remains robust across heterogeneous speech corpora.

The base classifier provides recognition capabilities on the “old” accents before expanding to new classes. We define an accent label space \mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{base}} by collapsing the 16 fine-grained accent categories in CommonAccent into 5 broad accent categories: North American (American and Canadian), British Isles (British, Irish, Scottish, and Welsh), Australasian (Australian and New Zealand), South Asian (Indian), and Southeast Asian (Malaysian and Singaporean). This grouping preserves broad regional structure while avoiding unreliable distinctions between fine-grained labels with limited training data.

Given an input waveform x, we use the encoder of a pretrained Whisper-Large-v3 model as the acoustic feature extractor. We train only the downstream projection, pooling, and classification modules. Motivated by prior findings that intermediate layers of speech foundation models retain useful acoustic and phonetic information, we extract hidden states from multiple Whisper encoder layers rather than using only the final layer.

Namely, we select encoder layers \mathcal{S}=\{16,20,24,28\}, an evenly spaced middle-to-late subset chosen to cover multiple representation depths while limiting computation. For each layer \ell\in\mathcal{S}, let H^{(\ell)}=\{h_{t}^{(\ell)}\}_{t=1}^{T} denote the corresponding frame-level hidden sequence. We apply a layer-specific projection head q_{\ell}(\cdot) to reduce the encoder’s hidden dimension and map all selected layers to the same dimensionality: \tilde{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}=q_{\ell}\!\left(h_{t}^{(\ell)}\right),\qquad\tilde{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{P},\vskip-5.0pt where P=256 in our implementation. Each projection head consists of layer normalization followed by a linear projection, a ReLU activation, and dropout.

The projected layer representations are then concatenated at each frame to form a multi-level accent representation, i.e. u_{t}=\mathrm{Concat}_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}}\left(\tilde{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\right), where u_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|P}. The resulting sequence \{u_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} is passed to the attentive statistics pooling, which computes attention-weighted mean and standard-deviation statistics over time. The pooled representation is fed into an MLP to obtain a compact accent embedding, which is then passed to a linear classifier to predict the regional accent label.

For each training example (x_{i},y_{i},d_{i}), the model produces logits a_{i} and an accent embedding z_{i}. To account for class imbalance, we use logit-adjusted cross-entropy. Let \pi\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{base}}|} be the empirical class-prior vector in the training set. The classification loss is: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cls}}=\frac{1}{\mathcal{B}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}}\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}(a_{i}+\tau\log\pi,y_{i}),\vskip-5.0pt where \tau controls the strength of the logit adjustment. Setting \tau=0 recovers standard cross-entropy.

We also regularize the learned accent embedding space with a domain mean alignment (DMA) loss. Since the same regional accent may appear in multiple datasets with different recording conditions, speaker pools, or corpus collection protocols, this term encourages embeddings to remain consistent across sources while preserving accent-class separation. For accent class y and domain d, let \mu_{y,d} denote the mean embedding of samples, and let \mu_{y} denote the mean embedding of all samples with label y in the mini-batch. The alignment loss is computed over active class-domain groups: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}|}\sum_{(y,d)\in\mathcal{G}}\left\|\mu_{y,d}-\mu_{y}\right\|_{2}^{2},\vskip-5.0pt where \mathcal{G} is the set of active class-domain groups in the mini-batch, defined as groups with at least m samples whose accent class is represented in at least two domains. We set m=2 in our experiments. The final base-training objective is \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cls}}+\beta_{\mathrm{align}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}, where \beta_{\mathrm{align}} controls the strength of the alignment term.

To add a new accent class, we expand the classifier head of the base model f_{\mathrm{base}} from |\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{old}}| outputs to |\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{old}}|+1 outputs. The classifier’s weights for the old classes are copied from f_{\mathrm{base}}, while the new-class weights are randomly initialized. The expanded model, denoted by f_{\theta}, is then trained on the union of the new-class data and the replay memory, i.e. \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{new}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{mem}}.

For class-incremental training, we construct a fixed replay memory from the old accent classes. Let \mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{old}} denote the old label space. For each old class k\in\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{old}}, we select K_{k}=\min\left(K,|\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{old}}_{k}|\right) utterances, where K is the maximum number of replay samples per class and \mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{old}}_{k} denotes the old-training utterances with label k. Within each class, we stratify sampling by domain/corpus. We divide the K_{k} selections as evenly as possible across the domains represented in \mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{old}}_{k} and sample without replacement from each domain. If a domain has too few utterances, the remaining samples are drawn at random from the unused utterances of the same class. The resulting class-specific memories are combined to form \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{mem}}=\bigcup_{k\in\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{old}}}\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{mem}}^{k}. This yields a replay memory that is balanced across old accent classes while maintaining source diversity within each class.

Let \mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{old}}\cup\{y_{\mathrm{new}}\} denote the expanded label space, where y_{\mathrm{new}} is the newly added accent class. Given utterance x_{i}, the expanded model produces logits a_{i}=f_{\theta}(x_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{Y}|}. The primary objective is cross-entropy \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}} over the expanded label space.

To reduce forgetting on old accents, we keep a frozen copy of the base model f_{\mathrm{base}} and use it as a teacher on replay memory samples. Let \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{mem}}\subseteq\mathcal{B} denote the old-class replay samples in the mini-batch, and let C_{\mathrm{old}}=|\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{old}}|. Since the expanded classifier contains an additional new-class output, we restrict its logits to the old label space when computing the retention loss. For replay sample i, let a_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}=a_{i}[\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{old}}] and a^{\mathrm{base}}_{i}=f_{\mathrm{base}}(x_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{\mathrm{old}}} denote the old-class logits of the expanded model and the logits produced by the frozen base model, respectively. We use temperature-scaled knowledge distillation to preserve the base model’s old-class prediction distribution: p^{\mathrm{base}}_{i}=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{a^{\mathrm{base}}_{i}}{\tau}\right),\qquad p^{\mathrm{old}}_{i}=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{a^{\mathrm{old}}_{i}}{\tau}\right), where \tau is the distillation temperature. The retention loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ret}}=\tau^{2}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{mem}}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{mem}}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(p^{\mathrm{base}}_{i}\;\|\;p^{\mathrm{old}}_{i}\right). This loss encourages the expanded model to preserve the frozen base model’s old-accent decision structure on replay samples, while the supervised cross-entropy loss allows the model to learn the newly added accent.

Because \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ret}} ignores the newly added class logit, an old replay sample can still receive a high new-class score even when its old-class logits are preserved. Complementary to retention, we add an old-to-new margin loss that directly suppresses new-class overprediction on replay memory samples. For each replay sample, the loss encourages the true old-class logit to exceed the new-class logit by a margin m: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{old,new}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{mem}}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{mem}}}\max\left(0,\,a_{i,y_{\mathrm{new}}}-a_{i,y_{i}}+m\right).\vskip-5.0pt The final continual-training objective is: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CL}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}+\beta_{\mathrm{align}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}+\beta_{\mathrm{ret}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ret}}+\beta_{\mathrm{old,new}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{old,new}}. Here, \beta_{\mathrm{align}}, \beta_{\mathrm{ret}}, and \beta_{\mathrm{old,new}} control the strengths of domain alignment, retention, and old-to-new margin regularization, respectively.

We construct our accent classification dataset from multiple English speech corpora, including CommonVoice, GLOBE, AESRC, UK-Ireland, EdAcc, L2ARCTIC, ARCTIC, EmiliaYODAS, VoxPopuli, and EMIME. We assign each utterance to a regional accent group following our collapsed accent label mapping. The full dataset includes North American (NA), British Isles (BI), Australasian (AUS), South Asian (SA), Southeast Asian (SEA), Spanish (SPA), and Chinese (CHN) accent groups.

All splits are constructed at the speaker level to prevent speaker overlap among the training, validation, and test sets. Because several corpora contain many utterances from the same speaker, we also limit speaker dominance during training. For each accent group, we first cap each speaker at 50 utterances. We then limit the total number of utterances per accent group to 50,000. To preserve training dataset diversity, we sample across the datasets available for each accent group. This prevents the training subset from being dominated by a small number of frequent speakers or large corpora, while keeping variation in recording conditions across datasets. The resulting training data distribution is shown in Figure 2.

We train AccentCL sequentially. All models are trained for 10 epochs with a batch size of 40 using AdamW and cosine learning-rate annealing. All reported results use a single fixed seed of 42. First, we train the base regional accent classifier with a frozen Whisper-Large-v3 encoder and update only the downstream projection layers, attentive statistics pooling module, MLP, and classifier head. The base model uses an initial learning rate of 1\times 10^{-3}, domain mean alignment weight \beta_{\mathrm{align}}=20, and logit adjustment temperature \tau=1.0. We select the base checkpoint using validation macro-F1.

We then perform continual training by adding Spanish-accented English as a new class. The classifier head is expanded by copying the old-class weights and initializing a new output unit. The expanded model is trained with new-class data and source-stratified replay memory from the old classes. We set the replay budget to K=2{,}000 utterances per old accent class, corresponding to approximately 10% of the original training data. Continual training uses an initial learning rate of 1\times 10^{-4}, \beta_{\mathrm{align}}=20, retention temperature \tau=2, and retention weight \beta_{\mathrm{ret}}=1.0. The margin loss uses \beta_{\mathrm{old,new}}=0.2 and margin m=0.3.

We repeat the same procedure to add Chinese-accented English on top of the base-plus-Spanish model. For continual training stages, checkpoint selection uses the harmonic mean between old-class macro-F1 and new-class F1:

H_{\mathrm{old,new}}=\frac{2F^{\mathrm{old}}_{\mathrm{macro}}F^{\mathrm{new}}}{F^{\mathrm{old}}_{\mathrm{macro}}+F^{\mathrm{new}}+\epsilon}, which balances old-class retention and new-class learning, instead of selecting models that perform well on only one side of the incremental task.

We compare AccentCL against two existing accent classification systems: CommonAccent is a wav2vec2-XLSR-based English accent classifier trained on CommonVoice. Voxlect evaluates several architectures for English dialect classification and reports the best performance with Whisper-Large-v3. We therefore use its Whisper-Large-v3 variant as the Voxlect baseline. Since CommonAccent, Voxlect, and AccentCL use different output label spaces, all models are evaluated under the shared regional accent label mapping described in Section V. Predictions outside the evaluated label set are retained and counted as errors. For class-incremental experiments, we also report Frozen Base model before adding each new class. This gives the original performance on the old classes and is used as reference for measuring forgetting. We also include joint retraining on all available data as an upper bound and naive new-class-only fine-tuning with cross-entropy and no replay as a lower bound.

We report accuracy, balanced accuracy, and macro-F1 for regional accent classification. Balanced accuracy is computed as the mean per-class recall. Macro-F1 is the unweighted average of class-wise F1 scores. We report results under two evaluation settings. All evaluates all test utterances from our constructed benchmark whose labels fall within the target regional label set. OOD evaluates source-held-out generalization on Speech Accent Archive and IDEA, neither of which is used as a training source for any model.

For class-incremental learning, we report new-class F1 and old-class balanced accuracy, where old classes are those learned before the current incremental step. To measure forgetting, we compute the per-class accuracy change between the expanded model and the model before adding the new accent, i.e. \delta_{k}=\mathrm{Acc}^{\mathrm{after}}_{k}-\mathrm{Acc}^{\mathrm{before}}_{k}. We then report the average forgetting over all old classes and the worst-class change: \Delta_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{old}}|}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{old}}}\min(0,\delta_{k}),\qquad\Delta_{\mathrm{worst}}=\min_{k\in\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{old}}}\delta_{k}.\vskip-5.0pt More negative values indicate stronger forgetting.

Table I reports the performance of the 5-class base regional accent classifier. We evaluate each model on the full test set and on a source-held-out subset to assess generalization across recording sources. On the full evaluation set, AccentCL base achieves an accuracy of 76.0%, balanced accuracy of 77.1%, and macro-F1 of 76.9%. Compared with the mapped Voxlect baseline, AccentCL base improves accuracy by +11.2 points, balanced accuracy by +11.3 points, and macro-F1 by +8.8 points. These results show that the proposed regional classifier provides stronger overall and class-balanced performance under the shared five-class accent label space.

On the source-held-out subset, AccentCL base achieves an OOD accuracy of 89.7%, balanced accuracy of 79.6%, and macro-F1 of 83.0%. Compared with Voxlect, AccentCL improves OOD accuracy by +5.9 points, balanced accuracy by +2.1 points, and macro-F1 by +0.4 points. Although the OOD macro-F1 gain is modest, AccentCL maintains strong class-balanced performance while improving overall accuracy on held-out recording sources. Ablation results in Table I further show that both logit adjustment and DMA improve OOD robustness, with DMA having the larger individual effect and their combination providing the strongest generalization to unseen recording sources.

We next evaluate whether the regional accent inventory can be expanded without retraining the full model from scratch. Starting from the five-class base model, we incrementally add two accent classes: first Spanish-accented English, and then Chinese-accented English, yielding a class-incremental sequence of 5\rightarrow 6\rightarrow 7 classes.

Table II reports the class-incremental results. Voxlect is included as a fixed-label reference model rather than a continual-learning baseline. After adding Spanish-accented English, AccentCL achieves the best new-class F1 (83.3) and old-class balanced accuracy (77.3%), while showing only a small average old-class drop (-0.8 points). The retention-only variant gives the smallest forgetting in this step, suggesting that matching the previous classifier’s predictions helps preserve the performance of the original five regional classes. After adding Chinese-accented English, AccentCL again obtains the best new-class F1 (61.8) and old-class balanced accuracy (77.6%). The margin-only variant has the smallest degradation on old classes in this step, indicating that reducing confusions between old accents and the new class is important when adding Chinese-accented English. Overall, the ablations show that retention and the margin loss contribute to the two expansion steps. Combining both gives AccentCL the most consistent balance between learning the new accent and maintaining performance on old accents.

As lower and upper bounds, naive new-class-only fine-tuning and full joint retraining achieve 15.0/0.3 and 89.3/77.7 New F1/Old BAcc, respectively, for the 5\!\rightarrow\!6 step, and 5.7/5.7 and 70.3/80.0 for the 6\!\rightarrow\!7 step. These results show that naive fine-tuning suffers severe catastrophic forgetting, while AccentCL approaches full joint retraining using only limited replay.

Figure 3 compares per-class recall for Voxlect and AccentCL after adding Spanish-accented English. We evaluate on the held-out speakers from corpora used by both models. AccentCL shows higher recall for the newly added Spanish-accented English class and for old regional classes, which is consistent with the gains in Table II.

Fig. 4 shows t-SNE visualizations of learned embedding spaces. Compared with Voxlect, AccentCL forms clearer accent groups with weaker domain shifts. For example, Australasian samples in VoxLect are split into several clusters from different domains, while AccentCL keeps them more compact. Some domain shifts remain, suggesting that AccentCL reduces, but does not fully remove, variation across corpora.

We proposed AccentCL, a framework for English accent classification that supports class-incremental expansion. By combining data from new accents with replay memory stratified by dataset, AccentCL adds Spanish- and Chinese-accented English without retraining on the full old dataset. In our setting, only about 10% of the old training data is retained as replay memory and still maintains balanced accuracy on old accent classes across incremental steps.

The ablation results show that retention and old-to-new margin regularization provide complementary benefits. Retention preserves the previous classifier’s behavior while the margin loss reduces confusion between old accents and the newly added class. New-class F1, balanced accuracy on old classes, and worst-class forgetting further show that AccentCL balances learning new accents with retaining old accents. A limitation of the current study is that continual learning is evaluated over only two expansion steps, using a single class order and random seed. Future work will examine robustness across additional expansion sequences and random seeds.

Compared with the Voxlect state-of-the-art baseline, AccentCL achieves stronger regional accent classification and better adaptation to the expanded label space. These results show that AccentCL provides a practical pipeline for continually expanding accent classifiers to future accent categories without retraining from scratch or substantially degrading previously learned classes.
Generative AI tools were used only for editing to improve clarity and presentation. All experimental design, implementation, data analysis, and result interpretation were performed by the authors.

People Making Conversation: Evaluating How Naturally Speech Models Converse. A conversational speech model has to decide, at every pause, whether to speak. Existing evaluations test boundary detection, policy adherence, or aggregate statistics, not this decision. We place real-time speech systems at 427 pauses and 482 turn ends from 176 unscripted conversations in Seamless Interaction, give each the conversation so far, and score what it generates against what the person did: whether and how soon it speaks at a pause; its latency, length, and wording at a turn end; and whether it can answer a question about the preceding 30 to 120 seconds. Across six systems, the hosted APIs (GPT Realtime, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, Grok Voice) respond at almost every pause whichever endpointer they use; only their latency, about 1 to 4 s with silence-based endpointers and about 8 s with semantic turn detection, decides whether the words land inside the pause. The full-duplex models (PersonaPlex, Moshi) are the only systems that regularly stay silent and the only ones that interrupt within a human reaction time. Hosted systems reply longer than the person.

Given the history as text, hosted systems recall 41 to 60% of conversation facts under a Claude Opus 5.5 judge and 19 to 26% under a strict word matcher; hearing it as audio, full-duplex models recall 17 to 22% and 12 to 15%. We release the labels, points, harness, and every output.

A conversational model must know when to say nothing. A listener can take the floor, acknowledge without taking it, or keep listening. The choice depends on the conversation so far, not only on whether the other person has stopped speaking. A short response latency does not establish whether the system should have spoken. Natural here means doing what the person did at that moment: silent where they were silent, replying where they replied, with similar timing and length; no listener rates the outputs.

PeopleMakingConversation does that. From 176 casual conversations we select two kinds of moment. A pause point is a silence inside a speaker’s turn that a system might mistake for its cue; the person listening did not speak, and the speaker went on. A turn-end point is a boundary where the floor passed and the person replied. The system receives the conversation up to the moment, then hears the other speaker continue in real time (Figure 1). At a pause we score whether it stays silent or takes the floor, and how quickly. At a turn end we score how soon it begins, how long it speaks relative to the person, and how close its words are to theirs. After 30 to 120 seconds of history we also ask a spoken question about something said earlier, and a judge scores the answer.

We evaluate six real-time systems, two self-hosted full-duplex models and four hosted API configurations. Two things follow from the results. With the silence-based endpointers we tested, hosted systems almost always responded; their latency, 1 to 4 s, rather than a contextual turn-taking decision, determined whether speech began inside the pause. The full-duplex models are the only systems that regularly stay silent, and the only ones that interrupt within a human reaction time; at turn ends they do not stop, and no system says as little as the person did. We release the corpus selection, labels, evaluation points, the harness, and every system output at https://github.com/People-Make-Things/people-conversation-bench.

Moshi reports aggregate timing statistics. The Gemini 3.1 Flash Live and GPT-Live releases report audio reasoning, function calling, and human preference, but no boundary-level account of which decisions the model gets right. Model papers such as BayLing-Duplex and SALMONN-omni score scenario success.

Table 1 lists the corpora of two-party conversation and Table 2 the benchmarks. Turn-taking is measured in three ways. Detection benchmarks ask whether a system marks the events a human annotator marked: end of turn, pause, backchannel, interruption. TurnBench, Talking Turns, and Full-Duplex-Bench v1 do this, and each penalises firing at a pause within a turn. Policy benchmarks ask whether a system speaks when a rule says it should, or completes a task while conversing: Speak or Stay Silent, CoDeTT, Instruct-FD, Full-Duplex-Bench v2/v3, and MTR-DuplexBench. Aggregate evaluations ask whether generated dialogue resembles human dialogue in its statistics, or whether people prefer it. Each answers its own question; none asks ours.

The detection family is the nearest to ours. What it scores is whether a boundary event was emitted at the right time. What we score is what a generative system does at a boundary a person actually faced, in a conversation nobody staged, and what it retains from the minutes before. Their stimuli are elicited or synthetic by design, which buys controlled conditions; ours are casual by design, which buys the decisions we want to measure. The two are complementary, and a system should be run on both. Our hosted pause results differ from benchmarks where hosted systems appear to hold at pauses. Those evaluations let the provider’s turn detector decide when a turn ended and score the detection; we requested a response once a silence-based endpointer fired, so what we measure is that configuration’s behaviour and latency, not whether the model could hold under a different turn detector (§ 6).

The corpus is the naturalistic subset of Seamless Interaction: 1,395 prompted, casual sessions of at least seven minutes, in which two participants were given a topic card and talked. We select by liveliness alone. Six traits are computed from the released transcripts and voice activity (speech-time balance, speaker alternations per minute, short-utterance rate, question rate, one minus the longest single-speaker share, overlaps per minute); a conversation’s score is the mean of its six percentile ranks among the 1,395. The 176 at or above 0.75 are the corpus (35.9 hours, mean 12.2 minutes, median 8.7; Appendix A). No model selects conversations; the LLM judge of § 3.3 selects points within them. The score favours lively conversation, so rates reported here are not population estimates.

Each speaker’s channel is labelled with speech onsets and offsets, turns, pauses, backchannels, and overlaps. Voice activity and transcripts are the corpus’s own; voiced stretches of at least 350 ms with no transcript are transcribed and aligned by Qwen3-ASR and Qwen3-ForcedAligner. A deterministic rule engine places every label and records the rule and confidence behind it. Gaps of at most 250 ms inside one speaker’s activity are closed. A listener segment of at most 1 s and two words during the other speaker’s turn is a backchannel. At every offset the engine looks ahead 5 s: if the same speaker resumes it is a pause; if the other speaker starts substantively it is an end of turn; if the other speaker starts and yields it is a pause and a failed take; if nobody speaks it is an end of turn. A voice activity projection model and three heuristics flag labels for review: a turn ended while the projection keeps the speaker on the floor (P\geq 0.65), a backchannel where it hands the floor over (P\geq 0.60), a turn with half its words from gap-fill, and a lexical turn under 400 ms; 19,933 turns produce 5,447 flags (27.3%, Appendix B).

The points in this paper are built on the engine’s labels. Every pause and turn-end window in the run was played with its context to two annotators and accepted, an accept-or-reject check with no per-window log.

The 176 conversations contain about 46,000 candidate boundaries; the point set is curated from them in two stages. Hard gates reject events that cannot be scored cleanly: pauses shorter than 600 ms or overlapped by the listener, active turns shorter than 1 s or three words, turn ends whose reply starts more than 3 s later or has fewer than five words, and events whose audio fails the scorer’s speech gate. Survivors are ranked by a heuristic over pause length, turn context, and the last words before the boundary, keeping at most three per type per conversation. A GPT-4o judge then reads a transcript window around each survivor. It rejects incoherent windows, pauses that hand the turn to the listener, interrupted fragments, and unresponsive replies, and ranks the rest by how tempting the pause is. An event the judge scores zero is never selected. This gives 427 pause points and 482 turn-end points across 157 and 171 of the 176 conversations; the run reported here draws a seeded random 300 of each.

At a selected pause the engine found no listener words and at a selected turn end the person replied substantively, so the human reference is hold or take, never backchannel. Appendix A gives the funnel.

Recall points test memory. For each prefix of 30, 60, 90, and 120 seconds ending at a completed turn, a question is spoken to the system in the user’s voice, cloned by Qwen3-TTS from 20 to 40 s of their speech. Conversation recall asks, in the user’s words and addressed to the system, about a specific fact either speaker stated in the first 30 seconds. The system plays speaker 1; the question is spoken in speaker 2’s cloned voice, with “I” and “me” referring to speaker 2 and “you” to speaker 1. A correct answer states the fact from speaker 1’s position, whichever speaker originally said it (example in Table 10). GPT-4o extracts it, a judge checks it for specificity, and it is dropped if its spoken form leaks a speaker label. Answers are scored by Claude Opus 5.5 (temperature 0); GPT-4o scores of the same transcripts are kept for comparison (Table 12). The same question is asked at every history length. Fact recall is the control.

It asks one general-knowledge question from a fixed list of twelve, assigned per conversation, whose answer does not depend on the history; a system that fails it did not answer the question it was asked. A judge-approved conversation fact exists for 46 conversations, giving 184 conversation-recall points; fact recall has 669, a prefix being skipped when no turn completes before its target. The run uses all 184 and a seeded random 300.

A rollout has two phases: history preload, then a live stream that is scored. History is capped at 164 s before the active turn, PersonaPlex’s context window. Full-duplex models receive it as two audio channels, the other speaker’s and their own, teacher-forced with word timestamps. Hosted models receive completed turns as text and the trailing user audio; their APIs accept nothing else. Every system also receives a short identity prompt, written once per speaker by GPT-4o from the transcript: who it is, how it knows the other person, and that the assistant history is its own prior speech.

At a pause point every system is streamed the active turn, the recorded pause, and the speaker resuming, as real-time frames, so it hears the pause as real silence; a full-duplex model steps through it frame by frame, and a hosted model’s server-side endpointer fires on it. The endpointer is the system’s turn-taking policy. At a turn-end point the trigger differs by family: a hosted model receives an explicit end-of-turn signal and a requested response, with its endpointer off so a mid-turn pause cannot interrupt it; a full-duplex model must detect the end from the audio itself and then receives silence frames until it stops or reaches the cap. The person’s reply is not played back. Drain lengths, caps, and audio format are in Appendix C. We score the first rollout of each point; a second rollout from the same run is released but not reported. Every output is recorded with its input timing, so every score can be recomputed from the rollout.

Speech intervals are found by an energy gate calibrated against Whisper word timestamps on the systems’ own output (Appendix D). The gate alone is a weak classifier of speech, so a response requires transcribed words; above-gate audio with an empty transcript is wordless phonation, reported as its own category.

Pause recognition. On the stream of § 3.4, a takeover is a word-bearing interval overlapping the labelled pause; otherwise the system held, either silently or by speaking after the person resumed. We report the shares silent, takeover, and after, the wordless rate, and takeover latency from pause start to the first words, zero if the system was already speaking. Turn-end latency. Time from the turn end to the onset of the system’s first transcribed word, on the playback clock; a word that began before the turn end gives zero or less. Response length. Duration from first to last speech interval and word count, each as a ratio to the human reply. Response similarity. Token F1 and cosine similarity of all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings between the system’s transcript and the human reply. Recall. Whether the spoken answer is correct, judged by Claude Opus 5.5 against the gold answer or the conversation, reported by history length.

We evaluate six real-time speech systems in two families. Self-hosted full-duplex models listen and speak at once and run on Modal: PersonaPlex-7B and Moshi. Hosted real-time APIs take audio in and return audio out, with the provider’s server-side voice activity detection deciding when the user’s turn has ended: GPT Realtime (gpt-realtime-2025-08-28), Gemini 3.1 Flash Live (preview), and Grok Voice (grok-voice-latest). GPT Realtime is run at two silence settings, 300 ms and 500 ms, which isolates the endpointer’s contribution within one model. The 500 ms setting is OpenAI’s documented server-VAD default; 300 ms is the faster variant. For pause points only, GPT Realtime is also run with OpenAI’s semantic turn detection at eagerness low, the setting most willing to wait; turn-end and recall evaluations turn detection off and commit the turn explicitly, so this configuration has no results there. GPT Realtime and Grok use a detection threshold of 0.5, Gemini’s automatic detection closes on 500 ms of silence, and every hosted endpointer uses 300 ms of prefix padding. Versions, evaluation dates, and settings for every system are in Appendix C.

Every system sees the same points, the same history cap, the same identity prompt, the same live audio frames, and the same speech gate, and is scored by the same code. One thing differs and is not hidden: full-duplex models hear the history and hosted models read it, so cross-family recall comparisons carry that caveat (§ 6).

Two policies bound the pause and turn-end metrics without running anything: never speak holds every pause and takes no turn; always speak takes every pause at zero latency. The human, by construction of the point set, held every pause and took every turn end, with a length ratio of 1 and a similarity of 1. Similarity has a measured floor, the human reply from a different point in the same conversation (median token F1 0.08, cosine 0.12 over 240 pairs), and a measured ceiling, the human reply against its own label transcript (0.88, 0.89), the transcription noise every system is scored through. Recall has a ceiling too: a text model reading the transcript answers 97% of the conversation-recall questions under the GPT-4o judge (Appendix E), so a score is a fact about memory, not about the questions.

Every metric is reported per system and per point type, never pooled across types. Recall is pooled over history lengths only for the scorer comparison (Table 12 and the abstract). The semantic configuration ran on 475 curated pauses, two rollouts each; comparisons with the 300-point set use the 173 shared points. A rollout that returns no audio or times out is an outcome reported beside the scores, not an exclusion. Rates are over rollouts; latencies, ratios, and similarities are medians with interquartile ranges over rollouts with words; confidence intervals (Appendix E) come from a bootstrap over conversations, which share a speaker, a topic, and a recording. We report the metric vector and do not combine it.

Pause points (Figure 2, Table 3). The hosted systems almost never stayed silent (0 to 2% of points): their silence-based endpointers request a response once speech ends. Silent shares and no-audio outcomes are reported separately (Table 15). Hosted speech began a median 1.0 to 1.1 s after the pause began for GPT Realtime, 2.7 s for Gemini, and 3.9 s for Grok over all rollouts (Table 3 gives the median over takeovers only), against a median labelled pause of 0.97 s. Whether the words land inside the pause, a takeover on 7 to 26% of points, or after the person has resumed, on 72 to 86%, is set by the latency, not by a decision. Grok’s low takeover rate is its slowness, not restraint: its words arrive after the person has resumed on 86% of points. The full-duplex models are the only systems that stay silent, on 22% (PersonaPlex) and 39% (Moshi) of points, because nothing forces a full-duplex model to respond.

They are also the only ones that take the floor within a human reaction time, a median 216 and 373 ms in; three in ten of PersonaPlex’s takeovers and a quarter of Moshi’s were speech already under way at the pause. Raising GPT Realtime’s endpointer from 300 to 500 ms cuts its takeover rate from 26 to 17% and delays its speech by 80 ms: the endpointer is the policy. Semantic turn detection at low eagerness changes the timing more than the outcome: on the 173 pauses shared with the main set it produced no words on 5% (9 points, several with wordless audio), took the floor inside the pause on 6% (500 ms: 17%; 300 ms: 26%), and spoke after the person resumed on 88%, its first words a median 6 s after the pause ended (Table 3, Figure 2). Wordless phonation is a full-duplex phenomenon, 6% of PersonaPlex’s points and 1% of Moshi’s.

Turn-end points (Figure 3). GPT Realtime answers a median 0.5 s after the turn ends, Grok 0.9 s (of which 0.5 s is a protocol wait), PersonaPlex 1.1 s, Gemini 1.7 s. Moshi’s median is 86 ms because it was often already talking through the turn; on 19% of points it produced no words at all. Every system talks longer than the person, in seconds if not always in words. Among replies with words, the median duration ratio is 1.4 for Grok, 3.3 to 3.6 for Gemini, Moshi, and GPT Realtime, and 7.8 for PersonaPlex; the word ratios are 1.1, 2.6 to 3.0, 0.8 for Moshi, and 3.9. The full-duplex models do not stop: 90% of PersonaPlex’s rollouts and 92% of Moshi’s were still speaking at the 30 s cap. A harness audit found that reaching the cap does not by itself establish continued speech, so these durations are neither clean lower bounds nor single replies (§ 6). Gemini reached the cap on 24% of rollouts, GPT Realtime on 2 to 3%, Grok on 1%.

Similarity sits near its floor: median token F1 is 0.10 to 0.12 for every system that answers, against a floor of 0.08 and a ceiling of 0.88. The systems respond to the conversation, and barely more to the turn.

Recall (Figure 4). Judged by Claude Opus 5.5 and given the history as text, Grok answers 46 to 70% of questions about what was said, GPT Realtime 43 to 49%, and Gemini 38 to 42%, with no trend across history lengths from 30 to 120 s. Hearing the same history as audio, PersonaPlex answers 13 to 20% and Moshi 17 to 28%. The fact-recall control separates memory from attention: GPT Realtime answers the general-knowledge question 95 to 98% of the time, Grok 84 to 89%, and Gemini 62 to 73%, so their conversation-recall misses are misses of memory; PersonaPlex and Moshi answer it 16 to 40% of the time, so most of theirs are failures to answer the question at all. Rescoring the same transcripts with GPT-4o moves no system by more than 9 points and preserves the ordering (Table 12).

Hosted models read the history as text and full-duplex models hear it, so the cross-family recall gap is partly a gap between channels; streaming audio history to the hosted models is future work. The hosted systems’ near-zero silence is a property of the silence-based endpointer configurations we tested, which request a response once speech ends, not a decision their models failed to make. Semantic turn detection was tested at one setting, low eagerness, on pause points only. A harness audit found that scoring could stall the shared audio stream and the drain could outlast queued playback, so reaching the 30 s cap does not establish continued speech, full-duplex durations can include later resumptions, and latencies can reflect stalls. GPT-4o still selects the points and extracts the recall facts, sharing a provider with two systems under test. Turn-end comparisons depend on the family-specific response triggers of § 3.4; reply playback remains untested. The gate is an energy threshold, no score has a human-human variance, and we report one rollout per point.

Labels are rule-based and only spot-checked: on 42 re-annotated windows, 86 to 95% of boundaries fall within 250 ms of a human’s, a 250 ms shift can reorder individual systems but not families (Appendix E), and humans hear a backchannel in 7 of 20 pause windows labelled silent. Finally, the corpus is English and dyadic.
