HarnessSQL: Harness-Native Training for SQL Agents in Realistic Database Environments. Text-to-SQL models are commonly trained to map questions directly to static queries, whereas real-world database agents operate through stateful, multi-turn interaction with live databases -- inspecting schemas, executing probe queries, diagnosing errors, and revising hypotheses. This creates a critical train-deploy mismatch, as the execution harness that mediates this interaction is introduced only at inference time. To bridge this gap, we propose HarnessSQL, a harness-native post-training framework that preserves the full interaction structure throughout both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. HarnessSQL builds isolated, executable database environments paired with hidden execution oracles, rolls out teachers directly inside the target SQL harness, and retains only verified trajectories for full-sequence SFT, followed by execution-reward RL. Across Spider 2.0-SQLite, HarnessSQL dramatically boosts the execution accuracy of compact models, raising Qwen3-8B from 15.5% to 45.2% and Qwen3-14B from 22.2% to 54.8%, while transferring effectively to out-of-distribution interactive benchmarks such as BIRD-Interact and LiveSQLBench. Our findings demonstrate that training database agents directly within their execution harness is essential for mastering complex, long-horizon database workflows.

Text-to-SQL has traditionally been formulated as a direct mapping from a natural-language question and database schema to an executable SQL query (Yu et al., 2018; Li et al., 2023). This abstraction has enabled substantial progress, but it increasingly diverges from how modern systems solve realistic database tasks. Benchmarks such as Spider2.0 (Lei et al., 2025) place agents in large, unfamiliar database environments where the information required to solve a task cannot always be captured in a static prompt. An agent may need to inspect tables, examine schemas and values, execute intermediate queries, diagnose errors, and revise its solution over multiple turns. Recent systems have consequently begun to treat Text-to-SQL as an interactive problem, mirroring the broader rise of autonomous data agents (Zhu et al., 2026) that use tools and execution feedback to reason over databases rather than generating a query in a single pass (Deng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). This shift raises a corresponding question: how should such SQL agents be trained?

Figure 1 illustrates why interactive SQL agents require more than simply adding tools at inference time. Even for a seemingly simple request such as “How many unique customers purchased in 2023?”, the agent may not know in advance which tables, keys, or values are relevant (Pham et al., 2026). It may first inspect the schema, issue a plausible query, encounter an execution error such as referencing a nonexistent user_id column, and then use the returned database state to revise its hypothesis before submitting a correct query. This process exposes three coupled challenges. First, the environment must be executable and reproducible: the agent needs access to authentic schemas, values, query results, and runtime errors rather than a static textual approximation. Second, the harness itself shapes the policy: which inspection and execution tools are available, what observations are exposed, and how submission and termination are defined determine the sequence of decisions the model can make.

Third, the supervision must capture the interaction process rather than only the terminal SQL: a correct final query does not teach the model when to inspect the schema, how to interpret an execution failure, or how to recover from an incorrect intermediate hypothesis (Guo et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2025). Recent interactive SQL benchmarks and harness studies increasingly expose these requirements at evaluation time (Xu et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2026a), yet most SQL post-training still focuses on static question–SQL supervision or terminal execution correctness. This creates a fundamental train–deploy mismatch: models are trained to produce answers, but deployed as policies that must explore, execute, revise, and terminate through a concrete database harness.

To resolve these challenges, we introduce HarnessSQL, a harness-native post-training framework that aligns the supervision of database agents directly with their runtime execution interface. HarnessSQL consists of three core components: 1. Executable SQL Environment Construction. We instantiate isolated database sandboxes that provide authentic schemas, query execution, runtime feedback, and hidden executable verification, enabling agent trajectories to be generated and evaluated against real database states. 2. SQL-Specific Harness Adaptation. Rather than directly adopting a generic agent harness, we adapt its interaction interface and execution protocol to the characteristics of SQL tasks. The resulting harness exposes task-relevant observations and actions while reducing unnecessary interaction complexity, making teacher rollouts more reliable and the resulting trajectories easier for compact models to learn from. 3. Harness-Native Post-Training. We collect oracle-verified full interaction trajectories directly inside the adapted harness and use them for supervised fine-tuning, followed by execution-reward reinforcement learning in the same environment. This two-stage training process teaches the model not only to produce correct SQL, but also to acquire the complete interaction policy for exploration, execution, recovery, and submission.

Empirical results demonstrate that harness-native training substantially elevates compact models. On Spider 2.0-SQLite, HarnessSQL improves Qwen3-8B execution accuracy from 15.5% to 45.2% and Qwen3-14B from 22.2% to 54.8% after SFT and RL. Furthermore, the learned policies transfer effectively to out-of-distribution interactive environments, reaching 9.0%/11.3% on BIRD-Interact Mini and 24.8%/28.5% on LiveSQLBench Base-Lite for 8B/14B models. Controlled comparisons confirm that harness-native post-training significantly outperforms conventional non-harness fine-tuning, highlighting the importance of aligning training with the deployment interaction interface.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) Problem Formulation: We identify a train–deploy mismatch in database agents and formulate interactive Text-to-SQL as long-horizon policy learning grounded in an executable harness, highlighting the coupled roles of environment, interaction interface, and trajectory-level supervision. (2) HarnessSQL Framework: We develop a harness-native pipeline spanning sandbox environment construction, dedicated SQL harness design, and end-to-end full-trajectory post-training via SFT and execution-reward RL. (3) State-of-the-Art Compact Agents: We show that HarnessSQL substantially improves 8B/14B open-weight models on Spider 2.0 and transfers to out-of-distribution interactive benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of training database agents natively within their deployment environment.

section: SQL agents as partially observed policies
text: We formalize interactive Text-to-SQL as a partially observed Markov decision process (POMDP) mediated by an execution harness. A task instance is defined as a tuple x=(q,\mathcal{D},h,v), where q is the natural-language user instruction, \mathcal{D} denotes the underlying database instance, h specifies the execution harness, and v is a hidden executable oracle.

section: SQL agents as partially observed policies
text: At each turn t\in[1,T], the agent receives an observation o_{t}\in\mathcal{O} emitted by the harness and generates an action a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} according to its policy \pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}), where the visible state s_{t}=(q,a_{1},o_{1},\dots,a_{t-1},o_{t-1}) comprises the dialogue history. The action a_{t} consists of natural-language reasoning accompanied by either a tool call (e.g., schema lookup or query execution) or a terminal submission. An entire interaction episode is represented as: \tau=(q,a_{1},o_{1},a_{2},o_{2},\dots,a_{T},o_{T},y), where y is the final submitted SQL artifact extracted from a_{T}. Crucially, the agent never observes the full ground-truth state of \mathcal{D} directly; instead, o_{t}=h(\mathcal{D},a_{t}) is a harness-dependent projection bounded by system protocols (such as row truncations, query timeouts, and error message formatting).

section: SQL agents as partially observed policies
text: Task success is evaluated over the complete trajectory by a joint reward function: R(\tau;x)=R_{\mathrm{result}}(y,v)\cdot R_{\mathrm{protocol}}(\tau,h). Here, R_{\mathrm{result}}(y,v)\in\{0,1\} evaluates the denotational execution equivalence of the submitted artifact y against the hidden verifier v over \mathcal{D}, rather than relying on surface-form string matching. R_{\mathrm{protocol}}(\tau,h)\in\{0,1\} verifies compliance with harness invariants, including read-only query constraints, adherence to action schemas, absence of repeated redundant queries, and termination within the step budget T.

Existing SQL post-training frameworks predominantly conceptualize Text-to-SQL as a one-shot conditional generation task. Formally, conventional supervision maximizes the likelihood of the golden query y^{*} conditioned on the prompt and a static schema description \mathcal{S}: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{static}}(\theta)=-\log\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}\mid q,\mathcal{S}). Even recent reasoning-oriented methods that incorporate chain-of-thought traces c still formulate the objective as \pi_{\theta}(c,y^{*}\mid q,\mathcal{S}), terminating statically without environment interaction.
When deploying such a model as an interactive agent, a severe distributional and structural mismatch emerges across three orthogonal dimensions:

1. Marginalizing out intermediate states. By treating the final query y as the sole optimization target, static training marginalizes over the interaction trajectory: p(y\mid q,S)=\sum_{\tau\setminus\{y\}}p(\tau\mid q,S). Yet in interactive environments, transitions p(o_{t}\mid s_{t},a_{t}) are determined by live database execution. Discarding these intermediate states removes the procedural policy for exploration, execution, and termination, corroborating recent findings that intermediate trajectory traces, rather than terminal targets alone, causally govern model generalization (Wen et al., 2026).

2. Policy blindness to execution feedback. A deployed SQL agent operates under closed-loop control: a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{t-1},o_{t-1}). Static supervision never exposes the model to runtime observations such as execution errors or empty results, creating exposure bias when such feedback must be handled at inference time.

3. Harness-oblivious action spaces. Bridging this mismatch requires harness-native training: explicitly optimizing \pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}) over trajectories \tau collected directly within the deployment harness h, driven by execution-grounded rewards R(\tau;x).

Figure 2 illustrates the HarnessSQL pipeline. To resolve the environment, harness, and supervision mismatches identified in Section 2, HarnessSQL couples hermetic sandbox construction with an SQL-specific interaction contract, synthesizing verified trajectories for full-sequence SFT and execution-reward RL.

Catalog grounding and task synthesis. For each target database, we extract an execution-grounded catalog directly from the live engine, capturing runtime schemas, sample column values, and valid join paths. Rather than pairing questions with post-hoc queries, task construction follows an SQL-first blueprinting approach: the generator samples an executable SQL query adhering to difficulty controls (Appendix I) and derives both the natural-language prompt and the execution oracle from the ground-truth relation.

Hermetic sandboxing and deterministic gating. Each generated task packages public instruction fields (q,h) and a hidden oracle verifier v. Tasks are instantiated inside isolated container sandboxes enforcing strict read-only execution, single-statement dialect constraints, and child-process deadlines (60s). Candidate blueprints pass through automated deterministic gates that prune syntax errors, empty relations, degenerate joins, and uninformative edge cases. Mutation tests further perturb queries to ensure semantic discriminability before rollout.
Rather than exposing an unbounded coding environment, we specialize the DSH substrate (DeepSeek AI, 2026) to define a minimal, database-aligned state–action contract:

Action space (\mathcal{A}): The model-visible tool interface is restricted to four primitives: sql_list_tables (table and row enumeration), sql_schema (DDL inspection and sample values), sql_exec (bounded read-only query trial), and sql_submit (terminal artifact submission). Unrelated shell, filesystem, and code-runtime tools are disabled. Observation and protocol middleware (\mathcal{O}): The environment plane injects runtime guards around every turn, including deterministic row truncation to bound observation length, repeated-call reminders to mitigate loop deadlocks, and pressure-triggered context compaction for long-horizon episodes to prevent distraction and memory degradation under noisy multi-turn observations (Liang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). Detailed lifecycle hooks are elaborated in Appendix A.

Supervised fine-tuning (cold start). We collect demonstration experience by deploying an expert teacher directly within the target harness. For each task, the teacher interacts with the live database solely through the four-tool contract without access to the hidden oracle. Trajectories that pass denotational verification and protocol checks are preserved, yielding 2,512 verified episodes across 79 databases. We train the student policy via full-trajectory SFT: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}),\quad\text{where }s_{t}=(q,a_{1},o_{1},\dots,a_{t-1},o_{t-1}). Crucially, tokens originating from the harness observations o_{t} are masked out of the loss, training the model to orchestrate reasoning, tool invocation, and error recovery conditioned on runtime feedback.

Reinforcement learning (execution optimization). To encourage the agent to discover autonomous exploration and self-correction paths beyond teacher demonstrations, we continue training via reinforcement learning in the identical harness environment. We optimize the policy using Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO) (Yu et al., 2025). For each task rollout, the hidden verifier evaluates the submitted artifact against the oracle, providing a sparse, execution-based terminal reward R(\tau;x)\in\{0,1\}, in contrast to dense step-level process reward models (Chan et al., 2025). Token-level policy gradients are applied across all generated assistant segments. By preserving identical tool semantics, observation boundaries, and termination protocols across both SFT and RL, the policy natively masters the closed-loop decision process required at deployment. Complete training objectives and hyperparameters are detailed in Appendix C.

Corpus and Data Synthesis. We construct our training corpora from 79 databases originating from Spider 2.0-Lite (30 SQLite) and Spider 2.0-DBT (49 DuckDB ported to SQLite with full schema and column parity). For SFT, collecting verified teacher rollouts yields 2,512 multi-turn trajectories. For reinforcement learning, our training pool comprises 2,700 synthesized question–SQL prompts and 100 validation instances. Detailed database mappings, difficulty stratification, and corpus statistics are provided in Appendix D.

Harness Deployment. Evaluations and rollouts strictly follow the 4-tool DSH-SQL contract defined in Section 3.2. Each task runs in a fresh, isolated child process with read-only database bindings, a 60-second execution deadline, and bounded observation buffers. Tasks terminating without an explicit sql_submit call are marked as failures. Full runtime architecture, middleware hooks, and activation logs are detailed in Appendix A.

Model Training. We evaluate HarnessSQL across two compact base models: Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B. Models are trained sequentially via harness-native full-trajectory SFT and execution-reward RL using DAPO. Optimization is conducted over isolated DSH environments. Specific training hyperparameters, sequence length caps, and compute configurations are deferred to Appendix C.

Evaluation Benchmarks. We evaluate execution accuracy under both in-domain and out-of-distribution (OOD) settings: (i) Spider 2.0-SQLite (135 complex tasks from Spider 2.0-Lite) as the in-domain benchmark; (ii) BIRD-Interact Mini (Huo et al., 2025) (under the A-Interact interactive protocol with a GPT-4o user simulator) for multi-turn user/environment interaction transfer; and (iii) LiveSQLBench Base-Lite SQLite (BIRD Team, 2026) for cross-database and complex reasoning generalization. Comprehensive benchmark specifications are given in Appendix G.

Baseline Models and Evaluation Protocols. We compare against three groups of baselines in Table 1. General-purpose models include Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, providing coding-oriented and reasoning-capable references. SQL-specialized models include OmniSQL (Li et al., 2025) and Arctic-Text2SQL (Yao et al., 2026b) at both 7B and 32B scales. Multi-agent systems are represented by MARS-SQL (yang2026mars-sql), which coordinates three 7B models for SQL generation. To ensure fair comparison, all baselines are evaluated using their native inference protocols, avoiding performance degradation from forced harness interactions (see Appendix F for cross-harness ablations).

Table 1 compares our final harness-native agents against existing SQL baselines across in-domain (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks. Along with execution accuracy, we report model size, agentic interaction, explicit reasoning, and whether each model is trained within an interactive harness, making the differences in model scale and interaction paradigm explicit.

In-Domain Performance. On Spider 2.0-SQLite, HarnessSQL establishes a substantial advantage over both traditional non-agentic baselines and prior multi-agent setups. Our 8B variant achieves 45.2% execution accuracy, nearly tripling the performance of 32B-scale specialized models such as OmniSQL (14.8%), Arctic-Text2SQL (16.3%), and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B (16.3%). Scaling the policy to 14B yields further consistent gains, reaching 54.8%. This highlights that compact models, when natively grounded in the execution harness, can vastly outperform far larger open-loop models that lack trajectory-level interaction capabilities.

Out-of-Distribution Generalization. The performance gains transfer robustly to unseen environments and distinct interaction protocols. On BI-mini, which requires multi-turn dialogue with a user simulator, HarnessSQL reaches 9.0% (8B) and 11.3% (14B), well above the 1.7%–3.0% range achieved by existing 7B–32B baselines and the MARS-SQL multi-agent pipeline (3.0%). Crucially, on LSB-SQLite, our 8B and 14B models achieve 24.8% and 28.5% execution accuracy, respectively, outperforming all evaluated 32B baselines by a large margin (7.0%–8.9%). These trends confirm that harness-native post-training instills resilient procedural reasoning and closed-loop error-recovery capabilities rather than simply memorizing in-domain schema patterns.
Table 2 reports the performance progression across different post-training stages on Spider 2.0-SQLite, starting from the original Qwen3 base models.

Trajectory Supervision vs. Direct RL. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) substantially elevates execution accuracy, rising from 15.5% to 30.4% for the 8B model and from 22.2% to 37.8% for the 14B model (+14.9 and +15.6 percentage points, respectively). In contrast, applying execution-reward RL directly to the 8B base model achieves only 20.0% (+4.5 points). This demonstrates that while uninitialized RL provides modest exploration gains, cold-starting via verified harness trajectories is critical for establishing effective task grounding.

Execution-Reward RL after SFT. Continuing from the SFT checkpoints, RL yields a further substantial leap to 45.2% (+14.8 points) at 8B and 54.8% (+17.0 points) at 14B. The complete two-stage pipeline delivers total gains of 29.7 and 32.6 points over the respective base models. Notably, RL post-SFT yields over 3\times the accuracy increment compared to Direct RL on the 8B model, highlighting that trajectory supervision provides the structural foundation necessary for reinforcement learning to efficiently optimize complex execution-guided reasoning.

We next examine the design choices most closely tied to our formulation: alignment between post-training and the deployment harness, preservation of complete interaction trajectories, and sufficient context for long-horizon interaction. We additionally test the robustness of our results to the RL optimization algorithm. Further analyses of trajectory synthesis and learned interaction behavior are provided in Appendix B.
We first ablate the core premise of our framework: aligning post-training with the interactive execution harness. Table 3 separates the effects of interactive inference and harness-native training.

First, an executable interactive environment is already valuable without post-training: applying DSH-SQL to the base model improves S2-SQLite from 2.2% to 15.5%, with consistent gains on both OOD benchmarks. Second, with inference fixed to DSH-SQL, harness-native post-training substantially outperforms non-harness post-training across all three benchmarks, including 30.4% vs. 9.6% on S2-SQLite. Finally, non-harness post-training improves non-harness inference (2.2% to 14.1%) but transfers poorly to DSH-SQL (9.6%), demonstrating the importance of training–inference alignment. Additional comparisons between the generic Full DSH interface and our SQL-specific harness are reported in Appendix B.1.

We next investigate whether multi-turn interactions should be trained as unified long sequences or decomposed into turn-level instances. In our default full-trajectory setting, an entire episode is trained as a single sequence where all assistant actions are jointly supervised while environment observations are masked from the loss. In contrast, the turn-split variant decomposes each episode into separate training samples, optimizing the loss solely on each individual assistant turn conditioned on its preceding history prefix.

As shown in Figure 3, full-trajectory SFT consistently outperforms turn-split training across all three benchmarks. This result supports our central supervision hypothesis: preserving complete interaction structure provides a stronger learning signal for long-horizon database agents than decomposing trajectories into isolated decisions.

Long-horizon SQL agents impose substantially greater context demands than conventional Text-to-SQL systems, as a single trajectory must accommodate reasoning traces, tool calls, execution outputs, intermediate observations, and iterative revisions (He et al., 2026a). We therefore vary the maximum sequence length while keeping the context limit consistent across SFT and RL. As shown in Figure 4, performance improves consistently as the context window increases from 8K to 32K across both ID and OOD benchmarks. The improvement is particularly pronounced on S2-SQLite, where execution accuracy increases from 27.4% at 8K to 45.2% at 32K, while BI-mini and LSB-SQLite exhibit similar upward trends. These results suggest that sufficient context capacity is important for learning long-horizon agentic trajectories, where truncating earlier interactions can remove execution evidence and intermediate reasoning required for subsequent decisions.

Our main results use a fixed RL recipe. To determine whether the gains depend strongly on the specific optimization algorithm, we compare GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025), and DAPO (Yu et al., 2025) starting from the same SFT checkpoint and using identical rollout data, reward signals, context limits, and training budgets.

As shown in Table 4, both DAPO and GSPO consistently outperform GRPO across both in-domain and out-of-distribution suites, with DAPO achieving the highest accuracy on Spider2.0-SQLite (45.2% vs. 40.7%). This improvement is consistent with the more stable policy updates of DAPO and GSPO, which may be particularly beneficial for long-horizon trajectories with sparse execution rewards. The relatively small difference between DAPO and GSPO further suggests that the gains of HarnessSQL are not tied to a single RL algorithm.

Beyond execution accuracy, trajectory-level analysis shows that harness-native post-training substantially improves protocol adherence, error recovery, and valid termination, providing behavioral evidence that the model learns the intended interaction policy rather than only improving terminal accuracy (Appendix B.2).

Text-to-SQL has progressed from cross-domain semantic parsing benchmarks such as Spider (Yu et al., 2018) and BIRD (Li et al., 2023) to more realistic settings involving large schemas, external knowledge, and enterprise database workflows, as exemplified by Spider2.0 (Lei et al., 2025) and BIRD-Interact (Huo et al., 2025). Recent work improves LLM-based text-to-SQL through large-scale synthetic supervision and execution-based optimization, including OmniSQL and Arctic-Text2SQL-R1 (Li et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2026b), while systems such as CHESS (Talaei et al., 2024), ReFoRCE (Deng et al., 2025), and MARS-SQL (yang2026mars-sql) increasingly rely on retrieval, database exploration, execution feedback, and iterative refinement at inference time. Together, these developments suggest that performance on realistic SQL tasks depends not only on SQL generation ability, but also on effective interaction with the surrounding execution environment. Rather than proposing another SQL-specific inference strategy, HarnessSQL uses SQL as a challenging domain for studying how training data can be synthesized to teach models to operate effectively through an agent harness.

Modern language-model agents operate through harnesses that define their tools, observations, execution loops, and context management. ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) established the paradigm of interleaving reasoning and actions, while subsequent systems study richer interfaces for API use, executable code, and software environments (Qin et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024). Interactive benchmarks further expose the execution environment as part of the problem (Liu et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2024); most directly, Harness-Bench shows substantial performance variation across model–harness pairings even under controlled tasks and validators (Yao et al., 2026a). These findings motivate treating agent behavior as a property of the model–harness system rather than the backbone alone. HarnessSQL extends this perspective from evaluation to learning by making the deployment harness part of task generation, teacher rollout, post-training, and evaluation.

section: Synthetic instruction and agent trajectory data.
text: Synthetic supervision has evolved from bootstrapped instruction–response pairs (Wang et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2026) and self-supervised tool-use annotations (Schick et al., 2023) to multi-step tool-use data (Tang et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2023) and complete agent trajectories (Chen et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2023; Mitra et al., 2024; He et al., 2026b; Zheng et al., 2026). Recent work also emphasizes executable and semantic verification to improve the reliability of synthetic tool-use data (Liu et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2024a),as well as step-level confidence calibration for multi-step self-correction (He et al., 2025). HarnessSQL combines these directions through harness-native synthesis: tasks are grounded in executable environments, solved by teachers through the target harness, and retained only after outcome verification. Task construction, trajectory generation, and verification therefore share the deployment protocol, yielding supervision for the complete harness-conditioned interaction policy rather than isolated answers or tool calls.

Our current study focuses primarily on SQLite, while several realistic SQL benchmarks additionally involve dialects such as PostgreSQL, Snowflake, and BigQuery. This limitation is partly inherited from the underlying small models, whose initial capabilities are substantially weaker and less consistent across non-SQLite dialects. Prior work has similarly identified SQL dialect generalization as a major bottleneck for smaller text-to-SQL models, and has shown that execution-verified adaptation can substantially improve performance on previously underrepresented dialects (Zhang et al., 2025). In our setting, this challenge is further compounded by long-horizon interaction, where dialect-specific syntax, database clients, metadata commands, and execution behavior all become part of the agent trajectory. Our ongoing work therefore extends harness-native synthesis to dialect-specific execution environments, with the goal of closing the current performance gap between SQLite and other practically important SQL dialects.

We presented HarnessSQL, a harness-native framework for training long-horizon SQL agents. Our central finding is that closing the train–deploy gap requires alignment at three levels: an executable environment that exposes authentic database states and runtime feedback, a task-specific harness that defines the agent’s interaction protocol, and trajectory-level supervision that teaches the resulting closed-loop policy. HarnessSQL realizes these principles through isolated SQL sandboxes with hidden executable oracles, a minimal four-tool SQL harness, and harness-native full-trajectory SFT followed by execution-reward RL.

Across Spider 2.0-SQLite, BIRD-Interact Mini, and LiveSQLBench Base-Lite SQLite, harness-native post-training consistently improves both tested model scales and transfers to out-of-distribution interactive settings. On Spider 2.0-SQLite, Qwen3-8B improves from 15.5% to 45.2% and Qwen3-14B from 22.2% to 54.8%. Controlled analyses further show that these gains depend not only on access to an interactive execution environment, but also on aligning training with the deployment harness and preserving complete interaction trajectories during supervision. These results support a broader view of agent learning: the harness is not merely an inference-time wrapper, but part of the behavior distribution that training should reproduce. While broader dialect and harness coverage remains an important direction, our results provide a concrete path toward compact database agents that learn verified interaction policies rather than isolated terminal answers.

Appendix A specifies the harness composition and runtime hooks, Appendix C specifies the post-training objective and context budgets, Appendix H specifies the task and trajectory records, and Appendix J lists the verifier gates used in the current implementation. We record generation prompts, database identifiers, random seeds, raw rollouts, executed SQL, normalized result fingerprints, per-seed outcomes, selected-trajectory provenance, timing, and rejection reasons. The final submission will include an anonymized code snapshot, data manifests, training hyperparameters, environment versions, and evaluation commands; proprietary database contents and model endpoints will be replaced by documented public equivalents where redistribution is not permitted.

We used an AI assistant for grammar checking and translation during manuscript preparation. For grammar checking, we used the assistant to identify grammatical errors and suggest corrections to sentence structure, tense, and word usage. For translation, we used it to translate text, with attention to fluency, consistent technical terminology, and preservation of the original meaning.

PAINT: A Framework for Multilingual Pain Representation from Medical Licensing Exams to Real-World Clinical Texts. Pain is one of the most common and clinically important symptoms, reflecting disease onset, progression, and treatment response. However, pain is difficult to accurately capture and interpret from medical text, as its expression varies across languages, documentation types, and patient demographics, and is often embedded in terminology, negation, temporality, and contextual descriptions. Existing pain-related studies remain largely monolingual or limited to narrow clinical settings. In this study, we introduce PAINT, a multilingual framework for studying pain representation across medical exams and real-world clinical texts. PAINT includes nine pain-focused dataset partitions spanning English, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, with clinician annotations in all four languages. We curated a structured schema covering pain relevance, pain presence, anatomical location, pain descriptors, and demographic information. To capture multilingual pain representations, we leverage large language models (LLMs) and adopt an ensemble strategy to improve performance. Ten clinicians across four languages validate the labels: the ensemble reaches macro-F1 of 0.91-1.00 on pain relevance and pain presence and 92-100% accuracy on demographics, with inter-annotator $κ$ of 0.82-1.00.

We release the WorldMedQA-Pain ensemble labels, the extraction pipeline, validation scripts, and clinician annotation sheets for publicly licensed corpora, providing a foundation for pain-centered clinical NLP and for studying pain documentation across languages and healthcare contexts.

Pain is a common and consequential symptom in clinical care, and prior work has shown that its assessment, treatment, and documentation vary with patient race, gender, age, and language (Singhal et al., 2016; Hoffmann and Tarzian, 2001; Eccleston et al., 2021; Rambachan et al., 2023; Lor and Koleck, 2022). Such variation may affect clinical decision making. Studying these differences across languages, document types, and patient demographics is therefore relevant both to clinical practice and to the evaluation of robustness and fairness in large language model (LLM)-based clinical NLP systems.

Multilingual clinical NLP primarily relies on two types of resources. Medical licensing examination benchmarks, such as MedQA and WorldMedQA, evaluate structured clinical knowledge in standardized exam settings (Jin et al., 2021; Alonso et al., 2024; Matos et al., 2025). Real-world clinical corpora, including MIMIC and BRIDGE, capture how clinicians document patient encounters in routine practice (Johnson et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2026). The two offer different views of medical language: one reflects what medicine teaches, the other how medicine is practiced.

Despite growing interest in pain-related NLP, available resources remain limited in both linguistic and clinical diversity. A recent systematic review identified small sample sizes, monolingual datasets, and the underrepresentation of non-English populations as persistent challenges in the field (Rajwal, 2024). Existing annotated pain corpora have similarly focused on English clinical text, including UK mental health records annotated for pain relevance, anatomical location, and pain character (Chaturvedi et al., 2023), and US clinical notes annotated for chronic pain episodes, causes, locations, severities, and medications (Carlson et al., 2020). To date, no resource provides a unified multilingual representation of pain across both medical education and clinical practice.

In this work, we present PAINT, to our knowledge the first multilingual framework for analyzing pain representation across Portuguese, Japanese, Spanish, and English. PAINT is a data resource, and the LLM ensemble serves as its labeling methodology, with open-weight models benchmarked against clinician-annotated labels. We began from a clinical question, how pain is documented and how that documentation changes with language and patient demographics, and selected corpora accordingly. Cross-language corpora with matched documentation purpose for pain are scarce, so we work with the real-world clinical text that is available, in which pain appears incidentally rather than by design. PAINT comprises two resources: WorldMedQA-Pain, containing 2,963 medical licensing examination questions, and BRIDGE-Pain, containing 17,795 real-world clinical records. Pairing exam and clinical text within each language under a common schema, with clinician validation across all four languages, enables within-language comparisons between exam and clinical text. Figure 1 provides an overview of the PAINT framework.
Our contributions are threefold:

(1) Resource. A multilingual pain dataset that pairs medical-licensing-exam text with real clinical notes under one structured schema across four languages, with clinician-validated labels and a released extraction pipeline. The validated labels also serve as an evaluation set for pain extraction, useful for testing clinical NLP systems and LLMs, especially in non-English settings where such data are scarce.

(2) Methodology. A reproducible, clinician-validated labeling pipeline with three methodological strengths: generalizability, a cross-lingual, cross-corpus pain extraction and labeling framework; transferability, the pipeline validated on WorldMedQA-Pain transfers to BRIDGE-Pain, where clinician review confirms macro-F1 of at least 0.91 for pain relevance and pain presence and at least 92% accuracy for demographics across all five clinical corpora; and efficiency, the open-weight ensemble matches GPT-5 on the consensus subset and runs locally on a single GPU, making it usable on controlled-access clinical corpora and in resource-constrained settings.

(3) Documentation. We document the released labels per partition: sample sizes, consensus coverage, pain relevance and presence rates, and demographic field coverage, together with the annotation protocol, clinician instructions, and every inter-annotator disagreement, so that users can judge the reliability of each field and partition before reusing them.

Recent studies suggest that AI systems may reproduce the disparities in pain assessment and treatment documented across race, gender, age, and language (Singhal et al., 2016; Hoffman et al., 2016; Hoffmann and Tarzian, 2001; Eccleston et al., 2021; Rambachan et al., 2023). In knee radiography, radiologist-based severity grading explains only a small share of racial disparities in reported pain, whereas a model trained on patients’ own pain reports explains substantially more of them (Pierson et al., 2021); demographic bias has also been observed in LLM-assisted opioid prescribing and pain management (Omar et al., 2026; Omar et al., 2025). Beyond clinical prediction, Berke et al. (2026) propose a computational theory of intuitive pain reasoning, modeling how humans infer and describe pain through mechanisms analogous to intuitive physics and theory of mind.

Examination datasets such as MedQA (Jin et al., 2021), MedMCQA (Pal et al., 2022), MedExpQA (Alonso et al., 2024), and WorldMedQA-V (Matos et al., 2025) evaluate clinical knowledge across one or multiple languages. In parallel, clinical corpora such as MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV (Johnson et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2023) and the ICU databases unified by ricu (Pollard et al., 2018; Faltys et al., 2021; Thoral et al., 2021; Bennett et al., 2023) provide large-scale records of routine clinical documentation. More recently, BRIDGE (Wu et al., 2026) has expanded clinical benchmarking across institutions and languages, and DRAGON (Bosma and others, 2025) across Dutch clinical NLP tasks. However, none of these resources represents pain as a standardized, structured variable suitable for cross-lingual analysis.

Few-shot prompting makes large language models effective clinical information extractors without task-specific fine-tuning (Agrawal et al., 2022), and chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022) and self-consistency decoding (Wang et al., 2023) further improve their reasoning. Ensemble reasoning enhances the stability and consistency of structured clinical extraction (Chang et al., 2024). PAINT builds on this work by using two multilingual chain-of-thought prompting pipelines and requiring agreement among three models to generate high-precision silver annotations at scale.

WorldMedQA-Pain is constructed from the text-only national licensing examination partitions assembled by the WorldMedQA team as an extension of WorldMedQA-V (Matos et al., 2025), retaining four partitions in their original languages. The resulting corpus contains 2,963 instances spanning Brazilian Portuguese, Japanese, Spanish, and English. The four partitions correspond to REVALIDA (Brazil), the National Medical Licensing Examination (Japan), MIR (Spain), and PLAB (United Kingdom). Each instance carries clinician-annotated labels for pain relevance and pain presence, produced under the multilingual annotation protocol described in Appendix I.

BRIDGE-Pain is derived from the multilingual BRIDGE benchmark (Wu et al., 2026) and consists of five clinical-text partitions: MEDIQA 2023 Chat-A (English doctor–patient dialogues) (Abacha et al., 2023), MIMIC-III Outcome (English ICU discharge summaries) (van Aken et al., 2021), Cantemist (Spanish oncology reports) (Miranda-Escalada et al., 2020), Brateca (Brazilian Portuguese electronic health records) (Consoli et al., 2022), and IFMIR (Japanese medication-safety incident reports) (Wong et al., 2024). We retain the complete MEDIQA and Cantemist partitions and randomly down-sample MIMIC-III, Brateca, and IFMIR to 5,000 records each. The final BRIDGE-Pain corpus contains 17,795 clinical documents, all annotated with the same multilingual ensemble pipeline and validated by clinicians on sampled records.

We extract pain and demographic information using two chain-of-thought prompting pipelines (Wei et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022), one for pain attributes and one for demographic attributes. All source texts are processed in their original languages. Hierarchical constraints on the pain labels are enforced in the prompt. The complete prompts are provided in Appendix D.

Each record is described by five fields organized under a hierarchical schema. Pain relevance indicates that the text mentions pain in any way, including a pain term, synonym, or derivative (e.g., painful, painless, or painkiller), as well as an explicit denial of pain. Pain presence, conditioned on relevance, indicates that pain is asserted to be present in the patient at least once. A record in which the only pain mention is a denial or refers to an attribute of an intervention is therefore relevant but not pain-present. Anatomical location, conditioned on pain presence, records the anatomical site or sites of pain as stated in the text, in concise medical terminology, or unspecified when pain is present but no site is named. Pain descriptors capture free-text descriptions of pain quality. Demographics include age, gender, ethnicity, and occupation when stated in the text. The distinction between relevance and presence is the central design choice of the schema: it separates records that mention pain from those in which pain is actually present, ensuring that denials and intervention-related mentions are not counted as pain. Table 1 gives examples of such mentions in each language.

We evaluate five open-weight LLMs on WorldMedQA-Pain using native-language inputs, with GPT-5 (gpt-5-2025-08-07) included as a proprietary reference. As shown in Table 2, Gemma-4-E4B (4B), Qwen3-8B (8B), and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B (32B) perform best overall, with macro-F1 scores ranging from 0.87 to 0.97 for pain relevance and pain presence across the four partitions. LLaMA-3.1-8B and MedGemma-4B score lower across the partitions and are not included in the ensemble.
PAINT combines the three highest-performing open-weight models into a consensus ensemble; performance on non-consensus rows is reported in Table 3.

Let y_{i}^{(m)} denote the prediction of model m\in\{1,2,3\} for instance i, and let \bot denote abstention. For the binary tasks of pain relevance and pain presence, we use a strict three-way agreement rule: \hat{y}_{i}=\begin{cases}y_{i}^{(1)},&\text{if }y_{i}^{(1)}=y_{i}^{(2)}=y_{i}^{(3)},\\ \bot,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} The consensus subset is S=\{i:\hat{y}_{i}\neq\bot\}, and ensemble coverage is defined as |S|/N, where membership in S requires agreement on both pain fields. This rule prioritizes precision over recall by restricting downstream analyses to instances on which all three models agree.

For demographic attributes, we use majority voting over non-null predictions, retaining a value when at least two models agree and leaving the field missing when the predictions conflict without a majority. Thus, a value produced by only one model is retained only when no other model provides a conflicting prediction. Anatomical location and pain descriptors are represented as lists and aggregated item by item under the same two-of-three agreement rule. If only one model provides a list, its predictions are retained; otherwise, an item is retained only if at least two models include it. This strategy provides higher coverage for sparse attributes, such as ethnicity and occupation, for which requiring unanimous agreement across all three models would result in substantial data loss.

The strict agreement rule sets aside 7–11% of WorldMedQA-Pain rows and up to 31.8% of Brateca. Because WorldMedQA-Pain provides clinician-annotated labels for every row, including abstained rows, we can assess whether the abstain subset is systematically harder than the consensus subset. Table 3 reports macro-F1 for both pain fields on the abstain subset for each individual model, the 2-of-3 majority vote, and GPT-5, with the 0.92–0.99 performance on the consensus subset serving as a reference. Difficulty is concentrated in pain presence: no system exceeds 0.75, and GPT-5 reaches only 0.63–0.73, whereas pain relevance is more recoverable (GPT-5: 0.80–0.98). These results indicate that the disagreements leading to abstention are associated primarily with uncertainty about pain presence rather than pain relevance. Thus, the consensus subset is enriched for cases in which pain presence can be determined more reliably, rather than representing a random sample of the corpus.

We apply a deterministic post-processing pipeline to normalize demographic values across languages. Age is represented in years by the first numeric value in the extracted age field; ages under one year are recorded as 0. Gender is mapped to the binary labels male and female using a cross-lingual dictionary. Ethnicity and occupation are preserved as free text. Values that cannot be normalized are recorded as null.

The extracted annotations were validated by ten clinicians, two per dataset. For each BRIDGE-Pain dataset, each of its two annotators independently reviewed a random sample of 100 records, and for each WorldMedQA-Pain partition, 30 records.

For WorldMedQA-Pain, clinician validation covered the demographic attributes of age, gender, and occupation, while pain relevance and pain presence were evaluated against the clinician-annotated labels. For BRIDGE-Pain, clinicians validated pain relevance, pain presence, age, gender, and occupation; anatomical location, pain descriptors, and ethnicity were not validated. To assess inter-annotator reliability, the two annotators assigned to each partition independently annotated an overlapping subset of 50 BRIDGE-Pain records and 10 WorldMedQA-Pain records, without communication or access to each other’s labels. Annotation dates for all annotators are reported in Appendix G.

Metrics are defined under Tasks and metrics below. A blank value confirmed as correctly absent counts as correct, and agreement between clinicians requires an exact match of normalised values, with two blanks counted as a match. Percentage agreement is used for demographic fields because high-cardinality or single-category samples can make \kappa unstable or undefined; demographic \kappa values and the matching rules are given in Appendix E.

As shown in Table 5, the ensemble achieves macro-F1 scores of 0.91–1.00 on BRIDGE-Pain, comparable to its 0.92–0.99 performance on WorldMedQA-Pain. Demographic extraction reaches 92–100% accuracy across all five clinical datasets. Inter-annotator agreement is similarly high, with \kappa=0.88 –1.00 for pain relevance, \kappa=0.87 –1.00 for pain presence, and 90–100% agreement for demographic attributes across the BRIDGE-Pain and WorldMedQA-Pain overlaps. Wherever defined, demographic \kappa values range from 0.82 to 1.00, corresponding to almost-perfect agreement under the Landis and Koch (1977) scale. Detailed per-field results, confusion matrices, and all observed disagreements are provided in Appendix E.

PAINT is formulated as a multilingual information extraction benchmark. Table 4 lists each clinician-validated field with its task, definition, input, output, and evaluation metric. We report macro-F1 for the binary pain tasks, the unweighted mean over the True and False classes of F_{1}=\frac{2PR}{P+R}, and accuracy for demographic extraction, the fraction of records whose extracted value matches the clinician-confirmed value. Inter-annotator agreement is measured using Cohen’s \kappa=\frac{p_{o}-p_{e}}{1-p_{e}} for pain relevance and pain presence, where p_{o} is observed agreement and p_{e} the agreement expected from the two annotators’ marginals, and percentage agreement (p_{o}) for demographic attributes.

We release the extraction pipeline, prompts, schema, validation and agreement scripts, WorldMedQA-Pain labels, and clinician annotation sheets (source text removed) for the publicly licensed corpora; sheets for credentialed corpora are provided on request. The released consensus labels cover pain relevance and pain presence; anatomical location, pain descriptors, and demographic fields are provided as per-model raw outputs and can be aggregated with the released scripts. The clinician gold labels for WorldMedQA-Pain will be made available in a subsequent version. BRIDGE-Pain cannot be redistributed under the underlying corpus licenses, but users with access can regenerate the labels using the released pipeline. Every number in Tables 5, 10, 11 and 13 reproduces from the sheets with the released scripts, as documented in Appendix E.
Tables 6 and 7 summarise the released labels per partition. The label distributions differ substantially between partitions and are not comparable prevalence estimates.

We introduced PAINT, to our knowledge the first multilingual resource for pain representation across medical licensing examinations and real-world clinical text in English, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese. It contributes clinician-validated pain and demographic annotations and the open-weight labeling pipeline.

PAINT is intended as a benchmark for multilingual clinical information extraction and as infrastructure for studying how pain documentation, and the demographic detail attached to it, varies across languages and care settings, including whether large language models reproduce known disparities in pain assessment. The pipeline extends to further languages and document types with minimal adaptation.

Corpus purpose, language, country, and healthcare system co-vary across the nine partitions, so the label distributions in Table 6 characterise each corpus rather than estimate prevalence. Differences between partitions should be read as corpus-purpose effects rather than as cultural claims about pain experience.

PAINT captures pain as documented by clinicians and examination writers, not as reported by patients; none of the source corpora carry numeric pain scores. The schema is designed to accommodate structured pain-intensity scores and patient-reported pain once corpora with such data become available.
The five BRIDGE-Pain partitions cannot be redistributed, so the clinical half of the resource must be regenerated by users with access to the source data, using the released pipeline.

Unlike the Spanish and Japanese partitions, the English partitions are not country-matched: WorldMedQA-Pain uses the UK PLAB examination, whereas BRIDGE-Pain contains US clinical corpora (MEDIQA and MIMIC-III), so exam-versus-clinical differences in English are confounded with British versus American clinical language. Also, both Portuguese partitions are Brazilian, so European Portuguese pain vocabulary is not represented.

PAINT combines public medical licensing examinations with multilingual clinical corpora. WorldMedQA contains no patient-identifiable information, and the pain annotation study was granted IRB exemption by MIT. The annotation effort was conducted by ten clinicians (nine physicians and one pharmacist), all fluent in the source languages and listed as co-authors. Annotation procedures and timelines are documented in Appendix G.

The five BRIDGE-Pain corpora are used in accordance with their original licensing and ethical frameworks, including the PhysioNet Credentialed Health Data License for MIMIC-III. PAINT does not redistribute source clinical text. Clinician annotation sheets are released with all source text removed for corpora whose licenses permit it (WorldMedQA, Cantemist, IFMIR); for the remaining corpora (MIMIC-III, MEDIQA, Brateca) they are provided on request to users with access to the underlying corpus.

PAINT is designed to support multilingual clinical NLP research, information extraction, and fairness auditing. It is not intended for clinical diagnosis, treatment recommendation, or automated triage. Because demographic attributes may be sensitive, demographic results for restricted clinical datasets are reported as aggregate statistics; the only record-level values shown are the seventeen annotation disagreements in Appendix E, which carry no identifiers.
