Table 1 compares it with the competing predictors (§ 3.3), each configuration provides a different account of how a VLM could produce its joint preferences from the same probes. The best single probe trails by 0.22–0.35 in R^{2}, which supports the argument that VLMs integrate evidence rather than deferring to the more confident modality. Calibrated naive Bayes trails by 0.14–0.32, showing that fitting the modality weights substantially improves prediction over combining the evidence with no weights. Additional flexibility yields much smaller gains. Adding the bilinear interaction improves R^{2} by at most 0.001, while unconstrained linear regression improves it by at most 0.017. Although attention can mix the two modalities at any layer, and indeed does Kaduri et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2025a), we find that joint preferences are well approximated by an additive function of the unimodal evidence, as Assumption 1 predicts. The unconstrained regression also tests the restriction Bayes’ rule places on the prior. For three of the four VLMs, its fitted prior coefficient is close to one (Table 10).

The exception is Qwen3.5 (\beta_{\pi}=0.53 – 0.66), whose question-only prior contributes less to joint preferences than Bayes’ rule implies. Thus, enforcing the Bayesian constraint costs little predictive accuracy.

Linear cue combination separates evidence, which the probes measure separately for each input, from modality weights, which are fixed for each VLM and dataset. A challenging test of this separation is whether weights fit under one set of reliability manipulations still predict preferences under another. We introduce two new manipulations that alter the evidence differently from the original corruptions (§ 2.2). Pixel occlusion blacks out a growing fraction of the image, removing information locally while leaving the remaining pixels intact. Textual relevance weakens a passage’s support for the answer while preserving fluency and plausibility (details in Appendix A.5). After measuring the probes on the new relevance \times occlusion grid, we compare two sets of weights, each evaluated with the OOD protocol on the same held-out examples. Transferred weights are fit on text noise \times blur and applied without refitting to the new grid. Refitted weights are fit on the relevance \times occlusion grid and serve as a reference. If the weights are stable, the transferred weights should predict as well as the refitted ones, and the two sets of weights should be similar.

Strikingly, Table 2 shows that both predictions hold. Refitted weights reach R^{2} of 0.68–0.85, and transferred weights come within 0.021 of the refit value for every VLM. The refitted weights are also close to the transferred ones (App. Table 11), so the new manipulations recover nearly the same modality weights. This supports a key prediction of the model and suggests that the fitted modality weights are stable within each VLM–dataset pair.

Having shown that linear cue combination predicts joint preferences and that its weights transfer across reliability manipulations, we now turn to the interpretation it offers. Under the rule \hat{s}_{J}=\pi_{0}+\beta_{T}e_{T}+\beta_{V}e_{V}, a VLM’s modality preference reflects the evidence each modality supplies, the weight assigned to that evidence, and the prior. Table 3 summarizes the first two factors as the clean-input evidence ratio, |\bar{e}_{T}|/|\bar{e}_{V}|, and the integration bias, \beta_{T}/\beta_{V}.

On clean inputs, mean textual evidence exceeds mean visual evidence by a factor of 1.4–3.8 for every VLM on every dataset. This is expected given how the stimuli are constructed: the text states the answer while the image must be interpreted, though the ratio also depends on each model’s ability to extract this information. Stronger textual evidence can therefore lead a VLM to follow the text even with equal modality weights, unless the prior offsets this advantage. Gemma3 illustrates this: it leans toward text more than Qwen3.5 and GLM-4.6V (Fig. 2, right), yet weights the two modalities nearly equally or modestly favors text (\beta_{T}/\beta_{V}=0.96 – 1.27). Qwen3.5 and GLM-4.6V instead weight visual evidence more heavily on every dataset (\beta_{T}/\beta_{V}=0.56 – 0.68), counteracting the text advantage. This vision-favoring weighting holds under both example- and cell-level fitting, whereas some smaller integration biases for Qwen2.5-VL and Gemma3 depend on the fitting level. Strong text-following can thus coexist with only modest integration bias. By the same logic, the “blind faith in text” reported by Deng et al. (2025) and the visual preference reported in other models (Hua et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2026) do not necessarily reflect different integration strategies.

Under a single additive rule, which modality wins depends on how much evidence each supplies and how heavily it is weighted, and both vary across models and tasks. Consistent with this, Deng et al. (2025) also find that vision wins when it is the more certain modality.

The same decomposition explains how a single VLM’s preference changes across datasets. Qwen3.5 weights vision more heavily on all three datasets, but its evidence ratio rises from 1.44 on DocVQA to 2.03 on VQAv2 and 2.88 on RealworldQA. The magnitude ratio of its weighted mean text and vision contributions correspondingly rises from 0.95 to 1.14 and 1.94, so the growing textual advantage increasingly outweighs its vision-favoring bias, qualitatively matching its increasing text preference (Fig. 2, left). More generally, changes in evidence strength can reverse a VLM’s preference even under fixed modality weights. For example, Pezeshkpour et al. (2025) observe that VLM preferences shift toward images as textual queries grow more complex. Our decomposition separates two explanations for this shift: weaker textual evidence under fixed weights, or a genuine change in integration bias. Measuring e_{T} and e_{V} across query complexity would distinguish them.

We presented a Bayesian cue combination model that predicts how VLMs arbitrate between conflicting text and images. Despite its simple, two-parameter form, the model predicts per-example joint preferences across datasets, architectures, and held-out combinations of degradation, and its fitted weights transfer to new forms of unreliability without refitting. Together, these results characterize modality preference as a predictable interaction between evidence strength and stable, modality-specific integration biases. This distinction explains how apparent “blind faith in text” can arise even when visual evidence receives greater weight, reconciling reports of text and vision dominance under a single combination rule.

Our central claim is not that VLMs behave optimally or in a “perfectly rational” way, but that a Bayesian cue combination framework usefully explains their behavior. In particular, the modality weights \beta_{T} and \beta_{V} are fitted empirically rather than derived from a normative account, because models differ in how they weight text and vision evidence in ways our framework does not yet predict. Further, we measure modality preferences using differences in length-normalized candidate-answer log-likelihoods. Their correspondence to the posterior log-odds in our Bayesian derivation is approximate, and they do not directly measure open-ended generation frequencies. Although this is an approximation, Appendix B.5 shows good agreement when candidate answers are given as multiple choice options and a VLM reasons over them. Finally, we extensively manipulate the supplied evidence but do not systematically manipulate prior beliefs independently of that evidence. Conflicts between supplied evidence and parametric knowledge offer a complementary setting in which to test the prior’s contribution Golovanevsky et al. (2025); Ortu et al. (2026). Applying the framework to such counterfactual benchmarks would assess whether the elicited prior and measured evidence also account for preferences when external information conflicts with a model’s existing knowledge.

MemPilot: Orchestrating On-Demand Multimodal Memory Curation for LLM Agents. Memory has become integral to the LLM agent ecosystem, supporting information retention and reuse across interactions. However, most existing agent memory systems construct memory in a query-agnostic manner, which can incur unnecessary preprocessing cost and discard details that later prove essential. Recent studies have begun shifting memory processing toward runtime adaptation, but typically specialize in particular operations or fixed processing schemes, leaving flexible control over performance, cost, and latency largely underexplored. To address this challenge, we present \textbf{MemPilot}, a flexible framework that orchestrates on-demand memory curation under different performance--cost--latency preferences. Specifically, we optimize a multi-step LLM policy via reinforcement learning to iteratively choose between retrieving from query-agnostic memory and delegating query-specific curation of raw multimodal history to heterogeneous LLMs and VLMs. The policy jointly controls evidence amount, curation instructions, model selection, and visual access, enabling fine-grained allocation of runtime computation. To optimize this policy under competing objectives, we adapt objective-wise advantage decoupling by separately estimating each objective's advantage before aggregation. Moreover, we introduce prefix-based marginal utility estimation for fine-grained credit assignment across multi-step rollouts.

Experiments on five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks demonstrate favorable performance--cost--latency trade-offs across optimization preferences, with preference sweeps yielding broader frontiers than existing trade-off-aware baselines.

As large language model (LLM) agents evolve toward persistent, long-horizon interaction, memory becomes increasingly central to preserving and reusing past experience (Hu et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026). However, most existing agent memory systems construct memory from interaction histories in a query-agnostic manner, and relying solely on such pre-query construction can be wasteful and lossy, as it cannot reliably anticipate future query needs (Xu et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026c). To mitigate this limitation, a growing line of work moves memory adaptation to runtime through query-time evidence distillation, on-demand memory construction, and adaptive memory strategies (Yan et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2026d). Despite this progress, flexible orchestration of runtime memory adaptation remains underexplored, particularly when adapting runtime computation to query needs and multimodal evidence while balancing performance, cost, and latency (Zhang et al., 2026b). This raises a key challenge: how can runtime multimodal memory curation be adaptively orchestrated with controllable performance–cost–latency trade-offs?

Unfortunately, addressing this challenge is non-trivial due to three key limitations of existing approaches to runtime memory adaptation. 1 Runtime memory control remains structurally rigid: existing methods typically rely on hand-designed operations or fixed processing pipelines, with efficiency control hard-wired into predefined modules, budget tiers, or heuristics (Yin and Tang, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Yu et al., 2026a), leaving few degrees of freedom for query-specific adaptation and making fine-grained trade-off optimization difficult. 2 Trade-off optimization remains incomplete: existing approaches often target only a subset of efficiency objectives, such as token usage or monetary cost, while user-facing latency is rarely treated as an explicit optimization objective (Liu et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026d). 3 Existing methods largely assume a fixed processing backend for runtime memory adaptation, overlooking substantial variation in curation quality, cost, and latency across heterogeneous models and limiting adaptation to query difficulty and evidence modality, thereby constraining the achievable trade-off space (Yu et al., 2026a; Yan et al., 2025a). Collectively, these limitations call for a more flexible framework that can orchestrate runtime memory operations and processing backends according to both query needs and optimization preferences.

Building on these observations, in this work we introduce MemPilot, a flexible framework for orchestrating on-demand memory curation under different performance–cost–latency preferences. At a high level, MemPilot follows a simple design principle: retain query-agnostic memory, compatible with off-the-shelf agent memory systems, for efficient access, while preserving raw interaction history for query-specific runtime curation. Specifically, at inference time, a multi-step LLM policy constructs a query-adaptive orchestration trajectory by iteratively choosing between retrieving from the query-agnostic memory bank and delegating curation of the raw history to heterogeneous LLMs and vision-language models (VLMs), whose distinct capabilities naturally offer different quality, cost, and latency profiles. Rather than relying on hand-crafted pipelines or discrete budget tiers, the policy adaptively determines how much evidence to process, how it should be curated, which model to invoke, and whether visual evidences are needed, exposing fine-grained controls over runtime computation trade-offs. We optimize this policy with reinforcement learning under different performance, cost, and latency preferences. To better handle the resulting multi-objective optimization, we adapt objective-wise advantage decoupling by estimating each objective’s advantage separately before weighted aggregation. We further introduce prefix-based marginal utility estimation, which estimates the marginal contribution of individual curation steps for fine-grained credit assignment.

Experiments on five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks show that MemPilot achieves favorable performance–cost–latency trade-offs across different optimization preferences. Fine-grained preference sweeps further reveal broader trade-off frontiers than existing trade-off-aware baselines, while behavioral analyses show that MemPilot adaptively reallocates runtime computation as optimization preferences change. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce MemPilot, a systematic framework for preference-aware runtime memory orchestration that jointly controls memory access, query-specific curation, heterogeneous model delegation, and visual evidence usage. By unifying these decisions within a multi-step policy, MemPilot enables fine-grained performance–cost–latency control without relying on fixed processing pipelines, predefined budget tiers, or a fixed processing backend. To optimize the orchestration policy under competing objectives, we adapt objective-wise advantage decoupling and introduce prefix-based marginal utility estimation for fine-grained credit assignment in multi-step rollouts, enabling stable and effective optimization. Experiments on five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks demonstrate favorable performance–cost–latency frontiers across preferences, with analyses revealing shifts in model selection, visual access, and computation allocation as preferences change.

LLM agents increasingly rely on memory mechanisms to preserve and reuse information from long-term interaction histories (Zhong et al., 2024; Packer et al., 2023). Most existing text-centric systems construct memory before future queries are known, using either hand-designed mechanisms for extraction and organization (Chhikara et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026c) or learned policies for memory construction, updating, and retrieval (Yan et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a; Yu et al., 2026b; Yue et al., 2026). Beyond text-centric memory, recent work has extended agent memory to multimodal interactions, maintaining structured representations over textual, visual, and other sensory experiences (Feng et al., 2026a; Wang and Chen, 2025; Long et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026b). Despite increasingly adaptive and multimodal memory designs, they still construct memory in a largely query-agnostic manner.

A growing line of work instead shifts memory processing toward runtime adaptation. GAM (Yan et al., 2025a) performs just-in-time research over stored memory and raw history, while BudgetMem (Zhang et al., 2026b) learns query-aware runtime extraction under different computation budgets. MemGen (Zhang et al., 2025a) and AdaMEM (Zhang et al., 2026d) dynamically generate or refresh memory guidance according to evolving reasoning states, whereas MemRL (Zhang et al., 2026c) adapts the utility of stored experiences from interaction feedback. More recent work further explores query-time evidence distillation and deferred memory construction (Yin and Tang, 2026; Yu et al., 2026a). However, these approaches typically specialize in a particular form of runtime adaptation or follow a predefined processing pattern. MemPilot instead learns to orchestrate heterogeneous multimodal memory curation at runtime under controllable performance–cost–latency preferences.

LLM routing aims to match different queries with suitable models based on their heterogeneous capabilities and costs. Early approaches route queries through model cascades or select models based on estimated query difficulty (Chen et al., 2023; Ding et al., 2024). More recent work improves routing through preference learning (Ong et al., 2025), contrastive objectives (Chen et al., 2024), and graph-based modeling (Feng et al., 2024), while further extending routing to multi-agent settings (Yue et al., 2025) and unified routing frameworks (Feng et al., 2026b). Moving beyond one-shot routing, several methods employ reinforcement learning to enable multi-step model selection and orchestration (Zhang et al., 2025b; Qian et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026c). These advances highlight the potential of LLM routing as a general paradigm for adaptively allocating heterogeneous model computation according to task demands and resource constraints.

In this section, we first formulate on-demand memory orchestration as a multi-step decision process (Section 3.1). We then instantiate the factorized curation and delegation decisions that enable query-adaptive runtime control (Section 3.2). Finally, we introduce resource-aware reward modeling for optimizing quality–cost–latency trade-offs with fine-grained credit assignment (Section 3.3).

section: On-Demand Memory Orchestration as a Multi-Step Decision Process
text: Dual-view memory representation. To support flexible runtime adaptation while retaining efficient access to query-agnostic memory, MemPilot maintains two complementary views of the interaction history: a query-agnostic memory bank \mathcal{M} and the raw multimodal history \mathcal{H}. In this work, \mathcal{M} can be initialized with memories constructed by any off-the-shelf agent memory system (Xu et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026c) or a simpler memory construction scheme, keeping memory construction orthogonal to MemPilot’s runtime orchestration and ensuring broad compatibility with existing memory systems. Meanwhile, \mathcal{H} is segmented into fixed-length token chunks while preserving the original multimodal context within each chunk. These two views serve complementary roles: the former enables efficient memory access, whereas the latter retains fine-grained information that may be absent from the query-agnostic memory representation.

section: On-Demand Memory Orchestration as a Multi-Step Decision Process
text: Sequential decision formulation. As shown in Figure 1, given a query q, MemPilot formulates on-demand memory curation as a multi-step decision process governed by an orchestrator policy \pi_{\theta}. At step t, the orchestrator conditions on the query and previously acquired evidence, s_{t}=(q,a_{<t},o_{<t}), and produces a structured memory action: a_{t}=(z_{t},\phi_{t})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}), where z_{t} denotes the action type and \phi_{t} denotes its associated action arguments (for simplicity, we show one action per step, and multiple actions may be issued and run in parallel). Specifically, z_{t}\in\{\text{\hbox{\pagecolor{retrievebg}{\color[rgb]{0.1914,0.3711,0.5273}{{Retrieve}}}}},\,\text{\hbox{\pagecolor{curatebg}{\color[rgb]{0.543,0.3516,0.0859}{{Curate}}}}}\}. Here, Retrieve directly accesses the query-agnostic memory bank \mathcal{M}, while Curate performs query-specific runtime curation over the raw history \mathcal{H}. We abstract the resulting observation as: o_{t}=\begin{cases}\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{M}}(\phi_{t}),&z_{t}=\text{\hbox{\pagecolor{retrievebg}{\color[rgb]{0.1914,0.3711,0.5273}{{Retrieve}}}}},\\ \mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{H}}(\phi_{t}),&z_{t}=\text{\hbox{\pagecolor{curatebg}{\color[rgb]{0.543,0.3516,0.0859}{{Curate}}}}},\end{cases} where \mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{M}}(\cdot) denotes semantic-similarity retrieval over the compressed memory bank, while \mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{H}}(\cdot) denotes query-specific runtime curation over the raw history, including evidence retrieval and subsequent processing. In our instantiation, \mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{H}}(\cdot) delegates the retrieved evidence to a heterogeneous pool of external LLMs and VLMs (elaborated in Section 3.2), whereas the orchestrator itself remains text-only and never directly processes raw multimodal inputs (e.g., image pixels). After a variable number of steps, the policy terminates memory curation and produces the final answer y.

section: On-Demand Memory Orchestration as a Multi-Step Decision Process
text: This process yields a query-adaptive curation trajectory with at most T_{\max} steps: \tau=(q,a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{T},o_{T},y),\quad T\leq T_{\max}, whose behavior can vary substantially across queries and optimization preferences. We characterize each trajectory by its answer quality Q(\tau) and runtime resource consumption: \mathbf{R}(\tau)=\big(C(\tau),\,L(\tau)\big), where C(\tau) denotes monetary cost and L(\tau) denotes user-facing latency. Given an optimization preference \boldsymbol{\lambda}, our goal is to learn an orchestrator policy \pi_{\theta} that flexibly balances answer quality Q(\tau), monetary cost C(\tau), and latency L(\tau) rather than optimizing task performance alone. This formulation casts on-demand memory orchestration as a preference-conditioned sequential decision problem over answer quality and resources, laying the foundation for explicit trade-off optimization.

Factorized curation controls. We next instantiate the structured action arguments \phi_{t} to expose fine-grained control over runtime memory curation. Rather than relying on a fixed processing pipeline or predefined budget tiers, MemPilot factorizes each action into several controllable dimensions, allowing the orchestrator to adapt what evidence to retrieve, how much to retrieve, how it should be curated, which model should process it, and whether visual evidence is needed. These decisions jointly provide flexible control over runtime computation and its resulting quality–cost–latency trade-offs.

We factorize the action arguments according to the two action types: \phi_{t}=\begin{cases}(r_{t},k_{t}),&z_{t}=\text{\hbox{\pagecolor{retrievebg}{\color[rgb]{0.1914,0.3711,0.5273}{{Retrieve}}}}},\\ (r_{t},k_{t},i_{t},m_{t},v_{t}),&z_{t}=\text{\hbox{\pagecolor{curatebg}{\color[rgb]{0.543,0.3516,0.0859}{{Curate}}}}},\end{cases} where r_{t} is the retrieval query and k_{t} specifies the evidence count, allowing the orchestrator to adapt retrieval depth across steps rather than relying on a fixed top- k. For Curate, i_{t} further specifies a query-specific curation instruction, m_{t} selects the processing backend, and v_{t} determines whether original visual evidence is included. Importantly, we decouple what to retrieve (r_{t}, e.g., “Lena’s dress options") from how to curate it (i_{t}, e.g., “extract the two dress types she considered"), avoiding conflating two semantically distinct operations in a single textual field while keeping retrieval evidence-focused and curation task-directed.

Heterogeneous model delegation. Beyond deciding what evidence to retrieve and how to curate it, MemPilot also adapts which model performs the runtime curation, since heterogeneous models exhibit distinct capabilities, monetary costs, and latencies, making model choice a natural and effective control dimension for runtime trade-offs. Inspired by the LLM routing paradigm (Feng et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b), MemPilot therefore delegates runtime curation to a configurable pool of LLMs and VLMs, allowing the orchestrator to adaptively select a model for each curation step under different optimization preferences. To support this routing decision, the orchestrator is given anonymized model IDs together with lightweight profiles describing key characteristics such as parameter scale and supported input modalities. The selected model m_{t} then processes the retrieved evidence according to i_{t} and returns a textual observation to the orchestrator. For vision-capable routes, v_{t} further determines whether raw images should be included in the curation request.

Together, these factorized decisions allow each query to induce its own curation trajectory over evidence depth, processing strategy, model capacity, and modality access, providing flexible trade-off control without requiring a rigid processing pipeline or predefined budget tiers.

Having exposed multiple controls over runtime curation, we train the orchestrator to use them according to different optimization preferences. For a preference vector \boldsymbol{\lambda}=(\lambda_{Q},\lambda_{C},\lambda_{L}) (with \lambda_{Q}=1 throughout this work), we optimize the policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) over answer quality, monetary cost, and latency.

Resource-aware GRPO. For each query, the policy \pi_{\theta} samples a group of G curation trajectories \{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} and evaluates each trajectory with three objective-specific rewards: r_{i}^{Q}=Q(\tau_{i}),\qquad r_{i}^{C}=-C(\tau_{i}),\qquad r_{i}^{L}=-L(\tau_{i}), where Q(\tau_{i}) is the task-specific answer reward (e.g., F1-Score). Monetary cost accounts for token-based inference costs incurred by both orchestrator generation and delegated model calls, C(\tau_{i})=C_{\pi}(\tau_{i})+C_{\mathrm{ext}}(\tau_{i}). Latency similarly considers both sources of runtime delay. Since direct wall-clock measurements are sensitive to network and serving fluctuations, we use a proxy estimator L(\tau_{i})=\widehat{L}_{\pi}(\tau_{i})+\widehat{L}_{\mathrm{ext}}(\tau_{i}) to ensure training stability, with more details provided in Appendix A.1.

Objective-wise advantage decoupling. Since directly combining multiple rewards before group normalization can obscure their individual learning signals, inspired by (Liu et al., 2026d), we instead normalize each objective independently within the rollout group: A_{i}^{j}=\frac{r_{i}^{j}-\mu^{j}}{\sigma^{j}+\epsilon_{\mathrm{norm}}},\qquad j\in\{Q,C,L\}, where \mu^{j} and \sigma^{j} are the group-wise mean and standard deviation for objective j, and \epsilon_{\mathrm{norm}} is a small constant for numerical stability. We then aggregate the normalized advantages according to the preference \boldsymbol{\lambda} and further normalize the combined signal at the batch level: \bar{A}_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=\lambda_{Q}A_{i}^{Q}+\lambda_{C}A_{i}^{C}+\lambda_{L}A_{i}^{L},\qquad A_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=\frac{\bar{A}_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-\mu_{\bar{A}}}{\sigma_{\bar{A}}+\epsilon_{\mathrm{norm}}}, where \mu_{\bar{A}} and \sigma_{\bar{A}} are the batch-wise mean and standard deviation. The resulting advantage is used in the following clipped GRPO loss: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MemPilot}}=-\mathbb{E}_{i,k}\left[\min\!\left(\rho_{i,k}A_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{i,k},1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip}})A_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right)\right]+\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}), where \rho_{i,k} is the probability ratio between the current policy \pi_{\theta} and the rollout policy \pi_{\mathrm{old}} for token k of trajectory i, \epsilon_{\mathrm{clip}} is the clipping coefficient, \beta controls the KL regularization strength, and \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} denotes the reference policy. Varying \boldsymbol{\lambda} yields policies with different quality–cost–latency trade-offs while preserving objective-specific learning signals.

Prefix-based marginal utility. Trajectory-level advantages provide the same learning signal across curation stages, obscuring their individual contributions. We therefore probe the rollout after each stage t by truncating subsequent curation and directly generating an answer \hat{y}_{i,t}. Let u_{i,t}=Q(\hat{y}_{i,t}),\qquad\Delta u_{i,t}=u_{i,t}-u_{i,t-1}, where \Delta u_{i,t} estimates the marginal answer-quality improvement contributed by stage t. Since cost and latency are directly attributable and already captured at the trajectory level, prefix probing focuses only on answer quality to avoid double-counting resource penalties. We use this signal to refine credit assignment for the policy decisions associated with that stage: \widetilde{A}_{i,k}=A_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}+\eta\,\Delta u_{i,t},\qquad k\in\mathcal{S}_{i,t}, where \mathcal{S}_{i,t} contains the policy reasoning and action tokens that precede the corresponding curation response, and \eta controls the strength of the marginal credit. Other tokens retain the trajectory-level advantage A_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}. The stage-refined advantage \widetilde{A}_{i,k} replaces A_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}} in Eq. 11 for k\in\mathcal{S}_{i,t}, incurring little overhead due to short answer completions and largely shared prefix KV-cache reuse.

Benchmarks and Metrics. We mainly evaluate MemPilot in multimodal settings involving both textual and visual interaction histories. Specifically, we use five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks: Mem-Gallery (Bei et al., 2026), WorldMemArena (Liu et al., 2026a), H2HMem (Zhu et al., 2026), MemEye (Guo et al., 2026), and MemLens (Ren et al., 2026), with MemEye and MemLens further serving as out-of-distribution evaluation sets. We evaluate answer quality using F1 score and an LLM-judge score (L-J), with GPT-4o-mini as the judge model. Cost measures the total token-based monetary cost incurred by both the orchestrator and delegated external models. Latency measures their total inference latency in seconds. Appendix A.1 and A.4 provide further details.

Baselines. We organize baselines into two groups according to whether they support explicit trade-off control. The first group contains fixed-configuration methods used for the main comparison. It includes (1) text-centric memory systems including A-MEM (Xu et al., 2025) and SimpleMem (Liu et al., 2026c), (2) training-based memory methods including GAM (Yan et al., 2025a), AgeMem (Yu et al., 2026b), and Mem-T (Yue et al., 2026), and (3) multimodal memory systems including MIRIX (Wang and Chen, 2025), MemVerse (Liu et al., 2025), and M2A (Feng et al., 2026a). The second group contains (4) methods that explicitly expose performance–efficiency trade-offs, including LightMem (Fang et al., 2025), BudgetMem (Zhang et al., 2026b), and OmniSimpleMem (Liu et al., 2026b). Section 4.4 compares these methods separately through frontier analysis.

MemPilot is implemented based on VeRL, with Qwen3-4B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2025) as the default orchestrator policy. To disentangle gains from RL-enhanced answer generation, we additionally report a decoupled-answer evaluation where the curated context is passed to a separate, non-RL-trained answer model, using Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct and Qwen3.5-9B. External LLMs and VLMs are accessed through OpenRouter, with the heterogeneous model pool specified in Appendix A.2. We segment raw interaction histories into 256-token chunks and use Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Zhang et al., 2025c) for semantic retrieval. Unless otherwise specified, the query-agnostic memory bank is constructed with LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al., 2024) at a 0.4 compression ratio for policy training and main evaluation. We further examine compatibility with memory banks produced by other agent memory systems in Section 4.6. We retrieve at most five evidence items per step for both MemPilot and applicable baselines. Since memory items from different systems can vary substantially in length, we directly compare monetary cost and latency rather than memory-item counts. Remaining hyperparameters are provided in Appendix A.5.

For training, we adopt a 7/1/2 train/validation/test split. We merge the training portions of Mem-Gallery, WorldMemArena, and H2HMem into a joint training set and evaluate in-domain performance on their held-out test sets. We further use MemLens and MemEye exclusively for out-of-domain evaluation to assess generalization to unseen memory distributions. The same data protocol is applied to all applicable baselines, with detailed dataset statistics provided in Appendix A.4. For the main comparison, we evaluate three representative MemPilot preferences: Perf, Bal, and Cost, prioritizing answer quality, balanced quality–resource trade-offs, and inference cost, respectively. Additional preference settings are explored in Section 4.4.

As shown in Table 1, MemPilot spans distinct quality–cost regimes across both models and benchmarks. The results reveal several consistent trends across methods and settings. (1) Text-centric systems achieve low cost largely by avoiding additional multimodal processing and runtime curation, but this often comes with lower answer quality. In comparison, MemPilot-Bal generally achieves stronger overall quality at moderate cost, while MemPilot-Cost reaches similarly low-cost regimes on most datasets. (2) Runtime adaptation does not necessarily translate into controllable trade-offs. Although GAM, AgeMem, and Mem-T adapt memory processing at inference time, they largely expose a fixed operating regime rather than explicitly controlling the quality–cost balance. In contrast, MemPilot spans multiple operating points. MemPilot-Perf achieves the best L-J score across all five benchmarks under both models, while MemPilot-Bal substantially lowers cost and provides a distinct intermediate quality–cost trade-off. (3) Multimodal memory processing can be costly without adaptive allocation. MIRIX, M2A, and MemVerse often incur substantially higher inference cost without consistently translating that expense into better answer quality. In contrast, MemPilot selectively invokes external curation and achieves stronger performance at much lower cost in most settings, with the same trend extending to MemEye and MemLens.

Overall, MemPilot provides controllable quality–cost trade-offs rather than a single performance-oriented operating point. MemPilot-Perf prioritizes answer quality, MemPilot-Bal offers a balanced operating point, and MemPilot-Cost further reduces resource usage with greater quality sacrifice. We analyze latency and finer-grained performance–cost–latency frontiers in Section 4.4.

We further examine fine-grained trade-off frontiers by sweeping MemPilot’s optimization preferences. In addition to the main baselines, we include LightMem (Fang et al., 2025), BudgetMem (Zhang et al., 2026b), and OmniSimpleMem (Liu et al., 2026b), which explicitly support performance–efficiency trade-offs. For latency, we report representative fixed-inference baselines together with runtime-adaptive methods, since most query-agnostic systems exhibit nearly unchanged inference behavior and collapse to similar single operating points.

Performance–cost. As shown in Figure 2 (a), MemPilot forms a stronger frontier across a broad cost range and largely envelopes the competing methods. Compared with trade-off-aware baselines such as LightMem, BudgetMem, and OmniSimpleMem, MemPilot reaches higher quality as additional computation is allocated, while also covering competitive low-cost operating points. Most conventional memory systems expose only a fixed quality–cost point, highlighting the additional flexibility provided by learned runtime orchestration. Multimodal systems such as MIRIX, M2A, and MemVerse generally incur much higher cost due to visual processing, whereas MemPilot reduces unnecessary multimodal computation through on-demand curation and selective model delegation.

Performance–latency. Figure 2 (b) shows a similarly broad quality–latency frontier. MemPilot spans lightweight to performance-oriented configurations, whereas most baselines expose only a narrow region or a single operating point. Even among runtime-adaptive methods, the achievable latency range remains limited. MemVerse achieves competitive quality at relatively low latency, but lacks explicit trade-off control and incurs substantially higher monetary cost in Figure 2 (a). This further highlights that cost and latency capture complementary resource constraints.
Overall, MemPilot provides a broader, more controllable performance–cost–latency frontier through adaptive runtime orchestration, enabling flexible computation allocation under resource preferences.

section: How Does MemPilot Allocate Runtime Computation?
text: To better understand how MemPilot realizes different trade-offs, we analyze its learned runtime curation behavior in Figure 3. Panels (a) and (b) show that as the optimization preference shifts toward lower cost or lower latency, the policy adjusts multiple control dimensions in a coordinated manner rather than relying on a single knob. Moving from left to right, MemPilot generally reduces the number of policy steps, the frequency of Curate actions, image access, and policy output tokens. At the same time, evidence count also changes adaptively, indicating that the policy does not simply retrieve less information, but learns to reconfigure how memory is accessed and processed under different resource preferences.

section: How Does MemPilot Allocate Runtime Computation?
text: Panel (c) further shows that model selection is a key mechanism behind this adaptation. Under higher-cost settings, MemPilot relies more heavily on stronger VLMs and LLMs, while lower-cost settings shift computation toward cheaper model groups. Together, these results show that MemPilot learns a coherent allocation strategy over curation depth, modality access, and routed model capacity, which explains its ability to realize controllable performance–cost–latency trade-offs.

Ablation Study of Core Design Choices. We ablate four key components of MemPilot to examine their contributions to runtime orchestration and policy optimization, with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct as an answer model. As shown in Table 2, removing LLM/VLM delegation reduces the average Judge score from 37.40 to 14.58, highlighting the importance of adaptive external curation. Removing marginal utility or retrieval–instruction decoupling causes similarly large degradation, demonstrating the value of fine-grained credit assignment and separating evidence retrieval from curation instructions. Objective-wise advantage decoupling is also important for multi-objective training, with its removal reducing the Judge score to 21.94. Although all ablated variants consume less inference cost, their substantial quality losses indicate that simply reducing runtime computation does not yield a desirable trade-off.

Compatibility with Off-the-Shelf Memory Banks. To examine whether MemPilot depends on a particular query-agnostic memory construction, we replace its default memory bank with off-the-shelf agent memory banks and evaluate the performance–cost frontiers without retraining using Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct as an answer model. Figure 4 reports averages across five benchmarks. The resulting frontiers are clearly separated: the default bank occupies the lower-cost regime, SimpleMem provides an intermediate profile, while A-MEM incurs higher cost but reaches stronger performance. Each memory bank thus induces a distinct operating regime, while MemPilot improves performance as additional runtime computation is allocated. This demonstrates compatibility with diverse upstream memory systems while preserving their distinct performance–cost characteristics through runtime orchestration.

We presented MemPilot, a framework for orchestrating on-demand memory curation under controllable performance–cost–latency preferences. MemPilot formulates runtime memory adaptation as a multi-step decision process, combines query-agnostic memory with raw interaction history, and adaptively delegates curation to heterogeneous LLMs and VLMs. We further introduced resource-aware policy optimization with objective-wise advantage decoupling and prefix-based marginal utility for fine-grained credit assignment. Experiments across multimodal agent-memory benchmarks demonstrate that MemPilot achieves favorable trade-off frontiers while adapting computation to different optimization preferences. We hope this work encourages agent memory systems to move beyond performance-only optimization toward resource-aware runtime adaptation.

When Judges Agree and Are Wrong: Consistency-Accuracy Dissociation as a Blind Spot for Label-Free Evaluation. Label-free evaluation methods, such as self-consistency filtering, majority-vote aggregation, and agreement-based reliability scoring, rely on an implicit assumption that consistency can serve as a proxy for correctness when ground-truth labels are unavailable or expensive to obtain. In this paper, we test this assumption directly. Using four financial QA datasets (multiple-choice and free-form), ten consistency dimensions, and two frontier model families, we measure the joint distribution of consistency and accuracy at the level of individual examples rather than in aggregate. We find that 60% of all incorrect answers fall in the high-consistency region (consistency $\geq$ 0.8), and that 77.7% of these show complete answer collapse, i.e. identical wrong answers across all perturbation variants. This high-consistency/incorrect quadrant cannot be detected by any evaluation signal that is built on agreement alone, as the model appears maximally reliable while being wrong. We show that the phenomenon is robust to the choice of consistency threshold t (it persists from t=0.50 to t=1.00), is shared across model families, and is concentrated in specific intersections of perturbation dimension and domain.
We map where this quadrant occurs, analyze its stability properties, and discuss the implications for evaluation pipelines that use agreement-based signals in place of human labels.

A growing family of evaluation methods treats consistency as a load-bearing proxy for correctness. Self-consistency sampling, majority-vote filtering, and agreement-based reliability scores are deployed precisely in those settings where ground-truth labels are unavailable, and the underlying assumption is that a model which agrees with itself across meaning-preserving perturbations is more likely to be right. This assumption is rarely tested against ground truth at the resolution where it matters most: not on average across a benchmark, but conditionally, within the population of wrong answers. In this paper, we test it at that resolution and find that the assumption fails in the least desirable direction, as the majority of model errors are concentrated inside the high-consistency region that agreement-based methods would certify as reliable.

We situate this test in financial question answering, a domain in which the construct-validity question is both answerable and consequential. It is answerable because professionally validated exam items (CFA, CMT) provide unambiguous gold labels against which the dissociation can be measured. It is consequential because financial AI deployments are precisely the high-stakes, regulated settings in which consistency-based evaluation carries real operational weight: proprietary data constraints and compliance boundaries frequently prevent ground-truth labels from being shared, which makes agreement-based proxies load-bearing rather than supplementary. The financial domain additionally provides internal variation that allows us to isolate what drives the dissociation: a difficulty gradient (CFA Level 1 vs. CFA Level 2), format differences (multiple-choice vs. free-form numerical reasoning), and distinct subject areas within a single professional knowledge domain. As such, we are able to attribute the concentration of the phenomenon to question complexity and consistency dimension rather than to confounded differences across unrelated benchmarks.

We conduct our experiments across 4 financial QA datasets (CFA Level 1 and CFA Level 2, CMT, and FinQA), 10 consistency dimensions, 2 tested model families (GPT 5.5 and Claude Opus 4.5), and 6 distinct generator-validator pipeline configurations, measuring the joint consistency–accuracy distribution at the level of individual examples. We treat the high-consistency/incorrect quadrant (Figure 1) of this distribution as the primary object of study.

The contributions of this work are as follows. (1) We provide the comprehensive example-level characterization of the dissociation between consistency and accuracy in financial QA, and show that it is large and asymmetric: almost two-thirds (60%) of all incorrect answers meet or exceed a consistency threshold of 0.80, which is the standard operating threshold for agreement-based filters, and 77.7% of these Consistent But Inaccurate (CBI) examples show complete answer collapse, producing identical wrong responses across all perturbation variants. (2) We demonstrate that the phenomenon is structural rather than an artifact of experimental choices: it is threshold-invariant, with CBI rates moving only from 7.2% to 5.05% as the threshold increases from 0.50 to 1.00; it is shared across model families, which converge on the same wrong answers with consistency of 1.0 for specific questions and thereby defeat ensemble-based and cross-model agreement strategies; and it is stable across all 6 generator–validator configurations.

(3) We map where the phenomenon concentrates, showing that CBI rates increase with question complexity (5.22% for CFA Level 2 compared to 3.80% for CFA Level 1) and with answer format (7.49% for free-form numerical reasoning compared to 5.42% for multiple choice), while remaining diffuse across perturbation types, with rates between 0.2% and 9.7% in nine of ten dimensions and no single dimension dominating. (4) We quantify the implications for evaluation pipelines that substitute agreement-based signals for human labels, and derive from our analysis two practical recommendations: a low-cost pre-deployment diagnostic for estimating quadrant mass, and a structured disclosure format for reporting the failure modes of agreement-based evaluators. (5) Finally, we establish the direct practical consequence of the above findings: consistency-based filtering measurably improves the retained set, but any pipeline that uses it to certify data quality, to gate deployment decisions, or to substitute for human evaluation retains a majority of its errors inside the certified set, and those retained errors are disproportionately the deterministic ones that further sampling or ensembling cannot remove. The residual is therefore not incidental noise around a working signal but a stable and largely irreducible component of it.

Wang et al. [23] introduce self-consistency, replacing greedy decoding with sampling of multiple reasoning paths and returning the plurality answer, on the premise that complex problems admit several routes to a single correct answer while errors diverge. Taubenfeld et al. [22] propose CISC, which weights sampled reasoning paths by self-assessed confidence rather than counting votes equally, matching or beating standard self-consistency while reducing the required number of paths. A parallel line of work measures consistency not over samples but over inputs: Jang et al. [7] decompose behavioral consistency into negational, symmetric, additive, and semantic sub-categories, providing the typology our perturbation dimensions follow. Tan et al. [21] identify self-consistent errors, where a model repeatedly returns the same wrong answer, and show that consistency-based detectors collapse to worse than chance on them. Ding [4] audit self-consistency and cross-model agreement as confidence signals and conclude that agreement is a conditional proxy for correctness, with confident errors recurring across providers. Norman et al. [14] conduct a large judge meta-evaluation and report kappa deflation: exact-match agreement overstates chance-corrected discrimination. Krumdick et al. [10] introduce BFF-Bench, 160 business and finance questions authored by financial professionals, and VERDICTS, expert correctness annotations over 1,200 model responses.

Their central result is that without a reference answer, judges agree with human experts primarily on questions the judges could answer correctly themselves. This work establishes that consistent errors exist and that agreement overstates validity; what remains unmeasured is the fraction of the error population lying inside the certified region, its stability under threshold choice, and its concentration by perturbation type and difficulty.

Datasets. We scope our experiments to financial QA for three reasons. First, it is a domain in which consistency-based evaluation is frequently used, since regulatory and data-sharing constraints frequently preclude access to ground-truth labels and make agreement-based proxies necessary. Second, professionally validated exam items (CFA, CMT) provide unambiguous gold labels against which the dissociation can be measured; this is a requirement our design depends on, and one that many specialized domains cannot satisfy. Third, the available datasets vary in difficulty (Level 1 vs. Level 2) and format (multiple-choice vs. free-form numerical reasoning), which allows us to analyze the results through these lenses. We use four financial QA datasets: CFA Level 1 and CFA Level 2 contain multiple-choice questions from the Chartered Financial Analyst curriculum, with Level 2 requiring multi-step quantitative reasoning; CMT contains Chartered Market Technician exam items covering technical analysis and market structure; and FinQA contains free-form numerical reasoning questions that require extraction and calculation over financial tables. Both CFA Level 1, CFA Level 2 and CMT datasets are accessed through the FINESSE-Bench benchmark. We use subsets of randomly selected 200 examples from each dataset, resulting in 23,170 individual example-level observations after perturbation expansion, which we explain next.

Consistency dimensions. Following the broader taxonomy of consistency phenomena in language models, each base item is perturbed along up to 10 consistency dimensions, each producing 3 variants: option order (random permutation of answer labels), option relabel (substitution of label identifiers, e.g. A/B/C \to X/Y/Z), paraphrase (meaning-preserving restatement of the stem), factual (anchoring with additional true context), additive (insertion of irrelevant but plausible distractor text), crosslingual (translation to Spanish, French, or German), symmetric (swapping symmetric conditions in the problem), negation (semantic inversion of the question, requiring a different correct answer), distractor (rewording of incorrect options), and self-consistency (repeated presentation with varied reasoning prompts). Perturbations are generated by a dedicated generator model and validated by a validator model before being presented to the tested model, in order to ensure variant quality (98.8% validator pass rate across configurations).

Models. We test six distinct configurations (Table A.1) that combine two tested models (GPT 5.5, Claude Opus 4.5), two generators (GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5), and two validators (GPT-5.2, Claude Haiku 4.5). We assign the stronger model from each family to the generator role and the smaller model to the validator role, motivated by evidence that verification is a comparatively easier capability than generation for language models: models frequently produce correct outputs that weaker models can still validate reliably, even when those same weaker models could not have generated the output themselves. The factorial structure allows us to assess whether CBI patterns depend on the tested model alone or whether they interact with the perturbation-generation and validation pipeline.

Metrics and definitions. For each example (a base item \times dimension pair), we record the following. Consistency is an entropy-based measure of agreement across the baseline response and all variant responses, with range [0,1], where 1 indicates identical answers across all variants. Accuracy is a binary indicator of whether the model answer matches the gold label. Combining both, we define an example as CBI as \text{CBI}(x)=[\text{consistency}(x)\geq t]\wedge[\text{model\_answer}(x)\neq\text{gold}(x)],

with a default threshold of t=0.80. In addition, we measure answer collapse, i.e. whether all variant responses produce the identical (wrong) label. This is a stricter condition that indicates deterministic rather than stochastic error.

The joint consistency–accuracy space forms four quadrants (Figure 1): Q1 (high consistency, correct) corresponds to reliable behavior; Q2 (low consistency, correct) corresponds to accurate but inconsistent behavior; Q3 (low consistency, incorrect) corresponds to behavior that is unreliable but detectable; and Q4 (high consistency, incorrect) corresponds to CBI, which is not detectable by agreement-based signals.
We organize our findings around five questions, each answered directly from the experimental setup it required.

How large is the dissociation between consistency and accuracy, and where does the error mass concentrate? At the standard operating threshold for agreement-based filters (t = 0.80), 5.24% of all 23,170 observations fall in the high-consistency/incorrect quadrant (Q4, Consistent But Inaccurate, Table 1). This rate understates the practical problem: conditioned on being incorrect, 60% of all errors (1,213 of 2,014) fall in Q4, so an error is about 2.03x more likely to appear in Q4 than in the low-consistency/incorrect quadrant Q3 (1,213 vs. 801). The association between consistency stratum and correctness is highly non-random (\chi^{2}(1,N=23,170)=2085.38,p<0.001). Using odds ratio as effect size for the 2x2 table, the odds of being incorrect in high-consistency vs. low-consistency strata are OR=0.122, equivalently the low-consistency stratum has about 8.20x higher odds of error. Among CBI examples, 77.7% exhibit complete answer collapse — identical wrong answers across all three perturbation variants — indicating that the dissociation is not a marginal disagreement a majority vote could resolve, but a deterministic convergence on a single incorrect answer.

Is CBI an artifact of the consistency threshold, or a structural property of the model’s error distribution? We recompute CBI rates across thresholds from t = 0.50 to t = 1.00. The overall rate moves from 7.2% to 5.05%, a compression of only 2.15% across the full range, and the curve flattens at t = 0.6 (Figure 2). This indicates that CBI examples are not borderline cases pushed just over an arbitrary cutoff; the bulk sit at or near perfect consistency regardless of where the threshold is drawn. The pattern holds separately for each model family, with Claude Opus 4.5 showing a consistently higher CBI rate (5.54–8.15%) than GPT-5.5 (4.64-6.4%) at every threshold tested.

Does CBI depend on the tested model, or on the perturbation-generation pipeline? Across the 6 generator-validator configurations, the overall CBI rate ranges narrowly (from 4.2\% to 6.3\%), and switching validator family (GPT-5.2 vs. Claude Haiku 4.5) shifts CBI rates by 0.57% for Claude Opus 4.5 and 0.7% for GPT 5.5, which indicates the phenomenon is a property of the tested model’s learned preferences rather than an artifact of how perturbations were generated or validated. To test whether cross-model overlap could be explained by independent failures, we evaluated the common item set (N=4{,}264), where the independence baseline P_{\text{indep}}(\text{shared error})=0.01 implies an expected shared-error count of E_{\text{indep}}=44.92. Empirically we observe 159 shared CBI items (and 282 shared wrong items overall), i.e. 3.54\times the independence expectation, and a goodness-of-fit chi-square test strongly rejects the independence account, \chi^{2}(1)=292.76, p=1.24\times 10^{-65}. Because these failures are not independent, cross-model ensembling — the strongest available mitigation against single-model unreliability — does not detect them.

Where does CBI concentrate across domain difficulty, question format, and perturbation type? CBI rate increases with question complexity: 5.22% for CFA Level 2 (multi-step quantitative reasoning) versus 3.80% for CFA Level 1 (Table 2). Comparing formats, CMT (multiple-choice) shows a lower rate (5.42%) than FinQA (free-form numerical reasoning, 7.49%), and this gap does not depend on the model. Breaking down by perturbation dimension (Table A.2), CBI is broadly distributed rather than concentrated in any single dimension: rates fall between roughly 3.5% and 9.7% for nine of the ten dimensions and for both models, with additive perturbation the highest for each (9.65% for GPT 5.5, 7.83% for Claude Opus 4.5) and factual perturbation the next highest for Claude Opus 4.5 (9.48%). Aggregate CBI rates across dimensions are nearly identical for the two models (5.42% and 5.20%), but the dimension-level profiles differ.

Is CBI stochastic noise, or evidence of a stable, mechanistic failure? The 77.7% answer-collapse rate among CBI examples (RQ1) is the central piece of evidence here: a model producing the identical wrong answer across meaning-preserving perturbation is not exhibiting noisy disagreement that would wash out under resampling, but a stable, reproducible preference. The dimension-level breakdown (Table A.3) shows that this property is not driven by any single dimension. Collapse is complete (100%) for option order, option relabel, and distractor rewording, remains high for symmetric (93.0%), negation (85.7%), and crosslingual (79.5%) perturbation, and even at the low end retains roughly two-thirds for factual (74.8%), self-consistency (69.7%), and paraphrase (68.5%), so that for most CBI examples the model does not merely agree with itself at the level of a consistency score but returns the same specific wrong answer. That collapse is strongest precisely on the surface-form dimensions agreement-based filters are designed to probe is where a consistency signal would be most confidently and most wrongly reassuring.

Negation warrants separate interpretation, since its underlying failure may be an inability to detect semantic inversion rather than the trained-in wrong-preference mechanism driving the other dimensions, but the two are operationally indistinguishable to any consistency-based filter, which is the property that matters for downstream pipeline design.

Our findings are demonstrated within financial QA. Whether the same quadrant mass and the same concentration patterns hold in other specialized domains, such as legal, biomedical, or engineering QA, remains an empirical question, although the cross-model convergence we observe suggests that the mechanism is not specific to finance.

Our results do not show that consistency is uninformative; the concern is rather with what a consistency-based filter leaves behind. Such a filter certifies 89.7% of all items, and because almost all items fall in the high-consistency stratum, 60% of the total error mass ends up inside the certified set, so that gating buys approximately a one-third reduction in error rate while leaving most errors in the region it has labeled reliable. What is consequential about this residual is its character rather than its size: among CBI examples, 77.7% show complete answer collapse, returning the same specific wrong answer across every perturbation variant, so these are not borderline cases sitting just above the threshold but deterministic preferences against which the two standard responses to unreliable output, raising the threshold and cross-model ensembling, are both ineffective.

CBI is distributed across dimensions rather than concentrated in any one of them, which has a direct practical consequence: if a single perturbation type drove the dissociation, a pipeline could exclude that dimension and recover a usable signal, but our results indicate that no such dimension exists. Answer collapse is moreover highest on precisely those surface-form dimensions that agreement-based filters are designed to probe, reaching 100% for option order, option relabel, and distractor rewording, which is where a consistency signal is at once most reassuring and most misleading.

section: Bearing on the inter-judge agreement question.
text: Agreement and correctness are related, but the relationship is conditional on domain and dimension, so the quantity that determines deployment risk is not a single transportable threshold but the error mass that remains above it. Because our perturbations preserve meaning by construction, the failures we observe are categorically different from formatting sensitivity: the model is not reacting to surface form, but is stably wrong regardless of it, which is a harder case for any surface-sensitivity mitigation to catch.

We identify two concrete uses of quadrant analysis in the design of evaluation pipelines. First, as a diagnostic before deployment, the mass of Q4 should be estimated on a small labeled sample before a consistency-based filter is trusted in a new domain, rather than assuming that general-domain calibration transfers. Second, as a form of structured disclosure, the error mass remaining in the certified set should be reported alongside aggregate consistency, since it is this quantity that determines whether an agreement-based signal is adequate for a given deployment. We propose three fields for evaluation disclosure templates: the certified-set error rate, the CBI-within-inaccurate rate, and the answer-collapse rate, stratified by perturbation type.

Consistency carries real signal about correctness in financial QA, but it is not a substitute for it. Because almost all items fall in the high-consistency region, a standard agreement-based filter certifies 90% of our data while keeping 60% of its errors, and 77.7% of those retained errors are identical wrong answers repeated across every perturbation variant. Neither a stricter threshold nor cross-model ensembling removes them, since the rate is nearly flat across thresholds and the failures are shared across model families. Consistency-based gating should therefore be treated as an error-rate reduction with a largely irreducible residual rather than a stand-in for ground truth, and we suggest that this residual mass become a standard part of evaluation pipeline disclosure.

InsClaimBench: Benchmarking Insurance Claim Adjudication Across the Decision Chain. Recent advances in reasoning-oriented large language models (LLMs) have motivated increasing evaluation of their ability to perform professional decision tasks. Insurance claim adjudication is one such task, requiring models to connect case evidence, insurance rules, intermediate judgments, and payout calculations across a structured decision process. We introduce InsClaimBench, an end-to-end benchmark for evaluating insurance claim adjudication across the decision chain. Grounded in real claim materials and structured insurance rules, InsClaimBench contains 3,780 cases in 375 case families across auto, property, and health insurance, comprising 86,656 atomic rule judgments. It evaluates each claim from atomic rules through adjudication modules to payout decisions and amounts, with controlled factual variants testing whether required changes are correctly propagated across levels. Evaluation of six LLMs reveals a progressive loss of reliability along the decision chain. Payout-decision accuracy ranges from 74.23--80.19%, while joint decision--amount accuracy drops to 47.54--73.15%. Strong local performance also fails to ensure case-level correctness: atomic-rule accuracy reaches 95.48%, whereas rule-vector exact match peaks at only 36.90%, and the most frequent module errors are not necessarily those most associated with final-decision failure.

Under factual changes, these inconsistencies further become propagation failures: module updates are less reliable than rule updates, correct local judgments can still yield incorrect payouts, and correct payouts can conceal intermediate errors. These results show that reliable claim adjudication requires consistent composition and propagation across the decision chain.

Recent advances in reasoning-oriented large language models (LLMs) have substantially improved their performance on complex reasoning tasks (Guo et al., 2025). This progress has motivated increasing attention to LLM reasoning and decision-making in professional domains, including financial reasoning, clinical diagnosis, legal adjudication, and autonomous driving (Xie et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026). Such high-stakes professional decisions are rarely single predictions. They are chains of dependent judgments whose intermediate correctness and downstream consequences may diverge.

Insurance claim adjudication is one such professional decision task. It requires insurers to investigate case-specific facts, interpret applicable policy terms, determine coverage and causation, and assess the amount of loss or payment (Lin et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). These determinations are interdependent: insurance liability depends on whether the loss falls within the insured risk and is not excluded, while the final settlement further depends on loss assessment and applicable payment conditions (Asmat and Tennyson, 2014; Huynh et al., 2015). Whether LLMs can effectively navigate these interconnected judgments and reach appropriate claim decisions and settlement outcomes has therefore emerged as an important question for further investigation.

Existing insurance benchmarks have progressively moved beyond knowledge-oriented question answering toward reasoning tasks grounded in specific insurance scenarios and business workflows (Feng et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026). Despite this shift toward scenario-based decision-making, existing benchmarks typically focus on selected subtasks or partial decision processes; for example, Liu et al. (2026) evaluate clause-grounded reasoning from case facts to claim verdicts, while Lin et al. (2025) evaluate predefined reasoning steps within specific insurance workflows. They therefore do not yet capture claim adjudication as a unified end-to-end decision process that connects underlying judgments, intermediate decisions, final claim outcomes, and their financial consequences, limiting the ability to analyze where LLMs succeed or fail along the complete decision chain.

To address this gap, we introduce InsClaimBench, an end-to-end benchmark for structured insurance claim adjudication (see Figure 1). InsClaimBench represents each claim as a connected decision chain spanning atomic rule judgments, adjudication modules, claim-level decisions, and payout calculation, with expert-defined logic linking the reference decisions across these levels. Grounded in real claim materials and structured insurance rules, the benchmark contains 3,780 cases organized into 375 case families across auto, property, and health insurance, comprising 86,656 atomic rule judgments. Beyond evaluating performance at individual stages, InsClaimBench constructs controlled factual variants that modify selected claim facts while holding unrelated evidence fixed, enabling systematic analysis of whether LLMs update affected judgments, preserve unaffected ones, and correctly propagate these changes to downstream claim decisions and payment outcomes.

Our evaluation of six representative LLMs reveals four main findings. First, current LLMs do not yet achieve consistently reliable performance on insurance claim adjudication. Claim-decision accuracy ranges from 74.23% to 80.19%, while joint decision-amount accuracy varies more substantially from 47.54% to 73.15%. Second, strong performance on individual judgments does not reliably translate into correct end-to-end adjudication. Atomic rule accuracy reaches as high as 95.48%, yet the best model correctly resolves all applicable rules in only 36.90% of cases and reaches only 73.15% accuracy on final payout amounts. Third, the difficulty of claim adjudication is uneven across the decision chain, with Event and Causation emerging as a consistent bottleneck. It is the least accurate adjudication module for all six models, with accuracy ranging from 70.21% to 75.58%. Finally, models exhibit substantial failures in propagating judgments through the decision chain. Among cases requiring a module update, 28.57–39.98% of updates fail even when the original prediction is correct; moreover, correct payment outcomes can still conceal erroneous intermediate judgments.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) Decision-chain evaluation framework. We introduce InsClaimBench, connecting reference rule judgments, adjudication modules, payout decisions, and amounts through expert-defined logic for end-to-end evaluation and cross-level diagnosis. (2) Controlled counterfactual evaluation. We construct controlled case pairs to test required judgment updates, stability of unaffected judgments, and correctness of downstream decisions and payouts under factual changes. (3) Empirical diagnosis. Across six LLMs, we show that high local accuracy does not ensure case-level correctness, the most frequent module errors need not be most associated with final-decision failure, and correct payouts can conceal intermediate errors.

Insurance benchmarks have gradually expanded from domain knowledge and document-based question answering to scenario-level reasoning and business-oriented tasks (Feng et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). This shift has introduced richer evaluation settings, including multi-step workflows, policy-grounded reasoning, and claim-level decisions. Nevertheless, most benchmarks still define their evaluation targets around individual capabilities or selected components of an insurance task, rather than the relationships among successive decisions. As a result, how performance and errors evolve from underlying judgments to final decisions and financial outcomes remains insufficiently characterized.

Beyond domain-specific benchmarks, reasoning evaluation has increasingly moved from outcome-level scoring toward examining the decision process itself. Two complementary directions have emerged: process-level evaluation localizes errors and assesses intermediate steps, rule application, or dependent task stages (Zheng et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026b), while controlled counterfactual interventions test whether model reasoning and outputs respond consistently to prescribed changes (Roewer-Després et al., 2025; Han et al., 2026). These studies show that final-answer correctness can conceal deficiencies in intermediate reasoning and that errors may accumulate across dependent stages (Xie et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Han et al., 2026). However, the two perspectives are rarely integrated within a domain-defined professional decision process where changes in evidence have explicit implications for intermediate judgments and downstream consequences.

Figure 2 presents the overall pipeline of InsClaimBench, covering task decomposition, rule extraction and composition, case and reference-answer generation, and independent evaluation. We first define claim adjudication as a hierarchical decision task and extract atomic rules from domain materials, with expert-defined logic connecting these rules to adjudication modules, claim outcomes, and payout calculations. The resulting rules and logic guide the construction of complete claim files and controlled factual variants, after which models and human evaluators are independently assessed at different levels of the decision chain.

We define insurance claim adjudication as an end-to-end task from a complete claim file to a final payout amount. To ensure that our benchmark closely aligns with real-world insurance applications, we have developed a top-down hierarchical task definition methodology. This framework incorporates a three-layer hierarchy:

Claim outcome level. Given a complete claim file, the overall task is to determine the payout decision and amount owed under the policy. The task covers auto, property, and health insurance. A predicted no-payout claim is assigned a predicted payout amount of zero in all payout-based evaluations.

Module level. An insurance claim is a request for payment following a loss that may be covered under an insurance contract. Claim adjudication therefore requires determining what loss occurred and whether the policy provides coverage for that loss. These determinations can be organized into 3 legally and factually distinct modules. Contract and Claim Eligibility (CCE) checks whether the contract and claimant meet the requirements for a claim. Event and Causation (EC) identifies the event, the cause of loss, and the causal chain. Coverage and Exclusions (CE) applies coverage conditions, exclusions, and exceptions.

Atomic rule level. The adjudication modules are further decomposed into atomic rules that can be judged True or False from the claim evidence. For example, a disclosure provision may require separate judgments about truthful disclosure, intentional or grossly negligent omission, its effect on underwriting, and the insurer’s prior knowledge.

We then define a counterfactual pair as a base claim file and a variant whose selected facts are modified to reverse a targeted atomic judgment, while unrelated evidence and the governing rules remain fixed. Both cases have reference answers for atomic rules, adjudication modules, payment eligibility, and final amounts. The reference logic and calculation rules determine which downstream judgments and amounts should change and which should remain unchanged.

Atomic rule extraction. Claims experts and LLMs extract atomic rules from policy terms, insurance laws and regulations, and expert knowledge (Figure 3). Each rule specifies a proposition to judge from case evidence. Rules are organized into general, category-specific, and product-specific levels according to their applicability.

Expert-defined formulas. We combine the atomic judgments into module decisions and payment eligibility. The resulting judgments and case facts determine the reference payout amount under the applicable calculation rules. To improve transparency and enable limited replication of the reference-answer construction procedure, Appendix D provides a simplified and specified worked example from atomic judgments through module aggregation and payout calculation.

Case generation. An LLM (in this paper, GPT-5.6-sol) generates atomic scenarios from the extracted rules and combines them into complete claim files. Each atomic scenario supplies evidence that establishes a reference T/F label for its associated rule.

Case family organization. To construct a counterfactual variant, the generator revises the facts supporting a selected atomic judgment so that its reference label reverses, while preserving unrelated facts in the base case. For each base case and variant, we use the atomic reference labels and case facts to compute module decisions, payment eligibility, and final amounts under fixed expert logic and calculation rules. Comparing the reference answers at the two endpoints identifies the required changes and invariances at each level. We group each base case with its variants into a case family and pair every variant with its base case. The resulting dataset contains 375 families comprising 3,780 cases and 3,405 base–variant pairs. Table 1 summarizes the distribution of rules, rule judgments, and cases across insurance domains.

Four claims experts, organized into two pairs, independently review a stratified sample of approximately 10% of case families without access to the reference answers. Their atomic judgments match the reference labels with 93.99% accuracy, with module accuracies of 93.47–97.61%, payout decision accuracy of 96.79%, and amount accuracy of 96.32% (Table 2). This correspondence validates the correctness of the generated atomic scenarios and their associated answers, and the aggregation logic linking atomic judgments to downstream decisions and payouts. The two expert pairs achieve agreement rates of 91.54% and 91.30%, with Cohen’s \kappa of 0.822 and 0.805 (Appendix A), supporting consistent interpretation of the generated cases and rules.

We evaluate six models from different model families. These include GPT-5.6-sol from OpenAI (OpenAI, 2026), Gemini-3.8-Flash from Google DeepMind (Google DeepMind, 2026), Qwen-3.8-Flash from Alibaba (Qwen Team, 2026), Kimi-K2.6 from Moonshot AI (Moonshot AI, 2026), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (DeepSeek-AI and others, 2026), and Qwen3.5-27B model. We evaluate all models on the same cases and rules. All inputs are text.

Models and human evaluators complete the adjudication in separate steps. They first judge each atomic rule, then independently assess the three modules, CCE, EC, and CE, and finally decide whether the claim is payable. For rule-level evaluation, each request contains the complete claim file and the original text of the target atomic rule. Module judgments and claim-level payout decisions are obtained through separate requests containing the complete claim file, without supplying the atomic rule texts or predictions from the rule-level evaluation. When a model judges a claim payable, a separate request to the same model uses the claim file and its directly predicted payout decision to compute the payout amount. Human evaluators likewise provide an amount when they judge a claim payable.

Judgment scores. Rule accuracy pools all applicable rule judgments. Module accuracy and final T/F accuracy use all cases. Rule-vector Exact Match (EM) requires every rule in a case to be correct. R^{+} and R^{-} denote cases with all rules correct and at least one rule error. D^{+} and D^{-} denote correct and incorrect final decisions. The shares R^{+}D^{-} and R^{-}D^{+} use all cases as the denominator. Final fail. is the percentage of wrong final decisions among cases with an error in the given module, with the error-case count in parentheses. Top rules are ranked by error count, and their error rates use occurrences within the same subset.

Payout amounts. Let \mathcal{A}=\{i\mid\hat{c}_{i}=1\} contain cases predicted payable and \mathcal{A}_{+}=\{i\in\mathcal{A}\mid q_{i}>0\}. We report mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) as \mathrm{MAPE}=\frac{100}{|\mathcal{A}_{+}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}_{+}}\frac{|\hat{q}_{i}-q_{i}|}{q_{i}}.
