When the Weakest Language Keeps Moving: ARMOR-DP for Multilingual BabyLM. Multilingual BabyLM systems usually fix language sampling proportions even though the weakest language can change during training. We present ARMOR-DP, a modular framework that diagnoses imbalance arising from representation, exposure, capacity, and objective pressure, and uses per-language validation loss to update sampling. Controlled experiments show that equal character budgets create a severe representation artifact for Chinese; byte-level encoding removes much of it, while static Chinese protection can subsequently make English the weakest language. The dynamic controller tracks these transitions and achieves a better score--balance tradeoff than fixed protection. On official evaluation, curriculum-dynamic checkpoints outperform a matched static Chinese-protective baseline while using fewer Chinese epochs; scaling capacity yields the strongest internal ARMOR-DP system. These results support a simple conclusion: multilingual weakness is a training-time state rather than a fixed property of a language. ARMOR-DP therefore separates diagnosis from intervention, allowing protection to follow the current bottleneck instead of a predetermined language label.

The BabyLM challenge tasks a model with acquiring language from a developmentally plausible data budget, and the 2026 BabyBabelLM track extends this premise to the multilingual setting (BabyLM Organizers, 2026b; BabyLM Organizers, 2026a). Naturalistic linguistic input is not a fixed curriculum: properties of child-directed speech change over development and can track children’s emerging linguistic abilities (Vosoughi and Roy, 2012). We use this responsiveness as a motivating analogy, not as a claim that caregivers optimize explicit language proportions.

In contrast, standard multilingual pretraining relies on static sampling temperatures or predetermined corpus proportions, which are agnostic to the model’s evolving proficiency. Under BabyLM’s stringent capacity and data constraints, languages compete for a shared parameter budget, and a fixed ratio can underserve whichever language currently lags. A responsive artificial learner should therefore reallocate exposure online. Doing so requires first diagnosing why a language is weak at a particular moment—a question that cannot be answered by exposure alone.

Our central hypothesis is that a language can be weak for at least four different reasons. It can be weak because its script is poorly represented by the tokenizer (representation), because it receives insufficient effective exposure, because the shared model has insufficient language-private capacity, or because the objective allocates gradient pressure in a way that amplifies already frequent units (objective). Therefore, we propose ARMOR-DP (Armor for D evelopmental P ressure), a modular diagnostic and intervention framework.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we show that the identity of the weakest language moves as representation, exposure, and capacity interventions take effect. Second, ARMOR-DP separates four possible sources of weakness and turns per-language validation loss into an online sampling signal. Third, our official evaluations show that curriculum-dynamic training improves on a matched static Chinese-protective system while remaining within the challenge budget.

ARMOR-DP is a modular diagnostic and intervention toolkit. It separates four sources of multilingual weakness, each paired with a corresponding probe or intervention. Components can be enabled or omitted according to empirical evidence rather than treated as a mandatory stack.

We use UTF-8 byte units as a script-fair representation. It removes a key comparison artifact, in which Chinese characters are treated as sparse atomic symbols while Latin-script languages reuse a small alphabet. This choice is based on tokenization-free and byte-level models (Xue et al., 2022; Clark et al., 2022; Tay et al., 2022).

We compare balanced sampling with ZH-protective schedules. Our primary static baseline uses English/Dutch/Chinese ratios of 25/25/50. We also test a curriculum that starts balanced and switches to 25/25/50 halfway through training. This is related to temperature-based multilingual sampling and curriculum learning (Conneau et al., 2020; Bengio et al., 2009).

We test two lightweight capacity mechanisms: language adapters and a language-conditioned routing gate over attention heads. We employ the routing gate as an interpretable capacity intervention for multilingual adaptation. Rather than introducing a new routing mechanism, our goal is to analyze how capacity allocation interacts with language imbalance within the ARMOR-DP framework (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2022).

We test both a naive rare-token weighted objective and a pressure-aware objective that combines current excess loss, script pressure, and exposure. The rare-token diagnostic multiplies token-level cross-entropy by a weight derived only from that byte type’s frequency in the diagnostic corpus: less frequent types receive larger weights, clipped to the range reported in Appendix 10. It is included as a simple frequency-only analogue of loss reweighting (Lin et al., 2017), not as part of the final checkpoint. In our diagnostics it over-protects Chinese after exposure has already helped it, whereas pressure-aware weighting reduces this failure.

The dynamic controller is responsible for adapting the sampling distribution as multilingual learning progresses. Instead of assuming that the weakest language remains fixed throughout training, it continuously estimates the current learning pressure of each language and reallocates training probability accordingly. At each update step t, the controller measures language \ell ’s relative weakness by its validation loss deviation from the multilingual mean. Formally, the pressure score is defined as: \rho_{\ell}^{t}=\beta\log\frac{L_{\ell}^{t}}{\bar{L}^{t}}+\lambda_{s}\log s_{\ell}-\lambda_{e}p_{\ell}^{t}, The first term amplifies the language-specific loss gap; we set \beta=2.0 to make a moderate 10% loss difference translate into a meaningful sampling shift, while avoiding overreaction to early-training noise. The second term, \lambda_{s}\log s_{\ell} with s_{\ell} as bytes-per-character, is an optional script-complexity prior—we disable it for all final checkpoints (\lambda_{s}=0) because our ablations show that this static bias over-corrects Chinese in later training and widens the balance gap. The third term, -\lambda_{e}p_{\ell}^{t} with \lambda_{e}=0.5, acts as a negative feedback that gently penalizes languages already receiving high sampling probability, preventing the controller from chasing loss fluctuations too aggressively.

We then convert \rho_{\ell}^{t} into a target distribution q_{\ell}^{t} via softmax with temperature \tau, and smooth the update with momentum \eta: q_{\ell}^{t}=\frac{\exp(\tau\rho_{\ell}^{t})}{\sum_{k}\exp(\tau\rho_{k}^{t})},\qquad\tilde{p}_{\ell}^{t+1}=(1-\eta)p_{\ell}^{t}+\eta q_{\ell}^{t}. We set \tau=2.0 to produce moderate distributions (avoiding hard one-hot assignments) and \eta=0.5 to balance responsiveness to new signals against stability across updates. Finally, we clip \tilde{p}^{t+1} to [p_{\min},p_{\max}]=[0.18,0.50] and renormalize. The lower bound ensures that no language drops below 18% sampling probability (roughly half of uniform 33%), preventing starvation; the upper bound caps any single language at 50%, enforcing a balancing constraint that aligns with the 10-epoch BabyLM budget and prevents dominance by one language. The curriculum-dynamic schedule used by submission-facing runs is detailed in Algorithm B.

We first conduct diagnostic experiments to isolate the four challenges identified by ARMOR-DP before training submission-facing checkpoints. These probes use the official gated BabyBabelLM dataset rows available through the Hugging Face dataset viewer and construct equal-length 128-character windows with an equal number of samples for each language. Unless otherwise stated, the focused diagnostic probe uses 180 windows per language, sequence length 64, a 2-layer decoder-only Transformer with hidden size 56 and four attention heads, and is trained for 240 steps over five random seeds. These deliberately short runs isolate mechanisms; they are not used as estimates of full-scale language competence. All benchmark claims come from the 1M- and 100M-budget checkpoints described below. We report the mean validation loss across languages together with the balance gap \Delta=\max_{\ell}L_{\ell}-\min_{\ell}L_{\ell}, which measures cross-linguistic imbalance. These diagnostic experiments are intended to identify the dominant source of multilingual weakness and guide component selection rather than serve as the final benchmark evaluation.

Based on the diagnostic analysis, we train submission-facing checkpoints by instantiating the three most effective ARMOR-DP components, namely byte-level representation, exposure control, and the dynamic sampling controller. The objective layer is retained as an optional diagnostic module and is evaluated separately through ablation rather than included in the final submission. For byte-level representation, all Unicode text is encoded using standard UTF-8 byte sequences, where each byte is treated as an individual token without language-specific preprocessing or segmentation. Byte values are mapped to training ids by adding an offset of two to reserve ids 0 and 1 for padding and EOS tokens. This mapping is shared throughout training and Hugging Face export, ensuring complete consistency between training and official evaluation.

For the 100M frontier, we train curriculum-dynamic checkpoints with a context length of 512 at model sizes d64, d256, d512, and d768, together with a matched d512 static ZH50 baseline. Training metadata records the actual number of non-padding predicted tokens, wall-clock throughput, per-language consumed epochs, and the maximum consumed epoch, confirming that every reported competition candidate remains below the official ten-epoch limit.

We evaluate all checkpoints using the official BabyLM public zero-shot and fine-tuning pipelines. Before full evaluation, interface compatibility is verified using approximately 100k predicted tokens, 300 official rows per language, training sequence length 128, and exported context length 512. The released equal-trilingual GPT-2 baseline from the official evaluation README is included as a public horizontal reference (BabyLM Organizers, 2026c). Public-suite results are used for model selection because leaderboard-only tasks become available only after submission. The selected d768 checkpoint is finally submitted to the official leaderboard, and the returned multilingual score is reported separately.
Table 1 maps the checkpoint names used throughout the results to their active components.

section: Balanced input is not balanced pressure
text: Figure 1 compresses the first failure mode behind ARMOR-DP: a balanced multilingual budget is not automatically a balanced learning pressure. With the same 23,040-character budget per language, Chinese contains 66,228 UTF-8 bytes and 1,535 unique characters, while English and Dutch each have about 23,000 bytes and fewer than 60 unique characters.

section: Balanced input is not balanced pressure
text: This pressure is visible in Table 2. A character-level balanced baseline collapses on Chinese, with a mean loss of 3.066 and a balance gap of 1.858. Switching only the representation to byte units reduces mean loss to 2.362 and gap to 0.185. This is the clearest evidence for the first ARMOR-DP layer.

Exposure and capacity armor improve the average score but change which language needs protection. Figure 2 makes this tradeoff visible without requiring the reader to scan every loss column in Table 2. Byte + ZH50 adapters obtains the lowest mean loss in the controlled probe, but the worst language is English in all seeds. This transfer is not a failure of the framework; it is the phenomenon the framework should explain. A multilingual BabyLM system should not protect a fixed language. It should protect the language currently under the highest developmental pressure.

section: Dynamic control turns movement into signal
text: We therefore ran a dynamic probe. Every 24 steps, the controller evaluates per-language losses and updates sampling ratios with capped adaptive protection. The pure dynamic adapter system keeps the balance gap close to balanced training while slightly lowering mean loss. A script-prior variant pushes more mass to Chinese and achieves lower mean loss than pure dynamic control, but at a larger gap. Static ZH50 remains the lowest mean-loss configuration in this small run, but has the largest gap among the adapter systems.

section: Dynamic control turns movement into signal
text: The logged update points also provide a direct trace of weakest-language movement. In the objective probe, the weakest language often begins as Dutch, moves to Chinese during early byte-level learning, and then transfers to English after Chinese-protective exposure has taken effect. Across three seeds, the adaptive exposure controller shows two NL \rightarrow ZH transitions and three ZH \rightarrow EN transitions. This supports the main claim that “weakest language” is a training-time state, not a fixed label.

Before comparing objective variants, we distinguish genuine pressure weighting from a reduction artifact: averaging losses by language already equalizes languages even when explicit pressure weights are weak.

Table 4 compares objective variants under byte-level representation and language adapters. Naive rare-token weighting is the least attractive objective in this confirmation run: it lowers Chinese loss but widens the final gap by making English much worse. Pressure-aware weighting is more controlled. Under a fixed ZH50 exposure schedule, it reduces the gap from 0.348 to 0.232 with only a modest mean-loss cost. However, it still does not beat the balance-preserving adaptive exposure baseline. We therefore treat objective armor as necessary but not solved: the evidence favors a pressure-aware objective, while the final system should tune its strength so it does not duplicate exposure protection.

We later found that objective design has one additional pitfall. A language-level pressure loss can improve balance simply by changing the reduction unit from token means to language means, even when pressure weights are weak. To separate the objective layer from this hidden equalization effect, we added a token-level pressure reduction with warmup, end decay, and a capped maximum weight of 1.4. With strength 0.20, this scheduled objective reduces the local 1M validation gap from 0.253 to 0.240 while keeping mean loss essentially unchanged (2.264 to 2.262). On the public zero-shot suite, it reduces the curriculum-dynamic language gap from 0.0359 to 0.0330, but lowers overall accuracy from 0.4634 to 0.4612. We therefore keep curriculum-dynamic as the scorer and treat scheduled token pressure as evidence for the objective layer rather than as the final checkpoint.

section: Public evaluation separates score and diagnosis
text: Table 5 reports a full pass through the official multilingual zero-shot task groups for the original five 1M-token checkpoints plus the best scheduled token-pressure variant. These are not interface smoke tests: each checkpoint is loaded through the HuggingFace causal-LM path and evaluated with the official English, Dutch, and Chinese lm-eval task definitions. Hidden leaderboard tasks are not available locally, so the table should be read as public-suite evidence.

section: Public evaluation separates score and diagnosis
text: The official score changes the model-selection story. Static ZH50 remains the best local language-modeling-loss checkpoint, but it is not the strongest zero-shot system. Curriculum-dynamic protection obtains the best mean score by a small margin over balanced byte adapters, and dynamic+pressure obtains the smallest language gap and variance while sacrificing mean accuracy. This is the desired ARMOR-DP separation: the competition-facing scorer, the balance-preserving controller, and the diagnostic pressure objective need not be the same checkpoint.

section: Public evaluation separates score and diagnosis
text: We evaluate all checkpoints using the official multilingual fine-tuning pipeline over 22 public task-language pairs. Since fine-tuning losses are not directly comparable across task-specific classifiers, Table 6 reports the official accuracy metric. Curriculum-dynamic achieves the highest fine-tuning mean and the best average of zero-shot and fine-tuning performance, primarily driven by improved Chinese accuracy, which increases from 0.210 under balanced adapters and 0.207 under static ZH50 to 0.244. Pressure-aware variants instead prioritize cross-lingual balance, with curriculum-dynamic+pressure achieving the smallest fine-tuning gap while shifting the weakest language from Chinese to Dutch.

The next local experiment scales the most relevant systems from the 100k-token interface probe to 1M predicted tokens, using 600 cached official rows per language. Table 7 shows the 1M local validation losses and the actual consumed epochs logged by the training sampler. All runs remain below the 10-epoch competition limit. Static ZH50 obtains the lowest mean loss but does so by driving Chinese loss far below English and Dutch, making English the weakest language and widening the gap to 0.389. Curriculum-dynamic protection gives up 0.015 mean loss while reducing the gap to 0.253. Balanced byte adapters are also highly competitive, which reinforces the representation claim: script-fair representation is a prerequisite before exposure control can be interpreted.

Although dynamic+pressure and curriculum-dynamic+pressure improve cross-lingual balance, they incur a reduction in the overall mean score compared with curriculum-dynamic alone. We therefore retain pressure-aware weighting as an optional fourth-layer mechanism for diagnostic analysis rather than including it in the final submission, suggesting that its effectiveness depends on appropriate strength scheduling.

text: We include GPT-2 only as an external score reference, not as a controlled tokenizer comparison. Figure 5 turns this model-selection result into the frontier view used for the final submission decision: moving from d64 to larger curriculum-dynamic models improves score without returning to the large local gap of static ZH50.

We submit the d768 curriculum-dynamic checkpoint as the final challenge-facing ARMOR-DP system. The official leaderboard accepts the submission as challenge eligible and returns a multilingual average of 38.32. The language averages are 35.34 for English, 40.96 for Dutch, and 38.65 for Chinese. This result should be read as a final submission check rather than a new model-selection signal: all system choices above were made from public official evaluations, and the leaderboard result confirms the submitted checkpoint while preserving the paper’s main claim as diagnostic rather than leaderboard dominance.

ARMOR-DP builds on three lines of work. First, BabyLM studies sample-efficient pretraining under developmentally plausible data budgets (BabyLM Organizers, 2026b; BabyLM Organizers, 2026a; Warstadt and others, 2025). Our setting adds the multilingual constraint that a fixed token or character budget can interact with script and morphology. Second, token-free and byte-level models show that character and byte units can reduce tokenizer-specific assumptions (Xue et al., 2022; Clark et al., 2022; Tay et al., 2022); here we use bytes as a diagnostic representation, not as a claim that bytes are universally optimal. Third, multilingual sampling, adapters, curriculum learning, sparse routing, and loss reweighting provide tools for allocating exposure, capacity, and gradient pressure (Conneau et al., 2020; Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2020; Bengio et al., 2009; Fedus et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2017). ARMOR-DP’s contribution is to combine these tools around the moving identity of the weakest language.

Our experiments show that multilingual imbalance is an evolving training state: the dominant weakness shifts from representation to exposure and then capacity, so static language protection becomes progressively less effective. ARMOR-DP separates these factors and their interventions, allowing adaptation to follow the current learning state rather than a predetermined schedule.

For the BabyLM challenge, byte-level representation, exposure control, and the dynamic controller consistently improve multilingual performance and form our final system. The objective layer is optional: pressure-aware weighting reduces cross-lingual gaps but modestly lowers the mean score, suggesting that its strength should be scheduled rather than applied unconditionally. This modular separation also makes interactions and future combinations easier to analyze.

The final submission is the curriculum-dynamic d768 checkpoint, which has the best overall public performance while maintaining competitive cross-lingual balance. We retain the matched d512 checkpoint as the principal diagnostic control against static ZH50.

ARMOR-DP reframes multilingual BabyLM as protection of the language currently under greatest developmental pressure. Across diagnostics, 1M probes, and capacity scaling, representation establishes a script-fair foundation, exposure and capacity improve performance, and dynamic control tracks bottleneck transitions that fixed protection misses. By separating diagnosis from modular, empirically instantiable interventions, ARMOR-DP offers a flexible basis for future multilingual training.

The experiments use small diagnostic models and cached subsets of official dataset rows. The public official suite is complete for the checkpoints reported here, and we include the released GPT-2 equal-trilingual public baseline for orientation. Leaderboard-only tasks were not available during model selection; they were scored only after the final d768 checkpoint was submitted. We therefore treat the official leaderboard average as a post-selection submission result, not as a tuning signal. The 100M-budget runs use a 100M maximum-token training budget, but actual predicted non-padding tokens are lower because many cached examples are shorter than 512 tokens. The 100M capacity frontier is single-seed because of compute cost; diagnostic claims are supported by multi-seed small probes, but large-scale score variance remains unmeasured. The controller is evaluated on only three languages, and a larger language set may produce noisier pressure signals and require different update bounds. We also report one controller configuration rather than a full sensitivity sweep. The script-complexity prior was the most brittle component: it over-corrected Chinese later in training and was disabled in final runs. A scheduled prior that decays after early training remains an open direction.

Ontology-Guided Knowledge Graph Construction from Structured Metadata and Climate Science Publications. The rapid expansion of scientific literature far outpaces the speed of manual curation, creating a fundamental bottleneck in extracting structured knowledge from scientific texts. To address this, we introduce an agentic, ontology-guided framework for knowledge graph (KG) construction. Our framework utilizes specialized agents for document understanding, information extraction, ontology conformance, and entity linking. First, an LLM extracts factual knowledge in the form of triples with explicit textual evidence from research papers. Then the triplets undergo a multistage verification process to ground the triplets in the ontology. By enforcing schema constraints and requiring evidence in the form of text fragments, we ensure the data is both semantically consistent and traceable. In an agreement study over 1,000 extracted triplets, Gemini-2.5-flash achieves Cohen's $κ$ scores of 0.640--0.700 against three human annotators, matching the human--human agreement range of 0.616--0.689. We applied this framework to 2,000 scientific publications and construct a novel, ontology-grounded KG for climate science with 133,990 nodes and 755,308 relations; of the 23,327 triplets that the publications contribute after validation, 98.96\% are judged correct. The pipeline code and KG is publicly available https://github.com/aayushacharya/climatekg.

The volume and complexity of the scientific literature continue to grow at an unprecedented rate Hanson et al. (2024); Ding et al. (2025), challenging the ability of researchers to synthesize knowledge across publications, models, and domains. Knowledge graphs (KGs) provide a structured representation of scientific knowledge that can support semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation, and scientific reasoning Peng et al. (2023); Guan et al. (2025). From an NLP perspective, constructing such graphs from unstructured text requires robust information extraction (IE) systems capable of identifying entities, relations, and provenance while respecting domain semantics.

Recent progress in Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly improved IE performance Wei et al. (2024), enabling zero-shot and few-shot extraction of relational facts from scientific text Kartchner et al. (2023). The large context window of newer LLMs allows the processing of documents without the need to distribute them into chunks. Moreover, the shift from simple text processing to “native” understanding of document layouts, tables, and visual hierarchies without needing separate OCR greatly improves IE Ke et al. (2026). A parallel line of work has explored ontology-guided IE, where schemas constrain extraction to a fixed set of entity and relation types van Cauter and Yakovets (2024). Due to semantic consistency and interoperability, ontology-guided methods consistently show better extraction quality in domain specific setting Bhattarai et al. (2024); Cotti et al. (2025).

Climate science exemplifies both the opportunity and the challenge. Recent works Chen et al. (2025); Bulian et al. (2024) note that information about climate science is underrepresented in current LLMs. Climate models form the backbone of climate research and assessment, yet critical information about model genealogy, shared components, physical parameterizations, and experimental setups is dispersed across thousands of publications Kuma et al. (2023). While controlled vocabularies such as Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF), a global infrastructure that standardizes and distributes climate model datasets, and Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6), an international framework defining standardized climate model experiments and metadata, exist, they primarily describe datasets and metadata rather than the rich relational knowledge embedded in the scientific literature. To date, there is very little work done on comprehensive KG integrating these vocabularies with systematically extracted, literature-derived knowledge about climate models, which is the focus of this work.

Climate science further poses a distinctive challenge for LLM-based extraction due to its reliance on domain-specific, long-tail entities and implicit dependencies that are rarely stated explicitly. For example, in the statement: CESM2 shares atmospheric component with CAM6.

an extraction system must infer that CESM2 and CAM6 are climate models, that the relation corresponds to an ontology-defined predicate such as hasComponent, and that CAM6 represents an atmospheric component rather than a standalone system. Such inferences go beyond surface-level pattern matching and expose a key limitation of open extraction and general-purpose LLMs, which often lack familiarity with specialized climate terminology and its implicit semantics. This motivates the need for ontology-guided extraction that explicitly encodes domain knowledge, constrains relation semantics, and supports reasoning over long-tail scientific entities.

In this paper, we address these gaps by introducing an evidence-based, ontology-guided IE framework and using it to construct a novel climate KG. Our approach requires each extracted subject–predicate–object triplet to be accompanied by explicit textual evidence and applies automated LLM-based validation to verify both the triplet and its evidence. This design reduces human annotation effort by narrowing manual review to concise evidence spans rather than entire documents, while maintaining high quality through automated filtering. We show that LLM-based validation achieves high agreement with human annotators, enabling scalable KG construction with minimal human intervention. In summary, our contributions are: Formulation. We formalize domain-specific KG construction as an evidence-grounded extraction task. By first extracting triples with explicit textual evidence, we streamline complex literature curation into a more efficient verification process for domain-specific KGs. Framework. We propose an agentic, ontology-guided framework that utilizes specialized LLM agents for document understanding, schema conformance, and hybrid entity linking. The system integrates authoritative climate science vocabularies and a dedicated evidence validator, thereby ensuring that all extracted relations are traceable to the source text. Experiments. In a 1,000-triplet validation study, Gemini-2.5-flash achieves Cohen’s \kappa scores of 0.640–0.700 against three human annotators, comparable to human–human agreement.

Furthermore, 98.96% of the 23,327 triplets that survive validation are judged correct, and a stage ablation shows where that precision comes from, at a verification cost of roughly 1% of extraction. Climate KG. We introduce a novel climate KG that unifies ESGF metadata with CMIP6 controlled vocabularies, concepts from GCMD (Global Change Master Directory), a NASA-maintained controlled vocabulary that standardizes Earth science metadata to support consistent data discovery and interoperability, and GeoNames-based geolocation. It is further enriched with evidence-grounded relations extracted from 2,000 scientific publications, yielding 133,990 nodes and 755,308 relations that connect models, experiments, variables, institutions, and regions with literature-derived, text-verifiable links; 73,283 of those nodes and 298,747 of those relations come from the publication corpus rather than from the initialization sources.

Let \mathcal{O}=(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}) denote a domain ontology, where \mathcal{C} is the set of entity classes and \mathcal{R} is the set of typed relations with explicit domain and range constraints. Let \mathcal{D}=\{d_{1},\ldots,d_{N}\} be a corpus of scientific publications.

Our objective is to construct a domain-specific KG G=(V,E), where each edge r\in E is a triple (h,r,t) grounded in explicit textual evidence. For each document d_{i}, we aim to extract a set of evidence-backed triples \mathcal{T}_{i}=\{(h,r,t,\varepsilon)\}, where \varepsilon is a sentence or paragraph(s) in d_{i} that explicitly supports the relation. The KG is updated iteratively. Given a current KG G, the enriched KG is obtained as G=G\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{T}_{i}. The initial G is extracted from established, trusted scientific sources, as discussed in Section 3.4.

Purely open IE suffers from uncontrolled relation phrasing and weak schema alignment, resulting in inconsistent and difficult-to-curate outputs. Ontology-guided extraction mitigates these issues by constraining entity types and relations to a predefined vocabulary and by enforcing semantic consistency through domain and range validation. Recent work has shown that incorporating ontological structure into LLM-based extraction substantially improves relation consistency and downstream usability Nie et al. (2024).

We design a two-level ontology that combines standardized scholarly metadata with domain-specific concepts, using OpenAlex-derived paper-centric entities as a stable backbone. Domain-specific classes are introduced only for screened, domain-relevant publications, ensuring scalable extraction while minimizing noise and schema drift.

The domain ontology is constructed with input from a domain expert by unifying authoritative climate resources: ESGF metadata, GCMD Nagendra et al. (2001), CMIP6 Controlled Vocabularies, and GeoNames. These sources provide standardized model, experiment, variable, component, institution, and geographic concepts; additional details are provided in Appendix A.18. The resulting ontology \mathcal{O} defines domain and range constraints such as \text{dom}(\texttt{hasComponent})=\texttt{Model} and also \text{range}(\texttt{hasComponent})=\texttt{Component}. These constraints serve as soft structural priors during information extraction.

We assemble a targeted corpus of domain-specific scientific literature to ensure coverage of authoritative and highly relevant sources. The first phase begins with a small seed set of core papers and expands through two levels of citation mining with LLM-based relevance filtering. After the first phase selected 1,007 papers, we used the top OpenAlex concepts from this set to retrieve recent, context-matched candidates and applied the same screening procedure, adding 993 papers for a 2,000-paper corpus; further details are in Appendix A.1. The small seed of core papers for climate-domain task was taken from the following sources. The sources were selected on consultation with climate experts: (1) curated references from the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (2023) and (2) CMIP6 publications.

We propose an ontology-guided IE pipeline that integrates semantic constraints and explicit evidence grounding throughout the extraction process. The agentic system is presented in Figure 1. Now we give a brief overview of the role of each agent represented by an LLM.

The detailed architecture for information extraction pipeline is given in Figure 1. For each document d\in D, we predict triplets (h_{1},r_{1},t_{1}),\dots,(h_{N},r_{N},t_{N}) with evidence spans \epsilon_{1}\ldots\epsilon_{n} supporting each triplet. For each triplet (h,r,t), we also predict its ontology classes c_{h} and c_{t}.

Example. From a single sentence the agent may predict \displaystyle(h_{1},r_{1},t_{2})=(\displaystyle\text{CESM2},\ \texttt{hasComponent}, \displaystyle\text{CAM6}), \displaystyle(h_{2},r_{2},t_{2})=(\displaystyle\text{CAM6},\ \texttt{appliesToRealm}, \displaystyle\text{atmos}) together with ontology-aligned type assignments c_{h1}=\texttt{Source},\quad c_{t1}=\texttt{SourceComponent}, c_{h2}=\texttt{SourceComponent},\quad c_{t2}=\texttt{Realm} and an explicit supporting evidence span
\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}= CESM2 uses CAM6 as its atmospheric component to simulate large-scale atmospheric circulation.
The agent uses Gemini’s native document understanding to extract these features. Beyond the triplets, there are other features extracted during this stage which is provided in Appendix A.2.

Candidate triples are first checked for ontology conformance: \mathbb{I}(h,r,t\mid\mathcal{O})=\textbf{1}[\text{dom}(r)=c_{h}\land\text{range}(r)=c_{t}]. Only if \mathbb{I}(h,r,t\mid\mathcal{O})=1, a triplet is passed to the evidence validator agent. The check is deterministic and is specified in Appendix A.19.

Example. Assume the ontology \mathcal{O} defines the relation \texttt{hasComponent}: \texttt{Source}\rightarrow\texttt{SourceComponent}. Consider the following sentence in document d: CAM6 is the atmospheric component used within the CESM2 climate modeling framework. From this sentence, an LLM-based extractor may plausibly generate the triple: (h,r,t)=(\text{CAM6},\ \texttt{hasComponent},\ \text{CESM2}), by incorrectly assigning the syntactic subject as the head entity. The inferred ontology classes are: c_{h}=\texttt{SourceComponent},\quad c_{t}=\texttt{Source}.

However, this assignment violates the ontology constraints for relation hasComponent. As a result, the ontology conformance agent returns: \mathbb{I}(h,r,t\mid\mathcal{O})=0, and the triplet is discarded before any evidence or semantic check is run on it.

Unlike other multi-agent information extraction frameworks Lu and Wang (2025), which enforce ontology-level constraints without explicitly verifying textual grounding, our framework introduces a dedicated evidence validator agent. It ensures that the extracted sentence/paragraph is not introduced through hallucination or paraphrasing. Given a candidate evidence span \varepsilon and the parsed content of the paper \mathcal{P}(d), the agent verifies whether \varepsilon occurs verbatim or as a faithful substring within the document. Formally, we define an evidence presence function \mathbb{E}(\varepsilon,d)=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }\varepsilon\subseteq\mathcal{P}(d),\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} Only triples (h,r,t,\varepsilon) satisfying \mathbb{E}(\varepsilon,d)=1 are forwarded to the validator agent, so that every triple reaching semantic validation carries an evidence span that is present in the source document. Triples with missing or hallucinated evidence are discarded at this point. Conformance and evidence grounding are independent tests, so applying them in either order yields the same surviving set; we run conformance first because it is the cheaper of the two and removes the largest share of candidates.

It receives the triples that pass both the ontology conformance agent and the evidence validator agent. It validates whether each triplet (h,r,t) of classes c_{h} and c_{t} is indeed supported by evidence \varepsilon: \mathbb{V}(\varepsilon,h,r,t)=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }\varepsilon\text{ supports }(h,r,t),\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} Triples with \mathbb{V}(\varepsilon,h,r,t)=0 are discarded.

We initialize the KG G from over four million ESGF dataset metadata records, deterministically mapping standardized model, experiment, variable, institution, and spatial attributes into ontology-aligned entities and relations. This trusted backbone grounds subsequent literature-derived enrichment by giving the entity linker canonical climate identifiers instead of relying on the LLM to generate or memorize standardized names. Additional construction details are provided in Appendix A.3.

This section describes the Entity Linking agent (Figure 7, Appendix). For each triple (h,r,t) and evidence \epsilon, we consider (h,t) as candidate entities to be linked to existing nodes of G=(V,E). For linking, we consider string-based similarity or embedding-based similarity, depending on the type of entity.

We use NV-Embed-V2 Lee et al. (2025) to produce deep embeddings, since it showed consistently good performance in MTEB benchmark Muennighoff et al. (2022); Enevoldsen et al. (2025) and was also utilized by Pan et al. (2025b) for Climate tasks. In general, the embedding model performs well, but the embedding distance is widely inconsistent for similar items. Given a deep embedding function \psi, let \hat{v} be the most similar graph node to an entity e: \hat{v}=\arg\max_{v\in V}\text{sim}(\psi(e),\psi(v)), If \text{sim}(\psi(e),\psi(\hat{v}))\geq\tau, \hat{v} is linked to e. However, if \text{sim}(\psi(e),\psi(\hat{v}))<\tau, we retrieve the top- k candidates {v_{1},\ldots,v_{k}} using a fallback threshold \tau_{f} and ask an LLM to identify the best match given the provided evidence. We use LLM-based candidate selection, as shown in Figure 2, because embedding similarity can be unreliable for specialized climate terms, where distributional proximity does not always reflect ontological compatibility.

Each design choice in the pipeline is settled empirically rather than by preference: the linking thresholds come from the sensitivity analysis of Appendix A.5 (Table 10), the composition of verification stages from the ablation of Table 4, and the choice of a deterministic test over an LLM call for ontology conformance and evidence grounding from the cost comparison in Appendix A.11. We empirically set the automatic linking threshold \tau=0.80 and the LLM fallback threshold \tau_{f}=0.55. These thresholds are selected using the sensitivity analysis(refer to Appendix, Table 10), where match rates rise sharply above 0.80 and bins down to 0.55 still recover useful LLM-confirmed matches. For strict identifiers such as climate model names, we use string matching rather than embedding similarity; details are provided in Appendix A.4.
It is possible that some facts are repeated by multiple papers during this stage. The handling is provided in Appendix A.7.

To assess whether LLM-based validation can scale KG quality control, we compare Gemini-2.5-flash with three human annotators on 1,000 extracted triplets sampled from IPCC-linked climate-science papers Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (2023) of the corpus of Section 3.2. The sample is drawn from the raw output of the triplet and evidence extractor agent, before any verification stage, so it contains triplets that the pipeline later keeps as well as triplets it removes. Each decision is the binary judgement of whether the evidence span supports the triplet, which is the task of the validator agent in Figure 1. As shown in Table 2, Gemini-human Cohen’s \kappa scores range from 0.640–0.700, comparable to the human-human range of 0.616–0.689; against the human majority vote, Gemini reaches \kappa=0.798 and 0.977 observed agreement. This supports its use as a scalable surrogate validator for large-scale KG construction.

We evaluate extraction quality using a triplet precision, which we call triplet correctness metric and denote as C_{\text{triplet}}. It measures the proportion of triplets generated by the system that are judged to be correct by an evaluator.

Let T denote the set of triplets output by a given extraction stage, and let T_{\text{valid}}\subseteq T denote the subset of those triplets validated as correct by the evaluator. A triplet is considered correct if the relation between the source and target entities is supported by the corresponding paragraph in the source document, allowing for implicit references and anaphora resolution. The triplet correctness score is defined as: C_{\text{triplet}}=\frac{|T_{\text{valid}}|}{|T|}

The metric is precision-like in nature, as it evaluates correctness over generated triplets without assuming an exhaustively annotated gold standard. This makes C_{\text{triplet}} well suited to the evaluation of ontology-guided information extraction from scientific publications, where the emphasis is on producing high-quality, curator-ready KG assertions rather than maximizing coverage.

Table 3 shows the effect of each validation stage over 2,000 publications. The extractor produces 39,964 candidate triplets; ontology conformance, evidence validation, and final validation reduce this to 23,327 high-quality triplets with a final correctness score of 98.963%. The resulting KG contains 133,990 nodes and 755,308 relations across 55 node types and 59 relation types (Table 5). Separating the two sources of content, the deterministic initialization from ESGF, CMIP6 controlled vocabularies, GCMD, and GeoNames accounts for 60,707 nodes and 456,563 relations, while the publication corpus contributes 73,283 nodes and 298,747 relations, including 96,100 paper-to-entity mention edges and 6,530 distinct entity-to-entity relations asserted by the papers themselves.

Because every candidate triplet stores the verdict of every stage, we can evaluate all eight combinations of the three verification stages on the same 39,964 triplets with the same C_{\text{triplet}} judge, without re-running any agent (Table 4). The stages act on different axes rather than on a single quality dimension. The validator agent is the precision component: removing it from the full pipeline leaves 27,900 triplets at 94.72%, so it contributes +4.24 points of C_{\text{triplet}}. Ontology conformance contributes almost no precision, but that is not its function: 93.4% of the 11,050 triplets it removes are judged textually correct, yet their (source type, relation, target type) signature lies outside the ontology, so they cannot be typed into the KG at all. Its role is schema compatibility rather than error correction. Evidence validation likewise leaves final precision unchanged (24,172 at 98.96% without it), and instead supplies the traceability guarantee: without it, 845 triplets whose evidence span cannot be matched against the parsed source enter the KG. Precision, schema compatibility, and traceability therefore have to be read as three separate outcomes of the pipeline. The details about what the pipeline filters remove is given in Appendix A.8.
The verification stack is also inexpensive relative to what it corrects. Appendix A.11 reports cost, runtime, and ablation effect per stage.

We further measure knowledge saturation as papers are incrementally linked into the KG. Here, created entities are new KG nodes introduced during entity linking, while mentions are paper-level entity references resolved against the KG. Novelty is computed within each paper interval as the number of unique items not seen in earlier papers divided by the total number of unique items observed in that interval. As shown in Table 1 and Figure 3, the average number of new unique created entities per paper drops from 16.89 in the first 500 papers to 8.81 in the final 500 papers, while the entity novelty rate drops from 61.9% to 40.3%. Entity mention novelty shows a similar decline, from 43.3% to 24.1%, and relation assertion novelty declines from 84.4% to 73.1%. At the schema level, all 9 created entity types are observed by paper 4, 90% of the final 34 mention entity types are observed by paper 129, and 90% of the final 17 relation types are observed by paper 434. These trends indicate that additional papers increasingly reuse the existing climate KG vocabulary and schema, while continuing to add validated assertions.

The same redundancy is visible at the level of individual assertions: of the 6,530 distinct literature-derived edges, 11.0% are asserted independently by two or more papers, and 1.6% by five or more. Facts missed in one paper are therefore often recoverable from overlapping evidence in later papers, which partially mitigates per-document recall limitations at corpus scale.

Table 6 compares our framework with KARMA Lu and Wang (2025), the closest available agentic baseline because it is also a multi-agent framework for extracting KG-style assertions from scientific publications. We are not aware of an existing agentic KG construction system designed specifically for climate-science papers, so we adapt KARMA’s prompts to the climate domain and evaluate both systems on the first 1,007 publications after final validation. Our system extracts 17,141 triplets with 99.067% correctness, while KARMA extracts 3,820 triplets with 92.277% correctness, showing that explicit evidence grounding and ontology-conformance validation improve precision while producing a much larger validated KG.

We also compare against ClimateIE Pan et al. (2025a), a climate-specific IE benchmark rather than an agentic KG-construction system. For this experiment, we run our pipeline on the 25-paper ClimateIE human corpus using the ClimateIE ontology for both systems, and evaluate source–relation–target triples with the same Gemini-2.5-flash validator. As shown in Table 7, our system produces fewer triplets but reaches substantially higher correctness: 92.936% compared with 75.004%. This indicates that the proposed evidence-centered agents trade some raw extraction volume for much cleaner curator-ready assertions, outperforming both the general agentic baseline and the climate-specific IE baseline in precision.

The 1,000 human-annotated triplets of Section 4.1 support the same conclusions with human labels, since they were sampled from raw extractor output and therefore cover triplets at every filter outcome. Against the majority vote of three annotators, triplets kept by the full pipeline are 99.0% correct (625 of 631), which closely tracks the 98.96% judged by the LLM evaluator.

C_{\text{triplet}} is precision-like, so we complement it in two ways: we measure entity-level recall against external gold that we did not produce, and we decompose what the verification stages remove.

The CMIP Publication Hub hosts publication metadata submitted through a form by the papers’ own authors, who select projects, activities, experiments, frequencies, sources, realms, and variables from controlled checkbox lists. This gives an independently curated annotation that is not derived from our pipeline. We scraped the hub for DOIs, queried OpenAlex for open-access PDFs, and retained the 139 papers that both downloaded and carried entity metadata. Because a curator can tag a paper with an entity that is never written in the paper (a related model family or a nearby variant, for instance), we first check whether each gold entity occurs in the parsed papers. Only 50.78% of the curated gold entities appear in the paper text at all, which is itself evidence that exhaustive per-document gold is ill-posed in this domain. Over the entities that are recoverable from the text, our pipeline reaches 90.29% micro-averaged recall, as shown in Table 8.

Automatic KG construction from text is commonly treated as a pipeline of entity extraction, relation extraction, linking, and refinement, with persistent challenges around schema conformance, scalability, and factual reliability Zhong et al. (2023). Recent LLM-based systems address these challenges by decomposing KG construction into extraction, schema alignment, canonicalization, and validation stages Zhang and Soh (2024).

Ontology-guided benchmarks further emphasize that extracted facts must be evaluated not only for correctness but also for conformance to a target schema Mihindukulasooriya et al. (2023). SciER shows that entity and relation extraction over full-text scientific papers remains hard for both supervised models and LLMs, even for generic dataset, method, and task entities Zhang et al. (2024). ClimateIE provides a climate-specific benchmark for NER, relation extraction, and entity linking Pan et al. (2025a), and taxonomy-driven climate IE work shows that grounding extraction in curated vocabularies can reduce hallucination and improve precision Pan et al. (2025b). KARMA Lu and Wang (2025) uses multiple agents for scientific KG enrichment, but it is not designed for a climate-specific system with domain ontology grounding, evidence-level validation, and entity linking into a curated climate KG. Our work builds on this line of research by combining ontology-constrained extraction, explicit evidence grounding, hybrid entity linking, and scalable validation to construct a large climate-science KG from scientific publications.

We presented an evidence-based, ontology-guided framework for constructing climate-science KGs from scientific publications. By requiring explicit evidence, validating ontology conformance, and linking entities to a trusted climate KG backbone, the framework produces high-precision, traceable relations at scale. Across 2,000 publications, the pipeline constructs a KG with 133,990 nodes, 755,308 relations, while maintaining high triplet correctness after validation.

The results show that agentic extraction benefits from domain structure: ontology constraints reduce schema drift, evidence validation filters unsupported assertions, and hybrid entity linking connects literature-derived facts to canonical climate entities. Our agreement study supports Gemini-2.5-flash as a scalable validator, and comparisons with KARMA and ClimateIE show that the proposed framework achieves substantially cleaner curator-ready assertions than both a general multi-agent scientific IE baseline and a climate-specific IE baseline. These findings demonstrate the practicality of evidence-centered extraction for constructing auditable, domain-specific scientific KGs.
