Our pipeline performs evidence grounding, ontology checks, entity linking, and validation in addition to extraction. Two of these verification stages are deterministic and the third is a short call to a small model, so the added cost is about 1% of extraction (Appendix A.11); the pipeline is nevertheless more expensive than direct extraction, and it inherits the GPU cost of local parsing and screening. We do not compute triplet-level recall, since open-ended scientific text would require exhaustive gold triplets for each document. Instead we report entity-level recall against external curated gold restricted to what the text actually states (90.29% micro-average, Section 4.4), and we quantify how many judge-correct triplets each stage removes. These two measurements do not cover relations that no paper in the corpus states explicitly, nor triplets whose entities fall outside the CMIP metadata families. Finally, LLM validators may still over-accept plausible but unstated relations or reject relations requiring dispersed evidence or domain knowledge.

The work uses publicly available publications, bibliographic metadata, and community resources such as ESGF/GCMD, CMIP6 controlled vocabularies, and GeoNames. Human involvement is limited to low-risk validation of evidence-supported triplets from non-sensitive scientific text. We mitigate risks from third-party LLM extraction and validation by requiring explicit textual evidence, checking evidence grounding, and releasing derived resources with appropriate attribution and source-license constraints. We declare no conflicts of interest.

Byte Language Models: Scaling, Emergent Abstractions, and Information Allocation. Tokenizer-free language models remove the inductive bias of fixed tokenizers by modeling text directly as bytes, but the resulting longer sequences substantially increase computation and eliminate explicit text abstractions. We ask whether this additional computation can be useful, and whether standard Transformers can learn the abstractions that tokenization provides. We study these questions on Transformers without specialized tokenization-related architectures. With token-superposition training and hash embeddings, byte Transformers consistently outperform subword Transformers as model size scales. We further find that byte Transformers build local text abstractions as external tokenizers: a set of segmentation-like positions are used to collect local context representations, and restricting up to $25\%$ of intermediate layers to these local representations preserves downstream performance. Finally, these learned structures induce highly non-uniform generation difficulty, with uncertainty concentrated near local structure boundaries; exploiting them for speculative decoding yields $3.4\times$ more accepted tokens than in subword Transformers.

Tokenizer-free language models, or byte language models, aim to remove externally imposed tokenizers by modeling text directly as byte sequences (Xue et al., 2022; YU et al., 2023; Slagle, 2024; Tsiamas et al., 2025; Shah et al., 2026). This formulation provides a universal input space and a new joint learning setting. However, it also introduces two main challenges. First, byte sequences are longer than subword sequences. If a typical subword contains K (usually around 4) bytes, a byte model must process K times more sequence positions. Second, prior studies suggest that effective language modeling benefits from prior abstractions over raw text. Directly modeling bytes can therefore underperform tokenized models, despite having a more general input representation.

Recent works (BLT Pagnoni et al., 2025, H-Net Hwang et al., 2026, ByteFlow Deng et al., 2026) develop new network architectures with built-in tokenization mechanisms. For example, in BLT, local encoder layers first encode byte streams into variable-sized chunks, then global layers operate on the chunks, and local decoder layers decode chunks back to bytes. While these architectures demonstrate the promise of joint tokenization, they often need specialized training and optimization strategies, making it less clear how much of the observed gains are from the joint formulation. In this work, we retain the flat Transformer architecture (without the explicit local-global-local hierarchy) and investigate the two challenges underlying byte-level language modeling: Can the additional computation caused by longer sequences be beneficial, and how does a Transformer recover useful text abstractions directly from bytes?

We study the scaling behavior of byte Transformers, and the main findings are: 1) with two modeling ingredients (token-superposition training (Peng et al., 2026) and hash embeddings), byte Transformers consistently outperform subword Transformers when scaling the number of parameters (Figure 1 a). 2) Byte models remain effective as training data continues to scale. Given a fixed FLOPs budget (Figure 1 c), the optimal proportion between data and parameters is around 1.5 to 3 times that of subword models. These results motivate a different perspective on sequence length: rather than treating longer sequences as a defect, they can provide additional computation under the same parameter budget, which is a useful scaling axis for language models. Further evaluations on downstream text-only and vision–language tasks show that byte Transformers significantly improve performance on tasks that require fine-grained perception (around 40\% relative improvements over subword Transformers on CUTE scores, 20\% on OCRBench (Liu et al., 2024)).

We next investigate how a byte Transformer develops the abstractions that tokenization provides explicitly. By studying an input-copying task on byte models, we find that copying actions need to attend only to certain segmentation positions (not necessarily whitespace), where information from local text pieces can be read out. Based on this finding, we further constrain a range of intermediate layers (up to 25\% of all layers) to access only these locally aggregated representations, resembling a global modeling stage over learned local structures. The resulting model retains downstream performance without additional training. This suggests that the apparent hierarchy of local abstraction and global reasoning is not merely imposed by tokenizer-free architectures such as BLT and H-Net, but can also emerge implicitly in the byte Transformer.

Finally, we study whether these learned local structures can be exploited during inference. By plotting the per-byte loss distribution, we find that byte Transformers have much higher variance than subword models: many byte positions have near-zero loss (in bits per byte), while substantially larger losses concentrate near the boundaries of the learned local structures. This observation suggests that the extra generation steps are not uniformly expensive in terms of model uncertainty. We therefore apply speculative decoding to construct local structures during inference (Wang et al., 2024; Kallini et al., 2026), and show that a drafting model on byte Transformers can produce 3.4\times more accepted tokens than on subword Transformers.

To summarize, our results support a simple view of tokenizer-free language modeling: longer byte sequences provide useful additional computation. At the same time, the model can learn useful local abstractions internally rather than relying on a fixed tokenizer. This perspective suggests sequence length, learned abstraction, and computation allocation as closely connected dimensions for future language-model design.

We first ask how the additional tokens in byte sequences affect model quality under parameter and compute constraints. We then examine which task capabilities benefit from byte resolution and how shared depth and sparse capacity change these trade-offs.

We first establish a controlled comparison between byte- and subword-level Transformers. Both models are trained from scratch with a mixed attention model. The byte model uses a vocabulary of size 256, while the subword model uses a 49,152 token vocabulary from the cosmo2-tokenizer (Allal et al., 2025). We use “token” to refer to both byte and subword, depending on the model in context.

Directly applying the standard training recipe to bytes is suboptimal. Byte sequences contain substantially more tokens, while each byte token carries less local semantic context than a subword token. We find the following two ingredients are effective for training byte models.

First, we use token-superposition training (TST; Peng et al., 2026) to improve learning efficiency from the longer byte sequences. TST averages four consecutive token embeddings and predicts the corresponding next four-token bag. Applying TST during the first 30% of training provides 4\times token exposure in this stage, while reverting to standard next-token prediction for the remaining 70% results in 1.9\times total text exposure under the same number of training tokens (see Appendix A.2 for details).

Second, we augment byte embeddings with hash embeddings as (Pagnoni et al., 2025). The model learns representations for n -grams of bytes and combines them with byte embeddings, allowing each byte token to incorporate information from nearby multi-byte patterns (Appendix A.3). Similarly, we increase the convolution width of gated DeltaNet from 4 (for subword models) to 16 (for byte models), to build a broader local receptive field.

Unless otherwise specified, byte models apply TST and hash embeddings (denoted by Byte), while subword models don’t (denoted by Subword). We later ablate these components to separate the contribution of the training recipe from that of input granularity.

section: Parameter and Compute Efficiency under IsoFLOPs
text: A longer byte sequence can be viewed either as a computational burden or as an opportunity to allocate more computation to a model with the same number of parameters. To distinguish these effects, we study how byte and subword Transformers scale along three coupled axes: model size, data exposure, and training compute.

section: Parameter and Compute Efficiency under IsoFLOPs
text: Following the standard practice of model scaling analyses, we train families of byte and subword models with different training FLOPs per token M and cumulative training data volume V (measured in bytes consumed during training), record their validation loss L (measured in bits per byte, BPB), and fit the loss L as function of M and V. We adapt the Chinchilla law (Hoffmann et al., 2022), L(M,V)=E+AM^{-\alpha}+BV^{-\beta}, where \alpha,\beta,E,A,B are fiting coefficients. We also denote total training FLOPs C=MD, where D is the amount of training data in tokens.

section: Parameter and Compute Efficiency under IsoFLOPs
text: Following Hoffmann et al. (2022), we compare model performance in the compute-optimal manner. Given a FLOPs budget C, we collect loss L of models with various sizes N (or equally, M) under C, fit a curve for the obtained (N,L) pairs, and the optimal parameter count under the FLOPs budget N^{\star}(C) is located at the minimum loss L^{\star} (see Figure 6 and Appendix C for details). Similarly, we obtain the optimal training byte volume V^{\star}(C). By varying C, we trace the L^{\star} – N^{\star} and L^{\star} – C Pareto frontiers in Figure 1.

section: Byte has lower optimal loss at the same optimal parameter count
text: The L^{\star} – N^{\star} Pareto frontiers (Figure 1 a) of Byte consistently below Subword. It suggests that Transformers can transform additional computation to performance gains. Meanwhile, Figure 1 b shows a different story: under the same FLOPs budgets, Subword is always better. We defer discussion on scaling along computation to Section 2.4.

section: Byte optima allocate more source bytes per parameter.
text: Compared with Subword, at the same training-compute budgets, the fitted optima select smaller Byte models and generally allocate more (3.2\times) source bytes per parameter (Figure 1 c). It implies that Byte can reach lower BPB if training data continues to scale.

section: TST and hashing embeddings provide larger combined gains for Byte.
text: We ablate TST and hashing at matched depth and training compute within each family. Combining them consistently improves BPB over raw training, with larger gains for Byte.

section: Fine-Grained Capabilities in Text-Only and Vision–Language Tasks
text: We next examine whether the modeling advantages of byte-level representations translate into downstream text-only and vision-language tasks. We evaluate word manipulation with CUTE (Edman et al., 2024), and fine-grained OCR tasks with OCRBench and TextVQA (Singh et al., 2019).

section: Fine-Grained Capabilities in Text-Only and Vision–Language Tasks
text: The results in Table 1 show that Byte has a clear advantage in word manipulation capabilities over Subword. We think the better fine-grained modeling ability of Byte comes from stronger perception of inputs and stronger ability to generate byte-level sequences. We particularly expect better alignment among modalities in future byte language model-based multimodality learning.

section: Fine-Grained Capabilities in Text-Only and Vision–Language Tasks
text: We additionally evaluate both model families on broader standard text-only (21 tasks, Table 9) and vision-language benchmarks (5 tasks, Table 13) in Appendix D. On text tasks, Byte model consistently outputperforms Subword, due to more computation per parameter. On vision-language tasks, Byte is on par with Subword.

section: Controlling Computation with Shared Depth and Sparse Experts
text: The preceding results reveal a compute–quality trade-off between Byte and Subword. We therefore examine two complementary ways to shift this trade-off (Figure 2): increasing Subword computation through shared depth, and reducing Byte ’s activated computation at a given parameter capacity with sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE). Using the main model suite, we evaluate four-pass Subword models and Byte MoE models under the training schedules of their dense counterparts; architecture details are provided in Appendix A.

We follow the setting of LoopFormer (Jeddi et al., 2026) to increase Subword computation with four shared backbone passes. It closes most of the BPB gap to Byte in both the parameter and compute views, showing that repeated depth is an effective way to scale computation for subword models. The looped Subword models also achieve consistently higher QA RC than the standard dense Byte models across the evaluated scales.

section: Reducing activated computation with sparse experts.
text: Sparse MoE (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) consistently improves Byte BPB in both the parameter and compute views, showing that sparse activation is an effective way to reduce computation while retaining larger model capacity. Notably, the 1B Byte MoE achieves lower BPB than the 3B dense Subword model while reaching comparable QA RC.

section: Reducing activated computation with sparse experts.
text: Together, these results show that the byte–subword modeling gap depends strongly on how computation is allocated. Increasing computation through shared depth allows Subword models to recover much of the BPB gap, while sparse activation improves the compute efficiency of Byte models at comparable parameter capacity.

section: Emergent Local Abstractions in Byte Transformers
text: Tokenization provides explicit local abstractions that can organize text into useful computational units. In this section, we investigate whether similar structures can emerge implicitly in byte Transformers without an explicit tokenizer or hierarchical architecture. We study this question through two complementary experiments. First, we examine how byte models organize information during prediction using an input-copying task. Second, we evaluate whether the representations revealed by this analysis can support alternative computation patterns through a frozen layer intervention.

section: Copying as a probe of local information structure
text: To probe how text semantics are abstracted and accessed in models, we study the copying task by prompting the model with “Your task is to copy the string: X. Now copy it: X ”, where X is a short string composed of multiple meaningful English words. We evaluate Byte -1B by analyzing attention patterns during the copying process, focusing on how different layers access the source text when generating the copied sequence (see Appendix E.1 for details).

section: Copying as a probe of local information structure
text: As shown in Figure 3, Byte -1B exhibits a clear attention aggregation pattern during copying. In particular, attention in intermediate layers becomes concentrated on a small set of source positions that are repeatedly accessed by multiple consecutive target bytes. This aggregation occurs even without any whitespace in inputs, indicating that it does not simply arise from explicit separators. The repeated reuse of these positions suggests that the byte model internally develops a mechanism for consolidating local information into representative states, providing an implicit structure over the byte sequence.

section: Testing local abstractions with a frozen layer intervention
text: The copying task reveals that multiple byte predictions can repeatedly access a small set of locally aggregated source representations. However, attention patterns alone do not establish whether these representations are sufficient for subsequent computation. We therefore introduce a frozen layer intervention that forces a contiguous range of intermediate layers to operate on a shorter sequence of locally aggregated representations, while preserving full byte-resolution states before and after the intervention. No model parameters are updated.

section: Testing local abstractions with a frozen layer intervention
text: Concretely, following the external tokenizer applied in BLT (Pagnoni et al., 2025), we partition the text sequence into local spans using a frozen, architecturally matched 200M Byte model and compress non-image text tokens (for vision–language tasks) by approximately 4\times. We treat the selected intermediate layers as a temporary global stage (like the global model in BLT): each local span is mean-pooled into a single representation, processed at the compressed resolution, and then propagated back to the original byte-resolution sequence. This intervention introduces a coarse-grained computation stage into the pretrained Byte -1B model without modifying its parameters or retraining it. More details and results are in Appendix E.2.

section: Testing local abstractions with a frozen layer intervention
text: We apply the same intervention to Byte -1B and Subword -1B across several downstream tasks, sweeping the start and end layers of the compressed global stage G. As shown in Figure 4, Byte exhibits a clear recovery in performance when the global stage is placed sufficiently late in the network, with the trend becoming apparent for intervals starting around layer 17. More importantly, a stable compressible region emerges in the later layers: for G=[21,27], 7 of the model’s 28 layers (25%) operate only on the compressed local representations, while downstream performance remains close to the uncompressed baseline across tasks. In contrast, applying the same intervention to the subword model causes substantial degradation across nearly all layer intervals. This contrast suggests that the robustness to an intermediate compressed global stage is a property of the byte model rather than a generic consequence of pooling hidden states.

Locally aggregated representations can support part of Byte ’s computation on a shorter sequence (Section 3), while the model still predicts every byte separately. These additional modeling steps raise the question of where the extra computation (Section 2.2) is useful and where it could be reduced. For a given text source, deterministic, reversible tokenizations preserve total entropy (Proposition 1), so finer granularity distributes the same source information over more tokens. We therefore examine how BPB varies across these tokens, how token boundaries explain the distribution gap, and whether small drafts can handle the low-BPB continuations.

To compare local modeling difficulty across granularities, we use byte-weighted BPB: the random variable X gives the BPB at a uniformly sampled text byte. Following the BPB definition in Appendix D.1, a target token T_{i} spanning m_{i} original text bytes has BPB score x_{i}, x_{i}=-\frac{\ln p_{\theta}(T_{i}\mid\mathbf{T}_{<i})}{m_{i}\ln 2}. In the distribution statistics, each token’s BPB x_{i} has weight m_{i}, accounting for differences in token length. Our main comparison uses the 1B Byte and Subword models, and we extend the analysis to public models.

The BPB density f_{X} exhibits a near-zero power law and an exponential tail over finite ranges, connected by an empirical transition: f_{X}(x)\approx\begin{cases}k_{\rm pow}x^{\alpha},&\epsilon<x\leq u_{1},\\ f_{X}^{(\mathrm{trans})}(x),&u_{1}<x\leq u_{2},\\ k_{\rm exp}e^{-x/\beta},&u_{2}<x\leq v.\end{cases} Here \alpha is the near-zero power-law exponent and \beta is the exponential decay scale. The fitted ranges are (\epsilon,u_{1}] and (u_{2},v]; the transition f_{X}^{(\mathrm{trans})}(x) and values outside the fitted ranges remain empirical. Let F_{X} and S_{X} denote the CDF and survival function of X, with S_{X}(x)=1-F_{X}(x)=\Pr(X>x) (Figure 5 c). We set the normalization coefficients k_{\rm pow} and k_{\rm exp} so that each fitted density integrates to the measured probability mass in its fitting interval: k_{\rm pow}=\frac{F_{X}(u_{1})-F_{X}(\epsilon)}{\int_{\epsilon}^{u_{1}}t^{\alpha}\,dt},\qquad k_{\rm exp}=\frac{F_{X}(v)-F_{X}(u_{2})}{\int_{u_{2}}^{v}e^{-t/\beta}\,dt}.

section: Byte distributions place more mass at both low and high BPB.
text: Near zero, byte densities approach 1/x, with fitted power-law exponent \alpha\in[-0.97,-0.91], whereas subword densities are shallower, with \alpha\in[-0.8,-0.6] (Figure 5 a–b). In the tail, byte models have slightly larger decay scales \beta and more high-BPB mass overall than subword models (Figure 5 c). Together, these patterns show that Byte has more probability mass at both low and high BPB than Subword (Figure 5 b–c; Table 2). We also verify this law in public byte models, including BLT and H-Net, and widely used subword models. The byte models have nearly overlapping BPB distributions (Figure 11; Table 15).

section: Token boundaries explain the distribution gap.
text: We aggregate Byte BPB by averaging within each token span defined by a subword tokenizer. The aggregated distribution (dotted lines in Figure 5 b–c) closely matches the native Subword distribution. This result indicates that the distribution gap largely reflects how information is grouped into tokens. Subword tokenization provides a statistical prior for this grouping: it combines high-BPB bytes with predictable continuations into fewer tokens, reducing near-zero BPB mass while retaining the source’s total information (Proposition 1).

section: Byte modeling can allocate more computation to difficult tokens.
text: For the same total source information, Byte uses multiple modeling steps within a span that Subword handles in one step, retaining high-BPB bytes as separate tokens (Figure 5 c). This supports the argument in Section 2.2 that longer sequences can scale computation without increasing model size.

Maintaining a fixed byte granularity allows more computation for high-BPB tokens, but also adds modeling steps for the many low-BPB continuations (Figure 5; Table 2). We therefore examine whether speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023) can reduce this overhead.

We use existing 200M and 50M models as drafts and same-family 1B models as targets for both Byte and Subword. We do not train specialized drafts. On the validation dataset, we compare accepted bytes per target forward pass in an oracle simulation on the given evaluation text. Appendix G specifies the protocol.

section: Higher byte acceptance rates compensate for shorter token spans.
text: At both draft sizes, Byte accepts about 3.4\times as many tokens per target forward pass as Subword. Accepted bytes per forward are nearly identical with 200M drafts and slightly higher for Byte with 50M drafts (Table 3). The 200M drafts yield longer accepted text per forward in both families.

section: Higher byte acceptance rates compensate for shorter token spans.
text: These acceptance lengths suggest that many additional byte tokens can be verified together, reducing the need for separate sequential target calls. The comparable text coverage of the two families at both draft sizes suggests that joint verification could offset much of the extra sequential overhead introduced by byte granularity.

Tokenizer-free language models operate directly on fine-grained inputs such as bytes or characters, avoiding a separately constructed subword vocabulary. ByT5 (Xue et al., 2022) studies byte-to-byte pretraining, while MambaByte (Wang et al., 2024) models byte sequences with selective state-space models. Other works (Clark et al., 2022; YU et al., 2023; Pagnoni et al., 2025; Hwang et al., 2026), introduce hierarchical mechanisms that compress or aggregate fine-grained inputs for coarser-grained computation. In contrast, we study byte language modeling with Transformers with hybrid attention that preserves byte resolution throughout the network.

Model scale and computation can be varied independently through tokenization and architectural design. Compute Optimal Tokenization (Limisiewicz et al., 2026) studies how token granularity changes the relationship between raw data, sequence length, and compute. Repeated-depth models such as LoopFormer (Jeddi et al., 2026) increase computation while sharing parameters, whereas sparse MoE models such as DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) increase parameter capacity without proportionally increasing activated computation. Building on these directions, we use shared depth to increase Subword computation and sparse experts to reduce Byte activated computation at a given parameter capacity, examining how computation shapes the byte–subword modeling trade-off.

Our results provide a complementary perspective to recent byte-level approaches, which introduce explicit hierarchical or learned tokenization mechanisms to control the cost of long byte sequences. Using a flat Transformer, we show that this sequence-length overhead can instead provide useful computation: byte models benefit from scaling and favor substantially more training data per parameter under a fixed FLOP budget. Moreover, although we do not impose a hierarchy, byte Transformers develop segmentation-like positions that aggregate local text information, and intermediate layers can exploit these representations without loss in downstream performance. This connects flat byte Transformers to hierarchical architectures and suggests that local abstraction and global modeling can emerge implicitly from byte-level training. These learned structures also have inference-time consequences, as prediction difficulty concentrates near their boundaries and can be exploited by speculative decoding. Together, our results suggest that sequence length, learned abstraction, and computation should be viewed as coupled design dimensions, motivating future work on adaptive computation and learned computational granularity for byte language models.

Our study is limited to vanilla Transformer backbones and the evaluated training and task scales; whether the observed scaling behavior and emergent local structures generalize to other architectures, larger models, and broader modalities remains open.

Mixture of Phonetic Experts Based Low-Rank Adaptation of Conformer Models for Accented English Speech Recognition. We present Mixture of Phonetic Experts based Low-Rank Adaptation (MoPE-LoRA), a parameter-efficient adaptation framework for accented English speech recognition. Recent mixture-of-experts approaches typically allocate experts per accent, implicitly treating accent identity as the primary axis of variation. In contrast, we organize adaptation along phonetic categories, motivated by the observation that accent differences are often expressed as systematic distortions of phoneme realization. MoPE-LoRA introduces a fixed set of six low-rank experts aligned with manner-of-articulation classes and performs frame-level routing through a hybrid mechanism that combines phoneme supervision with learned acoustic gating. Because the expert set is shared across accents, the model does not require accent-specific modules and naturally extends to previously unseen accents. Experiments on L2-ARCTIC show that MoPE-LoRA consistently improves over single LoRA and full fine-tuning. In zero-shot evaluation where one accent is held out during training, the proposed method yields a 12.3% relative improvement over single LoRA. These results indicate that phonetic-category-based decomposition offers a scalable and transferable alternative to accent-level adaptation.

While modern ASR systems achieve high accuracy on native English speech, their performance often degrades on non-native or accented English, particularly in low-resource scenarios. Accented speech typically involves systematic shifts in pronunciation and phoneme realization, which models trained primarily on native speech do not fully capture. Improving robustness to such variation remains an important challenge.

A range of adaptation strategies have been explored. Domain adversarial training aims to learn accent-invariant representations, while multi-task learning introduces auxiliary objectives such as accent classification or phoneme prediction. While these methods can partially mitigate performance drops, they often require carefully balanced training objectives and additional annotated data, which may not be feasible in low-resource accented speech scenarios.

More recently, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods, particularly low-rank adaptation (LoRA), have become attractive for adapting large pre-trained ASR models with limited additional parameters. However, standard LoRA applies a single adaptation mechanism across all phonetic contexts, without explicitly modeling how accent variation manifests at the phoneme level.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches provide another direction by routing inputs through specialized sub-modules. In multi-accent settings, experts are often assigned per accent or language. While effective when accent identity is known, this formulation treats accent as the primary axis of variation and may require the number of experts to grow with the number of supported accents. In practice, however, accent differences are largely expressed through systematic distortions of phonetic realizations, such as vowel shifts or consonant substitutions, which may recur across multiple accents. Modeling adaptation strictly at the accent level may therefore overlook the shared phonetic structure underlying accent variability.

Motivated by this observation, we propose MoPE-LoRA, a phonetic routing-based adaptation framework for Conformer ASR models. Inspired by Switch Transformer and ST-MoE, our method introduces phoneme-aware expert routing, allowing the model to dynamically select experts based on phonetic content rather than accent or language identity. By integrating LoRA in selective layers with phonetic routing, our method adapts to accented speech using a fixed set of six low-rank experts aligned with manner-of-articulation classes. To our knowledge, this is the first use of phoneme-category-grounded LoRA experts with frame-level hybrid routing for non-native multi-accent ASR.

We evaluate our approach on the L2-ARCTIC dataset, a widely used benchmark for non-native English speech recognition. Our method improves WER over single LoRA adaptation, demonstrating that phoneme-aware MoE with phonetic routing provides an accurate, interpretable, and parameter-efficient solution for accented ASR. To further assess generalization, we conducted unseen-accent experiments by holding out one accent from the L2-ARCTIC dataset for testing while training on the remaining accents. Across all evaluated accents, our approach achieved the lowest error rates, highlighting its robustness to previously unseen accent variations.

To handle phonetic variations in accented speech, we use MoPE-LoRA, which decomposes adaptation into linguistically motivated experts. Each expert targets a phonetic category (e.g., vowels, fricatives) via low-rank adapters, providing inductive bias for phonetic correction. Unlike conventional MoE, MoPE-LoRA leverages phonetic priors for focused adaptation (Figure 1).

We group English consonants into five articulatory classes following standard manner-of-articulation distinctions, namely Stops/Plosives, Fricatives, Affricates, Nasals, and Liquids/Glides, and add Vowels as a sixth category, yielding six phonetic expert groups in total. Table 1 maps phonemes to the six linguistic expert categories used for routing and evaluation.

This decomposition ensures that each expert is responsible for a coherent set of sounds that share articulatory properties, under the hypothesis that sounds produced by similar mechanisms are subject to related accent-induced distortions. Each group corresponds to a dedicated LoRA expert, allowing the model to learn specialized weight adjustments for different articulatory classes.

For a given encoder layer, the e -th expert introduces a low-rank weight perturbation to the frozen weight matrix \mathbf{W}_{\text{base}}: \Delta W_{e}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\alpha}{r}\mathbf{B}_{e}\mathbf{A}_{e}\mathbf{x},\quad e=1,\dots,E, where \mathbf{A}_{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times D} is the down-projection matrix that maps the input from the original dimension D into a low-rank subspace of dimension r, and \mathbf{B}_{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times r} is the up-projection matrix that maps back to D. The rank r\ll D controls the capacity of each expert, and the scaling factor \alpha modulates the magnitude of the adaptation relative to the frozen weights. \mathbf{A}_{e} is initialized randomly and \mathbf{B}_{e} is initialized to zero, so that at the start of training each expert contributes no perturbation and the model preserves its pretrained behavior.

Each of the E=6 experts specializes in an articulatory category, using separate low-rank subspaces to capture category-specific phonetic distortions. For example, the vowel expert models formant shifts and duration changes, while the fricative expert adapts to spectral variations in sibilants and non-sibilants across L1 backgrounds. This decomposition reduces interference seen in standard LoRA, where a single adapter must handle all phonetic categories within the same parameter space.

These expert modules are inserted into the Query (\mathbf{W}_{Q}), Key (\mathbf{W}_{K}), and Value (\mathbf{W}_{V}) projection matrices of the self-attention modules in adapted encoder layers. This placement is motivated by the fact that attention projections jointly govern how acoustic context is aggregated across frames, a process directly affected by phonetic distortion in accented speech. By adapting all three projections, the experts can modify both what the model attends to (via Q and K) and the content that is propagated (via V).
To ensure that each expert specializes in its assigned phonetic category, we design a hybrid routing strategy that combines external linguistic supervision with internal acoustic learning.

A learnable gating network computes frame-level routing logits from the encoder’s intermediate representations, producing learned routing probabilities: \mathbf{p}^{\text{learn}}_{b,t}=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{z}_{b,t}}{\tau}\right), where \mathbf{z}_{b,t} are routing logits and \tau is a temperature hyperparameter.

When phoneme labels c_{b,t} are available from the frozen phoneme model (Section 3.2), supervised routing provides a direct assignment signal: \mathbf{p}^{\text{sup}}_{b,t,j}=\begin{cases}1,&c_{b,t}=j,\\ 0,&c_{b,t}\neq j\text{ and }c_{b,t}\neq-1,\\ \frac{1}{E},&c_{b,t}=-1,\end{cases} where j\in\{1,\dots,E\} indexes the experts, c_{b,t}=j indicates that the frame belongs to phonetic category j, and c_{b,t}=-1 denotes low-confidence or silence frames that are routed uniformly. This supervised component acts as a hard constraint during training: frames confidently classified into phonetic category e are deterministically assigned to expert e, ensuring that each expert is grounded in its intended articulatory class rather than learning arbitrary input partitions.

The final routing distribution combines both signals: \mathbf{p}_{b,t}=\beta\mathbf{p}^{\text{sup}}_{b,t}+(1-\beta)\mathbf{p}^{\text{learn}}_{b,t},\quad\beta\in[0,1], where \beta controls the strength of phonetic supervision. The learned component captures acoustic patterns not fully explained by the phoneme model, such as coarticulation effects and phoneme boundary ambiguity characteristic of non-native speech, and can adaptively compensate for prediction errors on accented pronunciations, making the routing robust to the inherent imprecision of CTC-based alignment on accented speech.

Only the top- k experts are activated per frame for computational efficiency: \mathcal{K}_{b,t}=\mathrm{TopK}(\mathbf{p}_{b,t},k). We set k{=}2 following ST-MoE, which demonstrated that top-2 routing achieves a good balance between expert specialization and model capacity. Additionally, k{=}2 allows frames near phoneme boundaries to activate experts from two relevant categories (e.g., a transition from a vowel to a fricative), which is particularly important for accented speech where phoneme boundaries may shift.

The selected expert outputs are combined via normalized routing weights: \mathbf{Y}_{\text{moe}}[b,t]=\sum_{j=1}^{k}w_{b,t,j}\Delta W_{e_{j}}(\mathbf{h}_{b,t}), where \mathbf{h}_{b,t} denotes the intermediate representation at frame t of batch element b produced by the current encoder layer, e_{j}\in\mathcal{K}_{b,t} is the index of the j -th selected expert, and w_{b,t,j} denotes its routing probability from \mathbf{p}_{b,t} normalized over the top- k activated experts. The final adapted representation is: \mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{Y}_{\text{base}}+\mathbf{Y}_{\text{moe}}.

Crucially, the expert set is shared across all accents. No accent-specific modules are introduced and no accent labels are required at test time; the model adapts to a given utterance purely through its frame-level phonetic routing decisions.
The model is trained end-to-end using the Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) loss as the primary objective: \mathcal{L}_{\text{CTC}}=-\log P(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{Y}).

To stabilize MoE training, we incorporate two auxiliary losses. The first is a load balancing loss, which encourages uniform expert utilization by penalizing imbalanced routing: \mathcal{L}_{\text{balance}}=E\sum_{i=1}^{E}f_{i}P_{i}, where f_{i} and P_{i} denote the assignment frequency and average routing probability of expert i, respectively. The second is a router Z-loss, which discourages overconfident routing decisions by penalizing large routing probabilities: \mathcal{L}_{\text{z}}=\frac{1}{BT}\sum_{b,t}\left(\max_{i}p_{b,t,i}\right)^{2}.

The total training objective combines all three terms: \mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{CTC}}+\lambda_{\text{balance}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{balance}}+\lambda_{\text{z}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{z}}, where the auxiliary loss weights are set to \lambda_{\text{balance}}=0.01 and \lambda_{\text{z}}=0.001.

We use the L2-ARCTIC dataset, containing approximately 24 hours of non-native English speech from 24 speakers (4 per accent) across Mandarin, Korean, Spanish, Hindi, Arabic, and Vietnamese L1 backgrounds. Following the evaluation protocol of, we enforce both speaker- and sentence-disjoint partitions across 4 splits, which is stricter than speaker-only disjointness as it prevents the model from memorizing sentence-level patterns during training. In each split, one speaker per accent (6 speakers) is held out for testing on sentences excluded from training, while the remaining 18 speakers are used for training and development. Speaker assignments rotate so that every speaker is evaluated exactly once, and results are averaged. Table 2 reports per-accent statistics. For zero-shot evaluation, one accent is entirely excluded from training and used only for testing.
For layer-wise representation analysis, we additionally use the TIMIT corpus, which provides time-aligned phonetic annotations.

We use the NeMo Conformer CTC Small model ({\sim} 13M parameters) as the base encoder, with audio resampled to 16 kHz. Models are trained for 50 epochs with batch size 16. MoPE-LoRA adapters with E{=}6 experts are applied to Q, K, V projections in layers 6–16, each with rank r{=}8 and \alpha{=}16. The routing network uses top-2 expert selection with hybrid routing (blend \beta is a learnable parameter, initialized to \sigma(0.5)). The learning rate is 1\times 10^{-3} with cosine annealing to 5\times 10^{-6}. Training is conducted on an NVIDIA RTX 5090.

Phoneme Model. To provide frame-level phoneme supervision for expert routing, we train a separate phoneme-level CTC model on LibriSpeech, using a Conformer CTC Small architecture (16 layers, dimension 176). Grapheme-to-phoneme conversion uses g2p-en. The model is trained for 25 epochs with Adam (\beta_{1}{=}0.9, \beta_{2}{=}0.999, weight decay 1\times 10^{-5}), learning rate 1\times 10^{-3} with cosine annealing and 10% warmup. During MoPE-LoRA training, this model remains frozen.
We first evaluate our phoneme model on LibriSpeech to establish a native-English baseline. As shown in Table 3, the results confirm strong performance on both clean and noisy speech.

Cross-domain evaluation on L2-ARCTIC reveals a substantial drop in frame-level phonetic accuracy, with 36.04% top-1 and 61.56% top-2 accuracy (Table 4), highlighting the challenge of cross-domain accented phoneme recognition. This motivates our k{=}2 expert routing strategy: dual expert activations help capture coarticulatory transitions and provide smoother gradient flow than strict top-1 sparse routing. Combined with the learned gating (1{-}\beta), this approach achieves 10.43% WER on accented speech (Table 5), demonstrating effective compensation for cross-domain phonetic variability.

Not all encoder layers contribute equally to phonetic adaptation. Prior studies suggest that early layers capture low-level acoustic features, middle layers encode most phonetic information, and upper layers focus on contextualized representations.

To verify this, we computed the mutual information (MI) between each Conformer layer and phoneme labels on TIMIT. Continuous embeddings were discretized via K-Means, and MI was calculated between cluster assignments and ground-truth phonemes (Figure 2). The MI shows an inverted-U trend: middle layers contain the most phonetic information, while early and upper layers contain less. t-SNE visualizations (Figure 3) confirm this pattern.
Based on these results, we focus phonetic adaptation on layer ranges that include the middle, phoneme-rich layers, while varying the inclusion of early and upper layers.

Table 5 reports WER across adaptation strategies and layer ranges. Among Single LoRA variants, adapting all three attention projections (QKV) across layers 1–16 achieves the best WER (11.33%), outperforming partial-projection LoRA and Full Fine-Tuning. Limiting adaptation to upper layers degrades performance, highlighting the importance of middle layers for phonetic correction.

MoPE-LoRA consistently surpasses Single LoRA across all tested layer ranges. The best configuration, MoPE-QKV (6–16), achieves 10.43% WER—a 2.37% absolute improvement over Full FT and 0.90% over Single LoRA-QKV (1–16)—while using only 13.6M parameters. This demonstrates that phoneme-category experts provide a linguistically motivated decomposition that generalizes across accents more efficiently than the 244M-parameter accent-level MAS-LoRA.

Consistent with our MI (Figure 2) and t-SNE (Figure 3) analysis, Layers 1–5 encode low-level, accent-invariant acoustic features contributing little to phonetic adaptation. Performance improves steadily as middle layers (6–12) are included, reflecting the emergence of phoneme-discriminative representations. Despite lower phonetic MI, late layers (13–16) remain essential for the contextual representations required by CTC decoding; extending adaptation to all layers (1–16) offers no gain over 6–16, and restricting to middle layers alone (4–12) proves detrimental.

As shown in Table 6, MoPE achieves the lowest WER on all unseen accents, with a 12.3% relative improvement over Single LoRA and 44.3% over the unadapted baseline (per-accent reductions on range: 9.2%–21.8%). Without accent-specific experts or labels, phoneme-category specialization addresses pronunciation variability at its root, enabling robust zero-shot generalization.

We introduce MoPE-LoRA, a Mixture of Phonetic Experts framework adapting Conformer ASR to accented English via phoneme-category experts and hybrid frame-level routing, with no accent-specific modules required. On L2-ARCTIC, it achieves 10.43% WER and 44.3% relative improvement over the unadapted baseline in zero-shot transfer, confirming phoneme-level decomposition as a principled, parameter-efficient solution for accent-agnostic ASR.
