Beyond Binary Labels: Diagnostic Evaluation of LLM Safety with Prompt-Level Rubrics. Current LLM safety benchmarks predominantly rely on binary safe or unsafe labels, lacking explanatory depth and suffering from low consistency across automated judges. To address this, we introduce DiagSafe, a diagnostic evaluation framework that moves beyond binary classification by employing prompt-level rubrics. Grounded in globally applicable AI safety policies, each rubric provides explicit criteria along two dimensions: safety, which targets concrete harms with specific exemptions to suppress false positives, and usefulness, which independently evaluates instruction fulfillment. To ensure a robust and realistic evaluation, we construct a bilingual (English-Chinese) benchmark grounded in a comprehensive 84-label safety taxonomy, consisting of two subsets: DiagBase, which covers single- and multi-turn prompts with direct harmful queries and template-based jailbreaks, and DiagAttack, which embeds harmful intents into complex instruction-following tasks to form challenging instruction attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiagSafe significantly enhances the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, achieving 95.34% agreement with human annotations -- substantially higher than the 69%-87% achieved by the baselines -- and high inter-judge consistency (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.864).

Furthermore, applying our framework reveals that leading LLMs differ markedly in their unsafe rates, and each model also exhibits unique vulnerabilities along different dimensions. In addition, we observe that models are particularly susceptible in Chinese and multi-turn contexts. Ultimately, DiagSafe provides a reliable and explainable tool for auditing and optimizing LLM alignment.

As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into real-world applications, they pose potential risks that make evaluating their safety crucial for responsible deployment. To systematically quantify these risks, the research community has developed various safety benchmarks. Recent efforts, including SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024b), Do-Not-Answer (Wang et al., 2024), DecodingTrust (Wang et al., 2023), AIR-Bench (Zeng et al., 2024), and SALAD-Bench (Li et al., 2024), have made significant progress by introducing finer taxonomies, supporting multilingual prompts, and broadening attack coverage.

Despite these advancements, existing benchmarks face three primary limitations. First, their evaluation granularity is often too coarse. Reducing responses to binary safe or unsafe labels lacks explanatory depth, leaving developers without actionable insights for targeted improvements. Second, current evaluation methods suffer from low consistency. Prior work shows that swapping the evaluation classifier can shift attack success rates by nearly 30 percentage points, with inter-judge agreement dropping to 22% in certain categories (Liu et al., 2026b). Third, data diversity remains restricted. No existing benchmark systematically integrates multilingual prompts, single- and multi-turn dialogues, and different attack types across a generalized and comprehensive taxonomy, resulting in unsystematic and incomplete safety evaluation (see Table 1).

To address these limitations, we introduce DiagSafe, a comprehensive and diagnostic safety benchmark. It comprises two core components: a novel evaluation framework (Figure 1) and a highly diverse dataset. First, inspired by the domain-specific rubrics in FORTRESS (Knight et al., 2025), our diagnostic evaluation framework moves beyond traditional binary classification by employing prompt-level rubrics. Instead of relying on generic instructions, we designed a dedicated rubric for every prompt with explicit, item-level criteria for both safety and usefulness. This dual-dimensional approach transforms subjective binary judgments into objective, explainable assessments.

Second, to ensure robust and realistic evaluation, the DiagSafe dataset is grounded in a comprehensive safety taxonomy. By systematically collecting and coding AI safety policies and regulations from various countries, we developed a three-level taxonomy comprising 84 safety labels, each with a detailed policy specifying its definition and boundaries. Built upon this rigorous foundation, the dataset is designed to capture a wide spectrum of real-world scenarios and adversarial threats. It consists of two bilingual (English and Chinese) subsets. DiagBase covers single- and multi-turn prompts, including both direct harmful queries and template-based jailbreaks. DiagAttack further embeds harmful intents into complex instruction-following tasks, forming instruction attacks (Jiang et al., 2023).

Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiagSafe significantly enhances the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge, achieving 95.34% agreement with human annotators and high inter-judge consistency (Cohen’s \kappa=0.864). Applying our benchmark to a series of LLMs (8B to 1.6T parameters) reveals critical vulnerabilities. While unsafe rates on DiagBase range from 2% to 33%, 8 of the 11 models exceed 40% on DiagAttack. In addition, models are generally more susceptible to unsafe behaviors in Chinese contexts and during multi-turn interactions. Furthermore, the fine-grained analysis effectively exposes the unique safety blind spots of each evaluated model. In summary, our main contributions are three-fold: Prompt-Level Rubric Evaluation: We propose a novel paradigm that shifts safety evaluation from generic binary classification to fine-grained, item-by-item assessment. By independently evaluating safety and usefulness, this approach yields highly consistent and explainable judgments. Comprehensive Safety Benchmark: We construct a diverse dataset grounded in a rigorous three-tier 84-label taxonomy. It integrates bilingual prompts, multi-turn dialogues, and various attack strategies to ensure realistic threat evaluation. Actionable Model Diagnostics: We conduct extensive evaluations on leading LLMs, uncovering specific vulnerabilities obscured by aggregate metrics. Our findings provide concrete guidance for LLM alignment.

Safety benchmarks are a crucial component of large language model evaluation (Gehman et al., 2020; Hartvigsen et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2022). Recent advancements have evolved along two primary dimensions: taxonomic scope and scenario diversity. To broaden taxonomic scope, benchmarks like SALAD-Bench (Li et al., 2024) and S-Eval (Yuan et al., 2025) introduce hierarchical risk categories, AIR-Bench (Zeng et al., 2024) designs risk categories based on actual regulatory documents, and Safety-Prompts (Sun et al., 2023) significantly scales up the data volume. To enhance scenario diversity, recent datasets incorporate adversarial jailbreak attacks (Mazeika et al., 2024; Chao et al., 2024), multilingual contexts (Deng et al., 2024), and multi-turn dialogues (Cao et al., 2026). Despite these expansions, most existing benchmarks lack precise, policy-level boundary definitions for their labels and rarely integrate these diverse elements into a single framework. DiagSafe bridges this gap by unifying diverse evaluation scenarios under a comprehensive taxonomy, providing a unified diagnostic resource with explicit, instance-specific rubrics (Table 1).

Regarding the evaluation methods, existing work mainly falls into three categories. The first category uses multiple-choice questions (MCQs) to assess safety, enabling fully automatic and reproducible scoring, as in SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024b) and CHiSafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024a). However, this paradigm measures a model’s ability to recognize harmful content rather than the safety of its actual generations. The second relies on trained safety classifiers, such as open-weight models (e.g., LlamaGuard4 (Meta AI, 2025)) and benchmark-specific evaluators (e.g., SALAD-Bench’s MD-Judge (Li et al., 2024)). Although fast, these classifiers provide only binary labels without evidence trails or actionable diagnostics. The third employs general-purpose LLM judges with generic prompts, as seen in EasyJailbreak (Zhou et al., 2024), but such judges are highly susceptible to stylistic variations (Eiras et al., 2025) and degrade on adversarial or multilingual inputs (Liu et al., 2024). Classifiers and LLM judges with generic prompts suffer from significant inconsistency (Liu et al., 2026b) because their scoring rules are either implicit or globally generic. To address this limitation, recent work by Knight et al. (2025) demonstrated that employing instance-specific rubrics can achieve high human alignment in specific high-risk domains (e.g., national security and public safety).

Building upon this insight, DiagSafe scales and generalizes this prompt-level rubric paradigm to a comprehensive safety evaluation. Whereas Knight et al. (2025) directly pair each prompt with a dedicated rubric, DiagSafe introduces an explicit and reusable intermediate layer, following a safety provisions \rightarrow label specification \rightarrow prompt-level rubric pipeline. Through systematic experiments, we provide the first evidence that automatically synthesized prompt-level rubrics are highly effective in safety scenarios. By providing explicit, per-sample criteria across a broad taxonomy, our approach effectively constrains judge behavior to yield highly consistent, explainable, and reliable judgments (§ 4.2).

We present a diagnostic safety evaluation method that relies on prompt-level rubrics to conduct fine-grained evaluation of LLMs. The rubrics are grounded in a three-level taxonomy comprising 84 safety labels. To instantiate this method, we construct two subsets, DiagBase and DiagAttack (Section 3.2).

DiagSafe is built on an intuitive idea: reliable safety judgments depend on explicit evaluation criteria. Rather than relying on generic instructions to classify responses as “safe” or “unsafe,” we equip each prompt with a dedicated, prompt-specific rubric. These rubrics contain verifiable items across two dimensions: safety and usefulness. Since both are fundamental requirements for deployed models, evaluating them jointly provides a more comprehensive picture of model behavior than assessing safety in isolation.

The safety dimension is made of S-items, each naming a concrete behavior. A rubric contains multiple S-items, each corresponding to one type of harm that the response to this specific prompt may produce. Each S-item also carries its own exemptions: behaviors under that same risk that must not be judged unsafe, such as objective conceptual discussion, an explicit refusal, or legal and common-sense knowledge. These exemptions delimit the legitimate boundary for that item and suppress false positives.

The usefulness dimension consists of U-items, which independently assess whether a response fulfills the given instruction. These items fall into three categories: instruction following, information quality (e.g., factual correctness and internal consistency), and response patterns (e.g., bare refusals or the provision of alternatives). This dimension comprises eight fixed U-items whose binary (Yes/No) answers map to a 0–3 score via a deterministic rule. For example, a score of 3 requires a direct, factually consistent answer, whereas a bare refusal scores 1.

In summary, this rubric forms the foundation of DiagSafe’s fine-grained and reliable evaluation, converting subjective “is this safe?” judgments into objective, item-level criteria. Furthermore, by treating safety and usefulness as independent dimensions, the rubric enables a more comprehensive assessment of LLM behavior than a single safety label can provide.

We build the dataset around a hierarchical label taxonomy. To ensure that the labels are scientifically grounded and complete, we collect a broad set of public safety standards as the basis for label design, and equip each label with a detailed definition and explicit criteria that delimit its boundary.

We collect public safety guidelines from countries and regions such as the European Union, the United States, and China, covering ethical principles, risk frameworks, industry taxonomies, and national technical policies. From these documents we extract and consolidate 204 safety provisions. Drawing on this multi-source, cross-jurisdictional base, rather than a single company’s internal policy, keeps the taxonomy from inheriting any one vendor’s blind spots.

We use an LLM agent to merge the collected provisions and expand them into individual safety labels, each accompanied by a detailed label specification. Safety-team experts then review and revise the draft, verifying source traceability, rule accuracy, and boundary clarity, and removing safety-irrelevant labels. Each label specification explicitly specifies four components: (1) a precise definition of the label, (2) value principles grounded in public safety standards, (3) dangerous behaviors that constitute violations, and (4) safe behaviors that are permitted. Compared with the taxonomies of existing benchmarks, ours offers broader coverage and finer granularity, as shown in Figure 2.

Using the label specifications as seeds, we synthesize prompts along three orthogonal attributes: language (Chinese or English), dialogue turns (single- or multi-turn), and attack form. We use an LLM as a generator, equipped with a general-purpose guide that enables it to simultaneously generate prompts covering two languages, two dialogue turn scenarios, and three attack types. The resulting dataset consists of two subsets. DiagBase comprises ordinary harmful queries (no-jailbreak) as well as two types of adversarial queries: template-based jailbreak prompts and combined-template jailbreak prompts. To further increase the challenge of the benchmark, we construct DiagAttack, which takes the no-jailbreak, single-turn prompts from DiagBase as seeds and rewrites them into challenging instruction attacks by embedding the harmful intent into task shells drawn from an external instruction-following dataset.

After constructing the DiagSafe dataset, we generated a corresponding rubric for each prompt. We used an LLM as the writer to generate the rubric based on the prompt and the label specification associated with that prompt’s label. For details of the synthesis pipeline, the general-purpose guide, and specific examples, see Figure 3 and Appendix C.3. The average length of a rubric is 4,060 characters; each rubric contains an average of 4.5 S-items and exactly eight usefulness items.

The DiagBase dataset contains 2,401 samples, while DiagAttack contains 1,088 samples, for a total of 3,489 samples. Among these, the ratio of Chinese to English samples is approximately 1:1, the ratio of single-turn to multi-turn samples is 7:3.
We first validate the reliability of DiagSafe (Section 4.2) and then use it to conduct a comprehensive safety diagnosis of recent LLMs (Section 4.3).

We evaluate 11 recent LLMs spanning a wide range of model scales, from 8B to 1.6T parameters: Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, Kimi-K2.6, GPT-OSS-120B, MiniMax-M3, DeepSeek-V4-Pro Preview (hereafter DeepSeek-V4-Pro), GLM-5.2, Gemma-4-31B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash Preview (hereafter DeepSeek-V4-Flash), Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-3.3-70B. All models are served locally from their released checkpoints, with no moderation filters, guard models, or other deployment-level safeguards in the loop. We further supply no system prompt, so that the observed refusal or compliance behavior can be attributed to safety alignment internalized by the model itself. All models are evaluated in the non-thinking (fast-response) mode, under a unified decoding configuration: temperature (0.7), top- p (0.8), top- k (20), and repetition penalty (1.05).
DeepSeek-V3.2 is used for prompt synthesis, while Hy3 is used for rubric synthesis and serves as the rubric-guided judge.

The primary model-level metric is the unsafe rate (UR), defined as the proportion of responses that trigger at least one S-item for which no exemption applies. We report agreement with human judgments to assess validity and Cohen’s \kappa to assess inter-judge consistency. The rubric additionally provides a usefulness score on a 0–3 scale and item-level diagnostic traces.
To validate the reliability of DiagSafe, we conduct a human evaluation via stratified sampling, covering two dimensions: (i) the quality of the data and rubrics, and (ii) the evaluation reliability.

To verify quality, we conduct a human review of both the prompts and the rubrics. For prompt harmfulness, we draw a stratified sample of 4 prompts per third-level label (336 prompts); 324 are judged qualified, a 96.4% qualification rate. For rubric reasonableness, we draw a stratified sample of 3 rubrics per third-level label (252 rubrics) for expert review; 251 (99.6%) are judged reasonable and actionable, confirming the reliability of the rubric. Full annotation guidelines are provided in Appendix E.

We further examine whether our evaluation paradigm produces reliable judgments. We collect human annotations on 236 sampled responses as the gold standard, and compare four evaluation paradigms against it: an LLM judge equipped with our prompt-level rubric, an LLM judge with a generic safety prompt (refer to Appendix D.1), an LLM judge with a label-specification prompt (refer to Appendix D.2), and trained safety classifiers (Qwen3Guard, S-Eval, LlamaGuard4, and MD-Judge). Qwen3Guard is a three-class classification model (Safe, Unsafe, Controversial). Based on the official Qwen3Guard usage guidelines, we report its results under “strict” conditions (where “controversial” is classified as “unsafe”) and “lenient” conditions (where “controversial” is classified as “safe”). The agreement results are reported in Table 3.

Treating the human labels as correct, the rubric-based evaluation method performs best: when Hy3 acts as the judge, its accuracy reaches 95.34%, outperforming methods based on generic prompts (87.29%) and label specifications (86.86%). This conclusion holds true not only for DeepSeek-V4-Pro but also for Qwen3.5-9B. Compared with the classifiers, the rubric-based evaluation not only achieves higher accuracy but also exhibits lower variance. This indicates that explicitly grounding the judge in prompt-level criteria produces more accurate safety assessments than either generic prompting or specialized guard models.

We compared the agreement rates of the three judge models across the three evaluation paradigms using the results from all tested models; the results are shown in Table 4. The results indicate that rubric-based evaluation is the most robust, with agreement rates between models consistently above 93% (93.33% – 94.78%) and Cohen’s \kappa values all above 0.82 (0.828 – 0.864). In contrast, for the other two evaluation paradigms, both of these metrics fluctuate considerably.

In this section, we demonstrate DiagSafe as a diagnostic tool through a coarse-to-fine analysis. We begin with the unsafe-rate contrast between DiagBase and DiagAttack (Figure 4), then examine models on the safety–usefulness plane (Figure 5) and at the taxonomy-label level (Figure 6), and finally zoom in on per-sample rubric reports that explain individual responses (Table 2). This analysis uncovers model-specific vulnerabilities that aggregate metrics alone would obscure.

Figure 4 reports the URs of the 11 models separately on DiagBase and DiagAttack, revealing a striking contrast: wrapping the same harmful intents in benign instruction shells increases the UR of every model to between 1.9\times and 8.4\times its corresponding value on DiagBase (median: 5.3\times), with 8 of the 11 models exhibiting URs above 40%. This disparity suggests that instruction following and safety refusal may operate as competing objectives in current model training. Once a strong instruction engages a model’s instruction-following capabilities—by prescribing a role, an output format, and a tone—its safety behavior degrades, increasing the likelihood that the underlying harmful intent is fulfilled. Yet existing benchmarks largely overlook this failure mode, as they typically rely on direct harmful queries or conventional template-based jailbreaks rather than embedding harmful intents in benign instructions. DiagSafe’s instruction-attack design brings this distinctive vulnerability to light.

section: Two-Dimensional Assessment of Safety and Usefulness.
text: To assess joint safety–usefulness performance, Figure 5 positions the 11 models on a safety–usefulness plane. Each point represents a model’s average usefulness score and UR on a top-level safety category. A safe and useful model should achieve high usefulness while maintaining a low UR, placing it near the lower-right region of the plane. Qwen3.6-27B (highlighted) is concentrated near this desirable region, with usefulness scores above 2.0 and a UR mostly below 15%. In contrast, GPT-OSS-120B achieves consistently low URs but also uniformly low usefulness scores, most of which are below 1.5. This pattern suggests that its apparent safety may partly reflect a tendency toward blanket refusal. Llama-3.1-8B performs poorly on both dimensions: its UR averages 41% and reaches 49%, among the highest of all evaluated models, while its usefulness score averages 1.43. Thus, its limited helpfulness does not translate into greater safety. These qualitatively different behavioral patterns cannot be distinguished using any single aggregate safety metric.

The fine-grained label taxonomy enables us to assess model safety by category, providing a substantially more detailed picture than the aggregate unsafe rate alone. To illustrate this benefit, we select three models with similar overall unsafe rates, ranging from 18.6% to 20.9%, and compare their category-level profiles in Figure 6. Despite their similar aggregate performance, the models exhibit markedly different risk profiles. At the first taxonomy level, MiniMax-M3 has the highest unsafe rate for Intellectual Property (27.3%, compared with 22.3% for Kimi-K2.6). DeepSeek-V4-Pro, by contrast, has the highest unsafe rate for Suicide & Self-Harm (20.1%, compared with 13.0% for Kimi-K2.6) but the lowest rate for CBRNE (13.7%, compared with a maximum of 18.8% among the three models). The second-level categories reveal even greater variation and, more importantly, expose differences obscured by their parent categories. For example, the unsafe rates for Crime & Violence differ by only 0.3 percentage points across the three models, whereas those for its Animal Welfare subcategory differ by 8.3 percentage points. The largest disparity occurs in Radiological & Nuclear, for which the unsafe rate ranges from 11.6% to 26.0%.

These results demonstrate that a single aggregate score cannot adequately characterize model safety: models with nearly identical overall unsafe rates may fail in substantially different categories, while reporting only top-level categories may still obscure important failure modes through aggregation.

Our rubric-based evaluation provides a fine-grained, interpretable assessment of every sample. Table 2 illustrates this capability through a representative DiagAttack prompt for which the models exhibit sharply different behaviors. Among the safe responses, the rubric identifies three qualitatively distinct strategies: constructive refusal accompanied by redirection to a harmless alternative (Qwen3.6-27B), bounded compliance that addresses the question about sensations while foregrounding the associated harms (Kimi-K2.6), and bare refusal without substantive content (GPT-OSS-120B). Among the unsafe responses, the triggered S-items reveal a clear progression in scope and severity. DeepSeek-V4-Pro triggers only S2 and S4, indicating positive portrayal without adequate warnings; GLM-5.2 and Llama-3.1-8B additionally trigger S1 by providing concrete production steps; and MiniMax-M3 triggers all four items, extending its response to acquisition channels. These item-level traces transform a binary verdict into an actionable diagnosis, allowing developers to determine not only that a model failed, but also which safety boundaries it crossed and how far its response progressed.

We use this case to illustrate the role and necessity of safety diagnostics. Coarse “safe” or “unsafe” labels provide limited actionable feedback for further safety improvement, because a model’s responses may exhibit substantially different behaviors even when assigned the same label. Without a fine-grained understanding of these behaviors, it is difficult to identify specific weaknesses and determine appropriate optimization strategies. DiagSafe addresses this limitation by providing prompt-level diagnostic feedback, thereby enabling targeted and efficient safety alignment. For example, GPT-OSS-120B receives a low average usefulness score because it frequently refuses requests outright, suggesting that its low unsafe rate may come at the cost of usability. By contrast, in this case, DeepSeek-V4-Pro describes drug-induced euphoria in violation of the safety guidelines, although it did not provide concrete instructions for drug production. This response suggests that the model maintains some boundaries when handling drug-related queries but fails to exercise sufficient caution or recognize the indirect harm of glorifying drug use.
After the main experiments, we additionally evaluate several recently released models under the same protocol; the results are reported in Appendix B.

We additionally evaluate these models on DiagSafe along three data dimensions—attack form, language, and dialogue turns—to examine how models behave on different types of data. The main findings are as follows.

We compare the unsafe rates under normal queries and template-based jailbreak attacks to evaluate the effectiveness of conventional jailbreak templates. As shown in Figure 7, these templates are not uniformly effective: they yield only marginal increases in UR for models such as Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, while the UR of MiniMax-M3 is even lower than that under normal queries. Although larger increases are observed for some models, the results suggest that conventional jailbreak templates have limited and model-dependent effectiveness, highlighting the importance of DiagAttack.
For most models, the unsafe rate is slightly higher on Chinese data than on English data, suggesting that safety coverage in Chinese still lags behind English. Figure 8 shows this result.

Embedding the harmful intent in a multi-turn dialogue and unfolding it gradually increases the unsafe rate: the per-turn unsafe rate rises steadily as the conversation progresses, indicating that an established conversational context erodes the model’s refusal boundary. For models with a high rate of unsafe behavior, the risks become more apparent during multi-turn conversations. Figure 9 shows this result.

In this paper, we introduce DiagSafe, a diagnostic evaluation framework that overcomes the limitations of coarse binary labels through prompt-level rubrics. To support this framework, we constructed a comprehensive safety benchmark featuring an 84-label taxonomy, bilingual (English-Chinese) contexts, and diverse prompt formats including single- and multi-turn dialogues as well as challenging instruction attacks. Compared with existing evaluation paradigms, rubric-based judging achieves substantially higher agreement with human annotations and greater consistency across judge models. Our evaluation of 11 LLMs also uncovers safety failures that are obscured by aggregate unsafe rates. In particular, the unsafe rate of every evaluated model on DiagAttack is 1.9\times – 8.4\times that on DiagBase, while models with similar overall unsafe rates exhibit markedly different category-specific vulnerabilities. By providing fine-grained diagnostics at both the category and individual-response levels, DiagSafe offers actionable evidence for identifying model-specific weaknesses and guiding targeted safety alignment.
Although DiagSafe offers many advantages, we must also acknowledge that it currently has the following limitations:

The construction of DiagSafe relies on a per-label label specification that grounds the synthesis of prompts and rubrics. Since the label is generated by an LLM, its coverage of the underlying risk space is inherently bounded. Consequently, the synthesized prompts and prompt-level rubrics may fail to capture rare, emerging, or highly localized harmful scenarios. In future work, we plan to incorporate continuously updated regulatory sources and human-in-the-loop refinement to progressively broaden specification coverage.

We evaluate 11 locally served open-weight LLMs spanning 8B to over 1T parameters. This setting reduces confounding from provider-side moderation and enables cleaner attribution to model-level alignment, but limits coverage of commercial systems. Each model is evaluated under a single inference mode, leaving differences between thinking and non-thinking modes unexplored. Future work will cover both modes and API-accessible commercial systems, evaluated with their deployed safeguards, and maintain DiagAttack as a continuously updated safety leaderboard.

At present, DiagSafe supports safety evaluation of standalone LLMs in dialogue settings and does not yet cover LLM-based agents. As agents increasingly interact with external tools and open environments, their safety and security risks have attracted growing attention; recent work such as AgentDoG (Liu et al., 2026a) shows that risks arising from autonomous tool use and multi-step execution require dedicated, trajectory-level diagnostic frameworks beyond dialogue-level assessment. In future work, we plan to extend DiagSafe’s rubric-based diagnostic paradigm to agent scenarios, evaluating not only final responses but also the safety of intermediate actions and tool-use trajectories.

DiagSafe contains genuinely harmful prompts, including jailbreak-style attacks and queries from sensitive categories such as child exploitation, weapons, and controlled substances. The dataset is constructed and released exclusively for evaluating the safety of LLMs and for developing better safeguards; it must not be used to train models to generate harmful content, to probe production systems without authorization, or for any purpose inconsistent with its research intent. To mitigate misuse, we release the benchmark for research use only.

All prompts and responses are synthesized by LLMs under our constructed taxonomy and instruction shells; no real user queries, private conversations, or personal data are collected or used. Prompts do not reference real, identifiable individuals, organizations, or events; any resemblance is coincidental. The small fraction of categories that could in principle involve personal information (e.g., privacy inference) contains only synthetic, non-functional examples.

We will release the dataset, rubrics, and evaluation code to facilitate auditing and reproduction, and will maintain a channel for reporting problematic items. If any item is found to contain real personal information or otherwise inappropriate content, we will remove it in a subsequent revision.

BAIT: Can LLMs Find What Biases a Reader? A Benchmark for Cognitive Bias Triggers in News. Persuasive writing exploits cognitive biases, recruiting a reader's mental shortcuts to shape belief, often without the reader noticing. We call the linguistic features exploiting such mental shortcuts cognitive bias triggers. As large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people encounter news, summarizing it, ranking it, and answering questions over it, a natural question is whether they can recognize the features of a text that bias a human reader. We introduce BAIT (Bias Annotation In Text), a resource for detecting cognitive bias triggers in news. BAIT pairs a schema of nine triggers, each specified in an annotator codebook, with 50 English news articles annotated by trained annotators at the article and span levels and adjudicated into a gold standard. On this data we define two tasks, detecting which triggers a text contains and locating the spans that carry them. We then benchmark six frontier LLMs zero-shot and with three or ten in-context examples.

The models approach human agreement on which triggers an article contains, but rarely recover its full set of triggers, and they reach less than half of human agreement in locating the passages that carry them. Moreover, they over-predict triggers that come with easy surface cues, and most of the passages they mark for these triggers are not triggers, yet carry the trigger's surface cue far more often than random text. These findings suggest that the evaluated LLMs respond to surface cues rather than to the mechanisms that make a passage manipulative. We release the schema, the codebook, standoff annotations, and the evaluation pipeline.

Cognitive biases are systematic deviations from rational reasoning that arise from the heuristic processes underlying everyday cognition (Tversky and Kahneman 1974). These heuristics help readers process information efficiently. However, they can also be exploited through persuasive writing.

Such writing recruits these cognitive heuristics to shape belief and form attitudes (Petty and Cacioppo 1986). Building on work on media bias and persuasion techniques in computational social science (Spinde et al. 2021a; Piskorski et al. 2023), we refer to such persuasive writing features as cognitive bias triggers.

Cognitive bias triggers are hard to annotate because they cannot be identified from wording alone. Quoting an expert, recounting one person’s story, or restating a claim are common in news writing, and each can appear in a passage that is a trigger and in one that is not. Telling the two apart depends on the rest of the article, for example whether the expert’s claim is supported by evidence anywhere in the text. Work on the creation of annotated datasets for closely related phenomena, such as propaganda (Da San Martino et al. 2019) and persuasion techniques (Piskorski et al. 2023), reports the same difficulty. Both of these datasets relied on professional or expert annotators, detailed guidelines, and a consolidation step in which annotators resolved their disagreements. These datasets, however, do not record which cognitive bias a passage engages in the reader, or whether the conditions for that bias are met. To the best of our knowledge, no existing resource is annotated for this, so it is not yet possible to test whether a system can identify the passages that would bias a reader.

This question has become pressing as large language models (LLMs) increasingly stand between readers and the news, summarizing, retrieving, ranking, and answering questions about it. A model in this role decides what readers see and how it is framed. If it cannot recognize the passages that would bias a reader, it may pass them on unexamined or reproduce them in its own output.

A growing literature establishes that LLMs are themselves subject to human-like biases in their own judgments, including anchoring, framing, and order effects (Echterhoff et al. 2024; Itzhak et al. 2024; Koo et al. 2024). That work characterizes the model as a biased reasoner. It leaves open whether a model can recognize, in text supplied to it, the features that would bias a human reader, and localize them precisely enough for the judgment to be inspected.
We introduce BAIT (B ias A nnotation I n T ext), a resource and evaluation pipeline for detecting cognitive bias triggers in news text. Our contributions are as follows.

We define a schema of nine cognitive bias triggers, each specified in an annotator codebook. Two trained annotators used it to annotate 50 English news articles at the article and span levels, and the annotations were consolidated into a gold standard. We release the schema, codebook, standoff annotations, and evaluation pipeline. We define two tasks, detecting which triggers an article contains and locating the spans that carry them, and benchmark six frontier LLMs zero-shot and with three and ten in-context examples. We show that models can often tell that an article contains triggers but cannot reliably point to the passages that carry them: the best model reaches a trigger-level F_{1} of 0.22, against 0.50 between two annotators. In-context examples narrow this gap without closing it. We find that models respond to the surface cue of a bias rather than to its mechanism. They over-predict the triggers with the easiest cues, namely Negativity Bias (39 articles on average against 23 in the gold standard), Authority Bias (30 against 19), and Declinism (10.5 against 6). Most of the passages they mark for these triggers are not triggers, yet carry the trigger’s surface cue far more often than random text.
No part of this paper has been published before.

section: Media bias and lexical bias detection.
text: A substantial line of work annotates bias in news and locates it in word choice. BABE (Spinde et al. 2021a) provides expert annotations of 3,700 news sentences, marking whether each sentence is biased and which words carry the bias, with higher inter-annotator agreement than earlier crowdsourced datasets such as MBIC (Spinde et al. 2021b). MBIB (Wessel et al. 2023) assembles nine media-bias tasks over twenty-two datasets, spanning linguistic, political, framing, hate-speech, and other bias types, to test how detection methods generalize across them. MBIB also includes a cognitive-bias task, which it defines as readers’ selective choice of which sources to read and trust. In practice, however, the labels come from proxies: the political leaning of an article’s outlet using the BIGNEWS dataset (Liu et al. 2022) and the fact-checked truthfulness of a statement with the LIAR dataset (Wang 2017).

A second line annotates the rhetorical devices a text uses to persuade. Da San Martino et al. (2019) annotate news articles at fragment level with eighteen propaganda techniques and cast the problem as joint detection and localization. The SemEval-2023 Task 3 shared task (Piskorski et al. 2023) extends this to twenty-three persuasion techniques across nine languages, adding genre and framing labels. Both datasets label the rhetorical devices a writer uses to persuade. Neither says which cognitive bias a passage might trigger in a reader, and a cue that relies on no named technique falls outside their label sets.

A growing body of work asks whether language models display human-like biases in their own outputs: anchoring and framing effects in decision tasks (Echterhoff et al. 2024), biases that emerge from instruction tuning (Itzhak et al. 2024), and order and egocentric effects when models act as evaluators (Koo et al. 2024). This work treats the model as a reasoner whose judgments can be distorted, and measures that distortion. A separate strand annotates reasoning defects in text directly, closest among them logical fallacy detection (Jin et al. 2022), which labels invalid argument structure as a property of the argument itself.
Across these lines of work, the question of how a text might bias its reader remains open. No resource marks the passages likely to trigger a cognitive bias, or which bias each one triggers.

BAIT targets cognitive biases that news text can trigger in a reader: well-documented tendencies in human judgment that a passage can set off through the way it presents information. We selected candidate biases from the psychological literature on judgment, persuasion, and social cognition, and filtered them against two criteria: Text-surface identifiability: a trigger must produce a linguistic signal that can be marked as a character span. This rules out biases realized only in the reader’s prior beliefs or mental state rather than in the text. Confirmation bias, for instance, depends on what a particular reader already believes, so no span of text carries it on its own. Annotation reliability: candidate biases whose surface signals annotators could not reliably distinguish from those of another category during calibration were removed (Section 4.2). The resulting schema comprises the nine trigger categories in Table 1.

The nine categories draw on four broad mechanisms. Illusory Truth, Bandwagon Effect, and Authority Bias concern credibility: each lends a claim weight through something other than evidence, whether repetition, popularity, or the standing of its source. Negativity Bias and the Identifiable Victim Effect concern affect, steering evaluation through emotional salience. Stereotyping concerns social categorization. Declinism, Illusory Correlation, and Hindsight Bias concern temporal and causal reasoning: how the past is evaluated, how events are linked, and how predictable outcomes are made to seem. Research on misinformation documents that persuasive and misleading writing exploits mechanisms of these kinds (Ecker et al. 2022), which makes these triggers relevant to assessing whether language models can recognize when text is working on its reader.

The nine categories sit at a single level and are non-exclusive: a single passage may carry several triggers at once, and an article typically contains instances of several categories. Each category is specified in an annotator codebook giving its definition, the psychological mechanism it recruits, the textual conditions that count as a trigger, positive and negative examples, and, where applicable, its most likely confusion pair. Four such pairs were made explicit during calibration: Illusory Truth and Negativity Bias (repetition versus asymmetric weighting), Bandwagon Effect and Authority Bias (the crowd versus a specific source), Declinism and Hindsight Bias (an evaluative versus an epistemic claim about the past), and Illusory Correlation and Hindsight Bias (a forward causal claim versus backward predictability). The full codebook is provided in Appendix C. Two rules govern span annotation across all categories: Under the minimal-span rule, a span is the shortest contiguous fragment that, if removed, would eliminate the trigger, so annotators mark that fragment rather than the surrounding sentence or paragraph. A single span may also carry more than one trigger, in which case it is annotated once per applicable category.

We build BAIT on the English subset of the SemEval-2023 Task 3 corpus (Piskorski et al. 2023), 523 news articles on topics including COVID-19, climate change, migration, and the war in Ukraine. These articles already carry persuasion-technique and framing labels. We annotate a random sample of 50 articles, with a mean length of roughly 750 word tokens.

Two annotators labeled the corpus. The first, a PhD candidate in our research group, holds an MSc in Psychology. The second, a Master’s student in Linguistics at our university, was recruited through the university’s student job platform and paid the standard university hourly student rate. Before annotating the released sample, they completed two calibration rounds, during which the schema was revised and the codebook finalized. A third annotator, the first author of this paper, then reviewed every label against the finalized codebook and adjudicated it into the consensus set.

During calibration, several cognitive biases with unreliable surface signals were removed from an earlier, larger candidate set, explicit confusion pairs were added to separate categories that annotators tended to conflate, and some definitions were sharpened. We also fixed the reader’s perspective as the unit of judgment: a trigger is annotated on the basis of the textual cue a passage supplies, not on any inference about the author’s intention.

Both annotators labeled each article independently in two passes. The first pass records, per category, whether the trigger occurs anywhere in the article. The second marks the minimal span or spans carrying each present trigger, assigns its category, and records a confidence rating on a three-point scale (1 low, 2 moderate, 3 high).

Confidence governed inclusion in the gold standard. High-confidence triggers were retained. Moderate- and low-confidence triggers were retained when both annotators marked them; where the annotators disagreed, the third annotator alone decided whether to include them. Annotators were instructed to prefer a lower confidence rating over omitting a suspected trigger, so that borderline cases survived to adjudication rather than being dropped silently at the annotation stage. Spans of a single discontinuous trigger share a group identifier. Annotators did not see the SemEval persuasion or framing labels, keeping BAIT’s labels independent of them.

We measure agreement between the two annotators before adjudication, so the figures reflect the difficulty of the task rather than agreement with the consensus labels. Agreement is computed separately for each category, at the two levels at which annotation took place.

In the first annotation pass, each annotator judges, for each article and category, whether the trigger occurs anywhere in the article. For each category we compute Cohen’s \kappa (Cohen 1960) over these binary judgments for the 50 articles, \kappa=\frac{p_{o}-p_{e}}{1-p_{e}},\qquad p_{e}=p_{A}\,p_{B}+(1-p_{A})(1-p_{B}), where p_{o} is the proportion of articles on which the two annotators agree, and p_{A} and p_{B} are the proportions of articles in which each annotator marks the category present. The term p_{e} is the agreement the two annotators would reach if each marked articles at random at their own rate, so \kappa measures agreement beyond what these rates alone would produce.

We split each article into whitespace-delimited tokens and, for each annotator and category, mark the tokens that overlap at least one of that annotator’s spans. With A and B the sets of tokens marked by the two annotators, pooled over all 50 articles, we compute F_{1}=\frac{2\,|A\cap B|}{|A|+|B|}. This measure is symmetric, so neither annotator needs to be treated as the reference. We use token F_{1} rather than \kappa because free-form span selection has no fixed set of negative items over which chance agreement could be defined (Hripcsak and Rothschild 2005). This measure does not consider how spans are grouped into triggers. Averages are unweighted means over the nine categories.

Table 2 reports per-category agreement. Averaged over the nine categories, agreement is \kappa=0.53 at the document level and F_{1}=0.50 at the span level. Document-level \kappa ranges from 0.23 (Bandwagon Effect) to 0.63 (Hindsight Bias), and span-level F_{1} from 0.33 (Hindsight Bias) to 0.66 (Declinism). The lowest \kappa belongs to the rarest category. The annotators marked Bandwagon Effect in only three and four of the 50 articles respectively, so chance agreement is high (p_{e}=0.87) and their raw agreement on 45 of 50 articles yields a \kappa of only 0.23. This sensitivity of \kappa to rare categories is well documented (Feinstein and Cicchetti 1990). Negativity Bias shows a different pattern: one annotator marked it in 24 articles and the other in 11, so its disagreements reflect a difference in threshold rather than scattered judgments.

We acknowledge that this agreement is moderate, and argue that it is the expected outcome rather than a sign of weak annotation. Each category is defined by the cognitive mechanism a passage sets off in a reader, not by a fixed surface form that annotators could match word for word. Two trained annotators reading the same passage can therefore disagree in good faith over whether it supplies the cue. We take the agreement they reach as the practical ceiling for the task, the level careful human annotators attain, and evaluate models against that level.

The consensus set holds 592 trigger spans, grouped into 398 triggers, across the 50 articles. Forty-six articles carry at least one trigger, and four carry none and are labeled none, giving negative examples for detection. Table 3 reports per-category coverage.

Because BAIT is built on the SemEval-2023 Task 3 corpus, its labels can be compared with the persuasion techniques annotated for that task (Piskorski et al. 2023). These techniques are available to us only at the article level, so we compare at that level, on the 32 articles that carry at least one technique.

Six BAIT categories have a natural counterpart among the techniques (Figure 1). Agreement between each category and its counterpart is low, with Cohen’s \kappa between 0.05 and 0.24, except for Negativity Bias and Appeal to Fear/Prejudice (\kappa=0.44). The differences follow from BAIT’s definitions. Every article labeled with Repetition also carries Illusory Truth, but Illusory Truth occurs in 16 further articles, because BAIT also counts reworded restatements of a claim. Of the 12 of these articles with Authority Bias, only 3 carry Appeal to Authority, because BAIT requires a credential that replaces evidence rather than any appeal to a source. Three BAIT categories have no counterpart at all and account for 18% of BAIT’s article-level labels on these articles. BAIT therefore does not duplicate the existing label set: describing what a passage does to a reader captures distinctions that a taxonomy of persuasion techniques does not.

We formulate bias-trigger annotation as two tasks of increasing difficulty: detecting which biases an article contains, and localizing and grouping the spans that trigger them. Both operate on a full news article and target the nine categories (B01–B09), and we evaluate each under zero-shot and few-shot prompting.

Every metric below compares a model’s output with the gold standard unit by unit, where the unit depends on the metric: a (document, category) decision, a character, a span, or a trigger. For each category b, a true positive (\mathrm{TP}_{b}) is a predicted unit that matches a gold unit, a false positive (\mathrm{FP}_{b}) is a predicted unit that matches none, and a false negative (\mathrm{FN}_{b}) is a gold unit that no prediction matches. We sum these counts over all 50 articles and all nine categories and compute a single micro-averaged F_{1} for the corpus, F_{1}=\frac{2\sum_{b}\mathrm{TP}_{b}}{2\sum_{b}\mathrm{TP}_{b}+\sum_{b}\mathrm{FP}_{b}+\sum_{b}\mathrm{FN}_{b}}.

Given an article, the model identifies which bias categories are present. This is multi-label classification over the nine categories, and an article may exhibit any subset of biases, including none (4 of the 50 articles contain no trigger). The task measures whether a model recognizes that an article employs a given bias, independently of where.

The unit is a (document, category) decision. A category the model predicts for an article is a true positive if the gold standard also lists it for that article and a false positive otherwise, and a gold category the model misses is a false negative. We report F_{1} (Equation 3) together with subset accuracy, the fraction of the N articles whose predicted category set \hat{Y}_{d} exactly matches the gold set Y_{d}, \mathrm{SubsetAcc}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{d=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\bigl[\hat{Y}_{d}=Y_{d}\bigr]. The gold category set of an article is exactly the set of categories with at least one gold trigger, so a model is not penalized for answering the two tasks consistently.

Given an article, the model extracts the spans that trigger each bias and groups them into trigger instances. This reflects BAIT’s central annotation decision that a single bias instance may be realized across several non-contiguous spans. Illusory-truth effects (B01), for example, arise from a claim repeated through an article, so the repeated mentions form one trigger of several spans rather than several independent triggers. Task 2 therefore requires both locating biased text and correctly partitioning spans into triggers. In our corpus, 143 of 398 gold triggers (36%) consist of more than one span.

As a human reference for both tasks, we score one annotator’s labels against the other’s, before adjudication, with exactly the metrics used for the models. Because every metric here is symmetric, the choice of reference annotator does not matter. We do not score the annotators against the gold standard, which was built from their own labels.

A span is a contiguous stretch of characters in the article, identified by its first and last character. Because models return spans as copied strings, we first locate each string in the article, trying four matchers in turn: an exact match, a case-insensitive match, a match that tolerates differences in whitespace, and a fuzzy match that accepts a window of the article with a character similarity of at least 0.80 to the string. When a string occurs several times, as repeated claims often do, we prefer an occurrence not yet used by another span of the same category in the same output, then one that overlaps a gold span of that category, then the leftmost. The gold standard thus only chooses between positions where the article contains exactly the returned string, and cannot turn a wrong string into a correct one. At least 95% of every model’s spans match exactly, and at most 0.4% cannot be located at all (Appendix G). A string that cannot be located is unlocated and counts against the model at every level below. We score localization at three levels of granularity, from most to least forgiving, each reported as F_{1} (Equation 3).

The unit is a character of the article. For each category, a character is a true positive if it lies inside both a predicted and a gold span, a false positive if it lies only inside a predicted span, and a false negative if it lies only inside a gold span. The characters of an unlocated span all count as false positives. This rewards partial overlap, in the spirit of the character-overlap scoring used for propaganda span identification (Da San Martino et al. 2020).

The unit is a span. We measure the overlap of a predicted span a and a gold span g by their intersection over union, \mathrm{IoU}(a,g)=\frac{|a\cap g|}{|a\cup g|}, where |\cdot| counts characters. This is the Jaccard index (Jaccard 1912), known as IoU in object-detection evaluation (Everingham et al. 2010). It is 1 when the two spans coincide and 0 when they do not overlap. Predicted and gold spans of the same category are paired one-to-one, taking the pairs with the highest IoU first, and a pair is a true positive when its IoU is at least \tau_{s}=0.5 (at this threshold the greedy pairing is optimal; Appendix B). Unpaired predicted spans, including unlocated ones, are false positives, and unpaired gold spans are false negatives. This penalizes boundary errors that the character level partly forgives.

The unit is a trigger, the set of spans that the model or the annotator assigns to one bias instance. For a predicted trigger \hat{T} and a gold trigger T, let C(\hat{T}) and C(T) be the sets of characters covered by their spans. We score their agreement by the character overlap F(\hat{T},T)=\frac{2\,\bigl|C(\hat{T})\cap C(T)\bigr|}{\bigl|C(\hat{T})\bigr|+\bigl|C(T)\bigr|}, where the length of any unlocated span in \hat{T} is added to |C(\hat{T})|. Predicted and gold triggers of the same category are paired one-to-one in decreasing order of F, and a pair is a true positive when F(\hat{T},T)\geq\tau_{t}=0.5. Unpaired predicted and gold triggers are false positives and false negatives respectively. This is the only metric that evaluates grouping. A model that locates every span correctly but splits one multi-span gold trigger into several single-span triggers can score well at the character and span levels, but is penalized here.

We evaluate six frontier models, Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.6, Grok 4.5, DeepSeek-V4, Kimi K3, and Mistral Medium 3.5, at three in-context settings. Every model receives the same system prompt in every setting. It describes the two tasks, gives a one-line definition of each bias, states the rule for multi-span triggers, and fixes the output format.

In the zero-shot setting (k=0) the model receives only the instructions. In the few-shot settings it additionally receives k=3 or k=10 fully annotated example articles, drawn from the rest of the corpus under a leave-one-out protocol so that no article appears among its own examples. Each few-shot setting is run with three random draws of the examples (seeds 17, 23, and 29), and we report the mean over the three draws. The system prompt, bias definitions, and output format are identical across settings, so the settings differ only in the in-context examples.

Because outputs varied across repeated queries, even with temperature set to 0, zero-shot scores are the mean over six runs, one accompanying each few-shot run. The article is the sampling unit, so we compare settings and models with paired t -tests over the 50 articles on per-article scores, Holm-corrected (Holm 1979) for the number of comparisons in each figure. Outputs that cannot be parsed are scored as empty predictions rather than excluded, so every model and setting is evaluated on the same 50 articles. Decoding settings and scoring details are in Appendices A and B.

Table 4 reports corpus-level scores for all six models at k\in\{0,3,10\}. Figures 2 and 3 show how much the examples add over zero-shot on each task, and Figure 4 breaks both tasks down by bias. We call a difference significant only if it survives Holm correction.

Zero-shot, detection micro-F1 ranges from 0.45 (DeepSeek-V4) to 0.62 (Grok 4.5). With ten examples the models converge on 0.64–0.69, led by Kimi K3 (0.685), Grok 4.5 (0.680) and Claude Opus 4.8 (0.679). The two annotators reach 0.745 against each other (Table 4), so the best models come within about six points of human agreement.

Figure 2 shows that the benefit of examples depends strongly on the model. The two weakest zero-shot models gain the most: with ten examples, DeepSeek-V4 improves by 22.5 points per article and Claude Opus 4.8 by 17.1. Kimi K3 (+11.6) and Grok 4.5 (+8.0) also improve significantly, whereas the gains of GPT-5.6 (+7.7) and Mistral Medium 3.5 (+5.4) do not survive correction. Three examples are not enough for most models. At k=3, only Claude Opus 4.8 (+9.5) and DeepSeek-V4 (+8.3) improve significantly.

Examples do not, however, help models reproduce an article’s complete bias profile. Subset accuracy is at most 0.13 for every model and setting, against 0.36 between the two annotators, and none of its gains is significant.

Key Finding 1. LLMs approach human agreement in recognizing which biases an article contains, but rarely recover its full set of biases, and in-context examples mainly lift the weakest models toward the others rather than closing this gap. A model that screens news for manipulative framing would flag many manipulative articles while often misreporting which mechanisms they rely on.

Table 4 shows that localization is much harder than detection. Zero-shot, trigger-F1 ranges from 0.06 (DeepSeek-V4) to 0.15 (Grok 4.5 and GPT-5.6), and with ten examples from 0.17 to 0.22, led by Grok 4.5 (0.223). At k=10, every model’s detection micro-F1 is 3.0 to 3.8 times its trigger-F1. The gap to human agreement is far larger than for detection. The two annotators reach a trigger-F1 of 0.50 against each other, more than twice the best model’s 0.22, and the same holds at the character level (0.57 against at most 0.28).

Examples help localization more consistently than detection (Figure 3). With ten examples, five of the six models improve significantly at every granularity. On trigger-F1, the gains are 14.2 points for DeepSeek-V4, 8.9 for Claude Opus 4.8, 7.7 for Kimi K3, 6.9 for GPT-5.6 and 6.8 for Grok 4.5. Mistral Medium 3.5 is the exception: its gains (2.3–3.8 points) are not significant at any granularity. Three examples are not enough. At k=3, no model improves significantly on trigger-F1, and only Grok 4.5 improves significantly at the character and span levels. These gains are averages over articles and hide variation between them: with ten examples, trigger-F1 improves on 28–36 articles per model but gets worse on 4–13.

Key Finding 2. LLMs largely fail to show where a bias trigger is. The best model reaches less than half the trigger-level agreement of two human annotators (0.22 against 0.50), and examples improve this only modestly.

The aggregate scores hide large differences between biases (Figure 4). Averaged over models, detection F_{1} ranges from 0.89 on Illusory Truth (B01) to 0.34 on Bandwagon Effect (B03). The high score on Illusory Truth largely reflects its prevalence: it occurs in 45 of the 50 articles, so a model that predicts it almost everywhere is rarely wrong. Localization is uniformly poor. Illusory Truth is localized best (mean trigger-F1 0.30), followed by Stereotyping (B05, 0.18) and Illusory Correlation (B08, 0.18). Declinism (B06, 0.06), the Identifiable Victim Effect (B07, 0.09) and Authority Bias (B04, 0.10) are localized worst. Relative to detection, the loss is also largest for these three: detection F_{1} is 4.6 to 9.2 times their trigger-F1, against 2.1 to 4.0 times for the other six biases. Authority Bias, for instance, falls from 0.55 to 0.10 and Declinism from 0.55 to 0.06. The annotators, by contrast, agree on Authority Bias spans at a token-level F_{1} of 0.46 and on Declinism spans at 0.66 (Table 2), so these passages are not inherently hard to delimit.

Because Illusory Truth accounts for 57% of gold spans and almost all multi-span triggers, we check that it does not drive the main results. Without it, detection micro-F1 at k=10 ranges from 0.55 to 0.60 against 0.64 between the annotators, and macro-F1 from 0.50 to 0.56 against 0.61. Localization falls further: trigger-F1 ranges from 0.12 to 0.16, against 0.44 between the annotators. Illusory Truth therefore flatters the models. On the remaining eight biases, they stay close to human agreement on detection but reach only about a third of it on localization.

The models’ errors point to an explanation. With ten examples, models predict Negativity Bias (B02) in 39 articles on average against 23 in the gold standard, Authority Bias in 30 against 19, and Declinism in 10.5 against 6. All three have an easy surface cue (negative vocabulary, a cited expert, a reference to the past) that the codebook explicitly does not accept as sufficient. It requires asymmetric negative weighting, a credential that replaces evidence, and an idealized past whose problems are omitted. Hindsight Bias (B09) shows the opposite failure. It is under-applied, predicted in 7.5 articles against 11, and Claude Opus 4.8 almost never predicts it (in 1.7 articles on average), which explains its detection F_{1} of 0.13 on this bias against 0.42 to 0.62 for the other models.

No model is best across the board. Claude Opus 4.8 has the best detection F_{1} on four biases, but the worst on Hindsight Bias and zero trigger-F1 on Declinism. Grok 4.5 localizes three biases best, and Mistral Medium 3.5 is weakest at localizing Bandwagon Effect and Illusory Correlation. With as few as six gold articles for some biases, most of these per-bias differences are within noise. Across whole tasks, comparing every pair of models with paired t -tests over articles (Holm-corrected over the 15 pairs), only two pairs differ significantly at k=10: Grok 4.5 and Kimi K3 each localize better than Mistral Medium 3.5, by 5.6 and 6.5 points of trigger-F1.

Key Finding 3. Model performance depends on the bias more than on the model. Detection ranges from 0.89 on Illusory Truth to 0.34 on Bandwagon Effect, and localization is weakest for Declinism, the Identifiable Victim Effect and Authority Bias. Models over-predict the three biases with the most recognizable cues (Negativity Bias, Authority Bias and Declinism) and under-predict Hindsight Bias, while differences between models on any single bias are mostly within noise.

Section 7.3 showed that models over-predict the three biases with the easiest surface cues. We test whether this reflects attention to the cue rather than to the mechanism by examining where the predicted spans land (Figure 5 a). Of all spans predicted at k=10 for Negativity Bias, Authority Bias and Declinism, only 9.2% match a gold span of the same bias, against 26.9% for the other six biases, and 60.8% fall on text that no annotator marked for any bias. For Authority Bias, 53% of predicted spans lie in articles that contain no Authority Bias trigger at all. The pattern holds for every model, with 8 to 11% of spans matched for these three biases, against 21 to 32% for the others.

These misplaced spans do carry the cue. We check each one for a simple lexical marker: a negative word from the VADER lexicon (Hutto and Gilbert 2014) for Negativity Bias; an authority term (e.g. “expert”, “study”, “according to”, a title or an institution) for Authority Bias; and a reference to the past (e.g. a year, “used to”, “no longer”) for Declinism. As a baseline, we draw five random stretches of article text of the same length for each prediction. The misplaced spans contain the cue far more often than chance (Figure 5 b): 59% of unannotated Negativity Bias predictions contain a negative word, 59% of Authority Bias predictions an authority term, and 35% of Declinism predictions a reference to the past, against 20%, 26% and 11% for random text.

The four articles without any gold trigger illustrate the pattern. In one of them, all six models mark a sentence attributing a factual claim to a public health agency as Authority Bias, and a plain report of a death toll as Negativity Bias. Neither passage meets the codebook’s conditions: the agency is cited as the source of a fact, not as a substitute for evidence, and the death toll is stated without elaboration or asymmetric weighting. Each passage carries the surface cue of its bias, a named institution or a negative fact, but not the mechanism.

Key Finding 4. Models respond to the surface cue of a bias rather than to its mechanism. Most of the spans they mark for Negativity Bias, Authority Bias and Declinism fall on text that no annotator marked, yet these spans contain the bias’s surface cue two to three times as often as random text. A bias detector built on current LLMs would thus flag these biases most readily where it is least able to show them.

BAIT covers 50 English news articles from a single source corpus, on a limited set of topics (COVID-19, climate change, migration, and the war in Ukraine). Because the sample is random, category frequencies follow the source corpus rather than a balanced design. Illusory Truth occurs in 45 articles, whereas the sparsest categories rest on six or seven, so per-bias scores for these categories are imprecise, and most per-bias differences between models fall within noise. Pooled scores are also dominated by the frequent categories, which is why we report per-bias results separately. Whether the findings hold for other languages, genres, and outlets remains to be tested.

Each category is defined by the effect a passage is likely to have on a reader, so annotation requires judgment, and agreement between the two annotators is moderate (\kappa=0.53, token F_{1}=0.50). The two annotators bring training in psychology and in linguistics, and a single adjudicator, who is also an author of this paper, resolved their labels into the gold standard. A larger and more varied pool of annotators, with independent adjudication, would give a more robust consensus and a better estimate of human agreement on each category. Triggers are also annotated for a generic reader. Whether a passage actually biases a particular person depends on what that person already knows and believes, and BAIT marks passages likely to trigger a bias, not measured effects on readers.

We evaluate six models through prompting alone, with one-line definitions of each bias rather than the full codebook used by the annotators, and with up to ten in-context examples. The models therefore received less guidance than the annotators did, and our results describe what current models do under this setup, not an upper bound on what they can learn. Model behavior is also not fully reproducible: outputs varied across repeated queries even with temperature set to 0, which we address by averaging over runs, and API-served models may change over time.

The articles belong to the SemEval-2023 Task 3 corpus, whose terms do not permit redistribution. We therefore release BAIT as standoff annotations, with article identifiers and character offsets, so that users with access to the source corpus can reconstruct the full dataset.

Three directions follow directly from these limitations. First, extending the annotation to more articles, languages and outlets would yield enough instances of the sparse categories to compare models on each bias reliably. Second, our results raise the question of whether the gap between detection and localization reflects missing knowledge or missing guidance. Giving models the full codebook, fine-tuning them on the gold spans, or asking them to justify each trigger against the codebook’s conditions would test whether they can learn to look past the surface cue to the mechanism. Third, conditioning trigger detection on an explicit model of the reader, and testing annotated triggers against reader responses in user studies, would connect BAIT’s labels to the effects they are meant to anticipate.

We introduced BAIT, a resource for detecting cognitive bias triggers in news: the features of a text that recruit a reader’s mental shortcuts to shape belief. BAIT pairs a schema of nine triggers, each specified in an annotator codebook, with article- and span-level annotations of 50 English news articles adjudicated into a gold standard. Its labels describe what a passage does to a reader, and they overlap only weakly with the persuasion techniques already annotated on the same articles. On this data we define two tasks, detecting which triggers an article contains and locating the spans that carry them.

Benchmarking six frontier LLMs on these tasks shows that models can tell that an article is manipulative, but not how or where. With ten in-context examples, detection micro-F1 reaches 0.64–0.69, close to the 0.75 that the two annotators reach with each other, yet no model recovers an article’s full set of biases in more than 13% of articles, against 36% for the annotators. Localization is much weaker: the best trigger-F1 is 0.22, less than half the trigger-F1 of 0.50 that the annotators reach with each other. In-context examples help most for the weakest models but do not close these gaps.

The errors point to a common cause. Models over-apply the biases with the easiest surface cues: negative vocabulary, a cited expert, a reference to the past. Most of the spans they mark for these biases fall on text that no annotator marked, yet these spans contain the cue two to three times as often as random text of the same length. Current LLMs thus respond to what a trigger looks like rather than to the conditions that make a passage one.

This matters for any system that relies on an LLM to screen, summarize, or rank news on a reader’s behalf. Such a system would flag many manipulative articles, but it would often misreport which mechanisms they rely on and could not point to the passages responsible, so its judgments could not be checked by the people they are meant to protect. We release the BAIT schema, codebook, standoff annotations, and evaluation pipeline to support work on models that can show, and not only state, why a text may bias its reader.
