We obtain 95% confidence intervals from 2,000 document-bootstrap samples, using the same resampled documents for each model and condition. Appendix C gives passage construction and paired comparisons.

section: Language modeling and cross-lingual context use
text: PPT alone obtains greater corresponding-source benefit than SPT but higher target-only loss (Figure 3). It uses shared information across languages more effectively, while predicting single-language text less accurately. At every matched budget, PPT→SPT has lower target-only loss than SPT and PPT, while retaining greater corresponding-source benefit than SPT in both languages. SPT→PPT also has lower target-only loss and greater corresponding-source benefit than SPT.

section: Language modeling and cross-lingual context use
text: To examine the second stage itself, we also compare each model with its starting checkpoint. During the 20B of SPT following PPT, target-only loss falls by 0.038–0.061 BpB across the three stages and two languages. The corresponding-source benefit decreases, while the final model retains a greater benefit than SPT at the same budget. In the reverse order, target-only loss falls by 0.020–0.029 BpB and corresponding-source benefit increases in all six comparisons. Both orders improve monolingual prediction, while changing the benefit of bilingual context in different directions. Appendix C.2 reports corresponding-source changes and matched-budget comparisons.

section: Language modeling and cross-lingual context use
text: We apply the same analysis to the aligned English–Swahili health documents in AfriDocMT (Alabi et al., 2025). We score every noninitial sentence under the three conditions across the complete collection of 61 documents. Both staged models achieve lower target-only loss and greater corresponding-source benefit than SPT in Swahili and English at 120B (Table 7). During SPT after PPT, target-only loss falls and corresponding-source benefit decreases from the PPT starting point, as in English–French. The final model thus combines improved monolingual language modeling with greater cross-lingual context benefit than SPT in the low-resource setting.

We measure how adding source sentences and blocking attention to them affect fixed-target prediction (Fernandes et al., 2021). Both analyses compare the four 120B models on all 133 WMT14 document pairs whose first eight aligned sentences contain at most 900 tokens per language.

For source extension, we fix target sentences 1–8, using the first as a prefix and scoring sentences 2–8. Extending the source from sentences 1–3 to 1–8 supplies counterparts for target sentences 4–8; those for sentences 2–3 were already available. We subtract the loss reduction from extending a length-matched unrelated source. For each target region, we average this adjusted reduction equally over documents, in nats per target token.

Figure 4 (a) shows that the loss reduction is concentrated on sentences 4–8 in both target languages. For these sentences, PPT and the staged models gain 1.00–1.32 nats per token, compared with 0.72–0.87 for SPT. For sentences 2–3, adjusted changes range from - 0.024 to 0.030 nats per token across all four models and both target languages.

To test the contribution of source access, we adapt the attention-knockout intervention of Geva et al. (2023). We retain the complete input and block attention from positions predicting target sentences 4–8 to source sentences 4–8. The loss increase is measured against the unmodified model on the same input, then adjusted by subtracting the increase under an unrelated source. The target-language prefix, preceding target tokens and source sentences 1–3 remain accessible. To test this dependence at different depths, we intervene separately in the early, middle and late thirds of the model, each comprising eight layers (1–8, 9–16 and 17–24). Figure 4 (b) shows the middle group, where blocking these connections has a larger effect on PPT and the staged models than on SPT. For French targets, the adjusted loss increase is 0.62–0.73 nats per token for PPT and the staged models, compared with 0.40 for SPT. For English targets, the corresponding values are 0.87–0.95 and 0.54. Appendix C.3 provides the input diagrams and the separate interventions on earlier and later layer groups. PPT→SPT therefore retains greater sensitivity to corresponding content than SPT on both measures; SPT→PPT also exceeds SPT.

The same interventions on all 61 AfriDocMT documents show this pattern in English–Swahili. On Swahili target sentences 4–8, the adjusted extension benefit is 0.62–0.69 nats per token for PPT and staged models, compared with 0.37 for SPT. Both languages show greater extension benefits and larger effects of blocking layers 9–16 for these models (Table 8).

We next examine how answers change on single-language commonsense tasks. We compare answers on English and French HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019) and paired English–Swahili XStoryCloze stories (Lin et al., 2022b). Both tasks ask for plausible continuations of single-language inputs. Comparing the same questions before and after training separates corrected errors from retained correct answers. Corrected and lost answers are reported as shares of all questions; their difference is the change in accuracy.

From 100B to 120B, both training orders retain more correct answers than continued use of the initial method on both tasks. On HellaSwag, they also correct more errors in English and French (Figure 7). On XStoryCloze, lost answers decrease by 0.79 percentage points for PPT→SPT and 1.16 for SPT→PPT, averaging English and Swahili. These reductions outweigh slightly fewer corrections, yielding higher accuracy in each language (Table 9).

The continuation tasks assess plausible outcomes in a given situation. We also examine whether models associate properties with appropriate concepts, using English COMPS-BASE minimal pairs (Misra et al., 2023) for the English–French models. Each pair tests whether a property phrase receives higher probability after an appropriate concept than after a distractor. At 120B, PPT→SPT reaches 75.15% accuracy, up from PPT’s 67.96% and close to SPT’s 75.52%. SPT→PPT reaches 77.27%. Both orders improve over continued use of their initial method in all five property categories (Table 10).

SPT and PPT have similar average language understanding throughout pretraining, while their English–French translation ranking varies. Following PPT with SPT improves both understanding and translation at matched budgets in both language settings. The prediction analyses clarify this contrast. In English–French, PPT alone benefits more from corresponding context than SPT but has higher monolingual prediction loss. Following PPT with SPT reduces this loss below both baselines at every tested English–French stage. Corresponding-context benefit decreases from the PPT starting point but remains above SPT. The English–Swahili PPT→SPT model similarly has lower monolingual loss and greater context benefit than SPT at 120B. Together, these results support developing cross-lingual context use through PPT and then adapting to independently sampled documents through SPT.

PPT→SPT retains greater use of corresponding content than SPT. Added source sentences help predict their target-language counterparts, and blocking attention to them raises loss. These observations extend analyses of related-document context (Shi et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024) to another language’s expression of the same content. On single-language tasks, greater retention of correct answers contributes to commonsense-reasoning gains in both language pairs, and subsequent SPT improves PPT’s concept–property judgments. These task-level gains accompany improved monolingual prediction.

Introducing PPT after SPT also improves monolingual prediction while increasing corresponding-context benefit. This order improves English–French translation and gives the highest language-understanding average at 80B and 180B. In English–Swahili, both orders reach the same understanding average. PPT→SPT gives the highest translation average across all tested stages and both language pairs. Its gains in both general language understanding and translation favor this order for multilingual pretraining across high- and low-resource settings.

Multilingual pretraining data. FineTranslations translates non-English FineWeb2 documents into English, producing over one trillion translated tokens (Penedo et al., 2025; Penedo et al., 2026). Translation into other languages also supports pretraining (Doshi et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). TransWebLLM uses independently sampled translations of English web documents and achieves competitive multilingual performance, including in Swahili (Wang et al., 2025).

Pretraining with parallel corpora. Translation language modelling predicts masked tokens in concatenated parallel sentences (Lample and Conneau, 2019), while document-level encoder–decoder objectives support document translation and cross-lingual generation (Lee et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2023). Recent decoder-only studies examine sentence ordering and parallel-data composition (Kondo et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2025). Qorib et al. (2025) obtain their strongest translation results with a short parallel-sentence stage after predominantly English pretraining. We compare both training orders at document scale, including long parallel pretraining followed by a short independent-sampling stage on the same bilingual corpus.

Sequence composition and multilingual context. Random cross-document context can interfere with prediction (Zhao et al., 2024). Grouping related documents improves language modeling and context use (Zhao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024; Staniszewski et al., 2025). For multilingual adaptation, Wu et al. (2025) concatenate title-matched Wikipedia articles in different languages and compare with using the same article pairs without concatenation. Removing naturally occurring bilingual documents reduces translation, and restoring their parallel content recovers much of that performance (Shao et al., 2026). Our analyses hold target content fixed to measure the predictive benefit of corresponding cross-lingual context.

PPT uses document correspondence in machine-translated corpora to improve cross-lingual context use, but does not consistently improve general language understanding. Following PPT with SPT improves language understanding and translation over standard pretraining at matched budgets in both high- and low-resource settings. Behavioral analyses show improved monolingual language modeling while retaining an advantage over SPT in using cross-lingual context. These findings support PPT followed by SPT for multilingual pretraining using large-scale document-level parallel corpora.

Our experiments use 1.3B-parameter models and two language pairs, English–French and English–Swahili. Extending the study to larger models and more language pairs would broaden our understanding of how the two-stage use of parallel data benefits multilingual pretraining.

Evaluating Context Compaction on the Questions That Come Later. Language-model agents compact their context for the question at hand, but the compacted context must also serve questions that come later. We evaluate compaction on these later questions, using four corpora that annotate the evidence of several questions per text and recorded agent trajectories, and compare every method with random deletion at the same budget. On MultiRC, keeping the sentences that gpt-6-luna (through the OpenAI Decisions API) judges necessary for the current question raises its accuracy on that question by 11.4 points at 25% of the tokens. On the later questions, however, no method that selects sentences for the current question does detectably better than deleting sentences at random. Deleting words instead of sentences does better: LLMLingua-2, which ignores the question, beats random sentence deletion at the same token count by 12.5 points on the later MultiRC questions. It keeps about twice random deletion's share of the evidence's content words, and at equal content-word retention its gain shrinks to 7.3 points (exploratory).

On FEVER, label accuracy can overstate what the kept text supports: the gain of sentence selection is no longer detected when answers are scored against the kept evidence, and the 21.0-point gain of LLMLingua-2 is not shown to rest on the kept text. The ranking also depends on the setting: on Evidence Inference sentence selection beats LLMLingua-2 at a nominal 25% budget, and on $τ$-bench trajectories, whose later tool calls need exact identifiers, it beats random deletion while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain. Scores on the question a compaction was made for do not reliably show how it serves later ones.

Applications that call a language model many times, such as agents, assistants and multi-step pipelines, carry text from one call to the next: documents read so far, conversation turns, tool outputs. We call this text the state. Every call pays for it in tokens and the context window bounds it, so applications compact it: they delete parts of it to fit a budget. At compaction time the application usually knows its current question, and the natural choice is to keep what that question needs. The state, however, outlives that question. Later questions, unknown when the deletion was made, must be answered from whatever survived, and a deleted sentence is gone for all of them. We call the question available at compaction time known and the later ones hidden. Query-aware compressors are usually evaluated on the question they compress for; we evaluate them on the hidden ones.

We compare query-aware selection, which keeps what the known question needs, with question-agnostic compressors. Our main instance uses typed decision models, which take a state and typed questions about it (a Boolean, a Choice among options or a Score) and return a probability for each answer (TypeSafe AI, 2026; OpenAI, 2026). Typed selection asks one Boolean per sentence, “is this sentence needed to answer the question?”, and keeps the most probable sentences; the same model then answers the questions, and in this role we call it the reader. Figure 1 shows the risk. We compare it with random deletion, question-agnostic selection by the same model, TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency) selection and lead (the first sentences). We also run LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al., 2024), which deletes individual words without any question, and, at token budgets, LongLLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2024) and maximal marginal relevance (MMR; Carbonell & Goldstein, 1998), two established compressors that use the question.

The corpora are MultiRC (Khashabi et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019), ERASER’s FEVER (Thorne et al., 2018; DeYoung et al., 2020), Evidence Inference (Lehman et al., 2019) and LoCoMo conversation memory (Maharana et al., 2024), in which several questions share one text and each question’s evidence is annotated, and recorded \tau -bench agent trajectories (Yao et al., 2024), whose questions ask for the identifiers that later tool calls pass. Our findings are: Selection for the known question beats random deletion on that question. On MultiRC, typed selection, MMR and LongLLMLingua raise known-question accuracy over random deletion at 25%, but none shows a detected advantage on hidden questions on average. On MultiRC, hidden questions gain only where they share the known question’s evidence. On FEVER, a gain in recovering a claim’s label is not detected when the kept text is scored for what it supports (Section 3). The label-accuracy gain of word-level compression there is not shown to rest on the kept text either (Section 4). On MultiRC, picking words beats picking sentences by the same scores.

With the same importance scores, picking words instead of sentences raises hidden-question accuracy, and LLMLingua-2 and a hybrid of typed sentences and LLMLingua-2 words lead on hidden questions. They keep about as many evidence words as random deletion but far more of the evidence’s content words, which partly explains the lead: at equal content-word retention it shrinks from 12.5 to 7.3 points with gpt-6-luna (Section 4). The ordering is not stable across settings. On Evidence Inference typed selection beats LLMLingua-2 on hidden claims at a nominal 25% budget. On agent trajectories, whose later calls need exact identifiers, typed selection beats random deletion and LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain (Section 5). Concurrent work shows that compaction can serve the current query and fail later ones (Liu et al., 2026; Zhang, 2026). We add an evaluation on annotated evidence that compares sentence- and word-level compression and locates where each serves later questions.
This section describes the MultiRC experiment; Sections 3 and 5 give the changes for the other settings.

Each MultiRC question has several candidate answers that annotators labeled correct or incorrect, and a question can have more than one correct answer. We use 300 paragraphs with at least three questions and 6–20 sentences, with 3,355 questions and 17,895 candidate answers, from the validation and training splits (validation alone has too few such paragraphs). The first listed question of each paragraph is known and the others are hidden. gpt-6-luna reads every corpus. Every gpt-6-luna read and selection in this paper goes through the OpenAI Decisions API (OpenAI, 2026), the typed decision interface: a request poses typed questions and returns a probability for each answer, with no generated text. Three open-weight models built for the typed decision interface, open-decider (2B), open-bosun (1.7B) and open-lumma (0.6B) (Mapika, 2026; Hanno Labs, 2026; FrontiersMind, 2026), also read MultiRC from their released weights, and qwen3.8-flash is a general instruction-tuned reader (Appendix B). We drop refused answers; counting them as wrong instead changes neither the sign of any typed - random contrast nor whether its interval excludes zero (Appendix B).

Both model-based selectors ask one Boolean per sentence, with the sentences numbered in the state. Typed selection puts the known question in the state and asks “is sentence i needed to answer the question?”. Question-agnostic selection gives no question and asks “does sentence i state a fact that a reader is likely to be asked about later?”. A policy keeps a budget b\in\{25,50,75\}\% of a paragraph’s sentences (rounded half to even, at least one). Typed and agnostic selection keep the most probable sentences, TF-IDF selection those closest to the known question, lead the first ones, and random deletion one seeded uniform sample. Kept sentences stay in document order. Token-matched tests cut every text, LLMLingua-2 ’s included, to the same o200k token count (Appendix G).

One request asks one Boolean per candidate answer: “given the passage, is this a correct answer to the question?”, where “no” is defined as “not supported or incorrect”. Once a compaction deletes the evidence for a correct answer, the reader is therefore asked to reject that answer. We score each candidate answer against the MultiRC labels, average within each paragraph, then over paragraphs, with paragraph-bootstrap 95% intervals; a difference is detected when its interval excludes zero. Answering “no” to every candidate already scores 55.6%, and of the four typed readers only gpt-6-luna (88.2%) and open-decider (75.3%) are detectably above it on the full text, so the main tables report these two. A hidden question is overlapping if its annotated evidence shares a sentence with the known question’s, and disjoint otherwise.

Hypotheses, tests and decision rules were specified before any model request for the Evidence Inference overlap test, the KEEP–DROP contrast, the LoCoMo test and four follow-ups under one plan (token-matched budgets, query-aware baselines, three-way labels and harder LoCoMo options). The same holds for the LLMLingua-2 granularity test, the hybrid compactor, a test with a different known question, a general-reader test, the \tau -bench test and the abstractive-summary test. Appendix A counts the outcomes and lists every prediction that was not fully met. The other analyses, including the content-word analysis and the FEVER evidence-support check of Section 4, are exploratory. The ancillary files contain the summary tables and the values of all reported numbers.

At a 25% budget, open-decider answers the known question at 70% after typed selection, against 61% after random deletion and 74% on the full text; for gpt-6-luna the same accuracies are 77%, 67% and 89% (compacted texts in Table 1).

section: Averaged over hidden questions, selection stays near random deletion.
text: Typed - random hidden accuracy is slightly below zero for both readers at 25% and 50%, and question-agnostic selection is similarly close to random (Table 1). The split holds when texts are cut to the same token count: typed - random at 25% with gpt-6-luna is +11.4 [+9.1, +13.8] points on the known question and - 0.4 [- 1.5, +0.6] on hidden ones. LongLLMLingua and MMR show the same split with both readers, and on hidden questions LongLLMLingua falls below random deletion (- 1.6 [- 2.6, - 0.6] with gpt-6-luna; Appendix G). With qwen3.8-flash as reader, typed - random is +10.4 [+7.4, +13.3] on the known question and - 0.6 [- 1.8, +0.6] on hidden ones.

section: Hidden questions gain where they share the known question’s evidence.
text: ERASER (DeYoung et al., 2020) marks evidence sentences for 3,300 of the 3,355 MultiRC questions. Typed selection at 25% keeps 50% of the known question’s evidence (gpt-6-luna) against 25% expected for a random subset, and about the random share for hidden questions. Hidden questions that share evidence with the known one gain +4.3 [+2.2, +6.4] points (gpt-6-luna) and +5.3 [+2.9, +7.7] (open-decider). Disjoint ones lose - 2.9 [- 4.3, - 1.4] and - 3.0 [- 4.5, - 1.4], with less of their evidence kept than under random deletion (18% against 25%; Figure 2).

A hidden answer that was right on the full text flips more often when its evidence was deleted. With gpt-6-luna, adding some of the deleted evidence back undoes more flips than adding as many sentences that are evidence for no question (+26.8 [+22.6, +31.5] points; Appendix D). A sufficiency check (“does the passage contain the information needed to answer this question?”) ranks questions with broken evidence first. Yet re-reading a random quarter of hidden questions on the full text recovers most of what re-reading the lowest-sufficiency quarter does (Appendix D).

section: FEVER and Evidence Inference: hidden claims gain in label recovery.
text: Each question here is a claim, and the reader judges whether the text supports it. We sample 200 FEVER documents with 5,433 hidden claims and 792 Evidence Inference clinical-trial articles (Appendix E); the first claim of each document is known. On FEVER at 25% typed - random hidden-claim accuracy is +17.2 points, and on Evidence Inference disjoint claims gain too, with more of their evidence kept than random deletion keeps (Figure 2).

section: Label recovery and support scoring disagree.
text: Label accuracy counts the document’s label as right even when a claim’s evidence was deleted. A prespecified three-way read therefore also scores each answer against what the kept text supports: the document’s label if all of the claim’s annotated evidence was kept and “not enough info” if all of it was deleted. In this read, with true and false claims weighted equally, typed selection on FEVER recovers the label 25.2 points more often than random deletion, while its support-target accuracy, with the three targets weighted equally, differs from random deletion by - 1.0 [- 3.9, +2.2] points (Appendix J). Prespecified KEEP–DROP tests give a hidden claim two texts with the same number of sentences, one with its evidence and one without; KEEP beats DROP by +50.0 [+47.4, +52.4] points on FEVER and +17.8 [+15.9, +19.7] on Evidence Inference (Appendix K).

section: For sentence selection, the gain follows the extra evidence kept.
text: Across the eight 25% groups of Figure 2 (corpus, reader, overlapping or disjoint), the typed - random hidden gain rises with how much more of the hidden questions’ evidence typed selection keeps than random deletion, at 0.37 points of gain per point of extra evidence. We fixed this line before a second experiment that repeats typed selection with a different, randomly drawn known question in every document. On the eight new groups it misses the observed gains by 3.4 points on average. The largest misses are 9.5 points (overlapping FEVER claims, under-predicted) and 6.9 (overlapping MultiRC questions read by open-decider, over-predicted); the other six are within 4.8 points (Appendix F).

section: On MultiRC, word-level compression serves later questions
text: LLMLingua-2 scores every word of the text without any question and keeps the highest-scoring words. A prespecified hybrid keeps typed whole sentences up to half the token budget and fills the rest with the highest-scoring LLMLingua-2 words of the other sentences (Appendix H). Table 2 compares them with sentence selection at 25% of the tokens.

section: Word-level compression leads on hidden questions.
text: LLMLingua-2 - random sentence deletion on hidden questions with annotated evidence, from the model of Appendix I without retention terms, is +12.5 [+11.3, +13.6] points on MultiRC with gpt-6-luna, +6.0 [+4.7, +7.3] with open-decider and +21.0 [+18.7, +23.4] in label accuracy on FEVER; the paired contrast over all hidden questions, dropping refusals pairwise, gives +12.1 and +21.0 for the two gpt-6-luna cells (Appendix G). LLMLingua-2 is also ahead of typed selection on hidden questions in all three cells (Table 2). The hybrid beats typed selection on hidden questions in all three cells, by 4.6 to 8.3 points with every interval above zero; it beats LLMLingua-2 on FEVER and stays below it on MultiRC (Appendix H).

section: The gain comes from picking words.
text: A prespecified test keeps the LLMLingua-2 scores and changes only the unit kept. Picking words instead of whole sentences raises hidden-question accuracy at 25% by +11.7 points (MultiRC, gpt-6-luna), +4.6 (MultiRC, open-decider) and +19.1 (FEVER). Whole sentences picked by the same scores are not detectably better than random sentence deletion in five of six cells (Appendix H). On the known MultiRC question LLMLingua-2 is ahead of typed selection with gpt-6-luna in all four comparisons. The two intervals at sentence budgets exclude zero, and the one at 50% of the tokens just does (upper end -0.02 points) (Appendices G and H).

section: Word-level compression keeps the evidence’s content words.
text: Counted over all words, LLMLingua-2, the hybrid and random sentence deletion keep similar shares of the hidden questions’ evidence on MultiRC, yet their accuracies differ by up to 12.5 points. Sentence deletion keeps a sentence’s content and function words together. LLMLingua-2 drops function words first, so it keeps 48.0% of the evidence’s content words against 26.1% for random sentence deletion (Table 2). For sentence policies the two counts agree within half a point, so the relation of Section 3 is unchanged.

section: Content-word retention accounts for part of the lead.
text: A model of each answer’s correctness, with document fixed effects, compares policies at equal content-word retention. It describes an association, since the policies produce the retention they are compared at. At equal retention the MultiRC LLMLingua-2 - random-sentence gap shrinks from 12.5 to +7.3 [+6.1, +8.4] points with gpt-6-luna and from 6.0 to +2.0 [+0.7, +3.2] with open-decider. Also conditioning on how many of each candidate answer’s content words survive leaves +4.9 points with gpt-6-luna and +0.6 [- 0.5, +1.8] with open-decider. The hybrid - typed gaps shrink the same way (Table 15). On FEVER binned retention leaves 1.3 points; a linear term leaves 14.9, because accuracy rises non-linearly with retention there.

section: Which words are kept matters too.
text: On FEVER typed selection keeps more of the hidden claims’ content words than LLMLingua-2 yet scores lower (Table 2). At the same content-word retention LLMLingua-2 still beats random word deletion by +6.7 [+5.5, +8.0] points on MultiRC with gpt-6-luna, +1.7 [+0.5, +2.9] with open-decider and +9.6 [+7.5, +11.7] on FEVER (Appendix I).

section: LLM-written summaries stay below word-level compression.
text: A compaction can also have an LLM rewrite the text. Two summarizers, qwen3.8-flash and gpt-6.1-sol, summarized each MultiRC paragraph within the same token budget, once for unknown later questions and once for the known question (Appendix O). On hidden questions the generic summaries beat random sentence deletion by 7.6 and 10.9 points but stay below LLMLingua-2: summary - LLMLingua-2 is - 4.5 [- 5.7, - 3.2] and - 1.3 [- 2.4, - 0.3] points. The summaries written for the known question answer it better than typed selection and LLMLingua-2 (88.5% and 89.2%), but on hidden questions they fall below random deletion (qwen3.8-flash, - 2.9 [- 4.0, - 1.8]) or show no detected gain (gpt-6.1-sol, +0.9 [- 0.2, +2.1]).

section: On FEVER, label accuracy overstates the word-level gain.
text: FEVER accuracy counts the document’s label, which Section 3 shows can be right without textual support. The LLMLingua-2 gain over random sentence deletion lies on true claims (+31.5 [+28.0, +35.0] points; false claims - 2.2 [- 3.7, - 1.0]). When at most a fifth of a true claim’s evidence content words survive, the reader still calls it supported for 56.0% of claims after LLMLingua-2 and 26.8% after random sentence deletion. An evidence-support target, scored on the binary reads, reproduces the three-way result for typed - random (- 0.2 [- 3.4, +3.0] points, label-balanced) and removes the hybrid’s gain over typed selection (- 3.7 [- 9.4, +1.3]). Under LLMLingua-2 it is undefined for 99% of hidden claims, whose evidence is partly kept, so its FEVER gain is not shown to rest on the kept text (Appendix I).

On Evidence Inference typed selection keeps more of even the disjoint claims’ evidence than random deletion (Figure 2). It beats LLMLingua-2 on hidden claims when LLMLingua-2 is set to the compression rate of 25% sentence deletion (+12.2 [+10.1, +14.4] points); at the 50% rate the difference is +1.0 [- 0.5, +2.6]. This comparison is not token-matched: at 25% the typed texts keep 28.9% of the article’s o200k tokens and the LLMLingua-2 texts 25.8% (Appendices G and L).

In the recorded \tau -bench retail trajectories an agent calls tools for a simulated user. The state is a trajectory up to its middle tool output, split into turns, tool calls and tool outputs. The known question asks which identifier (an order, item, product or payment-method ID, or a zip code) the next tool call passes; each hidden question asks the same for a later call, among same-shaped identifiers from the state. On 390 states with 837 hidden questions at 25% of the tokens, typed - random is +22.3 [+15.1, +28.9] points with gpt-6-luna and +21.7 [+15.7, +27.6] with qwen3.8-flash, while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain (+4.0 [- 1.1, +9.3]); token-level extractive compressors are known to strip the action syntax that agents need (Zhang & Sun, 2026). Typed selection keeps the hidden question’s identifier for 66.4% of hidden questions against 42.4% (random) and 52.3% (LLMLingua-2).

section: Anticipating later calls costs the known one.
text: Selectors that anticipate later calls trade the known call for the hidden ones: on a 120-state subsample, expected-coverage selection gains +12.8 [+5.2, +20.8] points over typed selection on hidden questions and - 10.6 (90% interval [- 17.8, - 2.9]) on the known one. About half of the hidden gain comes from fewer refusals: scored on answered questions only, it is +5.8 [- 1.4, +13.6] (Appendix N).

LoCoMo’s ten long conversations are compacted four times as they grow, so a dropped turn never returns. At the last checkpoint, a typed 25% memory with a hidden question’s evidence beats one with the same number of turns without it by 13.3 points (gpt-6-luna), in all 10 conversations. Typed versus random deletion is unresolved for both readers, and on the four-choice format empty memory already scores 81.4% (Appendix M).

Query-aware sentence selection raises the known question’s accuracy over random deletion. On later questions it helps those that share the known question’s evidence. On MultiRC, where many do not, it does no better than random deletion on average.

On MultiRC the compressors that lead on later questions delete words. They drop function words first, so the same token budget holds more of the evidence’s content words. At equal content-word retention two fifths to two thirds of LLMLingua-2 ’s MultiRC lead over random sentence deletion disappears, and LLMLingua-2 still beats random words, so which words are kept also matters. On FEVER, typed selection’s label gain is not detected under support scoring, and the word-level gain is not shown to rest on the kept text. The ordering is not general. On Evidence Inference, where even disjoint claims keep more evidence under typed selection, it beats LLMLingua-2 at a nominal 25% budget. On agent trajectories, whose later calls need exact identifiers, LLMLingua-2 keeps fewer of them than typed selection and shows no detected gain.

For evaluation, the results suggest scoring hidden questions as well as the known one, comparing with random deletion at matched tokens, measuring the hidden questions’ evidence kept in content words, and reporting support-based scoring next to label recovery. Compaction also costs tokens to build: for typed selection at 25% with gpt-6-luna, compacting once pays for itself in input tokens only with one request per later question, after about 6.6 to 11.0 of them on FEVER, Evidence Inference and LoCoMo. On Evidence Inference this is more than its mean of 3.7 later questions, and on MultiRC the extrapolated break-even, 14.0, exceeds its mean of 10.2 (Appendix L). Keeping the full state allows a re-read for a later question, but neither recovery we tested matches it. On MultiRC, re-reading the lowest-sufficiency quarter of hidden questions on the full text lifts accuracy over all hidden questions from 67% to 74%, against 89% on the full text (Appendix D). On agent trajectories, fetching dropped units on demand reaches 69.1% against 88.8% for the full state at 102.0% of its passage tokens, and the prespecified prediction that it would come close is not met (Appendix N).

Prompt compression removes tokens or sentences by perplexity (Jiang et al., 2023), by query-aware importance (Jiang et al., 2024) or by a learned task-agnostic importance (Pan et al., 2024), and key–value (KV) cache compression has the same split (Kim et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). Earlier agent-memory work studied the same write-before-query asymmetry. TierMem (Zhu et al., 2026) falls back to a raw log when a router judges pre-query summaries insufficient, and EMBER (Li et al., 2026) learns which evidence to retain before the query. Chen et al. (2026) find that query-aware KV eviction does not generalize across queries, and Yu et al. (2026) separate write-time from retrieval-time loss. We delete sentences (turns on LoCoMo) for one known question and test the questions hidden at deletion time with annotated evidence and KEEP–DROP substitutions. The closest work is concurrent.

Tirmazi et al. (2026) formalize compaction against later queries, with a set-membership case study, and Liu et al. (2026) find that compacting agent KV caches before later queries arrive hurts, and that deferring compaction recovers much of the cost; RestoreKV (Baek et al., 2026) adds learned restoration to query-agnostic eviction, and Luo et al. (2026) find that hiding the question at compression time reorders KV-cache compressors, with most no better than trivial baselines. These work on KV caches rather than on evidence-annotated text. Liu (2026) counts the extra retrieval calls an agent makes to re-acquire state that compression dropped, and Zhang (2026) tests whether compressed memory keeps what a later update needs on synthetic histories; we measure answer accuracy on later questions of existing corpora and locate the loss with evidence annotations. Wang et al. (2026) find that context compactors keep about a sixth of the constraints a user sets for the agent’s later behavior. Sadowski & Chudziak (2026) and Shen & Li (2026) optimize what is written when the later goal is known. Mnemon (Wang, 2026) uses the same per-record “is this needed” Boolean but keeps its raw records recoverable.

Shankaranarayana et al. (2026) find that asking whether the evidence suffices is more informative than answer confidence; we ask it after compaction has deleted part of the evidence. Ai et al. (2026) find that KV-cache eviction can keep final-answer accuracy while the reasoning that supports the answer degrades; on FEVER we find the analogous gap between label accuracy and the evidence the kept text retains.

The experiments use public text and conversation benchmarks and recorded agent trajectories, not live agents. Abstractive summaries are tested only on MultiRC at a 25% budget. In the \tau -bench test the actions and tool outputs are fixed by the recording, the questions ask only for identifiers, retail is the only domain with enough trajectories for inference, and the only budget is 25%. The relation between gain and evidence kept is tested by consistency across settings, KEEP–DROP interventions and one out-of-sample check on the three document corpora, for sentence selection; it could not be assessed on LoCoMo and holds only qualitatively on \tau -bench. The content-word analysis of word-level compression is exploratory, leaves part of the MultiRC gap unexplained and, on FEVER, does not separate content words from all words. The model-based sentence selectors are typed models, which usually also answer; qwen3.8-flash is the only general instruction-tuned reader, and it reads the texts that gpt-6-luna selected. Only two typed readers perform above the all-“no” baseline on MultiRC. On the three document corpora the known question is the first listed one or, in one test, one other randomly drawn question per document.
Evidence annotations are incomplete, so neither the retention tests nor the evidence-support target can account for unannotated evidence.

Budgets count sentences or conversation turns, except in the token-matched tests and the \tau -bench test; Appendix L counts input tokens. The KEEP–DROP comparison covers one budget and does not include MultiRC. LoCoMo has ten conversations and a four-choice format on which empty memory already scores 81.4%. Hosted reads taken at different times can differ slightly (Appendix C). Intervals are unadjusted for multiple comparisons. The benchmark texts predate the models, so contamination cannot be ruled out.

Compaction that deletes a question’s evidence can make supported answers “unsupported”. Without provenance, a downstream consumer may take them for answers that are genuinely unsupported or false, and the sufficiency check does not flag every such case. Recoverable full-state designs should be evaluated before compaction is used in consequential settings. Keeping the full state in turn carries the privacy and retention obligations of whatever it contains. The Evidence Inference articles are clinical-trial reports used only as a benchmark, and compaction and the sufficiency check remain unvalidated for clinical decision support.

SpecGuardBench: Can Coding Agents Construct Reliable Validation Harnesses from Natural Language Specifications? As coding agents become more capable, tests remain the primary evidence for judging whether their code is correct. Yet passing available tests does not establish that an implementation satisfies its natural language specification. Reliable validation requires checks that faithfully capture the specification and scenarios that thoroughly exercise the code, but current benchmarks provide limited insight into whether agents can construct such evidence themselves. We introduce SpecGuardBench, a benchmark of 291 tasks from 13 real-world repositories, covering 8 types of verification logic such as functional postconditions and interaction protocols. Given a natural language specification, repository context, and a reference implementation, an agent constructs a validation harness comprising executable checks and test scenarios. The checks should reject implementations that violate the specification while accepting those that satisfy it, and the scenarios should thoroughly exercise the code. Across four proprietary and open-weight coding agents, none constructs a harness scored as faithful on the benchmark's implementations for more than 63% of the tasks. The bottleneck lies less in exploring test scenarios than in constructing checks that faithfully reflect the specification.

Specifically, the agents show a clear tendency to write checks that mirror the reference implementation rather than the specification, and therefore reject implementations that the specification permits.

As coding agents take on increasingly complex changes and long-horizon tasks across software repositories, natural language specifications from humans or agents guide what they should accomplish and provide a basis for judging their outputs. Reliable validation of whether the code aligns with specifications is therefore essential and challenging for benchmark evaluation, interactive coding workflows, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Across these scenarios, finite executable test suites remain a primary mechanism for validation and supervision (Jimenez et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025b). Yet passing a test suite does not establish conformance to the underlying specifications: an incorrect implementation may satisfy the tested examples while violating specifications in untested situations (Liu et al., 2023; Ahmed et al., 2026). Moreover, scaling test suites is challenging, as test inputs are typically coupled with expected outcomes. A finite test suite is thus bound to be incomplete, making it an unreliable validation paradigm.

Reliable validation requires checks that faithfully capture the stated specifications and the exploration of test scenarios that thoroughly exercise the relevant code (Barr et al., 2015). Faithful checks should identify specification violations without rejecting behavior that the specifications permit, while thorough exploration of test scenarios should apply these checks to executions spanning a broad range of paths and program states. Although exhaustive testing is generally infeasible, exploration budget can be scaled to application-specific reliability requirements, with additional compute helping reduce the risk of undetected faults (Böhme and Falk, 2020). Expressing specifications as reusable executable checks decoupled from test scenarios lets the same checks assess newly generated test scenarios and real-world executions, supporting continued validation beyond the initial test suite and after deployment.

Existing benchmarks increasingly assess models’ ability to construct evidence for code validation, but only partially address whether the resulting evidence supports scalable, faithful validation against natural language specifications. Previous test-generation evaluations typically ask whether LLMs can generate tests that improve fault detection (Jain et al., 2025; Jing et al., 2026), reproduce bugs (Mündler et al., 2024; Ahmed et al., 2024), or exercise more program structure (Wang et al., 2025). However, these evaluations overlook the risk that generated tests overfit the reference implementation rather than faithfully capture the stated specifications. Verification-oriented benchmarks (Ye et al., 2025; Thakur et al., 2026) move beyond this paradigm by asking agents to construct machine-checkable specifications that characterize intended program behavior. Machine-checkable specifications are typically decoupled from specific inputs and exercised by a formal verifier. However, they often evaluate these specifications within predefined formal languages and verification interfaces, providing limited evidence about agents’ ability to validate code against diverse natural language specifications in real-world repositories. Such scenarios may involve complex dependencies and various types of verification logic (e.g., functional postconditions and interaction protocols).

To bridge this gap, we introduce SpecGuardBench, which evaluates whether LLM agents can construct evidence that supports thorough, faithful validation against natural language specifications in real-world repositories. SpecGuardBench consists of 291 validation problems, covering eight types of verification logic. As shown in Figure 1, given a natural language specification, repository context, and a reference implementation, an agent constructs a validation harness comprising comprehensive test scenarios and executable checks. The test scenarios supply concrete arguments that drive the code under validation through a broad range of program states. The executable checks perform invocations of the code under validation with whatever arguments they receive and assert the properties that the natural language specification requires of the resulting behavior, so the same checks apply across executions, even after deployment. Together, the checks and the scenarios should thoroughly exercise specification-relevant code and expose violations without rejecting implementations that satisfy the specification.

Using SpecGuardBench, we evaluate four coding agents spanning proprietary and open-weight models, and none constructs a validation harness scored as faithful on the benchmark’s implementations for more than 63% of the tasks. The primary bottleneck is the faithfulness of the checks, not the thoroughness of the scenarios. The agents detect the violations on most tasks, but their checks also assert requirements the specification does not impose, and the resulting false alarms leave every agent’s faithfulness 11 to 22 percentage points below its detection rate. Even when given scenarios that expose the violation, the checks of three of the four agents still accept most of the violations they missed, and the scenarios account for at most 33 to 42% of each agent’s failures. Moreover, the coding agents ground their checks in the reference implementation rather than in the specification: when shown a violating reference, every agent loses 19 to 31 points of faithfulness, because its validation harness then accepts the violation or rejects the gold implementation. These results reveal a gap in coding agents’ ability to validate code against a natural language specification.
Closing this gap depends above all on checks that assert no more and no less than the specification requires, which none of the agents we evaluate reliably produces.

In summary, we make the following contributions: We introduce SpecGuardBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether LLM agents can construct reliable evidence to validate code in real-world repositories against natural language specifications. We release a scalable data construction pipeline that converts code with relevant documentation into additional evaluation tasks. We evaluate four proprietary and open-weight LLMs and analyze the remaining challenges in depth.

Prior evaluations of LLM test generation score generated tests by the faults they detect, the reported bugs they reproduce, or the coverage they reach, and when a test is validated, it is validated only against the one correct implementation available, while overlooking whether the test overfits that implementation. TestEval (Wang et al., 2025) and TestGenEval (Jain et al., 2025) ask a model to write concrete test cases for a given program; the former measures the line, branch, and path coverage the tests reach, and the latter additionally measures the fraction of injected faults they detect, while SWT-Bench (Mündler et al., 2024) and TDD-Bench Verified (Ahmed et al., 2024) give a reported issue together with its repository and score an instance as solved when some generated test fails before the fix and passes after it. Since each concrete test couples one input with its expected outcome, it offers no reusable check for other inputs, and thoroughness can only be measured by the number of tests or the coverage they reach.

Property-based testing decouples the two by stating a property once and generating inputs separately, and prior studies ask whether LLMs can write such properties from a library’s documentation and code (Vikram et al., 2024; Maaz et al., 2025). PBT-Bench (Jing et al., 2026) is the closest to our task in form. Given a Python library with injected bugs and its documentation, an agent writes Hypothesis tests, each pairing a property drawn from the documentation with a random input distribution, and a bug counts as found when some test fails on the buggy library and passes on the fixed one. This design leaves two limitations. First, the fixed library is the only implementation a test must accept, so a test that overfits it still counts as finding a bug. Second, the agent describes only an input space, from which the testing framework draws random samples under a fixed budget, and is told to leave finding the violation to the sampler. The task thus limits how far the agent explores and constructs the scenarios that reach a violation, and whether a bug is found depends in part on random sampling, a process the agent neither takes part in nor observes.

SpecGuardBench fixes one atomic specification per task, scores the harness as a whole by its verdict on each implementation, and includes valid alternative implementations that satisfy the specification but differ from the reference in code the specification does not constrain, so that checks fitted to the reference rather than to the specification are exposed, and asks the agent to explore and construct the scenarios itself.

A second line of work asks a model to turn a natural language description into a machine-checkable specification in a fixed formalism, typically a pre- and postcondition contract, and scores the specification by whether it accepts correct behavior and rejects incorrect behavior. In formal settings, the specification is written in a verification language and checked by a verifier. Verina (Ye et al., 2025) and CLEVER (Thakur et al., 2026) generate Lean specifications from a natural language description and compare them with a ground-truth specification by proving implication or equivalence between the two, while nl2spec (Cosler et al., 2023) targets temporal logic. In executable settings, the specification is a set of runtime assertions, checked by execution rather than by formal proof. nl2postcond (Endres et al., 2024) generates postconditions, assertions over a function’s inputs and return value, from its docstring, and scores them by whether the reference implementation satisfies them on the test inputs and by the fraction of incorrect programs they reject. CodeSpecBench (Chen et al., 2026) extends this to preconditions, assertions over the inputs, and to repository-level tasks drawn from SWE-bench.

It scores a specification by whether it accepts executions of a reference implementation and rejects illegal inputs and outputs that differ from the reference implementation. A related line infers specifications from the implementation itself, but since the implementation is then the standard, a specification that mirrors it is the intended outcome rather than a failure (Ma et al., 2025a; Wen et al., 2024; Le-Cong et al., 2025). These benchmarks differ from ours in three respects. The formal line requires both the code and the specification to be written in a verification language, with ground truth formalized by hand, which limits it to standalone functions and excludes real repositories with their dependencies. The executable line reaches real repositories, but the inputs on which a specification is exercised are a curated test set supplied by the benchmark, so the model is never asked to explore the code and its thoroughness is never measured. Above all, most of these benchmarks define correct behavior by one implementation or by tests derived from it, and thus also overlook the risk that a specification overfits the reference implementation.

SpecGuardBench therefore asks the agent for both the checks and the scenarios, measures how thoroughly the scenarios exercise the relevant code, and scores the checks against valid alternative implementations, which distinguishes checks faithful to the specification from checks faithful to the reference implementation.

SpecGuardBench measures whether an agent can turn a natural language specification into evidence that supports thorough, faithful validation. Its tasks are produced by an automated pipeline built on top of FeatureBench (Zhou et al., 2026), described in Section 3.2.

Each task provides the agent with one atomic natural language specification, a reference implementation containing the specified functionality, and the code repository. The agent is not told whether the reference implementation aligns with the specification. It is therefore instructed to take the specification, not the implementation, as the standard and to produce executable checks that reject every violating implementation and accept every satisfying one, together with test scenarios that exercise the relevant code as thoroughly as possible. The agent submits a validation harness comprising two components: a generator of test scenarios, each specifying the concrete arguments of a single invocation of the code under validation, and scenario-agnostic executable checks that, given one scenario, perform the invocation and assert the properties required by the specification. Appendix D gives the contract that fixes the form of the two components, and a complete task.

We then evaluate the validation harness by running its checks against three kinds of implementations: the gold implementation, which satisfies the specification by construction; a violating implementation constructed for that specification; and valid alternative implementations, which modify only code that the specification does not constrain. Section 3.2 describes the construction of the latter two. We measure the faithfulness rate, the fraction of tasks whose checks reject the violating implementation and accept every satisfying one, and report its two conditions separately. The detection rate is the fraction of tasks whose checks reject the violating implementation, and the false alarm rate is the fraction whose checks reject the gold implementation or a valid alternative. Since no evaluation can exhaust the implementations that satisfy or violate a specification, the faithfulness rate measured on these implementations is an empirical upper bound. This bound errs only in the agents’ favor. A validation harness faithful to the specification is always scored as faithful, while every failure we report is witnessed by a concrete implementation that the harness misjudges, so our results can only understate how far the agents fall short.

We additionally record the edge coverage attained by the generated scenarios, which indicates how thoroughly they explore the relevant code and, when the checks pass, helps assess the residual risk of unexercised violation (Bishop, 2002; Malaiya et al., 2002). Edge coverage is the fraction of control-flow edges the scenarios execute in the gold-patch functions that implement the specification and in every gold-patch function reachable from them by calls.

Each validation task needs a natural language specification, code known to align with it, and code known to violate it. We build SpecGuardBench on FeatureBench, which already provides high-quality natural language specifications that align with the code implementing them. On top of each FeatureBench instance, we construct the violating implementations, as Figure 2 illustrates and the rest of this section describes. Each FeatureBench instance targets a feature of an open-source Python project and ships its specification as a task statement and interface descriptions describing the feature, together with the gold patch that implements it and the test suite that validates it. Compared with issue reports in bug-fixing benchmarks such as SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024), which describe a bug symptom and leave the intended behavior implicit, a FeatureBench specification explicitly states a feature’s intent, which executable checks must validate. From FeatureBench, we randomly sample 30 instances that do not require a specific GPU environment, covering 13 repositories.

A FeatureBench specification describes a whole feature and therefore includes many requirements, each of which an implementation can satisfy or break on its own, so each is a separate place to go wrong and a separate point to verify. We use an LLM (Claude Opus 5) to split it until each piece is a requirement that can be violated without violating another, and call these pieces atomic specifications (Figure 2 a). Each atomic specification must be copied from the original specification rather than inferred from the gold patch, is labeled as behavioral, structural, or an implementation constraint, and is paired with its implementation in the gold patch.

For each atomic specification, we then build the violating implementation that the checks must catch (Figure 2 b). Given the targeted atomic specification and the other specifications of the FeatureBench instance, the same LLM produces a candidate by injecting a violation of the targeted specification into its implementation, so that this atomic specification no longer holds while the others still do. The violation should produce an effect observable by executing the code rather than inspecting its source, so the task is solvable by executable checks, and the divergence should be deterministic rather than an effect of environmental noise. As evidence of the violation, the LLM also writes a differential witness: scenarios whose execution produces such an effect and diverges from the gold implementation.

The pipeline discards a candidate that fails either of two filters (Figure 2 c). First, we run it against the FeatureBench instance’s validating test suite. A surviving candidate is one the original test suite cannot catch, since it violates the specification only in situations the suite never exercises. It is therefore challenging by construction, and lies precisely in the gap between passing tests and conforming to the specification that motivates this work. Second, we run the witness against the gold implementation and against the candidate, and keep the candidate only when both runs finish and their outputs differ. A second LLM from a different model family (GPT-5.6-sol) then checks the divergence and confirms, by majority vote over three independent samples, that it indicates a genuine violation of the specification rather than an incidental difference. We use two LLMs from different model families, one to synthesize a candidate and the other to check it, to mitigate the ambiguity of the natural language specification: a candidate is kept only when both agree that it violates the target specification without violating the others.

We then check that the candidate violates only the targeted atomic specification, so that the other specifications of the FeatureBench instance still hold (Figure 2 d). Such a candidate still satisfies every other specification of the instance, so it can later test whether the checks written for those specifications overfit and reject an implementation they should accept. We check this in two complementary ways. We call a specification’s neighbors the other specifications whose implementation overlaps with its implementation, and run each of their witnesses against the candidate under check to see whether it diverges from the gold implementation, suggesting the neighboring specification no longer holds. Given the candidate and any divergence, the second LLM then decides for every other specification of the instance whether it still holds, and rejects the candidate by the same majority vote if any of them no longer holds. We keep an atomic specification only when both its own candidate and that of at least one neighboring specification survive this check, the neighbor’s candidate serving as a valid alternative implementation that faithful checks should not reject.

To validate these two LLM judgments, we manually reviewed a sample of 50 tasks from the final benchmark, stratified by instance. Two authors independently judged, for each task, whether the violating implementation violates the targeted atomic specification and whether each valid alternative implementation still satisfies it. The two annotators agreed on 94.7% of judgments, and their adjudicated judgment confirmed the pipeline’s decision on 98% of tasks.

Across the 30 instances, our decomposition and curation pipeline yields 291 atomic specifications, each with at least one valid alternative implementation. These tasks constitute the Full Set of SpecGuardBench. As shown in Figure 4, the task counts vary considerably across instances, with a median of 7.5 and an interquartile range from 4 to 11 tasks. To facilitate wider adoption of SpecGuardBench, we construct a Lite Set of 100 specifications by random sampling stratified by instance: every instance contributes at least one specification, and the remaining slots are allocated in proportion to each instance’s share of the full set.

We further performed open coding (Cruzes and Dyba, 2011) on a stratified sample of the specifications and their differential witnesses to examine whether the underlying properties map to existing formal verification logics. Through this process, we derived eight types of verification logic, ranging from postconditions on a return value to frame conditions, interaction protocols, and relations across executions, and each corresponds to a construct of an existing formal verification logic. Figure 4 shows their distribution across SpecGuardBench. Details are provided in Appendix A.

On SpecGuardBench, none of the four coding agents we evaluate produces faithful validation harnesses for more than 63% of the 291 tasks, and detection exceeds faithfulness by 11–22 points for every agent. Section 4.1 describes the setup and Section 4.2 reports the main results. Section 4.3 locates the failures. False alarms come from checks that assert more than the specification requires, and most missed violations persist even when we replace the scenarios with ones proven to expose the violation. Section 4.4 varies two conditions of the main experiment: which implementation is shown as the reference, and how many model calls the agent may make.

We evaluate four coding agents spanning proprietary and open-weight models: Codex with GPT-5.6-sol, Claude Code with Claude Opus 5, OpenCode with DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and OpenCode with GLM-5.3. Each agent runs with the default settings of its agent harness under a step budget of 80 model calls per task. The reference implementation shown to the agent is the gold implementation.

Table 1 reports the performance of the four coding agents we evaluate, and shows that the task is challenging not only in detecting implementations that violate the specification, but also in not rejecting those that satisfy it. Faithfulness, which requires both, ranges from 45% to 63% of the 291 tasks, so even the two most faithful agents fall short on more than a third of them. The agents miss the violation on 18% to 35% of the tasks and, sometimes on the same tasks, reject an implementation that satisfies the specification on 15% to 27%. Detection is the quantity a test-generation evaluation would report, and such an evaluation would underestimate the false alarm rate and rank the agents by differences that need not carry over to faithfulness. GPT-5.6-sol detects the violation on eight points more tasks than GLM-5.3 but also raises false alarms on eight points more, so the two agents reach a similar level of faithfulness (Appendix B reports the scores averaged over features). Conversely, DeepSeek-V4-Pro detects as often as Claude Opus 5 but raises false alarms on six points more tasks.
The two most faithful agents are also the two with the highest edge coverage, consistent with checks exercised through more thorough scenario exploration.

A validation harness can be unfaithful in two ways, by raising a false alarm or by missing the violation (Figure 5 a). These failures involve two components with different obligations. The scenario generator is only required to supply test scenarios that exercise the relevant code, while the checks are scenario-agnostic and must judge correctly on any scenario supplied to them. False alarms therefore arise from the checks. Since a false alarm rejects an implementation the specification permits, it means the checks assert requirements the specification does not impose. These false alarms account for the gap between detection and faithfulness for every agent in Table 1. This pattern suggests that agents tend to fit their checks to the reference implementation rather than the specification, a tendency that Section 4.4.1 further supports.

Missed violations can arise from insufficient exploration of test scenarios, checks too weak to catch the violation, or both. To separate these causes, we replace the generated scenarios with the differential witness scenarios from Section 3.2 whenever the harness and the witness invoke the same callable in the same form, leave the checks unchanged, and rerun the evaluation. These scenarios distinguish the gold implementation from the violating implementation. A validation harness that still misses the violation therefore fails to detect it on a scenario known to expose it. Among missed violations, the proportion repaired is about two thirds for GPT-5.6-sol and one half for GLM-5.3. For Claude Opus 5 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, roughly three quarters of missed violations persist with witness scenarios (Figure 5 b). Even counting every missed violation that the replacement cannot test as a failure of the scenarios, the scenarios account for at most 33–42% of each agent’s failures.

section: Showing the Violating Implementation as the Reference
text: In practice, the implementation a validation harness is written against may satisfy its specification or violate it, and a validation harness that merely mirrors whichever implementation it was shown, regardless of what the specification requires, is worthless. To test whether the agents’ checks are grounded in the specification rather than the implementation they are shown, we rerun the agents on the Lite Set (Section 3.3) with the violating implementation as the reference. The first value of each cell in Table 2 is the main experiment restricted to the Lite Set. We found that every agent’s validation harnesses show a clear tendency to mirror the implementation the agent is given, and that showing the violating implementation as the reference does not help the agent detect it. Faithfulness falls by 19 to 31 points and detection by 3 to 33 points (Table 2). False alarms rise from 12–23% to 24–48% of tasks, and most of the increase comes from rejections of the gold implementation, which rise from 0–15% to 12–41%.

section: Showing the Violating Implementation as the Reference
text: We further investigate how each agent responds when its own validation harness rejects the reference. Under the violating reference, such a rejection indicates that the implementation violates the specification or that the checks are wrong, and each agent consistently reads nearly all of its own rejections. Claude Opus 5 and GLM-5.3 read them as faults of the checks. As a result, their validation harnesses often accept the implementation they were shown, and their detection rate drops sharply. Moreover, although instructed to follow the specification rather than the implementation, Claude Opus 5 in particular constructs a validation harness that accepts the violating implementation and rejects the gold implementation, showing a clear tendency to follow the reference over the specification. GPT-5.6-sol and DeepSeek-V4-Pro read the rejections as faults of the implementation. Their detection is almost unchanged, but the checks they construct include requirements the specification does not impose, and they now reject the gold implementation, confirming the over-assertion discussed in Section 4.3.

To test whether an unfaithful validation harness reflects an inability to write the right checks rather than a step budget too small to finish, we compare the 80-step results of the 291-task main experiment, restricted to the Lite Set, with new runs on the Lite Set within 30 and 50 steps. Figure 6 reports the effect of the budget on each agent. Between 30 and 50 steps, the two open-weight coding agents submit a validation harness on 95% of the tasks, up from 68% and 77%. However, a validation harness submitted within 50 steps is no more likely to detect the violation or to be faithful than one submitted within 30 steps. Among submitted harnesses, both agents become more faithful only between 50 and 80 steps, and for GLM-5.3 the gain comes from fewer false alarms rather than more detections. GPT-5.6-sol is insensitive to the budget at every rate, and the faithfulness of Claude Opus 5 barely changes at any budget.

We have introduced SpecGuardBench, a benchmark of 291 validation tasks drawn from 30 features of 13 real-world Python repositories, each providing an atomic natural language specification, a reference implementation, a violating implementation that the original test suite cannot catch, and valid alternative implementations that satisfy the specification while differing from the reference. The benchmark measures whether a coding agent can construct a validation harness whose checks are faithful to the specification and whose scenarios thoroughly exercise the relevant code, and our evaluation of four proprietary and open-weight coding agents shows that none does so on more than 63% of the tasks, mainly because their checks assert requirements the specification does not impose and mirror the reference implementation they are shown. We hope that SpecGuardBench will serve as a resource for measuring and improving the ability of coding agents to produce evidence of specification conformance, a capability on which benchmark evaluation, interactive coding workflows, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards all depend.

Despite advancing the evaluation of code validation against natural language specifications, SpecGuardBench has several limitations. First, its 291 tasks come from a subset of FeatureBench instances and are unevenly distributed across repositories; future work can extend the automated pipeline to more instances and other programming languages, given various coding benchmarks that provide high-quality specifications and code aligned with them. Second, faithfulness is estimated by execution against a finite set of implementations that satisfy or violate the specification, so a check that over-asserts in a way none of them exercises passes undetected; a larger, more diverse pool of alternatives would provide a more precise estimation of the faithfulness. Finally, the repositories and gold patches are public and may appear in training data, but the violating and alternative implementations are newly synthesized, which mitigates the risk of contamination.

In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist with language polishing and code debugging. These tools did not contribute to formulating the research ideas or the paper’s conclusions. The authors reviewed all AI-assisted content and are responsible for all statements, interpretations, results, and artifacts in this work.
To ensure reproducibility, our complete code, prompts, dataset, and detailed evaluation settings are available at github.com/coxhin/SpecGuardBench and huggingface.co/datasets/coxhin/SpecGuardBench.

IdeaLens: Detecting AI Ideas in Long-form Writing. While modern AI detectors identify who wrote the words, emerging policies on AI use increasingly hinge on a different question: who came up with the ideas? We introduce IdeaLens, a detector that identifies whether a document's ideas came from a human or AI (idea provenance), regardless of who wrote its words. To focus IdeaLens on ideas rather than prose, we represent documents as outlines: lists of items that each pair a discourse role with a brief, paraphrased description of the content, minimizing word-level overlap with the raw text. We train IdeaLens on 1M FineWeb documents with silver labels from Pangram, a prose provenance detector. Since the outlines are largely stripped of surface-level information, the labels must be fit mainly through the ideas. In a controlled study, IdeaLens's AI flag rate drops from 95% to 7% as models write from increasingly detailed human plans, while Pangram 4 still flags 92%; from AI-derived plans, IdeaLens stays above 96%. Conversely, on a new dataset of 50 stories that human authors wrote from AI-generated plans, IdeaLens flags 68% of the stories as AI, compared to 8% for Pangram 4.

On a comprehensive suite of 19 existing detection benchmarks, we show that IdeaLens maintains strong detection rates at low false positive rates, suggesting that ideas themselves provide a powerful discriminative signal, and its performance holds across domains, formats, and languages. Finally, we examine 90K predictions from IdeaLens to characterize systematic differences between human and AI ideation. We release our models and labeled datasets to facilitate future research on idea provenance detection.

In August 2026, the AI detector Pangram flagged a Wall Street Journal op-ed (druckenmiller2026bond) by billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller as 100% AI-generated, to which Druckenmiller unapologetically responded: “Of course I used AI” (stein2026druckenmiller). Paul Gigot, the editor of WSJ’s editorial pages, defended Druckenmiller by arguing that what matters is whether an op-ed “reflects an author’s original argument” and that “nobody can doubt that his op-ed is his genuine opinion” (wapo2026wsjai), though he provided no supporting evidence from the writing process (e.g., chat logs). Detectors like Pangram answer only who wrote the words (prose provenance), while Gigot’s defense, like many emerging policies on AI use in writing (springernature2026ai; iclr2027aipolicy), hinges on who came up with the ideas (idea provenance).

Idea and prose provenance can differ within the same document: a human can brainstorm the ideas for a document and ask an AI to write it, or vice versa. Prior work separates the two by building detectors around simulated human–AI collaborations, such as human writing polished by AI or AI writing run through humanizers (Bao2025DecouplingCA; li-etal-2026-beyond-final). These simulations are expensive to create at scale, and detectors trained on them may not transfer to real collaborations. In contrast, prose detectors like Pangram are trained on documents whose ideas and words come from the same source, which are cheap to collect: human text can be sampled from the pre-ChatGPT era, and AI text can be generated on demand.

We propose IdeaLens, an idea provenance detector that learns from the same cheap labels as prose detectors and can therefore be trained at their scale. Our key methodological contribution is to change the classifier’s input. Following the cognitive process model of writing (FlowerHayes1981; hayes2012), we define a document’s ideas as what its author decided to say (e.g., its claims, events, and organization), as opposed to the words used to say it. We represent these ideas as an outline whose items each consist of a discourse role paired with a short description of its content, paraphrased to remove the original wording (Figure 2). We train IdeaLens on a dataset of 1M outlines extracted from FineWeb (penedo2024the) documents, with silver labels from Pangram. As a control, we also train a separate model, ProseLens, with the same backbone, documents, and labels, but on the raw text instead of outlines. Despite identical supervision, the two behave in opposite ways whenever a document’s ideas and words come from different sources, showing that the outline forces IdeaLens to fit the labels through ideas rather than words.

IdeaLens detects human ideas in AI-generated documents. On a dataset of AI documents generated from increasingly detailed human plans, IdeaLens ’s flag rate falls from 94.9% with minimal human input to 6.8% with a full human outline, while remaining above 96% when plans come instead from AI. ProseLens and Pangram 4 flag 86.5% and 92.4% of documents generated from full human outlines. This behavior is further supported by results on 10 external benchmarks of AI polishing, paraphrasing, and rewriting, where IdeaLens flags 5.6% of documents on average, versus 46.0% for ProseLens and 52.0% for Pangram. IdeaLens detects AI ideas in human writing. The opposite scenario is harder to study: prior work touches on it only through AI text that people or models edit. To this end, we collect the first dataset of long-form documents that people wrote from scratch following AI ideas. Our dataset contains 50 stories, each written from an outline extracted from an AI-generated story, without access to the raw text of that story.

IdeaLens flags 68.0% of the human-written stories and 96.0% of the AI originals, while ProseLens and Pangram flag all of the AI original stories but only 0% and 8.0% of the human-written stories, respectively (Figure 1). Despite not seeing the raw text, IdeaLens rivals the strongest open-source detector on conventional benchmarks and transfers across 24 languages. On 19 evaluations that require separating fully AI (ideas and writing) from fully human documents, IdeaLens flags 91.1% of AI documents on average with a false positive rate of 0.6%, compared to 81.8% and 0.2% for EditLens-3B, the strongest existing open-weight detector. ProseLens is even stronger here (98.9% and 0.7%), rivaling the commercial Pangram 4 at its published threshold (97.3% and 0.3%). Although trained only on English, IdeaLens transfers to 24 languages through English outlines, detecting 95.3% of AI documents on average at a false positive rate of 0.1% compared with 82.5% and 0.0% for ProseLens. IdeaLens flags ideas whose details could apply to anything or can’t be verified.

Based on an analysis of 90K item-level predictions, we find that IdeaLens scores ideas as more AI when they cite numbers or methods without the context needed to check them, or claim more than their evidence supports. IdeaLens scores ideas as more human when they include specific sources that a reader could look up or discuss downsides and open problems.
We publicly release both IdeaLens and ProseLens along with their training data, the evaluation datasets that we create, and our idea-level analysis.

The fundamental challenge in training an idea detector is that we have no large-scale labels for who came up with a document’s ideas, only for who wrote its prose. Thus, we train on prose labels while replacing each document with an outline that preserves its ideas but not its wording.
