To create these outlines (Figure 2), we identify discourse roles typical of each writing format, use them to extract an outline of each document, and paraphrase the outline to remove wording copied from the raw document. We train IdeaLens to predict each document’s Pangram label from its paraphrased outline, while ProseLens predicts the same labels from the raw document.

section: Web documents with silver labels from Pangram.
text: We sample a 1M subset from WildAI (russell2026aitoken), which labels documents from FineWeb (penedo2024the) with WebOrganizer (wettig2025weborganizer) formats and topics along with authorship labels from Pangram 3.3.2 (thai2026editlens). We focus on long-form writing, selecting English documents of at least 500 words that belong to one of eight relevant WebOrganizer formats (), and that Pangram labels as either human-written or AI-generated. We assume that the ideas and prose in these documents share the same source, which enables us to use them as noisy silver labels for idea provenance. We discard documents that Pangram labels as mixed, since AI only wrote part of these texts and thus idea provenance is unclear. We split WildOutlines, the full corpus of 1M documents into training (\sim 842k), validation (\sim 30k), calibration (\sim 80k, human documents only) and test (\sim 50k) sets ().

Cognitive models of writing (FlowerHayes1981; hayes2012) separate the act of planning from the act of translating these plans into prose. To build a document representation of the former without the latter, we turn to discourse theory, which describes the roles a passage plays within the broader context of the document, for example through rhetorical structure theory (MANNTHOMPSON+1988+243+281; Mann2006). We represent a document as an outline: an ordered list of discourse roles, each paired with brief descriptions of how those roles are implemented in the document. For example, the op-ed displayed in Figure 2 contains 17 items, starting with an Event Account of a Treasury announcement followed by an Evaluation of the market’s reaction. Many of these roles are format-specific (swales1990genre; SunWangXiong+2021+599+624; van2019macrostructures); for instance, creative writing uses different roles than nonfiction. Thus, we induce separate role sets for each of the eight formats in our dataset ().
We build a training dataset, WildOutlines, for IdeaLens by converting documents to outlines in three automated steps:

Role induction: We adapt the TopicGPT framework (pham2024topicgptpromptbasedtopicmodeling) by prompting GPT-5.6 Sol (openai2026gpt56) to propose base roles for each format given a detailed description of that format. Then, we label outlines of 200 documents in that format using those roles, while asking the model to invent new roles as needed. Afterwards, we deduplicate and prune the resulting role set (e.g., to 42 roles for nonfiction); more details in §. Outline extraction: Given a document, we prompt Gemini 3.7 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro (gemini2023; gemini37flash; gemini31pro) with its format’s role set (and few-shot demonstrations from the much more powerful Claude Fable 5 (anthropic2026fable5)) to produce an outline of the document’s ideas in order, where each item consists of a role and a short content description. Paraphrasing: Extracted outlines can copy phrasing from the original document, which a model could use as a stylistic shortcut to the label (i.e., human wording can leak into the outlines). Therefore, we prompt Gemini 3.1 Pro (gemini31pro) to paraphrase each outline. This pushes all outlines toward a homogeneous, AI-like style: for human-written documents, the fraction of outline text that Pangram 4 labels as human drops from 8.5% to 0.3% ().

Meaning is still preserved (), as paraphrased outlines have a cosine similarity of 0.93 with the originally extracted outlines (vs. 0.39 for unrelated outlines) and 0.76 with the source document (vs. 0.26). We paraphrase only for training, to keep the model from learning style; at inference, IdeaLens sees the unparaphrased outline.

Both of our models start from a backbone of Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B (nvidia2026nemotron35lightning), fine-tuned for one epoch with LoRA (hu2022lora) using Tinker (tml2026tinker). We threshold each model’s probability that a document is AI-generated at a 1% false positive rate on our calibration split. The only difference between the two models is that IdeaLens is trained on paraphrased outlines, whereas ProseLens is trained on the original documents. Since they share their backbone, training documents, and labels, any difference in their behavior is a direct result of transforming the input into our outline representation.

We evaluate IdeaLens and ProseLens against 17 existing detectors, including the state-of-the-art Pangram 4, on 19 external benchmarks and three datasets that we create ourselves: IdeaShift, IdeaShift-X, and TwiceTold. These datasets cover all four quadrants in Figure 1: documents with shared provenance (fully human or fully AI) as well as documents with mixed provenance (human ideas and AI prose, or AI ideas and human prose). Idea detectors should achieve high accuracy in all four quadrants, while prose detectors should fail in the two mixed quadrants.

We report accuracy at detecting AI ideas, which we define as the percentage of documents whose predicted label (AI or human) agrees with the source of their ideas. Our baselines include Pangram 4 (glickenhaus2026pangram4technicalreport), EditLens-Llama-3.2-3B (thai2026editlens), Fast-DetectGPT (bao2024fastdetectgpt), Binoculars (hans2024spotting), MELD (li2026meldmultitaskequilibratedlearning) and Desklib (desklib2025aitextdetector). For IdeaLens, ProseLens, and EditLens, we set a global threshold across all formats at 1% FPR on our calibration set. We binarize Pangram’s ternary labels (AI, AI-assisted, human) following its tech report, and other baselines use their default thresholds.

Of the 19 external detection benchmarks (see § for full list), 14 contain documents with shared provenance (fully human or fully AI). We evaluate accuracy on these documents and on our in-domain test set of 50K documents from our Pangram-labeled web corpus. We also measure FPR on a set of 10K documents from C4 (c4dataset), which was created prior to ChatGPT’s release and is thus much more likely to be human-written than our silver-labeled test set. Finally, 10 external benchmarks also contain documents written by humans but edited by an AI (e.g., via paraphrasing, polishing, or rewriting), which we use as instances of human ideas rendered in AI prose; this includes OpAI-Bench (Bsharat2026OperationGuidedPH) and GEDE (Gehring2025LimitsOL).

section: IdeaShift: AI writing from increasingly detailed human plans.
text: A common collaborative writing pattern is for a human to give an AI their ideas via a prompt, which it uses to write a document from scratch (10.1145/3698061.3726910). Only two external datasets we evaluate on contain instances of this pattern (saha2026policies; Gehring2025LimitsOL), and neither controls the amount of human input, so it is unclear how much of the final document’s ideas came from the human. Thus, we create IdeaShift from 500 seed documents (both human-written and AI-generated) sampled from our in-domain test set. For each seed document, GPT-5.6 Sol (openai2026gpt56) writes five progressively more detailed prompts: the level-0 prompt contains only the topic (e.g., “Write a dining and lifestyle blog post reviewing a restaurant visit.”), while the level-5 prompt contains the full outline extracted as per § 2 with instructions to add nothing else to it. GPT-5.6 models then generate a new document for each prompt. Since all of the prose in IdeaShift is AI-generated, prose detectors should flag every document as AI, and an idea detector should do the same for AI seeds. However, on documents generated from human seeds, idea detectors should flag fewer and fewer documents as the prompts carry more of the human plan.

section: TwiceTold: humans writing from AI plans.
text: We are also interested in the reverse pattern: a human obtains ideas from an AI and then writes the document themselves. Existing datasets approximate this pattern with AI-generated text that humans edit or AI tools humanize, but these edited documents are still largely AI-generated and thus do not cleanly separate idea and prose provenance. To fill this gap, we create TwiceTold, a dataset with 50 stories written from scratch by humans given only the outline of a 500-word story generated by GPT-5.6 Sol (see § for more details). Prose detectors should label these stories as human, while idea detectors should label them as AI. We also include the 50 original AI stories, which all detectors should label as AI.

section: IdeaShift-X: idea detection in multilingual documents.
text: While prose detectors rely on language-specific features (e.g., vocabulary choice, sentence structure), IdeaLens uses an LLM extractor that can generate English outlines for documents in any language. Thus, even though IdeaLens is trained only on English documents, we can apply it to documents in other languages without any additional training. To test this, we create IdeaShift-X by sampling 10K human-authored documents in 24 languages () from FineWeb2 (penedo2025fineweb), to measure FPR across different languages. For each, we follow the IdeaShift protocol to generate AI versions in the original language at level 0 (AI ideas) and level 5 (human ideas).

section: IdeaLens detects AI ideas, not AI prose
text: footnote 11 summarizes our main results across 51 evaluation splits from 22 benchmarks, where each point is a detector plotted by its aggregate idea detection accuracy on documents with shared vs. mixed provenance. IdeaLens is the only detector that achieves high accuracy in both shared (95.3%) and mixed (81.3%) settings. ProseLens and Pangram 4 are extremely accurate on documents with shared provenance (99.1% and 98.5%, respectively) but fail to identify the source of a document’s ideas in mixed settings (25.4% and 25.9%). Since ProseLens has the same backbone, training documents, and training labels as IdeaLens, this highlights the impact of our outline representation, which a ModernBERT-based pair (warner-etal-2025-smarter) replicates with a different backbone. IdeaLens also transfers unexpectedly well to raw text inputs at test time, exhibiting high shared provenance accuracy and substantially higher mixed provenance accuracy than ProseLens.

section: IdeaLens detects idea provenance on IdeaShift.
text: As the human plan in the prompts from IdeaShift becomes more detailed, IdeaLens ’s flag rate drops from 94.9% at level 0 to 6.8% at level 5 (4(a)). In contrast, ProseLens and Pangram 4 flag 86–100% of documents regardless of the level of human ideation. When the plans come from AI instead of humans, IdeaLens consistently flags more than 96% of documents at every level (), showing that it is sensitive to idea provenance rather than level of prompt detail. Finally, we observe that the biggest drop in flag rate occurs between levels 3 and 4, which is when the prompts begin including outlines with content in addition to structural role information ().

section: IdeaLens is insensitive to AI rewording of human ideas.
text: Aggregated over 12 benchmarks where AI makes surface-level changes to human text (e.g., polishing, paraphrasing), IdeaLens labels 94.7% of documents as human, compared to 50.7% for ProseLens and 43.8% for Pangram 4 (). In GEDE (Gehring2025LimitsOL), IdeaLens flags only 0.5% of human essays as AI after minor corrections made by an LLM (vs Pangram 4’s 54.6% and ProseLens ’s 45.8%) and 2.6% after a rewrite preserving the original content (vs Pangram 4’s 94.3% and ProseLens ’s 77.1%). In HART (Bao2025DecouplingCA), IdeaLens flags 4.9% of LLM paraphrases of human documents, compared to 42.8% by Pangram 4 and 44.5% by ProseLens. In the Academic Integrity dataset (Karr2026WhyAD), it flags 8.2% of abstracts that an LLM generated from a human-written reference abstract, compared to Pangram 4’s 96.4% and ProseLens ’s 83.9%.

section: IdeaLens detects AI ideas in TwiceTold ’s human-written prose.
text: IdeaLens flags 68% (95% CI 54–79%) of TwiceTold stories as AI, compared to 0% for ProseLens and 8% for Pangram 4. All detectors are reliable at flagging the AI-generated original stories (96% for IdeaLens and 100% for ProseLens and Pangram), but only IdeaLens sticks with its prediction for the majority of the human stories, even though the prose is completely different (4(b)). The stories that IdeaLens marks as human generally follow their outlines while adding new events or world-building details: 12 out of 16 errors are on stories that contain speculative or fantasy elements.

section: From ideas alone, IdeaLens outperforms the strongest existing open detectors.
text: On 19 evaluation splits with shared provenance, IdeaLens detects 91.1% of AI documents at 0.6% FPR compared with 81.8% at 0.2% FPR for EditLens-3B, the strongest existing open baseline (), with both calibrated to a 1% target. Training on full text does better: ProseLens reaches 98.9% at 0.7% FPR, rivaling Pangram 4 (97.3% at 0.3%) and making it the strongest open detector in our evaluations. To cleanly measure FPR, we collect 10K pre-ChatGPT documents from C4: IdeaLens flags only 0.01% compared to 0% for ProseLens and Pangram 4 (§). Against humanization and adversarial attacks, IdeaLens ’s detection rate drops 6.4 points on average, between Pangram’s 4.9 and ProseLens ’s 10.6 (). One weakness of IdeaLens is DIPPER paraphrasing (krishna2023paraphrasing) in GEDE (Gehring2025LimitsOL), where it detects 77.6% versus 97.1% for ProseLens and 95.1% for Pangram 4; we suspect this attack changes content as well as style (§).

section: IdeaLens detects idea provenance across 24 languages on IdeaShift-X.
text: IdeaShift-X contains documents generated in 24 different languages, and IdeaLens flags 95.3% of the level-0 documents but only 0.7% of the level-5 documents despite being trained only on English. These results show that signatures of AI ideas are largely invariant to the language in which they are written. In contrast, prose detectors like ProseLens and Pangram 4 flag 82–85% of level-0 and 45–62% of level-5 documents, and this gap between IdeaLens and these detectors widens in low-resource languages like Tamil and Amharic. Additionally, IdeaLens achieves a low FPR on non-English human-written documents: on 10K pre-ChatGPT documents in these 24 languages sampled from FineWeb2 (penedo2025fineweb), it flags only 0.1% as AI ().

DeclineCraft: A RAG Abstention Benchmark for Jointly Measuring Combined Retrieval and Parametric Knowledge. Reliable retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires recognizing when neither retrieved documents nor parametric knowledge supports an answer. We introduce DeclineCraft, a dynamic abstention benchmark whose unanswerable questions target Minecraft feature additions after a corpus cut-off, with audits of possible parametric exposure. Later cut-offs support evaluation of future models. Across 27 LLMs, we measure Correct Abstention Rate (CAR; how often models acknowledge insufficient knowledge on unanswerable questions), Answerable Attempt Rate and Answer Accuracy. We find that (1) single-shot retrieval significantly raises CAR in 38 of 40 configurations (model and thinking setting) versus no retrieval. (2) Iterative RAG, in which the model self-assesses its context and can request up to two further retrieval rounds, significantly lowers CAR versus single-shot RAG in 30 of 40 configurations (mean 46.4%), with little change in Answer Accuracy (68.5% to 69.3%). Adding query rewriting and reranking to hybrid (dense & sparse) retrieval lowers CAR for all 12 models tested. (3) Larger models answer more accurately (Spearman $ρ= +0.60$ with total parameters), but neither model size nor release date shows a significant association with CAR.

(4) Without retrieval, enabling thinking on the same weights lowers CAR significantly for 8 of 13 models (by 14% points on average), and the responses shift from acknowledged uncertainty to premise denial.

A player fleeing skeletons in Minecraft Java Edition asks an assistant whether copper horse armor would let a horse survive three arrows. Answering requires combining the rules for arrow damage, horse health points, and the protection supplied by this particular armor in a specific game edition. Suppose copper horse armor was introduced after both the model’s training and its retrieval corpus. Passages about horses, skeletons and other armor types may be relevant, yet the key fact about the horse’s armor is missing. The assistant must acknowledge this knowledge gap. For instance, when asked for the armor’s protection, Qwen3 32B with thinking enabled instead declares: “Since ‘copper horse armor’ is not a recognized item in the game, it would provide 0 armor points. If you meant golden horse armor, it provides 7 armor points.” (Table 1). This response treats a presupposition it cannot verify as false (Kim et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2023), a premise denial, then substitutes a different item for the one the user asked about.

For RAG systems, recognizing such a knowledge gap must remain part of the decision to answer as retrieval and thinking proceed. This matters most when the answers are consumed by AI agents, which may not notice that a premise denial is unsupported by the model’s available knowledge. A human user, by contrast, may know that a new law was just passed, or that copper horse armor was added to Minecraft, when posing their query. Evaluation must therefore distinguish an admission of missing knowledge from a premise denial that the model cannot verify.

Distinguishing abstention from premise denial matters for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) wherever documentation and the world it describes can change (Barnett et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024). RAG systems can combine retrieved documents with parametric knowledge, the information stored in a model’s weights (Lewis et al., 2020). Unless explicitly asked about a historical version, a system should allow for questions about a time after both the corpus cut-off and the model’s knowledge cut-off. An item absent from an earlier version may exist when the user asks about it; absence from the available sources does not establish present-day nonexistence. A reliable system should therefore abstain when these sources together cannot support an answer, identifying the knowledge gap, without categorically rejecting a premise it cannot verify.

Evaluating this behavior is challenging: an answer missing from retrieved passages may still be available in the model’s weights. Context-grounded benchmarks instruct models to answer only from supplied documents (Song et al., 2025; Ming et al., 2025; Muhamed et al., 2026). UAEval4RAG’s out-of-database questions include facts from newer news absent from its database, under a database-grounded answering protocol (Peng et al., 2025). AbstentionBench evaluates, without retrieval, questions whose answers changed after the models’ knowledge cut-offs (Kirichenko et al., 2025). Our study combines a time-partitioned corpus, whose later part postdates the models’ knowledge cut-offs, with related but insufficient retrieved evidence, and scores premise denial separately from acknowledged uncertainty.

To evaluate this setting, we introduce DeclineCraft, a dynamic benchmark of 700 answerable and 300 unanswerable questions built from the update history of Minecraft (Minecraft Wiki Contributors, 2026). The interacting game mechanics of Minecraft and its feature additions over time create facts that can only be learned from new wiki pages: e.g., knowing how existing armor works does not establish the protection of a newly introduced material against a pre-existing weapon. We construct a retrieval corpus (C_{\text{pre}}) from wiki pages as they stood at a corpus cut-off and generate unanswerable questions from pages created later (C_{\text{post}}). Answerable questions use the same generation pipeline as unanswerable ones, with their target facts drawn from the earlier corpus (Figure 1). We audit our unanswerable questions against the earlier documentation. To assess possible parametric exposure, we use published knowledge cut-offs and a leakage audit. The leakage audit tests whether models answer the unanswerable questions correctly without retrieval. The temporal design establishes a knowledge gap when the required facts postdate both parametric knowledge and the RAG corpus. The benchmark is dynamic: it can be regenerated with a later corpus cut-off as new game content becomes available.

We evaluate 27 LLMs from several families under three retrieval conditions, with thinking enabled and disabled where possible. Single-shot RAG retrieves five wiki passages (chunks) once, combining keyword and embedding search. Iterative RAG lets the model request up to two further retrieval rounds when it judges the chunks insufficient (Section 4.2). We measure Correct Abstention Rate (CAR) as the share of unanswerable questions on which a model acknowledges that it lacks the answer. Our experiments yield three main findings: Retrieval helps models recognize missing knowledge, but additions to the retrieval pipeline erode that benefit. Single-shot RAG raises CAR for almost every configuration. Iterative RAG, ten instead of five chunks per query, and query rewriting with reranking each lower it again (Section 4.2). Newer and larger models do not reliably acknowledge knowledge gaps. CAR has no significant association with release date or parameter count. Recent families such as Qwen3.5 and Qwen3-Next often deny the existence of the item or feature mentioned in the question (Section 4.3). Thinking can replace uncertainty with premise denial. Without retrieval, enabling thinking significantly lowers CAR for 8 of the 13 models with switchable thinking and raises it for none.
The lost abstentions most often become premise denials. With retrieval, the effect of thinking differs by model (Section 4.4).

SQuAD 2.0 evaluates abstention when a passage lacks the answer (Rajpurkar et al., 2018). Selective QA studies when to withhold answers to control error among answered questions (Kamath et al., 2020). R-Tuning trains models to acknowledge gaps in parametric knowledge (Zhang et al., 2024), while Feng et al. (2024) use collaboration between models to detect knowledge gaps and decide whether to abstain.

AbstentionBench includes stale-knowledge questions evaluated without retrieval (Kirichenko et al., 2025). RefusalBench perturbs question–passage pairs to test context-grounded abstention (Muhamed et al., 2026). On DeclineCraft, its context-only answer prompt makes models decline many answerable questions (Appendix B). Among its six categories, UAEval4RAG generates out-of-database questions from recent news and evaluates abstention when the database lacks support (Peng et al., 2025). Our setting permits both retrieved and parametric knowledge and distinguishes acknowledged uncertainty from premise denial, following (QA) 2 ’s distinction between false and unverifiable assumptions (Kim et al., 2023).

Mallen et al. (2023) show that retrieval helps answer questions about less popular facts that models struggle to recall. Joren et al. (2025) study whether the retrieved context alone suffices to answer, and how models behave when it does not. Their evaluation uses answerable questions; DeclineCraft adds questions designed to expose gaps in both sources. FLARE retrieves during generation using predicted upcoming sentences (Jiang et al., 2023); iterative RAG uses prompted self-assessment of context sufficiency (Appendix E). Related but insufficient passages can mislead models (Cuconasu et al., 2024), and prior work studies how further retrieval affects abstention (Xie et al., 2026).
Appendix L discusses uncertainty estimation, knowledge conflicts, temporal datasets, broader RAG evaluation and Minecraft-based evaluation.

section: DeclineCraft: A Dynamic Benchmark for Knowledge-Aware Abstention
text: DeclineCraft evaluates whether a RAG system recognizes when its parametric knowledge and retrieved documents together cannot support an answer. The questions use real Minecraft content, including additions documented after the corpus cut-off. When the required facts also postdate the model’s knowledge cut-off, the system should acknowledge the missing information. We distinguish such a response from premise denial, in which the model asserts, without support, that an item or feature named in the question does not exist. The issue is whether the model has enough knowledge to justify that claim, even if it happens to be correct. Table 1 shows an example of each, alongside a third outcome: an unsupported answer.
We collect two corpora from the Minecraft Wiki (minecraft.wiki), using 31 March 2025 as the corpus cut-off:

Pre-cut-off corpus (C_{\text{pre}}): The latest revision of each wiki page at or before the corpus cut-off: 2,642 pages split into 11,612 chunks as detailed in Appendix D. This is the only corpus available to the evaluated retrieval pipelines. By default they use a hybrid retriever that combines keyword (BM25) and embedding similarity (Appendix E). Post-cut-off corpus (C_{\text{post}}): Pages created after the corpus cut-off, stored at their latest revision when scraped on 8 September 2026: 170 pages split into 712 chunks. These supply facts for generating unanswerable questions.

We exclude pages that existed before the corpus cut-off from C_{\text{post}}, even if they were later updated, to focus on missing knowledge about later additions to the game. Appendix D provides details on data collection and filtering.

Excluding a fact from retrieval does not by itself exclude it from parametric knowledge. Temporal separation requires the fact to postdate the model’s knowledge cut-off as well as the corpus cut-off. We report each model’s knowledge cut-off when available in Table 11. Our leakage audit therefore asks models the 300 unanswerable questions without retrieval and scores their answers against reference answers that an oracle model writes from C_{\text{post}}. A model that often answers correctly may have seen the post-cut-off pages in training (Figure 19).

Figure 1 traces the generation of one answerable question (top, blue) and one unanswerable question (bottom, orange) through the same five steps. A generator LLM, Qwen3.5 122B-A10B, performs every writing step, each with its own prompt (Appendix J.1). Scenario. We draw three random chunks from C_{\text{pre}} and give them to the generator. It writes a player scenario of under 30 words about one or two related concepts in these chunks. Target chunk. For an answerable question, we embed the scenario with Qwen3-Embedding-8B and retrieve the ten chunks with the most similar embeddings in terms of cosine similarity from C_{\text{pre}}. For an unanswerable question, we follow the same procedure, except the chunks are retrieved from C_{\text{post}}. We drop chunks from technical pages and, for an answerable question, the scenario’s own three chunks. The target chunk is drawn uniformly at random from the five highest-ranked chunks that remain. Fact. The generator lists up to six facts that appear in the target chunk but not in the comparison text. For an answerable question, the comparison text is the scenario’s three chunks, so the scenario does not already contain the fact.

For an unanswerable question, it is the three C_{\text{pre}} chunks most similar to the target chunk, so the fact is new relative to C_{\text{pre}}. One listed fact is chosen uniformly at random. Question. The generator receives the scenario, the fact and the target chunk. It writes one candidate question from the player’s perspective whose answer is the fact, and the question is appended to the scenario. Verification. A separate LLM checks each candidate against C_{\text{pre}} (Section 3.3). Appendix G compares Qwen3.5 122B-A10B with two other generators on the same pipeline; we chose to use Qwen3.5 122B-A10B since the resulting answerable and unanswerable questions were the hardest to tell apart by wording alone. Appendix F details the algorithms, and Appendix C shows a generated question of each kind.

Scenarios make the benchmark harder in a realistic way, because they lead retrieval to familiar contexts with insufficient information. For 71.3% of the 300 unanswerable questions, the hybrid retriever returns at least one of the scenario’s own source chunks among its five retrieved chunks (Figure 24). Such a chunk is related to the scenario but says nothing about the missing fact. Removing the scenario raises Correct Abstention Rate for all 10 models tested with single-shot RAG (Section A.4).

Generation can go wrong in three ways: An answerable question whose answer is not in C_{\text{pre}}; An unanswerable question whose fact is already in C_{\text{pre}}, for example because a page created after the corpus cut-off restates an older fact; Many questions drawn from the same few pages. The first two mislabel a question, and the third lets a few pages dominate the benchmark. Three steps remove them.

A separate verifier LLM, Gemma 4 31B, checks each candidate scenario and question, so that no model judges its own questions. For each query, the verifier reads the 10 C_{\text{pre}} chunks retrieved with hybrid retrieval and reranking. Reranking uses a second model to reorder the retrieved chunks by their relevance to the query. An answerable candidate is kept only if both of the following hold: (1) the scenario does not state or directly imply the target fact, so it does not give the answer away; and (2) the chunks retrieved for the question contain the information needed to answer it. An unanswerable candidate is kept only if both of the following hold: (1) the C_{\text{pre}} chunks retrieved for the target fact do not state or directly imply it; and (2) the chunks retrieved for the question do not answer it. Appendix J gives the verifier’s prompts.

We reviewed all unanswerable questions against C_{\text{pre}} and dropped 21 malformed candidates (claiming fake in-game items like “steel” and fabricated game mechanics like “attacked by a creeper with a diamond sword”). We found no examples of questions which had answers in C_{\text{pre}}. We keep questions that can be answered only by assuming that an older mechanic carries over to a new item, such as whether new copper tools accept an enchantment that iron tools already accept: such a guess may be right, but neither C_{\text{pre}} nor the model’s training establishes it, so the model should still abstain.

The number of chunks per C_{\text{post}} page varies widely (median 2, up to 64), so without limits the questions concentrate on a few pages. We therefore allow at most 2 questions per chunk and at most 10 per page. We also drop candidates whose question sentence has a novelty cue (“new,” “recently”, a month or a year), which would reveal a post-cut-off subject.

The final benchmark contains 700 answerable and 300 unanswerable questions. For the 700 answerable questions, the default hybrid retriever returns the target chunk among its five retrieved chunks in 91.0% of cases. Answerability in the corpus therefore does not guarantee that the LLM receives the target passage.

In what follows, we introduce our results over 27 LLMs evaluated on DeclineCraft without retrieval, with single-shot RAG and with iterative RAG. We assess whether models acknowledge missing knowledge on unanswerable questions while attempting and correctly answering answerable questions. After describing the evaluation setup and metrics (Section 4.1), we compare retrieval conditions (Section 4.2), examine the associations of Correct Abstention Rate with model size and release date (Section 4.3), and measure the effect of enabling thinking (Section 4.4). Throughout these results, we distinguish acknowledged uncertainty from premise denial. Appendix A reports the results for every model and further analyses.

We use the 700 answerable and 300 unanswerable questions constructed in Section 3. A configuration is one model with one thinking setting. 13 models have switchable thinking (the same weights run with thinking enabled or disabled); running both gives 40 configurations per retrieval condition. Appendix H gives the API settings and statistical tests; Appendix K lists the models and their knowledge cut-offs, and Tables 2 and 3 report every model and thinking setting under each condition.

Correct Abstention Rate (CAR) is the percentage of unanswerable questions on which the model acknowledges insufficient knowledge without a premise denial or an unsupported answer. An LLM response judge labels each response as an abstention, a premise denial or an attempted answer (Appendix I). A premise denial followed by a guessed answer still counts as a premise denial, not a correct abstention. Premise denials of answerable questions count as attempts. Appendix I repeats the analyses under a lenient rule that also counts premise denials as abstentions: the retrieval findings hold, whereas the thinking and release-date findings change. Answerable Attempt Rate is the percentage of answerable questions the model attempts to answer. Answer Accuracy averages the scores of three LLM accuracy judges from different families on the answerable questions: 1 for correct, 0.5 for partly correct and 0 for incorrect answers or abstentions, against reference answers that an oracle model writes from each question’s source pages. Outputs that exhaust the output budget of 16,000 tokens, including thinking, without a final answer (1.9% of all answers; Appendix H) are excluded from the two rates and score 0 in Answer Accuracy. Appendix I details the scoring.

Three annotators independently label 70 responses and score 30 attempted answers for accuracy. The response judge matches the human majority on 96% of response labels; disagreements mainly concern an abstention sentence followed by a premise denial. For accuracy, mean judge–human agreement is \kappa=0.66, versus 0.42 between humans (quadratic-weighted Cohen’s \kappa). Samples are balanced across response labels and accuracy-score bins; Appendix I gives details and confidence intervals.

section: Retrieval Raises Correct Abstention Rate; Iterative RAG Lowers It Again
text: Single-shot RAG retrieves five chunks from C_{\text{pre}} using the default hybrid retriever (BM25 and dense retrieval, combined by reciprocal rank fusion; see details in Appendix E). Figure 2 plots Correct Abstention Rate (y-axis) against the retrieval condition (x-axis) for the subset of 11 models also evaluated with ten retrieved chunks; gray lines show individual models, and the blue line shows their mean. Across all 40 configurations, mean Correct Abstention Rate rises from 17.1% without retrieval to 56.4% with single-shot RAG. Relative to no retrieval, 38 configurations show a statistically significant increase in Correct Abstention Rate, and none shows a statistically significant decrease (q<0.05; see Appendix H for details on statistical analysis).

section: Retrieval Raises Correct Abstention Rate; Iterative RAG Lowers It Again
text: Our iterative RAG implementation uses prompted self-assessment, inspired by Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024) and query-level self-evaluation (Xie et al., 2026). In our experiments, it starts with the same five chunks and lets the model request up to two additional retrieval rounds when it judges the context insufficient (Algorithm 4; Appendix H). Relative to single-shot RAG, mean Correct Abstention Rate falls to 46.4%, with significant decreases in 30 of the same 40 configurations and no significant increases. Mean Answer Accuracy on the answerable questions changes from 68.5% to 69.3%, compared with 24.3% without retrieval. Figure 8 in the appendix shows both metrics for each configuration. Thus, in this pipeline, further retrieval lowers CAR while adding little accuracy.

section: Retrieval Raises Correct Abstention Rate; Iterative RAG Lowers It Again
text: The Sulfur Cube example in Appendix A.9 illustrates this failure: GPT-OSS 120B correctly abstains with single-shot RAG, then uses a retrieved passage about Magma Cubes to answer about the unfamiliar entity after further retrieval. The example shows how relevant-looking context can support an unwarranted substitution; the aggregate comparison does not isolate which component of iterative RAG causes the decrease, and the reflection prompt itself asks whether the context suffices to answer rather than whether to answer at all.

section: Retrieval Raises Correct Abstention Rate; Iterative RAG Lowers It Again
text: Appendix A.2 examines how retrieving five versus ten chunks affects Correct Abstention Rate for 11 models (Figure 2) and discusses why iterative RAG cannot isolate the effect of follow-up queries from that of additional context. Appendix A.3 compares six retrieval pipelines (Figure 3): adding both query rewriting and reranking to hybrid retrieval lowers Correct Abstention Rate for all 12 tested models. Appendix A.4 details the scenario-removal ablation introduced in Section 3.2: removing scenarios from both retrieval queries and model inputs raises Correct Abstention Rate for all 10 tested models under single-shot RAG.

section: Correct Abstention Rate Has No Significant Association with Size or Release Date
text: Under single-shot RAG, neither total parameters (Spearman \rho=-0.24, p=0.31) nor active parameters (\rho=+0.21, p=0.37) has a significant association with Correct Abstention Rate across the 20 open-weight models. Active parameters are those used for each token. A mixture-of-experts model uses only part of its total parameters for each token. Figure 5 (left) shows the comparison with total parameters, with thinking enabled where switchable; Figure 12 in the appendix shows active parameters. Release month likewise has no significant association across all 27 models (\rho=-0.16, p=0.42; Figure 5, right), or across the 14 families when selecting the model with the highest Correct Abstention Rate in each (\rho=-0.22, p=0.45). On the same open-weight models, Answer Accuracy is positively associated with total parameters (\rho=+0.60, p=0.005; Figure 13 in the appendix). Thus, the observed accuracy gains with scale do not establish better recognition of missing knowledge.

section: Correct Abstention Rate Has No Significant Association with Size or Release Date
text: The response categories matter for interpreting this result. Recent families such as Qwen3.5 and Qwen3-Next frequently respond with premise denial: they assert, without support, that the queried item does not exist. Figures 17 and 18 in the appendix separate premise denials from abstentions and attempted answers, by family and model. As the copper horse armor responses in Table 1 illustrate, a premise denial can also lead to a numerical answer or the substitution of a familiar item. Such a response does not establish recognition of a knowledge gap, even if its claim was true at the corpus cut-off.

section: Thinking Lowers Correct Abstention Rate Without Retrieval
text: Figure 4 compares thinking disabled (gray dots) and enabled (arrowheads) for the 13 models with switchable thinking, holding weights fixed, without retrieval (left) and with single-shot RAG (right). Orange indicates lower CAR, blue higher; faded arrows mark changes that are not statistically significant.

section: Thinking Lowers Correct Abstention Rate Without Retrieval
text: Without retrieval, we observe 8 statistically significant decreases in CAR and no statistically significant increases. Per question, enabling thinking without retrieval turns abstentions into premise denials more often than the reverse for 9 models (Figure 25). Appendix A.5 shows that Answer Accuracy can improve while CAR falls.

section: Thinking Lowers Correct Abstention Rate Without Retrieval
text: Across 40 single-shot RAG configurations, Answer Accuracy and CAR have no statistically significant unadjusted association (Spearman \rho=-0.28, p=0.08); Appendix A.6 reports a negative association after adjusting for release date.

section: Thinking Lowers Correct Abstention Rate Without Retrieval
text: With single-shot RAG, 33 of 40 configurations have both a higher CAR and a higher Answerable Attempt Rate than without retrieval (Appendix A.7).

Some models are fine-tuned specifically for abstention, such as Trust-Align 3B, Trust-Align 7B (Song et al., 2025), and Abstain-R1 3B (Zhai et al., 2026). We evaluate these three models against their corresponding base model (Appendix A.8). Figure 7 shows that fine-tuning raises CAR and lowers Answerable Attempt Rate. With single-shot RAG, fine-tuning raises CAR from 35.7% (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) to 89.3% (Trust-Align 3B), but Trust-Align 3B attempts only 43.6% of answerable questions. These models lie on or near the Pareto trade-off frontier of the other configurations, the highest CAR that they reach at or above each Answerable Attempt Rate. They trade a higher CAR for lower Answerable Attempt Rate and Answer Accuracy by abstaining on answerable questions that other models answer correctly (Figure 7). Fine-tuning moves these three models along the trade-off frontier rather than beyond it.

We introduced DeclineCraft, a dynamic benchmark built from dated Minecraft Wiki pages to evaluate recognition of missing knowledge and distinguish acknowledged uncertainty from premise denial. Across 27 LLMs, single-shot RAG produces statistically significant increases in Correct Abstention Rate in 38 of 40 configurations relative to no retrieval; our prompted iterative RAG pipeline produces statistically significant decreases in 30 of the same configurations relative to single-shot RAG, with little change in Answer Accuracy. Under single-shot RAG, Correct Abstention Rate has no statistically significant association with model size or release date. Enabling thinking produces statistically significant decreases in Correct Abstention Rate for 8 of 13 models without retrieval, with no statistically significant increases; its effect with single-shot RAG varies across models.

These results motivate evaluating and training recognition of missing knowledge explicitly. A premise denial does not establish this recognition when the model cannot verify its claim. Future work should improve judgments of evidence sufficiency across retrieval rounds and test whether these findings extend to other domains with dated documentation.
While DeclineCraft provides a controlled environment to evaluate the temporal adaptability and abstention capabilities of RAG-equipped LLMs, we identify several limitations to our work.

Our framework uses only the Minecraft Wiki, which may not represent the complexity of other domains where RAG systems are deployed. Other domains may have more erroneous chunks or poorly maintained version histories, or may not receive regular updates. Future work is needed to test whether our findings on knowledge unavailability at a corpus cut-off generalize to other domains.

We rely on LLMs throughout: Qwen3.5 122B-A10B writes the questions, Gemma 4 31B verifies them, the response judge Gemma 4 26B-A4B labels abstentions and premise denials, the oracle model DeepSeek V4.1 Flash writes reference answers, and three accuracy judges score the answers. These models may impart their own biases, such as preferring longer answers or asking underspecified questions. A human study on 100 shared items (Appendix I) finds that the judges agree with the annotators at least as well as the annotators agree with one another, but it covers a small sample. The two accuracy judges whose families we also evaluate show a small self-preference (Section A.1).

section: One Chunking Scheme and Embedding Model
text: We compare six retrieval pipelines, including reranking and query rewriting, but all of them search the same index: fixed-size chunks of about 1,500 characters split at line breaks, embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-8B. Hierarchical or semantic chunking, or other embedding models, may retrieve differently.

Our headline Correct Abstention Rate excludes premise denials, including premise denials followed by a guessed answer. We report these responses separately from acknowledged uncertainty (Appendix I). The answer prompt did not tell models that the game may contain items newer than their knowledge. We have not tested whether making this temporal uncertainty explicit changes the frequency of premise denials.

Because of cloud inference costs and limited local hardware, we selected models to cover a wide range of sizes, architectures and families. We chose the Qwen3 family because it offers many sizes and architectures within one family, which lets us vary one factor while holding the others fixed.
