Latent Coherence: Do Frontier Language Models' Probability Judgments Obey the Law of Total Probability? LawZero's Scientist AI trains a Predictor toward the Bayesian posterior, with an objective that penalizes inconsistent probabilities among latent explanations. We ask whether current frontier language models, with no such training, are already consistent in this sense zero-shot: do their probability judgments satisfy the law of total probability, $P(X)=\sum_z P(z)P(X|z)$, when the latent $z$ must be inferred from records in the context? In separate single-turn calls, models are asked for $P(X)$, for $P(z)$ over the latent's states, and for $P(X|z)$; a causal family applies the same test to $P(y|do(x))$ and the back-door adjustment. Every query has an exact ground-truth probability, and a subset of items is asked in three wordings to separate persistent incoherence from rewording noise. Across seven models, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 are the most coherent (mean absolute residual 0.08 and 0.12 log-odds, about 2 percentage points). Claude Haiku 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash and DeepSeek V4-Pro show persistent incoherence (0.27-0.35 log-odds) that is mostly item-specific rather than a shared offset.

Within every model, larger residuals go with larger errors against the truth (Spearman 0.40-0.62), so the residual, which needs no ground truth, flags unreliable answers. Reasoning length does not predict coherence, across models or within a model across rewordings of the same question. Simple consistency checks pass almost everywhere; the failures are specific to reasoning through a latent variable. Code and data: https://github.com/ppotash/latent-coherence

Many proposals for safer AI systems lean on calibrated probabilistic judgment rather than goal-directed action. LawZero’s Scientist AI is a prominent example: a non-agentic Predictor trained to approximate the Bayesian posterior over natural-language statements, including latent explanations of the data. It can answer a query directly or by Monte-Carlo averaging over latent statements proposed by an Explainer, with the Predictor itself supplying the probability of each latent and of the answer given it. Its training objective has the posterior as its unique minimizer and penalizes inconsistencies among the probabilities of latent statements, so a well-trained Predictor’s two routes agree. Their agreement is the law of total probability, P(X)\;=\;\sum_{z}P(z)\,P(X\mid z), and a predictor that violates it gives answers that depend on how a question is decomposed. The Scientist AI authors expect direct predictions to be “potentially incoherent” and introduce averaging over latents partly to improve coherence.

We ask whether current frontier language models, which receive no such training, already have this consistency zero-shot. Prior work has shown that language model probability judgments violate simple identities such as complementation and the conjunction rule, and that forecasters can be scored by the consistency of logically related forecasts. We target a specific and safety-relevant case: coherence under marginalization over a latent variable that the model must infer from evidence in context. The latent is never stated. It might be whether a news source is careful, judged from its track record, or which of three faults is present, judged from an inspection log.

An eval of latent coherence with four item families (§ 3.2). Three are synthetic, with exact ground truth. The fourth is built from HoVer multi-hop claims, fictionalized so that models cannot answer from memory. One synthetic family, causal, tests P(y\mid do(x)) against the back-door adjustment. A noise-corrected decomposition of each model’s residual into rewording noise and a persistent component (§ 3.3), so that unstable answers are not mistaken for incoherent judgments. Results for seven frontier models (§ 5). Two models are coherent to within about 2 percentage points on average. Three have persistent incoherence that varies from item to item. Large residuals mark inaccurate answers within every model. Reasoning length is not associated with coherence across models, nor within a model across rewordings of the same question. The code (MIT), data (CC BY-SA 4.0) and evaluation harness are at github.com/ppotash/latent-coherence.

Human probability judgments are famously incoherent, as in the conjunction fallacy; Zhu et al. [19] explain such deviations as the product of sampling-based inference. Zhu and Griffiths [18] find the same signatures in LLMs, testing identities over events stated directly in the prompt. We test a different identity, marginalization over a latent the model must infer, and we separate wording noise from persistent incoherence instead of pooling them.

Fluri et al. [8] evaluate models on tasks without ground truth by checking logical consistency, and Paleka et al. [14] turn this into arbitrage-based metrics for LLM forecasters. Our items have exact ground truth, which lets us relate incoherence to accuracy directly.

QUITE and BLInD test Bayesian-network reasoning from text against computed answers. CLadder tests causal queries across Pearl’s ladder. These benchmarks score accuracy. We score whether a model’s own answers agree with each other, which needs no ground truth, and we report accuracy separately. Calibration work asks whether stated confidence matches frequency, a property distinct from coherence across related queries.

For an item with target event X and latent Z with states z_{1},\dots,z_{K}, a model is asked for \hat{P}(X), \hat{P}(Z=z_{k}) and \hat{P}(X\mid Z=z_{k}) in 1+2K separate single-turn calls, so no answer is ever visible to another query. Its decomposition is D=\sum_{k}\hat{P}(z_{k})\,\hat{P}(X\mid z_{k}). The residual is the gap in log-odds, r\;=\;\operatorname{logit}\hat{P}(X)-\operatorname{logit}D, with probabilities clipped to [0.01,\ 0.99]. Between 6.6% and 9.6% of each model’s answers lie at or beyond these bounds; the conclusions do not depend on the clip level or on the log-odds scale (Appendix D.2). Log-odds treat a move from 1% to 2% as seriously as one from 33% to 50%. Near 50%, a residual of 0.1 is about 2.5 percentage points. A positive r means the direct answer exceeds the decomposition.

For causal items the target is P(y\mid do(x)): the probability of outcome y if treatment x were imposed, rather than merely observed. When Z is the only confounder and is not affected by X, the back-door adjustment gives P(y\mid do(x))\;=\;\sum_{z}P(z)\,P(y\mid x,z), and the residual compares the model’s interventional answer with its own adjustment. Normalization (\sum_{k}\hat{P}(z_{k})=1 and \hat{P}(X)+\hat{P}(\lnot X)=1) is checked separately. Rescaling a model’s \hat{P}(z_{k}) to sum to 1 before forming D lowers its mean residual by 0.004–0.07 log-odds (at most about a quarter, for Opus) and leaves the model ranking essentially unchanged, so the residuals are not an artifact of unnormalized latent probabilities.

Table 1 summarizes the families. In the full versions the item is a well-posed calculation. In the qualitative versions the model must form its own numbers. Coherence compares a model with itself, so it is meaningful at both levels. Every item has exact ground truth: computed from the generating parameters by exact enumeration for source and hover (validated against rejection sampling) and naive Bayes for diagnostic, and given by the empirical frequencies for causal, where the table is the population. Items are filtered so that targets and latent probabilities lie in [0.1,\ 0.9] and the conditionals differ across latent states by at least 0.10–0.15. Without the filter, coherence would hold trivially near 0 or 1.

The released data contain 1,500 synthetic items (300 in each of the five family–level groups: source and diagnostic at both levels, causal at the full level only) and 1,698 HoVer items built from 849 claims. For HoVer, Gemini 3.8 Flash decomposed each claim into logically independent sub-claims and replaced every named entity with an invented name. A second Gemini pass audited the decomposition, and Claude re-verified each accepted claim (Appendix B). The target claim is true exactly when all its sub-claims are, and sub-claim truths and source reliabilities are sampled from stated parameters, so HoVer items also have exact ground truth.

section: Metrics: rewording noise vs persistent incoherence
text: A nonzero residual has two possible sources. The model’s answers may vary with wording, so that r scatters around zero (instability), or its judgments may be inconsistent, so that r stays away from zero under every wording (incoherence). To separate them, a subset of noise-floor items is asked in three wordings (“What is the probability that…”, “How likely is it that…”, “Estimate the probability that…”).

section: Metrics: rewording noise vs persistent incoherence
text: Model each repeated residual as r_{ik}=\mu_{i}+e_{ik} for instance i (an item \times identity) and wording k\in\{1,\ 2,\ 3\}, where \mu_{i} is the instance’s true residual and e_{ik} is wording noise with variance \sigma^{2}. Then \displaystyle\widehat{\sigma^{2}} \displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum_{i}\operatorname{var}_{k}(r_{ik}) \displaystyle\text{(rewording noise}=\widehat{\sigma}), \displaystyle\widehat{\langle\mu^{2}\rangle} \displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum_{i}\bar{r}_{i}^{\,2}-\widehat{\sigma^{2}}/3 \displaystyle\text{(persistent residual}=\textstyle\sqrt{\max(0,\widehat{\langle\mu^{2}\rangle})}), where \bar{r}_{i} is the mean over wordings. The correction \widehat{\sigma^{2}}/3 removes the noise that remains in a three-wording average. The persistent residual is the root-mean-square size of the instances’ true residuals. Writing \langle\mu^{2}\rangle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\mu_{i}^{2} for the mean of their squares and \bar{\mu}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\mu_{i} for their mean, the square of the persistent residual satisfies \langle\mu^{2}\rangle=\bar{\mu}^{\,2}+\operatorname{var}(\mu), with \operatorname{var}(\mu)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}(\mu_{i}-\bar{\mu})^{2}, so it counts both a lean shared by all items (the direction, \bar{\mu}) and item-to-item variation (the spread, estimated as \sqrt{\max(0,\operatorname{var}_{i}(\bar{r}_{i})-\widehat{\sigma^{2}}/3)}). A model whose incoherence is a fixed offset has spread near 0; one whose errors point different ways on different items has direction near 0. A noisy but coherent model scores about 0. 95% intervals come from 2,000 bootstrap resamples of instances.

section: Metrics: rewording noise vs persistent incoherence
text: We also report the mean residual, the average |r| over all items using the first wording only, which reflects noise and persistent incoherence together, and the error vs truth, |\operatorname{logit}\hat{P}(X)-\operatorname{logit}P(X)|. Models are compared item by item with a paired sign-flip permutation test on mean |r| (20,000 permutations), Bonferroni-corrected over all 21 model pairs.

We sampled 20 items from each of the seven (family, level) groups and asked 60 of them in all three wordings: 3 from each full-spec synthetic group, and 12–13 from each qualitative and HoVer group, where wording effects are larger. Full-spec synthetic items are solved essentially exactly by every model, so all models except Haiku were capped at 5 items in each of those three groups. Claude Haiku 5.5 was run first, uncapped, as a low-cost end-to-end test of the harness ($0.62 for 1,890 prompts); we report it as a reference point for a small, fast model rather than as a planned comparison. All comparisons use the 95 items answered by every model: 90 with a latent total-probability identity (HoVer items carry two, over the bridge sub-claim and over a source’s kind) and 5 causal items with two back-door identities each. Every model answered the same 1,590 prompts; Haiku, being uncapped, also answered 300 more full-spec prompts, which are not shared and so are left out of all comparisons.

Table 2 lists the models. Each prompt was an independent single-turn call with the system prompt “Answer the question using only the information provided. Give your final answer as a single probability between 0 and 1.” Prompts contain no worked examples (zero-shot). The nominal reasoning effort was medium. GLM 5.3 and DeepSeek V4-Pro offer no medium setting and ran at high. Grok 4.7 ran at low because medium was projected to cost about $94; even so, it reasoned more than every model except DeepSeek. We verified that each provider honors its effort setting by comparing reasoning-token counts across levels on the same prompts. Claude, GPT and Gemini ran through their providers’ batch APIs; the others ran synchronously. Responses cut off by the token limit were re-asked with a higher limit (32K for Gemini, 65K for GLM and DeepSeek); none remained truncated. A parser extracts one probability per response, handling both answer-first and answer-last layouts, and was audited by hand on every answer whose reading changed (Appendix C).

Table 2 and Figure 1 give the main results. GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 are the most coherent: their direct answers differ from their own decompositions by 0.08 and 0.12 log-odds on average, or 1.5 and 1.9 percentage points on the probability scale (medians 0.3 and 0.5). Their difference is not significant (p_{\text{Bonf}}=1.0). Both are significantly more coherent than Gemini, GLM and Haiku (p_{\text{Bonf}}\leq 0.008), none of which can be separated from the others. DeepSeek V4-Pro (0.15) and Grok 4.7 (0.21) fall between. DeepSeek is significantly more coherent than Haiku but cannot be separated statistically from any other model. Grok is significantly less coherent than GPT (p_{\text{Bonf}}\leq 0.001) and more coherent than Haiku (p_{\text{Bonf}}=0.028), but cannot be separated from Opus (p_{\text{Bonf}}=0.13), DeepSeek, Gemini or GLM. All 21 comparisons are in Appendix D.1.

The two residual measures can disagree sharply. GLM and Gemini have the same mean residual (0.26) and similar rewording noise (0.53 and 0.50), but GLM’s persistent residual is 0.11 [0, 0.25] while Gemini’s is 0.28 [0.10, 0.40]. GLM’s residuals scatter around zero as the wording changes, so its incoherence is mostly instability that averaging several samples would reduce. Gemini’s residuals vary as much with wording, but around nonzero values that persist, so its judgments are inconsistent and re-asking does not remove the inconsistency. For a system that relies on composing judgments, the persistent kind is the more serious failure. Four models have a persistent residual whose interval excludes 0: Haiku (0.35), Gemini (0.28), DeepSeek (0.27) and, at a small magnitude, GPT (0.08). DeepSeek has the second-lowest noise (0.30), but 44% of its residual variance is persistent, the largest share of any model. It is exact on most items (median residual 0.013) and consistently off on a few.

For every model the spread nearly equals the persistent residual, and the shared lean accounts for at most a sixth of its square, except for GLM, whose small persistent residual is about 40% lean. The leans that do exist are model-specific. Haiku’s and DeepSeek’s direct answers sit above their decompositions (+0.14 and +0.08 overall, rising to +0.22 for Haiku on full HoVer items and +0.19 for DeepSeek on qualitative HoVer items), and Gemini’s sit below (-0.11 overall, -0.32 on qualitative HoVer items). On HoVer items X is a conjunction of sub-claims, so a positive lean is consistent with overestimating conjunctions relative to their parts; Gemini’s opposite sign shows that this is not a universal property of language models.

Residuals are near zero on full-spec synthetic items, which are calculations: every model’s mean residual there is at most 0.055 (Table 5). They grow on qualitative items and on HoVer, but verbal evidence alone is not the main difficulty. Qualitative diagnostic items also require turning words into numbers, but have a single three-state latent, and six of seven models stay at 0.04–0.11 there (GLM 0.28). Qualitative HoVer items, where the target is a conjunction of sub-claims linked through a bridge entity, reach 0.64 for Gemini and 0.80 for Haiku, against 0.075 and 0.110 for the same two models on qualitative diagnostic items. The by-spec persistent residuals (Table 6) add model-specific detail. Gemini’s is concentrated on qualitative items (0.35 [0.11, 0.51], vs 0.09 on full-spec ones), while DeepSeek’s is larger on full-spec items (0.36 [0.04, 0.57]): its persistent errors arise even when every number is given. GPT’s small pooled persistent residual comes almost entirely from qualitative items, where its interval excludes zero (0.11 [0.03, 0.16]). Opus’s estimate there is 0.00, but its interval [0, 0.17] is too wide to separate the two. Rewording noise is higher on qualitative items for six of the seven models.

Within every model, instances with larger residuals have larger errors against the truth (Table 3): Spearman correlations are 0.40–0.62, all with intervals well above zero, and the direct answer’s mean error on incoherent instances (|r|>0.5) is 2.2–4.8 times that on coherent ones (|r|\leq 0.1). Part of this relation is mechanical: since |r|\leq|\operatorname{logit}\hat{P}(X)-\operatorname{logit}P(X)|+|\operatorname{logit}D-\operatorname{logit}P(X)|, a large residual means that the direct answer or the decomposition must be far from the truth. The residual needs no ground truth, so it is a usable lower bound on combined error. Which estimate is wrong differs by model (Table 7). For Gemini it is mostly the direct answer: on its incoherent instances the direct error is 1.68 against 1.25 for the decomposition, which is closer to the truth on 64% of them. Grok leans the same way but only slightly (1.15 vs 1.03; decomposition closer on 50%). For Haiku and DeepSeek it is the decomposition (1.41 vs 0.89; 1.09 vs 0.75), and DeepSeek’s errors there sit mainly in the latent prior \hat{P}(z) (1.06, vs 0.63 for the conditionals). GLM’s two estimates are equally wrong (0.85, 0.86); Opus and GPT have too few incoherent instances (4 and 2) to say.

Pooled over models, the conditionals are nearly exact on full-spec items (error 0.07) and the latent prior carries the largest error (0.13); on qualitative items every component’s error is 0.63–0.72. Decomposing through the latent would thus rescue a bad holistic judgment for some models and introduce errors for others.

section: Reasoning length does not predict coherence
text: Across models (Figure 2), the two most coherent reasoned the least (about 400 and 500 tokens per answer). Grok, GLM and Gemini reasoned 9–18 times as much and were less coherent (0.21–0.26), while DeepSeek reasoned the most (about 16,900 tokens) and placed third. Because the seven models differ in developer and training, this comparison is only observational, so we also look within each model (Table 3, right). Across a model’s items, the correlation between |r| and reasoning tokens ranges from -0.22 (GPT, whose incoherent instances drew fewer tokens) to +0.25 (Haiku, whose incoherent instances drew more), and its interval excludes zero only for those two and, barely, DeepSeek. That correlation is confounded with difficulty, since a hard item can both lengthen reasoning and raise the residual. Comparing the three wordings of the same noise-floor instance holds the item fixed. There, the wording that elicited more reasoning was neither more nor less coherent: the centered correlation lies between -0.08 and +0.13, and its 95% interval includes zero for every model. We find no evidence that longer reasoning on a given question changes coherence.

section: Simple checks pass; decomposition rarely helps accuracy
text: Each model’s probabilities over a latent’s states sum to 1 (median |\Sigma-1|\leq 0.02 for every model). On causal items, each model’s interventional answer matches its own back-door adjustment, with mean residuals at most 0.002 except for DeepSeek (0.030) and GLM (0.047). Both exceptions are a single answer on the same item (Appendix D), and both treat an interventional question as an observational one. DeepSeek’s \hat{P}(y\mid do(\text{slow}))=0.6735 and GLM’s \hat{P}(y\mid do(\text{fast}))=0.375 equal the observational P(y\mid\text{slow})=132/196=0.6735 and P(y\mid\text{fast})=39/104=0.375 to every reported digit, while every piece of each model’s own adjustment was exactly right, giving the true 0.605 and 0.275. Apart from such slips, the failures are specific to marginalizing over an inferred latent. Over all instances, a model’s own decomposition D is closer to the truth than its direct answer on only 39–49% of them and improves the mean error only for Gemini, GPT and Grok, by at most 0.07.

Two frontier models judge probabilities through a latent coherently enough for many purposes, within about 2 percentage points on average. Others carry inconsistencies that persist under rewording, so a system that composes their judgments, as Scientist AI does when it averages over latent statements, inherits errors that sampling will not remove. Because the persistent part is mostly item-specific spread, it cannot be calibrated away with a fixed correction, and the absence of a common direction suggests these failures come from each model’s training rather than a shared heuristic. Because the residual needs no ground truth, it can also be used to flag unreliable answers: within every model, answers with a large residual have two to five times the error of coherent ones. Whether to trust the direct answer or the decomposition when they disagree, however, depends on the model.

Several design choices limit how far the results generalize. Settings. “Medium” effort is a vendor label, not a fixed amount of reasoning, and three models deviated from it (Grok low; GLM and DeepSeek high). Temperature is not controllable for most reasoning models, and each prompt was asked once (three times on noise-floor items). Sample size. The noise-floor estimates rest on 83 latent-identity instances from 57 items, so persistent-residual intervals are wide and per-group breakdowns (Appendix D) are suggestive only. Single framing. We used one conditioning framing (“Suppose you additionally learn, from a completely reliable check, the following”); the harness’s “assume” framing was not run. Ground truth on qualitative items. It comes from the hidden generating numbers. Error vs truth there partly measures how a model maps words like “usually” to numbers; coherence is unaffected. HoVer construction. Decomposition and fictionalization were done and audited by LLMs from two providers; remaining errors would affect ground truth but not coherence. Scope. We test seven API models at one point in time. Dedicated forecasting or decision models that output probabilities directly, and open-weight models run locally, are natural additions.

We introduced an eval of whether language models’ probability judgments obey the law of total probability over latent variables inferred from context. Across seven frontier models, coherence varies about 4.5-fold, and persistent incoherence is item-specific, unrelated to reasoning length, and a signal of error against the truth. For proposals that build safe systems from calibrated, composable probability judgments, measuring this kind of coherence directly seems a necessary step.

Closing the Loop: Practical Training Recipes for Looped Language Models. Looped language models increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared block of layers, but existing large-scale recipes require multi-stage training over trillions of tokens, while the benefits of recurrence remain difficult to separate from differences in data and training. In this work, we establish practical training recipes for looped language models, with three main results. (1) We develop a compute-efficient from-scratch pipeline that reduces the training budget from 7.7T tokens in Ouro to 310B tokens while retaining strong reasoning performance. Pretraining followed by high-quality mid-training, together with learning-rate warmup and stronger exit-gate regularization, enables stable recurrent training without prior multi-stage schedules. (2) Under controlled comparisons, our 1.4B LoopLM outperforms a parameter-matched dense model trained on the same data and token budget on all 12 evaluated benchmarks, including +14 points on GSM8K, +10 on MATH, and +22 on DROP. At matched inference compute, it approaches a 3.9B dense model on mathematical reasoning and reading comprehension while using only 36\% as many parameters. (3) We introduce a minimal recipe for converting pretrained dense models into looped ones: a single learned input-mixing scalar and a smoothed exit loss, with no step-specific parameters.

Applied to Qwen3-1.7B-Base, Looped Qwen improves over an identically continued dense baseline on every evaluated benchmark across two data regimes, with statistically clear gains on GSM8K, MATH, and MMLU-Pro on the curated mixture. Together, these results make looped language models substantially cheaper to train from scratch and practical to introduce into existing pretrained checkpoints, while isolating the gains due to recurrence itself.

Transformers spend the same computation on every token. Looped language models apply a shared transformer block repeatedly, which raises effective depth without adding parameters, and with adaptive exits they can spend extra computation only where it is needed (Dehghani et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2025).

Ouro showed that looped models can be pretrained at scale and compete with much larger dense models (Zhu et al., 2025). Its recipe runs through five stages and 7.7T tokens, it starts from scratch while pretrained dense checkpoints go unused, and its gains are measured against dense models trained on other data, so the share that comes from recurrence is unknown.

We address all three points: a simpler and much cheaper from-scratch recipe, a conversion of dense checkpoints into recurrent models with minimal architectural changes, and a comparison against dense counterparts trained on the same data with the same training stages, matched in parameters or in inference compute.

Our recipe has two stages where Ouro has five, one pretraining run and one high-quality mid-training stage, and trains on 310B tokens against Ouro’s 7.7T. At this budget the model is already competitive on reasoning benchmarks, while the 25 times longer training of Ouro-1.4B still shows on knowledge benchmarks (Table 3). Without the intermediate stages the exit gate can collapse early in training; a learning-rate warmup removes this early collapse, and a larger KL coefficient lets the gate recover if it does collapse. The resulting 1.4B LoopLM beats its parameter-matched dense twin on all 12 evaluated benchmarks, with the largest gains on DROP, CRUXEval-I and GSM8K, and at three recurrent steps, the inference cost of a 3.9B dense twin, it stays competitive with that model on math and reading comprehension while trailing it on knowledge and commonsense benchmarks.

Applying the Qwen3-1.7B-Base decoder (Yang et al., 2025) recurrently without further changes fails: each later step makes the representation worse. One learned scalar that mixes the original token embedding into every later step, with a smoothed exit loss that keeps every step training, is enough, and step-specific LoRA adapters are optional. Without step-specific adapters, Looped Qwen is ahead on every benchmark of Qwen3-1.7B-Base continued on the same data for the same number of steps, in two independent runs. On the curated mixture its gains on GSM8K, MATH and MMLU-Pro exceed two standard errors. An inference-compute-matched Qwen3-4B-Base stays ahead, as expected from a checkpoint more than twice the size.

The main contributions are: A simplified from-scratch recipe: one pretraining run and one mid-training stage, 310B tokens against Ouro’s 7.7T, with a learning-rate warmup that removes the early collapse of the exit gate and a larger KL coefficient that lets it recover. A dense-to-loop conversion with minimal architectural changes: one learned scalar and a smoothed exit loss, no step-specific parameters, and Looped Qwen, the converted Qwen3-1.7B-Base, improves on the source checkpoint given the same continued training. A controlled comparison in both regimes: every looped model is measured against dense counterparts that share its data, training stages and token budget, matched in parameters or in inference compute, for LoopLM and Looped Qwen alike. The large looped models so far report their headline numbers against published dense models.

Universal Transformers introduced the construction behind most looped models, a shared block applied repeatedly with adaptive halting (Dehghani et al., 2019; Graves, 2016); fixed-point formulations replace the halting with a convergence test on the hidden state (Movahedi et al., 2026). Looped Transformers use the shared block to extend depth and length generalization (Saunshi et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2025), recurrent-depth models gain from more test-time iterations (Geiping et al., 2025), and Mixture-of-Recursions gives each token its own depth (Bae et al., 2025b). At scale, Ouro pretrains looped models that match much larger dense models (Zhu et al., 2025), HRM-Text applies hierarchical recurrence to open-domain text (Wang et al., 2026), and Loop the Loopies loops a mixture-of-experts model (Gao et al., 2026).

Each of these works hits an instability of its own. Ouro saw loss spikes at eight recurrent steps and cut the depth to four and halved the KL coefficient; the first large run of Geiping et al. (2025) stalled with hidden states that became the same for every token; HRM-Text adds a normalization scheme and warms up its backward horizon; Mixture-of-Recursions needs balancing losses to keep its router alive. None gives a from-scratch recipe without a multi-stage schedule or names the ingredient that keeps the exit gate alive once that schedule is gone (Section 3).

Comparisons against dense models trained on the same data exist: Saunshi et al. (2025) and Mixture-of-Recursions train parameter-matched and compute-matched baselines, HRM-Text matches training FLOPs, Loop the Loopies matches pretraining cost, and Ouro’s own small-scale study finds a deeper dense model ahead of the looped one at matched forward FLOPs. Ouro and the recurrent-depth model report their headline numbers against published dense models trained on other data, so the share of the gain that comes from recurrence stays open. We measure the model we report against dense twins in both regimes, and do the same for Looped Qwen, our converted model, where prior work matched parameters only.

Relaxed Recursive Transformers tie the layers of a pretrained model into looping blocks with one LoRA adapter per iteration and distill from the original (Bae et al., 2025a); Think-at-Hard starts from Qwen3-Base and adds depth-specific adapters and a router for hard tokens (Fu et al., 2025). Both rely on step-specific adapters and compare against parameter-matched baselines only. We show that looping the pretrained decoder as it is degrades the representation, that one learned scalar stops this degradation and that adapters are optional.

GRPO and DAPO (Shao et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025) assume a fixed computation path; RLTT distributes credit across recurrent iterations (Williams & Tureci, 2026). Ouro reports no gain from RL on its final model. A separate study asks when RL adds to a looped model (Appendix C).

Ouro (Zhu et al., 2025) trains LoopLMs through five stages: pretraining at eight recurrent steps, continued pretraining at four, high-quality annealing, context extension, and supervised mid-training. Its exit gate is optimized jointly with the language model using an entropy-regularized ELBO objective with KL coefficient \beta.

We simplify this recipe by collapsing the pretraining stages into a single run, reducing the total token budget, and training the dense baselines of Section 5.1 through the same stages on the same data.

Ouro’s pretraining uses three regimes before fine-tuning: pretraining at T{=}8, continued pretraining at T{=}4, and annealing on a higher-quality mixture (Zhu et al., 2025). We replace all three with one run from random initialization on a fixed mixture dominated by filtered web text, with mathematics and instruction-following data (Table 12).
As in Loop the Loopies (Gao et al., 2026), high-quality data is present from the start. We keep only one mid-training stage afterwards (Section 3.4).
Our single run departs from Ouro’s first-stage configuration in depth and in schedule.

Ouro explores T{=}8 in its first stage and drops to four afterwards, citing loss spikes at the larger depth (Zhu et al., 2025). Our own T{=}8 run under that configuration points the same way: the per-loop loss stops improving after the third or fourth iteration, and the gate spreads its mass evenly over loops four to eight (Figure 2). The extra iterations cost compute without measurable gain, so depth is fixed at T{=}4 from the start.

Ouro also lowers \beta after its first stage and trains with a constant learning rate from then on. Our run has no such transition, so we ask what keeps the exit gate alive once the schedule is gone. The failure is a gate collapse: early in training the gate learns to exit after the first loop, later iterations stop receiving gradient, and the model trains on as a plain transformer. Figure 3 compares \beta{=}0.05, the value Ouro uses after its first stage, with our \beta{=}0.15, each trained without warmup and with our warmup-plus-cosine schedule. Without warmup the smaller \beta collapses for good and the larger one comes close before it recovers. With the warmup schedule the larger \beta never comes near the collapsed regime, while the smaller one stays near p_{0}=0.9 for its first thousand steps before recovering. Thus, warmup prevents early collapse at our \beta, while larger \beta enables recovery if collapse occurs: without warmup every \beta\geq 0.10 we tried recovers, and only \beta{=}0.05 stays collapsed (Appendix B). The main run therefore uses \beta{=}0.15 with warmup and cosine decay (Table 1).
Notably, the language-modelling loss does not reveal the collapse while it occurs, so the exit distribution must be monitored directly.

Despite the mathematics and instruction-following data in pretraining, the resulting checkpoint reaches only 35% accuracy on 5-shot GSM8K (Appendix C). We therefore add a high-quality mid-training stage using instruction–response pairs with loss on response tokens only. The mixture emphasizes mathematics and reasoning while retaining a knowledge-preserving component.

Mid-training continues for 100B tokens on the HRM-Text mixture (Wang et al., 2026), whose largest components are FLAN, SYNTH, and OpenMathInstruct-2 (Table 13). Recurrent depth, \beta, weight decay, optimizer, and architecture remain unchanged from pretraining. The same stage is applied to both dense baselines with identical data, schedule, and token budget.

The final recipe keeps Ouro’s shared recurrent architecture and trains it in two stages instead of five: a single 210B-token pretraining run from random initialization followed by 100B tokens of high-quality mid-training. The resulting 310B-token budget is 25 \times smaller than the 7.7T tokens used for Ouro-1.4B and needs about 3% of the training compute of Ouro’s schedule on the same architecture (Appendix I). Training uses T{=}4 from the start, a learning-rate warmup to prevent early exit-gate collapse, and \beta{=}0.15 to enable recovery if collapse occurs (Section 3.3). Table 1 summarizes the recipe; Appendix D provides the architecture, gate objective, and data mixtures.
The mid-training stage contributes most of the reasoning improvement: relative to the step-100,000 pretraining checkpoint, it more than doubles GSM8K accuracy and improves MMLU by about nine points.

section: Reinforcement learning as a separate study
text: None of the models compared in Section 5 uses reinforcement learning; we study it separately, since Ouro reported no gain from RL with verifiable rewards on its final checkpoint (Zhu et al., 2025). We use RLTT (Williams & Tureci, 2026), a GRPO variant for looped models that distributes policy gradients across recurrent iterations while keeping rollout and training execution paths consistent. With group-based methods a prompt contributes gradient only when its rollouts contain both successes and failures. A mid-trained checkpoint of an earlier run of this recipe already solved about three quarters of its MATH rollouts, and RLTT left MATH unchanged; the step-100,000 pretraining checkpoint of the main run solved about a third of its GSM8K rollouts, and the same method added twelve points. What separates the two runs is the solve rate at rollout time. Appendix C reports these two runs and their training dynamics, and summarizes four runs at a lower learning rate that did not move the policy.

Only a few pretrained looped checkpoints are publicly available, making dense-to-loop conversion an attractive alternative to training from scratch. We find that naive recurrence degrades later steps, while a single input-preserving scalar together with a smoothed exit loss is sufficient to convert Qwen3-1.7B-Base, at under 1% of its pretraining compute (Appendix I). Appendix G reports the corresponding training dynamics.

We start from Qwen3-1.7B-Base (Yang et al., 2025) and apply the full decoder recurrently for T{=}3 steps. Without input re-injection, later steps are consistently worse than the first: after the initial phase, the LM losses of steps 2 and 3 remain about 0.01 and 0.02 nats higher, respectively (Figure 9 a). A learned per-step projection of the original embedding and recurrent state also fails to produce refinement: the gate abandons the middle step and the final step does not improve over the first (Figure 9 c).

We instead preserve direct access to the original embedding with a single learned scalar. Let e denote the token embedding and h_{t-1} the output of the previous recurrent step. For t>0, z_{t}=we+(1-w)h_{t-1},\qquad w=\sigma(a), where a is the only additional parameter. With the same data, batch, and seed as the naive run, steps 2 and 3 finish about 0.02 nats below step 1 (Figure 9 b). We initialize w=0.99; it increases slowly throughout training in all runs (Figure 9 e; Appendix F).

The exit gate introduces a separate instability. Under the standard LoopLM objective (Zhu et al., 2025), \sum_{t}p_{t}\mathcal{L}_{t}, each step is trained in proportion to its current exit probability; once the gate assigns little mass to a step, that step receives little learning signal. In an unsmoothed run with rank-8 stepwise LoRA, the gate drops the middle exit and its loss rises to about 10 nats (Figure 9 d).

We therefore smooth only the exit distribution used for the LM loss: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LM}}^{\mathrm{smooth}}=(1-\epsilon)\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}p_{t}\mathcal{L}_{t}+\frac{\epsilon}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathcal{L}_{t}. Gate regularization and inference still use the original exit probabilities. With \epsilon{=}0.05 and T{=}3, every step retains at least 0.0167 LM weight, preventing the later-step losses from drifting (Figure 9 d).

We use a curated continued-training mixture covering mathematics, code, STEM, science, and instruction following, with final-answer supervision and no explicit chain-of-thought traces (Appendix F). To separate recurrence gains from data effects, we repeat the conversion on a second mixture dominated by filtered web text. Each mixture is shared unchanged between the looped model and its dense baselines.

We test whether step-specific parameters are necessary by adding independent rank-32 LoRA adapters to each recurrent step (Bae et al., 2025a). They provide little benefit: training losses nearly match the shared model (Figure 9 f), and benchmark differences stay within two points with neither variant consistently ahead (Section 5.3). We therefore use the fully shared model by default.

Figure 4 summarizes the final model: a shared pretrained decoder, scalar input injection from Eq. 1, and a shared LM head and exit gate trained with Eq. 2. Because the third step improves training loss by less than 0.001 nats over the second on the instruction mixture (Figure 9 f), evaluation uses a fixed exit after two steps.

We evaluate both from-scratch and converted looped models against dense baselines trained on the same data, stages, and token budget. For each track, we use a parameter-matched baseline and a larger inference-compute-matched baseline.

Both dense baselines remove recurrence (T{=}1) while retaining the same transformer block and two-stage training procedure. dense-ouro-1.4B uses one 24-layer block and matches LoopLM in parameter count; dense-ouro-3.9B stacks three such blocks into 72 layers and matches the inference compute of LoopLM at three recurrent steps. Because LoopLM trains with all four iterations, its per-token training compute is about 4\times that of dense-ouro-1.4B and 1.4\times that of dense-ouro-3.9B (Appendix I).

For conversion, Qwen3-1.7B-Base is the parameter-matched baseline and Qwen3-4B-Base the inference-compute-matched reference (Yang et al., 2025). All models are continued on the same conversion mixture with identical optimization and evaluation settings. At its two-step exit, Looped Qwen uses about 20% fewer inference FLOPs than Qwen3-4B-Base (Appendix I).

section: Against dense models trained on the same data
text: Table 2 compares LoopLM with both controlled dense baselines.

section: Against dense models trained on the same data
text: At equal parameter count, four-step LoopLM outperforms dense-ouro-1.4B on all 12 benchmarks. The gains are largest on reasoning-intensive tasks: +22 points on DROP, +17 on CRUXEval-I, +14 on GSM8K, and about +10 on MATH, MMLU, and CRUXEval-O. Thus, recurrence provides a consistent advantage over applying the same parameter budget only once.

section: Against dense models trained on the same data
text: At equal inference compute the larger dense model is ahead or level on every benchmark, and the advantage of LoopLM at this point is its size. With 1.4B parameters, 36% of those of dense-ouro-3.9B, three-step LoopLM comes within one standard error of the difference on GSM8K, MATH and MATH500 and within about one point on DROP. A fourth iteration, roughly one third more inference compute, moves it ahead on DROP and level on GSM8K. The gap that remains is in knowledge and commonsense benchmarks, 2 to 9 points, where the extra parameters of the dense model store more facts.

section: Against dense models trained on the same data
text: The depth sweep shows that these gains come from using recurrent computation rather than from the underlying 1.4B checkpoint alone. One iteration trails the parameter-matched dense model on every benchmark; two iterations outperform it on 11 of 12, three on all 12, and the fourth iteration improves 10 of 12 scores further.
Because published models differ substantially in evaluation protocol and pretraining budget, Table 3 is intended as contextual rather than controlled comparison.

Despite using only 0.31T training tokens, LoopLM remains competitive with models trained on substantially larger budgets. The four-step model achieves the highest DROP score in the table and the second-highest GSM8K score. Against Ouro-1.4B, trained on 25 \times more tokens, LoopLM is lower on MATH and MATH500 but higher by 4.4 points on GSM8K and 10.9 points on DROP. The controlled evidence for recurrence itself remains the comparison in Table 2.

We run the conversion twice from Qwen3-1.7B-Base using the same recipe: once on 84B tokens of web-scale data and once on 60B tokens of curated instruction data (Section 4.3). Each run has dense baselines continued on the same data for the same number of steps. Table 4 reports the instruction run; the web-scale run is in Appendix H. Looped Qwen trains with all three recurrent steps and is evaluated after two, where its inference cost is close to Qwen3-4B-Base.

The conversion result is consistent across both data regimes. Without step-specific adapters, Looped Qwen improves over Qwen3-1.7B-Base continued on exactly the same data for the same number of steps on every benchmark in both runs. Most gains are modest, but the curated instruction mixture produces clear reasoning improvements: +4.3 points on GSM8K, +3.8 on MMLU-Pro, and +2.2 on MATH, each exceeding two standard errors of the difference. On the web-scale mixture, gains remain within about two points, with only MMLU and HellaSwag exceeding that threshold.

The larger gains on the curated mixture suggest that the benefit of recurrence depends strongly on the continued-training data. Importantly, the effect does not require step-specific capacity: the shared and LoRA-32 variants differ by at most two points, with neither consistently ahead.

Looped Qwen still trails Qwen3-4B-Base on every benchmark. The conversion therefore does not replace the knowledge and capacity obtained from substantially larger pretraining; instead, it provides a lightweight way to improve an existing 1.7B checkpoint without repeating pretraining or adding per-step parameters.
This work gives two practical ways to build a looped language model: a short recipe for training one from scratch, and a conversion of a pretrained dense model with minimal architectural changes.

For from-scratch training, a two-stage recipe trains a looped model at a fraction of the token budget of earlier multi-stage pipelines, a learning-rate warmup removes the early collapse of the exit gate, and a larger KL coefficient lets the gate recover if it does collapse. The resulting LoopLM improves over a parameter-matched dense model on every evaluated benchmark and, at equal inference compute, comes within about a point of a dense model with three times its parameters on math and reading comprehension; the larger model keeps its lead where parameter count stores facts.

For pretrained models, applying a dense decoder repeatedly does not produce refinement. One learned scalar that mixes the token embedding into each recurrent step, together with a smoothed exit loss, is enough to turn Qwen3-1.7B-Base into Looped Qwen, which improves on the source checkpoint given the same continued training, with no step-specific parameters. At the inference cost of Qwen3-4B-Base it still trails that model, as a checkpoint more than twice its size should.
Both results are measured against dense baselines trained on the same data with the same training stages, matched in parameters or in inference compute.

We adhere to the ICLR Code of Ethics. This work studies the architecture, training, and evaluation of language models and does not involve human-subject experiments or the collection of new personal or sensitive data. Training uses existing language-model pretraining and instruction-tuning datasets; we do not release additional user data or construct datasets containing newly collected personal information.

The models studied in this work are general-purpose language models and therefore inherit the usual potential risks associated with such systems, including generation of inaccurate, biased, or harmful content and possible dual-use applications. Our work does not introduce mechanisms specifically designed for harmful use, nor does it evaluate or optimize models for such applications. The proposed methods primarily change how computation is reused across recurrent steps and do not remove the need for the same safety, fairness, privacy, and deployment considerations that apply to conventional language models.

To the best of our knowledge, this work raises no additional legal, privacy, or fairness concerns beyond those associated with the underlying public pretraining and instruction-tuning corpora and pretrained checkpoints. Explaining Chess and Go in Natural Language. Modern chess engines play far beyond human ability, often choosing moves whose underlying ideas are difficult for humans to understand. We propose an automatic metric for evaluating chess explanations, grounded in chess-engine evaluations. Evaluating state-of-the-art language models using this metric, we find that they perform surprisingly poorly, often relying on surface-level board observations rather than robust, transferable chess concepts. We then introduce BinProp, a training-free method that enables these same models to discover reusable chess concepts and use them to explain moves in natural language. BinProp improves explainability for every model tested, nearly tripling the average score compared with direct prompting. Beyond chess, the same method discovers useful concepts in Go, draughts, and shogi without additional tuning.

Modern chess-playing algorithms, called chess engines, are vastly superior to human players, but their decisions are often difficult to understand. Since Shannon’s formulation of computer chess (Shannon, 1950), engines have followed the same basic paradigm: search through possible continuations, evaluate the resulting positions, and choose the move whose continuation looks best using MiniMax (v. Neumann, 1928). Modern engines apply this framework at enormous scale: Stockfish 18 (The Stockfish developers, 2026), the strongest chess engine at the time of writing,, evaluates millions of positions per second using a neural-network evaluation function.

This gap between playing strength and understanding has recently attracted increasing attention (Björnsson, 2024; Spinnato, 2025; Barthelemy, 2025). An engine’s evaluation tells us which move it prefers, but not the chess ideas behind that choice. Our goal is to explain in natural language why a chess engine prefers one move over another.

Chess and Go engines are especially interesting to explain because they can reveal ideas that human players overlook. Chess masters highlighted AlphaZero’s “march of the rook’s pawn”: against a kingside-castled king, it often advances the h-pawn to h6 to restrict the king’s movement (Sadler and Regan, 2019). In Game 2 against Lee Sedol, AlphaGo’s Move 37 was so unusual that its team estimated only a one-in-10,000 chance of a human playing it (Hassabis, 2016). Understanding the ideas behind engine moves could help improve human play.

Explaining why an engine prefers one move over another is challenging because the quality of a move cannot be judged solely by looking at the current board. A position with a material advantage, for example, may still be losing if the opponent has a reply that leads to forced checkmate. Instead, the value of a move depends on the continuations it enables and those it prevents. We therefore frame explanations as contrastive: given two candidate moves, we ask what becomes true after the first move but not after the alternative. As shown in Fig. 1, these explanations take the form of concrete chess motifs, such as passed pawns, restricted pieces, or superior piece activity.

Our contributions are as follows. First, we propose an engine-grounded metric for measuring the quality of chess explanations. Second, we evaluate four open-weight and four frontier large language models and show that their explanations often rely on surface-level observations rather than robust, transferable chess concepts. Third, we introduce BinProp, a training-free method for discovering reusable concepts and using them to explain moves in natural language. BinProp improves explainability for every model tested on chess, raising Fable 5 ’s score from 3.1\% with direct prompting to 29.6\%, and GPT-5.6 Sol ’s from 6.2\% to 20.5\%. It also extends to Go, draughts, and shogi without additional tuning.

Our goal is to generate explanations such as: “If you play this move, your opponent’s king will come under pressure; after a weaker alternative, it will not.” In this work, we focus on binary concepts, or motifs, that are either present or absent in a position, making explanations easier to interpret. In this section, we describe how we build a test set of positions to evaluate the quality of a given explanation.

The main challenge is that a motif may not appear immediately after a move is played: a move can be good because of what becomes possible only several moves later. We therefore use Stockfish 18 to generate multiple plausible continuations after the best move and a weaker alternative. In evaluation, we give models these Stockfish-generated continuations, so the evaluation tests motif quality rather than move calculation.

Concretely, we sample positions where the engine’s top move gives a modest advantage, while an alternative move loses that advantage. We sample positive positions from continuations that begin with the top move and preserve the advantage, while negative positions come from continuations that begin with an alternative move. The task is to find a motif, written as a Python function, that returns True on positive positions and False on negative positions.

Separating positives from negatives is not enough: a motif may simply capture an irrelevant difference between the boards. Figure shows one example: Black has a pawn on d6 separates the two sets, but says little about why one side has an advantage. We call such motifs brittle. To catch them, we use nearby negatives: we keep the early moves of a positive continuation but replace a later move with a weaker one that loses the advantage. Because nearby negatives share a prefix of moves with positives, the resulting boards tend to be similar, helping catch brittle motifs.

We randomly sample 100 positions from master-level games in PGNMentor (64 Squares, 2026). We exclude positions with an overwhelming advantage, where the explanation is often trivial, and forced mates, where the engine’s mating line itself provides the explanation. The best move must evaluate between +75 and +125 centipawns for the side to move. The alternative must evaluate between -125 and +50 centipawns, at least 75 centipawns below the best move and within 50 centipawns of the second-best move.

For each starting position, we construct a set of 12 positives, 12 negatives, and 8 nearby negatives. We retain only quiet positions: neither king is in check and no immediate material tactic is visible. This requirement excludes boards midway through tactical exchanges (§ C.1). We sample these positions across several plausible continuations, rather than a single engine line (Figure 2).

We start two continuations from the same position: one with the best move and one with the weaker alternative. After each, Stockfish plays both sides for at least six plies, stopping at the first quiet position. If none is reached by ply 16, we discard the line.

To generate the set of boards, we branch into several continuations from each quiet position. We explore up to 12 additional plies, considering up to six highly ranked Stockfish moves at each turn. We retain 12 distinct quiet positions after each of the two moves: positives preserve the best move’s advantage, while negatives start with the worse move and keep roughly the same evaluation. Every retained position has the same player to move as in the starting position.

We start from a quiet position reached along a positive continuation, then have the advantaged player play a weaker move instead of Stockfish’s best move. After Stockfish’s best reply, we retain the position as a nearby negative only if it is quiet and the advantage is lost. We collect eight per starting position.

We show the model four positives and four negatives, called the support set. Nearby negatives are never shown to the model. We then evaluate its motifs on 24 positions it has not seen: eight positives, eight negatives, and eight nearby negatives. For each group, we compute the fraction of correct outputs: True for positives and False for either kind of negative. A motif’s explainability score is the lowest of these three fractions. Additional dataset construction details are in § C.1.

In this section, we introduce BinProp (short for Bin ary Prop erties), our method for explaining chess engine decisions. BinProp first finds general chess motifs that occur more often in winning than losing positions then uses them to explain why the engine prefers one move over another.

To find these motifs, we construct a set of 200k positions from the Lichess Elite Database (Noel, 2020). All evaluations are expressed from the perspective of the player to move: 100k positions evaluate between +125 and +250 centipawns, and 100k evaluate between -250 and -125 centipawns. We call these the winning and losing sets, respectively.

BinProp runs as an iterative loop. At each step, a language model proposes a motif: a Python function f that maps a board state to True or False. We evaluate f on both sets; a useful motif fires more often on winning positions. For example, consider the motif “the player to move is ahead in material.” It fires on 61.5\% of winning positions and 5.5\% of losing positions, a gap of 56 percentage points. In general, \Delta(f) is the difference between a motif’s firing rates on the winning and losing sets, and we retain only motifs with \Delta(f)>0.01, i.e., more than one percentage point.

We also want the motifs to be different from one another. To check this, we measure containment on the winning set. For a candidate motif, containment is its largest overlap with any existing motif: among winning positions where the candidate is True, what fraction also satisfy that existing motif? High containment indicates redundancy between motifs. We reject a candidate when containment exceeds 70\%, unless its \Delta(f) is larger than that of the overlapping motif; in that case, the candidate replaces the older motif.

We run the iterative loop (Algorithm 1) for 100 steps using each model’s maximum reasoning setting, a 61,440-token reasoning budget, and a 4,096-token visible-output budget. Additional details, including the full prompts, are given in § A.

Given an initial position, and a move we want to explain, we use the process detailed in § 2 to generate a set of positive and negative positions. Then, our goal is to find the most relevant motifs that explain the differences in positive and negative positions. For each motif, we ask two questions. First: how useful is the motif in general? This is measured by \Delta(f): motifs with larger \Delta(f) appear much more often in winning positions than losing ones. Second: how relevant is the motif for this particular move? We measure how often the motif is true on the given positives and how often it is false on the given negatives. Fit is the lower of these two percentages. We rank motifs by combining these two quantities, \Delta(f)\cdot\text{fit}(f), and return the top k. Lastly, an additional LM call converts the motifs into natural language (§ B).

We evaluate four open-weight models, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (Qwen Team, 2026), Kimi-K3 (Kimi Team and others, 2026), GLM-5.2 (GLM-5-Team and others, 2026), and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), and four proprietary models, GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026b), GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026a), Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026b), and Fable 5 (Anthropic, 2026a). For each model, we compare direct prompting (Baseline) with BinProp. For each position, Baseline is prompted to propose three motifs, while BinProp selects three from its discovered set. Both methods follow the same evaluation protocol. For each position in the test set, we score up to three motifs with at least 50\% support fit. The position’s score is the arithmetic mean of these motif scores. If none qualifies, we score the highest-ranked valid motif; if none is valid, the position scores zero. Table 1 reports the average across all 100 test positions and shows that BinProp improves explainability for all eight models (bootstrap intervals in § C.2). Even the lowest BinProp score, 0.174, exceeds the strongest baseline, 0.173; the highest BinProp score is 0.296.

Even when prompted to identify general chess concepts, direct prompting mostly yields motifs that rely on shallow board details. In Fig. 3, the Opus 5 motif requires only that each side has a queen and at least one rook; Fable 5 checks for White’s queen on d1 and Black’s on a5; and GPT-5.5 checks for White’s bishops on c1 and g2. All three fit the support examples but also hold on every nearby negative, so each scores zero. Still, a minority of baseline runs produce non-brittle motifs: one Opus 5 motif requires a White pawn on the fifth rank or beyond and no Black bishop or knight in White’s half. Another, from GPT-5.5, requires an advanced White bishop to attack a square next to Black’s king, both achieving an explainability score of 87.5\%.

BinProp discovers 192 motifs (§ H), ranging from 11 for Kimi-K3 to 44 for GPT-5.5. Median \Delta(f) ranges from 2.5\% for Fable 5 to 9.0\% for Qwen. The models also differ in how many chess ideas they combine within a motif. Most favor a single idea: 20 of Opus 5 ’s 30 motifs each focus on a single chess concept, such as material advantage or dangerous passed pawns. In contrast, Fable 5 and GPT-5.5 combine several ideas in 19 of 20 and 37 of 44 motifs, respectively. Such motifs can hold for different reasons in different positions. Fable’s concrete target motif, for example, can identify profitable captures, weak-pawn pressure, advanced passed pawns, or king attacks, subject to material and piece-safety conditions. Another example is GPT-5.5 ’s Material-parity forcing gain or mobile bishop pair.

Material advantage appears in most model motif sets. Qwen, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Opus 5 require at least a pawn advantage; GLM-5.2 requires two; Kimi-K3 accepts a material lead or, at equal material, more attacks on enemy pieces. GPT-5.5 requires a one-pawn material advantage, counting a 0.4 -pawn bonus for having two bishops. The bishop pair also appears in most motif sets: Qwen, GLM-5.2, Kimi-K3, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro require two bishops against at most one; GPT-5.6 Sol adds equal material and minor piece counts; Fable 5 adds safe pieces and king; and Opus 5 and GPT-5.5 include it in broader motifs.

We measure uniqueness by applying motifs to the winning set and finding each motif’s largest containment overlap with any motif from another model; lower overlap means more unique. Among motifs from Opus 5, Fable 5, GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.6 Sol with \Delta(f)\geq 5\%, the two most unique both come from Opus 5: Opponent pieces tied to passive defence finds pieces forced to defend or block passed pawns, while Opponent saddled with a bad minor piece finds a knight with few safe squares or a bishop trapped by its own pawns. Among these four models, the most unique accepted motif (\Delta(f)>1\%) is also from Opus 5: Line pressure with pins and x-rays (\Delta=1.16\%), which compares the two sides’ pins, x-rays, batteries, and potential discovered attacks.

With standard selection, Baseline scores 0.079 and BinProp scores 0.235 (Table 1). Selecting the highest-scoring motif among each model’s up to three already-selected motifs, using test labels, gives 0.164 and 0.356. Choosing the best of these motifs across all eight models gives 0.429 and 0.660. Both oracles use the maximum motif score rather than the mean. The cross-model BinProp oracle (0.660) more than doubles the best individual BinProp result (0.296), suggesting room for further improvements through better ranking, stronger motifs, or both.

Does a higher explainability score correspond to better chess knowledge? If better explanations capture more useful chess concepts, those concepts should also help choose better moves. To test this, we randomly sample motif sets with varying explainability scores and use each set as features in a simple position evaluator. If explainability is indeed tied to objective chess strength, motif sets with higher explainability scores should agree more often with Stockfish.

We use motifs from the four strongest BinProp runs: Fable 5, Opus 5, GPT-5.5, and GLM-5.2. We repeatedly sample sets of 10 motifs whose mean explainability ranges from 7.5\% to 27.5\%. Each set defines a 10-feature evaluator: feature j is one when motif j holds and zero otherwise. We fit a regularized linear model on the 200k winning and losing positions to predict Stockfish’s centipawn evaluation, learning one weight per motif. The test set contains 100 starting positions with eight unseen continuation pairs each. Both continuations in a pair begin from the same position: one follows Stockfish’s best move, while the other follows a lower-evaluated alternative. The evaluator agrees with Stockfish when it assigns the best continuation a higher score. As shown in Fig. 4, explainability strongly correlates with Stockfish agreement (\rho=0.66, p<10^{-4}).

Concept-Guided Chess Commentary (CCC) (Kim et al., 2025) is the closest reproducible prior method. It ranks 21 LeelaChessZero (Leela Chess Zero Contributors, 2018) concept probes and conditions commentary on the top five.

We use Fable 5, the highest-scoring BinProp model, at maximum reasoning and give CCC the same eight support boards as the baseline and BinProp. For evaluation, Fable 5 translates each commentary into up to three Boolean Python functions. Two additional Fable 5 calls check that converting the commentary into code preserves its meaning. Functions approved by both checks undergo the same 50% support-fit filter and scoring as BinProp. If no working function passes both checks, the commentary scores zero. On the test set, CCC scores 0.051, compared with 0.031 for the baseline and 0.296 for BinProp. Figure shows example explanations from CCC and BinProp.

section: Using BinProp to Explain Go, Draughts, and Shogi
text: We next ask whether BinProp extends beyond chess. We present our experiments on Go here, on draughts in § E, and on shogi in § F. For Go, we use 100k winning and 100k losing positions from JGDB (Redmon,), scored by KataGo (Wu, 2019), and evaluate on 100 held-out expert-game positions with positive, negative, and nearby-negative continuations (see § D.1). BinProp retains its chess discovery settings; engines, score bands, and continuation sampling are game-specific.

section: Using BinProp to Explain Go, Draughts, and Shogi
text: On Go, BinProp improves explainability scores for all eight models (Table 4). Like in chess, the few-shot baseline often produces brittle, coordinate-specific motifs: one Qwen motif requires three Black stones on a fixed board segment, while one GLM-5.2 motif examines only a fixed 3\times 3 region. BinProp instead finds reusable Go concepts (Fig.). Kimi-K3 ’s local stone density territory estimates territory from nearby stones, while Opus 5 ’s multi-scale box-majority area lead combines local influence at two scales. Beyond territory, BinProp finds motifs about the risk of losing groups of stones. GPT-5.5 ’s net low-liberty attack swing compares threatened and defended groups, while GPT-5.6 Sol ’s low-liberty burden advantage compares how many stones each side has in groups with only one or two liberties.

Prior work explains classifier outputs with textual or multimodal justifications (Hendricks et al., 2016; Park et al., 2018), counterexamples or absent features (Gulshad and Smeulders, 2020; Dhurandhar et al., 2018), and sensitivity to user-defined concepts (Kim et al., 2018). Natural-language explanations can also provide executable supervision. BabbleLabble (Hancock et al., 2018) lets a user explain why a training example has a label, then converts that explanation into a program that labels new examples. For instance, the phrase due to appearing between two entities becomes a rule for recognizing a causal relation. Related methods jointly learn language interpretation and classification or generate Python labeling functions with text-to-text models (Srivastava et al., 2017; Papanikolaou, 2021). Anchors finds short conditions under which a classifier almost always keeps the same prediction, while LORE also describes nearby changes that would flip it (Ribeiro et al., 2018; Guidotti et al., 2018).

Closest in structure to our work are methods that propose and score natural-language differences between groups of samples. This pattern has been used for text distributions and goal-directed corpus analysis (Zhong et al., 2022; Zhong et al., 2023), image sets (Dunlap et al., 2024), and language-model outputs (Dunlap et al., 2025). A language model can also evolve class-specific visual attributes, retaining those that improve a CLIP classifier (Chiquier et al., 2025). NLParam iteratively builds statistical models whose features are yes/no natural-language statements about individual examples (Zhong et al., 2024). VidDiff and ADIFF instead describe fine-grained differences between paired videos or audio recordings (Burgess et al., 2025; Deshmukh et al., 2025). BinProp likewise proposes and tests descriptions, but compiles each one into a deterministic board function.

Lee et al. (2022) generate commentary from an engine’s evaluation of move quality and its suggested continuations. Cui et al. (2026) turn selected engine lines into written plans and test whether humans and language models can use them against different replies. In concurrent work, ACT-Eval decomposes commentary into atomic claims, checks factual claims with chess tools, and measures coverage against expert annotations (Hebbar et al., 2026). BinProp automatically discovers motifs as Python functions and tests them on engine continuations.

McGrath et al. (2022) train simple linear models to detect human-defined chess concepts, such as material advantage and the bishop pair, in AlphaZero’s internal activations. They also look for concepts without predefined labels using matrix factorisation and correlations between activations and board features. This reveals patterns such as which squares an opponent’s pieces can reach, although most factors in later layers remain uninterpreted. Schut et al. (2025) compare AlphaZero’s internal representations along strong and weak search lines to find features that separate them. They keep features that a student agent can learn and that appear more clearly in AlphaZero games than in human games. They then show example positions to four grandmasters and test whether the players can infer these concepts. BinProp requires no engine activations or training: it iteratively discovers concepts that are associated more with winning positions than losing ones.

We introduce BinProp, a training-free method for finding natural-language explanations for chess, Go, draughts, and shogi moves. BinProp iteratively finds concepts that appear more often in winning positions than in losing ones. Beyond games, BinProp could explain agent rollouts spanning hundreds or thousands of steps (Press et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2026), showing why one trajectory succeeds and a similar one fails when manual review is impractical.

The First Token Is Not the Verdict: Hidden Costs of Reading LLM Judges Without Generating. Reading an LLM judge's verdict from the logits of its first generated token is cheap, requires no generation, and is exactly what constrained decoding and likelihood-scoring evaluation harnesses produce. We show that this readout distorts position bias in one direction: it overstates it in every condition we test, so figures obtained this way behave as upper bounds. The mechanism is that judges do not always lead with a verdict token, on 12% to 49% of pairs for three Qwen3 judges and under 3% for Llama-3.1-8B and Phi-3.5-mini, and forcing a read on those pairs returns whichever response was shown first rather than a judgment. Pooled over the 924 pairs where a judge did not commit, the forced read flips on 89.7% of them when the responses are swapped, against 47.5% read after generation (paired difference +0.422, 95% CI [+0.365, +0.467]). The distortion is specific to what is measured: it moves position bias by 42 points while moving judge accuracy by under one point in seven of ten conditions, so it misleads whoever audits a judge rather than whoever uses one.

A second, smaller failure occurs even when the judge does lead with a verdict token, since it sometimes opens with one letter and reasons its way to the other, on 0 to 5.5% of pairs at a rate uncorrelated with compliance. We recommend reporting the rate at which a judge leads with a verdict token, which costs one forward pass and no labels, alongside any position-bias figure.

Position bias is measured by presenting each pair of responses in both orders and counting how often the verdict flips, that is, reverses (Zheng et al., 2023; Norman et al., 2026). Obtaining that verdict requires choosing a protocol, and the two protocols in common use are not the same operation.

The first protocol generates a response and parses the verdict from the text, which is what judge audits do (Norman et al., 2026; Usami et al., 2026; Tan et al., 2024). The second reads the verdict from the logits of the first generated token. It is far cheaper because it requires no generation at all, it is what restricted-likelihood evaluation harnesses compute, and it is what constrained decoding produces by construction, since token masking guarantees a legal verdict at the first position (Gao et al., 2024; Willard and Louf, 2023). That guarantee is advertised as the point: one never gets a parse error and never has to retry.

Existing practice handles a non-verdict first token in one of three ways, and two of them are the forced read. Restricted-likelihood harnesses score only the candidate answers against each other and never ask what the model would have said (Gao et al., 2024). Constrained decoding masks every illegal token, so a verdict is produced by construction (Willard and Louf, 2023). The third way is to generate and, on a parse failure, retry or let the judge continue, which is what JudgeBench does (Tan et al., 2024). Only the third recovers what the judge would have answered.

Logit-based judging is in production use rather than hypothetical. Probability-weighted score aggregation is standard (Liu et al., 2023), and AlpacaEval 2.0 computes its headline win-rate from the logprobs of a single output token (Li et al., 2023). We did not identify a published position-bias figure obtained this way, so we ask a conditional question: if judge verdicts are obtained as this tooling obtains them, what does that cost when the quantity measured is position bias? The guarantee turns out to be the problem. A judge that was not going to commit still yields a verdict, and that verdict carries position rather than content.

A pair is two responses to one instruction, shown in two presentations, one per order, under a prompt ending “Answer with exactly one character”. We take two readouts of the same judge on the same pairs. The first-token readout takes the larger of the two verdict-token logits at the first generated position, whether or not either was what the judge would actually have emitted; we call it the forced read, and that property is what this paper is about. The generated readout lets the model write up to 500 tokens and parses the verdict using explicit decision patterns such as “the answer is X”, rather than bare mentions of the letters, because the judge names both responses repeatedly while reasoning; where none parses we regenerate once at 1{,}500 tokens. A pair is compliant when the judge would have led with a verdict token in both presentations, that is, when the argmax over its full vocabulary is one of the two verdict tokens.

The judges are Qwen3 at 1.7 B, 4 B and 8 B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini. The benchmarks are JudgeBench (Tan et al., 2024), 620 pairs, and LLMBar (Zeng et al., 2024), 419 pairs. Verdict tokens are X/Y, A/B and 1/2. We run the full benchmarks. Intervals are cluster bootstraps over benchmark sources. Qwen3 supports a hybrid thinking mode, which we disable (enable_thinking=False) so that all judges receive comparable single-turn prompts; the non-compliance we report is therefore not an artefact of an explicit reasoning mode being left on.

Two properties of this design make our numbers conservative. Our prompt asks for one character, so the generated readout measures the judge disobeying it; audits that invite reasoning would see lower compliance and a larger divergence. And the 88 presentations that still yield no verdict at 1{,}500 tokens are excluded from both readouts; every such pair is non-compliant, so the exclusion removes data from the arm that produces the effect. Recovery is uneven: the second pass resolves 95\% of the Qwen3-8B cases but 54\% for Qwen3-1.7B, which often reaches the cap without concluding.

section: Compliance varies widely and is not predictable
text: Compliance is a property of a model, a prompt and a task together, not of a model alone. Holding Qwen3-8B and the benchmark fixed and changing only the two verdict tokens moves it from 0.506 to 0.676. Holding the model and the prompt fixed and changing the benchmark moves it from 0.506 to 1.000, LLMBar items being short instruction-following comparisons while JudgeBench items are technical questions that invite step-by-step work. Across Qwen3 sizes compliance is non-monotone, running 0.663, 0.885, 0.506 at 1.7 B, 4 B and 8 B. Reported elsewhere for this same Llama-3.1-8B under a multiple-choice prompt, first-token validity is 9.5\% (Cappelletti et al., 2025), against 99.8\% under ours. A compliance rate cannot be inherited from another study.

section: A forced read on an undecided judge locks to a slot
text: The two readouts diverge only on pairs where the judge did not lead with a verdict token, and there they diverge sharply. Because both readouts are measured on the same pairs, the comparison is paired, and we pool it across conditions. Of 924 pooled non-compliant pairs, the forced read flips on 829 of them (0.897) and the generated read on 439 (0.475), a paired difference of +0.422 with a 95\% cluster-bootstrap interval of [+0.365,+0.467] over conditions. Of the 420 pairs on which the two readouts disagree about whether a flip occurred, 405 are flips seen only under the forced read and 15 only under generation (exact McNemar p=1.0\times 10^{-99}, which treats pairs as independent and so understates the true p; the clustered interval above is the one we rely on).

section: A forced read on an undecided judge locks to a slot
text: What the forced read is measuring follows by identity rather than by inference. With two verdict tokens and no ties, a flip occurs exactly when the same slot position is selected in both presentations, because the responses swap between them; we verify that this holds on all 5{,}720 pairs (the 11{,}596 order-presentations counted in Section 5 are the 5{,}798 pairs before exclusion, each presented twice). The flip rate on non-compliant pairs is therefore not evidence of a slot lock but is itself the rate at which the forced read locked to a slot, 0.897.

section: A forced read on an undecided judge locks to a slot
text: The slot it locks to is almost always the first one. Of the 829 locked non-compliant pairs, 827 locked to the first position (0.998; exact binomial against chance p=1.9\times 10^{-244}), and four of the five conditions lock to it without a single exception. The lock is to a fixed position at the logit level rather than being item-specific, and it makes the error one-sided: in all five conditions the forced read flips more, never less, so position-bias figures obtained from first-token logits are upper bounds on what a generate-and-parse audit would report.
