section: A forced read on an undecided judge locks to a slot
text: The choice of readout affects measurement rather than use. Against gold labels the two readouts differ in accuracy by nothing at all in four conditions and by more than a point in only three, the largest difference being 6.7 points (0.439 to 0.648 overall). Flip rate, by contrast, differs by up to 0.220. Both readouts are near chance on the non-compliant pairs that drive the divergence, because the judge does not know the answer there under either protocol. The forced read adds error that depends on order but not on the label, so it affects whoever audits a judge far more than whoever uses one.

section: A compliant first token is usually, but not always, the conclusion.
text: On 300 compliant pairs per judge we compared the first token to the parsed final verdict. Qwen3-4B disagrees on 15 of 271 parsed (5.5\%), Phi-3.5-mini on 14 of 257 (5.4\%), Qwen3-8B on 8 of 285 (2.8\%) and Llama-3.1-8B on 0 of 300 (0.0\%, Wilson 95\% CI [0.0\%,1.3\%]). The disagreements share a form: the judge opens with X, then writes “…Therefore, Response Y better follows the instruction.” This failure is independent of the first: across the four judges its rate is uncorrelated with compliance (r=0.01), and Phi-3.5-mini leads with a verdict token on 97.1\% of pairs yet changes its mind on 5.4\% of them. The judge that looks safest for a first-token readout is not the one least distorted by it.

section: A cheaper procedure, and what it is worth
text: The characterisation suggests a shortcut: read the first token, and generate only for the orders where the judge did not lead with a verdict. Adaptive computation of this shape is standard (Jung et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2024), but those cascades escalate to a stronger model under a calibrated threshold, whereas we escalate between two readouts of the same model and need no calibration set. The saving is large and the fidelity is high but not perfect. Across our ten conditions the procedure generates for 1{,}678 of 11{,}596 order-presentations, a reduction of 85.5\%, ranging from 58.9\% on the least compliant condition to 100\% where the judge always leads with a verdict. By Section 4 the substituted verdicts are wrong on 0 to 5.5\% of compliant pairs, so fidelity runs from about 0.945 to 1.00. It is an approximation with a measured error rate rather than a guarantee.

The divergence is measurable in only one of the three families we test. Compliance is so high for the other two that Phi-3.5-mini contributes 18 non-compliant pairs and Llama-3.1-8B one, too few to analyse, so the pooled comparison is Qwen3 only and the cross-family contrast is a difference in compliance rather than an independent replication of the effect. We also test only open-weight judges at 8 B and below, because frontier API judges do not expose logits.

Two measurement choices should be read with the result. The generated readout uses a heuristic parser and a capped budget, so even after the second pass it is a lower bound on how often a verdict is eventually reached. And we tested whether the two readouts reorder judges by position bias; the reordering was not stable under bootstrap (50.1\% of resamples) and we do not claim it.

Our question is conditional on a practice rather than a correction of a published number. That first-token reads fail when a model does not commit is already stated for multiple-choice settings (Cappelletti et al., 2025), and the readout is in production use (Li et al., 2023). Prompts engineered for single-token output may reach compliance close to 1, and output prefilling (Cappelletti et al., 2025) is a plausible remedy we have not tested; our point is that neither is usually verified or reported.

Three things belong in a judge deployment disclosure, all cheap and currently absent from reported evaluations. Report the compliance rate: it costs one forward pass per pair, needs no labels, varies from 0.506 to 1.000 across our conditions, and cannot be inherited from another paper. Rao and Callison-Burch (2026) ask the same of abstention and tie rates in generated outputs; ours applies that discipline one step earlier. Say which readout produced the verdict, because a figure obtained by constrained decoding and one obtained by generate-and-parse are not the same quantity when compliance is incomplete. And treat the answer format as an experimental variable: changing two characters moves compliance by 17 points here, and most papers do not report which verdict tokens they used.

The first token is a convenient place to read a judge’s verdict and an unreliable one. It is not a verdict at all on up to 49\% of pairs, and not its conclusion on up to 5.5\% of those where it looks like one. Both rates are measurable in advance and neither is reported.

Temporally-Resolved Token Attribution Reveals the Generation Dynamics of Diffusion Language Models. This work presents Diffusion Layer Integrated Gradients (DLIG), a token attribution method for diffusion language models (DLMs) that extends Integrated Gradients (IG~\cite{sundararajan2017axiomatic}) to arbitrary layers and denoising steps. DLIG attributes a DLM's progressive commitment to a self-generated or fixed completion for an input prompt. We establish direct correspondences between DLIG and the IG axioms of completeness, implementation invariance, linearity, and symmetry preservation. As a lightweight complement to interventional analysis, DLIG provides an inexpensive first check of mechanistic hypotheses across the denoising trajectory. We demonstrate this on word-sense disambiguation, multi-hop graph reasoning, and sentence infilling, revealing how DLMs draw on inputs across positions, layers, and denoising steps.

Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate by iterative refinement rather than left-to-right prediction, unmasking a sequence over a trajectory of denoising steps. This changes what it means to explain a generation: the same output token is arrived at gradually and the computation supporting it is distributed over both network depth and denoising time. Explaining a DLM’s output therefore requires locating support not only where in the network it lives but when along the trajectory it forms.

Yet post-hoc attribution for DLMs remains largely unaddressed. A recent taxonomy formalizes what an attribution contract for iterative generation should provide, but no concrete method instantiates one: existing token-attribution tools carry no notion of a denoising step, while DLM interpretability has primarily adapted expensive interventional analyses such as causal tracing.

We close this gap with Diffusion Layer Integrated Gradients (DLIG). DLIG scores the model’s commitment to its self-generated completion at a chosen layer and denoising step, and attributes that score to the prompt by integrating gradients along a path from a prompt-free baseline to the prompt-present state. Resolved over a grid of layers and steps, it yields a per-token attribution field exposing how output-driving support evolves through denoising. The construction admits an exact correspondence to Integrated Gradients applied at a fixed (\text{layer},\text{step}), which lets us carry the IG axioms over to DLIG. Crucially, this correspondence holds at a single coordinate; DLIG’s value comes from assembling these axiom-preserving scores across the layer–step grid to expose trajectory structure that single-pass attribution cannot reveal. This temporal resolution parallels recent causal-tracing approaches for DLMs, while providing a relatively light-weight first-pass analysis.

We demonstrate DLIG on word-sense disambiguation, multi-hop reasoning, and sentence infilling with DiffuGPT-M, using it to test concrete hypotheses about where and when output-driving evidence emerges. § 3 defines DLIG and extends the IG axioms to it (§ 3.1); § 5, § 6, and § 7 report the three tasks, with implementation checks and full statistics in Appendices A.1 and B. This positions DLIG as a lightweight first check that can identify or rule out candidate mechanisms before more expensive causal interventional analyses.

Diffusion, originating in nonequilibrium thermodynamics, has become the central algorithm behind modern image generation models. Recent work has applied diffusion to language models —generating text through iterative refinement over a denoising trajectory—as compared to standard next-token prediction language models, achieving competitive performance with substantially higher throughput. DLMs broadly fall into three families: continuous-space DLMs, which diffuse over continuous embeddings before mapping back to discrete tokens; discrete-space DLMs, which diffuse directly over tokens or vocabulary states via masking or transition matrices; and hybrid AR–diffusion models, which combine autoregressive generation with diffusion-based refinement. We propose DLIG, an attribution method for interpreting DLM behavior. Although instantiated on a discrete DLM, our approach is broadly applicable to iterative diffusion processes.

section: Explainable AI (XAI), Attribution Methods and Diffusion Explainability.
text: XAI encompasses post-hoc methods for explaining model decisions, including SHAP, LIME, and Integrated Gradients (IG). IG quantifies feature contributions to a model’s prediction and has been adapted to language models to measure the influence of individual input tokens on generated outputs. Attention and probe-based analyses can reveal information encoded by models and support hypothesis formation, but attribution methods more directly connect model behavior to specific inputs while remaining lightweight and interpretable. In diffusion models, post-hoc explanation has focused primarily on vision, either using diffusion to construct IG integration paths or deriving CAM-style visual attributions from denoising states in diffusion MLLMs. For DLMs, however, post-hoc explanation remains largely conceptual: a recent taxonomy formalizes attribution contracts for iterative generation, but no concrete method instantiates them. In particular, token-level attribution across layers and denoising steps remains open. We address this gap with DLIG, which extends IG to quantify a DLM’s progressive commitment to its completion at arbitrary layers and denoising steps.

Interpretability aims to reverse engineer the computations of machine learning models into human understandable algorithms. Mechanistic interpretability has emerged as a sub-domain that aims to interpret larger neural networks, typically large multimodal models. Standard techniques include observable methods such as training probes to decode linearly encoded information in the residual stream, causality driven interventions that identify the causal role of internal representations through activation patching and causal tracing, dictionary/concept-learning methods, and geometry and activation driven steering methods. Recent work has adapted these methods to interpret DLM behavior. Shnaidman et al. [39] extract a low-dimensional refusal direction from contrastive prompts and intervene on residual-stream activations during denoising, An and Han [40] steer DLMs by biasing token distributions with pre-computed attribute scores, Li et al. [41] analyze safety across denoising steps and introduce representation-based auditing and repair, Yao et al. [5] adapt the original causal tracing technique for masked DLMs, and Kong et al. [42] use hidden-state geometry to identify diffusion-friendly layers for diffusion-based replacement. Rather than competing with interventional methods, DLIG provides a lightweight complementary first check: inexpensive attribution can identify or rule out candidate mechanisms before more costly causal validation.

Let a masked diffusion language model denoise a sequence over T steps. At a fixed diffusion step t, let X_{t} denote the partially-unmasked sequence and C the conditioning prompt occupying positions 1,\dots,L. We attribute a scalar score F_{t} to the model’s internal computation at a chosen layer \ell, isolating the causal contribution of the prompt to that score.

The score reads out the model’s commitment to its own completion at step t. Let z_{t}(\cdot)\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|} be the logits the model emits at each generated position, and let y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{n}) be the target tokens occupying the generated region (positions L{+}1,\dots,L{+}n). We use the summed target log-probability F_{t}\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_{i}\,\log\mathrm{softmax}\big(z_{t}^{(L+i)}\big)_{y_{i}}, where m_{i}\in\{0,1\} masks out positions not yet scored. By default y is self-generated: y_{i}=(X_{t})_{L+i}, the tokens the model has itself committed to along its denoising trajectory, so the attribution targets actual model behavior. F_{t} then measures how strongly the layer- \ell activations drive the model toward the completion it is in the process of producing. We also implement the fixed-target framing where y is a supplied string held constant across prompts and diffusion steps, and F_{t} scores the model’s commitment to that string.

Let a=h^{(\ell)}_{t}(X_{t},C) be the layer- \ell activations under the true prompt, and let a^{\prime}=h^{(\ell)}_{t}(X_{t},\varnothing) be the activations under a null conditioning obtained by masking the prompt positions while holding the generated tokens X_{t} fixed. The pair (a^{\prime},a) defines a straight-line path in activation space from the prompt-free to the prompt-present state.

DLIG attributes F_{t} to layer- \ell activations by integrating the gradient of F_{t} along that path and weighting by the displacement: \mathrm{DLIG}^{(\ell)}_{t}\;=\;(a-a^{\prime})\;\odot\;\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\partial F_{t}}{\partial a}\Big(a^{\prime}+\alpha\,(a-a^{\prime})\Big)\,d\alpha, with \odot the elementwise product, so that \mathrm{DLIG}^{(\ell)}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times H} carries one attribution value per (position, hidden-dim). The integral is approximated by an m -point Riemann sum, \mathrm{DLIG}^{(\ell)}_{t}\;\approx\;(a-a^{\prime})\;\odot\;\frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{\partial F_{t}}{\partial a}\Big(a^{\prime}+\tfrac{k}{m}\,(a-a^{\prime})\Big).

The tensor \mathrm{DLIG}^{(\ell)}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times H} carries a value per (position, hidden-dim). To score attributions, we collapse the hidden axis to one score per token, s^{(\ell)}_{t}[i]=\sum_{j}\mathrm{DLIG}^{(\ell)}_{t}[i,j], and read a prompt token’s attribution off at its position i\leq L. Completeness (§ 3.1), \sum_{i}s^{(\ell)}_{t}[i]=F_{t}(X_{t},C)-F_{t}(X_{t},\varnothing), makes the summed per-token attribution an exact additive decomposition of the causal effect of inserting the prompt, with s^{(\ell)}_{t}[i] being position i ’s share of that total. Since the baseline masks the prompt, s^{(\ell)}_{t}[i]>0 means the token drives the model toward its target, while s^{(\ell)}_{t}[i]<0 means its presence suppresses the target at layer \ell.

Fix a layer \ell and step t, and let G_{t}^{(\ell)}:\mathbb{R}^{S\times H}\to\mathbb{R} denote the map that overrides the layer- \ell output with a candidate activation u, recomputes the layers above \ell, and reads out the score: G_{t}^{(\ell)}(u)\;=\;F_{t}\big(\,\text{layers }\ell{+}1,\dots\text{ applied to }u\,\big). Then, DLIG is exactly IG applied to the function G_{t}^{(\ell)} with input a=h^{(\ell)}_{t}(X_{t},C) and baseline a^{\prime}=h^{(\ell)}_{t}(X_{t},\varnothing): \mathrm{DLIG}^{(\ell)}_{t}[i,j]\;=\;\mathrm{IG}_{ij}\big(G_{t}^{(\ell)};\,a,\,a^{\prime}\big)\;=\;(a-a^{\prime})_{ij}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\partial G_{t}^{(\ell)}}{\partial u_{ij}}\big(a^{\prime}+\alpha\,(a-a^{\prime})\big)\,d\alpha.

section: Extending Axiomatic Properties of IG to DLIG
text: The axiomatic guarantees of IG are proved for an arbitrary almost-everywhere-differentiable scalar function of the integration variable. Next, we demonstrate that these guarantees transfer to DLIG by instantiating that function as G_{t}^{(\ell)}, which is differentiable almost-everywhere as a composition of transformer blocks and a softmax readout, along with direct implementation tests where required.

section: Extending Axiomatic Properties of IG to DLIG
text: (1) Completeness. The attribution summed over all coordinates equals the difference in the scored function between the endpoints of the integration path: \sum_{i,j}\mathrm{DLIG}^{(\ell)}_{t}[i,j]=G_{t}^{(\ell)}(a)-G_{t}^{(\ell)}(a^{\prime})=F_{t}(X_{t},C)-F_{t}(X_{t},\varnothing). The identity holds for any scalar F read off from h^{(\ell)} up to the O(1/m) error of the m -point Riemann sum, independent of how F consumes the logits; it is therefore agnostic to the shifted-readout convention, which is checked separately below. Completeness also implies the Sensitivity(a) axiom—if a and a^{\prime} differ only in coordinate (i,j) and G_{t}^{(\ell)}(a)\neq G_{t}^{(\ell)}(a^{\prime}), completeness applied to the pair forces \mathrm{DLIG}^{(\ell)}_{t}[i,j]\neq 0.

section: Extending Axiomatic Properties of IG to DLIG
text: (2) Implementation Invariance. The attribution depends on the network only through the function G_{t}^{(\ell)} and its gradients. For any two parameterizations realizing the same map, G_{t}^{(\ell)}\equiv\tilde{G}_{t}^{(\ell)} implies \mathrm{DLIG}^{(\ell)}_{t}=\widetilde{\mathrm{DLIG}}^{(\ell)}_{t} at every (a,a^{\prime}).

section: Extending Axiomatic Properties of IG to DLIG
text: (3) Linearity. For scalar weights \lambda_{1},\lambda_{2} and readouts G_{1},G_{2} of the same activation, \mathrm{IG}(\lambda_{1}G_{1}+\lambda_{2}G_{2})=\lambda_{1}\,\mathrm{IG}(G_{1})+\lambda_{2}\,\mathrm{IG}(G_{2}). Since F_{t} enters DLIG only through G_{t}^{(\ell)}, attributions toward two fixed targets y^{+},y^{-} may be differenced, \Delta\mathrm{DLIG}^{(\ell)}_{t}\;=\;\mathrm{DLIG}^{(\ell)}_{t}\big(y^{+}\big)-\mathrm{DLIG}^{(\ell)}_{t}\big(y^{-}\big)\;=\;\mathrm{IG}\big(G_{t}^{(\ell)}(\cdot\,;y^{+})-G_{t}^{(\ell)}(\cdot\,;y^{-});\,a,\,a^{\prime}\big), i.e. the difference is itself a valid path attribution of the contrast score F_{t}(\cdot\,;y^{+})-F_{t}(\cdot\,;y^{-}), and satisfies completeness with respect to \Delta F_{t}.

section: Extending Axiomatic Properties of IG to DLIG
text: (4) Symmetry Preservation. DLIG integrates along the straight-line path \gamma(\alpha)=a^{\prime}+\alpha(a-a^{\prime}), the unique path choice for which the theorem holds; the property is inherited unchanged.

We demonstrate DLIG’s utility in explaining DLM behavior across three tasks, all using DiffuGPT-M, a masked diffusion language model adapted from GPT-2-medium. Task-specific configurations, training details, and the per-task denoising-step grids used for attribution are in Appendix C.

Word-Sense Disambiguation. WiC asks whether a target word shares its sense across two context sentences (binary). We wrap each instance in a prompt querying sense-match, with the model generating Yes / No; answer tokens share no vocabulary with the disambiguating context, avoiding surface-form overlap. As the official test labels are private, we re-split the train set into 4,928 train / 638 val / 500 test and finetune DiffuGPT-M.

Multi-Hop Graph Reasoning. ProsQA is a synthetic multi-hop benchmark: each question states an ontology of typing facts (with off-path distractors), roots the queried subject, and poses a binary choice (“Is s a A or B?”) whose gold option is reachable by a k -hop chain. We finetune DiffuGPT-M on the 17,886 train / 300 val / 500 test split.

Sentence Infilling. ROCStories comprises five-sentence commonsense stories; we infill sentence three from the two preceding and two following sentences (1000 eval samples). The generated span attends bidirectionally to context on both sides, so DLIG can resolve how attribution mass splits between left and right context and evolves over denoising steps.
The main text reports each finding qualitatively; full quantitative results, effect sizes, and statistical significance testing for every experiment are in Appendix B.

Scored under the self-generated framing of § 3, the finetuned model is strongly Yes -biased (class-wise performance in Appendix C, Table 11). One possible explanation is that Yes and No decisions draw on prompt evidence at systematically different depths. DLIG provides an inexpensive test for this hypothesis directly from its layer-step attribution field. We contrast this attribution-based axis with a simple logit-based measure of when the model commits:

Attribution depth: Per denoising step t, we weight each layer \ell by its prompt-token attribution mass M^{(\ell)}_{t}=\sum_{i\leq L}|s^{(\ell)}_{t}[i]| and take the centroid \bar{c}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}^{\prime}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}^{\prime}}\big(\sum_{\ell}\ell\,M^{(\ell)}_{t}\big)/\big(\sum_{\ell}M^{(\ell)}_{t}\big), the mass-weighted mean layer index averaged over steps, measuring how deep the attribution sits. Commitment timing: As a behavioral comparator, we directly record the softmax probability of the committed answer token across denoising steps and define the commitment step as the earliest step from which it exceeds 0.5 and remains above it.
We report each axis as a Mann–Whitney AUC for Yes - vs. No -responses (0.5 chance), and additionally test each Yes -response population for latent structure with Hartigan’s dip test.

We first illustrate in Figure 1 a single DLIG map on a correctly answered example. The two occurrences of the pivot word channel (“the channel” and “the English Channel”) together with the content tokens of both sentences carry the dominant, positive attribution, largest in the shallow layers which decreases with depth, while function words and template scaffolding stay near zero. The one early dissenting signal is France: in the shallowest layers the model reads the geographic specificity of between France and England as mild evidence against the same-sense reading, but this is overridden with depth and flips to positive support by the mid layers, leaving the deep-layer map almost uniformly answer-aligned. Now, we analyze the attribution depth and commitment timing to ask whether the model’s Yes- and No-responses, grouped by predicted label, are mechanically distinguishable along the two axes (parseable-prediction counts per axis in Figure 2).

Yes- and No-responses read out from the same depth: The two response types are distributed near-identically along this axis (Figure 2(a)): both center just above layer 7 of the 24-layer stack, and the pred-Yes and pred-No distributions overlap almost entirely; DLIG provides cheap evidence against the depth hypothesis.

Yes-responses commit stronger and hold it: Reading the model’s confidence in its own answer across the denoising trajectory (Figure 2(b)) separates the two response types clearly: pred-Yes examples are already confident in Yes at the first denoising step and stay there, whereas pred-No examples begin only just above threshold and slightly degrade towards the end. The per-example commitment is markedly stronger for Yes than for No.

We analyze success (correct or conceptually correct, n{=}286) & failure (incorrect option, n{=}69), excluding off-manifold generations (n{=}145). One hypothesis is that failures arise from answer-driving support being mislocalized onto distractors rather than the reasoning path; DLIG directly tests this over the prompt’s fact graph. We construct each prompt’s fact graph and mark two token sets: the gold path (BFS-recovered chain from subject to gold option), and the cited chain (facts named in the model’s generation and matched to graph facts via fuzzy string matching).

We define per-example targets (y^{+}) as the gold answer sentence and (y^{-}) as the same sentence with the gold option replaced by the incorrect choice, thereby isolating the answer concept. The per-token contrastive score d[i]=s^{(\ell)}_{t}[i](y^{+})-s^{(\ell)}_{t}[i](y^{-}) measures whether prompt token i supports the correct (d[i]>0) or incorrect (d[i]<0) option. We define path precision \mathrm{prec}=\sum_{i\in\mathrm{GOLD}}\max(d[i],0)\,/\,\sum_{i\in\mathrm{FACT}}\max(d[i],0) as the fraction of positive support attributable to gold-path tokens, measuring where positive support concentrates (facts or distractors). We report its gap over chance (|\mathrm{GOLD}|/|\mathrm{FACT}|) and against a random-edge null matched for path size.

Because d tracks the gold option, its sign tracks model behavior only on successes; on fails, we therefore use d_{\mathrm{behavior}}=-d, so that d_{\mathrm{behavior}}>0 always marks support for the generated option. Along the reasoning chain, we average d_{\mathrm{behavior}} per gold-path hop, normalizing within each example by its mean |d_{\mathrm{behavior}}| across hops (so that examples contribute equally regardless of overall magnitude). We also report the contrastive magnitude \overline{|d|}, the mean |d[i]| over fact tokens (total fact attention regardless of which option it supports).

Attribution concentrates on answer driving facts: d_{\mathrm{behavior}} ’s positive mass concentrates on gold-path tokens well above chance and the random-edge null (Figure 3(a)). Concentration is layer- and step-localized—rising towards later layers, decaying over denoising (Figure 3(b))—and increases from the root fact to the answer edge at every path length (Figure 3(c)). On fails, attribution likewise concentrates on the model’s cited chain rather than the remaining facts (Table 8); where cited and gold paths diverge, the two are indistinguishable.

Errors preserve attribution localization: Gold-path precision is nearly identical for successes and fails and carries no signal in a joint logistic model (Figure 4 right; Table 8). Fails show numerically higher contrastive magnitude \overline{|d|}, but this does not significantly discriminate outcomes overall or after difficulty controls. Thus, failures do not arise from attribution shifting onto distractors: DLIG shows that the relevant reasoning structure remains localized even when the model answers incorrectly.

The model infills sentence 3 from sentences 1–2 (left) and 4–5 (right), scored under the self-generated framing of § 3. If successful infilling increasingly relies on context as the span resolves, this dependence should emerge over denoising; DLIG tests this directly. The position axis is signed distance to the span (negative = left, positive = right). Infill quality is final-span ROUGE-1 vs. gold.

Context reliance predicts infill quality, increasingly over denoising: The association between how much the model draws on context and how well it infills is absent at the first denoising steps and strengthens through the denoising (Figure 5(a)). ROUGE only scores the final span, evidencing that only once the model’s committed span has sharpened toward that final output does the context become predictive of how well it reconstructs the span. Since there is no committed span early on, context reliance and eventual quality are unrelated. Pooling over steps hides this temporal structure (Appendix A.4).

Attribution is bidirectional, left-skewed, and strengthens late in denoising: The model draws on both sides of the span, peaking at each boundary and decaying outward, with a persistently stronger left pull (a DLM sees right context an autoregressive model cannot; Figure 5(b)). Context reliance grows as the model commits to its span later in denoising (Table 10). Neither the amount nor the direction of context mass tracks infill quality (Appendix A.4); the attribution field’s shape is therefore task-level, while its late strengthening tracks commitment.

We introduce DLIG, a token-attribution method for DLMs that resolves a model’s commitment to its output jointly across network depth and the denoising trajectory scored at any (layer, step), decomposing it into per-token contributions. DLIG exposes not just where in the model support for an output lives, but how it evolves through its denoising trajectory.

We evaluate DLIG across three tasks, revealing structure a single-pass attribution would miss. On word-sense disambiguation, DLIG cheaply rules out attribution depth as an explanation for the model’s Yes bias: Yes and No responses draw on similar depths, despite sharply different commitment dynamics. On multi-hop reasoning, the DLM locates the right fact chain even when it answers wrongly, so errors trace to how it uses the facts and not where it looked. On sentence infilling, the DLM draws on both sides of the gap, including right context an autoregressive model cannot see, with context reliance correlating with infill quality only late in denoising.

Across tasks, DLIG is not only useful for visualizing attribution, but also serves to complement interventional analyses as an inexpensive first check for mechanistic hypotheses—identifying or ruling out where and when output-driving evidence emerges before more expensive interventional validation. Broadly, since a DLM arrives at its output gradually, explaining it means reading the whole denoising trajectory, not just its end. DLIG makes this dynamic evolution of a DLM’s commitment as well as where it draws from directly observable.

DLIG is a post-hoc gradient attribution method: it identifies where and when a model’s committed output is gradient-sensitive to the prompt, not the causal circuit producing it, so its outputs are hypotheses to be confirmed, not mechanism at face value—future work should pair DLIG with interventional tests (activation patching, causal tracing) against causal ground truth. We also instantiate DLIG on a single 355M discrete masked-diffusion model (DiffuGPT-M); extending to continuous-space and hybrid AR–diffusion families (§ 2), and to larger, natively-trained DLMs, is left for future work.

AlphaPilot: Multi-Turn Tool-Using LLM Agents for Adaptive Alpha Mining with Reinforcement Learning. Formulaic alpha mining seeks interpretable expressions that rank assets by future returns. The task is challenging because it demands simultaneous processing of unstructured market descriptions, historical data, and quantitative evaluation of candidate factors, yet most existing methods exploit only a subset of these signals. We introduce AlphaPilot, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains multi-turn tool-using LLM agents for adaptive alpha mining. The agent conditions on market descriptions, proposes factor expressions, queries real-data evaluator feedback, and updates a retained factor pool across turns. This design jointly leverages market text, LLM financial knowledge, real data, and evaluation feedback. At inference time, AlphaPilot performs day-by-day search and pool updates to adapt to shifting market regimes. Across three independent runs in out-of-sample rolling backtests on CSI300 and CSI500, AlphaPilot achieves mean total returns of 42.93% and 54.19%, with mean Sharpe ratios of 2.46 and 2.86, respectively. It attains the highest mean total return, Sharpe, and RankIC among the evaluated methods on both universes.

Alpha factor mining is the task of discovering predictive signals that rank assets by their expected future returns (Ding et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2025). In formulaic alpha mining, these signals are written as mathematical expressions over market features, making them easy to inspect, combine, and deploy inside existing quantitative pipelines (Zhang et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2024). This setting poses several general challenges. First, the search space is combinatorial: even a small library of operators, features, and lookback windows can generate a huge number of candidate formulas (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu and Zhu, 2025). Second, the supervision is weak and unstable, since financial returns are noisy and market regimes change over time (Shi et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025). Third, a formula that performs well in isolation may become redundant once added to a larger factor set (Yu et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2025). A practical alpha-mining framework should therefore use every available information source, including market-regime descriptions, financial priors, executable market data, and evaluation feedback, to support efficient and effective pool-level search.

Existing methods only use subsets of this information. Genetic programming and related symbolic-regression methods produce closed-form expressions that are easy to inspect and deploy, but they search formula trees through combinatorial mutation or local search and are typically guided only by scalar historical fitness, making discovery inefficient and prone to overfitting (Zhang et al., 2020; Cranmer, 2023; Petersen et al., 2021; Ren et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2026). RL and generative systems such as AlphaGen (Yu et al., 2023) and AlphaForge (Shi et al., 2024) optimize search with historical market data and downstream rewards, but they do not use language priors to interpret regimes or explain why a search direction should change (Zhu and Zhu, 2025; Xu et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025a; Zhao et al., 2025b). LLM-based frameworks add financial knowledge and natural-language reasoning, but they still rely heavily on base-model capability and remain closer to proposal-and-filter pipelines than to practical alpha-mining policies (Li et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2025; Han et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026).

Alpha-R1 (Jiang et al., 2025) trains a context-aware financial reasoning model with GRPO, but it screens a predefined alpha pool from textual descriptions rather than proposing new formulas or refining them through executable evaluator feedback.

To address this gap, we introduce AlphaPilot, a multi-turn tool-using reinforcement learning framework for adaptive formulaic alpha mining that integrates the information sources summarized in Table 1. Like Alpha-R1 (Jiang et al., 2025), AlphaPilot uses an LLM policy conditioned on daily natural-language regime descriptions and trains it with GRPO. Unlike one-shot screening, AlphaPilot gives the agent executable market-data access and detailed turn-level feedback through a multi-turn tool-use loop. Figure 1 highlights the contrast with Alpha-R1 (Jiang et al., 2025). The agent proposes new factors, queries a factor evaluator, updates the factor pool, observes structured feedback, and refines its proposals through an interpretable search trajectory. At inference time, AlphaPilot mines factors day by day and converts the retained pool into a transparent stock-selection signal, so the discovered signal set can change with market conditions rather than remain frozen after a single mining stage.

Our main contributions are: We design a multi-turn tool-using framework for formulaic alpha mining. It inherits the ability of prior LLM-based methods to condition on market descriptions, while giving the agent executable real-data access through a factor-evaluator tool and detailed turn-level feedback for newly proposed factors. We use GRPO to train the agent, improving the financial decision ability embedded in a small base model while maintaining inference efficiency. This lets the policy learn from multi-turn evaluator feedback rather than relying only on the original capability of a large general-purpose model. We build a daily adaptive inference and benchmarking framework for alpha-mining methods. It updates factor pools day by day and evaluates methods with both factor-level diagnostics and portfolio-level backtests.

Automated formulaic alpha mining has long relied on symbolic search over expression trees. Genetic programming and related symbolic regression methods (Zhang et al., 2020; Cranmer, 2023; Petersen et al., 2021; Ren et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2026) produce closed-form expressions that are easy to deploy and can yield open-ended formulaic novelty through combinatorial search. However, their search is guided solely by a noisy, non-stationary scalar fitness, and they cannot incorporate structured evaluator feedback or learn an adaptive search policy across market regimes.

Reinforcement learning and generative-based methods improve this picture by learning search or combination policies rather than relying only on unguided symbolic mutation (Xu et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025a; Zhao et al., 2025b). AlphaGen (Yu et al., 2023) and AlphaQCM (Zhu and Zhu, 2025) formulate alpha discovery as sequential decision making and emphasize the utility of synergistic factor sets. AlphaForge (Shi et al., 2024) further introduces learned generation and dynamic combination mechanisms for formulaic factors. These methods motivate our daily pool-level view of alpha mining, but they still rely on weak, noisy, and non-stationary historical scalar rewards, are less transparent than formula-level language reasoning, and can overfit to backtest-specific feedback.

Recent financial LLMs, reasoning models, and evaluation benchmarks show that language models can provide financial priors, interpretable rationales, and more flexible proposal strategies (Wu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2026b; Qian et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026). In alpha mining, LLM-based methods have begun to emerge (Wang et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Kou et al., 2025; Weng et al., 2026; Han et al., 2026). Prompt-based systems such as FAMA (Li et al., 2024) and AlphaAgent (Tang et al., 2025) show that LLMs can support autonomous factor generation with natural-language reasoning and intermediate evaluator signals. However, these systems still rely heavily on base-model capability: stronger models are slower and more expensive, while insufficiently adapted models can produce hallucinated or weakly grounded proposals. Alpha-R1 (Jiang et al., 2025) is a reinforcement-learning framework tailored to LLM-based alpha mining: it uses GRPO-trained financial reasoning for context-aware screening.

This is an important step toward trainable financial reasoning, but it still screens a predefined alpha pool rather than designing new factors, relies on textual descriptions instead of executable data access, and does not provide turn-level evaluator feedback in a multi-turn refinement loop. Taken together, these limitations motivate a new method that can efficiently use all available information in the alpha-mining loop, including market descriptions, model priors, real data, and detailed evaluator feedback as summarized in Table 1.

Our formulation is also motivated by recent agentic RL methods that train multi-turn tool-using or memory-using LLM policies with downstream outcome rewards, including search-augmented reasoning and learned memory construction (Jin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025). However, alpha mining is different from the QA-style search and memory tasks used in much of this literature. Its reward comes from noisy, delayed, and non-stationary market signals rather than discrete answers, full backtesting is too slow for every multi-turn trajectory, and the agent must track both recent failures and how each new factor changes a retained pool. These differences motivate adapting agentic RL frameworks to pool-level factor design rather than standard tool-augmented QA.

We study formulaic alpha discovery over a stock universe observed on trading days t=1,\ldots,T. Let X_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{t}\times m\times\tau} denote the available market features for the tradable assets on day t, and let y_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{t}} denote the next-period return. A formulaic alpha is a domain-specific language (DSL) expression f\in\mathcal{F} that maps X_{t} to a cross-sectional score v_{t}=f(X_{t}). The usual single-factor objective asks whether v_{t} ranks assets consistently with y_{t}, often measured by the information coefficient and rank information coefficient: \displaystyle\mathrm{IC}_{t} \displaystyle=\mathrm{corr}(v_{t},y_{t}), \displaystyle\mathrm{RankIC}_{t} \displaystyle=\mathrm{corr}(\mathrm{rank}(v_{t}),\mathrm{rank}(y_{t})).

In deployment, however, alpha factors are rarely used alone. A general pool-level objective is to select a set of factors P_{t}=\{f_{t,1},\ldots,f_{t,K_{t}}\}\subset\mathcal{F} and combination weights w_{t}, producing a daily stock-selection signal vector s_{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{K_{t}}w_{t,i}f_{t,i}(X_{t}). The optimization task is therefore to construct a factor pool whose aggregated signal has future predictive utility while satisfying practical constraints such as validity, coverage, diversity: \displaystyle\max_{P_{t},w_{t}} \displaystyle\mathcal{J}(P_{t},w_{t};W_{t}^{\mathrm{future}})-\lambda\Omega(P_{t},w_{t};\mathcal{A}_{t}) \displaystyle\mathrm{s.t.} \displaystyle f\in\mathcal{F},\quad\forall f\in P_{t}. Here \mathcal{J} can be instantiated by future-window IC/RankIC, portfolio return, or other downstream utility measures, while \Omega denotes a generic regularization term over the candidate pool which encourages retained factors to be nonredundant and diverse, rather than repeatedly proposing variations of the same signal.

AlphaPilot instantiates the rolling alpha-mining workflow as the multi-turn tool-using pipeline shown in Figure 2. On each decision date, the system builds a daily market context, lets a language policy interact with an executable evaluator, and updates a retained factor pool. During offline training, it computes a reward from the pool’s future-window utility. Compared with prior formula-mining systems, this design is meant to close more of the information loop: it combines regime-aware language priors, executable real-market data, detailed turn-level evaluator feedback, and pool-level memory inside one trainable search process. Appendix Table 6 summarizes this high-level contrast.

For decision date t, the data pipeline constructs a prompt-level context c_{t}=(q_{t},\mathcal{S}_{t},\mathcal{O}), where q_{t} is the natural-language market-regime description shown to the agent, \mathcal{S}_{t} is the seed or carried-over factor manifest, and \mathcal{O} is the supported operator set. The seed factor manifest provides candidate factors as starting points, while the operator set defines the DSL that the agent is allowed to use.

AlphaPilot casts each daily search as a multi-turn tool-using process. At turn k, the small LLM policy observes the daily context c_{t}, compact memory of recently tried factors, the current retained-pool state, and available tool feedback from previous turns. It then proposes several DSL factors, a_{t,k}=\{(e_{t,k,j},g_{t,k,j})\}_{j=1}^{B}, where e_{t,k,j} is a formulaic alpha expression and g_{t,k,j} is a factor-family label. The system evaluates these factors with executable tools, updates the retained factor pool, and returns compact feedback to the agent before the next turn. This loop continues for at most H_{\max} turns.

Single-factor evaluation. The retained-pool module receives new candidate factors through the executable factor_evaluator, which is the bridge between language reasoning and market data. Given a candidate expression, the tool validates the DSL syntax, executes the factor on the current rolling training window, applies the universe and tradability filters, and returns single-factor feedback. The compact feedback shown to the policy includes the validated expression, factor family, IC, RankIC, stability, and any execution error.

Factor combination. Pool-level decisions in AlphaPilot are made from the utility of the retained set rather than from isolated factor quality. To score the current pool, we first combine retained factors into a meta-alpha by fitting nonnegative weights on the recent training segment: w_{t}^{\star}=\arg\min_{w\geq 0}\left\|Y_{t}^{\mathrm{train}}-F(P_{t,k})w\right\|_{2}^{2}+\rho\|w\|_{2}^{2}, where F(P_{t,k}) is the matrix of retained factor signals. The combined pool signal scores stocks by s_{t}(x)=\sum_{f_{i}\in P_{t,k}}w_{t,i}^{\star}f_{i}(x), and the scores are converted into cross-sectional ranks before computing the pool-level diagnostics used by the updater. Appendix A.2 gives the exact standardization and fallback details shared with the seed-factor baseline.

Pool updater. After single-factor evaluation, AlphaPilot applies a lightweight initial filter: invalid factors, factors with insufficient coverage, and factors with non-positive single-factor score are discarded. The remaining candidates are passed to the retained-pool updater, which decides whether each factor should be added, rejected, or used to replace an existing pool member according to its marginal effect on the current pool. Let \Gamma(P) denote the pool score on the recent training segment: \displaystyle\Gamma(P)= \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{IC}_{P}+\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{RankIC}_{P} \displaystyle+\eta_{\mathrm{div}}\mathrm{Div}(P)+\eta_{\mathrm{stab}}\mathrm{Stab}(P). Here \mathrm{IC}_{P} and \mathrm{RankIC}_{P} are computed from the combined pool signal above, while the auxiliary terms encourage diversity and stability. Following AlphaEval (Ding et al., 2025), we compute these regularization terms in the same way. The full definitions are given in Appendix A.1.

If the pool has free capacity, a surviving candidate is accepted when it improves \Gamma(P). If the pool is full, the candidate must improve \Gamma(P) after replacing the weakest or most redundant member. Thus the update P_{t,k+1}=\mathcal{U}(P_{t,k},a_{t,k},\xi_{t,k}) is driven by marginal contribution to the retained pool rather than by isolated factor quality alone.

Feedback. After all candidates in the current turn are processed, AlphaPilot returns three feedback views to the agent. First, a compact tool response reports the single-factor metrics and the pool decision for each submitted factor, including the update action, marginal pool gain, and similarity to the current pool. Second, a recent-tried memory summarizes prior evaluated candidates with their expression, family, score, stability, pool-update action, marginal gain, and similarity to the pool; the current turn’s submissions are already covered by the compact tool responses. This memory allows later turns to avoid repeated failures. Third, a current-pool memory summarizes the retained pool with its current pool score and each retained factor’s expression, family, score, IC, and RankIC. These feedback blocks form the history h_{t,k}. They are what make the search multi-turn rather than proposal-and-filter: the policy can condition its next proposal on both local evaluator outcomes and the evolving state of the factor pool.

At the terminal rollout length H, the final pool P_{t,H} is passed to a reward manager. Using the same nonnegative pool-combination rule defined above, the reward manager forms a final meta-alpha from P_{t,H}, converts it into cross-sectional ranks, and evaluates the ranked signal on the future window W_{t}^{\mathrm{future}}. We then compute \mathrm{PP}_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{IC}^{\mathrm{future}}_{\mathrm{pool}}+\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{RankIC}^{\mathrm{future}}_{\mathrm{pool}}. The trajectory reward is R_{t}=\sigma(\mathrm{PP}_{t}/\tau)\cdot C(P_{t,H}), where \sigma is the reward mapping used in training, \tau is a scale parameter, and C(P_{t,H}) is a pool-completeness term that penalizes trajectories ending with too few useful retained factors. Appendix A.5 gives their closed forms.

Finally, AlphaPilot trains the same tool-using policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), following recent reasoning-model training practice (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025). For each sampled decision context c_{t}, the rollout engine samples a group of G complete trajectories \{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} from the old policy \pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}. Each trajectory contains the model’s reasoning tokens, tool calls, evaluator observations, pool updates, and final reward R_{i}. GRPO forms a group-relative advantage without training a separate critic: \hat{A}_{i}=\frac{R_{i}-\mathrm{mean}(\{R_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G})}{\mathrm{std}(\{R_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G})+\epsilon}. Let \rho_{i,u}(\theta) be the probability ratio between the current policy and the old policy for generated token or action u in trajectory \tau_{i}. The clipped surrogate for each token or action is \displaystyle\ell_{i,u}(\theta)=\min\Big(\displaystyle\rho_{i,u}(\theta)\hat{A}_{i}, \displaystyle\mathrm{clip}(\rho_{i,u}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat{A}_{i}\Big). The training objective is \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\displaystyle\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|\tau_{i}|}\sum_{u\in\tau_{i}}\ell_{i,u}(\theta) \displaystyle-\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\Bigg]. Optimizing this objective increases the likelihood of proposal, tool-use, and revision decisions that lead to higher future-window pool rewards relative to other rollouts from the same market context. This is well matched to alpha mining: the evaluator metrics at each turn are noisy and local, but the useful learning signal is delayed until the final factor pool is combined and tested on future returns.

We use daily Chinese A-share panels for CSI300 and CSI500. Each decision example contains a 3-year rolling history window, natural-language regime descriptions, and a seed factor library. The 21- and 63-day future windows serve offline evaluation only and are unavailable to the inference policy. We split at 2024-01-01 for validation and 2025-07-01 for testing, sample train/validation examples every 5 trading days, and run daily test inference. Appendix Table 8 gives the exact date ranges, example counts, sampling schedules, and split objectives.

We compare AlphaPilot with deterministic LLM-agent baselines using Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, and Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507, all decoded with temperature 0. Following the benchmarking results in AlphaEval (Ding et al., 2025), we use AlphaGen (Yu et al., 2023) as the RL-based baseline and AlphaForge (Shi et al., 2024) as the generative-based baseline. For CSI300, we also include a controlled GRPO single-turn baseline with the same Qwen3-4B backbone, GRPO algorithm, data splits, and terminal pool-level reward as AlphaPilot. It generates the final factor pool in one response, removing iterative tool-based refinement while retaining RL training. We also include seed-factor linear regression and a DeepSeek-R1 direct-propose reference. We do not report a reproduced AlphaAgent baseline because the available open-source release does not provide enough detail for faithful replication in our setting. Appendix A.6 describes the baseline pipelines, seed factor library, and reproduction notes.

AlphaPilot is trained with GRPO in VERL Sheng et al. (2024) using Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. The main setup samples eight rollouts per prompt, allows up to 40 assistant turns, and uses a sigmoid-mapped future-window IC/RankIC reward with a minimum-positive-factor completeness penalty. At inference time, we preserve each baseline’s original factor-generation design as much as possible and evaluate all methods under a common day-by-day portfolio protocol. AlphaPilot uses recent-window NNLS/ridge-style factor weights; AlphaGen and AlphaForge retain their native weights (Appendix A.6). All signals are traded as long-only top- K portfolios with 10 bps transaction costs.

The main tables report total return, Sharpe, maximum drawdown, IC, and RankIC. Returns and drawdowns are percentages; IC and RankIC are daily cross-sectional metrics computed from the traded signal and next-day returns. We report three-run means for AlphaPilot, GRPO single-turn, AlphaGen, and AlphaForge, and single-run results for other methods; annualized returns and standard deviations are in Appendix Table 11. For the benchmark-relative analysis, we construct an equal-weight benchmark from the same tradable universe over the same test period and compute daily excess returns as portfolio returns minus benchmark returns. Cumulative excess return is the difference between cumulative portfolio and benchmark returns.

Table 2 shows that AlphaPilot is the strongest method on CSI300 by mean total return, Sharpe, and RankIC. It achieves 42.93% total return, 2.46 Sharpe, 0.0403 IC, and 0.0595 RankIC. The seed-factor linear-regression baseline remains substantially below AlphaPilot in portfolio return, Sharpe, and signal quality. The deterministic LLM baselines are much weaker, suggesting that prompting alone does not reliably turn a base model into a useful daily alpha-mining policy.

Table 3 gives the corresponding CSI500 results. AlphaPilot obtains the highest mean total return, Sharpe, IC, and RankIC among the reported main-table methods, reaching 54.19% total return and 2.86 Sharpe. AlphaGen and AlphaForge show substantial variation across runs on this universe, while AlphaPilot produces the strongest average signal quality in the table.

Against an equal-weight benchmark from the same tradable universe, AlphaPilot achieves 21.49% cumulative excess return with a 1.65 excess Sharpe on CSI300, and 18.22% cumulative excess return with a 1.36 excess Sharpe on CSI500. Appendix Table 12 reports the complete results.

Figure 3 plots cumulative return over the test period. On CSI300, its mean trajectory recovers from a mid-period decline and rises strongly in the final months. On CSI500, it closes the gap with AlphaGen late in the test period. It therefore records the highest final value on both CSI300 and CSI500.

The controlled-comparison block of Table 4 isolates the contribution of iterative refinement beyond RL training. Compared with GRPO single-turn, the three-run AlphaPilot result improves mean total return by 7.31 percentage points, Sharpe by 0.43, maximum drawdown by 6.98 percentage points, and RankIC by 0.0099, while achieving comparable IC (0.0403 versus 0.0407). Differences are computed from the unrounded run means. Both settings use the same backbone, GRPO algorithm, data splits, and terminal pool-level reward.

The design-ablation block of Table 4 compares the full method with three single-run design ablations on CSI300. In this comparison, the full method obtains the strongest portfolio return and Sharpe among the reported variants.

Removing memory feedback lowers total return from 48.64% to 26.40% and increases average rollout length from 5.24 to 15.75 turns. This suggests that compact tried-factor and retained-pool feedback is not only useful for selecting better factors, but also for steering the agent away from longer, less productive search trajectories.

Adding a separate reward-side auxiliary term gives comparable but slightly weaker portfolio results: 44.49% total return and 2.50 Sharpe, compared with 48.64% and 2.74 for the full setting. We therefore keep auxiliary terms in the retained-pool score, where they directly affect pool selection, but omit the extra reward-side auxiliary term in the main configuration for efficiency.

The no-pool-auxiliary variant has the best IC and RankIC in Table 4, but weaker total return and Sharpe than the full method. This gap shows that the training proxy need not align with realized portfolio return after weighting, selection, and transaction costs. We therefore prioritize pool-level utility over IC or RankIC alone.

Beyond aggregate metrics, we inspect the CSI300 AlphaPilot rollout on the first formal test trading day, 2025-07-11. The market description suggests a supportive uptrend, so momentum and trend-following factors are plausible first hypotheses. However, the evaluator assigns weak or negative RankIC to the pure momentum/trend proposals, after which the agent pivots toward reversal and liquidity-sensitive factors. Table 5 lists the factors that are actually added to the retained pool.

The trajectory highlights four behaviors. First, tool feedback corrects the initial regime prior: although the market description suggests momentum, the pool is ultimately dominated by reversal-style factors. Second, the strongest retained factors are interpretable liquidity-driven reversal signals, including -rank(vwap_spread), -rank(close / volume), and -rank(ts_delta(volume, 10)). Third, several volatility-adjusted variants receive high standalone IC/RankIC but are rejected because their marginal pool gain is negative (see Table 20 in Appendix C). The final pool therefore reflects ensemble utility rather than single-factor strength alone, reaching a pool score of 0.0938 with 14 retained factors in 4 turns. Fourth, only 4 of these 14 accepted factors come directly from the seed library, while the other 10 are newly proposed mutations, showing that the agent actively expands the factor set rather than merely selecting from seeds.

We presented AlphaPilot, a multi-turn tool-using RL framework for formulaic alpha mining that combines market descriptions, LLM financial priors, executable market data, and turn-level evaluator feedback while optimizing a retained factor pool. Across CSI300 and CSI500 rolling backtests, it achieves the highest mean total return, Sharpe, and RankIC among the evaluated methods on both universes, offering a scalable path for agentic alpha-mining policy training and inference.

Our experiments are limited by the scale of the models and benchmarks we can afford to run. Because GRPO training with multi-turn tool use is computationally expensive, we train AlphaPilot with a small open-weight LLM instead of scaling the same procedure to larger policies. Similarly, due to API and financial constraints, we do not benchmark top proprietary LLMs in the full multi-turn tool-using setting. Evaluation covers one contiguous period (July 2025–March 2026) in two Chinese equity universes; broader historical and cross-market generalization remains untested.

Our reward uses short-term future-window IC/RankIC proxy metrics rather than executing a full backtest inside every training trajectory. This proxy keeps training tractable, but it may miss deployment objectives such as drawdown control, capacity, liquidity, transaction-cost sensitivity, and risk exposure. An important direction is to design efficient reward pipelines that incorporate richer backtesting signals during alpha mining without making RL training prohibitively slow.

Finally, our goal is to study multi-turn tool-using RL training for LLM-based alpha mining, not to optimize a complete trading strategy. We therefore use a simple and transparent evaluation protocol—recent-window factor combination, a long-only top- K portfolio, daily rebalancing, and stylized transaction costs—to test whether the discovered factor pools are useful under common conditions. Designing stronger portfolio construction rules and trading strategies is left for future work.

This work studies LLM-assisted alpha factor discovery for research purposes. The proposed framework is intended for offline factor exploration and analysis, rather than as investment advice or an autonomous trading system. Any real-world deployment would require additional validation, risk control, compliance review, transaction-cost modeling, market-impact analysis, and live monitoring.

Our experiments use historical market data and do not involve personal or user-level private information. The future-window evaluation is used only to compute offline training rewards and is not available to the agent during deployment.

Same Judgment, Different Yes: Measuring Multilingual Judgment Profiles in Language Models. Multilingual evaluations often score a model's opening yes or no, a token that also carries model and language answering conventions. We ask when different ways of eliciting and reading an answer recover the same judgment, and when they measure an answer habit. We collect 1.1 million replies from eight models in six languages on up to 105 moral vignettes, varying the question's form, the answer constraint, and the reading of the reply, token or sentence, in both wordings (the FAR-6 battery). Story-level judgment profiles converge across the tested readouts and question forms, except for the yes/no token after a negative interrogative read under a preset mapping: on the same replies, token and sentence profiles agree at a median r = 0.67 across cells, while sentence profiles agree with free-sentence profiles at 0.94, a known linguistic variability. With each language's story consensus removed, a model's profile is nearest to its own in another language for 39 of 48 model-language cells under proposition labels and 15 under free sentences, against 5 expected by chance. Particle, position, and named-term preferences follow their own patterns.
A model can keep its judgment and change its yes: scoring that token requires establishing which proposition it affirms.

Language models are now asked for judgments, moral, social, and political, in many languages, and the usual instrument is a question with a fixed set of answers whose chosen option becomes a number: count yes as endorsement and no as rejection, then compare the number across models and languages (Moore et al., 2024; Labat et al., 2026), a number that is cheap, comparable, and looks language-neutral.

Nevertheless, the role of the language cannot be assumed to be null. A classic case is the negative question: an answer can address the polarity of the question or the truth of the state of affairs asked about, and which of the two yes and no pick depends on the language and, within a language, on the construction. To “Do you not agree?”, an English speaker who does not agree may answer “Yes” or “No” and mean the same thing (Goodhue and Wagner, 2018; Holmberg, 2016); a Japanese \cjkfont はい (hai, “yes”) to a neutral negative question confirms the negative, that the speaker does not agree (Kuno, 1973); German doch and French si exist to reject a negative antecedent (Claus et al., 2017; Kameyama, 2013). The particle is an answering convention, not the judgment; a model trained on these languages inherits conventions of its own, such as preferring no, the second-listed option, or the term the question names. A yes/no score therefore mixes the judgment with the way of answering, and the mixture can differ by language. A model can keep its judgment and change its yes.

This is well described for human speakers but elusive in the evaluation of language models, where the form of the question, the constraint on the answer, and the rule that reads the reply are fixed by convenience rather than varied by design (§ 2). We ask when different ways of eliciting and reading an answer recover the same judgment, and when they measure an answer habit instead. We distinguish a judgment profile, the vector of story-level judgments of one model in one language under one readout, from an answer habit, a systematic preference in the way of answering. The battery (§ 3) crosses the form of the question, including both wordings and the negative interrogative, the constraint on the answer, and the reading of the reply on the same stories in six languages for eight models, and reads the same replies twice.

We report four findings. (1) Story-level judgment profiles converge across readouts and question forms, except for the yes/no token after a negative interrogative, which disagrees with the sentence it opens on the same replies (§ 4, Figure 2). (2) The same model in another language is closer than another model in the same language, and its consensus-removed profile identifies it across languages for 39 of 48 cells (§ 5, Figure 3). (3) Preferences for no, for the second-listed option, and for the named term have patterns of their own by model and language (§ 6, Figure 4). (4) After a negative interrogative, the token maps to its own sentence by construction, language, and model (§ 7, Figure 5).

The study is motivated by how humans answer, but it measures models: a judgment measure must allow the same judgment to come with a different yes, and scoring the token requires establishing which proposition the model uses it to affirm (§ 8).

Table 1 places the battery among the closest measurement studies: option order, labels, and prompt format move multiple-choice and benchmark answers (Zheng et al., 2024; Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024; Sclar et al., 2024), and survey answers carry label, ordering, and acquiescence biases of their own, the last probed with negated-agreement questions whose ambiguity is noted but not resolved (Dominguez-Olmedo et al., 2024; Tjuatja et al., 2024; Braun, 2025). Consistency studies vary paraphrase, topic, format, and translation (Moore et al., 2024), option order, symbols, and language on human-translated survey items (Labat et al., 2026), or the prompting language of moral-reasoning tests (Khandelwal et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024); none crosses the interrogative construction with the evaluative keying, and each reads its outputs once. On what a score reads, much of the prompt sensitivity measured on English benchmarks with reference answers comes from rule-based scoring rather than from the generated answers (Hua et al., 2025); a crossed English design separates the stance on moral dilemmas from order and label effects across three instruments (Huang, 2026); and a desirability-matched format mitigates instruction-induced socially desirable responding on English personality items (Okada et al., 2026).

Model identity has been recovered by classifiers from psychometric profiles across two languages (Sha et al., 2026) and from generated text (Sun et al., 2025). The battery differs on three counts: question form and wording polarity are factors alongside the answer constraint in six languages; the same reply is read by a token rule and by a sentence judge; and identity is tested on consensus-removed profiles across six languages without a trained classifier.

section: The battery and the measurement contract
text: The battery (FAR-6; Figure 1) varies three things about a yes/no question put to a model. The first is the form of the question, covering the general ways of posing one. A plain polar question (“Was what Finn did wrong?”) is the default; the negative interrogative (“Wasn’t what Finn did wrong?”) negates it, the construction on which answer systems differ; the alternative question lists both terms (“wrong or right?”); and the or-not question (“…, or not?”) is natural in some of our languages and marked in others (Appendix A3). The second is the answer constraint, the standard ways of requesting a reply, from the least to the most constrained: a free sentence, a sentence that starts with a verdict word, a sentence that starts with yes or no (with language-specific particles), and one letter that stands for an explicit proposition, with both letter orders presented (Appendix A1). The third is the reading: the opening token or letter, read by a fixed rule, or the whole sentence, read by a judge; each form and each constraint is asked about the same stories in six languages and in both wordings of every question.

section: The battery and the measurement contract
text: The stories combine 85 Moral Foundations Vignettes with published wrongness ratings (Clifford et al., 2015) and 20 authored stories, spanning acceptable, contested, and violation cases. English, Chinese, German, and Japanese cover up to 105 stories, Korean and French 45. Language-specific concept pairs such as wrong/right and oppose/support express opposing evaluations of the act (Appendix A8); keying denotes which term the question names. Concept pair, keying, option order, and repetition (a subset of prompts receives three independent generations) stay separate throughout (Table 2).

section: The battery and the measurement contract
text: A readout combines a question form, answer constraint, and reading; a cell combines a model and a language. The fixed token rule reads yes as affirming the term named in the question and no as its opposite, counting German doch and French si with yes. After a negative interrogative this is the polarity-based mapping of the linguistic literature, one human answer system among others, which we retain as the hypothesis to be tested against the sentence it opens (§ 7). The verdict word is read by a fixed rule extended in four stated ways (Appendix A11; the figures label the rules R and R+). The sentence judge (Claude Sonnet 5, one uniform prompt) instead codes whether the reply asserts the reference proposition, asserts its opposite, takes both sides or conditions, or takes no position (P and not-P in the figures); only the first two readings are decisive and enter the shares.

section: The battery and the measurement contract
text: We orient both question wordings toward the same reference proposition before averaging, so that an answer to “right?” can be compared with an answer to “wrong?” Let q_{p} and q_{np} be the shares of decisive replies asserting the reference proposition when the question names that term and when it names its counterpart. With q_{k}=\mathrm{mean}_{\text{orders}}\Pr(\text{reference}\mid k,\text{decisive}) for the term k named in the question, judgment s=(q_{p}+q_{np})/2 averages the shares, whereas keying bias b=(q_{p}-q_{np})/2 measures their difference; repeated generations are averaged within the exact item before available orders receive equal weight. Both wordings (or both orders of an alternative question) must have decisive support, and the story score averages s over concept pairs.

section: The battery and the measurement contract
text: We compare profiles on their common stories through three quantities: story-level r, their Pearson correlation; residual-profile r, the same correlation after removing each language’s story consensus over models and each model’s mean, which asks whether a model’s departures from its peers stay distinctive; and mean \lvert\Delta\rvert, the mean absolute difference between corresponding story scores, which retains changes in individual judgments that a high correlation can conceal. Class means use 95% story-bootstrap intervals with models and languages fixed, and class differences the same resampled stories.

section: The battery and the measurement contract
text: The battery holds 1,104,574 replies, 839,230 of them in the analyzed answer constraints; the rest are additional conditions and a control stratum excluded from all analyses, and not every combination of form and constraint is run. We evaluate Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 5, GPT-6 luna, GPT-6.1 sol, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, Qwen3.8-27B, and Mistral Medium 3.5 (prompts, settings, and coverage in Appendices A1 and A2). Every free and verdict-first reply has a judged sentence, as does every yes/no-first reply to the plain question and to the negative interrogative; about 4% of the other token and label replies are judged (Appendix A2). Two other judge models agree with the sentence reference on 95.5% and 97.2% of audited replies, native readers on 95.5% of 400 replies in four languages with no opposite decisive label, and repeated runs of the same judge on 96.3% and 97.7% of two sets of 300 identical prompts (Table 7).

section: The battery and the measurement contract
text: Two readouts of one cell can differ for three reasons: sampling variability across repeated generations, which more draws reduce (Appendix A9); systematic effects of wording, keying, order, and constraint, which the balanced design averages over and § 6 measures one by one; and the mapping from an opening token to a proposition, which no amount of sampling can settle, because the same yes accompanies opposite propositions in different constructions. Reading the same replies twice isolates the third: both readings of the same replies with identical weights hold the generated text fixed, so a difference lies in the reading; comparing those sentences with free sentences on the same stories then checks whether the constraint changed the profile.
Figure 2 a gives each comparison’s median over the 48 cells and its 10–90% range on the stories common to the compared readouts (Appendix A3).

The plotted readout pairs converge except for those red rows, with median story-level r at least 0.90. Under plain questions, free sentences agree with proposition labels at 0.92 and with verdict-first sentences at 0.93; the comparisons across question forms preserve the profile likewise (Table 3). Median residual correlations among the convergent pairs range from 0.46 to 0.93: agreement retains how individual models depart from the consensus.

Under the fixed rule, the negative-interrogative token changes that picture: against the plain-question token its median story-level correlation falls to 0.73, with mean absolute story difference 0.22 and some cells below zero. On the same 71,282 replies with both readings decisive (§ 3), the token and sentence profiles agree at 0.67, with absolute difference 0.25, whereas the profiles of those judged sentences agree with free-sentence profiles from other replies on common stories at 0.94 (absolute difference 0.07); the same double reading of the plain-question replies agrees at 0.99 with absolute difference 0.02. Requiring a yes/no opening still produces sentences whose story profiles reproduce the free-sentence profile; the change lies in the opening’s mapping to its sentence.

Reply-level disagreement supports this reading without aggregation (Figure 2 b): among replies with both readings decisive, mean disagreement across cells rises from 3.3% for plain-question yes/no-first replies to 31.3% after a negative interrogative. A targeted audit by three judge configurations at high reasoning effort upholds the sentence reading in 93–96% of the conflicting negative-interrogative replies but in only about half of the conflicting plain-question replies (Appendix A1), so the plain-question rate partly reflects the judge. Verdict openings also depart more under negation; proposition letters do not (Appendix A11).

With the readouts agreeing except where noted, profiles can be compared across models and languages: is the same model in another language closer than another model in the same language? Figure 3 compares proposition-label profiles under plain questions over pairs of model–language cells, grouped by what changes: language, model, or both.

The most direct test treats the 48 cells (eight models in six languages) as unlabeled profiles and asks which other cell each one resembles most (Table 6). Under residual r, a cell’s nearest neighbor is another language of the same model for 39 of 48 proposition-label cells (per model in Figure 3 b), against 5 under a uniform-random-neighbor benchmark that gives each of the 47 other cells equal probability and ignores the language structure of the cells; under story-level r the count is 25, and under mean \lvert\Delta\rvert it is 30.

The same-model class has higher mean story-level correlation than the same-language class, 0.88 against 0.81, and a mean absolute story difference of 0.10 against 0.15; both contrasts have joint bootstrap intervals that exclude zero (+0.075 [0.047, 0.096] and -0.052 [-0.065, -0.040]). Story-level r is dominated by structure every cell shares (violations high, acceptable stories low), which keeps the gap modest. Within one story group the gap widens where models disagree, 0.79 against 0.69 on acceptable stories and 0.70 against 0.62 on contested stories, and vanishes on violations (0.43 against 0.46), where every cell condemns and little remains to tell models apart (Appendix A10).

The same model across languages retains a mean residual correlation of 0.56; within-language centering couples the different-model residuals, so their negative mean is a constrained reference, and the informative result is the positive same-model association.

The strength of that signature differs across models and language pairs (Figure 3 b). Residual correlations span 0.69–0.97 for sol against 0.14–0.50 for Qwen and about zero to 0.54 for luna. Under free sentences the residual profiles identify the model for 15 of 48 cells, against 39 under proposition labels. One candidate explanation is granularity: free-sentence story scores sit at an endpoint for 81% of model–language–story observations against 49% for labels (Appendix A9), leaving less graded structure to carry a model’s departures; the comparison does not establish this. A model thus retains a distinctive judgment profile across languages, with story-level changes of 0.10 (labels) and 0.07 (free sentences) per story.

section: Answer habits and their change under negation
text: We now return to the constrained readouts, the yes/no token under the plain question and the proposition letter, whose story profiles converge with the sentence profile while measurable answering preferences remain, attached to the question’s wording or option order rather than to the story. We measure three such habits on the same reference proposition. Yes/no keying bias is b, half the difference between the shares under the two wordings (negative for a preference for no; the sign is kept when the named term sits inside negation). Second-listed preference, measured on proposition-label choices, is half the difference between choosing the second- and the first-listed proposition. Named-term pull, a term of ours for the same choices, is the preference for the proposition that contains the term the question names, a lexical echo of the question (Figure 4).

section: Answer habits and their change under negation
text: Yes/no keying bias favors no in every plain-question cell, averaging -0.11, but its magnitude belongs to a model–language combination: the interaction accounts for 0.56 of the cell-mean matrix’s variance (cells in Appendix A4).

section: Answer habits and their change under negation
text: Second-listed preference averages +0.05 and follows the model more closely; named-term pull is positive in every plain-question cell, averaging +0.08 (Table 4). Position balance and opposing wordings therefore address distinct preferences: reversing the options alone leaves the named-term association free to move the answer (Appendix A4).

section: Answer habits and their change under negation
text: Negation separates the habits’ trajectories (hollow against filled markers): second-listed preference remains similar, named-term pull approaches zero, and the fixed reading of the yes/no opening changes the sign of b in 19 of the 48 cells. The changing sign points to the token’s mapping to its sentence.

Figure 5 a illustrates the alternatives for “Do you not agree with what X did?”: under the polarity mapping, yes accompanies “I agree”; under the truth/agreement mapping, yes accompanies “I do not agree.” The polarity share is the fraction of usable particle replies following the former mapping given their judged sentence (selection in Appendix A2).

Judged free sentences under negative interrogatives have median story-level correlation 0.94 with their plain-question counterparts, and against the published English human reference the token’s mean correlation falls from 0.60 to 0.25 while the sentence and label associations remain similar (Appendix A6).

For Japanese \cjkfont 反対しないんですか (hantai shinai n desu ka, “Do you not oppose?”), Sonnet, Opus, and Qwen favor polarity, while Haiku, luna, and Mistral favor truth/agreement. In English, “Do you not agree / oppose?” has mean polarity share 0.22 against 0.99 for “Don’t you think?” (Appendix A5).

Families of corresponding constructions, defined from the prompts before inspecting their values (Figure 5 c), show the negated evaluative adjective ranging from mean polarity shares 0.97 in English and 0.91 in French to 0.21 in Chinese (wordings and support in Table 5).
