Human linguistics distinguishes a few answer systems for negative questions: polarity-based ones, in which yes affirms the term the question names; truth- or agreement-based ones, in which yes confirms the negative proposition; and mixed ones with a dedicated reversal particle such as German doch or French si (Holmberg, 2016; Claus et al., 2017; Kameyama, 2013). English is usually placed in the first group and Japanese in the second (Kuno, 1973), and in Mandarin \cjkfont 是/ \cjkfont 不 (shì / bù) track the answerer’s opinion against the polarity of the question’s main point (Lu, 2002); our two mappings operationalize the first two systems. Speakers are less clear-cut than the classification, with both answers attested in one language depending on construction and context (Goodhue and Wagner, 2018; Park, 2023); the models show the same complexity. Appendix A7 sets the model mappings beside the literature and dialogue corpora; a matched human study is future work. We therefore identify the mapping from the model’s own sentence: a changed yes can reflect a changed way of relating to a negative question while the sentence preserves the judgment.

Read the sentence, or balance proposition labels across opposing wordings and orders; both reproduce the story profile. Report keying bias beside a yes/no score; the preference for no varies by model and language. Do not score the opening token after a negative interrogative as a judgment. A judgment measure must allow the same judgment to come with a different yes.

Same-model comparisons retain per-story differences, and residual structure reproduces with substantial variation across models and language pairs; the model signature is sharper under proposition labels than under free sentences. Medians over cells for readout comparisons and class means over cell pairs for identity comparisons summarize different units.

Korean and French contain fewer stories. Undecided sentences that take both sides, add conditions, or take no position are excluded from decisive shares, and the other token and label conditions are judged on a sample. The English, Chinese, German, and Japanese instruments were reviewed by native readers; the Korean and French instruments and story renderings were not (Appendix A1).

The sentence judge is one model, supported by two other judge models, a targeted audit at higher reasoning effort, test–retest checks, and native-reader labels on 100 replies per language in Chinese, English, German, and Japanese; Korean and French replies have no human labels, and the audited negative-interrogative yes/no-first strata hold 19–33 replies per language. These audits measure agreement between judgment procedures, leaving shared labeling biases possible; on plain-question replies where token and sentence conflict, stronger judges side with the token about half the time.

The models and languages are fixed, and intervals resample stories rather than model or language populations. The measurements concern the forms, constraints, reading rules, and wordings represented in the battery. The construction groups retain available language-specific wordings and therefore do not isolate syntax from every lexical or pragmatic difference.

Published MFV ratings provide an English reference set used across languages. The dialogue corpora span different registers and collection settings from the model prompts and provide linguistic background, without establishing that models match or mismatch speakers; no human study on the same stories exists.

s and b are an operational decomposition, not pure judgment and pure bias; the judge is a reference rather than ground truth; and cross-language identifiability is a property of the measured profiles, not evidence of a language-free internal state.

ReAnchor: Reusing Rejected Verifier States for Diffusion Drafting. Block diffusion drafters accelerate speculative decoding by generating multiple draft tokens in a single forward pass. However, each pass produces only a fixed-length block from a single target-generated anchor, limiting how far the draft can extend. Meanwhile, target verification computes hidden states even at positions beyond the first rejection, but these states are typically discarded rather than reused. We propose ReAnchor, a training-free method that reanchors a pretrained drafter at shifted positions using discarded verifier states to generate parallel draft blocks. These blocks improve predictions within the original block and extend coverage beyond its endpoint. At sampling temperature of T=0, ReAnchor achieves its largest average gains on Gemma 4-12B, improving acceptance length by 19.4% and decoding speed by 17.9% across eight benchmarks. Averaged equally over four target models and eight benchmarks, it improves acceptance length by 15.2% and decoding speed by 13.4% with pretrained DFlash drafters.

Autoregressive large language models generate tokens sequentially, making decoding a major source of inference latency. Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) reduces this cost by using a lightweight drafter to propose multiple tokens and verifying them in parallel with the target model. Many existing methods use autoregressive drafters (Li et al., 2026b; Cheng et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024a), whose token-by-token generation introduces sequential work into the drafting stage. Block diffusion drafters such as DFlash (Chen et al., 2026) remove this sequential dependence by predicting multiple draft tokens in a single forward pass.

This single-pass block generation comes at the cost of flexibility in how draft proposals are used and extended. Unlike autoregressive drafters, which can extend proposals one token at a time and stop when further drafting is unlikely to be worthwhile (Huang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), block diffusion drafters generate a fixed-length block determined by their training configuration. When verification encounters an early rejection, hidden states computed for the remaining draft positions are typically discarded. Conversely, when the entire block is accepted, no further proposals are available beyond its endpoint. Simply increasing the block length at inference time forces the drafter outside its training configuration and degrades acceptance performance (Chen et al., 2026). Thus, block diffusion drafting leaves verifier computations underutilized when proposals are rejected early, while limiting draft coverage when the entire block is accepted.

Our observation is that verifier hidden states computed at discarded draft positions retain useful information for subsequent drafting (Table 1). Although these states depend on rejected tokens and cannot be reused as valid target-model states, they can still serve as conditioning signals for the pretrained drafter. This suggests that otherwise discarded verifier computations can be leveraged for additional drafting without further target-model evaluations.

Building on this finding, we introduce ReAnchor, a training-free method that reuses verifier hidden states from the discarded post-rejection suffix to reanchor the same pretrained drafter at those later positions. The reanchored blocks are generated in parallel with the baseline draft, each preserving the drafter’s trained block length. To combine these blocks, ReAnchor matches their starting tokens to the baseline and attaches their continuations at the matched positions. By reanchoring at later positions (Figure 1), these blocks provide alternative predictions for nearby tokens within the original block, while also extending draft coverage beyond its endpoint. All attached continuations are verified by the target model under their new prefixes, preserving lossless decoding.

With DFlash drafters, ReAnchor improves average acceptance length by 15.2% and decoding speed by 13.4% across four target models and eight benchmarks at T=0. The largest average gains are observed on Gemma 4-12B, with improvements of 19.4% in acceptance length and 17.9% in decoding speed. These improvements also extend to three DFlash-based drafter variants, Domino, DSpark, and Draft-OPD, which employ different training and prediction mechanisms. Across 48 comparisons spanning two Qwen3 target models and eight benchmarks, ReAnchor improves average acceptance length by 11.8% and end-to-end decoding speed by 9.8% over their respective baselines. Component-wise ablations further show that both in-block refinement and block extension contribute to these gains.

Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce ReAnchor, a training-free method that reuses verifier hidden states as shifted anchors for block diffusion drafting. ReAnchor improves DFlash by refining predictions within the original block and extending draft coverage beyond it, achieving consistent gains in acceptance length and decoding speed across diverse settings. We demonstrate that ReAnchor can be directly applied to three DFlash-based variants, Domino, DSpark, and Draft-OPD, without additional training or variant-specific algorithmic modifications.
We review DFlash-style block diffusion drafting and speculative decoding, introducing the notation and key concepts used throughout this work. Related work is discussed in Appendix D.

A block diffusion drafter generates multiple draft tokens in a single forward pass. The drafter receives two inputs: an anchor token, i.e., the bonus token that the autoregressive target model produces at the last verified position as a byproduct of its verification pass, and prefix context derived from the target model’s hidden states over the accepted prefix. Given these inputs, the drafter simultaneously predicts a fixed number of tokens at the positions immediately following the anchor.

We now formalize this procedure. Let p denote the target model and q the diffusion drafter. We write B for the block size: one anchor followed by B-1 drafted tokens. All positions are absolute; i denotes the anchor position. The anchor token a_{i}=x_{i}\sim p(\cdot\mid x_{<i}) is the target-generated bonus token, where x_{<i} is the accepted prefix. The target model’s hidden states \mathbf{H}_{<i}=(\mathbf{h}_{j})_{j<i} are projected into the drafter’s hidden space by a learned linear projection \Pi_{\phi} to form the prefix context \mathbf{C}_{<i}=\Pi_{\phi}(\mathbf{H}_{<i}). The drafter takes the anchor followed by B-1 mask tokens \mathbf{m}_{i+1:i+B-1} and produces a distribution over each masked position: \mathbf{z}^{[i]}=(a_{i},\;\mathbf{m}_{i+1:i+B-1}),\quad\mathbf{q}^{[i]}_{j}=q(\mathbf{C}_{<i};\;\mathbf{z}^{[i]})_{j}, \hat{x}^{[i]}_{j}\sim\operatorname{Cat}(\mathbf{q}^{[i]}_{j}),\quad j=i{+}1,\ldots,i{+}B{-}1. The superscript [i] identifies the anchor.

Given a draft block \hat{\mathbf{x}}^{[i]}_{i+1:i+B-1}, the target model p evaluates all proposed positions in a single forward pass. Verification then proceeds from left to right, accepting draft tokens as long as they match tokens independently sampled from the target distribution at each position. At the first mismatch, verification stops and accepts the target-sampled token.

Unlike standard probabilistic verification, which uses importance ratios and residual sampling, this sample-wise verification does not require evaluating proposal probabilities. It preserves the target distribution because each accepted token is sampled from p under its verified prefix.

Let \tau denote the average number of tokens accepted per round, including the target-generated token at the stopping position. The average decoding latency per accepted token is L=\frac{T_{\mathrm{draft}}+T_{\mathrm{verify}}}{\tau}. The drafter therefore aims to generate low-cost proposals that match the target’s sampled trajectory for as many consecutive positions as possible.

Block diffusion drafting removes the sequential bottleneck of autoregressive drafters, but the fixed-length parallel block introduces constraints that do not arise in the sequential setting. We now revisit this formulation and examine where its fixed-block design leaves room for improvement. We present two observations that together motivate ReAnchor: (i) the native block endpoint is frequently the binding constraint on acceptance length and no proposal exists beyond it, yet naively extending the block degrades acceptance; (ii) verifier states computed over rejected draft suffixes retain substantial predictive information and can condition additional drafts without retraining.

The native draft length frequently limits the accepted prefix, but simply increasing the proposal length at inference time does not resolve this issue. Figure 2 shows the acceptance-length distribution on representative math and code tasks for drafters trained with B=16. Both distributions exhibit a clear concentration at the maximum length. All drafted tokens are accepted in 16.4% of rounds on MATH-500 and 12.7% on HumanEval. In these rounds, every drafted position is consumed and no further proposal is available. Full-block acceptance does not establish that the next token would also be accepted, but the concentration at the final bin shows that the block endpoint is the binding constraint in a substantial fraction of decoding rounds.

A direct solution is to increase the proposal length at inference time. We test this by evaluating drafters trained with B=16 at B=24 and B=32 on Qwen3-8B across MATH-500, GSM8K, HumanEval, and MBPP. Despite the additional positions, the average accepted length decreases by 0.3 and 1.1 respectively compared to the native block size. The longer block forces the drafter to predict at offsets beyond its training range from the same anchor, under a masked input configuration it was not trained on. Extending coverage therefore motivates while preserving the native block size. We next examine whether the rejected portion of the preceding verification pass provides the conditioning information needed at these later starting points.

A rejection at position r prevents the remaining draft suffix from being accepted, but does not render every subsequent draft token incorrect. Table 1 reports the fraction of draft tokens after r that match the target model’s top-1 prediction. Across the evaluated tasks, 60–66% of these agree with despite following a rejected prefix. This indicates that the suffix is invalidated as a contiguous sequence rather than on a per-token basis, and that the discarded positions still carry substantial predictive information. Since the target model has already computed hidden states at these positions during verification, these states are available as conditioning signals for subsequent drafting at no additional target-model cost. Motivated by these observations, the next subsection introduces ReAnchor, which reuses these rejected-prefix verifier states as shifted anchors for the same pretrained drafter to generate additional fixed-length proposals.

ReAnchor constructs draft proposals by combining the standard baseline draft with additional shifted blocks conditioned on verifier hidden states discarded after rejection in the preceding round (Figure 3). These drafts are generated in parallel using the same pretrained drafter at its trained block length. Each shifted block is aligned with the baseline by matching its starting token, and its continuation is attached at the matched position. The resulting paths are merged into a token trie and jointly verified by the target model. This construction provides alternative predictions within the original block while extending draft coverage beyond its endpoint.

section: Parallel drafting from discarded verifier states.
text: Section 3.1 shows that verifier states from rejected prefixes remain useful for drafting. ReAnchor reuses a subset of these states as conditioning points for the same pretrained drafter. The resulting shifted blocks improve predictions within the original block and extend the draft beyond its endpoint without retraining the drafter.

section: Parallel drafting from discarded verifier states.
text: The baseline drafter uses the anchor a_{i} and \mathbf{C}_{<i} to generate \hat{\mathbf{x}}^{[i]}_{i+1:i+B-1}. Let i^{\prime} and r denote the anchor and the first rejected position of the preceding round; the token accepted at r becomes the current anchor, so i=r. We retain the otherwise discarded verifier states \widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{j} over the rejected suffix r\leq j\leq i^{\prime}+B-1, and let \widetilde{x}_{j} denote the token decoded from \widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{j-1} through the target LM head. Let \mathcal{D}\subseteq\{\,d\in\{1,\ldots,B-1\}:i+d\leq i^{\prime}+B\,\} denote the selected offsets from the current anchor. For each d\in\mathcal{D}, we define the shifted anchor \widetilde{a}_{i+d}=\widetilde{x}_{i+d} and its context \widetilde{\mathbf{C}}_{<i+d}=\Pi_{\phi}(\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}_{<i+d}), where \widetilde{\mathbf{H}}_{<i+d}=(\mathbf{H}_{<r},\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{r},\ldots,\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{i+d-1}), mirroring the baseline pair (a_{i},\mathbf{C}_{<i}). The same pretrained drafter takes \widetilde{a}_{i+d} followed by B-1 masked positions and predicts them in parallel. The baseline and shifted blocks are \displaystyle g(0) \displaystyle=\bigl(a_{i},\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{[i]}_{i+1:i+B-1}\bigr), \displaystyle g(d) \displaystyle=\bigl(\widetilde{a}_{i+d},\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{[i+d]}_{i+d+1:i+d+B-1}\bigr), each consisting of one anchor and B-1 proposed tokens. The entry g(d)_{k}, k\in\{0,\ldots,B-1\}, nominally corresponds to absolute position i+d+k.

section: Parallel drafting from discarded verifier states.
text: The 1+|\mathcal{D}| drafting calls are independent and can be batched together. Each block attends only to its own verifier context and masked input, and reusing states from the preceding verification pass requires no additional target evaluation. The subset \mathcal{D} controls the number of additional drafting calls; in this work, we use every available offset, \mathcal{D}=\{1,\ldots,i^{\prime}+B-i\}. When the preceding round accepts its entire block, no states are retained, \mathcal{D} is empty, and only the baseline draft is generated.

ReAnchor produces one baseline block and several shifted blocks, which must be combined into a single proposal set. A shifted block g(d) is drafted from a reused anchor at offset d, so it would naturally be appended to the baseline at that position. However, correcting the rejected token changes the continuation that follows it, so the tokens drafted in g(d) may now appear at a different position in the new baseline g(0), or not at all. Rather than fixing g(d) at its original offset d, we therefore search the baseline for a position at which g(d) aligns and attach its continuation there.

We say that g(d) has a positive overlap at baseline position t if its anchor matches the baseline token there, i.e., g(0)_{t}=g(d)_{0}. We attach g(d) at the earliest such position t^{\star}, so that its continuation follows the baseline prefix g(0)_{0:t^{\star}} (Algorithm 1). This gives every matched shifted block a unique, deterministic attachment point without a secondary ranking rule, and in practice it selects a path with high accepted length (Appendix C.1).

The overlapping prefix is represented only once in the concatenated path, and shifted blocks with no positive-overlap match are discarded; each shifted block therefore contributes at most one attached path. We collect the baseline and at most one attachment per shifted block into \mathcal{Y} and merge them into a token trie. Since a token match only identifies a candidate attachment rather than validating its continuation, we jointly verify the trie in a single target forward pass using tree attention (Miao et al., 2024), so that each continuation is evaluated under its attached prefix.

We evaluate ReAnchor with Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025) models at 4B and 8B scales, Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) and Gemma 4-12B (Team et al., 2026). Experiments cover GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH-500 (Lightman et al., 2024), AIME25, HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021b), LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025), MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023), and Alpaca (Taori et al., 2023). We report average acceptance length \tau and end-to-end decoding speedup relative to autoregressive decoding with the target model. We evaluate on 100 examples per dataset, sampled with random seed 0, using the full set for AIME25 (30) and MT-Bench (80). In all experiments, ReAnchor uses every retained rejected-suffix state as a shifted anchor.

Unless otherwise specified, our main experiments and ablations use pretrained DFlash (Chen et al., 2026) checkpoints. We additionally apply ReAnchor to three DFlash-based variants to assess its compatibility with different training and prediction mechanisms. Draft-OPD (Lei et al., 2026) post-trains DFlash through on-policy distillation with error-position replay. Domino (Huang et al., 2026) adds a GRU-based causal correction head. DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026) uses a lightweight Markov head for sequential token prediction. Further details on the drafter variants are provided in Appendix A.

We measure end-to-end wall-clock decoding latency with batch size one on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU. All compared methods use the same target model, drafter checkpoint, hardware, and generation settings. We exclude model loading and tokenization time while including measured latencies for both drafting and target verification for end-to-end latency evaluation. GPU execution is synchronized before timing, and we report results after warm-up runs. More details of the setup are provided in Appendix B.

At T=0, ReAnchor improves both average acceptance length \tau and end-to-end speedup in all 32 target–benchmark comparisons, achieving average gains of 15.2% and 13.4%, respectively (Table 2). The largest relative gains occur on Gemma 4-12B, with improvements of 19.4% in \tau and 17.9% in speedup, despite its shorter baseline accepted prefixes than Qwen3. At T=1, the improvements remain substantial, with \tau increasing in 31 of 32 comparisons and speedup in 27, averaging 11.8% and 6.9%, respectively. The smaller gains under stochastic sampling may stem from increased token mismatches between independently sampled draft and target continuations, reducing the benefit of additional proposals relative to their verification cost. Overall, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of reanchoring across different target models and decoding settings.

We further evaluate ReAnchor on three DFlash-based variants, Domino, DSpark, and Draft-OPD, with different training and prediction mechanisms. At T=0, ReAnchor improves both \tau and end-to-end speedup in all 48 comparisons, with average gains of 11.8% and 9.8%, respectively (Table 3). At T=1, the improvements remain consistent, increasing \tau in all 48 comparisons and speedup in 45, with average gains of 11.5% and 8.1%. These results demonstrate that ReAnchor generalizes across different drafting mechanisms without additional training or variant-specific modifications.

We analyze where the gains of ReAnchor come from: which draft positions benefit, how much is due to reusing rejected states versus token matching, and how the attachment rule affects performance. All ablations use Qwen3-4B with the DFlash drafter at T=0.

We separate the gains of ReAnchor into improvements within the native draft block and extensions beyond its endpoint. We consider two partial variants while keeping the same shifted anchors and drafter evaluations. In-block only uses predictions from shifted anchors only at positions up to i+B-1 and discards all predictions beyond the native block. Extension only retains the original DFlash predictions within i+1:i+B-1 and uses ReAnchor only to provide additional predictions after i+B-1. The full method uses both.

Table 4 shows that both components improve over the DFlash baseline. In-block refinement increases acceptance by providing later positions with predictions conditioned from closer verifier states. Block extension provides additional accepted tokens in rounds where verification reaches the native endpoint. Combining the two gives the largest improvement in both acceptance length and decoding speed, showing that ReAnchor benefits from improving existing draft positions as well as extending the draft beyond its original length.

We next examine how often a shifted block g(d) remains aligned with its original offset d after a rejection. Correcting the rejected token can alter the continuation that follows it, so the anchor g(d)_{0} may appear at a different position of the new baseline draft g(0). Table 5 reports two statistics over shifted blocks whose anchor matches at least one position t, i.e., g(0)_{t}=g(d)_{0}. Shifted only counts blocks that do not match at t=d but match at some t\neq d; Multiple counts blocks that match at more than one t. The two categories may overlap.

Across the evaluated tasks, 45.5–51.2% of matched shifted blocks fall into the shifted-only category, indicating that enforcing the original offset would discard a substantial fraction of otherwise usable continuations. In addition, 34.7–40.6% admit multiple candidate attachment positions, showing that alignment is frequently ambiguous rather than fixed. These results motivate searching over baseline positions when attaching shifted blocks. We next quantify the effect of this design choice by comparing fixed-offset attachment with the full token-matching strategy of ReAnchor.

We compare our default earliest-overlap rule with fixed-offset, random-match, and longest-prefix attachment on Qwen3-4B with DFlash (Table 6). All matching rules clearly outperform fixed-offset attachment (7.51–7.56 vs. 7.24 in \tau), while differing from one another by at most 0.05 in \tau and 0.02 \times in speedup. Re-alignment itself thus matters more than the specific attachment site. We adopt the earliest rule because it matches the best results while being the simplest: a single-token comparison that yields a unique, deterministic attachment point.

We isolate the contributions of shifted drafting and token matching with a cumulative ablation (Table 7). Starting from DFlash, which uses only the native anchor and draft block, we first add shifted blocks drafted from the retained rejected-suffix states, attaching each block to the baseline at its original offset t=d. We then replace this fixed attachment with token matching, which attaches each block at the earliest positive-overlap position. All configurations share the same offsets \mathcal{D}, drafter evaluations, and verification rule; only the proposal assembly differs. Shifted drafting alone raises \tau on every benchmark, from 5.38 to 5.87 on average, showing that rejected verifier states provide useful conditioning. Token matching further raises it to 6.22, accounting for roughly 40% of the total gain, as many shifted continuations become usable only at a position other than their original offset (Table 5).

We introduced ReAnchor, a training-free method that reuses verifier hidden states discarded after rejection to reanchor block diffusion drafting at later positions. By drafting multiple fixed-length blocks in parallel and attaching their continuations through token matching, ReAnchor refines predictions within the original block and extends draft coverage beyond its endpoint, while preserving lossless decoding. It consistently improves acceptance length and decoding speed across target models and benchmarks, and applies directly to DFlash-based drafter variants, including Domino, DSpark, and Draft-OPD. These results show that otherwise discarded verifier computations can be effectively reused to improve speculative decoding.

Like speculative decoding in general, ReAnchor is limited by how well the drafter aligns with the target model. Shifted blocks are drafted from verifier states conditioned on rejected tokens, so their benefit depends on how much the post-rejection drafts still agree with the target’s continuation. The gains therefore vary across tasks and decoding settings. At T=0, the average speedup gain is 9.9% on MT-Bench and Alpaca, compared with 14.5% on math and code tasks. Under stochastic sampling (T=1), independently sampled drafts agree less often with the target, and ReAnchor is slower than the baseline on four Llama-3.1-8B tasks and on LiveCodeBench with Qwen3-4B, where the additional verification cost outweighs the extra accepted tokens. In addition, ReAnchor has no retained states to reuse after a round in which the entire block is accepted, so it cannot extend the draft in consecutive full-acceptance rounds. Finally, all latency measurements use batch size one, where verifying additional trie tokens is nearly free; at larger batch sizes, where verification becomes compute-bound, the extra candidates may reduce the net speedup.

From Writing Advice to Manuscript Governance: A Constrained-Transformation Framework for Academic Revision. Academic revision presents a governance problem when legitimate writing objectives conflict. Writing-process and social-science research show that revision is recursive and that wording carries epistemic and disciplinary commitments. Those literatures identify important constraints but do not settle which objective should prevail when concision, outlet form or stylistic variation conflicts with evidence and claim boundaries. This paper models revision as an admissibility problem under ordered constraints. Task-relative invariants, contextual constraints and mutable presentation choices define the admissible space; a claim-preservation contract links evidence and judgement to an authorised claim boundary. Four governance propositions specify preservation, precedence, context and sufficiency. The Academic Writing Filter implements the model by screening candidate revisions; it is not a universal definition or classifier of good academic writing. The contribution is a technology-independent mechanism for changing presentation without silently changing the research argument.

section: Academic revision as a constrained transformation
text: Writing-process research has long rejected a linear model in which ideas are completed first and prose is polished afterwards. Flower and Hayes model writing as a recursive, goal-directed process in which planning, translating and reviewing interact with the task environment and the writer’s evolving goals (Flower and Hayes, 1981). Revision research likewise distinguishes local editing from changes that alter meaning, organisation and the writer’s representation of the text (Sommers, 1980; Faigley and Witte, 1981; Fitzgerald, 1987). These accounts establish that revision can reorganise an argument rather than merely smooth sentences.

section: Academic revision as a constrained transformation
text: Social-science scholarship makes the problem more specific because wording can carry epistemic and disciplinary commitments. Hedges and boosters communicate degrees of commitment, caution and certainty, and that their use varies across disciplinary communities (Hyland, 1996; Hyland, 1998). Organisation studies further shows that contribution and theory are constructed through argument rather than supplied by citations, data or novelty claims alone (Locke and Golden-Biddle, 1997; Whetten, 1989; Sutton and Staw, 1995; Alvesson and Sandberg, 2011). A revision can therefore alter more than style when it changes a qualifier, collapses a conceptual distinction or rewrites the relationship between evidence and contribution.

section: Academic revision as a constrained transformation
text: Revision becomes a governance problem when individually reasonable objectives conflict. Concision may compete with a qualification needed to delimit inference. Stylistic variation may compete with a technical distinction whose repeated wording is analytically necessary. An outlet convention may shape presentation but cannot make the underlying research design support a stronger claim. Treating every instruction as an equivalent writing preference leaves those conflicts unresolved.

section: Academic revision as a constrained transformation
text: This paper conceptualises revision as an admissibility problem under ordered constraints. A proposed revision is admissible only when it preserves properties fixed for the current revision task, satisfies applicable scholarly-context constraints and changes presentation within the remaining permissible space. Three classes of manuscript property structure the model: task-relative invariants, contextual constraints and mutable presentation choices. Reporting and discourse scholarship already establishes that scholarly communities differ in what must be reported, how knowledge claims are qualified and how conventions are adapted across methods and disciplines (American Educational Research Association, 2006; Levitt et al., 2018; Lupia and Elman, 2014; Nosek et al., 2015). Context therefore cannot be reduced to a universal style layer applied after the argument has been formed.

section: Academic revision as a constrained transformation
text: The term manuscript governance is used throughout this paper in a deliberately narrow operational sense: the allocation of decision rights among competing revision constraints. Governance specifies what must be preserved, what the scholarly context constrains, what may be optimised for clarity or economy, and which requirement prevails when two legitimate revision objectives conflict. No institutional, editorial or research-governance theory is claimed.

section: Academic revision as a constrained transformation
text: Four linked governance propositions define the model rather than making empirical claims about its effectiveness.

section: Academic revision as a constrained transformation
text: Preservation. When the underlying research argument is held fixed, a presentation revision is admissible only if claim-defining invariants are preserved. Precedence. Revision constraints are heterogeneous: evidential and inferential boundaries have decision rights over lower-order stylistic or house preferences when the two conflict. Context. Discipline, manuscript type and outlet constrain admissible expression, but those contextual requirements cannot legitimately override verified evidence or authorised inferential boundaries. Sufficiency. Economy is a lower-order presentation objective; deletion is not an improvement when it removes context, conceptual distinction or qualification required to warrant or interpret the contribution.

section: Academic revision as a constrained transformation
text: Existing literatures supply important parts of this architecture without being treated here as incomplete precursors. Cognitive models explain how writing and revision proceed (Flower and Hayes, 1981); social-science scholarship explains how contribution, theory and epistemic commitment are constructed in scholarly texts (Locke and Golden-Biddle, 1997; Sutton and Staw, 1995; Hyland, 1998); and reporting standards specify warrants, transparency and discipline-sensitive expectations (American Educational Research Association, 2006; Levitt et al., 2018; Lupia and Elman, 2014; Nosek et al., 2015). A recent AI-specific framework also restricts generative AI to post-draft diagnostic auditing in order to preserve authorial judgement and epistemic control (Nussbaum and Bekerman, 2026). This paper’s narrower conceptual claim concerns the relation among these kinds of requirement during revision: task-relative invariants define an authorised claim boundary, contextual constraints shape admissible expression, and an explicit precedence hierarchy determines which revision objective yields when requirements conflict.

section: Academic revision as a constrained transformation
text: An operational implementation, the Academic Writing Filter, makes that governance logic usable (Rudkin, 2026). The term filter is used operationally: candidate revisions are screened against evidence, the claim-preservation contract, contextual scholarly requirements and lower-order presentation rules. It does not denote an automatic quality classifier, a universal theory of good academic writing or a claim that the general writing advice contained in the file is novel. Conceptually, the artefact remains secondary to the governance mechanism. No claim is made here that the architecture improves writing quality, publication outcomes or reviewer evaluations.

section: Writing process and the scope of governance
text: Flower and Hayes describe writing as a hierarchy of recursive processes governed by goals rather than as a fixed sequence of planning, drafting and correction (Flower and Hayes, 1981). Reviewing can interrupt other processes, and writers can revise their goals as composing proceeds. Later revision scholarship similarly distinguishes surface correction from transformations that change meaning or organisation (Sommers, 1980; Faigley and Witte, 1981; Fitzgerald, 1987). These models explain how revision occurs and why it can be cognitively substantive.

section: Writing process and the scope of governance
text: Manuscript governance addresses a different question. Once a revision episode holds the underlying evidence and research argument fixed, which proposed changes remain admissible? Accordingly, manuscript governance does not compete with cognitive models of composing. Its starting point is a defined presentation-revision task in which some properties are temporarily fixed, others are context-dependent and the remainder stay open to optimisation. Crossing that boundary is permitted, but it should be recognised as substantive reconsideration rather than hidden inside prose editing.

section: Contribution and theory in the social sciences
text: Social-science scholarship cautions against treating contribution as a property that can be generated by editorial form alone. Locke and Golden-Biddle show empirically how organisation scholars construct opportunities for contribution through intertextual positioning and problematization (Locke and Golden-Biddle, 1997). Whetten distinguishes the components and boundary conditions of theoretical contribution, while Sutton and Staw argue that references, data, variables and hypotheses cannot substitute for explanatory logic (Whetten, 1989; Sutton and Staw, 1995). Alvesson and Sandberg further distinguish conventional gap-spotting from problematization that challenges assumptions in an existing literature (Alvesson and Sandberg, 2011).

section: Contribution and theory in the social sciences
text: These arguments place a limit on what generic writing guidance can legitimately do. An operational revision filter can make a contribution visible, test whether its wording remains coherent and remove material that obscures it, but it cannot decide by stylistic rule what the substantive contribution should be. Project-specific substantive judgement must establish the authorised argument first. Manuscript governance then protects that argument during presentation revision rather than manufacturing novelty through rhetoric.

Claim strength is partly encoded in apparently small linguistic choices. Hyland’s study of hedging in research articles treats tentativeness and qualification as resources for expressing uncertainty, precision and the writer’s epistemic commitment (Hyland, 1996). His cross-disciplinary analysis of hedges and boosters shows that statements of doubt and certainty also vary with the epistemological and interactional conventions of disciplinary communities (Hyland, 1998). Qualifiers such as “may”, “suggests” or “is associated with” can therefore be claim-defining rather than ornamental.

Disciplinary context also shapes which forms of argument and evidence are legible. Broader work on academic discourse reaches the same conclusion: scholarly language is not a neutral vocabulary layered onto otherwise identical arguments (Swales, 1990; Hyland, 2004). Together, these studies provide the basis for distinguishing a fixed inferential boundary from a contextual rhetorical convention. Governance must preserve the former while allowing the latter to shape expression where compatible with the evidence.

section: Reporting standards, warrants and methodological pluralism
text: Social-science reporting standards supply a further foundation. The American Educational Research Association (AERA) identifies sufficiency of warrants and transparency as overarching principles, while explicitly rejecting literal checklist compliance and allowing different methodological traditions to vary in form and order of presentation (American Educational Research Association, 2006). Levitt and colleagues develop qualitative and mixed-method reporting standards that are sensitive to diverse inquiry traditions and intended for use by authors, reviewers and editors across psychology and potentially the wider social sciences (Levitt et al., 2018). Levitt and colleagues also document a practical source of conflict: qualitative authors can face manuscript expectations or rhetorical forms that are inappropriate for their methods.

section: Reporting standards, warrants and methodological pluralism
text: Political-science and open-science frameworks make a similar distinction between shared principles and contextual implementation. Lupia and Elman describe data access and research transparency as general commitments that different research communities instantiate through their own standards of warrant and legitimacy (Lupia and Elman, 2014). TOP uses modular standards and explicitly allows different levels of adoption because not every standard is equally applicable across disciplines and journals (Nosek et al., 2015). Together, these frameworks specify important reporting and transparency constraints. Neither is designed to allocate decision rights among a project’s authorised claim boundary, outlet demands, disciplinary rhetoric and lower-order style preferences; that cross-level relation is the narrower problem addressed here.

Relations between propositions and warrants provide the immediate argumentative foundation. Toulmin makes explicit the connection between claims, grounds and warrants, while The Craft of Research translates similar logic into practical research writing (Toulmin, 2003; Booth et al., 2016). Sutton and Staw’s distinction between evidence and theory reinforces the same point within the social sciences: citations or findings do not substitute for the reasoning that connects them to a claim (Sutton and Staw, 1995). A simple audit question operationalises that relation within the Academic Writing Filter: what exact evidence licences this wording?

Four forms of warrant are distinguished. Table 1 makes their roles explicit. Prior scholarship can warrant inherited concepts, empirical regularities and methodological properties. Evidence produced by the current manuscript can warrant new empirical, qualitative, formal or simulation-based propositions. Authoritative primary material can warrant external factual propositions for which official statistics, legal texts, administrative documentation, archival records or technical standards are more appropriate than journal articles. Transparent analytic warrant can support a definition, a logical implication or a design principle introduced and reasoned within the paper itself. Evidence is therefore not synonymous with citation. Responsible referencing requires the cited source to support the proposition for which it is cited (Penders, 2018).

Cochrane’s writing advice supplies an operational rather than epistemic layer. Cochrane advocates a concrete contribution, newspaper-style organisation, rapid movement to the intellectual payoff, economy, active prose and removal of research-process narrative (Cochrane, 2005). Editorial and style guidance likewise favours direct, reader-centred prose (Nature Methods, 2017; Sword, 2012). Such advice is valuable inside the admissible revision space, but it cannot determine whether a design identifies a causal effect, whether a qualitative interpretation is warranted or whether a conceptual distinction may be removed. Those judgments arise from the research and the disciplinary context.

Nussbaum and Bekerman provide the closest framework-level neighbour in the assembled literature (Nussbaum and Bekerman, 2026). Nussbaum and Bekerman require a human-authored draft before generative AI enters the manuscript-revision process and restrict AI to diagnostic post-draft auditing. Authors retain epistemic authority while AI probes coherence, alignment and reconstructability; interpretation and evidentiary significance remain non-delegable scholarly judgments. At the level of human–AI interaction, that framework therefore addresses a closely related preservation problem.

The manuscript-governance framework shares the concern with epistemic authority but has a different unit of analysis. Manuscript governance is technology-independent: a proposed revision may originate with the author, a collaborator, a reviewer, an editor or an AI system. Governance instead asks whether that revision respects the authorised claim boundary and the precedence hierarchy. No human-first drafting requirement is built into the conceptual model. Nussbaum and Bekerman’s post-draft diagnostic constraint can instead be understood as a specialised policy for AI participation, while manuscript governance specifies the more general constraints against which any accepted revision is judged.

section: Task-relative invariants, contextual constraints and mutable choices
text: Three manuscript-property classes organise revision. An invariant is a property treated as fixed for a specified presentation-revision episode in which the underlying evidence and research argument are held constant; the term does not imply that a sentence or interpretation can never change. Reconsidering an invariant is possible, but doing so marks a move from presentation revision into substantive reconsideration. Table 2 defines the three classes and the different revision principles attached to them.

section: Task-relative invariants, contextual constraints and mutable choices
text: The three classes are distinct rather than nested sets. Task-relative invariants determine what must remain fixed within the revision episode; contextual constraints govern how that fixed argument is expressed in a particular scholarly setting; mutable presentation choices remain open to optimisation only where they are compatible with the first two classes. The operational filter maps these classes onto specific controls: verified evidence and the claim-preservation contract protect invariants; binding requirements and outlet overlays implement contextual constraints; cross-project defaults and local house-style preferences govern mutable choices.

section: Task-relative invariants, contextual constraints and mutable choices
text: Separating presentation revision from substantive reconsideration gives the architecture its operational boundary. Hyland’s analyses show why this distinction matters at sentence level: changing a hedge can change the degree of commitment attached to a proposition rather than merely change its style (Hyland, 1996; Hyland, 1998). A writer may change an invariant after new analysis, theoretical reconsideration or a deliberate change in the paper’s argument, but the change should then be recognised as substantive rather than smuggled in through prose optimisation. That distinction gives the preservation proposition an operational boundary.

Explicit ordering resolves conflicts that cannot be settled by treating every instruction as an equivalent preference. Reporting frameworks already recognise that standards vary in applicability and strength across methods, disciplines and journals (American Educational Research Association, 2006; Levitt et al., 2018; Nosek et al., 2015). Manuscript governance adds a cross-level ordering. Verified evidence and mathematical or statistical correctness come first. A project-specific claim-preservation contract occupies the second priority because it records the authorised claim boundary for the current revision episode. Binding outlet, editor or referee requirements come next where they are compatible with those first two levels. An outlet-specific corpus or style overlay, cross-project general writing heuristics and local house-style preferences then govern progressively more mutable presentation choices.

The Academic Writing Filter implements the hierarchy as a whole; only the cross-project default writing heuristics occupy Priority 5. Distinguishing the artefact from that one layer prevents inherited writing advice from being mistaken for the framework’s conceptual contribution.

Decision rights, rather than preference ranking alone, structure the hierarchy. A lower-priority objective remains legitimate until it conflicts with a higher-priority constraint. Concision may therefore govern between two equally accurate formulations, but it loses decision rights when shortening deletes a required qualification. Stylistic variation may improve prose, but it loses decision rights when variation collapses a fixed technical distinction. P2 therefore turns such conflicts into explicit revision decisions rather than matters of taste.

A claim-preservation contract bridges substantive evidence and admissible wording. For a specified revision episode it records authorised claims, prohibited claims, inferential boundaries, required qualifications and frozen conceptual or terminological distinctions. Verified facts and mathematical/statistical correctness remain separately protected at the first level of the hierarchy rather than being duplicated inside the contract. Hyland’s work on claim qualification provides a concrete reason to record such boundaries: apparently small changes in hedging can alter epistemic commitment (Hyland, 1996; Hyland, 1998). In compact form, the mechanism is: research evidence and substantive judgement \rightarrow authorised claim boundary \rightarrow revision decision. Table 4 gives a synthetic example.

A proposed rewrite is tested against that record before lower-order style preferences are considered. Changing “is associated with” to “reduces” crosses from the authorised associational claim to a prohibited causal claim. Alternating “exposure” and “participation” merely to avoid repetition collapses a declared distinction. Either change can become admissible only if the underlying evidence or argument is substantively reconsidered and the contract is deliberately updated. Accordingly, the contract governs a revision episode rather than declaring that a manuscript can never change.

The Academic Writing Filter is not solely a style guide because its implementation also screens proposed revisions against evidential, inferential and terminology constraints; nor is it a reporting guideline. AERA, JARS–Qual, TOP and health-research guidance specify information or standards needed for transparent reporting within particular research contexts (American Educational Research Association, 2006; Levitt et al., 2018; Nosek et al., 2015; Moher et al., 2010); the Academic Writing Filter does not reproduce those domain-specific items or their development processes. Outlet-agnostic core rules also distinguish it from a journal rubric. AI systems can use the file as contextual instructions, but the file is not itself an AI prompt or a substitute for substantive expertise: correctness of the underlying analysis, interpretation or proof remains outside its authority.

Conceptually, the manuscript-governance framework specifies admissible revision. Its intellectual contribution is an ordering principle for revision under conflict and a mechanism for preserving claim boundaries while presentation changes. Operationally, the public Academic Writing Filter screens candidate changes against that specification. Its warrant taxonomy, rule table and software-neutral file format support the mechanism rather than constitute separate theoretical claims.

First application begins with five decisions (Rudkin, 2026). Users establish the broad discipline, classify the manuscript type, identify a target outlet when one exists, retrieve or create the project claim-preservation contract, and write the central contribution in one concrete paragraph. These decisions turn otherwise generic writing advice into a manuscript-specific revision environment.

Revision then proceeds across four scales (Rudkin, 2026). Manuscript-level rules govern contribution and architecture. Section-level rules ask what necessary question each section answers. Paragraph-level rules require an appropriately warranted proposition or a genuine procedural/reproducibility function. Sentence-level rules favour concrete subjects, early verbs and wording that does not exceed the evidence. A final audit checks the interaction among those levels rather than assuming that locally polished sentences produce a coherent paper.

The October 2026 implementation contains thirteen default revision rules (Rudkin, 2026). They are not offered as thirteen novel propositions about academic writing; their role is to operationalise the governance hierarchy by combining inherited guidance, established scholarly principles and practice-derived defaults. Reproducing their full text here would duplicate the public artefact; Table 5 identifies their function and epistemic status.

Table 5 reports justificatory bases rather than mutually exclusive classes: a rule may draw on Cochrane-derived guidance, broader scholarly principles and practice-derived filter rules at the same time. Distinguishing those bases prevents a local preference from masquerading as a universal epistemic rule. A heuristic against habitual openings with “The”, “This”, “It”, “There”, “They” or “Their”, for example, encourages concrete subjects. Readability or disciplinary convention can override that heuristic when either provides a better reason. A prohibition on converting a descriptive association into a causal effect does not have the same optional status.

Several rules deliberately inherit rather than originate familiar social-science principles. Contribution framing is already a substantive problem in organisation studies (Locke and Golden-Biddle, 1997; Whetten, 1989; Alvesson and Sandberg, 2011); references and data cannot stand in for theoretical logic (Sutton and Staw, 1995); and reporting standards already require warrants, transparency and method-sensitive presentation (American Educational Research Association, 2006; Levitt et al., 2018). Within the present manuscript-governance framework, the Academic Writing Filter places those requirements inside one revision hierarchy rather than relabelling established disciplinary knowledge as new writing guidance.

Post-revision sufficiency follows from the hierarchy rather than operating as an exception to it. Economy and paragraph reduction belong to mutable presentation choices, whereas a required qualification can be invariant and disciplinary positioning can be a contextual constraint. A substantial deletion therefore requires a check that a lower-order optimisation has not damaged a higher-order requirement. After major compression, the October 2026 implementation checks literature coverage, necessary conceptual distinctions, Discussion depth and the navigation value of exhibits (Rudkin, 2026). Literature-led problem framing, short warranted paragraphs and navigation exhibits can survive when they perform a higher-priority argumentative or contextual function. Under the sufficiency proposition, shorter is better only inside the admissible revision space.

Markdown provides an inspectable, portable specification independent of a particular model or word processor. Users can compare dated releases, add discipline-specific terminology or an outlet overlay, and supply the same rules to a human collaborator or an AI-assisted system. Its role remains implementational: plain text exposes governance rules to inspection and adaptation but does not create the conceptual contribution.
Synthetic examples show how ordered constraints govern revision decisions; they make no empirical claims about the substantive topics mentioned.
Consider a hypothetical observational study whose draft states:
Exposure to the programme reduced subsequent non-participation.
Under the claim-preservation contract in Table 4, a causal interpretation is prohibited. An admissible revision therefore reads:
Programme exposure was associated with lower subsequent non-participation.

Adding “may”, “suggests” or “is consistent with” would not by itself repair an unsupported causal claim. Hyland shows that hedges legitimately calibrate epistemic commitment, but they do not supply evidence that the design lacks (Hyland, 1996; Hyland, 1998). Causal wording should therefore be aligned with the causal question and the design used to identify it rather than softened through euphemism (Hernán, 2018). Higher-order evidential constraints determine the claim class before sentence style is optimised.
Suppose the authorised claim is followed by a qualification required by the contract:
Programme exposure was associated with lower subsequent non-participation. Because exposure was not randomly assigned, the association does not identify a programme effect.

A compression pass proposes deleting the second sentence because the first is already associational. Concision is a legitimate objective, but the contract marks the qualification as required for interpretation. Because the qualification is an invariant, the second sentence remains. Governance does not declare concise prose undesirable; it specifies that concision has decision rights only among formulations that preserve the authorised claim boundary.

section: Conflict resolution: variation versus a fixed distinction
text: A copy-editing pass may also propose alternating “exposure” and “participation” to avoid repetition. Table 4 defines those terms as different analytical objects. Lexical variation is therefore rejected even when it would improve surface rhythm. Repetition remains because a house preference for variation cannot override a claim-defining distinction. Rejecting the substitution illustrates why an unranked checklist is insufficient when two reasonable writing objectives point in different directions.

That scope is sufficient for the paper’s claim about spatial concentration, but it does not identify the mechanisms that produce individual participation decisions. section: From confessional limitation to scope boundary
text: Work on limitations reporting likewise argues that limitations should explain consequences for interpretation rather than function as ritualised disclosures (Tsagkaris and Sevik, 2026). Governance adds a further condition: future work cannot rescue a present validity problem. If missing evidence is necessary to establish the central claim, the design or the claim must change in the current manuscript; otherwise, the limitation defines the boundary of what the present design authorises.

Technology independence allows the same hierarchy to govern several revision settings. Individual researchers, supervisors, co-authors and writing groups can use the hierarchy to test whether a proposed rewrite changes the authorised claim, conflicts with disciplinary terminology or applies a lower-priority preference too aggressively. An AI-assisted writing system can use the same specification as contextual instructions, but the system does not acquire authority to redefine the evidence or claim-preservation contract.

Nussbaum and Bekerman offer a complementary, AI-specific design (Nussbaum and Bekerman, 2026). Their “conversational companion” begins from a human-authored draft and limits generative AI to post-draft diagnostic work on coherence, alignment and reconstructability. A further distinction between delegable assistance and non-delegable interpretation reserves decisions about evidentiary meaning and conclusions to human scholarly judgement. Manuscript governance accepts the same general concern with epistemic responsibility but does not prescribe a particular agent or drafting sequence. Its unit of analysis is the revision decision: regardless of who proposes a change, acceptance depends on the evidence, the claim-preservation contract and the contextual hierarchy.

AI-assisted scientific writing can support organisation, drafting and language editing while creating risks of inaccuracy, inappropriate attribution and over-reliance on fluent output (Salvagno et al., 2023). Current ICMJE guidance places responsibility for AI-assisted content on human authors and requires disclosure of AI-assisted technologies used in manuscript production (ICMJE, 2026). Applicable disclosure requirements remain unchanged by use of the Academic Writing Filter. Its narrower role is to make revision constraints explicit and repeatable across editing contexts; no text file guarantees compliance by a human or a model.

As a design artefact, the Academic Writing Filter operationalises the manuscript-governance model but is not a validated reporting guideline or a universal standard of academic writing quality. No effectiveness study or consensus process has been undertaken. No present evidence establishes that using the filter improves manuscript quality, publication probability, reviewer agreement or writing speed. Those outcomes could be evaluated separately, but they are not part of the present claim.

No claim of disciplinary universality is made. Social-science reporting and discourse research shows why such a claim would be inappropriate: standards, rhetorical practices and evidential conventions differ across methodological and disciplinary communities (Hyland, 1998; American Educational Research Association, 2006; Levitt et al., 2018; Lupia and Elman, 2014; Nosek et al., 2015). Discipline, manuscript type and outlet therefore enter as contextual constraints rather than after-the-fact style adjustments. Contextual constraints must shape expression while preserving higher-order evidence and claim boundaries.

Nor does this paper claim to invent revision, contribution framing, hedging, transparent reporting or AI-assisted auditing. Those elements have established literatures (Flower and Hayes, 1981; Locke and Golden-Biddle, 1997; Hyland, 1996; American Educational Research Association, 2006; Nussbaum and Bekerman, 2026). This paper claims a narrower contribution: an explicit integration in which a task-relative claim boundary and a precedence hierarchy govern what may change when legitimate revision requirements conflict.

Cochrane provides the principal architectural starting point for the operational writing rules (Cochrane, 2005), but the manuscript-governance framework remains independent. Controls over evidential warrant, discipline, claim preservation, terminology and limitations combine broader scholarly principles with practice-derived rules. No endorsement by John H. Cochrane is implied.

Open release is intended to make the implementation inspectable and contestable. A stable repository or DOI can preserve the dated Markdown file and this working paper after the provenance and licence review is complete. Release mechanics are deliberately secondary to the conceptual claim: manuscript governance concerns ordered revision constraints regardless of where the implementation is stored.

Revision research, social-science writing scholarship and reporting standards establish that rewriting is recursive, epistemically consequential and context-dependent (Flower and Hayes, 1981; Hyland, 1998; American Educational Research Association, 2006; Levitt et al., 2018). Manuscript governance addresses the narrower problem created when those legitimate requirements conflict during a presentation-revision episode. Prose improvement alone cannot decide whether concision should remove a qualification, whether stylistic variation may alter a fixed term, or whether an outlet convention may strengthen a claim beyond the evidence.

The model created in this paper separates task-relative invariants from contextual constraints and mutable presentation choices, then assigns decision rights among them. A claim-preservation contract operationalises the central mechanism: evidence and substantive judgement define an authorised claim boundary; proposed wording is tested against that boundary before outlet form, economy or local house style are optimised. Changing an invariant remains possible, but doing so marks substantive reconsideration rather than ordinary presentation revision. That ordering also explains the post-revision sufficiency audit because lower-order compression cannot count as improvement when it removes a higher-order qualification, conceptual distinction or disciplinary requirement.

A portable Markdown file, the Academic Writing Filter, implements this architecture by screening candidate revisions through the hierarchy. Its thirteen rules combine inherited writing guidance, established scholarly principles and practice-derived controls; they are not presented as novel general writing guidance and are not the paper’s principal intellectual claim. Conceptually, the contribution is the ordering mechanism that connects claim preservation, context and presentation choice under conflict. That mechanism is technology-independent, although AI-specific frameworks such as Nussbaum and Bekerman’s post-draft diagnostic model illustrate one setting in which explicit boundaries around epistemic responsibility are especially salient (Nussbaum and Bekerman, 2026). Open release can make the mechanism available for use, criticism and adaptation without claiming an effectiveness that has not been demonstrated.
The October 2026 release of the companion implementation, Academic_Writing_Filter_10_2026.md, is available from the public project page at https://sites.google.com/view/simonrudkin/ai.

OpenAI’s ChatGPT was used during development of the Academic Writing Filter to consolidate successive drafts, identify candidate literature, test internal consistency and assist with preparation and revision of this working paper and its L a T e X source. Candidate sources used in the present revision were retained only after full-text copies were obtained and inspected. Author review and revision followed, and responsibility for the arguments, citations and final text remains with the author.
