EdgeWise: Bringing Long-Horizon Agents to the Edge via Selective Cloud Delegation. Complex and long-horizon agent tasks often rely on frontier models deployed in the cloud to achieve strong performance. However, using these models for every step of a long-horizon trajectory incurs substantial inference cost, even though not all steps may require the same level of model capability. In this paper, we find that allocating the LLM to only a small subset of key steps can achieve performance comparable to full LLM execution while significantly reducing inference cost. Motivated by this observation, we propose EdgeWise, an edge-cloud collaboration framework that deploys an SLM on the local device as the primary solver and selectively delegates critical steps to a cloud LLM when stronger model capacity is needed. To enable autonomous delegation without additional models at inference time, we introduce a step-level RL method that jointly optimizes task solving and delegation, with fine-grained credit assignment for individual delegation decisions. We also introduce an external judge-based delegation strategy and use it to systematically investigate key design choices in edge-cloud collaboration, including when to delegate, how delegation decisions should be made, what context should be shared, and how frequently the cloud LLM should be invoked.

Experiments show that EdgeWise matches or outperforms pure-LLM execution while reducing inference cost up to 62% on SWE-Rebench and 34% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. We further deploy EdgeWise on a local workstation, demonstrating comparable cost savings in a practical edge-cloud setting.

LLM-based agents have achieved strong performance on increasingly complex long-horizon tasks. However, frontier LLMs require substantial computation and are typically served through cloud infrastructure, making it costly to rely on them throughout long-horizon task execution. Importantly, model capability requirements can vary across intermediate steps, and many simpler steps can be handled by smaller models deployed locally. Recent works have explored allocating queries of different difficulty levels to models with varying capabilities.. Beyond single-query routing, Router-R1 and MERA extend model selection to multi-step settings, dynamically determining which model should handle intermediate invocations as the task progresses. However, existing methods still have critical limitations. (1) Limited Long-Horizon Evaluation: As noted by TwinRouterBench, most existing methods are evaluated on single-query reasoning or multi-hop QA, leaving real-world long-horizon tasks such as coding and deep research largely unexplored. (2) Model-Pool Dependency: Existing approaches typically rely on additional decision models trained over predefined model pools, making their decisions dependent on specific model capabilities and potentially less reliable as the model pool evolves.

Motivated by these limitations, as well as recent advances in SLM capabilities and edge computing hardware that make it increasingly practical to deploy capable SLMs directly on local devices, such as the NVIDIA DGX Spark, we consider an edge–cloud setting where a locally deployed SLM serves as the primary solver for long-horizon tasks and selectively leverages a stronger cloud LLM when needed. Based on this setting, we propose EdgeWise, a step-level edge–cloud collaboration framework in which the local SLM continuously interacts with the environment and selectively delegates critical steps to the cloud LLM. We explore two delegation mechanisms: an external judge-based strategy that dynamically determines when the cloud LLM is needed, and a self-delegation strategy that integrates this capability directly into the SLM through step-level RL with fine-grained credit assignment. Beyond these mechanisms, we systematically analyze the key design factors of edge–cloud collaboration, including when to delegate, what context should be shared, and how delegation frequency should be controlled. Our analysis reveals that the benefit of the cloud LLM is concentrated in a small subset of critical steps, enabling EdgeWise to reduce cloud-model usage while preserving the performance of full LLM execution.

Experimental results show that our methods, particularly RL-based self-delegation, maintain competitive performance while reducing inference cost by an average of 46% across models and benchmarks. We further validate EdgeWise in a practical edge–cloud deployment, where the locally deployed SLM achieves comparable performance and cost savings. shows the Pass@3–cost trade-off and demonstrates that our method selectively delegates harder steps to the LLM, with further analysis in Appendix E. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: We propose EdgeWise, a step-level edge–cloud collaboration framework for long-horizon agents, where an SLM deployed on the local device serves as the primary solver and selectively leverages a stronger cloud LLM when needed. We systematically investigate the key design factors of EdgeWise, including when the cloud LLM is needed, how delegation decisions should be made, what context should be shared between local and cloud models, and how frequently the cloud LLM should be invoked. Our analysis reveals that the benefit of the cloud LLM is concentrated in a small subset of critical steps. Within EdgeWise, we introduce two cloud delegation mechanisms: external-judge-based delegation and self-delegation.

In particular, our step-level RL method with fine-grained credit assignment enables the local SLM to jointly learn task solving and when to leverage the cloud LLM, without an additional decision model at inference time. Extensive experiments on long-horizon coding-agent benchmarks demonstrate that our self-delegation method maintains competitive task performance while reducing inference cost by an average of 46% across different LLMs and benchmarks. We further conduct a real-world deployment evaluation, demonstrating the practical feasibility of our edge–cloud collaboration framework for long-horizon agents.

section: Observation: Delegating Only Key Steps Matches Large-Model Performance
text: Long-horizon coding tasks typically involve a sequence of heterogeneous steps, including problem understanding, root-cause localization, code editing, testing, and result inspection. These steps differ in complexity and may therefore require different levels of model capability. Nevertheless, existing agent harnesses typically rely on a large model throughout the entire trajectory, allocating the same level of model capability to every step. This raises a natural question: Does every step in a long-horizon trajectory require a large model? To investigate this question, we first conduct a random delegation experiment. We use the SLM as the primary solver and randomly delegate a subset of steps to the LLM. Before each step, a delegation decision is independently sampled according to a predefined probability. If selected, the LLM executes the current step, after which control returns to the SLM for subsequent execution; otherwise, the SLM handles the step locally. This setup allows us to examine how task performance changes when the LLM participates in only a subset of steps, and whether the placement of these LLM calls affects the overall performance.

section: Observation: Delegating Only Key Steps Matches Large-Model Performance
text: In our experiments, we use Qwen3.5-9B as the local model and GPT-5.5 with xhigh reasoning effort as the cloud model, with a maximum of 80 turns per trajectory. We follow the default settings of each benchmark, including the original execution-time constraints, and evaluate on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Rebench using two agent harnesses, Terminus2 and OpenHands. To investigate whether the allocation of cloud intelligence matters, we randomly select a fixed proportion of steps to be handled by the cloud model. As shown in Figure 2, when the cloud-model ratio reaches 40%, performance exhibits substantial variation across different random allocations. Notably, some allocations achieve performance comparable to using the cloud model throughout the entire trajectory, while reducing inference cost by at least 25%. This suggests that a relatively small number of well-placed cloud-model calls can be sufficient for strong task performance, with the local model effectively handling the remaining steps. Overall, these results indicate that effective edge SLM–cloud LLM collaboration depends not only on how much stronger model capacity is used, but more importantly on where it is allocated along the trajectory.

section: EdgeWise: A Framework for SLM–LLM Collaboration in Problem Solving
text: Based on this finding, we introduce EdgeWise, an edge SLM and cloud LLM collaboration framework that uses the SLM as the primary solver and selectively delegates challenging steps to the LLM when stronger capability is needed. In this section, we systematically investigate the key design choices of such collaboration, including when and how to delegate, with the goal of maintaining strong task performance while reducing LLM usage and inference cost.

section: When Should the SLM Delegate to the LLM?
text: In Section 2, we observe that delegating only a subset of steps to the LLM can substantially reduce inference cost, with some random allocations achieving performance comparable to full LLM execution. However, at a 40% delegation ratio, performance varies considerably across random allocations, suggesting that where to delegate is critical under a limited budget. This motivates the first key question in designing EdgeWise: Which steps along the trajectory should be delegated to the large model? To investigate this question, we analyze 2.4k coding-agent trajectories and categorize each step into six action types: Write/Edit, Read/Search, Diagnose/Reproduce, Test/Validate, Discover/Navigate, and Wait/Poll. For each type, we measure its cloud coverage, defined as the fraction of steps delegated to the cloud model. To control for task difficulty and delegation budget, we group trajectories by benchmark, task, and random-selection budget, and center both cloud coverage and binary reward within each group. We then pool the centered observations and compute the Pearson correlation: r_{a}=\frac{\sum_{i}\widetilde{C}_{a,i}\widetilde{R}_{i}}{\sqrt{\sum_{i}\widetilde{C}_{a,i}^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{i}\widetilde{R}_{i}^{2}}}, where \widetilde{C}_{a,i} and \widetilde{R}_{i} denote the centered cloud coverage of action type a and task reward, respectively. This measures whether greater cloud coverage of a particular action type is associated with higher task success under the same task and delegation budget.

section: When Should the SLM Delegate to the LLM?
text: We estimate 95% confidence intervals using cluster bootstrap over task-and-budget groups.

section: When Should the SLM Delegate to the LLM?
text: As shown in the left panel of Figure 3, Write/Edit is the action type whose cloud coverage is most strongly associated with task success, with a correlation of 0.200 and a 95% confidence interval of [0.099,0.297]. Read/Search shows a weaker positive association, while the remaining action types have smaller correlations with confidence intervals overlapping zero. The right panel further supports this finding: successful trajectories allocate more cloud coverage to Write/Edit, with gaps of 9.4 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 5.6 on SWE-ReBench, while differences for other action types remain small. Together, these results identify Write/Edit as the action type most strongly associated with task success, suggesting that under a limited delegation budget, performance depends more on delegating critical steps than on uniformly increasing cloud-model usage.

section: Who Should Decide Whether to Delegate?
text: Our analysis suggests that different steps benefit differently from stronger model allocation, motivating a more selective delegation strategy. This raises a practical question: how should the delegation decision be made at each step? We explore two mechanisms. The first uses an external judge to dynamically determine whether the current step should be delegated, while the second integrates this capability directly into the SLM, enabling it to jointly learn task solving and delegation.

section: Key-Step-Aware Delegation with an External Judge
text: Building on the key-step analysis in Section 3.1, we design a key step-aware delegation mechanism that selectively delegates critical steps to the cloud LLM. Specifically, based on the patterns observed in Figure Figure 3, we use Write/Edit and complex Read/Search operations as guidance for identifying key steps in our delegation mechanisms, and translate these patterns into delegation criteria. We then introduce an external judge to dynamically identify such key steps and determine whether the current step should be delegated to the cloud LLM throughout the trajectory. Given the trajectory history h_{t} at step t, the judge determines whether the next step exhibits the characteristics of a key step and makes a binary delegation decision: a_{t}=J(h_{t}),a_{t}\in\{\text{Local},\text{Cloud}\}. If the current state is identified as requiring stronger model, the next step is delegated to the cloud model; otherwise, the local model continues execution. After each step, the judge reevaluates the updated trajectory, allowing key-step identification and model allocation to adapt dynamically as the task progresses. We instantiate GPT-5.4-mini as the external judge and incorporate the key-step patterns identified in Figure 3 into its delegation criteria.

section: Key-Step-Aware Delegation with an External Judge
text: As shown in Figure 4, this key step aware delegation strategy preserves most of the performance of the pure cloud-model baseline while reducing cloud-model usage. These results validate that the identified key-step patterns can effectively guide delegation, further supporting our finding in Section 3.1 that delegating Write/Edit and complex Read/Search steps to the LLM benefits SLM task solving. We therefore use this mechanism as the training-free variant of EdgeWise and further investigate its design choices, including LLM context (Section 3.3), delegation context (Section 3.3), and delegation frequency (Section 3.4).

In the previous section, we use an external judge to determine whether each step should be handled by the SLM or delegated to the LLM. To eliminate the need for an additional model, we formulate self-delegation as a joint task-solving and delegation problem, where the SLM learns to solve the task while selectively invoking the cloud LLM when additional model capability is useful. We adopt a two-stage training pipeline: SFT first teaches the SLM the delegation format, followed by RL that encourages efficient task solving while learning to delegate only critical steps to the LLM.

Stage1: SFT training on based model. Specifically, we use GPT-5.5 to generate task-solving trajectories. At each step, GPT-5.5 additionally considers whether the step would require delegation if executed by a smaller model, and generates the corresponding delegation label. Importantly, these labels are not intended to indicate that a step must be delegated to the LLM. Instead, they serve as format supervision, enabling the SLM to learn delegation as a valid action. Given the constructed dataset \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, we optimize the standard language modeling objective: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=-\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{SFT}}}\log p_{\theta}(y\mid x), where y contains both the task-solving trajectory and the corresponding delegation actions.

Stage 2: RL Training for Self-Delegation. After the first-stage training, we observe that although the SLM learns how to delegate to the LLM, it does not yet learn how to allocate cloud-model usage effectively across different steps, leading to suboptimal delegation behavior Section C.3 and degraded task performance Section B.1. To address this issue, we introduce an RL-based training method that jointly encourages successful task completion and selective allocation of LLM calls to critical steps, as identified in Section 3.1. During training, we follow the output format introduced in the SFT stage. At each step, the SLM first decides whether to delegate to the LLM. For local execution, the SLM generates the analysis and action itself; otherwise, the LLM generates the subsequent output. Since the delegated output is generated by the LLM, these tokens are excluded from the policy loss. Our trajectory-level reward combines an outcome reward for task correctness with a cloud-usage regularization term: R_{i}=V_{i}+\mathbb{I}(V_{i}=1)\frac{1}{1+\lambda C_{i}}, where V_{i} indicates whether the final answer is correct and C_{i} is the number of LLM calls. \lambda is a hyperparameter determined by the typical number of cloud calls per trajectory.

A larger number of cloud calls requires a smaller \lambda, and vice versa, to maintain an appropriate scale for the cost reward. In our experiments, we set \lambda=0.1 based on the cloud call statistics of the training data. The second term favors successful trajectories that use fewer cloud invocations, serving as a regularizer on overall cloud usage rather than directly optimizing monetary inference cost. Importantly, this trajectory-level signal only controls the overall amount of delegation and does not specify which steps should receive the limited cloud-model capacity. To explicitly learn where to allocate LLM calls, we introduce step-level credit assignment for individual delegation decisions. In standard GRPO, tokens within a sampled response typically share the same trajectory-level advantage, making it difficult to distinguish critical delegation decisions from routine ones. Based on the criteria derived in Section 3.1, we use GPT-5.4-mini as a lightweight critic model. Given the full rollout trajectory, the critic model evaluates each delegation decision according to the key-step criteria defined in Section 3.1. Decisions consistent with the critic model’s assessment receive a positive advantage, while unnecessary delegation or missed delegation receives a negative advantage. No additional advantage is assigned when local execution is sufficient.

In this way, the step-level signal does not simply encourage fewer delegations; instead, it encourages SLM to concentrate cloud-model usage on steps where delegation is most valuable. For delegation tokens at step i, its final advantage is A_{t}=A_{\text{traj}}+\beta\frac{N_{\text{trajectory}}}{N_{\text{route}}}A_{i}^{\mathrm{del}}, where A_{\text{traj}} is the trajectory-level GRPO advantage, N_{\text{trajectory}} is the number of training tokens in the trajectory, A_{i}^{\mathrm{del}} is the token level advantage on delegation tokens and N_{\text{route}} is the number of delegation tokens. The scaling factor prevents the step-level signal from being diluted when delegation tokens are sparse, while \beta controls its relative contribution to the policy loss. We evaluate the effectiveness of this step-level credit assignment in Section B.2 and further compare the SFT and RL models in Section B.1. We can see our method not only reduces the number of delegations but also allocates cloud model capacity more selectively to critical steps. We show the agreement between SLM and critic model in Appendix D.

section: What Context Should Be Provided for Collaboration?
text: Effective SLM–LLM collaboration depends not only on when cloud model is introduced, but also on what information is available to different components when making their decisions. In EdgeWise, context serves two distinct purposes. The LLM requires sufficient information to understand the current task state and effectively perform a delegated step, while the judge requires appropriate information to determine whether delegation is necessary in the first place. We therefore investigate the context provided to these two components separately and we empirically compare these configurations in Section 4.3.

section: What Context Should Be Provided for Collaboration?
text: What Information Should Be Passed to the LLM? When a step is delegated, the LLM requires sufficient context to understand the current task state, while longer context also increases inference cost. We therefore investigate five context configurations: (1) Full History, which provides the complete preceding trajectory; (2) Previous Step, which provides only the analysis, action, and observation from the preceding step; (3) Recent History, which provides the most recent k turns; (4) No SLM Reasoning, which removes the SLM’s analysis while retaining executed commands and observations; and (5) Relevant Steps, where the judge selects previous steps most relevant to the upcoming delegated step. These configurations examine the trade-off between context completeness and inference cost.

section: What Context Should Be Provided for Collaboration?
text: What Information Should Be Passed to the Judge? Unlike the LLM, the judge only determines whether the next step should be delegated and may therefore require different contextual information. We consider three configurations for step n: (1) Full History, containing steps 1 to n-1; (2) Full History + Current Analysis, which additionally includes the SLM’s analysis for step n; and (3) Current Analysis Only, which provides only the SLM’s current analysis.

section: What Context Should Be Provided for Collaboration?
text: We empirically compare these configurations in Section 4.3 and adopt Full History as the default context for the judge in EdgeWise.

section: How Frequently Should the LLM Be Invoked?
text: Beyond determining which steps should be delegated, another important design choice is how frequently the LLM should be invoked. More frequent delegation provides greater access to stronger model capabilities but also increases inference cost, whereas overly conservative delegation may prevent the LLM from intervening at critical steps. Therefore, EdgeWise requires a mechanism to explicitly control LLM involvement and balance task performance against inference cost.

section: How Frequently Should the LLM Be Invoked?
text: In Section 3.2.1, the external judge makes a binary decision at each step, determining whether the next step should be handled by the SLM or delegated to the LLM. While effective for identifying potential delegation opportunities, binary decisions provide limited control over the overall delegation frequency. To address this limitation, we extend the judge to produce a continuous delegation score. Given the trajectory history h_{t} at step t, the judge produces s_{t}=J(h_{t}), where s_{t} represents the estimated necessity of invoking the LLM for the next step. The delegation decision is then determined by a predefined threshold \tau: a_{t}=\begin{cases}\text{Cloud},&s_{t}>\tau,\\ \text{Local},&s_{t}\leq\tau.\end{cases} After each step, the judge reevaluates the updated trajectory and produces a new delegation score, allowing the decision to adapt as task execution progresses. By adjusting \tau, we can directly control the level of LLM involvement: a lower threshold results in more frequent delegation, while a higher threshold keeps more steps on the local SLM. This mechanism enables EdgeWise to operate under different cloud budgets and provides a flexible way to explore the trade-off between task performance and inference cost. Appendix F shows the relationship between the delegation threshold and the resulting cloud-call budget.

For training, we use SWE-Smith with Qwen3.5-9B as the SLM and Kimi-K3 as the LLM. We use 2K examples for SFT, followed by RL training on 40 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs for 175 steps, with a batch size of 8 and 16 rollouts per example. We refer to the resulting trained checkpoint as EdgeWise-9B. We evaluate on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-ReBench-03 using the Terminus2 harness, limiting each trajectory to 80 turns while retaining the default benchmark settings. Learning curve and cloud usage are shown in Appendix D and Section C.3, respectively.

We evaluate our delegation strategies against several multi-turn baselines, including LLM-only, random delegation, RSD, STEER, and MTRouter. We use Qwen3.5-9B as the SLM and GPT-5.5 (xhigh) or Claude Opus 4.8 via Bedrock as the cloud LLM, and evaluate on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-ReBench with a maximum of 80 turns. We report Pass@1, Pass@3, and inference cost in Table 1. Cost is computed from cloud LLM API usage based on input and output token pricing; local SLM computation is excluded, while judge API cost is included for binary delegation. Our methods consistently achieve better performance–cost trade-offs than the baselines. In particular, self-delegation reduces Pass@3 cost by 53%/63% on SWE-ReBench and 35%/33% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with GPT-5.5/Opus 4.8, respectively, while maintaining performance comparable to LLM-only. This trend is consistent across both cloud LLMs and benchmarks, suggesting that the gains are not tied to a particular model or task distribution. Moreover, the substantial cost reduction indicates that only a fraction of the trajectory requires access to the stronger cloud model, while the remaining steps can be effectively handled by the local SLM.

The advantage is more pronounced under Pass@3: with Opus 4.8 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, self-delegation trails LLM-only in Pass@1 but matches it in Pass@3. We hypothesize that SLM–LLM collaboration mitigates overthinking and increases exploration diversity across trajectories. We further study generalization in Appendix C across different harnesses, SLMs and judge models.

section: Effect of Context Passing on SLM/LLM Collaboration
text: Context Provided to LLM. In this section, we evaluate the context-passing strategies from the SLM to the LLM introduced in Section 3.3. For the recent- k -steps strategy, we set k=3. As shown in the results, passing the full context achieves the best performance but incurs the highest inference cost. We attribute this to long-horizon tasks, where critical steps delegated to the LLM often require more complete historical information. Full context minimizes information loss during the SLM-to-LLM transition. This is further supported by the no SLM reasoning strategy, which preserves nearly the full interaction history while excluding the SLM’s reasoning, achieving the second-best performance at a lower cost. These results suggest that effective SLM–LLM collaboration requires not only deciding when to switch models, but also what information to transfer. Preserving sufficient context during model transitions is critical, and context should therefore not be compressed indiscriminately.

section: Effect of Context Passing on SLM/LLM Collaboration
text: Context Provided to the Judge. In this section, we evaluate the three judge context configurations introduced in second part of Section 3.3. The results are shown in the left panel of Figure 5. Among the three configurations, Full History achieves the best performance. We attribute this advantage to the complete trajectory information available to the judge, which provides a more comprehensive view of previous actions, observations, and task progress. In contrast, incorporating the SLM’s current analysis may introduce additional bias when its interpretation is inaccurate, potentially causing the judge to miss critical steps that require LLM intervention. Although this reduces LLM usage and inference cost, it also leads to lower task performance. These results suggest that the complete trajectory provides a more reliable context for delegation decisions.

Budget-Aware Cloud Delegation. Following Section 3.4, we introduce a threshold into the external-judge-based method to explicitly control the delegation budget. We first split a validation set from SWE-Smith and evaluate thresholds of 0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8. As shown in Figure 6 (a), thresholds around 0.2 – 0.4 achieve better performance–cost trade-offs on the validation set. Based on this observation, we further evaluate the method on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-ReBench with different LLMs, as shown in Figures (b) and (c). The results exhibit a similar trend, where thresholds around 0.2 – 0.4 maintain strong task performance while substantially reducing inference cost compared with the LLM-only baseline. We further analyze the relationship between the threshold and delegation budget in Appendix F.

Real-World Edge Deployment. In this section, we deploy EdgeWise on a real-world edge device to evaluate its practical feasibility. Specifically, our self-delegation model is deployed on an NVIDIA DGX Spark as the primary solver, selectively delegating steps to a cloud LLM via API when stronger capability is needed. We follow the same experimental configuration as in the previous evaluation. As shown in Figure 6 (d), the edge deployment achieves Pass@3 performance comparable to our A100-based evaluation while reducing inference cost by approximately 50% compared with the vanilla LLM. These results demonstrate that EdgeWise preserves its performance-cost benefits in a practical edge–cloud setting. Additional details are provided in Section G.2.

Real-World Edge Deployment. In this section, we deploy EdgeWise on a real-world edge device to evaluate its practical feasibility. Specifically, we deploy our self-delegation model on an NVIDIA DGX Spark, which serves as the primary solver throughout task execution. When the local model determines that a step requires stronger intelligence, it delegates the step to a cloud LLM via an API request and subsequently continues execution locally. We follow the same experimental configuration as in the previous evaluation. As shown in Figure 6 (d), the edge deployment achieves Pass@3 performance comparable to our A100-based evaluation while reducing inference cost by approximately 50% compared to vanilla model. These results demonstrate that EdgeWise maintains its performance–cost benefits when deployed in a practical edge–cloud setting.

With the increasing inference cost of large language models, recent studies have explored model routing to reduce computational cost while maintaining model performance. Early methods mainly focus on query-level routing, where the router selects a model before solving the query. DiSRouter further allows candidate LLMs to estimate whether they are suitable for solving the current query. Beyond deciding which model to use, R2-Router jointly determines the model and its output-length budget. However, query-level routing makes the routing decision before solving the problem, while the initial query alone may not accurately reflect the actual difficulty encountered during problem solving. This motivates cascade routing, which dynamically determines whether a stronger model is needed based on the output of a smaller model. Conformal Cascade uses conformal prediction to estimate the reliability of the small model’s answer and escalates to a larger model when the answer is considered unreliable. RLCascadeRouter formulates model invocation as an MDP and uses reinforcement learning to optimize the performance-cost trade-off.

Beyond response-level cascading, other studies explore fine-grained routing during generation. CITER dynamically determines whether the small or large model should generate the next tokens. R2R uses a router to identify reasoning-divergent positions and invokes the large model only at these critical positions. While the above methods mainly focus on reasoning generation, routing becomes more challenging in agentic and multi-step tasks, where models need to handle new observations at each step. Router-R1 trains a router to dynamically invoke different models from a model pool for multi-hop QA. MasRouter trains a router to determine the collaboration mode among multiple agents and allocate an LLM to each agent. MERA assigns easier model invocations to smaller models and falls back to larger models for more difficult ones, while further using successful large-model invocations to train the smaller model.

Despite this progress, existing approaches still have several limitations. First, long-horizon agent tasks, such as coding and deep-research tasks, can involve complex and lengthy trajectories, and existing routing approaches may not scale effectively to such settings. Second, existing methods typically rely on an additional router that selects models from a predefined model pool. Such routers are therefore tied to the specific candidate models considered during routing, making it difficult to generalize when the underlying models are updated or replaced.

In this work, we present EdgeWise, an efficient agent framework that enables collaboration between local SLMs and stronger cloud models for long-horizon tasks. Our analysis shows that stronger intelligence is primarily needed at a small number of critical steps. Based on this observation, EdgeWise selectively delegates these steps to the cloud model while retaining the remaining execution locally. Across agentic coding benchmarks, EdgeWise substantially reduces cloud-model usage while maintaining competitive task performance, demonstrating the potential of step-level model collaboration for building efficient and practical agent systems.

MeddeX: A Retrieval-Augmented LLaMA-3 System with Gemini Vision for Evidence-Backed Medical Report Analysis. Modern healthcare generates increasingly complex medical reports that challenge clinical professionals in terms of time and interpretive burden. Manual review processes are slow, error-prone, and difficult to scale. This paper presents MeddeX, a Medical Report Analyzer that combines a QLoRA fine-tuned LLaMA-3 (8B) model with Retrieval-Augmented Gen eration (RAG) and a multimodal Gemini Vision layer to deliver accurate, concise, and evidence-backed summaries of medical documents. The system handles text-native PDFs, scanned image based PDFs, and direct radiological images through an intelligent hybrid extraction pipeline that includes a novel garbage-text detection mechanism for corrupted and UTF-16-encoded doc uments. Beyond single-report Q&A, MeddeX introduces report scoped retrieval for precise contextual grounding, an automated longitudinal report comparison engine, and a self-healing backfill pipeline that lazily processes legacy documents on demand. A FastAPI backend, Supabase vector store, and Next.js fron tend complete the end-to-end architecture. Evaluation against the base LLaMA3-Med42-8B model demonstrates consistent improvements across ROUGE-1 (+9.2%), ROUGE-2 (+10.0%), ROUGE-L (+11.8%), BLEU (+71.4%), and BERTScore (+0.8%), validating the benefit of domain-specific fine-tuning. MeddeX represents a practical and robust step toward AI-assisted clinical decision support.

Healthcare professionals routinely contend with lengthy, complex medical reports encompassing diagnostic results, patient histories, lab values, and clinical recommendations. The cognitive load imposed by manual review slows clinical workflows and increases the risk of oversight-related errors. With the exponential growth of digital health records, intelligent systems capable of rapid, reliable medical document interpretation have become a clinical necessity.

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) have opened new possibilities for automated medical report analysis. However, existing solutions suffer from well-documented limitations: poor handling of long-context documents, absence of verifiable evidence linking, inadequate adaptation to specialized medical terminology, and limited support for multimodal inputs such as scanned reports or radiological images.

This paper presents MeddeX, a system that directly addresses these limitations. MeddeX integrates: A QLoRA fine-tuned LLaMA-3 (8B) model (based on LLaMA3-Med42-8B) for domain-adapted generation. A RAG pipeline with report-scoped dense retrieval to ground outputs in specific source evidence. A Gemini Vision multimodal layer for OCR on scanned PDFs, UTF-16-encoded documents, and direct image inputs. A garbage-text detection module that identifies and re-routes corrupted or hex-encoded page extractions. A longitudinal comparison engine (/compare_reports) enabling AI-driven analysis of change across multiple reports over time. A lazy backfill pipeline that transparently processes legacy documents uploaded before the chunking system was in place. A FastAPI backend with Supabase vector and document storage, and a Next.js frontend for clinician-friendly interaction.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work and identifies research gaps. Section III details the proposed architecture. Section IV describes key implementation components. Section V presents experimental results. Section VI concludes and outlines future directions.

Natural Language Processing for clinical text has been studied extensively. Early systems relied on rule-based extraction and keyword matching, which lacked generalizability. The introduction of transformer architectures, beginning with BERT, enabled contextual understanding of medical language. Subsequent models such as BioBERT, ClinicalBERT, and PubMedBERT demonstrated that domain pretraining significantly improves downstream clinical NLP tasks including named entity recognition, relation extraction, and question answering.

Summarization-specific models including BART and Longformer have been applied to medical documents, with Longformer’s sliding-window attention providing a partial solution to the long-context problem. However, these models generate summaries without grounding claims in verifiable source passages, limiting clinician trust.

RAG, introduced by Lewis et al., combines a dense retriever with a seq2seq generator to produce factually grounded responses. The formulation conditions generation on retrieved passages: P(y\mid x)=\sum_{z\in\mathcal{D}}P(y\mid x,z;\,\theta)\,P(z\mid x;\,\phi) where x is the input query, z represents retrieved document chunks, and \phi, \theta are the retriever and generator parameters respectively. This joint framework enables outputs to be traced to source evidence, a critical requirement in clinical settings.

Large language models such as LLaMA-3 have demonstrated strong general-purpose generation but require domain adaptation for reliable clinical use. Med42, built on LLaMA-3, provides a medically pre-adapted checkpoint. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning via QLoRA allows further task-specific adaptation at a fraction of full fine-tuning cost by quantizing base weights to 4-bit and training only low-rank adapter matrices.

A substantial portion of clinical documents—including scanned lab reports, discharge summaries, and radiology images—exist as images rather than machine-readable text. Recent vision-language models such as Google Gemini have demonstrated strong OCR and medical image interpretation capabilities, enabling hybrid pipelines that process both textual and visual content.

A review of the literature reveals the following unresolved challenges that MeddeX targets: Long-document handling: Most LLMs degrade beyond their context window; chunked retrieval is necessary. Evidence-backed outputs: Summaries without source attribution are insufficient for clinical trust. Domain adaptation: Generic LLMs misinterpret subtle clinical terminology and lab value contexts. Multimodal support: Scanned documents and radiology images are not handled by text-only pipelines. Document integrity: Real-world PDFs frequently contain UTF-16 encoding artifacts or corrupted pages that silently produce garbled text, undermining downstream analysis. Longitudinal analysis: Existing systems treat each report in isolation; clinicians need automated comparison across visits to track patient health trends. End-to-end usability: Clinical adoption requires seamless, low-latency interfaces integrated with secure storage.

MeddeX is organized into four modular layers as illustrated in Fig. 1: a Frontend layer, a Backend API layer, a Model layer, and a Storage layer. The backend exposes three primary endpoints — /upload_report, /consult, and /compare_reports — each supported by shared processing modules for extraction, chunking, embedding, and generation.
The end-to-end pipeline proceeds as follows:

Ingestion: A user uploads a PDF or image via the frontend. The backend receives the file through the /upload_report endpoint. Garbage Detection: Before extraction, each page’s text is evaluated by _is_garbage_text() for UTF-16 hex artifacts or high non-printable character ratios. Corrupted pages are automatically re-routed to Gemini Vision. Smart Extraction: The hybrid extraction module routes text-native pages through PyPDF2, and scanned, garbled, or image-based pages through Gemini Vision OCR. Chunking: Extracted text is split into overlapping chunks (500 characters, 50-character overlap) to preserve local context at retrieval boundaries. Embedding & Indexing: Each chunk is encoded using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and stored with its 384-dimensional embedding vector in Supabase. Report-Scoped Retrieval: At query time, the question is embedded and the top- k most similar chunks are retrieved via match_chunks_by_report RPC, scoping results to the active report. A global match_chunks fallback is used when no report is selected. Generation: Retrieved chunks plus recent chat history are concatenated as context and passed to the fine-tuned LLaMA-3 model, which generates an evidence-grounded answer. Response & Persistence: The answer is returned to the frontend and stored in the chats table with report_id for session continuity.

The system implements the RAG objective defined in Eq. 1. The retriever uses dense embeddings to score chunk relevance, and the fine-tuned LLaMA-3 generator is conditioned on the concatenated top- k retrieved passages. This grounding mechanism ensures that factual claims in generated summaries can be traced to specific source chunks, improving clinical trustworthiness.

A critical robustness addition in MeddeX is the _is_garbage_text() function, which guards against silently corrupted text extractions from UTF-16-encoded or otherwise malformed PDFs. PyPDF2 may extract text from such pages, but the output is a stream of hex-like characters rather than readable content. Without detection, this garbage would be embedded and retrieved as if it were valid clinical text.

Two heuristics are applied: (1) if more than 30% of characters belong to contiguous runs of 20+ uppercase hex digits — a reliable signature of UTF-16 binary leakage — the page is flagged; (2) if more than 20% of characters are non-printable or non-ASCII, the page is similarly rejected. Flagged pages are silently re-routed to Gemini Vision OCR, maintaining extraction quality without user intervention.

Building on garbage detection, MeddeX routes each page through one of three paths: direct text extraction (PyPDF2), garbage-detected Gemini fallback, or full-image Gemini OCR for scanned pages. The updated routing logic is shown in Listing 2.

The updated /consult endpoint accepts an optional report_id parameter, enabling retrieval to be scoped to a specific document. This prevents context bleed across multiple uploaded reports for the same user — a significant correctness improvement for patients with a history of several uploaded documents.

Chat history is now also correctly formatted before injection into the context window, resolving a prior bug where raw database rows were passed to generate_answer() without a chunk_text key, causing them to be silently dropped.

The /compare_reports endpoint is a significant clinical feature that enables AI-driven longitudinal analysis. Given two report_id values, the system retrieves full text for each report, constructs a structured comparison prompt, and generates a comprehensive summary covering parameter-by-parameter changes, clinically significant findings, stable values, and an overall health trend.

The endpoint handles two ID formats robustly: valid UUIDs are queried directly against the reports table, while filename-style IDs fall back to a file_name search. The comparison result is saved to the chats table for audit and session continuity.

The get_or_extract_report_text() helper enables MeddeX to process reports that were uploaded directly to Supabase Storage without going through /upload_report. On first access, it fetches the raw file, runs the full extraction and chunking pipeline, and backfills embeddings under a new UUID — so subsequent calls resolve instantly from the database. Cached chunks that fail the garbage-text check are also purged and re-extracted, ensuring data integrity across the system.

Text chunks are encoded using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 SentenceTransformer model, producing 384-dimensional dense vectors. Vectors are stored in Supabase alongside chunk text and report metadata. Two RPC functions handle retrieval: match_chunks_by_report for scoped search and match_chunks for global search, both using cosine similarity via pgvector.
The generation module uses a QLoRA fine-tuned checkpoint of LLaMA3-Med42-8B. The model is invoked using the LLaMA-3 chat template format:
Inference uses nucleus sampling (\text{top-}p=0.9, temperature =0.3) with a maximum of 300 new tokens for Q&A and 600 for report comparisons, balancing response coherence and clinical conciseness.

The FastAPI backend exposes three primary endpoints: POST /upload_report — Accepts a file and user_id; runs garbage detection, smart extraction, chunking, embedding, and stores all data in Supabase. POST /consult — Accepts user_id, question, and optional report_id; performs report-scoped or global retrieval, injects chat history, and returns a generated answer. POST /compare_reports — Accepts user_id, report_id_1, and report_id_2; retrieves full text for both reports via the backfill pipeline and returns a structured longitudinal comparison summary.

Evaluation compared the base LLaMA3-Med42-8B model against the QLoRA fine-tuned MeddeX variant. The dataset consisted of de-identified medical reports and curated clinical Q&A pairs. Metrics computed include ROUGE-1/2/L (n-gram overlap), BLEU (precision-based phrase similarity), and BERTScore (semantic similarity via RoBERTa-large embeddings).
Table I presents the complete evaluation results. The fine-tuned model consistently outperforms the base model across all five metrics.

Table II compares the computational footprint and inference characteristics of the base LLaMA3-Med42-8B model against the QLoRA fine-tuned MeddeX variant. QLoRA quantizes base weights to 4-bit precision and trains only low-rank adapter matrices, dramatically reducing memory requirements while retaining generation quality.

The QLoRA configuration reduces VRAM requirements for fine-tuning by approximately 4\times compared to full BF16 fine-tuning, enabling training on a single consumer-grade RTX 3090 GPU rather than requiring an enterprise A100. Inference VRAM is similarly reduced, making deployment on mid-range clinical workstations feasible. The lower sampling temperature (0.3 vs. 0.7) used in MeddeX reflects a deliberate design choice to favour factual consistency over generative diversity in clinical contexts.
Fig. 2 visualizes the side-by-side metric comparison, and Fig. 3 shows percentage improvements per metric.

The most pronounced gain is in BLEU score (+71.4%), indicating that fine-tuning substantially improves the model’s ability to generate precise, phrase-level matches to reference clinical answers. This is clinically significant as it reflects the model’s improved fluency with medical terminology and structured reporting conventions.

ROUGE improvements of 9–12% demonstrate better content recall and answer structure. BERTScore improvement, while smaller in absolute terms (+0.8%), is meaningful given that the base model’s BERTScore of 0.8765 already reflects strong semantic similarity; marginal gains at this range indicate genuine refinement of clinical language understanding.

The modest absolute ROUGE values reflect the inherent difficulty of open-ended medical Q&A, where multiple valid phrasings exist for the same clinical answer. The relative improvements are what validate the fine-tuning approach.
These results validate the core design choices in MeddeX:

Domain-specific fine-tuning via QLoRA is effective and resource-efficient, yielding measurable gains without full model retraining. As shown in Table II, QLoRA reduces fine-tuning VRAM by \sim 4 \times and inference VRAM by half compared to the full-precision base model. RAG grounding with report-scoped retrieval ensures generation is conditioned on relevant, per-document context, reducing both hallucination risk and cross-report contamination. Gemini Vision with garbage-text detection extends the system to the full diversity of real-world medical documents — scanned reports, UTF-16-encoded PDFs, and radiological images — that text-only systems silently mishandle. Longitudinal comparison addresses a clinical need unmet by existing systems: automated, structured analysis of how a patient’s health parameters evolve across multiple visits. Lazy backfill pipeline improves system resilience by handling legacy documents transparently, ensuring no report is inaccessible due to missing preprocessing history.

Limitations include the relatively small evaluation dataset and the absence of a large-scale multi-site clinical trial. Occasional hallucinations on rare terminology were observed, consistent with known LLM behavior on out-of-distribution inputs. The comparison endpoint currently truncates each report to 1,500 characters of context for the prompt, which may omit details from very long documents; future work will address this with hierarchical summarization.

This paper presented MeddeX, a modular medical report analysis system combining a QLoRA fine-tuned LLaMA-3 (8B) model with RAG, a Gemini Vision multimodal OCR layer, and a suite of robustness and clinical-utility features developed through iterative engineering. Beyond the core summarization and Q&A pipeline, MeddeX introduces garbage-text detection for corrupted PDF handling, report-scoped retrieval for precise contextual grounding, an automated longitudinal comparison engine for tracking patient health trends, and a lazy backfill pipeline for transparent processing of legacy documents. Quantitative evaluation demonstrates consistent improvements over the base LLaMA3-Med42-8B model across all five metrics, with a particularly strong BLEU improvement of +71.4%, validating the domain fine-tuning approach. Together, these contributions position MeddeX as a comprehensive, production-oriented clinical AI system.

Planned extensions include: Large-scale clinical validation: Multi-center trials across specialties and languages to assess generalizability. Hierarchical summarization for comparison: Replace fixed 1,500-character truncation in /compare_reports with a multi-pass summarization strategy for very long reports. EHR integration: Real-time summarization within electronic health record systems for seamless clinical workflow adoption. Model distillation: Quantization and distillation to support inference on edge servers or low-VRAM GPUs for resource-constrained settings. Explainability: Calibrated confidence scores and claim-level source attribution surfaced directly in the frontend UI. Expanded multimodal support: End-to-end radiology report generation from raw imaging inputs, extending beyond OCR to full vision-language understanding.

From Retrieval to Typed Decisions: Calibrated System One Models from Biomedical Sentence Encoders. Typed decision models answer schema-constrained questions about a text in one forward pass and return probabilities meant to be thresholded. We ask whether biomedical sentence encoders trained for retrieval are good starting points for such models. We present SBERT2S1, which converts Sentence-Transformers encoders into bi-encoder, cross-head (C) and prior-fused residual (PFR) decision models, together with BIODECIDE, a biomedical typed-decision suite, and MEDLINE-S1, 243k training decisions derived from NLM indexing. Across six parent-retriever pairs, retrieval training improves zero-shot matching of content-bearing options. After fine-tuning, its effect depends on the head: across five pairs and three training-set sizes, retrieval training significantly helps PFR, which keeps the retrieval prior, in 10 of 15 comparisons, but helps C in one and hurts it in five. A matched grid of two heads and five training objectives shows that C outperforms PFR under every objective, and that the released RLCD recipe of open System One models trails cross-entropy by 2.5-3.0 points. The deficit stems mainly from its reward normalisation, which inflates the noisy score-function term 3.6-15-fold; an unbiased leave-one-out estimator recovers most of the gap.
After temperature scaling, no objective is clearly better calibrated than cross-entropy. We release the code, the MEDLINE-S1 labels and a model.

Much of the language processing in biomedical software consists of small, bounded decisions: does this abstract report a randomised trial, does the evidence support the claim, how severe are the side effects a patient describes? Because the answers are consumed by code, a decision is only useful if it respects a schema and comes with a confidence that can be thresholded to act, defer or escalate.

System One models were proposed for exactly this interface (TypeSafe AI, 2026). A request pairs a text (the state) with typed questions of three kinds (choice, score and noul), and the model returns, in one forward pass, a distribution over the options each question allows. The open model Laya (Convai Innovations, 2026) pairs an encoder with a mask-slot head and trains it with RLCD, a mixture of cross-entropy and a policy gradient against proper scoring rules (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). All existing System One models are general-domain and start from masked-language-model (MLM) or decoder checkpoints. Most biomedical encoders are MLMs too, such as BioBERT (Lee et al., 2020) and PubMedBERT (Gu et al., 2021). A smaller group has been further trained contrastively as Sentence-Transformers encoders for retrieval: S-PubMedBERT-MS-MARCO (Deka et al., 2022) is PubMedBERT fine-tuned on MS MARCO (Nguyen et al., 2016), and MedCPT (Jin et al., 2023) is trained on PubMed search logs. A typed decision resembles retrieval, since it asks whether a hypothesis formed from a question and an option matches the state, but retrieval similarity need not encode negation, ordinal judgement or calibrated truth.

This study tests whether biomedical sentence encoders can be converted into System One models, and what the result depends on: Initialisation: when does retrieval training improve zero-shot or fine-tuned decisions? Conversion: how do bi-encoder, cross-head and prior-fused conversions trade accuracy, robustness to option order, cost and retrieval retention, under matched objectives? Objective: which ingredient of RLCD matters once temperatures are fitted: the proper score, the noise smoothing, or the policy-gradient estimator?

(1) sbert2s1, a framework that turns Sentence-Transformers encoders into typed decision models with four conversions, including a prior-fused residual (PFR) head that starts from the calibrated zero-shot retriever; (2) BioDecide, a biomedical typed-decision suite with public and credentialed clinical tracks, and MEDLINE-S1, multi-question training data labelled from NLM indexing rather than an LLM teacher; (3) a controlled study over eleven encoders, six parent-retriever pairs, and a matched grid of two heads and five objectives; and (4) an analysis showing that RLCD optimises a noise-smoothed proper score, that the released estimator is biased and rescaled, and that a simple leave-one-out baseline removes both problems. Code, MEDLINE-S1 and the released model are available at https://github.com/pritamdeka/sbert2s1, https://huggingface.co/datasets/pritamdeka/MEDLINE-S1 and https://huggingface.co/pritamdeka/S1-PubMedBERT.

Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026) introduced typed decisions with three primitives: choice (one option from a schema), score (a distribution over an ordinal rubric) and noul (the probability that a statement holds); its training objective is not public. Laya (Convai Innovations, 2026), the first open implementation, pairs ModernBERT-large (Warner et al., 2025) with a two-layer head that scores one [MASK] slot per option, trained with cross-entropy plus a group-baselined policy gradient (as in GRPO; Shao et al., 2024) on noise-perturbed logits rewarded by proper scores. Decider (Marosi, 2026) fine-tunes decoders, and the Decision Index (Decision Index contributors, 2026) benchmarks typed-decision engines. Concurrent work applies or probes System One models in security agents, annotation, crash-report coding, distracting contexts and active questioning (dos Santos, 2026; Ibrahim and Zaki, 2026; Rafe and Das, 2026; Xu, 2026; Yilmaz et al., 2026) (Appendix A). These studies do not evaluate biomedical conversions, retrieval initialisation, or RLCD ablations.

A strictly proper scoring rule is uniquely optimised in expectation by the true distribution (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007); examples include the log, Brier (Brier, 1950), spherical and ranked-probability (Epstein, 1969) scores. Neural networks, including pre-trained transformers, are often miscalibrated, and temperature scaling is a strong post-hoc remedy (Guo et al., 2017; Desai and Durrett, 2020). A calibration benefit claimed for a training objective must therefore survive temperature scaling.

Siamese encoders trained so that cosine similarity reflects relatedness (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019), on query-passage data such as MS MARCO (Nguyen et al., 2016), are standard for dense retrieval; cross-encoders re-rank more accurately at higher cost (Nogueira and Cho, 2019). Comparing a text with label descriptions underlies entailment-based zero-shot classification (Yin et al., 2019). In biomedicine, domain pre-training (Gu et al., 2021) followed by contrastive training on search logs (Jin et al., 2023) or MS MARCO (Deka et al., 2022) yields strong retrievers. We use such encoders as the initialisation of decision models and measure what the contrastive stage adds.

A request consists of a state s (text or a serialised record) and questions q=(\tau,x,o_{1:K}), where \tau\in\{\texttt{choice},\texttt{score},\texttt{noul}\} is the type, x the instruction and o_{1},\dots,o_{K} the options: schema keys with optional descriptions for choice, ordered rubric levels for score, and (\textit{false},\textit{true}) for noul. We use the request schema shared by Jev and Laya. A model maps (s,q) to logits z\in\mathbb{R}^{K} and reports p(\cdot\mid s,q)=\operatorname{softmax}\big(z/T_{\tau,K}\big), where T_{\tau,K}>0 is a post-hoc temperature shared by all questions of type \tau in one option-count bucket (§ 3.4). The answer is \argmax_{k}p_{k} for choice, the expected level \sum_{k}(k-1)\,p_{k} for score, and p_{2} (true) for noul. The confidence \max_{k}p_{k} is the quantity that is thresholded and that expected calibration error (ECE) measures.

Let E_{\theta} be the transformer of a Sentence-Transformers model and e_{\theta}(\cdot)=\frac{\operatorname{pool}(E_{\theta}(\cdot))}{\lVert\operatorname{pool}(E_{\theta}(\cdot))\rVert_{2}} its normalised embedding, with the checkpoint’s pooling (mean or [CLS]). For option k we form the hypothesis h_{k}=x\oplus o_{k} (instruction followed by the rendered option) and define the retrieval prior c_{k}=\langle e_{\theta}(s),e_{\theta}(h_{k})\rangle; the hypothesis plays the query and the state the passage. We compare four conversions: Z, B: \displaystyle z_{k}=\alpha_{\tau}\,c_{k}, C: \displaystyle z_{k}=r_{\theta,\phi}(s,q)_{k}, PFR: \displaystyle z_{k}=r_{\theta,\phi}(s,q)_{k}+\alpha_{\tau}\,c_{k}. Z keeps \theta frozen and fits only the per-type scale \alpha_{\tau}. B trains \theta and \alpha; state embeddings can be pre-computed, so screening a corpus costs one embedding of K hypotheses and a matrix product. C is a cross-encoder head: E_{\theta} encodes \displaystyle\texttt{[CLS]}\,\tau\,x\,\texttt{[SEP]}\;\texttt{[MASK]}\,o_{1}\cdots\texttt{[MASK]}\,o_{K} \displaystyle\qquad\texttt{[SEP]}\;s\,\texttt{[SEP]}, a two-layer transformer \phi with a type embedding contextualises it, and an MLP scores the hidden state at the k -th [MASK]. The head replicates Laya’s, so the two load each other’s weights: the public Laya checkpoint run through our implementation reproduces its reported zero-shot accuracy on typed-decisions (0.3615 vs. 0.362). PFR adds this cross score to the retrieval prior. The last layer of the scorer is zero-initialised, so the untrained PFR model equals Z and training learns a cross-attention residual on top of the retriever.

The prior shares \theta by default; a frozen copy preserves the original retriever at twice the memory. The prior scale is initialised at \alpha_{\tau}=20, the usual similarity scale of contrastive encoders, has its own learning rate and no weight decay.

section: Training objectives and the RLCD estimator
text: All objectives compare the reported distribution p with a target distribution t (one-hot for most items). The simplest is cross-entropy (CE). Laya’s reward S(p,t) adds two further proper scoring rules to the log score: the spherical score for every question and, for score questions, the ranked probability score, which also penalises probability placed on distant rubric levels. A scoring rule is proper when reporting the true distribution maximises its expected value, so a high S rewards honest probabilities (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007).

section: Training objectives and the RLCD estimator
text: RLCD does not maximise S directly. For each item it adds Gaussian noise to the logits G=4 times, scores each noisy prediction with S, and moves the logits towards the noise directions that scored above average. This is a policy-gradient (REINFORCE) step, and CE is added to it with weight one. The reward part of the update for one item is \hat{g}=\frac{1}{G\sigma^{2}}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\frac{R^{(g)}-\bar{R}}{d}\,\varepsilon^{(g)}, where \varepsilon^{(g)} is the g -th noise draw, \sigma its scale (annealed from 0.4 to 0.1), R^{(g)} its reward, \bar{R} the mean reward of the item’s G draws, and d the standard deviation of the centred rewards in the minibatch.

section: Training objectives and the RLCD estimator
text: Without \bar{R} and d, \hat{g} would be an unbiased estimate of the gradient of the expected reward under noise, a smoothed version of S that tends to S as \sigma\to 0. The two choices change this. First, \bar{R} contains the draw’s own reward, so on average the estimate is shrunk by (G-1)/G=3/4. Second, the reward differences shrink roughly in proportion to \sigma, so dividing by d makes the estimate grow roughly as 1/\sigma while the noise is annealed. Because CE keeps a fixed weight, the noisy reward term gradually dominates it. Appendix C states this formally (Proposition 1) and proves it, and Appendix D measures it.

section: Training objectives and the RLCD estimator
text: To remove these biases, use the mean of the other G-1 rewards as the baseline and do not divide by d. We call this PG-LOO (leave-one-out). We compare six objectives with identical data and schedule: CE; Proper, which maximises S without noise; PG, the released RLCD recipe; PG w/o CE, its reward term alone; PG-LOO; and Reparam, which differentiates the smoothed reward directly through the noise (the reparameterisation trick) and adds CE. PG-LOO and Reparam estimate the same gradient on the same scale and differ only in variance.

After training, one temperature per type and option-count bucket (K=2, 3 – 5, 6 – 10, {\geq}11) is fitted by minimising negative log-likelihood on a calibration split carved from the training data before training, with a per-type fallback for buckets with fewer than ten items. Every metric is reported before and after this step.

Clinical notes exceed the 512-token context of base encoders. Besides truncation and sliding windows, we evaluate retrieve-then-decide: the model’s own embedding e_{\theta} selects the m=3 note chunks most similar to the instruction x, and the decision is made on those chunks in document order. This requires the converted model to remain a retriever.

We convert existing biomedical datasets into typed decisions over a state (Table 1; conversions in Appendix B). In the grounded track the state determines the answer: evidence QA (PubMedQA; Jin et al., 2019), claim verification (SciFact, HealthVer and PUBHEALTH; Wadden et al., 2020; Sarrouti et al., 2021; Kotonya and Toni, 2020), drug–drug interactions (DDI; Herrero-Zazo et al., 2013), cancer hallmarks with ten noul questions per abstract (HoC; Baker et al., 2016), adverse drug events (ADE; Gurulingappa et al., 2012), patient drug reviews with three score questions each (Druglib; Gräßer et al., 2018), sentence similarity (BIOSSES; Soğancıoğlu et al., 2017) and specialty routing (MTSamples). In the knowledge track (MedQA, MedMCQA and MMLU-medical; Jin et al., 2021; Pal et al., 2022; Hendrycks et al., 2021) the state is an exam vignette whose answer depends on memorised knowledge; it is reported but does not drive headline numbers. PUBHEALTH, BIOSSES and MMLU are never trained on, and MTSamples is a held-out task family. We also evaluate on the general-domain typed-decisions set used by Laya.

Each source example becomes one record: a state (the text the decision is about), one or more typed questions, and a gold distribution over each question’s options (Figure 1; a full record is in Figure 4). The dataset’s question or label set becomes the instruction, and each label gets a short description, written once per task, so that options carry content rather than bare label words. Multi-label annotations become one noul per label (HoC), multi-aspect ratings become several questions about one state (Druglib), a graded score becomes a score question whose target splits its mass between the two nearest levels (BIOSSES), and exam items become choice questions with the answer texts as descriptions. Answer-revealing fields are removed (PubMedQA conclusions, PUBHEALTH explanations). Official splits are kept where they exist, and before any training a calibration slice (about 10% of training, at most 400 states) is carved off, grouped by claim or topic where the source groups items. Appendix B details every dataset.

Existing corpora pose one question per text, whereas System One requests typically ask several heterogeneous questions about one state. Multi-question training data is usually produced by an LLM teacher, whose errors then become targets. We instead derive labels from MEDLINE indexing, which NLM curates: study design (six classes from publication types, with a fixed precedence for overlapping tags); disease area (the single MeSH disease-tree category among major topics, against 3–7 randomly drawn distractors, so that no encoder is favoured by model-mined negatives); human or animal subjects; whether adverse effects or drug therapy are reported; and, for human studies, two sampled age or sex groups. We keep 2005–2021 citations with manual or human-curated indexing and exclude every PMID in any BioDecide evaluation set. Tags are weak labels: absence need not mean false, and indexers may use the full article. The training set has 40k abstracts (242,986 decisions); the test set has 5k abstracts from disjoint files.

Under PhysioNet credentialed access (Pollard et al., 2026) we convert MedNLI (Romanov and Shivade, 2018; Shivade, 2019); 1,000 human-reviewed trial-eligibility questions over MIMIC-III discharge notes (Woo et al., 2024; Woo et al., 2025; Johnson et al., 2016), posed as yes / no / not stated and as an answerability noul; and a name-mention noul over windows of MIMIC-IV notes with inserted surrogate names (Lim et al., 2023; Johnson et al., 2023), including a split of names that are also common words. The MIMIC-III notes average 12.9k characters and form our long-state test. Credentialed data were processed only on institutional hardware and never sent to a hosted API; the released model is trained on public data only.

We evaluate eleven base-size checkpoints: PubMedBERT and its retrieval children S-PubMedBERT-MS-MARCO and MedCPT-Query; MPNet and all-MPNet-base-v2; ModernBERT-base and its Nomic and GTE embedders; BioClinical-ModernBERT and its embedder; and BGE-base-v1.5 as an unpaired retriever (Gu et al., 2021; Deka et al., 2022; Jin et al., 2023; Song et al., 2020; Sentence Transformers, 2021; Warner et al., 2025; Nussbaum et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Sounack et al., 2025; NeuML, 2025; Xiao et al., 2024). This gives six parent-retriever comparisons with shared parents and different retrieval corpora; they are not six independent replications of one intervention. Model-specific query/document prefixes are used.

Training tasks are sampled with probability \propto n_{t}^{1/2}. The budget is 8,000 steps at batch size 32 (at most eight epochs), with AdamW, bf16 autocast over fp32 weights and gradient clipping at norm 1. Options are shuffled except for ordinal rubrics. All encoders are trained with C and PFR under the released RLCD recipe (PG), three seeds each, plus 2% and 10% learning curves for the ten paired checkpoints, also with three seeds. On S-PubMedBERT-MS-MARCO we run the full head \times objective grid: C and PFR with CE, Proper, PG, PG-LOO and Reparam (and PG w/o CE for PFR), three seeds per cell, identical data, schedule and seeds. Appendix K lists hyperparameters.

Laya-large (421M) is evaluated zero-shot and fine-tuned on our mixture with the same recipe. Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026) and Gemma-4-31B (Gemma Team, 2026) score option letters in one forward pass with thinking disabled (Appendix J). All systems are temperature-scaled on the same calibration splits. Exam questions are likely present in LLM pre-training data, so LLM scores on the knowledge track are descriptive only.

The headline metric is chance-normalised accuracy \mathrm{acc}_{\text{cn}}=(\mathrm{acc}-1/K)/(1-1/K), averaged over (question, K) groups within a task and then over tasks. Seen denotes the eight grounded training tasks; held-out PUBHEALTH, BIOSSES and MTSamples. We also report top-label ECE and NLL before and after temperature scaling, ordinal error, option-order flips and retrieval retention (nDCG@10 on BEIR SciFact and NFCorpus; Thakur et al., 2021; Boteva et al., 2016). Confidence intervals come from a paired bootstrap (10,000 draws) over document clusters within each task: all records sharing a normalised text are resampled together. Intervals condition on the observed tasks and on seed-averaged correctness; seed sd is reported separately. Holm correction is applied within each research question across both tracks (Appendix F). Non-significance is not read as equivalence.

An exact-input audit found a few training duplicates in calibration (nine DDI and seven Druglib records) and test (two SciFact and 13 Druglib records) splits, and repeated inputs within some test sets. Removing all affected test inputs lowers seen-task scores by 0.3–0.4 points for every model and changes no ranking (Appendix I).

Retrieval improves zero-shot content matching. Without training, every contrastive checkpoint reaches 15–24 chance-normalised points on questions whose options differ in content (disease areas, study designs, specialties, rubrics, exam answers), against 0–7 for their MLM parents and 20.3 for Laya-large (Table 3). On options that differ only by a label word (yes/no, true/false), cosine gaps are of order 10^{-3} and no encoder is reliably above chance.

After fine-tuning, retrieval benefits depend on the head. With full data and the cross head the contrastive stage is roughly neutral: S-PubMedBERT and PubMedBERT reach 67.7 and 67.3, both MPNet checkpoints 66.4, and the BioClinical-ModernBERT pair 72.9 and 73.1 (Table 2); the only Holm-significant difference is negative (GTE-ModernBERT -2.5; Table 8). With PFR, which keeps the retrieval prior, the retriever is better in three of five pairs (all-MPNet +4.5, Nomic +2.7, GTE +2.9), worse for S-PubMedBERT (-1.6), and the ModernBERT embedders gain +10.9 on held-out tasks (Holm p\leq.014 for each). With less data the heads diverge further (Figure 2). For PFR, retrievers are ahead in four of five pairs at both 10% and 2% (significant in three and four; e.g. Nomic +5.3 and +9.2, GTE +4.7 and +7.4, and up to +16.3 on held-out tasks). For C, the ModernBERT-family retrievers are 2.5–3.7 points behind their parents at 10%, BioClinical-ModernBERT’s embedder is 8.5 points behind at 2%, and the only gain is S-PubMedBERT at 10% (+1.9). MedCPT-Query illustrates the dependence on the conversion: its [MASK] states are identical within an input, so the cross head reaches only 17.9, but PFR reaches 60.4.

The strongest base-size model is BioClinical-ModernBERT with a cross head (73.1), close to fine-tuned Laya-large (75.0) at about a third of its size. Over all 15 pair and data-size comparisons (Table 8), retrieval training is significantly better in ten and worse in one with PFR, and better in one and worse in five with C.

The cross head achieves higher accuracy. In the matched grid (Table 4), C exceeds PFR by 1.3–2.4 seen-task points for all five shared objectives (Holm p\leq.011 for CE, Proper and PG;.08 and.14 for PG-LOO and Reparam) and by 3.8–10.2 points on held-out tasks. The bi-encoder B matches C on seen tasks (-0.6, n.s.) but loses 9.4 held-out points; its value is that state embeddings can be precomputed for corpus screening. A frozen prior improves PFR by 2.5 points.

Prior fusion reduces option-order sensitivity. Prior fusion makes decisions almost invariant to option order: averaged over all evaluation splits, a random permutation changes 0.3% of S-PubMedBERT PFR answers versus 15.7% for C, whose flips concentrate on unseen inputs (held-out 17%, exams 28%, seen tasks 3%; Appendix H). PFR also has lower ordinal error on Druglib for every objective (Table 7).

Fine-tuning reduces retrieval performance. SciFact nDCG@10 of the pooled embedding falls from 67.6 (Z) to 43.3 (C), 35.6 (PFR), 34.3 (B) and 24.6 for C trained with CE (Table 14 in Appendix K); only a frozen prior keeps the retriever intact. A ten-question request takes 6.6 ms for C, 15.2 ms for PFR and 22.7 ms for Laya-large (forward pass, batch 1, MI300X).

section: RQ3: Does RLCD improve accuracy or calibration?
text: The released RLCD recipe trails cross-entropy. With either head, CE, Proper and Reparam are within one point of each other, while the released PG recipe trails CE by 3.0 (PFR) and 2.5 (C) points (Holm p=.005), with a fourfold larger seed sd for PFR (1.5 vs. 0.4). Adding the spherical and RPS terms does not significantly improve accuracy (Proper - CE +0.2 and +0.5, n.s.), and removing CE from PG has little effect on accuracy (+0.2).

section: RQ3: Does RLCD improve accuracy or calibration?
text: An unbiased estimator reduces the accuracy deficit. PG-LOO, which differs from PG only in its baseline and in dropping the reward normalisation, gains 2.5 (PFR) and 1.5 (C) points over PG (Holm p=.005) and is within 0.8 points of Reparam (n.s.). A matched probe on fixed checkpoints and batches explains why (Appendix D): the released estimator points in the right direction (cosine 0.98 with the true smoothed gradient) but is 3.6–3.8, 5.7–6.1 and 14–15 times too large at \sigma=0.4, 0.25 and 0.1, so the score term outweighs CE by 5–20 \times instead of 1.3 \times. Since the global gradient norm exceeds the clipping threshold at every step for every objective, step length is fixed and the objectives differ only in direction; under PG that direction is dominated by a score-function term with a per-item signal-to-noise ratio below one. The pathwise estimator is 100–1,500 times less noisy at matched scale, yet PG-LOO trains nearly as well, so estimator variance is a secondary factor.

section: RQ3: Does RLCD improve accuracy or calibration?
text: No clear calibration benefit after scaling. PG has the lowest raw ECE (7.0 vs. 9.3 for CE with PFR), but after temperature scaling all objectives lie between 3.6 and 4.4 and PG has the worst NLL (Table 7, Figure 7). On the three held-out tasks the ordering is noisier and differs from seen tasks (e.g. C with Reparam is 7 points below C with PG), so we do not generalise the objective ranking beyond the training distribution.

Fine-tuned encoders are competitive on seen tasks: S-PubMedBERT C trained with CE (70.2) and Laya-large (75.0) exceed zero-shot Gemma-4-31B (65.7) and Qwen3.8-27B (57.4), with better calibration (ECE after scaling 3.8–4.3 vs. 8.5–9.1). The LLMs achieve higher accuracy on held-out tasks (Gemma 52.6 vs. 31.0), the clinical track (81.6–83.4 vs. at most 38.4 zero-shot, 55.2 with clinical training) and exams. The two are complementary (Figure 3): routing the 20% least confident questions to Gemma raises macro accuracy over seen and held-out tasks from 59.5 to 68.4 for S-PubMedBERT C (CE) and from 64.3 to 69.1 for Laya-large, against 62.1 for Gemma alone. This is a retrospective fixed budget on the test set, not a validated deployment threshold.

section: Retrieval benefits depend on the head.
text: Retrieval training helps zero-shot and helps a prior-fused head, more so with scarce labels, but is close to neutral for a cross head with full data and can cost accuracy with few labels. Retrieval initialisation is therefore most beneficial when the conversion retains the retrieval prior (PFR), particularly with scarce labels; it offers no consistent accuracy gain for a cross head.

For per-request decisions, we recommend a cross head with cross-entropy (70.2 on S-PubMedBERT). BioClinical-ModernBERT with a cross head reaches 73.1 under PG. PFR is preferable when low option-order sensitivity is important or when the encoder’s mask-slot states are degenerate, and B when a corpus must be screened against many questions. Every trained conversion degrades the embedding as a retriever unless the prior is frozen.

Biomedical sentence encoders trained for retrieval can be converted into System One models: with a cross head they reach 66–73 seen-task points with top-label ECE below 6 after temperature scaling (MedCPT-Query excepted), close to fine-tuned Laya-large (75.0) at about a third of its size. Whether retrieval training itself helps depends on the conversion: it helps PFR in 10 of 15 comparisons, most clearly with little labelled data, but does not consistently help C. Plain cross-entropy with temperature scaling matches or outperforms the released RLCD recipe, whose deficit comes from its reward normalisation; implementations of RLCD should use an independent baseline such as leave-one-out. Fast encoders and LLMs are complementary, so a calibrated System One model is a natural first stage that answers confident cases and escalates the rest.

Results cover base-size encoders, one fixed training budget and hyperparameters inherited from Laya; objectives were not tuned separately, and the head \times objective grid was run on one encoder. The six parent-retriever comparisons share parents and differ in retrieval corpora, so they are not independent replications. Intervals condition on the observed tasks and seed-averaged correctness; no mixed-effects or equivalence analysis is claimed.
