MEDLINE-S1 labels are weak: indexing can omit tags and uses the full article. A few exact training inputs recur in calibration and test splits; we report the (small) sensitivity of test scores but did not retrain or refit temperatures on de-duplicated splits. Text-level identity cannot establish patient-level independence or exclude near-duplicates. Exam contamination of the LLMs is unmeasured.

Low ECE on seen tasks does not imply calibration on new tasks: on held-out tasks several models are poorly calibrated, and option-order sensitivity of cross heads grows under shift. Thresholds should be validated on in-domain samples before use.

The clinical tests are small, come from one hospital system and use surrogate names; long-note strategies remain close to chance for base encoders. Nothing here is a validated clinical device, and the released model is not trained on clinical notes.

Credentialed PhysioNet data (MedNLI, MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV derivatives) were used under their data use agreements, processed only on institutional infrastructure, and never sent to a hosted model or API; only aggregate metrics leave that infrastructure, and examples in this paper are paraphrased. Public datasets are used under their published licences or terms of use; for them we release conversion code and per-record hashes rather than the data. For MEDLINE-S1 we release PMIDs, questions and labels under CC BY 4.0 without the abstracts, which a script retrieves from PubMed. The released model is trained only on public data and inherits the non-commercial licence of S-PubMedBERT-MS-MARCO. Calibrated confidences can encourage automation; we recommend human review of escalated and low-confidence decisions in any health-related deployment.

We thank the creators and maintainers of the publicly released datasets, pretrained encoders, language-model checkpoints and open-source software used in this study, including Laya, Sentence-Transformers, PyTorch and Hugging Face Transformers. We also acknowledge the National Library of Medicine for PubMed and MeSH, and PhysioNet and the contributors to the clinical resources accessed under their respective data use agreements.
Computational experiments used Kelvin2 GPU resources provided by Queen’s University Belfast through the Northern Ireland High Performance Computing (NI-HPC) service.

LatentRiskBench: Measuring State-Dependent Risks in Enterprise Agents. Enterprise agents face safety risks that cannot be determined from individual actions alone. Existing safety benchmarks largely evaluate action-local risks, overlooking failures whose safety depends on workflow state. In such state-dependent risks, the same action may be safe in one context but violate policy in another. Hence, we introduce LatentRiskBench for evaluating such state-dependent risks in enterprise settings. It pairs risky trajectories with benign counterparts that share the same terminal action but differ in latent policy-relevant states, requiring models to reconstruct workflow context rather than rely on action-level cues. We also introduce new metrics for state-dependent risk evaluation, including a suite of residual risk (RR) measures. Experiments on the benchmark show that action-level evaluation detects only 0.09 of state-dependent violations, whereas state-level evaluation reaches 0.96. Existing guardrail methods largely overlook such risks unless they are explicitly applied to workflow states. Case studies on a commercial deployed scenario further show that the safety metrics embedded in the benchmark provide a more realistic measure of safety for enterprise agents. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/JingyueCong/LatentRiskBench.

Agent evaluation is increasingly shifting from isolated tasks toward operational workflows in which agents read, transform, and dispatch business artifacts (Yao et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023; Debenedetti et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Ensuring the safety of such agents requires more than evaluating individual actions. In many enterprise settings, whether an action is compliant or risky depends on the workflow state established by prior steps. An action that appears routine at the point of execution may become policy-violating because of earlier decisions, approvals, or information accumulated throughout the workflow.

Consider an enterprise agent on an e-commerce platform, tasked with preparing a marketing campaign. Each individual action appears harmless, so the risk is invisible to action-level auditing. Yet whether the same action is safe may flip depending on the workflow state established by prior steps: it can violate policy if a required approval is missing or restricted content is involved. Similar situations arise across enterprise workflows, including document sharing, report distribution, customer communication, and access management.

Current agent-safety benchmarks do not isolate this observability regime. Prior benchmarks cover important settings, including tool-use security, prompt-injection robustness, web-agent safety, and risk awareness from interaction traces (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024; Levy et al., 2024). However, many of their tasks expose the decisive evidence in a step-local output, the proposed action itself, or a recognizable trace pattern; they do not directly test routine-looking terminal actions whose violations depend on workflow state induced by prior steps.

We refer to this regime as state-dependent risk (Figure 1), in which a terminal action appears benign or ambiguous under action-level auditing but becomes policy-violating once the underlying workflow state is taken into account. The central distinction is not trajectory length but risk-signal location: the same action may be safe in one trajectory yet unsafe in another, because prior steps induce different policy-relevant states.

Designed to address this gap, LatentRiskBench is a risk-observability benchmark for enterprise agents. Each agent trace contains a task intent, committed trajectory prefix, proposed terminal action, applicable policy set, and risk label. Its core design principle is constant-action pairing, in which risky and benign trajectories share the same terminal action while differing in underlying policy-relevant states. It includes a 100-task state-dependent core, visible-risk controls, matched benign twins, and an e-commerce marketing instantiation.

Using LatentRiskBench, we find that state-dependent violations are largely invisible to action-level evaluation: an action-level checker flags only 0.09 of these violations, whereas an auditor that reconstructs workflow state flags 0.96. Representative guardrails inherit this blind spot. They suppress locally observable risk but leave most state-dependent risk unresolved unless they explicitly reconstruct and reason over states. Finally, auditing a deployed enterprise e-commerce marketing agent shows the practical stakes: conventional outcome-level summaries (Outcome Violation Rate and Task Success Rate) appear reassuring even though state-dependent residual risk remains high.

Our contributions are: Regime. We formalize state-dependent risk as a risk-observability regime in which the same terminal action can be safe or unsafe depending on reconstructed workflow state. Benchmark and metrics. We introduce LatentRiskBench, with constant-action risky/benign twins, visible-risk controls, an e-commerce instantiation, and the SRG, CAS, and residual-policy-risk metrics. Evaluation. We evaluate representative guardrails and auditor backbones, showing that state reconstruction is the key capability separating strong state-dependent auditing from action-local or prefix-only screening.

Recent agent benchmarks evaluate increasingly realistic forms of web navigation, tool use, computer use, prompt-injection robustness, and policy compliance (Zhou et al., 2023; Koh et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Mialon et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2025; Schick et al., 2023; Debenedetti et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Zhan et al., 2024; Andriushchenko et al., 2025; Evtimov et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025; Levy et al., 2024; Naik et al., 2026). These benchmarks are important for measuring whether agents can complete tasks and avoid unsafe behavior. However, those safety failures are detectable from a local signal: sensitive content returned by a tool, an explicitly unsafe action, or a trace pattern.

Enterprise workflows introduce a different risk regime. The same terminal action can be policy-compliant in one workflow and policy-violating in another, depending on the state accumulated across business records, approvals, prior actions, and policy constraints. In this setting, the decisive risk signal is not the action surface form or a single observation, but the policy-relevant workflow state that must be reconstructed from the trajectory. Fig. 2 shows that such risks are poorly covered by existing benchmarks. A broader discussion of related agent benchmarks is provided in Appendix A.

Each instance consists of labeled risky trajectories, matched with benign twins, and visible-risk controls. To assess risks, it employs a state-dependent auditor as the evaluation instrument, drawing on world-model consequence prediction (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018) and the predictive-guardrail framing of prior work (Chen et al., 2026).

We call h_{<t}=\langle(a_{1},o_{1}),\dots,(a_{t-1},o_{t-1})\rangle the committed prefix, including the actions already taken and the observations already returned before t. The trajectory state s_{t}\in\mathcal{S} summarizes the workflow state over a fixed set of policy-relevant variables, including accumulated content, generated artifacts, outbound destinations, authorization or approval status, data-sensitivity tags, and goal alignment with respect to the user intent I. Formally, state s_{t} at time t is reconstructed from the committed prefix and the available environment context c_{t}: s_{t}=R(I,h_{<t},c_{t}),\qquad s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}, where c_{t} denotes the current environment context (such as artifact metadata, destination metadata, access-control state, approval records, data-sensitivity annotations, and policy-specific task parameters). Reconstruction is limited to facts supported by the committed prefix or the provided environment context. Thus, s_{t} is the policy-relevant workflow state induced by the trajectory and its environment, not a copy of the full working logs.

We start by curating benign workflows. Each test instance is seeded from an enterprise-common task, for which we script a policy-compliant workflow. We then construct an unsafe counterpart with the same task structure and terminal action. Specifically, we sample a timestep t, reconstruct the trajectory state s_{t}=R(I,h_{<t}), and bind the relevant policies in \mathcal{P} to the state variables that determine compliance. To make the injected risk invisible to action-local auditing, we target state-specific leverage points: policy-gating variables that are not apparent from the action surface or from any single prefix step. Earlier steps are then edited so that the selected variable becomes policy-violating while the terminal action remains unchanged. In the core set of LatentRiskBench, we balance the state-dependent risk across four mechanisms: state accumulation, destination dependence, authorization dependence, and goal-shift dependence.

We manually validate each paired trace for authenticity and state dependence. A valid item must satisfy three criteria: the violation is invisible from every individual agent action, detectable from the reconstructed state, and invariant under path perturbations that preserve the same policy-relevant state. If changing the wording, ordering, or intermediate observations while preserving s_{t} changes the label, the item is classified as composite rather than state-dependent.

The 24 cases identified as short-horizon or locally visible risks are retained separately as a control set. After filtering, the benchmark contains 124 domain-general enterprise-agent traces, denoted LatentRiskBench-Core. We further develop the LatentRiskBench-E-commerce set, consisting of 40 e-commerce-specific traces extracted and refined from real-life agent logs of industry deployment (Section 5). Data scheme, example trace, and human evaluation are detailed in Appendix B.

Let \mathcal{P} be the applicable policy, the state-dependent auditor takes the audit instance (I,h_{<t},c_{t},a_{T},\mathcal{P}), reconstructs the trajectory state s_{t}, and judges whether a_{T} would violate \mathcal{P} under that state. We write its output as (\hat{y},\hat{v},e)=W(I,h_{<t},c_{t},a_{T},\mathcal{P}), where \hat{y}\in\{0,1\} is the predicted violation label, \hat{v} is the predicted violated policy class, and e is a short evidence trace linking reconstructed state, terminal action, and policy.

As a contrasting view of the state-dependent auditing, we use an action-local evaluator E(a_{T},\mathcal{P}). It receives the same full terminal action, including arguments and visible content, but not the committed prefix or environment context. Since both evaluators judge the same a_{T}, their detectability gap quantifies the contribution of reconstructed trajectory state rather than differences in action content. The full auditor prompt and output schema are provided in Appendix C.
We propose three state-dependent risk metrics: Residual Risks (RRs), State-Reconstruction Gain (SRG), and Constant-Action Specificity (CAS).

RR shifts from the auditor to the methods under evaluation. For a candidate safety-control method, RR is the fraction of risky trajectories on which it still leaves a policy violation, i.e., it neither blocks the violating terminal action nor otherwise removes the violation. We report overall RR together with stratum-specific values for short/local-visible (S-RR), action-revealing (AR-RR), and state-dependent (SD-RR) cases. We also report each method’s benign admission: unnecessary blocking of a matched benign twin is counted as a false positive, and benign admission is one minus this false-positive rate.

SRG measures the additional detection rate of the state-dependent auditor over an action-local evaluator: \mathrm{SRG}=D_{\mathrm{state}}-D_{\mathrm{action}}. Here, D_{\mathrm{action}} is the detection rate of E(a_{T},\mathcal{P}), and D_{\mathrm{state}} is the detection rate of W(I,h_{<t},c_{t},a_{T},\mathcal{P}) on the same risky terminal actions. SRG is a benchmark diagnostic: it quantifies the detectability gained from reconstructing trajectory state.

CAS measures whether matched benign twins with the same terminal action are admitted as policy-compliant. CAS is computed on benign twins whose a_{T} matches a risky item but whose reconstructed state makes the action compliant. This metric ensures that high SRG is not achieved by labeling the shared terminal action as universally unsafe.

We evaluate representative guardrails spanning lexical, rule-based, LLM-judge, and trajectory-level defenses: Vanilla, Keyword (Rebedea et al., 2023), StepRule (Rebedea et al., 2023), LLMJudge (Zheng et al., 2023), and TrajRule. TrajRule observes the committed prefix but does not explicitly reconstruct policy-relevant state, allowing us to separate trajectory access from state reasoning. We also include LlamaGuard3 as a moderation-style boundary baseline (Llama Team, 2024) and GuardAgent as a stronger trajectory-reasoning baseline (Xiang et al., 2024).

Evaluation Metrics. In addition to metrics proposed in Sec. 3.4, we also report conventional metrics: Outcome Violation Rate (OVR) and Task Success Rate (TSR). OVR (akin to attack success rate) measures the fraction of workflows whose outcome violates policy, while TSR measures task completion. Because RR and CAS rely on the state-dependent auditor, we validate its verdicts against blind human labels and robustness checks. Formal metric definitions are provided in Appendix E.

Table 1 compares guardrails on LatentRiskBench -Core. Conventional risk evaluation metrics, such as OVR, appear reassuring even when residual risk remains high under the state-dependent auditor. Action- and moderation-style guardrails reduce local-visible risk, but leave much of the state-dependent risk unresolved.

The results also confirm that safeguarding agents simply based on trajectory of actions may not be suffient. For example, TrajRule safeguard agents by checking the committed prefix, but it still leaves high residual risk (RR). LLMJudge provides strong semantic judgment over the current action, but its remaining errors concentrate in the SD regime. Guardrails with stronger trajectory reasoning reduce SD-RR the most, yet state-dependent residual risk remains non-trivial.

Additional guardrails, including Llama Guard 3 (Llama Team, 2024) and GuardAgent/ShieldAgent trajectory guardrails (Xiang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025), do not close the SD gap unless they reconstruct and reason over state. A prefix reader that observes the full committed trajectory but does not reconstruct policy-relevant state also fails to close the gap. Thus, SRG reflects state reconstruction, not mere prefix access. Full validation and robustness analyses are provided in Appendix F.2 and Appendix F.3. Utility remains high across the non-trivial guardrails, as reflected by TSR. On the 100 same-action benign twins, benign false-positive rates are low, indicating that lower RR is not achieved by broad blocking. Policy-class and mechanism breakdowns are reported in Appendices F.1 and F.6.

Figure 3 compares violation detection using only action-local signals, denoted D_{\text{action}}, with detection using reconstructed workflow state, denoted D_{\text{state}}. This comparison tests whether policy risks that are not evident from the terminal action become detectable once the policy-relevant trajectory state is recovered. On the 100 state-dependent trajectories in LatentRiskBench -Core, action-local detection identifies only 0.09 of violations, whereas the state-dependent auditor identifies 0.96, yielding a State-Reconstruction Gain of \mathrm{SRG}=0.87. This large gap indicates that action-local screening substantially underestimates residual risks in enterprise workflows. Because both evaluators are applied to the same trajectories, we further assess the paired difference using McNemar’s exact two-sided test, which shows a big difference between action-local and state-dependent decisions (p<10^{-15}) (McNemar, 1947). The Wilson 95% confidence intervals for the two detection rates are also well separated: 0.09 [0.05,0.16] for D_{\text{action}} versus 0.96 [0.90,0.98] for D_{\text{state}}. More details in Appendix F.

Because the state-dependent auditor is the load-bearing measurement instrument, we validate it against human labels and robustness checks. Two annotators independently labelled all agent traces and report risk detection. They reached high agreement (\kappa=0.90) (Cohen, 1960). Against the human majority, the auditor reaches \kappa=0.88 overall, with \kappa=0.83 on the SD regime and \kappa=1.00 on AR. Its main weakness is mild over-conservatism on short/local-visible tasks, rather than failure on the headline SD regime.

The conclusions are stable across instruments and backbones. The primary auditor used in the main results is gpt-4o-mini; other LLM backbones are evaluated as robustness checks under the same audit protocol. As shown in Table 2, action-local detection remains low across backbones, while state-dependent detection remains substantially higher. This suggests that the observed SRG reflects the state-dependent risk regime rather than a gpt-4o-mini -specific artifact.

section: External-Validity Audit of an E-commerce Marketing Agent
text: LatentRiskBench was motivated by a manual audit of an enterprise e-commerce marketing agent. We revisit this setting as an external-validity case study, applying the same audit to anonymized committed trajectories from its workflow.

The audited system is the marketing assistant of an anonymized e-commerce enterprise. It supports growth workflows such as drafting promotional copy, summarizing product performance, reading customer segments, preparing and pushing email marketing campaigns, and syncing campaign drafts to a marketing platform. The agent follows a ReAct -style tool-calling loop (Yao et al., 2023) with access to product sales data, customer-segment files, campaign briefs, discount-strategy documents, and marketing-platform tools. The audit uses the same enterprise policy family as the benchmark.

Table 3 summarizes the audit. Conventional outcome-level summaries appear reassuring: Outcome Violation Rate is low (OVR= 0.08) and Task Success Rate is high (TSR= 0.92). However, these summaries do not capture pre-execution risk that has not yet produced a realized harmful outcome, such as a campaign draft that has absorbed restricted information but has not yet been sent externally. The state-dependent audit exposes this gap. Residual Risk remains high (RR= 0.61): many proposed terminal actions would violate policy when judged under the accumulated workflow state. State-Reconstruction Gain is also high (SRG= 0.49), showing that much of the risk is not visible from the terminal action alone. The benign false-positive rate is low (0.025; admission 0.975), suggesting that the audit is not simply flagging routine marketing actions broadly. Thus, the audit reproduces the benchmark pattern: outcome-level summaries can appear safe while state-dependent residual risk remains high.

Because the audit is run over committed trajectories rather than enforced inline, we validate flagged actions through inert sandbox replay. Each flagged terminal action is replayed under the reconstructed state, and deterministic event-log rules determine whether the transition would realize a policy violation. The reported RR therefore counts only flags backed by a policy-violating transition.

A representative promotional-email workflow is described in Appendix J: a routine campaign-sync action becomes risky only after reconstructing that the draft contains internal pricing information and is being sent to an external marketing platform.

The audit incurs a median latency overhead of 430 ms and a p95 overhead of 1.9 s per audited action, with an estimated cost of $0.0028 per action. This overhead is non-negligible but compatible with selective deployment: actions with external side effects can be audited inline, while lower-risk internal actions can be audited asynchronously or through sampling. Additional latency and cost details are provided in Appendix J.

This case study is an external-validity audit, not a production enforcement study. Verdicts were computed offline over anonymized committed trajectories and were not used to block the live agent. The controlled benchmark remains the primary quantitative evidence.

We presented LatentRiskBench, a deployment-oriented benchmark for auditing state-dependent residual risk in enterprise agents. The benchmark targets policy violations whose decisive evidence is not visible from the terminal action or any single local observation, but from the policy-relevant workflow state accumulated across the trajectory. Our results show that action-local evaluation substantially underestimates this risk: state-dependent violations are rarely detected from the action alone (0.09), but are largely recovered by state-dependent auditing (0.96, \mathrm{SRG}=0.87). Representative guardrails reduce locally visible risks but leave substantial residual risk when they fail to reconstruct and reason over workflow state. Matched benign twins further show that the auditor responds to state differences rather than action surface form. Human validation, robustness checks, and an offline audit of a real enterprise marketing agent support the reliability and practical relevance of the benchmark. LatentRiskBench provides a pre-deployment evaluation resource for testing whether agent guardrails can detect state-dependent policy risk before being trusted in enterprise workflows.

Our benchmark is designed to isolate state-dependent risk, so the SD trajectories are authored such that the final action appears benign in isolation and becomes risky only after reconstructing environment state. This makes the State-Reconstruction Gain measurable, but also means SD difficulty is partly a property of the benchmark design rather than a purely organic empirical finding. In addition, the world-model auditor is itself the measuring instrument; although we hold it out from the defense matrix and validate its judgments against independent LLM and human annotations, shared LLM bias cannot be fully ruled out. Finally, the study is instantiated in an e-commerce marketing sandbox with modest per-category sample sizes, so absolute numbers, policy coverage, and inline deployment costs may not transfer directly to other domains without re-validation.

RealControlBench: A Benchmark for Interpretability-Informed Fine-Grained Control of LLMs and Agents. Existing steering benchmarks are built around simplified, isolated generation tasks and evaluate a single behavioral attribute under controlled settings that do not reflect the diversity and complexity of practical deployment. As a result, performance on these benchmarks provides only a limited picture of how steering methods perform in the real world. We therefore introduce RealControlBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating fine-grained steering of LLMs and LLM agents across diverse behavioral targets and interaction settings. RealControlBench extends steering evaluation beyond isolated generations to complex, execution-grounded, multi-turn agent interactions, covering five complementary dimensions: instruction-following control, agentic tool-use decision control, reasoning-performance steering, reasoning-length control, and trajectory-conditioned safety awareness. Rather than measuring steering success alone, the benchmark jointly evaluates target controllability and capability preservation, including instruction following, reasoning performance, and downstream agent utility and safety. It further examines whether steering effects remain specific and robust across prompt variations, domains, and model architectures. Our evaluation shows that existing steering methods remain unreliable across realistic control objectives: they often fail to consistently induce the intended behavior and can substantially degrade the model's underlying task performance.

These results suggest that strong steering effects in controlled settings do not necessarily translate into reliable control in more realistic evaluations. By providing a unified, model-agnostic steering evaluation framework, RealControlBench aims to support the development of steering methods that are not only effective but also precise, robust, and useful in realistic AI deployments.

Large language models (LLMs) are arguably the first systems we have built that combine an open-ended natural-language interface with broad competence in writing, reasoning, programming, and tool use (Wei et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023, inter alia). This flexibility makes it easy to tell a model what we want it to do. Ensuring that it does so precisely and reliably, however, is a different matter. Reliable control over model behavior is therefore becoming a fundamental requirement for deploying LLMs in practice. This challenge is becoming more important as the adoption of agentic LLM systems continues to accelerate and the technology becomes increasingly ubiquitous and embedded in more critical, high-risk real-world settings (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Han et al., 2025).

While multiple approaches exist, from prompting and constrained decoding to fine-tuning and preference optimization, steering has recently shown particular promise owing to its distinct advantages (Zou et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Liu and Han, 2026; Han et al., 2026). It allows us to adjust a model’s behavior during inference by intervening directly on its internal representations, without retraining the model. In practice, most steering methods simply add a scaled vector to the model’s activations, with little computational overhead and a single coefficient controlling the intervention’s strength (Turner et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026). The same basic approach has been applied to truthfulness (Li et al., 2023), refusal and sycophancy (Rimsky et al., 2024), instruction following (He et al., 2026), mathematical reasoning (Ouyang et al., 2026), and agentic tasks (Chen et al., 2026).

Nevertheless, steering also faces a crucial challenge that existing benchmarks do not fully capture. Method papers often focus on whether an intervention increases or suppresses a small set of target behaviors, leaving unclear whether these changes translate into useful control in realistic settings. In practice, steering must induce the intended behavior without compromising the model’s ability to complete the underlying task, and remain appropriate as the interaction evolves. Can existing steering methods provide reliable control without sacrificing task performance?

Therefore, we introduce RealControlBench, which, to our knowledge, provides the first unified evaluation of steering across instruction following, reasoning, and safe control and execution in multi-turn agent interactions, measuring target success together with utility retention. We design the benchmark around three criteria. First, it should provide broad coverage across control objectives and models, rather than focusing on a single behavior or setting. Second, evaluation should be execution-grounded, measuring not only whether steering induces the intended behavior but also whether the model retains its ability to complete the underlying task. Third, the benchmark should be model-agnostic, allowing the same tasks, environments, and evaluation criteria to be applied across models without reconstructing model-specific benchmark data. Together, these criteria shift steering evaluation from isolated behavioral changes toward practical control under realistic task demands.

As summarized in Table 1, RealControlBench evaluates steering across instruction following, tool-use decisions and execution, reasoning performance, reasoning-length control, and safety. Beyond isolated response-level behaviors, it examines whether steering remains useful for downstream task execution and multi-turn interaction. Our results show why this distinction matters: improvements on individual metrics do not always translate into stronger end-to-end performance. On Qwen3-8B, for example, PCA (Zou et al., 2023) achieves a higher Decision score than prompting (42.00% vs. 40.50%) but a lower FollowUp score (16.25% vs. 24.50%), a difference that first-turn evaluation alone would miss. A similar pattern appears in reasoning, where gains on the in-distribution (ID) benchmark do not consistently carry over to out-of-distribution (OOD) problems, suggesting that fixed steering directions may not provide reliable improvements across problem distributions.

We make three main contributions: We introduce a unified benchmark spanning instruction following, tool use, reasoning and reasoning-length control, safety, and multi-turn agent execution. To our knowledge, RealControlBench is the first steering benchmark to evaluate both multi-turn agent execution and safety, moving beyond response-level control to assess whether interventions remain effective throughout agent trajectories. We benchmark prompting and representative steering families across multiple models, providing a common empirical basis for comparing practical steering behavior.
This framing enables more meaningful comparisons between steering methods and highlights the need for interventions that remain effective and reliable under realistic deployment conditions.

Mechanistic interpretability studies how model behaviors and concepts are represented and computed internally, with the goal of identifying features, directions, circuits, or components associated with particular behaviors (Zhao et al., 2024; Elhage et al., 2021; Olsson et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023). Recent work has shown that some high-level behaviors can be localized to relatively simple internal structures. For example, linear directions have been used to characterize properties such as truthfulness, refusal, and other behavioral attributes, while sparse autoencoders decompose dense activations into more interpretable feature dictionaries (Arditi et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025). These observations naturally motivate representation-level control: if a behavior is encoded in an identifiable internal representation, intervening on that representation may provide a direct way to steer model outputs. Representation-level interventions have been instantiated at multiple granularities: contrastive and PCA-based methods derive global activation directions, linear probes use learned decision boundaries as steering directions, and ITI localizes interventions to a small subset of informative attention heads (Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023).

More recently, ODESteer moves beyond static one-step interventions by formulating activation steering as an ODE-based control process, enabling adaptive multi-step steering along the activation trajectory (Zhao et al., 2026). In parallel, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) factorize dense model activations into a sparse set of latent features, where each feature is associated with a direction in activation space and is intended to capture a more localized component of the model’s internal representation (Huben et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025; Karvonen et al., 2025). This decomposition provides a finer-grained intervention interface: rather than steering along a single global direction, SAE-based methods can identify and manipulate individual features associated with the target behavior (Fang et al., 2026; Arad et al., 2025). However, directly manipulating individual SAE features may still provide limited or unstable control, and SAE-SSV therefore identifies a sparse, task-relevant subspace using supervised signals and explicitly optimizes a steering vector within that subspace (He et al., 2025). SAE features can also support targeted behavioral editing; for example, ablating bias-associated sparse features can mitigate demographic stereotypes while largely preserving demographic recognition (Shan and Mueller, 2026).

Recent work uses representation-level interventions to improve reasoning performance and control reasoning behavior. DenseSteer steers model activations toward patterns associated with stronger reasoning, improving mathematical reasoning without updating model parameters (Ouyang et al., 2026). SEAL extracts reasoning steering vectors to calibrate chain-of-thought generation, reducing redundant reasoning while improving answer accuracy (Chen et al., 2025b; Sheng et al., 2025). Beyond overall performance, Venhoff et al. (2025) identify activation directions associated with specific reasoning behaviors, including backtracking, expressing uncertainty, and generating examples, and use steering vectors to modulate these behaviors. At the feature level, SAE-Steering identifies sparse autoencoder features associated with specific reasoning strategies and intervenes on these features to control behaviors such as backtracking and cross-verification (Fang et al., 2026; Azizi et al., 2026). RISER further explores adaptive steering by constructing a library of reasoning vectors and training a lightweight router to compose them for each input using task-level rewards (Ye et al., 2026).

Existing benchmarks evaluate LLM steering across a range of concepts and behavioral attributes. AxBench benchmarks concept detection and steering, evaluating whether generated responses express a target concept while preserving instruction following and fluency (Wu et al., 2025). TruthGen and TwinViews-13k provide paired statements for studying truthfulness and political bias (Fulay et al., 2024), while STEER-BENCH evaluates alignment with community-specific norms and viewpoints (Chen et al., 2025a). CLaS-Bench measures target-language control alongside semantic relevance across languages (Gurgurov et al., 2026). SteerEval organizes behavioral targets at increasing levels of specificity, covering language features, sentiment, and personality, with additional experiments on reasoning patterns (Xu et al., 2026). These benchmarks provide useful measures of behavioral control and response quality. Evaluating steering in reasoning and agentic tasks also requires checking its consequences for task completion: whether a shorter reasoning trace still yields the correct answer, whether a tool-use decision leads to successful execution, and whether control remains effective over subsequent interactions. MAS, introduced with AgentLens, addresses part of this problem through annotated multi-turn coding-agent trajectories for runtime safety detection and mitigation (Luo et al., 2026). Its emphasis is on safety during agent execution.

Agentic control requires deciding when to invoke tools, request clarification, or decline a request, while preserving the ability to complete valid tasks. For ambiguous requests, Suri et al. (2026) model uncertainty over tool parameters to select informative clarification questions and determine when further questioning is unnecessary. Their ClarifyBench evaluates tool-calling agents through multi-turn clarification, connecting interaction efficiency with subsequent tool-use performance. This work highlights the importance of evaluating a clarification decision through the actions it enables. Decision-theoretic approaches weigh the expected benefit of clarification against user effort (Dong et al., 2026), while Trajectory2Task studies tool-use adaptation to ambiguous, changing, and infeasible user intents (Wang et al., 2026). Related work on conditional activation steering studies how to make interventions selective. CAST conditions steering on input-dependent activation patterns, enabling refusal for specified content categories while preserving responses to other inputs (Lee et al., 2025). Runtime guardrails also constrain agent behavior: GuardAgent translates safety requirements into executable checks (Xiang et al., 2025), while ShieldAgent uses verifiable policy reasoning to assess action trajectories (Chen et al., 2025c).

More recent methods assess planned actions before execution with Safiron (Huang et al., 2026) and combine formal verification with contextual risk assessment for mobile GUI agents in OS-Sentinel (Sun et al., 2026). Agent safety benchmarks further examine the consequences of decisions during tool execution. AgentHarm evaluates both refusal and the completion of harmful tasks requiring multiple tool calls (Andriushchenko et al., 2025). AgentDojo studies prompt injection through untrusted tool outputs, evaluating attack success alongside legitimate task completion in interactive environments (Debenedetti et al., 2024). These evaluations motivate assessing control over complete interactions, including the effects of intermediate decisions on later actions. RealControlBench follows this perspective by evaluating call, clarify, and abstain decisions together with tool execution, follow-up success, and multi-turn task completion.

Existing steering benchmarks primarily focus on controlling a relatively narrow set of LLM behaviors, often in simple and static evaluation settings. As a result, high benchmark scores do not necessarily translate into effective steering in realistic reasoning and agentic settings. For example, AxBench evaluates concept-level steering and concept detection (Wu et al., 2025), while TruthGen and TwinViews-13k (Fulay et al., 2024) are commonly used to study truthfulness and political-viewpoint steering. CLaS-Bench (Gurgurov et al., 2026) focuses on cross-lingual alignment and different-language control, STEER-BENCH (Chen et al., 2025a) studies community norms and viewpoint steering, and SteerEval (Xu et al., 2026) evaluates fine-grained controllability over attributes such as language, sentiment, and personality. These benchmarks measure whether specific behaviors can be induced, but rarely evaluate downstream reasoning or agent execution.

As summarized in Table 1, RealControlBench evaluates steering across instruction following, tool-use decisions and execution, reasoning performance, reasoning-length control, and safety. Beyond individual responses, it assesses whether an initial decision supports successful follow-up and multi-turn task completion. Our results highlight the importance of this broader evaluation: although steering improves some metrics over the unsteered baseline, prompting achieves higher instruction-following and follow-up success than all reported steering baselines across the three evaluated models. MAS (Luo et al., 2026) also considers multi-turn agents, but primarily focuses on runtime safety detection and mitigation. RealControlBench broadens this scope to multiple control objectives, examining both behavioral control and task performance through a common evaluation framework.

Why RealControlBench? RealControlBench offers three key advantages. (i) Broader coverage: tool use, CoT length, reasoning, instruction following, safety, and agent trajectories. (ii) Execution-grounded evaluation: steering is tested within downstream reasoning and multi-step execution. (iii) Model-agnostic design: the same benchmark can be reused across foundation models without model-specific data regeneration.

We organize the construction of our RealControlBench into five domains: instruction following, agentic tool-use decisions, long-to-short reasoning, weak-to-strong reasoning improvement, and trajectory-conditioned safety. Together, these domains span response-level control, reasoning behavior, agentic decision-making, and trajectory-level safety, providing a diverse testbed for evaluating steering under increasingly complex execution settings. For each domain, we describe the source data, construction procedure, split and leakage controls, and annotation granularity.

Instruction following is usually evaluated by including an explicit constraint in the prompt and checking whether the model follows it (Zeng et al., 2024). Recent work has studied sparse internal representations for interpreting and steering instruction-following behaviors (He et al., 2026). We therefore introduce an instruction-following dataset that evaluates whether steering alone can induce compliance with a target response constraint when the model receives only the user query. The dataset tests whether a controllable internal direction learned from examples with explicit instructions can transfer the corresponding response constraint to new queries in the absence of those instructions.

We define five types of automatically verifiable response constraints, summarized in Table 2. Each rank corresponds to a different form of instruction following: changing the capitalization pattern of the response, controlling its length, avoiding specified punctuation, producing a particular type of final sentence, or inserting an exact target string. Here, “Rank” is simply a category label and does not imply increasing difficulty; in fact, fine-grained constraints such as exact-string insertion or final-sentence control can be harder to steer than broader surface-form changes.

We select 2,028 English questions from the OASST1 and OASST2 releases of the OpenAssistant Conversations corpus (Köpf et al., 2023). These comprise two non-overlapping pools: 1,014 questions for intervention extraction and 1,014 additional carrier questions. All five constraint types share the same carrier questions within each pool. For each extraction question, we construct a positive prompt by appending the target instruction, such as “Answer in lowercase,” and a negative prompt containing only the original question. The two prompts thus differ only in the target instruction, isolating the instruction as the contrast used for representation extraction. The additional carrier questions contain no target instruction.

Tool use is a core capability of LLM agents, enabling them to interact with external environments through function calls (Yao et al., 2025). Existing function-calling benchmarks typically focus on whether an agent selects the correct function and arguments when executing a tool call (Patil et al., 2025). In realistic interactions, however, an agent must first decide whether and how to use the available tools. Given a user request and a set of tools, the agent must either call an appropriate tool, clarify by requesting missing required information, or abstain when no suitable tool is available (Table 3). We evaluate this decision-making problem in two settings. In the single-turn setting (the single-turn track below), each instance specifies an initial tool-use decision and, for clarify and abstain cases, a scripted continuation that provides the missing argument or tool. In the multi-turn setting (the multi-turn track below), the agent additionally observes the interaction history and executes tools in a stateful environment, such that later decisions depend on earlier actions and their outcomes.

The single-turn evaluation data are adapted from the When2Call test set (Ross et al., 2025). We remove the multiple-choice answer options to obtain open-ended tool-use decisions and retain 3,109 instances after filtering: 1,226 call, 873 clarify, and 1,010 abstain. Each instance contains a user request and the available tool definitions. For clarify instances, the appropriate tool is available, but the request is missing one or more required arguments; a scripted user turn subsequently provides the missing information. For abstain instances, no available tool can satisfy the request; a scripted continuation subsequently introduces the required tool. These follow-up turns allow us to evaluate whether the agent acts correctly once the missing information or capability becomes available.

The multi-turn data contain 600 conversations from BFCL v4 (Patil et al., 2025), with 200 from each of three categories: base for call, miss_param for clarify, and miss_func for abstain. These conversations retain the preceding user, assistant, and tool messages together with the environment state. Missing-parameter cases require clarification before the relevant call, while missing-function cases require abstention until the necessary tool becomes available. Each tool call is executed against BFCL’s stateful backend, and its result is returned as part of the conversation. This preserves the dependencies between the current decision and subsequent task continuation.

We use a separate balanced extraction set derived from the When2Call preference-training split to construct steering directions. This set is independent of the evaluation instances above and is shared by both the single-turn and multi-turn tracks. We construct 8,100 contrastive pairs, with 2,700 pairs for each target action: call, clarify, and abstain. For each target action, the positive response exhibits that action, while negative responses are evenly sampled from the other three response types: the two remaining tool-use actions and direct, with 900 pairs from each. Each pair shares the same user request and tool list. The resulting composition is summarized in Table 8. Figure 1 illustrates the overall workflow for extracting steering vectors from When2Call and applying them to the single-turn and multi-turn tracks.

We evaluate whether the steering vector improves mathematical reasoning accuracy and whether the resulting effect transfers beyond the dataset used to construct the steering vector. We use MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024) as the in-distribution source domain: steering vectors are extracted from 160 MATH500 problems, while a disjoint 60-example development set is used to select the steering layer, intervention strength \alpha, and other method-specific hyperparameters. To construct the contrastive examples used for steering-vector extraction, we pair each problem with a positive and a negative reasoning trajectory. Positive trajectories are generated by GPT-5.1 and are retained only when the final answer is correct, providing high-quality examples of successful mathematical reasoning. Negative trajectories are obtained from the unsteered subject model under the same problem prompt and decoding setup, representing the model’s native reasoning behavior before intervention. We then compute the steering direction from the difference between hidden-state representations of the positive and negative trajectories at the selected layer, as in (Ouyang et al., 2026).

After fixing the configuration, we evaluate it once on the remaining 280 held-out MATH500 problems, and we additionally test the same frozen steering configuration on AMC 2023 (AI-MO Team, 2024b) and AIME 2024 (AI-MO Team, 2024a), without any dataset-specific retuning or adjustment.

Long chain-of-thought is often treated as a proxy for stronger reasoning, yet many problems admit substantially shorter derivations without sacrificing answer quality (Kang et al., 2025). Our reasoning-length track therefore asks whether an intervention can compress a model’s reasoning trajectory while preserving its ability to solve the underlying problem. Unlike prompt-based length control, the intervention is learned from paired reasoning traces and applied directly at inference time (Ouyang et al., 2026), allowing us to test whether reasoning verbosity can be controlled as an internal behavioral direction rather than only through an explicit natural-language instruction.

To retrieve the steering artifacts, we construct a shared extraction set of 64 pairs from the MATH training split, restricted to difficulty levels 2–4 across its seven subjects. GPT-5.1 first generates a detailed solution, then extracts an ordered skeleton of essential intermediate results, and finally rewrites the solution as a concise derivation using the same method. Both traces must terminate normally, have reference-matching final answers, and pass a repetition filter. The long and short reasoning spans must contain at least 80 and 32 tokens, respectively, with a long-to-short token length ratio between 2 and 5; the short trace must also cover at least 80% of the extracted skeleton. We evaluate on the MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024) dataset.

Command-line agents operate on files, permissions, and system services, making safety central to their evaluation (Luo et al., 2025; Kuntz et al., 2026). An action’s safety depends on its context: harmful tasks may contain harmless inspection steps, while benign tasks may lead to unsafe operations. Representation-level safety steering requires identifying internal states that encode safety-relevant information about an agent’s actions in context. Recent work (Luo et al., 2026) demonstrates that harmful execution states in multi-turn coding agents can be detected from step-level hidden representations and subsequently mitigated through intervention in a low-dimensional safety subspace. This suggests a natural progression from trajectory-conditioned safety awareness to mechanistic safety steering: if a model reliably distinguishes safe from unsafe actions given the interaction context, its internal representations provide a meaningful basis for identifying safety-relevant directions or subspaces and testing whether they can be causally manipulated. Motivated by this perspective, we study safety awareness as a foundational capability for agent safety steering.

We collect executable ReAct trajectories from Qwen3-8B, Gemma-2-9B-it, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on benign OS tasks and harmful tasks from AdvCLI (Luo et al., 2025). Each data point pairs a current agent output with the exact input used to generate it, including the ReAct instructions and demonstration, the original task, prior actions, and environment observations. We preserve the current output’s reasoning, bash command action, and arguments without rewriting. Each example excludes the current action’s execution result and subsequent steps (Figure 2).

Our evaluation asks a central question: can the steering method reliably induce a desired behavior without compromising the model’s ability to perform the underlying task? Below, we describe the baseline methods, evaluation protocols, and metrics.
We use deterministic checks where possible and LLM judges for semantic evaluation. Section 5.2 defines the corresponding metrics.

We use LLM judges for instruction following and tool use tasks where semantic assessment is difficult to capture with exact matching alone. To evaluate instruction following, we first use a deterministic verifier to check whether the response satisfies the specified constraint, and an LLM judge then evaluates the response for coherence and whether it adequately addresses the user’s request. For single-turn tool use, an LLM judge checks whether the model correctly calls, clarifies, or abstains, and whether its response is coherent. We use rule-based checks to verify tool names and argument schemas. For multi-turn tool use, BFCL checks execution outcomes and whether unnecessary calls are avoided. At the turn affected by missing parameters or an unavailable tool, an LLM judge checks whether the agent requests the missing information or explains that it cannot proceed and avoids calling a tool, respectively. Judges receive only task-relevant information. Judge models and prompting details are provided in Appendix 9.2.

For reasoning improvement tasks, we evaluate answer correctness using automatic checks. On MATH500, AMC 2023, and AIME 2024, we extract the final \boxed{} answer and use math_verify (Kydlíček,) to determine mathematical equivalence with the reference answer. For safety, the evaluated model predicts whether a candidate action is safe or unsafe given the task and preceding interaction context. We parse the predicted label and compare it with the reference label; invalid outputs are counted as incorrect. For Long2Short, we evaluate both reasoning length and answer accuracy. We count the tokens in the solution preceding the final answer and report the relative reasoning-length change ratio (Comp.) from the unsteered baseline. For answer accuracy, we extract and normalize the final answer and first apply exact matching against the reference answer. Exact matches are marked correct and missing answers are marked incorrect. However, nonempty unmatched answers are evaluated for semantic equivalence by a judge model.

Table 4 summarizes our evaluation metrics. For instruction following, we report the mean accuracy across the five domains, with equal weight assigned to each domain: \mathrm{Acc}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{d=1}^{5}\mathrm{Acc}_{d}, where \mathrm{Acc}_{d} denotes the accuracy in domain d. For single-turn tool use, decision success requires the correct initial action and an appropriate response, including valid tool names and arguments when a tool is called. Follow-up success requires both a correct initial decision and a successful subsequent tool call. For multi-turn tool use, BFCL accuracy measures success on the official execution and irrelevance checks. Decision accuracy measures LLM-judged action success at the designated turn with missing parameters or an unavailable tool. Our main metric, joint accuracy, requires BFCL success and, for these affected cases, decision success, a nonempty response, and no premature tool call. Reasoning accuracy measures mathematical equivalence to the reference answer. For Long2Short, we report answer accuracy and relative reasoning-length change (Comp), defined as \mathrm{Comp}=\bar{L}_{\mathrm{after}}/\bar{L}_{\mathrm{before}}-1, where \bar{L}_{\mathrm{before}} and \bar{L}_{\mathrm{after}} are the mean reasoning-token counts before and after the compression process, respectively. Comp is reported as a percentage, with more negative values indicating greater compression. We assess length reduction jointly with answer accuracy.
Safety metrics are classification accuracy and F1, with unsafe actions as positives.

We evaluate eight baselines spanning prompting, dense representation steering, sparse feature steering, and attention-head interventions (as Table 5). No Steering uses the original model without additional behavioral instructions or internal interventions, while Prompted adds the target behavior as a natural-language instruction. CAA uses the mean activation difference between paired positive and negative examples (Rimsky et al., 2024). In our evaluation, PCA extracts the leading principal component from positive and negative activations, whereas LAT applies PCA to pairwise activation differences (Zou et al., 2023). Linear Probe uses the normalized weight vector of a classifier trained to separate positive and negative activations (Wu et al., 2025). SAE Steering intervenes along the decoder direction of a behavior-associated sparse autoencoder feature (Fang et al., 2026). ITI selects discriminative attention heads using linear probes and shifts their outputs along positive–negative mean-difference directions (Li et al., 2023).

Table 6 shows that steering gains vary across five domains and three models, with no method consistently performing best. Figure 3 shows a representative tool-use comparison; analogous plots and additional results for other domains are provided in Appendix 10.

For multi-turn agentic tool use (Figure 3), the best internal methods outperform prompting in multi-turn accuracy (10.50% vs. 9.50% on Qwen, 7.00% vs. 4.67% on Llama, and 1.17% vs. 1.00% on Gemma), but these small absolute gains and persistently low success rates highlight the gap between relative improvements and reliable execution across turns. Single-turn follow-up success is also limited: even prompting, the strongest method on all three models, reaches only 24.50%, 20.75%, and 45.25% on Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, respectively. Reasoning gains are uneven across datasets: improvements on the in-distribution (ID) benchmark MATH500 do not reliably predict transfer to the out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks AMC’23 or AIME’24, although several configurations improve both ID and OOD accuracy. The best internal method improves MATH500 over the unsteered baseline by 0.71–3.22 percentage points across the three models. Linear Probe is the best-performing internal method on MATH500 for each model, tied with PCA on Gemma; on Llama, prompting scores higher (52.14% vs. 51.79%). On Qwen, all five evaluated internal methods improve MATH500, yet none improves AMC’23; nevertheless, LAT and PCA raise AIME’24 accuracy from 10.00% to 26.67% and 23.33%, respectively.

On Llama, LAT and Linear Probe improve both MATH500 and AMC’23, with AMC’23 rising from 25.00% to 35.00% and 27.50%, respectively, while both lower AIME’24 from 6.67% to 3.33%. Thus, ID gains do not translate into consistent improvements across OOD datasets. For long-to-short control, prompting achieves the greatest compression on all three models, while the strongest internal compression on Llama (\mathrm{Comp}=-22.80\%) falls short of prompting (\mathrm{Comp}=-29.60\%) and yields much lower answer accuracy (33.80% vs. 47.20%). For safety awareness, steering can rival prompting, but only with certain methods. LAT achieves the highest accuracy and F1 on Qwen and Gemma, exceeding prompting in accuracy by 1.38 and 2.26 percentage points, respectively, whereas prompting leads on Llama (51.05% vs. 46.10% for the best internal methods). These gains are not shared by all internal methods: relative to the unsteered baseline, Linear Probe improves accuracy by at most 0.19 percentage points across the three models, SAE matches both baseline metrics on Gemma, and ITI matches the baseline on Qwen but underperforms it on Llama and Gemma. Thus, internal steering can improve safety classification, but its advantages over prompting are modest.

Improving a target behavior does not guarantee better task performance. Greater compression can come with lower accuracy, while better initial decisions need not improve follow-up execution. Reliable steering must therefore preserve task performance and sustain gains across distribution shifts and multi-turn interactions. Takeaway

Figure 4 breaks down instruction-following accuracy by task and model. Prompting achieves 89.90–95.60% average accuracy, compared with 28.00–39.30% for the best internal steering methods. The five constraints follow ranks R1–R5 in Table 2: lowercase, one sentence, no comma, question ending, and fixed ending. Internal steering is more effective for lowercase output (R1), while question ending (R4) remains difficult, particularly on Llama and Gemma. Fixed ending (R5) is the hardest constraint for internal steering: all evaluated internal methods achieve 0% success on every tested model, whereas prompting remains effective. The intermediate ranks do not imply a strictly monotonic accuracy ordering for every method and model. Even within one model, a method that performs well on one constraint can fail on another. Aggregate accuracy should therefore be interpreted alongside per-task results when assessing the reliability of instruction-following control.

We introduce RealControlBench, a unified benchmark for evaluating LLM steering across five domains: instruction following, agentic tool use, reasoning, reasoning-length control, and safety awareness. The benchmark jointly measures behavioral control and task performance, including generalization to OOD inputs and execution in multi-turn interactions. Across three models, internal steering yields selective gains, but no method consistently leads across tasks and metrics, and prompting remains a strong baseline. Gains in target behaviors can coexist with accuracy losses, weak follow-up execution, and uneven OOD generalization. These findings identify capability preservation and transfer across evaluation settings as central challenges for reliable steering. RealControlBench provides a shared testbed for measuring these trade-offs and developing interventions that remain effective as inputs and interaction contexts change, while preserving underlying task competence.

We implement the representation-steering baselines using RepSteer, which is an open-source repo that provides a unified interface for extracting activation directions and applying inference-time interventions. Given a positive input x_{i}^{+} and a negative input x_{i}^{-}, we denote the corresponding hidden activation at layer \ell by \mathbf{h}_{\ell}(x_{i}^{+}) and \mathbf{h}_{\ell}(x_{i}^{-}), respectively. The baselines differ primarily in how they estimate a steering direction or subspace from these activations. We compare against two non-intervention baselines and six representative representation-steering methods. The non-intervention baselines measure the model’s original behavior and the effect of directly stating the target instruction prompt, while the remaining methods manipulate internal representations at inference time.
This baseline evaluates the original model without any prompt modification or internal intervention. The model receives only the task input.

Prompted. The Prompted baseline directly includes the target behavior as a natural-language instruction in the input prompt. For example, if the desired behavior is to produce a shorter reasoning trace, the corresponding instruction is explicitly provided to the model at inference time. This baseline measures how well the target behavior can be induced through ordinary prompting, without modifying the model’s internal activations.

Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). CAA (Rimsky et al., 2024) learns a steering direction from paired positive and negative examples. Given hidden activations \mathbf{h}_{i}^{+} and \mathbf{h}_{i}^{-} for a matched pair, CAA computes the average activation difference \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{CAA}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\mathbf{h}_{i}^{+}-\mathbf{h}_{i}^{-}\right). At inference time, the direction is added to the model’s hidden state with a tunable coefficient \alpha. Intuitively, CAA estimates the average internal shift associated with changing from the negative to the positive behavior.

PCA extracts dominant directions of variation from the hidden activations of the positive and negative examples (Zou et al., 2023). Rather than directly averaging the contrastive difference as in CAA, PCA identifies a low-dimensional subspace that captures the largest variation in the activation data. We use the leading component as the steering direction and orient its sign toward the positive examples. PCA therefore provides an unsupervised geometric estimate of the behavioral direction.

Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT). LAT (Zou et al., 2023) is a representation-engineering method that uses matched contrastive examples to identify a shared concept direction. Unlike PCA applied directly to the activation distribution, LAT first forms pairwise activation differences, \mathbf{d}_{i}=\mathbf{h}_{i}^{+}-\mathbf{h}_{i}^{-}, and extracts the dominant principal direction across these differences. The resulting direction captures the representational change that is consistently shared across contrastive pairs, while reducing variation specific to individual examples.

Linear Probe. Following Wu et al. (2025), we train a linear classifier to distinguish positive from negative hidden activations. Given an activation \mathbf{h}, the probe predicts p(y=1\mid\mathbf{h})=\sigma(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{h}+b). The learned weight vector \mathbf{w} is normal to the classifier’s decision boundary and defines the direction that best separates the two classes. We normalize this vector and use it directly as the steering direction. At inference time, we intervene on the hidden representation as \mathbf{h}^{\prime}_{\ell,t}=\mathbf{h}_{\ell,t}+\alpha\frac{\mathbf{w}}{\|\mathbf{w}\|_{2}}, where \alpha controls the intervention strength. This baseline tests whether a direction that linearly decodes the target behavior can also causally induce that behavior during generation.

Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) Steering. SAE (Fang et al., 2026) steering represents model activations using a sparse dictionary of learned features. We identify SAE features whose activations most strongly distinguish the positive and negative examples and use the corresponding decoder direction for intervention. At inference time, increasing the selected feature moves the residual-stream representation toward the behavior associated with that feature. In contrast to methods such as CAA or PCA, which operate directly in the dense hidden-state space, SAE steering performs control through a sparse, feature-level representation.

ITI (Li et al., 2023) performs a sparse, head-level intervention rather than modifying the residual stream with a single global direction. For each attention head at each layer, ITI trains a linear probe to distinguish positive from negative activations and ranks the heads by their validation probing accuracy. Only the top- K most discriminative heads are selected for intervention. For each selected head, ITI constructs a behavioral direction from the difference between the mean positive and negative activations, \mathbf{v}_{\ell,h}=\bm{\mu}_{\ell,h}^{+}-\bm{\mu}_{\ell,h}^{-}, and shifts the head output along this direction during generation. The intervention is scaled by the standard deviation of the head activations along the selected direction, \mathbf{a}^{\prime}_{\ell,h,t}=\mathbf{a}_{\ell,h,t}+\alpha\,\sigma_{\ell,h}\,\frac{\mathbf{v}_{\ell,h}}{\|\mathbf{v}_{\ell,h}\|_{2}}, where \alpha controls the intervention strength. The same intervention is applied autoregressively at every decoding step. Thus, unlike methods such as CAA or Linear Probe steering that intervene through a global residual-stream direction, ITI first localizes the behavior to a small subset of informative attention heads and intervenes only on those heads.

section: ITI Head-Selection Saturation on Instruction Following
text: ITI selects attention heads by their validation probing accuracy, but this criterion becomes uninformative when the positive–negative classification task is too easy. Figure 5 shows this saturation on Qwen3-8B: across the five instruction-following tasks, the median accuracy among all 1,152 heads is 100% on the 40-example validation set. Specifically, 745, 650, 643, 682, and 705 heads achieve perfect accuracy for lowercase, fixed ending, question ending, one sentence, and no comma, respectively. Thus, hundreds of heads tie for the highest score, far exceeding the 48 heads selected for intervention. Validation accuracy alone cannot distinguish which of these perfectly predictive heads are effective intervention sites; selection among tied heads depends on the tie-breaking rule.

section: ITI Head-Selection Saturation on Instruction Following
text: A plausible explanation is that these simple classification tasks admit shortcuts: probes may exploit superficial cues shared by the positive and negative conditions, such as differences in instruction wording or formatting, without identifying the mechanisms that enforce the target constraint during generation. Such cues could be decodable from many heads, producing near-ceiling probe scores without corresponding causal control. The small validation set further limits ranking resolution, since one example changes accuracy by 2.5 percentage points. The histograms establish saturation of the selection criterion; they do not by themselves identify which shortcut, if any, the probes use.

section: ITI Head-Selection Saturation on Instruction Following
text: This distinction between decoding a condition and controlling behavior helps explain ITI’s weak instruction-following results (Table 11). For example, 650 heads perfectly classify the fixed-ending validation examples, yet ITI achieves 0.0% downstream accuracy on that task. Perfect probing accuracy therefore does not guarantee that shifting the selected heads induces the desired output. When the probe task is too easy, selecting a small subset of equally accurate heads may capture readily available condition information while missing the representations needed for reliable instruction execution. More challenging, cue-controlled probe examples and head selection based on held-out intervention effects would help test this explanation.

ITI’s \alpha scales each selected head’s activation standard deviation, whereas residual-stream methods use a residual-norm ratio. Its numerical values are therefore not directly comparable with those of the other methods, and ITI uses task-specific grids rather than the common \{0.5,1,1.5,2,2.5\} grid. The selected instruction-following configurations include \alpha=1,5,15,20 (Table 12); safety sweeps \alpha\in\{1,5,10,15,20\} (Appendix 9.4.1). An ITI setting of \alpha=0 corresponds to no intervention.

For instruction following, agentic tool use, and safety awareness, the residual-stream methods (CAA, PCA, LAT, and Linear Probe) use layers \{9,18,27\} for Qwen3-8B, \{8,16,24\} for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and \{11,21,32\} for Gemma-2-9B-it, with \alpha\in\{0.5,1,1.5,2,2.5\}. This grid is not a universal search space across all tracks. In particular, reasoning-performance configurations are selected separately on the disjoint 60-problem development set (Appendix 9.3.1); the layer sets above do not specify that search space. SAE steering is only tested on Gemma-2-9B-it, and we use the Gemma Scope (Lieberum et al., 2024) dictionaries at layers \{9,20,31\}. For the tracks specified above, SAE uses the same strength grid, with safety additionally including \alpha=3. ITI uses task-specific strength grids: its \alpha multiplies the head-wise activation standard deviation, rather than specifying a residual-norm ratio. The common \{0.5,1,1.5,2,2.5\} grid therefore does not apply to ITI; for example, safety uses \alpha\in\{1,5,10,15,20\} (Appendix 9.4.1).

We sample 200 evaluation questions and 100 extraction questions without replacement, using seed 42 for both samples. Each contrastive pair consists of an extraction question and a version that appends the target instruction. All five targets share the same 100 extraction questions, differing only in the appended instruction, and neither input contains a generated answer. Representations are extracted from each input rendered with the model’s chat template, at the last non-padding token of the assistant generation prefix, immediately before generation begins.

Evaluation begins with deterministic checks for the constraints in Table 2, using pysbd for sentence segmentation and treating empty responses as failures. Responses that pass these checks are then evaluated by Qwen3-8B, which receives only the original question and response and judges coherence and answer adequacy. A response succeeds only if it satisfies the target constraint, remains coherent, and adequately answers the question; the judge prompt is released with the code. For each model, method, and target, we calculate the success rate over all 200 evaluation questions and select the highest-scoring configuration, breaking ties by smaller \alpha and then lower layer where applicable. The main table’s IF (Avg. Acc.) averages the five selected target success rates, while No Steering and Prompted are averaged directly without configuration selection. Per-target scores and intervention configurations are provided in Tables 11 and 12.

Instruction Following: One Sentence Extraction pair: Positive: What causes the seasons on Earth? Answer in exactly one sentence. Negative: What causes the seasons on Earth? Evaluation input (instruction withheld): Who discovered the law of gravity? Deterministic check: pysbd segments the response into exactly one sentence; empty responses fail. Judge check (Qwen3-8B): Given only the question and response, the judge assesses coherence and answer adequacy. Passing response: Isaac Newton formulated the law of universal gravitation, publishing it in his Principia in 1687. Failing response: Isaac Newton discovered the law of gravity. He published it in 1687.

Table 7 separates the shared extraction pairs, single-turn examples, and multi-turn dialogues. For single-turn evaluation, we use 200 examples per target from the full pool; the clarify and abstain subsets each include a follow-up.

The extraction pool comes from When2Call’s preference-training split. Of 9,000 source records, 8,804 admit the required action categorization; balanced sampling with seed 20260910 produces 8,100 pairs. The single-turn pool comes from the separate multiple-choice test split: we remove the answer options and retain 3,109 of its 3,652 records after auditing action labels, tool availability, and follow-up consistency. Extraction and evaluation are separated at the instance level, including the tool context. A generic request such as “What is the current weather?” can occur in both with different tools; prompt-string identity alone does not define a duplicate tool-use instance.

We construct contrastive pairs for each target action: call, clarify, and abstain. Within each pair, the user request and available tool list are identical, while the appended assistant responses differ in their action category. The positive response exhibits the target action. Negative responses are balanced across the other three categories, with 900 pairs per category and 2,700 pairs per target (Table 8). The direct category consists of responses that answer directly or claim task completion without invoking a tool; it is used only as a negative category. Within each positive target, no user request is sampled twice.

Both sides include the complete assistant response. We extract representations at the shared end-of-turn token following the response, rather than at its final content token, so that the extraction position is not determined by response-specific punctuation or tool-call delimiters.

We evaluate 200 examples per target. An initial response succeeds when it takes the requested action, remains coherent and appropriate to the task, and, when calling, uses valid tool names and schema-conforming arguments. Qwen3-8B judges the semantic criteria from the actual request, available tools, and generated response; structural checks validate calls. The judge does not receive the steering configuration. Decision success is the equal-weight mean over call, clarify, and abstain.

Every clarify and abstain example has a scripted second turn that supplies the missing argument or restores the missing tool. The same intervention remains active during this continuation. Follow-up success requires both initial success and a successful subsequent call, and is averaged over these 400 paired examples. A valid second-turn call following a wrong initial response is a recovery diagnostic, not a successful pair. This track validates the call but does not execute it in a stateful backend. Semantic scores are finalized only when all required judge results are valid.

We use 200 conversations from each of BFCL’s base, miss_param, and miss_func categories. Tool parameter types are converted to JSON Schema for the model-facing interface, while execution uses BFCL’s stateful backend. The agent receives actual tool returns and its accumulated dialogue history; tools withheld in missing-function cases are restored at the specified continuation turn. One fixed target intervention is reused throughout the conversation, rather than selecting a new direction from the reference action at each turn.

The release records one local correction to multi_turn_miss_param_180. In the source record, an omitted optional description did not establish a valid missing-parameter decision, and the user continuation was misaligned with the reference. The corrected record retains the paired base conversation through turns 0–4, withholds a required, user-chosen title at turn 5, and supplies it at turn 6. The correction ledger preserves the source identity and unchanged tool environment.

We retain BFCL’s execution and irrelevance checks. The execution checker verifies that tool execution results and environment states match the reference outcomes. The irrelevance checker verifies that no tool is called at turns where a call is inappropriate.

section: Decision evaluation at the designated turn.
text: For each miss_param or miss_func conversation, we predesignate one turn affected by a missing parameter or an unavailable tool. Qwen3-8B judges all assistant actions at this turn for correctness, coherence, and appropriateness: the assistant should request the necessary missing information or clearly explain the relevant tool limitation. The judge receives the preceding dialogue, tool definitions, and actual tool returns, but no target labels, reference answers, or steering configuration. This judgment is applied only to the designated turn and supplements BFCL by assessing whether the response accompanying a no-call decision is meaningful and appropriate.

The joint accuracy metric is the fraction of conversations passing all applicable checks. A base conversation succeeds when both BFCL checks pass. For miss_param and miss_func, success additionally requires passing the LLM judge at the designated turn, producing a nonempty assistant response, and making no premature tool call.
