Explicit demographic labels improve personalization but also amplify stereotypical associations already present in the textual backbones. These findings highlight the need to train speech LLMs not only to perceive demographic cues, but to learn when they should shape their responses.

Speech LLMs are increasingly capable of leveraging not only linguistic content but also information conveyed by the speaker’s voice, enabling more natural and personalized interactions. In particular, speech provides demographic cues such as age and gender that are unavailable from linguistic content alone. This creates a new challenge: a capable speech assistant should exploit these cues when appropriate, while ignoring them when they are irrelevant or could lead to unfair, stereotypical, or otherwise inappropriate behavior. Personalization and stereotypical bias are therefore not independent phenomena, but two outcomes of the same underlying sensitivity to speaker characteristics, distinguished by whether demographic cues are used when relevant or irrelevant to the task.

Yet, existing speech LLMs evaluations do not always cleanly disentangle these aspects. Bias benchmarks typically assess demographic disparities under controlled linguistic content, encompassing stereotypical bias towards demographic groups as well as performance and recommendation disparities. Meanwhile, some personalization and paralinguistic-aware benchmarks reward demographic-dependent changes in model responses even when such adaptation is not explicitly requested by the user. Thus, similar demographic-dependent behavior may be rewarded as personalization or penalized as stereotyping across evaluations. Motivated by Kantharuban et al. [26], we distinguish these outcomes by considering demographic personalization desirable only when explicitly requested.

Building on this distinction, we introduce BASIS-Bench (B ias A nd per S onalization I n S peech LLMs Bench mark). We define three evaluation axes: (1) demographic robustness, measuring disparities in content-related tasks across speakers and demographic classification capabilities; (2) stereotypical bias, measuring whether perceived demographic cues trigger stereotypical behavior when they are irrelevant to the task; and (3) personalization, measuring whether models can tailor responses to demographic characteristics when explicitly requested. To characterize the sources of demographic-dependent behavior along these axes, we further distinguish three potential effects: the acoustic effect, arising from speech encoding; the backbone effect, inherited from the underlying language model; and the interaction effect, arising from their interaction. Together, this framework allows us to isolate different sources of demographic disparity and distinguish failures to process speech and perceive demographic information from its appropriate or inappropriate use.

Our results show that recent speech LLMs achieve similar content-based task performance across demographic groups and often correctly identify speakers’ demographic characteristics. Yet, consistent with previous work, most models show limited personalization across age and gender when demographic information must be inferred from speech. Providing them explicitly via text substantially improves personalization, suggesting that these failures primarily reflect difficulty translating speech demographic cues into appropriate behavior changes rather than an inability to personalize. Conversely, models consistently exhibit stereotypical behavior toward female and elderly speakers. This behavior is amplified by explicit demographic information but persists when speech is replaced by its transcription, suggesting that much of it originates in the backbone rather than from the use of speech. Together, these findings suggest that speech LLMs are not yet reliable at deciding when and how demographic information should shape their behavior: they struggle to turn perceived demographic cues into appropriate personalization, yet readily reproduce stereotypes when such information is irrelevant.

Our contributions are the following: (1) We introduce BASIS-Bench to disentangle stereotypical bias from personalization while diagnosing three potential sources of demographic-dependent behavior: acoustic, backbone, and interaction effects. (2) We release data resources, including Spoken StereoSet+, a manually filtered version of the original dataset with explicit definitions of stereotypical bias and associated harms; ELIP-Pair, an age personalization dataset based on ELIP; and BASIS-Health and BASIS-Product, synthetic gender personalization datasets. (3) We provide a comprehensive evaluation of eight popular speech LLMs across demographic robustness, stereotypical bias, and personalization, revealing systematic gaps in how models perceive and use demographic information.

Following the success of text-only LLMs, numerous speech-native assistants have been proposed for end-to-end spoken interaction, progressively expanding from modeling linguistic content, to jointly modeling acoustic and paralinguistic information such as speaker identity, prosody, emotion, and speaking style. This evolution reflects the growing recognition that effective spoken language interaction requires modeling both linguistic content and acoustic characteristics.

Bias evaluation in speech systems has been extensively studied in recent years. We highlight that while speech LLMs are subject to the same sources of demographic disparity as single-purpose systems (e.g., transcription and translation systems), their broader capabilities introduce additional ways in which demographics can affect model behavior. Assessing disparities arising from speech encoding alone is therefore insufficient to capture their potential harms.

section: Data for Speech LLM Bias Evaluation
text: The majority of existing bias datasets for speech LLMs are repurposed from existing textual datasets. Consequently, most evaluate bias primarily through lexical content rather than on acoustic features and their interaction. For example, Choi et al. [11] resynthesize contexts from the text-based BBQ dataset, thus stereotypical associations are primarily encoded in lexical rather than acoustic cues. We argue that this approach fails to capture the modality-specific biases embedded in end-to-end speech LLMs. A more compelling evaluation protocol must investigate how model behavior shifts in response to demographic information conveyed through speech. Datasets where semantic content remains fixed, but the speaker’s acoustic attributes vary thus provide a more realistic measure of bias in speech LLMs.

Recent speech LLM benchmarks such as SD-Eval, ParaS2S, and EchoMind evaluate whether speech LLMs can leverage paralinguistic cues for generating speaker-aware responses, covering cues such as emotion, accent, age, gender, sarcasm, and environmental sounds. SD-Eval and EchoMind take broader approaches spanning multiple paralinguistic and reasoning capabilities, while ParaS2S focuses on speaker traits through incongruent speech scenarios where linguistic content alone cannot determine the appropriate response. Overall, these works show that current models have substantial room for improvement in leveraging paralinguistic cues. In parallel, recent work in the textual domain has investigated to what extent LLMs can derive implicit demographic cues from the user interaction and provide unprompted personalization. Kantharuban et al. [26] show that LLM recommendations can be influenced by explicit or implicit racial identity, producing stereotypical recommendations even when personalization is not requested, while Entezami and Endres [17] find that demographic attributes unrelated to the task can influence AI-assisted software development outputs. In this work, we focus on speech LLMs, jointly evaluating their ability to reliably perceive demographic cues, personalize based on them when requested, and avoid unprompted stereotypical behavior.

We introduce BASIS-Bench (B ias A nd per S onalization I n S peech LLMs Bench mark), a benchmark designed to disentangle personalization from stereotypical bias in speech LLMs and diagnose the factors underlying demographic-dependent disparities. Focusing primarily on age and gender, we first introduce three complementary evaluation axes (§ 3.1 - 3.3), then define a framework that disentangles the sources of demographic disparity along them (§ 3.4). Figure 1 provides an overview, and Appendix B describes additional inference and evaluation settings.

We use demographic robustness to assess whether speech LLMs can reliably process and perceive speech across speakers with diverse demographic characteristics. We evaluate two complementary capabilities: whether models can perceive demographic cues through age and gender classification, and whether they exhibit performance disparities across speakers on content-based tasks, namely automatic speech recognition (ASR) and spoken question answering (SQA). Together, these evaluations provide context for interpreting the subsequent stereotypical bias and personalization axes by establishing whether models can reliably process speech and perceive demographic cues.

For ASR, we use Fair-Speech, Spoken StereoSet+ (ASR Age Split), and SD-QA. Fair-Speech covers different genders and accents; we do not use its age labels, which span 18-65 years and therefore do not cover children or elderly speakers. We use the Spoken StereoSet+ ASR Age Split (Appendix A.1.3) to assess performance across age groups; we describe its construction in § 3.2. SD-QA covers different accents and it is also used for SQA, while LibriSQA assesses SQA performance across gender categories. For demographic classification, we use the same data as the other axes, enabling direct comparisons across axes.

For ASR, we report word error rate (WER) between the gold and generated transcripts after applying the Whisper normalizer. We cap WER at 100 and report accuracy (100-\mathrm{WER}) averaged for each demographic (accent, gender, and age) and dataset (SD-QA, Fair-Speech, Spoken StereoSet+). For SQA we use LLM-as-judge evaluation, computing mean accuracy for each demographic category (accent and gender) and dataset (SD-QA and LibriSQA) before aggregating across them. We then average the resulting ASR and SQA scores to obtain the context-based score for each model. For demographic classification, we explicitly provide the possible categories in the evaluation prompt, reducing the task to implicit MCQA, and reporting exact-match accuracy per-label. We then average across labels, obtaining the final classification score.

We use stereotypical bias to refer to harmful forms of stereotyping, where a demographic group is associated with particular characteristics, attributes, or behaviors, and these associations are used to draw unwarranted inferences about individual members. In speech LLMs, this can manifest when speech demographic cues, such as gender or age, influence a model’s response based on stereotypical assumptions about a speaker’s characteristics, preferences, abilities, or social roles. Such behavior can reinforce social stereotypes and lead to differential treatment across speakers with equivalent requests. This axis thus assesses whether models exhibit stereotypical behavior based on perceived demographic cues when their use is not explicitly requested.

We build on Spoken StereoSet, introducing a manual filtering stage to align the dataset with our definition of stereotypical bias for age and gender. We consider adult and elderly male speakers for age, and female and male speakers for gender. We detail our definitions and post-processing in Appendix A.1, and refer to the resulting dataset as Spoken StereoSet+.

We follow the context association test (CAT) from StereoSet, reporting the proportions of stereotypical and anti-stereotypical continuations. Since irrelevant continuations are negligible, we omit them for brevity. To mitigate positional bias in the MCQA setting, we evaluate all answer-option permutations and report mean accuracy for both stereotypical and anti-stereotypical continuations. We additionally adopt the idealized CAT (ICAT) score from StereoSet, which jointly captures continuation relevance and the skew between stereotypical and anti-stereotypical choices. ICAT ranges from 0 (maximally biased) to 100 (unbiased). We report the per-demographic mean ICAT score as a single number measuring bias per model, rather than an overall ICAT, to prevent opposing stereotypical and anti-stereotypical behaviors across demographics from balancing out and producing an apparent unbiased score.

This axis assesses whether models can use demographic information conveyed through a speaker’s voice to tailor their responses. A key challenge is determining when such adaptation is appropriate, as inferring preferences from age or gender can itself constitute stereotyping. Motivated by Kantharuban et al. [26], we thus consider personalization appropriate only when explicitly requested.

For age personalization, we focus on developmental differences between children and adults, adapting the complexity, style, or presentation of information based on cognitive development differences rather than socially constructed stereotypes. We do not treat elderly speakers as a separate personalization category, as defining age-based adaptations for this group would require assumptions about their cognitive abilities or needs that may themselves be stereotypical. Instead, the adult category spans young to elderly adult speakers. During inference, the model receives a spoken question along with textual descriptions of the adult and child profiles and is asked to answer in the same style as the speaker’s demographic profile.

For gender personalization, we similarly find that existing formulations are difficult to disentangle from stereotypical bias. We thus formulate it as a constrained gender recognition task: when explicitly instructed to personalize based on the speaker’s voice, the model must select the only response containing the speaker’s gender marker. We introduce two datasets: BASIS-Health, covering health questions whose answers depend on biological sex, and BASIS-Product, covering product recommendations where identical options differ by the gender marker (e.g., Men’s vs. Women’s razor). These datasets assess whether models exploit gender information when explicitly requested, while minimizing reliance on stereotypical associations.

For age personalization, we follow Thonet et al. [42] and create and manually validate an expanded version of ELIP, ELIP-Pair, containing 521 questions, each associated with two responses tailored to distinct personas: child and adult. We synthesize child and adult speech by cloning other synthetic voices, and then automatically filtering the result based on both ASR quality and age classification. Outliers are then manually verified. For gender personalization, we create BASIS-Health and BASIS-Product using Claude-Opus, followed by GPT-5.6 filtering, speech synthesis, and similar automatic and manual post-processing from ELIP-Pair. Detailed generation pipelines for these datasets are provided in Appendix A.2 and § A.3.

For gender personalization, we report per-demographic accuracy and, as for stereotypical bias, we evaluate all answer-option permutations to mitigate positional bias. For age personalization, we classify the response as child- or adult-oriented using LLM-as-judge.

Although bias in speech systems is well studied and textual LLMs have been extensively evaluated for demographic bias, existing evaluations of speech LLMs lack a systematic framework for distinguishing whether demographic-dependent behavior originates from the speech encoder, the backbone, or their interaction. We therefore distinguish three sources of demographic disparity, and design our evaluation framework to disentangle their contributions.

The acoustic effect originates from disparities in the speech encoding process, where speaker characteristics may affect how reliably linguistic content or demographic cues are represented and perceived. For example, strongly accented or non-standard dialectal speech may be less reliably processed than speech varieties overrepresented in training data, resulting in performance gaps.

The backbone effect refers to biases and personalization capabilities inherited from the language model, independently of the speech modality. Recent work has shown that LLMs can infer demographic characteristics from implicit cues and exhibit demographic stereotypes and disparate treatment across sensitive attributes. A speech LLM may therefore inherit tendencies such as occupational gender stereotypes or culturally skewed recommendations, from its backbone.

The interaction effect arises from the interaction between speech representations and the backbone. Even when speech is faithfully encoded, demographic and other paralinguistic cues may introduce demographic-dependent behavior or amplify or attenuate biases already present in the backbone. This effect captures how speech shifts behavior relative to the backbone. For example, a speech LLM may adopt a more patronizing tone, or make different recommendations solely because the same utterance is spoken by different speakers.

For the stereotypical bias and personalization axes (§ 3.2 and § 3.3), we must distinguish whether a model can perceive demographic information from how it uses it. We therefore evaluate these axes under four modes, combining two modalities (speech / text) and two demographic-marker settings (implicit / explicit). In the speech modes, speech-implicit represents the target setting, where demographic information is available only through speech and may influence model behavior; speech-explicit additionally provides the demographic label in text, bypassing its inference from speech. Their comparison reveals whether behavioral differences arise from perceiving demographic cues or their subsequent use, and therefore allows to disentangle acoustic from interaction effect. The text modes isolate behavior from the backbone: text-implicit provides only the query transcript, removing acoustic and demographic information; while text-explicit additionally provides the demographic label. Their comparison reveals the effect of explicit demographic information on the backbone (backbone effect), while comparison with the corresponding speech modes reveals the effect of acoustic information (interaction effect).

Models are eligible for our benchmark evaluation if they (1) support speech input, (2) accept textual instructions alongside speech, and (3) produce textual responses. We evaluate the following speech LLMs: audio-flamingo AF-3 and AF-Next, DeSTA2.5, MOSS-Audio, Qwen2.5- and Qwen3-Omni, Step-Audio2, and Voxtral.

Figure 2 and Appendix Table 7 summarize the three axes and four evaluation modes. Appendix Tables 8, 9 and 10 provide additional details for demographic robustness (§ 4.1), stereotypical bias (§ 4.2) and personalization (§ 4.3) axes respectively.

Most models perform robustly on content-based tasks (ASR/SQA) across demographic groups, with DeSTA2.5 showing the largest degradation on accented audio (Appendix Table 8). For classification, we observe that gender is considerably easier than age, with most models achieving high gender classification accuracy. Exceptions include Voxtral for male and Step-Audio2 for female speakers in BASIS-Health/Product, although the latter performs well on Spoken StereoSet+, suggesting dataset-dependent behavior. Age classification is harder. AF-Next and MOSS-Audio struggle with young adults, while AF-3, DeSTA2.5, Qwen2.5-Omni, Step-Audio2, and Voxtral struggle with elderly speakers. Child speakers also challenge DeSTA2.5 and Voxtral, but elderly speakers remain harder overall. Notably, Qwen3-Omni substantially improves over Qwen2.5-Omni on both elderly and child classification, suggesting better age perception. These measurements help isolate the acoustic effect when interpreting stereotypical bias and personalization, distinguishing failures to perceive demographic cues from how they are used.

Figure 2 presents mean ICAT scores, while Appendix Table 9 reports per-demographic behavior. An ICAT score of 100 corresponds to perfectly balanced (50/50) stereotypical and anti-stereotypical selections across test samples.

text-implicit captures baseline behavior without demographic information, while text-explicit isolates the effect of providing speaker demographics to the backbone. Under text-implicit, some models slightly prefer female stereotypical continuations and, symmetrically, anti-stereotypical male ones. For age, behavior is more balanced, with only two models slightly favoring anti-stereotypical continuations for elderly speakers. Making demographics explicit (text-explicit) substantially increases stereotypical selections, especially for female and elderly speakers, though selections also rise for male and young speakers. Notably, the prompt does not instruct models to condition on the demographic attribute shared, yet models systematically incorporate it in a way that reinforces stereotypes. Qwen3-Omni, MOSS-Audio, and Voxtral exhibit the strongest bias across gender and age, while Step-Audio2 is particularly biased for gender. Characterizing these textual priors isolates stereotypical behavior inherited from the LLM from that arising through speech integration.

Comparing speech-explicit with text-explicit and speech-implicit with text-implicit reveals whether speech amplifies or dampens backbone disparities. In explicit mode, speech generally reduces stereotypical behavior relative to text. For gender, text-explicit produces more stereotypical continuations than speech-explicit, except for AF-3 and AF-Next (male), and MOSS Audio (female), all with small differences (\leq 1.1). Age follows a similar pattern, except for AF-Next, MOSS-Audio and Qwen3-Omni (elderly; 3.4/1/5.6), and Qwen2.5-omni (young; 0.6), where speech increases stereotypical selections. In implicit modes, gender shows no consistent trend: text-implicit is more stereotypical for male speakers in 5/8 models, while speech-implicit is more stereotypical for female speakers in 5/8. Age exhibits a clearer interaction effect: speech-implicit increases stereotypical selections for elderly speakers in all models except AF-Next (-0.5). On average, speech shifts stereotypical selections by +4/-3.2 points for elderly/young speakers, compared with +2.1/-1.4 for female/male speakers. Overall, equivalent speech and text conditions remain closely aligned, suggesting that stereotypical behavior is largely inherited from the backbone. Interaction effects are small, but more consistent for age in the implicit mode.

We contrast speech-implicit, where models infer speaker demographics, with speech-explicit, where they are provided in the prompt. In the center column of Figure 2, the shift from hollow to filled circles shows that explicit demographics consistently increase stereotypical selections. Appendix Table 9 shows increases of 4.7/3.4 points in stereotypical selections for female/male speakers, versus 20.1/9.2 points for elderly/young speakers, with Qwen3-Omni showing the largest increases (32.2/21.0). More broadly, increased stereotyping under speech-explicit suggests that relatively balanced speech-implicit behavior may reflect limited ability to perceive and translate demographic cues into behavioral changes, rather than genuine fairness.

Demographic classification distinguishes limited reliance on demographic cues from failures to perceive them. For elderly speakers, MOSS-Audio and Qwen3-Omni classify well (96.3/88.1; Appendix Table 8), yet show little stereotypical behavior under speech-implicit (60.4/53.1; Appendix Table 9). Once age is explicit, however, they become the most biased (78.7/85.3). Conversely, AF-3 and Voxtral poorly classify elderly speakers (0/13.4) and appear balanced under speech-implicit (44.3/48.8). Under speech-explicit, however, Voxtral shifts strongly toward stereotypical selections (75.7), suggesting that its apparent balance partly reflects limited perception, whereas AF-3 remains balanced (54.2). For gender, classification is more reliable (95.2/83.2 on average for female/male speakers), yet the slight text-implicit asymmetry in stereotypical bias largely persists under speech-implicit, with a smaller shift than for age, suggesting demographic cues are not considered. Overall, apparently balanced speech-implicit behavior may reflect limited reliance on demographic information rather than limited perception, while stereotypical trends largely mirror backbone priors.

Figure 2 presents mean personalization accuracy. Appendix Table 10 reports per-dataset gender results. text-implicit measures preferences among age profiles or gender answers without demographic information. For age, we additionally report text-baseline, which captures default behavior without a specified response style, whereas text-implicit includes child/adult profiles and their preferences. Comparing the two reveals how default responses align with these profiles, distinguishing default behavior from personalization.

For gender, text-implicit reveals a puzzling preference for female personalization across backbones, despite the BASIS-Health/Product datasets providing equally probable options differing only in gender-specific content. This preference is stronger for BASIS-Health (77.9 on average) than BASIS-Product (58.5). As chance-level accuracy is expected in this setting, these results suggest an underlying backbone tendency toward female personalization. In contrast, text-explicit yields near-ceiling performance, supporting the dataset design and showing that gender personalization is straightforward when gender is provided textually. For age, text-baseline shows that most models default to more adult-like responses, while Qwen3-Omni is the most balanced. Under text-implicit, most models show no strong profile preference, although DeSTA2.5 and Qwen3-Omni lean toward the adult profile and AF-Next toward the child profile. text-explicit reveals the backbone’s personalization capabilities: child personalization is straightforward for all models but AF-3 (64.1%), whereas adult personalization remains challenging. Only DeSTA2.5, Qwen3-Omni and Voxtral exceed 77%, while AF-Next and Step-Audio2 perform worst (34.9/42.1%, respectively). Once age is explicit, models readily personalize toward children but remain substantially less effective at adapting toward adults.

Therefore, models default toward adult but show no consistent profile preference under text-implicit, then, when age is explicit, they readily personalize toward children but remain substantially less effective for adults.

We assess the interaction effect by comparing speech-implicit with text-implicit. For gender, speech-implicit is highly asymmetric, with substantially higher accuracy for female than male speakers (Appendix Table 10). Female performance is largely driven by BASIS-Health (82.6 on average), compared with BASIS-Product (66.4), while male personalization remains poor on both datasets (51.1/31.9 for BASIS-Product/Health). This closely resembles text-implicit, both in overall trends and, for several models, absolute performance, suggesting that models largely reproduce backbone preferences rather than exploit demographic cues in speech. Thus, speech does not reliably induce behavioral adaptation from demographic cues despite high gender classification accuracy (Appendix Table 8). A different pattern emerges for age: no model successfully adapts to both age groups under speech-implicit, with speech instead consistently shifting responses toward the child profile. Relative to text-implicit, personalization accuracy increases substantially for child speakers (+61.1 on average), while decreasing for adults (-47.2). This effect is particularly pronounced for DeSTA2.5, Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, and Voxtral, whose relatively adult-oriented backbone behavior shifts strongly toward the child profile under speech. Rather than speaker-aware personalization, this shift may reflect a modality-induced style preference: speech-oriented training favors conversational answers aligned more closely with the child than the adult profile.
Thus, unlike gender, age exhibits a strong interaction effect, but one that does not reliably track speakers age.

Under speech-implicit, personalization remains asymmetric for both age and gender despite their contrasting classification performance: age classification is relatively weak, whereas gender classification is generally reliable. In both cases, personalization largely resembles the backbone behavior under text-implicit, suggesting that models make limited use of speech demographic cues. When gender is explicitly provided under speech-explicit, personalization rises sharply for both groups, with all models achieving high accuracy. Thus, models can personalize based on gender when it is directly available, but struggle to translate speech demographics into the intended adaptation. Age reveals a different pattern. Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni classify both adult and child speakers reasonably well (79.1/85 and 75.5/99, respectively), yet strongly favor the child profile under speech-implicit, yielding low adult personalization accuracy. Voxtral shows the same preference despite accurately classifying adults but not children (92.2/14.4), suggesting that this behavior is not reliably speaker-aware. Under speech-explicit, child personalization becomes nearly trivial for most models, whereas adult personalization remains considerably harder. The same asymmetry under text-explicit indicates that this difficulty is not solely perceptual, but also reflects limitations already present in the backbone.

Taken together, our results reveal two fundamental limitations in how speech LLMs use demographic information. (1) Recognizing demographic information does not imply using it effectively. Models often fail to translate speech demographic cues into the requested personalization: gender behavior remains shaped by backbone preferences, while age induces a broad shift toward the child persona that does not reliably track the speaker’s age. Stereotypical behavior similarly mirrors backbone priors. Crucially, this pattern emerges both in models that classify demographics well and in those that do not, revealing a gap between demographic perception and its translation into behavior. (2) Models do not reliably distinguish when demographic information should shape their behavior. Personalization explicitly requests demographic-dependent adaptation, whereas stereotypical bias evaluates behavior when such adaptation is neither requested nor relevant. Yet the gender Pareto frontier in Figure 2 shows that less stereotypical models tend to personalize less, while stronger personalization coincides with more stereotypical behavior. Explicit demographic information under speech-explicit shifts this trade-off but does not change the behavior: personalization improves, yet stereotypical behavior increases. Age exhibits a similar but weaker trade-off that also becomes clearer when demographics are explicit.
Thus, improving demographic perception alone is insufficient: models must learn when to use this information and when to turn a deaf ear to it.

We introduced BASIS-Bench to jointly evaluate stereotypical bias and personalization in speech LLMs while disentangling the sources of disparities. Across eight models, our results show that perceiving demographic information does not imply using it appropriately. Demographic-dependent behavior often remains shaped by language model priors, and models struggle to ignore demographic information when it is irrelevant. These findings call for more multi-dimensional evaluations covering demographic perception and its use.

Our evaluation focuses on stereotypical bias, capturing only one form of representational bias and not intersectional bias. Similarly, while our demographic robustness axis evaluates disparities across groups, it does not characterize all their sources. A comprehensive evaluation requires datasets covering broader forms of bias.

Our evaluation adopts a binary categorization of gender, distinguishing between male and female speakers. We acknowledge that this does not capture the diversity of gender identities and expressions. Following recommendations for using gender as a variable in NLP, we make this categorization explicit and justify it by the requirements of our evaluation: it enables a controlled task isolating whether speech LLMs exploit gender-related information for personalization and stereotypical bias evaluation. We thus use these categories as an experimental abstraction rather than a comprehensive representation of gender.

Our evaluation assumes that demographic categories can be associated with speech samples. However, attributes such as gender and age cannot always be reliably inferred from speech, and acoustic cues may reflect perceived rather than self-identified characteristics. Our results therefore measure models’ use of demographic cues in speech, rather than their ability to determine speakers’ demographic identities.

We evaluate accent only for demographic robustness and exclude it from the personalization and stereotypical bias axes. Defining appropriate personalization based on accent is challenging without making assumptions about a speaker’s linguistic background, preferences, or cultural identity. We leave accent-based personalization and bias evaluation to future work.

Blodgett et al. [5] argue that annotators recruited through crowd-sourcing platforms may be detached from the intended measurement construct, potentially resulting in annotations that do not faithfully capture the target notion of bias. For the reannotation of Spoken StereoSet (Appendix A.1), a dataset that passed through two rounds of crowd-sourcing annotations, we chose to perform the annotation ourselves. This decision does not come without limitations. While it allowed us to consistently apply the proposed annotation criteria, it substantially reduced the diversity and number of annotators involved in the process. As all annotators were contributors to this work and shared the same annotation guidelines, the resulting labels may still reflect common assumptions or blind spots that differ from those of other populations. Future work could validate and refine our annotation protocol through larger-scale studies involving annotators from more diverse backgrounds.

We generated our own personalization data, as existing datasets for speech personalization were either unavailable or entangled with stereotypes and other sources of bias. For age personalization, ELIP-Pair uses a friendlier and more playful tone for children and a professional and more expert tone for adults. This formulation captures only a coarse form of age-based personalization. Our evaluation therefore tests whether speech LLMs can exploit coarse age-related cues when instructed to personalize, rather than whether they can provide comprehensive age-aware personalization. For gender personalization, BASIS-Health and BASIS-Product frame personalization as implicit binary gender classification, testing whether a speech LLM can infer gender from speech and select the corresponding response. In BASIS-Health, however, the relevant medical distinction is biological sex, which is not equivalent to perceived gender inferred from speech. BASIS-Product instead uses otherwise identical products differing only in an explicit gender marker. These datasets should thus not be used for comprehensive evaluations of gender-aware personalization or healthcare reasoning.

Our speech sources for the personalization and stereotypical bias axes are restricted to synthetic voices. Although we carefully ensure content quality and appropriate demographic representation, synthetic speech may not fully capture the acoustic variability and naturalness of human speech, and its demographic cues may differ from naturally occurring ones.

This work studies whether speech LLMs can personalize based on speech demographic cues when explicitly requested, while refraining from demographic-dependent stereotypical behavior when unprompted. The ability to infer demographic characteristics from speech does not justify their use in real-world applications: inferred attributes should not be treated as ground truth, and unsolicited inference may enable profiling, inappropriate adaptation, or discrimination. We thus consider demographic information appropriate to use only when explicitly requested.

Our evaluation uses simplified demographic categories: binary gender does not comprehensively represent gender identity or expression, while child, adult, and elderly categories do not capture within-group diversity. We use these categories as controlled abstractions, not to suggest that demographic characteristics can or should be reduced to them. BASIS-Health warrants particular care. It is a controlled diagnostic task assessing whether speech LLMs can exploit a binary sex-related distinction when explicitly required. It is not a benchmark for clinical reasoning or an endorsement of inferring gender or sex for medical advice. Real-world recommendations depend on many factors beyond demographics, and incorrect inference may have consequential effects.

Finally, our datasets and protocols are evaluation tools, not recommendations for inferring or using demographic information in deployed systems. We hope this work supports the creation of capable speech LLMs that use demographic information only when appropriate.

RSIPO: Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Skill-Policy Co-Evolution. Recent focus in agentic reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to improve credit assignment in long-horizon tasks. One promising direction combines reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), integrating trajectory-level advantages with dense token-level supervision. This line of work often conditions a teacher model on privileged context, such as agentic skills, to score tokens generated by the student policy. Despite their progress, they largely overlook the on-policy evolution of agentic skills and the reliability of teacher supervision. Towards this end, we introduce Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization (RSIPO), a self-evolving agentic RL framework that enables agentic skills and the policy model to co-evolve throughout the training process. Specifically, RSIPO enables the policy itself to extract skills from completed trajectories and explicitly optimizes its skill-generation capability through trajectory replay. It further employs empirical Bayes shrinkage to dynamically calibrate the student's trust in teacher scores, accounting for the fact that skill-enhanced teacher guidance can sometimes be less reliable. Experiments with Qwen-family models on embodied interaction and search-based agentic tasks demonstrate that RSIPO outperforms all the compared baseline approaches.

With Qwen2.5-7B as the base model, RSIPO achieves an average success rate of 98.6\% on ALFWorld, yielding absolute improvements of 2.5\% and 17.4\% over the second-best baseline and standard GRPO, respectively.

Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) Zhang et al. (2025a); Zhang et al. (2025b) has emerged as a key component of large language model (LLM) post-training, substantially improving model performance on long-horizon multi-turn tasks. Unlike conventional RL for static and single-turn scenarios Guo et al. (2025), agentic RL aims to train models through interactions with dynamic environments, where they iteratively reason, invoke tools, and incorporate observations across multi-turn conversations Lu et al. (2026b); Singh et al. (2025). This requires learning sequential decision-making policies that reliably guide agents toward successful task completion.

As shown in Figure 1, recent agentic RL approaches have explored reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), and hybrid training frameworks that combine the two. Among them, RLVR-based methods provide effective outcome-based trajectory-level advantages, whereas OPSD-based methods offer dense and fine-grained token-level supervision. Hybrid methods seek to combine these complementary signals, typically coupling an RLVR branch with an OPSD branch for joint optimization. In the OPSD branch, a teacher model conditioned on privileged context scores student-generated tokens, and the student is trained to reduce the token-level log-probability gap between the two models. For example, SDAR Lu et al. (2026a) uses agentic skills retrieved from an external skill library as privileged context for the teacher model, whereas OPID Yang et al. (2026b) and SEED Wu et al. (2026) explore generating such skills with external or internal analyzers.

Despite their progress in advancing agentic RL, existing hybrid approaches face two key limitations. First, agentic skills are either retrieved from a static external library or produced by a skill generator trained off-policy in advance. Consequently, while the policy improves at task execution during training, skill generation is not explicitly optimized on-policy to evolve alongside it. Following the experimental setup of SEED Wu et al. (2026), we find that only 0.25% of the trajectories in the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data used to train the skill generator are successful, mainly because the base model follows the required action format in just 11.0% of its steps, whereas the policy’s rollout success rate rapidly exceeds 80% during subsequent RL training (Figure 2 (a)). As a result, 86.8% of the skills in the SFT data concern action format or syntax, even though 99.7% of the policy’s actions are already valid in the first 10 RL steps. The trajectories that the skill generator must summarize thus shift from almost exclusively failures to predominantly successes, creating a distribution shift that its initial off-policy training does not explicitly address.

Second, the OPSD objective encourages the student to align with a skill-enhanced teacher, implicitly assuming that the teacher consistently provides more reliable guidance than the student’s own decisions. However, access to skills does not guarantee better performance. As shown in Figure 2 (b), the skill-enhanced teacher underperforms the student on 5.5%–22.4% of tasks across different levels of student competence. Its advantage is most pronounced on tasks that the student solves in one to three of four rollouts. By contrast, for tasks with zero or four successful student rollouts, the proportions of tasks on which the teacher outperforms and underperforms the student differ only slightly (16.0% vs. 13.6% and 6.9% vs. 5.5%, respectively). Figure 2 (c) further shows that, during the first 15 RL training steps, the teacher underperforms the student on more tasks than it outperforms the student (22.9% vs. 15.0%) and continues to underperform on 4%–11% of tasks thereafter. Therefore, uniformly trusting teacher guidance exposes the student policy to unreliable supervision.

These observations motivate Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization (RSIPO), a self-evolving agentic RL framework that jointly improves skill generation and task execution while calibrating the student’s trust in teacher supervision. Building on the RLVR and OPSD branches, RSIPO uses the student policy to rewrite skills and replays half of its rollouts with these skills, measuring the resulting gains relative to the remaining half, which serves as a control group. Each replay gain is centered by subtracting the mean gain for the same task type, and the resulting reward is assigned to the generated skill tokens. This explicitly optimizes the policy’s skill-generation capability on-policy without requiring auxiliary judge models or additional evaluation data. Beyond skill evolution, RSIPO dynamically adjusts the student’s reliance on the teacher in the OPSD branch. Specifically, it applies empirical Bayes shrinkage to the replay gains to obtain robust and task-dependent trust coefficients that weight the OPSD objective. These coefficients increase the student’s reliance on reliable teacher guidance, downweight unreliable supervision, and can disable distillation entirely on tasks where the teacher is particularly unreliable.

We conduct extensive experiments across multiple base models on ALFWorld Shridhar et al. (2021) for embodied interaction and seven datasets for search-based agentic tasks. The results show that RSIPO substantially outperforms a wide range of baselines, including RLVR-based, OPSD-based, and hybrid agentic RL methods. On ALFWorld, RSIPO achieves average task success rates of 95.7% and 98.6% with Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B Yang et al. (2024), respectively, surpassing the strongest prior method, SEED Wu et al. (2026), by 3.9% and 2.5%. The performance improvements over the standard GRPO+OPSD baseline are even larger, reaching 14.5% and 18.2%, respectively.

To summarize, our main contributions of this paper are threefold: Co-Evolving Perspective. We identify limitations in skill generation and teacher supervision in existing agentic RL methods and propose a co-evolving perspective that couples on-policy skill improvement with adaptive trust in the teacher. Self-Evolving Framework. We introduce RSIPO, a self-evolving framework that uses skill-induced performance gains measured through trajectory replay to drive skill-policy co-evolution and applies empirical Bayes shrinkage to calibrate the student’s trust in teacher supervision. Empirical Validation. Extensive experiments across multiple models and datasets demonstrate that RSIPO outperforms existing agentic RL methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance on ALFWorld and search-based agentic tasks.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has demonstrated substantial gains in single-turn reasoning. Critic-free methods such as GRPO Guo et al. (2025) and DAPO Yu et al. (2025) estimate advantages from group-normalized outcome rewards, eliminating the need for the learned value network used in PPO Schulman et al. (2017). In agentic settings, policies interact with embodied Shridhar et al. (2021), shopping Yao et al. (2022), or search Jin et al. (2025) environments over multiple turns. Attributing a single terminal reward to a long sequence of decisions poses a credit assignment challenge, motivating multi-turn training frameworks Wang et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2025b) and step-level advantage estimation Feng et al. (2025). A complementary line of work equips agents with reusable natural-language experience, including reflections, insights, and skill libraries Shinn et al. (2023); Zhao et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2023), with recent methods incorporating such skills into agentic RL training Xia et al. (2026); Lu et al. (2026b). These approaches, however, typically rely on fixed skill libraries, frozen external generators, or skill-generation objectives that do not explicitly account for the utility of generated skills in task execution.

In on-policy distillation (OPD), a teacher model scores sequences sampled from the student policy, allowing the student to learn from its own generation distribution rather than a fixed corpus Agarwal et al. (2024); Gu et al. (2024). On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the same model as the teacher by conditioning it on privileged training-time context unavailable to the student, such as worked solutions or feedback on the student’s attempts Zhao et al. (2026); Hübotter et al. (2026). Hybrid approaches combine this supervision with RLVR, often using agentic skills as privileged context for the teacher Wang et al. (2026a). For example, SDAR retrieves skills from an external library Lu et al. (2026a), OPID uses an external analyzer to extract skills from completed episodes Yang et al. (2026b), and SEED trains the policy itself to generate skills through supervised fine-tuning Wu et al. (2026). Other methods modify how the teacher–student log-probability gap contributes to optimization, for example by aggregating it at the action-step level or annealing the distillation signal over training Zhang et al. (2026); Wang et al. (2026b); Tan et al. (2026).

We consider an agent that solves a task x by interacting with an environment for at most T_{\max} turns. At turn t, the policy \pi_{\theta} receives a context c_{t} that contains the task instruction, a window of recent observations and actions, and the current observation. Then it generates a response y_{t}=(y_{t,1},\dots,y_{t,|y_{t}|}) consisting of reasoning and action tokens. The environment executes the action and returns the next observation. An episode produces a trajectory \tau=(c_{1},y_{1},\dots,c_{T},y_{T}) with T\leq T_{\max} and a verifiable outcome reward R(\tau)\in\{0,1\} that indicates task execution success.

For each task, G trajectories \{\tau^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{G} are sampled from the current policy. Following GRPO Shao et al. (2024), trajectory \tau^{(i)} receives the group-normalized advantage A^{(i)}=\bigl(R(\tau^{(i)})-\mu_{R}\bigr)/\sigma_{R}, where \mu_{R} and \sigma_{R} are the mean and standard deviation of the rewards in the group, and this advantage is shared by all tokens of \tau^{(i)}. The policy is optimized with the clipped surrogate objective \mathcal{L}_{\text{PPO}} Schulman et al. (2017) and a KL penalty \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}} toward a reference policy: \mathcal{L}_{\text{RLVR}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{PPO}}+\lambda_{\text{KL}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}.

Following SEED Wu et al. (2026), the policy itself summarizes each completed trajectory into an agentic skill s, prompted with an analysis template that presents the trajectory and asks for an episode summary and a reusable skill. The skill-enhanced teacher is the same policy with the skill inserted into its context, \pi_{T}(\cdot\mid c_{t})=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c_{t}\oplus s). For each token generated by the student, the two log-probabilities define a gated distillation term: \displaystyle\ell_{t,j} \displaystyle=g_{t,j}\bigl(\log\pi_{T}(y_{t,j})-\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t,j})\bigr), \displaystyle g_{t,j} \displaystyle=\sigma\bigl(\beta\bigl(\log\pi_{T}(y_{t,j})-\operatorname{sg}[\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t,j})]\bigr)\bigr), where the conditioning on c_{t} and y_{t,<j} is omitted, \operatorname{sg}[\cdot] stops gradients, and the teacher log-probabilities are treated as constants. The gate g_{t,j} focuses distillation on tokens for which the teacher is more confident than the student. Let \mathcal{L}_{\text{OPSD}} denote the average of \ell_{t,j} over all response tokens, the hybrid objective is: \mathcal{L}_{\text{hybrid}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{RLVR}}+\lambda_{\text{OPSD}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{OPSD}}. Following SEED Wu et al. (2026), the policy is initialized by supervised fine-tuning on skills that an external LLM writes for the base model’s own trajectories, so that it can generate skills before RL begins. No skill is provided at test time.

RSIPO keeps both RLVR and OPSD branches of the hybrid agentic RL framework and adds an execution check that measures how much a self-generated skill actually improves the policy’s execution for every training task. The measured gains are used twice: ❶ they reward the policy model for writing helpful skills, so that skill generation co-evolves with task execution, and ❷ they calibrate the student’s trust in the skill-enhanced teacher. Figure 3 illustrates the overall RSIPO framework.

Before any outcome is inspected, the G rollouts of task x are split uniformly at random into an evidence set \mathcal{E}_{x} and a control set \mathcal{C}_{x} of equal size, so that \mathcal{C}_{x} is an unbiased sample of the student’s current performance. RSIPO picks one trajectory from \mathcal{E}_{x}, preferring a successful one when available, and lets the policy rewrite a skill s_{x} from it with the analysis template. If s_{x} is valid, the skill-enhanced teacher \pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\cdot\oplus s_{x}) is replayed K times from exactly the same initial state of the task. Each episode is scored by the utility: u(\tau)=\mathbb{I}\bigl[R(\tau)=1\bigr]\Bigl(1-\alpha\,\frac{T(\tau)}{T_{\max}}\Bigr), where T(\tau) is the number of turns and \alpha favors faster successes. The replay gain compares the K replays \{\tilde{\tau}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} with the control rollouts: \Delta_{x}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}u(\tilde{\tau}_{k})-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{x}|}\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{C}_{x}}u(\tau). Since both the replay and control groups contain only a few episodes, \Delta_{x} could be noisy. We approximate its sampling variance by v_{x}=\sum_{a\in\{\text{rep},\,\text{ctl}\}}\tilde{u}_{a}(1-\tilde{u}_{a})/n_{a}, where n_{a} is the number of episodes in group a and \tilde{u}_{a}=(n_{a}\bar{u}_{a}+1)/(n_{a}+2) is its Laplace-smoothed mean utility.

To obtain reliable estimates from such noisy measurements, RSIPO pools the gains of tasks of the same type c, such as a task category in ALFWorld or a source dataset in search-based tasks, across training steps. For each type present in the current batch, it updates the moving averages as: \mathbf{m}_{c}\leftarrow(1-\eta)\,\mathbf{m}_{c}+\eta\,\bigl(\overline{\Delta},\ \overline{\Delta^{2}},\ \overline{v},\ 1\bigr), where the averages are taken over the tasks of type c in the batch and the last entry corrects the bias of the zero initialization. Writing \mathbf{m}_{c}=(m_{c}^{(1)},m_{c}^{(2)},m_{c}^{(v)},m_{c}^{(0)}), the type mean \bar{\Delta}_{c}=m_{c}^{(1)}/m_{c}^{(0)} and the between-task variance \hat{\sigma}^{2}_{c}=\max\bigl(0,\,m_{c}^{(2)}/m_{c}^{(0)}-\bar{\Delta}_{c}^{2}-m_{c}^{(v)}/m_{c}^{(0)}\bigr), i.e., the total variance minus the noise variance, specify a Gaussian prior over the true gains of type c. Following empirical Bayes estimation Efron and Morris (1975), the posterior mean of the gain of task x shrinks its own estimate toward the type mean according to its reliability: \hat{g}_{x}=w_{x}\Delta_{x}+(1-w_{x})\bar{\Delta}_{c},\quad w_{x}=\frac{\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{c}}{\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{c}+v_{x}}, with c=c(x). Gains that are noisy or belong to types without genuine variation across tasks are pulled toward the type mean, whereas reliable and distinctive gains are largely preserved. When a task has no valid replay, the corresponding replay gain falls back to the prior mean \hat{g}_{x}=\bar{\Delta}_{c}.

RSIPO uses the execution check to train skill generation directly. Each task contributes one sample, whose input is the analysis prompt q_{x} of the selected evidence trajectory and whose output y^{(x)} is the rewritten analysis containing s_{x}. The reward is defined as the replay gain centered by the type mean: r_{x}=\Delta_{x}-\bar{\Delta}_{c(x)}, where r_{x} is positive only if s_{x} yields a larger replay gain than the policy’s skills achieve on average for tasks of the same type, and negative otherwise. In contrast to the trust coefficient below, r_{x} is not shrunk, because a policy-gradient signal should be unbiased and shrinkage would suppress all rewards whenever the between-task variance cannot be separated from noise. An invalid skill receives the penalty r_{x}=-\rho, and a task whose replay does not reproduce the initial state receives r_{x}=0. The skill-generation loss is a reward-weighted log-likelihood over the tokens of the skill: \bar{\ell}_{x}=\frac{\sum_{j}m_{x,j}\log\pi_{\theta}\bigl(y^{(x)}_{j}\mid q_{x},y^{(x)}_{<j}\bigr)}{\max\bigl(1,\sum_{j}m_{x,j}\bigr)}, \mathcal{L}_{\text{skill}}=-\frac{1}{|X|}\sum_{x\in X}r_{x}\,\bar{\ell}_{x}, where X is the task batch and m_{x,j}=1 marks the tokens inside the skill string of a valid output, or all tokens of an invalid one.

Because the skills are written by the current policy from its own trajectories and rewarded by their effect on its own execution, skill generation is optimized on-policy and evolves together with task execution.

The shrunk gain \hat{g}_{x} estimates how much the skill-enhanced teacher outperforms the student on task x. RSIPO maps it to a trust coefficient: \omega_{x}=\operatorname{clip}\bigl(1+\kappa\,\hat{g}_{x},\ 0,\ \omega_{\max}\bigr), which weights the OPSD terms of all rollouts: \mathcal{L}_{\text{OPSD}}(\bm{\omega})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\sum_{t,j}\omega_{x(i)}\,\ell^{(i)}_{t,j}, where \ell^{(i)}_{t,j} is the term in Eq. (2) for the j -th token of turn t in rollout i, x(i) is the rollout task, and N is the number of response tokens. Setting \omega_{x}=1 for all tasks recovers the original OPSD loss. With \kappa=2 and \omega_{\max}=2, distillation is disabled when \hat{g}_{x}\leq-0.5 and doubled when \hat{g}_{x}\geq 0.5. We use \hat{g}_{x} rather than \Delta_{x} because a noisy per-task estimate would directly distort the loss weight.

RSIPO optimizes all components in a single update: \displaystyle\mathcal{L}={}\mathcal{L}_{\text{RLVR}}+\lambda_{\text{OPSD}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{OPSD}}(\bm{\omega})+\mathcal{L}_{\text{skill}}. The gradient of \mathcal{L}_{\text{skill}} is accumulated with the last PPO mini-batch so that both share one optimizer step, and the type statistics are committed only after the update succeeds. Algorithm 1 in Appendix C summarizes one training step of RSIPO.

We evaluate the proposed RSIPO framework and baseline approaches on embodied interaction tasks using ALFWorld Shridhar et al. (2021) and search-based agentic tasks. Following Search-R1 Jin et al. (2025), we employ three single-hop datasets, NQ Kwiatkowski et al. (2019), TriviaQA Joshi et al. (2017), and PopQA Mallen et al. (2023), and four multi-hop datasets, HotpotQA Yang et al. (2018), 2WikiMultiHopQA Ho et al. (2020), MuSiQue Trivedi et al. (2022), and Bamboogle Press et al. (2023) for search-based tasks. We report success rates on ALFWorld and exact-match accuracy on search-based tasks.

We compare RSIPO with 13 baselines, including training-free methods like Vanilla and Skill-Prompt*, and methods from the three paradigms in Figure 1, namely the RLVR-based GRPO Shao et al. (2024), Skill-GRPO, and Skill-GRPO*, the OPSD-based OPSD Zhao et al. (2026), and the hybrid GRPO+OPSD, Skill-SD Wang et al. (2026a), RLSD Yang et al. (2026a), SDAR Lu et al. (2026a), StepOPSD Zhang et al. (2026), OPID Yang et al. (2026b), and SEED Wu et al. (2026). Skill-Prompt* adds skills from the SkillRL library Xia et al. (2026) to the prompt at test time, while Skill-GRPO uses them during training and Skill-GRPO* also keeps them at test time. All other methods, including RSIPO, act without skills at test time.

We employ various Qwen-family models, including Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct Yang et al. (2024), and Qwen3-1.7B Yang et al. (2025) as base models. Following SEED Wu et al. (2026), we first fine-tune each model to generate agentic skills using trajectory-skill pairs that are annotated by GLM-5.2 Z.ai (2026) on training data. RSIPO then runs for 150 steps with G=8 rollouts per task and 16 tasks per step on ALFWorld or 128 on search-based tasks, using a learning rate of 10^{-6}, and a KL coefficient of 0.01 on ALFWorld and 0.001 on search-based tasks. We keep the OPSD setting with \lambda_{\text{OPSD}}=0.01 and \beta=5. For RSIPO, the evidence and control sets each contain half of the rollouts, and we set K=4, \alpha=0.5, \eta=0.1, and \rho=0.2. Each run uses 8 \times NVIDIA H20 GPUs.
Table 1 and Table 3 compare RSIPO with all baselines on three base models. From these results, we can derive the following observations.

On ALFWorld, RSIPO achieves the highest average success rate across all three backbones, reaching 95.7%, 98.6%, and 95.0% with Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Qwen3-1.7B, respectively. These results correspond to gains of 3.9%, 2.5%, and 3.0% over the strongest baseline, SEED, and 20.7%, 17.4%, and 48.9% over standard GRPO. Adding OPSD to GRPO does not consistently improve performance, as GRPO+OPSD underperforms GRPO with both Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3-1.7B. This finding is consistent with our preliminary analysis in Figure 2, which suggests that uniformly trusting teacher guidance can hinder student learning. In contrast, RSIPO outperforms GRPO+OPSD by 14.5%, 18.2%, and 63.0% with Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Qwen3-1.7B, respectively.

RSIPO attains the highest average accuracy with Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3-1.7B, at 50.8% and 42.6%, and ranks second with Qwen2.5-3B, only 0.4% below SEED. It improves over GRPO by 8.9%, 8.8%, and 1.8% on the three backbones. The margins are smaller than on ALFWorld, likely because answering these questions relies more on retrieved evidence than on procedural skills, so the skill-enhanced teacher provides less additional guidance, as reflected by trust values close to one in Figure 4 (a).

Despite using no agentic skills at test time for inference, RSIPO consistently outperforms baselines that receive skills during evaluation, including Skill-Prompt* and Skill-GRPO*, across both benchmarks and all evaluated backbones. With Qwen2.5-7B, RSIPO surpasses Skill-GRPO* by 10.3% on ALFWorld and 3.3% on search-based agentic tasks. These results suggest that trust-calibrated self-distillation helps the policy internalize knowledge from agentic skills generated during training, rather than relying on explicit skill guidance at inference.

Figure 4 (a) shows the training curves of RSIPO with Qwen2.5-3B. The training success rate rises from 63% to over 90% on ALFWorld and from 32% to 53% on search-based tasks, while the OPSD loss is roughly halved on search-based tasks and stays stable on ALFWorld. The dynamic trust tracks the reliability of the teacher. On ALFWorld, it exceeds 1.1 within 20 steps as the skill-enhanced teacher increasingly outperforms the control rollouts. On search-based tasks, where the teacher offers little extra benefit, it stays close to one, showing that even in such unfavorable cases the calibrated distillation degrades gracefully to approximately standard OPSD.

Figure 4 (b) reports a cumulative ablation on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-3B. OPSD alone improves the base model only from 21.9% to 28.1%, whereas GRPO reaches 75.0%, and combining the two yields 81.2%. With SFT initialization, the hybrid pipeline reaches 86.4%. On top of it, dynamic trust and skill evolution bring gains of 3.6% and 5.6%, respectively, and the full RSIPO reaches 95.7%. Removing either component from RSIPO costs 3.7% to 5.7%, showing that the two components are complementary.

Figure 5 traces the self-generated skills on ALFWorld using three non-exclusive keyword-based categories: Procedure (numbered steps), Format (action syntax), and Recovery (handling “Nothing happens”). Early skills inherited from SFT often fall into Format or Recovery, with a negative average replay gain. Procedure skills then exceed 94% in the last 45 steps, and the replay gain turns positive. For example, the step-0 skill only advises checking the syntax, whereas the step-150 skill specifies a systematic search-and-place procedure.

In this work, we presented RSIPO, a self-evolving agentic RL framework that enables agentic skills and the policy to co-evolve throughout training. RSIPO evaluates the utility of self-generated skills by comparing skill-enhanced teacher replays with control rollouts. The resulting replay gains reward the policy for generating useful skills and calibrate the student’s trust in teacher supervision. Experiments on embodied and search-based tasks demonstrate RSIPO’s advantages over existing agentic RL methods. Future work will extend RSIPO to larger models and a broader range of agentic tasks, including coding and co-working scenarios.

Despite its effectiveness, RSIPO has two main limitations. First, although trajectory replay requires neither additional evaluation data nor auxiliary evaluation models, the extra rollouts increase training costs. This introduces a trade-off between training effectiveness and computational efficiency. Second, RSIPO relies on environments that can be reset to a specified state, such as simulators and search environments backed by offline retrieval corpora. Extending RSIPO to non-resettable settings, such as interactions with live websites, remains a challenge, which we leave as future work.

Capable Teacher, Myopic Scorer: Reward-Free Teacher Repair for Agentic On-Policy Distillation. Agentic on-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student agent on its own trajectories while a teacher scores every token. A natural explanation of where it goes wrong is compounding error: the student's mistakes carry its trajectories beyond the region where the teacher is reliable, so recent methods keep training inside that region, through episode-length curricula, teacher-guided turns, prefix replay, or teacher intervention where the two disagree. We show this explanation is incomplete. From the states where the student departs most from the teacher, the teacher's own takeovers still finish the task, yet the student trained on its token scores keeps running out of turns. We attribute this to the myopia of next-token scoring. The teacher rates each token without seeing where the episode ends, so its scores let through the safe, delaying moves that outcome-based RL would punish with zero reward, a penalty agentic OPD lacks. We call this difference between what the teacher does and what it scores the rollout-scorer gap.

We propose Rollout-to-Scorer Distillation (R2S), which repairs the scorer before distillation by mining high-disagreement states from the untrained student, running teacher takeovers from them, keeping the states where enough takeovers pass a reward-free check such as consensus or an LLM judge, and fine-tuning the teacher to give its takeover-informed scores on every assistant token from the divergence turn onward, without the takeover in context. The repaired teacher is frozen as the sole scorer for standard OPD, requiring no task reward during repair or training. Across three environments, two teachers and four students, R2S outperforms three state-of-the-art agentic-OPD methods in all twelve teacher-student-environment cells, by 12.8 success points on average over the best of them in each cell. Project page: https://tree-shu-zhao.github.io/r2s/.

Agentic on-policy distillation (OPD) trains an agent on its own trajectories. The student acts in a live environment, and a stronger teacher scores every token it produces (Liao et al., 2026). The teacher never acts in this loop; it only scores, and its next-token distribution on the student’s histories is the whole training signal. This form of dense supervision also underlies the multi-teacher post-training pipelines of MiMo-V2-Flash and Nemotron-Cascade 2 (Xiao et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026).

A natural explanation of where agentic OPD goes wrong is compounding error. The student’s mistakes carry its trajectories beyond the region where the teacher is reliable, and its scores there are noise. Recent agentic-OPD methods act on this reading and keep training inside the trusted region, by shortening the student’s episodes (Wang et al., 2026), handing turns to the teacher (Li et al., 2026a), replaying teacher prefixes (Liao et al., 2026), or intervening where the two disagree (Chen et al., 2026), and report gains in their own settings.

We show this explanation is incomplete. We take the states where the untrained student disagrees most with the teacher, late in its episodes, the states that compounding error should place furthest outside the teacher’s region, and let the teacher act from them. Its takeovers still finish the task. In every environment they beat the student’s own outcome from the same states, and they rescue many of the states the student went on to lose. The student has not drifted beyond what the teacher can handle. Yet the teacher’s plain scores let the student’s delay pass: only with one of its finishing takeovers in context do they mark down the student’s hedging and searching, and the student trained on the plain scores keeps running out of turns. Figure 1 illustrates this.

We attribute this to the myopia of next-token scoring. Acting, the teacher writes the whole episode itself: each action is followed by its consequences and by the teacher’s own next action, and the episode runs to an outcome. Scoring, it rates each of the student’s tokens one at a time, on a history it did not write, without seeing where the episode ends. Under that uncertainty another look or another search keeps options open and is reasonable on its own, so the teacher’s scores let it pass. Outcome-based RL punishes such delay with zero reward when the episode runs out, while agentic OPD has no such penalty. We call this difference between what the teacher does and what it scores the rollout–scorer gap. This motivates informing the scores with selected teacher continuations.

Rollout-to-Scorer Distillation (R2S) repairs the scorer before distillation. First, the teacher takes over from the untrained student’s highest-disagreement states. Second, we keep the states where enough takeovers pass a reward-free check, consensus among them or an LLM judge, and pick the shortest passing one as the reference. Third, we fine-tune the teacher to give its takeover-informed scores on every assistant token from the selected divergence turn onward, without the takeover in context. The repaired teacher is frozen for standard OPD. Student training retains the ordinary OPD objective and rollout recipe, and no task reward enters repair or training. We evaluate R2S across three environments, two teachers and four students under a fixed final-checkpoint protocol. R2S outperforms three state-of-the-art agentic-OPD methods in every cell. The gain over the best of them in each cell averages +17.0 points from the 9B teacher and +8.5 from the 30B-A3B teacher.

Our contributions are: (1) The rollout–scorer gap. Section 3 shows that the teacher’s takeovers still finish from the states where the student departs most from it, while its plain scores let the student’s delay pass; only a finishing takeover in context turns them against it. (2) R2S. Section 4 introduces a reward-free repair that moves the teacher’s rollout competence into the scores OPD consumes, then freezes the teacher for standard OPD. (3) Evaluation. We evaluate R2S against three state-of-the-art agentic-OPD methods across twelve model–environment cells under a shared protocol, and measure target fidelity, out-of-turn rates and searching turns in a long-horizon analysis.

On-policy distillation for agents. ReOPD identifies a prefix trap: histories closer to the student’s distribution can make the teacher’s targets less reliable, motivating a curriculum over replayed teacher prefixes (Liao et al., 2026). Our compared methods address related trajectory-level difficulties: TCOD-F2B schedules rollout depth, Guided-OPD allocates teacher-controlled turns, and FutureBridge validates teacher bridges from high-disagreement states (Wang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026). These methods retain the original scorer. R2S repairs its token scores before student training, a change that can be combined with student-side curricula.

Context and self-distillation. SDFT and Self-Distilled Reasoner use demonstration-conditioned self-teachers to supervise student rollouts (Shenfeld et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026b). SDPO instead conditions on textual feedback or successful attempts (Hübotter et al., 2026), while OPCD internalizes experiential knowledge and system prompts through on-policy context distillation (Ye et al., 2026). CANON selects privileged solutions by consensus without gold labels (Gkountouras et al., 2026). These works establish that useful distillation signals need not come from task rewards. R2S uses teacher takeovers to repair an external scorer, then freezes it for a separate student’s OPD.

Teacher quality and repair. Li et al. (2026b) show that a higher-scoring teacher need not transfer better: compatible reasoning patterns and new capabilities matter. Kaur et al. (2026) find that privileged context can suppress self-correction and degrade thinking models. These results motivate checking what the teacher’s local signal teaches, beyond its standalone performance. Distillation Traps and Guards directly calibrates an external teacher with utility and calibration rewards (Zhan et al., 2026). R2S instead fits takeover-informed token targets without task reward and evaluates the repaired scorer through target fidelity and downstream completion. Sections A.1 and A.2 give the detailed comparisons and extended discussion.

Agentic on-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student \pi_{\theta} to match a teacher T. The student acts in the environment: at each turn t it reads the history h_{t} (the task, the observations so far and its own earlier responses) and emits a response y_{t}; the environment returns the next observation. In vanilla OPD the teacher does not act; it scores every token the student produces, given the same history.

The training signal is the teacher’s next-token distribution on the student’s own histories. The student minimizes a token-level divergence to it; we use the reverse KL, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{h\sim\pi_{\theta}}\;\mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h)\,\|\,T(\cdot\mid h)\big), estimated at the sampled token (Xiao et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b). Other OPD variants use forward KL or Jensen–Shannon divergence (Shenfeld et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026); what follows concerns the per-token scoring, not the choice of divergence. The loss reports how closely the student matches the teacher’s scores. Nothing in this objective looks past the current token: the teacher scores h without seeing how the episode ends. The analysis below studies one teacher, Qwen3.5-9B, and its Qwen3.5-4B student.

section: Where the Student Drifts, the Teacher Still Finishes
text: Where the student trains is not the whole story. Recent methods trace what goes wrong in agentic OPD to long horizons. The student’s early mistakes compound (Ross et al., 2011) and carry it into states beyond the teacher’s reach, where the teacher’s scores can no longer guide it, so the student learns the wrong thing there. TCOD-F2B, Guided-OPD and FutureBridge therefore keep training within that reach, by shortening the student’s episodes, handing turns to the teacher, or intervening where the two disagree.

section: Where the Student Drifts, the Teacher Still Finishes
text: The explanation assumes that the states the student drifts into lie beyond what the teacher can handle. If so, the teacher acting from them should fail as well. We test this on the states the explanation points to: the turns at which the untrained student’s next-token distribution departs most from the teacher’s. From each state the teacher takes over eight times. As the success columns of Table 1 show, in every environment its takeovers finish more often than the student did from the same states. The student has not drifted beyond what the teacher can handle.

section: Where the Student Drifts, the Teacher Still Finishes
text: Its plain scores let the student’s delay pass. Once one of its finishing takeovers is in context, the teacher’s scores turn against the student’s delay: in the drop columns of Table 1, its probability of the student’s hedging and searching words falls two to three times as much as that of the rest of the student’s thinking. The plain scores OPD trains on lack this direction: these states are within the teacher’s reach, yet the student learns from the teacher’s next-token scores there, not from its rollouts. As a result, the student trained on these plain scores to its final checkpoint still runs out of turns in a third of its held-out ALFWorld and ScienceWorld episodes and in more than half of its WebShop ones, about twice as often as when it trains on the repaired teacher.

section: Where the Student Drifts, the Teacher Still Finishes
text: Takeaway: recoverable states, cautious student At the states where the student departs most from the teacher, even late in its episodes, the teacher’s own takeovers still finish the task. The teacher’s plain scores let the student’s delay pass, and the student trained on them keeps running out of turns.

section: The Scorer Never Sees Where the Episode Ends
text: Outcome-based RL punishes delay with zero reward when the episode runs out of turns; plain scoring lacks this continuation signal. Acting, the teacher generates a continuation from the student’s state, observes the consequences of its actions, and reaches an outcome. Scoring, it rates the student’s tokens given the observed history, without that continuation in context. Its probabilities may encode expectations about future outcomes, but ordinary OPD supplies no explicit feedback from the realized task outcome. This distinction matters when useful information gathering and costly delay look similar locally. Another look or search keeps options open, but it spends one turn of a fixed budget, which the student trained on plain scores often uses up. Plain next-token scores carry no penalty for delay: each extra look is scored on its own, and on its own it is reasonable. Conditioning the scorer on a selected teacher continuation changes its supervision on the same student text. We call the distinction between the teacher’s demonstrated rollout competence and its token-level supervision the rollout–scorer gap.

section: The Scorer Never Sees Where the Episode Ends
text: Design implications. We mine the untrained student’s high-disagreement states and use selected teacher takeovers to inform the scores supplied there. Agreement on an observable outcome or an offline filter supplies the selection rule without reading task reward. We train the teacher to reproduce takeover-informed distributions on every assistant token from the divergence turn onward, without the takeover in context. The repaired teacher then becomes the sole scorer for ordinary OPD.

R2S targets the rollout–scorer gap of Section 3. The teacher’s rollouts from the student’s states carry the judgment its scores lack. As illustrated in Figure 2, we therefore let the teacher take over from those states, read off the scores it gives with its own ending in view, and fine-tune it to give those scores closed-book, with no takeover in context; the refrozen teacher then scores ordinary OPD. The student never sees a takeover.

The teacher takes over where the student departs most from it. We first let the untrained student play the training tasks. In each of its episodes we mine the divergence turn: the turn where the student’s thinking departs most from the teacher’s, measured by OPD’s own per-token divergence averaged over that thinking, \Delta_{t}=\frac{1}{|y^{\mathrm{think}}_{t}|}\sum_{i\in y^{\mathrm{think}}_{t}}\left[\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t,i}\mid h_{t},y_{t,<i})-\log T_{0}(y_{t,i}\mid h_{t},y_{t,<i})\right], where y^{\mathrm{think}}_{t} is the thinking of turn t, the part of y_{t} before the action, and T_{0} is the original teacher; the divergence turn has the largest \Delta_{t}. Only the thinking is compared, because it decides the action that follows. From the state at each mined turn, the teacher takes over K times and plays the episode to its end. The choice among these takeovers is general: any check that tells a finishing takeover from a failing one will do, such as consensus among the takeovers, an LLM-as-a-judge, or the ground truth, which is the task’s own 0–1 reward.
