Consensus and a judge need no reward, so R2S can also run where no reward is available. A state is kept when at least m of its takeovers pass the check, and the shortest of them is selected as \tau_{h}.

The judgment supervises the complete suffix from the divergence state. For a kept state h, the frozen teacher T_{0} scores the rest of the student’s own episode, every token of its thinking and actions from h to the end, with the takeover \tau_{h} in context. These informed scores are the targets q^{+}. The takeover only informs them; its tokens never replace the student’s. A trainable copy T_{\phi} sees the same episode without the takeover and learns to give the same scores: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{R2S}}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{h}\,\mathbb{E}_{h^{\prime}}\Big[\mathrm{CE}\big(\underbrace{T_{0}(\cdot\mid\tau_{h},h^{\prime})}_{q^{+}},\;T_{\phi}(\cdot\mid h^{\prime})\big)\Big], where h^{\prime} runs over the student’s histories from h to the end of its episode, one per token the student wrote, and \mathrm{CE} is the cross-entropy. Refrozen, T_{\phi} is an ordinary next-token scorer, and OPD uses it in place of T_{0}.

Our experiments ask four questions. RQ1: does repairing the scorer improve OPD across teachers, students and environments? RQ2: can the takeovers be selected without reward? RQ3: which parts of R2S are necessary? RQ4: what does the repaired scorer change in long-horizon behavior? We answer these questions below.

Teachers and students. Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026) teaches Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-4B on three environments, and Qwen3.5-4B teaches itself in Table 3. Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (Yang et al., 2025) teaches Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on the same three environments. We chose these pairs to vary three things: model size, from 2B to 30B parameters; model generation, Qwen3.5 and Qwen3; and architecture, a dense 9B teacher and a mixture-of-experts 30B-A3B teacher. Every prompt carries one fixed worked demonstration per environment; native reasoning mode is off, and each turn opens with one to three sentences of plain-text deliberation before the tool call, as detailed in Appendix D.

Environments. ALFWorld (household tasks), WebShop (shopping) and ScienceWorld (science experiments) are scored by success (%). ALFWorld and ScienceWorld have a seen and an unseen split, and the main text reports their mean; WebShop is evaluated on its 500 canonical goals. Following TCOD, the held-out splits hold 140 seen and 134 unseen games on ALFWorld and 140 seen variations and 134 unseen task rows on ScienceWorld. An episode has 30 turns, 15 on WebShop, under one full-history tool-call protocol.

Protocol. Each teacher–student–environment cell is one 150-step training run. Its final checkpoint is evaluated in three sampled decodes, with no checkpoint selection. The teacher and the untrained student acting alone follow the same prompt and evaluation protocol. In every cell, R2S mines up to 2{,}400 states, takes K{=}8 takeovers from each and fine-tunes the teacher for one epoch.

Training and evaluation. Each step trains on 16 episodes, 128 on WebShop, sampled at temperature 0.4 within a 32{,}768 -token context; the distillation log-ratio of the sampled estimator enters a clipped PPO surrogate as the per-token advantage, with no additional KL or entropy term, and Adam runs at a constant learning rate of 10^{-6}. Reasoning mode is off for acting, scoring and distillation; a turn is capped at 512 tokens in training and 4{,}096 at evaluation, and student responses are copied byte-identically into the separately served teacher context. Table entries are the mean \pm std over the three decodes of the final checkpoint: its in-training evaluation and two re-loads under further decoding seeds. The teacher acting alone is evaluated through the same path, prompts and seeds.

Repair settings. A turn is eligible for mining when its thinking has at least three tokens and ends in a tool call; we keep the eligible turn with the largest \Delta_{t} in each episode, at most three states per goal, and the N states with the largest \Delta_{t} overall. In the privileged pass the selected takeover enters as one reference message before the student’s first turn, listing the teacher’s thinking and action at each of its steps; T_{\phi} sees the same stream without that message. The targets q^{+} keep the teacher’s sixteen most probable tokens at each position, renormalized, and are computed once from T_{0}; T_{\phi} is initialized from T_{0} and fine-tuned full-parameter for one epoch at learning rate 2\times 10^{-6}, in batches of eight states, with 10% of goals held out. Appendix C lists every remaining setting.

Baselines. Vanilla OPD minimizes Eq. 1 with the sampled estimator against the original teacher T_{0}; R2S runs the same OPD against the repaired teacher T_{\phi}, so vanilla OPD is its direct control. The other three are recent agentic-OPD methods, chosen because, like R2S, they train the student by distillation alone, without a task-reward RL objective such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024). TCOD-F2B (Wang et al., 2026) trains the student on shortened episodes that lengthen over training, Guided-OPD (Li et al., 2026a) hands part of the turns to the teacher, and FutureBridge (Chen et al., 2026), the closest prior method, trains the student on validated teacher bridges from the states where the two disagree most. Their code is public, so all three run under the same models, prompts, estimator and protocol as vanilla OPD and R2S. We leave out methods that combine distillation with reward-based RL, such as SDAR (Lu et al., 2026): their students also learn from task reward, which would confound the comparison; a repaired teacher could serve as the distillation term of such a hybrid.

R2S beats every baseline in all twelve cells of Table 2 and ends above the teacher acting alone. The gain over vanilla OPD averages +17.8 points from the 9B teacher and +9.8 from the 30B-A3B teacher, and R2S exceeds every baseline in mean on all 24 splits of Table 12. Averaged over the ten cells outside the 30B-A3B teacher’s WebShop pair, the vanilla student ends within a point of the teacher acting alone. On WebShop the 30B-A3B teacher acting alone seldom completes a purchase: on 13.7 of its 15 turns per episode, on average, it answers without calling the action tool, so 94\% of its episodes run out of turns, and every student ends above it. Figure 3 follows the Qwen3.5-9B-to-4B students of all five methods over three training runs each: the R2S student separates from every baseline well before the final checkpoint. The three R2S runs share the one repaired teacher of Table 2, so the width of its band comes from student training alone.

The teacher’s takeovers from the untrained student’s highest-disagreement states finish more often than the student does in eleven of the twelve cells (Table 11 in Appendix B), so what Section 3.2 found for one pair holds for all four.

The teacher can be the student’s own base model. Table 3 repeats the Qwen3.5-4B cells with the 4B as its own teacher. In all three environments, the R2S student taught by the repaired 4B passes the vanilla student that the 9B teaches in Table 2. Since the teacher and the student are the same model, the student–teacher gap that ranks states is zero, so the pipeline draws one turn per episode of the untrained student at random under the same goal cap and budget; the 4B itself runs the takeovers and the selection, so no larger model enters the pipeline. In all three environments this self-taught student also ends above the 9B teacher acting alone in Table 2. Taught by the unrepaired 4B, the four other students gain about six points on ALFWorld and at most about a point on WebShop and ScienceWorld: a model’s plain scores of its own tokens teach it little. What lifts the student is not a larger model’s knowledge but scores informed by the ending, which its own base model can supply.
Each ablation below varies one part of R2S in the Qwen3.5-9B-to-4B cells of Table 2, on all three environments.

Takeover selection. Table 4 repairs the teacher with three rules for picking the winning takeovers. Ground truth reads the task reward; the consensus vote and the LLM judge do not. With either reward-free rule the student ends above vanilla OPD in all three environments, so the repair depends neither on reading the reward nor on one particular rule.

Effect of informed targets. Table 5 separates the takeovers from the informed targets built on them. The label-SFT control fine-tunes the teacher on the selected takeovers by standard SFT. Its student already ends well above vanilla OPD in all three environments, so the takeovers carry signal of their own; fitting the informed targets instead lifts the student further. The takeovers help most as context for the teacher’s scores of the student’s own tokens, not as SFT data.

Supervised turns. R2S fits the informed targets on the suffix of the student’s episode, from the divergence turn to its end. Table 6 supervises instead the divergence turn alone or the prefix up to it. Every span lifts the student well above vanilla OPD in all three environments, so the informed targets help whichever turns they cover. Vanilla OPD, whose teacher scores each token without seeing how the episode ends, trails them all by a wide margin.
We compare the Qwen3.5-9B-to-4B R2S teachers and students of Table 2 with vanilla OPD.

Repair brings the teacher closer to its informed targets, and its student runs out of turns less often. Scored against the same q^{+} targets over the complete assistant suffix of held-out states, the repaired teacher is closer to them than the unrepaired teacher in every environment, as the left panel of Figure 4 shows. In the evaluation episodes behind Table 2, the student trained on the repaired teacher runs out of turns about half as often as the vanilla OPD student, as the right panel shows.

The vanilla student inherits the teacher’s endings. Table 7 counts, for the same evaluation episodes, how often each policy runs out of turns and how many turns it takes, beside the teacher acting alone and the untrained student. On ALFWorld every failure is a timeout, since the wrapper ends an episode only on success. In every environment the vanilla student takes about the teacher’s number of turns and runs out of turns almost as often as the teacher does. The R2S student finishes in fewer turns and runs out of turns far less often than the teacher that scores it.

The saved turns are searching turns. Table 8 splits the turns of the students’ training rollouts into searching, that is moving, opening and looking, or searching and paging on WebShop, and acting on the task. The R2S student spends fewer turns searching than the vanilla OPD student in every environment and about as many on the task. Counting only the episodes each student wins, it still searches less: 8.4 turns against 10.5 on ALFWorld, 2.0 against 3.0 on WebShop and 7.1 against 9.1 on ScienceWorld. On ALFWorld it opens fewer receptacles, on ScienceWorld it looks, reads and waits less, and on WebShop it searches and pages less and buys more. This matches the direction of the informed scores in Table 1, which fall most on the student’s hedging and searching words.

The teacher’s takeovers can still finish from the states where the student departs most from it, yet its plain scores let the student’s delay pass; only a finishing takeover in context turns them against it. R2S transfers information from selected teacher continuations into the scores used by ordinary OPD. Its repair supervises every assistant position from the divergence turn onward with takeover-informed targets, then freezes the repaired teacher as the student’s sole scorer. Under a shared protocol, R2S outperforms three state-of-the-art agentic-OPD methods in all twelve model–environment cells, and it also leads when the teacher is the student’s own base model.

Compute. Before distillation, R2S spends the untrained student’s episodes, N{\times}K=19{,}200 takeover episodes, the selection step and one teacher fine-tune. Every method then trains for 150 steps; Guided-OPD and FutureBridge also spend teacher generation inside training. One model family. Evidence comes from text-agent benchmarks and Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 models. Replayable environments. Takeovers start from the student’s own states, so R2S needs an environment that can be replayed to a given state; all three benchmarks here can.

OPRD: On-Policy Reminder Distillation for Long-Horizon Coding Agents. Reliable repository-level coding requires agents not only to generate correct code but also to preserve constraints and respond to tool feedback across long interactions. However, our diagnostic analysis shows that agents often fail to act on relevant information already available in context, while final Pass/Fail outcomes provide only sparse process supervision. We introduce On-Policy Reminder Distillation (OPRD), which combines Multi-Scope Reminder supervision with outcome-based routing on reminder-free student rollouts. Successful rollouts provide autoregressive self-imitation targets, whereas failed rollouts receive Reminder-conditioned reverse-KL supervision from a teacher that re-evaluates the same student-generated prefixes. A Global Reminder converts final-test diagnostics into trajectory-level guidance, while Turn-local Reminders apply only to the next decision following the relevant environment observation. The teacher and student share a two-stage initialization from Coding SFT and Instruction-Following (IF) SFT. At inference, the student operates without Reminders. On SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, and SWE-bench Multilingual, OPRD improves the benchmark-averaged task resolution rate by 11.3 points over the open-source Qwen3.5-4B base model. Under the same diagnostic protocol, it reduces the aggregate error-event count from 446 to 222, a 50.2% reduction.

Large language models have advanced in reasoning (Zhan et al. 2025a; Deng et al. 2025a; Xu et al. 2026b; Miao et al. 2026) and repository-level software engineering (Yang et al. 2025b; Jimenez et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2024a; Zhang et al. 2024; Ouyang et al. 2025; Xia et al. 2025). Reliable long-horizon coding nevertheless requires agents to preserve task constraints and adapt to tool and execution feedback (Yao et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2024). We examine this challenge on 200 SWE-rebench V2 validation tasks (Badertdinov et al. 2026), using two Qwen3.5-4B rollouts per task under identical inference settings (Qwen Team 2026). In the reminder-free rollout, deterministic rules identify explicit tool and execution failures, while GPT-5.4 classifies remaining context-dependent events from the task and complete trajectory (OpenAI 2026). Each event belongs to one of four categories in Table 6: Tool-Feedback Recovery, Scope and Source Grounding, Scenario-Condition Reasoning, and Post-Edit Control and Validation. In the second rollout, the agent restarts from the task under the same settings, and the Reminder mechanism examines each environment observation to decide whether to insert a Turn-local Reminder before the next action.

Applying the same annotation protocol reveals fewer error events across all four categories (Fig. 1). Post-hoc annotation audits completed trajectories, while runtime Reminder selection uses only the currently visible interaction prefix. This finding suggests that reliable long-horizon coding requires models to preserve task-level constraints across a trajectory and use local interaction feedback at appropriate decision points. A natural direction is therefore to provide process-level corrective information with explicit temporal scope.

However, coding-agent training relies on supervised imitation of successful trajectories or executable-outcome optimization (Pan et al. 2025; Jain et al. 2025; Wei et al. 2025). These signals improve task completion but do not indicate which constraints should persist or which observation should guide the next decision. At inference time, agents can adapt to feedback (Yao et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2024) or recover missed information through reflection and self-critique (Shinn et al. 2023; Madaan et al. 2023; Gou et al. 2024). Runtime reminders require deployment-time construction and injection, consume context, and tie behavior to an agent scaffold. On-policy distillation trains students on self-generated outputs to reduce train–inference mismatch (Agarwal et al. 2024; Gu et al. 2024). Related work uses context- and feedback-conditioned distillation to internalize behavior induced by auxiliary instructions or environment feedback (Ye et al. 2026; Hübotter et al. 2026). Applying these ideas to long-horizon coding leaves two challenges. First, training-time corrective information can encode persistent constraints and local corrections from observations relevant to one decision. Without explicit scopes, local corrections may be diluted in long contexts or propagated to unrelated decisions.
Second, models without instruction-following adaptation may ignore constraints and feedback, so teacher reminders may not produce reliable distillation targets.
This raises a practical question: Can we internalize scope-specific corrective information during training so that a coding agent can operate without reminders at inference time?

We address this with On-Policy Reminder Distillation (OPRD), which combines Multi-Scope Reminder supervision with outcome-based routing on rollouts from a reminder-free student. For failed trajectories, we construct reminders from task, trajectory, and execution/validation records. A Global Reminder converts final-test diagnostics into trajectory-level guidance. A Turn-local Reminder is anchored to an observation and applies only to the next decision. This combines trajectory-level feedback with local correction without propagating local feedback to unrelated decisions. For reliable supervision, our two-stage cold start uses Coding SFT to establish coding capabilities and Instruction-Following (IF) SFT to improve responsiveness to constraints, feedback, and reminders. Both models are initialized from the IF checkpoint. Based on executable verification, OPRD routes successful rollouts to autoregressive self-imitation and failed rollouts to reminder-conditioned distillation without reinforcing erroneous decisions. For failures, the teacher re-evaluates student-generated prefixes under reminders, while the student matches the teacher distribution through Top-100 reverse KL. OPRD internalizes scope-specific corrections, enabling the student to act on corresponding constraints and feedback without reminders at inference time. We evaluate OPRD on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, and SWE-bench Multilingual (OpenAI 2024; Deng et al. 2025b; Yang et al. 2025a).

OPRD improves the benchmark-averaged task resolution rate by 11.3 points over the open-source Qwen3.5-4B base model. Under the same diagnostic protocol, the trained OPRD model reduces the aggregate error-event count across the four categories from 446 to 222, a 50.2% reduction relative to the base model.

Our main contributions are threefold: Multi-Scope Reminder supervision for long-horizon coding. We combine a Global Reminder that provides guidance across the trajectory with Turn-local Reminders that target only the next decision, enabling process-level supervision at complementary temporal scopes. On-Policy Reminder Distillation with Outcome-Based Routing. We propose OPRD, which learns from verified successful rollouts through autoregressive self-imitation and from failed rollouts through reminder-conditioned reverse KL distillation. A two-stage supervised cold start for reliable reminder distillation. Coding SFT followed by IF SFT provides a shared teacher–student initialization that improves responsiveness to constraints, execution feedback, and reminders, thereby providing a stronger starting point for subsequent reminder-conditioned distillation.

Repository-level evaluation covers code completion (Deng et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2024b), executable issue resolution (Jimenez et al. 2024), broad agent capabilities (Xu et al. 2025), and multimodal web coding (Lei et al. 2026). SWE-agent, AutoCodeRover, and Agentless provide tool-based issue-resolution pipelines (Yang et al. 2024a; Zhang et al. 2024; Xia et al. 2025). Training uses trajectories, verifiers, and generated or freshly collected tasks (Pan et al. 2025; Jain et al. 2025; Yang et al. 2025a; Badertdinov et al. 2025), alongside executable-outcome optimization (Wei et al. 2025) and multi-stage coding-agent training (Zhan et al. 2025b). Evaluation also considers engineering-constraint compliance beyond functional correctness (Zhu et al. 2026).

ReAct, Reflexion, and self-refinement use observations or feedback to guide actions and revisions (Yao et al. 2023; Shinn et al. 2023; Madaan et al. 2023). FTTT studies test-time feedback optimization (Li, Lyu, and Wang 2025); tool-grounded critique, search, and execution verification guide correction (Gou et al. 2024; Zhou et al. 2024; Chen et al. 2024; Zhong, Wang, and Shang 2024). Complementary work explores code-critique evaluation (Zhang et al. 2025), failure diagnosis in agent traces (Li et al. 2026), visual feedback for web-code refinement (Li et al. 2025), and generative process rewards (Xu et al. 2026a). Structured failure feedback also guides refinement in autonomous driving (Luo et al. 2026a).

On-policy distillation supervises student-generated sequences (Agarwal et al. 2024), with reverse/skew KL objectives (Gu et al. 2024; Ko et al. 2024) and entropy-aware or black-box extensions (Jin et al. 2026; Ye et al. 2025). Context and privileged-information distillation internalize behavior induced by auxiliary instructions or training-only information (Snell, Klein, and Zhong 2022; Zhao et al. 2026; Penaloza et al. 2026). OPCD uses a context-conditioned teacher on student trajectories (Ye et al. 2026). Reflective driving guidance can also be internalized through outcome-routed on-policy self-distillation (Luo et al. 2026b). OPRD studies this training–inference separation with explicitly scoped Reminders for long-horizon coding.

Long-horizon coding agents must not only generate correct code, but also consistently follow user constraints throughout multi-turn interactions and adapt their behavior to tool responses and execution feedback. However, final verification outcomes provide limited process-level supervision for constraint adherence and feedback use at different scopes. To address this limitation, we propose O n- P olicy R eminder D istillation (OPRD), which distills the behavior of a teacher conditioned on Multi-Scope Reminders into a student that operates without reminders at inference time. As illustrated in Fig. 2, we formulate the long-horizon coding task (Sec. 3.1), then introduce Multi-Scope Reminders (Sec. 3.2) and a two-stage supervised cold start (Sec. 3.3), and present Multi-Scope Reminder-Conditioned Distillation (Sec. 3.4).

Given a repository-level coding task x, an agent interacts with a code execution environment over multiple turns. We denote the k -th assistant turn by a_{k} and the resulting environment observation by o_{k}. The complete interaction trajectory is \tau=(x,a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{K},o_{K}). An executable verifier evaluates the final repository state and returns c(\tau)\in\{0,1\}, where c(\tau)=1 indicates that the trajectory passes verification and c(\tau)=0 indicates failure. We denote the trainable student by \pi_{\theta} and the teacher by \pi_{\phi}. The token sequence of the k -th assistant turn is a_{k}=(y_{k,1},\ldots,y_{k,L_{k}}), where L_{k} is the number of tokens in that turn. The interaction history preceding the k -th assistant turn and the student context for generating its j -th token are defined as H_{k}=(x,a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1},o_{k-1}),\qquad h_{k,j}^{S}=(H_{k},y_{k,<j}), where y_{k,<j} denotes the token prefix preceding y_{k,j} within the current turn. System messages, user messages, and tool responses provide generation context but are not prediction targets. Training is restricted to valid assistant tokens, whose index set is \Omega(\tau)\subseteq\{(k,j)\mid 1\leq k\leq K,\ 1\leq j\leq L_{k}\}.

The constraints and feedback received by a long-horizon coding agent operate over different temporal scopes. Task-level constraints, such as permitted modification scope, interface requirements, and output format, must hold throughout the trajectory. In contrast, test errors, tool responses, and file inspection results typically pertain to a specific decision point. Nevertheless, the final verifier compresses the entire trajectory into a binary outcome and cannot represent these distinct scopes. Treating all corrective information as a single trajectory-wide prompt may cause local errors to be diluted by the long context, whereas propagating local feedback to all subsequent turns may introduce irrelevant or conflicting supervision as the interaction state evolves. We therefore organize corrective information from a failed trajectory into a Multi-Scope Reminder. A Global Reminder provides persistent task-level guidance across turns, while a Turn-local Reminder is aligned with a specific decision point and highlights environmental feedback that the model ignored or misinterpreted at that point. For a failed trajectory \tau, its Multi-Scope Reminder is represented as R(\tau)=\left(r^{G},\{(k,r_{k}^{L})\}_{k\in\mathcal{I}_{\tau}}\right),\qquad\mathcal{I}_{\tau}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,K-1\}, where r^{G} denotes the Global Reminder, r_{k}^{L} denotes the Turn-local Reminder anchored to environment observation o_{k}, and \mathcal{I}_{\tau} is the set of observation indices associated with local corrective signals.

The Global Reminder remains visible throughout the teacher’s evaluation of assistant turns. In contrast, r_{k}^{L} is visible only when the teacher evaluates the assistant turn a_{k+1} following o_{k}, and does not propagate to later turns. Instruction-Following (IF) SFT first strengthens the model’s ability to understand and respond to explicit constraints and feedback. During OPRD, Multi-Scope Reminders serve as training-time privileged information available only to the teacher, and the behavior they induce is distilled into a student that does not observe reminders.

When a trajectory contains a correctable failure, we construct reminders post hoc from the task, trajectory, interaction feedback, and final test results. We determine the scope of each corrective signal and then assign its functional category. The Global Reminder contains one category, Test-Outcome Feedback, which converts final-test diagnostics into trajectory-level guidance. Turn-local Reminders target correctable decisions identified from each environment observation and assistant action. They comprise four categories: Tool-Feedback Recovery for responding to explicit tool feedback; Scope and Source Grounding for evidence-grounded localization and modification; Scenario-Condition Reasoning for task-specific execution conditions; and Post-Edit Control and Validation for controlled post-edit verification. We retain grounded and actionable candidates, discarding ambiguous, redundant, unverifiable, reference-patch-revealing, or unsupported content. Detailed category definitions, generation prompts, trigger rules, and filtering procedures are provided in Appendix C.

The base model first acquires capabilities for repository understanding, tool interaction, and code editing through Coding SFT. However, coding competence alone does not ensure that the model will follow constraints and feedback that arise during an interaction. A standard coding model may still ignore user requirements, tool responses, test errors, or harness rules that are already present in the context. Given a base model \psi_{0}, we first train on successful coding trajectories \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{code}} to establish core agentic coding capabilities. We then use IF data \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{IF}} to improve the model’s responsiveness to user constraints, interaction feedback, execution outcomes, and reminders, yielding an IF checkpoint \psi_{\mathrm{IF}} that combines coding and instruction-following capabilities: \psi_{\mathrm{code}}=\operatorname{SFT}(\psi_{0},\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{code}}),\qquad\psi_{\mathrm{IF}}=\operatorname{SFT}(\psi_{\mathrm{code}},\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{IF}}).

OPRD uses shared initialization. The teacher \pi_{\phi} and student \pi_{\theta} use the same model architecture and are initialized with the parameters of the same IF checkpoint \psi_{\mathrm{IF}}, such that \theta^{(0)}=\phi^{(0)}=\psi_{\mathrm{IF}}. During training, the teacher is periodically updated toward the student, while the student is optimized at every step. The teacher additionally receives reminders as training-time privileged information. For a task x\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{task}}, the current student interacts with the coding environment without access to reminders to sample \tau\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x). As the student is updated, subsequent rollouts expose different states and errors, keeping reminder supervision aligned with the distribution visited by the current policy.

After each rollout, an executable verifier determines whether it succeeds but does not provide fine-grained credit assignment. A successful rollout provides executable evidence that the student’s current behavior can solve the task and can therefore serve directly as an autoregressive self-imitation signal. Applying the same objective to a failed rollout would instead increase the likelihood of erroneous decisions. OPRD thus routes successful rollouts to a self-imitation branch and failed rollouts to a reminder-conditioned distillation branch. For the current rollout batch \mathcal{B}, we define \mathcal{B}_{+}=\{\tau\in\mathcal{B}\mid c(\tau)=1\} and \mathcal{B}_{-}=\{\tau\in\mathcal{B}\mid c(\tau)=0\}.

For each \tau\in\mathcal{B}_{+}, we compute the autoregressive loss over all valid assistant tokens to increase the likelihood that the student reproduces successful behavior discovered through its own on-policy sampling: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pass}}(\tau)=-\frac{1}{|\Omega(\tau)|}\sum_{(k,j)\in\Omega(\tau)}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{k,j}\mid h_{k,j}^{S}).

For each \tau\in\mathcal{B}_{-}, reminders are constructed after the rollout and provided only to the teacher. The student always uses the original context without reminders. The teacher does not resample the trajectory. Instead, it evaluates the same student-generated token prefix y_{k,<j}, ensuring that the distillation targets remain aligned with the states visited by the current policy. For the k -th assistant turn, the teacher history is defined as \widetilde{H}_{k}^{T}=\begin{cases}\operatorname{Inject}(H_{k},r^{G},r_{k-1}^{L}),&\begin{subarray}{c}k\geq 2,\\ k-1\in\mathcal{I}_{\tau}\end{subarray},\\ \operatorname{Inject}(H_{k},r^{G}),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} The corresponding teacher token context is h_{k,j}^{T}=(\widetilde{H}_{k}^{T},y_{k,<j}). The teacher augments the student’s original context with the reminders active at the current scope. The Global Reminder is visible at every assistant turn, whereas r_{k-1}^{L} is injected only when the teacher evaluates a_{k} and is removed from subsequent turns. Reminder scope is determined by its visibility in the teacher context, while the loss for a failed trajectory still covers all valid assistant tokens in \Omega(\tau). Within this unified distillation signal, the Global Reminder provides task-level correction across turns, while the Turn-local Reminder provides fine-grained guidance at the corresponding decision point. Let \mathcal{V} denote the full vocabulary, and let z_{\theta} and z_{\phi} denote the student and teacher logits, respectively. For v\in\mathcal{V}, their token distributions at temperature \mathcal{T} are \begin{split}p_{\theta,k,j}^{(\mathcal{T})}(v)&=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{z_{\theta}(h_{k,j}^{S})}{\mathcal{T}}\right)_{v},\\ p_{\phi,k,j}^{(\mathcal{T})}(v)&=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{z_{\phi}(h_{k,j}^{T})}{\mathcal{T}}\right)_{v}.\end{split}

We then compute the reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence over the Top-K-vocabulary distributions: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fail}}(\tau)=\frac{\mathcal{T}^{2}}{|\Omega(\tau)|}\sum_{(k,j)\in\Omega(\tau)}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left[p_{\theta,k,j}^{(\mathcal{T})}\;\middle\|\;\operatorname{sg}\!\left[p_{\phi,k,j}^{(\mathcal{T})}\right]\right], where \operatorname{sg} stops gradients through the teacher branch and \mathcal{T}^{2} compensates for gradient-scale changes from temperature scaling. Reverse KL weights discrepancies by the student distribution, prioritizing corrections to tokens to which the student assigns high probability in visited states.

After training, only the student is deployed. The teacher, the reminder-construction module, and all reminders are removed at inference time. Let \lambda_{+} and \lambda_{-} control the relative strengths of self-imitation on successful rollouts and reminder distillation on failed rollouts, respectively. The OPRD objective is \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPRD}}=\lambda_{+}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\in\mathcal{B}_{+}}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pass}}(\tau)]+\lambda_{-}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\in\mathcal{B}_{-}}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fail}}(\tau)].

We use Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B as base models (Qwen Team 2026). Training consists of three stages. Coding SFT uses 8,000 verified successful trajectories, including 7,262 from SWE-rebench V2 (Badertdinov et al. 2026) and 738 from Multi-SWE-RL (Zan et al. 2025). IF SFT then uses 2,000 reminder-following examples from SWE-rebench V2. OPRD operates on a pool of 3,630 SWE-rebench V2 tasks and 370 Multi-SWE-RL tasks, from which the student generates reminder-free rollouts online. In the OPRD variant without IF SFT, both teacher and student are initialized from the Coding SFT checkpoint while all other settings remain unchanged.

Table 1 summarizes the three stage-specific data configurations. Coding SFT and IF SFT operate on trajectories or reminder-following examples, whereas OPRD uses a task pool from which the current student generates new rollouts online. The OPRD counts therefore describe available training tasks rather than a fixed set of trajectories.

Figure 3 reports the programming-language composition of the three stages. Python is the largest source in every stage (43.5–45.8%), followed by TypeScript and JavaScript. Coding SFT and the OPRD task pool use nearly identical proportions by construction, while the IF set is slightly more concentrated in Python, JavaScript, and Rust and contains no Ruby example. The distribution nevertheless covers nine languages in IF SFT and all ten languages in Coding SFT and OPRD.
Training implementation and hyperparameters are detailed in Appendix B.

We evaluate task resolution rate on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, and SWE-bench Multilingual (OpenAI 2024; Deng et al. 2025b; Yang et al. 2025a). All models use the same agent harness and inference configuration. Except for the controlled Reminder interventions in the scope and functional-category analyses, all main results and training ablations use reminder-free inference.

All models are evaluated with a shared Claude Code agent scaffold and the executable verifier associated with each benchmark. Every subtask is allocated 16 CPU cores and 32,768 MiB of memory, with a maximum of 200 agent turns. Decoding uses temperature 1.0 and top- p 0.95. The vLLM deployment permits at most 128 concurrent sequences, a maximum model length of 262,144 tokens, and 8,192 batched tokens.

section: OPRD provides consistent gains across software engineering benchmarks.
text: Table 2 compares the base and supervised checkpoints with the OPRD variants to assess whether Reminder-conditioned process supervision transfers to reminder-free inference. The complete training recipe reaches an average resolution rate of 47.9, improving over the Qwen3.5-4B base model by 11.3 points and over the IF SFT checkpoint by 6.3 points. Gains are consistent across all three benchmarks, with the largest improvement on SWE-bench Multilingual. Removing IF SFT before OPRD reduces the average by 3.6 points. This gap suggests that coding adaptation alone is insufficient for fully exploiting Reminder-conditioned supervision, whereas IF SFT provides a more suitable shared initialization for teacher and student. Because all entries in Table 2 use reminder-free inference, the improvement does not depend on test-time Reminder injection.

section: OPRD gains persist with the 9B backbone.
text: As shown in Table 2, the complete Qwen3.5-9B training recipe reaches an average resolution rate of 55.9, improving over the open-source checkpoint by 11.5 points and over the IF SFT checkpoint by 5.4 points. The improvement over the open-source model is consistent on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, and SWE-bench Multilingual, with gains of 10.4, 8.6, and 15.4 points, respectively. Removing IF SFT before OPRD lowers the average by 2.6 points, showing that the supervised instruction-following preparation remains useful at the larger model scale.

We examine the distillation design, loss balance, teacher refresh, supervised preparation, and Reminder scope and functional categories, followed by a process-level error analysis. Training ablations use the same task pool and on-policy rollout protocol; Reminder interventions are compared under shared inference settings.

The OPRD variant without IF SFT initializes both the teacher and student from the Coding SFT checkpoint and otherwise retains the complete OPRD configuration. In the distillation-formulation ablation, All-Rollout OPSD applies the selected KL objective to both successful and failed on-policy rollouts. Outcome-Routed OPRD instead applies autoregressive self-imitation to verified successes and Multi-Scope Reminder-conditioned KL to failures. The compared rows use the same training tasks, on-policy rollout budget, Top-100 support, and distillation temperature.

The teacher-refresh ablation compares a frozen teacher, periodic refresh schedules, and shared teacher–student parameters. The frozen teacher remains at its initial checkpoint. Our four-refresh setting copies the current student parameters to the teacher at 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80% of training. Under shared parameters, the teacher context is evaluated with the current student parameters at every update while gradients remain stopped through the teacher branch.

section: Effect of KL support and distillation temperature.
text: The KL-support ablation compares full-vocabulary and Top-100 supports and varies the distillation temperature to identify an effective distributional target for OPRD. At the shared temperature of \mathcal{T}=0.6, Top-100 and full-vocabulary KL perform similarly, with Top-100 obtaining a slightly higher average score. This indicates that a sparse high-probability support is sufficient for effective distillation in this setting. Among the Top-100 variants, \mathcal{T}=1.0 performs best with an average score of 47.9, while both lower and higher temperatures perform worse, suggesting that a moderate temperature balances teacher preferences with useful alternatives.

section: Effect of outcome-based routing and KL direction.
text: A paired comparison of All-Rollout OPSD and Outcome-Routed OPRD under forward and reverse KL isolates the effects of outcome-based routing and KL direction. Reverse KL outperforms forward KL under both training strategies. At a fixed KL direction, OPRD consistently improves over OPSD, with a 1.9-point gain under reverse KL. These results support assigning verified successes to autoregressive self-imitation and failures to Reminder-conditioned distillation, rather than applying a single KL objective uniformly to all rollouts. Reverse KL further focuses the update on candidates that the student assigns high probability but the Reminder-conditioned teacher considers inappropriate.

The balanced 1{:}1 setting performs best on all three benchmarks and obtains a 47.9 average. Reducing \lambda_{+} over-concentrates training on correcting failed states and weakens retention of successful behavior already discovered by the current policy. Increasing \lambda_{+} gradually shifts the objective toward successful-trajectory self-imitation and underuses the process supervision supplied by Reminders on failed states. SWE-bench Pro and SWE-bench Multilingual are more sensitive to this imbalance because they contain more tasks that require correction from tool feedback and cross-file context.

section: Effect of the teacher refresh schedule.
text: Varying the teacher refresh schedule examines the trade-off between adapting to the evolving student and maintaining a stable distillation target. As shown in Fig. 4, periodic refreshes exhibit a non-monotonic trend, with four evenly spaced refreshes performing best on every benchmark and reaching an average resolution rate of 47.9. This pattern suggests that a frozen teacher may become misaligned with states visited by the evolving student, whereas overly frequent refreshes may reduce target stability. The Shared Parameters setting performs worst, further supporting the importance of a relatively stable teacher target for Reminder-conditioned distillation.

A controlled comparison of four Reminder conditions across the Base, Coding SFT, and IF SFT checkpoints measures Reminder utility and model responsiveness. Both Global-only and Turn-local-only conditioning improve every checkpoint on all benchmarks, while combining them consistently performs best. Turn-local Reminders generally provide larger gains, while the additional improvement from Global Reminders shows that persistent cross-turn guidance complements feedback aligned with a specific environment observation. The average benefit of Multi-Scope Reminders grows across preparation stages and reaches 4.9 points after IF SFT, indicating that IF SFT improves the model’s ability to use corrective information at different scopes.

section: Effect of IF SFT on Reminder responsiveness.
text: As shown in Fig. 6, the aggregate Reminder-following rate increases from 45.8 for the open-source base model to 49.3 after Coding SFT, and then to 77.1 after IF SFT. Relative to Coding SFT, IF SFT improves the rate by 27.8 points overall and by 25.9–30.4 points across the four functional categories. Its category-level rates are consistently high, ranging from 75.4 for Scenario-Condition Reasoning to 80.0 for Post-Edit Control and Validation. The largest gain over Coding SFT occurs for Scope and Source Grounding, which increases from 46.3 to 76.7. These results isolate behavioral adherence to an inserted Reminder rather than end-to-end task resolution, and support using the IF checkpoint as the shared teacher–student initialization for OPRD.

Grouping Reminders by content rather than temporal scope evaluates the contribution of each functional category. All four categories in Fig. 8 outperform reminder-free evaluation, with Post-Edit Control and Validation providing the strongest individual result. Enabling all categories raises the average resolution rate from 36.6 to 39.2, suggesting that they provide complementary corrective signals and broader coverage when combined.

Applying the same four-category taxonomy as Fig. 1 tests whether OPRD’s task-level gains coincide with fewer process errors. Each checkpoint generates one reminder-free trajectory for the same 200 SWE-rebench V2 validation tasks under identical inference settings, and we record case-level triggers from the resulting trajectories. As shown in Fig. 7, the total number of triggers falls from 446 for Qwen3.5-4B to 378 after Coding SFT and 222 after OPRD, a 50.2% reduction relative to Qwen3.5-4B. Trigger counts decline by 43.1–58.0% across categories, with the largest decrease in Post-Edit Control and Validation. These results show that OPRD improves both final task resolution and intermediate process behavior.

Long-horizon coding agents must preserve task constraints and respond to interaction feedback while producing correct code. Our diagnostic analysis highlights process-level failures throughout repository-level problem solving. We introduce OPRD, which uses Multi-Scope Reminders as training-time privileged information and applies outcome-based routing to on-policy rollouts. A Global Reminder converts final-test diagnostics into trajectory-level guidance, while Turn-local Reminders anchor observation-derived corrections to the next assistant decision. OPRD routes successful rollouts to autoregressive self-imitation and failed rollouts to Reminder-conditioned reverse-KL distillation. Its two-stage supervised cold start, consisting of Coding SFT followed by Instruction-Following SFT, improves responsiveness to these corrective signals. Experiments show that OPRD improves task resolution and reduces adherence failures. By internalizing trajectory-level feedback and local corrections into model parameters, OPRD enables long-horizon coding agents to operate without Reminders at inference time.

Compositional Activation Steering Across Languages and Behaviors with Contextual Gates. Activation steering has emerged as an effective and precise way to influence the behaviours of language models. However, composing multiple steering directions to control several behaviours simultaneously remains challenging, particularly in multilingual settings and with training-free steering vectors. We address this challenge with contextual steering, jointly training gates that adapt the strength of fixed steering directions to the current hidden state and interactions between interventions. Across a broad range of languages, behavioural attributes, and models, our approach outperforms constant-strength steering and four strong baselines, including prompting. It also better preserves general knowledge and keeps the model's internal computation closer to that of the prompted model. Our analysis further shows how jointly trained gates adapt their contributions during composition, explaining the mechanisms underlying effective compositional steering.

Inference-time steering shifts a model’s activation trajectory toward a desired behaviour without updating its weights (Turner et al., 2025). It has been used to control a range of attributes, including style (Konen et al., 2024), factuality (Rimsky et al., 2024), truthfulness (Li et al., 2023), language identity (Gurgurov et al., 2026), and refusal (Arditi et al., 2024). For language control in particular, recent work shows that steering remains effective across variation in input language and content (Sterz et al., 2025; Chou et al., 2025; Michaelov et al., 2026; Gurgurov et al., 2026), suggesting that it can serve as a form of adaptation (Ostermann et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). Yet, most existing work considers only one attribute at a time. In realistic settings, models often need to satisfy several constraints simultaneously, such as generating text in a specified language while adhering to a behavioural requirement.

Although several approaches to compositional steering have been explored (Nguyen et al., 2025; Oozeer et al., 2025; Ghasemi et al., 2026), effectively composing multiple attributes remains challenging, particularly in multilingual settings (Scalena et al., 2024; Kang et al., 2026). A central difficulty is that interventions that work well in isolation may interact when combined in the residual stream, making their effects difficult to predict. Moreover, fixed intervention strengths cannot adapt to the current context, where an attribute may already be expressed to varying degrees. Effective composition therefore requires interventions that account for both the current hidden state and the interactions between attributes

Contextual steering offers a way to address these challenges by using gates to determine intervention strengths from the current state (Hsu et al., 2026). We extend this idea to compositional steering by jointly training such gates for multiple attributes while keeping their steering directions fixed, allowing each gate to adapt its contribution in the presence of other interventions. We evaluate this approach across languages, behavioural attributes, and models, analyse its effects on knowledge retention, and investigate why contextual steering works by examining internal representations, output distributions, and interactions between interventions.

Our contributions are as follows: We establish a cross-lingual evaluation setup for composing language steering with general- and safety-related behavioural attributes, covering variation in both language and meaning. We introduce a compositional steering method that jointly trains context-dependent gates while keeping steering directions fixed. Across 9 models, 9 target languages, and 14 behavioural directions, it outperforms constant-strength steering and four additional strong baselines. We show that contextual composition substantially improves knowledge retention over constant-level steering, while maintaining strong performance across languages, including languages unseen during training. We analyse the internal dynamics of steering, showing that contextual interventions keep representations and intermediate output distributions closer to those of the prompted model, while jointly trained gates adapt their contributions during composition.

Two common bottlenecks in steering are layer selection and steering-strength tuning, which are typically resolved through manual sweeps (Turner et al., 2025; Konen et al., 2024; Rimsky et al., 2024). Our method avoids both, by applying interventions at every layer and learning a gate that determines the intervention strength from the current hidden state. Figure 1 provides an overview of our approach.

For an attribute a, we extract one steering direction per layer, d_{\ell}^{(a)}, as the unit-normed difference in means (Marks and Tegmark, 2024; Wu et al., 2025) of the last-token residual activations h_{\ell} between texts that exhibit a and those that do not.
Constant-strength steering, referred to as CAA in prior literature (Rimsky et al., 2024; Radevski et al., 2026; Ghasemi et al., 2026), applies the same scalar intervention strength at every layer
h_{\ell}\leftarrow h_{\ell}+\gamma^{(a)}\,d_{\ell}^{(a)},
where \gamma^{(a)} (\boldsymbol{\gamma}) is selected once per attribute by a grid search over a predefined range. The same value is used at all layers.

We build on the contextual steering method of Hsu et al. (2026), referred to as CLAS, keeping d_{\ell}^{(a)} fixed while learning a per-layer, per-attribute affine gate: \alpha_{\ell}^{(a)}=w_{\ell}^{(a)\top}h_{\ell}+b_{\ell}^{(a)},\qquad h_{\ell}\leftarrow h_{\ell}+\underbrace{\alpha_{\ell}^{(a)}\,d_{\ell}^{(a)}}_{\nu^{(a)}(h_{\ell})}. Here, {\color[rgb]{0.3516,0.5508,0.3516}\boldsymbol{\nu}^{(a)}(h_{\ell})} is a context-dependent intervention in place of the constant {\color[rgb]{0.7461,0.3125,0.2734}\boldsymbol{\gamma}^{(a)}}. The gate is the only trainable component; the language model and steering directions remain frozen. Training minimizes next-token cross-entropy on the completion tokens of prompt-completion pairs exhibiting a. Since the steering direction is fixed and the gate is a rank-one linear projection, the method requires little training data and introduces few trainable parameters (see Appendix M for details on efficiency). Training data and hyperparameters are described in Appendices A.1 and A.2.

We additionally regularize the training objective with an anchor to prevent the gates from collapsing to minimal intervention strengths or not firing at all. Specifically, we add a quadratic penalty that pulls the gate outputs at each layer \ell and token position t toward a fixed target \alpha_{\star}:
\mathcal{L}=\mathrm{CE}+\lambda\cdot\mathbb{E}_{\ell,t}\big(\alpha_{\ell,t}^{(a)}-\alpha_{\star}\big)^{2}.

The anchor weight \lambda and the gate learning rate are swept over a small grid, and the best configuration is selected using a held-out score. Setting \lambda=0 reduces the objective to unconstrained cross-entropy. Training uses small train and validation splits with early stopping on validation loss; further details are provided in Appendix A.1.

We compose n attributes by summing their interventions in the same residual stream: h_{\ell}\leftarrow h_{\ell}+\sum_{a=1}^{n}\nu^{(a)}(h_{\ell})=h_{\ell}+\sum_{a=1}^{n}\alpha_{\ell}^{(a)}\,d_{\ell}^{(a)}. Each \alpha_{\ell}^{(a)} is computed from the current h_{\ell} before the interventions at layer \ell, so all attributes are evaluated in the same residual state. The single-attribute gates from § 2.1 can therefore be composed without modification; we refer to this as the independent-gate baseline (§ 3). However, during inference, each gate receives a residual state that has already been affected by the other attributes, which differs from the states observed during its single-attribute training.

We, thus, propose an alternative, more robust composite-steering method by training the gates for each attribute combination jointly, with all composed interventions active during training. This allows each gate to adapt to the residual produced by the other attributes. We consider two variants.

Let \theta^{(a)}=\{(w_{\ell}^{(a)},b_{\ell}^{(a)})\} denote the gate parameters for attribute a. Each gate is initialized from its single-attribute checkpoint, and all n gates are then optimized jointly using a shared next-token cross-entropy objective, with the composed steering active during the forward pass: \displaystyle\min_{\theta^{(1)},\dots,\theta^{(n)}} \displaystyle\mathrm{CE}\Big(y\;\Big|\;x;\;\;h_{\ell}\leftarrow h_{\ell}+\sum_{a=1}^{n}\alpha_{\ell}^{(a)}d_{\ell}^{(a)}\Big), \displaystyle\text{where }\alpha_{\ell}^{(a)}=w_{\ell}^{(a)\top}h_{\ell}+b_{\ell}^{(a)}\text{ for each }a. Here, x is the prompt and y is a completion exhibiting all n attributes, obtained as in Section § 2.1. The shared loss updates all gate parameters simultaneously, so each gate is trained against a residual carrying the compounded effect of every attribute’s earlier-layer deltas.

For multi-attribute combinations, we also consider a sequential variant. We keep the pretrained gate for the first attribute fixed and optimize only the second gate using the same cross-entropy objective, with both interventions active during the forward pass. Unlike joint setup, this approach allows the second gate to adapt to the first while leaving the first gate unchanged.

We evaluate on nine instruction-tuned models spanning five model families and three sizes: Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.2-3B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen-2.5-{3B,7B,14B} (Yang et al., 2025b), Gemma-2-{2B,9B} (Team et al., 2024), Mistral-7B (Jiang et al., 2023), and Aya-Expanse-8B (Dang et al., 2024).

We select attributes that have been widely studied in the steering literature, but mostly in isolation. We consider nine target languages from FLORES (NLLB Team et al., 2024): English, German, Japanese, Russian, Korean, Spanish, Italian, Arabic, and Polish. We additionally evaluate seven behavioural attributes: chain-of-thought, formality, humour, truthfulness (Lin et al., 2022), refusal (Arditi et al., 2024), bias (Parrish et al., 2022), and toxicity (Hartvigsen et al., 2022). Each single attribute is steered toward one of its two poles (e.g., funny vs. serious for humour). Two-way composition pairs each of the 9 languages with each of the 14 behaviour poles (126 compositions); three-way composition pairs each language with one style pole (chain-of-thought, formality, or humour) and one safety pole (refusal, truthfulness, bias, or toxicity), for 108 triples.

We evaluate every attribute and attribute combinations on held-out prompts from either CLaS-Bench (Gurgurov et al., 2026), a parallel collection of open-ended questions across 32 languages, or an attribute-specific dataset where needed: harmful and harmless instructions for jailbreak from Arditi et al. (2024), TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2022) for truthfulness, BBQ (Parrish et al., 2022) for bias, and ToxiGen Hartvigsen et al. (2022) for toxicity. For most attributes, we use a mixed-language source distribution, with questions pooled across several languages rather than restricted to English. This provides a more challenging setting than using a single source language. Further details are in Appendix A.3.

Each attribute has a task-specific score, e.g. a FastText-LID language-fidelity score (Joulin et al., 2017), an LLM-judged register score for style attributes, or a safety-classifier or reference-match rate for the corresponding behavioural attributes. Every run additionally reports Output Relevance (OR), a judged score in \{0,1.0,2.0\} measuring whether the completion still answers the question faithfully; OR is omitted when the task score already subsumes relevance. We use Qwen-3-8B (Yang et al., 2025a) as the judge for task scores and OR, and Qwen-3-Guard (Zhao et al., 2025) for safety-related attributes; the exact prompts are provided in Appendix E. We additionally validate these judgments using larger 30B-MoE and 32B judges, finding high agreement (Appendix E.2). The main scores reported for single- and multi-attribute results are the harmonic means (HM) of all active scores (task score(s) + OR), following Wu et al. (2025) and Gurgurov et al. (2026). The HM penalizes the final score when any individual sub-score is low.

We compare against five baselines: (1) prompting (\boldsymbol{\pi}) as a token-space reference (Appendix E.4); (2) constant-level steering (CAA; \boldsymbol{\gamma}) composed additively across independently-tuned attributes (Rimsky et al., 2024; Kang et al., 2026); (3) contextual CLAS (\boldsymbol{\nu}(x)) composed from independently trained gates; (4) K-Steering (\boldsymbol{\kappa}(x)) Oozeer et al. (2025), which derives intervention directions from gradients of a learned multi-label classifier; and (5) ORBIT (\boldsymbol{\omega}(x)) (Ghasemi et al., 2026), a training-free method that rotates activations within a shared multi-attribute subspace, gated per token. For each baseline, we perform extensive method-appropriate hyperparameter sweeps (Appendix A.1).
We report single-, double, and tripple-attribute results, with significance tests in Appendix I.

We first evaluate language and behavioural attributes independently, averaging scores over all 9 languages and 14 behaviours for each model. Figure 2 compares prompting, constant-strength CAA, and contextual CLAS. CLAS consistently outperforms CAA across all nine models, with gains ranging from 1.3 to 21.9 points. The largest gains are observed for Aya-8B (21.9 points), Mistral-7B (20.0), and Llama-3.1-8B (17.0). The advantage is also consistent across attributes (Table 11 in Appendix F). Removing the anchoring objective substantially degrades performance (Appendix B), highlighting its importance for robust contextual steering in this setting.

CLAS also compares favourably with prompting, which we use primarily as a token-space reference rather than as a steering baseline. It outperforms prompting on seven of nine models and remains within two points on the other two. These results show that residual-stream interventions can provide competitive attribute control without modifying the model weights or relying solely on input-level instructions.

We next evaluate the composition of language and behavioural steering across all languages and 14 behavioural directions. Table 1 reports scores averaged across behaviours and models, broken down by target language. Joint-CLAS substantially outperforms the other steering approaches, achieving an overall average of 82.5%, compared with 78.3% for sequential CLAS, 72.4% for prompting, and 49.6% for CAA. K-Steering achieves 43.2%, comparable to CAA, while ORBIT achieves 48.2%, outperforming K-Steering; both results are consistent with their reported performance (Oozeer et al., 2025; Ghasemi et al., 2026). Joint-CLAS also performs consistently across models, reaching at least 77.1% on every model and exceeding 80% on seven of nine. Independently trained gates, in contrast, do not reliably preserve single-attribute performance. Joint-CLAS addresses this mismatch by jointly training all gates with the composed interventions active, allowing each gate to adapt to the residual stream produced by the other attributes. Sequential CLAS also improves over independent composition but remains below Joint-CLAS, highlighting the benefit of jointly optimizing interacting attributes. We investigate these interactions and their effects on the residual stream in Section 5. The results extend to three-attribute composition.
Joint-CLAS again outperforms the competing methods across models, achieving at least 80% on every model; see the radar plots in Figure 3.

Importantly, the behavioural directions are extracted entirely from English-only data, yet compose successfully with language-specific directions across multiple target languages. This suggests that behavioural steering directions can transfer across languages, consistent with previous findings on shared multilingual representations (Mousi et al., 2024; Riemenschneider and Frank, 2025; Yang et al., 2026). Our results extend this observation to steering directions across languages and behavioural attributes.

The jointly trained gates and their corresponding directions also generalize to languages not seen during their construction. We evaluate the composition configurations on Chinese, Portuguese, Hindi, French, Norwegian, and Czech. Results in Appendix J show that the learned interventions transfer beyond the languages used during training.

We additionally evaluate how well steering preserve the model’s general knowledge by measuring accuracy on MMLU Hendrycks et al. (2021), ARC-Easy and -Challenge Clark et al. (2018), and Winogrande Sakaguchi et al. (2020). Figure 3 (right) reports results averaged over Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.2-3B. Joint-CLAS achieves an average accuracy of 63.9%, substantially outperforming composed CAA (41.6%) and single-attribute CAA (62.3%), although it remains below single-attribute CLAS (68.1%) and the unsteered baseline (70.7%). Three-way Joint-CLAS also outperforms its CAA counterpart with 61.2% over 39.2%. This advantage highlights the benefit of contextual steering: by adapting intervention strength to the current state, Joint-CLAS can avoid unnecessary interventions and better preserve general knowledge than constant-strength composition. Some degradation relative to the unsteered model is expected, as steering necessarily modifies the model’s representations to enforce additional output constraints.

We next investigate what happens inside the model when steering succeeds, both for individual attributes and under composition. We hypothesize that contextual steering is more compatible with the model’s natural computation than constant steering, allowing it to enforce target attributes while minimizing unnecessary changes to the residual stream.

Figure 4 (A) shows the gate activity across layers and token positions for an example of language steering. Rather than intervening uniformly, the gate concentrates its activity at particular positions and depths. This suggests that it selectively reinforces the target attribute depending on the current context. Additional examples in Appendix L show similar patterns.

We next examine whether this selective intervention keeps the model’s internal computation closer to its natural behaviour. We use the prompted model as a reference, since it produces activations without residual-stream interventions. Figure 4 (B) compares the projection of generated-token representations onto the steering direction across layers. For representation h_{\ell} and steering direction d_{\ell}, we compute p_{\ell}=h_{\ell}^{\top}d_{\ell}. We then quantify the deviation from the prompted model as |p_{\ell}-p_{\ell}^{\mathrm{prompt}}|. Compared with CAA, CLAS produces a trajectory closer to the prompted model while still shifting the representation in the desired direction.

We similarly compare the model’s output distributions using the logit lens (Nostalgebraist, 2020). Figure 4 (C) shows the KL divergence between the intermediate next-token distribution P_{\ell} and that of the prompted model P_{\ell}^{\mathrm{prompt}}: \sum_{y}P_{\ell}(y)\log\frac{P_{\ell}(y)}{P_{\ell}^{\mathrm{prompt}}(y)}. We average this divergence over the last five layers, where logit lens predictions are more closely aligned with the model’s final output (Wendler et al., 2024). Lower divergence indicates that intermediate predictions remain closer to those of the prompted model. CLAS again exhibits lower divergence than CAA.

Finally, Figure 4 (D) visualizes the geometry of generated-token representations at early, middle, and late layers using principal component analysis (PCA) (Pearson, 1901). We quantify the distribution shift between steered and prompted representations using the Earth Mover’s distance (EMD) (Villani, 2009) in the first two principal components, following Grant et al. (2026). Table 2 aggregates the three measures across attributes and models for both single- and multi-attribute steering. Across all three metrics, contextual steering remains closer to the prompted model than constant-strength steering. The differences are particularly pronounced under composition, where Joint-CLAS achieves the lowest values for every metric. This suggests that contextual gates do more than simply reduce the overall intervention strength: they adapt interventions in ways that better preserve the model’s existing computational trajectory.

We next examine how gates change when two attributes are trained jointly. Figure 5 (A) compares generation-time gate activity before and after joint training for an example composition. Joint training substantially changes intervention strengths, particularly in later layers, rather than simply preserving the independently learned gate activities. This indicates that the gates adapt to the presence of the other intervention. Figure 5 (B) provides a more direct view of this co-adaptation. Joint training increases gate coactivation while reducing sign agreement (Table 3). We define coactivation as the mean product of the gate magnitudes, |a_{A}a_{B}|, across layers and generated tokens. Sign agreement is the fraction of layer-token pairs for which a_{A}a_{B}\geq 0. The interference ratio measures the magnitude of the combined intervention relative to the sum of the individual magnitudes, \frac{\lVert\Delta_{A}+\Delta_{B}\rVert}{|a_{A}|+|a_{B}|}, where values closer to 1 indicate less cancellation between the two interventions.

Thus, the gates do not learn to avoid interacting with one another; instead, they tend to activate more strongly together, with more frequent opposing signs. At the same time, the interference ratio increases, indicating that a larger fraction of the combined intervention strength is retained despite these stronger interactions. Joint training, therefore, changes not only how strongly each attribute is applied, but also how their interventions combine in the residual stream.

These findings suggest that successful composition depends on coordinating intervention strengths, rather than simply combining individually effective interventions. This is consistent with the low cosine similarity between steering directions shown in Figure 5 (C), indicating that the directions themselves are largely separated in representation space. Similar observations have been made for the composability of steering directions (Kang et al., 2026). The main challenge, however, lies not only in the directions themselves, but also in how the interventions interact in the residual stream, which Joint-CLAS addresses by adapting the gates to the composed setting.

Marks and Tegmark (2024) show that true and false representations exhibit a linear structure, motivating linear steering directions such as difference-in-means. Activation steering has since been applied to a range of behaviours, including style (Konen et al., 2024), factuality and sycophancy (Rimsky et al., 2024), truthfulness (Li et al., 2023), refusal (Arditi et al., 2024), and language (Michaelov et al., 2026). These approaches typically use a constant steering strength and require manual selection of the intervention layer and strength. Hsu et al. (2026) instead introduce sensing-vector gates that adapt the steering strength to the context, demonstrating their effectiveness with directions learned by the Recursive Feature Machines (Beaglehole et al., 2026).

Compositional steering has been explored in the embedding space through learned steering tokens (Radevski et al., 2026), in the unembedding space through learned output transformations (Han et al., 2024), and in activation space (Scalena et al., 2024; Nguyen et al., 2025; Oozeer et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026), which is the setting we study.

In activation space, Scalena et al. (2024) steer behaviours across attention heads using a gating function that compares the outputs of two parallel model passes through their KL divergence. Nguyen et al. (2025) jointly learn steering vectors and per-token intervention strengths with orthogonality, sparsity, and related objectives, operating at the attention-output level; such multi-objective optimization can be difficult to optimize robustly in practice. In contrast, we keep the steering directions fixed and train only the gates, keeping our method close to training-free steering while operating directly in the residual stream. Oozeer et al. (2025) propose K-Steering, which trains a non-linear multi-label classifier on activations and uses its gradients at inference time to derive intervention directions. Ghasemi et al. (2026) propose ORBIT, which rotates activations within a shared multi-attribute subspace at inference time, gated per token, without training. Kang et al. (2026) instead compose constant-strength steering directions and show that composition can succeed when intervention layers and strengths are appropriately selected, but is not reliable across settings.

Other studies investigate composition as a side experiment. van der Weij et al. (2024) find that injecting multiple vectors at the same layer can be destructive, and Stolfo et al. (2025) find greater success when vectors are injected at separate layers. Cao et al. (2024) show that vectors learned through preference optimization can also be combined, with partial success for a single combination.

Among prior work, Scalena et al. (2024) and Kang et al. (2026) most directly study multilingual composition in activation space. Scalena et al. (2024) dynamically assign intervention strengths to individual properties using a reference model, without accounting for the residual changes induced by simultaneously steering other properties. Their method requires two forward passes per step at inference, operates at the attention level, and is evaluated on a single model across four languages. Kang et al. (2026) use constant-strength steering and rely on per-model, per-layer, and per-attribute grid search, finding that composition depends strongly on the choice of intervention layers and strengths.

In contrast, we train a contextual gate for each attribute and then jointly train the gates for each attribute combination. Each gate therefore learns in the same residual-stream context in which it is used at inference, while requiring no additional forward passes. We evaluate the resulting method across a much broader range of attribute combinations, languages, and models, and additionally provide a representational account of why it succeeds.

In this work, we showed that simple training-free steering vectors can be composed effectively when their interactions are accounted for through contextual steering and jointly trained gating functions. The resulting approach is robust across attribute combinations, languages, and models, while preserving more general knowledge than constant-strength composition. We further investigated why contextual steering is effective and found that gate-based interventions produce internal dynamics that remain closer to those of the prompted model, suggesting that contextual steering can achieve stronger attribute control while better preserving the model’s existing computation.

Our approach requires computing steering directions and gates separately for each model; transferring them across models remains an interesting direction for future work. We also use next-token cross-entropy to train the gates, although contrastive or other task-specific objectives may prove more suitable. A further limitation is that joint training requires first training the single-attribute gates used for warm-starting, introducing an extra training stage, though the overall procedure remains efficient in practice (Appendix M). Our experiments also focus on a single method for extracting steering directions; although difference-in-means vectors are simple and effective in our setting, it would be valuable to investigate alternatives, including SAE-derived features and probe weights. Finally, we attempted to reproduce MAT-Steer (Nguyen et al., 2025), but found its multi-objective optimization difficult to tune in our setting; in particular, the second attribute often had little observable effect. This is consistent with the optimization challenges of this method discussed by Ghasemi et al. (2026), although it does not establish that the method is ineffective more generally.

The harmful attributes explored in this work (i.e., jailbreak, bias, and toxicity) are studied solely for scientific purposes, to understand and expose how easily current models can be steered toward harmful behaviours. Methods for improving model robustness against such steering should be developed alongside these techniques.

Dynamic Positional Attention Modulation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has become a standard approach for adapting large language models to downstream tasks. However, most existing PEFT methods rely on uniform and static adaptations, without accounting for the structured heterogeneity of attention across dimensions, heads, layers, and input tokens. In practice, attention representations exhibit non-uniform behavior, and positional encoding mechanisms such as rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) induce dimension-dependent positional structure, making uniform adaptation suboptimal. In this work, we propose DyPAM (Dynamic Positional Attention Modulation), a PEFT method that adapts how positional information contributes to attention by operating directly on the query and key representations. DyPAM combines input-conditioned, dimension-wise modulation with head-wise and layer-wise structural modulation, performing fine-grained adaptation of positional attention aligned with the RoPE-induced structure without modifying the pretrained backbone. Extensive experiments on mathematical and commonsense reasoning benchmarks across multiple backbone models demonstrate that DyPAM consistently outperforms existing strong PEFT baselines.

Large language models (LLMs) have been widely adopted across a broad range of real-world applications, including question answering, code generation, and mathematical reasoning (Wang et al., 2023b; Wu et al., 2026; Cheng et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025). Despite their strong general-purpose capabilities, different application scenarios and downstream tasks often impose substantially different requirements on model behavior. Effectively adapting an LLM to diverse task-specific requirements is essential in practical deployment (Zhao et al., 2023b; Li et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2025b).

Full-parameter fine-tuning for a specific task is effective but computationally and storage intensive, which limits its practicality in many settings. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) addresses this issue by updating only a small subset of parameters while keeping the backbone model frozen, achieving a favorable balance between efficiency and performance (Mangrulkar et al., 2022; Han et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). Representative PEFT methods include LoRA (Hu et al., 2021), which reparameterizes weight updates into a low-rank subspace, IA 3 (Liu et al., 2022), which modulates intermediate activations via lightweight scaling vectors, BOFT (Liu et al., 2023), which applies orthogonality-constrained multiplicative transformations with butterfly factorization, and Bone (Kang and Yin, 2024), which introduces block-wise affine updates with shared parameters.

Despite their strong empirical performance, most existing PEFT methods apply additional parameters in a largely uniform manner across layers, attention heads, and feature dimensions (i.e., individual dimensions of the hidden representations), and therefore lack mechanisms to account for the structured and heterogeneous roles of different model components in a fine-grained manner.

Figure 1 visualizes attention activation patterns of Llama-3.2-3B, focusing on the query (Q) representations used in self-attention. Similar heterogeneous patterns are also observed for key (K) representations, while such patterns are not significant for value (V) representations. Activations vary substantially across query dimensions, attention heads, and layers. As shown in Figure 1 (a), attention exhibits distinct activation patterns across dimensions at different layers, indicating that different dimensions contribute differently to attention. Figure 1 (b) further shows clear head-wise variation within the same layer, indicating that different attention heads exhibit distinct activation patterns. Figures 1 (c) and (d) show that activation patterns also depend on the input tokens. Tokens with different semantic roles induce systematically different activation distributions, both when aggregated across dimensions and when examined at the level of individual dimensions for a fixed head and layer. Together, these visualizations demonstrate that attention in pretrained LLMs operates in a structured and heterogeneous manner across dimensions, heads, layers, and input tokens.

Such heterogeneous activation patterns are consistent with the fact that different components of LLMs play distinct functional roles (Zhang et al., 2023). Recent studies have shown that Transformer modules are not functionally uniform, with different layers and components specializing in different aspects (Geva et al., 2021). For example, feed-forward networks have been shown to primarily store factual information (Meng et al., 2022), while attention mechanisms are more closely associated with contextual interaction (Clark et al., 2019b). Within the attention module, architectural design choices further introduce structured differences in how information is processed. In particular, positional encoding mechanisms in Transformer-based LLMs introduce structured differences in internal representations, resulting in non-uniform usage of attention dimensions across layers and heads (Barbero et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025). Beyond structural differences across model components, attention behavior also varies with the input, where different tokens can induce different activation patterns depending on their semantic roles and contextual requirements (Wang et al., 2023a; Ji et al., 2026). Taken together, these findings suggest that LLMs exhibit intrinsic functional heterogeneity across components and inputs, and effective adaptation methods should account for such fine-grained structural differences.
