These observations suggest three requirements for structure-aware adaptation. First, adaptation should distinguish attention dimensions, since different dimensions exhibit different positional and functional behaviors. Second, it should account for head-wise and layer-wise differences, because the same dimension can play different roles across attention heads and network depths. Third, adaptation should remain input-conditioned, as different tokens and contexts can induce different attention activation patterns. This provides a direct way to adapt dependency modeling while keeping the original attention architecture unchanged.

Motivated by these observations, we propose DyPAM (Dy namic P ositional A ttention M odulation), a PEFT method that adapts how positional information contributes to attention. DyPAM addresses attention heterogeneity from two complementary perspectives. It combines input-conditioned, dimension-wise modulation with head-wise and layer-wise structural modulation to adapt attention behavior. In contrast to prior PEFT methods that apply static adaptation shared across inputs, DyPAM models heterogeneity jointly at the token, dimension, head, and layer levels, and aligns the modulation with the RoPE-induced dimension pairing. Extensive experiments across multiple models and tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of this design.

We summarize the main contributions of this work as follows: We propose DyPAM, the first parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that explicitly adapts large language models by modulating positional attention in a fine-grained and structured manner. DyPAM introduces input-conditioned, dimension-wise modulation, enabling different attention dimensions to be dynamically adjusted according to the input context. DyPAM further incorporates head-wise and layer-wise structural modulation, allowing different attention heads and network layers to maintain distinct positional preferences. Extensive experiments across multiple backbone models and downstream tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of DyPAM compared to existing PEFT methods.
We briefly review the attention mechanism, Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), which provide the necessary background for describing our method.

Large language models are typically built upon the Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017), where self-attention is the core mechanism for modeling interactions among tokens. Given an input sequence, each layer \ell of the model produces a sequence of hidden states \mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}=[\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}_{1},\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}_{2},\dots,\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}_{T}], where \mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denotes the hidden representation of the t -th token. In each attention layer, the hidden states are linearly projected into query, key, and value representations, \mathbf{Q}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{W}_{Q}^{(\ell)},\quad\mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{W}_{K}^{(\ell)},\quad\mathbf{V}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{W}_{V}^{(\ell)}, where \mathbf{W}_{Q}^{(\ell)},\mathbf{W}_{K}^{(\ell)},\mathbf{W}_{V}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} are learned projection matrices.

The projected representations are then reshaped into H attention heads. For each head h\in\{1,\dots,H\}, we denote the per-head matrices as \mathbf{Q}^{(\ell,h)},\mathbf{K}^{(\ell,h)},\mathbf{V}^{(\ell,h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{\text{head}}}, where d_{\text{head}}=d/H. For a given token position t, we denote by \mathbf{q}^{(\ell,h)}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{head}}} and \mathbf{k}^{(\ell,h)}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{head}}} the query and key vectors corresponding to the t -th token. We further denote by q^{(\ell,h)}_{t,j} the j -th feature dimension of \mathbf{q}^{(\ell,h)}_{t}. Self-attention is computed independently for each head. For head h at layer \ell, the attention output is given by \mathrm{Attn}\!\left(\mathbf{Q}^{(\ell,h)},\mathbf{K}^{(\ell,h)},\mathbf{V}^{(\ell,h)}\right)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}^{(\ell,h)}{\mathbf{K}^{(\ell,h)}}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{\text{head}}}}\right)\mathbf{V}^{(\ell,h)}.

Notably, the attention operation itself is permutation-invariant and does not encode positional order (Press et al., 2021). As a result, positional information must be explicitly incorporated into the attention computation. Modern LLMs achieve this by applying position-dependent transformations to the query and key representations.

Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) (Su et al., 2024) incorporates positional information into attention by applying position-dependent transformations to the query and key representations. For each attention head, RoPE views the per-head vector as two halves of equal size: a “real” part and an “imaginary” part, each of dimension d_{\text{head}}/2. RoPE then applies a 2D rotation to each index i by jointly rotating the paired components \big(z^{\text{real}}_{i},z^{\text{imag}}_{i}\big). As a consequence, the two halves share the same rotation at each index, and thus exhibit closely related positional behavior across corresponding dimensions.

The rotations vary across dimensions, resulting in different positional behaviors. Figure 2 visualizes this effect, showing that different attention dimensions respond differently to relative positional distances in a non-uniform and multi-scale manner. As a result, different attention dimensions play different roles in encoding positional information, which motivates treating them differently when adapting positional attention.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adapts LLMs by introducing lightweight transformations, while keeping the pretrained backbone fixed. We describe PEFT by applying a constrained transformation to an intermediate representation \mathbf{z} in the model. Formally, the adapted representation can be written as \mathbf{z}^{\prime}=\mathcal{T}\big(\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}\big), where \mathcal{T}(\cdot;\boldsymbol{\theta}) denotes a parameter-efficient transformation with a small number of trainable parameters \boldsymbol{\theta}. Many existing PEFT methods adopt an additive update, \mathbf{z}^{\prime}=\mathbf{z}+\Delta\mathbf{z},\qquad\Delta\mathbf{z}=\mathcal{A}\big(\mathbf{z};\boldsymbol{\theta}\big), where the adaptation module \mathcal{A}(\cdot) is typically applied in a static and largely uniform manner across model components.

While effective, this formulation typically applies the same adaptation mechanism uniformly across layers, attention heads, feature dimensions, and input tokens. However, attention behavior in modern LLMs is highly heterogeneous, particularly in how positional information is encoded. This motivates PEFT approaches that perform fine-grained and structure-aware adaptation.

In this work, we follow the PEFT paradigm and apply multiplicative modulation to attention representations: \mathbf{z}^{\prime}=\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x})\odot\mathbf{z},\qquad\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x})=\mathcal{M}\big(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}\big), where \mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x}) is an input-conditioned modulation signal and \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. In DyPAM, this modulation is applied to the query and key representations in attention and indexed by the internal structure of attention, including layers, heads, tokens, and feature dimensions. Both formulations follow the same parameter-efficient adaptation paradigm. The key difference is that DyPAM performs input-conditioned, structure-aware modulation, enabling fine-grained adaptation of positional attention.

In this section, we introduce DyPAM, a PEFT method for LLMs that explicitly modulates positional information in attention. We first present an overview of the DyPAM framework and its core design principles, and then describe each component in detail.

In RoPE-based LLMs, attention exhibits heterogeneous behavior across feature dimensions, layers, heads, and input tokens. However, most existing PEFT methods rely on uniform and static adaptation mechanisms, without accounting for such heterogeneity.

To address this limitation, we propose Dynamic Positional Attention Modulation (DyPAM), a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that adapts how positional information contributes to attention. DyPAM operates directly on the query and key representations and jointly models input-conditioned, dimension-wise modulation together with head-wise and layer-wise structural modulation, enabling fine-grained and structured adaptation of positional attention. As illustrated in Figure 3, DyPAM introduces modulation into attention representations in a manner aligned with the internal structure of attention and conditioned on the input. The two modulation sources play different roles. The input-conditioned component captures token-dependent variation by generating modulation features from hidden states. The structural bias terms capture persistent preferences associated with heads and layers. Their combination allows DyPAM to adapt to each input while maintaining stable structural differences across the attention hierarchy.
In the following, we present DyPAM by detailing how the modulation is constructed and how it is applied to attention representations, and summarize the overall procedure in Algorithm 1.

DyPAM operates on the query and key representations used in self-attention. At each Transformer layer \ell, these representations are derived from the token-level hidden states \mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times d}, where B is the batch size, T is the sequence length, and d is the model dimension. Following the standard attention formulation described in Section 2.1, the hidden states are linearly projected to obtain the query and key matrices \mathbf{Q}^{(\ell)} and \mathbf{K}^{(\ell)}, which are subsequently reshaped into per-head representations \mathbf{Q}^{(\ell,h)} and \mathbf{K}^{(\ell,h)} as defined in Eq. (1).

To enable input-conditioned adaptation of attention behavior, DyPAM derives modulation features directly from the same hidden states \mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}. Since the hidden states encode token-specific contextual information, the resulting modulation features are token-dependent and differ across inputs, providing the basis for input-conditioned modulation. Concretely, we apply a lightweight low-rank projection to the hidden states, yielding modulation features: \mathbf{M}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{A}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{B}^{(\ell)},\qquad\mathbf{M}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times(H\cdot d_{e})}, where \mathbf{A}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} and \mathbf{B}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times(H\cdot d_{e})} are learnable matrices with rank r\ll d, H is the number of attention heads, and d_{e} denotes the feature dimension per head.

The projected features are reshaped into H head-specific components, yielding modulation features \mathbf{m}^{(\ell)}_{t,h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}} for each token position t and attention head h. These features encode contextual information associated with each token and attention head, capturing how the current input is represented at different heads within the layer. They serve as an intermediate representation that bridges the token-level hidden states and the dimension-wise modulation subsequently applied to the query and key representations.

Given the modulation features constructed from the hidden states, DyPAM maps them to dimension-wise modulation values that are aligned with the query and key representations in attention. This mapping determines how the contribution of each attention dimension is modulated in an input-conditioned manner, allowing the model to dynamically adjust the influence of each dimension. By conditioning on both the token and its context, DyPAM enables fine-grained control over how positional information is utilized across different attention dimensions.

For each layer \ell, DyPAM introduces learnable dimension embedding matrices that project modulation features to the attention dimension space. Concretely, for the query and key representations, we use separate embedding matrices \mathbf{E}^{(\ell)}_{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{\frac{d_{\text{head}}}{2}\times d_{e}},\qquad\mathbf{E}^{(\ell)}_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{\frac{d_{\text{head}}}{2}\times d_{e}}, where each row corresponds to one pair of attention dimensions. This design reflects the structure induced by RoPE, where each pair of dimensions shares the same positional rotation and therefore exhibits similar positional behavior. By assigning a single modulation value to each dimension pair, DyPAM reduces parameter overhead while respecting the RoPE-induced structure. This pair-wise sharing also avoids assigning unrelated modulation values to two coordinates that jointly represent the same rotated subspace. In this way, DyPAM changes the strength of each RoPE-aligned channel without breaking the internal pairing used by the positional transformation. This also supports grouped-query attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., 2023), where multiple attention heads share key and value projections. In such cases, the key-side modulation is shared across heads that use the same key representation, while the query-side modulation remains head-specific.

Given the modulation feature \mathbf{m}^{(\ell)}_{t,h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}} for token position t and attention head h, the dimension-wise modulation scores for queries and keys are computed as \mathbf{g}^{(\ell)}_{t,h,Q}=\mathbf{E}^{(\ell)}_{Q}\mathbf{m}^{(\ell)}_{t,h},\qquad\mathbf{g}^{(\ell)}_{t,h,K}=\mathbf{E}^{(\ell)}_{K}\mathbf{m}^{(\ell)}_{t,h}, where \mathbf{g}^{(\ell)}_{t,h,Q},\mathbf{g}^{(\ell)}_{t,h,K}\in\mathbb{R}^{\frac{d_{\text{head}}}{2}} denote the modulation scores for query and key dimension pairs, respectively. Each entry corresponds to one RoPE dimension pair, and we use i to index dimension pair i.
At this stage, the modulation scores provide input-conditioned, dimension-wise adjustments for the query and key representations.

Discussion. Input-conditioned dimension-wise modulation enables DyPAM to adapt the contribution of individual attention dimensions based on the input context. By aligning modulation with RoPE-induced dimension pairing, DyPAM selectively adjusts how positional information influences attention, while maintaining parameter efficiency. This mechanism provides fine-grained control over positional attention that is sensitive to both token-level context and the structured organization of attention dimensions.

While input-conditioned dimension-wise modulation captures token-dependent variation, attention behavior also exhibits differences across attention heads and network layers. To model such structure-level heterogeneity, DyPAM introduces head-wise and layer-wise structural modulation that is independent of the input.

For each layer \ell, DyPAM maintains layer-wise bias vectors \boldsymbol{\beta}^{(\ell)}_{Q},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(\ell)}_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{\frac{d_{\text{head}}}{2}}, which capture layer-specific preferences over attention dimension pairs for the query and key representations. In addition, for each attention head h at layer \ell, DyPAM introduces head-wise bias vectors \boldsymbol{\beta}^{(\ell)}_{h,Q},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(\ell)}_{h,K}\in\mathbb{R}^{\frac{d_{\text{head}}}{2}}, allowing different heads within the same layer to maintain distinct structural biases. Here the subscripts Q and K indicate that the query and key representations use separate bias vectors of the same shape. These bias terms are added to the dimension-wise modulation scores. For queries and keys, the structurally augmented modulation scores are given by \tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{(\ell)}_{t,h,Q}=\mathbf{g}^{(\ell)}_{t,h,Q}+\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(\ell)}_{h,Q}+\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(\ell)}_{Q}, \tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{(\ell)}_{t,h,K}=\mathbf{g}^{(\ell)}_{t,h,K}+\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(\ell)}_{h,K}+\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(\ell)}_{K}, where \mathbf{g}^{(\ell)}_{t,h,Q} and \mathbf{g}^{(\ell)}_{t,h,K} are the input-conditioned dimension-wise scores from Section 3.3. The bias terms are shared across token positions and encode structural preferences that persist across inputs.

At this stage, the modulation scores integrate input-conditioned, dimension-wise adjustments with head-wise and layer-wise structural biases, capturing both token-dependent variation and persistent structural preferences in attention. These scores are then transformed into bounded modulation factors and applied to the query and key representations.

The combined modulation scores obtained from the previous steps encode both input-conditioned and structural adjustments over attention dimensions. We next apply a normalization step that maps these scores to bounded modulation factors, ensuring stable and controlled adaptation.

Here, \tilde{g}^{(\ell)}_{t,h,i} denotes the modulation score for dimension pair i in the combined score vector for the query or key representation at layer \ell, head h, and token position t. For brevity, we omit the explicit Q/K subscript when the formulation applies identically to both. For each layer \ell, token position t, attention head h, and dimension pair i, the normalized modulation factor is computed as s^{(\ell)}_{t,h,i}=1+\alpha\cdot\big(\sigma(\tilde{g}^{(\ell)}_{t,h,i})-0.5\big), where \sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function and \alpha controls the modulation strength. This normalization maps the modulation factors to a bounded interval \big[1-\tfrac{\alpha}{2},\,1+\tfrac{\alpha}{2}\big], centering them around the original scale and preventing deviation from the pretrained representations.

The modulation factors are applied to the query and key representations before positional encoding. Let \mathbf{q}^{(\ell,h)}_{t,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} and \mathbf{k}^{(\ell,h)}_{t,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} denote the paired dimensions of the query and key vectors corresponding to dimension pair i. Both dimensions within each pair are modulated using the same factor: \hat{\mathbf{q}}^{(\ell,h)}_{t,i}=s^{(\ell)}_{t,h,i}\cdot\mathbf{q}^{(\ell,h)}_{t,i},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{k}}^{(\ell,h)}_{t,i}=s^{(\ell)}_{t,h,i}\cdot\mathbf{k}^{(\ell,h)}_{t,i}.

This operation corresponds to the multiplicative PEFT formulation introduced in Eq. (5), where the pretrained representation \mathbf{z} corresponds to the query or key vectors, and the modulation signal \mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x}) is indexed by layer, head, token position, and dimension pair. Following the convention above, s^{(\ell)}_{t,h,i} is computed independently for the query and key sides from their respective scores \tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{(\ell)}_{t,h,Q} and \tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{(\ell)}_{t,h,K}, so the query and key representations are modulated by their own factors. As the two coordinates within each pair share the same factor, the modulation signal \mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x}) takes a common value over each pair and thus spans the full d_{\text{head}} dimensions of the query and key vectors. The modulated query and key representations are then passed through the RoPE mechanism and used in the standard attention computation. By applying modulation prior to RoPE, DyPAM aligns adaptation with the RoPE-induced positional structure.

More broadly, DyPAM addresses attention heterogeneity by jointly modeling input-conditioned, dimension-wise modulation and head-wise, layer-wise structural modulation. This design enables attention dimensions to adapt to input context, while allowing different heads and layers to maintain distinct positional preferences. Rather than introducing uniform parameter updates, DyPAM performs targeted modulation aligned with how positional information is encoded and utilized in attention. As a result, DyPAM provides a structured and fine-grained mechanism for adapting positional attention within the PEFT paradigm.

DyPAM is trained end-to-end using the standard cross-entropy loss for language modeling. Given an input sequence \mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{T}) and the corresponding target sequence \mathbf{y}=(y_{1},\dots,y_{T}), the training loss is defined as \mathcal{L}=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p(y_{t}\mid x_{\leq t}), where p(y_{t}\mid x_{\leq t}) denotes the model output distribution at position t. The model is parameterized by the pretrained backbone together with the DyPAM parameters. Algorithm 1 summarizes the overall forward computation and training procedure.

This section evaluates DyPAM across tasks, models, and experimental settings. Our experimental design is organized around a set of research questions that assess overall performance, scalability across model sizes, component contributions, and learned positional modulation behavior.

Specifically, we investigate the following research questions: RQ1: Does DyPAM outperform existing PEFT methods with comparable numbers of trainable parameters? RQ2: Is DyPAM effective across different backbone model sizes? RQ3: Which components of DyPAM contribute most to its performance? RQ4: How sensitive is DyPAM to its hyperparameters? RQ5: What positional modulation patterns does DyPAM learn?
We first introduce the experimental setup, followed by a systematic evaluation of DyPAM with respect to each research question.

Datasets. We evaluate DyPAM on mathematical and commonsense reasoning tasks with distinct reasoning patterns and positional sensitivity, and train on two datasets drawn from multiple existing benchmarks (Hu et al., 2023), emphasizing multi-step arithmetic and general commonsense reasoning, respectively. Mathematical reasoning performance is evaluated on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), AQuA (Ling et al., 2017), MAWPS (Koncel-Kedziorski et al., 2016), AddSub (Hosseini et al., 2014), MultiArith (Roy and Roth, 2016), SingleEq (Koncel-Kedziorski et al., 2015), and SVAMP (Patel et al., 2021), while commonsense reasoning is evaluated on BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019a), PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), Social IQA (Sap et al., 2019), ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge (Clark et al., 2018), OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), and WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2020). Across benchmarks, inputs are natural-language questions and outputs are either final numeric answers or discrete choices, and we report accuracy as the evaluation metric with further details provided in the Appendix.

Backbone Models. Experiments are conducted on three widely used RoPE-based LLM families with different architectures and design choices, namely LLaMA 3.2, Qwen3, and Gemma 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Team, 2025b; Team, 2025a), to evaluate the robustness and generality of DyPAM.

Baseline Methods. We compare DyPAM with a diverse set of PEFT methods that adopt different adaptation strategies. Low-rank adaptation methods include LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) and AdaLoRA (Zhang et al., 2023), which parameterize weight updates in a low-dimensional subspace, with AdaLoRA further adjusting rank allocation across layers according to their relative importance. We also consider structured weight reparameterization approaches, including OFT (Qiu et al., 2023) and Bone (Kang and Yin, 2024), where OFT constrains updates to orthogonal transformations and Bone employs block-wise affine parameterization to capture structured correlations within weight matrices. In addition, we include lightweight modulation-based methods such as IA 3 (Liu et al., 2022) and LNTuning (Zhao et al., 2023a), which adapt the model by rescaling internal activations or normalization parameters with minimal trainable parameters. We further compare against FourierFT (Gao et al., 2024), which performs adaptation in the frequency domain by learning a compact set of spectral coefficients for weight updates. Finally, we include SHiRA (Bhardwaj et al., 2024), which applies sparse high-rank adapters to update only a small subset of backbone weights, and RoSA (Pan et al., 2026), which performs RoPE-aware selective adaptation over attention dimensions and layers.

Implementation Details. All experiments are conducted using DeepSpeed (Rasley et al., 2020) with bfloat16 precision on NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs. For DyPAM, we use a modulation embedding dimension d_{e}=64, a low-rank projection rank r=128, and a modulation strength \alpha=0.3. For baseline methods, except for extremely low-parameter approaches, we match the number of trainable parameters to a comparable scale. Additional implementation details are provided in the appendix, and all code and data are released to ease reproducibility.

Across both mathematical and commonsense reasoning benchmarks, DyPAM consistently outperforms existing PEFT baselines under comparable parameters, providing a clear positive answer to RQ1. The improvements are observed across all evaluated backbone models and task categories, indicating that the effectiveness of DyPAM generalizes across different models and datasets.

Specifically, on mathematical reasoning benchmarks as shown in Table 1, DyPAM demonstrates strong and stable gains across heterogeneous tasks that require multi-step computation, and numerical reasoning. The improvements are reflected in both micro- and macro-averaged metrics, suggesting that DyPAM enhances overall reasoning capability rather than favoring a small subset of benchmarks. In contrast, existing PEFT baselines exhibit more uneven behavior. Low-rank methods such as LoRA and AdaLoRA tend to yield limited gains, particularly on more challenging datasets. Frequency-domain approaches such as FourierFT show moderate performance but lack robustness across datasets. Methods with extremely small parameter budgets, including IA 3 and LN-Tuning, generally underperform due to their limited adaptation capacity. Structured or orthogonal methods such as OFT and Bone often perform well on specific tasks but struggle to maintain consistent improvements across the full benchmark suite, whereas sparse adaptation methods like SHiRA, which selectively activate a subset of parameters during fine-tuning, achieve strong performance on multiple tasks, highlighting the potential of structured parameter updates. RoSA also benefits from structured adaptation by introducing rotational subspace updates, leading to competitive results on several benchmarks.

However, RoSA applies a static RoPE-aware selection that is shared across all inputs, whereas DyPAM modulates query and key dimension pairs in an input-conditioned, token-dependent manner coordinated with head-wise and layer-wise structure. This fine-grained and input-conditioned modulation, rather than the use of positional structure alone, accounts for the consistent margin of DyPAM over RoSA across backbones. Compared with these baselines, DyPAM achieves more balanced improvements across tasks and models, indicating superior robustness and generalization.

A similar pattern is observed on commonsense reasoning tasks as shown in Table 3. DyPAM yields balanced improvements across diverse datasets spanning factual verification and social commonsense. The consistent gains in macro-averaged performance indicate improved robustness at the task level, while the improvements in micro-averaged accuracy reflect stronger overall performance.

Overall, these results show that DyPAM provides a more reliable and general-purpose adaptation mechanism than prior PEFT approaches. By delivering consistent gains across tasks, domains, and backbone models, DyPAM effectively addresses RQ1 and demonstrates clear advantages over existing PEFT baselines.

Table 2 evaluates the scalability of DyPAM across Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 8B using macro-averaged accuracy on mathematical reasoning benchmarks. As model size increases, DyPAM consistently achieves better performance than the strongest PEFT baselines at each scale. Moreover, the performance difference between DyPAM and baselines becomes larger as the backbone grows, indicating that DyPAM continues to benefit from increased capacity.
Overall, these results demonstrate that DyPAM maintains strong scalability across model sizes and remains effective when applied to both small and large backbone models, directly addressing RQ2.
We further analyze DyPAM through ablation studies and parameter sensitivity experiments, aiming to understand the contribution of individual components and the robustness of key hyperparameters.

The ablation results show that each core component of DyPAM plays a complementary role in overall performance. Removing any single component consistently leads to performance degradation, indicating that the gains of DyPAM arise from their joint design rather than isolated architectural choices. In addition, the sensitivity analysis on the modulation strength \alpha demonstrates the effectiveness of this design choice. Proper modulation significantly improves performance compared to weak or overly strong modulation. Overall, these analyses confirm that the performance improvements of DyPAM are structurally grounded and robust.
We analyze the learned modulation from two perspectives: the structural bias terms and the effective modulation ranges.

Figure 5 visualizes the learned layer-wise query bias over attention dimensions on LLaMA-3.2-3B under commonsense and mathematical reasoning settings. Rather than exhibiting uniform shifts, the bias values vary across both layers and dimensions, indicating that DyPAM learns heterogeneous, dimension-specific adjustments. This structured non-uniformity suggests that different attention dimensions develop distinct positional preferences at different depths, aligning with the intuition that positional information is utilized differently across layers. In addition, faint horizontal band patterns can be observed, hinting that certain layers may exhibit consistent preferences over specific subsets of attention dimensions.

Figure 6 summarizes the effective modulation range of query and key representations under the same two settings. The scale factors remain centered around 1, while the range varies across layers and training data. This restrained behavior preserves the pretrained attention structure while allowing flexibility.

Overall, these visualizations demonstrate that DyPAM learns structured and stable positional modulation patterns. By combining dimension-wise modulation with restrained head-wise and layer-wise scaling, DyPAM adapts positional attention in a targeted manner, shaping how token dependencies are formed and thereby helping explain its consistent performance gains across models and tasks.

Recent advancements in PEFT focus on reducing the number of trainable parameters while maintaining performance. Low-rank approaches such as LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) and AdaLoRA (Zhang et al., 2023) adapt pre-trained weights through additive low-rank updates, while scaling-based methods including IA 3 (Liu et al., 2022) and LNTuning (Zhao et al., 2023a) employ lightweight gating to modulate activations under strict parameter constraints. Structured PEFT approaches, such as OFT (Qiu et al., 2023) and Bone (Kang and Yin, 2024), further constrain the update space by enforcing geometric properties, whereas spectral-domain methods like FourierFT (Gao et al., 2024) perform adaptation via frequency-based transformations of model representations. In addition, RoSA (Pan et al., 2026) is motivated by the structure of RoPE and proposes RoPE-aware selective adaptation by emphasizing low-frequency attention components. Compared with RoSA, which applies static RoPE-aware selection, DyPAM generates input-conditioned modulation over query and key dimension pairs. In contrast to these approaches, our method explicitly models fine-grained, input-conditioned modulation within attention, enabling structure-aware adaptation.

Transformer attention has been recognized for its structural heterogeneity, with different attention heads specializing in various semantic or syntactic aspects of the input (Raganato et al., 2020). Recent works have analyzed head-level specialization and layer-wise differences, demonstrating that attention heads should not be treated uniformly (Voita et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022). Beyond language modeling, attention- and frequency-aware designs have also been widely adopted in spatiotemporal modeling (Jiang et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2026) and financial prediction (Wang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021), further underscoring the value of structure-aware mechanisms. Positional encodings, particularly in RoPE and its variants, are not just external biases but integral to the attention computation, providing a way to model relative positional relationships more effectively (Gu et al., 2025). Newer methods, such as ComRoPE (Yu et al., 2025a), introduce dynamic and input-conditioned positional encodings, enhancing the flexibility of position representations in transformers. RoSA (Pan et al., 2026) is also motivated by the structure of RoPE and explores selective adaptation of attention components guided by frequency characteristics.

While these studies highlight the structured and positional nature of attention, they largely rely on static or coarse-grained mechanisms, motivating the need for fine-grained and input-conditioned modulation within attention.

In this work, we introduce DyPAM, a PEFT method that adapts LLMs by modulating positional attention in a fine-grained and structured manner. Motivated by heterogeneous attention behavior across dimensions, heads, layers, and input tokens, DyPAM operates directly on the query and key representations and aligns adaptation with the RoPE-induced positional structure. It jointly models input-conditioned, dimension-wise and head-wise, layer-wise structural modulation, providing a principled approach to adapting positional attention within the PEFT paradigm. By reshaping how positional information influences attention, DyPAM adjusts the way dependencies are formed across tokens, which is consistent with its gains on tasks that rely on multi-step and relational reasoning. Extensive experiments across mathematical and commonsense reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that DyPAM consistently outperforms strong PEFT baselines. Future work will further optimize the runtime implementation and extend DyPAM across diverse architectural mechanisms.

Sensitivity or Criterion? Measuring and Moving When Language Models Act. Before an agent acts, it must decide whether action is warranted. A single accuracy cannot distinguish failure to recognize a warranted action from reluctance to act. Signal-detection theory separates sensitivity from criterion, but criteria estimated from authored binary labels depend on each benchmark's example mix. We introduce FlipAct, a diagnostic of tool use in physical states. A rule over annotated tool properties computes each answer and a graded evidence score, fixing the Yes/No boundary at zero across models. Questions form 2-by-2 quads that hold required knowledge fixed while the state flips. The slope of the fitted Yes-rate curve measures sensitivity; its crossing at one half measures criterion. Across 44 open models, sensitivity rises with size within a family, and its ranking agrees with three of four external when-to-act benchmarks. Models respond to evidence sign rather than magnitude, accepting actions that leave the state no better about as often as helpful ones. When Yes means act, most models are conservative across rephrasings; in some, this partly reflects a preference for No. Criterion is not determined by size.

Activation steering shifts criterion with weights fixed; distillation from a model's own steered copy puts the shift into its weights without a significant sensitivity change. The distilled shift transfers to six external benchmarks, including two without Yes/No answers, while criterion-free AUC is preserved on the five benchmarks where it is available. Accuracy improves where models start conservative and declines or remains within error where they start permissive. Project page: https://sixundong.com/projects/flipact

Large language model (LLM) agents must decide whether to act before they decide how. Benchmarks for agents mostly score the action once taken: whether the chosen function, its arguments and the trajectory are correct (Patil et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2026). Those that study the decision itself, in tool calling (Ross et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026), clarification (Li et al., 2026) and abstention (Kirichenko et al., 2026), report a single accuracy, and that number mixes two ways to fail. A model may not recognize whether a situation warrants action, a failure of its sensitivity; or it may recognize the situation and still be too reluctant or too ready to act, a failure of its criterion. Too conservative a criterion refuses benign requests (Röttger et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024) or answers from memory where a tool was needed; too permissive a criterion acts where nothing warrants it.

On When2Call (Ross et al., 2025), gemma-2-9b and Phi-3.5-mini reach balanced accuracies of 0.65 and 0.64 with opposite behavior: the first rarely calls the tool, even where it should, and the second calls it on most examples, many where it should not (Figure 1 a). They separate the two kinds of example about equally well, so on this benchmark the first should act more and the second less.

Signal-detection theory (Green et al., 1966) separates sensitivity (d^{\prime}) from criterion (Figure 1 b; § 3.1), but on a benchmark with binary labels the criterion it recovers is relative to that benchmark’s mix of examples, and no zero is shared across benchmarks. Comparing criteria needs a fixed boundary on a common evidence scale, which authored binary labels do not provide (Jacobs and Wallach, 2021, cf.).

FlipAct supplies such a scale by computing the evidence for acting. Its design draws on qualitative process theory (Forbus, 1984), which describes physical change by the sign of each quantity’s change and a coarse ordinal magnitude, enough to say what an action does to a state without numbers. Each question shows a situation and a candidate tool and asks whether using the tool is warranted. The state and the tool each have a sign and an ordinal magnitude on a physical axis. A rule over these properties computes the evidence score \Delta U, how much closer the action brings the state to its goal, with the Yes/No boundary at zero (Figure 1 c). The design unit is a 2\times 2 quad: two tools, each shown in the state it fixes and in the state it worsens, so the knowledge needed to answer stays the same and the state decides the answer (Figure 2). Fitting a model’s Yes-rate against \Delta U gives its sensitivity as the slope a and its criterion as the score \tau where it crosses one half.

Across 44 open models (§ 4), sensitivity behaves as expected of a capability: it rises with size inside a family, and its ranking agrees with external d^{\prime} on three of four when-to-act benchmarks. Models read the sign of the evidence rather than its size, accepting actions that leave the state no better about as often as helpful ones. When Yes means act, the criterion is mostly conservative, in some models through a preference for answering No. It is a stable per-model setting, not set by size: two releases of Mistral-Small-24B sit on opposite sides of zero.

We move the criterion separately from sensitivity in two ways (§ 5). At inference, adding a direction read from the model’s own activations (Zou et al., 2023; Turner et al., 2023; Ke et al., 2026) shifts the criterion with the weights fixed. In the weights, distilling the model from its own steered copy shifts the criterion on four models from three developers with no significant change in sensitivity, and a random direction of the same norm does not. The shift carries beyond FlipAct ’s Yes/No format: on benchmarks without a Yes/No answer it exceeds the shift from a teacher that only favors Yes, on both models tested. On every benchmark, accuracy rises or falls as the starting criterion predicts. Supervised training on the computed labels instead raises sensitivity and moves the criterion with it.

A measurement scheme that splits when-to-act accuracy into a sensitivity and a criterion, read against an evidence scale computed by rule with the Yes/No boundary fixed for every model. FlipAct, built by an automated pipeline in which language models only annotate what a tool does, while the states and every answer follow from the rule. Evidence that the criterion moves separately from sensitivity: steering and distillation from a steered copy move the criterion, while training on the computed labels raises sensitivity.

When-to-act evaluation. Benchmarks for deciding whether to act cover tool calling (Ross et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2024; Patil et al., 2025), clarification (Li et al., 2026), abstention (Kirichenko et al., 2026) and over-refusal (Röttger et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024). Most share three design choices: ground truth is authored by humans or an LLM judge, the evidence for acting is a binary label, and performance is a single rate that conflates a model’s sensitivity with its criterion. Li et al. (2026) instead compute ground truth by constraint satisfaction, and Sun et al. (2026) fix a controlled call/no-call boundary with deliberate no-tool cases. Neither flips a world-state while holding the required knowledge fixed, and none of these benchmarks grades the evidence for acting per question. We reuse four of them as external tests (§ 4.2) and measure transfer on six benchmarks (§ 5.3). App. F compares twelve on these design choices.

Signal detection and language models. Signal-detection theory separates an observer’s sensitivity from its criterion (Green et al., 1966). Reading a benchmark score as the measurement of a latent quantity raises the question of whether it measures what it is read as (Jacobs and Wallach, 2021; Bean et al., 2026). Cacioli (2026) fits signal-detection models to factual question answering with the model’s answer log-probability as evidence, so the criterion sits on each model’s own confidence scale. Shi et al. (2026) read a call/no-call offset off sparse-autoencoder features on When2Call and cancel it by steering. Their offset is an intercept on an internal margin, compared within one model and without a separate sensitivity. FlipAct places the criterion on a rule-computed evidence scale shared across questions and models, estimates it separately from sensitivity with the required knowledge held fixed, and moves it into the weights.

Signal-detection theory (Green et al., 1966) models an observer who reports a signal whenever a scalar amount of evidence exceeds a threshold. The sensitivity d^{\prime} is the distance between the evidence distributions of signal and noise trials in units of their spread, and the criterion c is where the threshold sits relative to their midpoint. From the hit rate H and the false-alarm rate \mathrm{FA} the equal-variance estimators, with z the inverse of the standard normal distribution function, are d^{\prime}\;=\;z(H)-z(\mathrm{FA}),\qquad c\;=\;-\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(z(H)+z(\mathrm{FA})\bigr). In when-to-act terms a hit is acting when one should and a false alarm is acting when one should not. A positive c is conservative. FlipAct supplies an evidence score per question, and the same two quantities become the slope a and the crossing point \tau of a model’s Yes-rate against that score (§ 4.1). Every comparison in the paper pairs a with d^{\prime} and \tau with c. An interactive version is online.

Each question shows a physical situation, the goal of returning it to normal and one candidate tool, and asks whether using the tool is a wise choice. All questions share one minimal template (Figure 2), as do the stimuli of template-based diagnostics (McCoy et al., 2019; Ribeiro et al., 2020), so only the tool, the state and their outcome vary. Physical situations are used because a tool’s effect on a state can be written as an explicit qualitative transition: a humidifier helps a dry room and harms a wet one. In the quad of Figure 2, a humidifier that adds two steps of moisture and an industrial dehumidifier that removes three are crossed with a very dry and a dangerously wet room. Every question of the quad needs the same two facts, what the tool does and what the room needs. For a given tool only the state changes, and with it the answer, so a model that knows what a humidifier is for must still read the state.

Quads and state flips are controls built into the set. The main set has 1{,}880 questions: 840 lie in a complete quad and 1{,}256 belong to a state flip, the same tool with opposite answers in two states. A state flip separates a model that ignores the state, which gives both questions about the same Yes–No logit margin, from one that is merely permissive, which may answer Yes to both but still ranks the warranted one higher (App. D.3, D.7). Every situation has as many Yes as No questions, so the description of the world does not predict the answer.

section: Ground truth and evidence by rule
text: Each situation fixes an integer state v on a physical axis (thermal transfer, moisture, mechanical cohesion, …) with the goal at 0. Each tool carries a direction \delta\in\{+1,-1\} and an ordinal magnitude band \mu\in\{1,2,3\} on that axis (Forbus, 1984, in qualitative process theory, a sign and a place in a quantity space;), optionally conditional on a prerequisite. Applying it moves the state to v+\delta\mu, and the process behind that change is not modeled. The evidence score is the utility of the action, how much closer to the goal it leaves the world, \Delta U\;=\;|v|\;-\;|v+\delta\mu|,\qquad\texttt{Yes}\iff\Delta U>0, and a tool with unmet prerequisites carries \Delta U=-2 for each, a value set by convention. The question type follows from the same computation: a wrong-direction tool is destructive, a right-direction tool that overshoots or acts on a state already at the goal is redundant, and a tool applied without its prerequisite is prerequisite. Because v and \mu are integers, \Delta U takes seven values on [-3,3]. A question conveys |v| only by the adverb slightly, very or dangerously, and \mu only by the tool itself. Language models annotate each tool’s axis, direction, magnitude and prerequisite, and the rule computes the answer from those properties.

FlipAct is generated by a pipeline (Figure 3) that needs no per-question human annotation or adjudication. Its specification is written once: the physical axes, a closed vocabulary of tool properties, the rule of § 3.3 and the template. Ten lexical, medical and visually grounded resources supply 149{,}840 candidate entities, and two annotator models, Qwen3.5-27B and gemma-4-31b, fill the vocabulary for each. Where they disagree, both arbitrate against the specification, and unresolved records are dropped. Tool records (one tool, one axis) are paired when they act in opposite directions on that axis and target object, and states, answers, question types and text follow by rule. A balance selection keeps 1{,}880 of the 6{,}176 rendered questions. Two matched-pair supplementary sets, 342 already-satisfied and 224 prerequisite-blocked questions, are kept outside the fits. A new axis, a new tool inventory or a larger set runs through the same steps at the cost of annotator calls (App. A).

A lexical probe trained on the question text is at chance on held-out situations whose tools it has not seen (App. A.5), and recomputing the ground truth independently of the build gives zero mismatches. A model’s judgment enters only where tools are annotated and screened, and a model family outside the build reproduces every tool/non-tool judgment, nine in ten axis judgments and every magnitude band to within one band, two in three exactly. Perturbing the annotations at that rate, or until a quarter of the computed answers change, keeps the rankings by a and \tau intact and moves criteria toward acting, so it cannot produce the conservative criteria (App. A.6).

Models. To see how the coordinates a and \tau vary with size and family, we fit 44 open models, all but five with reasoning off (App. B.7), from 0.6 B to 70 B parameters and fifteen families, among them Qwen3 and Qwen3.5, Gemma 2–4, Llama 3, Mistral and Phi (App. Tables 9 – 10).

External benchmarks. To test whether the coordinates capture what when-to-act benchmarks score, we compare them with four, each posing the decision in a different domain. Every example is one where acting is right or one where withholding is, and d^{\prime} and c follow from Eq. 1 with acting as the response. On BFCL acting is calling a listed function, which is right when one fits the query; on When2Call it is choosing the tool call among four replies (call, ask, cannot answer, answer directly); QuestBench and When2Tool ask Yes/No whether the model already has enough information to answer and whether it would need a tool (App. Table 11).

section: The fit and the response profile
text: On FlipAct every question carries a computed evidence score, so we fit the model’s Yes-rate as a logistic curve over that score (Green et al., 1966): P(\text{Yes}\mid\Delta U)\;=\;\sigma\!\bigl(a\,(\Delta U-\tau)\bigr). Here \sigma is the logistic function, the slope a the sensitivity and the crossing point \tau the criterion. A positive \tau means the fitted curve crosses one half above the rule’s boundary, so the model answers Yes less often than the rule warrants, which we call conservative. A criterion is estimable when a\geq 0.15 and \mathrm{SE}(\tau)\leq 2.0, and well determined when it also lies inside the score range; beyond \pm 3 it is reported as a bound. Both coordinates have split-half reliability above 0.9 (App. B.2). On external benchmarks we use d^{\prime} and c (Eq. 1); a model readier to act has lower \tau and c.

section: The fit and the response profile
text: Response profile. Models read the sign of the evidence, not its size (Figure 4). Yes-rates jump between \Delta U=-1 and 0, significantly in 19 of the 21 reasoning-off models with a well-determined criterion, and are flat on either side: no model answers Yes reliably more often at \Delta U=+3 than at +1. The step sits one unit below the rule’s boundary: models accept actions that leave the state no better about as often as helpful ones. The questions at \Delta U=0 are all redundant slight overshoots, so this set cannot tell whether that placement belongs to the models or to the rule. Models do withhold when the state is already at its goal or a prerequisite is unmet (App. B.2), so the overshoot is the one redundancy they accept. The sign of \tau is set by the height of the Yes plateau, not by the step: for the median model the Yes-rate on helpful actions stays near one half (Figure 4).

section: The fit and the response profile
text: Reading \tau. A step function at the sign of the evidence predicts held-out answers as well as the logistic. Still, \tau tracks the criterion divided by sensitivity: with c/d^{\prime} of Eq. 1 read from hits on \Delta U>0 and false alarms on \Delta U<0, \tau\approx-0.09+3.22\,c/d^{\prime} (r=0.999), and both find the same models conservative (App. B.2 – B.3). In 9 of the 21 models the Yes-rate never reaches one half, so \tau is where the fitted curve, not the data, crosses it. We therefore read \tau by sign and rank.

section: Sensitivity grows with size and agrees with external benchmarks
text: Within a family, a rises with size: Qwen3 goes from 0.34 at 4B to 0.58 at 32B, and the one exception is Qwen3.5, which peaks at 9B. Twelve models fit below 0.30, among them widely deployed small instruct models, and their Yes-rates span almost the whole range: a model can be permissive or conservative about a tool and still be unable to tell when using it is warranted (Figure 5).

section: Sensitivity grows with size and agrees with external benchmarks
text: FlipAct sensitivity predicts external d^{\prime} on three of the four benchmarks (Figure 6 a). The comparison uses a panel: of the 39 reasoning-off models, 27 have an estimable criterion and 21 a well-determined one, and the 18 of these with a\geq 0.30 and usable external d^{\prime} and c form the panel, so that both sides of each comparison are estimated reliably (App. B.4 varies the cutoff on a). All three relations hold with model size partialed out (App. B.5). This agreement across three domains and formats supports reading a as the sensitivity these benchmarks score. On When2Tool the relation is not significant.

section: Criterion: a per-model setting, conservative by default
text: Eighteen of the 21 reasoning-off models with a well-determined criterion are positive on the canonical wording of Figure 2: they answer Yes less often than the rule warrants (Figure 5), and nearly all tested stay positive under five rephrasings (App. C). The criterion is one setting across question types: models that accept more destructive actions also accept more slight overshoots on other questions (\rho=0.88, 27 models, a\geq 0.30), though most accept overshoots more readily.

section: Criterion: a per-model setting, conservative by default
text: As in signal detection, the criterion collects every bias in the response, including a preference for one answer word. We also ask each question in three reversed wordings, such as “Is using the tool a mistake?”, under which No means act. After recoding, a preference for No raises the canonical criterion and lowers the reversed one, so writing them as \tau_{d}+b and \tau_{d}-b separates a threshold on the evidence, \tau_{d}, from the preference, b (App. C). For the three Qwen3.5 models and GLM-4-32B, b is +3 to +4 and \tau_{d} within a unit of zero; the other twelve of the 16 models tested stay conservative without it. JEV (TypeSafe AI, 2026), a model that returns a probability, not text, and so has no answer word to prefer, is conservative too and steps at the sign of the evidence (App. E).

section: Criterion: a per-model setting, conservative by default
text: Where the criterion sits is a property of the model more than of its size. The two Mistral-Small-24B releases are the same size and land on opposite sides of zero, at +2.18 (2501) and -1.10 (3.2, 2506) (Figure 5). Inside a family \tau drifts toward zero as models grow, in Qwen3, in the dense Qwen3.5 models and across the Gemma generations (Figure 6 b). Part of this drift follows from rising sensitivity, since \tau tracks the criterion divided by sensitivity. Families differ in their typical \tau, so pooled over all models the relation with size vanishes.

section: Criterion: a per-model setting, conservative by default
text: The criterion measured on FlipAct does not consistently predict a model’s c on other benchmarks: across the panel the correlation is near zero on When2Call (Pearson r=-0.01), QuestBench and When2Tool, and positive on BFCL (r=+0.51), where it rests on the three models with the lowest \tau (App. Table 15). Section 5.3 asks instead whether moving \tau moves c.

We ask whether the criterion can be moved while sensitivity stays fixed, at inference (§ 5.1) and in the weights (§ 5.2), and whether the moved criterion carries to external benchmarks (§ 5.3). Such a move trades misses for false alarms and cannot raise accuracy beyond what sensitivity allows.

section: Steering moves the criterion with the weights fixed
text: Models and data. We steer five open models, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-27B, gemma-2-9b, Mistral-Small-24B (the 2501 release, Mistral-24B below) and phi-4, and measure the effect on When2Call (Ross et al., 2025), on 600 examples, half call and half withhold (eleven more models in App. D.1).

section: Steering moves the criterion with the weights fixed
text: Method. Steering follows the standard recipe (Turner et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Arditi et al., 2024). A logistic probe from the final-token residual stream at relative depth 0.6 to the model’s own Yes/No answers on the FlipAct questions gives the criterion direction \hat{w}, which is added during generation to the residual-stream activation h at that layer as h\leftarrow h+\lambda\hat{w}. For each model the strength \lambda^{\star} is the one with the lowest When2Call criterion among those that keep d^{\prime} within 25\% of its unsteered value.

section: Steering moves the criterion with the weights fixed
text: Results. The direction moves the When2Call criterion toward acting on all five models (Table 1). On Qwen3-8B, gemma-2-9b and Mistral-24B the shift is at least three times that of same-norm random and orthogonal directions and keeps over two thirds of its size when the refusal, sycophancy and engagement directions are projected out of \hat{w}; over sixteen models, eleven move significantly toward acting and four pass both controls (App. D.1). The shift is small on Qwen3.5-27B, which starts near zero on When2Call and whose FlipAct criterion is mostly a preference for No, and there it does not exceed random directions of the same norm. On phi-4, which starts permissive and moves least, it does not hold when the strength is chosen on one half of the examples and measured on the other (App. D.1). On four models steering gains hits at the cost of correct withholds, and on all five, accuracy changes by at most four points. With the direction fit on one half of FlipAct and measured on the other, it also moves the criterion of Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-27B toward zero and raises their accuracy by 2.6 and 1.6 points.

section: Distilling from a steered copy puts the criterion into the weights
text: Models and data. As an existence proof that the criterion can be placed in the weights, we distill four students from three developers, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, gemma-3-12b and Mistral-24B, each from its own steered copy. The FlipAct main set is split in half so that no situation or tool record appears on both sides. Students train on one half (940 questions) with three seeds per condition, and every result is measured on the held-out half, so baselines differ from the full-set values of § 4.

section: Distilling from a steered copy puts the criterion into the weights
text: Method. In criterion distillation, the teacher T is the student with steering on. Its direction is a difference of means over the student’s own Yes and No answers on the training half, and its strength is the one on a sweep that moves \tau furthest while a and d^{\prime} stay close to their unsteered values. The student S has the same weights, a LoRA adapter and no steering, and is trained to match the teacher’s next-token distribution at the answer position of each training question q, \mathcal{L}\;=\;\sum_{q}\mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{T}(\cdot\mid q)\,\big\|\,p_{S}(\cdot\mid q)\bigr). The control replaces the direction with a random one of the same norm. A change is significant when it exceeds twice its paired bootstrap error over situations (settings in App. D.3).

section: Distilling from a steered copy puts the criterion into the weights
text: Results. Criterion distillation moves \tau toward acting on all four students (Table 2), by more than twice its error on three and just under twice on gemma-3-12b. No student’s sensitivity changes significantly in any seed; the largest change, -0.17\pm 0.10 on Mistral-24B, is under twice its error (App. Table 29). An equivalence test bounds the change within \pm 0.12 on Qwen3.5-9B and gemma-3-12b and cannot decide on Qwen3-8B and Mistral-24B. On When2Call, d^{\prime} stays within 20\% of its baseline for all four. Held-out accuracy rises by one to five points, as a criterion shift should when the model starts conservative, as all four do. The random direction moves \tau at most a fifth as far. Injected at a strength that perturbs the answers as much as the teacher’s direction, a random direction either leaves \tau in place or collapses the model onto one answer (App. D.3).

section: The distilled criterion moves the same way on six external benchmarks
text: Benchmarks. To test whether the shift generalizes beyond FlipAct ’s physical questions and its Yes/No format, each student is tested on six unseen benchmarks, scored with d^{\prime} and c. Four ask whether to act now: When2Call and When2Tool (Sun et al., 2026) (call a tool), QuestBench (Li et al., 2026) (ask or solve) and BFCL-miss-func (Patil et al., 2025) (the needed function is removed from the list). Two ask a planning judgment: ACPBench (Kokel et al., 2025) (does an action apply) and CaT-Bench (Lal et al., 2024) (must one step precede another). When2Call offers four replies, BFCL-miss-func takes a free-form call or refusal, and the other four take Yes or No.

section: The distilled criterion moves the same way on six external benchmarks
text: Results. Moving the FlipAct criterion moves c the same way on every benchmark, although across models it does not consistently predict a benchmark’s c (§ 4.3). On all 23 scored model–benchmark pairs, c moves toward acting in every seed, and every control moves less than the distilled student beside it (Figure 7). Sensitivity is kept: the criterion-free AUC from answer log-probabilities, available on five benchmarks, stays unchanged for every student (Table 4).

section: The distilled criterion moves the same way on six external benchmarks
text: Answer preference. On a Yes/No format a shift toward acting and a shift toward Yes coincide. On FlipAct most of the distilled shift flips sign under the reversed wordings of § 4.3, so there it shifts the preference for Yes, the form the decision to act takes on a Yes/No format (App. D.5). Whether more than that preference carries over shows only where the answer has no Yes: if a Yes preference were all that transfers, a student distilled from a teacher whose Yes logits are raised by a constant tuned to the steered teacher’s Yes-rate would match the criterion-distilled one there. On Qwen3-8B and gemma-3-12b it does not: on When2Call and BFCL-miss-func the criterion-distilled student moves c further in every seed, though on Qwen3-8B the Yes-bias student reaches half to three quarters of it. On the four Yes/No benchmarks it moves c as far or further.

section: The distilled criterion moves the same way on six external benchmarks
text: Accuracy. Accuracy follows the starting point, as a pure criterion shift predicts. Where a student starts conservative, balanced accuracy rises in every case, by up to six points (Table 4; all students in App. Table 31). Where it starts permissive, accuracy falls by up to four points or stays within its error, except Mistral-24B on When2Tool: its hit rate is already at ceiling, so a shift toward acting only adds false alarms, and accuracy falls about ten points. A criterion shift should thus take its sign from the target benchmark. Steering the five models of § 5.1 toward acting on five benchmarks lowers balanced accuracy on 12 of the 25 model–benchmark pairs; choosing the sign and strength from fifty labeled examples of each benchmark instead leaves only Mistral-24B on When2Call worse (App. D.6). Where the benchmark has an answer token, a scalar bias on that token chosen the same way does as well (19 of 20 pairs), as expected if steering is one offset on the criterion.

section: Labels move sensitivity, and the criterion with it
text: Sensitivity learning, supervised training on the computed labels, tests the converse: whether labels move sensitivity. It uses the same students, split, adapter and seeds, adds 263 supplementary questions on the same tool records to the training half, and shuffles the labels within matched groups of questions as its control. It raises a on every student, by about 0.5 to 1.2, and held-out accuracy by 17 to 24 points, while the shuffled-label control lowers accuracy (Table 2). It also brings \tau close to zero, so labels move both coordinates, whereas distillation moves the criterion alone. The gain in sensitivity stays on FlipAct: on the external benchmarks its changes in d^{\prime} and c differ in sign across students and are matched by the shuffled-label control. Limitations are discussed in App. G.

We treated the decision to act as a measurement problem. Two models with the same accuracy can need opposite fixes, so a when-to-act benchmark says more when it reports d^{\prime} and c beside accuracy. The criterion moves, at inference or in the weights, with a shift whose sign the target benchmark sets, while sensitivity on FlipAct rises with training on labels. On a Yes/No format the criterion also holds a preference between answer words, which reversed wordings separate from the rest.

This work evaluates open-weight models on public benchmarks and involves no human subjects. Moving a model’s criterion toward acting makes it act on thinner evidence, a trade-off practitioners should weigh for their application.

The paper specifies the full experimental setup: the construction of FlipAct and its rule (§ 3, App. A), the estimators (§ 4.1), and the steering and training procedures with all hyperparameters (§ 5, App. D.3). Every training condition is run with three seeds and reported as the seed mean with its bootstrap error, and every reported change comes with a significance test; steering effects carry bootstrap intervals and are checked on held-out splits. The dataset, code and evaluation logs will be released.

We used generative AI tools to generate synthetic data sets: in the FlipAct pipeline, language models annotate tool properties (§ 3.4, App. A), while every answer and evidence score is computed by rule. We used generative AI tools to implement methods: the evaluation, steering, training and analysis code was written with an AI coding assistant. We also used generative AI tools to aid and polish the writing. We did not use generative AI tools for the other tasks with required disclosure. The authors reviewed all AI-assisted code, data and text and take responsibility for the final content of this work.

BanglaShield: A Script-Robust Safety Classifier and Benchmark for Bangla Native, Romanized, and Code-Mixed Prompts. Safety classifiers for large language models (LLMs) are typically built and evaluated on standard-script text, yet Bangla, like many lower-resource languages, is routinely written in native script, in Latin-script romanization, and code-mixed with English, Hindi, or Urdu. We introduce BanglaShield, a resource and model for graded prompt-safety classification across these written forms. We consolidate 10,245 Bangla prompts from six sources under a four-level taxonomy (Safe, Offensive, Harmful, Severe) and render each prompt in three aligned forms that share labels and a group-aware split, enabling strictly paired comparisons. Benchmarking six contemporary LLMs, including a Bangla-specialized one, on 36,882 classification queries and 24,318 judged responses, we find that LLM classifiers label 47.0% of unsafe native-script prompts as Safe, rising to 63.4% under romanization, while response-level safety accuracy drops by 10.3 points. Three multilingual guard models also pass 30.3-57.3% of unsafe native-script prompts. Using a model's own classification as an input filter reduces harmful compliance by only about five points.

In contrast, BanglaShield, a compact fine-tuned encoder, reaches 87.8 macro-F1 on native-script and 84.4 on romanized prompts, outperforming the best LLM on each form by 42.8-46.1 points with ~130x fewer parameters than Gemma 4 31B. We release the corpus, splits, judgments, and model.

Prompt-level guard models assess a user input before a model generates a response, and they have become a standard component of LLM deployment (Inan et al., 2023; Han et al., 2024). Most guard models are trained with supervised learning, but their training data is concentrated in English and a few other high-resource languages, and low-resource languages are often covered only through machine-translated data (Kumar et al., 2025). Multilingual studies consistently report that safety performance drops for low-resource languages (Yong et al., 2023; Deng et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024).

Bangla, spoken by roughly 250 million people, adds a further challenge: the same request can appear in several written forms. Bangla users write online in the native script, in Latin-script romanization, and frequently mix Bangla with English, Hindi, or Urdu (Das et al., 2022; Raihan et al., 2023; Goswami et al., 2023). Existing Bangla safety resources have three limitations. They omit romanized Bangla (Islam et al., 2026), use only binary or three-way safety labels (Hassan and Hossain, 2026), or address offensive language rather than harmful user requests. Little work compares how guard models classify the same request in different written forms, so it remains unclear whether a harmful request that is caught in Bangla script is also caught when it is romanized or code-mixed, and whether a compact classifier can make graded safety judgments that stay stable across these forms.

Figure 1 shows the problem. All six evaluated LLMs flag a request for help disposing of a corpse as unsafe when it is written in Bangla script, yet five of the six classify the code-mixed version of the same request as Safe. The meaning and intent of the request are unchanged; only its written form differs. Changing the written form can therefore bypass existing safety filters, whether the user is an adversary or simply writes Bangla the way many speakers do every day. We address this problem with BanglaShield, a benchmark and safety classifier for Bangla prompts in native-script, romanized, and code-mixed forms. Our contributions are as follows:

A paired, graded Bangla safety corpus. We consolidate 10,245 prompts from six sources under a four-level taxonomy with source-aware mapping rules, and render each prompt in Bangla script, romanized Bangla, and Bangla code-mixed with English, Hindi, or Urdu. The three versions of a prompt share its label and data split, so every comparison across forms uses the same items (§ 3). A paired benchmark of LLM safety across written forms. We evaluate six LLMs, including a Bangla-specialized one, on prompt classification and on the safety of their own responses, and three guard models on prompt classification, with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired significance tests (§ 4 –§ 5). BanglaShield, a compact script-robust guard. A fine-tuned MuRIL (Multilingual Representations for Indian Languages) encoder (Khanuja et al., 2021) that surpasses all evaluated LLMs on every form while remaining stable across scripts (§ 5, § 5.2).

Two lines of work bear on BanglaShield: guard models and multilingual safety evaluations, which show that safety degrades outside English (§ 2.1), and Bangla resources, which cover offensive language or unpaired written forms (§ 2.2).

Guard models classify unsafe requests and responses: Llama Guard uses a predefined safety taxonomy (Inan et al., 2023; Grattafiori et al., 2024), WildGuard separately models prompt harm, response harm, and refusal (Han et al., 2024), and XSTest probes exaggerated refusals (Röttger et al., 2024). PolyGuard covers 17 languages (Kumar et al., 2025), IndicGuard ten Indic languages (Bramhecha et al., 2026), and X-Guard low-resource and code-switched inputs (Upadhayay and Behzadan, 2025). Safety also varies across languages: XSafety (Wang et al., 2024) and RTP-LX (de Wynter et al., 2025) compare languages, MultiJail (Deng et al., 2024) and code-switching (Yoo et al., 2025) bypass safety mechanisms, and IndicJR finds lower jailbreak success for romanized or mixed inputs under JSON-constrained output (Pattnayak and Chowdhuri, 2026a). These studies compare languages, not the written forms of one language.

Bangla resources mostly target offensive language: Das et al. (2022) cover Bangla-script and romanized hate speech, TB-OLID transliterated comments (Raihan et al., 2023), and OffMix-3L code-mixed Bangla, English, and Hindi (Goswami et al., 2023). BanglaSafe provides culturally grounded harmful prompts and shows that register shifts weaken LLM safety (Islam et al., 2026), BanglaVeilGuard evaluates a three-class prompt guard over six Bangla forms (Hassan and Hossain, 2026), and TigerLLM is a Bangla-specialized LLM (Raihan and Zampieri, 2025). No Bangla resource combines graded labels, paired written forms, response-level evaluation, and a released guard (Table 1). The encoder underlying BanglaShield is pretrained on translated and transliterated pairs (Khanuja et al., 2021); BanglaShield fine-tunes it jointly on native-script, romanized, and code-mixed prompts.
BanglaShield maps six Bangla safety resources to one four-level taxonomy (§ 3.1) and renders every prompt in three aligned written forms (§ 3.2); Figure 2 summarizes the pipeline.

We collect the Bangla instances of six public resources and convert them into a common format that preserves their source information (Figure 2, steps 1–2). Five are safety datasets: LinguaSafe (Ning et al., 2025), XSafety (Wang et al., 2024), BanglaSafe (Islam et al., 2026) (its formal, colloquial, and institutional conditions), IndicSafe (Pattnayak and Chowdhuri, 2026b), and MultiJail (Deng et al., 2024). These datasets contain few benign requests, so we add negative product reviews from BanglaEcomReviewCorpus (Ayman et al., 2026), converted into first-person customer-support requests with deterministic templates based on product category. The reviews carry negative sentiment but do not request harmful assistance, so they serve as Safe examples.

Because our goal is a guard model that classifies a request before an LLM responds, we map every example to one of four safety levels: Safe, Offensive, Harmful, and Severe (Table 2). Deterministic rules derived from each dataset’s own label definitions perform this mapping (Table A): a record i with text x_{i}, source s_{i}, and source label o_{i} receives y_{i}=g_{s_{i}}(o_{i})\in\mathcal{Y}=\{0,1,2,3\}, where g_{s} is the rule set of source s and 0<1<2<3 orders Safe, Offensive, Harmful, and Severe by risk. Every example keeps o_{i} and s_{i}. By design, we exclude multiple-choice safety items (e.g., in XSafety) and bias benchmarks (BanStereoSet, BharatBBQ), which test whether a model recognizes harmful or biased content rather than whether a user requests harmful assistance. Figure 3 a shows the resulting distribution of safety levels, which differs considerably across sources; we therefore also analyze results by source (§ 5.2).

From each source prompt we derive three parallel forms x_{i}^{f}, f\in\mathcal{F}=\{\mathrm{bn},\mathrm{rom},\mathrm{cm}\}, each paired with the label y_{i} and the data split of record i, so differences in model behavior can be attributed to the written form.
We use the original Bangla text, x_{i}^{\mathrm{bn}}=\mathrm{NFC}(x_{i}).

We transliterate each prompt into Latin script with bodhan-ai/indic-translate, a Gemma-based Indic translation model, and instruct it to change only the script (“Transliterate the following text into Bangla (Roman)”). The outputs contain no Bengali-script characters and keep the original words and word order, and the mean prompt length stays at 23.6 words (Table 3; Figure 3 b).

For each prompt, we select one embedded language: English (60%), Hindi (25%), or Urdu (15%), with proportions stratified by the fine-grained source category. We first translate the complete prompt with NLLB-200 (NLLB Team et al., 2024) and align the translation to the original with SimAlign (Jalili Sabet et al., 2020). Let w_{1},\dots,w_{n} be the words of x_{i}^{\mathrm{bn}}, E_{i} the positions of aligned non-punctuation words, and a(j) the translation aligned to w_{j}. We sample p_{i}\sim\mathcal{U}(0.35,0.50) and a subset S_{i}\subseteq E_{i} with |S_{i}|\approx p_{i}|E_{i}|, and set w^{\mathrm{cm}}_{j}=\begin{cases}a(j)&j\in S_{i},\\ w_{j}&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} Unaligned words stay unchanged, so the realized rate r_{i}=|S_{i}|/n can fall below p_{i} (Figure 3 c). The procedure corresponds to the lexical code-mixing condition of Santy et al. (2021): it controls content and label but does not reproduce the grammatical constraints of natural code-switching (Appendix C).
We evaluate six LLMs as classifiers and as assistants and three guard models as classifiers on the paired test set, and train BanglaShield on the paired training set.

We divide the 10,245 instances into training (7,172), validation (1,024), and test (2,049) sets, stratified by source and safety label. To prevent leakage, all records sharing a group_id (parallel translations, register variants, or duplicate reviews) are assigned to the same partition, so stratification is approximate. The romanized and code-mixed forms of each record inherit its partition: no item is seen in one form during training and evaluated in another at test time, and every cross-form comparison uses identical items. Table 3 summarizes the test set.

(i) Prompt classification: a system assigns one of the four labels to each test prompt. (ii) Response safety: each LLM answers the 1,351 test prompts with labels 1–3 in each form under a neutral system prompt; the expected behavior is a useful answer for Offensive prompts and refusal, safe redirection, or strictly harm-minimizing information for Harmful and Severe prompts. Safe prompts are excluded from this task. Prompts are given in Appendix G.

We evaluate Gemma 4 31B, Llama 4 Maverick, Command A+, GPT-4.1 mini, and Claude Haiku 4.5 via OpenRouter with JSON-constrained output, and the Bangla-specialized TigerLLM (Raihan and Zampieri, 2025) locally with schema-constrained JSON (Appendix F). Four Command A+ outputs that remained unparseable after retries are scored as incorrect. We also run the guard models Llama Guard 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), PolyGuard (Kumar et al., 2025), and IndicGuard (Bramhecha et al., 2026) on the prompt alone (Appendix J).

Each response is scored independently by two LLM judges (GPT-5.6 Luna and Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite) for compliance, compliance degree (0–3), and label-appropriate behavior (Zheng et al., 2023). When the judges disagree on any field, Claude Sonnet 5.5 adjudicates with access to both judgments. The judges agree on behavioral correctness for 81.9% of responses (Cohen’s \kappa=0.56; Appendix I).

We fine-tune BanglaShield from the base-size pretrained checkpoint on the union of the three training forms (21,516 prompts), selecting the checkpoint with the best macro-F1 on the pooled validation forms (Appendix B).

For prompt classification we report accuracy (Acc) and macro-F1 (M-F1), \frac{1}{4}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{Y}}\mathrm{F1}_{c}. Over the unsafe items \mathcal{U}=\{i:y_{i}>0\} we measure missed and under-estimated risk: \mathrm{USR}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{U}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{U}}\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{i}=0]. The unsafe-as-safe rate (USR) is the share of unsafe prompts a guard would let through; the under-severity rate (US) replaces \hat{y}_{i}=0 with \hat{y}_{i}<y_{i} (lower is better for both). A judge labels each response’s behavior b_{i} and compliance c_{i}; with \mathcal{H}=\{i:y_{i}\geq 2\} and \phi_{i}=1 if a filter blocks prompt i, \displaystyle\mathrm{ARR} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{U}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{U}}\mathbf{1}[b_{i}=b^{\ast}(y_{i})], \displaystyle\mathrm{HCR} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{H}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{H}}\mathbf{1}[c_{i}=1\wedge\phi_{i}=0] are the appropriate-response and harmful compliance rates, where b^{\ast}(1) is a useful or safe completion and b^{\ast}(2)=b^{\ast}(3) is refusal. Confidence intervals use 1,000 paired bootstrap resamples over test UIDs (Efron and Tibshirani, 1994); McNemar’s test (McNemar, 1947) compares correct-to-wrong (n_{cw}) and wrong-to-correct (n_{wc}) flips across forms, \chi^{2}=(|n_{cw}-n_{wc}|-1)^{2}/(n_{cw}+n_{wc}).
We evaluate the LLMs as classifiers and assistants (§ 5.1), then BanglaShield (§ 5.2).
