section: LLMs under-detect risk in Bangla script, and romanization makes it worse.
text: LLM classifiers reach only 33.0–43.9 macro-F1 on Bangla-script prompts (Table 4); the Bangla-specialized TigerLLM scores lowest and never predicts Severe. Almost all errors are under-estimates. Across all models, 70.9% of unsafe prompts are assigned a lower severity label, and 47.0% are classified as Safe (unsafe-as-safe rate, USR). As shown in Figure 4, only 12.3% of Severe prompts are correctly classified, while 47.5% and 34.1% are classified as Harmful and Safe, respectively. In contrast, only 0.8% of Safe prompts are incorrectly classified as unsafe.

section: LLMs under-detect risk in Bangla script, and romanization makes it worse.
text: Romanization further reduces performance. Relative to Bangla script, mean macro-F1 falls by 7.8 points on romanized prompts, and USR rises to 63.4%. The drop is significant for five of six models. Command A+ is the most affected: it loses 19.9 points and labels 87.8% of romanized unsafe prompts Safe. Code-mixing has a smaller effect (- 2.4 points), and Gemma 4 is the only model with no significant change under either form. The loss again concentrates on the Severe class (20.4 \rightarrow 11.1 F1), where errors are most costly (Figure 5).

section: LLMs under-detect risk in Bangla script, and romanization makes it worse.
text: Finding 1. LLMs label 47.0% of unsafe Bangla-script prompts Safe. Romanization raises this to 63.4% and costs 7.8 macro-F1 points on average.

section: Response safety also deteriorates across written forms.
text: As shown in Table 5, the average ARR decreases from 78.3% on Bangla-script prompts to 77.0% and 68.0% on code-mixed and romanized prompts, respectively. The largest reduction is observed for GPT-4.1 mini on Severe prompts, where ARR decreases from 68.3% to 51.9% under romanization. Although Command A+ and TigerLLM rarely comply with romanized harmful requests, they achieve only 25.2% and 32.8% ARR on Offensive prompts, respectively, suggesting that they fail to understand the input rather than identify harmful content. Furthermore, between 5% and 22% of responses to Harmful and Severe prompts provide material or direct assistance (Figure 13). Classification macro-F1 and ARR are strongly correlated across the 18 model–form combinations (r=0.84; Figure 6), so models that classify better also respond more appropriately. Appendix H presents examples where changing the written form changes refusal behavior.

section: Response safety also deteriorates across written forms.
text: Finding 2. The written forms that hide risk from LLM classifiers also weaken their responses: mean ARR falls from 78.3% to 68.0% under romanization.

A natural mitigation is to let the LLM classify its own input and refuse whenever it predicts Harmful or Severe; we simulate this from our logged predictions and judgments (Table 6). Self-guarding lowers the mean harmful compliance rate by only about 5 points in each form, a relative reduction of roughly 15%, so models still comply with about 30% of Harmful and Severe prompts. The same under-estimation that hurts classification lets most unsafe prompts through the filter, while the filter also blocks 5–29% of Offensive prompts that warrant an answer. Without any guard, Haiku 4.5 complies less often than every other model with self-guarding on script and code-mixed prompts, so the choice of model matters several times more than the guard. Dedicated guards filter more: PolyGuard and IndicGuard lower mean HCR to 16.5–22.6%, but block up to 63% of Offensive prompts (Appendix J).
Finding 3. Self-classification removes only about 5 points of harmful compliance; models still comply with about 30% of Harmful and Severe prompts.

section: Dedicated guard models do not close the gap.
text: Llama Guard 3 passes more than half of the unsafe prompts in every form, and the USR of PolyGuard and IndicGuard roughly doubles under romanization (32.7 \rightarrow 60.4% and 30.3 \rightarrow 62.9%; Table 4).

section: BanglaShield is accurate and stable across forms.
text: BanglaShield achieves the best accuracy, macro-F1, and USR on all three forms. It is also far less sensitive to form (Figure 7). Its macro-F1 rises by 0.4 points under code-mixing and falls by 3.5 under romanization, against mean LLM drops of 2.4 and 7.8, and its USR stays at or below 1.0% on every form.

section: BanglaShield is accurate and stable across forms.
text: Finding 4. BanglaShield reaches 84.4–88.3 macro-F1 with a USR of at most 1.0% on every form, outperforming the best LLM on each form by 42.8–46.1 points and every guard model in USR.

section: BanglaShield is accurate and stable across forms.
text: The aggregate scores hide how unstable LLM predictions are on individual items. When only the form of a prompt changes, LLMs change their label on 9–31% of items, and for every LLM and form, flips from correct to wrong outnumber flips from wrong to correct (Table 8). As a result, only 34.5–45.9% of items are classified correctly in all three forms. BanglaShield classifies 81.7% of items correctly in all three forms, and under code-mixing it is the only system whose flips favor the correct label (2.3% wrong-to-correct vs. 1.8% correct-to-wrong).

section: Effect of linguistic form on evaluation and training.
text: Code-mixing lowers mean LLM macro-F1 by a similar margin whether the inserted words are English (38.9 \rightarrow 36.3), Hindi (38.0 \rightarrow 35.8), or Urdu (37.0 \rightarrow 35.2), and the accuracy gap to Bangla script stays between 1.5 and 2.0 points across substitution-rate bins (Figure 10; Appendix C). The degradation therefore comes from the change of form itself rather than from one embedded language or heavily mixed prompts. We train single-form variants of BanglaShield on each form alone and evaluate each variant on all three forms of the test set (Figure 8; full results in Table 13). Bangla-script and code-mixed training transfer well to each other, with both models reaching 76.3–87.2 macro-F1 on script and code-mixed prompts, but neither transfers to romanized prompts (39.4 and 42.9). Romanized training shows the mirror pattern, reaching 80.2 on romanized prompts but only 44.7 on script and 34.6 on code-mixed prompts. No single form is sufficient. Stable performance requires romanized training data together with at least one Bangla-script or code-mixed form.

section: BanglaShield handles culturally grounded harms that LLMs miss.
text: Table 7 breaks down LLM accuracy by source. Benign customer prompts are classified almost perfectly in every form, so the overall degradation comes almost entirely from the unsafe sources. Most of these are translated or adapted from English datasets. BanglaSafe, in contrast, is written natively from Bangladeshi court records and news reports, and it is the hardest source: on Bangla-script prompts, LLMs classify only 9.0% of its items correctly on average and respond appropriately to only 53.9%. Romanization also hurts the translated sources, lowering ARR most for MultiJail (19.3 points), followed by XSafety (11.9) and IndicSafe (10.1). BanglaShield improves accuracy on every source, and on BanglaSafe it reaches 84.3%, compared with 9.0% for the LLMs.

We introduced BanglaShield, a paired, four-level Bangla safety corpus in native-script, romanized, and code-mixed forms, together with a benchmark of six LLMs and three guard models, and a compact encoder-based safety classifier. Our results show that LLMs underestimate the severity of harmful Bangla prompts, classifying nearly half of unsafe prompts as Safe even in native script. Romanization further degrades both classification and response safety, and self-classification and existing multilingual guards offer limited improvement. BanglaShield closes most of this gap with a single 237M parameter encoder that is stable across written forms. We release the corpus, splits, judge outputs, and model to support script-robust safety research for Bangla and other multi-script languages.

Our study has several limitations. First, the romanized and code-mixed prompts are generated automatically without manual validation, so they may not fully represent natural romanization and code-switching patterns, and some may contain grammatical errors. However, these transformations preserve the original meaning and safety label while changing the written form, following previous multilingual safety studies (Deng et al., 2024; Yoo et al., 2025), and even these controlled transformations reduce LLM safety performance (Tables 4 and 5). Second, the safety labels are assigned using deterministic mappings from the original dataset categories rather than individual annotations, and the benign prompts are not manually validated. Nevertheless, the mappings follow the original datasets’ label definitions and preserve their annotations, making the labeling transparent and reproducible (Appendix A).

The corpus contains requests for harmful and severe assistance, drawn from previously published safety benchmarks. We release it for research on safety classification under the licenses of the original resources. Model responses and judge rationales are released in full to support auditing and replication; because some responses contain harmful or offensive content, they are distributed with a content warning and are intended solely for safety research. The benign controls derive from a CC BY 4.0 product-review corpus and contain no personal identifiers. A guard model reduces but does not eliminate risk, and BanglaShield should be deployed alongside other safeguards and human oversight.

Causal Edit Serialization. Standard autoregressive language models generate text sequentially, but revision requires referring back to tokens in the input context or those already generated. Causal Edit Serialization (CES) is introduced as a framework for expressing such revisions within the same causal token stream. Special pointer tokens are paired with predicted source addresses, allowing insertion, deletion, replacement, copying and movement to be localized explicitly. A lightweight localization head and dual-index rotary position encoding support both address prediction and conditioning on previously emitted pointers, while retaining a standard causal attention mask. A pretraining procedure combines ordinary language modeling with serialized repairs derived from random corruptions, model-generated edits and repeated text. Across model scales and editing baselines, CES models demonstrate complete applied edits with modestly higher clean-text bits per byte than clean autoregressive models. Supervised and reinforcement-learning post-training provide a grammatical-error-correction proof of concept, producing more beneficial than harmful changes under reference-blind model judging. Correct repair programs also improve subsequent text prediction while the original context and its cached states are retained. CES provides a common interface for generation and localized revision, with potential extensions to iterative refinement and additional pointer-addressed transformations.

Editing is fundamental in natural language and code: humans revise spans, replace phrases, move clauses, duplicate content, and repair earlier generations (Mallinson et al., 2020; Reid and Neubig, 2022). Standard autoregressive language models, however, are optimized to emit the next token from left to right (Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020). Regenerating a revised passage preserves causal decoding, but re-emits unchanged text, spending output tokens and decoding work on content already available. Emitting a localized edit avoids this repetition. The challenge is to identify the affected source spans and make those references available to subsequent predictions.

Denoising encoder–decoder models reconstruct text from corrupted inputs (Raffel et al., 2023; Song et al., 2019). FELIX combines tagging and insertion (Mallinson et al., 2020), while insertion-based and iterative editing models relax left-to-right output construction (Stern et al., 2019; Patel et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2019). Here, explicit edit programs are generated within a single causal token stream. Source locations are predicted directly, and subsequent decisions condition on those references, while the standard causal attention mask is retained. Replacement, copy, and move should be available alongside insertion and deletion.

This paper presents Causal Edit Serialization (CES). CES appends a structured edit stream after the base sequence and factors each edit into a short causal chain: predict an operation token, localize the relevant source span or destination, and then emit any payload tokens. A dual-index rotary scheme lets the model reason both about global token order and about edit addresses in the source sequence, while a lightweight localization head predicts source positions directly from the hidden states. The formulation supports insert, delete, replace, move, and copy, all inside the same decoder-only model.

The contributions are: A representation and training procedure for causal editing. CES combines source-address pointers and dual-index positional encoding with training on random corruptions, model-generated edits, and mined copy examples. A comparison of pretrained editing models. Three depths and three training seeds compare CES with autoregressive edit scripts using numeric addresses (AR-DSL, an autoregressive domain-specific language) or relative-distance tokens, full-text regeneration, infilling with given or predicted spans, iterative insertion/deletion, and adaptation of a clean decoder. Beneficial grammatical correction after post-training. Supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning produce positive net improvement on grammatical error correction (GEC) under reference-blind GPT-5 Mini judging. Continuation conditioned on edit programs. Supplied correct repairs improve subsequent clean-text likelihood while the source and edit program remain in the causal history.

The Insertion Transformer (Stern et al., 2019), Insertion Language Models (Patel et al., 2025), and Levenshtein Transformer (Gu et al., 2019) support generation orders or refinement operations beyond appending text. FELIX (Mallinson et al., 2020) combines tagging and insertion, while Reid and Neubig (2022) model editing processes. EditNTS (Dong et al., 2019) autoregressively generates edit operations with a cursor that advances through the source. CES makes source addresses explicit within the generated edit stream. The contribution of CES is the integration of explicit source addressing with causal edit generation.

T5 (Raffel et al., 2023) and MASS (Song et al., 2019) use reconstruction objectives with encoder–decoder architectures. Fill-in-the-middle training can also use a standard causal decoder by rearranging prefix, suffix, and middle (Bavarian et al., 2022); causal attention alone therefore does not distinguish CES from FIM. The distinction is predicting source locations and heterogeneous operations together, rather than receiving a hole to fill. Learned hole selection is also tested through the predicted-span FIM baseline. LintSeq (Piterbarg et al., 2025) constructs synthetic edit sequences for training autoregressive models to generate code as textual diffs. Patch interfaces used in coding-agent workflows likewise separate a generated edit description from deterministic application; CES makes token addressing a learned channel inside the decoder. Agent workflows are not evaluated, and superiority over mature coding assistants is not claimed.

Pointer networks (Vinyals et al., 2015) use attention to select input positions. CES combines source-address prediction with conditioning on emitted pointers, partitioning rotary features (Su et al., 2023) between serialization order and source addressing. A leave-one-out policy-gradient baseline (Ahmadian et al., 2024) is used over executed token-and-pointer trajectories in the post-training extension.

Consider a sequence of standard tokens x=(x_{0},\ldots,x_{T-1}) from a causal language model, with prompt x_{0:t-1} and generated continuation x_{t:T-1}. Suppose the span x_{i:j}, where t\leq i\leq j<T, is to be replaced. One approach is to regenerate the entire continuation with that span changed, re-emitting the text outside the edit. An edit program can instead specify the span and emit only its replacement. The question is how the model should identify positions in text it has already generated.

A textual patch can locate a span by emitting short search strings around its boundaries. Such anchors require matching rules and can be ambiguous when the same text appears more than once. Alternatively, the model can emit an absolute token index or a backward offset. Written as ordinary numbers, these addresses may occupy several BPE tokens and require decoding and interpreting the number; dedicated offset tokens instead require a predefined vocabulary of distances. Both encode addresses through vocabulary prediction; CES instead scores available source positions directly.

CES makes locations explicit through special pointer-role tokens paired with predicted source addresses. The vocabulary head chooses a role, such as the start of a replacement, and a separate localization head scores legal preceding positions. When that token is fed back into the model, dual-index RoPE encodes both its stream position and its source address. Thus the model both predicts locations and conditions on them while retaining ordinary causal attention. The source is not retroactively changed inside the decoding history: the model appends a program, which an interpreter applies to produce the edited text.

Five operations are defined: \mathcal{D}, \mathcal{I}, \mathcal{R}, \mathcal{C}, and \mathcal{M}, for delete, insert, replace, copy, and move. Each edit is decomposed into smaller causal decisions: first the edit type, then its source location or span, followed by any payload or destination address. Each decision conditions on the preceding ones. Supplying a partial program therefore allows the remaining decisions to be conditioned on a chosen edit type or location.

A program containing K edits is delimited by \mathcal{E}_{\text{S}} and \mathcal{E}_{\text{E}}: \bigl(x_{0:t-1},\ \mathcal{E}_{\text{B}},\ x_{t:T-1},\ \mathcal{E}_{\text{S}},\ \ser(e_{1}),\ldots,\ser(e_{K}),\ \mathcal{E}_{\text{E}}\bigr). The boundary marker \mathcal{E}_{\text{B}} separates the protected prefix from the editable suffix. Edits are ordered left-to-right and refer to the original source positions, which do not shift as earlier edits are applied.

An operation symbol without a subscript denotes its opener token. The subscripts S, E, and L denote start, end, and location; EOS marks the end of a payload. Superscripts give predicted source addresses. Figure 1 shows the full token names alongside this concise representation.

\ser(e)=\begin{cases}(\mathcal{D}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}{\color[rgb]{0.5352,0.4531,0.7031}\mathcal{D}_{\text{S}}^{i}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}{\color[rgb]{0.5352,0.4531,0.7031}\mathcal{D}_{\text{E}}^{j}}),&e=\operatorname{Delete}(i,j),\\[4.0pt] (\mathcal{I}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}{\color[rgb]{0.5352,0.4531,0.7031}\mathcal{I}_{\text{L}}^{\ell}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}{\color[rgb]{0.1016,0.4961,0.2148}y_{1}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}\ldots\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}{\color[rgb]{0.1016,0.4961,0.2148}y_{m}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}\mathcal{I}_{\text{EOS}}),&e=\operatorname{Insert}(\ell,y),\\[4.0pt] (\mathcal{R}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}{\color[rgb]{0.5352,0.4531,0.7031}\mathcal{R}_{\text{S}}^{i}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}{\color[rgb]{0.5352,0.4531,0.7031}\mathcal{R}_{\text{E}}^{j}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}{\color[rgb]{0.1016,0.4961,0.2148}y_{1}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}\ldots\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}{\color[rgb]{0.1016,0.4961,0.2148}y_{m}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}\mathcal{R}_{\text{EOS}}),&e=\operatorname{Replace}(i,j,y),\\[4.0pt] (\mathcal{C}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}{\color[rgb]{0.5352,0.4531,0.7031}\mathcal{C}_{\text{S}}^{i}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}{\color[rgb]{0.5352,0.4531,0.7031}\mathcal{C}_{\text{E}}^{j}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}{\color[rgb]{0.5352,0.4531,0.7031}\mathcal{C}_{\text{L}}^{\ell}}),&e=\operatorname{Copy}(i,j,\ell),\\[4.0pt] (\mathcal{M}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}{\color[rgb]{0.5352,0.4531,0.7031}\mathcal{M}_{\text{S}}^{i}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}{\color[rgb]{0.5352,0.4531,0.7031}\mathcal{M}_{\text{E}}^{j}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0},}}{\color[rgb]{0.5352,0.4531,0.7031}\mathcal{M}_{\text{L}}^{\ell}}),&e=\operatorname{Move}(i,j,\ell).\end{cases}
Purple symbols pair a token role with a predicted source address; green symbols are standard payload tokens. Commas separate tokens in the notation.

For insertion, emitting \mathcal{I} selects the insertion edit type, and \mathcal{I}_{\text{L}}^{\ell} specifies insertion after the source token x_{\ell} at position \ell. The model then emits y_{1},\ldots,y_{m} and closes the payload with \mathcal{I}_{\text{EOS}}. It can next begin another operation or finish the edit program with \mathcal{E}_{\text{E}}.

For deletion, \mathcal{D} is followed by \mathcal{D}_{\text{S}}^{i} and \mathcal{D}_{\text{E}}^{j}, identifying the first and last tokens to remove. The span [i,j] is inclusive and no payload is needed. Replacement uses the same span description followed by its new content.

Copy retains its source span; move removes it and reinserts it elsewhere. Their destination-position tokens, \mathcal{C}_{\text{L}} and \mathcal{M}_{\text{L}}, specify where the span is inserted. The boundary marker also allows insertion before the first editable token. Grammar masks restrict illegal addresses and overlapping spans.

The illustrated programs use \mathcal{I}_{\text{EOS}} and \mathcal{R}_{\text{EOS}} to mark payload completion. Including these terminators is a design choice: they separate payload completion from the choice of the next operation, whereas a convention without them uses the next operation opener or edit-end token to delimit the payload.

Each token at stream position i carries a global index i and an address index p_{i}. Pointer-role tokens use their source address; insertion and replacement payloads inherit the insertion location and replacement start, respectively. Other tokens use their global index. RoPE (Su et al., 2023) is applied to both indices using two disjoint channel groups, one for generation order and one for source-address relations.

For each attention head of width d_{h}, its query and key are split into equal halves, q_{i}=[q_{i}^{\mathrm{seq}};q_{i}^{\mathrm{addr}}] and k_{i}=[k_{i}^{\mathrm{seq}};k_{i}^{\mathrm{addr}}]. The two RoPE matrices act on these halves independently: R_{i}=\operatorname{diag}\!\bigl(R(i),R(p_{i})\bigr),\qquad\widetilde{q}_{i}=R_{i}q_{i},\qquad\widetilde{k}_{i}=R_{i}k_{i}, where each block is a d_{h}/2 -dimensional rotation. After Q/K RMS normalization and scaling, these rotated queries and keys enter ordinary causal attention (Vaswani et al., 2017); values are unchanged. Their dot product combines generation-order and source-address relations. Concatenation restores the original head width d_{h}. The pretrained-decoder adaptation baseline instead appends an address branch (Appendix F).

In addition to the vocabulary head, a pointer head scores legal source positions. With projected queries q_{t}=\operatorname{RMSNorm}(W_{q}h_{t}) and keys k_{i}=\operatorname{RMSNorm}(W_{k}h_{i}), normalized across channels without learned affine parameters, it computes p(i\mid h_{t},\mathcal{S}_{t})=\frac{\exp(q_{t}^{\top}k_{i}/\sqrt{d})}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\exp(q_{t}^{\top}k_{j}/\sqrt{d})},\quad i\in\mathcal{S}_{t}, where \mathcal{S}_{t} contains legal preceding source addresses for the current grammar state. The vocabulary head predicts the pointer’s role token; the address channel predicts its coordinate. This requires two small learned projections and an auxiliary source-key cache. The head and its dual-index encoding add 0.34–0.41% parameters relative to the regeneration models at the tested depths.

Edit-training streams are constructed from ClimbMix text (Diao et al., 2025). A modified source is paired with a causal program that recovers its target. Random corruptions insert, delete, replace, or move token spans. Their spacing and lengths are sampled from geometric distributions under a token budget; inserted content mixes spans from other documents or the current sequence with randomly sampled tokens.

To add more naturalistic revisions, localized edits proposed by GPT-5 Mini are also serialized. A separate copy-mining pipeline removes later occurrences of repeated spans and trains the model to restore them by referring to the earlier occurrence. Complementary edit types and lengths are provided by these sources; the training settings are selected through source-mixture and corruption sweeps. Appendix B gives the sampling procedure, corpus provenance, operation counts, and quality checks.

The model is trained with a standard autoregressive cross-entropy loss over the serialized token stream. For location-bearing tokens, an additional cross-entropy loss is applied over the address distribution produced by the localization head. Writing each component as a mean over its supervised targets, the objective is \mathcal{L}=\frac{\sum_{t}\delta_{t}\mathcal{L}_{\text{token}}(t)}{\sum_{t}\delta_{t}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{addr}}\frac{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{addr}}(t)}{|\mathcal{A}|}, where \mathcal{A} denotes the set of address-predicting tokens and \delta_{t} masks out corrupted source tokens whose next-token targets no longer lie on the clean language-modeling distribution. The address term is zero for a batch without pointer targets. \lambda_{\mathrm{addr}}=0.01 is selected from the three-seed sweep. In practice the address-loss weight is important: too much pressure on the position head hurts base language modeling, while too little pressure weakens edit localization.

The interpreter applies a completed program to the original source coordinates and returns the edited text. Subsequent generation can retain the source-plus-program history and its existing KV cache, or use the materialized edited text as its prefix. The latter requires recomputing causal states from the first change; the former preserves the cache but requires the model to interpret the appended edits (Section 4.5). Appendix C details edit decoding and cache management; Appendix I reports measured editing and continuation costs.

The CES model is further trained for grammatical error correction without changes to its architecture or edit language. Balanced supervised fine-tuning mixes edit programs, clean no-op examples, and ordinary continuations. Broad corruption-recovery RL then precedes GEC-focused RL on localized corruptions of clean CoEdIT sentences. Sampled programs are executed, and recovery of the known target is rewarded using edit-distance reduction and exact recovery, with penalties for invalid or excessive edits. Policy updates use leave-one-out REINFORCE (Ahmadian et al., 2024) over vocabulary and pointer decisions, alongside supervised losses. Appendix J details the training and evaluation procedures; Section 4.4 reports the resulting editing performance.

For controlled repair, a clean passage y^{*} from the held-out ClimbMix validation shard is synthetically corrupted to give source x. Each model receives x in its native prompt format and produces an edit program or revised text. Programs are applied to x, regenerated text is used directly, and FIM completions are inserted into their selected spans. The resulting \hat{y} is compared with y^{*}. The target is withheld during decoding, except that oracle-span FIM receives target-derived span boundaries.

Table 1 summarizes eight NanoChat-based editing methods (Karpathy, 2025). Three depths (12/18/24) and three seeds give 72 model runs, evaluated before and after supervised CoEdIT fine-tuning. CES has approximately 287M/705M/1.389B parameters. Clean AR provides additional language-model references. Exact baseline specifications are in Appendix F; budgets and evaluation protocols are in Appendix A.

The main comparison uses mixed random and GPT-generated edits, corruption control 1.0, address-loss weight \lambda_{\mathrm{addr}}=0.01, and greedy decoding. These settings balance language modeling and repair; Appendix D reports the source-mixture, address-loss-weight, and corruption-exposure ablations; Appendix E compares decoding policies.

Figure 2 compares pretrained models and representation costs. The controlled suite is balanced across insertion, deletion, replacement, movement, and mixed repair, with 1, 2, 4, or 8 operations. The eight-operation stratum is a denser stress condition. These tests measure recovery of known targets, not whether a reference is the only acceptable revision of natural text.

Clean AR has lower validation bits per byte (BPB) than from-scratch CES at all three depths, while CORE differences vary with depth. BPB measures ordinary next-token prediction on clean ClimbMix text (lower is better); the centered CORE aggregate (Li et al., 2025) measures sampled language-understanding and knowledge-task performance. At depth 24, CES obtains 0.7629 BPB versus 0.7484 for clean AR, a relative increase of approximately 1.9%.

CES usually produces executable programs, but exact target recovery remains difficult: depth-24 pretrained CES achieves 90.53\pm 1.85 % valid programs and 5.27\pm 0.45 % exact recovery. AR-DSL and flat-relative addressing produce no valid controlled programs in this setting. This supports the combined CES addressing design under the evaluated recipe; it does not isolate the pointer head from dual-index RoPE or establish that textual patches generally fail.

CES brings more inputs closer to the target than iterative Levenshtein at depth 24 (53.40\pm 3.75 % versus 39.03\pm 0.21 %), but its mean similarity gain is smaller (0.00941\pm 0.00147 versus 0.01062\pm 0.00046). Similarity change is \Delta S=S(\hat{y},y^{*})-S(x,y^{*}), where S is Python’s difflib.SequenceMatcher similarity ratio, based on matching character blocks (autojunk=False). Panel E reports \Pr(\Delta S>0); F reports \mathbb{E}[\Delta S], retaining both helpful and harmful changes. These target-recovery metrics do not measure the semantic quality of unrestricted revision.

Across the three tested depths, CES improves in clean-language modeling, CORE, program validity, and both the frequency and mean magnitude of partial repair; exact recovery also rises, but remains low at 5.27% at depth 24.

Supplying edit locations does not solve content generation. Oracle FIM still produces harmful payloads, and a separate seed-42 CES diagnostic obtains only 7.3% depth-24 exact recovery with gold pointers and 8.4% with the gold operation envelope as well (Table 6 in Appendix G). Predicting locations remains difficult: predicted-span FIM achieves exact span accuracies of 4.67%, 3.93%, and 2.37% at the three depths, although its poor BPB also indicates a weak trained comparator.

In a matched single-seed depth-12 ablation, sharing one pointer token across roles yielded similar language-modeling and editing scores, while synthetic pointer accuracy fell from 48.64% to 45.81% (Appendix K).

Adapted CES retains much of its initial clean-language performance, but its short adaptation schedule gives weak repair. It establishes compatibility with pretrained weights, not a compute-matched advantage of adaptation.

CES preserves text outside its selected operations and represents sparse revisions without regenerating unchanged text. On CoEdIT pairs (Raheja et al., 2023), minimum insert/delete/replace completions average 41.8 tokens for CES versus 56.0 for whole-target regeneration; including prompts gives approximately 100.0 versus 132.1 tokens. These reference-based costs assume fixed prompts and BPE boundaries; compactness does not establish edit quality or a quality-matched speedup.

Terminal editing requires no cache rebuild, and generation can continue from the appended source-plus-program history. Continuing instead from materialized edited text requires cache recomputation; its cost depends on context length and rebuild frequency. Full sequence accounting and measured editing and continuation costs are given in Appendix I.

Appendix G evaluates supervised CoEdIT fine-tuning using reference-distance metrics and ERRANT (the grammatical Error Annotation Toolkit) (Bryant et al., 2017), which compares predicted edits with reference edits to compute precision, recall, and F_{0.5}. After supervised fine-tuning, regeneration scores higher on reference-based GEC metrics while CES retains positive controlled repair, motivating targeted post-training; the separate judged evaluation below does not establish a reversal of this baseline ranking.

CoEdIT pairs source sentences with grammatical corrections (Raheja et al., 2023), but acceptable revisions can differ from the reference. The selected d24 seed-42 checkpoint is therefore assessed by reference-blind GPT-5 Mini judging after the curriculum in Section 3.7. Figure 3 compares unfiltered decoding and a conservative acceptance policy, reporting improvement, harm, coverage, and nominal-clean preservation together.

A custom 5,000-pair CoEdIT confirmation partition is used, with its recorded targets supplied as 5,000 nominal-clean identity inputs. The judge sees the source and anonymous model/human candidates, without identifying the human edit as an answer key. Appendix J describes the partition and source-overlap checks. An optional threshold \tau controls whether editing begins: unlike plain greedy, the gate combines probabilities across edit openers, so \tau=0 is not equivalent to greedy decoding (Appendix J).

Plain greedy yields positive net judged improvement of +4.74 percentage points (95% CI [3.52,5.96]), changing 22.74% of inputs: 619 improve, 136 are neutral and 382 worsen. It changes 3.48% of nominal-clean inputs. More aggressive editing increases harm: at \tau=-1, coverage reaches 59.62% but net improvement falls to -4.38 points. At \tau=0.75, net improvement is +5.18 points with 19.66% coverage; this threshold is exploratory rather than independently validated. Appendix J.2 gives decoding limits and replay checks; Figure 3 F illustrates successes, neutral changes, and failures.

Filtering yields more selective positive results. At \tau=0.5, candidates are accepted only if they change at most four removed-plus-inserted characters across at most one region and have mean program-decision log probability at least -0.6; rejections return the source. At 17.60% coverage, 68.30% of retained changes improve and 15.68% worsen, giving all-input net improvement of +9.26 points. Only 1.48% of nominal-clean inputs change. The human control has 100% changed coverage and +61.94 points, so it is not coverage-matched. Together, the unfiltered and filtered results establish positive judged editing capability in a CES model, but do not isolate the contribution of RL or establish superiority to general GEC systems; full-curriculum/filter-matched controls and independent human judging remain absent.

CES can also condition subsequent predictions on an appended edit program while retaining the original source history. On 540 held-out ClimbMix documents, a source prefix is corrupted and a correct repair program is supplied. The next 128 tokens of the original document are then scored under teacher forcing. Relative to the same corrupted prefix followed by an empty program, the repair lowers mean negative log likelihood (NLL) by 0.02123 nats/token. The reduction is 0.00641 nats/token relative to a valid sham program with the same operation family and span size that leaves the prefix incorrect. Thus the supplied correction makes the original continuation more likely, providing evidence that the model uses the repair content. This tests interpretation of supplied repairs, not autonomous repair or sampled continuation quality. Appendix H gives the protocol and uncertainty; Appendix I reports cache-rebuilding costs when continuing from materialized edited text.

CES integrates explicit source addressing and edit programs into a causal decoder. The experiments establish controlled repair, beneficial post-trained edits under model judging, and continuation conditioned on supplied repairs. These results support causal referencing as a practical modeling interface; reliable unrestricted revision and transfer to larger pretrained models remain open.

Experiments use one NanoChat model family up to 1.389B parameters and a 2,048-token context. Exact repair remains low, dense edits are difficult, and insertion recovery is a persistent weakness. Generated training edits are replacement-heavy and copy/move coverage is uneven. The trained regeneration, FIM, and iterative baselines do not represent state-of-the-art editing systems. Transfer to modern LLM families remains untested.

The selected confirmation policy permits only small local changes and abstains on 82.4% of editing inputs. Its positive semantic direction is specific to a GPT-5 Mini judge, candidate panel, custom holdout, and one post-training seed. The same model family generated some supervision and judged the outputs. Changing the set of candidates presented to the judge changed scores for identical CES outputs, and pair-based splitting allowed 24 repeated sources. Example bootstraps do not capture training or judge uncertainty. There is no independent blinded human audit or confirmation-set comparison with continued SFT or regeneration matched for the full training curriculum and acceptance filters.

Appending programs preserves caches but does not reclaim context; materializing edited text requires rebuilding. Timings depend on hardware, kernels, and context. Source-grouped splits, coverage-matched comparisons with stronger editors, and broader copy/move and long-context evaluations are needed.

A shared pointer token could support more general source references whose roles are specified through instructions or in-context examples, extending the ablation in Appendix K. Improved initialization and adaptation training for the localization head and dual-index attention could help integrate these mechanisms into pretrained LLMs. Joint training on programs and pointers could teach models to generate code that reads referenced spans and writes computed results back to selected locations. Better teacher repairs and task distributions could develop strong referencing with less corruption training. Equal-FLOP comparisons and scaling studies could examine how model capacity and corruption exposure affect editing ability and ordinary autoregressive performance. Larger models and practical text, code, and agent-context tasks would test these capabilities beyond controlled repair.

References could remain unexpanded until the model requests materialization of a region for editing, with addresses remapped to the expanded content. This makes cache reuse, faster partial rebuilding, and approximate KV-cache updates important systems directions. An edit-based discrete diffusion model is another possibility: training across noise levels could support generation from random text through repeatedly generated and applied edit programs, with the aim of approximating the training distribution.

Explicit edit programs can make text and code revision easier to inspect. They can also support subtle document manipulation or introduce harmful changes into otherwise correct text. Structural validity and model confidence are insufficient safeguards for semantic correctness. The current models are research artifacts; downstream applications should expose proposed changes for review and preserve provenance. Generated data and derivatives retain applicable upstream restrictions.

From Long Context to Selective Memory:A Survey of Memory-Centric Compression for Large Language Models. Long-context capability has become essential for large language models (LLMs) to handle complex tasks, yet continuously expanding the context window does not remove the computational, storage, and information-selection pressures incurred at inference time. Existing work on prompt compression, KV-cache management, efficient serving, retrieval augmentation, and agent memory is usually discussed in isolation, leaving the flow of information between storage and computation insufficiently understood. This survey reframes long-context compression as a memory-management problem for allocating inference-time resources. We distinguish compute-active memory, which directly participates in model computation, from compute-inactive memory, which lies outside the computation path but can be stored, retrieved, updated, or forgotten, and we characterize offloaded KV caches, persistent prefix caches, and precomputed KV states as intermediate states on the activation path. On this basis, we formulate writing, offloading, recall, retrieval-and-injection, materialization, eviction, consolidation, and forgetting as state transitions within an information lifecycle, and introduce a budgeted cost model that places these operations in a single cost account.

The resulting framework unifies short-term context compression, long-term memory management, and the transitions between them, and shows that the central challenge is not merely reducing information volume but deciding which information should participate in costly inference, when, and in what form. We further summarize evaluation dimensions, benchmark gaps, and open challenges, and argue that future research should move from static, pointwise compression toward dynamic, governable, lifecycle-aware memory management.

Long-context capability has become a prerequisite for large language models (LLMs) on complex tasks. As context windows have grown from several thousand to hundreds of thousands or even millions of tokens (Xu et al., 2026a; OpenAI, 2026; Google, 2026), long-document understanding, codebase analysis, multi-turn dialogue, tool-use trajectories, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and long-term personalized assistance increasingly depend on a model’s ability to receive and exploit large amounts of contextual information (Liu et al., 2025a).

A larger window, however, does not by itself yield more effective use of information (Liu et al., 2024c; Hsieh et al., 2024). Long inputs increase prefill computation and place growing pressure on key-value (KV) cache memory, memory bandwidth, and latency during decoding (Zhang et al., 2023; Kwon et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2026a), while realistic contexts contain repeated, obsolete, or irrelevant content that dilutes critical evidence. The long-context problem is therefore not only one of capacity but also one of management: how a system selects, compresses, and uses information under a finite computational budget.

Several research directions address this problem at different levels, including prompt compression, latent memory representations, KV-cache compression, architecture-level selective computation, efficient serving, retrieval augmentation, and external long-term memory (Jiang et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2024; Mu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Kwon et al., 2023; Lewis et al., 2020; Packer et al., 2023). Existing surveys usually organize them by technical origin or application scenario (Liu et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025c; Verma, 2024), which obscures a question they share: which information should enter the expensive attention-computation path, and which should instead be compressed, externalized, reused, updated, or forgotten?

This survey answers this question from a memory-centric perspective. We call information that directly participates in the current model computation compute-active memory, and information that lies outside the current computation path but can be stored, retrieved, updated, or forgotten compute-inactive memory. The distinction concerns an item’s participation in computation at a given inference step rather than its storage location: the same content may be stored externally, later retrieved and injected into the context, and finally written back after inference. Between the two lie intermediate states, in which information has left the attention path but can be restored without re-retrieval or re-encoding, as with offloaded KV caches and precomputed prefix caches. Long-context compression thus becomes the management of an information lifecycle across these states. Recent surveys have also proposed unified views of LLM memory based on memory operations, context engineering, or agent memory (Du et al., 2025; Mei et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025); we instead organize the field by the computational participation of information and its cost. The main contributions are as follows.

We propose a framework that distinguishes compute-active from compute-inactive memory, incorporates intermediate states on the activation path, and casts long-context compression as lifecycle management under a finite computational budget. We formulate writing, offloading, recall, retrieval-and-injection, materialization, eviction, consolidation, and forgetting as state-transition operators and introduce a budgeted cost model that places these operations in a single cost account. We review representative work up to 2026 along this lifecycle, from input, representation, and KV-cache compression to external long-term memory, learned memory policies, and transition mechanisms such as retrieval-and-injection, KV offloading and materialization, and agent-side context folding. We summarize evaluation dimensions, benchmark gaps, and open challenges, and pose a concrete research question for each challenge.

This survey focuses on the intersection of long-context modeling, KV-cache management, retrieval augmentation, and agent memory: how a system decides which information enters the current inference path, compresses its representation, controls its cost, and later updates or forgets it. Methods that only extend the context window without changing information selection, cache management, or memory mechanisms are treated as background. Parametric memory is included only in a limited way, because knowledge editing, continual pre-training, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning incur their cost mainly at training time and do not selectively activate information within a single inference; methods that blur this boundary, such as test-time neural memory (Behrouz et al., 2025) and self-study-trained KV caches (Eyuboglu et al., 2025), are discussed where they affect inference-time memory allocation.

The remainder of the survey is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the costs of long-context inference and positions this survey relative to prior reviews. Section 3 presents the framework. Sections 4 and 5 review compute-active and compute-inactive memory, Section 6 discusses state transitions, Section 7 covers evaluation, Section 8 discusses open challenges, and Section 9 concludes.

section: From Context Extension to Context Management
text: Early work on long-context LLMs focused on enlarging the input that a model can accept, through positional-encoding extrapolation, sparse and sliding-window attention, recurrent-state modeling, retrieval augmentation, and long-context fine-tuning (Chen et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2023; Ding et al., 2024; Beltagy et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020; Dai et al., 2019; Borgeaud et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2024a). These methods allow a model to access more complete task background in a single inference, which matters for long-document understanding, cross-file code analysis, multi-turn dialogue, and tool use, where relevant information is scattered across texts, knowledge bases, interaction histories, and execution states (Bai et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2024d; Lewis et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Packer et al., 2023). As windows reach hundreds of thousands or millions of tokens (Ding et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2026a), the central question has shifted from how much information a model can receive to which information deserves to enter the current inference path, and at what cost (Liu et al., 2025c; Liu et al., 2025a).

section: From Context Extension to Context Management
text: This shift is driven by two kinds of cost. The first is computational. Prefill cost and time-to-first-token grow with input length; during decoding, the KV cache grows with context length, model size, and batch size and consumes GPU memory and bandwidth; and information kept in external indexes becomes costly again once it is retrieved and injected into the prompt. The second is informational. Long inputs mix key evidence with background, repetition, outdated states, and noise, and models do not use information uniformly across positions (Liu et al., 2024c); when evidence is dispersed or appears in the middle of the input, omissions, evidence mismatch, and inconsistent reasoning become more likely. Long-context compression therefore differs from generic model acceleration: besides reducing computation, cache usage, and latency, it must preserve evidence coverage, fidelity, temporal consistency, and future recoverability. Over-compression breaks evidence chains, whereas over-retention increases latency, memory pressure, and noise.

section: Existing Surveys and the Gap Addressed by This Survey
text: Prior surveys fall into four groups. Surveys of long-context LLMs (Liu et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025c; Liu et al., 2025b) cover positional extension, sparse attention, training, infrastructure, and evaluation; compression is one topic among many, and transitions of information between internal states and external storage are rarely analyzed. Surveys of prompt compression (Li et al., 2025c), KV-cache management (Li et al., 2024a; Xu et al., 2026b), and efficient serving (Zhou et al., 2024; Miao et al., 2023) focus on the cost of the current inference path, but give little attention to how long-term memory is written, organized, and forgotten, and seldom relate KV offloading to external-memory retrieval. Surveys of RAG and agent memory (Gao et al., 2023; Verma, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024b; Du, 2026) emphasize external knowledge and long-term history; Hu et al. (2025) organize agent memory by form, function, and dynamics; they include KV compression as latent working memory but assign model-internal cache management to LLM memory, outside the scope of agent memory.

section: Existing Surveys and the Gap Addressed by This Survey
text: The survey of context compression for LLM agents by Wang et al. (2026a) is closest in spirit: it describes a select–compress–store–recover pipeline, discusses recoverability and control overhead, and formulates learned compression control as task reward minus cost. Its scope, however, is application-level trajectory compression, and it excludes KV-cache and model-level methods. Neither group distinguishes re-encoding retrieved text from recalling states that are already encoded, or accounts for online activation, offline materialization, cross-request reuse, and invalidation within one cost structure.

section: Existing Surveys and the Gap Addressed by This Survey
text: The fourth group, closest to this survey, proposes unified views of LLM memory. Du et al. (2025) distinguish parametric from contextual memory and define six atomic operations across long-term memory, long context, and parametric modification; Wu et al. (2025b), Shan et al. (2025), and Jia et al. (2025) organize LLM memory by analogy to human memory; and the context-engineering survey of Mei et al. (2025) places memory hierarchies and context compression under context management. On the system side, MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) manages context through an operating-system analogy, and MemOS (Li et al., 2025b) schedules plaintext, activation, and parametric memory within one system. These works organize the field by cognitive analogy, functional role, or operation type.

section: Existing Surveys and the Gap Addressed by This Survey
text: This survey differs in three respects. First, it organizes methods by whether and when information participates in inference computation, which allows system-level mechanisms such as offloaded KV caches, persistent prefix caches, and offline-compressed KV to be compared with external memory within one lifecycle. Second, it treats state transitions as first-class objects of analysis, in particular the distinction between re-encoding retrieved text (retrieve-and-inject) and recalling states that are already encoded (recall), which fetch memory at very different costs. Third, it compares methods through a budgeted cost model that separates online, offline, and amortized costs, so that costs moved from the current context into background maintenance are not hidden. Table 1 summarizes the comparison.

We treat long-context compression as a memory-management problem of allocating inference-time computation: the goal is to decide when information should participate in inference, in what form, and at what cost. This section defines memory states, the operators that move information between them, the resulting lifecycle, and a cost model that underlies the taxonomy of later sections. Figure 1 gives an overview.

We distinguish memory states by participation in inference computation, because this criterion corresponds directly to the main costs of a long-context system. We fix its granularity at a single request: information is compute-active if it is encoded for the current model and addressable by attention during the request, that is, resident in accelerator memory as tokens, latent states, or KV caches. Such information incurs prefill computation, accelerator memory, memory bandwidth, and decoding latency. Methods that attend to only part of it at each decoding step, such as page-level sparse attention, reduce reads and attention computation within compute-active memory rather than moving information out of it.

Compute-active memory is information that the model accesses during the current inference: prompt tokens, soft prompts or latent states, intermediate activations, and KV caches, including prefix caches reused by the current request. Its size and access pattern directly determine efficiency and generation quality. Compute-inactive memory is information that does not currently participate in computation but can be stored, retrieved, updated, or forgotten: document collections, vector indexes, knowledge graphs, summary memories, user profiles, dialogue histories, and tool trajectories. It is cheaper to hold and suited to long-term maintenance, but influences generation only after being retrieved, compressed, and injected. The two are states rather than fixed categories: retrieved content becomes compute-active, and answers, plans, or reflections produced during inference return to the compute-inactive state when written back.

section: Intermediate states on the activation path.
text: KV offloading, persistent prefix caching, and retrieval-based attention give rise to information that lies between these two states. Such information has already been encoded into a form the model can consume directly (KV blocks, compressed latent states, or precomputed prefixes) and is kept in host memory, SSDs, or remote cache pools; it is not addressable by attention in the current request, yet it can be restored with low latency without re-retrieval or re-prefilling. Examples include offloaded KV states in InfiniGen (Lee et al., 2024), ShadowKV (Sun et al., 2025a), and RetrievalAttention (Liu et al., 2024b), and compressed KV caches trained offline by Cartridges (Eyuboglu et al., 2025). A prefix cache retained for later requests is likewise in an intermediate state; it reaches this state either by being kept after a prefill (A \to S) or by precomputation from text (I \to S). We regard these as intermediate states on the transition path rather than as a third kind of memory. The criterion is the activation path: information that can return to computation through data movement and light correction is in an intermediate state, whereas information that additionally requires retrieval, compression, and re-encoding is compute-inactive.

section: Intermediate states on the activation path.
text: A transition between active and inactive memory may therefore pass through, and remain for some time in, an intermediate state with its own holding cost.

Long-context compression methods can be described by a small set of operators, each specifying the direction in which information moves among compute-active (A), intermediate (S), and compute-inactive (I) states, possibly together with a change of representation such as summarization, structuring, or encoding into KV states (Table 2).

These operators are related to the atomic memory operations of Du et al. (2025), but are defined by changes of computational state rather than by memory function. This distinguishes retrieve-and-inject (I \to A, requiring re-prefilling) from recall (S \to A, mainly data movement), which both fetch memory but have very different cost structures. Compression, in turn, is not a separate operator but a representation change attached to the operators: eviction discards information within active memory, writing may summarize, retrieve-and-inject may filter and rewrite, and consolidation reorganizes representations within one state. Two further conventions apply. Writing copies rather than moves: written content usually remains in active memory for the rest of the request, so A \to I creates a new representation in I without removing its source. Transformations that stay within compute-active memory, such as pruning, encoding into latent states, and architectural sharing or sparsification of KV states, change the representation or the accessed subset without changing state; Table 3 marks them as A \to A.

Composing these operators yields an information lifecycle of writing, storage, retrieval, selection, compression, injection, computation, updating, and forgetting. A system first decides what to write and how to organize it as summaries, indexes, structured representations, or embeddings. For a given task, external memory is retrieved, but retrieved results are not yet effective context: they must be filtered, reranked, compressed, and formatted before entering the inference path. After inference, new facts, plans, tool feedback, user corrections, and reflections may be written back, while outdated, conflicting, low-value, or sensitive memories are updated, down-weighted, or forgotten. Long-context compression is therefore a continuous process rather than one-time input pruning, and different methods act at different stages of this lifecycle.

The aim of compression in this view is to improve information utilization under limited budgets, and the relevant objectives differ by state: for compute-active memory, prefill, KV memory, bandwidth, and throughput; for compute-inactive memory, preserving the retrievability and temporal validity of stored information; and for transitions, evidence traceability, recoverability, and long-term consistency. To make these objectives comparable, let M be the set of memory units held at an inference step, and let each unit m have a state s(m)\in\{A,S,I\}. The total cost is C=\sum_{s(m)=A}c_{A}\,|m|+\sum_{s(m)=S}c_{S}\,|m|+\sum_{s(m)=I}c_{I}\,|m|+\sum_{\tau\in T}c_{\tau}, where |m| is the size of a unit (e.g., tokens or KV bytes); c_{A}, c_{S}, and c_{I} are per-unit holding costs, typically with c_{A}\gg c_{S}\gg c_{I}, covering respectively prefill computation, KV memory, and decoding bandwidth; host-memory or SSD storage; and external storage and index maintenance; T is the set of transitions performed for the current inference; and c_{\tau} is the cost of each transition (retrieval, reranking, compression, data movement, recomputation, or write-back), which also depends on the representations before and after the transition.

Long-context compression can then be written as \max_{s(\cdot),\,T}\;U(y\mid M_{A})-\lambda C\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{s(m)=A}|m|\leq B_{A},\quad\sum_{s(m)=S}|m|\leq B_{S}, where U(y\mid M_{A}) is the utility of generating output y from active memory M_{A}, \lambda trades cost against utility, and B_{A} and B_{S} are the active and intermediate-state budgets.

The model exposes a common structure across method families. Prompt compression shrinks M_{A} in text form; KV eviction removes units from A at the price of recoverability; offloading and recall move units between A and S, exchanging active budget for transfer cost; retrieval augmentation keeps information in I and pays a retrieve-and-inject cost on demand; materialization pays an offline cost to move information from I to S, lowering the cost of each later activation; and long-term memory management acts mainly on the I term and its future activation cost. It also explains why compression ratio alone is misleading: a method may reduce the c_{A} term while shifting cost into c_{\tau} or offline maintenance.

The following sections compare methods along shared dimensions: the memory state and operators involved; the compression target (text, structured fragments, continuous vectors, attention states, cache blocks, or indexes); the selection signal (query semantics, attention distributions, temporal state, task goals, retrieval scores, or heuristics); system requirements (access to internal states, training, compatibility with closed-model APIs, and cross-request reuse); and evaluation criteria (computational and storage cost, task utility, evidence fidelity, recoverability, and long-term consistency). Figure 2 organizes representative methods by memory state and transition, and Table 3 codes a subset of them along these dimensions.

Compute-active memory compression reduces the cost of information that is already on the inference path, and therefore acts directly on prefill overhead, decoding latency, GPU memory, and throughput. We organize methods by where compression occurs: text before model input, compact latent representations, the KV cache during decoding, the model architecture, and the serving system. For each family we consider which cost is reduced, what information is preserved, and what the method requires of model access, training, and deployment. KV states that leave the attention path through offloading are discussed with other state transitions in Section 6.3.

Input and prompt compression filters or rewrites context before it enters the model, acting as admission control for compute-active memory. Inputs that concatenate documents, interaction histories, retrieved passages, and instructions often contain repeated background, templated text, and weakly relevant passages that raise prefill cost and dilute useful information. Methods differ in how they estimate information value: redundancy-based methods such as Selective Context (Li et al., 2023) remove locally repetitive or low-information tokens, sentences, or passages; LLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2023) formulates compression as coarse-to-fine selection under a token budget; and LongLLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2024) conditions compression on the query to retain relevant evidence in long contexts.

Because the output remains natural language, these methods are inspectable and require no change to model internals. Readability does not by itself ensure evidence traceability, however: token-level pruning may produce ungrammatical text detached from its source, so applications such as RAG and knowledge-base question answering also need to retain the original positions, sources, and timestamps of the selected content. Their limitation is that compression precedes reasoning: content that appears unimportant locally may be needed for multi-hop reasoning, long-range coreference, code dependencies, or cross-turn consistency. They work best when task goals are clear, redundancy is high, and evidence can be located from the query, and otherwise need to be combined with reranking, structured evidence preservation, or downstream verification.

section: Compressed Representations: Gist Tokens, Latent States, and Summary Memory
text: Compressed-representation methods encode long contexts into denser computable states, such as special tokens, soft prompts, summary vectors, or compressed activations, which still participate in inference but occupy far less of the context budget. Three directions can be distinguished. Gist Tokens (Mu et al., 2023) train a model to store prompt information in a few learned tokens that later generation attends to; AutoCompressors (Chevalier et al., 2023) process long texts segment by segment and pass summary vectors forward; and Activation Beacon (Zhang et al., 2025b) and Infini-attention (Munkhdalai et al., 2024) compress Transformer activations or combine local attention with a bounded long-term compressed memory. More recent work scales encoder–decoder context compression to large-scale training, improving the trade-off among task performance, compression speed, and peak memory (Li et al., 2026).

section: Compressed Representations: Gist Tokens, Latent States, and Summary Memory
text: These representations increase information density and avoid repeated encoding when the same background is accessed many times. They are, however, difficult to interpret: it is hard to determine which facts or constraints a latent state preserves, or where information was lost when generation fails. They are also tied to specific architectures and training objectives, which limits transfer across models and to closed APIs. They are best viewed as high-density intermediate representations to be combined with task-aware compression or traceable retrieval.

During autoregressive decoding, the keys and values of past tokens are cached to avoid recomputing the prefix, and this cache grows with context length, depth, number of heads, and batch size until it dominates GPU memory and bandwidth. The KV cache is thus a high-cost form of short-term compute-active memory, and KV compression seeks to retain the states most useful for future generation within a fixed budget. Methods differ mainly in how they estimate future utility: by recency, accumulated attention, or attention sinks (Zhang et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2024b); by query-, head-, or layer-aware importance (Li et al., 2024b; Jo et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2025; Rehg, 2024); or by reducing representation cost through quantization, merging, low-rank reconstruction, or reuse across queries (Zhang et al., 2025c; Yang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024a; Chang et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b). Not all methods discard states: Quest (Tang et al., 2024) keeps the full cache resident and loads only the pages with the highest attention upper bounds for the current query, reducing reads and attention computation rather than memory capacity.

Systematic analyses further show that compression can degrade capabilities unevenly, even when aggregate scores are preserved (Liu et al., 2026b). These methods exploit internal signals unavailable to text-level compression, but require access to model states and inference-system support, and their decisions rest on imperfect predictions: states that received little attention so far may become critical later.

A fast-growing branch targets reasoning models, for which long chains of thought shift the main source of KV growth from the prompt to the model’s own generations, and redundancy arises from repeated verification and self-correction. R-KV (Cai et al., 2025) compresses reasoning-trace KV states by jointly considering attention importance and redundancy, and ThinKV (Ramachandran et al., 2026) allocates cache budgets and quantization precision according to the type of thought segment. These methods show that compute-active memory grows not only with external input but also with the reasoning process itself.

Architecture-level methods reduce the cost of long contexts by changing how the model represents and accesses history, rather than by deleting input or post-processing the cache. Multi-Query and Grouped-Query Attention (Shazeer, 2019; Ainslie et al., 2023) share keys and values across query heads, and Multi-head Latent Attention (DeepSeek-AI, 2024a; DeepSeek-AI, 2024b) compresses KV states into latent vectors. Sparse attention has since become native and trainable: NSA (Yuan et al., 2025) combines compression, selection, and sliding-window branches in a hardware-aligned design, MoBA (Lu et al., 2025) routes queries to attention blocks in a mixture-of-experts fashion, and DeepSeek-V3.2 (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) introduces sparse attention driven by a lightweight indexer; DeepSeek-V4 (Xu et al., 2026a) further integrates compressed attention, shared KV, and local windows into the attention mechanism. Other designs reduce reliance on full attention altogether: InfLLM (Xiao et al., 2024a) retrieves from an efficient context memory, state-space and hybrid models such as Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023) and Hymba (Dong et al., 2024) maintain recurrent states, and Kimi Linear (Kimi Team, 2025) pairs a few full-attention layers with linear-attention layers to shrink the KV cache substantially.

These methods build the selection or compaction of compute-active memory into the attention mechanism itself. Most require pre-training or continued training, although GQA can also be obtained by uptraining an existing multi-head checkpoint (Ainslie et al., 2023), and InfLLM is training-free and operates on a pre-trained model at inference time (Xiao et al., 2024a). We include context-extension techniques only when they change the access pattern, state representation, or cost structure of inference. Their main limitation is cost of adoption: they require changes to the architecture or attention kernels and to cache management, usually together with training, and cannot be applied to closed-model interfaces.

Serving-level methods do not change semantic content or internal representations; they determine how computed states are placed, reused, scheduled, and released across GPU memory, cache blocks, batches, and requests. vLLM/PagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023) manages KV caches in pages to reduce fragmentation and enable sharing, and vAttention (Prabhu et al., 2024) achieves similar benefits by decoupling virtual and physical memory. Prefix caching stores the KV states of stable contexts for reuse, reducing time-to-first-token, and SGLang/RadixAttention (Zheng et al., 2024) automatically identifies and reuses shared prefixes across multi-call programs, branching, and multi-turn interaction. Because prefill is compute-bound and decoding is bandwidth-bound, systems also schedule across phases: Orca introduces iteration-level scheduling (Yu et al., 2022), Sarathi-Serve uses chunked prefill (Agrawal et al., 2024), DistServe disaggregates prefill and decoding (Zhong et al., 2024), and Mooncake builds a disaggregated KV cache across CPU, DRAM, and SSD resources (Qin et al., 2025). TokenLake extends prefix caching to a segment-level cache pool, and Jenga manages memory under heterogeneous cache layouts (Wu et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025a).

Serving-level management is what converts the local savings of other methods into end-to-end latency, throughput, and memory gains. Its benefits depend strongly on frameworks, hardware, workloads, and cache hit rates, so evaluation should report throughput, memory utilization, hit rates, and tail latency rather than single-request speed alone.

Not all valuable information needs to remain in the attention window. Source documents, dialogue histories, user preferences, tool outputs, task states, and reflections are often stored externally and retrieved when needed. Such compute-inactive memory incurs no prefill or KV cost at the current step, but determines whether a system can maintain continuity and reuse experience over long-term operation. Compressing it therefore means turning large histories into memory structures that remain retrievable, updatable, and reactivatable, not merely reducing storage. This section follows the external-memory lifecycle: writing, organization, retrieval, maintenance, and learned policies that govern these steps; how retrieved memory is compressed and injected into the inference path is discussed in Section 6.

Writing determines which parts of the current interaction, task execution, or tool feedback become long-term memory units, and is the first selection boundary of an external-memory system. Writing complete histories reduces omission but enlarges the store, adds retrieval noise, and amplifies privacy risks and the accumulation of stale or erroneous content. Written objects can be grouped into five types: factual memory of user preferences and stable states (Zhong et al., 2023; Kang et al., 2025a); episodic memory of temporally grounded experiences (Park et al., 2023; Shu et al., 2026); trajectory memory of reasoning steps, tool calls, and feedback (Yao et al., 2023); reflective memory that abstracts experiences or failures into lessons (Shinn et al., 2023); and skill memory that consolidates successful experience into callable procedures (Wang et al., 2023a). Recent systems make writing an explicit decision: Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) extracts candidate facts after each interaction and decides whether to add, update, delete, or keep them, and LightMem (Fang et al., 2025) pre-compresses and topically segments input before writing and defers consolidation to an offline stage.

Writing is a selection made under uncertainty about future tasks: overly conservative writing weakens continuity, whereas overly aggressive writing lowers the signal-to-noise ratio of the store on which all later stages depend.

Organization determines how written memories are indexed, related, and later updated. Appending memories to a linear log preserves history but lets redundancy, staleness, and retrieval noise grow with interaction length. Existing systems use serialized memory streams that preserve temporal order (Park et al., 2023), vector indexes for semantic retrieval (Lewis et al., 2020; Borgeaud et al., 2022), external stores of independently accessible units (Zhong et al., 2023; Packer et al., 2023), graph-structured memory of entities and relations (Jimenez Gutierrez et al., 2024; Jimenez Gutierrez et al., 2025), hierarchical and multi-granularity memory across time scales (Kang et al., 2025a; Sun and Zeng, 2025; Xu et al., 2025a), structured semantic compression of memory units (Liu et al., 2026a), and stores of reflections and skills (Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a). Recent systems refine these forms: A-MEM (Xu et al., 2025b) organizes memories as linked atomic notes that evolve with new information, Zep (Rasmussen et al., 2025) uses a temporal knowledge graph with validity intervals for facts, and MIRIX (Wang and Chen, 2025) separates core, episodic, semantic, procedural, and resource memory managed by multiple agents.

Organization is itself a form of compression: without necessarily reducing the number of entries, structuring, indexing, and hierarchization reduce the noise faced by later retrieval and injection. The cost is maintenance: richer structures make updating, deletion, and conflict correction harder, and memory units that are too coarse import irrelevant content while units that are too fine break contextual integrity.

Retrieval decides which memories are relevant to the current query, task state, or agent goal. Vector retrieval relies on semantic similarity (Lewis et al., 2020; Borgeaud et al., 2022); interactive agents additionally weight recency and importance (Park et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2023); memory controllers schedule access across memory tiers (Packer et al., 2023; Kang et al., 2025a); graph-based retrieval follows entity and relation paths for multi-hop and temporal questions (Jimenez Gutierrez et al., 2024; Jimenez Gutierrez et al., 2025); episodic retrieval recalls specific past experiences (Shu et al., 2026; Chhikara et al., 2025); and agent memory may be triggered by task goals, tool states, or prior failures (Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a). Retrieval compresses the candidate space so that the full history need not be exposed in context, and its quality bounds every later step: retrieving too little causes forgetting and inconsistency, whereas retrieving too much reintroduces noise and increases the cost of later compression and injection. We refer to this stage as activation readiness because retrieved memories remain candidates; they become compute-active only after the selection, compression, and injection steps discussed in Section 6.

Long-term memory does not remain correct indefinitely: preferences change, task states evolve, facts become stale, and sources conflict. Updating reconciles new information with stored memory, reinforcing consistent entries and, for conflicts, replacing, revising, versioning, or deferring until confirmation; without it, stale information is repeatedly reactivated. Consolidation merges repeated or similar memories into summaries, topics, structured facts, or higher-level reflections, increasing density at the risk of losing details, temporal order, or conditions that later tasks need. Forgetting removes, down-weights, expires, hides, or archives memories that are low-value, stale, erroneous, or sensitive, serving both noise control and privacy and safety governance. Together these operations determine whether compute-inactive memory keeps a high signal-to-noise ratio over time; a system that only writes and retrieves gradually degrades into a store of historical noise.

The mechanisms above mostly rely on hand-designed rules or prompts. A recent trend is to learn memory-management policies with reinforcement learning, so that what to store, revise, and use is optimized by task reward. Memory-R1 (Yan et al., 2025) trains a memory manager to add, update, delete, or skip entries in an external memory bank and an answer agent to filter retrieved memories, turning the write, consolidate, and forget operators into learned policies that maximize utility under a budget, as in Eq. (2). Related methods learn to maintain a bounded memory inside the context window; because that memory is compute-active by our criterion, we discuss them with agent-side activation control (Section 6.4). Because rewards usually come only from final answers, however, such learned policies do not directly constrain the faithfulness, traceability, or privacy of memory, and may exploit benchmark regularities; incorporating cost and reliability terms into the reward remains open.

section: State Transitions: Retrieval, Injection, and Intermediate States
text: This section examines how information moves between memory states, which is where the memory-centric view departs most from existing reviews. Retrieved memory is not equivalent to information the model has used: it affects generation only after selection, compression, formatting, and injection into the attention path. Injecting every candidate reintroduces the cost and noise of long contexts, whereas aggressive filtering can remove evidence, temporal relations, or task state. We first discuss the transition from retrieved memory to active context and the forms of injection, then intermediate states on the activation path, agent-side activation control, and the feedback loop created by write-back.

section: From Retrieved Memory to Active Context
