text: Retrieval is often presented as a way to avoid placing all history in the input, but it is not a cost-free extension of context: as soon as retrieved content is concatenated into the prompt, it consumes prefill computation, context length, and subsequent cache budget. If candidates are injected wholesale, redundant, weakly relevant, or stale content re-enters the inference path and erodes the gains of compression. The transition from candidates to active context therefore requires three judgments: which candidates are relevant to the current task, which can be summarized, structured, or merged, and which must be kept as original evidence. The answer depends on the task: long-document question answering needs verifiable evidence, personalized dialogue needs consistent user state, code tasks need structural dependencies, and agent tasks rely on tool results and action histories. Retrieval-conditioned compression and injection is thus an activation-control process that connects the external memory of Section 5 with the active memory of Section 4.

Post-retrieval compression operates at several granularities: filtering removes weakly relevant candidates, reranking orders evidence, summarization merges candidates into shorter text, structured extraction produces entities, attributes, temporal or causal relations, and task states, graph-path compression keeps the key nodes and edges of multi-hop relations, and more aggressive methods encode retrieved content as special tokens, latent vectors, or cache states. Each choice carries its own risk: summaries are inspectable but may omit detail, structured facts are compact but depend on extraction quality, and latent representations compress most but are least interpretable.

The injection form determines the computational state in which external memory participates. Concatenating passages is simple and interpretable but costly; summaries are shorter but lossy; structured facts and graph paths suit relational, temporal, and multi-hop reasoning; and in more integrated systems, external memory enters as soft prompts, latent vectors, prefix states, or KV caches. At the KV level, TurboRAG (Lu et al., 2024) precomputes KV caches for document chunks offline and concatenates them online to skip prefilling of retrieved content; Block-Attention (Ma et al., 2025) encodes retrieved blocks independently, lets only the final query block attend to all blocks, and fine-tunes the model to this pattern; and CacheBlend (Yao et al., 2025) restores cross-document attention lost by naive concatenation by recomputing KV states for a small set of tokens with the largest deviation. No injection form is uniformly superior: traceable evidence favors text or structured facts, extreme compression favors latent representations, and multi-turn reuse favors prefix or cache states, so injection must be chosen jointly by cost, utility, and verifiability.

section: Intermediate States on the Activation Path: Offloading and Materialization
text: Retrieve-and-inject requires retrieval, compression, and re-encoding before external memory can be used. Intermediate states avoid the last two steps: the information already has a form the model can use and returns to computation through data movement and light correction. Such states arise in two directions, by offloading active KV states from the attention path (offload and recall in Table 2) or by materializing external memory in advance into loadable forms (materialize).

When historical KV states exceed the GPU budget, a system can move them to host memory or lower storage tiers instead of evicting them, and recall a small relevant subset during decoding. The key problem is to decide what to recall without touching all states. InfiniGen (Lee et al., 2024) predicts important tokens of the next layer from the previous layer’s input and partial query–key projections and prefetches their KV states; RetrievalAttention (Liu et al., 2024b) builds attention-aware vector indexes that account for the distribution mismatch between queries and keys; MagicPIG (Chen et al., 2025) estimates attention by locality-sensitive-hashing sampling rather than top- k selection; and ShadowKV (Sun et al., 2025a) keeps low-rank keys on the GPU, offloads values to the CPU, and reconstructs selected keys during decoding. LongMem (Wang et al., 2023b) applies the same idea beyond a single input, caching attention key–value pairs of past inputs in a memory bank that a trained side network retrieves from. Quest (Tang et al., 2024) uses query-aware page selection as well but keeps the full cache in accelerator memory, so it changes which states are read rather than where they reside (Section 4.3).

These methods are mechanistically isomorphic to external-memory retrieval—both index information beyond the active budget, select candidates for the current query, and reactivate them at a cost—but KV recall requires no re-prefilling. KV-level retrieval-based attention and text-level retrieval augmentation can thus be viewed as instances of one activation problem over different representations. They remain sensitive to host–device bandwidth, index construction, and recall precision, and mostly operate within a single request.

In the other direction, external memory can be moved in advance from the compute-inactive state into an intermediate state, so that each later activation pays only for loading and correction. Cross-request prefix caching (Section 4.5) is the simplest case, and the KV-level injection methods of Section 6.2 follow the same idea, facing the mismatch between independently encoded chunks and joint reasoning. Cartridges (Eyuboglu et al., 2025) take a different route: the model generates synthetic conversations about a corpus and distills it into a much smaller trainable KV cache, showing that materialization can be a lossy, learned compression targeted at the expected query distribution rather than lossless storage of raw KV states. Materialized states raise their own problems: they are bound to a specific model version and must be rebuilt after updates, they occupy far more storage than raw text, and they are hard to inspect or edit, so invalidating the derived states of a deleted or corrected document becomes a system-level instance of the governance problems in Section 8.

In long-horizon agent tasks, activation control also applies to the agent’s own trajectory: as tool calls, observations, and intermediate reasoning accumulate, the agent must decide which history stays in active context and which is summarized, folded, or externalized. ACON (Kang et al., 2025b) refines compression guidelines from trajectories in which the full context succeeds but the compressed context fails, and distills the resulting compressor into smaller models; Context-Folding (Sun et al., 2025b) lets an agent branch into sub-tasks and fold each completed sub-trajectory into a summary, learning the folding behavior with reinforcement learning; MEM1 (Zhou et al., 2025) lets an agent merge its previous internal state with each new observation into a compact state, keeping memory nearly constant in long-horizon tasks; and MemAgent (Yu et al., 2025a) reads long documents segment by segment and learns to overwrite a bounded in-context memory, allowing a limited-context model to handle very long inputs. Here the decision-maker shifts from external retrieval modules to the agent policy, and when and what to compress becomes part of the action space.

A dedicated survey (Wang et al., 2026a) reviews these methods in detail; from the lifecycle perspective, the open questions are whether folded trajectories should be written back to long-term memory, in what form, and whether information lost in folding can later be recovered.

Transitions form a loop: injected memory shapes current inference, and model outputs, tool feedback, user corrections, and reflections are written back as new memory. The loop allows experience to accumulate, but it also allows errors to persist. Retrieval may return stale or weakly relevant memories, compression may delete critical evidence, injection may use a format the model cannot exploit, inference may over-rely on injected content, and write-back may store erroneous outputs or low-quality reflections, which are then retrieved again in future tasks. The loop also has a security dimension: memory-poisoning attacks implant malicious entries into memory or knowledge bases that are later retrieved under specific triggers, as demonstrated by AgentPoison (Chen et al., 2024b), and a recent survey on long-term memory security (Lin et al., 2026) organizes such threats across the write, store, retrieve, execute, share, and forget phases and notes that compression can amplify poisoned content. Since every transition is a potential point of error or attack, validation must cover writing, materialization, injection, and write-back.

Evaluating long-context compression requires more than measuring how much information is removed. A method that shortens the input, shrinks the cache, or retrieves less is not effective if it damages evidence, reasoning chains, user state, or long-term consistency. Because costs arise at different stages—prefill for input compression, decoding memory for KV compression, recall and summarization for retrieval-conditioned compression, and writing, indexing, and maintenance for long-term memory—evaluation should report cost–quality curves across context lengths and budgets, so that genuine improvements can be distinguished from costs shifted into external storage or background maintenance.

Cost should be reported beyond compression ratio: input tokens, cache size, peak GPU memory, prefill latency, time-to-first-token, decoding latency, retrieval and compression latency, end-to-end latency, and throughput. Following the cost model in Section 3.4, we recommend reporting separately the active holding cost (prefill tokens and peak KV memory), the intermediate-state holding cost (offloaded or materialized storage), the transition cost (retrieval, transfer, compression, and recomputation), and offline maintenance cost, together with the number of requests over which each cost is amortized; vectorization, graph construction, consolidation, and prefix precomputation can otherwise move inference cost into unreported background processes.

Task utility should extend beyond final accuracy to evidence retention, faithfulness, reasoning consistency, hallucination rate, and task success. Question answering should be grounded in the correct evidence, structured and graph memory should preserve relation paths and state constraints, and agent tasks should additionally be assessed on planning, tool use, failure recovery, and skill reuse.

Long-term reliability distinguishes memory-centric compression from generic input or cache compression. Evaluation should test whether a system writes new memories correctly, retrieves old ones at the right time, updates stale states, consolidates repeated memories, and down-weights or forgets low-value, erroneous, sensitive, or retracted information. A method that optimizes single answers while accumulating erroneous reflections, stale preferences, or conflicting states is not a reliable long-term solution.

Existing benchmarks cover important but partial capabilities (Table 4). Comprehensive long-context benchmarks test understanding, question answering, summarization, code, and reasoning over long documents; synthetic retrieval tasks test localization at extreme lengths; and long-term memory benchmarks examine cross-session recall, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and implicit conflicts. Recent benchmarks address further gaps. InfiniteBench (Zhang et al., 2024a) extends evaluation beyond 100K tokens; HELMET (Yen et al., 2025) shows that synthetic tasks correlate weakly with downstream performance and adds application-oriented tasks; NoLiMa (Modarressi et al., 2025) removes literal overlap between questions and evidence and reveals sharp degradation when semantic association is required; BABILong (Kuratov et al., 2024) embeds multi-fact reasoning in long distractor text; SCBench (Li et al., 2025a) evaluates shared-context, multi-request settings across the generation, compression, retrieval, and loading of KV caches; MemoryAgentBench (Hu et al., 2026) evaluates retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, and conflict resolution in incremental interaction; and STALE (Chao et al., 2026) tests whether agents recognize memories that are no longer valid.

These benchmarks remain dominated by static inputs or isolated capabilities. Success on needle-style retrieval does not imply multi-evidence reasoning, accuracy on long-document question answering does not imply maintenance of user state, and recalling historical facts does not imply correct updating or forgetting. Evaluation protocols should therefore separate context comprehension, evidence localization, memory retrieval, state updating, forgetting, and agent execution, and should vary context length, evidence position, compression, cache, retrieval, and injection budgets, memory scale, and interaction rounds jointly while reporting both stage-level and end-to-end cost.

Most methods rely on fixed policies, such as a fixed compression ratio, number of retrieved items, cache budget, or summary granularity, although memory requirements vary with the task: factual question answering needs verifiable evidence, summarization needs coverage, code tasks need interfaces and dependencies, long-term dialogue needs temporally valid user state, and agents need goals, tool results, and reusable experience. Components are also optimized in isolation even though they interact: excessive retrieval enlarges the current context, aggressive context compression degrades both generation and subsequent write-back, and KV eviction determines whether activated information remains usable. Allocation should therefore be decided jointly across input compression, KV retention and offloading, retrieval, post-retrieval compression, and injection form, according to task goals, model uncertainty, and the available budget.

Can a single allocation policy be trained with the cost model of Section 3.4 as its objective, jointly choosing the prompt compression ratio, the fraction of KV states retained or offloaded, the number of retrieved items, and the injection form within a request? The learned policies in Sections 5.5 and 6.4 show that memory decisions can be learned, but their rewards include no explicit cost terms and do not cover KV- or serving-level decisions.

section: Trustworthy Write-back, Security, and Governable Forgetting
text: Errors in long-term memory are dangerous because they persist. Stale or irrelevant retrievals, compression that drops conditions, misattributed reflections, and misread tool results can be written back and reactivated in later tasks, turning a local error into a lasting bias; poisoning attacks exploit the same path deliberately. Memories should therefore not be retained merely because they appear in dialogue, model output, or tool logs; write-back requires evidence checking, conflict detection, provenance tracking, and versioning, and must distinguish stable facts from temporary states and uncertain inferences. Long-term memory also stores preferences, histories, and potentially sensitive personal information, so users need to know what is remembered, why, and when it is used, and to correct or delete it. Because memory is compressed into summaries, embeddings, graph nodes, profiles, reflections, skills, and KV states, governance must extend from source text to all derived representations.

When a memory is deleted or corrected, how can all of its derived representations—summaries, embeddings, graph nodes, materialized KV states (Section 6.3), and learned compressed caches—be located and invalidated, and how can poisoned content be detected at write-back time at acceptable cost? Verifiable deletion and the tracking of derived representations are among the least studied stages of the memory lifecycle (Lin et al., 2026).

section: Lifecycle-Level Evaluation with Full Cost Accounting
text: Current evaluation is largely based on single inputs, single answers, or fixed compression ratios, whereas memory-centric compression concerns a lifecycle in which a system must decide what to write, how to organize and retrieve it, how to compress it before injection, how to update it after inference, and what to forget. Evaluation must therefore ask not only whether a compressed system answers correctly, but whether its memory remains usable, trustworthy, and governable over time, under the stress conditions and cost reporting described in Section 7.

Can a single benchmark cover writing, materialization, activation, updating, and forgetting, and require methods to report the itemized costs of Section 3.4? SCBench (Li et al., 2025a) covers the KV lifecycle, and LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2024), MemoryAgentBench (Hu et al., 2026), and STALE (Chao et al., 2026) cover memory recall and updating, but no benchmark evaluates both within one workload.

section: Emerging Frontiers: Reasoning Traces, Multimodality, and the Parametric Boundary
text: Three developments are changing the problem. In reasoning models, long chains of thought shift the main source of active memory from input to the model’s own generations, and it is not yet understood which reasoning steps can be compressed without breaking correctness. Multimodal long contexts from video, document images, and embodied interaction produce far more tokens than text and have different redundancy structures, which affects both compression and cross-modal memory writing and retrieval. At the parametric boundary, test-time training, on-demand adapters, and learned compressed KV caches make the choice between holding memory in context or in weights no longer binary.

Under what query frequencies, corpus sizes, and update rates should information be kept as text, materialized as KV states, or compressed into parameters? The cost model of this survey offers a starting point, but the training and update costs of parametric representations must be brought into the same account.

Long-context compression is evolving from a problem of length reduction into a problem of managing information for inference-time computation: the bottleneck is no longer how much input a model can accept, but which information should be retained, when it should be activated, in what form it should participate in inference, and when it should be updated or forgotten. This survey addressed this problem from a memory-centric perspective. We distinguished compute-active from compute-inactive memory, characterized intermediate states on the activation path, and described long-context compression as a lifecycle of state transitions with a budgeted cost model. Within this framework, prompt compression, latent memory, KV-cache compression, architecture-level selective computation, serving-level cache management, external long-term memory, retrieval augmentation, agent memory, and learned memory policies regulate storage cost, computational cost, and task utility at different points of one lifecycle.

Future systems need to move from static, pointwise, and modular compression toward dynamic, joint, and governable memory management: allocating memory across tiers according to task and budget, preventing errors from accumulating through write-back, supporting verifiable forgetting, and being evaluated over the full lifecycle with complete cost accounting.

Epi: Towards a Persistent, Self-Improving Agent for Autonomous Research. We present Épi, an autonomous research agent that sustains investigations across model sessions and evolves its methods through accumulated experience. Épi combines persistent research history, hierarchical memory, branching and independent review to maintain research continuity, learn from experiments, and explore and revisit alternative approaches. Its experiments run across session boundaries, and a fixed verifier evaluates their outputs. Épi produced 120 record-setting results, comprising 20 numerical bound records across 12 families and 100 construction records across eight families. These include an approximately 84-fold narrower interval for the $n$-queens constant and a more than 3.6-million-fold narrower rigorous interval for the quartic Feigenbaum attractor dimension. Exact dual certificates establish that the Cohn-Elkies linear-programming bound cannot be sharp in dimensions 10 and 11. Beyond numerical improvements, Épi gives a computer-assisted proof of Tuza's conjecture for split graphs with an eight-vertex clique part and at most three triangle-active neighborhood types, with arbitrary multiplicities. We extend this research process to algorithmic coding with Épi-turbo, a lightweight configuration that develops executable solvers for tasks including vehicle routing, scheduling and production planning.

On 30 FrontierOR tasks, Épi-turbo achieves a 5.4% higher total benchmark score than Codex at 64% of its model cost, using the same underlying model and reasoning effort. Épi is designed to support human understanding by connecting computational results to explicit methods and mathematical arguments that researchers can examine and build upon.

Autonomous research agents must conduct experiments, interpret results and revise their methods over many interactions. FunSearch and AlphaEvolve demonstrate how agents can combine code generation with executable evaluation to discover new programs and constructions (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025). The AI Scientist-v2 extends automation to an experimental workflow (Yamada et al., 2025). When an investigation requires more work than one model session can support, however, the agent must manage three additional challenges.

Experiments and research decisions span multiple model sessions. To continue an investigation, the agent needs access to running jobs, code, intermediate results and reasons for earlier decisions. Kosmos maintains a shared research state, InternAgent-1.5 organizes long-horizon memory, and ScienceFlow archives recoverable execution states (Mitchener et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). These mechanisms preserve information across steps. As the history grows, the agent must also select what a bounded model context needs: the current experimental state, relevant lessons and reasons an earlier approach failed. This need motivates hierarchical memory that separates immediate context from reusable experience.

An agent needs to turn experimental observations into knowledge that guides subsequent decisions. This requires identifying which choices produced a result, under what conditions the method applies and which evidence supports the lesson. The agent must retain this knowledge and retrieve it for relevant tasks. MemoHarness addresses experience reuse by building a memory bank during training and retrieving execution diagnoses and reusable patterns to adapt the harness at test time (Huang et al., 2026). In an ongoing research investigation, the agent must also update its memory as new experiments arrive, linking each lesson to the conditions and evidence that support it.

A single research direction explores only part of the available methods. The AI Scientist-v2 uses agentic tree search to develop experimental alternatives, and ScienceFlow can resume from archived executable states (Yamada et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026). These systems demonstrate the value of branching and backtracking. For research with checkable outputs, the agent must preserve each alternative’s implementation and evidence, compare candidates under a common evaluation rule and recover earlier work when new findings make it useful.

To address these challenges, we introduce Épi, a persistent and evolving autonomous research agent. Épi uses hierarchical memory to resume investigations and retrieve experience from earlier work. It maintains versioned branches to develop alternative methods and backtrack to saved implementations, and incorporates independent review when assessing evidence and choosing its next experiment. The agent operates in verifiable research environments that evolve between campaigns, where a campaign is a complete investigation that may span multiple model sessions. Within a campaign, every branch uses the same feasibility checks, objective and comparison value. A verified finding can then establish a new reference or motivate a new task for the next campaign. Persistent execution and storage carry the research state across sessions.

Mathematical discovery provides a concrete demonstration of this research process: the agent develops methods whose outputs can be checked as constructions, bounds or proofs. We also evaluate its applicability to algorithmic coding, where the agent must design and implement a solver that handles new problem instances efficiently. Our lightweight configuration, Épi-turbo, achieves a 5.4% higher total benchmark score than Codex on 30 FrontierOR tasks at 64% of its model cost, using the same underlying model and reasoning effort (Section 6). These tasks include routing, scheduling, production planning and graph optimization.

Our contributions are an autonomous research agent that integrates hierarchical memory, branching and independent review to sustain and refine its investigations; a verification protocol that evaluates changing research methods under a fixed ruler and gain floor; and a collection of 120 record-setting results, comprising 100 improved constructions and 20 numerical bounds. Each record improves a documented literature or registry reference for the same problem and normalization; we count one final result per instance or parameter setting, as detailed in Section 4. These results include an approximately 84-fold narrower interval for the n -queens constant and a more than 3.6-million-fold narrower rigorous interval for the quartic Feigenbaum attractor dimension. Exact certificates establish that the Cohn–Elkies bound is not sharp in dimensions 10 and 11. Épi also proves Tuza’s conjecture for split graphs with an eight-vertex clique part and at most three triangle-active neighborhood types, with arbitrary multiplicities. We release the constructions and supporting certificates (Epi Team, 2026).

Our goal is to connect self-improvement with human understanding: researchers should be able to inspect how a method evolves, explain why a result holds, and use that knowledge to guide further work. Épi retains implementations, experimental artifacts, and research notes across branches and sessions, allowing researchers to inspect the development of a method and assess its supporting evidence. Its constructions, certificates, and mathematical arguments further connect computational outputs to findings that researchers can examine and build upon (Section 8).

We study research tasks with a reference result, an explicit budget and outputs that can be checked. A curator supplies the question and source material; the agent chooses the methods and experiments. To compare the agent’s output with the reference, we specify an evaluation rule, called a ruler. The ruler defines the submission format, feasibility conditions, objective, normalization and comparison value.

The agent submits the information required to check its claim. For a packing task, it supplies coordinates and orientations. For an optimization bound, it may supply a dual vector or another certificate. For a proof task, it supplies witnesses and an argument explaining why the checked objects establish the stated claim.

For a minimization problem, we write V(x)\in\{0,1\} for the verifier’s feasibility decision, f(x) for the objective and b for the reference value. We define the improvement as \Delta(x)=b-f(x). We also specify a positive gain floor \delta>0, the smallest improvement that the task counts as meaningful. Épi accepts an improvement when V(x)=1,\qquad\Delta(x)\geq\delta. For maximization, we instead define \Delta(x)=f(x)-b. The positive floor excludes ties and admits an improvement exactly equal to the threshold. If a task imposes no minimum gain (\delta=0), we instead require \Delta(x)>0. We fix the feasibility tolerances and gain floor before the investigation. The verifier uses the tolerances to check constraints, while Épi uses the floor to decide whether the improvement counts. For a rigorous numerical bound, we additionally require exact arithmetic or outward rounding that controls the numerical error.

We establish a new record by verifying feasibility and improvement over the best established result for the same problem and normalization. Each final artifact retains its comparison value, source and any rounding convention. For a theorem, the proof connects the verified objects to the full stated claim.

We call a complete investigation a campaign. A campaign may contain several agent sessions and concurrent experiments. Each session gives the agent a bounded context in which to inspect evidence, modify code and choose its next action. Épi stores the research state outside that context and keeps experiments running across session boundaries. A later session retrieves the saved state and resumes the investigation.

The curator may provide a published construction as the initial reference. The agent can consult the literature, implement alternative methods and select experiments within the campaign’s budget. We keep model weights fixed in the campaigns reported here. The agent adapts its methods through experimental feedback, retrieved memory and independent review.

Figure 1 shows Épi’s research loop. The agent conducts experiments in verifiable environments and improves its methods through branching, hierarchical memory and independent review. We describe the evolving environments and the mechanisms supporting the agent’s self-improvement below.

Comparing research methods requires a common objective and consistent validity checks. We establish these before search by checking that the scorer reproduces the reference result, testing input validation and fixing the configuration, feasibility checks and gain criterion. The verifier then evaluates every branch under this shared rule. This gives Épi a consistent basis for comparing methods throughout the investigation.

We also specify the evidence needed for each type of claim. The verifier checks geometric constraints for a construction. For a rigorous bound, we require a certificate with exact arithmetic or controlled numerical error. For a computer-assisted theorem, we require both the finite checks and a mathematical reduction showing why those checks establish the full statement. The agent must develop this reduction or certificate when the task requires one.

Épi’s research environments evolve with verified findings. Improved results provide new reference values for subsequent investigations, while new research questions motivate changes to task formulations, representations and verification requirements. We incorporate these changes when defining the next campaign. For example, a numerical estimate can lead to a certification task whose environment includes certificate representations and rigorous error control. Each campaign uses a fixed evaluation rule to compare methods, and successive campaigns build on the verified findings of earlier work.

Épi improves its research methods through accumulated experience. The agent develops and compares alternatives on versioned branches, retains and retrieves experience through hierarchical memory, and uses independent review to reassess its research decisions. Together, these mechanisms allow Épi to refine its approach across experiments and campaigns.

A single approach restricts which formulations and search regions the agent explores. Épi maintains branches to develop alternatives while preserving each method’s code and evidence. Each branch stores an implementation, tests and notes in a versioned repository. The agent saves changes as commits and can create a new branch from an earlier commit. It compares the resulting experiments under the same ruler.

The agent backtracks by returning to a saved implementation and trying a different continuation. It can also revisit an existing branch and extend the work already recorded there. When the agent abandons a branch, it records the reason and retains the branch for later inspection. For a packing problem, the agent might refine coordinates on one branch and change the contact pattern on another. It can compare both methods before allocating more compute.

Drawing on work on human and agent memory (Atkinson and Shiffrin, 1968; Packer et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023), Épi uses hierarchical memory to accumulate and reuse research experience. Short-term memory supports the current investigation, while long-term memory retains experience for subsequent research. As illustrated in Figure 1, memory records include research context, lessons that capture reusable findings, and dead ends that document unproductive approaches and why they were abandoned. The agent retrieves these records to guide its next experiment and updates them as new evidence becomes available.

Épi stores code, artifacts and detailed research notes in a persistent filesystem and keeps retrievable lessons and dead ends in a memory store outside the model context. At a session boundary, the agent records its findings and a handover note identifying the current state and next steps. A subsequent session receives relevant memory records and can open the referenced files as needed. This supplies a bounded working context without replaying the full history of earlier sessions.

The agent that develops a method also chooses which evidence to examine, giving its assessment a limited perspective. Prior work on self-correction motivates adding feedback from outside the agent’s own reasoning process (Huang et al., 2024); research on reward hacking further motivates checking whether a score increase reflects the intended task (Denison et al., 2024). Épi combines a separate review of research progress with artifact verification under the fixed ruler.

Épi supplies a review model with the score trajectory, attempted approaches, retrieved findings, comparison baseline and resource use. The reviewer assesses what the evidence supports and whether the agent’s interpretation of progress is justified. Épi records this assessment for subsequent sessions, and the agent uses it when selecting further experiments or revisiting a branch. We use a different model for an independent review and record the reviewer’s identity. The reviewer evaluates the research direction; the isolated verifier checks the candidate’s validity and gain.

Épi records alternative implementations, their experimental outcomes, and the assessments used to guide subsequent work. These records allow researchers to compare branches, inspect the evidence associated with a methodological change, and revisit the implementation on which a conclusion depends. Lessons summarize reusable findings, while references to code and experimental artifacts let researchers examine the evidence behind those summaries.

We use Breadboard as Épi’s execution infrastructure. Breadboard provides isolated experimental environments, supports long-running jobs across model sessions and stores research history, including code, branch states and experimental outputs. It also runs the fixed verifier and preserves the state needed to recover and continue an investigation. The agent uses these services to execute experiments, inspect results and resume its research across sessions.

We ran Épi over a few days using OpenAI frontier models (GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6-Astra). Computational budgets were set per problem. Published methods and constructions supplied starting points for several campaigns, including the packing case in Section 5.1. Each comparison uses the same task and evaluation convention for the reference and final artifact. All record comparisons are based on literature and registry references available as of September 16, 2026.

The current collection contains 120 record-setting results: 20 numerical bound records across 12 families and 100 construction records across eight families. A separate Tuza theorem extension brings the report to 21 families in total and is excluded from the record count.
We count one final result per distinct instance or parameter setting. An enclosing interval counts once, and intermediate improvements do not add records. Figure 2 gives the family breakdown.

The results repository retains the final artifacts and comparison values (Epi Team, 2026). Some evolving registries already list the new results. Our tables retain the earlier values used for comparison so the improvement remains traceable after those updates.

Of the 100 construction records, 97 concern geometric packing. The remaining three improve vehicle routing, the signed-maximum variant of the third autocorrelation inequality and a Zhang–Zagier construction. Figure 2 gives the counts for all eight families. Packing references come from Packomania and Erich Friedman’s Packing Center (Specht, 2026; Friedman, 2026). Appendix B defines the objectives and gives these three comparisons.
Table 1 summarizes the 12 numerical families and how their bounds are verified. Appendix A states the claims with their precise values and supporting witnesses.

The task is to place 34 non-overlapping regular pentagons of unit side length inside an equilateral triangle of minimum side length. Each pentagon has a center and orientation. The evaluator checks containment and overlap and measures the required triangle size.

Épi starts from a published arrangement with triangle side length approximately 12.9814 (Friedman, 2026). It jointly refines the pentagons’ centers and orientations, checking containment and overlap after each candidate update. The final side length is approximately 12.9756, a reduction of 0.0445\%. The released coordinates specify the construction at full precision.

Figure 3 shows nine retained geometric constructions. For pentagons, the objective reduces the size of the enclosing triangle. The circle-packing tasks increase the common radius inside a fixed container (Specht, 2026). Each panel is drawn directly from the released coordinates.

section: 5.2 Separating the Cohn–Elkies Bound from Packing Density
text: The Cohn–Elkies method bounds sphere-packing density from above by optimizing an auxiliary function. We ask whether its best possible bound can equal the actual packing density. A strict separation would establish a limitation of the method itself.

section: 5.2 Separating the Cohn–Elkies Bound from Packing Density
text: Let \rho_{d} be the optimal sphere-packing center density in dimension d, and let C_{d} be the best upper bound attainable by the Cohn–Elkies linear program in the same normalization. Then \rho_{d}\leq C_{d}. To prove that the method is not sharp, it is enough to find a packing upper bound U_{d} and a lower bound L_{d} on the linear program’s optimum such that \rho_{d}\ \leq\ U_{d}\ <\ L_{d}\ \leq\ C_{d}. The middle inequality creates a separation between the true packing problem and the best answer available from this method.

section: 5.2 Separating the Cohn–Elkies Bound from Packing Density
text: Li (2022) obtains such lower bounds through a discrete reduction of the infinite-dimensional linear program. The reduction yields a finite optimization problem whose dual witnesses can be checked. Épi sets new records in dimensions 9, 10, 11, and 13, retaining one final dual vector for each. Table 2 reports the resulting lower bounds on C_{d}.

section: 5.2 Separating the Cohn–Elkies Bound from Packing Density
text: In dimensions 10 and 11, the new lower bounds cross the independently established packing upper bounds of Cohn et al. (2022). Equation (2) therefore holds in both dimensions. The relative separations, L_{d}/U_{d}-1, are approximately 0.35\% and 1.92\%, respectively.

section: 5.2 Separating the Cohn–Elkies Bound from Packing Density
text: The separation identifies a structural limit of the Cohn–Elkies formulation in dimensions 10 and 11. Even exact optimization of this formulation cannot recover the true packing density; a sharp bound requires additional constraints or a different bounding method.

section: 5.3 Narrowing the Interval for the n -Queens Constant
text: The number Q(n) of placements of n non-attacking queens on an n\times n board has an asymptotic form governed by a constant \alpha, Q(n)=\left(ne^{-\alpha+o(1)}\right)^{n}. Bounds on \alpha can be obtained from finite convex optimization problems. Nobel et al. (2023) develop a scalable Newton method for these formulations and report the interval [1.944000752,\;1.944001082].

section: 5.3 Narrowing the Interval for the n -Queens Constant
text: Épi refines the lower and upper bounds separately. Rational feasibility checks and directed rounding give 1.9440010223327\ \leq\ \alpha\ \leq\ 1.9440010262694. The interval width decreases from 3.30\times 10^{-7} to approximately 3.94\times 10^{-9}, a factor of approximately 84. Figure 5 places the two intervals on a common axis.

section: 5.3 Narrowing the Interval for the n -Queens Constant
text: The two formulations have different computational costs, so Épi uses a higher resolution for the lower bound. Each endpoint has a retained witness that can be checked separately. Appendix A gives the resolutions.

Épi starts from the MAX-4-CUT gadget framework of Nagda et al. (2025) and optimizes its edge weights. With the gadget structure and relevant completeness assignments fixed, the competing colorings have objectives that are linear in those weights.
This allows the agent to normalize one side of the hardness ratio and optimize the other through a linear program. Coloring constraints enforce the required properties of the gadget.

The reference ratio follows from the gadget parameters in Lemma C.2 and the reduction in Theorem C.2 of Nagda et al. (2025). The final integer weighted gadget changes it from \frac{195581}{198140}\approx 0.987085\quad\text{to}\quad\frac{84931}{86101}\approx 0.986411. The released weighted edge list and finite checks recover this ratio exactly. Substituting the new gadget into the published reduction gives the improved hardness bound. This formulation provides a reusable optimization procedure: researchers can fix the gadget structure, optimize its weights subject to explicit coloring constraints, and verify the resulting ratio exactly.

section: 5.5 A Finite Construction for the Spencer Constant
text: The square-matrix discrepancy problem asks how well signs can balance the rows of a real matrix with entries in [-1,1]. Épi found an 8\times 8 matrix whose discrepancy is exactly five. Exhausting its 256 sign assignments gives row-maximum norms of five or seven, so the minimum is five. The matrix therefore raises the record lower bound on the universal constant from 7/\sqrt{17} to 5/\sqrt{8} (Tao et al., 2026).

section: 5.5 A Finite Construction for the Spencer Constant
text: Figure 5 shows the entire matrix. Its entries lie in \{-1,0,1\}, within the allowed range [-1,1], and the claim can be checked by enumerating its sign assignments.

The waterund36 instance in MINLPLib minimizes the cost of a water-using network under nonlinear flow and concentration constraints (MINLPLib, 2026). A feasible network costing approximately 662.807 was already known, but the listed global lower bound was only about 655.544.

Épi tightens the lower bound to within approximately 10^{-5} of that same feasible value, closing more than 99.999\% of the MINLPLib gap. This certifies the near-optimality of the existing network. The full-precision comparison appears in Appendix A.12.

To establish the bound, the agent constructs a relaxation containing every feasible network. Exact rational inequalities then rule out objective values below the stated cutoff. The certificate therefore applies to the original nonlinear problem. Appendix A.12 explains this argument and relates the instance to earlier optimization work.

section: 5.7 From Numerical Optimization to Proof: Tuza’s Conjecture
text: For a finite simple graph G, let \nu_{\triangle}(G) be the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint triangles and \tau_{\triangle}(G) the minimum size of a triangle cover: a set of edges meeting every triangle in G. Equivalently, deleting a triangle cover makes the entire graph triangle-free. Tuza’s conjecture, proposed in 1981 (Bonamy et al., 2022), asserts \tau_{\triangle}(G)\leq 2\nu_{\triangle}(G). Thus, if G contains no k+1 pairwise edge-disjoint triangles, deleting at most 2k edges suffices to eliminate every triangle in G.

Kőnig’s theorem equates the maximum matching size and minimum vertex-cover size in a bipartite graph (Kőnig, 1931). Tuza’s conjecture concerns a matching–cover relation in the triangle hypergraph, whose vertices are the edges of G and whose hyperedges are its triangles. Taking all edges of a maximum triangle packing gives the elementary bound \tau_{\triangle}\leq 3\nu_{\triangle}: any uncovered triangle could be added to the packing. The conjectured factor of two is attained by K_{4}, where \nu_{\triangle}=1 and \tau_{\triangle}=2.

A split graph has a partition V(G)=C\sqcup I, where C induces a clique and I is independent. Known cases include threshold graphs, whose independent-side neighborhoods are nested by inclusion (Bonamy et al., 2022), and K_{8} -free chordal graphs, which include K_{8} -free split graphs (Botler et al., 2021). Our eight-vertex clique part puts the family beyond the latter theorem’s K_{8} -free hypothesis.

For x\in I, let S_{x}=N_{G}(x)\cap C. Since C is a clique, every pair u,v\in S_{x} forms a triangle xuv. Thus x is triangle-active exactly when |S_{x}|\geq 2; vertices with identical S_{x} share one neighborhood type. Zeng (2026) proved the conjecture for |C|=8 and at most two types. Épi extends this to three types with unrestricted overlaps. Their triangles can compete for the same clique edges, requiring joint covers and packings.

Let G be a finite simple graph with a specified partition V(G)=C\sqcup I, where G[C]=K_{8} and I is independent. Suppose that the sets N_{G}(x)\cap C, over vertices x\in I with at least two neighbors in C, take at most three distinct values. Then \tau_{\triangle}(G)\leq 2\nu_{\triangle}(G).

Up to clique relabeling and type permutation, there are 872 three-type profiles: 35 have nested neighborhoods and 277 further profiles satisfy Zeng’s maximum-cut criterion. Épi constructs exact cover and packing certificates for the remaining 560 profiles, using 18,444 multiplicity boxes. An independent checker verifies the witnesses and complete profile enumeration. Zeng’s truncation lemma extends the checks to arbitrary multiplicities, establishing the result for an infinite graph family (Appendix A.13).

The proof separates the finite certificate checks from the argument extending them to arbitrary multiplicities, making explicit how the computational evidence establishes the infinite-family statement.

Algorithmic coding extends Épi’s research process to the development of executable solvers. Given a problem specification and a fixed evaluator, the agent designs, implements and tests an algorithm whose solution quality and runtime are measured on new instances. Épi-turbo is a lightweight configuration for these tasks, designed to develop effective algorithms within a short campaign and a small model budget.

Épi-turbo keeps the parts of Épi that make a result reliable. The verifier checks each candidate under a fixed ruler, and Épi keeps the research state across sessions. Branches keep each method with its code and evidence, so the agent can return to an earlier version. Memory records keep lessons and dead ends for later sessions. Épi-turbo changes how the agent uses its model budget and when the campaign stops.

The task instructions tell the agent how the benchmark measures a program. They give the complete score formula, which includes the quality term and the runtime term. They also tell the agent that the final score comes from instances that the agent does not see. When a program uses a large part of its time limit, Épi-turbo tells the agent. Thus the agent can find a good balance between solution quality and runtime. The instructions do not contain methods or hints for a specific problem.

Each model call has a cost, and a short task has a small number of calls. Épi-turbo tells the agent that every call costs money, which includes a check on an active job. The agent does short experiments with a time limit in its own session. It sends an experiment to the execution infrastructure only when the experiment needs more time than a session gives. It examines active jobs only when a result can change its next decision. As a result, most of the budget goes to the design and test of algorithms.

Épi-turbo runs each campaign as one continuous session if possible. The session continues the best method so far and does not restart from an empty context. Before a session ends, the agent records its state, its best candidate and its next steps. The next session reads this record and continues the work. Épi-turbo stops the campaign when more sessions do not improve the best verified score. Thus the agent does not use more budget on a task where it finds no improvement.

Épi-turbo reserves the maximum cost of a model call before the call starts. It also keeps a small part of the budget for the end of the campaign. Thus the cost of a campaign is never more than its budget, and the final steps always have funds. The reservation uses the price limits of the model, so the agent can use almost all of its budget.
Independent review and extra validation are optional in Épi-turbo. On short tasks, their cost was larger than their benefit in our tests. Both components were off in the runs below.

We use FrontierOR, a benchmark of 180 operations-research tasks from the literature (Kong et al., 2026). Each task asks for a standalone program that solves new instances of one problem class. The program must not call an external optimization solver. The baseline is Codex (OpenAI, 2026), a widely used coding agent, with GPT-6-Astra as its model. Épi-turbo uses the same model with the same reasoning effort.

We selected 30 tasks that were new to both systems. We took them in the official hardness order of the benchmark and excluded tasks with unreliable reference values. Of these tasks, 13 are in the hard split, and 17 have hardness ranks 51 to 70. For each task, each system had a model budget of $20. We did one run for each task and system, so we do not report statistical significance.

The evaluator first runs each program on two development instances. The agent sees these results during the campaign. After the campaign, the best development program runs once on four held-out instances. Each held-out run has a time limit of one hour. The benchmark score has a quality term and a speed term.

The quality term decreases as the gap to the reference value increases. The speed term compares the runtime of the program with the runtime of the reference solver. It counts only when the solution is within 1% of the reference value. Outside this 1% band, the score is the quality term alone. The reference values come from a commercial solver, and some of them are weak. Thus we also compare the two systems on each instance directly, with their objective values only.

Table 3 gives the main results. Épi-turbo gets the higher total score, 53.96 against 51.21. It has the higher score on 18 tasks, and Codex has the higher score on 12. On 10 of these tasks, the difference is less than 0.01. Épi-turbo uses 64% of the model cost of Codex. Its median research time per task is approximately 22 minutes, and the median for Codex is 37 minutes.

Figure 7 shows the results for each task. The gains of Épi-turbo are larger than its losses. On the 18 tasks where Épi-turbo is higher, the total gain is 4.54. On the other 12 tasks, the total loss is 1.79. Épi-turbo also costs less on 27 of the 30 tasks.

Table 4 splits the tasks into two groups. On the 13 tasks of the hard split, Épi-turbo has the higher score on 9 tasks, and its total score is 10% higher. On the 17 tasks with ranks 51 to 70, the two systems are close. On 15 of the 30 tasks, Épi-turbo has both the higher score and the lower model cost.

The higher score comes mainly from the speed term. The programs of Épi-turbo usually stop when their search finds no better solution. On the held-out instances, the median runtime of an Épi-turbo program is 2.9 seconds, and the median for Codex is 9.3 seconds. No held-out run of Épi-turbo used more than 30 minutes. Codex used more than 30 minutes on 17 of the 120 held-out runs, in 7 tasks. A long run can improve the solution, but it decreases the speed term.

Table 5 lists the ten algorithmic coding tasks with the largest score difference in favor of Épi-turbo. The tasks span vehicle routing, cooperative crane scheduling, production planning, facility location, clustering and graph optimization. Each row evaluates a generated program on unseen instances of its problem class. This breadth makes the connection to the mathematical campaigns explicit: Épi’s research process supports both constructing mathematical artifacts and developing algorithms with measurable gains in practical optimization settings. The four cases below show how solution quality and execution speed contribute to these gains.

section: Clique interdiction: better solutions and faster programs (furini2021)
text: The Épi-turbo program solves each held-out instance in less than 17 seconds. On one instance, its solution has an objective value of 8, and the Codex solution has 20. The Codex program also runs for 20 to 60 minutes on three of the four instances. Thus Épi-turbo has both the higher quality term and the higher speed term.

Épi-turbo has the better solution on three instances and the same solution on the fourth. On one instance, the Codex solution is 1.19% above the reference value, and the Épi-turbo solution is 0.89% above it. Thus only Épi-turbo gets the speed term on that instance. The Épi-turbo programs are also 2 to 7 times faster.

Épi-turbo matches the reference value on all four instances. The Codex solution is 5% worse on one instance. On another instance, the Codex program needs 34 seconds, which is more time than the reference solver needs. Thus Codex loses the speed term on that instance, and Épi-turbo keeps it.

Both systems beat the reference values by 5% to 17%. The Codex solutions are slightly better on three instances, by at most 2.6%. But the Codex program uses the full hour on three instances, and the Épi-turbo program needs at most 36 seconds. Here the speed term decides the result.

Autonomous research systems differ in how they organize the search for a useful next experiment. The AI Scientist-v2 explores experimental directions through agentic tree search (Yamada et al., 2025). Co-Scientist uses model-generated critique to refine hypotheses around a research goal (Gottweis et al., 2026), and InternAgent-1.5 coordinates generation with verification across computational and empirical tasks (Feng et al., 2026). These systems share Épi’s need to revise a research direction in response to feedback. AIRA 2 addresses a related execution challenge through asynchronous experiments and a consistent evaluation protocol (Hambardzumyan et al., 2026). In Épi, the verifier stays fixed within a campaign as the agent changes its approach.

Continuing research also depends on how previous work is represented. Kosmos uses a shared world model to connect literature search and data analysis (Mitchener et al., 2025). ScienceFlow preserves executable research states that can be resumed or revisited (Zhao et al., 2026). Knowledge can also pass between investigations through reports, as in AgentRxiv (Schmidgall and Moor, 2025), or through AutoKD’s persistent graph of accepted findings (Ge et al., 2026). Épi retains both the experimental state needed to resume a campaign and lessons intended for reuse on another problem. Branches preserve alternative histories within that campaign.

For tasks with executable evaluation, FunSearch and AlphaEvolve guide program generation using measured performance (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025). SimpleTES scales search through independent trajectories and reuse of evaluated histories (Ye et al., 2026). Dream-RSI turns recorded discovery trees into replay environments for evaluating and revising exploration policies before deploying them in further searches (Zheng et al., 2026). TTT-Discover adapts model weights at test time (Yuksekgonul et al., 2026). Épi keeps model weights fixed and uses stored lessons and branch histories to guide its next experiment. Released Hyra constructions offer starting points for further refinement (Hyra Team, 2026). Épi’s investigations can also extend beyond refinement to finding a certificate or proving a statement, as in the Tuza case study.

Our goal with Épi is to make autonomous research contribute to human understanding: researchers should be able to explain why a result holds, identify what it reveals about the problem, and use that knowledge to guide further work. Achieving this goal requires connecting computational artifacts to explicit formulations, mathematical arguments, and the scientific questions they resolve. Épi builds on existing theory and retains the implementations, experiments, and assessments through which its methods develop. The case studies illustrate how this process can produce knowledge that researchers can use: the Cohn–Elkies separation identifies a structural limit of an established method; the MAX-4-CUT formulation provides a reusable procedure for optimizing gadget weights; and the Tuza proof makes explicit how finite certificates establish a statement about an infinite graph family. These examples express our broader aim for self-improvement: an agent should accumulate both the ability to obtain better results and knowledge that helps people understand and extend those results.

Épi is an autonomous research agent that sustains investigations across model sessions and improves its methods through memory, branching and independent review. Its campaigns produced 120 record-setting results and a computer-assisted proof of a new case of Tuza’s conjecture. The released constructions and certificates provide concrete, checkable evidence for these advances. Épi-turbo extends this research process to algorithmic coding across routing, scheduling, planning and graph optimization. On 30 FrontierOR tasks, it achieves a 5.4% higher total benchmark score than Codex with the same model while using 64% of its model cost.

Épi couples method improvement with a persistent record of implementations, experiments, and review. This record supports inspection of the research process, while explicit constructions and proof arguments make the resulting findings available for further scientific work. Together, these evaluations demonstrate the applicability of persistent, feedback-driven method development to mathematical discovery and efficient algorithm design.
